units.la: ADIVRO vos, qui hoc DOCTRINÆ CHRISTIANÆ CORPVS, Scholarum & Ecclesiarum reformatarum utilitati, bonorum desiderio, labore non exiguo, à nobis restitutum, vel primi nunc evulgatis, vel porrò evulgaturi estis: per Dominum nostrum JESUM CHRISTUM, & gloriosum adventum eius, in quo veniet iudicare vivos & mortuos: ut quoties illud deinceps recudendum erit, non nisi ad exemplum ULTIMA CURA à me recognitum (addità semper hac Adiurationis formulâ) recudatis, vel recudendum ab aliis curetis. Quos ego eadem obtestor religione, ne vel citra voluntatem meorum hæredum, ac librariorum, quorum impensis nunc prodit, falcem suam in messem mittant alienam: vel cum consensu, aut ratione quavis alia licita, diversum ab hac adiuratione faciant. VA-LETE. Heidelbergæ è Pareano meo, Calendis Iunii; Anno salutis recuperatæ ∞ IDC XXII. Ætatis meæ LXXIV.
units.tr: I adjure you, who now publish or will hereafter publish this CORPUS DOCTRINAE CHRISTIANAE, restored by me with no small labour for the use of the schools and reformed churches, out of a good desire, through OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, and his glorious coming, when he will come to judge the living and the dead: that whenever it must be reprinted from now on, you reprint it only on the model of the ULTIMA CURA revised by me (always with this form of adjuration added), or see that it is reprinted by others. I beg you by that same religion not to put his sickle into another's harvest, without the consent of my heirs and of the booksellers at whose expense it now appears; nor, with consent or by some other lawful means, to do otherwise than this adjuration. FARE WELL. From my Pareanum at Heidelberg, on the Kalends of June, in the year of recovered salvation 1622, in my seventy-fourth year.

units.la: SI memoriam paucorum illorum annorum animo nobiscum recolamus, quibus vniuersa CHRISTI Ecclesia, à fermento Anti-Christiano virtute Numinis divini, atque ministerio virorum DEI expurgata, à jugo & tyrannide Episcoporum Romanensium liberata, laudes solemnes DEO cum JUBILO magno cecinit: utiqi comperiemus, non minori voto hoc ipso tempore DEO nostro vehementer obnoxios nos manere, quando ad lustri unius atque alterius interstitium supremus ille Phosphorus lucernam Veritatis cœlestis de candelabro removit quidem, sed humilitate gregis sui paternè commisertus, iterum illam nunc nuper accendit, & clarum splendere fecit. O miseram illam Patrum nostrorum ætatem, quâ sæculis anteactis sub opicâ superstitionum caligine tam diu cæcutire cos necesse fuit, antequam radiis Veritatis
units.tr: If we call to mind in our hearts those few years when the whole Church of Christ, cleansed of Antichristian leaven by the power of the divine Majesty and through the ministry of the men of God, freed from the yoke and tyranny of the Roman bishops, sang solemn praises to God with great jubilation, we shall find that at this very time we ought to be no less deeply bound by vows to our God. For within the space of one or two lustra that supreme Morning Star indeed removed the lamp of heavenly truth from the lampstand, but, mercifully taking pity on the humility of his flock, he has now lately lit it again and caused it to shine clearly. O the wretched age of our fathers, in which, for many centuries past, they were obliged to remain blind for so long under the thick darkness of superstition, before they were at last enlightened again by the rays of truth!

units.la: Anno 1617. celebratum Jubilæi restitutionis Evangelij. tatis tandem illuminarentur rursum! O miseriorem illam filiorum nostrorum sortem, quâ, jam tenellarum animarum suarum facibus accensis, tam subitò in Germaniam, eiusq; potiores provincias irrumpentibus Babyloniis, densâ quasi nube falsitatum velut ex inopinato fuerunt circumfusi, atq; ad pedes qui antea Christianorum Gamalielum proni sederunt, præter omnium opinionem in ipsius Belialis Romani sinum penitus fuerunt conjecti! Sed ô iterùm iterumq; felices eosdem filios nostros, qui Orcino Meretricis Babylonicæ felle repudiato ad ubera beatæ Matris Ecclesiæ sunt reducti, sugentes denuò æternæ salutis lac: quo salutariter pasti in virum adultum crescere nunc incipiunt! Nimirum Medea Romana annis præterpropter duodecim puerulis illis, quos unicus Ecclesiæ Pastor Jesus Christus iccircò ad se vocarat, ut eis regnum cœlorum donaret, nil nisi Babylonica propinavit venena, quibus miserè intoxicati decreta desperatæ damnationis avidâ aure imbiberunt, & aliquandiu esse avulsi à corpore veræ Ecclesiæ fermè visi sunt: atque ita sermones fidei, in quibus erant innutriti, ac præclaram doctrinā, quam semel illis traditam fuerant affectati, præfractè deseruerunt. Intelligo elementa illa initii eloquiorum Dei, quæ vocat Apostolus, & principium veri Christianismi, quod gustauerant quidē, sed turpiter sub Papatu novo abiecerunt. Neq; verò adeò expertes sanorum Dei verborum, rum, aut tam faciles nos esse oportet, ut patia-mur nobis oblini os, quasi nihilo minus in Papa-tu catecheticæ doctrinæ capita, ad salutē æter-nam necessaria, absq; errore doceantur: Sym-bolum, inquam, Apostolicū, Decalogus, Ora-tio Dominica, ac verus deniq; usus Sacramen-torum. Nullum mendacium, inquit D. Johannes, est ex veritate. Huius cùm vix retineant imagi-nem Romani Papicolæ, Tridentinæ suæ Synodi mendaciis singula profecto illa Christianæ doc-trinæ tirocinia abominandis traditionum hu-manarum fæcibus infandùm contaminarunt: adeò ut tamenetsi C A'TECHESIN aliquam splendidè profiteantur: non tamen illa Christi præcipiat ἀπλότητα & simplicitatem, sed Anti-Christi instillet πανουργήματα atq; astutias. Fieri potest, dicit Augustinus, ut quis integra verba te-neat Symboli,& tamen non recte credat. Pariter Sal-vator noster objurgat falsos adoratores: Vos ne-scitis,inquit,quid adoretis. Deus in veritate vult ad-orari, & coli. PAPATUS verò est mendacium: & quicquid in eo est, id omne ex præscripto sui Dictatoris Veritati primigeniæ aut sopiendæ aut abolendæ inservire necessū est. Exprimam Ignatij Martyris sententiâ indolem Papatūs.
units.tr: In the year 1617 the jubilee of the restoration of the Gospel was celebrated. ...that they might at last be enlightened again! O the more wretched lot of our sons, when the Babylonians suddenly burst into Germany and its chief provinces, and they, their tender souls already kindled, were as if unexpectedly enveloped by a thick cloud of falsehoods, and those who had once sat humbly at the feet of the Gamaliel of the Christians were, beyond all expectation, thrust deep into the bosom of Belial himself, the Roman one! But oh, again and again happy those same sons of ours, who, having rejected the gall of the Babylonian harlot's Orcus, have been led back to the breasts of blessed Mother Church, sucking again the milk of eternal salvation, by which, wholesomely nourished, they now begin to grow into grown men! Indeed the Roman Medea, for about twelve years, gave those little children, whom Jesus Christ, the sole Pastor of the Church, had called to himself so that he might give them the kingdom of heaven, nothing but Babylonian poisons. Wretchedly intoxicated by them, they drank in with eager ears the decrees of hopeless damnation, and for some time they seemed almost torn away from the body of the true Church. And so they stubbornly abandoned the words of faith in which they had been brought up, and the excellent doctrine once handed down to them, which they had cherished. I mean those elements of the beginning of God's oracles, as the Apostle calls them, and the principle of true Christianity, which they had indeed tasted, but shamefully cast away under the new Papacy. Nor indeed ought we to be so inexperienced in the sound words of God, or so easy-going, as to suffer ourselves to have our mouths stopped, as though under the Papacy the heads of catechetical doctrine necessary for eternal salvation were taught without error: I mean the Apostles' Creed, the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and finally the true use of the sacraments. No lie is of the truth, says John. Since the Roman Papists scarcely retain an image of this truth, they have with the lies of their Synod of Trent unspeakably defiled each of those rudiments of Christian doctrine with the abominable dregs of human traditions, so that although they profess some catechism with great show, it does not teach the simplicity [ἀπλότης] of Christ, but instils the craftiness [πανουργήματα] and cunning of Antichrist. It is possible, says Augustine, that someone holds the words of the Creed entire, and yet does not believe rightly. In the same way our Saviour rebukes false worshippers: You do not know, what you worship. God wills to be worshipped and served in truth. But the Papacy is a lie, and whatever is in it must, by the prescription of its Dictator, serve either to lull to sleep or to abolish the primal Truth. I shall express the character of the Papacy in the words of Ignatius the martyr.

units.la: Οὐκ εἰσὶ χριστιανοί, ἀλλὰ χρισέμποροι, ἀπιστὴ ᾧ ἐιφέροντες τὸ ὄνομα χριστοῦ, καὶ τὸν οἶον ᾧ ὁ πλέγοντες τῆς πλαγῆς τῇ γλυκεία ᾧ θηγορία, ᾧ ἁπερ οἶνομελίῃ κώνοντες κεράμιῶν τες, ἵνα ὁ οἶνων τῇ γλυκυτάτῃ κλαπεῖς ᾧ ποιοῦμ τῶν γευσικῶν ἀϊδησιν, ἀφυλάκῃως τῷ ἡμιάτῳ ᾧ ἐπιπαρῇ. PAPISTÆ non sunt Christiani, sed CHRISTI institores, qui ex nomine CHRISTI quæstum faciunt, fraude circumferentes illius nomen: & erroris venenum alli- entes dulcib. alloquiis, velut mulso aconitū miscentes, ut suavissimo sapore deceptus qui gustat, incautè morte hauriat. Habeant igitur Papistæ (qui meretricio fuco nomen CATHOLICORUM invaserunt) Catechesin Christianam: jactitent symbolum fidei: ferociant meritoriis Decalogi operibus: debuccinent canonicas suas precum horas: Sacramentorū deniq; septeno typho superbiant: vana mehercules pietatis hæc sunt ϑεογεῖα & monstra, quorum fundus unicè veræ debetur Ecclesiæ, cuius caput est JESVS CHRISTUS. Hoc Baptisma, ait Augustinus, non est Ecclesiæ illius, quæ se separat, sed eius, unde se separat. Et rursum scitè: Olim Idumæis nulli erant capitaliores hostes Iudæorum: qui tamen erant participes eorundem Sacramentorum, & sanguinum communionē habebant. Veruntamen fieri potest, ut homo integrum habeat Sacramentum, & perversam fidem. Absq; verborum ambitu dicam, quod sentio. Quicquid in Papatu censebimus verum esse, adeoq; etiam verbo DEI consentaneum, illud Pontificiorum proprie doctrinam haudquaquam dici posse arbitramur; quandoquidem id omne tanquam bonum DEI verbum sibi vendicat vera DEI Ecclesia, ab ipso capite CHRISTO fundata: quod Papatus deinde putrido illo suo impurauit fermento. Pharisæi nonne quæso crediderunt, esse angelos, esse spiritus, esse resurrectionem mortuorum: & id genus fidei Articulos ? num propterea illos, quia sedere se fecerunt in cathedrâ Mosis, judicabimus veram tenuisse doctrinam? Fermentum, inquit Beda, Pharisaorum propria fuit doctrina: à quâ Christus cavere nos voluit. Quin potius audimus grave illud monitum Domini nostri: Sinite illos: caeci sunt, & caecorum duces. Tales omninò fuerunt tempore desolationis nostrae Romanenses Catechetae, qui quasi conjuratim viam perditionis ingredi jusserant seductos Catechumenos in patrio nostro Palatinatu: ubi Corpus illud Doctrinae Sanae Neophytis junioribus juxtà ac grandioribus, ignorantibus scilicet sermonem iustitiae, fuerat palam ademptum: quod olim aeternae memoriae Princeps Palatinus Fridericus III. pro incredibili suâ Pietate in brevem hypotyposin à summis Theologiae Doctoribus comprehendi demandaverat: quodque postea ab omnibus Scholis pariter atq; Ecclesiis, quotquot à Romano Papatu DEI clementiâ sunt reformatae, religioso consensu fuit approbatum atque susceptum. In illo non solùm piè conservando, sed etiam ad posteros jugiter propagando, quantum venerabilis meus pater ὁ μακάριος Doctor David Pareus perpetuò desudaverit, tota jam novit Ecclesia Christi: neque meo ulterius praeconio opus habet. Tanta verò sanctissimi senis in Corpore hoc doctrinæ Catholicæ expoliendo erat sollicitudo, ut ad extremū usq; vitæ spiritum circa illud fuerit occupatus: eò quidem avidius, quòd non sine dolore sæpenumero expertus esset, extra Archi-Palatinatum nostrum à sciolis quibusdam, sanæ huius doctrinæ pertæsis, atque in cerebelli sui commenta mirum quantū inclinantibus, fuisse alienis typis evulgatum: ac quidem sub nominibus puriorū nostrorum Theologorum, Vrsini & Parei, ceu sacrilegā quadam injuriā fœdatum. Proinde cùm nunc sub pristinam Evangelismi αἰανεχγίνωσιν incomparabile hoc Sanæ Doctrinæ corpus in Ecclesiæ ædificationem iterum foret excudendum, de supremo desiderabilis mei patris elogio, Posthumam hanc Editionem, novâ meâ limâ exasciatam, librariis haud gravatè elargitus sum: istâ meâ industriâ publicitùs confirmans, genuinā hanc esse γνησιώτατον illius doctrinæ euangelicæ, quæ à fidissimis Dei servis, ac cummaximè Dn. D. Zacharia Vrsino, & Davide Pareo, in Archi. Palatinâ Academiâ Heidelbergensi, juxta indubitatum sacræ Scripturæ canonem ad salutem æternam ore scriptisque fuit contradita, nobisque, atque adeò illis, qui post nos eandem sitituri sunt beatitudinem, relicta. Scilicet duo illi Ecclesiæ φωστῆρες Catechesin hanc reformatæ à Papatu doctrinæ iccircò tradere voluerunt, ἵνα καὶ διὰ τῶν αὐτῶν, ὁ λόγ⊙ αὐτῶν τῶν τῶν ἐνεχῇ τῆς διανοίας ἡμῶν: ut & absentibus ipsis ser- mo ipsorum mentes nostras institueret: quemadmo- dum de sua Catechesi loquitur Divus Chry- sostomus.
units.tr: They are not Christians, but merchants of Christ, who bear the name of Christ faithlessly, and who with fraud carry it about, and mix the poison of error with sweet words, as men mix aconite with honeyed wine, so that the one who tastes it, deceived by the sweetest flavour, drinks death unwarily. [Οὐκ εἰσὶ χριστιανοί, ἀλλὰ χρηστέμποροι, ἀπιστὰ ἐκφέροντες τὸ ὄνομα Χριστοῦ, καὶ δόλῳ περιφέροντες αὐτό, καὶ τὸ φάρμακον τῆς πλάνης μετὰ γλυκέων λόγων ἐγκιρνῶντες ὡς οἶνον μελίτι κίρνασθαι...] So let the Papists, who have usurped the name of CATHOLICS with a harlot's paint, have a Christian catechism; let them boast of the creed of faith, make a show of the meritorious works of the Decalogue, sound out their canonical hours of prayer; and finally let them be proud of their sevenfold display of Sacraments. These are, by Hercules, empty pretences of piety and monstrous things, whose foundation belongs solely to the true Church, whose head is JESUS CHRIST. This baptism, says Augustine, does not belong to that Church which separates itself, but to that from which it separates itself. And again, wisely: Once the Idumeans were the bitterest enemies of the Jews; yet they were partakers of the same Sacraments and had communion of blood. It is however possible that a man has the Sacrament entire and a perverse faith. Without a long preamble I will say what I think. Whatever we judge to be true in the Papacy, and therefore consistent with the Word of God, we do not think can properly be called the doctrine of the Papists, since the true Church of God, founded by Christ the head himself, claims all of it as the good Word of God, which the Papacy afterwards defiled with its rotten leaven. Did not the Pharisees, I ask, believe that there are angels, spirits, and the resurrection of the dead, and articles of that kind of faith? Shall we therefore judge that they held the true doctrine, because they sat in the seat of Moses? The leaven, says Bede, was the proper doctrine of the Pharisees, against which Christ wished us to be on guard. Rather, let us hear that grave warning of our Lord: Let them alone: they are blind, and blind leaders of the blind. Such were without question the Roman catechists at the time of our desolation, who as if by agreement had ordered the deceived catechumens in our native Palatinate to take the road to perdition. There the body of sound doctrine, for young and old neophytes alike, who were ignorant, of course, of the word of righteousness, had been openly taken away. Our Prince Palatine Frederick III, of eternal memory, had with his incredible piety commissioned the highest doctors of theology to compile this into a short outline, and afterwards all schools and churches, however many were reformed by God's mercy from the Roman Papacy, approved and received it with united consent. How much my venerable father, the blessed Doctor David Pareus, laboured without ceasing, both in preserving it piously and in propagating it continually to posterity, the whole Church of Christ already knows, and it has no need of my further praise. So great was the care of that most holy old man in polishing this body of Catholic doctrine that he was occupied with it until the last breath of his life, the more eagerly because he had often found, not without grief, that outside our Archpalatinate it had been published with foreign type by certain smatterers, weary of sound doctrine and strongly inclined to the inventions of their own little brains, and, under the names of our purer theologians, Ursinus and Pareus, defiled by a sort of sacrilegious injury. Therefore, when this incomparable body of sound doctrine was now to be printed again for the building up of the Church, restored to its former ἀναγνώρισις of the Gospel, I, mindful of my dear father's supreme praise, freely granted this posthumous edition, refined by my own file, to the booksellers, confirming by my own diligence before the public that this is the most genuine γνησιώτατον of that evangelical doctrine which was handed down, by word and writing, by the most faithful servants of God, and especially by Dr Zacharias Ursinus and David Pareus, in the Archpalatine Academy of Heidelberg, according to the indubitable canon of Holy Scripture, for eternal salvation, and left to us, and to those who after us will thirst for the same blessedness. Clearly those two φωστῆρες lights of the Church wished to hand down this Catechism of the doctrine reformed from the Papacy for this reason: ἵνα καὶ διὰ τῶν αὐτῶν, ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν τὰς διανοίας ἡμῶν ἐνάγῃ, that their words might instruct our minds even in their absence, as Divine Chrysostom says of his own Catechism.

units.la: Quare cùm incomparabile hoc depositum nobis omni studio custodiendum sit: neq; ullo modo committendum, ut vel ab haereticis manifestis, vel ab iis, qui foedas etiamnum haereticorum lacunas puritati Euangelicae veritatis immiscere satagunt, ullâ ratione convellatur, aut labefactetur: non dubitavi, Serenissime Princeps Ludovice-Philippe, Domine clementissime, idem hoc Sanae Doctrinae Corpus, summo zelo pietatis à sanctae memoriae patre meo ad ipsos supremos vitae illius dies extremâ operâ recognitum, Celsitudini Tuae devotâ animi mei submissione offerre: eâ fini, ut quoniam Celsitudo Tua non minori Pietatis zelo, quàm laudatissimę memoriae Principes maiores Tui, obryzū Evangelii aurum, sepositis omnibus errorum stipulis, lignis, atq; foeno, ex singulari illuminatione Spiritus sancti & agnovit, & palàm profitetur; eâdem quoque fortitudine, atque animi constantiâ coelestem illam veritatem in Ecclesiis & Scholis Palatinis, à novo Papatus fermento divinâ clementiâ nuperrimè repurgatis, suo patrocinio tueatur atque defendat.
units.tr: Therefore, since this incomparable deposit must be guarded by us with all zeal, and must in no way be allowed to be shaken or weakened, either by manifest heretics or by those who strive to mix foul remnants of heretical error into the purity of the evangelical truth, I did not hesitate, most serene Prince Ludovic-Philip, most gracious Lord, to offer this same Body of Sound Doctrine, which my father of holy memory revised with the highest zeal of piety and with his final labour in those last days of his life, to Your Highness with devoted submission of mind. My purpose is this: since Your Highness, with no less zeal for piety than your most renowned ancestors, has both recognised and openly professes the pure gold of the Gospel, with all the straw, wood and hay of error set aside, through the singular illumination of the Holy Spirit, Your Highness may likewise, with the same courage and steadfastness of mind, protect and defend that heavenly truth in the churches and schools of the Palatinate, which have lately been purged by divine clemency of the new leaven of the Papacy, under your patronage.

units.la: Hanc verò nuncupationem meam Celsitudini Tuae acceptam fore, cùm multa alia argumenta me confirmatiorem reddunt, tum vel maximè fiduciam meam stabilit insignis illa clementia, quâ me indignum servum Celsitudo Tua non ita pridè Heidelbergæ affecit, quando non solùm, post tam mirabiliter coeptam afflictissimi Palatinatûs ἀπολύτρωσιν, augustissimâ suâ præsentiâ cohonestavit publicam Panegyrin, in quâ μεγαλεῖα D E I solemni ac votivâ Oratione in redivivæ A C A D E M I Æ Theatro celebravi; sed etiam alterum meum Hymenæum eâ clementiâ atque munificentiâ prosequuta est, ut lætitiâ non unâ cor meum sit circumfusum. Quam quidè Heroicam virtutem atque clementiam erga Ecclesiam, & Scholas, literatosque viros, ut Celsitudo Tua innumerabiles annos salva & incolumis perseveret, sacrosanctam D E I Trinitatem supplicibus meis votis dies atque noctes adoro. Cui soli sit laus, honor & gloria in omnia sæcula! Scripsi Hanoviæ a. d. III. Kall. April. Anno Christi Salvatoris 1634.
units.tr: That this dedication will be acceptable to Your Highness, many other considerations make me more confident, but above all my confidence is strengthened by that remarkable kindness with which Your Highness, not long ago at Heidelberg, favoured me, an unworthy servant. For when, after the so wonderfully begun deliverance of the sorely afflicted Palatinate, Your Most August Presence graced the public panegyric, which I delivered in a solemn and votive oration on the greatness of God in the theatre of the restored Academy, Your Highness did not stop there, but also showered my second wedding poem with such kindness and generosity that my heart was filled with joy on more than one count. For this heroic virtue and clemency towards the Church, the schools and men of learning, I adore the most holy Trinity of God day and night with my suppliant prayers, that Your Highness may continue safe and unharmed for countless years. To Him alone be praise, honour and glory for ever! Written at Hanau, 3 days before the Kalends of April, in the year of Christ our Saviour 1634.

units.la: NE mireris, mi charissime fili PHILIPPE, postremæ recognitioni explicationum Catecheticarum, hoc ipso anno nundinis Paschalibus editæ, ULTIMAM hanc CVRAM κατὰ πόδας insuper à me additam. Pretiosa margarita manu gemmarii vix elimatur aut expolitur satis, quin semper ille nitidiorem dare cupiat, & quouis obtutu videat, quod elegantiæ additum velit. Ita hic THESAVRUS CATECHETICVS nunquam mihi in manus sumitur, quin quasi rediviua Præceptoris voce audiam, & discam, quod prius me fugerat: numquam etiam de manibus ponitur, quin hic-ibi mentem subeat, quod elimatius redditum velim, &, prout hodie postulat sæculum, explicatius. Verè autem confirmo, post SACRA BIBLIA vix alium librum frequentius me manibus trivisse, quàm hunc THESAVRVM CATECHETICVM; vix alium, immò nullum, esse in hoc genere, cui plus nervosioris doctrinæ tribuam, tribuitque iure posse existimem: nullum, cui ego quidem plus operà studiisque lubens meritoque impenderim: nullum, ex quo sacrosanctæ Theologiæ studiosis plus utilitatis spondere ausim: præ quo omnes lucubrationes meas alias vix cassæ nucis æstimo: quique vnus commentariorum aliorum iacturam Theologicis Scholis pensare bona parte possit. Quare & hunc tibi quoque diligentissimè habebis commendatum: inprimis verò postremam istam meam recognitionem, in exilio meo factam, si quid interea humanitus mihi accidat, Typographis sic edendam trades, habitâ ratione ADIVRATIONIS illius, quam novissimæ editioni præfixeram. &c. VALE. Ex Patmo in Lievvna, vbi furente in Palatinatu Marte, & milite Hispano, Bavaroque grassante, exulabam. Anno 1621. ad diem 30. Decemb. Natalitieo
units.tr: Do not be surprised, my dearest son Philipp, that I have added this final care, made immediately [κατὰ πόδας] after the latest revision of the Catechetical Explanations, published this year at the Easter fair. A precious pearl is scarcely polished or finished enough by the jeweller's hand; he always wants to give it more brilliance, and at every glance he sees something he would like to add to its elegance. So it is with this CATECHETICAL TREASURY. It is never taken into my hands without my hearing, as if from the revived voice of a teacher, something I had earlier overlooked; and it is never put down without some thought occurring to me here and there that I would like it rendered more polished and, as the present age demands, more explicit. I truly affirm that, apart from the HOLY BIBLE, I have hardly worn any other book more often in my hands than this CATECHETICAL TREASURY. I scarcely know of another book of this kind, indeed of none, to which I would or could rightly ascribe more solid teaching; none on which I have gladly and rightly spent more labour and study; none from which I would venture to promise more usefulness to students of most sacred Theology; and compared with it I hardly value all my other writings at the worth of an empty nutshell. This one book alone can, for the most part, make up for the loss of other commentaries in the theological schools. Therefore you will keep this book also carefully commended to you. Above all, if anything should happen to me in the course of human affairs, you will hand over to the printers this final revision, made in my exile, to be published in such a way as to take account of that Dedication which I had prefixed to the latest edition. Farewell. From Patmos in Lievvna, where I was in exile while Mars raged in the Palatinate and the Spanish and Bavarian soldiery ran riot. In the year 1621, on the 30th day of December, on my birthday.

units.la: VERITATEM dico. Magnâ iniuriâ affecit D. Vrsinum, quicunque Commentarios in Catechismum sub eius nomine N. primùm edidit. Aut enim eius sententiam de Iustificatione hominis ignoravit, aut malignè adulteravit. Testabuntur hoc omnes illi, quicunque D. Vrsinum cum aliqua attentione docentem olim audiverunt. Benè igitur & de Ecclesia, & de communi nostro Præceptore meritus es, quòd aliis Commentariis eundem Catechismum illustrasti. *** Vale. Franeccerae a.d. 3. Octob. Anno 1591.
units.tr: I speak the truth. Whoever first published the commentaries on the Catechism under the name of D. Ursinus has done him a great wrong. For either he was ignorant of his teaching on the justification of man, or he corrupted it maliciously. All those who once heard D. Ursinus teaching with some attention will bear witness to this. You have therefore deserved well both of the Church and of our common teacher, in that you have illustrated the same Catechism with other commentaries. Farewell. Franeker, 3 October 1591.

units.la: PROLEGOMENA IN CORPVS DOCTRINÆ ECCLESIARVM A PAPATV ROMANO REFORMATARVM.
units.tr: PROLEGOMENA TO THE BODY OF DOCTRINE OF THE CHURCHES REFORMED FROM THE ROMAN PAPACY.

units.la: PROLEGOMENA partim sunt generalia, de doctrina Ecclesiæ; partim specialia, de Catechesi.
units.tr: PROLEGOMENA are partly general, concerning the doctrine of the Church, and partly special, concerning the catechism.

units.la: Prolegomena generalia de doctrina Ecclesiæ sunt quinque.
units.tr: There are five general prolegomena concerning the doctrine of the Church.

units.la: I. Quid & qualis sit doctrina Ecclesiæ. II. Qua sint eius partes, quaque partium discrimina. III. Quid differat à doctrina aliarum sectarum, itemq; à Philosophia: & cur hæc discrimina tenenda sint. IV. Quibus testimoniis confirmetur eius certitudo. V. Quotuplex ratio sit eam tradendi & discendi.
units.tr: I. What the doctrine of the Church is and what kind of doctrine it is. II. What its parts are and how the parts differ. III. How it differs from the doctrine of other sects, and likewise from philosophy, and why these distinctions must be maintained. IV. By what testimonies its certainty is confirmed. V. In how many ways it is to be taught and learned.

units.la: I. Quid, & qualis sit doctrina Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: I. What the doctrine of the Church is, and what kind of doctrine it is.

units.la: DOCTRINA Ecclesiæ est integra & incorrupta doctrina Legis & Euangelij, de vero Deo eiusque voluntate, operibus & cultu à Deo patefacta, & comprehensa libris Prophetarum & Apostolorum, & confirmata miraculis ac testimoniis diuinis, per quam Spiritus sanctus est efficax in cordibus electorum, & colligit sibi in genere humano æternam Ecclesiam, à qua in hac & in futura vita celebretur.
units.tr: The doctrine of the Church is the whole and uncorrupted teaching of the Law and the Gospel, concerning the true God and his will, works and worship, revealed by God, contained in the books of the Prophets and Apostles, and confirmed by divine miracles and testimonies. Through this doctrine the Holy Spirit is effective in the hearts of the elect, and gathers for himself from the human race an eternal Church, by which he is celebrated in this life and in the life to come.

units.la: Hæc doctrina est prima & præcipua nota veræ Ecclesiæ, quam Deus in mundo vult esse conspicuam, & separari à reliquo genere humano, juxta dicta: Fugite idola. Exite è medio eorum, & separamini. Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non affert, ei nec Aue dicite. Sancti estote, immundum ne tangitote, qui fertis vasa Domini. Exite ex ea populE mi, ne ex plagis eius accipiatis. Vult autem hanc separationem Deus fieri. Primò, propter suam gloriam. Vt enim non vult ipse commisceri cum idolis diabolis: ita vult suam veritatem discerni à mendaciis, & suos domesticos ab hostibus Ecclesiæ, & filiis diaboli segregari. Contumeliosum est Deo, cogitare, quod velit tales filios habere, qui eum persequantur. Blasphemum est, Deum facere authorem doctrinæ impiæ, & patronum blasphemiarum. Quæ enim concordia Christo cum Belial? Deinde, propter consolationem & salutem electorum. Necesse est enim Ecclesiam in hoc mundo conspici, ut sciant electi in toto genere humano dispersi, cui cœtui se adiungere debeant in hac vita, & ad Ecclesiam aggregati hac certa consolatione fruantur, se esse in eo cœtu, qui Deo placet, & qui habet promissiones vitæ æternæ. Vult enim Deus omnes salvandos aggregari Ecclesiæ in hac vita, quia extra Ecclesiam non est salus.
units.tr: This doctrine is the first and chief mark of the true Church, which God wills to be conspicuous in the world and set apart from the rest of the human race, according to the sayings: "Flee from idols. Come out from among them, and be separate" (2 Cor. 6:17). "If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not even greet him" (2 John 10). "Be holy, touch nothing unclean, you who bear the vessels of the Lord" (Isa. 52:11). "Come out of her, my people, lest you receive of her plagues" (Rev. 18:4). God wills this separation to be made. First, for his own glory. For just as he does not wish to be mixed with idols and demons, so he wills his truth to be distinguished from lies, and his own household to be separated from the enemies of the Church and from the children of the devil. It is an insult to God to think that he would want to have such children as persecute him. It is blasphemy to make God the author of impious doctrine and the patron of blasphemies. "For what concord has Christ with Belial?" (2 Cor. 6:15). Second, for the comfort and salvation of the elect. For the Church must be visible in this world, so that the elect, scattered through the whole human race, may know to which assembly they ought to join themselves in this life; and, joined to the Church, may enjoy this sure consolation, that they are in that assembly which pleases God and which has the promises of eternal life. For God wills all who are to be saved to be gathered into the Church in this life, because outside the Church there is no salvation.

units.la: Unde autem Ecclesia agnoscatur, & quæ sint eius notæ, quibus ab aliis sectis discerni possit, in loco de Ecclesia docetur. Tres notæ sunt. 1. puritas doctrinæ. 2. legitimus sacramentorum usus. 3. obedientia erga Deum secundum omnes doctrinæ partes in fide & moribus.
units.tr: How the Church is recognised, and what its marks are by which it can be distinguished from other sects, is taught in the locus on the Church. There are three marks: (1) purity of doctrine; (2) the lawful use of the sacraments; (3) obedience to God in all parts of doctrine, in faith and in morals.

units.la: At etiam in Ecclesia sæpè grassantur magna vitia. Resp. Grassantur quidem aliquando, sed non defenduntur, ut in aliis sectis. Immò Ecclesia prius ea reprehendit & damnat, quàm alij. In Ecclesia sunt peccata cum improbatione & emendatione. Dum hoc manet, tantisper manet Ecclesia.
units.tr: But great vices often rage also in the Church. I reply: they indeed sometimes rage, but they are not defended, as they are in other sects. Indeed, the Church first rebukes and condemns them, before others do. In the Church there are sins together with disapproval and amendment. So long as this remains, the Church remains.

units.la: II. Quæ sint doctrinæ Ecclesiæ partes, & quæ partium discrimina.
units.tr: II. What the parts of the doctrine of the Church are, and how the parts differ.

units.la: Partes doctrinæ Ecclesiæ sunt duæ, Lex & Euangelium: quibus summa totius scripturæ sacræ continetur. Lex vocatur decalogus. Euangelium est doctrina de Christo Mediatore, & de gratuita remissione peccatorum per fidem. Hæc doctrinæ divisio probatur evidentibus argumentis.
units.tr: The parts of the doctrine of the Church are two, Law and Gospel, in which the sum of the whole of Holy Scripture is contained. The Law is called the Decalogue. The Gospel is the doctrine concerning Christ the Mediator, and concerning the free forgiveness of sins through faith. This division of doctrine is proved by clear arguments.

units.la: I. Omnis doctrina sacris literis comprehensa, est aut de natura Dei, aut de eius voluntate, aut de eius operibus, aut de peccato, quod diabolorum & hominum opus est proprium. Atqui de his omnibus vel in Lege, vel in Euangelio, vel in utroq; docetur. Ergo Lex & Euangelium sunt duo summa capita, quæ omnem doctrinam scripturæ continent.
units.tr: I. Every doctrine comprised in the sacred writings concerns either the nature of God, or his will, or his works, or sin, which is the proper work of devils and men. But all of these are taught either in the Law, or in the Gospel, or in both. Therefore Law and Gospel are the two chief heads which contain all the doctrine of Scripture.

units.la: II. Christus ipse facit hanc divisionem doctrinæ, quam suo nomine vult prædicari, inquiens: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere à mortuis tertio die, & prædicare in nomine eius pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Hoc autem totum Lege & Euangelio continetur.
units.tr: II. Christ himself makes this division of doctrine, which he wills to be preached in his name, saying: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name" (Luke 24:46-47). But all of this is contained in the Law and the Gospel.

units.la: III. Scriptura prophetica & apostolica continent vetus & novum testamentum, seu fœdus inter Deum & homines. Ergo necesse est, in illis explicari præcipua capita fœderis, nempe, quid nobis promittat & præstet Deus: videlicet, gratiam, remissionem peccatorum, justitiam, & vitam æternam: & quid à nobis vicissim requirat, videlicet fidem & obedientiam. Hæc autem sunt, quæ in Lege & Euangelio docentur.
units.tr: III. The prophetic and apostolic Scriptures contain the Old and New Testament, or covenant, between God and men. Therefore it is necessary that the principal heads of the covenant be explained in them: namely, what God promises and gives to us, that is, grace, forgiveness of sins, righteousness, and eternal life; and what in turn he requires from us, namely faith and obedience. These, however, are what are taught in the Law and the Gospel.

units.la: IV. Totius scripturæ summa & fundamentum est Christus. Ad Christi verò & beneficiorum eius agnitionem necessaria est doctrina Legis & Euangelij. Lex enim est pædagogus noster ad Christum, cogens nos ad Christum confugere, & ostendens, quæ sit illa justitia, quam Christus nobis restituit. Euangelium verò de Christi persona, officio & beneficiis ex professo concionatur. Tota igitur scriptura & doctrina cœlestis in Lege & Euangelio consistit.
units.tr: IV. The sum and foundation of the whole of Scripture is Christ. But for the knowledge of Christ and of his benefits the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel is necessary. For the Law is our schoolmaster to Christ, compelling us to flee to Christ and showing what that righteousness is which Christ restores to us. The Gospel, however, preaches expressly concerning the person, office and benefits of Christ. Therefore all Scripture and heavenly doctrine consists in the Law and the Gospel.

units.la: DISCRIMINA harum partium præcipua sunt tria.
units.tr: There are three chief distinctions between these parts.

units.la: I. In subiectis, (seu ipso doctrinæ genere: quod Lex est doctrina præcipiens facienda, & prohibens omittenda: Euangelium est concio de gratuita remissione peccatorum, per & propter Christum.
units.tr: I. In the subject matter (or the very kind of doctrine): the Law is a doctrine commanding what is to be done and forbidding what is to be left undone; the Gospel is a proclamation of the free forgiveness of sins, through and on account of Christ.

units.la: II. In modo patefactionis: quod Lex est natura nota: Euangelium diuinitus est revelatum.
units.tr: II. In the mode of revelation: the Law is known by nature; the Gospel has been revealed from God.

units.la: III. In promissionibus: quod Lex promittit vitam, cum conditione perfectæ obedientiæ nostræ: Euangelium eandem promittit cum conditione fidei nostræ in Christum, & inchoationis novæ obedientiæ. Sed de his infra suo loco fusius dicendum erit.
units.tr: III. In the promises: the Law promises life on the condition of our perfect obedience; the Gospel promises the same on the condition of our faith in Christ and the beginning of new obedience. But these matters will be discussed more fully below in their proper place.

units.la: III. Quid differat doctrina Ecclesiæ à doctrina aliarum sectarum: quid item à philosophia: & cur hæc discrimina tenenda sint.
units.tr: III. How the teaching of the Church differs from the teaching of other sects, and also from philosophy, and why these distinctions must be maintained.

units.la: Discrimina doctrinæ Ecclesiæ, & aliarum religionum, sunt quatuor.
units.tr: There are four differences between the teaching of the Church and the teaching of other religions.

units.la: 1. Doctrina Ecclesiæ habet authorem Deum, à quo per Prophetas & Apostolos est tradita: aliarum sectarum religiones ab hominibus, instinctu diaboli, sunt excogitatæ.
units.tr: (1) The teaching of the Church has God as its author, and it was handed down by him through the Prophets and Apostles. The religions of other sects were devised by men, at the prompting of the devil.

units.la: 2. Solius Ecclesiæ doctrina habet testimonia divina, certa & infallibilia, quæ conscientias pacant, & alias sectas erroris convincunt.
units.tr: (2) Only the teaching of the Church has divine testimonies that are certain and infallible. These calm consciences and refute the other sects of error.

units.la: 3. In Ecclesia lex Dei integra & incorrupta retinetur: aliæ religiones & sectæ legē Dei mutilant, vel corrumpunt. Primæ enim tabulæ doctrinam de vera Dei agnitione & cultu omnino abijciunt, fingentes alium Deum, quam qui se verbo & operibus in Ecclesia patefecit, & quærentes cognitionem Dei extra Filium, vel aliter Deum colentes, quam se coli in verbo præcepit: secunsecundæ item tabulæ interiorem ac spiritualem obedientiam prorsus ignorant. Quicquid verò in his boni aut veri habent reliquum, pars est præceptorum secundæ tabulæ, de disciplina externa, & de ciuilibus officiis erga homines.
units.tr: (3) In the Church the law of God is retained whole and uncorrupted. Other religions and sects either mutilate or corrupt the law of God. For they entirely reject the teaching of the first table concerning the true knowledge and worship of God, inventing another God than the one who has revealed himself in the Church by word and deeds, and seeking knowledge of God apart from the Son, or worshipping God in a way other than he has commanded in his Word. Likewise they are completely ignorant of the inward and spiritual obedience of the second table. Whatever good or truth they still have is a part of the precepts of the second table, concerning external discipline and civil duties towards men.

units.la: 4. In sola Ecclesia Euangelium de Christo docetur integrum, & rectè intellectum: aliæ verò sectæ, vel prorsus illud ignorant & abijciunt, vt Ethnici, Philosophi, Iudæi, Turcæ: vel tantum aliquam eius particulam ex doctrina Apostolica excerptam suis erroribus assuunt, cuius tamen vsum neque norunt, neq; percipiunt, vt Ariani, Papistæ, Anabaptistæ, & omnes hæretici, quorum alij de persona, alij de officio Christi Mediatoris errores tuentur.
units.tr: (4) In the Church alone the Gospel concerning Christ is taught whole and rightly understood. Other sects either altogether ignore and reject it, as do the heathen, philosophers, Jews and Turks, or they attach to their errors only some small part of it taken from the Apostolic doctrine. Yet they neither know nor perceive its use, as with the Arians, Papists, Anabaptists and all heretics, some of whom defend errors about the person of Christ the Mediator, and others about his office.

units.la: Hæc maxima discrimina ostendunt, Ecclesiæ doctrinam solam discendam & retinendam, aliarum verò sectarum religiones & doctrinas, cum ea pugnantes, tanquam diaboli mendacia, cauendas & fugiendas esse, juxta dicta: Cauete à Pseudoprophetis. Item: Fugite idola.
units.tr: These greatest differences show that the teaching of the Church alone is to be learned and retained, while the religions and doctrines of other sects, which fight against it, are to be regarded as lies of the devil, to be guarded against and fled from, according to the words: Beware of false prophets. Also: Flee from idols.

units.la: Philosophia diuersa est ratio. Vera enim Philosophia, etsi & ipsa à doctrina Ecclesiæ multum differt, tamen nec pugnat cum ea, nec est mendacium, vt aliarum sectarum falsæ doctrinæ, sed est veritas, & quidam quasi radius sapientiæ DEI, mentibus hominum in creatione impressus. Est enim doctrina de Deo, & de creaturis, aliisque rebus bonis, & generi humano vtilibus, ex luce naturali, & ex principiis natura notis à sapientibus exstructa. Vnde Christianis philosophiæ operam dare non modo est licitum, sed etiam vtile: cum contra aliarum sectarum doctrinis operam dare non liceat, sed omnes, tanquam ipsius diaboli mendacia, sint fugiendæ.
units.tr: Philosophy is a different matter. True philosophy, although it too differs much from the teaching of the Church, nevertheless neither fights against it nor is a lie, as the false doctrines of other sects are. Rather it is truth, and a certain kind of ray of God's wisdom, impressed on the minds of men at creation. For it is a teaching about God, about creatures, and about other good things useful to the human race, built up from the natural light and from principles known by nature to wise men. Hence it is not only lawful but also useful for Christians to devote themselves to philosophy, whereas it is not lawful to devote oneself to the doctrines of other sects, but all of them must be fled from as the very lies of the devil.

units.la: Differunt autem philosophia, & doctrina Ecclesiæ, his præcipuè modis.
units.tr: Philosophy and the teaching of the Church differ, however, chiefly in the following ways.

units.la: I. Principiis. Philosophia tota est naturalis, & è natura notis exstruitur atque confirmatur. In doctrina Ecclesiæ etsi multa etiam sunt naturalia, tamen præcipua eius pars, nempe Euangelium, præter & supra naturam est, adeò vt nisi Filius Dei nobis è sinu Patris eam reuelasset, nulla neque hominum, neque Angelorum sapientia eam invenire potuerit.
units.tr: I. In principles. Philosophy is wholly natural, and is built up and confirmed from things known by nature. In the teaching of the Church, although many things are also natural, its chief part, namely the Gospel, is above and beyond nature, so that unless the Son of God had revealed it to us from the bosom of the Father, no wisdom of men or of angels could have discovered it.

units.la: II. Subiectis. Doctrina Ecclesiæ continet integram & incorruptam sententiam Legis & Euangelij: Philosophia Euangelium prorsus ignorat, & Legis præcipuas partes omittit, & eas, quas retinet de disciplina & officiis externis, ex paucis tantum legis diuinæ præceptis excerptas, imperfectè & obscurè proponit. Tradit verò etiam alias artes & scientias humanæ vitæ vtiles, logicen, physicen, & mathematicen, quæ in doctridoctrina Ecclesiæ non docentur, sed tamen in ea tradenda & discenda aliquem vsum habent.
units.tr: II. In subject matter. The teaching of the Church contains the whole and uncorrupted sense of the Law and the Gospel. Philosophy is entirely ignorant of the Gospel, omits the chief parts of the Law, and sets forth imperfectly and obscurely those parts of it that it retains concerning discipline and external duties, taken from only a few precepts of the divine law. Yet philosophy also teaches other arts and sciences useful for human life, such as logic, physics and mathematics, which are not taught in the teaching of the Church, but which nevertheless have some use in teaching and learning it.

units.la: III. Effectus. Sola doctrina Ecclesiæ detegit fontem omnis mali, & miseriæ humanæ, nempe lapsum & inobedientiam primorum parentum, seu peccatum. Præterea conscientiis veram & viuam consolationem suggerit, ostendens modum, quo ex miseria peccati & mortis eluctari possimus, & reddens nos certos de vita æterna per Christum: Philosophia causam nostrorum malorum ignorat, & consolationem veram neque intelligit, neque præstat.
units.tr: III. In effect. The teaching of the Church alone uncovers the source of every evil and of human misery, namely the fall and disobedience of our first parents, that is, sin. Moreover, it offers consciences true and living comfort, showing the way by which we can struggle out of the misery of sin and death, and making us certain of eternal life through Christ. Philosophy does not know the cause of our evils, and neither understands nor provides true comfort.

units.la: Habet quidem philosophia consolationes quasdam cum theologia communes, vt sunt prouidentia Dei, necessitas obtemperandi Deo, bona conscientia, dignitas virtutis, causæ finales eiusdem, exempla aliorum, spes compensationis, collatio euentuum, qua minus malum confertur cum maiori, & boni rationem videtur habere. Sed veræ consolationes contra peccatum & mortem, sunt Ecclesiæ propriæ: videlicet, remissio peccatorum gratuita per & propter Christum, gratia & præsentia Dei in ipsis malis, liberatio finalis, & vita æterna.
units.tr: Philosophy does indeed have certain consolations in common with theology, such as the providence of God, the necessity of obeying God, a good conscience, the dignity of virtue, its final causes, the examples of others, the hope of compensation, and the comparison of outcomes, by which a lesser evil is weighed against a greater and seems to take account of good. But the true consolations against sin and death belong to the Church alone: namely, the free forgiveness of sins through and for the sake of Christ, the grace and presence of God in the very evils themselves, final deliverance, and eternal life.

units.la: Vera igitur philosophia, etsi respectu theologiæ est imperfecta, & in his, quæ dicta sunt, deficit: tamen cum theologia nunquam pugnat. Quæ verò in philosophorum libris erronea, vel cum doctrina Ecclesiæ pugnantia occurrunt, aut ab hæreticis ex philosophia contra scripturam afferuntur: ea vel philosophica non sunt, sed inanes argutiæ humani ingenij, & vlcera veræ philosophiæ; vt opinio Aristotelis de mundi æternitate, Epicuri de animæ mortalitate, &c. vel philosophica quidem sunt, sed perperam ad theologiam accommodata.
units.tr: True philosophy, therefore, although in comparison with theology it is imperfect and falls short in the points just mentioned, nevertheless never fights against theology. But whatever is erroneous in the books of the philosophers, or is found to conflict with the teaching of the Church, or is brought forward by heretics from philosophy against Scripture, is either not philosophical at all but the empty subtleties of human wit and the ulcers of true philosophy, such as Aristotle's opinion on the eternity of the world, or Epicurus' on the mortality of the soul, and so on; or it is indeed philosophical but has been wrongly applied to theology.

units.la: Hæc discrimina doctrinæ Christianæ, & aliarum religionum atque philosophiæ, tenenda sunt:
units.tr: These distinctions between Christian doctrine, the religions of others, and philosophy must be maintained:

units.la: I. Vt sua gloria Deo tribuatur integra: quod non fit, nisi & quicquid ille de se & voluntate sua vult credi, sciamus ac profiteamur, & nihil ipsius patefactionibus affingamus. Commisceri enim Deus cum idolis, & veritas diuina cum diaboli mendaciis absque summa nominis eius contumelia non potest.
units.tr: I. That the whole glory be ascribed to God. This does not happen unless we know and profess whatever he wishes to be believed about himself and his will, and attribute nothing to his revelations. For God cannot be mixed with idols, nor divine truth with the lies of the devil, without the greatest insult to his name.

units.la: II. Ne nos ipsi in periculum salutis nostræ incidamus: quod fieret, si decepti sectæ alicuius doctrinam vel philosophiam pro vera religione amplecteremur.
units.tr: II. That we do not fall ourselves into danger to our salvation. This would happen if, deceived, we embraced the doctrine or philosophy of some sect as the true religion.

units.la: III. Vt in nobis fides & consolatio sit firmior: quod fit, cum videmus, quanto doctrina Ecclesiæ reliquis omnibus sit perfectior, quam multa in nostra religione sint, quæ in aliis desiderantur, & quæ sint causæ, cur hanc doctrinam profitentes tantum saluentur, aliæ verò omnes cum suis sectatoribus dam-nentur, & à Deo abijciantur.
units.tr: III. That faith and comfort may be firmer in us. This comes about when we see how much more perfect the teaching of the Church is than all the rest, how many things there are in our religion that are lacking in others, and what the causes are why only those who profess this doctrine are saved, while all others, with their followers, are condemned and cast off by God.

units.la: IV. Vt nos separemus ab Epicureis & Academicis, qui om-nem religionē contemnunt, vel ita convelluntur, vt quemlibet in sua religione conseruari arbitrentur, trahentes huc illud Apostoli: Iustus fide sua viuet. At illi quidem (Epicurei) indigni sunt refutatione: isti verò (Academici) sententiam Apostoli manifeste corrumpunt, & facilè refutantur. Nam pronomen sua nequaquam significat eam fidem, quam quisque sibi fingit, sed veram fidem cuiusque propriam, & opponitur fidei alienæ etiam veræ nec non opinionibus de iustitia operum: & sensus est: iustus iustificatur non operibus legis, sed sola fide in Christum, & quidem sua propria, non aliena.
units.tr: IV. That we may separate ourselves from the Epicureans and the Academics, who either despise all religion, or are so shaken that they think anyone may be preserved in his own religion, dragging in here that saying of the Apostle: The just shall live by his own faith. The former (the Epicureans) are unworthy of refutation; the latter (the Academics) plainly corrupt the Apostle's meaning and are easily refuted. For the pronoun his own by no means signifies the faith that each person fashions for himself, but the true faith proper to each, and it is opposed to another's faith, even a true one, and also to opinions about the righteousness of works. The sense is: the righteous man is justified not by the works of the law but by faith alone in Christ, and indeed by his own faith, not another's.

units.la: IV. Quibus testimoniis confirmetur religionis Christianæ seu doctrinæ Ecclesiæ certitudo.
units.tr: IV. By what testimonies the certainty of the Christian religion, or of the doctrine of the Church, is confirmed.

units.la: Argumenta veritatem ac certitudinem doctrinæ Ecclesiæ confirmantia sunt plurima, quorum alia conscientias de veritate convincunt, vt priora XII, alia etiam persuadent atque convertunt, vt postremum.
units.tr: There are very many arguments confirming the truth and certainty of the doctrine of the Church. Some of them convince the conscience of the truth, as the first twelve do, and others also persuade and convert, as the last one does.

units.la: I. Est integritas & puritas Legis: Impossibile est enim, religionem fingentem idola, vel approbantē scelera, contra legem Dei, & iudicium rectæ rationis, veram & diuinam esse. Atqui omnes religiones, præter eam, quæ in sacris literis est tradita, & ab Ecclesia colitur, manifestè illud faciunt. Omnes enim primam legis diuinæ tabulam de vno vero Deo, & de huius veri Dei vero cultu, vel abijciunt, vel suis mendaciis contaminant: secundæ verò aliquam tantum partem de externa honestate, & officiis ciuilibus retinent, vt supra est dictum. Sola Ecclesia vtramque legis tabulam puram & integram secundum scripturam amplectitur. Quare sola Ecclesiæ doctrina est vera & diuina.
units.tr: I. The first is the integrity and purity of the Law. For it is impossible that a religion which devises idols or approves crimes, contrary to the law of God and the judgment of right reason, should be true and divine. But all religions, apart from the one that is set out in the sacred writings and worshipped by the Church, plainly do this. For all of them either reject the first table of the divine law, concerning the one true God and the true worship of him, or they contaminate it with their own falsehoods. As for the second table, they retain only some part of it, namely outward decency and civil duties, as was said above. The Church alone embraces both tables of the law, pure and whole, according to Scripture. Therefore the doctrine of the Church alone is true and divine.

units.la: II. Euangelium ostendens exitum & liberationem à peccato & morte. Procul dubio enim ea doctrina & religio, quæ modum euadendi ex peccato & morte, citra violationem iustitiæ diuinæ ostendit, & firmam consolationem de vita æterna conscientiis præbet, vera est & diuina. Sola autem Ecclesiæ doctrina in Euangelio explicat liberationem à miseria, & firmam consolationem conscientiis ostendit. Sola igitur vera est & diuina.
units.tr: II. The Gospel, which shows the way out of sin and death and the deliverance from them. Beyond doubt, that doctrine and religion which shows a way of escaping from sin and death without violating divine justice, and which gives the conscience a firm consolation about eternal life, is true and divine. But the doctrine of the Church alone, in the Gospel, explains deliverance from misery and shows the conscience a firm consolation. Therefore it alone is true and divine.

units.la: III. Antiquitas huius doctrinæ, quæ reperitur vetustissima. Sola enim Ecclesiæ doctrina in scripturis tradita originem suam ad ipsum Deum referre potest, & propagationem continuam tinuam ac certam in de ab initio mundi ostendere. Alias vero religiones omnes aliis temporibus post illam exortas ac recentiores esse, collatio historiarum totius mundi cum historia sacra ostendit. Cum igitur antiquissima religio haud dubie sit verissima, (primam enim religionem homines a Deo acceperunt) sequitur, Ecclesiae doctrinam solam veram & diuinam esse.
units.tr: III. The antiquity of this doctrine, which is found to be the most ancient. For the doctrine of the Church alone, handed down in the Scriptures, can trace its origin back to God himself and show a continuous and sure propagation from the beginning of the world. The comparison of the histories of the whole world with sacred history shows that all other religions arose at later times than that one and are more recent. Since, then, the most ancient religion is undoubtedly the truest (for men received the first religion from God), it follows that the doctrine of the Church alone is true and divine.

units.la: IV. Miracula, quibus Deus inde ab initio mundi hanc doctrinam confirmauit, & quae diabolus non potest imitari, ne per speciem quidem: vt sunt suscitatio mortuorum, status & regressus solis, diuisio maris & fluminum, partus virginis, & similia, quae cum solius Dei sint opera ad confirmandam Prophetarum & Apostolorum doctrinam edita, Deus vero mendacio testimonium non perhibeat, doctrinam eam a Deo profectam & verissimam esse euincunt.
units.tr: IV. The miracles by which God, from the beginning of the world, confirmed this doctrine, and which the devil cannot imitate, not even in appearance: such as the raising of the dead, the standing still and going back of the sun, the dividing of the sea and of rivers, the virgin birth, and similar things. These were wrought as works of God alone, to confirm the doctrine of the prophets and apostles. And since God does not bear witness to a lie, they prove that this doctrine came from God and is most true.

units.la: V. Oracula & praedictiones rerum futurarum euentibus comprobatae, cuiusmodi plurimae in vtriusq; testamenti libris continentur, & coelestem eorum originem euidenter confirmant, cum oracula vera edere Dei sit proprium.
units.tr: V. The oracles and predictions of future events, confirmed by their outcomes, of which very many are contained in the books of both Testaments, and which clearly confirm their heavenly origin, since it is proper to God to utter true oracles.

units.la: VI. Consensus partium doctrinae Ecclesiae. Doctrina enim sibi contraria, non est vera ac diuina, cum verum vero consonet, & Deus sibi non contradicat. At praeter solam propheticam & apostolicam doctrinam religiones aliae omnes a seipsis & inter se variè dissident, etiam in fundamento & praecipuis capitibus. Sola igitur Ecclesiae doctrina vera est & diuina.
units.tr: VI. The agreement of the parts of the doctrine of the Church. For a doctrine that contradicts itself is not true and divine, since truth agrees with truth and God does not contradict himself. But apart from the prophetic and apostolic doctrine alone, all other religions differ widely both from themselves and from one another, even on the foundation and the chief heads. Therefore the doctrine of the Church alone is true and divine.

units.la: VII. Hostium confessio, quod ipse diabolus clamare cogitur: Tu es Christus ille Filius Dei: & alij hostes fateri coguntur, doctrinam nostram esse veram. Quicquid enim boni & veri in suis religionibus habent alij, id etiam & quidem multo clarius ac solidius habet nostra religio: & possunt conuinci, quod ex nostra sint suffurati, & suis figmentis admiscuerint, vt solet diabolus, Dei simia, quaedam vera suis mendaciis miscere, quo facilius hominibus imponat. Vnde quae alij nostrae doctrinae habent consentanea, ea non possunt refutari, qui ex nostra sumserunt: quae habent pugnantia, ea facile euertuntur, quia sunt hominum figmenta.
units.tr: VII. The confession of enemies. The devil himself is forced to cry out, "You are the Christ, the Son of God," and other enemies are compelled to confess that our doctrine is true. For whatever good and true things other religions have, our religion has them too, and far more clearly and solidly. And they can be convicted of having stolen them from ours and mixed them into their own inventions, as the devil, the ape of God, is accustomed to mix some true things with his lies, the more easily to deceive men. Hence, whatever other religions have that agrees with our doctrine cannot be refuted by those who took it from ours; whatever they have that conflicts with it is easily overthrown, because it is the invention of men.

units.la: VIII. Odium Satanae, & instrumentorum eius aduersus hanc doctrinam. Ea enim religio haud dubie vera est & diuina, quam omnes mali & ipse Satan vno consensu oderunt, & extinctam cupiunt. Nam veritas odium parit: & diabolus est mendax ab initio, & in veritate non stetit. Atqui nullam doctrinam Satan & mundus impensius oderunt & oppugnant, quam doctrinam Ecclesiæ, quia nimirum doctrina Ecclesiæ longè rigidius eos accusat, mendacia eorum sub examen vocat, fraudes detegit, omniaq; idola & vitia damnat, quam aliæ sectæ, quæ ista concedunt, vel etiam defendunt. Mundus me odit, quoniam testificor de eo, quod opera eius mala sint. Si de mundo essetis, mundus, quod suum est, amaret, &c.
units.tr: VIII. The hatred of Satan and of his instruments against this doctrine. For that religion is undoubtedly true and divine which all the wicked and Satan himself hate with one accord and desire to extinguish. For truth breeds hatred, and the devil "was a liar from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth." But Satan and the world hate and assail no doctrine more fiercely than the doctrine of the Church, because, of course, the doctrine of the Church accuses them far more sharply, calls their lies into question, exposes their frauds, and condemns all idols and vices, more than other sects do which concede these things or even defend them. "The world hates me, because I testify of it that its works are evil. If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own," and so on.

units.la: IX. Mirabilis defensio & conseruatio huius doctrinæ contra furores Satanæ & aliorum hostium. Cùm enim nulla religio grauius à tyrannis & hæreticis perpetuò sit oppugnata, & sine intermissione oppugnetur, quàm hæc ipsa, Deus nihilominus eam, inuitis hostibus & inferorum portis, mirabiliter adhuc defendit, vt sola inuicta permanserit, cùm interim aliæ religiones, vel omnino non, vel leuius oppugnatæ, citò perierint. Hinc doctrinam Ecclesiæ Deo probari, & curæ esse, firmissimè concludimus.
units.tr: IX. The wonderful defence and preservation of this doctrine against the rage of Satan and of other enemies. For although no religion has been more constantly and severely assailed by tyrants and heretics, and is assailed without interruption, yet God, against the will of its enemies and the gates of hell, still defends it wonderfully, so that it alone has remained unconquered, while other religions, either not assailed at all or assailed more lightly, have quickly perished. Hence we conclude most firmly that the doctrine of the Church is approved by God and is his concern.

units.la: X. Pœna hostium. Nam dubium non est, eam religionem à Deo approbari & defendi, ob cuius oppugnationem aduersarios puniit. Testantur autem historiæ veteres & recentes, atrociter à Deo punitos esse, qui Prophetarum & Apostolorum doctrinam oppugnarunt. Ergo eam Deus approbat.
units.tr: X. The punishment of enemies. For there is no doubt that that religion is approved and defended by God for whose opponents he inflicts punishment. Ancient and recent histories bear witness that those who assailed the doctrine of the prophets and apostles have been terribly punished by God. Therefore God approves that doctrine.

units.la: Etsi autem impij aliquando in mundo florent, & Ecclesia oppressa iacere videtur: tamen id neque casu fieri, neque quod illi Deo placeant, vel Ecclesia non placeat, euentus testantur, & scriptura passim docet. Perpetuò enim Ecclesia in persecutionibus seruatur, & tandem liberatur: cùm contra tyrannorum & impiorum breuem felicitatem tristissimus interitus excipiat. Nec refert, quod non omnes persecutores Ecclesiæ tragicè hic puniantur, sicut Antiochus & Herodes, &c. Dum enim Deus plerosque in hac vita vlcisciitur, satis ostendit, quid de aliis similibus æstimari velit, eos nimirum esse hostes suos, in æternas pœnas abijciendos nisi resipiscant.
units.tr: Although the wicked sometimes flourish in the world and the Church seems to lie oppressed, yet the outcome shows, and Scripture teaches everywhere, that this does not happen by chance, nor because those wicked men please God or the Church does not. For the Church is always preserved in persecutions and at last is delivered, whereas the brief happiness of tyrants and the impious is followed by a most miserable end. Nor does it matter that not all persecutors of the Church are punished here in a tragic way, as Antiochus and Herod were, and so on. For while God takes vengeance on many in this life, he sufficiently shows what he wishes to be judged about others like them: that they are his enemies, to be cast into eternal punishments unless they repent.

units.la: XI. Testimonia & constantia martyrum, qui suo sanguine doctrinam Ecclesiæ obsignantes, inter læuissima tormenta testantur, se vere sic sentire, & in cordibus suis de veritate doctrinæ, quam sunt professi, firmissimè persuasos esse, atq; eam consolationem, quam aliis prædicarunt, ex ea vere percipere, quod propter Christum vere sint filij Dei, & quod sint Deo curæ in media morte. Deus igitur hac viua consolatione eos sustentans testatur, se doctrinam Ecclesiæ, propter quam illi patiuntur, approbare.
units.tr: XI. The testimony and constancy of the martyrs, who, sealing the doctrine of the Church with their blood, bear witness amid the most cruel torments that they truly think so, that they are most firmly persuaded in their hearts of the truth of the doctrine they have professed, and that they truly receive from it that consolation which they preached to others: namely, that for Christ's sake they are truly children of God, and that they are cared for by God even in the midst of death. God, therefore, by sustaining them with this living consolation, testifies that he approves the doctrine of the Church, for which they suffer.

units.la: XII. Pietas & sanctitas eorum, qui libros sacros scripserunt, & doctrinam in illis comprehensam professi sunt. Quæ enim religio homines facit sanctos, Deoque placentes, eam necesse est sanctissimam & diuinam esse. At Patriarchæ, Prophetæ, Apostoli & alij, qui doctrinam eorum serio amplexi sunt, & amplectuntur, vera virtute & sanctitate longissimè superant aliarum religionum homines: id quod collatio ostendit. Quare Ecclesiæ potius quam aliarum religionum doctrinam veram esse ac diuinam, est consentaneum.
units.tr: XII. The piety and holiness of those who wrote the sacred books and professed the doctrine contained in them. For a religion that makes men holy and pleasing to God must be most holy and divine. But the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and others, who earnestly embraced and still embrace their doctrine, far surpass the men of other religions in true virtue and holiness, as comparison shows. Therefore it is consistent that the doctrine of the Church, rather than that of other religions, is true and divine.

units.la: XIII. Candor eorum in detegendis suis & suorum vitiis, per quos Spiritus sanctus doctrinam hanc literis commendauit.
units.tr: XIII. The candour of those through whom the Holy Spirit commended this doctrine in writing, in disclosing their own faults and those of their people.

units.la: XIV. Spiritus sancti, cuius inspiratione scriptura est tradita, in cordibus credentium testificatio, seu certa persuasio, scripturam sacram esse verbum Dei, & Deum nobis juxta scripturæ huius vocem velle propitium esse: quæ persuasio est ipsa fides, quam sequitur lætitia in Deo acquiescens, & eum invocans, eum certa spe impetrandi cum alia bona, quæ ex verbi ipsius præscripto petimus, tum ipsam vitam æternam. Hæc πληροφορία, & hæc viva consolatio piorum, neque hominum neque vllius creaturæ testimonio nititur, sed est effectus Spiritus sancti proprius: quem per solam Prophetarum & Apostolorum doctrinam lectam, auditam, & mentibus impressam, ab eo accendi & confirmari, omnes pij viuo & certo suorum cordium sensu experiuntur. Hac igitur testificatione Spiritus sancti omnes ad Christum conuersi de certitudine doctrinæ cœlestis firmissimè confidunt & obsignantur.
units.tr: XIV. The testimony of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers, by whose inspiration Scripture was handed down, or the certain persuasion that the sacred Scripture is the Word of God and that God wishes to be gracious to us according to the voice of this Scripture. This persuasion is faith itself, which is followed by joy resting in God and calling upon him with the certain hope of obtaining both other good things, which we ask according to the precept of the Word itself, and eternal life. This full assurance [πληροφορία] and this living consolation of the godly rests not on the testimony of men or of any creature, but is the proper effect of the Holy Spirit. All the godly experience, by the living and certain sense of their hearts, that it is kindled and confirmed in them by him through the doctrine of the prophets and apostles alone, when read, heard, and impressed on their minds. By this testimony of the Holy Spirit, therefore, all who have been converted to Christ are most firmly assured and sealed in their confidence in the certainty of the heavenly doctrine.

units.la: Atque hoc argumentum, vt est renatorum proprium, ita solum corda eorum non solum de veritate & authoritate scripturæ sacræconuincit, sed etiam persuadet, vt assentiantur, & in ea firmiter acquiescant: reliqua omnia communia sunt etiam non conuersis, quos quidem etiam conuincunt, atque ora contradicentibus obturant, sed sola non persuadent, nec mouent ad assentiendum, nisi intus testimonium Spiritus sancti accedat.
units.tr: And this argument, as it is proper to the reborn, so it alone not only convinces their hearts of the truth and authority of Holy Scripture, but also persuades them to assent to it and rest firmly in it. All the other arguments are common even to the unconverted: these indeed convince them too and stop the mouths of those who contradict, but they alone do not persuade or move them to assent, unless the testimony of the Holy Spirit comes in inwardly.

units.la: V. Quotuplex sit ratio tradendi & discendi doctrinam Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: V. What is the manner of teaching and learning the doctrine of the Church.

units.la: Triplex est studij Theologici ratio.
units.tr: There is a threefold method of theological study.

units.la: Prima est institutio catechetica, seu summaria & rudis doctrinæ Christianæ & præcipuarum eius capitum explicatio, quæ Catechesis appellatur. Hæc omnibus est necessaria, quia fundamentum religionis omnibus, doctis pariter & indoctis, cognitum esse oportet.
units.tr: The first is catechetical instruction, that is, the brief and rudimentary summary of Christian doctrine and the explanation of its main heads, which is called Catechesis. This is necessary for everyone, since the foundation of religion ought to be known by all, learned and unlearned alike.

units.la: Secunda est tractatio locorum communium, qui continent prolixiorem explicationem singularum partium, & quæstionum num difficiliorum, cum suis definitionibus, diuisionibus, ra-tionibus, antithesibus, & porismatis.
units.tr: The second is the treatment of the common topics (loci communes), which contain a fuller explanation of the individual parts and of the more difficult questions, together with their definitions, divisions, arguments, antitheses and corollaries.

units.la: Haec ad scholas Theologicas praecipuè pertinet, & est necessaria:
units.tr: This belongs chiefly to the theological schools, and it is necessary:

units.la: 1. Vt qui in scholis educantur, & ad docendum aliquando accessuri sunt, sacram Theologiam facilius & plenius cognoscant. Nam vt in aliis, ita in hoc studio difficilius & tardius discitur, immò omnis cognitio manet confusa & imperfecta, nisi omnes doctrinae partes certo ordine tradantur, & mente concipiantur.
units.tr: 1. So that those who are educated in the schools, and who will one day come to teach, may know sacred theology more easily and fully. For in this study, as in others, learning is more difficult and slow; indeed, all knowledge remains confused and imperfect unless all parts of doctrine are taught in a fixed order and grasped by the mind.

units.la: 2. Vt Theologiae studiosi suis aliquando auditoribus summam integrae doctrinae ordine ac perspicuè tradere possint, necesse est ipsos prius perfectum doctrinae systema, quasi corpus quoddam mente conceptum habere.
units.tr: 2. So that students of theology may one day be able to present the sum of the whole doctrine to their hearers clearly and in order, they must first have the complete system of doctrine, as it were a body conceived in the mind.

units.la: Est 3. necessaria ad veram & genuinam scripturarum interpretationem inveniendam & judicandam, quae cum fidei analogia esse, & nulli doctrinae sacrae capiti repugnare debeat, omnia eius capita integre perfecta esse oportet.
units.tr: Third, it is necessary for finding and judging the true and genuine interpretation of Scripture, which ought to agree with the analogy of faith and contradict no head of sacred doctrine; for this, all its heads must be whole and perfect.

units.la: 4. Requiritur ad formanda judicia de controversiis Ecclesiasticis, quae & variae sunt, & difficiles ac periculosae, ne a vero ad errores & mendacia abripiamur.
units.tr: 4. It is required for forming judgments on ecclesiastical controversies, which are many, difficult and dangerous, lest we be carried away from the truth into errors and lies.

units.la: Tertia studij theologici ratio est diligens lectio & meditatio ipsius scripturae, seu textus sacri. Atque hic est summus studij theologici gradus, cuius causa catechesis & loci communes discuntur: nempe vt ad sacram scripturam legendam, intelligendam atque tradendam aliis parati accedamus. Doctrina enim Catechetica & loci communes sicut ex scriptura petuntur, & ad scripturarum veluti normam dirig untur, sic rursus ad scripturam nos quasi manu ducunt. Ad primam studij Theologici tationem pertinet Catechesis, de qua sequuntur
units.tr: The third method of theological study is diligent reading and meditation on Scripture itself, that is, the sacred text. This is the highest level of theological study, and the sake for which catechism and the common topics are learned: namely, that we may come to reading, understanding and teaching Holy Scripture to others, well prepared. For catechetical doctrine and the common topics are drawn from Scripture and are directed by it as by its rule, and in turn they lead us by the hand back to Scripture. To the first method of theological study belongs the Catechism, of which the following is concerned.

units.la: Prolegomena specialia de CATECHESI.
units.tr: Special prolegomena on the CATECHISM.

units.la: Sequuntur prolegomena specialia quinque de Catechesi. I. Quid sit Catechesis. II. An semper fuerit, seu de eius origine in Ecclesia. III. Quae sint eius praecipua capita. IV. Cur sit necessaria. V. Quis sit eius scopus.
units.tr: There follow five special prolegomena on the Catechism. I. What the Catechism is. II. Whether it has always existed, or concerning its origin in the Church. III. What its principal heads are. IV. Why it is necessary. V. What its aim is.

units.la: 1. Quid sit Catechesis.
units.tr: 1. What the Catechism is.

units.la: Κατήχησις est à κατηχέω, vt κατηχισμὸς, à κατηχίζω: vtrumque significat insono, viua voce instituo, & dicta repeto: proprie verò prima alicuius doctrinae rudimenta doceo: & magis proprie, in ecclesiae sermone prima elemen a religionis Christianae trado, vt Luc.1, 4. Act.18, 25. Gal.6, 6. & alibi vsurpatum legitur. Hinc catechesis generaliter significat primam breuem & elementarem in quacunque doctrina institutionem rudiorum, quae fit viua voce. In Ecclesia autem significat talem institutionem rudiorum in elementis doctrinae Christianae.
units.tr: Katechesis [κατήχησις] comes from katecheo [κατηχέω], as katechismos [κατηχισμὸς] comes from katechizo [κατηχίζω]. Both mean to sound in the ears, to instruct by the living voice, and to repeat what has been said; strictly, to teach the first rudiments of some doctrine; and most properly, in the language of the Church, to deliver the first elements of the Christian religion, as is found used in Luc.1, 4. Act.18, 25. Gal.6, 6. and elsewhere. Hence generally catechesis means the first brief and elementary instruction of beginners in any doctrine, given by the living voice. In the Church, however, it means such instruction of beginners in the elements of Christian doctrine.

units.la: Catechesis igitur Christianae religionis est, breuis, perspicua, & ad captum rudiorum accommodata doctrinae Christianae ex scriptis propheticis & apostolicis collecta, & in certas quaestiones ac responsiones digesta explicatio & recitatio: seu est compendium doctrinae propheticae & apostolicae, quod rudioribus viua voce traditur, & ab iisdem rursus exigitur.
units.tr: The catechesis of the Christian religion is therefore a brief, clear explanation and recital of Christian doctrine, gathered from the prophetic and apostolic writings and adapted to the understanding of beginners, arranged in set questions and answers. In other words, it is a compendium of prophetic and apostolic doctrine, delivered by the living voice to beginners and in turn required back from them.

units.la: Catechumeni in primitiua Ecclesia dicebantur, qui Catechismum discebant, hoc est, qui jam erant in Ecclesia, & in rudimentis doctrinae Christianae instituebantur. Erant autem duplices. Alij grandes, qui ex Judaeis aut Gentibus ad Christianismum accedebant, sed nondum erant baptizati. Hi prius erudiebantur in catechesi, deinde baptizabantur, & ad coenam Domini admittebantur. Talis catechumenus fuit Augustinus, cum ex Manichaeo fieret Christianus, & multos libros scripsit catechumenus, antequam ab Ambrosio baptizaretur. Talis etiam fuit Ambrosius, cum in Episcopum eligeretur, sic postulante necessitate Ecclesiae Mediolanensis propter Arianos, qui eam inuaserant. Alioqui Paulus vetat deligi Episcopum neophytum, hoc est, nouitium & catechumenum. Neophyti enim dicebantur catechumeni, nondum vel recens baptizati, a νέος & φυτόν, quasi nouae plantae, hoc est, nouitij auditores & discipuli Ecclesiae. Alij catechumeni erant paruuli, in Ecclesia nati, seu liberi Christianorum. Hi statim post partum, vt membra Ecclesiae, baptizabantur, & postquam nonnihil adoleuissent, in catechesi instituebantur, quam tenentes cum impositione manuum e coetu catechumenorum dimittebantur, vt deinceps eis liceret cum adultis ad coenam accedere. Vide quaedam de catechumenis apud Eusebium lib. 10. histor. Eccles. cap. 4. non procul a fine. Catechetae vero seu catechistae dicebantur, qui catechismum docebant, hoc est, praeceptores catechumenorum.
units.tr: In the early Church those were called catechumens who learned the Catechism, that is, who were already in the Church and were being instructed in the rudiments of Christian doctrine. There were two kinds. Some were adults, who came to Christianity from Jews or Gentiles but had not yet been baptized. These were first trained in catechesis, then baptized, and then admitted to the Lord's Supper. Such a catechumen was Augustine, when he passed from Manichaeism to Christianity, and he wrote many books while still a catechumen, before being baptized by Ambrose. Such also was Ambrose, when he was chosen bishop, the need of the Church of Milan demanding it because of the Arians, who had invaded it. Otherwise Paul forbids a bishop to be chosen from a neophyte, that is, a novice and catechumen.
