For catechumens who were not yet baptized, or had only recently been baptized, were called neophytes, from new [νέος] and plant [φυτόν], as it were new plants, that is, new hearers and disciples of the Church. Others, who were catechumens, were infants born in the Church, that is, children of Christians. These were baptized straightaway after birth, as members of the Church, and when they had grown somewhat they were instructed in catechesis; having learned it, they were dismissed from the company of catechumens with the laying on of hands, so that thereafter they might be allowed to come to the Supper with adults. On some matters concerning catechumens see Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 10, chapter 4, not far from the end. Catechists, however, were called catechetae or catechistae, those who taught the Catechism, that is, the instructors of catechumens.

units.la: II. De origine Catecheseos, & an semper in Ecclesia fuerit.
units.tr: II. On the origin of catechesis, and whether it has always been in the Church.

units.la: De origine catecheseos in Ecclesia idem quod de toto ministerio sentiendum est, a Deo ipso esse institutam, & in Ecclesia semper fuisse. Nam cum Deus jam inde ab initio fuerit non modo adultorum, sed etiam paruulorum Deus, juxta formulam foederis: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui: utrosque etiam in doctrina salutis pro ipsorum captu voluit erudiri; adultos quidem per publicam vocem ministerii, juniores vero per domesticam & scholasticam catechizationem. Ac de adultorum quidem institutione satis constat.
units.tr: The origin of catechesis in the Church is to be understood in the same way as that of the whole ministry: it was instituted by God himself and has always existed in the Church. For since God from the beginning has been the God not only of adults but also of children, according to the formula of the covenant, I will be your God and the God of your seed, he willed that both should be taught the doctrine of salvation in a manner suited to their capacity: adults by the public voice of the ministry, and the younger ones by domestic and school instruction. Concerning the instruction of adults, enough is certain.

units.la: De puerorum vero catechizatione in Ecclesia Judaica passim exstant in sacris scripturis mandata. Exod. 12. & 13. jubet Deus pueros & familias erudiri de origine & de usu paschatis. Deut. 4. praecipit parentibus, ut repetant parvulis historiam promulgatae legis. Deut. 6. jubet pueris inculcari doctrinam de unitate Dei, & de perfecta dilectione Dei: & Deut. 11. iisdem explicari totam legem sive decalogum. Erudiebantur ergo pueri in veteri testamento domi a parentibus, & in scholis a Prophetis, de praecipuis doctrinae propheticae capitibus: nempe de Deo, de lege, de promissione Euangelij, de usu sacramentorum & sacrificiorum, quod essent typi venturi Messiae & beneficiorum eius, &c. Nam in hunc usum non est dubium fuisse apertas scholas Prophetarum, Eliae, Elisaei, & aliorum. Huc faciebat brevis summa legis a Deo tradita: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Et summa Euangelij: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Habebant item sacrificia, precationes & alia, quae Deus voluit, ut Abraham eiusque posteri suos liberos & familias docerent: proinde accommodata fuit haec doctrina puerorum rudiumque captui.
units.tr: Concerning the catechizing of children in the Jewish Church, commands are found throughout the sacred Scriptures. In Exodus 12 and 13 God orders children and households to be taught the origin and use of the Passover. In Deuteronomy 4 he charges parents to repeat to their little ones the history of the giving of the law. In Deuteronomy 6 he orders the doctrine of the unity of God and of the perfect love of God to be impressed upon children, and in Deuteronomy 11 the whole law, or the Decalogue, is to be explained to them. Children in the Old Testament were therefore taught at home by their parents, and in the schools by the prophets, in the chief heads of prophetic doctrine: namely concerning God, the law, the promise of the Gospel, and the use of the sacraments and sacrifices, which were types of the coming Messiah and of his benefits, and so on. For there is no doubt that open schools of the prophets existed for this purpose, those of Elijah, Elisha, and others. To this purpose served the brief summary of the law given by God: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc., and your neighbour as yourself. And the summary of the Gospel: The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent; in your seed shall all the nations be blessed. They also had sacrifices, prayers, and other things, which God willed that Abraham and his posterity should use to teach their children and households. Accordingly this doctrine was adapted to the capacity of children and the untaught.

units.la: In novo testamento exstat mandatum de pueris Christo adducendis, quibus manus imposuit & benedixit: Sinite pueros ad me venire, & ne prohibete eos: talium enim est regnum Dei. Et in Ecclesia apostolica catechizationem puerorum diligenter observatam fuisse, testatur exemplum Timothei, quem Paulus scribit a puero didicisse literas sacras: & epistola ad Hebraeos, quae aliquot capita catecheseos apostolicae recenset, & hac puerorum appellat: de resipiscentia: de fide in Deum: de baptismo & sacramentorum doctrina: de impositione manuum: de resurrectione mortuorum: & de judicio aeterno. Haec & similia capita solebant a catechumenis grandibus exigi in baptismo, a parvulis in impositione manuum, ideo Apostolus ea vocat doctrinam baptismatum & impositionis manuum. Similiter & patres scripserunt breves summas doctrinae, quarum reliquias videmus adhuc in Papatu. Eusebius scribit de Origene, quod doctrinam catecheticam Alexandriae sub persecutionibus collapsam instauraverit. Augustinus scripsit totum librum de catechizandis rudibus. Tom IV. Socrates etiam de catechesi: Nostra, inquit, formula ad hunc modum se habet, sicut ab episcopis, qui nos antegressi sunt, accepimus: sicut cum fidei fundamenta iecimus, cumque baptizati sumus, audivimus: sicut à divinis scripturis didicimus, &c. Papa Gregorius idola & imagines in templa locavit, ut essent libri laicorum & puerorum. Post ea tempora doctrina Ecclesiæ, negligentia episcoporum, & astu Pontificum Romanorum, paulatim corrupta est, & catechesis collapsa, tandemque in ludicrum confirmationis situm transformata, quem hodie vocant die Firmuna. Videtur Distinct. IV. de consecratione apud Gratianum. Hæc de origine & exercitiis catecheseos in Ecclesia.
units.tr: In the New Testament there is a command concerning bringing children to Christ, upon whom he laid his hands and whom he blessed: Suffer the little children to come to me, and forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of God. And that in the apostolic Church the catechizing of children was carefully observed is witnessed by the example of Timothy, whom Paul writes to have learned the holy letters from childhood, and by the Epistle to the Hebrews, which lists several heads of apostolic catechesis and calls these the teaching of children: repentance, faith in God, baptism and the doctrine of the sacraments, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. These and similar heads were customarily required of adult catechumens at baptism, and of children at the laying on of hands; therefore the Apostle calls them the doctrine of baptisms and of the laying on of hands. Likewise the Fathers wrote brief summaries of doctrine, the remnants of which we still see in Papacy. Eusebius writes of Origen that he restored the catechetical teaching at Alexandria, which had fallen during the persecutions. Augustine wrote an entire book on catechizing the uninstructed. Tom. IV. Socrates also speaks of catechesis: Our formula, he says, is in this manner, as we have received it from the bishops who went before us: as when we laid the foundations of faith, and when we were baptized, we heard it; as we learned it from the divine Scriptures, etc. Pope Gregory placed images and idols in the churches, so that they might be books for the laity and children. After those times the doctrine of the Church, through the negligence of bishops and the craft of the Roman Pontiffs, was gradually corrupted, and catechesis fell, and was at last transformed into a sort of ceremony of confirmation, which they today call the Firmuna day. See Distinction IV, on consecration, in Gratian. These things concern the origin and practice of catechesis in the Church.

units.la: III. Quæ sint partes seu præcipua capita doctrinæ catechetica.
units.tr: III. What are the parts, or principal heads, of catechetical doctrine.

units.la: Partes præcipuæ rudimentorum Catecheticorum (ut patet ex loco citato ad Hebræos) erant pœnitentia & fides in Christum, hoc est, Lex & Euangelium. Primò igitur & communissimè catechesis dividitur, sicut doctrina Ecclesiæ, in Legem & Euangelium. Catechesis enim & doctrina Ecclesiæ non differunt subjecto & re, sed tantum ratione & modo rei: sicut non differunt subjecto, sed modo tantum, cibus solidus adultorum, cui doctrina Ecclesiæ, & cibus præmansus, & lac puerorum, cui catechesis à Paulo confertur. Hæ partes vulgo vocantur decalogus & symbolum apostolicum, quia decalogus complectitur summam legis, symbolum, Euangelij: item doctrina fidei & operum, seu doctrina credendorum & faciendorum.
units.tr: The principal parts of the catechetical rudiments (as is clear from the passage cited in Hebrews) were repentance and faith in Christ, that is, Law and Gospel. First, then, and most commonly, catechesis is divided, like the doctrine of the Church, into Law and Gospel. For catechesis and the doctrine of the Church do not differ in subject matter and substance, but only in the manner and mode of the matter: just as solid food for adults, which is the doctrine of the Church, and chewed food and the milk of infants, which is catechesis as Paul gives it, do not differ in substance but only in manner. These parts are commonly called the Decalogue and the Apostles' Creed, because the Decalogue comprises the summary of the law, and the Creed the summary of the Gospel; likewise the doctrine of faith and of works, or the doctrine of what is to be believed and what is to be done.

units.la: Alij dividunt in doctrinam de Deo, de voluntate Dei, & de operibus Dei. Et opera Dei rursus distinguunt in opera creationis, conservationis & redemptionis. Sed de his tribus membris agitur vel in lege, vel in Euangelio, vel in utroque. Itaque hæc divisio facile revocatur ad priorem.
units.tr: Others divide it into the doctrine of God, of the will of God, and of the works of God. And they again distinguish the works of God into works of creation, preservation, and redemption. But these three members are treated either in the law, or in the Gospel, or in both. Thus this division is easily traced back to the former one.

units.la: Alij faciunt quinque partes: decalogum, symbolum apostolicum, baptismum, eucharistiam & precationem: quarum partium aliæ à Deo ipso immediatè sunt traditæ, ut decalogus: aliæ mediatè, idque per Filium in carne manifestatum, ut precatio dominica, baptismus, eucharistia: vel per Apostolos, ut symbolum apostolicum. Sed & hæ partes ad duas illas revocantur. Nam decalogus est summa legis: symbolum est summa Euangelij: sacramenta sunt Euangelij appendices; ideo ad Euangelium referuntur, quatenus sunt sigilla gratiæ, in Euangelio promissæ; quatenus verò sunt testimonia nostræ erga Deum obedientiæ, sacrificiorum rationem habent, & ad legem pertinent. Precatio est pars cultus Dei; ideo ad legem refertur.
units.tr: Others make five parts: the Decalogue, the Apostles' Creed, baptism, the Eucharist, and prayer. Of these parts some were delivered immediately by God himself, as the Decalogue; others mediately, and that through the Son manifested in the flesh, as the Lord's Prayer, baptism, and the Eucharist; or through the Apostles, as the Apostles' Creed. But these parts too are reduced to those two. For the Decalogue is the summary of the law; the Creed is the summary of the Gospel; the sacraments are appendices of the Gospel, and so are referred to the Gospel, insofar as they are seals of the grace promised in the Gospel; but insofar as they are testimonies of our obedience toward God, they have the character of sacrifices and pertain to the law. Prayer is a part of the worship of God, and so it is referred to the law.

units.la: Nostra catechesis tribus partibus constat. 1. De hominis miseria. 2. De eiusdem liberatione. 3. De gratitudine. Quæ diuisio à superioribus reipsa non discrepat, quia aliæ partes ad has referuntur. Decalogus pertinet ad primam partem, quatenus est speculum peccati & miseriæ nostræ, & ad tertiam, quatenus est regula veræ gratitudinis & vitæ Christianæ. Symbolum, quia liberationis modum explicat, ad secundam refertur. Eodem pertinent sacramenta, tanquam appendices & sigilla doctrinæ fidei. Precatio denique, tanquam præcipua pars cultus spiritualis & gratitudinis, ad tertiam refertur.
units.tr: Our catechesis consists of three parts: 1. Concerning the misery of man. 2. Concerning his deliverance. 3. Concerning gratitude. This division does not in fact differ from the above, because the other parts are referred to these. The Decalogue belongs to the first part, insofar as it is a mirror of our sin and misery, and to the third, insofar as it is the rule of true gratitude and of the Christian life. The Creed, since it explains the manner of deliverance, is referred to the second. To the same part belong the sacraments, as appendices and seals of the doctrine of faith. Finally, prayer, as the chief part of spiritual worship and gratitude, is referred to the third.

units.la: IV. Cur sit necessaria Catechesis in Ecclesia.
units.tr: IV. Why catechesis is necessary in the Church.

units.la: Necessaria est diligens exercitatio doctrinæ catechecticæ in Eeclesia:
units.tr: Careful exercise in catechetical teaching is necessary in the Church:

units.la: I. Propter mandatum Dei. Acues ea filiis tuis, &c.
units.tr: I. On account of the command of God: "You shall teach them diligently to your sons, etc."

units.la: II. Propter gloriam Dei, quæ postulat, vt Deus non solum ab adultis, sed etiam à pueris recte agnoscatur & celebretur, juxta dictum: Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem tuam.
units.tr: II. On account of the glory of God, which requires that God be rightly acknowledged and celebrated not only by adults but also by children, according to the saying: "Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected your praise."

units.la: III. Propter nostram consolationem & salutem. Nam sine vera agnitione Dei & Filii eius Iesu Christi, hoc est, sine fide & pœnitentia, nemo adultus seruatur, neq; habet firmam consolationem, quod placeat Deo. Hæc est enim vita æterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Et: Sine fide impossibile est Deo placere. Nemo autem credit in eum, quem non nouit, vel de quo nunquam audiuit. Quomodo credent ei, de quo nunquam audierunt? Fides ex auditu est: auditus per verbum Dei. Quotquot ergo seruari cupiunt, eos necesse est tenere fundamentum, quod est doctrina de Christo. Omnes igitur oportet institui, proinde & talem doctrinæ summam in Ecclesia oportet tradi, cuius etiam rudes & juniores sint capaces.
units.tr: III. For our consolation and salvation. For without the true knowledge of God and of his Son Jesus Christ, that is, without faith and repentance, no adult is saved, nor has he firm comfort that he pleases God. "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." And: "Without faith it is impossible to please God." But no one believes in him whom he does not know, or of whom he has never heard. "How will they believe in him of whom they have never heard? Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God." Therefore, all who desire to be saved must hold the foundation, which is the doctrine concerning Christ. It is necessary, then, that all be instructed, and so the summary of this doctrine must be taught in the Church in such a way that even the unlearned and the young are able to grasp it.

units.la: IV. Propter Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ conseruationem in hac vita. Nam vt Ecclesia & respublica consistat, opus est religione & cultu Dei, disciplina, studiis & exercitiis pietatis, honestatis, justitiæ & veritatis inter homines. At hæc frustra quæruntur inter barbaros, qui nulla pietatis aut virtutis disciplina imbuti sunt. Imbui autem oportet à teneris: quia cor hominis prauum & peruersum est à juuentute: immò tanta est naturæ nostræ corruptio, vt nisi mature fiat emendatio, serò medicina paretur,
units.tr: IV. For the preservation of the Church and the commonwealth in this life. For in order that the Church and the commonwealth may stand, there is need of religion and the worship of God, of discipline, and of zeal and exercises of piety, honesty, justice and truth among men. Yet these things are sought in vain among barbarians, who have been imbued with no discipline of piety or virtue. But they must be imbued from tender years: "because the heart of man is evil and perverse from youth; indeed, so great is the corruption of our nature that unless correction is made early, the remedy is prepared too late, when evils have grown strong through long delays."

units.la: Ex.12. &13. Deut.4,6. 11.12. Psal.8,3. Ioh.17,3. Hebr.11,7. Rom.10,7. Genef.8,21. Ierem.17,9. cum mala per longas inualuere moras. Nisi ergo de Deo & voluntate eius inde à pueris rectè ex verbo Dei erudiamur, & ad pietatem assuefiamus, difficulter aut nunquam ab erroribus, qui nobiscum quasi nascuntur, vel quos pueri imbibimus, & à viitiis, quibus innutriti sumus, nos retrahi patiemur. Tempestiuè itaque occurrendum est prauitati humanæ, ne Ecclesia & Respublica perdatur.
units.tr: Ex. 12 and 13; Deut. 4:6; 11:12; Ps. 8:3; John 17:3; Heb. 11:7; Rom. 10:7; Gen. 8:21; Jer. 17:9. Unless, therefore, we are rightly taught from childhood, out of the Word of God, about God and his will, and are accustomed to piety, we will with difficulty, or never, allow ourselves to be drawn back from the errors which seem to be born with us, or which we drink in as children, and from the vices in which we have been nourished. Human depravity must therefore be met in good time, lest the Church and the commonwealth be ruined.

units.la: V. Normam judicandi de dogmatibus oportet omnibus notam esse, ne errent, aut seducantur, juxta mandatum: Cauete à pseudoprophetis: Omnia probate: Probate spiritus, an ex Deo sint. Hæc autem norma sunt præcipua capita catechetica, decalogus & symbolum Apostolicum.
units.tr: V. The rule of judging doctrines ought to be known to all, lest they err or be led astray, according to the command: "Beware of false prophets; test all things; test the spirits, whether they are from God." Now the chief catechetical heads, the Decalogue and the Apostles' Creed, are this rule.

units.la: VI. Qui catechesin discunt, etiam conciones rectius intelligunt, quoniam ea, quæ ex verbo Dei audiunt, facilè ad sua quæq; capita catecheseos, quam didicerunt, reuocare possunt. Quod cum non fit, conciones plerumque non magno cum fructu audiuntur.
units.tr: VI. Those who learn the catechism also understand sermons more correctly, since what they hear from the Word of God they can easily refer to the several heads of the catechism which they have learned. When this does not happen, sermons are for the most part heard with little profit.

units.la: VII. Propter ruditatem & infirmitatem discentium. Juventuti enim & incipientibus, difficilis & inutilis est prolixa & vaga institutio. Debet ergo breuis esse, simplex & perspicua, qualis est catechetica.
units.tr: VII. On account of the rudeness and weakness of the learners. For a long and rambling instruction is difficult and useless for the young and for beginners. It ought therefore to be brief, simple and clear, such as the catechism is.

units.la: VIII. Omnibus etiam rudibus & junioribus necessaria est discretio à sectis & gentibus prophanis, quam necesse est fieri per catechesin.
units.tr: VIII. Discrimination from the sects and profane peoples is also necessary for all the unlearned and the young, which must be done through catechesis.

units.la: IX. Denique scholasticis maximè necessaria est catechesis: quia his doctrina Christiana notior esse debet, quam aliis; tum propter vocationem, vt aliquando alios doceant, tum propter occasiones discendi, quas habent, & quas non debent negligere, exemplo Timothei.
units.tr: IX. Finally, catechesis is most necessary for students: because Christian doctrine ought to be better known to them than to others, both on account of their calling, that they may sometimes teach others, and on account of the opportunities for learning which they have, and which they ought not to neglect, following the example of Timothy.

units.la: His addi possunt etiam aliæ causæ impulsiuæ, præcipuè ad populum: à fine creationis nostræ: à causa prorogatæ & conseruatæ nobis vitæ à Deo, vsque ad annos adolescentiæ, juventutis, &c. item, à præstantia obiecti doctrinæ catecheticæ, quod est summum bonum, Deus: & ab effectu, qui est, huius summi boni cognitio & σωτηρία, quæ præstat omnibus mundi thesauris. Hæc enim est pretiosa illa margarita, in agro Ecclesiæ defossa, de qua Christus Matth.13. & cuius gratia olim Christiani vnà cum suis paruulis martyria læti adibant. Videatur exemplum Origenis apud Eusebium lib.6. histor. cap.3. Legatur Theodoretus lib.4. histor. cap.16. Quid verò nos pro Christi doctrina & gloria pateremur, si eam ignoremus? Quomodo autem non ignorabimus, si à teneris non didiceri-mus? Neglectus ergo catecheseos causa est non postrema, cur hodie multi quouis doctrinæ vento circumferantur, vel à Christo ad Antichristum deficiant.
units.tr: Other moving causes may also be added, especially with regard to the people: from the end of our creation; from the cause of the life prolonged and preserved for us by God, up to the years of adolescence and youth, etc.; likewise from the excellence of the object of catechetical doctrine, which is the highest good, God; and from its effect, which is the knowledge of this highest good and salvation [σωτηρία], which surpasses all the treasures of the world. For this is that precious pearl, buried in the field of the Church, of which Christ speaks in Matthew 13, and for whose sake Christians of old, together with their little children, joyfully went to martyrdom. Let the example of Origen in Eusebius, book 6 of the History, chapter 3, be seen. Let Theodoret, book 4 of the History, chapter 16, be read. But what would we suffer for the doctrine and glory of Christ if we were ignorant of it? And how shall we not be ignorant of it, if we have not learned it from tender years? Neglect of catechesis is therefore no small cause why today many are carried about by every wind of doctrine, or fall away from Christ to Antichrist.

units.la: V. Quis sit scopus catecheseos & doctrina Christiana.
units.tr: V. What is the aim of the catechism and Christian doctrine.

units.la: Scopus huius doctrinæ est consolatio & salus nostra. Salus in fruitione summi boni consistit. Consolatio est fiducia & exspectatio certa vitæ æternæ, cum inchoata quadam fruitione coniuncta. Summum bonum est, quod habentes beati, & quo destituti infelices & miseri sumus. Porrò hæc unica consolatio, quæ & qualis sit, prima quæstione catecheseos explicatur, ad quam nunc transeamus.
units.tr: The aim of this doctrine is our consolation and salvation. Salvation consists in the enjoyment of the chief good. Consolation is the confident and certain expectation of eternal life, joined with a certain inchoate enjoyment of it. The chief good is that which the blessed possess and which the wretched and miserable lack. Moreover, this single consolation, what it is and of what kind, is explained in the first question of the catechism, to which we now pass.

units.la: Hucusque Prolegomena.
units.tr: Hitherto the Prolegomena.

units.la: CATECHESIS RELIGIONIS Christianae.
units.tr: CATECHISM OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.

units.la: QVÆSTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: QUESTION 1.

units.la: Qua est vnica tua consolatio in vita & in morte?
units.tr: What is your only comfort in life and in death?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: QVOD animo a pariter & corpore, siue viuam, b siue moriar, non c meus, sed fidissimi Domini, & Seruatoris mei d IESU CHRISTI proprius sum: qui pretioso sanguine suo e pro omnibus peccatis meis plenissimè satisfaciens, me ab omni potestate Diaboli f liberauit; meque ita g conseruat, vt sine voluntate Patris mei coelestis h ne pilus quidem de meo capite possit cadere: immò verò etiam i omnia saluti meæ seruire oporteat. Quocirca me quoque k Spiritu sancto de vita æterna certum facit: vtque ipsi deinceps viuam, l promtum ac paratum reddit.
units.tr: That I, body and soul alike, whether I live or die, am not my own, but belong to my faithful Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ: who, with his precious blood, has fully satisfied for all my sins and has delivered me from all the power of the devil; and so preserves me that without the will of my heavenly Father not a hair can fall from my head; indeed, all things must work together for my salvation. Wherefore, by his Holy Spirit he also assures me of eternal life, and makes me ready and willing to live for him from now on.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: QVÆSTIO de consolatione ideò primo loco est posita, quia continet scopum & summam totius Catechismi. Scopus est, vt habeamus sitam consolationem in vita & in morte. Propterea enim tota doctrina coelestis à Deo est reuelata, & à nobis potissimum est discenda. Summa in eo consistit, quod sumus Christo per fidem insiti, per eum dilecti & reconciliati Deo, vt ab eo curemur & seruemur in æternum.
units.tr: This question about comfort is placed first for the reason that it contains the aim and the sum of the whole Catechism. The aim is that we may have comfort set before us in life and in death. For this is the reason why the whole heavenly doctrine has been revealed by God, and it is above all to be learned by us. The sum consists in this, that we are through faith ingrafted into Christ, loved by him and reconciled to God, so that we may be cared for and preserved by him for ever.

units.la: De hac Consolatione tenendum:
units.tr: On this consolation, what must be held:

units.la: I. Quid sit. II. Quibus partibus constet. III. Quare hæc unica sit solida. IV. Quæ ad eam habendam requirantur.
units.tr: I. What it is. II. Of what parts it consists. III. Why this alone is a solid consolation. IV. What is required in order to have it.

units.la: I. Quid sit.
units.tr: I. What it is.

units.la: CONSOLATIO est quædam ratiocinatio, qua malo alicui bonum aliquod opponimus, & consideratione huius boni dolorem mitigamus, & malum patienter toleramus. Quanto igitur gravius est malū, tanto maius ac certius requiritur bonum: & quia hic quæritur consolatio contra summum malum, quod est peccatum & mors æterna: non quoduis, sed summum bonum hic remedium sufficiens esse potest. De hoc autem summo bono extra verbum Dei tot fere inveniuntur sententiæ, quot capita. Epicurei id posuerunt in voluptate: Stoici in recta affectuum moderatione, vel in habitu virtutis: Platonici in ideis: Peripatetici in actione virtutis: Vulgus in honoribus, divitiis, potentia. Sed hæc omnia nimis sunt evanida, quia vel in vita amittuntur, vel morte abrumpuntur. Quæritur verò bonum, quod in morte non evanescat. Est quidem virtutis immortale decus, & vivit post funera virtus, ut Poëta ait: sed apud alios potius quàm apud nos: ac recte dictum est à quodam, virtutes ut summa bona jactari non posse, cum eas habeamus calamitatum nostrarum testes. Hypocritæ in Ecclesia & extra eam Iudæi, Pharisæi, Mahumetani, in suis meritis, vel in ceremoniis & ritibus externis, mortis remedium quærunt. Papistæ non dissimiliter faciunt. Sed ritus externi conscientias munere non possunt: neque Deus satisfactiunculis humanis deluditur.
units.tr: Consolation is a certain reasoning by which we set some good against an evil, and by considering this good we ease our grief and bear the evil patiently. The greater the evil, therefore, the greater and surer the good that is needed. Since the consolation sought here is against the greatest evil, which is sin and eternal death, only the supreme good can serve as a sufficient remedy. Outside the Word of God there are almost as many opinions about this supreme good as there are heads. The Epicureans placed it in pleasure; the Stoics in the right ordering of the emotions, or in the habit of virtue; the Platonists in the ideas; the Peripatetics in the exercise of virtue; the common people in honours, riches and power. But all these are far too fleeting, for they are either lost in life or cut off by death. What is sought is a good that does not fade in death. Virtue has an immortal glory, and virtue lives on after the funeral, as the poet says; but it lives on among others rather than among us. And someone has rightly said that virtues cannot be boasted of as the highest goods, since we have them as witnesses of our calamities. Hypocrites within the Church and outside it, Jews, Pharisees, Mohammedans, seek a remedy for death in their own merits, or in ceremonies and external rites. The Papists do not act much differently. But external rites cannot calm consciences, and God is not deceived by human trifling satisfactions.

units.la: Etsi igitur Philosophia, & omnes aliæ sectæ quærunt & promittunt tale bonum, quod sit solida consolatio hominis in vita & in morte: tamen nec habent, nec præstant, quin conscientiæ subinde fluctuent, & sensus reclamet. Sola doctrina Ecclesiæ tale bonum ostendit, & solidam consolationem præstat, ita, ut conscientiæ requiescant. Sola enim detegit fontem omnium miseriarum, quibus genus humanum est obnoxium: sola quoque explicat modum eluctandi ex ea per Christum.
units.tr: Although philosophy and all the other sects seek and promise such a good as would be a solid consolation for man in life and in death, they neither have it nor provide it, so that consciences keep wavering from time to time and the senses protest. Only the teaching of the Church shows such a good and provides a solid consolation, so that consciences rest. For it alone uncovers the source of all the miseries to which the human race is subject; it alone also explains the way of escaping from them through Christ.

units.la: Est igitur consolatio Christiana unica & solida in vita & in morte, fiducia gratuitæ remissionis peccatorum, & reconciliationis cum Deo per & propter Christum, & certa expectatio vitæ
units.tr: Therefore the Christian consolation is the only and solid one in life and in death: the confidence of the free forgiveness of sins and of reconciliation with God through and for the sake of Christ, and the sure expectation of eternal life

units.la: Opiniões variæ de summo bono hominis. vitæ æternæ, à Spiritu sancto per Euangelium cordibus nostris impressa, vt non dubitemus, nos esse Christi proprios, & propter eum à Deo amari, ac seruatum iri in æternum juxta illud: Quis nos separabit à dilectione Christi? num oppressio? num an-gustia? &c.
units.tr: Various opinions on the highest good of man. Eternal life, impressed on our hearts by the Holy Spirit through the Gospel, so that we do not doubt that we are Christ's own, and that for his sake we are loved by God and will be kept for ever, according to that saying: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation? or distress? etc.

units.la: II. Quibus partibus constet.
units.tr: II. Of what parts it consists.

units.la: Partes huius consolationis sunt sex.
units.tr: This consolation has six parts.

units.la: I. Reconciliatio nostri cum Deo per & propter Christum, vt non amplius simus hostes, sed filij Dei, nec nostri juris, sed Christi proprij. 1 Cor. 3. v 23.
units.tr: I. The reconciliation of ourselves with God through and for the sake of Christ, so that we are no longer enemies but sons of God, and belong not to ourselves but to Christ. 1 Cor. 3. v 23.

units.la: II. Modus reconciliationis cum Deo per Christi sanguinem, hoc est, passionem, mortem, satisfactionem pro nostris peccatis. 1 Pet. 1, 18. & 1 Joh. 1, 7.
units.tr: II. The manner of reconciliation with God through the blood of Christ, that is, his passion, his death, and his satisfaction for our sins. 1 Pet. 1, 18. and 1 John 1, 7.

units.la: III. Liberatio ex miseriis peccati & mortis. Nam Christus non tantum nos Deo reconciliat, sed etiam à potestate diaboli liberat, vt peccatum, mors, Satan, nihil juris in nos habeant. Heb. 2, 14. 1 Joh. 3, 8.
units.tr: III. Deliverance from the miseries of sin and death. For Christ not only reconciles us to God, but also frees us from the power of the devil, so that sin, death and Satan have no right over us. Heb. 2, 14. 1 John 3, 8.

units.la: IV. Conseruatio perpetua reconciliationis, liberationis, & omnium bonorum, quæ Christus semel nobis acquisiuit. Suumus eius proprii: ergo custodit nos tanquam peculium suum, vt ne pilus quidem de capite nostro possit cadere sine voluntate Patris nostri cœlestis. Salus nostra non consistit in manibus aut viribus nostris: alioqui millies singulis momentis eam amitteremus.
units.tr: IV. The perpetual preservation of the reconciliation, the deliverance, and of all the good things that Christ has once for all acquired for us. We are his own; therefore he keeps us as his special possession, so that not even a hair of our head can fall without the will of our heavenly Father. Our salvation does not rest in our own hands or strength; otherwise we would lose it a thousand times at every moment.

units.la: V. Conuersio omnium malorum in bonum. Pij quidem in hac vita affliguntur, immò interficiuntur: sunt velut oues macationis. Sed hæc non nocent, immò juuant nostram salutem: quia Deus omnia in bonum convertit; Diligentibus Deum omnia simul conferunt ad bonum.
units.tr: V. The turning of all evils into good. The godly indeed are afflicted in this life, even put to death; they are like sheep for the slaughter. But these things do not harm them; rather they help our salvation, because God turns all things to good: All things work together for good to those who love God.

units.la: VI. πληροφορία & certitudo nostra de his tantis bonis, & de vita æterna. Ea est 1. ex testimonio Spiritus sancti efficientis in nobis veram fidem & conuersionem, & contestantis spiritui nostro, nos esse filios Dei, & ista bona vere ad nos pertinere: quia est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ. 2. Ex effectis veræ fidei, quæ in nobis sentimus, vt sunt vera pœnitentia, & firmum propositum credendi & obediendi Deo, secundum omnia eius mandata. Ex serio enim studio obediendi Deo, certi sumus de vera fide: ex fide autem de benevolentia Dei & de salute æterna, juxta promissionem Euangelij, qua fides nititur: Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet vitam æternam. Hæc est basis reliquarum partium, sine qua omnis consolatio in tentationibus euanesceret. Summa igitur consolationis nostræ breuiter hæc est: nos esse Christi, per eum Patri reconciliatos, ab eo diligi, & seruatum iri, dato Spiritu sancto & vita æterna.
units.tr: VI. Our full assurance [plērophoria, πληροφορία] and certainty about these great goods and about eternal life. This comes (1) from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who works true faith and conversion in us and bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God and that these goods truly belong to us: for he is the pledge of our inheritance; (2) from the effects of true faith which we perceive in ourselves, such as true repentance and a firm purpose of believing and obeying God in all his commandments. For from a earnest zeal to obey God we are certain of true faith; and from faith we are certain of God's goodwill and of eternal salvation, according to the promise of the Gospel on which faith rests: He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life. This is the basis of the remaining parts, without which all consolation would vanish in temptations. The sum of our consolation, then, is briefly this: that we are Christ's, reconciled to the Father through him, loved by him and to be kept, with the Holy Spirit given and eternal life.

units.la: III. Cur hæc vnica sit solida consolatio.
units.tr: III. Why this alone is solid consolation.

units.la: Hanc vnicam esse solidam consolationem, patet 1. quia hæc sola in morte non evanescit. Nam siue viuimus, siue morimur, Domini sumus: &, Quis nos separabit à dilectione Christi? 2. Quia sola aduersus omnes tentationes Satanæ manet inuicta, & nos sustentat.
units.tr: That this alone is solid consolation is evident: (1) because this alone does not vanish in death: "Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's" [Rom. 14.8], and "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" [Rom. 8.35]; (2) because it alone remains unconquered against all the temptations of Satan and sustains us.

units.la: Satan obijcit: Tu es peccator. Consolatio respondet: Christus pro meis peccatis satisfecit, & me pretioso suo sanguine redemit, vt jam non meus, sed Christi sim proprius.
units.tr: Satan objects: "You are a sinner." Consolation answers: "Christ made satisfaction for my sins and redeemed me with his precious blood, so that I am no longer my own but belong to Christ."

units.la: Inst. Es filius iræ, hostis Dei. Resp. Sum quidem talis natura ante reconciliationem: sed sum Deo per Christum reconciliatus, & in gratiam receptus.
units.tr: Objection: "You are a son of wrath, an enemy of God." Answer: "I was indeed such by nature before reconciliation, but I have been reconciled to God through Christ and received into favour."

units.la: Inst. At tibi est moriendum. Resp. Christus redemit me à potestate mortis, & scio me ex morte emersurum in vitam æternam.
units.tr: Objection: "But you must die." Answer: "Christ has redeemed me from the power of death, and I know that I shall emerge from death into eternal life."

units.la: Inst. At multa mala tibi interim tibi eueniunt. Resp. Defendit & tuetur me in illis Dominus noster, & facit, vt mihi cooperentur in bonum.
units.tr: Objection: "But many evils befall you in the meantime." Answer: "Our Lord defends and protects me in them, and makes them work together for my good."

units.la: Inst. Quid si gratia Christi excidas? Potes enim peccare & deficere: & longum atq; arduum est iter in cœlum. Resp. Christus sua beneficia mihi non tantum est meritus, & semel contulit, sed etiam perpetuò conseruabit, & donabit me perseuerantia, ne deficiam, aut excidam à gratia.
units.tr: Objection: "What if you fall away from the grace of Christ? For you can sin and fail, and the way to heaven is long and steep." Answer: "Christ has not only merited his benefits for me and bestowed them once, but will also preserve them forever and grant me perseverance, so that I do not fail or fall away from grace."

units.la: Inst. Quid si ad te non pertineat gratia, & tu non sis ex eorum numero, qui sunt Domini? Resp. Scio, gratiam ad me pertinere, & me esse Christi, quia 1. Spiritus sanctus contestatur spiritui meo, quod sim filius Dei. 2. quia habeo veram fidem. Promissio autem est vniuersalis pertinens ad omnes verè credentes.
units.tr: Objection: "What if grace does not pertain to you, and you are not among those who belong to the Lord?" Answer: "I know that grace pertains to me and that I am Christ's, because (1) the Holy Spirit bears witness to my spirit that I am a son of God; (2) I have true faith. The promise is universal, pertaining to all who truly believe."

units.la: Inst. Quid si non habeas veram fidem? Resp. Scio me habere veram fidem, ex effectis veræ fidei: quia habeo conscientiam in Deo acquiescentem, & voluntatem ac studium seriùm credendi & obsequendi Deo.
units.tr: Objection: "What if you do not have true faith?" Answer: "I know that I have true faith from the effects of true faith: because I have a conscience resting in God, and a will and zeal to believe earnestly and to obey God."

units.la: Inst. Fides tua infirma est, & conuersio imperfecta. Resp. Est tamen vera, & non simulata. Habenti autem dabitur. Credo Domine, opem fer incredulitati meæ.
units.tr: Objection: "Your faith is weak and your conversion imperfect." Answer: "It is nevertheless true and not feigned. 'To him who has, more will be given.' 'Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.'"

units.la: In hac lucta grauissima & periculosissima, quam omnes filij Dei non raro experiuntur, manet immota consolatio Christiana, & tandem concludit: Ergo Christus cum omnibus suis beneficiis etiam ad me pertinet.
units.tr: In this most grievous and dangerous struggle, which all the children of God not infrequently experience, Christian consolation remains unshaken and at last concludes: "Therefore Christ, with all his benefits, also pertains to me."

units.la: IV. Cur sit necessaria.
units.tr: IV. Why it is necessary.

units.la: Ex his liquet, nobis hanc consolationem valde esse necessariam: 1. Propter nostram salutem, ne videlicet in tentationibus, & luctā conscientiæ deficiamus & desperemus. 2. Propter celebrationem Dei. Nam vt Deum in hac & futura vita celebrare possimus, ad quod conditi sumus, oportet nos emergere ex peccato & morte, nec ruere in desperationem, sed firma consolatione sustentari vsque ad mortem.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that this consolation is very necessary for us: (1) for our salvation, namely that in temptations and struggles of conscience we may not fail and despair; (2) for the glory of God. For in order that we may celebrate God in this life and in the life to come, for which we were created, we must emerge from sin and death, and not fall into despair, but be sustained by firm consolation until death.

units.la: V. Qua ad hanc consolationem habendam sint necessaria.
units.tr: V. What things are necessary for obtaining this consolation.

units.la: De hoc sequitur
units.tr: On this there follows

units.la: QVÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: Quot sunt tibi scitu necessaria, vt illa consolatione fruens, beatè viuas & moriaris?
units.tr: How many things must you know in order to enjoy that consolation and live and die blessedly?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Tria. aPrimum, quanta sit peccati mei & miseriæ meæ magnitudo b. Alterum, quo pacto ab omni peccato & miseria liberer c. Tertium, quam gratiam Deo pro ea liberatione debeam d.
units.tr: Three. a First, how great my sin and my misery are. b Second, how I may be freed from all sin and misery. c Third, what gratitude I owe God for that deliverance. d

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hæc est propositio & partitio totius Catechismi, coincidens cum diuisione scripturæ in Legem & Euangelium, & cum harum partium discriminibus, vt supra ostensum est.
units.tr: This is the proposition and division of the whole Catechism, coinciding with the division of Scripture into Law and Gospel, and with the distinction between these parts, as was shown above.

units.la: Miseriæ agnitio est necessaria ad consolationem, non quod ipsa per se nos consoletur, aut sit pars consolationis, (per se enim potius terret, quam consolatur) sed:
units.tr: Knowledge of misery is necessary for consolation, not because it comforts us in itself, or is part of consolation (for in itself it terrifies rather than consoles), but:

units.la: Primò, quia excitat in nobis desiderium liberationis, sicut agnitio morbi affert ægroto desiderium medicinæ: miseriâ vero non agnitâ non quæritur medicus. Si autem liberatio non expetitur, etiam non quæritur: si non quæritur, non obtinetur: quia Deus tantum quærentibus dat liberationem: tantum pulsanti aperitur, sicut dicitur: Pulsanti aperietur. Petite & dabitur vobis. Beati qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam. Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis, &c. In spiritu contrito habitabo. Quod ergo necessarium est ad desiderium liberationis in nobis excitandum, id etiam necessarium est ad consolationem. Agnitio miseriæ necessaria est ad excitandum liberationis desiderium. Ergo ad consolationem est necessaria, vt causa sine qua non & quædam veluti ἀφορμὴ ad consolationem quærendam. Per se quidem terret: sed terror fit salutaris, cum accedit fides.
units.tr: First, because it stirs up in us a desire for deliverance, just as knowledge of a disease gives the sick person a desire for medicine. But if misery is not known, no physician is sought. If deliverance is not desired, it is not sought either; and if it is not sought, it is not obtained, because God gives deliverance only to those who seek it. He is opened only to the one who knocks, as it is said: "To him who knocks it will be opened. Ask, and it will be given to you. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. Come to me, all you who labour, etc. I will dwell in the contrite spirit." What is therefore necessary to stir up the desire for deliverance in us is also necessary for consolation. Knowledge of misery is necessary to stir up the desire for deliverance; therefore it is necessary for consolation, as a cause without which the effect does not occur, and as a kind of starting point [ἀφορμή] for seeking consolation. In itself it indeed terrifies, but the terror becomes salutary when faith comes alongside.

units.la: Secundò, vt pro liberatione Deo simus grati. Essemus enim ingrati futuri, si mali magnitudinem, ex quo liberati sumus, non agnosceremus: quia magnitudinem beneficij nunquam recte æstimaremus, & sic liberationem non consequeremur, cum ea tanquam gratis contingat.
units.tr: Second, so that we may be grateful to God for the deliverance. For we would be ungrateful if we did not acknowledge the greatness of the evil from which we have been freed; we would never rightly estimate the magnitude of the benefit, and so would not obtain the deliverance, since it comes to us as a free gift.

units.la: Tertiò, quia sine agnitione peccati & miseriæ non sumus idonei auditores Euangelij. Nisi enim concione Legis de peccato & de ira Dei fiat præparatio ad concionem de gratia, sequetur securitas carnalis, fitque consolatio instabilis: quia firma consolatio cum securitate carnali non consistit. Hinc patet, à prædicatione Legis inchoandum esse, sicut videmus Prophetas & Apostolos fecisse, vt deijciantur homines de præsumptione propriæ justitiæ, & præparentur ad agnitionem sui, & ad veram pœnitentiam. Hoc enim nisi fiat, concione gratiæ redduntur magis securi & contumaces, & porcis objiciuntur margaritæ pedibus conculcandæ.
units.tr: Third, because without knowledge of sin and misery we are not fit hearers of the Gospel. For unless the sermon on the Law, concerning sin and the wrath of God, prepares the way for the sermon on grace, carnal security follows and the consolation becomes unstable, because firm consolation does not stand together with carnal security. Hence it is plain that we must begin with the preaching of the Law, as we see the Prophets and Apostles did, so that men may be cast down from presumption of their own righteousness and be prepared for knowledge of themselves and for true repentance. For unless this is done, sermons on grace make men more secure and stubborn, and pearls are thrown to pigs to be trampled underfoot.

units.la: Liberationis cognitio ad consolationem est necessaria.
units.tr: Knowledge of deliverance is necessary for consolation.

units.la: Primò, ne desperemus. Agnitâ enim miseriâ mergeremur in desperationem, nisi præsto esset liberationis spes & fiducia.
units.tr: First, so that we do not despair. For once misery is known, we would be plunged into despair unless the hope and confidence of deliverance were at hand.

units.la: Deinde, vt eam desideremus. Nam bonum non agnitum non expetitur: quia ignoti nulla cupido. Si ergo bonum liberationis ignoremus, etiam non expetemus, proinde nec consequemur, immò etiam oblatum & inventum non agnoscemus.
units.tr: Then, so that we may desire it. For a good that is not known is not desired, since there is no desire for the unknown. If therefore we do not know the good of deliverance, we will not desire it, and so will not obtain it; indeed, even when it is offered and found, we will not recognise it.

units.la: Tertiò, vt nos consoletur. Bonum enim non agnitum non consolatur.
units.tr: Third, so that it may console us. For a good that is not known does not console.

units.la: Quarto, ne cum nominis divini contumelia, & salutis nostræ jactura, modum liberationis ipsi fingamus, aut ab aliis confictum amplectamur.
units.tr: Fourth, so that we do not, to the dishonour of God's name and the loss of our salvation, devise for ourselves some manner of deliverance, or embrace one invented by others.

units.la: Quintò, vt fide eam accipere possimus. Fides enim non est sine cognitione. Liberatio autem sola fide accipitur.
units.tr: Fifth, so that we may receive it by faith. For faith is not without knowledge, and deliverance is received by faith alone.

units.la: Denique, vt possimus Deo esse grati. Nam bonum incognitum vt non desideramus, ita nec magnifacimus, nec de gratitudine cogitamus. Ingratis autem beneficium liberationis non datur, cum Deus iis tantum dare velit, in quibus assequitur eius finem, qui est gratitudo. Propter has igitur causas ad solidam consolationem necessariò requiritur liberationis cognitio, quæ & qualis sit, per quem nobis præstetur, &c. Petitur autem hæc cognitio ex solo Euangelio, audito, lecto, & fide apprehenhenso: quia id solum promittit liberationem credentibus in Christum.
units.tr: Finally, so that we may be grateful to God. For a good that is unknown is neither desired nor esteemed, nor do we think of gratitude. But the benefit of deliverance is not given to the ungrateful, since God wishes to give only to those in whom his end, which is gratitude, is attained. For these reasons, then, knowledge of deliverance is necessarily required for solid consolation: what it is, by whom it is provided to us, and so on. This knowledge is sought from the Gospel alone, heard, read, and grasped by faith, because it alone promises deliverance to those who believe in Christ.

units.la: Gratitudinis cognitio est necessaria ad consolationem: Primò, quia Deus liberationem praestare vult tantum gratis. In his enim solis assequitur eius finem, nempe celebrationem sui, & gratitudinem. Gratitudo igitur est praecipuus finis, & scopus liberationis. In hoc apparuit Filius Dei, ut destrueret opera diaboli. Adoptauit nos ad laudem gloriosa suae gratiae.
units.tr: Knowledge of gratitude is necessary for consolation: first, because God wishes to grant deliverance only for the sake of gratitude. For in these alone is his end attained, namely the celebration of himself and gratitude. Gratitude is therefore the chief end and aim of deliverance. "In this the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil. He adopted us to the praise of his glorious grace."

units.la: Deinde, ut possit praestari, & quidem talis, quae Deo placeat. Deus enim non vult nos sibi aliter gratos esse, quàm ipse in verbo suo praescripsit. Vera igitur gratitudo non est fingenda, sed ex verbo Dei discenda.
units.tr: Then, so that it may be rendered, and rendered in such a way as pleases God. For God does not wish us to be grateful to him in any other way than he has prescribed in his word. True gratitude, therefore, is not to be invented but learned from the word of God.

units.la: Tertiò, ut sciamus, quaecunque Deo, & proximo officia praestamus, non esse merita, sed esse declarationem gratitudinis debitae. Pro quo enim gratias agimus, id fatemur non esse meritum, sed donum.
units.tr: Third, so that we know that whatever duties we perform towards God and neighbour are not merits, but a declaration of the gratitude owed. For for that for which we give thanks, we confess it is not a merit but a gift.

units.la: Denique, ut ex gratitudine fides & consolatio in nobis confirmetur, seu, ut ex ea de liberatione, quod eam habeamus, tanquam ex effectu de causa certi simus. Qui enim sunt grati, agnoscunt & profitentur, se de bono accepto certos esse. Discitur autem vera gratitudo, ex Euangelio quidem in genere, quia Euangelium requirit fidem & poenitentiam in salvandis: Resipiscite & credite Euangelio, quia appropinquauit regnum Dei. Ex Lege verò in specie, quia Lex distincte monstrat, quae opera, & qualis obedientia Deo placeat. Necessario igitur etiam de gratitudine in catechesi docetur.
units.tr: Finally, so that from gratitude faith and consolation may be confirmed in us, or so that from it we may be certain, as from an effect about its cause, that we have deliverance. For those who are grateful acknowledge and profess that they are certain of the good they have received. True gratitude is learned indeed from the Gospel in general, since the Gospel requires faith and repentance for salvation: "Repent and believe the Gospel, for the kingdom of God is at hand." But it is learned from the Law in particular, since the Law clearly shows which works and what kind of obedience please God. Therefore gratitude too is necessarily taught in the catechism.

units.la: Obiect. Quod vltrò sequitur, id non necesse est doceri. Gratitudo vltrò sequitur ad agnitionem miseriae & liberationis. Ergo non necesse est eam doceri.
units.tr: Objection. What follows of its own accord need not be taught. Gratitude follows of its own accord upon knowledge of misery and deliverance. Therefore it need not be taught.

units.la: Resp. Est fallacia secundum quid, &c. Gratitudo sequitur, sed modus gratitudinis non item: hoc est, agnità liberatione à miseria, intelligimus quidem, nos pro tanto beneficio debere gratos esse: sed quae sit vera & Deo placens gratitudo, nescimus, nisi doceamur. De modo igitur ex verbo Dei docendi sumus.
units.tr: Answer. This is a fallacy of qualification, etc. Gratitude follows, but the manner of gratitude does not. That is, having known deliverance from misery, we indeed understand that for so great a benefit we ought to be grateful; but what true gratitude, pleasing to God, is, we do not know unless we are taught. We must therefore be taught from the word of God about the manner.

units.la: Deinde nec maior est vniuersalis. Nam etiam id, quod vltrò sequitur, doceri potest, amplioris cognitionis & confirmationis gratia. Et Deus per hoc ipsum medium, hoc est, per doctrinam traditam & cognitam, vult in nobis excitare, augere & confirmare gratitudinem.
units.tr: Then, the major premise is not universal either. For even what follows of its own accord can be taught, for the sake of greater knowledge and confirmation. And God, through this very means, that is, through doctrine delivered and known, wishes to stir up, increase and confirm gratitude in us.

units.la: PARS PRIMA. DE MISERIA HOMINIS.
units.tr: PART ONE. CONCERNING THE MISERY OF MAN.

units.la: QVÆSTIO III.
units.tr: QUESTION III.

units.la: Vnde tuam miseriam agnoscis? RESPONSIO. Ex lege Dei a.
units.tr: How do you recognise your misery? ANSWER. From the law of God.^a

units.la: a Rom. 3. vers. 10.
units.tr: a Rom. 3. vers. 10.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: IN hac parte de miseria hominis præcipuè tractatur locus communis de peccato, & de effectibus seu pœnis peccati. Huic admiscentur alij minus principales, de creatione hominis, de imagine Dei in homine, de lapsu & primo peccato hominis. De miseria verò in genere tenendum, quid sit, unde agnoscatur, & quomodo.
units.tr: In this part, the common topic concerning sin, and concerning the effects or punishments of sin, is chiefly treated. Mixed in with it are other, less principal matters: the creation of man, the image of God in man, and the fall and first sin of man. As to the misery of man in general, we must hold what it is, whence it is recognised, and how.

units.la: Miseria nomen latius patet, quam nomen peccati. Complectitur enim malum culpæ, & malum pœnæ. Malum culpæ est omne peccatum: malum pœnæ est omnis afflictio, cruciatus, & destructio naturæ rationalis propter peccatum: omnia item peccata sequentia, quibus vniuntur præcedentia: vt numeratio populi à Dauide facta erat peccatum, & simul pœna peccati antecedentis, videlicet adulterij & homicidij Dauidis, hoc est, simul erat malum culpæ, & malum pœnæ. Est igitur miseria hominis misera hominis conditio post lapsum in duobus maximis malis consistens. 1. Quod natura humana per peccatum est à Deo auersa & tota praua. 2. Quod propter hanc prauitatem rea est æternæ maledictionis, & à Deo abiecta.
units.tr: The name misery extends more widely than the name sin. For it embraces the evil of guilt and the evil of punishment. The evil of guilt is every sin; the evil of punishment is every affliction, torment and destruction of the rational nature on account of sin; likewise all the sins that follow, to which the preceding ones are joined. Thus the numbering of the people made by David was a sin and at the same time a punishment for the preceding sin, namely David's adultery and murder; that is, it was at once an evil of guilt and an evil of punishment. Therefore the misery of man is the wretched condition of man after the fall, consisting in two greatest evils: (1) that human nature, through sin, has been turned away from God and is wholly depraved; (2) that, on account of this depravity, it is liable to eternal damnation and cast off by God.

units.la: Hanc miseriam agnoscimus ex lege Dei. Per legem Dei agnitio peccati, inquit Paulus. Et legis vox est: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, quæ sunt scripta in libro legis, &c.
units.tr: We recognise this misery from the law of God. "Through the law is the knowledge of sin," says Paul. And the voice of the law is: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things that are written in the book of the law, etc."

units.la: Quomodo autem ex lege fiat miseriæ agnitio, sequentes duæ quæstiones docent.
units.tr: How the recognition of misery comes from the law, the following two questions teach.

units.la: QVÆSTIO IV.
units.tr: QUESTION IV.

units.la: Quid à nobis postulat Lex Dei? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What does the law of God require of us? ANSWER.

units.la: Id docet nos Christus summatim, Matthæi 22. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo, ex tota anima tua, ex tota cogitatione tua, & ex omnibus viribus tuis. Istud est primum & maximum mandatum: secundum autem est simile huic: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Ab istis duobus mandatis tota Lex & Prophetæ pendent a.
units.tr: Christ teaches us this in summary, Matthew 22: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."^a

units.la: a Deut. 6. verf. 5. Leuit. 19, 18. Marci 12, 30. Luc. 10, 27.
units.tr: a Deut. 6. vers. 5. Lev. 19:18. Mark 12:30. Luke 10:27.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hanc summam legis Christus repetit Matth. 22. 37. & Luc. 10, 27. ex Deut. 6, 5. & Leuit. 19, 18. Explicat autem, quid sit illud: Qui non manserit in omnibus quæ, &c. hoc est, qui Deum non dilexerit ex toto corde, ex tota anima, ex tota cogitatione, & ex omnibus viribus suis; & proximum suum sicut seipsum. Hæc paulò latius explicanda sunt.
units.tr: Christ repeats this summary of the Law at Matt. 22:37 and Luke 10:27, taken from Deut. 6:5 and Lev. 19:18. He explains what the words "He who does not abide in all that is written, etc." mean, that is, he who does not love God with his whole heart, his whole soul, his whole mind and all his strength, and his neighbour as himself. These points need to be explained a little more fully.

units.la: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum. Diligere Deum ex toto corde, &c est, ex agnitione infinitæ bonitatis Dei reuerenter de Deo sentire, & pro summo bono Deum habere, & ideo Deum summè amare, nec non in Deo lætari & acquiescere omniaque Dei gloriæ postponere, adeò ut ne minima quidem cogitatio, vel inclinatio, vel appetitio vllius rei, in nobis sit, quæ Deo displiceat, ac potius etiam omnia charissima amittere, vel durissima perpeti velimus, quam à Dei communione auelli, aut Deum vlla in re offendere; denique omnia eò dirigere, vt Deus solus celebretur.
units.tr: "You shall love the Lord your God." To love God with the whole heart, etc., is, from knowledge of God's infinite goodness, to think of God with reverence, to hold God as the highest good, and therefore to love God above all, to rejoice and rest in God, and to set the glory of God above everything. So much so that not even the smallest thought, inclination or desire for anything that displeases God should be in us. Rather, we should be willing to lose all our dearest possessions, or to suffer the harshest things, rather than be torn from communion with God or offend God in any matter. In short, we should direct everything so that God alone is honoured.

units.la: Dominum Deum tuum. Quasi dicat, illum Deum diliges, qui est Dominus tuus, & Deus tuus, qui tibi benefacit, & cui tu ad seruiendum obstrictus es. Est ergo antithesis falsorum Deorum.
units.tr: "The Lord your God." As if to say: you shall love that God who is your Lord and your God, who does you good, and to whose service you are bound. Therefore this is set against the gods of the false religions.

units.la: Ex toto corde tuo. Cor Hebræis significat affectus, appetitus & inclinationes. Deus ergo cor nostrum totum requirens, vult se solum agnosci & haberi pro summo nostro bono, se solum supra omnia amari, in se solo cor nostrum totum acquiescere, nec partem eius sibi, partem alteri tribui, ita vt nihil sit, quod ei æquare, ne dum anteponere vel in amoris partem admittere velimus. Hoc vocat scriptura perfecto corde ambulare coram Deo: cuius oppositum est, ambulare coram Deo, non toto, non perfecto, sed diuiso corde coram Deo, hoc est, claudicare, nec se totum Deo dedere.
units.tr: "With your whole heart." Among the Hebrews, "heart" signifies the affections, desires and inclinations. God, then, requiring our whole heart, wills to be acknowledged and held as our highest good, to be loved alone above all things, and our whole heart to rest in him alone. Part of it is not to be given to him and part to another, so that we are not to set anything equal to him, much less to prefer anything to him or admit anything to a share of our love. Scripture calls this "to walk before God with a perfect heart." Its opposite is to walk before God not with the whole or perfect heart, but "with a divided heart", that is, to limp, and not to give oneself wholly to God.

units.la: Obiect. Solus Deus est diligendus. Ergo non proximus, non parentes & cognati. Resp. Fallacia accidentis, à negatione modi ad negationem rei. Solus Deus est diligendus summè, & supra omnia, hoc est, sic vt nihil prorsus sit, quod ei vel præferamus, vel æquemus, quodq; ipsius causa amittere non parati simus: Proximum verò & parentes & alia diligere debemus non summè, non supra omnia, nec ita, vt malimus Deum quam parentes. tes offendere, sed infra Deum, & propter Deum, non supra Deum.
units.tr: Objection. Only God is to be loved. Therefore not the neighbour, nor parents and relatives. Reply. This is the fallacy of the accident: an inference from the denial of a manner to the denial of the thing itself. Only God is to be loved supremely and above all things, that is, so that there is absolutely nothing that we prefer to him or set equal to him, and we should not be unwilling to lose anything for his sake. But we ought to love the neighbour, parents and others not supremely, not above all things, and not so that we would rather offend God than parents, but beneath God and for God's sake, not above God.

units.la: Ex tota anima tua.] Anima significat partem volentem, & motus voluntatis, quasi dicat: tota voluntate & proposito diliges.
units.tr: "With your whole soul." The soul signifies the willing part and the movements of the will. As if to say: you shall love with your whole will and purpose.

units.la: Ex tota cogitatione tua] Cogitatio significat mentem, seu partem intelligentem, quasi dicat: quantum de Deo cognoscis, tantum etiam eum diliges. Omnes vero cogitationes tuas intendes, ut Deum recte & perfecte cognoscas, & sic etiam amabis. Quantum enim cognoscimus, tantum diligimus. Nunc imperfecte cognoscimus, quia ex parte cognoscimus. In altera vita perfecte cognoscemus, ideo perfecte etiam diligemus, & id quod ex parte, cessabit. Nunc cognoscimus in speculo, tunc videbimus eum a facie ad faciem.
units.tr: "With your whole mind." The mind signifies the understanding part. As if to say: you shall love God as much as you know him. Moreover, you shall direct all your thoughts to knowing God rightly and perfectly, and so you will also love him. For we love as much as we know. Now we know imperfectly, because we know in part. In the other life we shall know perfectly, and therefore we shall also love perfectly, and what is in part will cease. "Now we see through a glass darkly; then we shall see face to face."

units.la: Ex omnibus viribus tuis.] Intelligimus omnes actiones simul, internas & externas, ut cum Lege Dei sint congruentes.
units.tr: "With all your strength." We understand all actions together, internal and external, so that they agree with the Law of God.

units.la: Iste est primum & maximum mandatum.] Dilectio Dei dicitur mandatum primum: quia est fons aliorum mandatorum, hoc est, causa impulsiva, efficiens, & finalis totius obedientiae reliquae. Ideo enim diligimus proximum, quia diligimus Deum, & ut amorem nostrum erga Deum in proximo declaremus. Maximum. 1. Quia circa obiectum maximum, nempe Deum immediate versatur. 2. Quia finis est, ad quem omnia alia mandata dirigantur. Huc enim omnis nostra obedientia spectat, ut Dei dilectionem ostendamus, & eum honore afficiamus. 3. Quia est cultus Dei principalis, cui servire & cedere debuit ceremonialis. Pharisei ceremoniale cultum anteponebant morali. Contra Christus dilectionem vocat maximum mandatum, & cultum moralem anteponit ceremoniis, quia haec propter dilectionem fuerunt instituta, eique cedere debuerunt.
units.tr: "This is the first and great commandment." The love of God is called the first commandment because it is the source of the other commandments, that is, the moving cause, the efficient cause and the final cause of all the rest of obedience. For we love our neighbour because we love God, and so that we may show our love for God in our neighbour. Great. (1) Because it is concerned directly with the greatest object, namely God. (2) Because it is the end to which all the other commandments are directed. For all our obedience looks to this: that we show our love of God and honour him. (3) Because it is the principal worship of God, to which ceremonial worship ought to serve and yield. The Pharisees put ceremonial worship before moral worship. Christ, on the contrary, calls love the great commandment and puts moral worship before the ceremonies, because these were instituted on account of love and ought to give way to it.

units.la: Obiect. Dilectio Dei est maximum mandatum: Ergo dilectio est maior fide: proinde magis justificat, quam fides. Resp. Dilectio hic sumitur pro tota obedientia, quam Deo debemus, sub qua comprehenditur fides, quae justificat, non per se, ut est virtus, sed correlative, ut apprehendit & sibi applicat meritum Christi. Dilectio vero quae in specie sic dicta, fidei opponitur, non justificat, quia non dilectione, sed sola fide fit applicatio justitiae Christi: immo dilectio nascitur ex fide: fides enim est causa omnium aliarum virtutum.
units.tr: Objection. The love of God is the great commandment. Therefore love is greater than faith, and so it justifies more than faith does. Reply. Here love is taken for the whole obedience we owe to God, under which faith is included. Faith justifies, not in itself as a virtue, but relatively, inasmuch as it apprehends and applies to itself the merit of Christ. But love, taken in the specific sense in which it is opposed to faith, does not justify, because the application of Christ's righteousness is made not by love but by faith alone. Indeed, love is born of faith, for faith is the cause of all the other virtues.

units.la: Secundum est simile huic: Diliges proximum &c.] Diligere proximum sicut seipsum, est ex dilectione Dei, hoc est, ideo quia diligimus Deum, proximo bene velle facere, secundum omnia Dei mandata: seu proximo ea optare & facere, quae nobis ab ipso fieri secundum Legem vellemus. Proximus autem est omnis homo.
units.tr: "The second is like it: You shall love your neighbour, etc." To love one's neighbour as oneself arises from the love of God. That is, because we love God, we wish our neighbour well and do him good in accordance with all the commandments of God; or we desire and do for our neighbour those things which we would wish to be done to us by him according to the Law. Now the neighbour is every man.

units.la: Dicitur mandatum secundum. 1. Quia continet summam secundæ tabulæ, seu officia, quæ immediatè proximo præstantur. Si enim dilexeris proximum sicut te ipsum, non occides, non lædes eum. 2. Quia dilectio proximi debet promanare ex dilectione Dei, ideo est natura posterior.
units.tr: It is called the second commandment. (1) Because it contains the sum of the second table, or the duties that are performed directly towards the neighbour. For if you love your neighbour as yourself, you will not kill him or harm him. (2) Because love of the neighbour ought to flow from love of God, and so it is posterior in nature.

units.la: Dicitur simile primo tripliciter. In genere cultus moralis, seu spiritualis & principalis, quia hic non minus in secunda tabula quam in prima sancitur, & ceremoniis opponitur. 2. In genere pœna: quia hæc propter utriusque tabulæ violationem æquè à Deo infligitur. 3. In coherentia: quia neutra tabula sine altera potest servari.
units.tr: It is called like the first in three ways. (1) In the kind of worship, moral or spiritual and principal, because this is enacted in the second table no less than in the first, and it is set against the ceremonies. (2) In the kind of punishment, because God inflicts it equally for the violation of either table. (3) In coherence, because neither table can be kept without the other.

units.la: Est etiam dissimile primo. 1. In obiecto immediato, quod in prima tabula est Deus, in secunda proximus. 2. In ordine causæ & effectus: quod dilectio proximi ex dilectione Dei oritur, non contrà. 3. In gradibus dilectionis. Deum enim supra omnia: proximum non supra omnia, nec supra Deum, sed ut nos ipsos, diligere debemus.
units.tr: It is also unlike the first in three ways. (1) In the immediate object, which in the first table is God, and in the second the neighbour. (2) In the order of cause and effect, because love of the neighbour arises from love of God, not the reverse. (3) In the degrees of love. For we ought to love God above all things, but the neighbour not above all things, nor above God, but as ourselves.

units.la: Hinc patet responsio ad obiectionem. Secundum est simile primo: Ergo primum non est maximum: vel: Ergo proximus est æquandus Deo, & similiter colendus. Est enim simile primo non simpliciter, sed tantum in quibusdam, manente dissimilitudine in aliis, ut dictum est.
units.tr: Hence the reply to the objection is plain. "The second is like the first; therefore the first is not the greatest"; or else: "therefore the neighbour is to be equated with God and similarly worshipped." For the second is like the first not simply, but only in certain respects, the dissimilarity remaining in others, as has been said.

units.la: Ab istis duobus mandatis tota Lex & Prophetæ pendent. Hoc est, tota doctrina Legis & Prophetarum ad hæc duo capita revocatur, & tota obedientia Legis in Mose & Prophetis comprehensa, ex dilectione Dei & proximi oritur. Obj. Atqui in Prophetis etiam multæ sunt promissiones Evangelij: Ergo doctrina Prophetarum videtur male ad ista restringi. Resp. Christus loquitur de doctrina legali, non de promissionibus Evangelij: quod liquet ex quæstione Pharisæi quærentis, quodnam sit præcipuum mandatum non autem, quæ sit principalis promissio in Lege.
units.tr: "On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets." That is, the whole teaching of the Law and the Prophets is reduced to these two heads, and the whole obedience of the Law comprehended in Moses and the Prophets arises from love of God and of the neighbour. Objection. But in the Prophets there are also many promises of the Gospel. Therefore the teaching of the Prophets seems wrongly restricted to these. Reply. Christ is speaking of the teaching of the Law, not of the promises of the Gospel. This is clear from the question of the Pharisee, who asked which was the chief commandment, not which was the principal promise in the Law.

units.la: QVÆSTIO V. Num hæc omnia perfectè servare potes?
units.tr: QUESTION V. Can you keep all these things perfectly?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Minimè 4. Naturâ enim propensus sum ad odium Dei & proximi. b
units.tr: By no means. 4. For by nature I am inclined to hatred of God and of my neighbour. b

units.la: a Rom. 8. verf. 10. 20. 13. 1 Ioh. 1. v. 8. 10. b Rom. 8. v. 7. Ephes. 2. verf. 5. Tit. 3. verf. 3. Genes. 6. v. 5. & 8. verf. 21. Ierem. 17. verf. 9. Rom. 7. verf 23.
units.tr: a Rom. 8. verse 10. 20. 13. 1 John 1. verse 8. 10. b Rom. 8. verse 7. Ephes. 2. verse 5. Tit. 3. verse 3. Genes. 6. verse 5. & 8. verse 21. Jer. 17. verse 9. Rom. 7. verse 23.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hæc quæstio conjuncta cum præcedente ostendit, miseriam ex lege cognosci dupliciter, prout etiam duæ sunt miseriæ partes: primò collatione nostri cum lege: deinde applicatione maledictionis legis ad nos.
units.tr: This question, taken together with the preceding one, shows that misery is recognised from the law in two ways, corresponding to the two parts of our misery: first by comparing ourselves with the law, and then by applying the law's curse to ourselves.

units.la: Collatio nostri cum lege, seu legis ad nos, est consideratio, quam puritatem lex flagitet, & an ea sit in nobis. Hæc collatio ostendit, nos non esse tales, quales lex requirit. Lex postulat perfectam dilectionem Dei: in nobis est odium & fuga Dei. Lex postulat perfectam dilectionem proximi: in nobis est φιλαυτια, amor sui, & odium proximi. Sic igitur ex lege cognoscitur prior miseriæ pars, nempe prauitas nostra, de qua etiam scriptura nos arguit. Rom. 8, 7. Ephes. 2, 3. Tit. 3, 3. &c.
units.tr: The comparison of ourselves with the law, or of the law with us, consists in considering what purity the law demands and whether it is found in us. This comparison shows that we are not such as the law requires. The law demands perfect love of God; in us there is hatred and flight from God. The law demands perfect love of neighbour; in us there is philautia [φιλαυτία], self-love, and hatred of the neighbour. So from the law we recognise the first part of our misery, namely our corruption, of which Scripture also accuses us. Rom. 8, 7. Ephes. 2, 3. Tit. 3, 3. &c.

units.la: Applicatio maledictionis legis ad nos fit per syllogismum practicum, cuius maior est vox legis: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, ut ea faciat. Conscientia nobis dictat minorem: Ego non mansi in omnibus, &c. Conclusio est approbatio sententiæ legis: Ergo sum maledictus. Talem syllogismum omnibus hominibus dictat sua conscientia: immò conscientia nihil est aliud, nisi talis syllogismus practicus in cuiusq; mente, cuius maior propositio est lex Dei, minor est cogitatio facti nostri discrepantis à lege, conclusio est approbatio sententiæ legis, damnantis nos propter peccatum: quam approbationem sequitur dolor & desperatio, nisi accedat consolatio Euangelij, & fiat remissio propter Filium Dei Mediatorem. Sic igitur etiam reatus æternæ maledictionis, qui est altera miseriæ pars, ex lege cognoscitur. Omnes enim hoc argumento convincimur. Lex omnes obligat ad obedientiam, vel si hanc non præstent, ad pœnam seu maledictionem temporalem & æternam. At nemo præstat obedientiam. Omnes ergo lex obligat ad maledictionem temporalem & æternam.
units.tr: The curse of the law is applied to us by a practical syllogism, whose major premise is the voice of the law: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them." Our conscience supplies the minor premise: "I have not abided in all things," and so on. The conclusion is the approval of the law's sentence: "Therefore I am cursed." Such a syllogism our conscience dictates to all people. Indeed, conscience is nothing other than such a practical syllogism in each person's mind, whose major premise is the law of God, whose minor is the thought of our deed differing from the law, and whose conclusion is the approval of the law's sentence condemning us on account of sin. This approval is followed by sorrow and despair, unless the consolation of the Gospel intervenes and forgiveness is granted for the sake of the Son of God, our Mediator. In this way also the guilt of eternal curse, which is the other part of our misery, is recognised from the law. For we are all convinced by this argument: the law obliges all to obedience, or, if they do not render it, to punishment or curse, temporal and eternal. But no one renders obedience. Therefore the law obliges all to temporal and eternal curse.

units.la: QVÆSTIO VI.
units.tr: QVÆSTIO VI.

units.la: Num ergo Deus hominem ita prauum & perversum condidit?
units.tr: Did God therefore create man so depraved and perverse?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: RESPONSE.

units.la: Nequaquam: immò verò bonum a, & ad imaginem sui condidit eum b, hoc est, vera justitia & sanctitate præditum, ut Deum Creatorem suum recte cognosceret, ex animo diligeret, cum eo beatus in æternum ternum viueret : idque ad eum laudandum & celebrandum c.
units.tr: By no means! Rather, God created him good a, and made him in his own image b, that is, endowed with true righteousness and holiness, so that he might rightly know God his Creator, love Him from the heart, and live blessed with Him for ever; and this so that he might praise and celebrate Him c.

units.la: a Genes 1. verf.31. b Genes.1,26.27. c Ephes.6,24. Coloss.3,16. 2 Cor.3. verf.18.
EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Constituta hac propositione: Natura humana obnoxia est peccato: statim quæritur, an à Deo talis sit condita? & si non talis, qualis igitur? & unde existat peccatum in homine? Pertinet itaque huc locus de creatione hominis, & de imagine Dei in homine.
units.tr: With this proposition laid down, that human nature is subject to sin, the question arises at once: was it created like this by God? And if not, what was it like then? And whence does sin come into man? The topic therefore belongs here: the creation of man, and the image of God in man.

units.la: Et quidem antithesis miseriæ & præstantiæ originalis instituenda hic fuit. 1. Ut nota esset causa & origo miseriæ, ne Deo imputetur. 2. Ut magis elucesceret miseriæ magnitudo. Tantò enim hæc magis conspicua est, quantò magis de excellentia originali constat: sic ut tanto illustrius sit liberationis beneficium, quanto magis de malorum, ex quibus liberati sumus, magnitudine constat.
