units.tr: Indeed, the contrast between original misery and original excellence ought to be set out here. (1) So that the cause and origin of the misery may be known, and it may not be imputed to God. (2) So that the greatness of the misery may stand out more clearly. For it is the more evident the more clearly the original excellence is established; so that the benefit of deliverance shines the more brightly the more the greatness of the evils from which we have been freed is understood.

units.la: De Creatione hominis.
units.tr: On the Creation of Man.

units.la: De hominis creatione præcipuè quæritur: I. Qualis. II. Ad quid homo à Deo sit conditus.
units.tr: Three questions are chiefly asked about the creation of man: (I) what kind of man God made; (II) for what purpose God created him.

units.la: I. Qualis à Deo sit conditus homo.
units.tr: I. What Kind of Man God Created

units.la: Hæc quæstio iisdem ferè de causis proponitur, ob quas totus ipse locus: nempe 1. ut constet hominem à Deo conditum esse sine peccato, ideoq; Deum non esse authorem peccati, vel prauitatis & miseriæ nostræ. 2. Ut intelligamus, ex quanto dignitatis fastigio, in quam profundam miseriæ voraginem per peccatum præcipitati simus, eoq; agnoscamus misericordiam Dei, qui nos ex ea extrahere & liberare dignatur. 3. Ut agnoscamus nostram ingratitudinem pro acceptis beneficiis, & indignitatem in accipiendis. 4. Ut restitutionem amissæ dignitatis & felicitatis tanto ardentius expetamus & quæramus in Christo. 5. Deniq; ut pro eius restitutione Deo grati simus.
units.tr: This question is raised for almost the same reasons as the whole topic: (1) so that it is established that God created man without sin, and therefore that God is not the author of sin, or of our depravity and misery; (2) so that we understand from what height of dignity, into what deep abyss of misery we have been plunged through sin, and so acknowledge the mercy of God, who deigns to draw us out of it and set us free; (3) so that we recognise our ingratitude for the benefits received and our unworthiness in receiving them; (4) so that we may seek and pursue with greater ardour the restoration in Christ of the dignity and happiness we lost; (5) and finally, so that we may be thankful to God for that restoration.

units.la: Qualis autem homo à Deo initio sit conditus, hæc quæstione docetur, vbi dicitur: Bonum & ad imaginem sui condidit eum, &c. quod declarandum est fusius.
units.tr: What kind of man God originally made is taught in this question, where it is said: God made him good and in his own image, etc. This must be explained more fully.

units.la: Creatus igitur est homo à Deo sexto die creationis mundi. 1. E tertâ corpore immortali, si maneret in iustitia, mortali, si deficeret. Mortalitas enim peccatum secuta est tanquam pœna. 2. Animâ ex nihilo immediatè à Deo inspiratâ, rationali, spirituali & immortali: Deus inspiravit spiraculum vitæ in faciem eius, Gen.1. {*} & sic factus est homo in animam viventem. Creauit & vniuit animam corpori, vt cum eo esset vnum ψυχοσώματον, exercens actiones internas & externas naturae humanae proprias in corpore & cum corpore, organicas & inorganicas, justas, sanctas, & Deo placentes. 3. Ad imaginem Dei, hoc est, perfectè bonus, sapiens, justus, sanctus, beatus, & dominus aliarum creaturarum. De hac imagine D E I in homine paulò post fusius dicetur.
units.tr: Man was therefore created by God on the sixth day of the creation of the world. (1) As to his body, it was from the earth; immortal if he remained in righteousness, mortal if he fell away, for mortality followed sin as a punishment. (2) As to his soul, it was breathed in immediately by God out of nothing, rational, spiritual and immortal: God breathed into his face the breath of life, Gen. 1. {*} and so man became a living soul. God created the soul and joined it to the body, so that it was one psychosomaton [ψυχοσώματον] with it, exercising the internal and external actions proper to human nature, in and with the body, organic and inorganic, just, holy and pleasing to God. (3) In the image of God, that is, perfectly good, wise, just, holy, blessed, and lord of the other creatures. The image of God in man will be discussed more fully a little later.

units.la: II. Ad quid homo sit conditus.
units.tr: II. For What Purpose Man Was Created

units.la: Respondet catechesis: Vt Deum Creatorem suum rectè cognosceret, ex animo diligeret, cum eo beatus in aeternum viveret, idq; ad eum laudandum & celebrandum. Vltimus ergo & principalis finis creationis hominis est celebratio Dei. Ideo enim Deus creauit naturas rationales, angelos & homines, vt ab eis agnitus in aeternum celebretur. Homo igitur conditus est principaliter ad celebrationem Dei, hoc est, ad professionem & invocationem nominis divini, ad laudes & gratiarum actionem, dilectionem & obedientiam, quae constat officiis erga Deum & homines. Haec enim omnia celebratio Dei complectitur.
units.tr: The catechism answers: That he might rightly know God his Creator, love him from the heart, live blessed with him for ever, and do this to praise and celebrate him. The ultimate and principal end of the creation of man, therefore, is the celebration of God. For God created rational natures, angels and men, so that, being known by them, he might be celebrated for ever. Man was therefore created chiefly for the celebration of God, that is, for the profession and invocation of the divine name, for praises and thanksgiving, for love and obedience, which consist in duties towards God and men. For all these things the celebration of God embraces.

units.la: Obiect. Etiam caelum, terra, & irrationales creaturae aliae, dicuntur Deum celebrare. Ergo ad id non erat opus hominem condere. Resp. Res brutae dicuntur Deum celebrare, non quod ipsae Deum agnoscant aut celebrent, sed quia sunt materia celebrationis, quae fit à creaturis rationalibus. Ex earum enim intuitu angeli & homines, Dei sapientiam, bonitatem atque potentiam agnoscunt, & occasionem habent enim celebrandi. Opus igitur erat intelligentibus creaturis, & cernentibus ordinem naturae. Si enim hic ordo à nemine agnosceretur, & non intelligeretur, qualem causam requirant huiusmodi effectus; tam non celebrarent Deum, quàm si planè non essent. Itaque prosopopoeiae sunt, cum Dauid dicit: Laudate Deum caelum, mare, terra, &c.
units.tr: Objection: Heaven, earth and the other irrational creatures are also said to celebrate God. Therefore there was no need to create man for this. Answer: The lifeless things are said to celebrate God not because they themselves acknowledge or celebrate him, but because they are the matter of the celebration which is done by rational creatures. For from the sight of them angels and men recognise the wisdom, goodness and power of God, and have occasion to celebrate him. There was therefore need of creatures that understand and perceive the order of nature. For if this order were recognised by no one and not understood, what kind of cause such effects require, they would no more celebrate God than if they did not exist at all. Thus they are personifications when David says: Praise God, heaven, sea, earth, etc.

units.la: Huic fini principali plures alij subordinantur. Celebrationi subserviunt agnitio Dei: quia Deus non agnitus non potest celebrari. Propria autem hominis actio est Deum agnoscere & celebrare, in quo vita aeterna consistit. Haec est vita aeterna, vt te solum agnoscant esse verum Deum.
units.tr: Several other ends are subordinated to this principal end. Knowledge of God serves the celebration, since a God who is not known cannot be celebrated. The proper action of man, however, is to know and celebrate God, in which eternal life consists. This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God.

units.la: Agnitioni Dei subordinatur felicitas & beatitudo hominis, quae est communicatio Dei & fruitio bonorum caelestium. Ex his enim agnoscitur Dei bonitas, misericordia & potentia.
units.tr: Subordinated to the knowledge of God is the felicity and blessedness of man, which is the communion of God and the enjoyment of heavenly goods. For from these is recognised the goodness, mercy and power of God.

units.la: Obiect. Atqui felicitas, agnitio & celebratio sunt qualitates, & conditiones, cum quibus & in quibus Deus hominem condidit, didit, hoc est, sunt pars imaginis Dei & formae hominis. Ergo non sunt fines: & potius ad priorem, quam ad hanc quaestionem pertinent. Resp. Sunt pars formae & finis, diverso respectu. Nam & talem Deus hominem condidit, qui beatus & felix cum recte agnosceret ac celebraret: & in hunc finem condidit, ut ab eo in aeternum agnosceretur & celebraretur, & ut se ei perpetuo communicaret. Conditus igitur est homo integer & beatus, Deum recte agnoscens & celebrans: haec fuit accidentalis eius forma, quam in creatione accepit: & simul conditus fuit ad hoc, ut talis esset. Recte ergo dicitur utrumque: & quod sit creatus talis, & quod sit creatus ad hoc, ut talis esset. Prius pertinet ad quaestionem qualis, respectu principij: posterius ad quaestionem, ad quid, respectu perseverantiae. Unde apparet, non esse absurdum, idem diverso respectu dici formam & finem. Quod enim respectu creaturae fuit forma: idem intentione Creatoris fuit finis.
units.tr: Objection: But felicity, knowledge and celebration are qualities and conditions with which and in which God created man, that is, they are part of the image of God and the form of man. Therefore they are not ends, and belong rather to the earlier question than to this one. Answer: They are part of the form and also the end, in different respects. For God made man such that he, being blessed and happy, would rightly know and celebrate him; and he made him for this end, that he might be known and celebrated by him for ever, and that he might perpetually communicate himself to him. Man was therefore created whole and blessed, rightly knowing and celebrating God; this was his accidental form, which he received at creation; and at the same time he was created for this purpose, that he should be such. Both are therefore rightly said: that he was created such, and that he was created in order that he should be such. The former pertains to the question what kind, with respect to the beginning; the latter to the question for what purpose, with respect to perseverance. From this it appears that it is not absurd for the same thing to be called both form and end in different respects. For what was the form with respect to the creature was the end in the intention of the Creator.

units.la: Obiect. Si Adam conditus fuit ad vitam aeternam: fuit etiam electus. Omnes autem homines conditi fuerunt in Adamo. Omnes igitur homines videntur conditi ad vitam aeternam: proinde omnes electi; nulli reprobati.
units.tr: Objection: If Adam was created for eternal life, he was also elect. But all men were created in Adam. Therefore all men seem to have been created for eternal life, and so all are elect, and none reprobate.

units.la: Resp. Negatur consequentia; quia est fallacia a secundum quid. Fuerunt quidem omnes homines conditi in Adamo ante lapsum, quoad communem naturam: sed non etiam quoad speciale m gratiam. Secus dicendum, electionem factam fuisse in Adamo; non in Christo: quod est falsum. Adam igitur speciali gratia fuit conditus in integritate, sub conditione, ut si quidem in integritate perseveraret, beatus cum Deo in aeternum viveret. Sin autem, ipse cum posteris beatitate excidheret: nec nisi in Christo eandem recuperaret: quorum posterius fuisse consilio Dei definitum, eventus declarauit, & scriptura testatur. Vide uberiorem huius argumenti explicationem in D. Parei Epistola ad Mosen Vasarhelinum Hungarum, quae exstat in volum. epist. Theol. D. Dav. Parei.
units.tr: Answer: The inference is denied, because it is the fallacy of arguing from what is true in a certain respect to what is true absolutely. Indeed all men were created in Adam before the fall, as to common nature; but not also as to special grace. The opposite would have to be said, that the election was made in Adam and not in Christ, which is false. Adam, therefore, was created in integrity by special grace, under this condition: if he persevered in integrity, he would live blessed with God for ever. But if he fell away, he with his posterity would lose the blessedness, and could recover it only in Christ; which latter was determined by the counsel of God, as the outcome has shown and Scripture testifies. For a fuller explanation of this argument see the letter of Dr. Pareus to Moses Vasarhelius the Hungarian, which is found in the volume of letters of the Theology of Dr. David Pareus.

units.la: Fuit etiam Adam speciali gratia electus, non quidem in se, vel in sua integritate, sed hac amissa in Christo. Inter posteros vero Adami Deus discrimen fecit, & elegit in Christo, quos voluit: reprobavit item, quos voluit: sicut Isaac personaliter electus fuit: electio vero divina inter gemellos, quos genuit, discrimen fecit. Rom. 9, 11. Genes. 25, 23. Mal. 1, 2.
units.tr: Adam was also elected by special grace, not indeed in himself, or in his integrity, but in Christ after that was lost. Among the posterity of Adam, however, God made a distinction, and elected in Christ whom he willed, and likewise reprobated whom he willed; as Isaac was elected personally, and divine election made a distinction between the twins whom he begot. Rom. 9, 11. Gen. 25, 23. Mal. 1, 2.

units.la: Agnitioni & felicitati subordinatur patefactio Dei, seu declaratio misericordiae Dei in seruandis electis: & iustitiae in puniendis reprobis. Ut enim Deus agnoscatur, & se nobis communicet, necesse est, ut ipse se nobis patefaciat,
units.tr: Subordinated to knowledge and felicity is the manifestation of God, or the declaration of the mercy of God in saving the elect, and of his justice in punishing the reprobate. For that God may be known, and communicate himself to us, it is necessary that he should reveal himself to us.

units.la: Quintus finis est conservatio societatis in genere humano patefactioni subordinata. Nisi enim essent homines, non haberet Deus, quibus se patefaceret in terris. Psal. 22. v. 23. Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis.
units.tr: The fifth end is the preservation of society in the human race, subordinated to the revelation. For if there were no men, God would have no one to whom he might reveal himself on earth. Ps. 22. v. 23. I will declare your name to my brothers.

units.la: Sextus est communio officiorum, & mutuæ beneficentiæ inter homines, conservationi societatis humanæ subserviens. Nam vt conservetur societas humana, necesse est esse pacem, & mutua officia, inter homines.
units.tr: The sixth end is the sharing of duties and mutual kindness among men, serving the preservation of human society. For in order that human society may be preserved, there must be peace and mutual services among men.

units.la: De Imagine Dei in homine.
units.tr: The Image of God in Man.

units.la: De hac præcipuè quæritur: I. Quid sit, & qua eius partes. II. Quatenus sit amissa, & reliqua in homine. III. Quomodo reparetur.
units.tr: Here the following questions are chiefly asked: (1) what it is and what its parts are; (2) how far it has been lost, and what remains of it in man; (3) how it is restored.

units.la: I. Quid sit imago Dei in homine.
units.tr: I. What the image of God in man is.

units.la: Imago Dei in homine est mens recte agnoscens Dei naturam, voluntatem & opera Dei: & voluntas liberè obtemperans Deo; omniumque inclinationum, appetitionum & actionum congruentia cum voluntate Dei; & denique spiritualis ac immortalis animæ natura, totiusque hominis puritas & integritas, perfecta beatitudo & laetitia acquiescens in Deo, & dignitas hominis ac maiestas, quæ cæteris naturis sub cœlo antecellit ac dominatur.
units.tr: The image of God in man is a mind that rightly recognises the nature, will and works of God; and a will that freely obeys God; and the agreement of all inclinations, appetites and actions with the will of God; and finally the spiritual and immortal nature of the soul, together with the purity and integrity of the whole man, perfect blessedness and joy resting in God, and the dignity and majesty of man, which excels and rules over all other natures under heaven.

units.la: Imago igitur Dei complectitur: 1. Ipsam animæ substantiam incorpoream aut immortalem cum suis potentiis intelligendi & volendi. 2. Omnes notitias naturales de Deo & eius voluntate atque operibus, hoc est, perfectam sapientiam in mente. 3. Iustas & sanctas inclinationes & motus partis volentis, hoc est, perfectam iustitiam & sanctitatem in voluntate & corde, & externis actionibus omnibus. 4. Felicitatem, beatitudinem & gloriam, cum summa laetitia acquiescente in Deo, & copia omnium bonorum conjunctam, sine miseria & corruptione. 5. Dominium hominis in omnes creaturas, pisces, aves, & animantia alia sub cœlo. His omnibus natura rationalis homo Creatorem tanquam imago Archetypum, aliquo modo referebat, non tamen æquabat. Paulus Ephes. 4. vers. 24. imaginem Dei nominans veram iustitiam & sanctitatem, tanquam præcipuas partes, non excludit felicitatem & gloriam. Hæc enim illas ex ordine iustitiæ divinæ consequitur. Vbi enim est vera iustitia & sanctitas: ibi est absentia omnium malorum culpæ & poenæ: præsentia verò felicitatis & gloriæ. Possunt verò iustitia & sanctitas vel pro eodem sumi: sicut in Deo & Angelis reuereuera idem sunt: vel ita discerni, vt iustitia intelligatur de actionibus externis & internis, congruentibus cum mente recte iudicante & cum lege DEI: sanctitas de ipsis qualitatibus.
units.tr: The image of God therefore comprises: (1) the incorporeal or immortal substance of the soul itself, with its powers of understanding and willing. (2) All natural knowledge of God and of his will and works, that is, perfect wisdom in the mind. (3) Just and holy inclinations and motions of the willing part, that is, perfect righteousness and holiness in the will and heart, and in all external actions. (4) Happiness, blessedness and glory, with the highest joy resting in God, and joined with an abundance of all good things, without misery or corruption. (5) Dominion of man over all creatures, fish, birds and other living things under heaven. By all these things the rational nature of man referred to its Creator, as to its archetype, in a certain way, though it did not equal him. Paul, in Ephes. 4. vers. 24, calling the image of God true righteousness and holiness, as its chief parts, does not exclude happiness and glory; for these follow from the order of divine righteousness. For where there is true righteousness and holiness, there is the absence of all evils of guilt and punishment, and the presence of happiness and glory. Moreover, righteousness and holiness may either be taken as the same thing, as in God and the angels they are indeed the same; or they may be distinguished so that righteousness is understood of external and internal actions agreeing with a mind that judges rightly and with the law of God, and holiness of the qualities themselves.

units.la: Obiect. Perfecta iustitia est solius Dei, nec cadit in vllam creaturam: & omnium creaturarum, etiam Angelorum beatorum sapientia potest crescere, & crescit. Quomodo igitur imago Dei in homine fuit perfecta sapientia & iustitia? Resp. Perfecta sapientia hic vocatur, non quae nihil ignorer, sed quae perfecta sit ea perfectione, quae potest in naturam creatam competere, seu quam Creator vult in creatura esse, quaeque ad creaturae felicitatem sufficit: vt Angelorum sapientia & beatitudo est perfecta, quia talis est, qualem Deus vult esse: & tamen ei aliquid potest accedere: alioqui esset infinita. Sic homo erat perfecte iustus, quia erat conformis Deo in omnibus, quae ab eo Deus requirebat: non quod esset Deo aequalis, aut iustitiam haberet perfectam, eo gradu, quo Deus habet, sed quod nihil ei deesset ad eam perfectionem, quam Deus in eo condidit, & esse vohomonymia in vocabulo perfectionis. Et hoc quidem sensu homo dicitur imago Dei, seu ad imaginem Dei conditus in scriptura.
units.tr: Objection. Perfect righteousness belongs to God alone, and does not fall to any creature; and the wisdom of all creatures, even of the blessed angels, can increase, and does increase. How then was the image of God in man perfect wisdom and righteousness? Answer. Perfect wisdom is here called not that which knows nothing unknown, but that which is perfect with the perfection that can belong to a created nature, or which the Creator wills to be in the creature, and which suffices for the creature's happiness; just as the wisdom and blessedness of the angels is perfect, because it is such as God wills it to be, and yet something can still be added to it; otherwise it would be infinite. So man was perfectly righteous, because he was conformed to God in all the things that God required of him; not that he was equal to God, or had perfect righteousness to the degree that God has it, but that nothing was lacking to him for that perfection which God established in him. There is a homonymy in the word perfection. And in this sense man is called the image of God, or is said in Scripture to be created after the image of God.

units.la: Longè diuersa ratione Christus vocatur imago Dei, nimirum: 1. respectu diuinae naturae, qua est imago aeterni Patris coaeterna, consubstantialis & aequalis Patri proprietatibus essentialibus, & operibus, & persona illa, per quam Pater se immediatè patefecit, creando & conseruando omnia, praecipuè autem seruando electos. Et quidem vocatur imago non suiipsius, aut Spiritus sancti, sed Patris: quia non est à seipso, nec à Spiritu sancto, sed à Patre genitus ab aeterno. 2. Respectu humanae naturae, qua est imago Dei creata quidem, sed gradibus & numero donorum, sapientia, iustitia, potentia & gloria, omnibus angelis & hominibus in immensum antecellens, & peculiari ratione Patrem nobis referens, doctrina, virtutibus, & actionibus, sicut ipse dicit: Philippe, qui vidit me, vidit & Patrem meum.
units.tr: In a very different way Christ is called the image of God, namely: (1) with respect to the divine nature, in which he is the image of the eternal Father, coeternal, consubstantial and equal to the Father in essential properties, in works, and in that person through whom the Father revealed himself immediately, creating and preserving all things, but especially saving the elect. He is called image not of himself, or of the Holy Spirit, but of the Father, because he is not from himself, nor from the Holy Spirit, but was begotten from the Father from eternity. (2) With respect to the human nature, in which he is the image of God, created indeed, but surpassing all angels and men immeasurably in the degrees and number of his gifts: wisdom, righteousness, power and glory; and he presents the Father to us in a special way, by his teaching, virtues and actions, as he himself says: Philip, he who has seen me has seen my Father also.

units.la: Angeli verò & homines nominantur imago Dei, tam Filij & Spiritus sancti, quam Patris respectu, vbi dicitur: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram: non propter essentiae similitudinem vel aequalitatem, sed propter quandam proprietatum conuenientiam, non gradibus vel essentia, sed generatione & imitatione. Sunt enim quaedam à Deo in angelis & hominibus creatum analogum ad diuinae essentiae archetypum.
units.tr: Angels and men are called the image of God with respect to the Son and the Holy Spirit as well as the Father, where it is said: Let us make man in our image and likeness. This is not because of a likeness or equality of essence, but because of a certain agreement of properties, not in degrees or essence, but by generation and imitation. For there are certain things created by God in angels and men which are analogous to the archetype of the divine essence.

units.la: Quae verò contra haec de imagine Dei in homine olim ab Anthro-
units.tr: As for the things disputed against these views concerning the image of God in man, formerly by the Anthropomorphites, and recently by Osiander, which

units.la: C thropomorphitis, & recens ab Osiandro disputata sunt, legantur vol. 1. D. Vrsini pag. 154. 155.
units.tr: may be read in vol. 1 of D. Ursinus, pp. 154, 155.

units.la: 11. Quatenus amissa & reliqua sit imago Dei in homine.
units.tr: 11. How far the image of God was lost, and what of it remains in man.

units.la: Hæc igitur fuit imago Dei, ad quam Deus initio hominem condidit, & quam homo in se lucente habuit ante lapsum. Sed post lapsum homo per peccatum hac pulcherrima imagine Dei amissa, transformatus est in tetram imaginem diaboli. Manserunt quidem aliquæ illius reliquiæ & scintillæ post lapsum, quæ etiam in non renatis hominibus adhuc restant. 1. Substantia animæ incorporea, rationalis, & immortalis cum suis potentiis: & in his libertas voluntatis, ut quicquid vult, libere velit homo. 2. Multæ notitiæ in mente de Deo, de natura, de discrimine honestorum & turpium, quæ sunt artium principia. 3. Vestigia quædam & semina virtutum ethicarum, & disciplinæ extemporalis qualiscunq; possibilitatis. 4. Fruitio multorum temporalium bonorum. 5. Denique dominium aliquod in creaturas. Nam ne hoc quidem totum amissum est: sed multæ manent hominis imperio subiectæ: multas regere & vsurpare potest. Hæc, inquam, reliquiæ imaginis Dei in homine, etsi & ipsa per peccatum vehementer sunt obscuratæ & labefactatæ, seruatæ tamen sunt aliquo modo in natura. Idq; 1. Vt essent testimonium misericordiæ Dei erga nos etiam indignos. 2. Vt Deus his vtere-tur ad instaurationem imaginis sui in nobis. 3. Vt improbos redderet ἀναπολογήτους, hoc est, inexcusabiles.
units.tr: This, then, was the image of God in which God first created man, and which man possessed shining within himself before the Fall. But after the Fall, man lost this most beautiful image of God through sin and was transformed into the hideous image of the devil. Yet some remnants and sparks of it remained after the Fall, and these still persist even in unregenerate men: (1) the incorporeal, rational, and immortal substance of the soul with its faculties, and in these the freedom of the will, so that a man freely wills whatever he wills; (2) many notions in the mind about God, about nature, and about the distinction between honourable and shameful things, which are the first principles of the arts; (3) certain traces and seeds of ethical virtues, and some kind of possibility of external discipline; (4) the enjoyment of many temporal goods; (5) finally, some dominion over creatures. For even this has not been wholly lost: many creatures remain subject to human rule, and man can govern and make use of many of them. These remnants of the image of God in man, I say, although they too have been greatly obscured and weakened by sin, have nevertheless been preserved in some measure in nature. And this was done (1) so that they might be a testimony of God's mercy towards us even though we are unworthy; (2) so that God might use them for restoring his image in us; (3) so that he might render the wicked ἀναπολογήτους [anapologētous], that is, inexcusable.

units.la: Sed amissa sunt de imagine Dei longe plura & maiora bona. 1. Vera, perfecta, & salutaris agnitio Dei & voluntatis eius. 2. Integritas notitiarum de diuinis operibus, & lumen clarissimum in mente: cui successit ignorantia, cæcitas, tenebræ. 3. Omnium inclinationum, appetitionum, & actionum rectitudo & conformitas cum Lege Dei in voluntate & corde, & membris externis: cui successit horribilis ἀλογία & prauitas inclinationum & motuum cordis & voluntatis, unde pullulant actualia peccata, &c. 4. Dominium in creaturas merum & perfectum. Nam quæ bestiæ prius metuebant hominem, nunc ei repugnant, insidiantur, ac nocent: agri spinas ac tribulos proferunt. Jus utendi creaturis, quod Deus non hostibus, sed filiis suis concessit. 6. Denique felicitas huius & alterius vitæ: cui successit mors æterna & temporalis cum omnis generis calamitatibus.
units.tr: But far more and greater goods were lost from the image of God: (1) the true, perfect, and saving knowledge of God and of his will; (2) the integrity of knowledge about the divine works, and the most clear light in the mind, which has been succeeded by ignorance, blindness, and darkness; (3) the rectitude and conformity of all inclinations, desires, and actions with the Law of God, in the will and heart and external members, which has been succeeded by a horrible ἀλογία [alogia], that is, unreasonableness, and by the depravity of the inclinations and movements of the heart and will, whence actual sins spring forth, etc.; (4) complete and perfect dominion over creatures. For the beasts that once feared man now resist him, lie in wait for him, and harm him; the fields bring forth thorns and thistles; (5) the right to use creatures, which God granted not to enemies but to his sons; (6) finally, happiness in this life and the next, which has been succeeded by eternal and temporal death with every kind of calamity.

units.la: Obiect. Ethnici magnis virtutibus excelluerunt, & res præclaras gesserunt: ergo non videtur in illis imago Dei extincta. Resp. Eximiæ virtutes & res gestæ Ethnicorum pertinent quidem ad reliquias & ruderia imaginis Dei conseruatæ in naturâ hominis: sed tantum abest, vt sint vera illa & integra imago Dei, quæ in homine luxit, vt vix sint vmbræ, vel tantum larvæ quædam disciplinæ externæ, sine obedientia cordis interna erga Deum, quem ignorant & fugiunt: ideo nec placent Deo, cum neque ex vera Dei agnitione proficiscantur, neque ad gloriam eius referantur.
units.tr: Objection: The heathen excelled in great virtues and performed notable deeds; therefore the image of God does not seem to have been extinguished in them. Answer: The outstanding virtues and deeds of the heathen do indeed belong to the remnants and ruins of the image of God preserved in the nature of man. But so far are they from being that true and whole image of God which shone in man, that they are scarcely shadows, or merely certain masks of external discipline, without inward obedience of heart towards God, whom they do not know and flee from. Therefore they do not please God either, since they neither proceed from the true knowledge of God nor are referred to his glory.

units.la: III. Quomodo imago Dei in nobis reparetur.
units.tr: III. How the image of God is restored in us.

units.la: Reparatio imaginis Dei in homine fit à solo Deo, qui eam homini dederat. Eiusdem enim est vitam dare, & amissam restituere. Restituit eam Deus Pater per Filium: quia hunc fecit nobis sapientiam, iustitiam, satisfactionem & redemptionem: Filius per Spiritum sanctum: Transformamur in eandem gloriam, tanquam à Domini Spiritu: Spiritus sanctus per verbum & vsum sacramentorum: Euangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem. Sic autem tantum inchoetur, confirmetur & crescat vsque ad finem vitæ: quoad totum hominem perficiatur in resurrectione corporum. Notandum ergo, quo authore, quo ordine, & quo modo fiat hæc reparatio.
units.tr: The restoration of the image of God in man is effected by God alone, who had given it to him. For it belongs to the same one to give life and to restore what was lost. God the Father restores it through the Son, because he has made him for us wisdom, righteousness, satisfaction and redemption (1 Cor. 1). The Son restores it through the Holy Spirit: We are transformed into the same glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3). The Holy Spirit restores it through the Word and the use of the sacraments: The gospel is the power of God unto salvation (Rom. 1). This restoration is only begun, strengthened, and grows in this way until the end of life, until the whole man is perfected in the resurrection of the body. It is to be noted, therefore, by whose authority, in what order, and in what manner this restoration takes place.

units.la: QVÆSTIO VII.
units.tr: QUESTION VII.

units.la: Vnde igitur existit hæc natura humanæ pravitas?
units.tr: Whence, then, does this depravity of human nature arise?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Ex lapsu & inobedientia primorum parentum Adami & Euæa. Hinc natura nostra ita est depravata, vt omnes in peccatis concipiamur & nascamur.
units.tr: From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve. From this our nature has been so corrupted that we are all conceived and born in sins.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hic primum de lapsu, & primo peccato hominis, ex quo prauitas naturæ humanæ orta est; deinde de peccato in genere præsertim de peccato originali est cogitandum.
units.tr: Here we must consider first the fall and the first sin of man, from which the depravity of human nature arose; then we must consider sin in general, and especially original sin.

units.la: De Lapsu & primo Peccato hominis.
units.tr: On the Fall and the First Sin of Man.

units.la: I. Quod & quale peccatum fuerit. II. Qua eius causa. III. Qui effectus. IV. Cur Deus permiserit.
units.tr: I. What the sin was and of what kind. II. Its cause. III. Its effects. IV. Why God permitted it.

units.la: I. Quod & quale peccatum fuerit Lapsus.
units.tr: I. What the Fall was, and what kind of sin it was.

units.la: Lapsus siue primum peccatum hominis fuit inobedientia primorum parentum Adami & Euae in paradiso, siue esus pomi a Deo prohibiti: De omni fructu horti comedes: sed de arbore scientiæ boni & mali non comedes. Quocunque verò die comederis, morte morieris. Hoc mandatum Dei homo suasu diaboli violauit. Inde prauitas & miseria nostra.
units.tr: The Fall, or the first sin of man, was the disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in paradise, that is, the eating of the fruit forbidden by God: "Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die." Man violated this commandment of God at the persuasion of the devil. From this come our depravity and misery.

units.la: Sed an tantum nefas raptus pomi? Sanè grauissimum: quia in eo multa horrenda peccata concurrunt. 1. Incredulitas. Arguebat enim Deum mendacij. Dixerat Deus: Morte morieris: Hoc negauit diabolus, inquiens: Nequaquam moriemini: Accusauit Deum invidiæ: Sed nouit Deus, quod in die, qua comedetis ex ea, aperientur oculi vestri, eritisq; sicut dij, scientes bonum & malum. Diabolo Adam plus credidit quàm Deo: comedit de fructu vetito, nec credidit futurum, vt propterea puniretur. Deo autem non credere sed contrà credere diabolo, est Deum habere pro non Deo, immò est diabolum substituere in locum Dei. Hoc fuit supra modum horribile peccatum & principium reliquorum peccatorum. 2. Superbia, ambitio, admiratio sui: quia homo non contentus sua dignitate, voluit Deo esse æqualis. Hanc ei Deus e probrauit, dicens: Ecce homo factus est quasi vnus ex nobis. 3. Contumacia & inobedientia aduersus Deum: quia contra mandatum Dei edit de pomo. 4. Ingratitudo pro acceptis beneficiis. Erat conditus ad imaginem Dei, & ad vitam æternam: pro quo hanc gratiam rependit, quod diabolo magis auscultauit, quàm Deo. 5. A' ἀσέγεια & neglectus dilectionis erga posteros: quia miser homo non cogitauit, sicut sibi & posteris bona illa acceperat; sic se ea sibi & posteris peccando amisserum. 6. Apostasia seu defectio manifesta à Deo ad diabolum, cui credidit, & obtemperauit magis, quàm Deo, quem in Dei locum substituit, auellens se à Deo. Non expetit bona à Deo, quæ accepturus erat, sed consilio diaboli vult consequi æqualitatem cum Deo. Lapsus igitur hominis, nec simplex, nec leuc, sed multiplex & horrendum peccatum fuit, propter quod Deus hominem cum tota posteritate merito abjecit.
units.tr: But was it only the crime of plucking the fruit? Certainly it was a most grievous one, since many horrible sins concur in it. (1) Unbelief. For it accused God of lying. God had said, "Thou shalt surely die"; the devil denied this, saying, "Ye shall not surely die"; and he charged God with envy: "God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil." Adam believed the devil rather than God: he ate of the forbidden fruit and did not believe that the punishment would follow. To disbelieve God and instead believe the devil is to regard God as not God; indeed, it is to put the devil in the place of God. This was an exceedingly horrible sin and the beginning of all the other sins. (2) Pride, ambition, self-admiration: man, not content with his own dignity, wished to be equal to God. God rebuked this in him, saying, "Behold, the man is become as one of us." (3) Stubbornness and disobedience against God: he ate of the fruit contrary to God's command. (4) Ingratitude for the benefits received: he had been made in the image of God and for eternal life, and in return for this grace he repaid God by listening more to the devil than to God. (5) Impiety and neglect of love towards his posterity: the wretched man did not consider that he had received those good things for himself and his posterity, and that by sinning he lost them for himself and for them. (6) Apostasy, or a plain defection from God to the devil, whom he believed and obeyed rather than God, whom he set in God's place, tearing himself away from God. He did not seek the good things from God which he was about to receive, but by the counsel of the devil he wished to attain equality with God. The fall of man was therefore neither a simple nor a light sin, but a manifold and horrible one, on account of which God justly cast man off, together with his whole posterity.

units.la: Hinc facilè respondetur ad Obiect. Justus judex non infligit magnam poenam pro paruo peccato. Deus est justus judex. Ergo esum pomi non debuit tam grauiter punire. Resp. Non fuit peccatum paruum, sed grauissimum & varium, superbia, ingratitudo, apostasia, &c. vt dictum est. Iustè igitur Deus magnam poenam inflixit. Inst. Saltem posteris parcendum fuit: quia filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Resp. Modo filius non sit partuparticeps iniquitatum patris. Omnes autem filij Adæ culpæ eius participant: merito igitur & pœnæ.
units.tr: From this an answer to the objection is readily given. A just judge does not inflict a great penalty for a small sin. God is a just judge. Therefore he ought not to have punished the eating of the fruit so severely. Answer: It was not a small sin, but a most grievous and varied one: pride, ingratitude, apostasy, and so on, as has been said. Therefore God justly inflicted a great penalty. Objection: At least the posterity should have been spared, since "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father." Answer: Now, the son is not a partaker of the iniquities of the father. But all the sons of Adam share in his guilt, and therefore also in the punishment, and rightly so.

units.la: II. Qua causa primi peccati.
units.tr: II. The cause of the first sin.

units.la: Ortum habuit primum peccatum hominis, non à Deo, sed ab impulsu diaboli, & à libera voluntate hominis. Diabolus enim instigauit hominem ad defectionem à Deo, & homo instigationi diaboli assentiens, liberè sese auertit à Deo. Etsi autem Deus hominem in tentatione deseruit: tamen propterea non est causa lapsus vel peccati, vel exitij hominis: quia in illa defectione nihil horum Deus intendit, vel effecit, sed hominem probauit; ostendere volens, quam nihil possit creatura facere aut retinere boni, Deo eam non seruante & gubernante; cum sua verò probatione hominis peccatum concurrere justo judicio permisit.
units.tr: The first sin of man arose not from God but from the impulse of the devil and from the free will of man. For the devil incited man to fall away from God, and man, assenting to the devil's instigation, freely turned himself away from God. Although God forsook man in the temptation, he is nevertheless not on that account the cause of the fall, or of the sin, or of man's ruin: for in that defection God intended and effected none of these things, but tested man, wishing to show how little a creature can do or retain of good when God does not preserve and govern it; and with his own testing he permitted the sin of man to concur by a just judgment.

units.la: Ratio humana contra disputat. Qui subtrahit in tentatione gratiam, sine qua non potest euitare lapsus, is est causa lapsus. Deus homini in tentatione subtraxit gratiam, sine qua non poterat non labi: Ergo fuit causa lapsus. Resp. Maior vera est duntaxat de eo, qui subtrahit gratiam, quam est obligatus non subtrahere; & qui subtrahit inuito, nec vltro eam abijcienti: & qui subtrahit ex inuidia. Non autem est vera de eo, qui nec obligatus est ad seruandam gratiam, quam dederat: nec subtrahit inuito, sed volenti, immò vltrò abijcienti gratiam datam: nec subtrahit ideo, quod inuideat peccanti justitiam & vitam æternam, aut quod peccato delectetur, sed vt eum exploret. Qui enim sic aliquem deserit, nequaquam est causa peccati, etiamsi hanc desertionem & gratiæ subtractionem necessariò sequatur peccatum in eo, qui sic deseritur. Atqui Deus non illo priore: sed hoc posteriore modo homini in tentatione gratiam suam subtraxit. Non ergo Deus eam subtrahens, sed homo vltro eam abijciens peccati & exitij sui causa extitit.
units.tr: Human reason objects: whoever withdraws, in a temptation, the grace without which one cannot avoid falling, is the cause of the fall. God withdrew from man in temptation the grace without which he could not avoid falling. Therefore God was the cause of the fall. Answer: The major premise is true only of one who withdraws grace which he is bound not to withdraw, and who withdraws it from one unwilling, not from one who freely casts it away, and who withdraws it out of envy. But it is not true of one who is not bound to preserve the grace he had given, nor withdraws it from one unwilling but from one willing, indeed from one who freely casts away the grace given, nor withdraws it because he envies the sinner justice and eternal life, or because he takes pleasure in the sin, but in order to test him. For one who thus forsakes someone is by no means the cause of the sin, even though the sin in the one so forsaken necessarily follows this desertion and withdrawal of grace. But God did not withdraw his grace from man in temptation in the former manner, but in the latter. Therefore it was not God who withdrew it, but man who, of his own accord, cast it away, and so became the cause of his own sin and ruin.

units.la: Inst. Qui tentari vult eum, quem certò scit esse lapsurum, si tentetur, is vult peccatum eius, qui labitur. Deus voluit à diabolo tentari hominem, quem certò sciuit esse lapsurum, alioqui tentari homo non potuisset. Ergo Deus est causa lapsus. Resp. Negatur & hæc maior simpliciter intellecta. Non enim est causa peccati, qui lapsurum tentari vult explorandi, & creaturæ infirmitatem manifestandi causa. Sic autem Deus hominem tentari, hoc est, probari voluit. Diabolus verò tentans hominem hoc fine, vt peccaret atque à Deo auelleretur, & homo sponte obtemperans tentatori contra præceptum Dei, veræ fuerunt causæ primi peccati. Sed de causis peccati generatim postea dicetur.
units.tr: Objection: whoever wishes a man to be tempted, whom he certainly knows will fall if tempted, wishes the sin of the one who falls. God wished man to be tempted by the devil, whom he certainly knew would fall; otherwise man could not have been tempted. Therefore God is the cause of the fall. Answer: This major premise, taken simply, is denied. For one who wishes a creature to be tempted, knowing it will fall, in order to test it and to show the creature's weakness, is not the cause of the sin. And so God wished man to be tempted, that is, to be proved. But the devil, tempting man with the end that he should sin and be torn away from God, and man, obeying the tempter of his own accord against the command of God, were the true causes of the first sin. But concerning the causes of sin in general, it will be said later.

units.la: III. Qui effectus primi peccati.
units.tr: III. What were the effects of the first sin?

units.la: Effectus primi peccati sunt: 1. Reatus mortis & priuatio ac destructio imaginis Dei in ipsis parentibus. 2. Peccatum originale in posteris, hoc est, reatus æternæ mortis, & prauitas atque auersio totius naturæ à Deo. 3. Omnia peccata actualia, quæ ex originali nascuntur. Nam quod est causa causæ, est etiam causa effectus. At primum peccatum est causa peccati originalis, & hoc actualium. 4. Omnia mala pœnæ, quæ propter peccata infliguntur. Primum igitur peccatu est causa omnium aliorum peccatorum & pœnarum. An verò conueniat iustitiæ Dei, propter peccata parentum punire posteros, postea in loco de peccato originali explicabitur.
units.tr: The effects of the first sin are: (1) guilt of death, and the loss and destruction of the image of God in the parents themselves; (2) original sin in their posterity, that is, guilt of eternal death, and the corruption and aversion of the whole of nature from God; (3) all actual sins, which arise from original sin. For what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of its effect. But the first sin is the cause of original sin, and so of actual sins. (4) All the punishments of evil that are inflicted on account of sins. The first sin is therefore the cause of all other sins and punishments. Whether it is consistent with the justice of God to punish posterity for the sins of their parents will be explained later, in the place on original sin.

units.la: IV. Cur Deus permiserit.
units.tr: IV. Why God permitted it.

units.la: Poterat Deus hominem seruare, ne laberetur, si voluisset: permisit vero eum labi, hoc est, non dedit ei gratiam resistendi aut resistere volendi tentationibus diaboli, duas ob causas: Primum quidem, vt esset manifestatio infirmitatis creaturæ, si in rectitudine originali à Creatore non seruaretur. Deinde verò vt hac occasione Deus ostenderet suam bonitatem, misericordiam & gratiam in seruandis electis per Christum; iustitiam verò & potentiam in puniendis propter peccata impiis & reprobis, juxta dicta: Conclusit Deus omnes sub peccato, vt omnium misereatur, & obturetur omne os. Item: Volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, pertulit multa lenitate vasa irae coaptata ad interitum, & vt notas faceret diuitias gloriæ suæ erga vasa misericordiæ, quæ præparauit ad gloriam.
units.tr: God could have kept man from falling, had he wished to. Instead he permitted him to fall, that is, he did not give him the grace to resist the temptations of the devil, or the will to resist them, for two reasons. The first was so that the weakness of the creature might be made manifest, if he was not preserved in his original uprightness by the Creator. The second was so that on this occasion God might show his goodness, mercy and grace in saving the elect through Christ, but his justice and power in punishing the wicked and reprobate for their sins, according to the words: God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy on all, and every mouth may be stopped. Likewise: Willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, which he has prepared for glory.

units.la: De Peccato in genere.
units.tr: De Peccato in genere.

units.la: De peccato in genere præcipuè quæritsoler: I. An sit, seu vnde constet, peccatum esse in mundo, & in nobis. II. Quid sit. III. Quotuplex sit. IV. Vnde sit, seu quæ eius causa. V. Quæ sint eius effecta.
units.tr: Concerning sin in general, these questions are customarily raised: I. Whether there is sin, or how it is established that sin exists in the world and in us. II. What sin is. III. Of how many kinds it is. IV. Where it comes from, or what its cause is. V. What its effects are.

units.la: I. An sit peccatum in nobis.
units.tr: I. Whether there is sin in us.

units.la: Peccatum esse in mundo, & in nobis, variè conuincimur: 1. Asseueratio diuina nos omnes pronunciat reos peccati. Deo autem asseueranti, vt Greek & veracissimo, est credendum. Genef. 6. v. 5. & cap. 8. v. 21. Ier. 17, 9. Rom. 1, 21. & c. 3. v. 10. & c. 7. v. 18. Psal. 14. & 53. Iesa. 59. II. Ex Lege Dei peccatum integrè cognoscitur, vt supra ad quæstionem catechet. 3. & 5. ostendi.
units.tr: That sin exists in the world and in us is proved in several ways. 1. The divine assertion pronounces all of us guilty of sin. And God, who is unlying and most true, when he asserts something, must be believed. Gen. 6:5; ch. 8:21; Jer. 17:9; Rom. 1:21; ch. 3:10; ch. 7:18; Ps. 14 and 53; Isa. 59. II. From the law of God sin is fully known, as I showed above under the catechism questions 3 and 5.

units.la: Rom.11, 32. / Rom. 9, 22. ostensum est, juxta dicta : Per Legem agnitio peccati. Lex iram efficit : siquidem ubi non est lex, ibi nec est transgressio. Lex introiit, ut augeretur offensa. Peccatum non cognoui, nisi per legem. III. Con- scientia nos convincit peccati. Servavit enim Deus etiam praeter scriptam legem, notitias quasdam legis naturalis in mentibus, sufficientes ad homines accusandos & damnandos, juxta dicta: Quoniam id, quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est in eis. Et: Gentes natura, quae legis sunt, faciunt, & ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, una testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus. IV. Mors & poenae, quibus subiecti sunt omnes homines, omnia, inquam, coemeteria, cranaria, patibula sunt totidem conciones de peccato: quia Deus, cum sit justus, non infligit poenas, nisi propter peccatum; juxta dictum Mors manavit ad omnes, eo quod omnes peccaverunt. Item: Stipendium peccati mors est. Item: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, &c.
units.tr: Rom. 11:32; Rom. 9:22. This has been shown by the sayings: "Through the law comes the knowledge of sin" (Rom. 3:20). "The law works wrath" (Rom. 4:15). "Where there is no law, there is no transgression" (Rom. 4:15). "The law entered that the offence might abound" (Rom. 5:20). "I had not known sin except through the law" (Rom. 7:7). III. Conscience convicts us of sin. For God has preserved, even beside the written law, certain notions of the natural law in men's minds, sufficient to accuse and condemn them, according to the saying: "Because what may be known of God is manifest in them" (Rom. 1:19). And: "The Gentiles, who have not the law, do by nature the things of the law, and show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another" (Rom. 2:14-15). IV. Death and the punishments to which all men are subject: all the cemeteries, charnel houses and gallows, I say, are so many sermons about sin. For God, being just, inflicts punishments only on account of sin, according to the saying: "Death passed upon all men, because all have sinned" (Rom. 5:12). Likewise: "The wages of sin is death" (Rom. 6:23). Likewise: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things," etc. (Gal. 3:10).

units.la: Usus huius quaestionis est: 1. Ut habeamus materiam perpetuae humilitatis & poenitentiae. 2. Ut aversemur furores Anabaptistarum & Libertinorum, qui negant in se peccatum esse, contra expressum Dei verbum: Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus: & contra omnem experientiam. Nam & multa subinde admittunt, quae Deus in Lege pronunciat esse peccata: ipsi vero dicunt esse motus Spiritus sancti, sed mentiuntur: & in miseriis viuunt, morbis & morti obnoxii non minus, quam alij: quod certe, si essent ἀναμάρτητοι, fieret contra regulam: Vbi non est peccatum, ibi nec mors est.
units.tr: The use of this question is: 1. That we may have matter for constant humility and repentance. 2. That we may shun the frenzies of the Anabaptists and Libertines, who deny that sin is in them, against the express word of God: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 John 1:8), and against all experience. For they also at times admit many things that God in the Law pronounces to be sins, yet they call them movements of the Holy Spirit, and they lie. They live in miseries, subject to diseases and death no less than others; which would certainly not be so, if they were ἀναμάρτητοι [sinless], contrary to the rule: "Where there is no sin, there is no death either."

units.la: Sed quaeritur, an non etiam ex Euangelio fiat agnitio peccati. Nam Euangelium jubens nos quaerere justitiam non in nobis, sed extra nos in Christo, pronunciat nos peccatores: Ergo etiam ex Euangelio est agnitio peccati, & non tantum ex Lege. Resp. Euangelium pronunciat nos peccatores, sed non in specie, sicut Lex, neque ex professo docet, vel tractat de peccato: quod Legis est proprium: sed tantum hoc facit in genere, & minus principaliter, & ex hypothesi Legis, sicut inferior scientia principium aliquod assumit ex superiore. Postquam enim Lex nos convicit, quod sumus peccatores, & damnati, Euangelium hoc principium assumit & infert, cum simus peccatores & damnati in nobis, quaerendam igitur esse justitiam extra nos in Christo, ut serviemur.
units.tr: But it is asked whether knowledge of sin does not also come from the Gospel. For the Gospel, bidding us seek righteousness not in ourselves but outside ourselves, in Christ, pronounces us sinners. Therefore knowledge of sin comes also from the Gospel, and not only from the Law. Answer. The Gospel pronounces us sinners, but not in the particular way the Law does, nor does it teach or treat of sin professedly, which is the proper office of the Law. It does this only in general and less principally, and on the hypothesis of the Law, just as a lower science assumes some principle from a higher one. For after the Law has convicted us that we are sinners and damned, the Gospel takes up this principle and infers that, since we are sinners and damned in ourselves, righteousness must be sought outside ourselves, in Christ, so that we may be saved.

units.la: Sic igitur quinque modis cognoscitur in nobis esse peccatum. 1. Ex asseveratione divina. 2. Ex Lege Dei principaliter & in specie. 3. Ex Euangelio minus principaliter, & in genere. 4. Ex sensu conscientiæ. 5. Ex poenis, quas Deus justus non nisi propter peccatum infligit.
units.tr: Thus, then, in five ways it is known that sin exists in us. 1. From the divine assertion. 2. From the Law of God, principally and in particular. 3. From the Gospel, less principally and in general. 4. From the sense of conscience. 5. From the punishments which the just God inflicts only on account of sin.

units.la: II. Quid sit peccatum.
units.tr: II. What sin is.

units.la: Peccatum est ἀνομία, seu quicquid cum lege Dei pugnat, hoc est, defectus, vel inclinatio, vel actio, pugnans cum Lege Dei, offendens Deum, & ream faciens creaturam æternæ iræ Dei, nisi fiat remissio propter Filium Dei Mediatorem. Genus peccati est defectus, inclinatio vel actio, proprie tamen defectus: inclinatio vel actio potius sunt materiale peccati. Differentia seu formale, est pugnantia cum lege, quam Johannes vocat ἀνομίαν. Proprium necessario ei adhærens, est reatus creaturæ peccantis, seu obligatio ad poenas temporales & æternas, ex ordine justitiæ divinæ. Hinc vulgò dicitur peccati esse geminum formale, pugnantia cum lege, & reatus: seu geminus respectus, quorum prior est pugnantia cum Lege, alter ordinatio ad pœnam. Accidentalis conditio est: nisi fiat remissio &c. quia non ex natura peccati, sed per accidens fit, ut credentes in Christum non puniantur morte æterna; quia peccatum iis propter Christum non imputatur, & ex gratia remittitur.
units.tr: Sin is ἀνομία [lawlessness], or whatever is at odds with the law of God; that is, a defect, or an inclination, or an action, conflicting with the Law of God, offending God, and making the creature liable to the eternal wrath of God, unless remission is granted on account of the Son of God the Mediator. The genus of sin is defect; inclination or action, but properly defect; inclination or action are rather the material of sin. The difference, or formal element, is conflict with the law, which John calls ἀνομία. The property, necessarily adhering to it, is the guilt of the sinning creature, or obligation to temporal and eternal punishments, arising from the order of divine justice. Hence it is commonly said that sin has a twofold formal element: conflict with the law, and guilt; or a twofold respect, of which the first is conflict with the Law and the second is ordination to punishment. The accidental condition is: "unless remission is granted," etc., because it is not from the nature of sin but happens by accident that believers in Christ are not punished with eternal death; sin is not imputed to them on account of Christ, and is remitted by grace.

units.la: Portò DEFECTUS nominantur, in mente ignorantia & dubitatio de Deo, ejusq; voluntate, & in corde privatio dilectionis Dei & ardentis desiderij ac studij obtemperandi Deo secundum omnia ipsius mandata, & omissio actionū internarum & externarum, quæ in Lege Dei præcipiuntur. INCLINATIONES pravæ sunt contumacia cordis & voluntatis adversus Legem Dei, & judicium mentis de actionibus honestis & turpibus: Item pravitas & propensio naturæ ad faciendum ea, quæ Deus prohibet, quod malum nominant concupiscentiam.
units.tr: Moreover, defects are named: in the mind, ignorance and doubt concerning God and his will; in the heart, the lack of love for God and of ardent desire and zeal to obey God in all his commandments, and the omission of internal and external actions which are commanded in the Law of God. INCLINATIONS are evil: the obstinacy of heart and will against the Law of God, and the judgment of the mind about honourable and shameful actions; likewise the perversity and propensity of nature to do what God forbids, which they call concupiscence, an evil.

units.la: Hos autem defectus & inclinationes esse peccata, & à Deo damnari, probatur. I. Ex Lege Dei, quæ hos defectus & inclinationes expresse damnat, cum dicit: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, &c. Non concupisces: & illis opposita dona & facultates, perfectam nimirum agnitionem & dilectionem Dei & proximi, in hominibus requirit; Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, &c. Non habebis Deos alienos, &c. II. Ex plurimis scripturæ testimoniis, accusantibus hæc mala tanquam peccata: Omne figmentum cogitationum cordis humani duntaxat malum est à pueritia. Pravum est cor hominis & inscrutabile. Concupiscentiam non nossem (scilicet esse peccatum) nisi Lex dixisset: Non concupisces. Sic Johan.3. v.5. 1 Corinth.2,14. & 15, 50. Rom.1,21. & 8,6. III. Ex poenis & morte infantium, qui etsi bonum vel malum
units.tr: That these defects and inclinations are sins, and are condemned by God, is proved. I. From the Law of God, which expressly condemns these defects and inclinations when it says: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things," etc. (Deut. 27:26). "You shall not covet" (Exod. 20:17). And it requires in men the opposite gifts and capacities, namely a perfect knowledge and love of God and of neighbour: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," etc. (Deut. 6:5). "This is eternal life, that they know you the only true God," etc. (John 17:3). "You shall have no other gods before me," etc. (Exod. 20:3). II. From many testimonies of Scripture which accuse these evils as sins: "Every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil from childhood" (Gen. 6 and 8). "The heart of man is deceitful and desperately wicked" (Jer. 17:9). "I had not known concupiscence (that is, to be sin) unless the Law had said: You shall not covet" (Rom. 7:7). So also John 3:5; 1 Cor. 2:14; 15:50; Rom. 1:21; 8:6. III. From the punishments and death of infants, who, although they do neither good nor evil, and do not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression (Rom. 5:14; Rom. 9:11), nevertheless have sin, on account of which death reigns over them (Rom. 5:12). This sin is the blindness and aversion of nature from God, of which we have spoken.

units.la: Deut.27,26 Exo.20,17. Deut.6,5. Joh.17,3. Exod.20,3. Gen.6.&8. Jarem.17,9. Rom.7,7. Rom.9,11. Rom 5,12. malum non faciunt, & ad similitudinem transgressionis Adami non peccant, tamen habent peccatum, propter quod mors in eos regnat. Hoc vero est cœcitas & aversio naturæ à Deo, de qua dictum est.
units.tr: Though they do not do evil and do not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression, they nevertheless have sin, on account of which death reigns over them. This is indeed the blindness and aversion of nature from God, of which we have spoken.

units.la: Obijcitur contra. 1. Quod non est voluntarium, nec potest evitari, id non est peccatum, nec meretur pœnas. Defectus & inclinationes non possunt à nobis vitari. Non igitur sunt peccata. Resp. Maior vera est in judicio civili, sed non in judicio Dei, coram quo peccatum est, & pœnas meretur, quicquid cum Lege eius pugnat: sive vitari possit, sive non. Utrumque enim scriptura docet, & carnis intelligentiam non posse Legi Dei subjici, & quicunque Legi non subjiciuntur, maledictioni esse obnoxios.
units.tr: It is objected against this. (1) What is not voluntary and cannot be avoided is not sin and does not deserve punishment. Defects and inclinations cannot be avoided by us. Therefore they are not sins. Answer: The major premise is true in civil judgment, but not in the judgment of God, before whom whatever conflicts with his Law is sin and deserves punishment, whether it can be avoided or not. For Scripture teaches both: that the mind of the flesh cannot be subjected to the Law of God, and that all who are not subject to the Law are liable to the curse.

units.la: Obiect 2. Natura bona est. Inclinationes & appetitiones sunt naturales. Ergo sunt bonæ. Resp. ad maiorem: 1. natura est bona: scilicet ante corruptionem: quia dicitur: Omnia quæ fecerat Deus, erant valde bona. 2. Etiam nunc natura bona est, quoad substantiam, & quatenus à Deo est condita: non autem, quoad qualitates, & quatenus est corrupta per lapsum.
units.tr: Objection 2. Nature is good. Inclinations and appetites are natural. Therefore they are good. Reply to the major premise: (1) nature was good, namely before the corruption, since it is said: "God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good." (2) Nature is still good even now as to its substance, and insofar as it was created by God; but not as to its qualities, insofar as it has been corrupted by the fall.

units.la: Obj. 3. Pœnæ non sunt peccata. Inclinationes vitiosæ & defectus sunt pœnæ primi lapsus: ergo non sunt peccata. Resp. Maior vera est in judicio politico: non semper in divino. Nam Deus sæpe peccata peccatis punit: quod ostendit Apostolus Rom. 1, v. 27. 1 Thess. 2, 11. Habet enim Deus potestatem priuandi creaturas suo spiritu, quam potestatem creaturæ non habent.
units.tr: Objection 3. Punishments are not sins. Vicious inclinations and defects are punishments of the first fall; therefore they are not sins. Reply: The major premise is true in the civil judgment, but not always in the divine judgment. For God often punishes sins with sins, as the Apostle shows in Rom. 1:27 and 2 Thess. 2:11. For God has the power of depriving creatures of his Spirit, a power which creatures do not have.

units.la: III. Quotuplex sit peccatum.
units.tr: III. How many kinds of sin there are.

units.la: Præcipuæ diuisiones peccati sunt quinque.
units.tr: The principal divisions of sin are five.

units.la: PRIMA. Omne peccatum aut est originale, aut actuale. Hæc distinctio expressa est Rom. 5, 14. Rom. 7, 20, Rom. 9, 11.
units.tr: FIRST. Every sin is either original or actual. This distinction is expressed in Rom. 5:14, Rom. 7:20, and Rom. 9:11.

units.la: De peccato originali.
units.tr: Concerning original sin.

units.la: Originale peccatum est corruptio & reatus totius generis humani, ex lapsu primorum parentum; hoc est, priuatio agnitionis Dei & voluntatis diuinæ in mente, & inclinationes ad obediendum Deo in voluntate & corde: & in his inclinatio ad ea, quæ Lex Dei vetat, & aversio ab iis, quæ Deus præcepit, secuta lapsum primorum parentum, & ab his deriuata in omnes posteros, ac totam eorum naturam sic depravans, ut omnes propter hanc prauitatem rei sint æternæ iræ Dei, neque quicquam Deo placens facere possint, nisi fiat remissio, propter filium Dei Mediatorem, & renouatio naturæ per Spiritum sanctum. De hoc peccato dicitur: Mors regnauit in eos quoque, qui non peccauerant. rant ad similitudinem transgressionis Adami. In peccatis concepit me mater mea. Duo igitur complectitur peccatum originis. 1. Pravitatem naturæ humanæ ex lapsu primorum parentum. 2. Reatum æternæ damnationis propter eundem lapsum parentum. De utroque dicit Paulus: Per unum hominem peccatum intrôit in mundum, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pertransiit, eò quod omnes peccaverunt. Eadem complectitur, licet obscurius, definitio vulgata, quæ tribuitur Anshelmo: Peccatum originis est carentia justitiæ originalis, debita inesse. Justitia enim originalis non modò erat conformitas naturæ cum Lege Dei, sed etiam acceptatio seu approbatio divina. Conformitati autem pravitas approbationi reatus opponitur, & per lapsum in natura humana successit. Item illa Hugonis: Peccatum originis est, quod trahimus à nativitate per ignorantiam in mente, & per concupiscentiam in carne.
units.tr: Original sin is the corruption and guilt of the whole human race, arising from the fall of our first parents; that is, the privation of the knowledge of God and of the divine will in the mind, and inclinations in the will and heart against obeying God; and in these, an inclination toward what the law of God forbids, and an aversion from what God has commanded, which followed the fall of our first parents and has been derived from them into all their posterity, depraving their whole nature in such a way that all, because of this depravity, are liable to the eternal wrath of God, and can do nothing pleasing to God unless remission is granted on account of the Son of God as Mediator, and the renewal of nature through the Holy Spirit. Of this sin it is said: "Death reigned even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression." "In sin my mother conceived me." Original sin therefore embraces two things: (1) the depravity of human nature arising from the fall of our first parents; (2) the guilt of eternal damnation on account of that same fall of the parents. Paul speaks of both: "Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed upon all men, because all have sinned." The same things, though more obscurely, are included in the common definition ascribed to Anselm: "Original sin is the lack of original justice, which ought to be present." For original justice was not only the conformity of nature with the law of God, but also divine acceptance or approval. Depravity is opposed to conformity, and guilt to approval, and both came into human nature through the fall. Likewise there is that definition of Hugh: "Original sin is what we draw from birth, through ignorance in the mind and through concupiscence in the flesh."

units.la: Contra hanc de peccato originali doctrinam olim contendebant Pelagiani, sicut hodie Anabaptistæ; nullum esse peccatum originis, neque ex lapsu primorum parentum reos vel pravos esse posteros, neque in eos peccatum vel reatum vllum à maioribus deriuari vitio naturæ, sed singulos tantum imitatione parentum peccare, & cum culpa reatum contrahere. Hos Avgvstinvs multis libris confutauit. Alij dixerunt, esse quidem reatum ex lapsu parentum: sed nullam pravitatem singulis innatam, quæ damnationem mereatur.
units.tr: Against this doctrine of original sin, the Pelagians once contended, as the Anabaptists do today: that there is no original sin, that posterity is not made guilty or depraved by the fall of the first parents, and that no sin or guilt is derived into them from their ancestors through a vice of nature; but that each person sins only by imitating his parents, and incurs guilt by his own fault. Augustine refuted these in many books. Others have said that there is indeed guilt arising from the fall of the parents, but no depravity innate in individuals that deserves damnation.

units.la: Aduersus hos tenenda sunt hæc quatuor theoremata. 1. Totum genus humanum esse reum æternæ iræ Dei, propter inobedientiam primorum parentum. 2. Præter hunc reatum in nobis esse defectus & inclinationes cum Lege diuina pugnantes, quamptimum nascimur. 3. Hos defectus & inclinationes esse peccata merentia æternam iram Dei. 4. Hæc mala non imitatione tantum attrahi, sed propagatione naturæ vitiosæ à primis parentibus in omnes posteros, excepto Christo, deriuari.
units.tr: Against these, the following four propositions must be held. (1) The whole human race is liable to the eternal wrath of God on account of the disobedience of our first parents. (2) Besides this guilt, there are in us, as soon as we are born, defects and inclinations at odds with the divine law. (3) These defects and inclinations are sins that deserve the eternal wrath of God. (4) These evils are derived not merely by imitation, but by the propagation of a vicious nature from the first parents into all their posterity, except Christ.

units.la: Primum, secundum, & tertium supra sunt confirmata: quartum probatur.
units.tr: The first, second, and third of the above have been confirmed; the fourth is proved.

units.la: I. Testimoniis scripturæ. Eramus natura filij iræ, sicut & caeteri. Per vnam offensam reatus venit in omnes homines, ad condemnationem. Per vnius hominis inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi. Quis dabit mundum de immundo? In iniquitate natus sum. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non poterit ingredi in regnum Dei.
units.tr: I. By testimonies of Scripture. "We were by nature children of wrath, as others were." "Through one offence guilt came upon all men, to condemnation." "Through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners." "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" "I was brought forth in iniquity." "Unless a man is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."

units.la: II. Infantes moriuntur, & sunt baptizandi. Ergo habent peccatum. At non possunt peccare imitatione. Habent ergo peccapecatum ingenitum; unde dicitur: Transgressorem ab utero vocaui te. Cor hominis prauum à pueritia. Et Ambrosius ait: Quis justificatur in conspectu Dei, cum unius quoque diei infans mundus à peccato esse non possit.?
units.tr: II. Infants die, and they are to be baptized. Therefore they have sin. But they cannot sin by imitation. Therefore they have innate sin; hence it is said: "I called you a transgressor from the womb." "The heart of man is wicked from his youth." And Ambrose says: "Who is justified in the sight of God, when an infant of even one day old cannot be free from sin?"

units.la: III. Omne genitum habet naturam gignentis, quoad substantiam & accidentia speciei propria. At omnes nascimur ex parentibus corruptis & reis. Omnes ergo nascendo trahimus corruptionem & reatum per naturam.
units.tr: III. Everything begotten has the nature of the one who begets it, both in substance and in the accidents proper to the species. But we are all born of parents who are corrupt and guilty. Therefore we all, by being born, draw corruption and guilt through nature.

units.la: IV. Per mortem Christi, qui est secundus Adam, gemina nobis gratia contingit, justificatio & regeneratio. Ergo & geminum malum ex primo Adamo in nos manavit: reatus & depravatio naturæ: alioqui gemina illa gratia & medicina non fuisset opus.
units.tr: IV. Through the death of Christ, who is the second Adam, we receive a twofold grace, justification and regeneration. Therefore a twofold evil also flowed into us from the first Adam: guilt and depravity of nature. Otherwise that twofold grace and remedy would not have been necessary.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Si peccatum originis transit ex parentibus in sobolem, aut per corpus aut per animam transit. Non per corpus, quia est brutum: nec per animam, quia anima non propagatur per traducem, cum sit substantia spiritualis, impartibilis, nec creatur à Deo vitiosa, cum Deus non sit author peccati. Ergo omnino non transit per naturam. Resp. 1. Negatur minor: quia anima condita à Deo non vitiosa, potest vitium contrahere à corpore, licet bruto, cui infunditur. Neque enim absurdum est dicere, temperamentum corporis vitiosum, & ad mala pronum, ineptum esse animæ ad actiones bonas organum, & animam in rectitudine non confirmatam depravare, vt à sua integritate deficiat, quam primum corpori infunditur. 2. Negatur consequentia, quia non est sufficiens enumeratio in maiore. Transit enim neque per corpus, neque per animam, sed per totius hominis generationem immundam, propter culpam primorum parentum, propter quam Deus iusto judicio, animas dum creat, simul priuat originali rectitudine & donis, quæ parentibus hac lege contulerat, vt & posteris ea conferrent vel perderent, si ipsi ea retinerent vel amitterent. Neque Deus hoc faciens fit injustus vel causa peccati. Nam hæc priuatio respectu Dei eam infligentis ob culpam parentum, non peccatum, sed justissima pœna est: etsi respectu parentum, sibi & soboli suæ eam attrahentium, peccatum sit. Si ergo maior integra ponatur: Peccatum originis transit in posteros, vel per corpus, vel per animam, vel per totius hominis generationem immundam, propter culpam parentum, & meritum priuationis; ex justo judicio Dei; vitium argumenti manifestum est. Sicut enim peccatum originis ortum est in parentibus per culpam: sic per eandem transit in posteros. Hæc non est rimula, de qua Scholastici tam anxiè disputant, tradux videlicet, & contaminatio animæ per corpus, sed amplissima porta, per quam peccatum originale in naturam nostram irruit, vt testatur Paulus : Per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi,
units.tr: Objection 1. If original sin passes from parents to offspring, it passes either through the body or through the soul. Not through the body, because the body is brute matter; nor through the soul, because the soul is not propagated by traducianism, since it is a spiritual, indivisible substance, nor is it created by God as vicious, since God is not the author of sin. Therefore it does not pass through nature at all. Reply: (1) The minor premise is denied, because a soul created by God, though not vicious, can contract a vice from the body, even though it is a brute body into which it is infused. For it is not absurd to say that a vicious bodily temperament, prone to evils, is an unfit instrument for the soul's good actions, and that it corrupts a soul not yet confirmed in uprightness, so that it falls from its integrity as soon as it is infused into the body. (2) The inference is denied, because the enumeration in the major premise is not sufficient. For it passes neither through the body nor through the soul alone, but through the whole unclean generation of the man, on account of the fault of the first parents; on account of which fault God, by a just judgment, when he creates souls, at the same time deprives them of original uprightness and the gifts which he had bestowed on the parents on this condition: that they should pass these on to their posterity, or lose them, if the parents kept or lost them. Nor does God become unjust or the cause of sin by doing this. For this privation, inflicted by God on account of the parents' fault, is not sin with respect to God who inflicts it, but a most just punishment; although with respect to the parents, who draw it upon themselves and their offspring, it is sin. If therefore the major premise is taken in full: "Original sin passes to posterity, either through the body, or through the soul, or through the whole unclean generation of the man, on account of the parents' fault and the merit of the privation, by the just judgment of God," the flaw in the argument is obvious. For just as original sin arose in the parents through fault, so through the same fault it passes to posterity. This is not a narrow crack, over which the Schoolmen dispute so anxiously, namely traducianism and the contamination of the soul through the body, but a wide gate through which original sin rushed into our nature, as Paul testifies: "By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners."

units.la: Inst. 1. Priuatio originalis justitiæ est peccatum. Deus infligit priuationem hanc, creans in nobis animam non ornatam illis donis, quæ ei contulisset, si Adam non peccasset: Ergo Deus est author peccati. Resp. Est fallacia accidentis in maiore. Priuatio peccatum est, respectu Adam & nostri, quatenus illius & nostra culpa attrahitur, & cupidè recipitur. Creaturam enim carere rectitudine & conformitate cum Deo, pugnat cum Lege, & est peccatum. Respectu verò Dei est inobedientiæ Adami & nostræ justissima pœna cum natura & Lege Dei congruens.
units.tr: Objection 1. The privation of original justice is sin. God inflicts this privation, creating in us a soul not adorned with those gifts which he would have bestowed on it had Adam not sinned. Therefore God is the author of sin. Reply: This is a fallacy of accident in the major premise. The privation is sin with respect to Adam and to us, insofar as it is drawn upon us by his fault and ours, and is eagerly received. For for a creature to lack uprightness and conformity with God is contrary to the law, and is sin. But with respect to God, it is the most just punishment of the disobedience of Adam and of ours, agreeing with the nature and law of God.

units.la: Inst.2. At non debuit Deus culpam Adami tali pœna punire, ex qua sciebat secuturum esse totius naturæ humanæ interitum. Resp. Fiat justitia, & pereat mundus. Debuit Deus contumaciam hominis hoc modo vlcisci, propter suam justitiam: quia summi boni offensio merebatur summam pœnam, hoc est creaturæ æternam destructionem: & propter suam veritatem : quia dixerat : Morte morieris. Misericordiæ verò est, quod Deus ex communi exitio aliquos eripit & seruat per Christum, videlicet electos.
units.tr: Objection 2. But God ought not to have punished Adam's guilt with such a penalty, since he knew that the destruction of the whole human nature would follow from it. Answer: Let justice be done, though the world perish. God had to avenge man's obstinacy in this way, because of his justice: an offence against the highest good deserved the highest punishment, that is, the eternal destruction of the creature. And he had to do so because of his truth, since he had said, "You shall surely die." It is an act of mercy that God rescues and preserves some from the common ruin through Christ, namely the elect.

units.la: Obiect.2. Appetitiones obiectorum sunt naturales: Ergo non sunt peccata. Resp. Appetitiones obiectorum ordinatæ, seu quæ Deus illis ordinauit, non sunt peccata. Inordinatæ verò, & quæ sunt contra Legem, sunt peccata. Appetere quidem per se non est peccatum: appetitus enim per se bonus est, quia naturalis. Appetere verò contra Legem, est peccatum.
units.tr: Objection 2. The appetites for objects are natural; therefore they are not sins. Answer: Appetites for objects that are ordered, or that God has ordered, are not sins. But those that are disordered and contrary to the Law are sins. To desire something in itself is not a sin, for the appetite in itself is good because it is natural. But to desire contrary to the Law is a sin.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Peccatum originis tollitur in sanctis: Ergo sancti non possunt id propagare in sobolem. Resp.1.
