Maior omissa est falsa, quod parentes non possint propagare per naturam, quod in eis tollitur per gratiam. 2. Ad minorem : Peccatum originis tollitur in sanctis, quoad reatum, qui eis remittitur per Christum; manet verò, quoad formale, vitium pugnans cum Lege. Etsi enim regenerantur Spiritu sancto, quibus remittitur peccatum: tamen renouatio non perficitur in hac vita. Propagant igitur naturam adhuc vitiosam in posteros, qualem ipsi habent.
units.tr: Objection 3. Original sin is taken away in the saints; therefore the saints cannot propagate it to their offspring. Answer: 1. The major premise, which was left unstated, is false: parents cannot propagate by nature what is taken away in them by grace. 2. As to the minor: original sin is taken away in the saints as to its guilt, which is forgiven them through Christ; but as to its formal nature, the vice that conflicts with the Law remains. For although those who have their sins forgiven are regenerated by the Holy Spirit, the renewal is not completed in this life. They therefore propagate to their posterity a nature that is still vicious, such as they themselves have.

units.la: Inst. Quod non habent parentes, id non possunt propagare in posteros. Reatus tollitur in parentibus renatis: Ergo saltem reatus non propagatur. Resp. Maior distinguenda est. Parentes in sobolem non transmittunt id, quod non habent naturâ. A reatu autem non natura, sed gratia, sed beneficio Christi immunes sunt. Noa igitur justitiam, sed damnationem, cui naturâ sunt obnoxij, parentes in posteros naturâ propagant. Causa autem, cur reatum & non justitiam propagent, haec est, quia non secundum gratiam, sed secundum naturam nascuntur ex illis posteri: neque propagationi naturali, sed liberrimae electioni gratia & justificatio alligata est. Exemplo sunt Jacob & Esau, &c. Hoc Augustinus duplici similitudine declarauit. Vna est de granis tritici, quae cum a folliculis, paleis, aristis & spicis, per trituration em purgata seminentur, tamen cum illis omnibus renascuntur. Id fit, quia purgatio granis non accidit naturâ, sed industriâ humanâ. Altera est de patre circumciso, qui cum praeputium non habeat, tamen filium procreat cum praeputio. Id etiam fit, quia circumcisio in patre non fuit a natura, sed ex foedere.
units.tr: Objection. What parents do not have, they cannot propagate to their posterity. Guilt is taken away in regenerate parents; therefore at least guilt is not propagated. Answer: The major premise must be distinguished. Parents do not transmit to their offspring what they do not have by nature. But they are free from guilt not by nature but by grace, by the benefit of Christ. Parents therefore propagate by nature not righteousness but damnation, to which they are liable by nature. The reason why they propagate guilt and not righteousness is this: children are born from them not according to grace but according to nature, and grace and justification are bound not to natural propagation but to the most free election. Jacob and Esau are examples, etc. Augustine explained this by a twofold comparison. One is of grains of wheat, which, though cleansed of husks, chaff, awns and ears by threshing, when sown are still reborn with all those things. This happens because the cleansing of the grain did not come about by nature but by human effort. The other is of a circumcised father, who, though he has no foreskin, nevertheless begets a son with a foreskin. This too happens because the circumcision in the father was not from nature but from the covenant.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Si radix sancta, etiam rami sancti: Ergo liberi sanctorum nascuntur sancti, absque peccato originis. Resp. Est fallacia homonymiae. Sanctitas enim radicis & ramorum Apostolo non significat integritatem naturae, vel immunitatem a peccatorum jus foederis Dei: quod omnes posteri Abrahae jus foederis obtinerent, quodque Deus propter foedus cum Abrahamo initum, semper aliquos ex eius posteris converteret, & interna sanctitate donare vellet: ideoque de Judaeorum conversione desperandum non esset.
units.tr: Objection 4. "If the root is holy, so are the branches" (Rom. 11). Therefore the children of saints are born holy, without original sin. Answer: This is a fallacy of equivocation. For the holiness of the root and the branches does not mean, in the Apostle, the integrity of nature or immunity from sins, but the right of God's covenant: that all the posterity of Abraham obtained the right of the covenant, and that God, because of the covenant made with Abraham, would always convert some of his posterity and wished to bestow on them inward holiness; and therefore the conversion of the Jews was not to be despaired of.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Liberi vestri sancti sunt: Ergo, &c. Resp. Est eadem fallacia. Sunt sancti, non quod careant peccato originis: sed quod unus tantum altero parente Christiano nascantur, tamen sint cives Ecclesiae, & Christiani censendi, ac baptizandi: quin etiam pro electis habendi, donec adulti incredulitate vel impietate diversum de se testentur.
units.tr: Objection 5. "Your children are holy" (1 Cor. 7). Therefore, etc. Answer: It is the same fallacy. They are holy not because they are free from original sin, but because, although only one parent is Christian, they are citizens of the Church and are to be counted and baptized as Christians; indeed they are also to be regarded as elect, until, grown up, they show by their unbelief or impiety that they are otherwise.

units.la: Obiect. 6. In quos peccata omnium maiorum transeunt, miseriores erunt illis, in quos tantum aliquorum peccata propagantur. At si peccatum in posteros transit, in postremos homines omnia maiorum, in priores eorum tantum, qui praecesserunt, peccata deriuantur. Ergo posteriores erunt miseriores. Hoc vero absurdum videtur, & cum justitia Dei pugnans. Resp. Non foret absurdum, etiamsi Deus posteriores magis desereret ac puniret. Nam quanto plura peccata a genere humano cumulantur: tanto magis ira Dei accenditur, & exasperatur poena, juxta illud: Nondum completae sunt iniquitates Amorrhaeorum, &c. Ut veniat super vos omnis sanguis justus, &c. Sed & minor negatur. Etsi enim Deus propter justitiam suam peccatum originis, hoc est, vitium naturae & reatum in omnes posteros transfire sinit: tamen simul ex misericordia metas figit peccato, vt non semper maiorum peccata actualia imitentur & luant posteri, nec semper malorum parentum mali aut deteriores ac miseriores liberi existant.
units.tr: Objection 6. Those on whom the sins of all their forefathers pass will be more wretched than those on whom only the sins of some pass. But if sin passes to posterity, the sins of all forefathers are derived to the last of men, and only those of the earlier ones to the earlier men who went before. Therefore the later ones will be more wretched. This, however, seems absurd and in conflict with the justice of God. Answer: It would not be absurd even if God abandoned and punished the later ones more. For the more sins are heaped up by the human race, the more the wrath of God is kindled and the punishment made severe, according to the words: "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full," and "That upon you may come all the righteous blood," etc. But the minor premise is also denied. For although God, because of his justice, allows original sin, that is, the corruption of nature and guilt, to pass to all posterity, yet at the same time out of mercy he sets limits to sin, so that the posterity do not always imitate and expiate the actual sins of their forefathers, nor do the children of wicked parents always become wicked or more wretched.

units.la: Obiect.7. Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris: Ergo injustum est, posteros luere peccatum Adami. Resp. ad locum. Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris: seu, non luet propter patrem: nempe si iniquitatem patris non approbet, nec imitetur, sed damnet ac vitet. Nos vero Adami culpam juste luimus. 1. Quia culpa sic est Adami, vt etiam sit nostra. Omnes enim in Adamo peccante peccauimus: quia omnes in lumbis Adami fuimus. 2. Quia culpam Adami omnes natura trahimus, probamus, imitamur. Quis dabit mundum ex immundo? 3. Cum tota Adami natura sit rea, nos vero ex massa eius propagati simus, non possumus non etiam ipsi esse rei. Omnes enim sumus natura filij irae. 4. Adam dona Dei acceperat ea lege, vt nobis ea communicaret, si retineret: vel perderet, si amitteret. Quia igitur amisit, non sibi tantum, sed & posteris omnibus amisit.
units.tr: Objection 7. "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (Ezek. 18). Therefore it is unjust that posterity should pay for the sin of Adam. Answer to the passage: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father; that is, he shall not suffer on account of the father, namely if he does not approve nor imitate the father's iniquity, but condemns and avoids it. But we justly bear Adam's guilt. 1. Because the guilt is Adam's in such a way that it is also ours. For all sinned in Adam when he sinned, since we were all in the loins of Adam. 2. Because we all draw, prove and imitate Adam's guilt by nature. "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" (Job 14). 3. Since the whole nature of Adam is guilty, and we have been propagated from his mass, we cannot but be guilty ourselves too: "For we are by nature children of wrath" (Eph. 2). 4. Adam had received God's gifts on this condition, that he would communicate them to us if he kept them, or lose them for us if he lost them. Because therefore he lost them, he lost them not only for himself but for all his posterity.

units.la: Obiect. 8. Omne peccatum voluntate committitur. Infantes carent voluntate. Ergo peccatum non commiserunt vel committunt. Resp. 1. Datur totum de peccato actuali: non de originali, quod est vitium non voluntatis, sed naturae. 2. Negatur minor: quia infantes non carent facultate volendi: licet vero peccatum non velint actu, dici tamen potest, quod velint inclinatione, quia scriptum est: Cor hominis prauum, & tantum ad malum a iuuentute, Genes. 8, 21.
units.tr: Objection 8. Every sin is committed by the will. Infants lack will. Therefore they have not committed sin, nor do they commit it. Answer: 1. The statement holds of actual sin, not of original sin, which is a vice not of the will but of nature. 2. The minor is denied: for infants do not lack the faculty of willing; and although they do not will sin actually, it can nevertheless be said that they will it by inclination, because it is written: "The heart of man is evil and inclined to evil from his youth" (Gen. 8:21).

units.la: Inst. ad primam responsionem: Vitia naturae veniam potius, quam reprehensionem & poenam merentur: Aristotele teste in Ethicis: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ φύσεως ἀρχὰς ἔχει... Peccatum originis est vitium naturae: Ergo non meretur poenam. Resp. Maior est vera de vitiis naturae, at non negligentia nostra, vel malitia accersitis: vt si quis a natura, vel ex morbo, vel ex plaga caecus factus sit, non vituperio, sed commiseratione dignus est. Vitia vero malitiose attracta, quale est vitium originale, omnes jure reprehendunt, Aristotele ibidem testante, cum addit: τὰ δὲ τυφλῷ ἐξ εἰνοφλυξίας ἢ ἄλλης ἀνάλογίας ... Hactenus de peccato originis.
units.tr: Objection, against the first answer: Vices of nature deserve pardon rather than reproof and punishment, as Aristotle testifies in the Ethics: "For some things have their origin in nature [τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ φύσεως ἀρχὰς ἔχει...]." Original sin is a vice of nature; therefore it does not deserve punishment. Answer: The major premise is true of vices of nature, but not of those brought on by our negligence or malice: as when someone has been made blind by nature, or by disease, or by a wound, he deserves pity rather than blame. But vices that have been maliciously drawn in, such as original vice, all rightly reprove, as Aristotle testifies in the same place when he adds: "But blindness that comes from debauchery or some other such cause [τὰ δὲ τυφλῷ ἐξ εἰνοφλυξίας ἢ ἄλλης ἀνάλογίας ...]." So far concerning original sin.

units.la: De peccato actuali: & de reliquis peccati distinctionibus, causis & effectibus.
units.tr: On actual sin, and the other distinctions, causes and effects of sin.

units.la: Peccatum actuale est omnis actio interna & externa, pugnans cum Lege Dei, tam in mente, voluntate, & corde, quam in externis actionibus: & omissio eorum, quae Lex praecipit: vt cogitare, gitare, velle, prosequi, facere mala; ignorare, nolle, fugere; omittere bona. Huc pertinet diuisio in facti & omissionis peccata.
units.tr: Actual sin is every action, internal and external, that conflicts with the law of God, whether in the mind, the will and the heart or in outward deeds; and it is also the omission of what the law commands. Thus it is to think, plan, will, pursue or do evil, and to fail to know, to be unwilling, to flee, or to leave undone good things. To this belongs the division into sins of commission and omission.

units.la: Secunda distinctio. Peccatum aliud est regnans, aliud non regnans.
units.tr: Second distinction. One sin is reigning, another is not reigning.

units.la: Peccatum regnans est, cui peccans non repugnat per gratiam Spiritus sancti, ideoq; fit obnoxius æternæ morti, nisi pœnitentiam agat, & veniam per Christum consequatur. Seu, est omne peccatum, quod non deploratur, & cui non resistitur gratiâ Spiritus sancti, & propter quod non tantum ex ordine justitiæ Dei, sed ex re ipsa æternarum pœnarum reus est, qui illud habet. De hoc dicitur: Ne regnet igitur peccatum in mortali corpore vestro. Item: Qui facit peccatum, id est, qui data opera, & cum delectatione peccat, ex diabolo est: vbi de peccato regnante loquitur Johannes. Vocatur regnans, 1. quia ei indulgetur & seruitur ab homine. 2. Quia imperium tenet in hominem, & eum æternæ damnationis reum facit. Talia sunt omnia peccata in non renatis: quædam etiam in renatis; vt errores in fundamento fidei, & lapsus contra conscientiam, cum quibus fiducia remissionis peccatorum, & consolatio vera non consistit, donec resipiscant. Quod enim etiam renati possint ruere in peccatum regnans, satis ostendunt tristissimi lapsus sanctissimorum hominum, vt Aaronis, Dauidis. Quæ contra afferri solent, videantur volum. 1. D. Vrsini. pag. 207.
units.tr: A reigning sin is one which the sinner does not resist through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and for which he therefore is liable to eternal death, unless he repents and obtains pardon through Christ. Or: it is every sin that is not lamented and is not resisted by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and on account of which the one who holds it is guilty of eternal punishments, not only by the order of God's justice but in very fact. Of this it is said: Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body (Rom. 6:12). Likewise: He who commits sin, that is, he who sins deliberately and with delight, is of the devil (1 John 3:8), where John speaks of reigning sin. It is called reigning (1) because it is indulged and served by a man, and (2) because it holds dominion over the man and makes him liable to eternal damnation. Such are all sins in the unregenerate; some also in the regenerate, such as errors against the foundation of faith and lapses against conscience, with which confidence in the forgiveness of sins and true consolation do not stand, until they repent. That even the regenerate can fall into reigning sin, the most grievous falls of the holiest men clearly show, such as those of Aaron and David. For the objections usually raised against this, see vol. 1 of Dr. Ursinus, p. 207.

units.la: Non regnans peccatum est, cui peccans repugnat per gratiam Spiritus sancti, ideoque non est obnoxius æternæ morti, quia pœnitentiam agit, & veniam consequitur per Christum. Talia peccata sunt omnes defectus, inclinationes & cupiditates prauæ, & multa peccata ignorantiæ, omissionis & infirmitatis, reliqua in sanctis, quamdiu sunt in hac vita: quæ tamen agnoscunt, deplorant & oderunt, & repugnant eis, & petunt assiduè sibi ea remitti propter Christum Mediatorem, dicentes: Dimitte nobis debita nostra: ideoque in his fidem & consolationem retinent: Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus. Non amplius id ego perpetro, sed peccatum, quod in me habitat. Nulla condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, qui secundum Spiritum incedunt. Erata quis intelligit? Ab occultis meis munda me.
units.tr: A non-reigning sin is one which the sinner resists through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and therefore he is not liable to eternal death, because he repents and obtains pardon through Christ. Such sins are all defects, evil inclinations and desires, many sins of ignorance, omission and weakness, and the remnants of sin in the saints as long as they are in this life. Yet these they acknowledge, lament and hate, they resist them, and they continually ask that these be forgiven them for the sake of Christ the Mediator, saying: Forgive us our debts (Matt. 6:12). Therefore in these they retain faith and consolation: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). It is no longer I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me (Rom. 7:17). There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk according to the Spirit (Rom. 8:1). Who understands his errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults (Ps. 19:12).

units.la: [Ad hanc distinctionem referri potest illa vulgaris, in peccatum mortale & veniale. Etsi enim omne peccatum natura sua est mortale, hoc est, æterna morte dignum: tamen recte sic vocari potest peccatum regnans, in quo qui persequerat, finaliter perit. Fit autem veniale, hoc est, veniam consequitur, cum fit non veniale. non regnans in renatis, qui ei resistunt per gratiam Christi: non quod per se mereatur veniam, aut sit indignum poenâ, sed quia credentibus propter Christi satisfactionem ex gratia condonatur, nec imputatur ad condemnationem, sicut dicitur: Nulla condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, &c. Hoc sensu distinctio mortalis & venialis peccati tolerari potest: non autem eo, quo a Pontificiis vsurpatur: quasi mortale sit, quod sua grauitate mortem æternam mereatur; veniale, quod propter leuitatem suam non æterna morte, sed tantum temporali poena dignum sit coram Deo: quod est falsum: quia de quouis peccato dicitur: Stipendium peccati mors est. &: Qui in vno deliquit, est omnium reus. Qui soluerit vnum ex minimis istis mandatis, &c. minimus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Videtur autem distinctio nata ex disciplina veteris Ecclesiæ: apud quam venalia peccata erant, pro quibus non exigeretur satisfactio ecclesiastica. Quod verò tolerabile erat in foro Ecclesiæ, Sophistæ postea malè traxerunt ad forum Dei, & conscientiæ. Itaq; distinctio hæc à Theologis Orthodoxis hodie rectius improbatur, & omittitur, quàm retinetur: tum, quia est obscura & valde ambigua: tum, quia repugnat Scripturæ, quæ quoduis peccatum morte dignum pronunciat coram Deo: tum denique, ne si cum Sophistis loquamur, cum iisdem etiam sentire videamur.]
units.tr: [This distinction may be connected with the common one into mortal and venial sin. For although every sin is by its nature mortal, that is, worthy of eternal death, nevertheless a sin may rightly be called reigning when the one who persists in it perishes in the end. It becomes venial, that is, it obtains pardon, when it is non-reigning in the regenerate, who resist it through the grace of Christ; not because it deserves pardon in itself or is not worthy of punishment, but because it is freely forgiven to believers on account of Christ's satisfaction and is not imputed for condemnation, as it is said: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, etc. In this sense the distinction between mortal and venial sin can be tolerated, but not in the sense in which it is used by the Papists: as if that is mortal which by its gravity merits eternal death, and venial that which, because of its lightness, deserves before God not eternal death but only temporal punishment. This is false, because of every sin it is said: The wages of sin is death (Rom. 6:23); and: Whoever has offended in one point is guilty of all (James 2:10); and: Whoever breaks one of these least commandments, etc., shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:19). Now the distinction seems to have arisen from the discipline of the early Church, in which there were venial sins, for which no ecclesiastical satisfaction was required. But what was tolerable in the forum of the Church, the Schoolmen later wrongly transferred to the forum of God and of conscience. Therefore this distinction is today rightly rejected and omitted by orthodox theologians rather than retained, (1) because it is obscure and very ambiguous; (2) because it contradicts Scripture, which pronounces every sin worthy of death before God; and finally (3) lest, if we speak with the Schoolmen, we seem also to agree with them in their opinions.]

units.la: Tertia distinctio. Peccatum aliud est contra conscientiam, aliud non contra conscientiam.
units.tr: Third distinction: some sin is against conscience, and some sin is not against conscience.

units.la: Contra conscientiam est, cùm sciens Dei voluntatem, ex proposito contra eam facit: Seu est, quod à scientibus & volentibus committitur. vt Dauid sciens & volens committit adulterium & cædem contra Legem. Non contra scientiam est, quod vel non scientes, vel non volentes committimus: seu, quod quidem peccatum esse agnoscitur, & deploratur à peccante, sed tamen vitari perfectè non potest in hac vita: vt peccatum originis, & multa peccata omissionis, ignorantiæ, infirmitatis. Multa enim bona omittimus, & mala facimus, subitò victi infirmitatibus: vt Petrus ex infirmitate in periculo superatur, & abnegat Christum, sciens quidem, sed non volens: ideo flet amare: nec penitus amittit fidem, juxta promissionem: Oraui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Non erat peccatum regnans, multò minus in Spiritum sanctum: quia amabat Christum non minus, cùm negatet, quàm cùm fleret: licet ob metum periculi affectum illum non posset exercere. Tale peccatum Paulus in se agnoscit & deflet: Non facio bonum quod volo, sed malum, quod nolo, hoc ago &c. Ignorantiæ etiam peccatum fuit eius blasphemia & persecutio Ecclesiæ, de qua dicit: Ignorans feci: propterea Deus mei misertus est.
units.tr: A sin against conscience is what someone commits knowingly and deliberately against the known will of God. That is, it is what is committed by those who know and who are willing, as David knowingly and willingly committed adultery and murder against the Law. Not against conscience is what we commit without knowing or without willing it; that is, what is recognised as sin and lamented by the sinner, but still cannot be avoided perfectly in this life, such as original sin and many sins of omission, ignorance and weakness. For we leave undone many good things and do evil things, suddenly overcome by our infirmities. Thus Peter, through weakness in a time of danger, was overcome and denied Christ; he knew what he did but did not will it, and so he wept bitterly. Yet he did not utterly lose his faith, according to the promise: I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. It was not a reigning sin, much less a sin against the Holy Spirit, because he loved Christ no less when he denied him than when he wept, although out of fear of danger he could not exercise that affection. Paul acknowledges and laments such a sin in himself: I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, that I do, and so on. His blasphemy and persecution of the Church was also a sin of ignorance, of which he says: I did it ignorantly, therefore God had mercy on me.

units.la: Quarta distinctio. Peccatum aliud est irremissibile, seu in Spiritum sanctum, seu ad mortem: aliud remissibile, seu non in Spiritum sanctum, seu non ad mortem. Haec sumta est ex Matth. 12,31. Marci 3, 29. 1 Joh.5,16.
units.tr: Fourth distinction. Some sin is unforgivable, either against the Holy Spirit or unto death; another is forgivable, either not against the Holy Spirit or not unto death. This is taken from Matt. 12:31, Mark 3:29 and 1 John 5:16.

units.la: Peccatum irremissibile, seu in Spiritum sanctum, & ad mortem, est abnegatio & oppugnatio agnitae veritatis de Deo eiusque voluntate & operibus, de qua testimonio Spiritus sancti mentes certò edoctae & convictae sunt, non ex metu aut infirmitate, sed destinato consilio, & odio veritatis, animoque hostili adversus eam suscepta: quod peccatum qui committunt, puniuntur à Deo caecitate finali, ut nunquam resipiscant in hac vita, proinde nec remissionem consequantur. Vocatur igitur irremissibile, non quod gravitate sua meriti Christi magnitudinem superet; sed quia à Deo caecitate finali punitur, qui id perpetrat, nec datur ei poenitere. Quia enim singulare genus peccati est, etiam singularis poena infligitur, finalis caecitas & impoenitentia. Sine poenitentia autem nulla datur remissio. De hoc peccato dicitur: Quisquis locutus fuerit verbum adversus Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur, neque in hoc seculo, neque in futuro. Et: Quicunque blasphemarit Spiritum sanctum, non habet remissionem in aeternum, sed tenetur aeterno judicio.
units.tr: The unforgivable sin, that is, against the Holy Spirit and unto death, is the denial and opposition of a truth acknowledged concerning God, his will and his works, a truth of which minds have been certainly taught and convinced by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. It is undertaken not from fear or weakness, but from a settled purpose, hatred of the truth and a hostile mind against it. Those who commit this sin are punished by God with final blindness, so that they never repent in this life and therefore never obtain forgiveness. It is called unforgivable not because it exceeds the merit of Christ in its gravity, but because the one who commits it is punished by God with final blindness, and it is not given to him to repent. For since it is a singular kind of sin, a singular punishment is also inflicted: final blindness and impenitence. Yet without repentance there is no forgiveness. Of this sin it is said: Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come. And: Whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is liable to eternal judgment.

units.la: In Spiritum sanctum vocatur hoc peccatum, non quod Spiritus sanctus offendi à quoquam possit, quin simul in Patrem & Filium peccetur, sed κατ' ἐξοχὴν, quia singulari modo admittitur contra Spiritum sanctum, hoc est, contra proprium atque immediatum Spiritus sancti officium, seu operationem, quae est mentium illuminatio.
units.tr: This sin is called against the Holy Spirit not because the Holy Spirit can be offended by anyone without sinning at the same time against the Father and the Son, but by way of eminence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], because it is committed against the Holy Spirit in a singular way, that is, against the proper and immediate office or operation of the Holy Spirit, which is the illumination of minds.

units.la: Ad mortem vocatur à Johanne, non quod hoc solum sit mortale, seu mortem mereatur, sed κατ' ἐξοχὴν, quod mereatur maximè, & in hoc peccato omnes moriantur, qui illud admittunt, quia nulli agunt poenitentiam. Ideo Johannes non vult pro eo orati: quia nimirum remissio eius frustra à Deo petitur. De hoc peccato etiam alibi loquitur scriptura; Hebr. 6, 4.5.6.7.8. &c.10. v.26.27.28.29. & Tit. 3. v.10.11.
units.tr: It is called unto death by John not because this is the only mortal sin, or the only one that deserves death, but by way of eminence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], because it deserves death most of all, and all who commit it die in it, since they do not repent. Therefore John does not want prayer to be offered for it, because its forgiveness is sought from God in vain. Scripture also speaks of this sin elsewhere: Heb. 6:4–8, 10:26–29, and Titus 3:10–11.

units.la: Regulae de peccato in Spiritum sanctum tenenda.
units.tr: Rules to be held concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 1. Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum non in quosvis reprobos, sed in eos tantum cadit, qui a Spiritu sancto illuminati, & de veritate in conscientiis convicti sunt: ut Saul, Judas, Pharisaei, &c.
units.tr: 1. The sin against the Holy Spirit does not fall upon just any reprobate, but only upon those who have been enlightened by the Holy Spirit and convinced in their consciences of the truth, such as Saul, Judas, the Pharisees, and so on.

units.la: 2. Omne peccatum in Spiritum sanctum est peccatum regnans, & contra conscientiam: sed non contra. Fieri enim potest, ut quis ignorans, vel etiam sciens & volens, errores alit-
units.tr: 2. Every sin against the Holy Spirit is a reigning sin and against conscience, but not every sin against conscience is against the Holy Spirit. For it can happen that someone, through ignorance, or even knowingly and willingly, nourishes and defends certain errors

units.la: D aliquos tueatur, aut mandatum aliquod violet, ex imbecillitate, aut cruciatu, aut metu periculi, non tamen ex consilio & odio agnitam veritatem oppugnet, aut à religione & pietate totaliter deficiat, & in Epicureo contemptu perseueret, sed ad pœnitentiam redeat in hac vita. Differunt ergo, vt genus & species.
units.tr: or violates some commandment, from weakness, from anguish, or from fear of danger, yet does not from deliberate counsel and hatred assail the truth acknowledged, nor wholly fall away from religion and piety and persist in Epicurean contempt, but returns to repentance in this life. They differ, therefore, as genus and species.

units.la: 3. Pecatum in Spiritum sanctum non cadit in electos, & verè conuersos: quia electi perire non possunt, sed certò à Deo seruantur. Oues meas nemo rapiet ex manu mea. Sic 2 Tim. 2, 19. 1 Pet. 1, 5. 1 Ioh. 5, 16. Qui igitur in Spiritum sanctum peccant, nunquam fuerunt verè conuersi & electi. Ex nobis egressi sunt, quia ex nobis non erant.
units.tr: 3. The sin against the Holy Spirit does not fall upon the elect and truly converted, because the elect cannot perish but are certainly kept by God. No one will snatch my sheep out of my hand. So also 2 Tim. 2:19, 1 Pet. 1:5, 1 John 5:16. Therefore those who sin against the Holy Spirit were never truly converted and elect. They went out from us, because they were not of us.

units.la: 4. De hoc peccato non temerè pronunciandum est: quia nos non sumus καρδίας ὑπερ. Plura de hoc peccato disputata legantur vol 1. Vrsini pag. 213. &c.
units.tr: 4. One should not rashly pronounce about this sin, since we are not searchers of hearts [καρδιογνῶσται]. More on this sin disputed may be read in the first volume of Ursinus, p. 213 and following.

units.la: Peccatum remissibile, seu non in Spiritum sanctum, est quoduis aliud peccatum, cuius aliqui homines pœnitentiam agunt, & veniam consequuntur.
units.tr: The forgivable sin, that is, not against the Holy Spirit, is any other sin for which some men do repent and obtain pardon.

units.la: Quarta distinctio. Peccatū aliud est per se, aliud per accidens. Per se & suo genere peccata sunt omnia, quæ Lege Dei prohibentur, vt omnes inclinationes, motus & actiones contra Legem Dei: non tamen quatenus sunt motus, nec respectu Dei omnia mouentis (motus enim, quatenus motus, per se boni, & à Deo sunt, in quo viuimus, mouemur & sumus) sed respectu nostri, quatenus à nobis contra Legem Dei fiunt. Sic enim per se & suo genere sunt peccata.
units.tr: Fourth distinction. Some sin is through itself, and some is through accident. Sins through themselves and by their own kind are all those things forbidden by the Law of God: all inclinations, motions and actions against the Law of God. Not, however, insofar as they are motions, nor with respect to God, who moves all things (for motions, insofar as they are motions, are good in themselves and come from God, in whom we live, move and have our being), but with respect to us, insofar as they are done by us against the Law of God. In this way they are sins through themselves and by their own kind.

units.la: Per accidens peccata sunt actiones non renatorum & hypocritarum, quæ præceptæ quidem sunt à Deo, sed tamen Deo displicent, quia fiunt sine fide & conuersione ad Deum: actiones item adiaphoræ, quæ fiunt cum scandalo. Quicquid enim non fit ex fide, peccatum est. Et: Sine fide impossibile est Deo placere. Omnes ergo virtutes non renatorum, vt castitas Scipionis, fortitudo Julij, fides Reguli, iustitia Aristidis, &c. etsi per se sunt actiones bonæ, & à Deo præceptæ: tamen per accidens sunt peccata, ac Deo displicent: tum quia personæ, à quibus fiunt, non placent Deo, tum quia non eo modo & fine fiunt, quo Deus vult fieri, hoc est, non ex fide, neque ad gloriam Dei; quæ conditiones ad bonum opus requiruntur, & sine quibus etiam optimæ actiones peccata fiunt: vt, peccatum est, cùm impius vel hypocrita precatur, dat eleemosynam, offert sacrificia, &c. quia non ex fide, & non ad gloriam D ei facit. Hypocritæ dant eleemosynam in synagogis & plateis, vt gloriam consequantur ab hominibus. Amen dico vobis, receperunt ferunt mercedem suam. Qui macTat bouem, est ac si hominem occi- dat ; &c.
units.tr: Sins through accident are the actions of the unregenerate and hypocrites, which indeed are commanded by God, but still displease God because they are done without faith and conversion to God; likewise indifferent actions which are done with scandal. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. And: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Therefore all the virtues of the unregenerate, such as the chastity of Scipio, the courage of Julius, the faithfulness of Regulus, the justice of Aristides, and so on, although in themselves they are good actions and commanded by God, are nevertheless sins through accident and displease God: partly because the persons by whom they are done do not please God, and partly because they are not done in the manner and for the end in which God wills them to be done, that is, not from faith and not for the glory of God. These conditions are required for a good work, and without them even the best actions become sins. For example, it is a sin when the ungodly or hypocrite prays, gives alms, offers sacrifices, and so on, because he does not act from faith and not for the glory of God. Hypocrites give alms in the synagogues and the streets, so that they may win glory from men. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward. He who slaughters an ox is as if he killed a man, and so on.

units.la: Ingens igitur est discrimen inter virtutes renatorum & non renatorum. Nam 1. renatorum bona opera fiunt prælucente fide, & placent Deo: non renatorum non item. 2. Renati operta sua faciunt ad gloriam Dei: non renati & hypocritæ ad gloriam suam. 3. Renatorum opera sunt coniuncta cum interna obedientia seu studio obtemperandi Deo. Non renati & hypocritæ tantum externam disciplinam præstant sine interna obedientia: ideo virtutes eorum tantum sunt larvæ & hypocrisis, non veræ virtutes. 4 Imperfectio operum in renatis tegitur satisfactione Christi, & peccata inhærentia eis non imputantur, nec obijcitur eis, quod dona Dei suis peccatis inquinent. Non renatorum virtutes per se bonæ, sunt & manent peccata per accidens, & multis aliis inquinantur. 5. Bona opera non-renatorum ornantur à Deo præmiis tantum temporalibus: idque non quod Deo pareant, sed vt Deus ipsos & alios ad honestatem & disciplinam externam generi humano necessariam inuitet. Piorum verò opera Deus acceptat per Christum, & ornat præmiis temporalibus & æternis, sicut dicitur: Pietas habet promissionem huius & futuræ vitæ. 6 Denique non renati præstando opera à Deo præcepta, consequuntur mitigationem pœnarum, ne cum aliis facinorosis in hac vita grauiora patiantur: Renati verò non tantum, vt leuiora patiantur, sed etiam vt prorsus liberentur.
units.tr: There is, therefore, a great difference between the virtues of the regenerate and those of the unregenerate. For first, the good works of the regenerate are done with faith shining before them, and they please God; the works of the unregenerate are not so. Second, the regenerate do their works for the glory of God; the unregenerate and hypocrites do theirs for their own glory. Third, the works of the regenerate are joined with inner obedience, or zeal to obey God. The unregenerate and hypocrites provide only outward discipline without inner obedience; therefore their virtues are only masks and hypocrisy, not true virtues. Fourth, the imperfection of works in the regenerate is covered by the satisfaction of Christ, and the sins that dwell in them are not imputed to them, nor is it held against them that they defile God's gifts with their sins. The virtues of the unregenerate, though good in themselves, remain sins through accident and are polluted by many other things. Fifth, the good works of the unregenerate are rewarded by God only with temporal rewards, and this not because they obey God, but so that God may invite them and others to the honesty and outward discipline necessary for the human race. But God accepts the works of the pious through Christ and crowns them with temporal and eternal rewards, as it is said: Godliness has the promise of this life and of the life to come. Sixth, finally, by performing the works commanded by God, the unregenerate obtain a lessening of punishments, so that in this life they do not suffer more severely than other criminals; the regenerate, however, obtain not only that they suffer lighter punishments, but that they are wholly set free.

units.la: Obiect. Peccata non sunt facienda. Opera non-renatorum ciuiliter bona sunt peccata. Ergo non sunt facienda. Resp. Est fallacia accidentis. Maior de peccatis per se, minor de peccatis per accidens vera est. Iam quæ per se peccata sunt, simpliciter omitti, quæ verò per accidens, non omitti, sed corrigi & præstari eo modo ac fine debent, quo Deus præcepit.
units.tr: Objection. Sins must not be committed. The works of the unregenerate are civilly good, yet they are sins. Therefore they must not be done. Answer. This is the fallacy of accident. The major premise is true of sins in themselves, and the minor is true of sins only by accident. Sins that are sins in themselves must simply be omitted. Those that are sins only by accident must not be omitted, but corrected, and performed in the manner and for the end that God has commanded.

units.la: Est autem disciplina externa necessaria etiam in non renatis. 1. Propter mandatum Dei. 2. Vt vitentur pœnæ, quæ disciplinæ violationem sequuntur. 3. Vt pax & societas humana conserueatur. 4. Denique ne perseuerantia in manifestis sceleribus adiuum ad conuersionem eis intercludat.
units.tr: External discipline is necessary even for the unregenerate. (1) On account of God's command. (2) So that the punishments that follow the violation of discipline may be avoided. (3) So that peace and human society may be preserved. (4) Finally, so that persistence in open wickedness does not cut off their access to conversion.

units.la: Sic & ingens discrimen est inter peccata renatorum & non renatorum. Nam vt supra, præcipuè distinctione secunda, dictum est, in omnibus renatis manent adhuc multæ reliquiæ peccati: vt 1. Peccatum originis. 2. Multa peccata actualia ignorantiæ, omissionis & infirmitatis: quæ tamen ipsi agnoscunt & deplorant, eisque repugnant, ideoque non amittunt bonam conscientiam, & remissionem peccatorum. 3. Nonnulli etiam aliquando ruunt in errores pugnantes cum fundamento, aut in peccata contra conscientiam, propter quæ amittunt bonam conscientiam, & dona Spiritus sancti, & damnantur, si in illis usque ad finem perseverarent: sed in illis non pereunt, quia in hac vita pœnitentiam agunt.
units.tr: There is likewise a great difference between the sins of the regenerate and those of the unregenerate. As was said above, especially in the second distinction, many remnants of sin remain in all the regenerate: (1) original sin; (2) many actual sins of ignorance, omission and weakness, which they nevertheless acknowledge and lament, and which they resist, and so they do not lose a good conscience or the forgiveness of sins; (3) some at times also fall into errors that conflict with the foundation, or into sins committed against conscience, on account of which they lose a good conscience and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and are condemned if they persevere in them to the end. Yet they do not perish in these, because in this life they practise repentance.

units.la: Interim triplex manet discrimen, quo renati peccantes ab impiis differunt. 1. In Deo est propositum æternum seruandi electos. 2. In renatis, cum peccant, certa est pœnitentia finalis. 3. In iisdem, cum labuntur, manet aliquod semen veræ fidei, & conuersionis reliquum: quod alias est maius & firmius, & sic reluctatur peccato, ut in errores contra fundamentum, aut in peccatum regnans non labantur, alias est minus & languidius, ac vincitur tentationibus ad tempus, sed tamen facit, ne in universum à Deo deficiant, qui semel verè fuerunt conuersi, ut in Davide, Petro, &c. Rom. 7, 16. Luc. 22, 32. 1 Ioh. 3, 9. 1 Pet. 1, 23. Iesa. 42, 3. Psal. 37, 24. Nihil horum est in non renatis peccantibus, sed omnia diuersa.
units.tr: Meanwhile there remains a threefold difference by which regenerate persons who sin differ from the ungodly. (1) In God there is an eternal purpose of saving the elect. (2) In the regenerate, when they sin, final repentance is certain. (3) In the same persons, when they fall, some seed of true faith and of conversion remains. In some it is greater and firmer, so that it resists sin in such a way that they do not fall into errors against the foundation or into a sin that reigns. In others it is smaller and feebler, and for a time they are overcome by temptations, yet it keeps them from wholly falling away from God, those who once were truly converted, as in David, Peter, etc. Rom. 7:16; Luke 22:32; 1 John 3:9; 1 Pet. 1:23; Isa. 42:3; Ps. 37:24. None of these things holds for the unregenerate who sin; everything in them is the opposite.

units.la: IV. Quæ sint peccati causæ.
units.tr: IV. What are the causes of sin?

units.la: Deus nullius peccati causa est. Probatur: 1. Testimoniis scripturæ: Omnia erant valde bona. Non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es, &c. 2. Deus summè & perfectè bonus est & sanctus. 3. Deus omne peccatum in lege sua prohibet. 4. Deus omne peccatum seuerissimè punit. 5. Deus imaginem suam in homine ipse non destruit.
units.tr: God is the cause of no sin. This is proved: (1) by the testimonies of Scripture: "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Gen. 1:31); "For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness" (Ps. 5:4). (2) God is supremely and perfectly good and holy. (3) God forbids every sin in his law. (4) God punishes every sin most severely. (5) God himself does not destroy his image in man.

units.la: Propria verò & per se causa efficiens peccati est, voluntas diabolorum & hominum, quà liberè à Deo defecerunt, & se imagine Dei spoliarunt. Invidiâ diaboli mors intrauit in mundum. Mors autem est pœna peccati. Vos ex patre diabolo estis, & cupiditates patris vestri vultis explere. Ille fuit homicida à principio, & in veritate non perstitit. Non est enim veritas in eo: quoties loquitur mendacium, de suo loquitur, quia mendax est, & mendacij pater. Qui committit peccatum, ex diabolo est, quoniam à principio diabolus peccat. Ad hoc apparuit Filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli. Per unum hominem peccatum intrauit in mundum.
units.tr: The proper and direct efficient cause of sin, however, is the will of devils and of men, by which they freely fell away from God and stripped themselves of the image of God. By the envy of the devil death entered the world (Wisdom 2:24). Death, moreover, is the punishment of sin. You are of your father the devil, and you want to fulfil the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, for there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and the father of lies. He who commits sin is of the devil, for the devil has sinned from the beginning. The Son of God appeared for this purpose, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Through one man sin entered into the world (Rom. 5:12).

units.la: Primi igitur peccati seu lapsus primorum parentum in paradiso, causa fuit diabolus, impellens hominem ad peccandum, & hominis voluntas liberè sese à Deo auertens, & diabolo obtemperans. Originalis peccati in Adamo & posteris causa efficiens fuit primus ille lapsus Adami. Per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi. Actualium peccatorum omnium peccatores constituti sunt multi. Peccatum in posteris causa ... est, originale peccatum. Peccatum quod in me habitat, perpetrat malum, &c. Cupiditas postquam conceconcepit, parit peccatum. per accidens sunt obiecta ad peccandum sollicitantia. Peccatum occasione sumpta genuit in me omnem cupiditatem per illud mandatum. Per se sunt diabolus & mali homines. Actualium peccatorum sequentium causæ sunt actualia peccata præcedentia: quia DEUM peccata peccatis punire, & peccata sequentia pœnas præcedentium esse, scriptura docet. Propterea tradidit eos Deus cupiditatibus cordium ipsorum, ad impuritatem, perpetrantes fœda, & ἀκαθαρσίαν, hoc est compensationem, quam oportuit, erroris sui in se recipientes. Propterea mittet illis Deus efficaciam deceptionis, ut credant mendacio, &c.
units.tr: The cause of the first sin, or fall, of our first parents in paradise was the devil, who impelled man to sin, and the human will, which freely turned itself away from God and obeyed the devil. The efficient cause of original sin in Adam and his posterity was that first fall of Adam. By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners (Rom. 5:19). Many were made sinners by all actual sins. In posterity the cause of sin is original sin. Sin that dwells in me works evil (Rom. 7:17), etc. Desire, once it has conceived, gives birth to sin (James 1:15). Objects that stir up sin are causes by accident. Sin, having seized the occasion, produced in me every kind of desire through that commandment (Rom. 7:8). The devil and wicked men are causes in themselves. The causes of subsequent actual sins are the preceding actual sins, since Scripture teaches that God punishes sins by sins, and that subsequent sins are the punishments of earlier ones. Therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, to commit shameful deeds, and to uncleanness [ἀκαθαρσία] (Rom. 1:24), that is, receiving in themselves the recompense that was due for their error. Therefore God will send them a working of deception, so that they believe a lie, etc. (2 Thess. 2:11).

units.la: V. Quæ sint effecta peccati.
units.tr: V. What the effects of sin are.

units.la: Effectus peccati sunt pœnæ temporales & æternæ: & quia Deus peccata peccatispunit, etiam sequentia peccata sunt præcedentium effectus. Rom. 1, 24. 2 Thess. 2, 11. Matth. 13, 12. Hoc ut magis intelligatur, speciatim est explicandum.
units.tr: The effects of sin are temporal and eternal punishments. And because God punishes sins by sins, the sins that follow are also effects of those that went before. Rom. 1, 24. 2 Thess. 2, 11. Matth. 13, 12. To understand this better, it must be explained in detail.

units.la: 1. Primi lapsus in paradiso effectus fuit peccatum originale, totius naturæ humanæ corruptio, seu imaginis divinæ destructio & reatus; ut supra dictum est.
units.tr: 1. The effect of the first fall in Paradise was original sin: the corruption of the whole of human nature, or the destruction of the divine image, and guilt, as was said above.

units.la: 2. Peccati originalis effectus sunt omnia peccata actualia. Rom. 7, 17, &c.
units.tr: 2. The effects of original sin are all actual sins. Rom. 7, 17, &c.

units.la: 3. Peccatorum actualium præcedentium effectus sunt peccata actualia sequentia, eorumque incrementum: cùm nempe homines justo Dei judicio ex uno peccato ruunt in aliud, ut docetur de gentibus, Rom. 1.
units.tr: 3. The effects of earlier actual sins are the actual sins that follow, and their increase; since, by the just judgment of God, men fall from one sin into another, as is taught of the Gentiles in Rom. 1.

units.la: 4. Peccatorum actualium effectus sæpe etiam sunt aliena peccata, ratione scandali & mali exempli, quo alij ab aliis deteriores redditi, ad peccandum alliciuntur, juxta illud: Colloquia prava corrumpunt mores bonos.
units.tr: 4. The effects of actual sins are often also the sins of others, by way of scandal and bad example, by which others, made worse by them, are enticed to sin, according to the saying: Evil company corrupts good morals.

units.la: 5. Peccatum perpetuò sequitur mala conscientia, & metus judicij divini. Rom. 2, 15. Esa. 57, 21.
units.tr: 5. Sin is always followed by a guilty conscience and the fear of divine judgment. Rom. 2, 15. Isa. 57, 21.

units.la: 6. Omnes calamitates huius vitæ, & mors ipsa corporalis, effectus peccati sunt: quia propter hoc generi humano à Deo infliguntur, juxta dictum: Morte morieris.
units.tr: 6. All the calamities of this life, and bodily death itself, are effects of sin, because they are inflicted by God on the human race for this reason, according to the word: You shall surely die.

units.la: 7. Mors æterna extremus & summus effectus est peccati in omnibus, qui ab eo Christi merito non liberantur: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus. Multi resurgent ad opprobria & abominationem sempiternam. Ite maledicti in ignem æternum.
units.tr: 7. Eternal death is the final and highest effect of sin in all who are not freed from it by the merit of Christ: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things. Many shall rise to shame and everlasting contempt. Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire.

units.la: Omnia igitur peccata, qualiacunque sint, suâ naturâ merentur mortem æternam, idque testantur hæc & alia scripturæ dicta: Maledictus omnis, &c. Qui offenderit in uno, factus est omnium reus. est reus omnium. Non exibis, donec persolueris extremum quadrantem.
units.tr: Therefore all sins, of whatever kind, by their nature deserve eternal death, and this these and other sayings of Scripture bear witness to: Cursed is everyone, &c. Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all. He is guilty of all. You shall not come out until you have paid the last farthing.

units.la: Et tamen peccata non sunt paria, sed gradibus distincta, etiam in judicio Dei, juxta dicta: Quodvis peccatum remittitur, sed blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum non remittetur. Qui me tibi tradidit, gravius peccatum habet.
units.tr: And yet sins are not equal, but differ in degrees, even in the judgment of God, according to the words: Every sin will be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. He who handed me over to you has the greater sin.

units.la: Ideo & poenarum infernalium erunt gradus, ut seruetur poenarum & peccatorum proportio: etsi duratione omnes poenae erunt aeternae. Seruus sciens voluntatem Domini, & non faciens, pluribus plagis caedetur. Tyro & Sidon tolerabilius erit in die judicii, quam Chorazin, &c.
units.tr: Therefore there will also be degrees of infernal punishments, so that there is a proportion between punishments and sins, although in duration all punishments will be eternal. The servant who knew his master's will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows. It will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for Chorazin, &c.

units.la: QVÆSTIO VIII.
units.tr: QUESTION VIII.

units.la: An vero adeo corrupti sumus, ut ad bene agendum prorsus non simus idonei, & ad omne vitium proclives.
units.tr: Are we indeed so corrupted that we are wholly unfit to do good, and inclined to every vice?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Certè a, nisi per Spiritum sanctum regeneremur b.a Genes.8, 21. & 5, 6. Joh.14, 4. & 15, 14.16.35. Joh.3, 6. Esa.53, 6. b Joh.3,3.5. 1 Cor.3,5.
units.tr: Certainly we are, unless we are regenerated by the Holy Spirit. a Gen. 8, 21. and 6, 5. John 14, 4. and 15, 14.16.35. John 3, 6. Isa. 53, 6. b John 3, 3.5. 1 Cor. 3, 5.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Cum tractatione de miseria hominis cohaeret quaestio de libero arbitrio, seu de viribus humanae voluntatis ad bene agendum, & ad obtemperandum Deo. Necesse enim est scire, quid homo ante lapsum potuerit, & quid post lapsum possit, ut effecta primi peccati recte agnoscentes, ad humilitatem ac desiderium gratiae & gubernationis divinae, nec non ad gratitudinem erga Deum magis instigemur. Est enim doctrina de libero arbitrio non facultatis & praestantiae, sed imbecillitatis ac miseriae humanae contemplatio.
units.tr: Connected with the treatment of the misery of man is the question of free choice, or of the powers of the human will to do good and to obey God. For it is necessary to know what man could do before the fall and what he can do after the fall, so that, rightly recognising the effects of the first sin, we may be the more stirred to humility and to a desire for the grace and government of God, and also to gratitude towards God. For the doctrine of free choice is not a contemplation of human ability and excellence, but of human weakness and misery.

units.la: DE LIBERO ARBITRIO.
units.tr: ON FREE CHOICE.

units.la: Principalis huius disputationis quaestio & scopus est: An homo, sicut seipsum a Deo quaerit, sic etiam suis viribus redire ad Deum, accipere gratiam a Deo oblatam, & se ipse corrigere possit: atque adeo, an hominis voluntas causa sit praecipua, cur alij convertantur, alij in peccatis perseverent, ac tam conversorum, quam non conversorum, alij plus, alij minus, boni aut mali, deni, siue bona siue mala, hoc vel illo modo faciant.
units.tr: The principal question and aim of this disputation is: whether man, just as he seeks himself from God, can also by his own powers return to God, receive the grace offered by God, and correct himself; and therefore whether the human will is the chief cause why some are converted and others persist in sins, and why, of those converted and not converted, some do more and some less good or evil, and finally whether they do these or those things in this or that way.

units.la: Ad hanc quaestionem respondent Pelagiani & similes, omnibus hominibus tantum gratiae a Deo datum, ac in natura relireliquum esse, vt ad DEVM redire, eique obedire possint, nec aliam causam voluntate humana priorem aut superiorem quæri oportere, propter quam alij accipiant aut retineant, alij repudient aut abijciant auxilium diuinum in vitandis peccatis, & hoc vel illo modo consilia & actiones suas instituant.
units.tr: The Pelagians and those like them answer this question by saying that enough grace has been given by God to all men, and that enough remains in nature, for them to return to God and obey him; and that no other cause prior or superior to the human will ought to be sought, on account of which some receive or retain, and others reject or cast off, the divine help in avoiding sins, and in this or that way plan and carry out their counsels and actions.

units.la: Contrà verò scriptura docet, nullum opus Deo placens, sine regeneratione & singulari Spiritus sancti beneficio, ab vllo hominum suscipi aut perfici, neque plus vel minus in cuiusquam consiliis aut actionibus boni existere posse, quam Deus gratuita bonitate sua in eis efficere voluerit, nec alio voluntatem vllius creaturæ inclinari, quam quò æterno & optimo Dei consilio visum fuerit. Quod vt melius intelligatur, considerandum est:
units.tr: On the contrary, Scripture teaches that no work pleasing to God is undertaken or completed by any man without regeneration and the singular benefit of the Holy Spirit; nor can there be more or less of good in anyone's counsels or actions than God, by his free goodness, has willed to work in them; nor is the will of any creature inclined except in the direction that seemed good to God's eternal and best counsel. So that this may be better understood, the following must be considered:

units.la: I. Quid sit libertas voluntatis, & liberum arbitrium.
units.tr: I. What the freedom of the will and free choice are.

units.la: II. Quid sit discrimen libertatis in Deo, & in creaturis rationalibus, angelis & homine.
units.tr: II. What the difference of freedom is in God and in rational creatures, angels and man.

units.la: III. Sitne aliqua libertas voluntatis humanæ.
units.tr: III. Whether there is any freedom of the human will.

units.la: IV. Qualis sit libertas voluntatis in homine, seu, qui sint gradus liberi arbitrij secundum quatuor status hominis.
units.tr: IV. What kind of freedom of the will there is in man; or, what degrees of free choice there are according to the four states of man.

units.la: I. Quid sit libertas voluntatis & liberum arbitrium.
units.tr: I. What liberty of the will and free choice are.

units.la: Libertas communiter significat relationem, hoc est, facultatem seu jus personæ aut rei, ad agendum proprio arbitratu & motu, secundum honestas leges, vel ordinem naturæ suæ congruentem, ad fruendum item bonis sibi convenientibus absque prohibitione & impedimento, & ad non sustinendum defectus aut onera naturæ suæ non propria. Hæc libertas ab obligatione & à miseria dici potest, & opponitur seruituti. Sic DEVS est libertimus, quia nemini est obligatus: sic Romani & Judæi erant liberi, hoc est, immunes à dominiis & oneribus alienis: sic ciuitas est libera à tyrannide & seruitute, libertate ciuili: sic justificati fide liberi sumus ab ira Dei, à maledictione Legis, & à ceremoniis Mosaicis per Christum. Hæc significatio libertatis ad disputationem de libero arbitrio non pertinet. Constat enim, nos omnes esse seruos Dei, & Lege obligari ad obedientiam, vel ad pœnam. Multa etiam voluntas nostra liberè vult, quæ tamen perficiendi facultatem non habet. Alias libertas opponitur coactioni, & est qualitas voluntatis, seu potentia naturalis naturæ intelligentis, coniuncta cum potentia volente: hoc est, facultas eligendi aut repudiandi obiectum ab intellectu monstratum, suo ac proprio motu, sine coactione. existente & manente voluntate sua natura idonea ad oppositum vel diversum eligendum, vel ad actionem suspendendam: ut homo potest velle ambulare, vel non ambulare. Atque hoc est agere ἐx προαιρέσεως, hoc est, ex praeunte deliberatione, qui est modus agendi voluntatis proprius.
units.tr: Liberty commonly signifies a relation, that is, the power or right of a person or thing to act by its own judgment and motion, in accordance with honourable laws or the order proper to its nature; likewise to enjoy the goods suited to it without prohibition or hindrance, and not to bear the defects or burdens that are not proper to its nature. This liberty can be called freedom from obligation and from misery, and it is opposed to slavery. Thus God is free, because He is bound to no one. Thus the Romans and the Jews were free, that is, exempt from the dominion and burdens of others. Thus a state is free from tyranny and servitude, with civil liberty. Thus we who are justified by faith are free from the wrath of God, from the curse of the Law, and, through Christ, from the Mosaic ceremonies. This sense of liberty does not pertain to the dispute about free choice. For it is evident that we are all servants of God, and bound by the Law either to obedience or to punishment. Likewise our will freely wills many things which it nonetheless lacks the power to accomplish. In another sense, liberty is opposed to coercion, and it is a quality of the will, or a natural power of an intelligent nature, joined with the power of willing: that is, the faculty of choosing or rejecting an object presented by the intellect, by its own and proper motion, without coercion, the will remaining, while its nature is still fit to choose the opposite or a different thing, or to suspend action; as a man can will to walk or not to walk. And this is to act ἐκ προαιρέσεως [ek proaireseōs], that is, from prior deliberation, which is the proper mode of the will's acting.

units.la: Haec libertas voluntatis est in Deo, angelis & hominibus: & libera horum voluntas vocatur liberum arbitrium, hoc est, facultas seu potentia volendi aut nolendi, eligendi, aut repudiandi obiectum ab intellectu monstratum, proprio motu, sine coactione. Ac nominatur arbitrium, respectu mentis monstrantis voluntati obiectum eligendum aut repudiandum: liberum respectu voluntaris ultro & sponte sequentis judicium intellectus sine coactione. Liberum enim vocatur ἑκούσιον, spontaneum: quod opponitur ἀκουσίῳ involuntario & coacto, non semper ἀναγκαίῳ necessario. Potest enim ἑκούσιος consistere cum ἀναγκαίῳ, sed non cum ἀκουσίῳ; ut Deus & sancti angeli ἀναγκαίως, necessario sunt boni: non tamen ἀκουσίως, coacte, sed libertate: quia principium suae bonitatis habent in seipsis, liberam voluntatem. Coactum vero dicitur, quod principium & causam sui motus habet tantum externam, non etiam internam, qua ipsum se moveat ad hoc vel alio modo agendum.
units.tr: This liberty of the will is in God, in the angels and in men; and the free will of these beings is called free choice, that is, the faculty or power of willing or not willing, of choosing or rejecting an object presented by the intellect, by its own motion, without coercion. It is called choice with respect to the mind presenting to the will an object to be chosen or rejected, and free with respect to the will following the judgment of the intellect readily and willingly, without coercion. For that is called free which is ἑκούσιον [hekousion], spontaneous, and it is opposed to ἀκουσίῳ [akousiō], involuntary and coerced, but not always to ἀναγκαίῳ [anankaiō], necessary. For what is ἑκούσιον can consist with what is ἀναγκαῖον, but not with what is ἀκούσιον. Thus God and the holy angels are good ἀναγκαίως [anankaiōs], necessarily, yet not ἀκουσίως [akousiōs], by coercion, but by liberty, because they have the principle of their goodness in themselves, namely a free will. That is called coerced, however, which has only an external principle and cause of its motion, and not also an internal one by which it moves itself to act in this or that way.

units.la: Est proinde discrimen inter necessarium & coactum, ut inter genus & speciem. Omne enim coactum est necessarium: sed non omne necessarium est coactum. Unde gemina dicitur necessitas: immutabilitatis & coactionis: illa cum voluntario consistere potest: haec non potest.
units.tr: There is therefore a distinction between necessary and coerced, as between genus and species. For everything coerced is necessary, but not everything necessary is coerced. Hence necessity is said to be twofold: of immutability and of coercion. The former can consist with a voluntary act; the latter cannot.

units.la: II. De discrimine libertatis in Deo & creaturis.
units.tr: II. On the difference between liberty in God and in creatures.

units.la: Duo sunt communia Deo & creaturis rationalibus, quod ad libertatem voluntatis attinet. Unum, quod Deus & creaturae rationales ex deliberatione & consilio agunt, hoc est, eligunt aut repudiant obiecta, praeunte rationis judicio, comitante voluntate. Alterum, quod eligunt aut repudiant proprio motu sine coactione, hoc est, voluntas sua natura idonea existens ad volendum oppositum eius quod vult, aut ad suspendendam actionem, sua sponte in alteram partem inclinat. Psal.104. 24. & 115.3. Gen.3.6. Esa.1.19.20. Matth.27.37.
units.tr: There are two things common to God and rational creatures as regards liberty of the will. The first is that God and rational creatures act from deliberation and counsel, that is, they choose or reject objects, the judgment of reason going before and the will following. The second is that they choose or reject by their own motion without coercion, that is, the will, being by its nature fit to will the opposite of what it wills, or to suspend action, inclines of its own accord to the one side. Ps. 104:24; 115:3. Gen. 3:6. Isa. 1:19, 20. Matt. 27:37.

units.la: Discrimina vero libertatis in Deo & creaturis sunt tria. Primum est in intellectu: quod Deus omnia ex se ipso perfectissime ab aeterno intelligit ac intuetur, sine ulla ignorantia & judicij errore. Creaturae vero neque ex sese, neque omnia, neque eadem quovis tempore sciunt: sed tantum ac tum demum de Deo eiusque voluntate & operibus intelligunt, quantum quando ipsis revelare Deus vult; ideoque multa ignorant, & læpe errant. Testimonia huius discriminis sunt: De die illa & hora nemo scit, nisi solus Pater. &c. Qui dat sapientiam sapientibus, &c. Quis erudiit Spiritum Iehova? Nec est ulla res creata, quæ non manifesta sit in conspectu ipsius. Illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.
units.tr: The differences between liberty in God and in creatures are three. The first lies in the intellect: God knows and beholds all things from Himself, most perfectly and from eternity, without any ignorance or error of judgment. Creatures, however, neither know from themselves, nor know all things, nor know the same things at all times; but they understand concerning God, His will and His works only so much, and only then, as God wills to reveal to them. Therefore they are ignorant of many things and often err. The testimonies to this difference are: Of that day and hour no one knows, except the Father alone, etc. He who gives wisdom to the wise, etc. Who has taught the Spirit of Jehovah? Nor is there any created thing which is not manifest in His sight. He enlightens every man coming into this world.

units.la: Secundum est in voluntate: quod Dei voluntas non aliunde regitur aut pendet. Angelorum verò & hominum voluntates sic sunt actionum suarum causæ; ut nihilominus arcano Dei consilio & providentiâ, ad obiectorum electionem aut repudiationem flectantur, sive immediatè à Deo, sive per media, aliàs bona, aliàs mala, quibus uti Deo est visum; ac præter æternum & immutabile Dei consilium eas agere quicquam, sit impossibile. Itaque vocabulum ἀυτεξούσιον, quo Græci Theologi liberum arbitrium appellant, magis proprie in Deum competit, qui perfectè & similiter est sui juris. De creaturis reliquis usurpatur ἐξουσία, quo etiam scriptura utitur ad Philc. v.14. Heb.10. v.26. 1 Pet.5,2. Testimonia & argumenta huius discriminis in doctrina de providentia explicantur.
units.tr: The second lies in the will: God's will is not governed or dependent from anything else. The wills of angels and of men are indeed causes of their own actions, yet by God's hidden counsel and providence they are nonetheless turned to choose or reject objects, whether immediately by God or through means, some good and some evil, as it has pleased God to use them; and it is impossible for them to do anything beyond the eternal and unchangeable counsel of God. Hence the term αὐτεξούσιον [autexousion], by which the Greek theologians call free choice, belongs more properly to God, who is perfectly and in the same way His own master. Of the remaining creatures ἐξουσία [exousia] is used, which Scripture also employs: Philem. 5:14; Heb. 10:26; 1 Pet. 5:2. The testimonies and arguments for this difference are explained in the doctrine of providence.

units.la: Ac Deum esse primam consiliorum suorum causam, docent hæc & similia dicta: Omnia quæcunque voluit, fecit. Qui pro sua voluntate agit, tam in exercitu cœlesti, quam inter habitatores terræ, &c. Creaturarum verò voluntates & consilia à Dei nutu & consilio pendere, hæc & alia probant: Dominus mittet angelum suum coram te. &c. Vade & congrega senatores Israel, &c. Hunc definito consilio & providentia Dei deditum interemistis, &c. Scio per ignorantiam fecisse vos, &c. Deus autem hæc implevit, &c. Coacti sunt Herodes & Pontius Pilatus, ut facerent, quæcunque manus tua & consilium tuum prius definierat facienda. Novi Domine, quod non est hominis via sua, neque ut dirigat gressus suos. Cor Regis in manu Dei, &c. Voluntas igitur angelorum & hominum, & omnes aliæ causæ secundæ, sicut à Deo ut prima causa sunt, sic à Deo reguntur. Dei verò voluntas à nulla creaturarum regitur: quia ut non efficientem, sic neq; movencem, aut flectentem causam ullam extra se habet Deus: alioqui non esset Deus, hoc est, prima & suprema operum suorum causa; & creaturæ in locum Dei substituerentur. Regit autem & flectit voluntates creaturarum, non rapit aut cogit, hoc est, ostensis menti obiectis, efficaciter movet voluntatem ad volendum, quod mens tunc bonum judicat, & repudiandum, quod malum videtur.
units.tr: That God is the first cause of His own counsels is taught by these and similar sayings: Whatever He willed, He did. He who acts according to His will, both among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, etc. That the wills and counsels of creatures depend on God's nod and counsel is proved by these and other passages: The Lord will send His angel before you, etc. Go and gather the elders of Israel, etc. Him, delivered up by the set purpose and foreknowledge of God, you have slain, etc. I know that you did it in ignorance, etc. But God fulfilled these things, etc. Herod and Pontius Pilate were gathered together to do whatever Your hand and Your counsel had determined beforehand to be done. I know, O Lord, that a man's way is not his own, nor is it in man who walks to direct his steps. The heart of the king is in the hand of God, etc. Therefore the will of angels and of men, and all other secondary causes, as they are from God as first cause, so they are governed by God. But God's will is governed by no creature, because God has no cause outside Himself, either efficient or moving or inclining; otherwise He would not be God, that is, the first and supreme cause of His works, and creatures would be substituted in the place of God. Yet God governs and inclines the wills of creatures without snatching or compelling them; that is, by setting objects before the mind, He effectively moves the will to will what the mind then judges good, and to reject what seems evil.

units.la: Tertium discrimen est in intellectu & voluntate simul: quod Deus sicut immutabiliter omnia scit, sic etiam decreuit ab æterno, & vult immutabiliter omnia, quæ fiunt, quatenus bona sunt, & permittit, quatenus peccata sunt. Creaturarum autem sicut notitiæ & judicia de rebus, sic etiam voluntates mutabiles sunt, ut velint, quod antea nolebant, & nolint, quod antea volebant. Cùm enim Dei consilia omnia sint optima, justissima, & sapientissima, nunquam ea improbat, corrigit aut mutat, ut saepe faciunt homines, cùm se imprudenter antea statuisse agnoscunt. Huc pertinent dicta: Non est homo Deus, ut mentiatur, & quasi filius hominis, ut mutetur. Ergo Deus & non mutor. Volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, &c.
units.tr: The third difference lies in the intellect and the will together: just as God knows all things unchangeably, so He has also decreed from eternity, and unchangeably wills, all things that come to pass, insofar as they are good, and permits them insofar as they are sins. But creatures' knowledge and judgments about things are changeable, and so also their wills are changeable: they come to will what they formerly were unwilling, and to be unwilling what they formerly willed. For since all God's counsels are most good, most just and most wise, He never disapproves, corrects or changes them, as men often do when they recognise that they earlier decided something imprudently. To this belong the sayings: God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should change. Has He said, and will He not do it? Or has He spoken, and will He not make it good? Therefore God is not changed. Willing to show wrath and to make His power known, etc.

units.la: Obiect. I. Qui non potest mutare consilium, non habet liberam voluntatem. Deus consilium suum mutare non potest. Ergo eius voluntas non est libera. Resp. ad maiorem per distinction. Non habet liberam voluntatem is, qui consilium mutare non potest, impeditus à causa externa, etsi mutare velit. Deus autem consilium suum non mutat, nec mutare potest, non propter impedimentum causæ externæ, nec propter naturæ aut facultatis defectum: sed quia non vult, nec velle potest consilij sui mutationem, propter immutabilem rectitudinem voluntatis suæ, in quam neque error, neque ulla mutationis causa potest cadere.
units.tr: Obiect. I. He who cannot change his purpose does not have a free will. God cannot change his purpose. Therefore his will is not free. Resp. to the major by distinction. He who cannot change his purpose, although he wishes to, is not free, because an external cause hinders him. God, however, does not change his purpose, nor can he change it, not because of any hindrance from an external cause, nor because of any defect of nature or power, but because he does not will, and cannot will, a change of his purpose, on account of the unchangeable rectitude of his will, into which neither error nor any cause of change can fall.

units.la: Obiect. II. Quod immutabili Dei voluntate regitur, non agit liberè. Voluntas angelorum & hominum agit liberè. Ergo non regitur aliunde. Resp. ad maiorem per distinct. Non agit liberè, quod à Deo regitur, sine deliberatione & electione propria. Voluntas verò angelorum & hominum ita regitur à Deo, monstrante intellectui obiectum, & efficaciter per id movente atque afficiente voluntatem eorum, ad illud eligendum, ut nihilominus propria deliberatione & electione id velit & eligat, proinde & liberè. Liberè enim agere in creaturis non est ex nullius gubernatione, sed ex deliberatione & spontaneo voluntatis motu agere, quantumuis hic motus aliunde excitetur & regatur.
units.tr: Obiect. II. What is governed by the unchangeable will of God does not act freely. The will of angels and men acts freely. Therefore it is not governed by anything else. Resp. to the major by distinction. That does not act freely which is governed by God without its own deliberation and choice. But the will of angels and men is so governed by God, who shows the object to the understanding and efficaciously moves and affects their will through it to choose that object, that nevertheless by their own deliberation and choice they will and choose it, and therefore freely. For to act freely in creatures does not mean to act under no one's governance, but to act from deliberation and a spontaneous motion of the will, even though this motion is stirred up and directed from elsewhere.

units.la: Obiect. III. Si voluntas, dum convertitur à Deo, aut ad alia obiecta flectitur, non potest repugnare, habere se pure passiuè. At hoc falsum. Ergo & illud. Resp. Non est sufficiens enumeratio in maiore. Potest enim voluntas mota à Deo non tantum pugnare, sed etiam assentiri & obsequi Deo moventi suo ac proprio motu: quod faciens non tantum patitur, sed etiam agit & eiet ipsa suas actiones: etsi vim assentiendi & obsequendi non ex se habeat, sed ex gratia Spiritus sancti accipiat.
units.tr: Obiect. III. If the will, when it is turned away from God or bent toward other objects, cannot resist, then it has a purely passive part. But this is false. Therefore that is false too. Resp. The enumeration in the major is not sufficient. For a will moved by God can not only resist, but also assent to and obey God who moves it by his own proper motion; and in doing so it not only suffers but also acts, and by its own acts it performs its actions, although it does not have the power of assenting and obeying from itself, but receives it from the grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Obiect. IV. Quod repugnat divinæ voluntati, id non regitur ab ea. Voluntas hominum repugnat Deo in multis actionibus. Ergo non regitur à Deo. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini. Maior enim
units.tr: Obiect. IV. What opposes the divine will is not governed by it. The human will opposes God in many actions. Therefore it is not governed by God. Resp. There are four terms. For the major is true only of the will of decree and of the hidden will; the minor only of the will of sign, or revealed will. For the decrees of God's will are always fulfilled, and are carried out in all things, even in those who most oppose the divine precepts.

units.la: Contra id, quod creaturarum voluntates regantur à Deo.
units.tr: Against the claim that the wills of creatures are governed by God.

units.la: Liberè agere quid sit in creaturis. enim vera est de voluntate decreti & arcana: minor tantum de voluntate signi seu patefacta. Decreta enim voluntatis Dei semper sunt rata, & in omnibus perficiuntur, etiam in iis, qui praeceptis divinis quàm maximè aduersantur.
units.tr: What it is to act freely in creatures. For it is true of the will of decree and the hidden will; the minor only of the will of sign, or the revealed will. For the decrees of God's will are always fulfilled, and are carried out in all things, even in those who most oppose the divine precepts.

units.la: Obiect. V. Si omnes motus voluntatum etiam malarum Dei voluntate excitantur & reguntur: multi autem ex his sunt peccata: Ergo Deus constituitur author peccati. Resp. Est fallacia accidentis in minore. Motus enim malorum sunt peccata, non quatenus sunt motus, & à voluntate Dei ordinantur aut producuntur, (hactenus enim sunt boni, & cum Lege Dei congruunt, sed quatenus à diabolis & hominibus fiunt, qui in agendo aut voluntatem Dei non agnoscunt, aut non eo fine agunt, ut Deo sic volenti obtemperent.
units.tr: Objection. 5. If all motions of the wills, even of evil wills, are stirred up and governed by the will of God, and many of these motions are sins, then God is made the author of sin. Answer. This is a fallacy of accident in the minor premise. For the motions of evil men are sins not insofar as they are motions, and not because they are ordered or produced by the will of God (in that respect they are good and agree with the law of God), but insofar as they are done by devils and men, who in acting either do not acknowledge the will of God, or do not act with the aim of obeying God in so willing.

units.la: III. Sitne aliqua libertas humanae voluntatis.
units.tr: III. Whether there is any freedom of the human will.

units.la: Esse in hominibus aliquam libertatem voluntatis, probatur: 1. Quia homo est conditus ad imaginem Dei. Imaginis autem Dei pars est voluntas libera. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Deus ab initio constituit hominem, & reliquit eum in manu consilii sui. 2. Ex definitione libertatis eius, quae homini convenit. Nam homo facit ex deliberatione, cognoscens, appetens & repudians hoc vel illud obiectum. Si autem definitio convenit, etiam definitum.
units.tr: That there is some freedom of the human will in men is proved as follows: (1) Because man was created in the image of God, and freedom of the will is part of the image of God. Let us make man in our image and likeness. God from the beginning made man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. (2) From the definition of that freedom which belongs to man. For man acts from deliberation, knowing, desiring and rejecting this or that object. But if the definition applies, so does the thing defined.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Si est in homine libertas voluntatis, evertitur doctrina de peccato originis. Pugnat enim non posse obedire, & habere libertatem. Resp. Non pugnat: quia post lapsum habemus voluntatis libertatem tantum ex parte, non autem talem, qualem ante lapsum, neque eodem gradu.
units.tr: Obiect. 1. If there is freedom of will in man, the doctrine of original sin is overthrown. For it is inconsistent to be unable to obey and yet to have freedom. Resp. It is not inconsistent, because after the Fall we have freedom of will only in part, not such as we had before the Fall, nor to the same degree.
