units.la: Obiect. 2. Qui non aequè habet voluntatem ad bonum & ad malum, non habet liberam voluntatem. Sed homo post lapsum non habet aequè voluntatem ad bonum atq; ad malum. Ergo, &c. Resp. Negatur maior, quia est mala definitio libertatis. Sic enim Deus quidem haberet liberam voluntatem.
units.tr: Obiect. 2. He who does not have an equal will toward good and toward evil does not have a free will. But after the Fall man does not have an equal will toward good and toward evil. Therefore, etc. Resp. The major is denied, because it is a bad definition of freedom. For on that definition God alone would have a free will.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Quod aliunde pendet, non est liberum. Voluntas nostra aliunde pendet. Ergo non est libera. Resp. ad maiorem distinct. Quod ab alio pendet & regitur tantum, & non etiam à se, id non est liberum. Voluntas humana regitur ab alio non tantum, sed etiam à se. Deus enim sic movet homines, ut tamen non vi rapiantur, sed & ipsi se moveant. Quae autem naturaliter à se movetur, est solius Dei, cuius infinitè maior est libertas, quam creaturarum. Sufficit interim ad libertatem hominibus, quod quicquid volunt, velint liberè & deliberatò moru. Obiect. 4. Quod est seruum, non est liberum. Arbitrium nostrum post lapsum est seruum: Ergo non est liberum. Resp. Conceditur totum, si liberum capitur pro eo, quod habet facultatem eligendi bonum & Deo placens: hactenus enim voluntas serua est, nec potest eligere & velle nisi malum. Ego carnalis sum, venditus sub peccato. &c. Si vero liberum capitur pro spontaneo seu αὐτεξούσιον, maior est falsa. Non enim seruitus, sed coactio voluntatis libertatem tollit.
units.tr: Obiect. 3. What depends on something else is not free. Our will depends on something else. Therefore it is not free. Resp. to the major by distinction. What depends on and is governed only by another, and not also by itself, is not free. The human will is governed not only by another but also by itself. For God so moves men that they are not carried off by force, but also move themselves. What is moved naturally by itself, however, belongs to God alone, whose freedom is infinitely greater than that of creatures. Meanwhile it is enough for men's freedom that whatever they will, they will freely and with deliberate motion. Obiect. 4. What is a slave is not free. Our free choice after the Fall is a slave. Therefore it is not free. Resp. The whole is granted if "free" is taken to mean that which has the power of choosing good and what pleases God; for insofar as this is concerned the will is a slave, and can choose and will only evil. I am carnal, sold under sin, etc. But if "free" is taken to mean spontaneous, or autexousion, the major is false. For it is not slavery but compulsion of the will that removes freedom.

units.la: IV. Qualis sit libertas in homine, seu, qui sint gradus libertatis humanæ, secundum quatuor status hominis.
units.tr: IV. What kind of liberty there is in man, or, what are the degrees of human liberty, according to the four states of man.

units.la: Porro quæritur, & ad nostri cognitionem est necessarium, qualis & quanta, siue ad quas actiones sese extendens libertas ante lapsum generis humani in voluntate hominis fuerit: & aliqua ne an nulla, & si aliqua, qualisnam post lapsum sit reliqua: an item & quomodo & quatenus in nobis restituatur. Unde manifestum est, rectissime liberi arbitrij gradus considerari, & distingui secundum quatuor status hominis: videlicet nondum lapsi in peccatum, lapsi, renati & glorificati: hoc est, qualis & quanta libertas humanæ voluntatis fuerit ante lapsum, qualisnam post lapsum sit reliqua ante regenerationem: qualis sit in hac vita post regenerationem: & qualis futura sit in altera vita post regenerationem.
units.tr: Furthermore, it is asked, and it is necessary for our knowledge, what kind and how great the liberty was in the will of man, extending itself to which actions, before the fall of the human race; whether there was any liberty at all or none; and if there was some, what kind of it remains after the fall; and likewise whether and how and to what extent it is restored in us. Hence it is clear that the degrees of free choice are most rightly considered and distinguished according to the four states of man: namely, of man not yet fallen into sin, of man fallen, of man reborn, and of man glorified. That is, what kind and how great the liberty of the human will was before the fall; what kind of it remains after the fall and before regeneration; what kind it is in this life after regeneration; and what kind it will be in the other life after regeneration.

units.la: Primus gradus libertatis in homine nondum lapso, fuit mens illustrata perfecta Dei agnitione, & voluntas inclinatione sua & motu spontaneo præstans integram obedientiam Deo: sed tamen in hac agnitione & inclinatione non ita confirmata, quin obiecta aliqua specie boni, ad deficiendum ab illa obedientia inclinari, atque etiam ab ea deficere spontaneo motu posset: hoc est, voluntas hominis erat libera ad bonum & ad malum, seu, liberè eligebat bonum, sed ita, ut etiam posset eligere malum: posset persistere in bono, Deo eam seruante: & posset etiam deficere ad malum, Deo deserente. Prius confirmatur ex perfectione imaginis Dei, in qua homo erat conditus. Posterius nimis cuidenter patet ex euentu, & ex scripturæ testimoniis. Deus fecit hominem rectum: ipsi autem inquisiuerunt inuentiones multas. Conclusit Deus omnes in contumacia, ut omnium misereretur: quibus verbis testatur Paulus, singulari consilio Deum non confirmasse primum hominem contra lapsum, nec ei tantum gratiæ contulisse, ut non posset tentatione diaboli seduci, & ad peccandum permoueri, sed permisisse eum seduci, & labi in peccatum & mortem, ut quicunque ex communi interitu seruarenuarentur, sola eius misericordia seruarentur. Probatur etiam euidenti ratione. Si enim nihil sine æterno & optimo Dei consilio fieri potest, sane lapsus primorum parentum tanto minus ab eo potest excipi, quanto magis Deus de præcipuo suo opere, genere videlicet humano, quid fieri vellet, accurate ab initio constitutum habuit. Quæ hic ratio humana contra obijcere solet, videantur vol. 1. Vrsini pag. 42. &c.
units.tr: The first degree of freedom in man before the fall was a mind enlightened with the perfect knowledge of God, and a will which, by its own inclination and spontaneous movement, rendered complete obedience to God. Yet this knowledge and inclination were not so firmly established that the will could not be drawn, by some appearance of good set before it, to fall away from that obedience, and could not also turn away from it by its own spontaneous movement. That is, the human will was free to good and to evil; it freely chose the good, but in such a way that it could also choose evil. It could persist in good, with God preserving it; and it could also fall into evil, with God forsaking it. The former is confirmed from the perfection of the image of God in which man was created. The latter is made quite plain by the outcome and by the testimonies of Scripture: God made man upright, but they have sought out many inventions. God has shut up all under disobedience, that he might have mercy on all. In these words Paul testifies that, by a singular counsel, God did not confirm the first man against the fall, nor bestow on him such grace that he could not be seduced by the devil's temptation and moved to sin; rather he allowed him to be seduced and to slip into sin and death, so that those who were to be saved from the common ruin might be saved by his mercy alone. It is also proved by a clear argument: if nothing can happen without the eternal and best counsel of God, then certainly the fall of our first parents could not be excluded from it, all the more so since God had from the beginning carefully determined what he wished to be done with his chief work, the human race. The objections that human reason usually raises against this may be seen in vol. 1. Ursinus, p. 42, etc.

units.la: Secundus gradus liberi arbitrij est in homine lapso, ex parentibus corruptis nato, & nondum regenerato. In hoc statu liberè quidem agit voluntas, sed fertur tantum ad malum, & nihil nisi peccare potest. Ratio est, quia lapsum secuta est priuatio agnitionis Dei, in mente, & inclinationis ad obedientiam in voluntate & corde; successit cæcitas & auersio à Deo, quam homo exuere non potest, nisi per Spiritum sanctum regeneretur. Breuiter. Post lapsum in homine non-regenerato est aptitudo tantum ad malum eligendum. De hac cæcitate & prauitate naturæ humanæ post lapsum dicitur: Omne figmentum cordis humani tantum est malum. Si potest Æthiops mutare pellem suam, &c. Omnis homo ex iuuentute ad mala pronus est, & non possunt corda sua ex lapideis facere carnea. Non potest arbor mala bonos fructus ferre. Eramus mortui in peccatis: natura filij irae. Non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum quicquam velut ex nobis ipsis. Cum his testimoniis congruit singulorum experientia, & ipse conscientiæ sensus, qui clamat: nos nullam ad bona, nimis vero magnam ad mala facienda libertatem & propensionem voluntatis habere, nisi regeneremur, sicut dicitur: Conuerte me, & conuertar. Nullus igitur amor Dei in nobis est naturâ, ac proinde nullam habemus naturâ propensionem ad obediendum Deo.
units.tr: The second degree of free choice is in man who has fallen, born of corrupt parents, and not yet regenerated. In this state the will acts freely, but it is carried only toward evil, and can do nothing but sin. The reason is that the fall was followed by the loss of the knowledge of God in the mind, and of the inclination to obedience in the will and heart; blindness and aversion from God followed, which man cannot cast off unless he is regenerated by the Holy Spirit. In brief: after the fall, in the man who is not regenerated, there is only an aptitude for choosing evil. Of this blindness and perversity of human nature after the fall it is said: Every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart is only evil. Can the Ethiopian change his skin? … Every man from his youth is inclined to evil, and they cannot make their hearts of stone into flesh. A bad tree cannot bear good fruit. We were dead in sins, by nature children of wrath. We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything, as of ourselves. The experience of each person agrees with these testimonies, and so does the sense of conscience itself, which cries out that we have no freedom or inclination of the will toward doing good, but a very great one toward doing evil, unless we are regenerated, as it is said: Convert me, and I shall be converted. Therefore no love of God is in us by nature, and consequently we have by nature no inclination to obey God.

units.la: Obj. 1. Nihil facilius (inquit Erasmus ad Lutherum) quàm continere manus à furto. Item: Socrates, Aristides, & plures alij fecerunt multas virtutes. Ergò in ipsis fuit liberum arbitrium ad bonum ante regenerationem. Resp. 1. Est mala definitio liberi arbitrij & boni operis, seu libertatis ad bonum, quæ est facultas præstandi obedientiam Deo placentem. Hanc non-renati non habent. Furantur intus cupiditate, etsi foris continent manus à furto. 2. Deus suâ prouidentia etiam non-renatorum corda gubernat. Hinc verò non sequitur, eis ex se facile esse inchoare obedientiam internam vel externam, Deo placentem. Carent enim fide, cum sint non-renati. Absq; fide autem quod fit, peccatum est, & Deo placere est impossibile.
units.tr: Objection 1. Nothing is easier (says Erasmus to Luther) than to keep one's hands from theft. Likewise: Socrates, Aristides and many others performed many virtues. Therefore free choice to good existed in them before regeneration. Answer 1. It is a wrong definition of free choice and of a good work, or of freedom to good, which is the ability to perform obedience pleasing to God. The unregenerate do not have this. They steal inwardly by desire, even though they keep their hands from theft outwardly. 2. God by his providence governs the hearts even of the unregenerate. But it does not follow from this that it is easy for them, by themselves, to begin inward or outward obedience pleasing to God. For they lack faith, since they are unregenerate. But without faith whatever is done is sin, and it is impossible to please God.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Opera legis sunt bona. Ethnici fecerunt opera legis. Ergo ethnicorum opera fuerunt bona etiam ante regenerationem. Resp. ad maiorem per distinct. Opera Legis sunt bona per le: fiunt autem mala per accidens, cum fiunt à non-renatis: quia non fiunt eo modo & fine, quo Deus justit.
units.tr: Objection 2. The works of the law are good. The heathen performed works of the law. Therefore the works of the heathen were good even before regeneration. Answer to the major, by distinction. The works of the law are good in themselves, but they become evil by accident when they are done by the unregenerate, because they are not done in the manner and for the purpose that God commanded.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Quod Deus optat, vt faciamus, id est penes nos. Deus optat, vt simus idonei ad bonum agendum. Ergo per nos bonum agere possumus: & per consequens non egemus operatione Spiritus sancti. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini. In maiore optandi verbum proprie sumitur, in minore improprie. Deus enim optare dicitur per ἀνθρωπομόρφως. Ideo mutatur genus praedicationis. Optat autem dupliciter. 1. Mandato & invitatione. 2. Quod ad amorem erga creaturas, & cruciatum pereuntium, quo non delectatur: non autem, quod ad executionem suae justitiae attinet, qua summe delectatur. Inst. Qui invitat alios ad bene agendum, & laetatur bona eorum actione, id facere est penes alium, & non penes eum, qui invitat. Sed Deus invitat nos ad bene agendum, & delectatur, &c. Ergo penes nos est, aliquid bene agere. Resp. Negatur maior, quia non est satis, Deum invitare, sed oportet etiam nostram voluntatem bene agendi accedere, quam habere non possumus, nisi à Deo.
units.tr: Objection 3. What God wishes us to do is within our power. God wishes us to be fit for doing good. Therefore we can do good through ourselves, and consequently we do not need the working of the Holy Spirit. Answer. There are four terms. In the major premise the word wish is taken properly, in the minor improperly. For God is said to wish in a human manner [ἀνθρωπομόρφως]. Hence the kind of predication changes. He wishes in two ways: 1. by command and invitation; 2. with regard to love toward creatures and the torment of those who perish, in which he takes no delight; but not with regard to the execution of his justice, in which he takes supreme delight. Further: he who invites others to do good, and rejoices in their good action, does not make it happen by his own power, but by the power of the one invited. But God invites us to do good, and delights in it, etc. Therefore it is within our power to do something good. Answer. The major is denied, for it is not enough that God invites; our will to do good must also come to it, and we cannot have that unless it is given by God.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Si nihil nisi peccare possumus ante regenerationem, Deus injuste nos punit, peccantes necessario. Respond. ad maiorem per distinct. Qui necessario peccat, injuste punitur, nisi scilicet ipse attraxerit sibi necessitatem peccandi. Nos vero ipsi nobis attraximus peccandi necessitatem in primis parentibus: quin & ipsi eam volumus. Juste igitur punimur. Caetera, quae hic objici solent à liberi arbitrij patronis, videantur vol. 1. Vrsini pag. 245.
units.tr: Objection 5. If before regeneration we can do nothing but sin, God punishes us unjustly, since we sin of necessity. Answer to the major, by distinction. He who sins of necessity is punished unjustly only if he himself has brought upon himself the necessity of sinning. But we ourselves brought upon ourselves the necessity of sinning in our first parents; indeed we even want it ourselves. Therefore we are justly punished. The other objections usually raised here by the defenders of free choice may be seen in vol. 1. Ursinus, p. 245.

units.la: Tertius gradus liberi arbitrij est hominis in hac vita regeneram quidem, sed nondum perfecti & glorificati. In hoc statu voluntas sua libertate utitur non tantum ad bene, sed partim ad malè operandum. Ad bene operandum. Quia singulari gratia Spiritus sancti per verbum Dei renovatur natura hominis, accenditur in mente nova lux & cognitio Dei, in corde novi motus, in voluntate novae inclinationes cum Lege divina congruentes: & voluntas efficaciter movetur à Spiritu sancto, ad agendum secundum has notitias & inclinationes, atq; ita ad facultatem volendi, quod Deus approbat: & facultatis eius usum recuperat, incipitque Deo obedire, juxta dicta: Circumcidet Deus cor tuum. Dabo vobis cor novum & spiritum novum. Vbi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. Quisquis ex Deo natus est, non peccat.
units.tr: The third degree of free choice is that of man in this life, regenerate indeed but not yet perfected and glorified. In this state the will uses its freedom not only to act well but partly also to act badly. To act well. Because by the singular grace of the Holy Spirit, through the Word of God, the nature of man is renewed: a new light and knowledge of God is kindled in the mind, new motions in the heart, and new inclinations in the will agreeing with the divine Law; and the will is effectively moved by the Holy Spirit to act according to these understandings and inclinations. Thus it recovers the ability to will what God approves, and the use of that ability, and it begins to obey God, according to the words: The Lord will circumcise your heart. I will give you a new heart and a new spirit. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. Whoever is born of God does not sin.

units.la: Partim ad bene, partim ad malè operandum. 1. Quia renovatio mentis & voluntatis in hac vita non fit perfecta: sed etiam in sanctis
units.tr: Partly to do good, partly to do evil. 1. Because the renewal of the mind and will is not made perfect in this life, but even in the saints

units.la: Deut. 30, 6. Ezec. 36, 20. 2 Cor. 3, 1. 1 Ioh. 3, 9. sanctis manent multæ reliquiæ peccati: unde opera, quæ faciunt, sunt imperfecta, & peccatis inquinata: Scio, quod non habitet in me, hoc est, in carne mea, bonum. 2. Quia renati non semper à Spiritu sancto reguntur, sed interdum à Deo vel examinandi vel humiliandi ipsos causa ad tempus deseruntur: sed tamen ad pœnitentiam revocantur, ut non pereant. Spiritum tuum sanctum ne auferas à me. Quare errare nos fecisti à viis tuis?
units.tr: Deut. 30, 6. Ezec. 36, 20. 2 Cor. 3, 1. 1 Ioh. 3, 9. some great remnants of sin remain in the saints, so that the works they do are imperfect and tainted by sin: I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good thing. 2. Because the regenerate are not always governed by the Holy Spirit, but are sometimes left by God for a time, either to test them or to humble them; yet they are called back to repentance so that they do not perish. Take not your Holy Spirit from me. Why have you made us stray from your ways?

units.la: Breviter. Post regenerationem inchoatam in homine est aptitudo partim ad bonum, partim ad malum eligendum. Ad bonum: quia mens & voluntas illuminatæ à Spiritu sancto incipiunt aliquo modo flecti ad bonum, & inchoare novam obedientiam. Ad malum: quia sancti in hac vita imperfecte regenerantur, retinent multas infirmitates & malas inclinationes, propter inhærens originale peccatum: ideo bona opera, quæ faciunt, sunt imperfecte bona. Quæ ab anabaptistis & aliis contra imperfectionem renovationis & bonorum operum in renatis disputari solent, videantur eodem vol. Vrsini p. 256. & infra ad quæstionem catechet. 114.
units.tr: In brief. After regeneration has begun, there is in a person an aptitude partly to choose good and partly to choose evil. To good: because the mind and will, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, begin in some measure to be bent toward good and to begin a new obedience. To evil: because the saints are regenerated imperfectly in this life, they retain many infirmities and evil inclinations on account of the indwelling original sin; therefore the good works they do are imperfectly good. As to the objections which the Anabaptists and others usually raise against the imperfection of renewal and of good works in the regenerate, see the same volume of Ursinus, p. 256, and below on catechism question 114.

units.la: Quartus gradus liberi arbitrii est hominis posthanc vitam glorificati, seu perfecte regenerati: in quo voluntas hominis erit libera tantum ad bonum, non ad malum eligendum. Atqui hæc erit integra voluntatis nostræ libertas perfecte & semper obediendi Deo, qua non tantum non peccabimus, sed à nulla re magis abhorrebimus, quam a peccato, atq; etiam amplius peccare non poterimus. Primo: quia in mente lucebit perfecta Dei agnitio, in voluntate & corde perfectissima & summa alacritas ad obediendum Deo. Idcirco nullus tunc erit locus ignorantiæ aut dubitationi de Deo, aut minimæ contumaciæ adversus Deum. Deinde: quia nunquam deserentur, sed continuè regentur beati in vita cœlesti a Spiritu S., ut in vlla actione eos à rectitudine aberrare fit impossibile. Vnde dicitur: Erunt sicut Angeli in cælo. Similes erimus. Angeli boni tantum ad bonum propensi sunt, quia sunt boni: sicut contra angeli mali tantum ad malum, quia sunt mali. Nos autem similes erimus angelis bonis. Erit ergo conditio nostra longe præstantior, quam fuit Adam ante lapsum. Eratis quidem perfecte conformis Deo: sed poterat velle bonum & malicet potentia deficiendi à Deo, & amittendi bona, hoc est, erat bonus mutabiliter. At nos non poterimus velle nisi bonum: & sicut mali tantum feruntur ad malum, quia mali sunt; sic nos tantum feremur ad bonum, tantum bonum amabimus & eligemus, quia erimus boni immutabiliter, erimus in rectitudine pleplenè confirmati, vt deficere à Deo non possimus. Impossibile erit nos tunc velle vllum malum: quia seruabimur diuinâ gratiâ in libertate integra voluntatis ad bonum.
units.tr: The fourth degree of free choice belongs to a person glorified after this life, or perfectly regenerated: in which the will of the person will be free only to choose good, not evil. Now this will be the complete freedom of our will, to obey God perfectly and always, by which we will not only not sin, but will shrink from nothing more than from sin, and will no longer be able to sin any more. First, because in the mind the perfect knowledge of God will shine, and in the will and heart the most perfect and highest eagerness to obey God. Therefore there will then be no place for ignorance or doubt about God, or the least stubbornness against God. Next, because the blessed in the heavenly life will never be forsaken but will be constantly governed by the Holy Spirit, so that it will be impossible for them to stray from uprightness in any action. Hence it is said: They will be like the angels in heaven. We will be like him. Good angels are inclined only to good because they are good; likewise evil angels are inclined only to evil because they are evil. But we will be like the good angels. Our condition will therefore be far more excellent than was Adam's before the fall. He was indeed perfectly conformed to God, yet he could will good and evil, with the power of falling away from God and losing good things; that is, he was good in a mutable way. But we will be unable to will anything except good; and just as evil spirits are carried only toward evil because they are evil, so we will be carried only toward good, will love and choose only good, because we will be good immutably, will be fully confirmed in uprightness, so that we cannot fall away from God. It will then be impossible for us to will any evil, because we shall be preserved by divine grace in the complete freedom of the will toward good.

units.la: Ex his, quæ de gradibus libertatis humanæ dicta sunt, appareret, calumniam esse, quod tollamus in homine liberum arbitrium, eò quod docemus, hominem in statu peccati nihil posse eligere, nisi malum coram Deo. Nam & malum liberrimè eligunt non-renati in statu peccati. Non tollitur liberum arbitrium in Deo, & in angelis, qui nihil nisi bonum, neque in malis spiritibus, qui nihil nisi malum eligere possunt: quoniam liberrimo voluntatis proposito illi tantum bonum, isti tantum malum eligunt. Sic non-renati liberrimè eligunt malum: & moralia etiam, quæ externè faciunt, sunt mala: quia odium Dei in corde retinent.
units.tr: From what has been said about the degrees of human freedom it appears that it is a slander to say that we take away free choice from man, because we teach that a person in the state of sin can choose nothing but what is evil before God. For even the unregenerate choose evil most freely in the state of sin. Free choice is not taken away in God, or in the angels, who can choose nothing but good, nor in evil spirits, who can choose nothing but evil, since by the most free purpose of the will the former choose only good and the latter only evil. So the unregenerate freely choose evil, and even their moral acts, which they perform outwardly, are evil, because they retain hatred of God in their heart.

units.la: QVÆSTIO IX.
units.tr: QUESTION IX.

units.la: An igitur Deus homini iniuriam facit, qui ab eo in Lege sua flagitat, quæ præstare non queat? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Does God then do wrong to man when he demands of him in his Law what man cannot perform? ANSWER.

units.la: Minimè a. Nam Deus hominem talem condiderat, vt ea præstare posset: verum homo, impulsore diabolo b, sua ipsius contumacia, se & omnem posteritatem diuinis illis donis orbauit c.
units.tr: Certainly not a. For God had created man such that he was able to perform those things; but man, through the instigation of the devil b and by his own obstinacy, deprived himself and all his posterity of those divine gifts c.

units.la: a Genes.1.v.17. Eccles.7,30. Ephes.4,24. b Genes.3,1.7. 2 Cor.11, v.3. c Genes.3,6.7. Rom.5,12.
units.tr: a Genes.1.v.17. Eccles.7,30. Ephes.4,24. b Genes.3,1.7. 2 Cor.11, v.3. c Genes.3,6.7. Rom.5,12.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Est obiectio humanæ rationis contra præcedentem quæstionem. Si homo adeo est corruptus, vt non sit idoneus ad aliquid benè agendum, videtur Deus injustè ab eo requirere perfectam obedientiam in Lege. Qui enim postulat impossibile, est injustus. Deus ab homine in Lege postulat perfectam obedientiam, quam præstare non potest. Ergo videtur injustus. Resp. ad maiorem. Qui præcipit impossibile, est injustus, videlicet nisi prius dederit possibilitatem. Deinde, nisi homo impossibilitatem sibi sponte attraxerit, & eam etiam velit. Postremò, nisi præceptio impossibilis sit stimulus ad agnoscendam & deplorandam impossibilitatem. Deus verò homini creato ad imaginem suam dederat facultatem præstandi ea, quæ pro suo jure ab eo requirit. Quod si homo sua voluntate & culpa abjecit suum bonum, & sibi impossibilitatem obediendi Deo attraxit; non propterea etiam Deus amisit suum jus ab eo exigendi obedientiam debitam. Immò quia nos illud bonum abjecimus, mandatum Dei transgrediendo, & quia Deus transgressoribus minatus est poenas, ideo juste nos luimus.
units.tr: This is an objection raised by human reason against the preceding question. If man is so corrupted that he is not fit to do anything well, it seems that God unjustly requires of him perfect obedience in the Law. For he who demands the impossible is unjust. God demands of man in the Law perfect obedience, which man cannot render. Therefore God seems unjust. Answer to the major premise: he who commands the impossible is unjust, namely unless he has first given the possibility; and further, unless man has voluntarily drawn the impossibility upon himself and is willing to have it; and lastly, unless the impossible command serves as a goad to make him acknowledge and lament his impossibility. But God had given to man, created in his own image, the ability to perform those things which he by his right requires of him. If man by his own will and fault cast away his good and drew upon himself the inability to obey God, God has not on that account lost his right to demand the obedience owed to him. Indeed, because we cast away that good by transgressing God's command, and because God has threatened punishments to transgressors, we have therefore justly paid the penalty.

units.la: Inst. 1. Atqui nos peccatum non attraximus. Resp. Primi parentes lapsi amiserunt possibilitatem sibi & omnibus posteris: quia eam pro se & pro posteritate acceperant. Vasallus deficiens à Principe, feudum sibi & posteris amittit: & Princeps liberis eius non facit injuriam, si non restituit feudum patris culpâ amissum: si restituit, ex gratia facit.
units.tr: Objection 1. But we did not bring sin upon ourselves. Answer. Our first parents, having fallen, lost the ability for themselves and for all their posterity, because they had received it for themselves and for their posterity. A vassal who revolts from his prince loses the fief for himself and his descendants; and the prince does no wrong to his children if he does not restore a fief lost through the father's fault; if he restores it, he does so out of grace.

units.la: Inst. 2. Qui præcipit impossibilia, frustra præcipit. Deus præcipit impossibilia homini post lapsum. Ergo frustra. Resp. Primò est fallacia à dicto secundum quid. Deus non frustra præcipit, etsi nos non præstemus, quod præcipit: quia sunt etiam alij fines præcepti, tam in piis, quàm impiis. A piis enim postulat, 1. Ut agnoscant suam impossibilitatem. Per legem agnitio peccati. 2. Ut sciant, quales fuerint ante lapsum. 3. Ut sciant, quid principaliter à Deo petere debeant, nempe renovationem naturæ. 4. Ut intelligant, quid Christus nobis præstiterit, nempe, quod pro nobis satisfecerit; & nos regeneret. 5. Ut inchoetur in nobis nova obedientia, quia docet, quomodo nos vicissim erga Deum pro liberationis beneficio gerere debeamus, seu, quid Deus vicissim à nobis postulet. Impiis vero præcipitur obedientia, 1. Ut manifestetur justitia Dei in eis damnandis, quia sciunt, quid facere debeant. Quando igitur id non faciunt, juste damnantur: Servus sciens voluntatem Domini, & non faciens, &c. 2. Ut conservetur externa disciplina. 3. Ut convertantur conuertendi.
units.tr: Objection 2. He who commands impossible things commands in vain. God commands man after the fall impossible things. Therefore in vain. Answer. First, this is the fallacy of arguing from a statement taken without qualification. God does not command in vain, even though we do not perform what he commands, because there are other ends of the command, both in the godly and in the ungodly. In the godly, indeed, he requires: (1) that they acknowledge their own inability, Through the law comes the knowledge of sin; (2) that they know what they were like before the fall; (3) that they know what they ought chiefly to ask of God, namely the renewal of nature; (4) that they understand what Christ has done for us, namely that he made satisfaction for us and regenerates us; (5) that a new obedience may begin in us, because the law teaches how we in turn ought to conduct ourselves toward God for the benefit of deliverance, or, what God in turn requires of us. In the ungodly, however, obedience is commanded: (1) that the justice of God may be shown in condemning them, because they know what they ought to do; therefore when they do not do it, they are justly condemned: The servant who knows his lord's will and does not do it, etc.; (2) that external discipline may be preserved; (3) that those who are to be converted may be converted.

units.la: Secundò, ad maiorem per distinctionem. Qui præcipit impossibilia, scilicet non simul dans impossibilitatem, frustra præcipit. At Deus præcipiendo electis, etiam dat facultatem obediendi, per doctrinam Euangelij, eam nunc inchoans, & tandem perficiens. Augustinus: Da quod jubes, & jube quod vis, & non frustra jubebis. Ergo hæc postulatio impossibilis est maximum beneficium, quia est via ad recipiendam possibilitatem.
units.tr: Secondly, as to the major premise, by distinction. He who commands impossible things, that is, without at the same time giving the ability, commands in vain. But God, in commanding the elect, also gives them the ability to obey through the doctrine of the Gospel, beginning it now and at length bringing it to perfection. Augustine: Give what you command, and command what you will, and you will not command in vain. Therefore this demand, though impossible, is the greatest benefit, because it is the way to receiving the ability.

units.la: QUÆSTIO X. Num Deus hanc contumaciam & defectionem hominis dimittit impunitam?
units.tr: QUESTION X. Does God leave this contumacy and defection of man unpunished?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Immò verò horrendis modis infcitur a, cùm obin-nata nobis peccata, tum ob ea, quæ ipsimet committi-mus: eaque justissimo judicio temporalibus & æternis supplicis punit b: quemadmodum ipse pronunciat: Maledictus omnis, qui non permanet in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, ut ea faciat c.
units.tr: Indeed, God inflicts punishment in dreadful ways, both for the sins we are born with and for those we ourselves commit. In his most just judgment he punishes them with temporal and eternal torments, as he himself declares: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things that are written in the book of the Law, to do them."

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Sequitur de altera parte humanæ naturæ, seu de malo pœnæ & docetur, quod Deus grauissimè, justissimè & certissimè puniat peccata. Grauissimè: quia præsentibus & æternis pœnis, propter magnitudinem peccati, quo infinitum bonum offensum est. Iustissimè: quia omne etiam minimum peccatum violat Legem Dei, ideoque ex ordine justitiæ diuinæ pœnam æternam & abiectionem meretur. Certissimè: quia Deus est verax, nec mutat sententiam semel pronunciatam in Lege: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, &c.
units.tr: Next comes the other side of human nature, namely the evil of punishment, and it is taught that God punishes sins most severely, most justly and most certainly. Most severely, because he inflicts present and eternal punishments on account of the greatness of sin, by which an infinite good is offended. Most justly, because every sin, even the smallest, violates the Law of God, and therefore by the order of divine justice deserves eternal punishment and rejection. Most certainly, because God is true and does not change a sentence once pronounced in the Law: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things," and so on.

units.la: Obj. 1. Impij hic florent, & multa impunè faciunt. Ergo non omnia peccata puniuntur. Resp. Tandem punientur: immò & hic puniuntur: 1. In conscientia, cuius morsibus torquentur impij. 2. Etiam in iis, quibus vtuntur cum maxima voluptate: & quidem tanto magis, quanto minus agnoscunt se puniri. 3. Sæpe etiam aliis grauissimis pœnis: grauioribus vero in altera vita; vbi erit perpetua mors, non mortuum esse.
units.tr: Objection 1. The wicked flourish here and do many things with impunity. Therefore not all sins are punished. Answer: They will be punished in the end; indeed, they are punished even here: (1) in their conscience, by whose stings the wicked are tormented; (2) also in those things which they enjoy with the greatest pleasure, and all the more so the less they recognize that they are being punished; (3) often also with very grievous punishments, and more grievous ones in the next life, where there will be perpetual death, not the state of being dead.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Deus non fecit mortem. Ergo non punièt peccata tam grauiter. Resp. Deus quidem mortem non fecit in principio: quia mors non est creatura Dei, nec est ens, sed destructio entis. Peccato tamen admisso Deus mortem pro pœna justo judicio inflixit peccantibus, juxta comminationem: Morte morieris. Genes.2,17.
units.tr: Objection 2. God did not make death. Therefore he will not punish sins so severely. Answer: God indeed did not make death in the beginning, because death is not a creature of God, nor is it a being, but the destruction of being. Yet once sin had been committed, God, according to his threat, "Thou shalt die the death" (Gen. 2:17), inflicted death as a punishment on those who sinned, by a just judgment.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Deus non est injustus: nec idem bis punit. Ergo non puniet peccata præsentibus & æternis supplicis. Respond. Maior omissa est falsa. Pœna enim, quam Deus impiis in hac & altera vita infligit, est vna pœna, gradus vel partes habens. Præ-sensentes enim poenæ sunt tantum initium æternarum, nec sunt poena separata vel integra, quia non sunt sufficientes ad satisfaciendum justitiæ Dei.
units.tr: Objection 3. God is not unjust, nor does he punish the same thing twice. Therefore he will not punish sins with present and eternal torments. Answer: The major premise omitted is false. For the punishment which God inflicts on the impious in this life and in the other is one punishment, having degrees or parts. For the punishments felt now are only the beginning of the eternal ones, and they are not a separate or complete punishment, because they are not sufficient to satisfy the justice of God.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Imparia peccata non sunt pari poena punienda: ergo non omnia peccata sunt punienda æternis suppliciis Resp. Est plus in conclusione, quàm &c. Tantum hoc sequitur: Ergo non omnia peccata sunt pari poena punienda: quod est verum. Omnia verò peccata etiam minima merentur æternâ poenam, quia omnia delinquunt in æternũ & immensum bonum. Ergo quoad durationem, omnia quidem peccata pariter punientur, sed non quoad poenarum gradus. Grauiora enim grauioribus poenis, leniora lenioribus in æternum punientur.
units.tr: Objection 4. Unequal sins are not to be punished with equal punishment; therefore not all sins are to be punished with eternal torments. Answer: The conclusion says more than this does. What follows is only this: therefore not all sins are to be punished with equal punishment, which is true. But all sins, even the smallest, deserve eternal punishment, because all offend against an eternal and immense good. Therefore, as regards duration, all sins are indeed punished alike, but not as regards degrees of punishment. For greater sins will be punished with greater punishments, and lesser ones with lesser punishments, for ever.

units.la: Obj. 5. Si Deus peccata punit æternis poenis: Ergo perimus omnes, aut justitiæ Dei non satisfit. R. Sanè cogeremur omnes perire, si Deus peccata in nobis puniret. Verum non punit ea in nobis suppliciis æternis, nec tamen violatur eius justitia, quoniam peccata nostra poena æternis suppliciis æquivalente punit in Christo. Hæc est ιπσεxια, quam Euangelium addit Legi. Inst. Si punit in Christo, & est justus, non debet amplius punire in nobis. Injustè igitur pij affliguntur in hac vita. Resp. Afflictio- nes piorum non sunt poena aut satisfactio pro peccatis, sed tantum erux & castigationes paternæ, quibus ad humilitatem erudiuntur. Hic igitur de afflictionibus dicendum: sed prius explicanda est sequens quæstio.
units.tr: Objection 5. If God punishes sins with eternal punishments, then either we all perish or the justice of God is not satisfied. Answer: Certainly we would all have to perish if God punished sins in us. But he does not punish them in us with eternal torments, and yet his justice is not violated, since he punishes our sins in Christ with a punishment equivalent to eternal torments. This is the exchange (antidosis) which the Gospel adds to the Law. Objection: If he punished in Christ and is just, he ought not to punish again in us. Therefore the godly are unjustly afflicted in this life. Answer: The afflictions of the godly are not punishment or satisfaction for sins, but only the fatherly chastisements and corrections by which they are trained to humility. Therefore the afflictions must be discussed here; but first the following question must be explained.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XI.
units.tr: QUESTION XI.

units.la: An non igitur Deus etiam est misericors? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Is not God therefore also merciful? ANSWER.

units.la: Est ille quidem misericors a, sed ita, ut etiam sit justus b. Quapropter postulat eius justitia, ut quod adversus summam Dei maiestatem commissum est, id etiam summis, hoc est, sempiternis cum animi tum corporis suppliciis luatur.
units.tr: He is indeed merciful a, but in such a way that he is also just b. Therefore his justice requires that what has been committed against the supreme majesty of God be atoned for with supreme, that is, eternal, punishments of both soul and body.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Obiectio contra id, quod Deus omne peccatum æternis suppliciis puniat. Summè misericordis est, remittere aliquid de summo iure. Deus est summè misericors. Ergo aliquid remittet de summo iure. jure, nec puniet peccata æternis pœnis. Resp. ad maiorem. Est misericordis aliquid remittere, sed citra violationem suæ justitiæ, idem sit summè justus. Sic igitur vult exercere misericordiam, vt justitiam non violet. Postulat autem Dei justitia, vt omnia peccata aduersus summam eius maiestatem admissa, summis, hoc est, sempiternis animi & corporis supplicis luantur, vt sit culpæ & pœnæ proportio. Crimen n. tanto est grauius, & tanto grauiorem meretur pœnam, quanto maior est is, qui eo lœditur.
units.tr: The objection against the claim that God punishes every sin with eternal punishments runs: It belongs to supreme mercy to remit something of supreme right. God is supremely merciful. Therefore he will remit something of his supreme right, and will not punish sins with eternal penalties. Answer to the major premise: it belongs to mercy to remit something, but without violating his justice, since he is equally supremely just. So God wills to exercise mercy in such a way that he does not violate justice. Now God's justice requires that all sins committed against his supreme majesty be atoned for with supreme, that is, eternal, punishments of soul and body, so that there is a proportion between guilt and punishment. For a crime is the more grave, and deserves the more grave punishment, the greater the one who is injured by it.

units.la: Inst. 1. Stricta justitia non consistit cum summa misericordia. In Deo est summa misericordia. E. cum ea non consistit in Deo summa justitia. Resp. Maior negatur. Probatur. Summa misericordia admittit ἐπιείκειαν. Sed hanc non admittit stricta justitia, qualis in Deo est. Ergo, &c. Resp. Etiam Dei justitia admittit ἐπιείκειαν, non omittendo, sed transferendo pœnam in alium.
units.tr: Objection 1. Strict justice does not agree with supreme mercy. In God there is supreme mercy. Therefore supreme justice does not agree with it in God. Answer: the major is denied. Proof: supreme mercy admits of epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν], but strict justice, such as is in God, does not admit it. Therefore, etc. Answer: God's justice also admits of epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν], not by omitting the punishment but by transferring it to another.

units.la: Inst. 2. Qui stricte vult jus suum exequi, apud eum non habet locum ἐπιείκειαν. Deus stricte exsequitur jus suum. Ergo &c. Vel hoc modo: Qui nihil remittit de summo jure, is non misericors, sed tantum justus est. Deus nihil remittit de summo jure: quia omnia peccata punit sufficienti pœna. Resp. Primo negatur minor. Deus enim de stricto jure multum remittit, tametsi æternis pœnis omnia peccata puniat. Nam quod ad reprobos attinet, magnam adhibet ἐπιείκειαν, dum & nunc pœnas differt, & multis eos beneficiis ad pœnitentiam inuitat, & in ipsa pœnarum æternitate lenius, quam merebantur, eos puniet, &c. Quod ad electos, summam rursus ἐπιείκειαν adhibet, quia dat nobis Filium suum, & hunc pro nobis pœnæ subijcit, ex mera misericordia, nullo jure aut merito nostro ad hoc obligatus. Deinde maior negatur de eo, qui ea sit sapientia præditus, vt possit invenire modum exercendi misericordiam, salua sua justitia: item de eo, qui dum exequitur justitiam, non gaudet tamen hominis destructione, sed mallet eum esse salvum: vt cum judex latronem equuleo dignum contundit rota; nec gaudet eius supplicio; & licet summum jus videatur exequi, tamen ἐπιείκειαν adhibet. Multo magis Deus cum justitia ἐπιείκειαν adhibet. Nam destructione impiorum non delectatur (quia non vult mortem peccatoris) & electorum peccata puniuit in Filio.
units.tr: Objection 2. He who wishes to enforce his right strictly has no room for epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν] with him. God enforces his right strictly. Therefore, etc. Or in this way: he who remits nothing of his supreme right is not merciful but only just. God remits nothing of his supreme right, because he punishes all sins with a sufficient penalty. Answer: first, the minor is denied. For God remits a great deal of his strict right, although he punishes all sins with eternal punishments. As for the reprobate, he shows great epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν], since he both defers their punishments now, and invites them to repentance by many benefits, and in the very eternity of their punishments he will punish them more leniently than they deserved, etc. As for the elect, again he shows supreme epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν], since he gives us his Son and subjects him to punishment for us, out of pure mercy, himself bound by no right or merit of ours to do so. Next, the major is denied concerning one who is endowed with such wisdom that he can find a way of exercising mercy while keeping his justice intact; likewise concerning one who, while executing justice, nevertheless does not rejoice in the destruction of a man, but would prefer him to be saved. For example, when a judge who has condemned a thief to the wheel does not rejoice in his punishment, and although he seems to enforce the supreme right, nevertheless shows epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν]. Much more does God show epieikeia [ἐπιείκειαν] together with justice. For he takes no delight in the destruction of the wicked (because he does not desire the death of a sinner), and he has punished the sins of the elect in his Son.

units.la: De Afflictionibus.
units.tr: On Afflictions.

units.la: De afflictionibus tres sunt præcipuè quæstiones: I. Quæ sint earum genera. II. Quæ sint causa. III. Quæ consolationes iis opponenda.
units.tr: There are three principal questions about afflictions: I. What kinds of them there are. II. What their causes are. III. What consolations are to be set against them.

units.la: Quæ sint afflictionum genera?
units.tr: What kinds of afflictions are there?

units.la: Afflictionum aliæ sunt æternæ, aliæ temporales. Æterna sunt cruciatus animi & corporis perpetuò duraturi, & nunquam finiendi, in quos abijciendi sunt omnes diaboli & homines impij, qui in hac vita ad Deum non conuertuntur. Vocantur in scriptura gehenna, ignis, vermis, cruciatus, mors æterna: quia cruciatus erunt perpetui, & quales sunt morientium, qui semper-moriendo mori nunquam possunt. Nam mors æterna erit sem-per-mori, & nunquam mortuum esse: seu continuatio mortis cum accessione cruciatuum in infinitum. Testimonia scripturæ, quod sint pœnæ æternæ: Vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur. Bonum est tibi ad vitam ingredi mancum potius, quàm duas habentem manus abire in gehennam, in ignem inextinguibilem, vbi vermis eorum non interit, & ignis non extinguitur. Abite in ignem æternum, qui paratus est diabolis & angelis eius. Si justus vix seruatur, impius & peccator vbi comparebunt? Ratio etiam est euidens: quia pro peccato in bonum infinitum commisso postulatur infinita pœna, quandoquidem per pœnam creaturæ temporalem, non satisfieret infinitæ justitiæ DEI.
units.tr: Some afflictions are eternal, others temporal. The eternal ones are torments of soul and body that will last forever and never end, into which all the devil's angels and all impious men who are not converted to God in this life will be cast. In Scripture they are called gehenna, fire, worm, torment, eternal death: because the torments will be perpetual, and like those of the dying, who, though always dying, can never die. For eternal death will be an always-dying and never being dead: that is, a continuation of death with the addition of torments without end. Scripture testifies that the punishments are eternal: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched. It is better for you to enter life maimed rather than, having two hands, to go into gehenna, into the unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels. If the righteous are scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear? The reason is also plain: for a sin committed against an infinite good an infinite punishment is required, since a temporal punishment of a creature would not satisfy the infinite justice of God.

units.la: Pœnas æternas esse animæ & corporis, testatur Christus: Metuite eum, qui potest perdere corpus & animam in gehenna ignis, &c. Anima est fons peccatorum. Corpus organum animæ exsequitur, quod anima suggerit. Ergo author & instrumentum simul puniuntur.
units.tr: Christ testifies that the punishments are of both soul and body: Fear him who can destroy both body and soul in the fire of gehenna, etc. The soul is the fountain of sins. The body carries out what the soul prompts, as its organ. Therefore author and instrument are punished together.

units.la: Obiect. Qui est summè misericors, non potest videre æternos cruciatus suarum creaturarum, nedum infligere. Dei misericordia est summa, & maior peccatis, &c. Ergo, &c. Resp. Maior vera est de eo, qui non simul est summè justus. De Deo summe & misericorde & justo, est falsa, vt supra est demonstratum.
units.tr: Objection. He who is supremely merciful cannot look upon the eternal torments of his creatures, much less inflict them. The mercy of God is supreme and greater than sins, etc. Therefore, etc. Answer. The major premise is true of one who is not at the same time supremely just. It is false of God, who is supremely merciful and also just, as has been shown above.

units.la: Temporales afflictiones communes sunt piis & impiis, morbi, paupertas, contemtus, calumniæ, oppressiones, exilia, & aliæ huius vitæ miseriæ, denique mors ipsa temporalis. Hæc sunt vel pœna, vel crux. POENA est destructio & cruciatus à DEO inflictus ex ordine justitiæ propter peccatum. Estque reproborum propria, quia infligitur eis hoc fine, vt satisfiat justitiæ DEI. Lex enim omnes obligat ad obedientiam, vel ad pœnam.
units.tr: Temporal afflictions are common to the godly and the ungodly: sicknesses, poverty, contempt, slander, oppressions, exiles, and the other miseries of this life, and finally temporal death itself. These are either punishment or cross. PUNISHMENT is destruction and torment inflicted by God in the order of justice on account of sin. It belongs properly to the reprobate, because it is inflicted on them with this end, that the justice of God may be satisfied. For the law binds all men either to obedience or to punishment.

units.la: Obiect. Impiorum pœnæ in hac vita sunt longè minores, quàm vt satisfaciant justitiæ Dei. Resp. Etsi non sunt tota pœna, sunt tamen pars pœnæ, & initium satisfactionis, quæ ab eis in æteræternum exigitur. Sicut autem pars aëris dicitur aër, sic pars pœnæ dicitur pœna. Sunt autem gradus pœnarum Primus est in hac vita. Nam cum impios rodit conscientia, jam incipit vermis infernalis. Secundus in morte temporali. Nam tunc incipiunt sentire iram Dei, quando anima separatur à corpore sine consolatione, & in locum tormenti detruditur. Tertius erit in judicio extremo, quando corpus & anima simul abijcietur in gehennam; & in omnes impios, infernales & æternæ pœnæ quasi agmine facto irruent.
units.tr: Objection. The punishments of the impious in this life are far too small to satisfy the justice of God. Answer. Although they are not the whole punishment, they are nevertheless a part of the punishment and a beginning of the satisfaction which is demanded from them to all eternity. Just as a part of the air is called air, so a part of punishment is called punishment. There are, however, degrees of punishment. The first is in this life: for when conscience gnaws at the impious, the infernal worm already begins. The second is in temporal death: for then they begin to feel the wrath of God, when the soul is separated from the body without consolation and is thrust into the place of torment. The third will be at the final judgment, when body and soul together are cast into gehenna, and, as in a gathered host, eternal infernal punishments rush upon all the impious.

units.la: CRVX est piorum afflictio, quæ proprie non est pœna: quia non infligitur, vt fit satisfactio pro peccatis. Crucis autem piorum sunt quatuor species, finibus distinctæ.
units.tr: The CROSS is the affliction of the godly, which is not properly punishment, because it is not inflicted so as to make satisfaction for sins. There are four kinds of the godly's cross, distinguished by their ends.

units.la: 1. Τιμωρίαι, sunt castigationes, quas Deus infligit propter ipsorum peccata, sed secundum misericordiam suam, vt pater filium delinquentem leniter castigat, secundum παιδείαν: ideoq; proprie non sunt pœnæ, sed castigationes paternæ, quibus admonentur pij suæ immunditiei, suorum peccatorum & lapsuum peculiarium, excitantur ad pœnitentiam, & revocantur in viam; vt Dauid ejicitur in exilium propter lapsum. Singularia enim peccata sequuntur singulares & graues τιμωρίαι etiam in sanctis. Neque sunt compensatio peccati, sed sunt opera diuinæ justitiæ, per quæ Deus nos & alios vult admonere de sua justitia, se verè irasci peccatis, & non solum in hac vita, verum etiam in altera, morte ea puniturum esse, nisi fieret ad Deum conuersio. Apostolus 1 Cor.11, 32. vocat παιδεία castigationem seu disciplinam filialem. Κρινόμενοι δὲ παιδευόμεθα: Cum judicamur, à Domino castigamur.
units.tr: 1. Timoriai [τιμωρίαι] are chastisements which God inflicts because of their sins, but in his mercy, as a father gently chastises a erring son, in the manner of paideia [παιδεία]. Therefore they are properly not punishments but paternal corrections, by which the godly are admonished of their uncleanness, of their particular sins and falls, are stirred to repentance, and are called back into the way; as David was driven into exile because of his fall. For particular sins are followed by particular and grievous timoriai even in the saints. Nor are they a compensation for sin, but they are works of divine justice, by which God wishes to admonish us and others of his justice: that he truly is angry at sins, and that he will punish them not only in this life but also in the next, with death, unless conversion to God takes place. The Apostle, 1 Cor. 11:32, calls paideia [παιδεία] castigation or filial discipline: Κρινόμενοι δὲ παιδευόμεθα [Krinomenoi de paideuometha]: When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord.

units.la: 2. Δοκιμασίαι, sunt examina & probationes fidei, spei, invocationis, timoris Dei, & patientiæ sanctorum, vt in his virtutibus proficiant. Sæpe etiam, vt infirmitas eorum ipsis & aliis innotescat. Talis fuit afflictio Jobi.
units.tr: 2. Dokimasiai [δοκιμασίαι] are examinations and trials of faith, hope, invocation, fear of God, and the patience of the saints, so that they may make progress in these virtues. Often also so that their weakness may be made known to themselves and to others. Such was the affliction of Job.

units.la: 3. Μαρτύρια, sunt testificationes sanctorum de doctrina: cum pij suo sanguine obsignant doctrinam, quam sunt professi, quod sit vera & divina, & quod ipsi in media morte experiantur inde consolationem, quam aliis docendo promittebant, quodq; restet alia vita, & aliud judicium post hanc vitam.
units.tr: 3. Martyria [μαρτύρια] are the testimonies of the saints concerning doctrine: when the godly seal with their own blood the doctrine which they have professed, that it is true and divine, and that they themselves in the midst of death experience from it the consolation which they had promised to others by teaching, and that another life remains, and another judgment after this life.

units.la: 4. Λύτρον, est solius Christi obedientia, qua satisfecit pro peccatis nostris, & quæ in tota eius humilitate, inde ab articulo conceptionis, ad extremum usque agonem in cruce consistit.
units.tr: 4. Lytron [λύτρον] is the obedience of Christ alone, by which he made satisfaction for our sins, and which consists in the whole of his humiliation, from the article of his conception to the last agony on the cross.

units.la: II. Quæ sint afflictionum causæ.
units.tr: II. What are the causes of afflictions?

units.la: In impiis causæ pœnarum sunt: 1. Peccatum, causa impulsiva. Puniuntur enim, vt peccatum justa pœna compensetur. 2. Ju2. Justitia Dei, causa efficiens principalis, infligens poenas propter peccatum. 3. Instrumentales sunt variæ, angeli & homines, boni vel mali, & aliæ creaturæ, quæ omnes aduersus peccantes armantur, & Deo militant
units.tr: The causes of punishments in the wicked are: 1. Sin, the impelling cause. For they are punished so that sin may be repaid with a just penalty. 2. The justice of God, the principal efficient cause, inflicting punishments on account of sin. 3. The instrumental causes are various: angels and men, good and bad, and other creatures. All of these are armed against sinners and fight on God's side.

units.la: Crucis piorum causæ sunt:
units.tr: The causes of the crosses of the godly are:

units.la: 1. Peccatum: aliter tamen quàm in impiis. Pij enim affliguntur propter peccatum, non vt satisfiat justitiæ Dei, sed vt peccatum ab iis agnoscatur, & per crucem expurgetur: castigantur paternè, vt agnoscant lapsus: sunt conciones poenitentiæ: Gott zeigt ihnen em wenig/was sie verdient hatten: hoc est, Deus illis ostendit, quid promeriti sint. Cùm judicamur, à Domino corripimur, ne cum mundo pereamus. Bonum est mihi Domine, quod humiliasti me. Impiis Deus laxat fræna, vt ruant in exitium. Afficit eos commodis huius vitæ, breui quidem cum gaudio, quia sunt creaturæ, vt conuincat eos ingratitudinis, & reddat ἀνάπο- λογήτους. Pios verò per crucem emendat.
units.tr: 1. Sin, though in a different way than in the wicked. For the godly are afflicted on account of sin, not so that God's justice may be satisfied, but so that they may recognise their sin and have it purged away through the cross. They are chastised as a father chastises, so that they may acknowledge their lapses. These afflictions are sermons of repentance: God shows them a little of what they had deserved. When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not perish with the world. It is good for me, O Lord, that you have humbled me. God loosens the reins for the wicked, so that they rush headlong to ruin. He indulges them with the comforts of this life, indeed with joy for a short time, because they are creatures, so that he may convict them of ingratitude and make them inexcusable [ἀνάπολογήτους]. But he amends the godly through the cross.

units.la: 2. Vt discamus odisse peccatum, diabolum & mundum. Si de mundo essetis, mundus vos diligeret. Non est nobis lucta aduersus carnem & sanguinem, sed aduersus imperia & potestates. Ne diligatis mundum.
units.tr: 2. That we may learn to hate sin, the devil and the world. If you were of the world, the world would love you. Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers. Do not love the world.

units.la: 3. Exercitatio seu probatio, vt proficiamus in fide, spe, patientia, obedientia, inuocatione, seu vt habeamus materiam nos exercendi, & vt manifesta fiat nobis & aliis spes, fides & patientia nostra. Nam rebus secundis facilis est gloriatio de fide: in aduersis elucet virtutis decus: Qui non est tentatus, qualia scit? Probatio spem efficit.
units.tr: 3. Exercise, or trial, so that we may make progress in faith, hope, patience, obedience and prayer; or so that we may have material for exercising ourselves; and so that our hope, faith and patience may become manifest to ourselves and to others. For in prosperity it is easy to boast of faith; in adversity the glory of virtue shines forth. He who has not been tested, what does he know? Trial produces hope.

units.la: 4. Lapsus peculiares in sanctis. Manasses sua habuit peccata, sua Josaphat, & alij alios habent lapsus: ideo castigationes sunt diuersæ, quibus ostendit Deus, quod etiam sanctorum peccatis irascatur, & ea grauius sit vlturus, nisi resipiscant. Servus sciens voluntatem domini, nec faciens, cædetur multis plagis.
units.tr: 4. Particular lapses in the saints. Manasseh had his sins, Jehoshaphat had his, and others have other lapses. Therefore the chastisements differ, by which God shows that he is angry even at the sins of the saints, and that he will avenge them more severely unless they repent. The servant who knows his master's will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows.

units.la: 5. Patefactio & illustratio gloriæ Dei in liberationibus ecclesiæ & piorum. Vt enim liberatio sit gloriosior, sæpe Deus suos adducit in extrema pericula: vt in Ægypto Babylone, &c. vt gloriosè liberet, & ostendat, se inuenisse liberationis modum, vbi nulla creatura poterat sperare. Dominus deducit ad inferos, & reducit.
units.tr: 5. The disclosure and illustration of God's glory in the deliverances of the Church and of the godly. For so that a deliverance may be more glorious, God often brings his people into the greatest dangers, as in Egypt, in Babylon, and so on, so that he may deliver them gloriously and show that he has found a way of deliverance where no creature could hope for one. The Lord brings down to the grave, and brings up again.

units.la: 6. Conformitas membrorum cum capite Christo in æru- mnis & in gloria. Si toleramus, etiam cum eo regnabimus. Quos præscivit, eosdem & prædestinauit, vt conformes fiant imaginì Filij sui. Non est seruus maior Domino suo, nec discipulus supra magistrum.
units.tr: 6. The conformity of the members with their head, Christ, in sufferings and in glory. If we endure, we shall also reign with him. Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. The servant is not greater than his lord, nor the disciple above his teacher.

units.la: E 4 7.Testi7.Testificatio de doctrina in martyriis. Dum enim pij confessionis causa mala & ipsam mortem patiuntur, satis ostendunt se de huius doctrinæ veritate ita esse convictos, ut sine offensione Dei ab ea nullo modo discedere possint: & hanc doctrinam in ipsa morte firmam suppeditare consolationem; eoque veram esse. Petro prædicitur, qua morte Deum esset glorificaturus. Ergo martyria sunt Dei glorificatio.
units.tr: 7. Testimony to the doctrine in martyrdoms. For when the godly suffer evils, and even death itself, for the sake of confession, they sufficiently show that they are so convinced of the truth of this doctrine that they cannot in any way depart from it without offending God; and that this doctrine supplies firm comfort even in death itself, and is therefore true. It was foretold to Peter by what death he would glorify God. Therefore martyrdoms are the glorification of God.

units.la: 8. Afflictiones piorum sunt ὑπόδειγμα futuri judicij & vitæ æternæ. Postulat enim justitia & veritas Dei, ut tandem boni bene, malis male sit. Hoc non fit in hac vita: restat igitur alia. Quæres manifesto est in licio justi judicij Dei.
units.tr: 8. The afflictions of the godly are an example [ὑπόδειγμα] of the future judgment and eternal life. For the justice and truth of God demand that at last it go well with the good and badly with the wicked. This does not happen in this life; something else therefore remains. This becomes manifest in the light of God's just judgment.

units.la: Ex his causis respondendum est ad argumentum mundi contra providentiam Dei. Ecclesia in toto mundo concutitur & conculcatur ab omnibus: Ergo non est vera ecclesia, nec à Deo curatur. Resp. Immò quia affligitur ab impiis, Ecclesia vera esse deprehenditur. Si enim de mundo esset, mundus quod suum esset, amaret. Causæ crucis Ecclesiæ manifestæ sunt: mundum verò exitus aliquando refutab t.
units.tr: From these causes we must answer the argument of the world against God's providence. The Church is shaken and trampled upon by everyone throughout the whole world; therefore it is not the true Church, nor is it cared for by God. Answer: On the contrary, because it is afflicted by the wicked, the true Church is shown to be such. For if it were of the world, the world would love what was its own. The causes of the Church's cross are plain; but the outcome will one day refute the world.

units.la: III. Consolationes afflictionibus opponendæ.
units.tr: III. Consolations to be set against afflictions

units.la: Consolationes in afflictionibus aliæ sunt Ecclesiæ propriæ, aliæ Ecclesiæ cum Philosophia communes. Propriæ sunt prima & duæ postremæ. Reliquæ communes: idque tantum, quoad titulos, non quoad explicationem. Propriæ igitur sunt:
units.tr: The consolations in afflictions are some proper to the Church and others common to the Church and philosophy. The first and the last two are proper. The rest are common, and that only as to their headings, not as to their explanation. The proper ones, therefore, are:

units.la: 1. Remissio peccatorum. Hæc est prima & fundamentum reliquarum: quia sine hac aliæ nos non consolantur, incertos de reconciliatione cum Deo: semper alioqui dubitamus, an etiam ad nos pertineat promissio gratiæ. Si autem hæc bene sit posita, reliquæ sponte sequuntur. Si enim Deus est Pater noster, nihil nobis immittet damnosum, & in malis nos defendet. Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Ratio est: quia sublatâ causâ tollitur effectus. Sublato igitur peccato tolluntur pœnæ & mors.
units.tr: 1. The remission of sins. This is first and is the foundation of the rest; for without it the others do not console us, since we are uncertain of reconciliation with God. We always doubt whether the promise of grace pertains to us too. But if this is rightly laid down, the rest follow of their own accord. For if God is our Father, he will send us nothing harmful and will defend us in evils. If God is for us, who is against us? The reason is that when the cause is removed, the effect is removed. Therefore, sin being taken away, punishments and death are taken away.

units.la: 2. Voluntas Dei & providentia, seu necessitas obediendi Deo in secundis & adversis, quia Deus vult. Ratio consequentiæ est non solum, quia non possumus ei resistere, sed præcipuè, quia Pater noster. Ergo debemus ei obtemperare. 2. Quia sic debemus ei nobis est meritus, ut multo etiam graviora ferre in eius gratiam velle debeamus. 3. Quia mala, quæ immittit, sunt castigationes. Hæc consolatio placat animum: quia significat, Patrem nostrum velle hoc pati. Etsi occiderit me, tamen sperabo in eum. Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est: sit nomen Domini benedictum. dictum. Tacui, quia tu fecisti. Philosophi dicunt, patienter ferendum, quod mutari non potest: statuunt fatalem necessitatem: non igitur contra stimulum calcitrandum esse. Sed in calamitatibus non subijciunt se Deo, non agnoscunt iram Dei, nec aduersa patiuntur, vt Deo obtemperent, sed quia excutere non possunt.
units.tr: 2. The will of God and his providence, that is, the necessity of obeying God in prosperity and adversity, because God wills it. The ground of this consequence is not only that we cannot resist him, but chiefly that he is our Father; therefore we ought to obey him. Second, because we owe him so much that we ought to be willing to bear even much heavier things for his grace. Third, because the evils he sends are chastisements. This consolation calms the mind, because it signifies that our Father wills us to suffer this. Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him. As it has pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass: blessed be the name of the Lord. I was silent, because you did it. The philosophers say that what cannot be changed must be borne patiently; they posit a fatal necessity, and so one should not kick against the goad. But in calamities they do not submit themselves to God, nor do they acknowledge the anger of God, nor do they suffer adversity in order to obey God, but because they cannot shake it off.

units.la: 3. Dignitas virtutis, seu obedientia erga Deum, quae est vera virtus, propter quam non est abijciendus animus in cruce. Temporalia bona sunt magna beneficia Dei: sed longe maiora bona sunt, obedientia, fides, spes, &c. Ergo non praeferamus minora maioribus, nec propter jacturam minorem abijciamus maiora. Qui non odit patrem & matrem, &c. Qui quaerit animam seruare, perdet eam. Hanc philosophi vrgent, sed frigide: quia veris virtutibus destituuntur.
units.tr: 3. The dignity of virtue, or obedience towards God, which is true virtue, on account of which the mind is not to be cast down in the cross. Temporal goods are great benefits of God, but obedience, faith, hope and so on are far greater goods. Therefore let us not prefer lesser things to greater, nor on account of a smaller loss cast away greater things. He who does not hate father and mother, etc. He who seeks to save his life will lose it. The philosophers press this point, but coldly, because they lack true virtues.

units.la: 4. Bona conscientia, quae non est vera, nisi in piis, scientibus Deum sibi placatum esse per & propter Christum Mediatorem. Deo autem propitio non possumus non esse animo tranquillo. Philosophi hoc modo suos non consolantur: nam afflicti cogitant, cur bonam conscientiam bona fortuna non sequitur, ideo fremunt aduersus Deum, vt Cato, &c.
units.tr: 4. A good conscience, which is not genuine except in the godly, who know that God is reconciled to them through and on account of Christ the Mediator. But when God is propitious, we cannot help being of a tranquil mind. The philosophers do not console their own in this way; for the afflicted think about why a good conscience is not followed by good fortune, and so they rage against God, as Cato did, and so on.

units.la: 5. Causa finales. 1. Gloria Dei, quae elucescit in nostri liberatione: 2. Salus nostra. A Domino enim corripimur, ne damnemur cum mundo. 3. Conuersio aliorum, & propagatio Ecclesiae. Apostoli laetabantur, quod digni essent habiti, qui pro nomine Iesu contumelia afficerentur propter bonum illud, hoc est, conuersionem aliorum, & confirmationem multorum in fide. Philosophi dicunt: bonus est finis, propter quem pateris, vt serues patriam, & gloriam nominis aeternam consequaris. Sed interim miser cogitat: quid mihi ista proderunt, dum ego pereo.
units.tr: 5. Final causes. First, the glory of God, which shines forth in our deliverance; second, our salvation, for we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world; third, the conversion of others and the propagation of the Church. The apostles rejoiced that they were counted worthy to be dishonoured for that good cause, that is, the conversion of others and the confirmation of many in faith. The philosophers say: the end is good, on account of which you suffer, so that you may save your country and obtain eternal glory of name. But meanwhile the wretched man thinks: what will those things profit me, while I am perishing?

units.la: 6. Collatio euentuum. Melius est ad breue tempus castigari a Domino, quam in abundantia rerum viuere, a Deo auelli, & in aeternum exitium ruere. Philosophi conferentes mala inter se, exiguum bonum deprehendunt, quod ex collatione malorum prouenit, praecipuum vero bonum, cuius consequendi causa patiendum est, ignorant.
units.tr: 6. The comparison of outcomes. It is better to be chastened by the Lord for a short time than to live in abundance of goods, be torn away from God, and rush into eternal ruin. The philosophers, comparing evils with one another, find only a small good arising from the comparison of evils, but they do not know the chief good, for the sake of obtaining which one must suffer.

units.la: 7. Spes compensationis seu praemiorum in hac & altera vita. Merces vestra copiosa est in coelis. Nos scimus, nobis restare alia bona minime conferenda cum afflictionibus praesentis vitae: Et in hac etiam vita pij accipiunt maiora bona, quam alij homines: habent pacem cum Deo, & alia dona spiritualia. Corporalia bona si sunt exigua, sunt tamen eis salutaria: Nullus est, qui reliqueris domum, &c. quin accipiat centuplicia nunc isto tempore, & in sein seculo venturo vitam aeternam. Melius est modicum iusto, quàm peccatorum diuitiæ infinitæ. Gloriamur in afflictionibus, &c. Compensatio in exiguis malis aliquo modo consolatur philosophos, in magnis minimè: quia cogitant, se malle illa compensatione carere, quàm eam tanti emere, propterea quod incerta, exigua & temporaria est.
units.tr: 7. Hope of compensation, or of rewards, in this life and the next. Your reward is great in heaven. We know that other goods remain for us which are in no way to be weighed against the afflictions of this present life. Even in this life the godly receive greater goods than other people: they have peace with God and other spiritual gifts. If their bodily goods are small, they are still useful to them: There is no one who has left house, &c., who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, and in the age to come eternal life. It is better to have a little with righteousness than great riches with sin. We glory in afflictions, &c. Compensation for small evils consoles the philosophers to some extent, but for great evils not at all, because they reason that they would rather do without such compensation than buy it at so high a price, since it is uncertain, small and temporary.

units.la: 8. Exempla Christi & aliorum sanctorum. Non est seruus supra Dominum. Et Deus vult nos conformes fieri imagini Filij sui. Comitemur ergo Christum in ignominia, & in gloria. Requirit hoc gratitudo: quia mortem subiit nostræ salutis causa. Sancti martyres passi sunt, nec perierunt in malis. Non debemus nobis postulare fortunam peculiarem aut meliorem, cùm non simus meliores ipsis, immò etiam deteriores: ne simus tam iniusti. Illi sunt passi, & liberati à Deo. Ergo & nos expectemus similem euentum, quia amor Dei erga nos est immutabilis. Sic persecuti sunt Prophetas, qui fuerunt ante vos. Resistite firmi per fidem, scientes, eandem afflictiones à vestra, quæ in mundo est, fraternitate impleri.
units.tr: 8. Examples of Christ and of the other saints. The servant is not above his master. And God wills that we be made conformed to the image of his Son. Let us therefore accompany Christ in dishonour and in glory. Gratitude requires this, because he underwent death for the cause of our salvation. The holy martyrs suffered, and they did not perish in their afflictions. We ought not to demand for ourselves a special or better lot, since we are not better than they, indeed we are even worse, lest we be so unjust. They suffered, and were delivered by God. Therefore let us also expect a similar outcome, because God's love towards us is unchanging. So they persecuted the prophets who were before you. Resist, firm in faith, knowing that the same afflictions are being fulfilled in your brotherhood throughout the world.

units.la: 9. Præsentia & auxilium Dei in afflictionibus. Deus adest nobis suo Spiritu, corroborat, consolatur in cruce, nec finit nos tentari supra vires, sed præstat cum tentatione euasionem, ut possimus sufferre; seruabit semper proportionem virium & afflictionum. Habemus primitias Spiritus. Cum ipso sum in tribulatione. Dabit vobis alium Paracletum, ut maneat vobiscum in aeternum. Ego & Pater veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Non relinquam vos orphanos. Nunquid obliuiscetur mulier infantis sui, ita, ut non misereatur filij veteris sui? etiamsi isti obliuiscentur, sed ego non obliuiscar tui.
units.tr: 9. The presence and help of God in afflictions. God is present with us by his Spirit: he strengthens us, comforts us in the cross, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but with the temptation he provides a way of escape, so that we may be able to bear it; he will always keep a proportion between our strength and our afflictions. We have the firstfruits of the Spirit. I am with him in tribulation. He will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever. I and the Father will come, and make our home with him. I will not leave you orphans. Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? Yet even these may forget, but I will not forget you.

units.la: 10. Liberatio filialis & totalis. Hæc colophon erit omnium reliquarum. Prima est fundamentum, & præcipua: hæc erit absolutio & consummatio. Sicut enim poenarum, sic & liberationis sunt gradus. Primus est in hac vita, vbi habemus primitias Spiritus, & initia vitæ æternæ: de quibus infra Quæst. LVIII. Secundus est in morte corporali, vbi anima Lazari defertur in sinum Abrahæ. Luc.16,22. Tertius erit in resurrectione, quando corpore & animâ erimus perfectè beati. Tunc enim Deus abstergèt omnem lachrymam ab oculis nostris.
units.tr: 10. Filial and complete deliverance. This will be the crown of all the rest. The first is the foundation and the chief, and this will be the completion and consummation. For just as there are degrees of punishments, so there are degrees of deliverance. The first is in this life, where we have the firstfruits of the Spirit and the beginnings of eternal life, concerning which see below, Question LVIII. The second is at bodily death, when the soul of Lazarus is carried into Abraham's bosom (Luke 16:22). The third will be at the resurrection, when we shall be perfectly blessed in body and soul. For then God will wipe away every tear from our eyes.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS. DE LIBERATIONE Hominis.
units.tr: SECOND PART. CONCERNING THE LIBERATION OF MAN.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XII.
units.tr: QUESTION XII.

units.la: Quoniam igitur iusto Dei iudicio, temporalibus & æternis pœnis obnoxii sumus: estne reliqua ullaratio aut via, qua his pœnis liberemur, & DEO reconciliemur?
units.tr: Since, then, by the just judgment of God we are liable to temporal and eternal punishments, is there any remaining reason or way by which we may be freed from these punishments and reconciled to God?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vult Deus suæ iustitiæ satisfieri a: quocirca necesse est, vel per nos, vel per alium satisfaciamus. b
units.tr: God wills that his justice be satisfied; therefore it is necessary that we satisfy it, either by ourselves or by another.

units.la: a Genes. 2. v. 17, Exod. 23, 7. Ezech. 18, 4. Matth. 5, 26. 2 Thess. 1, 6. Luc. 16, 2. b Rom. 8, 3.
units.tr: a Gen. 2:17; Exod. 23:7; Ezek. 18:4; Matt. 5:26; 2 Thess. 1:6; Luke 16:2. b Rom. 8:3.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: POstquam ostensum est, homines propter non præstitam Deo obedientiam esse reos æternæ damnationis, quæritur porro an detur aliqua emersio ex ea. Ad hanc quæstionem respondet catechesis: dari liberationem, si iustitiæ Dei seu legi per sufficientem pœnam pro culpa admissa satisfiat. Obligat enim lex ad obedientiam, vel, si hæc non præstetur, ad pœnam: & utriusque præstatio est iustitia, quam sequitur approbatio eius, in quo est.
units.tr: Since it has been shown that men, on account of the obedience not rendered to God, are guilty of eternal damnation, the question follows whether there is any way out of it. To this question the catechism replies that deliverance is available, if satisfaction is made to the justice of God, or to the law, by a sufficient punishment for the fault committed.
