For the law binds to obedience or, if this is not rendered, to punishment; and the performance of either is justice, which is followed by its approval in the one in whom it is found.

units.la: Modi satisfaciendi per pœnam sunt duo. Vnus per nos: quem lex docet, & iustitia Dei flagitat: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, &c. Hic est legalis. Alter, per alium: quem Euangelium patefacit, & misericordia Dei admittit. Quod Legi erat impossibile, hoc fecit Deus missio Filio, &c. Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium daret, &c. Hic est evangelicus. In Lege quidem hic modus non docetur: sed nusquam etiam improbatur vel excluditur: neque cum iustitia Dei pugnat. Modo enim pro inobedientia hominis satisfactio præstetur ab homine per sufficientem pœnam, Lex est contenta, & iustitia Dei patitur, ut pars offendens absolvatur, & in gratiam recipiatur. Hæc est summa.
units.tr: There are two modes of satisfying by punishment. The one is through ourselves: this the law teaches and the justice of God demands: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things," etc. This is the legal mode. The other is through another: this the Gospel discloses and the mercy of God admits: "What was impossible for the Law, God did by sending his Son," etc.; "God so loved the world that he gave his Son," etc. This is the evangelical mode. Indeed, this mode is not taught in the Law, yet it is nowhere disapproved or excluded, nor does it conflict with the justice of God. For provided that satisfaction for man's disobedience is rendered by man through a sufficient punishment, the Law is content, and the justice of God permits the offending party to be absolved and received back into favour. This is the sum.

units.la: Porrò hac quæstione duo docentur: quod liberatio fieri possit, & quomodo. Hæc ut plenius intelligantur, consideran-dum est:
units.tr: Moreover, two things are taught in this question: that liberation can take place, and how. So that these may be understood more fully, the following must be considered:

units.la: DE LIBERATIONE HOMINIS.
units.tr: On the Deliverance of Man.

units.la: I. Quid & qualis sit liberatio hominis. II. An talis liberatio sit possibilis. III. An sit necessaria & certa. IV. An sit perfecta & exspectanda. V. Quomodo fieri possit.
units.tr: I. What deliverance of man is, and of what kind it is. II. Whether such a deliverance is possible. III. Whether it is necessary and certain. IV. Whether it is perfect and to be awaited. V. How it can come about.

units.la: I. Quid & qualis sit liberatio.
units.tr: I. What deliverance is, and of what kind.

units.la: Liberationis vocabulum est relatiuum. Omnis enim liberatio est ab aliquo, & ad aliquid, quasi à captiuitate ad libertatem. Homines verò natura captiui sunt peccati, satanæ, & mortis. Non rectius igitur, quid sit hominis liberatio, intelligitur, quàm si quid eius miseria, cogitetur. Miseria hominis primò consistit in amissione rectitudinis, & prauitate innata, hoc est, peccatis: deinde in peccatorum poenis: Liberatio igitur ab hac miseria requirit primò peccati condonationem & abolitionem, ac rectitutinis amissæ restitutionem in nobis: deinde liberatione à poenis ac miseriis omnibus. Vt igitur miseriæ sunt duæ partes, peccatum & mors: ita & liberationis duæ sunt partes, a peccato & à morte. Liberatio à peccato, est tum condonatio peccati, vt non imputetur, tum abolitio eius in nobis, per renouationem naturæ, vt non dominetur. Liberatio à morte, est liberatio à desperatione, & sensu iræ Dei, à calamitatibus & miseriis huius vitæ: deniq; à morte temporali & æterna.
units.tr: The word deliverance is relative. Every deliverance is from something and to something, as from captivity to liberty. Men by nature are captives of sin, of Satan, and of death. Therefore the nature of man's deliverance is best understood if we consider his misery. Man's misery first consists in the loss of righteousness and in innate depravity, that is, in sins; then in the punishments of sins. Deliverance from this misery therefore requires, first, the forgiveness and abolition of sin, and the restoration in us of the righteousness we have lost; then, deliverance from all punishments and miseries. So, since misery has two parts, sin and death, deliverance also has two parts: from sin and from death. Deliverance from sin is both the pardon of sin, so that it is not imputed to us, and its abolition in us through the renewal of our nature, so that it does not rule over us. Deliverance from death is deliverance from despair and from the sense of God's wrath, from the calamities and miseries of this life, and finally from temporal and eternal death.

units.la: Ex his liquet, quid & qualis sit liberatio: perfecta nimirum hominis lapsi vindicatio ab omni miseria peccati & mortis, & plena restitutio justitiæ, sanctitatis & vitæ, ac felicitatis æternæ per Christum, quæ in omnibus credentibus inchoatur in hac vita, & perficietur in altera.
units.tr: From these points it is clear what deliverance is and of what kind it is: namely, the complete vindication of fallen man from every misery of sin and death, and the full restoration of righteousness, holiness, life, and eternal happiness through Christ. This begins in all believers in this life and will be brought to completion in the next.

units.la: II. An talis liberatio sit possibilis.
units.tr: II. Whether such a deliverance is possible.

units.la: Fuit possibilis liberatio hominis lapsi.
units.tr: The deliverance of fallen man was possible.

units.la: 1. Propter immensam Dei bonitatem & misericordiam, quæ non passura erat totum humanum genus perire in æternum.
units.tr: 1. Because of the immense goodness and mercy of God, which would not allow the whole human race to perish for ever.

units.la: 2. Propter infinitam Dei sapientiam, qua poterat inuenire talem liberationis modum, quo & misericordiam suam erga genus humanum declararet, & justitiam non violaret.
units.tr: 2. Because of the infinite wisdom of God, by which he could devise a manner of deliverance that would both display his mercy towards the human race and not violate his justice.

units.la: 3. Propter Dei omnipotentiam, qua vt hominem ex nihilo ad imaginem suam creare, ita eundem ex lapsu instaurare, atqi à peccato & morte liberare potuit.
units.tr: 3. Because of the omnipotence of God, by which he could create man out of nothing in his own image, and likewise restore him after his fall and free him from sin and death.

units.la: Negare igitur liberationem hominis fuisse possibilem, esset Dei bonitatem, sapientiam & omnipotentiam negare. Deo autem neque consilium, neque bonitas, neque potentia deest, juxta dicta: Deus deducit ad inferos, & reducit. Domini sunt exitus ex morte. Non abbreviata est manus Iehova.
units.tr: To deny, then, that the deliverance of man was possible would be to deny the goodness, wisdom, and omnipotence of God. Yet God lacks neither counsel, nor goodness, nor power, according to the words: The Lord brings down to the grave and brings up again. To the Lord belong the issues from death. The hand of the Lord is not shortened.

units.la: Sed quaeritur, unde nos hoc sciam?: & an humana ratio sine verbo Dei scire possit? & an Adam post lapsum scire ac sperare potuerit? Resp. Liberationem fuisse possibilem nunc quidem patet ex eventu, & nos scimus ex Euangelio seu revelatione divina. Sed ratio humana de liberatione & eius modo nihil scit: etsi probabiliter opinari potest, non omnino fuisse impossibilem: eo quod non sit verisimile, creaturam praestantissimam fuisse condita m ad aeternas miserias: neque etiam, Deum tulisse legem, quae nunquam impleretur: quae duo argumenta sunt quidem per se firma, sed propter prauitatem suam ratio humana iis non assentitur. Sicut igitur liberationem nec scire, nec sperare possunt, quicunque extra Ecclesiam sunt, & Euangelium ignorant: sic Adam post lapsum, sine revelatione & promissione singulari, ex solo rationis judicio, eam nec scire ne sperare potuit. Admisso enim peccato nihil animo eius observari potuit, nisi summa Dei justitia, quae non patitur impune abire peccatum: & immutabilis Dei veritas, quae dixerat: Quacunque die comederis, morte morieris. Justitiae vero & veritati divinae intellexit Adam satisfieri oportere per aeternam destructionem peccantis. Itaque ex hac consideratione liberationem nullam sperare potuit. Potuit quidem probabiliter colligere, liberationem fieri posse, si huic justitiae & veritati Dei satisfieret: sed satisfactionem neque sperare, neque intelligere potuit, qualis & a quo posset praestari: immo ne angeli quidem modum eius excogitare aut invenire in aeternum potuissent, nisi Deus eum pro immensa sua sapientia & bonitate hominibus revelasset.
units.tr: But it is asked: how do we know this, and can human reason know it without the word of God? And could Adam, after the fall, have known and hoped for it? Answer: That deliverance was possible is now plain from the outcome, and we know it from the Gospel, or divine revelation. But human reason knows nothing of deliverance or its manner, although it can reasonably conjecture that it was not wholly impossible, because it is not probable that the most excellent creature was made for eternal miseries, nor that God gave a law that could never be fulfilled. These two arguments are indeed firm in themselves, but because of human reason's perversity, reason does not assent to them. Therefore, just as all who are outside the Church and ignorant of the Gospel can neither know nor hope for deliverance, so Adam after the fall, without a special revelation and promise, could neither know nor hope for it by the judgment of reason alone. For once sin was committed, nothing could present itself to his mind except the supreme justice of God, which does not suffer sin to pass unpunished, and the unchangeable truth of God, which had said: On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die. Adam understood that the justice and truth of God must be satisfied by the eternal destruction of the sinner. Hence, from this consideration, he could hope for no deliverance. He could indeed reasonably infer that deliverance might come about if this justice and truth of God were satisfied, but he could neither hope for nor understand the satisfaction, or by whom it could be made. Indeed, not even the angels could have devised or discovered its manner for eternity, unless God in his immense wisdom and goodness had revealed it to men.

units.la: Sed contra: Si Adamo visa est impossibilis liberatio, propter justitiam & veritatem divinam: ergo & nunc videtur esse impossibilis. Nam violatio justitiae & veritatis divinae non magis nunc fieri potest, quam olim potuit. Sed euasio peccatoris ex miseria erat violatura justitiam & veritatem Dei. Resp. Euasio peccatoris erat violatura justitiam & veritatem Dei, nempe, si fieret, non intercedente satisfactione pro culpa. Hanc solutionem si vidit Adam, potuit liberationem non simpliciter desperare, praesertim si simul naturam Dei, hoc est, immensam eius bonitatem, sapientiam atq; potentiam, & finem creati hominis consideraret: consentaneum nempe non esse, a Deo optimo, sapientissimo, & potentissimo, creaturam praestantissimam, ad per-
units.tr: But against this: If deliverance seemed impossible to Adam because of the justice and truth of God, then it seems impossible now too. For the violation of the justice and truth of God cannot happen now any more than it could then. But the escape of the sinner from misery would have violated the justice and truth of God. Answer: The escape of the sinner would have violated the justice and truth of God, namely, if it had happened without satisfaction being interposed for the guilt. If Adam saw this solution, he could not simply despair of deliverance, especially if he also considered the nature of God, that is, his immense goodness, wisdom, and power, and the end for which man was created. For it was not consistent that the most excellent creature should have been made by the best, wisest, and most powerful God for eternal misery, or that God should have given man a law that he could never fully keep.

units.la: Liberatio ratione humana ignota. perpetuas miserias conditam, vel talem ab eo legem homini latam esse, quam nunquam integrè præstare posset: certò tamen sperare non potuit, quoniam, vt dictum est, ante promulgatum Euangelium, neque ipse, neque vlla creatura modum euadendi ex pœnis, cum justitia Dei non pugnantem, videre vel imaginari sibi potuit, aut in æternum potuisset, nisi Deus eum per Filium reuelasset.
units.tr: Deliverance unknown to human reason. Yet he could not hope for it with certainty, because, as has been said, before the Gospel was proclaimed, neither he nor any creature could see or imagine, or could ever have seen, a way of escaping punishment that did not conflict with the justice of God, unless God had revealed it through the Son.

units.la: Summa igitur huc redit. Ante auditam promissionem de semine mulieris contrituro caput serpentis, homo lapsus liberationem à peccato & morte nullam sperare potuit: desperare verò etiam non debuit, vel simpliciter potuit. Etsi enim neque rationem necessariam habuit, ex qua liberationem futuram concluderet, neque modum satisfactionis intellexit, tamen non sequebatur: si nulla creatura eum inuenire posset, ideo etiam Deum non posse. Debuit ergo in Dei sapientia, bonitate & potentia acquiescere, nec desperare, licet ad desperationem omnia eum sollicitarent: quanquam nisi vox Euangelij accessisset, nihil sanè satis eum aduersus tentationes consolari poterat. Post auditam verò promissionem, etiam modum satisfactionis per Christum intellexit, & jam non tantum certò sperare liberationem potuit, sed & omnia argumenta obstantia soluere didicit, qualia erant:
units.tr: The sum, then, comes to this. Before the promise was heard concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head, fallen man could hope for no deliverance from sin and death; but he was not obliged to despair, or at least he was not necessarily driven to it. For although he had no necessary ground from which to conclude that deliverance would come, and did not grasp the manner of satisfaction, yet it did not follow that, if no creature could find it, God could not find it either. He ought therefore to have rested in the wisdom, goodness, and power of God, and not despaired, although everything urged him to despair. Still, unless the voice of the Gospel had come to him, he could certainly find no adequate comfort against temptations. But after the promise was heard, he understood also the manner of satisfaction through Christ, and now he could hope for deliverance not only with certainty, but he also learned to answer all the objections standing in the way, such as these:

units.la: I. Justitia Dei non finit impunè abire eos, qui sunt meriti æternam damnationem. Nos meriti sumus æternam damnationem. Ergo propter justitiam Dei impossibilis erit liberatio.
units.tr: I. The justice of God does not allow those who deserve eternal damnation to go unpunished. We deserve eternal damnation. Therefore, because of the justice of God, deliverance will be impossible.

units.la: Responsionem vidit ad Maiorem: justitiam Dei non dimittere impunè æternam damnationem meritos, nempe, non intercedente satisfactione per sufficientem pœnam pro culpa.
units.tr: He saw the answer to the major premise: the justice of God does not let those who deserve eternal damnation go unpunished, namely, unless satisfaction is interposed through a sufficient penalty paid for the guilt.

units.la: II. Cùm non fit quod justitia Dei postulat, & veritas minatur: vtraque violatur. At si homo peccator emerget ex malis, non fiet, quod justitia postulat, & veritas minatur, hoc est, non infligetur ei pœna & mors æterna. Ergo emersio hominis ex malis, erit cum vtriusque violatione coniuncta, quæ est impossibilis.
units.tr: II. When what the justice of God requires is not done, and the truth threatens, both are violated. But if sinful man emerges from evils, what justice requires and truth threatens will not be done, that is, eternal punishment and death will not be inflicted on him. Therefore the emergence of man from evils would be joined with the violation of both, which is impossible.

units.la: Rursus vidit Minorem tantum esse veram, si prorsus nulla infligatur pœna, vel nulli ipsi peccanti, vel alij pro ipso ad sustinendam pœnam se offerenti. Christum verò semen mulieris pro homine esse contriturum caput serpentis, ex promissione didicit.
units.tr: Again, he saw that the minor premise is true only if no punishment at all is inflicted, either on the sinner himself or on another who offers himself to bear the punishment on his behalf. He learned from the promise that Christ, the seed of the woman, would crush the serpent's head on behalf of man.

units.la: III. Quod postulat immutabilis Dei veritas & justitia, id est necessarium & immutabile. Abiectionem peccatoris in æternas pœnas postulat immutabilis Dei veritas & justitia. Ergo abiectio peccatoris est necessaria & immutabilis. ResponResponsionem vidit ad Maiorem: immutabile esse quod postulat justitia Dei, nempe simpliciter, & non alternatiuè, hoc est, ita vt vel fiat abiectio peccatoris in poenas, vel praestetur satisfactio pro eo per Christum.
units.tr: III. What the unchangeable truth and justice of God requires is necessary and unchangeable. The unchangeable truth and justice of God require the casting of the sinner into eternal punishments. Therefore the casting away of the sinner is necessary and unchangeable. Response: He saw in answer to the major premise that what the justice of God requires is unchangeable, namely, absolutely and not alternatively; that is, either the sinner must be cast into punishment, or satisfaction must be made for him through Christ.

units.la: IV. Ex quo non habemus facultatem emergendi, id est impossibile. Ex peccato & morte emergendi facultatem non habemus. Ergo est impossibilis.
units.tr: IV. From this it follows that we do not have the ability to emerge, that is, it is impossible. We do not have the ability to emerge from sin and death. Therefore it is impossible.

units.la: Responsionem rursus vidit ad Maiorem: impossibile esse, nisi videlicet Deus patefaciat viam eluctandi ex malis, rationi humanæ & omnibus creaturis incognitam, & inuentu impossibilem.
units.tr: He again answered the major premise: it is impossible, namely unless God should reveal a way of struggling out of evils, unknown to human reason and to all creatures, and impossible to discover.

units.la: Hæc & similia fulmina homo per promissionem Euangelij sustinere & elidere didicit. Nos verò solutiones istas hodie multò illustrius intelligimus, quàm olim Adam: quandoquidem liberationem hominis non modò possibilem, & aliquando futuram, vt ille, sed etiam jam factam & praestitam esse per Christum, ex Euangelio, & ipso euentu, ac sensu conscientiæ nostræ certo scimus. Est ergo & semper fuit Deo possibilis liberatio hominis.
units.tr: Man has learned to withstand and repel these and similar thunderbolts by the promise of the Gospel. We, however, understand those solutions far more clearly today than Adam once did, since we know with certainty from the Gospel, from the outcome itself, and from the perception of our own conscience, that the liberation of man is not only possible and will someday come, as it was for him, but has already been accomplished and bestowed through Christ. Therefore the liberation of man is, and always has been, possible for God.

units.la: III. An liberatio sit necessaria & certa.
units.tr: III. Whether liberation is necessary and certain.

units.la: Etsi Deus minimè fuit obstrictus, vt hominem liberaret, sed poterat pro sua libertate omnes in morte relinquere, & nullos seruare: Quis enim prior dedit Domino, vt retribuatur ei? tamen rectè dicitur, liberationem hominis fuisse & esse necessariam, nempe necessitate ea, quam vocant ex hypothesi.
units.tr: Although God was in no way bound to free man, but could by his freedom have left all in death and saved none (For who has first given to the Lord, that it should be repaid to him?), it is nevertheless rightly said that the liberation of man was and is necessary, namely by that necessity which they call necessity from hypothesis.

units.la: Probatur. 1. Deus liberrimè & immutabiliter eam decreuit & promisit. Impossibile est autem Deum fallere aut falli. Viuo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, &c.
units.tr: This is proved. (1) God decreed and promised it most freely and unchangeably. But it is impossible for God to deceive or be deceived. As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, etc.

units.la: 2. Deus vult ab hominibus in æternum celebrari. Creauit nos in laudem gloriæ suæ. Creastine frustra omnes filios hominum? Ergo necesse est, vt aliqui liberentur: quia Deus fine suorum consiliorum non frustratur.
units.tr: (2) God wills to be celebrated by men forever. He created us for the praise of his glory. Have you created all the sons of men in vain? Therefore it is necessary that some be liberated, because God is not frustrated in the end of his counsels.

units.la: 3. Deus filium suum non frustra misit in mundum, nec Christus frustra est mortuus. Descendi è cælo, vt faciam voluntatem eius, qui misit me. Hæc autem est voluntas eius, qui misit me, Patris, vt quicquid dederit mihi, non perdam ex eo, &c. Veni peccatores saluos facere. Veni seruare id, quod perierat. Mortuus est propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit propter justificationem nostri. Si per legem est iustitia, igitur Christus sine causa mortuus est.
units.tr: (3) God did not send his Son into the world in vain, nor did Christ die in vain. I came down from heaven to do the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, the Father, that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing, etc. I came to save sinners. I came to save what had been lost. He was put to death for our sins and raised for our justification. If justification comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.

units.la: 4. Deus magis propendet ad misericordiam, quàm ad iram. Atin puniendis impiis declarat iram. Ergo multò magis in seruandis piis declarabit misericordiam.
units.tr: (4) God is more inclined to mercy than to wrath. Yet in punishing the wicked he displays his wrath. Therefore much more, in saving the godly, he will display his mercy.

units.la: IV. An liberatio sit exspectanda perfecta.
units.tr: IV. Whether a perfect liberation is to be expected.

units.la: Liberatio in hac vita est perfecta in choatione: in altera erit perfecta etiam consummatione. Nunc est perfecta partibus liberatio ab utroque malo, poenae & culpae: tunc erit perfecta etiam gradibus, cum omnes lachrymae abstergentur ab oculis nostris, & imago DEI perfecte instaurabitur, & Deus erit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Liberation in this life is perfect in its beginning; in the other life it will be perfect also in its completion. Now the liberation is perfect in its parts, from both evils, punishment and guilt; then it will be perfect also in its degrees, when all tears are wiped from our eyes, the image of God is perfectly restored, and God will be all in all.

units.la: Probatur. 1. Quia Deus non tantum ex parte est liberator, sed perfecte servat & diligit, quos servat. Sanguis Iesu Christi mundat nos ab omni peccato. Salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis suis.
units.tr: This is proved. (1) Because God is not only a partial liberator, but perfectly preserves and loves those whom he preserves. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. He will save his people from their sins.

units.la: 2, Deus perfecte punit impios, ut justitiae ejus accurate satisfaciant poenis. Ergo & pios perfecte liberabit: quoniam magis propensus est ad misericordiam, quam ad iram. At Christi beneficium non est imperfectius aut infirmius peccato Adami. Esset autem infirmius, si non perfecte liberaret: quia omnem justitiam & salutem in Adamo amisimus. Est igitur expectanda perfecta liberatio, sed per gradus, ut dictum est: in hac vita, perfecta: in resurrectione perfectior: in glorificatione, perfectissima.
units.tr: (2) God punishes the wicked perfectly, so that they may fully satisfy the penalties of his justice. Therefore he will also liberate the godly perfectly, since he is more inclined to mercy than to wrath. But the benefit of Christ is not less perfect or weaker than the sin of Adam. Yet it would be weaker if it did not liberate perfectly, since we lost all righteousness and salvation in Adam. Therefore a perfect liberation is to be expected, but by degrees, as has been said: in this life, perfect; in the resurrection, more perfect; in glorification, most perfect.

units.la: V. Quomodo fieri possit liberatio.
units.tr: V. How liberation can come about.

units.la: Est possibilis eiusmodi liberatio: 1. Per satisfactionem sufficientem pro culpa admissa, hoc est, per poenam aeternam, vel aeternae aequivalentem. 2. Per expurgationem peccati & instaurationem naturae, hoc est, per restitutionem rectitudinis amissae & imaginis Dei in nobis, seu per regenerationem perfectam naturae. Utraque ad liberationem est necessaria.
units.tr: Such liberation is possible: (1) through a satisfaction sufficient for the guilt committed, that is, through eternal punishment or what is equivalent to eternal punishment; (2) through the purging of sin and the restoration of nature, that is, through the restoration of the righteousness lost and of the image of God in us, or through the perfect regeneration of nature. Both are necessary for liberation.

units.la: Satisfactio requiritur: quia misericordia Dei, ut supra ostensum est, non evertit Dei justitiam, cui oportet satisfieri. Lex autem obligat vel ad obedientiam, vel ad poenam. Per obedientiam satisfactio non potest fieri: quia praecedens obedientia jam est violata: sequens vero obedientia pro priore offensa satisfacere non potest, cum homo ad eam, tanquam ad praesens debitum, quovis momento obligetur. Obedientia igitur semel violata non restat alia satisfactio, nisi per poenam, juxta comminationem: Si comederis, morte morieris: quia poena sufficienter praestita, Deus peccatori reconciliatur, & potest sequi liberatio.
units.tr: Satisfaction is required, because the mercy of God, as shown above, does not overturn the justice of God, to which satisfaction must be made. The law binds either to obedience or to punishment. Satisfaction cannot be made through obedience: because the earlier obedience has already been violated; and a later obedience cannot make satisfaction for the earlier offence, since man is bound to it, as to a present debt, at every moment. Therefore, once obedience has been violated, no other satisfaction remains except through punishment, according to the threat: If you eat, you will surely die. For when the punishment has been sufficiently paid, God is reconciled to the sinner, and liberation can follow.

units.la: Requiritur etiam expurgatio peccati, & regeneratio naturae. Ea enim conditione Deus vult acceptare satisfactionem, & remittere peccata, si in posterum desinamus cum offendere, pro reconciliatione ei simus grati. Si enim vellen{-}à Deo in gratiam recipi, nec vellemus à peccatis desistere, illuderemus Deo. Non possumus autem à peccatis desistere, nisi natura instauretur. Hoc igitur modo possibilis est hominis liberatio: si fiat talis satisfactio, qua poena culpæ æqualis luatur, & quam nulla deinceps sequatur noua offensio.
units.tr: Purging of sin and regeneration of nature are also required. For God wills to accept the satisfaction and to remit sins on this condition: that in future we cease to offend, and are grateful to him for the reconciliation. For if we wished to be received back into favour by God, and did not wish to desist from sins, we would be mocking God. But we cannot desist from sins unless nature is restored. Thus liberation of man is possible in this way: if such a satisfaction is made, by which the punishment equal to the guilt is paid, and which no new offence afterwards follows.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XIII.
units.tr: QUESTION XIII.

units.la: Possumusne ipsi per nos satisfacere?
units.tr: Can we ourselves make satisfaction through ourselves?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Nulla ex parte: quin etiam debitum in singulos dies a augemus.
units.tr: In no way. Indeed, we even increase our debt every day.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Postquam constat, modum liberationis in satisfactione & expurgatione peccati consistere: amplius quæritur, à quo ista satisfactio & expurgatio peccati fieri possit, à nobisne, an ab alio: & si ab alio, an à nuda seu mera creatura, & si non à mera creatura, à quo igitur, & à quali mediatore. Ad primum respondetur hac quæst.13. ad duo reliqua qq.14.15.
units.tr: Having established that the manner of deliverance consists in satisfaction and the expiation of sin, the further question is by whom such satisfaction and expiation can be made: by us, or by another; and if by another, whether by a mere creature, and if not by a mere creature, then by whom, and through what mediator. The first point is answered in this question (13); the other two are taken up in questions 14 and 15.

units.la: A nobis igitur, & per nos satisfactio præstari non potest, neque per obedientiam, neque per pœnam.
units.tr: Satisfaction therefore cannot be made by us or through us, neither through obedience nor through punishment.

units.la: Non per obedientiam: quia quicquid boni præstamus, præsenti obligatione Deo debemus. Per id igitur pro peccatis prioribus satisfacere non possumus. Nihil enim possumus de Deo pro præsenti, ne dum pro præterito tempore mereri: nec potest vna satisfactione duplex debitum, præsens scilicet & futurum, exsolui.
units.tr: Not through obedience, because whatever good we do, we already owe to God by present obligation. So we cannot make satisfaction for our earlier sins by that means. For we cannot earn anything from God for the present, much less for past time; nor can one satisfaction pay off a double debt, the present and the future one together.

units.la: In catechesi additur alia ratio popularior, quia culpam seu debitum in singulos dies etiam augemus. Indesinenter enim peccamus, & peccando offensionem Dei atqui reatum cumulamus. Qui autem non definit offendere, nunquam placat offensum: sicut debitor nunquam se ære alieno exsoluit, qui ad priora debita subinde noua nomina accumulat.
units.tr: In the catechism another, more popular reason is added: we also keep increasing our guilt or debt every day. For we sin without ceasing, and by sinning we heap up offence against God, that is, guilt. But whoever does not stop offending never appeases the one offended. It is like a debtor who never clears his debt because he keeps piling new bonds on top of the old ones.

units.la: Nec per pœnam satisfacere possumus, quia culpa nostra infinita meretur pœnam infinitam, hoc est, æternam, vel æternæ æquivalentem. Peccatum enim est offensio infiniti boni, quæ meretur æternam damnationem, vel certè temporalem æternæ æqualem. Æternam sustinere non possumus, quia nunquam emergeremus. Perpetuò quidem lueremus, sed nunquam satisfaceremus, quia luitio & satisfactio nunquam esset perfecta: nec esset victoria de peccato & morte, sed imperfecta continuaretur in æternum: qualis satisfactio est æterna poena diabolorum & reproborum hominum, quæ nunquam absolvitur. Temporalem verò æternæ æquivalentem, qualis omnino requiritur, ut satisfactio sit victoria de morte, nulla creatura propter multiplicem imperfectionem sustinere potest, ut paulo post ostendetur.
units.tr: Nor can we satisfy through punishment, because our guilt deserves an infinite punishment, that is, eternal punishment, or something equivalent to eternal. For sin is an offence against an infinite good, and it deserves eternal damnation, or at least a temporal punishment equal to an eternal one. We cannot bear an eternal punishment, because we would never emerge from it. We would indeed be paying for ever, but we would never make satisfaction, since the payment would never be complete; there would be no victory over sin and death, but an unfinished struggle continuing for ever. Such is the satisfaction of the devil and of the reprobate, which is eternal punishment and never ends. A temporal punishment equal to an eternal one, which is completely required for satisfaction to be a victory over death, no creature can endure, because of its manifold imperfection, as will be shown shortly.

units.la: Cùm igitur nequeamus satisfacere per nos: necesse est, ut satisfaciamus per alium, si quidem liberari velimus.
units.tr: Since, then, we cannot satisfy through ourselves, it is necessary that we satisfy through another, if indeed we wish to be delivered.

units.la: Hinc ad objectionem facile respondetur. Nos neque ad obedientiam, neque per poenam Legi unquam satisfacimus. Ergo modus ille liberationis per satisfactionem est inanis. Resp. Non est inanis: quia licet satisfacere non possimus per obedientiam: possumus tamen per sufficientem poenam, luendo eam non quidem in nobis, sed in Christo, qui per obedientiam & per poenam Legi satisfecit.
units.tr: From this, an objection is easily answered. We never satisfy the Law, neither by obedience nor by punishment. Therefore that manner of deliverance by satisfaction is empty. Answer: it is not empty, because although we cannot satisfy through obedience, we can through a sufficient punishment, by bearing it not in ourselves but in Christ, who satisfied the Law both by obedience and by punishment.

units.la: Inst. 1. Lex requirit obedientiam vel poenam NOSTRAM: quia scriptum est: Qui fecerit ea, viuet in eis. Maledictus, qui non manserit in omnibus. Resp. Requirit obedientiam vel poenam nostram, sed non exclusiue. Nusquam enim excludit vel improbat satisfactionem alienam pro nobis, tametsi eam non docat, sed ignoret. Euangelium autem hanc revelat, & in Christo nobis ostendit.
units.tr: Objection 1: The Law requires obedience or punishment from OURSELVES, because it is written: "He who does these things shall live in them," and "Cursed is he who does not remain in all things." Answer: The Law does require obedience or punishment from us, but not exclusively. It nowhere excludes or disapproves of satisfaction made by another for us, although it does not teach this, but simply does not know of it. The Gospel, however, reveals this and shows it to us in Christ.

units.la: Inst. 2. Alium puniri pro nocente est injustum. Ergo Christus non poterat pro nobis puniri. Resp. Alium puniri pro nocentibus non pugnat cum Dei justitia, positis his conditionibus: 1. si, qui punitur, sit innocens: 2. si sit eiusdem naturæ: 3. si sponte se ad satisfactionem offerat: 4. si possit ipse emergere ex poena: (Ideo enim homines non possunt alium pro alio plectere, quia non possunt efficere, ut punitus non pereat in poena:) 5. si denique spectet & consequatur finem illum, quem Christus spectauit, nempe gloriam Dei, & salutem hominum. De hoc argumento vide etiam infra Quæst. 37. & 56.
units.tr: Objection 2: For one person to be punished for a guilty one is unjust; therefore Christ could not be punished for us. Answer: For another to be punished for the guilty does not conflict with God's justice, provided these conditions hold: (1) the one who is punished is innocent; (2) he is of the same nature; (3) he offers himself freely for satisfaction; (4) he is able himself to emerge from the punishment (this is why men cannot punish one person in place of another, since they cannot ensure that the one punished does not perish in the punishment); (5) finally, he aims at and attains that end which Christ aimed at, namely the glory of God and the salvation of men. On this argument see also below, questions 37 and 56.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XIV.
units.tr: QUESTION XIV.

units.la: Potestne vlla creaturarum in cœlo vel in terra, quæ tantum creatura sit, pro nobis satisfacere?
units.tr: Can any creature in heaven or on earth, being only a creature, make satisfaction for us?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Nulla. Nam principiò non vult Deus, quod homo peccauit, id in alia creatura plectere a. Deinde nec potest quidem, quod mera tantum creatura sit, iram Dei aduersus peccatum sustinere, & alios ab ea liberare b.
units.tr: None. For, first, God does not will that man, having sinned, should be punished for it in another creature (a). Next, a mere creature cannot, simply by being a creature, sustain the wrath of God against sin and deliver others from it (b).

units.la: a Ezech. 18,4. Genes. 3,17. b Nahum. 1,6. Psal. 130,3.
units.tr: a Ezek. 18, 4. Gen. 3, 17. b Nahum 1, 6. Psalm 130, 3.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: In quæstione additur exclusiua tantum, vt vera sit negatiua responsio. Nam oportebat quidem pro peccato creaturæ satisfacere creaturam, sed non talem, quæ esset mera, vel tantum creatura: quia talis satisfacere non poterat, vt patebit.
units.tr: The question adds the exclusive word "only," so that the negative answer is true. For it was indeed necessary that a creature should make satisfaction for the sin of a creature, but not one that was merely a creature, or only a creature, because such a one could not make satisfaction, as will become clear.

units.la: Quaeritur ergo, cum per alium sit satisfaciendum, an is alius possit esse aliqua creatura præter hominem, & quidem creatura mera vel nuda. Vtrumque negatur. Prioris ratio est: quia Deus non vult, quod homo peccauit, id in alia creatura plectere: idq; ex ordine suæ justitiæ, quæ non patitur, vt alia creatura peccet, alia luat. Anima quæ peccauerit, ipsa morietur. Hæc ratio probat, nullam creaturam, præter hominem, potuisse satisfacere pro homine: immò ne quidem cœli & terræ ipsorumq; angelorum & creaturarum omnium æterna destructione potuisse Deo satisfieri pro hominis peccato. Posterioris ratio est: 1. Quia nullius creaturæ tanta vis est, vt posset supplicium sustinere finitum, æquivalens infinito, pro infinita culpa hominis. Citius enim absumeretur, & in nihilum redigeretur creatura: quam Deo hoc modo satisfaceret: quia Deus ignis consumens est. Si iniquitates observaueris Domine, quis sustinebit? Quia Lex non poterat justificare, infirmata per carnem: misit Deus Filium suum in similitudinem carnis, &c. Hæc ratio probat, nullam in vniuersum creaturam potuisse sic Deo pro hominis peccato satisfacere per poenam, vt ex ea emergeret: qua emersione opus erat, vt fieret satisfactio & liberatio. Sic ergo propter infirmitatem creaturæ non fuisset proportio peccati & poenæ. 2. Quia supplicium nulla creaturæ non fuisset ἀξίωμα seu pretium satis dignum pro redemptione nostra. 3. Quia nuda creatura non potuisset naturam humanam à corruptione instaurare, & ne in posterum peccaremus efficere, quod liberatorem efficere oportuit.
units.tr: The question, then, since satisfaction must be made through another, asks whether that other could be some creature besides man, and indeed a mere or bare creature. Both are denied. The reason for the first is this: God does not will that man, having sinned, should be punished for it in another creature. This follows from the order of his justice, which does not allow one creature to sin and another to pay for it: "The soul that sins, it shall die." This reason proves that no creature other than man could satisfy for man; indeed, not even by the eternal destruction of heaven and earth, of the angels themselves and of all creatures, could God be satisfied for the sin of man. The reason for the second is: (1) no creature has such strength that it could endure a finite punishment equal to an infinite guilt of man. For a creature would be consumed more quickly and reduced to nothing than it would satisfy God in this way: "for our God is a consuming fire," and "If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, who could stand?" And because the Law could not justify, being weakened through the flesh, God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and so on. This reason proves that no creature at all could thus satisfy God for the sin of man through punishment in such a way as to emerge from it; and such an emergence was necessary for satisfaction and deliverance to take place. Thus, because of the weakness of the creature, there would not have been a proportion between sin and punishment. (2) Because no creature's punishment would have been a worthy price, sufficient for our redemption. (3) Because a bare creature could not restore human nature from corruption and bring it about that we should not sin in future, which the deliverer had to accomplish.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XV.
units.tr: QUESTION XV.

units.la: Qualis ergo quærendus est mediator & liberator?
units.tr: What sort of mediator and liberator must we seek, then?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Qui verus quidem homo sit a, ac perfectè sit justusb, & tamen omnibus creaturis potentior, hoc est, qui simul etiam sit verus Deus c.
units.tr: One who is truly a man a, perfectly just b, and yet more powerful than all creatures, that is, who is at the same time true God c.

units.la: a 1 Cor. 15. v. 21. b Heb. 7, 26. c Esa. 7, 14. & 9, 6. Ierem. 23, 6. Lucæ 11. vers. 12.
units.tr: a 1 Cor. 15. v. 21. b Heb. 7, 26. c Esa. 7, 14. & 9, 6. Ierem. 23, 6. Lucæ 11. vers. 12.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Cùm igitur nos ipsi satisfacere Deo non queamus, sed alio satisfactore pro nobis seu mediatore opus habeamus: quæritur porrò, qualem hunc esse oporteat. Nam aut erit tantum creatura, aut tantum Deus, aut utrumque. Tantum creatura esse non potest, propter causas jam explicatas. Tantum Deus etiam esse non potuit: tum quia non Deus, sed homo peccauit: tum quia Mediator pati & mori debuit pro hominis peccato. Deus autem in se nec pati nec mori poterat. Relinquitur ergo talem requiri, qui sit utrumque; hoc est, qui & homo sit & Deus. Causæ seqq. quæstionibus explicantur.
units.tr: Since we cannot satisfy God ourselves, but need another satisfier or mediator on our behalf, the further question is what sort of person he must be. He cannot be a creature alone, or God alone, or he must be both. A creature alone is impossible, for the reasons already explained. God alone was not possible either: first, because it was man, not God, who sinned; second, because the Mediator had to suffer and die for man's sin, and God in himself could neither suffer nor die. It remains, therefore, that we require one who is both, that is, who is both man and God. The reasons are explained in the following questions.

units.la: Tantū Deus pro nobis satisfacere non potuit.
units.tr: God alone could not satisfy for us.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XVI.
units.tr: QUESTION XVI.

units.la: Cur necesse est eum verum hominem, & quidem perfectè justum esse?
units.tr: Why is it necessary that he be a true man, and indeed perfectly just?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Quia justitia Dei postulat, ut eadem natura humana, quæ peccauit, ipsa pro peccato dependat a: qui verò ipse peccator esset, pro aliis dependere non posset b.
units.tr: Because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which sinned should itself make payment for sin a; and one who was himself a sinner could not make payment for others b.

units.la: a 1 Cor. 15. vers. 21. b Hebr. 7, 26. c Esa. 7, 14. & 9, 6. Ier. 23, 6. Lucæ 11. vers. 22.
units.tr: a 1 Cor. 15. vers. 21. b Hebr. 7, 26. c Esa. 7, 14. & 9, 6. Ier. 23, 6. Lucæ 11. vers. 22.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Mediatorem oportuit esse hominem verum, perfectè justum.
units.tr: The Mediator had to be a true man, perfectly just.

units.la: I. Hominem esse oportuit. 1. Vt quod homo peccauerat, homo luceret: Sicut per unum hominem peccatum introivit in mundum, &c. Per hominem mors, & per hominem resurrectio. 2. Vt posset mori. Debuit enim satisfacere pro nobis moriendo, quia dictum erat: Morte morieris. Sine sanguinis effusione non fit remissio.
units.tr: I. He had to be a man. (1) So that the man who had sinned might be made to atone: As by one man sin entered into the world, etc. By a man came death, and by a man the resurrection. (2) So that he could die. For he had to satisfy for us by dying, since it had been said: In dying you shall die. Without shedding of blood there is no remission.

units.la: II. Hominem verum esse oportuit, ex genere humano, quod peccauit, propagatum, non ex nihilo creatum, aut cœlitus delapsum, lapsum, quin & omnibus infirmitatibus nostris obnoxium, peccato excepto. 1. Propter justitiam Dei, quæ postulabat, vt eadem natura humana, quæ peccauerat, pro peccatis lueret. Anima enim quæ peccauit, ipsa morietur. Et: Quocunq; die comederis ex eo, morte morieris. Verus igitur homo ex posteritate Adami, qui peccauit, pro hominibus, quod ab ipsis exigebatur, dependere debebat. Hucfaciunt dicta: Quia per hominem mors, per hominem quoq; resurrectio mortuorum. Vnus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. Assumpsit semen Abrahæ: vnde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, &c. Ideo Apostolus dicit, nos esse consepultos Christo per baptismum, & cum Christo resurrexisse, &c. Augustinus de vera religione: Ipsa natura suscipienda erat, quæ liberanda. 2. Propter veritatem Dei, qui passim per Prophetas talem hominem descripsit Mediatorem nostrum, qui sit pauper, infirmus, contemptus, &c. qualis inprimis ab Esaia describitur cap. 53. 2. Propter consolationem nostram. Nisi enim sciremus, eum esse ex Adamo, non possemus statuere, eum esse promissum Messiam, & fratrem nostrum: quia dictum erat: Semen mulieris conteret caput Serpentis. In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terræ. Vnde Apostolus: Qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes (hoc est, eiusdem naturæ humanæ) quam ob causam non erubescit fratres ipsos vocare, &c. Ergo vt frater noster esset, oportuit eum propagari ab Adamo. Quoniam enim pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, &c. 4. Vt posset esse fidelis Pontifex, & succurrere iniquitatibus nostris. Debuit enim per omnia fratribus similis fieri, vt misericors esset, & fidelis Pontifex in iis, quæ apud Deum agenda forent ad expiandum peccatum populi: Nam ex eo, quod perpessus fuit, cum tentatus est, potest & iis, qui tentantur, succurrere.
units.tr: II. He had to be a true man, born of the sinning human race, not created out of nothing, nor come down from heaven, and subject to all our infirmities, sin excepted. (1) On account of the justice of God, which required that the same human nature which had sinned should make payment for sins. The soul that sins, it shall itself die. And: On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die. A true man, therefore, of the posterity of Adam, who sinned, had to make payment for men, as was demanded of them. The following sayings bear on this: For since by man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead. There is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. He took hold of the seed of Abraham; wherefore he had to be made like his brethren in all things, etc. Therefore the Apostle says that we are buried with Christ through baptism, and have risen with Christ, etc. Augustine, On True Religion: The very nature that was to be liberated had to be assumed. (2) On account of the truth of God, who throughout the Prophets described such a man as our Mediator, one who would be poor, weak, despised, etc., as Isaiah above all describes him in chapter 53. (3) On account of our comfort. For unless we knew that he was of Adam, we could not affirm that he was the promised Messiah and our brother, since it had been said: The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent. In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed. Hence the Apostle: He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one (that is, of the same human nature); for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren, etc. Therefore, that he might be our brother, he had to be descended from Adam. For since the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part in the same, etc. (4) So that he might be a faithful High Priest and succour our iniquities. For he had to be made like his brethren in all things, that he might be merciful and a faithful High Priest in those matters which had to be transacted before God to expiate the sin of the people. For because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.

units.la: III. Hominem perfectè justum, hoc est, nulla peccati originalis vel actualis labe infectum esse oportuit: vt sacrificium eius valeret non pro ipso, sed pro nobis.
units.tr: III. He had to be a man perfectly just, that is, free from the stain of original or actual sin, so that his sacrifice might avail not for himself but for us.

units.la: Si enim ipse fuisset peccator, pro suis peccatis et satisfaciendum fuisset. Seruus meus justus justificabit multos. Qui peccatum non fecit, nec est inventus dolus in ore eius. Christus semel pro peccatis passus est, justus pro injustis, vt nos ad Deum adduceret.
units.tr: For if he himself had been a sinner, he would have had to make satisfaction for his own sins. My righteous servant shall justify many. He who did not commit sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.

units.la: Qui vero ipse peccator.] Si enim vlli peccato Mediator fuisset obnoxius, ne ipse quidem iram Dei effugere, ne dum aliis impunitatem & gratiam Dei promereri potuisset: quia mors eius, qui nocens passus esset, ἀντὶ pro aliorum peccatis nullum fuisset. Idcirco Deus eum, qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis fecit peccatum, (hoc est, victimam pro peccato,) vt nos fieremus justitia. tia Dei in illo. Talis siquidem nobis conueniebat Pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatis, & sublimior cœlo factus, cui non sit quotidie necesse, quemadmodum illis Pontificibus, prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi.
units.tr: But he who was himself a sinner.] For if the Mediator had been subject to any sin, he could not even escape the wrath of God, much less obtain impunity and the grace of God for others; for the death of one who suffered as a guilty man could not be [ἀντὶ] in exchange for the sins of others. Hence God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (that is, a victim for sin), so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. For such a High Priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens, who does not need to offer sacrifices every day, as those priests did, first for their own sins and then for the sins of the people.

units.la: Quatuor verò modis Christus homo perfectè fuit justus, seu Legem impleuit. 1. Suâ ipsius justitiâ. Solus enim perfectam obedientiam, qualem Lex requirebat, præstitit. 2. Soluendo pœnam sufficientem pro peccatis nostris. Hanc geminam Legis impletionem oportuit in Christo esse. Nisi enim justitia eius fuisset perfecta; non potuisset pro alienis peccatis satisfacere: & nisi solutio pœnæ fuisset sufficiens, nos per eam à pœna æterna non potuissemus liberari. Prior vocatur impletio Legis per obedientiam: qua ipse fuit conformis Legi. Posterior, impletio Legis per pœnam: quam pro nobis dependit, ne nos manere mus damnationi æternæ obnoxii. 3. In nobis implet Legem suo Spiritu: dum per eum nos regenerat, & per Legem informat ad obedientiam internam & externam, quam Lex à nobis requirit, quamq; in hac vita inchoamus, integram præstabimus in vita æterna. 4. Impleuit Legem Christus docendo & repugando eam ab erroribus & corruptelis, ac restituendo veram eius doctrinam & intelligentiam, sicut dicit: Non veni soluere Legem, sed implere.
units.tr: Christ was perfectly just as a man, or fulfilled the Law, in four ways. (1) By his own righteousness. For he alone rendered the perfect obedience which the Law required. (2) By paying a penalty sufficient for our sins. These two fulfillments of the Law had to be in Christ. For unless his righteousness had been perfect, he could not have satisfied for the sins of others; and unless the payment of the penalty had been sufficient, we could not have been freed from eternal punishment by it. The first is called the fulfillment of the Law through obedience, by which he was conformed to the Law. The second, the fulfillment of the Law through penalty, which he paid on our behalf, so that we would not remain liable to eternal damnation. (3) He fulfills the Law in us by his Spirit, as he regenerates us through the Spirit and forms us through the Law to the inward and outward obedience which the Law requires of us, which we begin in this life and will render in full in eternal life. (4) Christ fulfilled the Law by teaching and by cleansing it from errors and corruptions, and by restoring its true doctrine and understanding, as he says: I came not to destroy the Law, but to fulfill it.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XVII. Quare oportet eum simul etiam verè Deum esse? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: QUESTION XVII. Why must he also be truly God? ANSWER.

units.la: Vt potentia suæ diuinitatis a, onus iræ diuinæ b, carne sua sustinere c, nobisque amissam justitiam & vitam reparare ac restituere possit d.
units.tr: So that, by the power of his divinity, a he might bear the weight of divine wrath b in his flesh c and might be able to repair and restore the righteousness and life we had lost. d

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Mediatorem oportuit esse non tantum hominem verum, & perfectè justum: sed etiam Deum verum; non ficticium, donis tantum e coelestibus ornatum, vt fingunt hæretici.
units.tr: The Mediator had to be not only a true man and perfectly righteous, but also true God, not a fictitious one endowed only with gifts from heaven, as the heretics imagine.

units.la: Deum esse oportuit. 1. Vt potentia sua diuinitatis infinitam Dei iram aduersus peccatum, & supplicium, quod duratione temporale, magnitudine & valore infinitum esse debuit, carne sua sustinere posset. Redactus enim fuisset in nihilum, qui homo mo tantum existens, molem iræ Dei in se suscepisset. Oportuit igitur Mediatorem robore infinito pollere, proinde Deum esse, qui supplicium immensum absque desperatione, & sui in nihilum redactione sustineret.
units.tr: He had to be God. (1) So that by the power of his divinity he could bear in his flesh the infinite wrath of God against sin, and the punishment, which, though temporal in duration, had to be infinite in magnitude and worth. For a man who merely existed as a man would have been reduced to nothing if he had taken upon himself the mass of God's wrath. The Mediator therefore had to possess infinite strength, and so had to be God, to endure an immense punishment without despair and without being reduced to nothing.

units.la: Debuit autem Mediatoris supplicium esse infiniti valoris, & æterno æquivalens: ut inter peccatum & pœnam esset proportio. Inter omnia enim, inde ab initio mundi usque ad finem, peccata commissa, nullum est tam parvum, quod mortem æternam non mereatur, omnia sunt tam mala, ut nullius creaturæ æterno exitio expiari possint.
units.tr: Moreover, the Mediator's punishment had to be of infinite worth and equal to an eternal punishment, so that there would be a proportion between sin and penalty. For among all the sins committed from the beginning of the world to its end, there is none so small that it does not deserve eternal death; all are so evil that they cannot be atoned for by the eternal destruction of any creature.

units.la: Tempore tamen finitum esse debuit: quia Redemptorem non oportuit manere in morte, sed ex ea eluctari, ut beneficium redemptionis absolvere, hoc est, perfecte mereri, & meritum efficacia sua nobis conferre & applicare posset. Utrumque enim facere debuit Mediator, mereri & conferre justitiam, ut esset perfectus Seruator, merito & efficacia. Hæc à nudo homine, quantocunq; esset præditus robore, non poterant præstari, quia nudus homo non poterat vi sua ex morte eluctari. Necesse igitur fuit, eum, qui alios à morte seruaret, mortem potentia sua vincere, & à se ipso prius depellere. Hoc verò non poterat, nisi Deus esset.
units.tr: Yet it had to be finite in time, because the Redeemer ought not to remain in death but had to struggle out of it, so that he could complete the benefit of redemption, that is, merit it perfectly, and could confer and apply the merit to us by his efficacy. For the Mediator had to do both: to merit and to confer righteousness, so that he would be a perfect Saviour, in merit and in efficacy. These things could not be accomplished by a mere man, however strong he might be, because a mere man could not by his own power struggle out of death. It was necessary, therefore, that he who would save others from death should overcome death by his own power and first drive it away from himself. This, however, he could not do unless he were God.

units.la: 2. λύτρον Mediatoris oportebat esse infiniti valoris, ut esset satis dignum & præstans ἀντίλυτρον pro animabus nostris, hoc est, ut satis valeret in judicio Dei ad expianda nostra peccata, & ad reparandam nobis justitiam & vitam amissam. Ergo etiam persona oportebat esse infinitæ dignitatis, hoc est, Deum. Dignitas enim huius λύτρου, cur Deo placeat, & quantumuis temporale, sit infiniti vigoris, consistit in duobus. 1. In dignitate personæ. 2. In gravitate pœnæ.
units.tr: (2) The ransom [λύτρον] of the Mediator had to be of infinite worth, so that it would be a sufficiently worthy and excellent counter-ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for our souls; that is, so that it would be sufficient in the judgment of God to expiate our sins and to repair the righteousness and life we had lost. Therefore the person also had to be of infinite dignity, that is, God. The dignity of this ransom, which pleases God, and which, though temporal, has infinite force, rests on two things: (1) the dignity of the person, and (2) the gravity of the punishment.

units.la: Dignitas personæ est, quod persona, quæ patitur, est Deus, creator ipse, quem pro mundi peccatis mori, in infinitum plus est, quàm omnium creaturarum destructio, & plus valet, quàm omnium angelorum & hominum sanctitas. Hinc Apostoli de Christo loquentes, fere semper deitatis ipsius mentionem faciunt: Deus suo sanguine redemit ecclesiam. Sanguis Iesu Christi Act.20,28. Filij Dei unigeniti mundat nos ab omni peccato. Ecce Agnus Dei, 1 Ioh.1,7. qui tollit peccata mundi. Immò Deus in paradiso hæc duo conjungit: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis, & serpens mordebit eius calcaneum. Ioh.1,29. Genes.3,15.
units.tr: The dignity of the person lies in this: the one who suffers is God, the Creator himself, and for him to die for the sins of the world is infinitely more than the destruction of all creatures, and is worth more than the holiness of all angels and men. Hence the apostles, when speaking of Christ, nearly always mention his deity: God purchased the church with his own blood. Acts 20:28. The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all sin. 1 John 1:7. Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. John 1:29. Indeed, God in paradise joined these two things together: The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent, and the serpent shall bruise his heel. Gen. 3:15.

units.la: Grauitas supplicij seu pœnæ fuit, quod Christus sustinuit horribiles inferni cruciatus, & iram Dei aduersus totius mundi peccata. Dolores inferni comprehenderunt me. Deus ignis consumens est. Coniecit in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Ex quo intellitelligitur, cur Christus tantopere mortem exhorruerit, cum martyres intrepidè jugulum praebuerint.
units.tr: The gravity of the punishment or penalty was that Christ endured the dreadful torments of hell and the wrath of God against the sins of the whole world. The sorrows of hell took hold of me. God is a consuming fire. He laid on him the iniquities of us all. From this it can be understood why Christ shrank so greatly from death, when the martyrs offered their throats fearlessly.

units.la: Obiect. Perfecta impletio legis per obedientiam poterat esse satisfactio pro nostris peccatis. At nudus homo, modo perfectè iustus esset, poterat perfectè implere legem per obedientiam. Ergo nudus homo perfectè iustus, poterat satisfacere pro nostris peccatis: proinde non necesse erat, mediatorem esse Deum. Respond. Maior negatur: quia, ut supra ostensum est, post obedientiam violatam iustitiae Dei non poterat satisfieri pro culpa, nisi per poenam sufficientem, propter comminationem diuinam: Quocunque die comederis, morte morieris. 2. Etsi minor concederetur, nudum hominem obedientia sua legem perfectè implere posse: tamen obedientia ea non posset esse pretium pro debito alieno: cum ad eam praestandam omnis obligetur. Requirebatur igitur, ut mediator poenam sufficientem pro nobis lueret, & ideo diuina potentia instructus esset. Nam ne diaboli quidem molem irae diuinae aduersus peccata sustinere possunt: nedum homo posset.
units.tr: Objection. A perfect fulfilment of the law through obedience could be a satisfaction for our sins. But a mere man, if he were perfectly righteous, could perfectly fulfil the law through obedience. Therefore a mere man who was perfectly righteous could satisfy for our sins, and so it was not necessary for the Mediator to be God. Answer. The major premise is denied: because, as has been shown above, after the violation of obedience, the righteousness of God could not be satisfied for the guilt except by a sufficient punishment, on account of the divine threat: On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die. (2) Even if the minor premise were granted, that a mere man could perfectly fulfil the law by his obedience, nevertheless that obedience could not be the price for another's debt, since every man is bound to render that obedience. It was therefore required that the Mediator pay a sufficient punishment for us, and so he had to be endowed with divine power. For not even the devils can bear the mass of God's wrath against sins, much less could a man.

units.la: Inst. Atqui diaboli & impii aeternam iram Dei sustinent, & sustinere coguntur. Resp. Sustinent quidem, sed non ita, ut vnquam iustitiae Dei satisfaciant, & ex poena emergant. Nam supplicium eorum in aeternum continuatur. Mediator verò onus irae Dei ita debuit perferre, ut absoluta satisfactione illud tum à se tum à nobis etiam tolleret.
units.tr: Objection. Yet the devils and the wicked bear the eternal wrath of God, and are compelled to bear it. Answer. They do indeed bear it, but not in such a way as ever to satisfy the righteousness of God and emerge from the punishment. For their punishment continues for ever. The Mediator, however, had to bear the burden of God's wrath in such a way that, once satisfaction was complete, he would remove it both from himself and from us.

units.la: 3. Oportuit esse Deum, ut arcanam Dei voluntatem de redemptione generis humani ex sinu aeterni patris nobis proferret, quod, nisi Deus esset, facere non poterat. Neque enim vlla creatura illam scrutari in aeternum potuisset, nisi filius Dei revelasset. Deum nemo vidit vnquam, vnigenitus ille filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse revelavit nobis.
units.tr: (3) God had to be God, so that he could reveal to us from the bosom of the eternal Father the secret will of God concerning the redemption of the human race, which he could not have done unless he were God. For no creature could have searched that will to eternity unless the Son of God had revealed it. No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known to us.

units.la: 4. Deum esse oportuit, ut posset dare Spiritum sanctum, colligere ecclesiam, ei adesse, & beneficia morte parta conferre & conseruare. Mediator enim non tantum debuit fieri victima, mortem à se depellere, apud Deum pro nobis intercedere, sed etiam spondere, ut aliquando desinamus peccatis Deum offendere. Hoc vero propter prauitatem nostram, sponderi de nobis à nullo poterat, qui non haberet facultatem donandi Spiritum sanctum, & nos per eum reformandi ad imaginem Dei. Donare autem Spiritum sanctum, & per eum regenerare corda, solius est Dei, cuius spiritus ille est proprius. Quem ego mittam vobis à patre. Solus enim Dominus naturae potest reformare naturam.
units.tr: (4) God had to be God, so that he could give the Holy Spirit, gather the church, be present with it, and confer and preserve the benefits won by death. For the Mediator had to become a victim, drive death away from himself, and intercede with God on our behalf; but he also had to promise that at last we would cease to offend God by our sins. Because of our perversity, however, no one could give this promise on our behalf who did not have the power to give the Holy Spirit and to reform us through him into the image of God. But to give the Holy Spirit and through him to regenerate hearts belongs to God alone, whose own Spirit he is. Whom I will send to you from the Father. For only the Lord of nature can reform nature.

units.la: 5. Denique Messiam oportuit esse Iehovam, iustitiâ nostram. Obiect. Obiect. Pars offensa non potest esse mediator, Christus est mediator. Ergo non potest esse pars offensa, hoc est, Deus. Resp. Maior vera est duntaxat de ea parte offensa, in qua non sunt plures personae. Vide volum. 1. Vrsini pag. 110.
units.tr: (5) Finally, the Messiah had to be Jehovah, our righteousness. Objection. The offended party cannot be the mediator; Christ is the mediator. Therefore he cannot be the offended party, that is, God. Answer. The major premise is true only of that offended party in whom there are not several persons. See Ursinus, volume 1, page 110.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XVIII. Quis autem est ille Mediator, qui simul est verus Deus a, & verus b perfectéq; iustus homo c?
units.tr: QUESTION XVIII. Who then is that Mediator who is at once true God and a true and perfectly righteous man?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus d, qui factus est nobis à Deo sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, & redemptio e.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who has been made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Qualis Mediator sit necessarius, dictum est. Iam quæritur, quis sit talis. Solus est Iesus Christus Filius Dei in carne manifestatus: quod his rationibus confirmatur:
units.tr: We have said what kind of Mediator is necessary. Now the question is who such a Mediator is. Jesus Christ alone, the Son of God manifested in the flesh, is he. This is confirmed by the following reasons:

units.la: 1. Mediatorem oportet esse verum Deum, ut est demonstratum. Deus Pater esse non poterat: quia Pater non agit per se, sed per Filium & Spiritum sanctum: nec fit ipse legatus, quia à nullo mittitur, sed ipse mittit Mediatorem. Nec Spiritus sanctus: quia hic à Mediatore in corda electorum mitti debuit. Solus igitur Filius est Mediator.
units.tr: 1. The Mediator must be true God, as has been shown. God the Father could not be the Mediator, because the Father does not act through himself but through the Son and the Holy Spirit; nor does he become the envoy, since he is sent by no one, but himself sends the Mediator. Nor can the Holy Spirit be the Mediator, because he ought to be sent by the Mediator into the hearts of the elect. Therefore the Son alone is the Mediator.

units.la: 2. Quod Mediator nobis debuit conferre, id oportebat ipsum habere. Debuit autem nobis conferre ius filiorum Dei, seu υἱοθεσίαν, qua excideramus, hoc est, debuit efficere, ut per & propter ipsum à Deo in filios adoptaremur: quia solus ipse hoc poterat, utpote solus ius filij habens. Non enim hoc habuit Spiritus sanctus, quia non est filius: Nec id habuit Pater, quia non est filius, & Pater debuit nos per Filium in filios adoptare. Ergo igitur, naturalis Dei Filius, solus est noster Mediator, in quo tanquam in primogenito, in filios Dei adoptamur: sicut dicitur: Si Filius vos liberaverit, verè liberi eritis. Quotquot receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem, filios Dei fieri. Quos adoptaret in filios per Iesum Christum. Fecit nos dilectos in illo dilecto.
units.tr: 2. What the Mediator was to bestow on us, he himself must have possessed. He was to bestow on us the right of the sons of God, or adoption [υἱοθεσία], which we had lost; that is, he was to bring it about that we are adopted as sons by God, through him and on account of him. Only he could do this, since he alone has the right of the Son. The Holy Spirit did not have this right, because he is not a Son; nor did the Father have it, because the Father is not a Son, and the Father was to adopt us as sons through the Son. Therefore the natural Son of God alone is our Mediator, in whom, as the firstborn, we are adopted as sons of God. So it is said: "If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed." "As many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God." "Whom he would adopt as sons through Jesus Christ." "He has made us accepted in the Beloved."
John 8:36. John 1:12.

units.la: 3. Solus Filius est λόγος, Orator Patris, ea persona missa ad genus humanum, per quam Pater consilium suum nobis patefacit, per quam operatur, dat Spiritum sanctum: per quam etiam fit secunda creatio. Per Filium enim efficimur novae creaturae. Ideo scriptura creationem primam & secundam passim coniungit, quia per eundem debuit fieri creatio secunda, per quem facta est prima. Per Filium omnia facta sunt. Mediatoris vero erat, esse talem internuncium Dei ad homines, nosq; per Spiritum regenerare, &c. Ergo solus Filius est Mediator.
units.tr: 3. The Son alone is the Word [λόγος], the Father's spokesman, that person sent to mankind through whom the Father reveals his counsel to us, through whom he works and gives the Holy Spirit, and through whom the second creation also takes place. For through the Son we are made new creatures. Therefore Scripture everywhere couples the first and the second creation, because the second creation had to be made through the same one through whom the first was made. All things were made through the Son. It belongs to the Mediator to be such an intermediary between God and men, and to regenerate us through the Spirit, and so on. Therefore the Son alone is the Mediator.

units.la: 4. Mediatoris est, immediatè mittere Spiritum sanctum. Solus Filius immediatè mittit Spiritum sanctum. Pater enim eum mittit per Filium: Filius immediatè à Patre, sicut dicit: Quem ego mittam vobis à Patre.
units.tr: 4. It belongs to the Mediator to send the Holy Spirit immediately. The Son alone sends the Holy Spirit immediately. For the Father sends him through the Son, while the Son sends him immediately from the Father, as he says: "Whom I will send to you from the Father."

units.la: 5. Mediatoris erat, pro nobis pati & mori. Solus Filius est is, qui, assumptâ carne, pro nobis est passus & mortuus. Deus manifestatus est in carne, &c. Mortificatus carne, &c. Ergo &c.
units.tr: 5. It was the Mediator's task to suffer and die for us. The Son alone is the one who, having taken on flesh, suffered and died for us. God was manifested in the flesh, etc. Put to death in the flesh, etc. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 6. Filium esse Mediatorem, probatur ex collatione patefactionum & oraculorum Veteris Testamenti, cum eorundem impletione in Novo.
units.tr: 6. That the Son is the Mediator is proved by comparing the revelations and oracles of the Old Testament with their fulfilment in the New.

units.la: 7. Idem probatur ex operibus & miraculis, quae Christus fecit. Opera, quae facio, testantur de me, quod Pater misit me. Operibus credite. Christus cùm venerit, num signa plura edet ius, quae hic edidit? Profecti renunciate Iohanni, quae videtis & auditis: caeci vident, claudi ambulant, &c.
units.tr: 7. The same is proved from the works and miracles which Christ performed. The works that I do bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. Believe the works. When Christ comes, will he perform more signs than those which he has performed here? Go and report to John what you see and hear: the blind see, the lame walk, etc.

units.la: 8. Ex scripturae apertis testimoniis: Unus est Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. Christus factus est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia & sanctificatio, & redemptio, id est, factus est nobis doctor sapientiae, iustificator, sanctificator, & redemptor, hoc est, Mediator & Seruator merito & efficacia. Abstracta enim in dicto Apostoli ponuntur pro concretis.
units.tr: 8. From the plain testimonies of Scripture: "There is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." "Christ was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." That is, he was made to us the teacher of wisdom, the justifier, the sanctifier, and the redeemer; that is, Mediator and Saviour by merit and efficacy. For abstract terms in the Apostle's saying stand for concrete ones.

units.la: Notandum, quod Christus Mediator dicitur nobis à Deo datus, datus, constitutus. Debuerat Mediator à nobis dari, & ex nobis prodire: quia nos offenderamus. Nos verò ex nobis aliquem dare non poteramus: quia omnes eramus filij irae. Necesse igitur fuit, Mediatorem nobis dari à Deo.
units.tr: It should be noted that Christ is said to be given to us as Mediator by God: given, appointed. The Mediator ought to have been given by us and to have come forth from us, because we had offended. But we could not give anyone out of ourselves, since we were all children of wrath. It was therefore necessary that a Mediator be given to us by God.

units.la: Notandum quoque, iustitiam & sanctitatem in Adamo ante lapsum fuisse eandem rem, nempe conformitatem cum Deo & Lege inhaerentem: ut nunc sunt res eadem in sanctis Angelis. Iam verò post lapsum non sunt res eadem in nobis. Nam iustitia nostra est Christus: & iustificatio nostra est impuratio iustitiae Christi, quia justi habemur coram Deo. Sanctitas verò est inchoata conformitas nostra cum Deo: & sanctificatio est effectio conformitatis cum Deo in nobis: quae hic imperfecta est, in aliis... in altera vita perficietur, vbi justitia & sanctitas rursus vna res erunt, etiam in nobis. Sequitur summa totius doctrinæ de Mediatore.
units.tr: It should also be noted that righteousness and holiness in Adam before the fall were the same thing, namely conformity with God and the Law inhering in him, as they are now the same thing in the holy angels. But after the fall they are not the same thing in us. For our righteousness is Christ, and our justification is the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, because we are held righteous before God. Holiness, however, is our inchoate conformity with God, and sanctification is the effecting of conformity with God in us, which is imperfect here. In the other life it will be perfected, where righteousness and holiness will again be one and the same thing, also in us. Here follows the sum of the whole doctrine of the Mediator.

units.la: DE MEDIATORE.
units.tr: ON THE MEDIATOR.

units.la: Doctrina de Mediatore tenenda est propter Dei gloriam, & propter nostram consolationem. 1. Vt celebremus misericordiam Dei, quod Filium suum nobis dedit Mediatorem, qui fieret victima pro nostris peccatis. 2. Vt sciamus, Deum esse justum, neq; leuiter remittere peccata, sed adeo grauiter irasci, vt ea non remittat, nisi intercedente Filij sui satisfactione. 3. Vt hoc Mediatore freti certi simus de vita æterna: quia vult & potest eam nobis dare. 4. Est fundamentum & summa totius Christianæ doctrinæ. 5. Propter hæreticos, quia eam omnibus temporibus grauissimè oppugnarunt, vt contra hos eam defendere possimus.
units.tr: The doctrine of the Mediator is to be held for the glory of God and for our consolation. 1. That we may celebrate the mercy of God, who gave us his Son as Mediator, to become the victim for our sins. 2. That we may know God to be just, and that he does not lightly remit sins, but is so gravely angry that he does not remit them unless his Son's satisfaction intervenes. 3. That, relying on this Mediator, we may be certain of eternal life, because he is willing and able to give it to us. 4. It is the foundation and sum of the whole Christian doctrine. 5. On account of the heretics, who have attacked it most severely in all ages, so that we may be able to defend it against them.

units.la: Videtur quidem pertinere ad locum de justificatione, quia ibi etiam officium Mediatoris explicatur. Verum aliud est docere, quid & quale sit beneficium justificationis, & quomodo accipiatur; quod fit in loco justificationis: aliud docere, cuius sit illud beneficium, à quo nobis conferatur; quod huc pertinet.
units.tr: It seems indeed to belong to the place on justification, because the office of the Mediator is explained there too. But it is one thing to teach what and of what kind the benefit of justification is, and how it is received, which is done in the place on justification; it is another to teach whose benefit it is, from whom it is conferred on us; and this belongs here.

units.la: Quæstiones de Mediatore præcipuæ sunt sex: I. Quid sit? II. An aliquo nobis sit opus? III. Quod eius officium? IV. Qualis esse debeat? V. Quis sit ille? VI. An possint esse plures?
units.tr: There are six principal questions concerning the Mediator: I. What is he? II. Is he necessary for us? III. What is the office of the Mediator? IV. What sort of person ought he to be? V. Who is he? VI. Can there be several?

units.la: I. Quid sit Mediator?
units.tr: I. What is a Mediator?

units.la: Mediator in genere significat eum, qui reconciliat duas partes dissidentes, interponens se, & placans offensam, vel deprecando, vel etiam satisfaciendo, & cauendo, ne amplius offendatur. Germanicè eim Schiedmann. Reconciliare enim est 1. intercedere pro eo, qui offendit, apud offensum. 2. Satisfacere pro injuria illata. 3. Promittere & efficere, vt pars offendens non amplius offendat.
units.tr: In general, a Mediator means one who reconciles two parties at variance, interposing himself and appeasing the offence, either by pleading or also by satisfying, and taking care that the offence is not repeated. In German, indeed, Schiedmann. For to reconcile means: 1. to intercede for the one who has given offence, with the one offended; 2. to make satisfaction for the injury inflicted; 3. to promise and bring it about that the offending party does not offend again.

units.la: Hoc loco, Mediator est persona reconcilians Deum irascentem peccatis, & genus humanum reum æternæ mortis propter peccatum, deprecans pro reis: & pro iisdem satisfaciens diuinæ justitiæ motiendo, applicans etiam credentibus sua merita per fidem, & regenerando eos per Spiritum sanctum, efficiens, vt peccare desinant, denique inuocantium preces & gemitus exaudiens. Seu: est pacificator inter Deum & homines, placans iram Dei, & restituens homines in gratiam Dei, intercedendo & satisfaciendo pro eorum peccatis, & faciens, vt Deus amet homines, & homines ament Deum, sitq; inter Deum & homines constans & æterna pax atque concordia.
units.tr: In this place, the Mediator is the person who reconciles God, angry at sins, and the human race, guilty of eternal death on account of sin; who pleads for the guilty and, on their behalf, satisfies divine justice by moving it; who also applies his merits to believers through faith, regenerates them through the Holy Spirit, bringing it about that they cease to sin, and finally hears the prayers and groanings of those who call upon him.
