Cur verò non omnes sibi applicent, nec omnes credant, sublimior est quæstio, quæ hùc non pertinet. Miseretur Deus cuius vult: quem autem vult, indurat. Et ita vult patefacere misericordiam, vt etiam exerceat justitiam.
units.tr: Objection 3. Adam subjected all to condemnation; Christ saves only some. Therefore the power of Adam's sin to condemn is greater than the power of Christ's satisfaction to save. Answer. The consequence is denied, because the force, excellence and efficacy of Christ's satisfaction are not measured by the multitude or number of men who are saved by it, but by the greatness of the benefit itself. And indeed it is a greater work to deliver one or another man from eternal death than to make all men guilty of eternal death through sin. Further, that the power of the efficacy of Christ's benefit does not reach all as the power of Adam's sin reached all, the fault lies in the men themselves, who do not apply the merit of Christ to themselves by faith as equally as they apply the sin of Adam to themselves by natural birth and imitation. But why not all apply it to themselves, and why not all believe, is a more lofty question, which does not pertain here. God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. And so he wills to display his mercy in such a way that he also exercises justice.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXI.
units.tr: QUESTION XXI.

units.la: Quid est vera fides? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What is true faith? ANSWER.

units.la: Est non tantum certa notitia, qua firmiter assentior omnibus, quæ Deus nobis in verbo suo patefecit a, sed etiam certa fiducia b, à Spiritu sancto c, per Euangelium in corde meo accensa d, qua in Deo acquiesco, certò statuens, non solum aliis, sed mihi quoque remissionem peccatorum, æternam justitiam, & vitam donatam esse, idque gratis, ex Dei misericordia, propter vnius Christi meritum f.
units.tr: It is not merely a certain knowledge by which I firmly assent to all the things God has revealed to us in his word a, but also a certain trust b, kindled in my heart through the Gospel by the Holy Spirit c d, by which I rest in God, firmly holding that forgiveness of sins, eternal righteousness and life have been given, and given freely, by God's mercy and on account of the merit of Christ alone f, not only to others but to me as well.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Doctrina de Fide sequitur: 1. Quia fides est medium, quo fimus Mediatoris participes. 2. Quia sine fide Euangelij prædicatio nihil prodest. De ea quæritur: I. Quid sit? II. Quas habeat species in scriptura. III. Quid à spe differat. IV. Quæ sint causæ efficientes fidei justificantis. V. Quæ eius effecta. VI. Quibus detur.
units.tr: The doctrine of faith follows for two reasons: 1. because faith is the means by which we become partakers of the Mediator; 2. because the preaching of the Gospel profits nothing without faith. Concerning it we ask: I. What it is; II. What kinds of it there are in Scripture; III. How it differs from hope; IV. What are the efficient causes of justifying faith; V. What are its effects; VI. To whom it is given.

units.la: I. Quid sit fides in genere.
units.tr: I. What faith is in general.

units.la: Fides à fiendo dicta, quia fiat, quod dictum est: juxta Ciceronem est dictorum conuentorumque constantia & veritas: & fundamentum justitiæ.
units.tr: Faith is so called from fiendo, becoming, because what was spoken comes to pass. According to Cicero, it is the steadfastness and truth of things said and agreed, and the foundation of justice.

units.la: Vulgò definitur, quod sit notitia certa propositionum seu conclusionum, quibus assentimur propter asseverationem testium veracium, de quibus fas non est dubitare, siue illi sint Deus, siue angeli, siue homines, siue experientia. Cùm verò alia sit diuina-rum, alia humanarum rerum fides, generalissima distinctione quæritur hic, quid sit fides rerum diuinarum, seu fides theologica. Danda est igitur definitio fidei generaliter sumptæ aliquanto restrictior: & tamen talis, quæ omnibus fidei speciebus in scri-ptura traditis competat.
units.tr: It is commonly defined as a certain knowledge of propositions or conclusions to which we assent on account of the assertion of trustworthy witnesses, whose testimony it is not right to doubt, whether they be God, angels, men, or experience. Since, however, faith in divine things is one thing and faith in human things another, the question here, by the most general distinction, is what faith in divine things is, that is, theological faith. A definition of faith taken in general, somewhat more restricted, must therefore be given; yet one such that it applies to all the kinds of faith handed down in Scripture.

units.la: In genere igitur fides, cuius sit mentio in sacris literis, est assensus, vel notitia certa propositionum de Deo, eiusque voluntate, operibus & gratia, quibus assentimur propter testimonium diuinum. Seu, est assentiri omni verbo Dei Ecclesiæ tradito in Lege & Euangelio, propter asseuerationem ipsius Dei.
units.tr: In general, then, faith, as it is mentioned in the sacred writings, is assent, or certain knowledge, of propositions concerning God and his will, works and grace, to which we assent on account of divine testimony. Or: it is to assent to every word of God handed down to the Church in the Law and the Gospel, on account of the assertion of God himself.

units.la: Sæpe autem fides accipitur pro ipsa doctrina Ecclesiæ, seu pro rebus, quibus ex Dei verbo ad fidem informamur: vt cum dicitur, fides Christiana, fides apostolica. Sæpe pro impletione vete-rum promissionum seu pro rebus ipsis, quæ creduntur. vt: Antequam venisset fides, sub legis præsidio tenebamur conclusi in eam fidem, quæ erat revelanda, &c. Plura fidei significata (septem nimirum) require in Comment. D. Parei ad Romanos cap.1. vers.17. & cap.11. dub.17.
units.tr: Often, however, faith is taken for the doctrine of the Church itself, or for the things by which we are instructed in faith from the Word of God: as when one speaks of Christian faith or apostolic faith. Often it is taken for the fulfilment of the old promises, or for the things themselves which are believed, as in: Before faith came, we were kept under the guard of the law, shut up to that faith which was to be revealed, etc. The several meanings of faith (seven, namely) are set out in D. Pareus's Commentary on Romans, chapter 1, verse 17, and chapter 11, dub. 17.

units.la: II. Quotuplex sit fides.
units.tr: II. Of how many kinds faith is.

units.la: Quatuor species fidei in scriptura commemorantur: historica, temporaria, miraculorum, & justificans, siue saluifica. Discrimen earum ex definitionibus constat.
units.tr: Four kinds of faith are mentioned in Scripture: historical, temporary, of miracles, and justifying or saving. The difference between them is clear from their definitions.

units.la: Historica fides est agnoscere & statuere, quod verum sit omne Dei verbum diuinitus traditum, siue per vocem, siue per oracula, siue per visiones, siue per alium revelationis modum, propter ipsius Dei authoritatem & asseverationem, de quo nobis constat. Nominatur historica: quia tantum est notitia historiæ, hoc est, eorum, quæ Deus dicitur fecisse, aut facere, aut facturus esse. De hac fide loquuntur dicta: Si habeam omnem fidem, &c. quod tamen etiam de quavis fide intelligi potest, excepta justificante. Dæmones credunt, & contremiscunt. Simon credidit: nempe doctrinam Petri veram esse. Sed non ideo habuit fidem veram justificantem.
units.tr: Historical faith is to acknowledge and hold as true every word of God delivered by divine inspiration, whether by voice, by oracles, by visions, or by another mode of revelation, on account of God's own authority and assertion, of which we are assured. It is called historical because it is merely knowledge of history, that is, of those things which God is said to have done, or to be doing, or to be going to do. Of this faith speak the words If I have all faith, etc., which, however, can be understood of any faith except justifying faith. The demons believe and tremble. Simon believed: namely, that the doctrine of Peter was true. But he did not thereby have true, justifying faith.

units.la: Temporaria fides est assentiri doctrinæ Euangelij, cum professione & lætitia, sed non vera & solida, hoc est, non orta ex sensu gratiæ Dei erga se, sed ex aliis quibuscunque causis, ideoque tantum ad tempus durat, & tempore afflictionum deficit. Seu, est assentiri doctrinæ cœlesti per Prophetas & Apostolos traditæ, eamque profiteri, de ea gloriari, & eius cognitione lætari ad tempus: non propter applicationem promissionis ad se, hoc est, non propter sensum gratiae in suo corde, sed propter alias causas. Haec definitio sumta est ex parabola & verbis Christi: Qui in petrosa semen excepit, is est, qui sermonem audit, & statim cum gaudio accipit, verum non habet radicem in semetipso, sed temporarius est, ortaq; oppressione vel persecutione propter sermonem statim offenditur. Causae gaudij quodammodo sunt infinitae, in aliis aliae: omnes tamen temporariae, quae cum mutantur, fides deficit. Hypocritae laetantur auditione Euangelij, vel quia eis est res nova, vel quia videtur blandiri eorum affectibus, dum leuat eos oneribus traditionum humanarum, ut doctrina de libertate Christiana, de justificatione, &c. vel quia quaerunt sub eius professione licentiam peccandi, compendia & commoda, priuata vel publica, diuitias, honorem, gloriam, &c. quod patet, cum ad crucem est ventum. Tum enim, quia radicem non habent, exuruntur. Non autem laetantur, sicut vere credentes, de sensu gratiae Dei, de bonorum in verbo oblatorum applicatione ad se: quae est causa solidae & verae laetitiae in vere credentibus, & cuius unius causae remotio sufficit ad hoc, ut fides sit temporaria.
units.tr: Temporary faith is to assent to the doctrine of the Gospel with profession and joy, but not true and solid; that is, not arising from a sense of God's grace toward oneself, but from some other causes, and therefore it lasts only for a time and fails in the time of afflictions. Or, it is to assent to the heavenly doctrine handed down by the Prophets and Apostles, to profess it, to glory in it, and to rejoice for a time in its knowledge; not on account of applying the promise to oneself, that is, not on account of a sense of grace in one's heart, but on account of other causes. This definition is taken from the parable and words of Christ: "He who received the seed on stony ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy, but has no root in himself, but is temporary; and when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, he is immediately offended." The causes of joy are in a way endless, and differ from person to person; yet all are temporary, and when they change, faith fails. Hypocrites rejoice at hearing the Gospel, either because it is new to them, or because it seems to flatter their feelings, while it relieves them of the burdens of human traditions (as the doctrine of Christian liberty, of justification, etc.), or because under its profession they seek licence to sin, advantages and profit, private or public, riches, honour, glory, etc. This becomes plain when the cross comes; for then, since they have no root, they are burned up. But they do not rejoice, as truly believing people do, in the sense of God's grace, in the application to themselves of the good things offered in the word. This is the cause of solid and true joy in true believers, and the removal of this one cause alone is enough to make faith temporary.

units.la: Haec fides temporaria differt ab historica sola laetitia comitante ipsam. Historica enim tantum habet notitiam. Temporaria vero etiam laetatur ea cognitione, quam habet. ἀσὐναυρσι enim accipiunt verbum cum gaudio. Daemones credunt historice, sed non gaudent, verum contremiscunt: non laetantur notitia, quam habent, sed vellent eam prorsus extinctam. Immo nec profitentur, se esse approbatores eius doctrinae, etsi sciunt veram esse, sed horribiliter eam oderunt & oppugnant. In hominibus tamen historica fides aliás coniuncta est cum professione; aliás non. Saepe enim homines quibusdam de causis ea profitentur, quae oderunt. Multi vero, qui sciunt doctrinam veram esse, nihilominus eam oppugnant, Sie wolten / daß die Bibel im Rhein schwimme: & hi peccant in Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: This temporary faith differs from historical faith only by the joy that accompanies it. For historical faith has only knowledge; temporary faith also rejoices in the knowledge it has. For these receive the word with joy [οὗτοι μετὰ χαρᾶς δέχονται τὸν λόγον]. Demons believe historically, but they do not rejoice; they tremble. They take no delight in the knowledge they have, but would wish it utterly extinguished. Indeed, they do not even profess themselves approvers of this doctrine, although they know it is true, but hate it horribly and attack it. In men, however, historical faith is sometimes joined with profession and sometimes not, for often people for certain reasons profess what they hate. Many, indeed, who know the doctrine to be true, nevertheless attack it: "They wanted the Bible to float down the Rhine"; and these sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Miraculorum fides est donum singulare, faciendi aliquod opus extraordinarium, aut praedicendi certum eventum, ex reuelatione divina. Seu est certa persuasio de futuro aliquo effectu miraculoso, quem fieri petit, & eventurum credit ac dicit, ex reuelatione, vel instinctu singulari. Haec enim fides non potest ex verbo generali concipi, nisi accedat specialis reuelatio. De hac fide ait Apostolus: Si habeam omnem fidem, adeo ut montes transferam.
units.tr: Faith of miracles is a special gift of doing some extraordinary work, or of foretelling a certain outcome, from divine revelation. Or it is a certain persuasion about some future miraculous effect, which one asks to be done and believes and says will come to pass, from a special revelation or singular inspiration. For this faith cannot be conceived from the general word unless a special revelation is added. Of this faith the Apostle says: "If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains."

units.la: 1 Cor. 13, 2. feram. Hoc dictum licet priore parte intelligatur de omnibus fidei speciebus, exceptâ justificante: tamen posteriore restringi- tur ad fidem miraculorum.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13, 2. feram. Although this saying, in its first part, may be understood of all the kinds of faith except justifying faith, its latter part is restricted to the faith of miracles.

units.la: Diuersam hanc esse ab aliis fidei speciebus, probatur:
units.tr: That this is different from the other kinds of faith is proved:

units.la: 1. Ex dicto Christi: Si habueritis fidem, quantulum est granum sinapis, dicetis monti huic: demigra hinc illuc, & demigrabit. Atqui multi sancti habuerunt firmam fidem, vt Abraham, Dauid, &c. & tamen non transtulerunt montes. Ergo haec est certa species fidei à justificante distincta.
units.tr: 1. From the saying of Christ: "If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, Move from here to there, and it will move." But many saints had firm faith, as Abraham, David, etc., and yet did not move mountains. Therefore this is a certain kind of faith distinct from justifying faith.

units.la: 2. Exorcistæ filij Sceuæ in actis conabantur eijcere dæmonia, cum non haberent donum id faciendi, quibus proinde res male succedebat.
units.tr: 2. The exorcists, the sons of Sceva, in Acts tried to cast out demons when they did not have the gift of doing so, and so things went badly for them.

units.la: 3. Simon magus dicitur credidisse, & tamen non potuit edere miracula. Nam ideo volebat hanc facultatem pecuniâ emere.
units.tr: Simon Magus is said to have believed, and yet he could not work miracles. For he wanted to buy this power with money.

units.la: 4. Diabolus nouit historiam: nec tamen edit miracula: Ergo nemo nisi Creator potest immutare rerum naturam.
units.tr: The devil knows the history, yet he does not work miracles. Therefore no one but the Creator can change the nature of things.

units.la: 5. Judas docebat, & edebat miracula, sicut alij Apostoli: ergo habuit fidem historicam (fortasse etiam temporariam) & miraculorum: & tamen non habuit justificantem. A Christo enim vocarur diabolus.
units.tr: Judas taught and worked miracles, as the other apostles did. Therefore he had historical faith (perhaps also temporary faith) and the faith of miracles, and yet he did not have justifying faith. For Christ calls him a devil.

units.la: 6. Multi dicent: Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo dæmonia ejecimus? quibus tamen respondebit Christus: Nunquam noui vos.
units.tr: Many will say: Lord, Lord, have we not cast out devils in your name? Yet Christ will answer them: I never knew you.

units.la: 7. Denique aliæ species fidei se extendunt ad omnia, quæ credenda in verbo proponuntur. Hæc verò ad certa tantum opera & euentus extraordinarios pertinet. Est ergo species fidei ab aliis distincta.
units.tr: Finally, the other kinds of faith extend to all the things that are proposed to be believed in the Word. This kind, however, pertains only to certain works and extraordinary events. Therefore this kind of faith is distinct from the others.

units.la: Iustificans fides proprie est ea, quæ definitur in catechesi, in qua definitione genus est notitia & assensus firmus. Doctrinæ enim incognitæ nulla fides: & oportet te doctrinam prius nosse, quam ei credas. Ideo Papistarum fides implicita non est fides, sed cæca opinio. Differentia est fiducia & applicatio gratiæ remissionis peccatorum, per & propter Christum. Proprium est acquiescere & lætari in Deo propter hoc tantum bonum. Causa efficiens est Spiritus sanctus. Instrumentalis est Euangelium, sub quo sacramentorum visus intelligitur. Subiectum est mens, voluntas & cor hominis.
units.tr: Justifying faith is properly that which is defined in the catechism, and in this definition the genus is knowledge and firm assent. For there is no faith in a doctrine that is unknown, and you must know a doctrine before you believe it. Hence the implicit faith of the Papists is not faith but blind opinion. The difference is trust and the application of the grace of forgiveness of sins, through and on account of Christ. The property is to rest and rejoice in God on account of this one good. The efficient cause is the Holy Spirit. The instrumental cause is the Gospel, under which the sight of the sacraments is understood. The subject is the mind, the will and the heart of man.

units.la: Differt ergo fides justificans & saluifica à reliquis speciebus:
units.tr: Justifying and saving faith therefore differs from the other kinds in the following ways:

units.la: 1. Quod hæc sola est coniuncta cum certa fiducia, qua nobis applicamus Christi meritum, hoc est, certò statuimus, justitiam seu meritum Christi nobis quoque donari & imputari. Fiducia verò est motus cordis & voluntatis persequens bonum cognitum, tum, eoq; gaudens & nitens : Germanicè vertrawen / sich gang vnd gar darauff verlassen. ϖίστις enim & ϖιστεύω est à ϖείθω: unde ϖιστεύειν etiam apud profanos authores significat fiduciam habere, niti re aliqua : ut apud Phocylidem: Λακῶ μὴ ϖίστευε, ϖα-λυτεγκὸς ἐπ' ἀμιλῶ. Et apud Demosthenem: Σαυτῷ ϖιστεύεις: confidis tibi ipsi, seu, te ipso niteris.
units.tr: 1. This faith alone is joined with a sure trust, by which we apply to ourselves the merit of Christ; that is, we firmly hold that the righteousness or merit of Christ is also given and imputed to us. Trust, however, is a movement of the heart and will that pursues a known good, and then rests in it, rejoices in it and strives toward it; in German, vertrawen, to rely wholly and entirely upon it. For [πίστις] and [πιστεύω] come from [πείθω]; whence [πιστεύειν] also among the secular authors means to have trust, to lean upon something, as in Phocylides: [Λακῶ μὴ πίστευε, παλυτεγκὲς ἐπ' ἀμιλλῶ], do not trust a Laconian... And in Demosthenes: [Σαυτῷ πιστεύεις], you trust yourself, or, you lean upon yourself.

units.la: 2. Differt etiam ab historica, quòd historicam semper in se complectitur: historica verò ad justificantem non sufficit; sicut nec aliæ duæ: & ab omnibus, quòd ex sola justificante est justitia & hæreditas. Nam si, ut Apostolus dicit, fide justificamur: fides imputatur ad justitiam: ex fide est hæreditas: ea fides utique erit una aliqua harum quatuor. Non verò est historica: alioquin & diaboli essent justi & hæredes: nec temporaria: quia hanc Christus reijcit: nec miraculorum: alioqui Judas etiam esset hæres. Ex sola igitur justificante est justitia & hæreditas: quidem proprie & simpliciter in scriptura fides appellatur, & electorum est propria.
units.tr: 2. It also differs from historical faith in that it always includes historical faith within itself, whereas historical faith is not sufficient for justification; nor are the other two. And it differs from all of them in that righteousness and inheritance come from justifying faith alone. For if, as the Apostle says, we are justified by faith, and faith is imputed for righteousness, and inheritance is by faith, then that faith must certainly be one of these four. It is not historical, for otherwise the devils too would be righteous and heirs; nor is it temporary, because Christ rejects this; nor is it the faith of miracles, for otherwise Judas would also be an heir. Therefore righteousness and inheritance come from justifying faith alone; and this is properly and simply what Scripture calls faith, and it belongs to the elect alone.

units.la: Quid verò sit fides justificans, nemo verè intelligit, nisi qui verè credit, seu qui veram fidem habet: sicut nemo intelligit, quàm dulce sit mel, etsi multa ei de mellis suavitate & dulcedine prædices, nisi mel ipse gustaverit. Credens verò scit & sentit se credere, & reperit in se hæc, quæ & aliis explicare potest.
units.tr: But what justifying faith is, no one truly understands except the one who truly believes, or who has true faith; just as no one understands how sweet honey is, however much you describe to him its smoothness and sweetness, unless he has tasted honey himself. The one who believes, however, knows and feels that he believes, and finds in himself the following things, which he can also explain to others.

units.la: 1. Credit vera & divina esse omnia, quæ in scriptura continentur.
units.tr: 1. He believes that all the things contained in Scripture are true and divine.

units.la: 2. Sentit se obligari ad ea firmiter credenda & amplectenda. Si enim vera & divina esse fatemur: æquum est utique & necessarium, ut eis assentiamur.
units.tr: 2. He feels himself bound to believe and embrace them firmly. For if we confess that they are true and divine, it is certainly right and necessary that we assent to them.

units.la: 3. Præcipuè intuetur amplectitur, & firma fiducia sibi applicat promissionem gratiæ, seu de gratuita remissione peccatorum, justitia, & vita æterna, per & propter Christum; sicut dicitur: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam.
units.tr: 3. Above all he looks upon and embraces the promise of grace, that is, of the free forgiveness of sins, righteousness and eternal life, through and on account of Christ, and applies it to himself with a firm trust; as it is said: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.

units.la: 4. Hac fretus fiducia firmiter acquiescit in præsenti gratia Dei, & ex ea sic concludit de futura: Cum jam me amet Deus, & mihi det tanta bona, etiam servabit me in æternum: quia est verax & immutabilis, & dona eius sunt absque pœnitentia.
units.tr: 4. Relying on this trust, he firmly rests in the present grace of God, and from it he thus concludes about the future: since God already loves me and gives me such great goods, he will also keep me forever, because he is true and unchangeable, and his gifts are without repentance.

units.la: 5. Sequitur lætitia in corde de his bonis, & pax conscientiæ omnem humanum intellectum superans.
units.tr: 5. There follows joy in the heart over these goods, and a peace of conscience surpassing all human understanding.

units.la: 6. Denique habet voluntatem & serium studium obediendi Deo, sine exceptione, in omnibus faciendis aut patiendis, quæ Deus jubet. Facit igitur homo præditus fide justificante officium mundo & diabolo reluctantibus. Hæc, qui verè credit, in se sentit, & qui in se sentit, verè credit.
units.tr: 6. Finally, he has a will and earnest zeal to obey God without exception in all the things that God commands to be done or suffered. The man endowed with justifying faith therefore performs his duty, though the world and the devil resist. This the one who truly believes feels in himself, and whoever feels it in himself truly believes.

units.la: III. Quid fides & spes differant.
units.tr: III. What faith and hope differ in.

units.la: Fides justificans non confunditur cum spe, etsi utraq; eadem bona respicit. Fides enim apprehendit praesentia, spes futura. Contra. Credimus vitam aeternam, quae est futura. Ergo fides etiam est futurorum. Resp. Vita aeterna est futurum bonum, quo ad consummationem, & sic jam non creditur simpliciter, sed speratur. Spe enim salui facti sumus. Nunc filij Dei sumus, sed nondum patefactum est, quod erimus, &c. Est vero etiam praesens bonum: 1. Quoad praesentem voluntatem Dei nobis eam dandi. 2. Quoad eius initium, etiam in hac vita: & sic non speratur, sed creditur vita aeterna, juxta dicta: Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet vitam aeternam, & transiuit a morte in vitam. Haec est vita aeterna, ut te solum cognoscant verum Deum, &c. Fide igitur statuimus, nostra esse bona, quae nondum habemus, propter promissionem divinam: sed spe certa expectamus, quoad impletionem. Et hoc sensu dicit Apostolus, fidem versari circa res speratas: Fides est substantia sperandarum, seu substantia bonorum sperandorum: hoc est, est illud, quod facit, ut extent quae sperantur: & quod demonstrat, quae non apparent: nempe quoad impletionem & consummationem, &c. Alij sic conciliant: Fides amplectitur propositiones symboli seu Euangelij praesentes de rebus futuris: spes autem res ipsas futuras. Sed minus popularis est haec conciliatio, quam altera. IV. Quae sint causa fidei. Causa efficiens prima & principalis fidei historicae, temporariae, & miraculorum, est Spiritus sanctus: sed actione divina generali: iustificantis vero actione speciali. Gratia Dei servati estis per fidem: non ex vobis: Dei donum est, &c. Obiectio: Diabolus habet fidem historicam. Ergo a Spiritu sancto. Resp. Etiam quae in daemonibus est fides, efficitur a Deo, sed generali & universali, ut dictum est, operatione, non speciali: quia tali operatione & modo Spiritus sanctus in solis electis operatur fidem justificantem. Nam etiam in daemonibus & hypocritis, quicquid est cogitionis, Deus per Spiritum suum efficit: sed non ita, ut eos regeneret aut justificet, sicut electos: neque ita, ut ipsi cum doni huius authorem agnoscant vel celebrent. Instrumentalis causa fidei in genere, est totum verbum Dei comprehensum libris veteris & novi testamenti, in quibus praeter verbum multa etiam opera & miracula Dei continentur.
units.tr: Justifying faith is not to be confused with hope, although both look to the same good things. For faith apprehends present things, and hope future ones. Objection. We believe eternal life, which is future. Therefore faith also concerns future things. Answer. Eternal life is a future good as to its consummation, and so it is not simply believed but hoped for. For we were saved by hope. Now we are the sons of God, but it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, etc. Yet it is also a present good: 1. As to God's present will to give it to us. 2. As to its beginning, even in this life; and so eternal life is not hoped for but believed, according to the sayings: He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life, and has passed from death to life. This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, etc. Therefore we hold by faith that those goods, which we do not yet have, are ours, on account of the divine promise; but we await their fulfilment with certain hope. In this sense the Apostle says that faith is concerned with things hoped for: Faith is the substance of things hoped for, or the substance of good things to be hoped for; that is, it is what makes the things hoped for subsist, and what demonstrates the things that do not appear: namely as to fulfilment and consummation, etc. Others reconcile it thus: faith embraces the present propositions of the creed or Gospel about future things, but hope embraces the future things themselves. But this reconciliation is less popular than the other. IV. What are the causes of faith. The primary and principal efficient cause of historical, temporary faith and of miracles is the Holy Spirit, by a general divine action; but of justifying faith, by a special action of justifying. By grace you have been saved through faith; and this not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, etc. Objection. The devil has historical faith. Therefore it comes from the Holy Spirit. Answer. The faith that is in demons is also produced by God, but by the general and universal operation, as has been said, not the special one; because it is by such an operation and manner that the Holy Spirit works justifying faith in the elect alone. For in demons and hypocrites too, whatever thought there is, God effects through his Spirit; but not in such a way that he regenerates or justifies them, as he does the elect; nor in such a way that they acknowledge or celebrate the author of this gift. The instrumental cause of faith in general is the whole Word of God contained in the books of the Old and New Testament, in which, besides the word, many works and miracles of God are also contained.

units.la: Proprium verò organum fidei justificantis est prædicatio Euangelij. Euangelium enim est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Fides ex auditu est: auditus per verbum DEI. Ordinariè igitur absque Euangelij prædicatione fides justificans non generatur in adultis.
units.tr: But the proper organ of justifying faith is the preaching of the Gospel. For the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. Ordinarily, therefore, justifying faith is not generated in adults without the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Fidei miraculorum organum non est simpliciter verbum Dei, sed requiritur promissio vel revelatio singularis.
units.tr: The organ of faith in miracles is not simply the Word of God, but a special promise or revelation is required.

units.la: Formalis causa fidei justificantis est differentia & proprium definitionis.
units.tr: The formal cause of justifying faith is its difference and the proper element of its definition.

units.la: Obiectum eiusdem est Christus, & promissio gratiæ.
units.tr: Its object is Christ, and the promise of grace.

units.la: Subiectum seu materia in qua, est intellectus, voluntas & cor hominis.
units.tr: The subject, or matter in which it resides, is the intellect, will and heart of man.

units.la: Finalis: 1. Est celebratio justitiæ, bonitatis ac misericordiæ Dei. 2. Salus nostra.
units.tr: The final cause: 1. It is the celebration of the justice, goodness and mercy of God. 2. Our salvation.

units.la: V. Qui sint effectus fidei.
units.tr: V. What the effects of faith are.

units.la: Effectus fidei justificantis sunt: 1. Justificatio coram Deo. 2. Lætitia acquiescens in Deo, & pax conscientiæ. Justificati ex fide pacem habemus cum Deo. 3. Conversio, regeneratio, & tota obedientia. Fide enim Deus purificat corda. 4. Ad effectus pertinent consequentia: incrementum donorum spiritualium & corporalium, & acceptio ipsarum rerum.
units.tr: The effects of justifying faith are: 1. Justification before God. 2. Joy resting in God, and peace of conscience. Justified by faith, we have peace with God. 3. Conversion, regeneration, and all obedience. For by faith God purifies the hearts. 4. Among the effects belong the consequences: the increase of spiritual and bodily gifts, and the receiving of these very things.

units.la: Primus itaq; effectus fidei justificantis est justificatio: ex hac deinde promanant alia beneficia, quæ fidem consequuntur, & quæ per fidem credimus nobis dari, quorum proinde fides est causa. Nam quod est causa causæ, est etiam causa effectus. Si igitur fides est proxima causa justificationis: etiam causa eorum, quæ justificationem consequuntur. Fides tua te seruauit. Summa. Effectus fidei sunt justificatio & regeneratio, inchoata in hac vita, & perficienda in altera. Romanor.3. v.28. & 10,10. Actorum 13,39.
units.tr: The first effect of justifying faith, then, is justification; from this there flow the other benefits which follow faith, and which we believe are given to us through faith, so that faith is their cause. For what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of the effect. If, therefore, faith is the proximate cause of justification, it is also the cause of those things which follow justification. Your faith has saved you. Summary: the effects of faith are justification and regeneration, begun in this life and to be perfected in the next. Romans 3:28 and 10:10. Acts 13:39.

units.la: VI. Quibus detur fides.
units.tr: VI. To whom faith is given.

units.la: Justificans fides est electorum propria, & quidem omnium. Datur enim omnibus & solis electis, etiam infantibus, inclinatione. Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater traxerit eum. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni cœlorum: reliquis autem non est datum. Credi derunt quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Quos prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit, justificauit, glorificauit. Fides donum Dei est. Non omnes auscultarunt Euangelio. Esaias enim dixit: Domine, &c. Non omnium est fides. Fides temporaria & miraculorum datur etiam iis, qui sunt tantum visibilis ecclesiæ membra, id est, hypocritis. Nonne in nomine tuo tuo fecimus virtutes multas? daemonia ejecimus? Jam tamen fides miraculorum desijt, quæ viguit in primitiva Ecclesia: siquidem doctrina miraculis jam satis est confirmata.
units.tr: Justifying faith is the proper possession of the elect, and indeed of all of them. For it is given to all and only the elect, even infants, by inclination. No one comes to me unless the Father draws him. To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to the rest it has not been given. As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Whom he predestined, these he also called, justified, glorified. Faith is the gift of God. Not all obeyed the Gospel. For Isaiah says: Lord, etc. Not all have faith. Temporary faith and faith in miracles is given also to those who are only members of the visible Church, that is, to hypocrites. Have we not in your name done many mighty works? cast out demons? Yet faith in miracles, which flourished in the primitive Church, has now ceased, since the doctrine has already been sufficiently confirmed by miracles.

units.la: Historica etiam omnibus extra Ecclesiam contingere potest, cum etiam sit diabolorum.
units.tr: Historical faith too can come to all outside the Church, since it is also the faith of the devils.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Fides historica est bonum opus. Diaboli habent fidem historicam. Ergo habent bona opera. Resp. ad maiorem: fides historica est bonum opus, si sit conjuncta cum applicatione & fiducia. Inst. Est effectum Spiritus Dei: ergo etiam sine applicatione est bonum opus. Resp. Est bonum opus per se: sed fit malum per accidens, cum non applicantur & accipiuntur ea, quæ agnoscit esse vera. Ideo diaboli dicuntur credere & contremiscere: quia quæ norunt de Deo, sibi non applicant: hoc est, non credunt; Deum ipsis quoque talem esse, qualem esse sciunt ex verbo, bonum, misericordem, &c.
units.tr: Obiect. 1. Historical faith is a good work. The devils have historical faith. Therefore they have good works. Resp. to the major: historical faith is a good work if it is joined with application and trust. Inst. It is an effect of the Spirit of God; therefore it is a good work even without application. Resp. It is a good work in itself, but it becomes evil by accident, since those things which one acknowledges to be true are not applied and received. Therefore the devils are said to believe and tremble: because what they know about God they do not apply to themselves; that is, they do not believe that God is to them also such as they know him to be from the word: good, merciful, etc.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Infantes multi sunt electi: nec tamen habent fidem. Ergo fides non est omnium electorum. Resp. ad maiorem: Infantes non habent fidem actualem, ut adulti: habent tamen potentiam seu inclinationem ad credendum, quam Spiritus sanctus etiam infantibus promittatur, non potest in eis esse otiosus ad fidem & salutem. Manet ergo quod dictum fuit, fidem esse omnium electorum.
units.tr: Obiect. 2. Many infants are elect, yet they do not have faith. Therefore faith is not of all the elect. Resp. to the major: infants do not have actual faith as adults do; yet they have the power or inclination to believe, and since the Holy Spirit is promised even to infants, he cannot be idle in them with regard to faith and salvation. It remains, therefore, that what was said stands: faith belongs to all the elect.

units.la: Quin & illud addo, non modò fidem, sed & professionem fidei omnibus electis adultis esse necessariam: 1. Propter mandatum Dei. Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum. Ergo recte assumes. Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, &c. 2. Propter gloriam Dei. Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, &c. 3. Quia fides non est otiosa, sed velut arbor frugifera per confessionem se prodit. 4. Propter salutem nostram. Ore fit confessio ad salutem. 5. Ut alios ad Christum adducamus. Et tu conversus, confirma fratres.
units.tr: Indeed I add this too: not only faith but also the profession of faith is necessary for all elect adults: 1. On account of God's command. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Therefore you shall rightly take it. Whoever confesses me before men, etc. 2. On account of the glory of God. Let your light shine before men, etc. 3. Because faith is not idle, but like a fruitful tree it shows itself through confession. 4. On account of our salvation. With the mouth confession is made unto salvation. 5. That we may lead others to Christ. And you, when you have turned, strengthen the brethren.

units.la: Scimus autem nos habere fidem: 1. Ex testimonio Spiritus sancti, & ex ipso fidei sensu, hoc est, vero & non simulato desiderio accipiendi beneficia à Christo oblata. Credens enim scit se credere: juxta illud Apostoli: Scio cui credidi. Et: Quia habemus eundem Spiritum fidei, secundum illud, quod scriptum est: Credidi, & ideo locutus sum: nos quoque credimus, quamobrem etiam loquimur. Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet testimonium in se ipso. 2. Ex lucta fidei cum dubitatione. 3. Ex effectis, hoc est, ex proposito & studio obediendi Deo secundum omnia eius mandata.
units.tr: We know that we have faith: 1. From the testimony of the Holy Spirit, and from the very sense of faith, that is, the true and unfeigned desire to receive the benefits offered by Christ. For the believer knows that he believes, according to that saying of the Apostle: I know whom I have believed. And: Since we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; we also believe, and therefore we also speak. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. 2. From the struggle of faith with doubt. 3. From its effects, that is, from the purpose and zeal of obeying God in all his commands.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Qui possunt labi & deficere ante finem vitæ, ij non possunt esse certi de vita æterna: quia certum esse de salute, & posse excidere salute, inter se pugnant. Atqui omnes nos possumus labi & deficere. Ergo non possumus de salute esse certi: & falsum est, quod fides sit certa fiducia, &c. Resp. Maior vera est de iis, qui possunt labi & deficere finaliter. Nam sic posse labi, pugnat cum certitudine salutis. Vera autem fide semel donati à Deo, non deficiunt, nec possunt deficere finaliter: quia qui ex Deo nati sunt, non peccant, nec possunt peccare finaliter: quia semen Dei manet in eis, 1 Ioh. 3. v. 9. & electi non possunt perire,
units.tr: Objection 3. Those who can slip and fall away before the end of life cannot be certain of eternal life, because being certain of salvation and being able to fall from salvation are mutually contradictory. But all of us can slip and fall away. Therefore we cannot be certain of salvation, and it is false that faith is a certain trust, etc. Answer: The major premise is true of those who can fall away finally. For to be able to slip in this way is inconsistent with certainty of salvation. But those who have once been given true faith by God do not fall away, nor can they fall away finally, because those who are born of God do not sin, nor can they sin finally, since the seed of God remains in them (1 John 3:9), and the elect cannot perish.

units.la: Inst. 1. Omnes infirmi possunt deficere finaliter. Nos omnes sumus infirmi, &c. Ergo, &c. Resp. ad maiorem, quæ vera est, nisi infirmos gratia Dei sustentet, ne labantur finaliter. Sic autem sustentat Deus electos. Si ceciderit iustus, non collidetur, quia Deus supponit manum.
units.tr: Objection 1. All the weak can fall away finally. We are all weak, etc. Therefore, etc. Answer to the major premise, which is true, unless God's grace sustains the weak so that they do not fall finally. But God sustains the elect in this way: "If the righteous falls, he will not be crushed, because God puts his hand under him."

units.la: Inst. 2. Deus non expressit, se nos seruaturum in gratia finaliter. Resp. Immò expressit loco dicto, & alibi. Ego vitam æternam do eis, nec peribunt in æternum, neque rapiet eas quisquam è manu mea. Pater, qui dedit eas mihi, maior est omnibus, neq; potest eas quisquam rapere è manu Patris mei. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Mihi persuasum est, neq; mortem, neq; vitam, neq; instantia, neq; futura, &c. posse nos separare à charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Objection 2. God has not expressly promised that he will keep us in grace to the end. Answer: On the contrary, he has expressly promised it in the passage cited and elsewhere: "I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. I and the Father are one" (John 10:28–30). "I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor things present, nor things to come, etc., can separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 8:38–39).

units.la: Inst. 3. Qui stat, videat, ne cadat. Ergo Deus perseuerantiam non promittit, sed nobis committit. Resp. Est fallacia non causæ. Hac ipsa enim hortatione Deus vult fidelium salutem fovere, conservare & perficere: non autem eorum viribus aut arbitrio perseuerantiam committere. Si igitur verè nunc credimus, stat tuere certò debemus, DEUM etiam deinceps nos seruaturum esse. Si enim vult nos esse certos de gratia præsente: vult etiam nos esse certos de gratia futura: quia est immutabilis, & ideo dat gratiam præsentem, quia decreuit etiam dare gratiam futuram, hoc est, salutem æternam.
units.tr: Objection 3. "Let him who stands see to it that he does not fall" (1 Cor. 10:12). Therefore God does not promise perseverance, but commits it to us. Answer: This is a fallacy of the non-cause. For by this very exhortation God wishes to foster, preserve and perfect the salvation of believers, not to commit perseverance to their own strength or choice. If therefore we now truly believe, we must surely hold firmly that God will also keep us from now on. For if he wills us to be certain of present grace, he also wills us to be certain of future grace, because he is unchangeable; and so he gives present grace precisely because he has also decreed to give future grace, that is, eternal salvation.

units.la: Inst. 4. Nescit homo, amore an odio sit dignus. Ergo non possumus esse certi de gratia præsente: & per consequens, nec de futura. Respond. ad antecedens: 1. Nescit homo, ex casus secundis, seu ex euentibus bonis vel malis. Externa enim fortuna non est fauoris vel odij DEI: quia est communis bonis vel malis. 2. Nescit ex sese: scit autem Deo docente per verbum & Spiritum suum.
units.tr: Objection 4. "Man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred" (Eccles. 9:1). Therefore we cannot be certain of present grace, and consequently not of future grace. Answer to the antecedent: 1. Man does not know this from prosperous circumstances or from good or bad events. For outward fortune is not a sign of God's favour or hatred, since it is common to both good and bad. 2. He does not know it of himself; but he knows it when God teaches him through his Word and his Spirit.

units.la: Inst. 5. Quis cognouit mentem Domini? Resp. Ante patefactionem nemo cognouit: sed post patefactionem cognoscimus mentem Domini, quantum ad salutem sufficit. Nos omnes retecta facie facie gloriam Domini vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur, &c.
units.tr: Objection 5. "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" (Rom. 11:34). Answer: Before the revelation no one knew it; but after the revelation we know the mind of the Lord, as far as is sufficient for salvation. "But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image, etc." (2 Cor. 3:18).

units.la: Obiect. 4. Si justus deflexerit à via sua recta, morietur in peccatis suis. Ergo etiam credentes possunt deficere à pietate, & perire. Resp. 1. Conditionalis nihil ponit. 2. Justus ibi dicitur non tantum qui verè est, sed etiam qui videtur esse justus, quales sæpe sunt hypocritæ ἀπόκριται, credentes ad tempus, & postea deficientes. Nam verè justus, est vt arbor plantata ad rivos aquarum, cuius folia non defluunt.
units.tr: Objection 6. "If the righteous turns aside from his right way, he shall die in his sins" (Ezek. 3:20). Therefore even believers can fall away from piety and perish. Answer: 1. A conditional proposition asserts nothing. 2. "Righteous" there is said not only of one who truly is, but also of one who seems to be righteous, such as hypocrites often are, apokritai, who believe for a time and afterwards fall away. For he who is truly righteous is "like a tree planted by streams of water, whose leaves do not wither" (Ps. 1:3).

units.la: Obiect. 5. Paulus hortatur Corinthios, ne frustra acceperint gratiam; & Christus, vt vigilemus & oremus. Resp. Prohibetur securitas carnalis, præcipitur vigilantia & precatio, quibus certitudo in electis fovetur & conservatur.
units.tr: Objection 7. Paul exhorts the Corinthians not to have received grace in vain (2 Cor. 6:1), and Christ bids us watch and pray. Answer: Carnal security is forbidden, and watchfulness and prayer are commanded, by which certainty is fostered and preserved in the elect.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Saul deficit finaliter; & fuit pius: Ergo quidam pij deficiunt finaliter. Resp. Saul non fuit verè pius, sed hypocrita. Minor igitur negatur. Inst. Habuit dona Spiritus sancti. Resp. Habuit dona communia cum electis & reprobis: non habuit dona regenerationis & νιοθεσίας, electis propria.
units.tr: Objection 8. Saul fell away finally, and he was pious. Therefore some pious people fall away finally. Answer: Saul was not truly pious but a hypocrite. The minor premise is therefore denied. Objection: He had gifts of the Holy Spirit. Answer: He had gifts common to the elect and the reprobate; he did not have the gifts of regeneration and adoption, which are proper to the elect.

units.la: Obiect. 7. Doctrina de perseverantia & de certitudine salutis parit securitatem. Resp. Parit securitatem spiritualem per se in electis, carnalem per accidens in reprobis.
units.tr: Objection 9. The doctrine of perseverance and of the certainty of salvation produces security. Answer: It produces spiritual security in the elect, through its own nature; carnal security in the reprobate, incidentally.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXII. Quænam sunt illa, quæ necesse est hominem Christianum credere?
units.tr: QUESTION XXII. What are those things which a Christian man must of necessity believe?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Omnia, quæ nobis in Euangelio promittuntur, quorum summa in symbolo apostolico, seu in capitibus catholicæ & indubitatæ omnium Christianorum fidei, breviter comprehenditur.
units.tr: All the things promised to us in the Gospel, the sum of which is briefly comprehended in the Apostles' Creed, or in the articles of the catholic and undoubted faith of all Christians.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Post tractationem de fide recte quæritur de credendorum summa seu de fidei obiecto. Fides igitur in genere refertur in omne Dei verbum, eique firmiter assentitur, vt ex definitione constat. Sed fides justificans proprie spectat promissiones Euangelij seu conceptionem gratiæ per Christum. Euangelium ergo proprie est obiectum fidei justificantis. Ideo & proprie dicitur doctrina credendorum: sicut Lex proprie est doctrina faciendorum. Excluduntur ergo traditiones humanæ, placita pontificum, decreta conciliorum. Fides enim solo Dei verbo, tanquam immoto fundamento, niti potest. Decreta verò hominum sunt incerta: quia omnis homo mendax: solus Deus est verax, & verbum eius veritas. Christiani igitur vt non debent sibi ipsi materiam fidei confingere, ita nec debent ab hominibus confictam aut traditam amplecti, sed debent credere Euangelio, juxta dicta: Agite pœnitentiam, & credite Euangelio. Ne fides vestra consistat in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei. Porrò Euangelij seu credendorum summa est symbolum apostolicum, de quo sequitur.
units.tr: After the treatment of faith, it is rightly asked what is the sum of the things to be believed, or the object of faith. Faith, then, in general refers to every word of God, and firmly assents to it, as the definition makes clear. But justifying faith properly looks to the promises of the Gospel, or to the offer of grace through Christ. The Gospel, therefore, is properly the object of justifying faith. For this reason it is also properly called the doctrine of things to be believed, just as the Law is properly the doctrine of things to be done. Human traditions, the decrees of popes and the decisions of councils are therefore excluded. For faith can rest only on the word of God, as on an immovable foundation. But the decrees of men are uncertain, since every man is a liar, and God alone is true, and his word is truth. Christians, therefore, as they ought not to devise the matter of faith for themselves, so neither ought they to embrace what has been devised or handed down by men, but they ought to believe the Gospel, according to the sayings: Repent, and believe the Gospel; Let your faith not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. Moreover, the sum of the Gospel, or of the things to be believed, is the Apostles' Creed, concerning which we proceed next.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXIII. Quod est illud symbolum?
units.tr: QUESTION XXIII. What is that creed?

units.la: 1. Credo in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, Creatorem cœli & terræ:
units.tr: 1. I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth;

units.la: 2. Et in Iesum Christum, Filium eius vnigenitum, Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: 2. And in Jesus Christ, his only begotten Son, our Lord;

units.la: 3. Qui conceptus est de Spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria virgine:
units.tr: 3. Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary;

units.la: 4. Passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus, & sepultus:
units.tr: 4. Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried;

units.la: 5. Tertia die resurrexit à mortuis:
units.tr: 5. On the third day rose again from the dead;

units.la: 6 Ascendit ad cœlos, sedet ad dexteram Dei Patris omnipotentis:
units.tr: 6. Ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty;

units.la: 7. Inde venturus est judicatum viuos & mortuos.
units.tr: 7. From thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: 8. Credo in Spiritum sanctum:
units.tr: 8. I believe in the Holy Spirit;

units.la: 9. Credo sanctam Ecclesiam catholicam, sanctorum communionem:
units.tr: 9. I believe in the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints;

units.la: 10. Remissionem peccatorum:
units.tr: 10. The forgiveness of sins;

units.la: 11. Carnis resurrectionem:
units.tr: 11. The resurrection of the flesh;

units.la: 12. Et vitam æternam, Amen.
units.tr: 12. And eternal life. Amen.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Symbolum in genere notam vel tesseram significat, qua quis discernitur ab alio: vt symbolum militare est tessera discernens socios ab hostibus. Germanicè eius Feldzeichen / oder Losung. Symbola, æ, est, quod confertur ad conuiuium, ἀπὸ τοῦ συμβάλλειν. Gay, Germanicè ʒusammen schiessin. In Ecclesia significat breuem& summariam fidei Christianæ formam, qua ecclesia eiusq; membra ab aliis sectis se discernunt. Sunt, qui putant, dictū esse symbolum, quia ab Apostolis sit collatum. Sed non potest proba-ri, singulos Apostolos aliquam eius partē contulisse. Probabilior est ratio, symbolum dici, quod articuli sunt nota Christianorum, & norma, ad quam omnium fides congruere debet, qui seruari volunt. Apostolicum dicitur: quia continet summam doctrinæ apostolicæ, quam cogebantur confiteri catechumeni: vel quia collegium Apostolicum eam summam discipulis suis tradidit, & ab his Ecclesia eam accepit. Dicitur & Catholicum, quia omnium Christianorum est vna fides.
units.tr: Symbolum in general means a mark or token by which one person is distinguished from another; thus a military symbolum is a token distinguishing comrades from enemies (in German, Feldzeichen or Losung). Symbola is that which is contributed to a banquet, from the verb symballein [ἀπὸ τοῦ συμβάλλειν]; in German, zusammenschiessen. In the Church it denotes a brief and summary form of the Christian faith, by which the Church and its members are distinguished from other sects. Some think it was called a symbolum because it was contributed by the Apostles. But it cannot be proved that each of the Apostles contributed some part of it. A more probable reason is that it is called a symbolum because its articles are the mark of Christians, and a rule to which the faith of all who wish to be preserved ought to conform. It is called Apostolicum because it contains the sum of apostolic teaching, which catechumens were required to confess; or because the college of Apostles handed this sum down to its disciples, and the Church received it from them. It is also called Catholicum, because there is one faith of all Christians.

units.la: Quaeritur hic, cur post symbolum apostolicum alia symbola, Nicenum, Athanasij, Ephesinum & Chalcedonense sint facta & recepta in Ecclesia? Resp. Hæc symbola proprie non sunt alia symbola ab apostolico, sed tantum sunt apostolici repetitio & declaratio, qua in aliis alia quædam verba sunt adiecta explicationis causa propter hæreticos, à quibus illud ob breuitatem deprauabatur.
units.tr: Here it is asked why, after the Apostles' Creed, other creeds, the Nicene, the Athanasian, the Ephesine and the Chalcedonian, were made and received in the Church. Answer: these creeds are not properly other creeds apart from the Apostles', but are only a repetition and declaration of the Apostles' Creed, in which certain other words have been added in others for the sake of explanation, on account of the heretics, by whom that creed, because of its brevity, was corrupted.

units.la: Fuerunt & aliæ graues causæ, quæ cogerent Episcopos & doctores ecclesiarum has breues confessionis formulas condere, præsertim crescentibus & ecclesiis, & hæresibus; nimirum: 1. Vt omnes tam iuuenes, quàm adulti fundamentum Christianismi breuiter comprehensum in animo circumferre possent. 2. Vt omnes fidei suæ confessionem & consolationem in conspectu semper haberent, scientes, quæ sit illa doctrina, propter quam persecutiones essent sustinendæ: sicut Deus olim summam legis & promissionum suarum breuiter complexus erat, vt omnes haberent in conspectu vitæ regulam, & consolationis fundamentum. 3. Vt fideles haberent certam notam seu tesseram, qua in præsentia, & deinceps omnibus seculis discernerentur ab infidelibus & hæreticis, vocem propheticam & apostolicam versute corrumpentibus: qua de causa hæ confessiones appellatæ sunt symbola. 4. Denique vt extaret regula perpetua, simplex, breuis, & omnibus cognitu facilis, ad quam omnem doctrinam & interpretationem scripturæ examinarent, vt cum ea congruentem reciperent, pugnantem repudiarent.
units.tr: There were also other weighty causes which compelled bishops and teachers of the churches to draw up these brief formulas of confession, especially as both the churches and heresies were multiplying; namely: (1) that all, both young and old, might carry about in their minds the foundation of Christianity briefly summed up; (2) that all might always have before them the confession and consolation of their faith, knowing what that doctrine is for which persecutions are to be endured; just as God of old briefly summed up the sum of his law and promises, so that all might have before them a rule of life and a foundation of consolation; (3) that the faithful might have a certain mark or token by which they could be distinguished, now and in all ages to come, from unbelievers and heretics, who craftily corrupt the prophetic and apostolic voice; for which reason these confessions were called symbola; (4) finally, that there might stand a perpetual rule, simple, brief, and easy for all to know, to which they could test all doctrine and interpretation of Scripture, so that they might accept what agrees with it and reject what conflicts with it.

units.la: Interim Apostolicum aliis symbolis longè antecellit authoritate. 1. Quia feré totum scripturæ verbis constat: 2. Quia omnibus aliis symbolis est antiquius, ab Apostolis, vel ab eorum discipulis vitis apostolicis, Ecclesiæ per manus ad nos usque propagatum. 3. Quia est fons & regula aliorum symbolorum, quæ, eius declarandi causa, ad vitandas hæreticorum fraudes corruptelas, in synodis œcumenicis, totius Ecclesiæ consensu, approbata fuerunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the Apostolicum far surpasses the other creeds in authority. (1) Because it consists almost entirely in the words of Scripture; (2) because it is older than all the other creeds, having been handed down to us by the hands of the Church from the Apostles, or from their disciples, the apostolic men; (3) because it is the source and rule of the other creeds, which, to explain it and to guard against the frauds and corruptions of heretics, were approved in the ecumenical synods with the consent of the whole Church.

units.la: Reliquorum vero symbolorum certitudo consistit non in authoritate hominum aut conciliorum, sed in perpetuo scripturæ sacræ consensu, & Ecclesiæ inde ab Apostolis retinentis doctrinam apostolicam, & testimonium edentis ad posteros, hanc doctrinam ab Apostolis & eorum auditoribus acceptam esse, qui consensus omnibus considerantibus est obuius. Certum est enim, nec angelorum, nec hominum ecclesiam habere potestatem condendi novas leges de cultu DEI, aut novos articulos fidei obligantes conscientiam. Idem enim est solius DEI. Neque Deo propter ecclesiæ, sed ecclesiæ propter Dei testimonium credendum est.
units.tr: But the certainty of the other creeds rests not on the authority of men or of councils, but on the perpetual agreement of holy Scripture, and on the Church, which from the Apostles onward has retained the apostolic doctrine and bears witness to posterity that this doctrine was received from the Apostles and their hearers; an agreement which is evident to all who consider it. For it is certain that neither the church of angels nor that of men has the power to make new laws concerning the worship of God, or new articles of faith binding the conscience. For this belongs to God alone. Nor is God to be believed on account of the Church, but the Church on account of the testimony of God.

units.la: Hæc de symbolorum causis & authoritate desumpta sunt ex Admonit. Neustad. anno 81. de Concordia Bergensi à D. Vrsino scripta: vbi plura de veritate & authoritate scriptorum ecclesiasticorum erudite disputata legant Theologiæ studiosi à pag. 117 vsq; ad pag. 142. Typum hic breuiter subjicio. Divina, hoc est, à Deo immediate Prophetis & Apostolis inspirata: vt sunt libri Veteris & Noui Testamenti. Hæc sola sunt tam verbis, quàm sententiis ... eoque sola omnium aliorum norma. Scripta de doctrina Ecclesiæ sunt vel Ecclesiastica; à doctoribus Ecclesiæ post Propheras & Apostolos edita: eaque sunt vel Publica, communi Ecclesiæ consensu & nomine edita: Quæ rursus sunt vel Catholica, seu vniuersalia: vt sunt symbola & confessiones totius Ecclesiæ orthodoxæ consensu & nomine scriptæ, & receptæ: vt sunt Apostolicum. Nicenum. Constantinopolitanum. Ephesinum. Athanasianum. Chalcedonense. Particularia, seu confessiones certarum Ecclesiarum vel conciliorum: vt Catecheses: Confessio Augustana; Wirtembergica, &c. Priuata, vnius vel plurium Doctorum vel Theologorum consilio & nomine scripta vel edita: vt loci Communes & Commentarij Philippi, Lutheri, Brentij, Bullingeri, Caluini, aliorum.
units.tr: These things about the causes and authority of the creeds have been drawn from the Admonition of Neustadt of the year 81, on the Concord of Bergen, written by Dr. Ursinus, where students of theology may read more learned disputation about the truth and authority of ecclesiastical writings, from page 117 to page 142. I briefly set out the outline here. Divine writings, that is, those inspired by God immediately to the Prophets and Apostles, such as the books of the Old and New Testaments. These alone are the norm of all others, both in words and in meaning. Writings on the doctrine of the Church are either ecclesiastical, published by the teachers of the Church after the Prophets and Apostles; and these are either public, published in the common consent and name of the Church; and these again are either catholic, or universal, such as the creeds and confessions written and received with the consent and in the name of the whole orthodox Church, such as the Apostles', Nicene, Constantinopolitan, Ephesine, Athanasian and Chalcedonian creeds. Or particular, that is, the confessions of certain churches or councils, such as the Catechisms, the Augsburg Confession, the Württemberg Confession, and so on. Or private, written or published by one or several teachers or theologians on their own counsel and name, such as the Common Places and Commentaries of Melanchthon, Luther, Brenz, Bullinger, Calvin and others.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXIV. In quotpartes distribuitur hoc symbolum?
units.tr: QUESTION 24. Into how many parts is this creed divided?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: In tres partes. Prima est de Deo Patre, & nostri creatione. Altera est de DEO Filio, & nostri redemptione, Tertia est de DEO Spiritu sancto, & nostri sanctificatione.
units.tr: Into three parts. The first concerns God the Father and the creation of us. The second concerns God the Son and our redemption. The third concerns God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Principales partes symboli apostolici sunt tres; 1. De Patre creatore.
units.tr: The principal parts of the Apostles' Creed are three: (1) concerning the Father, the Creator; (2) concerning the Son, the Redeemer; (3) concerning the Holy Spirit, the Sanctifier.

units.la: 2. De Filio redemptore.
units.tr: (2) Concerning the Son, the Redeemer.

units.la: 3. De Spiritu sancto sanctificatore.
units.tr: (3) Concerning the Holy Spirit, the Sanctifier.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Patri tribuitur creatio, Filio redemtio, Spiritui sancto sanctificatio. Ergo Filius & Spiritus sanctus non crearunt cœlum & terram, neque Pater & Spiritus sanctus redemerunt genus humanum, neq; Pater & Filius sanctificant fideles. Resp. Negatur consequentia: quia Patri tribuitur creatio, Filio redemptio, Spiritui sancto sanctificatio, non exclusiuè, hoc est, ita, vt hæc non etiam conueniant omnibus personis. Pater enim etiam nos redemit: quia tradidit Filium suum pro nobis: misit Filium in mundum, vt mundus seruetur per eum. Pater etiam nos sanctificat, quia emisit Deus Spiritum Filij sui in corda vestra, clamantem abba, Pater. Pater emittet eum in nomine meo. Ipse Deus pacis sanctificet vos totos. Filius etiam nos creauit: Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt: & nos sanctificat: quia factus est nobis sancti- ficatio à Deo: & sanctificat ecclesiam, purgans eam lauacro aquæ in verbo: & dat Spiritum sanctum: Cùm venerit Consolator ille, quem ego mittam vobis à Patre, &c. Effudit hoc, quod vos nunc spectatis & auditis. Idem sentiendum est de Spiritu sancto. Nam & is creauit cœlum & terram. Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas. Verbo Iehovæ facti sunt cœli, & Spiritu eris eius omnis exercitus eorum, &c.
units.tr: Objection 1. Creation is attributed to the Father, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit did not create heaven and earth, nor did the Father and the Holy Spirit redeem mankind, nor do the Father and the Son sanctify the faithful. Answer. The inference is denied, because creation is attributed to the Father, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Holy Spirit not exclusively, that is, in such a way that these things do not also belong to all the persons. For the Father also redeems us, since he gave up his Son for us, he sent his Son into the world that the world might be saved through him. The Father also sanctifies us, since God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The Father will send him in my name. May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly. The Son also created us, for all things were made through him, and he sanctifies us, since he has been made to us sanctification from God, and he sanctifies the Church, cleansing it by the washing of water in the word, and he gives the Holy Spirit: When that Comforter comes, whom I will send you from the Father, etc. He has poured out this which you now see and hear. The same must be understood of the Holy Spirit, for he also created heaven and earth. The Spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters. By the word of Jehovah the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host, etc.

units.la: Hac autem distinctione notatur discrimen & ordo agendi inter personas diuinitatis. Patri tribuitur creatio, non exclusiuè aut soli: sed quia fons est Deitatis, & diuinarum operationum, proinde & creationis. Omnia enim creauit à se per Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Redemptio tribuitur Filio non exclusiuè aut soli: sed quia Filius est is, qui immediatè opus redemptionis perfecit. Solus enim est factus λύτρον pro peccatis nostris. Solus pro nobis pretium soluit in cruce: non Pater, neq; Spiritus sanctus. Sanctificatio tribuitur Spiritui sancto, non exclusiuè aut solì: sed quia Spiritus sanctus est is, qui immediatè nos sanctificat, seu per quem fit immediatè sanctificatio.
units.tr: By this distinction, however, the difference and the order of working among the persons of the Godhead is noted. Creation is attributed to the Father, not exclusively or solely, but because he is the fount of the Godhead and of the divine operations, and therefore also of creation, for he created all things from himself through the Son and the Holy Spirit. Redemption is attributed to the Son, not exclusively or solely, but because the Son is the one who immediately accomplished the work of redemption. For he alone was made a ransom [λύτρον] for our sins. He alone paid the price on the cross; not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit. Sanctification is attributed to the Holy Spirit, not exclusively or solely, but because the Holy Spirit is the one who immediately sanctifies us, or through whom sanctification is immediately effected.

units.la: Obiectio 2. Opera diuinitatis ad extra sunt indiuisa. Creatio, redemptio, sanctificatio sunt opera diuinitatis ad extra. Ergo sunt indiuisa: & per consequens, non est opus distinctione.
units.tr: Objection 2. The works of the Godhead outwardly are undivided. Creation, redemption and sanctification are works of the Godhead outwardly. Therefore they are undivided, and consequently there is no need for a distinction.

units.la: Resp. Ad maiorem. Opera Trinitatis sunt indiuisa, seruato ordine & modo operandi, singulis personis proprio. Omnes igitur personæ omnia ad extra operantur, sed seruato hoc ordine, vt Pater agat à se per Filium & Spiritum sanctum: Filius à Patre per Spiritum sanctum, Spiritus sanctus à Patre & Filio per se. Sic igitur omnes personæ creant, redimunt, sanctificant: Pater mediatè per Filium & Spiritum sanctum: Filius mediatè per Spiritum sanctum: Spiritus sanctus immediatè per se: mediatè per Filium, quatenus est mediator. Quæ verò dicantur opera Trinitatis ad extra, vel ad intra in doctrina de Deo, quæstione penultima explicabitur paulò post.
units.tr: Answer to the major. The works of the Trinity are undivided, the order and manner of working being preserved, and proper to each person. All the persons therefore work all things outwardly, but in this order: the Father acts from himself through the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son from the Father through the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son through himself. Thus all the persons create, redeem and sanctify: the Father mediately through the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Son mediately through the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit immediately through himself, and mediately through the Son insofar as he is mediator. What are called the works of the Trinity outwardly or inwardly will be explained in the doctrine of God, a little later, in the penultimate question.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXV.
units.tr: QUESTION XXV.

units.la: Cum vna tantum sit essentia diuina a, cur tres istos nominas, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Since there is only one divine essence^a, why do you name these three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit? ANSWER.

units.la: Quia Deus ita se in suo verbo patefecit b, quod tres hæ distinctæ personæ sint vnus ille verus & æternus Deus.
units.tr: Because God has so revealed himself in his Word^b that these three distinct persons are that one true and eternal God.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hac quæstione continetur doctrina ecclesiæ de vno Deo & tribus personis diuinitatis. In ea præcipuæ quæstiones sunt: I. Vnde constet, quod sit Deus, II. Quid, & qualis sit Deus Ecclesiæ, & quomodo ab idolis gentium differat. III. An
units.tr: This question contains the Church's doctrine of the one God and the three persons of the Godhead. In it there are these principal questions: I. How it is established that there is God; II. What and what kind of God the Church teaches, and how he differs from the idols of the nations; III. Whether

units.la: Quaest. XXV.
units.tr: Question 25.

units.la: III. An sit vnus tantum, & quo sensu dicantur plures. IV. Quid essentia, persona, Trinitas, significent & differant. V. An haec vocabula in ecclesia sint vsurpanda. VI. Quot sint personae diuinitatis. VII. Quomodo haec discernantur. VIII. Cur necesse sit tenere doctrinam de Trinitate in Ecclesia.
units.tr: III. Whether there is only one, and in what sense several are spoken of. IV. What essence, person, and Trinity signify and how they differ. V. Whether these terms are to be used in the Church. VI. How many persons there are in the Godhead. VII. How these are distinguished. VIII. Why it is necessary to hold the doctrine of the Trinity in the Church.

units.la: I. An sit Deus,
units.tr: I. Whether there is God,

units.la: Esse DEUM, multis argumentis Philosophiae & Theologiae communibus probatur.
units.tr: That God exists is proved by many arguments common to philosophy and theology.

units.la: 1. Ordo naturae pulcherrimus, qui in mundo conspicitur, hoc est, partium dispositio, & motuum actionumque successio, ceterisque perpetuis legibus constans, non potest exsistere & conservari, nisi à natura aliqua intelligente & omnipotente, quae est Deus. Hoc argumentum prolixe testatur Psalmus 104. Item 8.19. 135.136.147.148. Rom.1. Act.14. & 17.
units.tr: 1. The most beautiful order of nature that is seen in the world, that is, the arrangement of its parts and the succession of its motions and actions, which holds by other perpetual laws, cannot exist and be preserved except by some intelligent and omnipotent nature, which is God. Psalm 104 bears witness to this argument at length. Likewise Ps. 8.19; 135, 136, 147, 148; Rom. 1; Acts 14 and 17.

units.la: 2. Rationalis natura habens causam, non nisi ab intelligente natura exsistere potest: quia causa non est toto genere deterior suo effectu. Mens humana est natura rationalis, & habet aliquam causam. Ergo à natura intelligente exsistit, quae est Deus. Prophetae spiritus est in homine, &c. Et dixerunt: non videbit Dominus, &c. Ipsius progenies sumus.
units.tr: 2. A rational nature that has a cause can exist only from an intelligent nature, because a cause is not inferior in its whole kind to its effect. The human mind is a rational nature and has some cause. Therefore it exists from an intelligent nature, which is God. "The spirit of the prophet is in man, etc." "And they said: the Lord will not see, etc." "We are also his offspring."

units.la: 3. Notitiae principiorum nobiscum nascentes, ut sunt, discrimen honestorum & turpium, numeratio, intellectus consequentiae in ratiocinando, &c. non possunt exsistere casu, aut a natura bruta, sed necessariò nobis sunt ingenitae à causa intelligente, quae est Deus. Gentes ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus, &c.
units.tr: 3. The notions of principles born with us, such as the distinction between honourable and base, number, the understanding of consequence in reasoning, etc., cannot exist by chance or from unthinking nature, but are necessarily implanted in us by an intelligent cause, which is God. "The Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts, etc."

units.la: 4. Ab hac notitia, quod sit Deus. Nulla enim gens tam est barbara, quin aliquam de religione opinionem tueatur, proinde & aliquem Deum esse statuat. Id quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est in ipsis, (hoc est, in animis hominum) Deus enim iis manifestum fecit.
units.tr: 4. From this notion, that God exists. For no nation is so barbarous that it does not hold some opinion about religion, and therefore it holds that some God exists. "What may be known of God is manifest in them (that is, in the minds of men), for God has made it manifest to them."

units.la: 5. Panores conscientiae, quibus impij post admissum peccatum corripiuntur, non possunt infligi, nisi à natura intelligente, & discernente honesta & turpia, intuente animos & corda, exercente judicium in animos hominum. Vermis eorum non moritur. Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus. Deus ignis consumens est. Ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus, vnà reddente testimonium ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus.
units.tr: 5. The stings of conscience, by which the wicked are struck after they have committed sin, cannot be inflicted except by a nature that is intelligent and discerns honourable from base, that sees souls and hearts, and that exercises judgment over the minds of men. "Their worm does not die." "There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord." "God is a consuming fire." "They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with them, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another."

units.la: 6. Praemia bonorum, & poena sceleratorum, ut diluuium, incendium Sodomae, submersio Pharaonis, excidia florentissimorum regnorum, &c. testantur, esse aliquem iudicem universauersalem & omnipotentem totius mundi, qui est solus Deus.
units.tr: 6. The rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked, such as the flood, the burning of Sodom, the drowning of Pharaoh, the overthrow of the most flourishing kingdoms, etc., testify that there is some universal and omnipotent judge of the whole world, who is God alone. "The Lord is known by the judgment he executes." "Surely you are the Lord who judges on earth."

units.la: Notus est Dominus judicium faciendo. Vtique es Dominus judicans in terra.
units.tr: The Lord is known by executing judgment. Surely you are the Lord judging on earth.

units.la: 7. Societas politica legibus sapienter ordinata non potuit nisi à mente intelligente & approbante hunc ordinem hominibus monstrari: & quoniam hanc societatem, & hunc ordinem diabolus cum impiis omnibus maximè odit, Deus sit oportet, qui adhuc cum defendit. Per me reges regnant, &c.
units.tr: 7. A political society wisely ordered by laws could not be made known to men except by a mind that is intelligent and that approves this order. And since the devil, with all the impious, hates this society and this order most of all, there must be a God who still defends it. "By me kings reign, etc."

units.la: 8. Motus heroici, hoc est, sapientia & virtus excellens in suscipiendis & efficiendis operibus, communem naturæ humanæ captum superantibus: vt est felicitas insignium artificum aut gubernatorum in perquestigandis aut excolendis artibus, & inveniendis consiliis: item magnitudo animi in præstandis actionibus, & in rebus gerendis, vt in Achille, Alexandro, Archimede, Platone, &c. ostendunt esse causam aliquam superiorem, omnipotentem, quæ hos motus excitet, &c. De Josua dicitur: Domi- nus præcedet te, ipse erit tecum. Excitavit Dominus spiritum Cyri. Irruit in eum spiritus Dei.
units.tr: 8. Heroic movements, that is, wisdom and excellent virtue in undertaking and accomplishing works that surpass the common grasp of human nature, such as the felicity of outstanding craftsmen or governors in investigating and cultivating the arts and in devising plans, and likewise greatness of spirit in carrying out actions and conducting affairs, as in Achilles, Alexander, Archimedes, Plato, etc., show that there is some superior, omnipotent cause that stirs up these movements, etc. Of Joshua it is said: "The Lord will go before you; he himself will be with you." "The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus." "The Spirit of God rushed upon him."

units.la: 9. Prædictiones certa & clara futurorum euentuum, qui neque humana acie vel perspicacia, neque ex causis vel signis naturalibus præsciri potuissent, vt sunt, vaticinia de diluuio, de posteritate Abrahami, de exhibitione Messiæ, &c. necessario ex eius tantum reuelatione cognoscuntur, qui & genus humanum, & naturam rerum omnium sic in sua potestate habet, vt sine eius motu nihil fieri possit. Is verè est Deus. Annunciate, quæ futura sunt in posterum, vt cognoscamus, quod dij sitis. Verbum quod locutus fuero, complebitur, dicit Dominus.
units.tr: 9. Certain and clear predictions of future events, which could not be foreknown by human sight or insight, nor from natural causes or signs, such as the prophecies about the flood, the posterity of Abraham, the coming of the Messiah, etc., are necessarily known only through the revelation of him who holds the human race and the nature of all things in such power that nothing can happen without his motion.
