He is truly God. "Declare what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods." "The word that I have spoken will be fulfilled, says the Lord."

units.la: 10. Finis & vtilitas omnium rerum non exsistit casu vel à natura bruta, sed à natura sapiente & omnipotente, quæ est Deus. Omnes verò res ad suos ac certos fines ordinatæ sunt sapientissimè.
units.tr: 10. The end and use of all things does not exist by chance or from unthinking nature, but from a wise and omnipotent nature, which is God. And all things are most wisely ordered to their certain ends.

units.la: 11. Series causarum & effectuum est finita, nec fieri potest, vt progressus causarum efficientium sese extendat in infinitum. Est igitur aliqua causa prima, quæ reliquas siue mediatè siue immediatè producat & moueat, & à qua omnes reliquæ causæ pendeant. In serie enim finita est aliquod primum.
units.tr: 11. The series of causes and effects is finite, and the progress of efficient causes cannot extend into infinity. Therefore there is some first cause, which produces and moves the rest, whether mediately or immediately, and on which all other causes depend. For in a finite series there is something first.

units.la: II. Quid & qualis sit Deus.
units.tr: II. What God is and what kind of being he is.

units.la: Deus definiri nequit: 1. quia immensus est: 2. quia essentia eius nobis est ignota. [De hoc vide Damasc. lib. 1. c. 4. Orthodox. fid. Basil. lib. 1. contra Eunom. Rustic. diaconum cap. 3. aduers. Acceph. Cyrill. lib. 11. Thesaur. cap. 1. Socrat. histor. eccles. lib. 3. cap. 5. Aristot. Metaph. lib. 12. cap. 7. Macrob. lib. 1. de somnio Scip.] Describi aliquo modo Deus potest ex patefactionibus diuinis, sic vt de- scriptio attributa, personas, & præcipua opera complectatur, quibus verus Deus à fictitiis numinibus discernitur. Philosophi- ca descriptio Dei est: quod sit mens æterna, ad felicitatem sibi suffi- ciens, optima, & causa boni in natura. Theologica vero & pleniot descriptio habetur in Ecclesia: quod Deus sit essentia spiritualis, intelligens, æterna, alia à creaturis omnibus, incomprehensibilis, in se ipsa perfectissima, immutabilis, immensa potentia, sapientia & bonita- tis, justa, verax, casta, misericors, benefica, liberrima, irascens peccatis: qui est Pater æternus, qui Filium ad imaginem suam ab æterno genuit: & Filius imago Patris coæterna: & Spiritus sanctus procedens à Patre & Filio: sicut patefacta est diuinitas certo verbo tradito per Prophetas & Apostolos, & testimoniis diuinis, quod Pater æternus cum Filio & Spiritu sancto cœlum & terram, & omnes creaturas in eis creauerit, & adsit omnibus creaturis, vt eas conseruet ac regat suâ prouidentiâ, & bona omnia in omnibus operetur, & quod in genere humano condito ad imaginem suam elegerit, & colligat sibi æternam ecclesiam propter filium & per eum, vt ab ea hac vna & vera diuinitas juxta verbum diuinitus agnoscatur ac colatur, & in vita æterna celebretur, & sit judex justorum & injustorum.
units.tr: God cannot be defined, (1) because he is immeasurable, and (2) because his essence is unknown to us. [On this see Damascene, Orthodox Faith, book 1, ch. 4; Basil, book 1 against Eunomius; Rusticus the deacon, ch. 3, against the Acephali; Cyril, Thesaurus, book 11, ch. 1; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, ch. 5; Aristotle, Metaphysics, book 12, ch. 7; Macrobius, on the Dream of Scipio, book 1.] God can be described in some way from his divine self-revelations, so that the description includes his attributes, his persons and his principal works, by which the true God is distinguished from fictitious deities. The philosophical description of God is: that he is an eternal mind, sufficient to his own happiness, the best, and the cause of good in nature. The theological and fuller description, however, is found in the Church: that God is a spiritual, intelligent, eternal essence, distinct from all creatures, incomprehensible, most perfect in himself, unchangeable, of immense power, wisdom and goodness, just, true, chaste, merciful, beneficent, most free, and angry at sins; who is the eternal Father, who from eternity begot a Son in his own image; and the Son is the image of the Father, coeternal; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; as this divinity has been revealed by the sure word handed down through the prophets and apostles, and by divine testimonies: that the eternal Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, created heaven and earth and all creatures in them, and is present to all creatures to preserve and govern them by his providence, and works all good things in all; and that, having made the human race in his own image, he has chosen and gathers for himself an eternal Church, for the sake of the Son and through him, so that by it this one and true divinity may be acknowledged and worshipped according to the divine word, and glorified in eternal life; and that he is the judge of the just and the unjust.

units.la: Hæc descriptio, quam ecclesia tradit, differt à philosophica. 1. Perfectione: quod ecclesia in sua descriptione addit quasdam partes naturæ ignotas, de tribus personis, de electione & colle- ctione Ecclesiæ per Filium, &c. & natura nota dilucidius ex-plicat: 2 Effectu seu fructu: quod homines luce naturali ad ve-ram Dei cognitionem peruenire nequeunt, quandoquidem ex ea nec veram & sufficientem notitiam Dei haurire possunt, nec mentes ad pietatem, hoc est, amorem & timorem Dei per-mouentur.
units.tr: This description, which the Church gives, differs from the philosophical one in two ways. (1) In its completeness: the Church, in its description, adds certain parts unknown to nature, concerning the three persons, the election and gathering of the Church through the Son, and so on, and explains more clearly what nature also knows. (2) In its effect or fruit: men cannot come by the light of nature to a true knowledge of God, since from that light they can draw neither a true and sufficient knowledge of God, nor are their minds moved to piety, that is, to the love and fear of God.

units.la: Eadem descriptio docet, verum Deum, quem ecclesia colit, à fictitiis numinibus aliarum gentium differre tripliciter: attribu- tu, personis, & operibus, ex quibus personæ patefiunt. Nam operi- bus declarauit Deus, se talem esse naturâ, qualis ex attributis de- scribitur: & simul ostendit in vna essentia esse tres personas, quandoquidem secundum opera, quæ sunt vel creationis, vel redemptionis, vel sanctificationis, varia Deus sortitur attribu-ta, personæque cognominantur.
units.tr: The same description teaches that the true God, whom the Church worships, differs from the fictitious deities of other nations in three ways: in attributes, in persons, and in works, from which the persons are made known. For by his works God has declared that he is by nature such as he is described by his attributes; and at the same time he has shown that in the one essence there are three persons, since God acquires various attributes according to his works, whether of creation, redemption or sanctification, and the persons are named accordingly.

units.la: Primò igitur Deus ab idolis differt attributis: quia extra eccle- siam nullam Dei attributum rectè & integrè intelligitur. Non misericordia: quia filius ignoratur, vel doctrina de eo corrum-pitur. Non justitia: quia impij non credunt, Deum adeò irascì peccatis, vt opus fuerit satisfactione pro illis, & redemptione per mortem Filij Dei. Non sapientia: quia præcipua pars est eius in ververbo, quod gentes non habent. Non veritas: quia ignorant promissiones. Sic de reliquis. In Ecclesia verò plena tribuitur Deo justitia, veritas, bonitas, misericordia, quæ attributa Dei aut corrumpunt aliæ sectæ, aut prorsus ignorant.
units.tr: First, then, the true God differs from idols in his attributes, because outside the Church no attribute of God is rightly and fully understood. Not mercy, because the Son is unknown, or the teaching about him is corrupted. Not justice, because the impious do not believe that God is so angry at sins that satisfaction had to be made for them, and redemption through the death of the Son of God. Not wisdom, because its principal part is in the Word, which the Gentiles do not have. Not truth, because they are ignorant of the promises. And so with the rest. In the Church, however, justice, truth, goodness and mercy are fully ascribed to God; and other sects either corrupt these attributes of God or utterly ignore them.

units.la: Secundò, personis: quia Ethnici & aliæ sectæ ignorant, vel negant tres personas in una essentia divina. Ecclesia verò agnoscit & invocat Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum unum Deum, tribus subsistentem personis, sicut se in verbo patefecit.
units.tr: Second, in persons, because the heathens and other sects either are ignorant of or deny the three persons in the one divine essence. The Church, however, acknowledges and invokes the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as one God, subsisting in three persons, just as he has revealed himself in his word.

units.la: Tertiò, operibus: quia extra ecclesiam ignorantur opera creationis & gubernationis rerum omnium, ac multo magis redemptionis & sanctificationis per Filium & Spiritum sanctum. His igitur modis verus Deus ab idolis discernitur: & cognitio Dei Ecclesiæ in verbo patefacta, ab ea differt, quam Ethnici habent ex natura haustam.
units.tr: Third, in works, because outside the Church the works of creation and of the governance of all things are unknown, and much more so the works of redemption and sanctification through the Son and the Holy Spirit. In these ways, then, the true God is distinguished from idols; and the knowledge of God revealed in the word, which the Church has, differs from that which the heathens have drawn from nature.

units.la: Breuis explicatio descriptionis Dei.
units.tr: A brief explanation of the description of God.

units.la: Deus est essentia. Res quæ à nullo alio sit orta vel sustentetur; sed à se & per se ipsam exsistat, & omnibus aliis rebus sit existendi causa. Ideo Iehova, quasi per se exsistens, & alia exsistere faciens.
units.tr: God is essence. A thing that has not arisen from anything else nor is sustained by anything else, but exists from itself and through itself, and is the cause of existence for all other things. Hence Jehovah, as if "self-existent" and "causing others to exist."

units.la: Spiritualis. Incorporea, invisibilis, nullo sensu perceptibilis; per se viuens, & alia viuificans.
units.tr: Spiritual. Incorporeal, invisible, perceptible by no sense; living of himself, and giving life to others.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Sæpe apparuit. Resp. Specie corporea ad tempus assumta. Obiect. 2. Visus est à facie ad faciem. R. Clara cognitione mentis, non oculis corporeis. Obiect. 3. Habet membra humana: Resp. Per ἀνθρωπομορφίας. Obiect. 4. Homo corporeus est imago Dei. Resp. Animæ essentia, facultatibus & rectitudine, non corporis figura.
units.tr: Objection 1: He has often appeared. Answer: In a bodily form, assumed for a time. Objection 2: He was seen face to face. Answer: By the clear knowledge of the mind, not by bodily eyes. Objection 3: He has human members. Answer: By anthropomorphism [ἀνθρωπομορφίας]. Objection 4: Man, a bodily being, is the image of God. Answer: In the essence of the soul, its faculties and uprightness, not in the shape of the body.

units.la: Intelligens. Ostendit hoc mens humana, & notitiæ in ea lucentes, quæ sunt à Deo. An qui plantauit aurem, non audiet?
units.tr: Intelligent. The human mind shows this, and the knowledge shining in it, which comes from God. He who planted the ear, shall he not hear?

units.la: Æterna. Nec principium, nec finem exsistendi habens. à æterno usque in æternum tu es Deus.
units.tr: Eternal. Having neither beginning nor end of existence. From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

units.la: Alia à creaturis. Non ipsa natura, non materia, non forma, non pars aliqua, sed efficiens rerum: nec permixta rebus, sed essentia alia à rebus, dissimilis omnibus. Obiect. 1. Omnia sunt ex Deo. Resp. Creatione ex nihilo. Obiect. 2. Dei progenies sumus. Resp. Similitudine proprietatum & creatione. Obiect. 3. Sancti sunt ex Deo nati. Resp. Regeneratione per Spiritum sanctum. Obiect. 4. Sumus participes diuinæ naturæ. Resp. Inhabitatione Deitatis & conformitate quadam. Obiect. 5. Christus Deus habet corpus diuinum. Resp. Vnione hypostatica & glorificatione: creatum tamen & verum.
units.tr: Other than creatures. Not nature itself, not matter, not form, not any part, but the efficient cause of things; not mixed with things, but an essence other than things, unlike all of them. Objection 1: All things are of God. Answer: By creation out of nothing. Objection 2: We are God's offspring. Answer: By likeness of properties and by creation. Objection 3: The saints are born of God. Answer: By regeneration through the Holy Spirit. Objection 4: We are partakers of the divine nature. Answer: By the indwelling of the Deity and a certain conformity. Objection 5: Christ as God has a divine body. Answer: By the hypostatic union and glorification; yet it is created and true.

units.la: Incomprehensibilis. 1. Cogitatione nostra. 2. Immensitate essentiæ. 3. Communicatione ejusdem numero in tribus personis.
units.tr: Incomprehensible. (1) By our thought. (2) By the immensity of his essence. (3) By the communication of the same numerical essence in the three persons.

units.la: In se ipsa perfectissima. 1. Sola habens omnia summa. 2. In se & à se ipsa. 3. Sufficiens omnibus aliis. Obiect. 1. Omnia facit propter se. Resp. Non juvandum, sed communicandum. Obiect. 2. Vtiuntur opera creaturarum. Resp. Non ex indigentia, sed honorans creaturas. Obj. 3. Tribuitur ei cultus à nobis. Resp. Ipsi debitus, & nostro bono. Obj. 4. Cui datur debitum, ei aliquid accedit. Resp. Negatur de debito ex ordine justitiæ, & spectante ad felicitatem dantis. Obj. 5. Lætatur nostra obedientia. Resp. Vt obiecto, non vt causa efficiente lætitiæ in eo.
units.tr: Most perfect in himself. (1) He alone has all supreme qualities. (2) He is in himself and from himself. (3) He is sufficient for all other things. Objection 1: He makes all things for his own sake. Answer: He is not helped, but he communicates himself. Objection 2: He uses the works of creatures. Answer: Not from need, but honouring the creatures. Objection 3: We render worship to him. Answer: It is due to him, and for our own good. Objection 4: Whatever is given to one to whom something is owed is added to him. Answer: This is denied of what is owed by the order of justice, and what concerns the happiness of the giver. Objection 5: Our obedience rejoices him. Answer: As its object, not as an efficient cause of joy in him.

units.la: Immutabilis. 1. Essentiâ. 2. Voluntate. 3. Loco: quia immensus. Obj. 1. Deum pœnitet factorum. Resp. Per ἀνθρωπομορφίαν. Obj. 2. Promittit, minatur, quæ non facit. Resp. Conditionaliter. Obiect. 3. Pendet a conditione mutabili. Resp. Respectu voluntatis humanæ, non sui consilj. Obiect. 4. Mutat præcepta & opera. Resp. Juxta æternum suum decretum.
units.tr: Unchangeable. (1) In essence. (2) In will. (3) In place, since he is immeasurable. Objection 1: God repents of what he has done. Answer: By anthropomorphism [ἀνθρωπομορφίαν]. Objection 2: He promises and threatens what he does not do. Answer: Conditionally. Objection 3: He depends on a changeable condition. Answer: With respect to the human will, not to his own counsel. Objection 4: He changes precepts and works. Answer: In accordance with his eternal decree.

units.la: Omnipotens. 1. Omnia potest & facit, quæ vult. 2. Solo nutu, sine difficultate. 3. Omnia habens in sua potestate. Obiect. Multa non potest. Resp. Quæ sunt imbecillitatis & imperfectionis, vt mentiri, mori.
units.tr: Almighty. (1) He can do and does all that he wills. (2) He does it by a mere nod, without difficulty. (3) He has all things in his power. Objection: There are many things he cannot do. Answer: Those which belong to weakness and imperfection, such as to lie or to die.

units.la: Immensa sapientia. 1. Intuens & intelligens seipsum, & totum mentis suæ ac naturæ ordinem uno intuitu, perpetuò & perfectissimè. 2. Causa omnis scientiæ in angelis & hominibus.
units.tr: Immense wisdom. (1) He sees and understands himself, and the whole order of his mind and nature, at one glance, constantly and most perfectly. (2) He is the cause of all knowledge in angels and men.

units.la: Immensa bonitatis. 1. Talis natura Dei, qualis in Lege & Evangelio est patefacta. 2. Causa & norma omnis bonitatis in creaturis. 3. Summum bonum. 4. Essentialiter.
units.tr: Of immeasurable goodness. 1. God's nature is such as it has been revealed in Law and Gospel. 2. He is the cause and norm of all goodness in creatures. 3. He is the highest good. 4. He is so essentially.

units.la: Iusta. 1. Justitia universali, immutabiliter talia volens & faciens, qualia in lege sua præcepit. 2. Justitia particulari immutabiliter tribuens præmia & pœnas convenientes. 3. Regula justitiæ ac rectitudinis in creaturis. Obiect. 1. Bonis male, malis bene facit. Resp. Non finaliter. Obiect. 2. Malos non statim punit. Resp. Differens pœnas ob certas causas. Obiect. 3. Bonis nunquam debebat male esse. Resp. Perfectè bonis in sese. Obj. 4. Facit quædam contraria legi. Resp. Generali derogans speciali voluntate. Obj. 5. Dat æqualibus inæqualia. Resp. Sed indebita. Inst. 1. Sunt debita ex ordine justitiæ. Resp. Deus nulli obligatur. Inst. 2. Promissum cadit in debitum. Resp. Promissio absoluta creaturarum, non Dei: quæ interdum est conditionata, libertimæ & gratuitæ voluntatis executio, sub conditione fidei & obedientiæ, Ezech. 18,9.10.
units.tr: Just. 1. By universal justice, always willing and doing, unchangeably, the things he has commanded in his law. 2. By particular justice, unchangeably bestowing fitting rewards and punishments. 3. He is the rule of justice and rectitude in creatures. Objection 1. He does good to the wicked and evil to the good. Reply Not ultimately. Objection 2. He does not punish the wicked at once. Reply He defers punishments for certain reasons. Objection 3. The good ought never to be in misery. Reply They are perfectly good in themselves. Objection 4. He does some things contrary to the law. Reply By a special will he sets aside a general one. Objection 5. He gives unequal things to equals. Reply But these are undeserved. Instance 1. Some things are owed by the order of justice. Reply God is under obligation to no one. Instance 2. A promise becomes a debt. Reply A promise is absolute when it comes from creatures, not from God; with God it is sometimes conditional, the execution of a free and gratuitous will, under the condition of faith and obedience (Ezek. 18:9, 10).

units.la: Verax. 1. Habens verissimas notitias rerum omnium. 2. Non volens nec dicens contraria. 3. Non simulans vel fallens. 4. Non mutans sententiam. 5. Euentu probans quod dicit. 6. Veracitatem præcipiens omnibus. Obiect.1. Quæ non vult fieri prædicit. Resp. Conditionaliter. Obj.2. Decipit Prophetas. Resp. Tradens eos diabolo decipiendos justo judicio.
units.tr: True. 1. He has most true knowledge of all things. 2. He neither wills nor says contrary things. 3. He does not pretend or deceive. 4. He does not change his mind. 5. By the outcome he proves what he says. 6. He commands truthfulness to all. Objection 1. He foretells what he does not wish to happen. Reply Conditionally. Objection 2. He deceives the prophets. Reply By handing them over to the devil to be deceived, through a just judgment.

units.la: Casta.] 1. Purissima natura sua. 2. Amans & præcipiens castitatem. 3. Seuerissimè detestans & puniens omnem immunditiem internam & externam. 4. Hac illustri nota se ab immundis & obscœnis spiritibus diabolis discernens. Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, vt abstineatis à fornicatione, & sciat vnusquisque vestrum vas suum possidere in sanctificatione, honore, &c. Nt polluamini in omnibus his. Per hæc omnia polluerunt se gentes.
units.tr: Chaste. 1. He is most pure in his own nature. 2. He loves and commands chastity. 3. He most severely detests and punishes every impurity, inward and outward. 4. By this distinguished mark he distinguishes himself from the unclean and obscene spirits, the devils. This is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication, and that each of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour, etc. That you be not defiled in all these things. For by all these the nations have defiled themselves.

units.la: Misericors.] 1. Volens omnium salutem. 2. Differens pœnas & inuitans omnes ad resipiscentiam. 3. Accommodans se nostræ infirmitati. 4. Liberans electos. 5. Tradens pro his Filium in mortem. 6. Gratuita bonitate hæc promittens & faciens. 7. Ignoscens, & hostibus benefaciens. Obj.1. Misericordia est dolor. Resp. In hominibus, non in Deo. Obiect.2. Lætatur vindicta. Respond. Quatenus est executio justitiæ suæ.
units.tr: Merciful. 1. He wills the salvation of all. 2. He defers punishments and invites all to repentance. 3. He accommodates himself to our weakness. 4. He delivers the elect. 5. For them he gave up his Son to death. 6. He promises and does these things by free goodness. 7. He forgives and does good to enemies. Objection 1. Mercy is a kind of grief. Reply In men, not in God. Objection 2. Vengeance rejoices. Reply In so far as it is the execution of his justice.

units.la: Obiect.3. Negat misericordiam impiis. Resp. Non resipiscentibus. Obiect.4. Non seruat omnes, cum possit. Respond. Vt cum misericordia etiam justitiam declaret. Obiect.5. Non misericordia sine satisfactione. Resp. Sed Filij satisfactionem gratis nobis donat.
units.tr: Objection 3. He denies mercy to the ungodly. Reply To those who do not repent. Objection 4. He does not save all, though he could. Reply So that, along with mercy, he may also display justice. Objection 5. There is no mercy without satisfaction. Reply But the Son freely gives us his satisfaction.

units.la: Benefica.] 1. Creans & seruans omnia. 2. Omnibus benefaciens. 3. Etiam malis. 4. Gratuito amore erga creaturas. 5. Præcipue erga electos, donans eos vita & gloria æterna. Obiect.1. Irascitur. Resp. Prauitati, non creaturæ. Obiect.2. Affligit homines. Resp. Impœnitentes.
units.tr: Beneficent. 1. He creates and preserves all things. 2. He does good to all. 3. Even to the evil. 4. He loves creatures with a free love. 5. Above all he loves the elect, giving them eternal life and glory. Objection 1. He is angry. Reply At wickedness, not at the creature. Objection 2. He afflicts men. Reply Those who do not repent.

units.la: Liberrima.] 1. Immunis ab omni culpa, miseria, obligatione, seruitute, coactione. 2. Volens & faciens omnia liberrimè & stissimè, quando & quomodo vult. Obi.1. Sine Deo non agunt causæ secundæ necessariò agentes. Resp. Necessitate consequentiæ. Obiect.2. Est bonus necessariò. Resp. Necessitate immutabilitatis, non coactionis. Obiect.3. Quæ semel decreuit, necessariò vult. Respond. Immutabiliter, non coacte. Obiect.4. Non fit quod vult. Quoties volui, & noluisti? Resp. Voluntate signi, non beneplaciti.
units.tr: Most free. 1. He is free from all guilt, misery, obligation, servitude and compulsion. 2. He wills and does all things most freely and most surely, when and how he wills. Objection 1. Without God, secondary causes, which act of necessity, do not act. Reply By the necessity of consequence. Objection 2. He is necessarily good. Reply By the necessity of immutability, not of compulsion. Objection 3. What he has once decreed he wills of necessity. Reply Unchangeably, not under compulsion. Objection 4. What he wills does not happen. How often would I have gathered you, and you would not? Reply By his will of sign, not of good pleasure.

units.la: Irascens peccatis.] Horribiliter detestans & puniens omnia peccata temporalibus & æternis pœnis.
units.tr: Angry at sins. He horribly detests and punishes all sins with temporal and eternal punishments.

units.la: III. Vnde constet vnum esse Deum.
units.tr: III. How it is established that there is one God.

units.la: Vnum esse Deum probatur. Primò, expressis testimoniis scripturæ pturæ : Audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster Deus vnus est. Videte, quod ego sum solus, & non est alius Deus praeter me. Ego primus & nouissimus : absque me non est Deus. Scimus idolum nihil esse in mundo, & nullum alium esse Deum, nisi vnum. Vnus Deus, vnus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. Similia legantur Deut. 4. verf. 35. 2 Samuelis 22, 32. Psalm. 18, 32. Esaiæ 45, 21. & 46, 9. Hoseæ 13, 4. Malach. 2, 1. Marci 12, 32. Rom. 3, 30. Ephes. 4, 5. Galat. 3, 20. Hæc sufficiant, quamuis innumera per totam scripturam sint sparsa.
units.tr: That there is one God is proved. First, by express testimonies of Scripture: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord." "See that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me." "I am the first and the last; besides me there is no God." "We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one." "There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Similar passages may be read at Deut. 4:35, 2 Sam. 22:32, Ps. 18:32, Isa. 45:21 and 46:9, Hos. 13:4, Mal. 2:10, Mark 12:32, Rom. 3:30, Eph. 4:5, Gal. 3:20. These will suffice, although countless passages are scattered through all Scripture.

units.la: Secundo, firmis rationibus, siue argumentis.
units.tr: Second, by firm reasons or arguments.

units.la: 1. Vnus tantum Deus, quem colit Ecclesia, talibus testimoniis patefactus est, quæ fallere non possunt : vt miraculis, variciniis, & operibus, quæ à sola natura omnipotente possunt prouidi ficisci. Quis sicut ego, qui vocet quod præterit, annunciet, illud, & ordinet &c. Non est sicut tu inter Deos, Domine, nec est secundum opera tua faciens.
units.tr: 1. The only God whom the Church worships has been revealed by such testimonies as cannot deceive: such as miracles, prophecies, and works which can proceed from almighty nature alone. "Who is like me? Let him call out, let him declare it and set it in order for me..." "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours."

units.la: 2. Qui solus imperet vniuersis, & solus gubernet omnia, ac proinde solus summam maiestatem obtineat, tantum vnus esse potest. Diuina verò maiestas sola summa ac tanta est, vt maior neque existere, neque cogitari queat. Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Regi seculorum immortali, invisibili, soli sapienti Deo honor, & gloria. Dignus es, Domine, qui accipias gloriam & honorem & virtutem : quia solus creasti omnia.
units.tr: 2. He who alone rules over all things and alone governs all, and therefore alone holds supreme majesty, can be only one. Divine majesty alone is so supreme and so great that a greater can neither exist nor be conceived. "I am the Lord, that is my name, and I will not give my glory to another." "To the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory." "You are worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power, for you have created all things."

units.la: 3. Perfectissimus tantum vnus esse potest. Qui enim solus habet totum & omnia, perfectus demum est. Deus est perfectissimus, quia causa omnium bonorum in natura. Itaque nihil est absurdius, quàm fingere, aliquid esse Deum, quod non sit summum & perfectissimum. Domine quis similis tibi?
units.tr: 3. Only one can be most perfect. For he who alone has all things and everything is at last perfect. God is most perfect, because he is the cause of all good things in nature. Therefore nothing is more absurd than to imagine that something is God which is not highest and most perfect. Lord, who is like unto thee?

units.la: 4. Omnipotens tantum vnus esse potest. Plures enim se mutuo impedire possent, & eo ipso omnipotentes non essent. Hoc argumento monarchia mundi vni Deo asseritur apud Daniclem, cum nullus esse dicitur, qui manui & voluntati eius resistere queat.
units.tr: 4. Only one can be almighty. For several could hinder one another and by that very fact would not be almighty. By this argument the sovereignty of the world is ascribed to the one God in Daniel, where it is said that there is no one who can resist his hand and will.

units.la: 5. Si plures dij ponantur, aut singuli regendis vniuersis impares, atque sic imperfecti, & non dij : aut reliqui otiosi & superflui erunt. At absurdum est talem Deum fingere, qui ad ministrandis vniuersis non sufficiat, aut superfluus sit & otiosus. Quare vnus tantum sit Deus necesse est, qui solus omnibus sufficiat.
units.tr: 5. If several gods are posited, either each is unequal to governing the universe, and so is imperfect and not a god, or the rest will be idle and superfluous. But it is absurd to imagine a God who is not sufficient to minister to the universe, or who is superfluous and idle. Therefore there must be only one God, who alone suffices for all.

units.la: 6. Infinitum seu immensum tantum vnum esse potest. Nam si darentur plura, nullum vlliq; esset, proinde nec plures dij, sed vnus tantum Deus esse potest, qui solus est infinitus.
units.tr: 6. The infinite or immeasurable can be only one. For if more were given, none would be infinite at all; therefore there cannot be several gods, but only one God, who alone is infinite.

units.la: 7. Non nisi vna esse potest omnium rerum causa prima. Deus autem est illa prima causa. Ergo tantum vnus est.
units.tr: 7. There can be only one first cause of all things. But God is that first cause. Therefore he is only one.

units.la: 8. Summum bonum tantum vnum esse potest. Si enim praeter illud etiam aliud esset summum bonum, esset aut maius, aut minus, aut æquale summo. Si maius, illud non esset summum: & hoc etiam Deus esset, quod Deo esset contumeliosum. Si minus, hoc non esset summum, proinde nec Deus. Si æquale, neutrum esset summum, neque Deus.
units.tr: 8. The highest good can be only one. For if beside it there were another highest good, it would be either greater, or less, or equal to the highest. If greater, the first would not be the highest, and this other would be God, which would be an insult to God. If less, this would not be the highest and so not God. If equal, neither would be the highest, nor God.

units.la: Usus quaestionis huius est: cum Deus sit vnus, non igitur colendi vel adorandi sunt alij, praeter hunc vnum Deum: neque aliunde, quàm ab eo solo bona omnia sunt expectanda, eique soli omnia accepta referenda.
units.tr: The use of this question is this: since God is one, others are not therefore to be honoured or worshipped besides this one God; nor are all good things to be expected from anywhere but from him alone, and all things are to be referred to him alone.

units.la: Obiect. At multi dicuntur dij in scriptura. Dixi ego, vos dij estis. Sunt dij multi, & domini multi. Moses dicitur Deus Aaronis & Pharaonis: immò diabolus dicitur Deus mundi. Resp. 1. Magistratus & judices aliquando vocantur dij, propter dignitatem & officium, quod gerunt Dei nomine, sicut dicitur: Per me reges regnant. Quia enim Deus gubernationem suam per magistratus & judices tanquam per organa & seruos in his terris exsequitur, etiam honore nominis sui eos dignatur, appellando deos: idque vt sciant subditi, cum Deo sibi negotium esse, siue obtemperent, siue repugnent magistratui; juxta illud: Qui se opponit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. 2. Angeli etiam vocantur dij, ob dignitatem & excellentiam naturae, potentiae, & sapientiae, qua longe nos antecellunt: & propter officium diuinum, quod sustinent in defendendis piis & puniendis malis. Fecisti eum paulo minus ab angelis. Angeli sunt administratorij spiritus. 3. Diabolus vocatur Deus huius seculi propter maximam potentiam, quam habet in homines & alias creaturas, justo Dei judicio. 4. Denique multi dij dicuntur opinione hominum, qui res aut creaturas aliquas habent & colunt pro diis. Ita dij dicuntur per mimesin omnia idola. Dij qui non creauerunt coelum & terram, peribunt de terra. Quorum Deus venter est. Sed hic agitur de vero Deo, qui naturâ est Deus, ex se, & per se, non aliunde potentiam habens, qualis tantum est vnus.
units.tr: Objection: Yet in Scripture many are called gods. "I have said, You are gods." "There are many gods and many lords." Moses is called God of Aaron and Pharaoh; indeed the devil is called God of the world. Reply 1. Magistrates and judges are sometimes called gods, on account of the dignity and office which they hold in God's name, as it is said: "By me kings reign." For since God executes his government in these lands through magistrates and judges as through instruments and servants, he also honours them with the title of his own name, calling them gods; and this so that subjects may know that they have to do with God, whether they obey or resist the magistrate, according to that saying: "Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God." 2. Angels also are called gods, on account of the dignity and excellence of their nature, power and wisdom, by which they far surpass us, and on account of the divine office they perform in defending the godly and punishing the wicked. "You have made him a little lower than the angels." "The angels are ministering spirits." 3. The devil is called god of this world, on account of the great power he has over men and other creatures, by the just judgment of God. 4. Finally, many are called gods in the opinion of men, who have certain things or creatures and worship them as gods. In this way all idols are called gods by metonymy. "The gods that did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth." "Whose god is the belly." But here we are speaking of the true God, who is God by nature, of himself and through himself, not having power from elsewhere, which only one God is.

units.la: IV. Quid essentia, persona, Trinitas sint & differant.
units.tr: IV. What essence, person, and Trinity are, and how they differ.

units.la: Essentia, Graecè οὐσία, in hac doctrina est res per se subsistens, non sustentata ab alio, etsi pluribus sit communicabilis. Communicabile vel communicatum dicitur, quod pluribus commune est, vel communicari potest: Incommunicabile est, quod nulli rei communicatur. Essentia hominis est communicabilis & communis munis multis hominib. specie, non indiuiduo. Dei autem essentia est communicabilis indiuiduo: quia deitas, seu Dei natura est in tribus personis eadem & tota existens.
units.tr: Essence, Greek οὐσία, in this doctrine is a thing subsisting in itself, not supported by another, although it can be communicated to several. Something is called communicable, or communicated, when it is common to several or can be communicated to them. Something is incommunicable when it is communicated to no thing. The essence of man is communicable and common to many men in species, not in the individual. But the essence of God is communicable in the individual, because the Godhead, or the nature of God, is the same and whole in the three persons.

units.la: Persona, [illegible, ~10 letters] (Greek), est subsistens indiuiduum, viuum, intelligens, incommunicabile, non sustentatum in alio, nec pars alterius. Subsistens: non accidens, cogitatio, decretū, sonus euanescens, qualitas, aut motus creatus. Indiuiduum: non brutum: quia bruta, etsi sunt viua animalia, non tamen sunt persona. Incommunicabile: ad differentiam essentiae, quae in pluribus esse potest, & pluribus esse communis: persona non potest. Non sustentatum in alio: quia per se subsistens. Nam humana Christi natura est subsistens, indiuidua, incommunicabilis, intelligens, sed non est persona: quia sustentatur a [illegible, ~3 letters]. Rursus anima hominis est per se subsistens, intelligens, non sustentata ab alio: & tamen non est persona, quia est pars alterius sustinentis indiuidui. Ideo additur: nec pars alterius.
units.tr: Person (Greek ὑπόστασις) is an individual subsisting being, living and intelligent, incommunicable, not supported by another, nor a part of another. Subsisting: not an accident, a thought, a decree, a fading sound, a quality, or a created motion. Individual: not a brute, because brutes, although they are living animals, are not persons. Incommunicable: in contrast to essence, which can exist in several and be common to several; a person cannot. Not supported by another: because it subsists in itself. For the human nature of Christ is subsisting, individual, incommunicable and intelligent, yet it is not a person, because it is sustained by the Person of the Word. Again, the soul of man subsists in itself, is intelligent and is not supported by another, and yet it is not a person, because it is a part of another individual that sustains it. Therefore the words nor a part of another are added.

units.la: Hinc apparet discrimen inter essentiam Dei, & personas essentiae diuinae. Essentia nomine intelligitur id, quod Pater aeternus, Filius & Spiritus sanctus singuli ad se absolute siue secundum naturam suam considerati, sunt, & dicuntur, ac tribus illis commune est. Persona vero nomine intelligitur id, quod singuli horum trium ad alios collati, seu relatiue, & secundum existendi modum cuique peculiarem considerati, sunt, & dicuntur, & eorum cuiq; est proprium. Hoc est, Essentia est ipsum Dei esse, seu ipsa aeterna atque unica deitas. Persona est id, quo illud Dei esse seu essentia diuina in singulis horum trium subsistit. Deus Pater est illud Esse a se: non ab alio. Filius est idem illud Esse non a se, sed a Patre. Spiritus sanctus est idem illud Esse, non a se, sed a Patre & Filio. Ita Esse seu essentia diuina horum trium eadem est, & numero una: sed esse a se vel ab alio, item esse ab uno vel a duobus, hoc est, essentiam illam unam habere a se, vel habere communicatam ab alio, ab uno, vel a duobus, est modus subsistendi, qui sunt tres numero distincti; a se esse, generatum esse; [illegible, ~2 letters] procedere: eoque tres sunt personae, quae Trinitatis nomine significantur.
units.tr: From this the difference between the essence of God and the persons of the divine essence appears. By the name essence is understood what the eternal Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each are and are called when considered absolutely, that is, in their own nature, and what is common to all three. By the name person, however, is understood what each of these three is and is called when compared with the others, or relatively, and considered according to the mode of existing peculiar to each, and what is proper to each one of them. That is, essence is the very being of God, that is, the eternal and single Godhead itself. Person is that by which this being of God, or the divine essence, subsists in each of these three. God the Father is that being which is from itself, not from another. The Son is the same being, not from himself but from the Father. The Holy Spirit is the same being, not from himself but from the Father and the Son. Thus the being, or divine essence, of these three is the same and one in number; but to be from oneself or from another, likewise to be from one or from two, that is, to have that one essence from oneself, or to have it communicated from another, from one or from two, is a mode of subsisting which makes them three distinct in number: to be from oneself, to be begotten, to proceed. And so there are three persons, who are signified by the name of Trinity.

units.la: Summa discriminis est. Essentia est absoluta & communicabilis: persona est relatiua & incommunicabilis. Pater exemplo hominis, quia aliud est hominem esse, aliud est, patrem esse: & tamen unus idemque est homo & pater sed homo absolute & secundum naturam suam, pater respectu alterius, nempe filii. Ita aliud est, Deum esse, aliud Patrem aut Filium, aut Spiritum sanctum esse, & tamen unus idemque est Deus, & Pater, aut Filius, aut Spiritus sanctus: illud respectu sui, hoc respectu alterius.
units.tr: The sum of the difference is this. Essence is absolute and communicable; person is relative and incommunicable. Take the example of a man: it is one thing to be a man, another to be a father; and yet one and the same is both man and father, but he is man absolutely and according to his nature, and father in respect of another, namely a son. So it is one thing to be God, another to be the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit; and yet one and the same is God and Father, or Son, or Holy Spirit: the former in respect of himself, the latter in respect of another.

units.la: Discrimen hoc essentiæ & personæ ideo tenendum est, ne aut unitas veri Dei distrahatur, aut personarum distinctio tollatur, aut denique aliud nomine personæ intelligatur, quam veritas verbi diuini ostendit. Itaque cautiones hæ diligenter sunt observandæ.
units.tr: This difference between essence and person must be held, lest either the unity of the true God be torn apart, or the distinction of the persons be removed, or finally something be understood by the name of person other than what the truth of the divine Word shows. Therefore these cautions are to be carefully observed.

units.la: 1. Personam in hac doctrina nequaquam significare duntaxat relationem vel officium: quemadmodum Latini dicunt, principis personam tueri, sicut olim Sabellius falso intellexit: multo minus vultum seu speciem visibilem, alterius formam & gestus repræsentantem, qualis est persona scenica, sicut his temporibus Servetus in vocabulo personæ lusit: sed intelligi subsistens, ab aliis, ad quos refertur, proprietate incommunicabili revera distinctum, hoc est, ipsum gignens, aut genitum, aut procedens: non officium, dignitatem, aut gradum gignentis vel geniti, vel procedentis.
units.tr: 1. In this doctrine person by no means signifies merely a relation or an office, as the Latins say, to maintain the person of the prince, as Sabellius once wrongly understood it; much less a visible face or appearance representing the form and gestures of another, as is a stage character, as Servetus in these times played with the word person. Rather it is to be understood as a subsisting being, really distinct from the others to whom it is related by an incommunicable property, that is, the one who begets, or who is begotten, or who proceeds; not the office, dignity, or rank of the begetter, or of the one begotten, or of the one proceeding.

units.la: 2. Personas non esse abstractum aut separatum aliquid ab essentia, quam communem habent, nec essentiam esse quartum aliquid separatum à tribus personis: sed singulas personas esse integram & eandem essentiam divinitatis. Discrimen autem inter est, quod personæ singulæ ab aliis distinctæ sunt, essentia vero est tribus personis communis.
units.tr: 2. The persons are not something abstracted or separated from the essence which they have in common, nor is the essence a fourth thing separated from the three persons; but each person is the whole and the same essence of the Godhead. The difference, however, is this: the individual persons are distinct from one another, whereas the essence is common to the three persons.

units.la: 3. De vocabulo essentia etiam hoc notandum est, quod Deus vel divinitas, vel essentia diuina non habent se ad personas, tanquam materia ad formam: quia Deus non componitur ex materia & forma: ideo non recte dicitur: Tres personæ sunt vel constant ex una essentia. Neque ut totum ad partes: quia Deus est indiuisibilis: ideo non recte dicitur, persona est pars essentiæ, aut essentia constat ex tribus personis: quælibet enim persona est tota essentia diuina. Neque ut genus ad species: quia essentia non est genus trium personarum, nec persona est species essentiæ. Sed Deus est nomen communius: quia Deitatis essentia tribus personis est communis, ideoque de singulis prædicari potest. Patris autem & Filij & Spiritus sancti nomina sunt angustiora: quia personæ revera sunt distinctæ, nec vna de aliis prædicari potest. Itaque recte dicitur: Deus vel essentia diuina est Pater, est Filius, est Spiritus sanctus. Item: Tres personæ sunt vna vel eadem essentia, natura Deus, vel in vno Deo: item, sunt vna vel eiusdem essentiæ, naturæ, diuinitas, &c. item, sunt vnius vel eiusdem essentiæ, naturæ, &c. Nec tamen recte, sunt vnius Dei: quia nulla est harum personarum, quæ non sit ipse Deus totus & perfectus. Quare essentia diuina habet se ad personas, vt singulari modo communimunicatum habet sed ea, quibus est commune. Neque enim simile est exemplum communicationis in vllis rebus creatis.
units.tr: 3. Concerning the word essence it must also be noted that God, or the Godhead, or the divine essence, does not stand to the persons as matter to form, because God is not composed of matter and form; therefore it is not rightly said: The three persons are, or consist of, one essence. Nor does it stand as the whole to the parts, because God is indivisible; therefore it is not rightly said that a person is a part of the essence, or that the essence consists of three persons; for each person is the whole divine essence. Nor does it stand as genus to species, because essence is not the genus of the three persons, nor is a person a species of essence. But God is the more common name, because the essence of the Godhead is common to the three persons and so can be predicated of each one. The names Father, Son and Holy Spirit, however, are narrower, because the persons are really distinct and one cannot be predicated of another. Therefore it is rightly said: God, or the divine essence, is the Father, is the Son, is the Holy Spirit. Likewise: The three persons are one and the same essence, nature God, or in one God; likewise, they are of one and the same essence, nature, divinity, etc.; likewise, they are of one essence, nature, etc. Yet it is not rightly said that they are of one God, because none of these persons is not himself the whole and perfect God. Therefore the divine essence stands to the persons in such a way that it is communicated to them in a singular manner, which it has with those to whom it is common. For there is no similar example of communication in any created things.

units.la: Trinitas, Græcè τριὰς, significat has tres personas tribus exsistendi modis distinctas in vna Deitatis essentia. Nec dicitur multiplicitas vel triplicitas, sed Trinitas personarum, ne cogitentur plures essentiæ, aut dissimiles personæ. Nec dicitur Deus multiplex vel triplex: quia Deus non est compositus vlla ratione, sed simplicissimus, vnus quidem ratione essentiæ, trinus verò ratione personarum.
units.tr: Trinity (Greek τριάς) signifies these three persons, distinguished by three modes of existing, in the one essence of the Godhead. It is not called multiplicity or triplicity, but Trinity of persons, lest several essences or dissimilar persons be thought of. Nor is God called manifold or triple, because God is not compounded in any way, but most simple: one indeed in respect of essence, but three in respect of persons.

units.la: V. An hæc vocabula sint vsurpanda.
units.tr: V. Whether these words ought to be used.

units.la: Hæretici iam olim impugnarunt hæc vocabula, eò quod non exstent in scriptura. Nos verò Ecclesiæ veteris & purioris sermonem rectè imitamur, & vocabula hæc retinemus.
units.tr: Heretics attacked these words long ago, on the ground that they do not occur in Scripture. We, however, rightly follow the language of the older and purer Church, and retain these words.

units.la: 1. Quia licet ipsa totidem syllabis non exstent: tamen cognatæ aut similes, aut idem certè significantes voces & locutiones inveniuntur in scriptura. Vt illud: Ego sum qui sum. Item: ὁ ὢν, qui est, misit me ad vos: item nomen יהוה negari non potest, quod respondeat vocabulo essentiæ. Sic nomen ὑποστάσεως, pro persona sumitur in epistola ad Hebræos, ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. Nec alio sensu Ecclesia personas Trinitatem dicit, quam Johannes Patrem, λόγον, & Spiritum sanctum tres esse pronunciat in cœlo testificantes.
units.tr: 1. Although the words themselves do not occur in Scripture in these exact syllables, related or similar words and phrases that certainly mean the same thing are found there. For example: I am who I am. Likewise: ὁ ὢν [ho ōn], "he who is," sent me to you. Likewise, the name Jehovah [יהוה] cannot be denied to correspond to the word "essence." So too the noun ὑπόστασις [hypostasis] is used for "person" in the Epistle to the Hebrews: ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ [hos ōn apaugasma tēs doxēs, kai charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs autou], "who being the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person" (Heb. 1.3). Nor does the Church call the persons a Trinity in any other sense than that in which John declares that the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit are three who bear witness in heaven.

units.la: 2. Quia interpretationis ratio postulat, vt verba scripturæ aliis idem significantibus, & sumptis ex communi vsu rudioribus exponantur. Alioqui tolleretur omnis interpretatio scripturæ. Licet ergo Ecclesiæ vsurpare verba & loquendi modos, quibus sensum scripturæ, & mentem suam commodè declaret.
units.tr: 2. The rule of interpretation requires that the words of Scripture be explained by other words of the same meaning, taken from common usage and simpler than the originals. Otherwise all interpretation of Scripture would be abolished. It is therefore lawful for the Church to use words and modes of speech by which she may suitably declare the sense of Scripture and her own mind.

units.la: 3. Quia corruptelæ & fraudes hæreticorum, quas plerumque scripturæ verbis tegere conantur, facilius deteguntur & cernuntur, si res eædem diversis verbis efferantur. Et propter brevitatem & perspicuitatem harum vocum fit, vt hæretici non possint occultare suas impostituras & sophismata. Si tamen consensus esset de re ipsa, facile conueniret de verbis. Abhorremus à λογομαχία. Nequaquam de vocabulis certamen est Ecclesiæ cum aliis gentibus & hæreticis, sed de hac doctrina, quod Pater æternus & Filius & Spiritus sanctus sint vnus Deus, & tamen nec Pater sit Filius, aut Spiritus sanctus, nec Spiritus sanctus sit Pater aut Filius, &c. Ab hac doctrina nisi abhorrerent hæretici, facilè etiam vocabula admitterent. Verum ideo vocabula auersantur, quia rem & fidem ipsam auersantur.
units.tr: 3. The corruptions and frauds of the heretics, which they generally try to cover with the words of Scripture, are more easily detected and exposed if the same things are expressed in different words. Because of the brevity and clarity of these terms, heretics cannot conceal their deceptions and sophisms. Yet if there were agreement about the thing itself, agreement about the words would easily follow. We abhor logomachy [λογομαχία]. The Church's dispute with other peoples and with heretics is in no way a quarrel about words, but about this doctrine: that the eternal Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God, and yet the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son, and so on. If the heretics did not shrink from this doctrine, they would readily accept the words too. But they reject the words precisely because they reject the thing and the faith itself.

units.la: Ex his ad obiectionem facilè respondetur: Vocabula quæ non sunt in scriptura, non sunt vsurpanda in Ecclesia. Hæc non sunt in scriptura. Non igitur sunt vsurpanda. Resp. ad maiorem: quae non sunt in scriptura, neque quoad voces, neque quoad sensum, omittenda sunt. At vocabula essentia, persona, Trinitatis, quoad rem ipsam in scriptura exstare, ostensum est. Item vocabula non exstantia in scripturis sunt omittenda, si scilicet omissis vocabulis res ipsa non periclitetur. At haeretici nihil aliud quaerunt, quam ut cum vocabulis ipsam doctrinam & fidem Trinitatis tollant vel depravent. Inst. At pariunt contentiones. Resp. Per accidens, apud haereticos contentiosos.
units.tr: From these points the objection is easily answered. The objection runs: words that are not in Scripture must not be used in the Church. These words are not in Scripture. Therefore they must not be used. Answer to the major premise: words that are not in Scripture, neither as to their wording nor as to their sense, are to be omitted. But the words essence, person, Trinity have been shown to occur in Scripture as far as the thing itself is concerned. Likewise, words not found in Scripture must be omitted if, when they are omitted, the thing itself is not endangered. But the heretics seek nothing else than to remove or corrupt, along with these words, the doctrine and the faith of the Trinity. Objection: But they produce contentions. Answer: Only incidentally, among contentious heretics.

units.la: VI. Quot sint personae divinitatis.
units.tr: VI. How many persons there are in the Godhead.

units.la: In una Dei essentia tres personae subsistunt, proprietatibus suis realiter distinctae, consubstantiales & coaeternae, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus: quae omnes & singulae sunt unus verus & aeternus Deus.
units.tr: In the one essence of God there subsist three persons, really distinct in their properties, consubstantial and coeternal: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. All of them, and each of them, are the one true and eternal God.

units.la: Confirmant hoc 1 Expressa testimonia scripturae veteris & novi testamenti plurima: Spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas: dixitque Deus: fiat lux. Verbo Iehova facti sunt caeli, & spiritu oris eius omnis exercitus eorum. Clariora sunt testimonia novi testamenti: Baptizate omnes gentes, in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti. Consolator ille Spiritus sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo (hoc est, per & propter me) ille vos docebit omnia. Cum venerit consolator ille, quem ego mittam vobis a Patre, qui a Patre emanat, ille testabitur de me. Tres sunt, qui testimonium perhibent in coelo, Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus sanctus, & hi tres unum sunt. Ex misericordia salvavit nos per lavacrum regenerationis, & renovationem Spiritus sancti, quem effudit in nos copiose per Iesum Christum. Per ipsum (Christum) habemus aditum utrique per unum Spiritum ad Patrem. Gratia Domini Iesu Christi, & charitas Dei, & communicatio Spiritus sancti, sit cum omnibus vobis. Emisit Deus Spiritum Filij sui in corda vestra. &c.
units.tr: This is confirmed, first, by very many express testimonies of the Old and New Testaments: The Spirit of God moved upon the waters; and God said, Let there be light. (Gen. 1.2–3) By the word of Jehovah the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. (Ps. 33.6) The testimonies of the New Testament are clearer still: Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. (Matt. 28.19) That Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name (that is, through and for my sake), he will teach you all things. (John 14.26) When the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me. (John 15.26) There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. (1 John 5.7) According to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ. (Titus 3.5–6) Through him (Christ) we have access in one Spirit to the Father. (Eph. 2.18) The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. (2 Cor. 13.13) God has sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts. (Gal. 4.6) etc.

units.la: 2. Idem probant ea scripturae loca, quae tribus, Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto nomen Iehovae & veri Dei tribuunt, quaeque de Iehova in veteri Testamento dicta, in novo ad Filium & Spiritum sanctum expresse & liberrime referunt.
units.tr: 2. The same is proved by those passages of Scripture which ascribe the name of Jehovah and of the true God to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and which refer to the Son and the Holy Spirit expressly and quite freely what is said of Jehovah in the Old Testament.

units.la: 3. Ea loca, quae tribus eandem & totam essentiam divinam tribuunt, & docent Filium esse Patris Filium proprium & unigenitum: & Spiritum sanctum esse Patris & Filij Spiritum ita proprium, ut ex utroque procedat.
units.tr: 3. Those passages which ascribe to the three the same and the whole divine essence, and which teach that the Son is the proper and only-begotten Son of the Father, and that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, so proper to them that he proceeds from both.

units.la: 4. Ea loca, quae tribus eadem attributa & perfectiones naturae divinae attribuunt, aeternitatem, immensitatem, omnipotentiam, &c.
units.tr: 4. Those passages which ascribe to the three the same attributes and perfections of the divine nature: eternity, immensity, omnipotence, etc.

units.la: 5. Ea loca, quæ tribus eadem opera deitatis propria tribuunt, nempe creationis, conseruationis & gubernationis mundi, miraculorum & redemptionis Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 5. Those passages which ascribe to the three the same works proper to deity, namely the creation, preservation and governance of the world, miracles, and the redemption of the Church.

units.la: 6. Ea loca, quæ tribus æqualem, & soli vero Deo competentem honorem, inuocationem & cultum tribuunt.
units.tr: 6. Those passages which ascribe to the three an equal honour, invocation and worship, such as belong to the one true God alone.

units.la: Ex hoc consensu veteris & noui Testamenti intelligitur & confirmatur, vnum Deum esse tres personas verè distinctas, & tres personas esse vnum Deum. Hinc illud quoque intelligitur, recte dici: Patrem esse alium à Filio & Spiritu sancto, Filium esse alium à Patre & Spiritu sancto: Spiritum sanctum esse alium à Patre & Filio: non recte autem: Patrem esse aliud, Filium aliud, Spiritum sanctum aliud. Nam alium esse, diuersitatem personæ; aliud esse, diuersitatem essentiæ declarat.
units.tr: From this agreement of the Old and New Testaments it is understood and confirmed that the one God is three persons truly distinct, and that the three persons are the one God. Hence it is also understood that it is rightly said that the Father is another (alius) than the Son and the Holy Spirit, that the Son is another than the Father and the Holy Spirit, and that the Holy Spirit is another than the Father and the Son; but not rightly that the Father is something else (aliud), the Son something else, and the Holy Spirit something else. For to say "another" (alius) indicates a diversity of person, while to say "something else" (aliud) indicates a diversity of essence.

units.la: Iam demonstrandum esset de singulis personis, quod verè sint ὑπόστασις[?], contra Samosatenum & Servetum: quod distinctæ contra Sabellium: quod æquales, contra Arium, Eunomium, Macedonium: quod denique ὁμοούσιοι[?], seu eiusdem essentiæ, contra eosdem. Ac de Patris quidem ὑπόστασις[?] nulla est controversia. De Filio autem & Spiritu sancto hæc suis locis infra commodius explicabuntur.
units.tr: It would now remain to demonstrate of each of the persons that they are truly subsistences [ὑπόστασις], against Samosatenus and Servetus; that they are distinct, against Sabellius; that they are equal, against Arius, Eunomius and Macedonius; and finally that they are homoousian [ὁμοούσιοι], that is, of the same essence, against the same heretics. Now there is no controversy about the subsistence [ὑπόστασις] of the Father. But concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit these points will be explained more fittingly in their proper places below.

units.la: VII. Quomodo discernantur tres personæ diuinitatis?
units.tr: VII. How are the three persons of the Godhead distinguished?

units.la: Hic tenendum est primò, quid scriptura Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto, qui tres sunt vnus Deus, & tamen personis distincti, tanquam tribus commune tribuat. Deinde, quid singulis tanquam cuique proprium ascribat, & quomodo personas inter se discernat.
units.tr: Here we must hold first what Scripture ascribes in common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are three and yet one God, distinct in persons. Then we must note what it ascribes to each as his own, and how it distinguishes the persons from one another.

units.la: Communes sunt tribus personis: 1. Omnes proprietates Dei essentiales, quas vno Deitatis nomine complectimur: vt æternitas, immensitas, omnipotentia, sapientia, bonitas, habere essentiam à se ipsa exsistentem.
units.tr: Three things are common to the three persons: (1) all the essential properties of God, which we comprehend under the one name of Deity, such as eternity, immensity, omnipotence, wisdom, goodness, and having essence from himself.

units.la: 2. Opera diuinitatis externa, quæ vulgo vocant ad extra, hoc est, ea, quæ Deus erga creaturas, & in eis, vel per eas exercet: vt sunt creatio, conseruatio, gubernatio mundi, collectio & seruatio Ecclesiæ, &c.
units.tr: (2) The external works of the Godhead, which are commonly called ad extra, that is, those which God performs towards creatures, and in them or through them: such as creation, preservation, the government of the world, the gathering and preservation of the Church, and so on.

units.la: Distinguuntur verò personæ dupliciter. 1. Operibus ad intra. 2. Operibus seu operandi modo ad extra. Operaseu actiones diuinitatis ad intra vocantur, quas habent, & exercent personæ erga se inuicem. His igitur operibus internis seu proprietatibus personæ primò inter se distinguuntur. Pater enim est à seipso, non ab alio exsistit. Filius à Patre est genitus ab æterno: hoc est, habet
units.tr: The persons are distinguished in two ways: 1. by works ad intra, and 2. by works, or the mode of operating, ad extra. The works or actions of the Godhead ad intra are those which the persons have and exercise towards one another. By these internal works, or properties, the persons are first distinguished from one another. The Father is from himself and does not exist from another. The Son is begotten of the Father from eternity: that is, he has the divine essence ineffably communicated to him by the Father.

units.la: silen-[?] essentiam diuinam sibi à Patre ineffabiliter communicatam. Spiritus sanctus à Patre & Filio procedit ab æterno: hoc est, habet eandem essentiam diuinam, sibi à Patre & Filio ineffabiliter communicatam. Testimonia: In principio erat λόγος: & λόγος erat apud Deum: & λόγος erat Deus. Vidimus gloriam eius tanquam unigeniti à Patre. Filius unigenitus, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarrauit nobis. Cùm venerit Consolator ille, quem ego mittam vobis à Patre, &c.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son from eternity: that is, he has the same divine essence, ineffably communicated to him by the Father and the Son. Testimonies: In the beginning was the λόγος, and the λόγος was with God, and the λόγος was God [ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος]. We have seen his glory, as of the only begotten of the Father. The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us. When that Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, etc.

units.la: Ordo itaq; personarum in exsistendo hic est. Pater est prima persona, & quasi fons diuinitatis Filij & Spiritus sancti: quia deitas ei à nullo est communicata, sed ipse deitatem communicat Filio & Spiritui sancto. Filius secunda persona: quia deitas ei à Patre communicatur per æternam generationem. Spiritus sanctus tertia persona: quia deitas ei à Patre & Filio communicatur per æternam spirationem. Quo ordine recensentur in his dictis: Baptizate omnes gentes, in nomine Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti. Tres sunt, qui testimonium dant in cælo, Pater, Sermo & Spiritus sanctus; & hi tres unum sunt. Ettamen Pater Filio, & Spiritu sancto, & Filius Spiritu sancto non est prior tempore, sed tantum ordine exsistendi. Nulla enim persona altera est prior aut posterior tempore, aut dignitate, aut gradu, sed tantum ordine, quo aliæ ab aliis exsistunt. Nunquam enim Pater fuit sine Filio, nec Pater & Filius sine Spiritu sancto fuerunt, quandoquidem nec augeri, nec minui, nec mutari diuinitas potest.
units.tr: The order of the persons in their existing is therefore this. The Father is the first person, and as it were the fountain of the deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the deity is communicated to him by no one, but he himself communicates the deity to the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Son is the second person, because the deity is communicated to him by the Father through eternal generation. The Holy Spirit is the third person, because the deity is communicated to him by the Father and the Son through eternal spiration. In this order they are listed in these sayings: Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. Yet the Father is not prior in time to the Son and the Holy Spirit, nor the Son to the Holy Spirit, but only in the order of existing. For no person is earlier or later than another in time, or in dignity, or in rank, but only in the order by which the others exist from the others. For the Father was never without the Son, nor did the Father and the Son ever exist without the Holy Spirit, since the deity can be neither increased, nor diminished, nor changed.

units.la: Quærunt hic curiosi: quid Filij generatio, & Spiritus sancti processio inter se differant? Etsi autem fatendum est, modum æternæ generationis & processionis, & formale utriusque discrimen nobis hominibus esse ἀρρητον, quod orthodoxi patres olim confessi sunt: tamen rem ipsam ex scriptura certo colligimus: Generationem esse communicationem essentiæ diuinæ, qua sola secunda persona diuinitatis à sola prima, tanquam Filius à Patre, essentiam accipit eandem & integram, quam Pater habet & retinet: Processionem verò seu emanationem esse communicationem essentiæ diuinæ, qua sola tertia persona diuinitatis à Patre & Filio, tanquam spiritus ab eo, cuius est spiritus, essentiam accipit eandem & integram, quam Pater & Filius habent & retinent.
units.tr: Both differ from creation in this: to be created by God is for something to be made out of nothing by the command of the divine will; but to be begotten or born, and to proceed or emanate, is for another, or another person, to be ineffably produced from eternity out of the substance of the begetter, and of him from whom the emanation comes; yet so that the Son exists by being born and the Holy Spirit by proceeding. Thus we understand the thing itself, that is, the fact of its being [τὸ εἶναι], as far as God willed us to know it for his glory and our salvation, although we do not grasp the that [τὸ ὅτι].

units.la: Vtraq; verò differt à creatione, quod creari à Deo, est aliquid ex nihilo fieri diuinæ voluntatis imperio: nasci autem siue gigni, & procedere siue emanare, est alium, siue personam aliam e substantia gignentis, & eius, à quo fit emanatio, ineffabiliter ab æterno produci: sic tamen, vt nascendo Filius, procedendo Spiritus sanctus exsistat. Sic igitur rem ipsam seu τὸ εἶναι intelligimus, quantum tum Deus ad gloriam suam & salutem nostram nos scire voluit: etsi τὸ ὅτι non assequamur.
units.tr: Moreover, both generation and procession differ from creation, in that to be created by God is for something to be made out of nothing by the command of the divine will; but to be born or begotten, and to proceed or emanate, is for another, or another person, to be ineffably produced from eternity out of the substance of the one begetting, or of him from whom the emanation comes; yet in such a way that the Son exists by being born and the Holy Spirit by proceeding. Thus we understand the thing itself, or τὸ εἶναι [the fact that it is], as far as God wished us to know it for his glory and our salvation, although we do not grasp τὸ ὅτι [the manner of it].

units.la: De illa porro quæstione, quæ inter Græcas & Latinas Ecclesias agitata est, an Spiritus sanctus rectè dicatur procedere à Patre & Filio, non à Patre tantum: infra in doctrina de Spiritu sancto dicendi locus erit.
units.tr: As for the question that has been debated between the Greek and Latin Churches, whether the Holy Spirit is rightly said to proceed from the Father and the Son, and not from the Father only, there will be a place to speak of it below, in the doctrine of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Observandæ verò sunt phrases scripturæ & veteris Ecclesiæ de hoc discrimine personarum ab intra. Rectè dicitur: Deus genuit: non rectè: Deus alium Deum, vel seipsum genuit. Rectè: Pater genuit alium: non rectè: genuit aliud vel alium Deum. Rectè: Filius est id, quod Pater est. Non rectè: est is, qui pater est. Rectè: Filius est genitus, Spiritus sanctus procedit sive emanat à Patre: item, Filius est à vel ex Patre, Spiritus sanctus est à vel ex Patre & Filio: item, Quicquid habet Filius, à Patre habet & accepit nascendo: quicquid Spiritus sanctus habet, à Patre & Filio habet & accepit emanando: item, Filius & Spiritus sanctus habent originem, quoad personam: & habent essentiam aliunde communicatam. Non rectè: habent originem, quoad essentiam: vel sunt essentia à Patre: vel habent essentiam aliunde productam. Rectè: prima persona divinitatis genuit secundam de sua essentia: tertia persona procedit ex prima & secunda. Non rectè: essentia divina genuit essentiam divinam, vel de essentia gignitur aut procedit persona. Rectè: essentia divina communicatur. Non rectè: essentia divina gignitur, procedit: quia communicari & gigni non sunt idem. Non enim id gignitur, quod communicatur genito, sed illud gignitur, cui substantia gignentis communicatur.
units.tr: The phrases of Scripture and of the ancient Church concerning this distinction of the persons within the Godhead are, however, to be observed. It is rightly said: God begat; it is not rightly said: God begat another God, or himself. Rightly: the Father begat another; not rightly: he begat another God or another God-person. Rightly: the Son is what the Father is; not rightly: he is the one who is the Father. Rightly: the Son is begotten, the Holy Spirit proceeds or emanates from the Father; likewise, the Son is from or out of the Father, the Holy Spirit is from or out of the Father and the Son; likewise, whatever the Son has he has from the Father and received by being begotten; whatever the Holy Spirit has he has and received from the Father and the Son by emanating; likewise, the Son and the Holy Spirit have their origin as to the person, and they have an essence communicated from elsewhere. Not rightly: they have their origin as to the essence; or they are the essence of the Father; or they have an essence produced from elsewhere. Rightly: the first person of the Godhead begat the second from his essence; the third person proceeds from the first and the second. Not rightly: the divine essence begat the divine essence, or a person is begotten or proceeds from the essence. Rightly: the divine essence is communicated. Not rightly: the divine essence is begotten or proceeds, because to be communicated and to be begotten are not the same. For that is not begotten which is communicated to the one begotten, but that is begotten to which the substance of the begetter is communicated.

units.la: II. Alterum personarum discrimen ex primo oritur, & in ordine operationum ad extra, hoc est, earum consistit, quas erga creaturas & in eis & per eas exercent. Fiunt enim hæc opera communi quidem Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti voluntate & operatione, sed eo tamen ordine personarum servato in agendo, quem habent personæ in exsistendo. Pater est fons ut persona, sic & operationis Filij & Spiritus sancti, agitque omnia non ab alio, hoc est, non alio per ipsum agente, seu præeunte alterius voluntate, & altero potentiam seu efficaciam suam ei communicante, sed à se ipso, ut exsistens, sic etiam intelligens, agens, &c. Filius & Spiritus agunt non à se, sed per se: Filius præeunte Patre agit per Filium & Spiritum sanctum, mittit eos, non mittitur ab eis. Filius agit per Spiritum sanctum, mittit eum in corda credentium à Patre, non mittitur ab eo, sed à Patre. Spiritus sanctus agit & mittitur à Patre & Filio, non à se. Omnia per ipsum facta facta sunt. Non potest Filius à se ipso operari, nisi viderit Patrem operantem; quæcunque enim ille facit, Filius similiter facit. Non à me ipso veni. Quem Pater mittet in nomine meo. Mittam eum vobis à Patre.
units.tr: II. The second distinction of the persons arises from the first, and consists in the order of the operations ad extra, hoc est, of those which they exercise towards creatures, in them and through them. For these works are done by the common will and operation of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, yet with that order of the persons kept in acting which the persons have in existing. The Father is the fountain of the operation of the Son and the Holy Spirit as he is a person, and he acts all things not from another, hoc est, not with another acting through him, or going before by the will of another, and another communicating to him his power or efficacy, but from himself, as he exists, so also as he understands, acts, etc. The Son and the Spirit act not from themselves but through themselves: the Son, the Father going before, acts through the Son and the Holy Spirit; he sends them, he is not sent by them. The Son acts through the Holy Spirit; he sends him into the hearts of believers from the Father; he is not sent by him, but by the Father. The Holy Spirit acts and is sent by the Father and the Son, not by himself. All things were made by him [Omnia per ipsum facta] were made. The Son cannot act of himself unless he sees the Father acting; for whatever that one does, the Son does likewise. I have not come of myself. Whom the Father will send in my name. I will send him to you from the Father.

units.la: Cæterum quando Filius & Spiritus sanctus dicuntur mitti, non intelligenda est missio localis, aut aliqua in ipso Deo mutatio, sed æterna voluntas & decretum aliquid per Filium & Spiritum sanctum perficiendi, & huius voluntatis per operationem Filij & Spiritus sancti exsecutio & patefactio. Sic Filius dicit, se à Patre missum esse in mundum: se de cœlo descendisse; & tamen cum in terris esset, se in cœlo esse. Et cum Spiritus sanctus jam ante esset & habitaret in Apostolis, tamen missus illis dicitur in Pentecoste. Missus est igitur in mundum utrque; non quia cœpit exsistere alicubi, ubi prius non erat, sed quia in mundo, quæ Pater voluit, effecit, seq; præsentem & efficacem juxta voluntatem Patris ostendit. Sicut dicitur: Misit Deus Filium suum, factum ex muliere. Quia vero estis filii, misit Deus Spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra clamantem: Abba Pater.
units.tr: Moreover, when the Son and the Holy Spirit are said to be sent, a local sending is not to be understood, nor any change in God himself, but an eternal will and decree to accomplish something through the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the execution and manifestation of this will through the operation of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Thus the Son says that he was sent by the Father into the world, that he came down from heaven, and yet, while he was on earth, he was in heaven. And although the Holy Spirit already existed and dwelt in the Apostles, he is nevertheless said to have been sent to them at Pentecost. Both, then, were sent into the world; not because they began to exist somewhere where they had not been before, but because they accomplished in the world what the Father willed, and showed themselves present and effective according to the will of the Father. As it is said: God sent his Son, made of a woman. And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father.

units.la: VIII. Cur necesse sit doctrinam de Trinitate retinere in Ecclesia.
units.tr: VIII. Why the doctrine of the Trinity must be retained in the Church.

units.la: Scienda & retinenda est hæc de Trinitate doctrina in Ecclesia: 1. Propter gloriam Dei, ut discernatur verus Deus ab idolis, quacum quibus non vult se confundi, sed agnosci & colitalis, quam lem se patefecit. 2. Propter nostram consolationem & salutem. Nemo enim servatur sine cognitione Dei Patris. Pater autem non cognoscitur sine Filio. Deum enim nemo vidit unquam: Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse revelavit nobis. Quisquis ergo negat Filium, is nec Patrem habet. Nemo enim servatur sine fiducia in Filium Dei mediatorem, qui est verus Deus & vita æterna. Quomodo autem invocabunt, in quem non crediunt? quomodo credent ei, de quo non audierunt? Similiter nemo sanctificatur & servatur sine cognitione Spiritus sancti. Qui enim non accipit Spiritum sanctum, non servatur; juxta illud: Qui Spiritum Christi non habet, non est eius. At nemo accipit eum, qui eum non novit; sicut dicitur: Quem mundus non potest accipere: quia non videt eum, neque novit eum. Quare, qui Spiritum sanctum non novit, non servatur. Omnes igitur salvandi, unum Deum, æternum Patrem, coæternum Filium, & coæternum Spiritum sanctum agnoscere oportet. Nisi enim agnoscatur talis, qualem se patefecit, non communicat se nobis, neque vita æterna ab eo sperari potest.
units.tr: This doctrine of the Trinity must be known and retained in the Church: (1) for the glory of God, so that the true God may be distinguished from idols, with which he does not wish to be confused, but to be acknowledged and worshipped as he has revealed himself; (2) for our consolation and salvation. For no one is saved without knowledge of God the Father, and the Father is not known without the Son. No one has ever seen God; the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known to us. Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either. No one is saved without trust in the Son of God as Mediator, who is the true God and eternal life. But how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? Likewise, no one is sanctified and saved without knowledge of the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not receive the Holy Spirit is not saved, according to that saying: Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But no one receives him who does not know him, as it is said: whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. Therefore whoever does not know the Holy Spirit is not saved. All who are to be saved must acknowledge one God, the eternal Father, the co-eternal Son, and the co-eternal Holy Spirit. For unless he is acknowledged as he has revealed himself, he does not impart himself to us, nor can eternal life be hoped for from him.

units.la: Obiectiones haereticorum contra doctrinam de Trinitate.
units.tr: Objections of the heretics against the doctrine of the Trinity.

units.la: 1. Vna essentia non sunt tres personae: quia vnum esse tria, implicat contradictionem. Iehoua est vna essentia Ergo, &c. Resp. Maior est vera de essentia creata & finita, quae non potest vna eadem & tota esse trium personarum substantia: falsa autem de essentia deitatis infinita simplicissima & individua.
units.tr: 1. One essence, three persons are not possible, because to be one and three involves a contradiction. Jehovah is one essence. Therefore, etc. Answer. The major is true of a created and finite essence, which cannot be one and the same whole substance of three persons; but it is false of the infinite, most simple and indivisible essence of the Godhead.

units.la: Inst. Essentia simplicissima non potest esse trium personarum. Dei essentia est simplicissima. Ergo, &c. Resp.
