Maior vera est de essentia, cuius pars alia aliam personam constituit, aut quae multiplicata est pro personarum numero: falsa autem de essentia tali, quae eadem est & integra in singulis personis. Huius enim summa simplicitas, personarum numero & distinctione minime violatur.
units.tr: Objection. A most simple essence cannot belong to three persons. The essence of God is most simple. Therefore, etc. Answer. The major is true of an essence of which one part constitutes one person and another part another, or which is multiplied according to the number of persons; but it is false of an essence which is the same and whole in each single person. For its supreme simplicity is in no way violated by the number and distinction of the persons.

units.la: 2. Vbi sunt tria & vnum, ibi sunt quatuor res distinctae. In Deo sunt tres personae, & vna essentia. Ergo in Deo sunt quatuor distincta, quod est absurdum. Respond. ad maiorem: Vbi sunt tria & vnum, scilicet realiter distincta, ibi sunt quatuor. At in Deo personae ab essentia nequaquam sunt realiter seu reipsa distinctae: quia singulae earum non sunt aliud quiddam reipsa diversum ab essentia, sed sunt ipsa essentia eadem atq; integra: differunt autem ab essentia tantum respectu sui ipsarum, & alterius personae seu subsistendi modo.
units.tr: 2. Where there are three and one, there are four distinct things. In God there are three persons and one essence. Therefore in God there are four distinct things, which is absurd. Answer to the major: Where there are three and one, namely really distinct, there are four. But in God the persons are by no means really or in fact distinct from the essence, because each of them is not something else in fact different from the essence, but is the very same and whole essence; they differ from the essence only in respect of themselves and of the other person, or in the mode of subsisting.

units.la: 3. Tria nomina vnius substantiae ponere, est Sabellianum. Sententia de Trinitate ponit tria nomina vnius substantiae. Ergo est Sabelliana. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini. Vel enim substantia in maiore personam, in minore essentiam significat, vel altera praemissarum falsa est.
units.tr: 3. To posit three names of one substance is Sabellian. The doctrine of the Trinity posits three names of one substance. Therefore it is Sabellian. Answer. There are four terms. For either "substance" in the major means person and in the minor means essence, or one of the premises is false.

units.la: 4. Qui est tota deitas, praeter eum non est alius, in quo similiter sit tota deitas. Pater est tota deitas. Ergo, &c. Resp. Negatur maior, quia eadem deitas, quae tota est in Patre, tota etiam est in Filio, & tota in Spiritu sancto, propter immensitatem essentiae diuinae, cuius nec plus nec minus est in personis singulis, quam in duabus vel tribus.
units.tr: 4. Whatever is the whole Godhead, there is no other besides him in whom the whole Godhead is likewise. The Father is the whole Godhead. Therefore, etc. Answer. The major is denied, because the same Godhead which is wholly in the Father is also wholly in the Son and wholly in the Holy Spirit, on account of the immensity of the divine essence, of which there is neither more nor less in each of the persons than in two or three.

units.la: 5. Quorum operationes sunt distinctae, eorum etiam essentiae sunt distinctae. Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti operationes internae sunt distinctae. Ergo & essentiae. Resp. Maior est vera de personis essentiam habentibus finitam: de personis vero diuinis falsa est.
units.tr: 5. Those whose operations are distinct, their essences are also distinct. The internal operations of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct. Therefore their essences also. Answer. The major is true of persons having a finite essence; but of the divine persons it is false.

units.la: 6. Essentia diuina est incarnata. Tres personae sunt essentia diuina. Ergo tres personae sunt incarnatae, quod est falsum. Resp. Maior non habet dici de omni: quia non quisquis est essentia diuidiuina, est incarnatus: sed essentia diuina in solius Filij verò est incarnata. Sunt igitur purae particulares.
units.tr: 6. The divine essence is incarnate. Three persons are the divine essence. Therefore three persons are incarnate, which is false. Answer. The major cannot be predicated of everything: for not whoever is the divine essence is incarnate, but the divine essence is incarnate in the Son alone. These are therefore merely particular propositions.

units.la: 7. Jehoua seu verus Deus est Trinitas. Pater est Jehoua. Ergo Pater est Trinitas, hoc est, omnes tres. Resp. Rursus maior non habet dici de omni. Non enim, quicquid vel quisquis est Jehoua, est Trinitas. Itaque ex puris particularibus nihil sequitur.
units.tr: 7. Jehovah, or the true God, is a Trinity. The Father is Jehovah. Therefore the Father is a Trinity, that is, all three. Answer. Again the major cannot be predicated of everything. For not whatever or whoever is Jehovah is a Trinity. Thus nothing follows from merely particular premises.

units.la: 8. Nullum nomen abstractum significat substantiam. Trinitas est nomen abstractum. Ergo, &c. Resp. Major falsa est. Nam deitas, humanitas, & abstracta sunt, & substantiam significant.
units.tr: 8. No abstract noun signifies a substance. Trinity is an abstract noun. Therefore, etc. Answer. The major is false. For deity and humanity are abstract nouns, and they do signify a substance.

units.la: De Deo Patre.
units.tr: On God the Father.

units.la: Quaestio XXVI.
units.tr: Question XXVI.

units.la: Quid credis, cùm dicis: Credo in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, Creatorem coeli & terrae? Responsio.
units.tr: What do you believe when you say: "I believe in God the Father almighty, Maker of heaven and earth"? Answer.

units.la: Credo, aeternum Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui coelum & terram, cum omnibus, quae in iis sunt, ex nihilo creauit, a, quique eadem aeterno suo consilio & prouidentia sustentat ac gubernat b: propter Christum, Deum meum & Patrem meum esse c. Itaque sic confido, sic in eo acquiesco, ut non dubitem, quin prorsus omnibus, cùm animo tum corpori meo neuisurus sit omnibus, cùm animo tum corpori meo necessariis d: tum etiam, quae mihi mala in hac aerumnosa vita immittit, ea in meam salutem sit conuersurus e: cùm & facere id possit, ut omnipotens Deus f, & facere id velit, ut benignus pater g.
units.tr: I believe in the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who created heaven and earth, with all that is in them, out of nothing, a and who by his eternal counsel and providence upholds and governs them b; and I believe that, for Christ's sake, he is my God and my Father c. Therefore I trust in him and rest in him so firmly that I do not doubt he will provide me with everything necessary, both for my soul and for my body d; and that he will turn to my salvation whatever evils he sends me in this troubled life e, since almighty God is able to do this f and fatherly goodness wills to do it g.

units.la: a Genes. 1.2. per totum. Exod. 20. verf. 11. Iob. 33,4. Iob. 38. & 39. per totum. Actor. 4,24. & 14,15. Psalm. 33,6. Esa. 45,7. b Heb. 1,3. Psalm. 104,2.3. & 115,3. Matth. 10,29. Ephes. 1,1. c Ioh. 1,12. Rom. 8. v. 5. Galat. 4, 5.6.7. Ephes. 1, 5. d Psalm. 55, 23. Matth. 6,26. Luc. 12,22. e Rom. 8,8. f Esa. 46.4. Rom. 10,17. g Matth. 6.32. 33. & 7, 9.10.11.
units.tr: a Gen. 1:2 throughout. Exod. 20:11. Job 33:4. Job 38 and 39 throughout. Acts 4:24, and 14:15. Ps. 33:6. Isa. 45:7. b Heb. 1:3. Ps. 104:2, 3, and 115:3. Matt. 10:29. Eph. 1:1. c John 1:12. Rom. 8:5. Gal. 4:5, 6, 7. Eph. 1:5. d Ps. 55:23. Matt. 6:26. Luke 12:22. e Rom. 8:28. f Isa. 46:4. Rom. 10:17. g Matt. 6:32, 33, and 7:9, 10, 11.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Credo in Deum. Differunt credo Deum, & credo in Deum. Illud declarat fidem historiae, hoc fiduciam. Nam credo Deum est, credo, quod do, quod sit Deus: & quod sit talis, qualem se in verbo patefecit, nempe essentia spiritualis, omnipotens, &c. æternus Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Credo in Deum est, credo quod mihi sit Deus, hoc est, quod quicquid est & habet, sit & habeat ad meam salutem. Seu, credere Deum proprie loquendo est, credere esse aliquem Deum secundum omnia sua attributa. Credere in Deum est, statuere, quod Deus omnia, quæ ipsi attribuuntur, conferat ad meam salutem propter Filium.
units.tr: "I believe in God." The phrases "I believe God" and "I believe in God" differ. The first expresses faith in history, the second trust. For "I believe God" means that I believe that he exists, and that he is such as he has revealed himself in his Word, namely a spiritual essence, almighty, and so on, eternal Father, Son and Holy Spirit. I believe in God means that I believe God to be mine, that is, that whatever he is and has, he is and has for my salvation. Or, to speak strictly, to believe God is to believe that there is a God with all his attributes. To believe in God is to hold that God bestows all the things attributed to him for my salvation, for the sake of the Son.

units.la: In Deum.] Nomen Dei hic sumi potest essentialiter pro Deo Patre, Filio & Spiritu sancto: quæ tres personæ ordine in symbolo subijciuntur, & ad singulas verbum credo cum particula in referetur. Nam non minus credimus in Filium & Spiritum sanctum, quàm in Patrem.
units.tr: In God. Here the name God (Dei) can be taken essentially, for God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. These three persons are set down in order in the creed, and the verb I believe with the preposition in is applied to each. For we believe in the Son and the Holy Spirit no less than in the Father.

units.la: Patrem.] Patris nomen oppositum Filio, sumitur personaliter, & significat primam personam deitatis, ut hoc loco: collatum vero cum creaturis intelligitur essentialiter, & significat totam essentiam diuinam, ut in oratione Dominica: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis. Sic Filius à Iesaia vocatur Pater æternitatis, id est, Deus æternus & fortis, sicut ibi nominatur. Prima persona vocatur PATER: 1. Respectu Christi filij unigeniti. 2. Respectu creaturarum, quatenus est creator & conseruator omnium. 3. Respectu electorum, quos sibi adoptauit in filios, & fecit dilectos in Filio suo dilecto: Eph. 1, 6.
units.tr: Father. The name Father, set against the Son, is taken personally and signifies the first person of the Godhead, as here. But when it is compared with creatures, it is understood essentially and signifies the whole divine essence, as in the Lord's Prayer: Our Father, who art in heaven. So also the Son is called by Isaiah Father of eternity, that is, the eternal and mighty God, as he is named there. The first person is called Father: (1) with respect to Christ, the only-begotten Son; (2) with respect to creatures, insofar as he is the creator and preserver of all things; (3) with respect to the elect, whom he has adopted as sons and made beloved in his beloved Son, Eph. 1:6.

units.la: Est igitur credere in Deum Patrem, credere in eum Patrem, qui est Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi: & credere, quod idem sit meus Pater, hoc est, sit paterna erga me affectus voluntate per & propter Christum, in quo me sibi adoptauit in filium. Breuiter: 1. est credere, quod sit Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi. 2. quod & mihi sit Pater propter Christum.
units.tr: Therefore to "believe in God the Father" is to believe in him as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to believe that he is also my Father, that is, that he has a fatherly disposition toward me through and for the sake of Christ, in whom he has adopted me as a son. In brief: (1) it is to believe that he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; (2) and that he is also my Father for Christ's sake.

units.la: Obiect. Credo in Deum Patrem. Ergo Filius & Spiritus sanctus non sunt Deus, sed solus Pater. Resp. Est fallacia compositionis & diuisionis. Nam vocabulum Deus ita coniungitur cum Patre, ut non separetur à Filio & Spiritu sancto. Ponenda est enim distinctio post εἰς ϑεὸν: hoc modo: Credo in Deum, Patrem, &c. Id probatur. 1. Quia Deus hic essentialiter tres personas complectitur, quæ velut per appositionem ordine ponuntur in symbolo: Credo in Deum, Patrem: & in Iesum Christum Filium eius unigenitum: credo in Spiritum sanctum: pro, credo in vnum verum Deum, qui est Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus: ita tamen, ut Pater non sit filius, neque Spiritus sanctus sit filius aut pater. 2. Expressè profitemur, nos credere in Filium & Spiritum sanctum, non minus, quàm in Deum Patrem. At non credimus, nisi in vnum verum DEUM. 3. Pleraque exemplaria graeca legunt: πιστεύω εἰς ἕνα Θεόν. Credo in vnum Deum: nempe Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum. Vt ergo credendum est in Patrem, quia Deus est: ita etiam credendum est in Filium & Spiritum sanctum: quia Deus sunt. Semel autem positum est nomen Dei: quia Deus tantum vnus est: nequaquam vero, quasi solus Pater sit Deus.
units.tr: Objection. "I believe in God the Father." Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit are not God, but only the Father. Answer. This is the fallacy of composition and division. For the word God is so joined with the Father that it is not separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit. A punctuation must be placed after εἰς θεόν [into God], thus: I believe in God, the Father, etc. This is proved as follows. (1) Because God here embraces essentially the three persons, who are set down in order in the creed by apposition: I believe in God the Father; and in Jesus Christ his only-begotten Son; I believe in the Holy Spirit, in place of I believe in one true God, who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit; yet so that the Father is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the Son or the Father. (2) We expressly profess that we believe in the Son and the Holy Spirit no less than in God the Father. But we believe in no one except the one true God. (3) Most Greek copies read: πιστεύω εἰς ἕνα Θεόν [I believe in one God], namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Just as we must believe in the Father because he is God, so we must also believe in the Son and the Holy Spirit because they are God. The name of God is mentioned once because God is only one, and by no means as if the Father alone were God.

units.la: Omnipotentem. ] Credere in Deum omnipotentem, est credere in talem Deum: 1. qui omnia quæ vult possit efficere, imo etiam ea quæ non vult, si non repugnent eius naturæ: vt, potuit Christum subtrahere morti, sed non voluit. 2. qui omnia sine difficultate solo nutu perficiat. 3. qui solus habeat potestatem omnia operandi, & author sit potentiæ eius, quæ est in omnibus creaturis. 4. qui mihi quoque sit omnipotens, & omnia ad salutem meam dirigere possit ac velit.
units.tr: Almighty. To believe in God almighty is to believe in such a God: (1) who can bring about all that he wills, and indeed even those things he does not will, provided they are not contrary to his nature; for example, he could have rescued Christ from death, but did not will to. (2) who accomplishes all things without difficulty, by a mere nod. (3) who alone has the power of working all things, and is the author of the power that is in all creatures. (4) who is also almighty for me, and is able and willing to direct all things to my salvation.

units.la: Obiect. Deus non potest mentiri, mori, factum reddere infectum. Ergo non potest omnia. Respond. Omnia potest, quæ sunt potentiæ. At posse mentiri, mori, &c. non est potentiæ. Defectus autem sunt in creaturis, non in Deo. Pugnant igitur cum natura Dei. Per inuersionem vero ita concludo: Non potest quæ sunt impotentiæ, & cum natura eius pugnant. Ergo est omnipotens.
units.tr: Objection. God cannot lie, die, or make what has been done undone. Therefore he is not able to do all things. Answer. He can do all things that belong to power. But to be able to lie, to die, and so on, does not belong to power. Defects, however, are in creatures, not in God. Such things therefore conflict with the nature of God. Conversely, I conclude thus: he cannot do what belongs to impotence and conflicts with his nature. Therefore he is almighty.

units.la: Creatorem cœli & terra. ] Credere in creatorem est, credere 1. quod sit creator omnium. 2. quod omnia à se creata sustineat & gubernet sua prouidentia. 3. quod me etiam creauerit, & me fecerit vas misericordiæ suæ ad salutem obtinendam in Christo, neque ad illam salutem speciali prouidentia & misericordia, qua electos complectitur, perducat. 4. quod omnia reliqua creauerit propter nos, vt seruiant ecclesiæ saluti, ad laudem gloriæ suæ. Breuius. Credere in creatorem est, credere, quod Deus creauerit me, vt seruiam gloriæ suæ, & omnia alia, vt seruiant saluti meæ. Omnia vestra sunt, vos autem Christi, Christus vero Dei: quasi dicat, omnia sunt creata propter nos: nos vero propter Deum.
units.tr: Maker of heaven and earth. To believe in the Creator is to believe (1) that he is the Creator of all things; (2) that he upholds and governs by his providence all the things created by him; (3) that he has also created me and made me a vessel of his mercy to obtain salvation in Christ, and that by the special providence and mercy with which he embraces the elect, he brings me to that salvation; (4) that he created all the rest for our sake, so that they may serve the salvation of the Church, to the praise of his glory. More briefly: to believe in the Creator is to believe that God created me to serve his glory, and all other things to serve my salvation. All things are yours; and you are Christ's; and Christ is God's [1 Cor. 3:22, 23]: as if to say, all things are created for our sake, and we for God's.

units.la: DE CREATIONE MVNDI.
units.tr: On the Creation of the World.

units.la: Doctrinæ de Deo commode subiicitur doctrina de Dei operibus, quemadmodum in symbolo factum videmus. Generaliter vero operationum Dei sunt quinque. 1. Creatio, cuius opera sunt, quæ in Genesi sex diebus perfecta leguntur. 2. Conservatio, qua Deus cœlum & terram, & res omnes creatas sustentat, ne corruant. 3. Gubernatio, qua omnia in mundo pro immensa sapientia sua gubernat. 4. Reparatio, qua omnia, quæ propter peccatum hominis obnoxia sunt corruptioni, reparat in Christo. 5. Perse5. Perfectio, qua omnia ad fines destinatos perducit, præcipuè verò Ecclesiam perfectè liberat & glorificat. Hic de operibus creationis seu de creatione mundi agitur, & præcipuè quæritur I. An Deus creauit mundum. II. Quomodo crearit. III. Quare.
units.tr: The doctrine of the works of God is fittingly placed after the doctrine of God, as we see was done in the Creed. In general there are five works of God. (1) Creation, whose works are those described as completed in six days in Genesis. (2) Preservation, by which God sustains heaven and earth and all created things, so that they do not collapse. (3) Government, by which he governs all things in the world with his immense wisdom. (4) Restoration, by which he restores in Christ all things that have become subject to corruption on account of human sin. (5) Perfection, by which he brings all things to the ends appointed for them, and especially by which he perfectly delivers and glorifies the Church. Here we are dealing with the works of creation, or the creation of the world, and we chiefly ask: I. Whether God created the world. II. How he created it. III. Why.

units.la: I. An Deus creauerit mundum.
units.tr: I. Whether God created the world.

units.la: Primùm vocabula intelligenda sunt. Creare est de nihilo aliquid producere. Mundus quatuor significat in scriptura. 1. Compagem totius universi, hoc est, cœlum, terram, & quæ in iis sunt: Mundus per ipsum factus est. 2. Mundanas cupiditates: Ne diligite mundum, &c. 3. Impios in mundo: Non oro pro mundo, &c. 4. Electos ex mundo: Non veni condemnare mundum, sed ut seruetur mundus, &c. Hic prima significatione mundus in quæstionem venit.
units.tr: First the terms must be understood. To create is to produce something out of nothing. In Scripture "world" has four meanings. (1) The whole fabric of the universe, that is, heaven, earth, and the things in them: "The world was made through him" (John 1). (2) Worldly desires: "Do not love the world," etc. (3) The wicked in the world: "I do not pray for the world," etc. (4) The elect out of the world: "I came not to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved," etc. Here the world is in question in its first meaning.

units.la: Hunc mundum à Deo esse in principio creatum, cognoscitur primò testimoniis scripturæ. Deinde rationibus.
units.tr: That this world was created by God in the beginning is known, first, from the testimonies of Scripture, and then from reasons.

units.la: TESTIMONIA Scripturæ præbet historia creationis à Mose descripta: In principio creauit Deus cœlum & terram. Cui accedunt alia plurima in Psalmis, & passim alibi, quibus admiranda Dei opera, & præcipuæ mundi partes à Deo creatæ nobis considerandæ proponuntur: ut ex earum contemplatione Deo fidere discamus. Verbo Domini firmati sunt cœli, & spiritu oris eius omnis exercitus eorum. Ipse dixit, & facta sunt: ipse mandauit, & facta sunt. Vide Psalm. 104. 113. 124. 136. 146. Et Deus ad demonstrandam iustitiam, potentiam & prouidentiam suam, mirabilia & incomprehensibilia opera sua in cœlo, terra, & rebus aliis à se conditis, conspicua proponit. Apostoli quoque in sua precatione dixerunt: Domine, tu es Deus ille, qui fecisti cœlum & terram, mare, & omnia, quæ in eis sunt.
units.tr: The history of the creation described by Moses provides the testimony of Scripture: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." To this are added many other passages in the Psalms and elsewhere, in which the wonderful works of God and the principal parts of the world created by God are set before us for consideration, so that from contemplating them we may learn to trust God. "By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. He spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast." See Psalms 104, 113, 124, 136, 146. And God, to demonstrate his justice, power and providence, sets before us his marvellous and incomprehensible works, conspicuous in heaven, in earth, and in the other things he has made. The apostles also said in their prayer: "Lord, you are the God who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them."

units.la: RATIONES confirmantes, mundum esse à Deo creatum, sunt plurimæ.
units.tr: There are many reasons confirming that the world has been created by God.

units.la: 1. Origines gentium à Mose traditæ, id ostendunt, quæ ab eo confingi non potuerunt, cum aliqua earum memoria tunc adhuc apud multos extaret, quæ tamen progressu temporis extincta est.
units.tr: (1) The origins of the nations handed down by Moses show this. These could not have been invented by him, since some memory of them still survived among many at that time, although it was in time extinguished.

units.la: 2. Nouitas omnium aliarum historiarum collata ad vetustatem historiæ sacræ.
units.tr: (2) The novelty of all other histories when compared with the antiquity of sacred history.

units.la: 3. Ætas hominum decrescens, quæ ostendit maius robur olim fuisse in natura recenti, nec sine principio hucusque decreuisse. 4. Certa series temporum inde ab initio mundi usque ad exhibitionem Messiæ.
units.tr: (3) The decreasing age of men, which shows that there was once greater strength in nature when it was new, and that it has not decreased without a beginning up to now. (4) The fixed sequence of times from the beginning of the world to the manifestation of the Messiah.

units.la: 5. Politiarum constitutio & conseruatio.
units.tr: (5) The constitution and preservation of states.

units.la: 6. Ordo in natura rerum, qui à mente aliqua intelligente, & rebus omnibus superiore productus sit necesse est.
units.tr: (6) The order in the nature of things, which must have been produced by some intelligent mind superior to all things.

units.la: 7. Mentis humanæ & angelicæ præstantia. Hæ mentes intelligentes habent originem. Ergo oriuntur ab aliqua causa intelligente.
units.tr: (7) The excellence of the human and angelic mind. These intelligent minds have an origin. Therefore they arise from some intelligent cause.

units.la: 8. Principia & notitiæ naturales mentibus nostris insitæ.
units.tr: (8) The principles and natural notions implanted in our minds.

units.la: 9. Pauores conscientiæ in impiis.
units.tr: (9) The terrors of conscience in the wicked.

units.la: 10. Fines omnium rerum sapienter ordinati.
units.tr: (10) The ends of all things wisely ordained.

units.la: 11. Denique omnia argumenta reliqua, quæ probant esse Deum, etiam probant, mundum esse à Deo creatum.
units.tr: (11) Finally, all the other arguments which prove that God exists also prove that the world was created by God.

units.la: PRÆTER has rationes etiam philosophorum argumentis ex media physica petitis obtineri potest, mundum esse creatum, & quidem à Deo: etsi ex his evinci nequeat, quando sit creatus.
units.tr: BESIDES these reasons, it can also be established by the arguments of the philosophers drawn from natural philosophy that the world has been created, and indeed by God, although it cannot be proved from these when it was created.

units.la: 1. Non est progressus causarum & effectuum infinitus in natura: alioqui nunquam peruenirent natura ad finem, seu effectus productionem. Ergo mundus cœpit aliquando esse.
units.tr: (1) In nature there is no infinite progression of causes and effects; otherwise nature would never arrive at its end, that is, the production of an effect. Therefore the world began to exist at some time.

units.la: 2. Mundus est effectus primus & præstantissimus. Ergo est à causa prima & præstantissima, quæ est Deus, &c.
units.tr: (2) The world is the first and most excellent effect. Therefore it is from a first and most excellent cause, which is God, etc.

units.la: Aliæ vero quæstiones: an fuerit à Deo creatus ab æterno: an in tempore, hoc est, an sit effectus coæternus suæ causæ: an vero inceperit aliquando esse, ut antea non fuerit? Item, si aliquando non fuit, an semper sit duraturus? item, an semper idem, an vero alius sit futurus? &c. non possunt in philosophia expediri. Ratio est: quia hæc omnia pendent ex sola voluntate primi motoris Dei, qui non agit ex necessitate, sed liberrime. Hæc vero Dei voluntas non est cognita ulli creaturæ, nisi cui Deus ipse patefacit. Ergo philosophis, hominibus ethnicis, non est nota, sed soli ecclesiæ. Nam ne quidem à posteriori, hoc est, ab effectu contingenti ad causam progrediendo, de his aliquid certi possunt colligere. Sequitur quidem, aliquam esse causam eorum effectuum; sed non sequitur, effectus illos hoc illo vel tempore, vel ab æterno, ab ea productos esse: quia causa libera potest agere, vel actionem suspendere. Summa demonstrationis hæc est: Effectus pendens à sola causa liberè agente, non potest ex ista demonstrari. Talis effectus est creatio mundi. Ergo creatio mundi ex voluntate primi motoris non potest demonstrari, quod ab æterno, vel in aliquo principio temporis facta sit.
units.tr: But other questions: whether it was created by God from eternity, or in time, that is, whether the effect is coeternal with its cause, or whether it began to exist at some time, as it previously did not exist? Likewise, if it did not always exist, will it always endure? likewise, will it always be the same, or will it be other? etc. cannot be resolved in philosophy. The reason is that all these depend solely on the will of God, the first mover, who does not act from necessity but most freely. This will of God is not known to any creature except to whom God himself reveals it. Therefore it is not known to the philosophers, the heathen men, but only to the Church. Nor can they gather anything certain about these matters even a posteriori, that is, by proceeding from a contingent effect to its cause. It indeed follows that there is some cause of these effects; but it does not follow that those effects were produced by it at this or that time, or from eternity, because a free cause can act or suspend its action. The sum of the demonstration is this: an effect that depends solely on a freely acting cause cannot be demonstrated from that cause. Such an effect is the creation of the world. Therefore the creation of the world cannot be demonstrated from the will of the first mover to have been done from eternity, or at some beginning of time.

units.la: Philosophorum argumenta contra mundi creationem, non ex vera philosophia, sed ex cerebro humano extructa esse, facilè perperspicere est, si ordo generationis ac mutationis rerum institutus à Deo in natura condita, à creatione discernatur.
units.tr: It is easy to see that the philosophers' arguments against the creation of the world were built not from true philosophy but from the human brain, if the order of generation and change of things established by God in nature once created is distinguished from creation.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Absurdum est (inquiunt philosophi) Deum fingere otiosum. Resp. Absurdum est otiosum dicere eum, qui gubernat mundum. Inst. Non potuit gubernare mundum nondum existentem. Fuit ergo otiosus. Resp. Negatur consequentia, quod, si Deus non gubernavit mundum ab æterno, fuerit otiosus: quia elegit nos in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Impiis vero, & curiosè in arcana D e i irrumpentibus inferos fabricavit: sicut Afer quidam joculariter quæstionis violentiam eludens olim respondit. Augustinus verò lib.11. Confess. cap.12. respondere maluit: Nescio quod nescio. Antequam faceret Deus cœlum & terram, non faciebat aliquid. Si enim faciebat, quid nisi creaturam faciebat? Et utinam (inquit ibidem Augustinus) sic sciam, quicquid vitiliter scire cupio: quemadmodum scio, quod nulla fiebat creatura, antequam fieret ulla creatura.
units.tr: Objection 1. It is absurd (the philosophers say) to imagine God idle. Reply. It is absurd to call idle him who governs the world. Inference. He could not govern a world not yet existing. Therefore he was idle. Reply. The consequence is denied, that if God did not govern the world from eternity, he was idle; because he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. But he has built hell for the impious and for those who rush curiously into the secrets of God, as a certain African once answered, jokingly, evading the violence of the question. Augustine, however, in book 11 of the Confessions, chapter 12, preferred to answer: I know not what I do not know. "Before God made heaven and earth, he did not make anything. For if he did, what else did he make but a creature? And would that (says Augustine in the same place) I might know as usefully whatever I desire to know, as I know that no creature was made before any creature was made."

units.la: Obiect.2. Omne quod ortum est, interit. Mundus non interit. Ergo non est ortus. Resp. ad maiorem: Omne ortum per generationem naturalem interit. Corruptio enim sequitur generationem vnius rei ex alia, naturali ordine: sed non creationem. Creatoris enim potentia tam quæ ex aliis formar, quàm quę ex nihilo producit, liberrimè in eodem statu vel seruare, vel mutare, vel in nihilum redigere poterat & potest.
units.tr: Objection 2. Whatever has arisen perishes. The world does not perish. Therefore it has not arisen. Reply to the major: Whatever has arisen through natural generation perishes. For corruption follows the generation of one thing from another in the natural order, but not creation. For the power of the Creator, which both forms things from others and produces them from nothing, could and can most freely preserve, change, or reduce to nothing in the same state.

units.la: Obiect.3. Qui est actu dominus, felicior est eo, qui tantum potentea dominus est. Deus ante creationem mundi tantum potentia fuit dominus. Ergo jam felicior factus est ex creatione. Hoc verò absurdum. Ergo mundus ab æterno fuit. Resp. ad maiorem: Felicior est, qui est actu dominus, si ex actuali dominio & gubernatione ei aliquid accedat boni vel commodi, quod ante non habuit. Deo autem, propter summam perfectionē ex creatione & dominio in creaturas nihil prorsus accedere potuit aut potest. Quod autem dicitur Dominus, id fit creaturarum respectu. Nam relationes in Deo non efficiunt mutationem, sed tribuuntur Deo creaturarum respectu.
units.tr: Objection 3. He who is actually lord is happier than he who is only lord in potential. God before the creation of the world was lord only in potential. Therefore he has now become happier through creation. But this is absurd. Therefore the world existed from eternity. Reply to the major: He is happier who is actually lord, if some good or advantage accrues to him from actual lordship and government which he did not have before. But to God, on account of his supreme perfection, nothing at all could accrue, or can accrue, from creation and dominion over creatures. What is said of him as Lord is said with respect to creatures. For relations in God do not produce change, but are attributed to God with respect to creatures.

units.la: II. Quomodo mundus sit conditus.
units.tr: II. How the world was created.

units.la: Mundus creatus est à Deo æterno Patre, per Filium & Spiritum sanctum. De Filio dicitur: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. De Spiritu sancto: Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas. Spiritus Domini formavit me.
units.tr: The world was created by God the eternal Father, through the Son and the Holy Spirit. Of the Son it is said: All things were made by him. Of the Holy Spirit: The Spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters. The Spirit of the Lord hath made me.

units.la: Mundum Deus creavit liberrimè, sine ulla coactione, non necessitate absoluta, sed tantum consequentiæ, hoc est, voluntatis suæ. Nam quamvis æterno & immutabili, tamen liberrimo decreto creto condidit omnia. Quoniam ipse dixit, & facta sunt. Certè Deus noster est in cœlis, omnia quæ voluit, fecit.
units.tr: God created the world most freely, without any compulsion, not by absolute necessity but only by a necessity of consequence, that is, of his own will. For although his decree is eternal and unchangeable, it is nonetheless most free, and by it he founded all things. For he spake, and it was done. But our God is in the heavens; whatever he pleased, he has done.

units.la: 3. Deus mundum creauit, solo nutu, verbo, voluntate, sine labore, fatigatione & mutatione sui. Nouitas enim vel mutatio in Deum nulla cadit, nec est in æterna eius voluntate, sed in rebus creatis. Esaiæ 40. vers. 28. Deus æternus Iehoua creator finium terræ, non lassatur, non fatigatur, & non est investigatio intelligentia eius.
units.tr: 3. God created the world by a mere nod, word, and will, without labour, weariness, or any change in himself. For novelty or change cannot fall upon God, nor is it in his eternal will, but in created things. Isaiah 40:28: The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary; there is no searching of his understanding.

units.la: 4. Omnia creata sunt ex nihilo, non ex Dei essentia, neque ex præjacente vel exsistente aliqua materia Deo coæterna. Si enim à Deo omnia creata sunt, nihil præter ipsum creatorem excipitur, ac ne materia quidem, ex qua omnia formantur.
units.tr: 4. All things were created out of nothing, not out of the essence of God, nor out of any pre-existing or existing matter co-eternal with God. For if all things were created by God, nothing is excepted besides the Creator himself, not even the matter out of which all things are formed.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Nos non sumus creati ex nihilo. Resp. Non sumus creati ex nihilo, respectu materiæ proximæ, quæ erat gleba terræ. Sumus autem ex nihilo, respectu primæ massæ, rudis & indigestæ, quam Deus principio creauit ex nihilo.
units.tr: Objection 1. We were not created out of nothing. Answer. We were not created out of nothing with respect to our proximate matter, which was a clod of earth. But we were created out of nothing with respect to the first mass, rough and undigested, which God at the beginning created out of nothing.

units.la: Obiectio 2. Ex nihilo nihil fit. Respond. 1. In ordine naturæ nunc constituto, ut aliud ex alio generetur & fiat. 2. Ab hominibus nihil ex nihilo fit. Sed quod hominibus est impossibile, Deo non est possibile. Principium ergo Philosophorum, ex nihilo nihil fit, non de Deo, sed de hominibus, nec de prima creatione, aut extraordinaria Dei operatione, sed de ordine in natura jam creata instituto accipiendum est. Ad nostram vero consolationem pertinet, quod ex nihilo Deus omnia creauit. Si enim creauit omnia ex nihilo, poterit & nos conseruare, & impiorum conatus retardare, immo in nihilum redigere.
units.tr: Objection 2. Out of nothing, nothing comes. Answer 1. This holds in the present order of nature, by which one thing is generated and made from another. 2. Nothing is made out of nothing by men. But what is impossible for men is not impossible for God. The principle of the philosophers, out of nothing, nothing comes, must therefore be understood not of God but of men, and not of the first creation or of an extraordinary operation of God, but of the order established in nature already created. It belongs, however, to our comfort that God created all things out of nothing. For if he created all things out of nothing, he can also preserve us, and check the attempts of the wicked, or even reduce them to nothing.

units.la: 5. Creauit omnia sapientissimè & optimè, hoc est, singula in suo genere atque gradu perfecta. Omnia erant valde bona, hoc est, absque deformitate & vitio, & sine omni malo culpæ vel pœnæ.
units.tr: 5. He created all things most wisely and best, that is, each thing perfect in its own kind and degree. All things were very good, that is, without deformity or fault, and without any evil of guilt or punishment.

units.la: Obiect. Atqui mors est mala. Resp. Deus mortem non fecit, sed inflixit creaturæ, ut justam pœnam propter peccatum. Isa. 45, 7. Amos 3, 6. Ego creans malum, &c. An erit malum in ciuitate, & Iehoua non fecerit illud? Resp. Hæc de malo pœnæ, non culpæ dicuntur. Est enim Deus pœnarum author: quia est judex mundi, & pœnæ habent rationem boni: peccatorum verò non est author, sed permissor.
units.tr: Objection. But death is evil. Answer. God did not make death, but inflicted it on the creature as a just punishment for sin. Isa. 45:7. Amos 3:6. I create evil, etc. Shall there be evil in the city, and the LORD hath not done it? Answer. These things are said of the evil of punishment, not of the evil of guilt. For God is the author of punishments, because he is the judge of the world, and punishments have the character of good; but he is not the author of sins, only their permitter.

units.la: 6. Non subito, nec uno momento mundus est à Deo conditus, sed sex dierum spatio: Die septimo perfecit Deus omne opus suum. Cur non momento? 1. Quia voluit manifestam & distinctam esse creationem ipsius materiæ à formatione corporum mundi, quæ ex ea constant. 2. Voluit potentiam & libertatem suam ostendere in pro-
units.tr: 6. The world was created by God not suddenly, nor in a single moment, but over a span of six days: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had made. Why not in a moment? 1. Because he willed the creation of matter itself to be manifest and distinct from the formation of the bodies of the world which consist of it. 2. He willed to show his power and freedom in producing whatever effects he wished,

units.la: Genes. 2, 2. Cur sex diebus Deus mundum creauerit. in producendis, quoscunque voluit, effectibus, etiam sine causis naturalibus: dum lucé præber mundo, fœcundat terram, stirpes ex ea alicit, ante Solem & Lunam conditam. 3. Voluit ostendere bonitatem & prouidentiam suam, qua creaturas suas fouet, iisq; nondum natis prospicit, dum animalia in terram stirpibus & pa-bulo, hominem in mundum rebus omnibus ad vitæ necessita-tem ac suauitatem pertinentibus instructissimum introducit. 4. Voluit nos illa creationis serie non in perfunctoria, sed dili-genti operum suorum consideratione retinere, quam & sabbathi consecratione toti generi humano consecrauit.
units.tr: Gen. 2:2. Why God created the world in six days. even without natural causes, while he gives light to the world, makes the earth fruitful, and draws plants out of it before the sun and moon were made. 3. He willed to show his goodness and providence, by which he cherishes his creatures and provides for them before they are born, while he brings the animals into the earth furnished with plants and pasture, and man into a world most fully equipped with everything pertaining to the necessities and pleasantness of life. 4. He willed that we should dwell on that series of creation not in a perfunctory way, but in a diligent consideration of his works, which he also consecrated to the whole human race by the hallowing of the sabbath.

units.la: Obiect. Qui viuit in æternum, creauit omnia simul. Ergo vno mo-mento. Resp. Non loquitur de momento temporis, sed de rerum vniuersitate: quasi dicat, vniuersa, quæ sunt, à Deo creata sunt, nullo excepto.
units.tr: Objection. He who lives for ever created all things at once. Therefore in one moment. Answer. Scripture does not speak of a moment of time but of the totality of things: as if it said that all things that exist were created by God, none excepted.

units.la: 7. Denique mundum Deus creauit non ab æterno, sed definito tempore, atque adeò in principio temporum. In principio enim creauit Deus cœlum & terram, &c. nempe hoc anno Christi vel-tente 1634. juxta Beroaldi quidem supputationem, quam judico sacræ historiæ maximè conuenire; ante annos 5562. Variant au-tem nonnihil eruditorum computi.
units.tr: 7. Finally, God created the world not from eternity, but at a defined time, and so at the beginning of time. For in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, etc. That is, in the year of Christ 1634, Christ willing, according indeed to the reckoning of Beroaldus, which I judge best agrees with sacred history; some 5562 years ago. Yet the reckonings of the learned differ somewhat.

units.la: Nam ab orbe condito vsque ad Christum natum Ex supputatione Melanchthonis Ex supputatione Lutheri Ex supputatione Geneuensium } sunt anni {3963. 3960. 3943. 3928. Ex supputatione Beroaldi Et sic mundus jam durauit Juxta Melanchthonem Juxta Lutherum Juxta Geneuenses } annos {5583. 5580. 5553. 5548. Juxta Beroaldum
units.tr: From the creation of the world until the birth of Christ: by the reckoning of Melanchthon 3963 years; by that of Luther 3960; by that of the Genevans 3943; by that of Beroaldus 3928. And so the world has now endured: according to Melanchthon 5583 years; according to Luther 5580; according to the Genevans 5553; according to Beroaldus 5548.

units.la: Hæ supputationes satis inter se conueniunt in numero maiore; etsi in minore aliquot annis variant. Neque mirum in retantæ antiquitatis, quam sacra historia non præcise expressit: multo autem minus historia profana. Constat saltem non au-te multo plures, vel pauciores, quam 5562. annos mundum à Deo fuisse conditum, ac proinde non esse ab æterno, sed initium habere.
units.tr: These reckonings agree fairly well with one another in the larger number, although in the smaller they vary by some years. Nor is this surprising in a matter of such great antiquity, which sacred history did not state precisely, and profane history much less so. It is at least certain that the world was created by God not many more or fewer than 5562 years ago, and therefore that it is not from eternity but has a beginning.

units.la: III. Quare mundus à Deo sit conditus.
units.tr: III. Why God created the world.

units.la: Fines creationis mundi, & omnium rerum alij sunt generales, alij speciales, & subordinati.
units.tr: The ends of the creation of the world and of all things are some general and some special and subordinate.

units.la: 1. Summus siue vltimus finis est, gloria & celebratio Dei, ad quam præcipuè conditi sunt angeli & homines. Vniuersa propter seipsum fecit Dominus. Benedicite Domino omnia opera eius. Ex eo, & per eum, & in eum sunt omnia.
units.tr: 1. The highest or ultimate end is the glory and celebration of God, for which angels and men above all were created. The Lord made all things for himself. "Bless the Lord, all his works." "From him, and through him, and to him are all things."

units.la: 2. Patefactio, agnitio & contemplatio diuinæ sapientiæ, potentiæ & bonitatis in ipsa rerum creatione elucentis. Si enim debuit celebrari Deus, debuit etiam creare naturas rationales, quæ ipsum agnoscerent, & agnitum celebrarent: & irrationales, quæ celebrationis materia essent. Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opera manuum eius annunciant firmamentum.
units.tr: 2. The disclosure, recognition and contemplation of the divine wisdom, power and goodness shining forth in the very creation of things. For if God was to be celebrated, he was also bound to create rational natures, which would acknowledge him and, having acknowledged him, celebrate him, and irrational ones, which would be the matter of that celebration. "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows forth his handiwork."

units.la: 3. Gubernatio mundi. Ideo mundum condidit, vt eum providentia sua semper gubernaret, regeret, conseruaret, atque in perpetuum patefaceret opera sua mirabilia, quæ inde ab initio fecit, facit, & faciet: præcipuè verò vt Ecclesiam angelorum & hominum electorum administraret. Et hic finis subseruit secundo. Leuate in sublime oculos vestros, & videte, quis creauit hæc.
units.tr: 3. The government of the world. He created the world so that by his providence he might always govern, rule and preserve it, and make known for ever his wonderful works, which he has done, does and will do from the beginning; and above all that he might govern the Church of angels and of elect men. This end serves as the second. "Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things."

units.la: 4. Vt ex genere humano colligeret sibi æternam ecclesiam, quæ Creatorem suum agnosceret & celebraret.
units.tr: 4. That from the human race he might gather for himself an eternal church, which would acknowledge and celebrate its Creator.

units.la: 5. Vt omnes aliæ res seruirent saluti, vitæ, necessitati & suauitati hominum, præcipuè verò, vt electis prodessent, suo quæque loco essent eis veluti ministri & organa, per quæ Deus eis benefaciens, ab ipsis celebraretur. Subycite vobis terram, & dominamini piscibus maris. Dominum eum constituisti super opera, quæ manus tuæ parauerunt: cuncta subdidisti sub pedibus eius. Siue vita, siue mors, siue præsentia, siue futura: omnia, inquam, vestra sunt. Hominem igitur propter se creauit Deus: reliqua omnia propter hominem, vt homini seruirent, & per hominem Deo. Quare cum nos constituimus creaturas Dei loco, deijcimus nos ipsos ex illo gradu, in quem constituti fuimus à Deo.
units.tr: 5. That all other things might serve the salvation, life, necessity and pleasure of men, and above all that they might profit the elect, each in its own place being to them as ministers and instruments, through which God, doing them good, might be celebrated by them. "Subdue the earth, and have dominion over the fish of the sea." "You have made him lord over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet." "Whether life or death, whether present things or things to come: all are yours." Man, therefore, God created for his own sake; all the rest for man's sake, that they might serve man, and through man God. Wherefore, when we set ourselves in the place of God's creatures, we thrust ourselves down from that rank in which God placed us.

units.la: Vsus doctrinæ de creatione est. 1. Vt creationis gloria integra Deo tribuatur, eiusque sapientia, potentia & bonitas ex operibus creationis agnoscatur. 2. Vt fiduciam nostram à rebus creatis, quæ sine Deo nihil sunt, abstrahamus, eamque in solo Deo collocemus, qui est author & dator salutis.
units.tr: The use of the doctrine of creation is this. 1. That the full glory of creation be ascribed to God, and his wisdom, power and goodness be recognised from the works of creation. 2. That we withdraw our trust from created things, which without God are nothing, and place it in God alone, who is the author and giver of salvation.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXVII.
units.tr: QUESTION XXVII.

units.la: Quid est Providentia Dei? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What is the Providence of God? ANSWER.

units.la: Omnipotens & vbique præsens Dei vis a, qua cælum ac terram cum omnibus creaturis tanquam manu sustinet ac gubernat b: vt quæ terra nascuntur, pluuia item & siccitas, fertilitas & sterilitas c, bona & aduersa valetudo d, diuitiæ & paupertas e, omnia deniq; non temerè aut fortuitò, sed paterno eius consilio & voluntate contingant f.
units.tr: God's almighty power, present everywhere, a by which he sustains and governs heaven and earth with all creatures as if with his hand, b so that whatever springs from the earth, and likewise rain and drought, fruitfulness and barrenness, c good and bad health, d riches and poverty, e in short all things, happen not by chance or accident, but by his fatherly counsel and will. f

units.la: a Actor. 17. verf. 25. Ierem. 23, 24. Esa. 29, 15. 16. Ezechielis 8, 12. b Hebr. 1, 3. c Ierem. 5, 24. Actor. 14, 17. d Ioh. 9, 3. e Prouerb. 22, 2. f Matth. 10, 29. Prouerb. 16, 33.
EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Cum doctrina de creatione mundi cohæret locus de providentia Dei, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm creationis continuatio: quia est gubernatio & conseruatio rerum creatarum. Non enim fingenda est talis creatio, qualis est exstructio nauis, quam architectus post fabrefactionem tradit regendam nauclero; sed certo certius est statuendum, sicuti Deus non creante res nunquam exstitissent, sic Deo res creatas prouidentia sua non gubernante & conseruante, eas ne ad momentum quidem consistere posse. Ideo non possumus recte intelligere creationem, nisi complectamur simul doctrinam de Providentia. De hac præcipuè quæritur: I. An aliqua sit prouidentia. II. Quid sit. III. Quis eius vsus.
units.tr: The locus on the providence of God is closely joined to the doctrine of the creation of the world, since providence is nothing other than the continuation of creation, because it is the governing and preserving of created things. For such a creation must not be imagined as the building of a ship, which the shipwright, once he has built it, hands over to the sailor to steer. Rather, it must be affirmed with the greatest certainty that, just as things would never have existed without God's creating them, so created things could not remain in being even for a moment without God's providence governing and preserving them. Therefore we cannot rightly understand creation unless we grasp at the same time the doctrine of providence. Three questions are asked about it in particular: I. Whether there is any providence. II. What it is. III. What its use is.

units.la: Duo priora hic explicantur: tertium quæstione sequente.
units.tr: The first two are explained here; the third in the following question.

units.la: I. An sit aliqua Dei prouidentia.
units.tr: I. Whether there is any providence of God.

units.la: Tres fuerunt opiniones philosophorum de Dei prouidentia. 1. Epicurei negarunt, vllam esse prouidentiam eorum, quæ sunt & fiunt in inferioribus mundi partibus. 2. Stoici prouidentiæ loco necessitatem absolutam omnium rerum & motuum commenti sunt, in ipsa rerum natura existentem, cui non modò aliæ res omnes, sed etiam ipse Deus sit obnoxius: quam necessitatem appellarunt fatum. 3. Peripatetici fixerunt, Deum quidem omnia intueri atque intelligere, non tamen omnia moderari & regere, verum cœlestes tantum motus ciere, & per eos inferioribus naturæ partibus agendi vim indere, &c.
units.tr: The philosophers held three opinions about the providence of God. (1) The Epicureans denied that there is any providence over those things which exist and happen in the lower parts of the world. (2) The Stoics, in place of providence, invented an absolute necessity of all things and motions, existing in the very nature of things, to which not only all other things but God himself is subject; this necessity they called fate. (3) The Peripatetics held that God indeed sees and understands all things, but does not govern and rule all things; rather, he sets in motion only the heavenly movements and, through them, implants a power of acting in the lower parts of nature, and so on.

units.la: Contra hos errores Ecclesia ex verbo Dei docet, nihil in vniuerso mundo nisi certo & definito quidem, sed tamen liberrimo atque optimo Dei consilio exsistere & euenire.
units.tr: Against these errors the Church teaches from the Word of God that nothing in the whole universe exists or comes about except by the certain and definite, yet most free and best, counsel of God.

units.la: Duo autem sunt probationum genera, quibus prouidentia diuina esse ostenditur: testimonia scripturæ, & argumenta.
units.tr: There are two kinds of proof by which divine providence is shown: the testimonies of Scripture and arguments.

units.la: 1. Testimonia scripturæ, vt: Ipse dat omnibus vitam, & halitum & omnia. In ipso viuimus, mouemur, & sumus. Nonnè duo passerpasserculi assario veneunt, & unus ex eis non cadit humi sine Patre vestro? Vestri vero etiam capillis capitis omnes numerati sunt. Deus omnia effecit secundum beneplacitum voluntatis suæ. Similia passim occurrunt in scriptura, quibus tum universalis, tum particularis providentia confirmatur. Vix enim ulla est pars doctrinæ cœlestis, quæ frequentius & diligentius inculcetur, quam doctrina de providentia Dei.
units.tr: (1) Testimonies of Scripture, such as: He himself gives to all life, and breath, and all things. In him we live, move, and have our being. Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. God works all things according to the counsel of his will. Similar passages occur everywhere in Scripture, by which both universal and particular providence are confirmed. For there is hardly any part of heavenly doctrine that is more often or more diligently impressed upon us than the doctrine of the providence of God.

units.la: 2. ARGUMENTA, quibus asseritur providentia, sunt duplicis generis. Alia sunt a posteriori, hoc est, ab effectis seu operibus Dei: alia a priori, hoc est, a natura & attributis Dei. Utraque sunt demonstrativa, & communia Philosophiæ & Theologiæ, nisi quod attributa & opera Dei plenius intelliguntur in hac, quàm in illa. Magis tamen obvia sunt illa a divinis operibus desumpta. Per hæc enim, quæ sunt a posteriori, penetramus ad ea, quæ sunt a priori.
units.tr: (2) ARGUMENTS by which providence is asserted are of two kinds. Some are a posteriori, that is, drawn from the effects or works of God; others are a priori, that is, drawn from the nature and attributes of God. Both are demonstrative and common to philosophy and theology, except that the attributes and works of God are understood more fully in theology than in philosophy. Nevertheless, those drawn from the divine works are more obvious. For through what is a posteriori we penetrate to what is a priori.

units.la: Argumenta ab effectis.
units.tr: Arguments from effects.

units.la: 1. Ordo non potest esse à causa bruta. Ubi enim est ordo, ibi est causa ordinans & disponens. In rerum natura est ordo, aptissima nimirum dispositio & successio rerum omnium, motuum, temporum, conservatio, & propagatio specierum, &c. Ergo hic ordo existit & conservatur ab aliqua mente: & cum hic ordo sapientissimus sit, etiam sapientissimus sit necesse est, qui eum constituit & providentia sua gubernat. Qui supputat numerum stellarum, omnes illas nominatim vocat.
units.tr: (1) Order cannot come from a senseless cause. For where there is order, there is a cause that orders and arranges. In the nature of things there is order, the most fitting arrangement and sequence of all things, of motions and times, the preservation and propagation of species, and so on. Therefore this order exists and is preserved by some mind; and since this order is most wise, the one who established it and governs it by his providence must also be most wise. He who counts the number of the stars calls them all by name.

units.la: 2. Homo, qui est μικρόκοσμος, regitur à mente. Ergo multò magis totus mundus. An qui plantat aurem, non audiet?
units.tr: (2) Man, who is a microcosm, is governed by a mind. Therefore much more the whole world is. Or will he who planted the ear not hear? (Ps. 94:9)

units.la: 3. Lex naturæ, notitiæ principiorum nobiscum nascentes, propositiones de discrimine honestorum & turpium mentibus nostris insitæ, docent esse providentiam. Qui præscribit regulam seu legem Deus indidit mentibus humanis. Vult igitur Deus homines secundum hanc normam viuere, ac proinde vitam, actiones, eventus eorum gubernat. Gentes ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, &c. Plautus: Est profecto Deus, qui quæ nos gerimus, audit, & videt. Homerus: ἐχει πάντα ἐκ Διὸς ὁμοίως.
units.tr: (3) The law of nature, the knowledge of first principles born with us, and the propositions about the difference between honourable and shameful things implanted in our minds, teach that there is providence. God, who prescribes the rule or law, has implanted it in human minds. He therefore wills that human beings live according to this norm, and consequently he governs their life, actions and outcomes. The Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts, and so on. Plautus: Surely there is a God who hears and sees what we do. Homer: [ἐχει πάντα ἐκ Διὸς ὁμοίως] (all things are alike from Zeus).

units.la: 4. Pavores conscientiæ. Vniversaliter sequitur peccatum trepidatio conscientiæ in scelestis. Ergo est numen arcana hominum cognoscens, peccato irascens, vindex scelerum & pavores peccantibus incutiens. Vna testimonium reddente conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus. Revelatur ira Dei super omnem impietatem. De his Juvenalis Satyr. XIII. Cur tamen hos tu Persuasisse putes, quos diri conscia fati Mens habet attonitos? & surdo verbere caedit Occulto quatiente animum tortore flagellum? Poena autem vehemens ac multo saevior illis, Quas & Caeditius gravis invenit & Rhadamanthus, Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem.
units.tr: (4) The terrors of conscience. Trembling of conscience generally follows sin in the wicked. Therefore there is a divine power that knows the hidden things of men, is angry at sin, avenges crimes, and strikes terror into those who sin. Conscience bears witness, and thoughts accuse or else excuse one another. The wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness. Juvenal, Satire XIII, speaks of this: Do you suppose that these men, whom a mind conscious of a dreadful fate holds stunned, have been persuaded? The hidden torturer strikes their soul with a whip that deafens them and beats them. The punishment is severe and far crueller than those which the stern Caeditius and Rhadamanthus have devised: to carry one's own witness in one's breast night and day.

units.la: 1. Praemia & poenae testantur, esse aliquem exsecutorem legis naturae. Placidiores sunt eorum exitus, qui moderate viuunt etiam extra ecclesiam. Atrocia vero delicta sequuntur atroces poenae. Ergo est aliquis judex mundi. Latabitur justus, cum viderit vindictam: pedes suos lavabit in sanguine impii, & dicet homo, verè est fructus justo: utique est Deus judicans in terra. An qui corripit gentes, non arguat? Sic olim ...
units.tr: (1) Rewards and punishments testify that there is someone who carries out the natural law. The ends of those who live moderately are more peaceful, even outside the Church. But atrocious crimes are followed by atrocious punishments. Therefore there is a judge of the world. The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he will wash his feet in the blood of the wicked; and man will say, surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth. Does not he who disciplines the nations rebuke? Thus formerly …

units.la: 6. Magna pars providentiae est constitutio, conservatio, & translatio imperiorum. Haec autem non fit sine Deo. Per me reges regnant. Ut cognoscant viventes, quod altissimus dominator in regno hominum, & cui voluerit, dabit illud. Cicero: Deorum ope & auxilio multo magis quàm ratione hominum & consilio respublica gubernatur, &c. Malorum semper est maior multitudo, quam bonorum: & plures vellent omnes leges sublatas, quàm conservatas. Nihilominus manet ordo politicus, respublicae, & regna. Ergo est aliquis major omnibus diabolis, tyrannis & impiis, qui contra istorum furores, ordinem politicum semper conservat.
units.tr: (6) A great part of providence is the establishing, preserving, and transferring of empires. But this does not happen without God. By me kings reign. So that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills. Cicero: The commonwealth is governed by the help and aid of the gods much more than by the reason and counsel of men, and so on. The multitude of the wicked is always greater than that of the good, and more would wish all laws abolished than preserved. Nevertheless the political order, commonwealths and kingdoms remain. Therefore there is someone greater than all devils, tyrants and impious men, who always preserves the political order against their furies.

units.la: 7. Virtutes excellentes, impetus & successus heroici, superantes communem naturam hominum, dona singularia & excellentia artificum, quae Deus aliquibus confert ad universale bonum, & conservationem societatis hominum, &c. sic esse Deum, & curari ab eo genus humanum testantur. Sunt enim hae res longè maiores, quàm ut existere queant à re bruta, & praestantiores, quàm ut humana industria acquirantur. Deus ergo est, qui cum vult gerere res magnas humano generi salutares, dat viros heroicis virtutibus praeditos, artium & consiliorum inventores, principes fortes, bonos, prudentes, & alia organa idonea & salutaria: eademque, cum vult punire, rursus tollit. Qui dat sapientiam sapientibus: &c. Excitavit Deus spiritum Cyri.
units.tr: (7) Excellent virtues, heroic impulses and successes that surpass the common nature of men, and the singular and outstanding gifts of craftsmen, which God bestows on some for the universal good and the preservation of human society, and so on, testify that God exists and that the human race is cared for by him. For these things are far too great to come from a senseless thing, and too excellent to be acquired by human industry. Therefore it is God who, when he wills to accomplish great things beneficial to the human race, gives men endowed with heroic virtues, inventors of arts and counsels, strong, good and prudent rulers, and other fitting and salutary instruments; and when he wills to punish, he again takes them away. He who gives wisdom to the wise, and so on. God stirred up the spirit of Cyrus.

units.la: Ovid. lib. 6. Fast. Est Deus in nobis, agitante calescimus illo: Impetus hic sacra semina mentis habet.
units.tr: Ovid, Fasti book 6: There is a God within us; we grow warm when he stirs. This impulse holds the sacred seeds of the mind.

units.la: Et: Sedibus aethereis spiritus ille venit.
units.tr: And: That spirit comes from the ethereal seats.

units.la: 8. A vaticiniis & praedictionibus eventuum. Deus est, qui Vaticinia signisignificat hominibus futura: nec potest falli prædictionibus: Ergo non tantum præuidet res futuras, sed etiam facit vt eueniant, vel effectione, vel permissione: eoq; curat res humanas, & mundum sua prouidentia regit. Dixit, & non faceret? Cicero: Non sunt dij, & non significant.
units.tr: 8. From prophecies and predictions of events. God is the one who signifies future things to men by prophecies, and he cannot be deceived in his predictions. Therefore he not only foresees future things but also brings it about that they come to pass, either by effecting them or by permitting them. So he cares for human affairs and governs the world by his providence. Has he spoken and will he not do it? Cicero: There are no gods, and they give no signs.

units.la: 9. Res omnes in mundo sunt ordinatæ ad certos fines & ad eas tendunt constanter. Ergo est aliqua natura sapientissima & omnipotens, suâ prouidentiâ omnia vniuersaliter sic ordinans, & singula ad fines destinatos deducens. Non ex solo pane vivit homo, sed ex omni verbo Dei, &c.
units.tr: 9. All things in the world are ordered to certain ends and constantly tend towards them. Therefore there is some most wise and almighty nature, which orders all things universally by its providence and brings each thing to its appointed end. Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God, etc.

units.la: 10. Deniq; iisdem fere argumentis probatur, quod sit Deus, quod creator, & quod conseruator: nisi quod aliqua immediatè, aliqua non nisi per consequens concludunt.
units.tr: 10. Finally, by almost the same arguments it is proved that there is a God, that he is creator, and that he is preserver; except that some of these arguments conclude immediately, while others conclude only by consequence.

units.la: Argumenta à natura Dei.
units.tr: Arguments from the nature of God.

units.la: 1. Deus est. Ergo est prouidentia. Hoc tam vere dicitur, quàm, Non est Deus. Ergo non est prouidentia. Nam fingere Deum, qui mundum non regat, est Deum negare. Et Deum esse, nec regere mundum, pugnat cum natura Dei: nec magis sine Deo mundus potest consistere, quàm creari.
units.tr: 1. God exists. Therefore there is providence. This is as true as the statement: there is no God, therefore there is no providence. For to imagine a God who does not govern the world is to deny God. To be God and not to govern the world is inconsistent with the nature of God; nor can the world subsist without God any more than it could have been created without him.

units.la: 2. Deus sic est omnipotens, vt nihil possit fieri, quod ipse simpliciter & nullo modo vult, necesse autem sit fieri, quicquid simpliciter vel aliquo modo vult fieri. Quæcunque igitur quotidie fiunt, Dei omnipotentis voluntate fiunt, atque ideo Dei prouidentia.
units.tr: 2. God is so omnipotent that nothing can happen which he simply and in no way wills, and whatever he wills to happen, either simply or in some respect, must necessarily happen. Whatever therefore happens every day happens by the will of almighty God, and so by his providence.

units.la: 3. Sapientis gubernatoris est, nihil sinere fieri in suo regno sine sua voluntate & certo consilio. Deus est sapientissimus, & potest rebus omnibus interesse. Nihil ergo fit in mundo sine Dei prouidentia.
units.tr: 3. It is the mark of a wise governor to allow nothing to happen in his kingdom without his will and deliberate plan. God is most wise and is able to be present in all things. Nothing therefore happens in the world without the providence of God.

units.la: 4. Deus est summè justus, & mundi judex. Ergo ipse bonis dat præmia, malis infligit pœnas.
units.tr: 4. God is supremely just and the judge of the world. Therefore he gives rewards to the good and inflicts punishments on the wicked.

units.la: 5. Deus est summè bonus. Summum autem bonum est maximè communicatiuum sui. Ergo vt Deus ex immensa bonitate mundum creauit, vt se ei communicaret: ita eadem bonitate mundum creatum conseruat & gubernat.
units.tr: 5. God is supremely good, and the highest good is most inclined to communicate itself. Therefore, just as God in his immense goodness created the world so that he might communicate himself to it, so by the same goodness he preserves and governs the world he has created.

units.la: 6. Omnium rerum fines sunt boni, & à Deo ordinati. Ergo etiam media ad fines sunt à Deo decreta ab æterno, vel simpliciter, vel secundum quid.
units.tr: 6. The ends of all things are good and ordained by God. Therefore the means to those ends also have been decreed by God from eternity, either absolutely or in some respect.

units.la: 7. Deus est causa omnium prima. Ergo à Deo omnes causæ secundæ pendent.
units.tr: 7. God is the first cause of all things. Therefore all secondary causes depend on God.

units.la: 8. Præscientia immutabilis pendet à causa immutabili. Deus omnia præscit immutabiliter ab æterno. Ergo præscit ex causa immutabili, quæ est consilium & decretum eius æternum. Summa. DEus est omnipotens, sapientissimus, justissimus, atq; optimus. Ergo nec sine certo fine instituit aut creauit, nec productionem suorum operum ad eos, quibus ea destinauit, fines intermittit, nec ea casu fieri patitur, quæ ad gloriæ suæ patefactionem condidit atq; ordinauit: Hac fecisti, & tacui, & putasti, Psal. 50, 21, me similem tibi, &c. Numquid obliuitus est misereri Deus? Consilium Psal. 77, 10. meum stabit, & omnem meam voluntatem faciam.
units.tr: 8. Immutable foreknowledge depends on an immutable cause. God foreknows all things immutably from eternity. Therefore he foreknows from an immutable cause, which is his eternal counsel and decree. In sum: God is almighty, most wise, most just and best. Therefore he neither establishes nor creates anything without a certain end, nor does he leave off bringing his works to the ends for which he has designed them, nor does he allow those things to happen by chance which he has founded and ordained for the manifestation of his glory: You did these things, and I kept silent, and you thought that I was like you, etc. Has God forgotten to be merciful? My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.

units.la: II. Quid & qualis sit prouidentia Dei.
units.tr: II. What and of what kind is the providence of God.

units.la: Præscientia, Prouidentia, & Prædestinatio Dei differunt. Præscientia est cognitio Dei, qua præcognouit ab æterno, non ea tantum, quæ ipse erat facturus, sed etiam ea, quæ ipsius permissione alij erant facturi, vt peccata. Prouidentia & Prædestinatio licet sint eorum tantum, quæ Deus ipse facturus erat: tamen in hoc differunt, quod Prouidentia ad omnes res, & opera Dei; Prædestinatio tantum ad creaturas rationales propriè extenditur. Est enim Prædestinatio sapientissimum, æternum & immutabile Dei decretum, quo vnumquemq; antequam crearetur, ad suum certum finem destinauit: vt infra pluribus ostendetur. Prouidentia verò est consilium Dei æternum, liberrimum, immutabile, sapientissimum, justissimum & optimum, secundum quod Deus omnia in omnibus creaturis efficit bona: mala etiam fieri permittit: & bona ac mala vniuersa ad suam gloriam & electorum salutem dirigit.
units.tr: Foreknowledge, providence and predestination of God differ. Foreknowledge is the knowledge of God by which he foreknew from eternity not only those things which he himself was going to do, but also those things which others were going to do by his permission, such as sins. Providence and predestination, although they concern only those things which God himself was going to do, nevertheless differ in this: providence extends properly to all the things and works of God, while predestination extends properly only to rational creatures. For predestination is the most wise, eternal and immutable decree of God, by which he appointed each one, before he was created, to his certain end, as will be shown more fully below. Providence, however, is the eternal, most free, immutable, most wise, most just and best counsel of God, according to which God brings about all good things in all creatures, permits evil things also to happen, and directs all good and evil things to his own glory and the salvation of the elect.

units.la: Definitionis explicatio & confirmatio.
units.tr: Explanation and confirmation of the definition.

units.la: Consilium. Prouidentia diuina nominatur in scriptura consilium Dei. Consilium Domini æternum stat. Consilium meum stabit. Deus volens ostendere immutabilitatem consilij sui. Sic Esa. 14, 26. & 19, 17. & 18, 29. Ierem. 32, 19. & 50, 44. Actor. 2, 23. Eph. 1, 11. &c. Ex quibus dictis manifestum est, prouidentiæ nomine non tantum scientiam vel notitiam præsentium & futurorum, sed etiam decretum seu voluntatem Dei efficacem intelligendam esse. Vtrumque enim nomen consilij complectitur: intellectum siue præscientiam faciendorum seu futurorum, & causarum propter quas facienda sint aut non facienda: & voluntate certis de causa aliquid statuentem. Prouidentia igitur non est nuda præuisio aut præscientia, sed præscientia & voluntas Dei simul: sicut apud Græcos notitiam & curam rerum significat. Sophocl. In Antigone.
units.tr: Counsel. In Scripture divine providence is called the counsel of God. The counsel of the Lord stands for ever. My counsel shall stand. God, wishing to show the immutability of his counsel. So Isa. 14, 26; 19, 17; 18, 29; Jer. 32, 19; 50, 44; Acts 2, 23; Eph. 1, 11, etc. From these passages it is clear that by the name of providence we must understand not only the knowledge or awareness of present and future things, but also the effective decree or will of God. For the one name of counsel embraces both: the understanding or foreknowledge of things to be done or to come, and of the causes on account of which they are to be done or not done; and the will deciding on something for certain reasons. Providence therefore is not bare foresight or foreknowledge, but the foreknowledge and will of God together; just as among the Greeks it signifies the knowledge and care of things. Sophocles, in Antigone.

units.la: Ἀεὶ ... (Greek quotation, illegible in scan)
units.tr: Ἀεὶ ... (Greek quotation, illegible in the scan)

units.la: Æternum. Quia cum nec vllius rei ignoratio, nec cognitionis incrementum, nec voluntatis mutario vlla in Deum cadat, necesse est ipsum omnia ab æterno sciuisse ac decreuisse. Dominus possedit me ab initio viarum suarum. Annuncians ab exordio mundi fundamenta. Loquimur sapientiam, quam praesinierat Deus ante secula.
units.tr: Eternal. Since no ignorance of anything, no increase of knowledge, and no change of will can fall upon God, he must necessarily have known and decreed all things from eternity. The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways. Declaring the foundations of the world from the beginning. We speak the wisdom which God foreordained before the ages.

units.la: Libertimum.] Quia ita decreuit ab æterno, sicut ipsi proinmensa sapientia & bonitate sua placuit, cum haberet integram potestatem, consilium aliter constituendi, vel etiam omittendi, vel res aliter perficiendi, quam consilio suo eas decreuit perficere. Omnia, qua voluit, fecit. Sicut lutum in manu figuli, sic vos in manu mea.
units.tr: Most free. Because he decreed from eternity as it pleased him, in his immeasurable wisdom and goodness, although he had full power to establish his counsel otherwise, or even to omit it, or to bring things to completion otherwise than he had decreed. Whatever he willed, he did. As the clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand.

units.la: Immutabile.] Quia nec error, nec mutatio in Deum cadit: sed quod semel ab æterno decreuit, id tanquam optimum & rectissimum in æternum vult & exsequitur. Ego Iehoua, & non mutor. Triumphator in Israel non mentitur, neque pœnitudine ducitur.
units.tr: Immutable. Because neither error nor change can fall upon God; rather, what he has once decreed from eternity, that he wills and carries out for ever as best and most right. I am the LORD, and I do not change. The Triumphant One of Israel does not lie, nor is he moved by repentance.

units.la: Sapientissimum.] Ostendit hoc rerum & euentuum in hoc mundo series admirabilis. Apud ipsum est sapientia & fortitudo. Ipse habet consilium & intelligentiam. O profunditatem diuitiarum & sapientia & cognitionis Dei. Sic 1 Sam.16,7. 1 Reg.8,39. Pf.33,11. Iob.36,23. Pf.33,15. & 139,1.2.3.4.5.6. & 147,5. Prou.8,30.
units.tr: Most wise. The admirable order of things and events in this world shows this. With him are wisdom and strength; he has counsel and understanding. O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! So 1 Sam. 16, 7; 1 Kings 8, 39; Ps. 33, 11; Job 36, 23; Ps. 33, 15; and 139, 1–6; 147, 5; Prov. 8, 30.

units.la: Iustissimum.] Quia voluntas Dei est fons & norma omnis iustitiæ. Non est apud Dominum Deum nostrum iniquitas, nec personarum acceptio. Sic Nehem.9,33. Job.9,2. Psal.36,7. & 119,137. Dan.9,7.14.
units.tr: Most just. Because the will of God is the fountain and norm of all justice. With the Lord our God there is no iniquity, nor respect of persons. So Neh. 9, 33; Job 9, 2; Ps. 36, 7; 119, 137; Dan. 9, 7, 14.

units.la: Secundum quod omnia efficit.] Hoc additur, ut sciamus, consilium Dei non esse otiosum, sed efficax, sicut Christus dicit: Pater usque huc operatur, & ego operor.
units.tr: According as he works all things. This is added so that we may know that the counsel of God is not idle but effective, as Christ says: My Father works until now, and I work.

units.la: Est autem operatio Dei duplex. Generalis, qua omnia, præsertim genus humanum, sustentat ac gubernat: & specialis, qua electorum salutem in hac vita inchoat, & in altera perficit. De vtraque dicitur: Deus est conseruator omnium hominum, maxime verò fidelium. Quotquot spiritu Dei ducuntur, ij sunt filij Dei. Oculi Domini super iustos, &c. Vtraque operatio Dei est vel immediata, vel mediata. Immediata est, cum sine mediis, præter vel contra consuetum naturæ ordinem, Deus quæ vult, operatur: vt, cum edit miracula, &c. Mediata est, cum per creaturas siue media & causas secundas effectus illos producit, ad quos consuetò naturæ ordine sunt idoneæ, & à Deo factæ: vt, cum per alimenta nos sustentat, per medicamenta morbos sanat. Non in solo pane viuit homo. Tollant massam ficuum, & ponant super vlcus, & sanabitur. Honora medicum propter necessitatem: etenim Altissimus creauit eum, &c. Ita mediatè per scripturam lectam, auditam, &c. se & voluntatem suam nobis patefacit Deus. Habent Mosen & Prophetas, audiant eos.
units.tr: The working of God is twofold. It is general, by which he sustains and governs all things, especially the human race; and special, by which he begins the salvation of the elect in this life and completes it in the next. Of both it is said: God is the preserver of all men, and especially of believers. As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, etc. Each working of God is either immediate or mediate. It is immediate when God works what he wills without means, beyond or against the customary order of nature, as when he works miracles, etc. It is mediate when he produces those effects through creatures, that is, through means and secondary causes, for which they are fitted by the customary order of nature and made by God: as when he sustains us through food, or heals diseases through medicines. Man does not live by bread alone. Let them take a lump of figs and lay it on the boil, and he will be healed. Honour the physician for the sake of his necessity, for the Most High created him, etc. In this way God reveals himself and his will to us mediately, through Scripture read, heard, etc. They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.

units.la: Hæc autem operatio seu actio Dei mediata peragitur aliquando per instrumenta bona, eaq; tam naturalia, quàm voluntaria: aliquando per mala & peccantia: ita tamen, ut Dei opus in illis & per illa semper optimum, justissimum & sanctissimum sit. Non enim ab instrumenti, sed ab ipsius Dei bonitate, sapientia & rectitudine, bonitas divinorum operum pendet. De bonis instrumentis, quod per illa Deus operetur optimè, non est inter pios controversia. De malis autem non omnes idem sentiunt.
