Nisi tamen negare velimus, probationes & castigationes piorum, & poenas impiorum, quæ per malos fiunt, & justas esse, & à voluntate atque efficacia divina proficisci, tum etiam virtutes & facta impiorum generi humano salutaria, Dei dona esse: oportet sanè fateamur, etiam per mala & peccantia organa Deum justa & sancta sua opera & judicia exequi. Sic enim per fratres & Midianitos impios mittit Josephum in Ægyptum, per Bileamum pseudoprophetam benedicit Israel, per pseudoprophetas tentat Populum, per Satanam exagitat Saulem, Dauidem punit per Absalomum, & per maledicta Simei, Salomonem per seditiosum Ierobeamum, Roboamum per populum deficientem, Iobum explorat per Sathanam & Chaldæos, transfert Iudam & Ierusalem per manus Nebucadnezaris, &c.
units.tr: This mediate operation or action of God is carried out sometimes through good instruments, both natural and voluntary, and sometimes through evil and sinful ones; yet God's work in them and through them is always most good, most just and most holy. For the goodness of God's works depends not on the instrument but on God's own goodness, wisdom and rectitude. On good instruments, that God works most excellently through them, there is no controversy among the godly. On evil ones, however, not everyone thinks alike. Yet unless we wish to deny that the trials and chastisements of the godly, and the punishments of the wicked which are inflicted by evil men, are just, and that they proceed from the divine will and efficacy, and also that the virtues and deeds of the wicked are gifts of God, which are useful to the human race, we must surely confess that God carries out his just and holy works and judgments even through evil and sinful instruments. Thus he sent Joseph into Egypt through his wicked brothers and the Midianites; he blessed Israel through Balaam the false prophet; he tested the people through false prophets; he harassed Saul through Satan; he punished David through Absalom and through the curses of Shimei; he punished Solomon through the seditious Jeroboam, and Rehoboam through the people who revolted; he tested Job through Satan and the Chaldeans; he carried Judah and Jerusalem away by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and so on.

units.la: Omnia bona efficit.] Ita videlicet, ut nulla creatura, magna vel parva, sine ipsius consilio & voluntate neq; fit, neq; moveatur, aut agat, vel patiatur quicquam. Boni enim nomine, intelliguntur non tantum ipsæ substantiæ rerum, sed & earū quantitates, qualitates & motus: quia hæc omnia sunt res à Deo conditæ, ac proinde eius providentiæ necessariò subiectæ.
units.tr: He works all good things. That is to say, in such a way that no creature, great or small, comes into being, is moved, acts or suffers anything without his counsel and will. For by the name of good are understood not only the substances of things but also their quantities, qualities and motions, because all of these are things created by God and therefore necessarily subject to his providence.

units.la: Mala etiam fieri permittit.] Malum duplex est: aliud culpæ, quod est peccatum: aliud pœnæ, quod est omnis destructio, aut afflictio, aut desertio creaturæ rationalis, quia Deus punit peccata. Exemplum utriusq; significationis est in dicto Jeremiæ: Sin autem convertatur gens ipsa à malo suo, contra quod locutus sum: pœnitebit me mali, quod cogitaveram facere eis.
units.tr: He also permits evils to happen. Evil is twofold: one kind is of guilt, which is sin; the other is of punishment, which is any destruction, affliction or abandonment of a rational creature, because God punishes sins. An example of both senses is in the saying of Jeremiah: "If that nation turns from its evil, against which I have spoken, I will repent of the evil that I had intended to do to them."

units.la: Malum pœna est à Deo authore & effectore, non tantum quatenus est actio seu motus aliquis, sed etiam quatenus peccantium destructio, vel afflictio; quod sic probatur: 1. Omnis boni causa prima & effector est Deus. Omnes autem pœnæ, seu mala pœnæ, habent rationem boni moralis: quia sunt executio & declaratio justitiæ divinæ. Ergo Deus est author pœnarum. 2. Deus est judex mundi, & vindex gloriæ suæ, & talis vult agnosci. Ergo est author praemiorum & poenarum. 3. Vniuersa scriptura maximo consensu & poenas impiorum, & castigationes, exercitia atque martyria sanctorum, ad efficacem Dei voluntatem refert. Ego Dominus faciens pacem, & creans malum. Non est malum (nempe poenae) in ciuitate, quod non fecerit Dominus. Timete potius eum, qui potest animam & corpus perdere in gehenna.
units.tr: Evil of punishment has God as its author and effector, not only insofar as it is some action or motion, but also insofar as it is the destruction or affliction of sinners. This is proved as follows: (1) God is the first cause and effector of every good. But all punishments, or evil punishments, have the character of moral good, because they are the execution and declaration of divine justice. Therefore God is the author of punishments. (2) God is the judge of the world and the avenger of his own glory, and he wishes to be acknowledged as such. Therefore he is the author of rewards and punishments. (3) The whole of Scripture, with the greatest agreement, refers both the punishments of the wicked and the chastisements, trials and martyrdoms of the saints to the effectual will of God: "I, the Lord, make peace and create evil"; "There is no evil (that is, of punishment) in the city which the Lord has not done"; "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell."

units.la: Mala vero culpae quatenus talia, hoc est, peccata sunt, non habent rationem boni: ideo Deus ea nec vult, nec probat, nec efficit, nec adjuuat, sed fieri a diabolis & hominibus permittit, hoc est, non impedit, quo minus fiant, quamuis impedire posset. Cadunt ergo ea quidem etiam sub prouidentiam Dei, verum non effectiue, sed tantum permissiue. Fiunt enim non voluntate aut effectione, sed permissione diuina.
units.tr: But evils of guilt, insofar as they are such, that is, insofar as they are sins, do not have the character of good. Therefore God neither wills them, nor approves them, nor effects them, nor assists them, but permits them to be done by devils and men; that is, he does not hinder them from being done, although he could hinder them. These things therefore also fall under the providence of God, but not effectively, only permissively. For they come to pass not by his will or effecting, but by divine permission.

units.la: Nec abijciendum est permissionis vocabulum, cum in scriptura quandoque vsurpetur. Non permisit, vt tangeres eam. Non permisit ei Deus, vt noceret mihi. Ista sunt gentes, quas reliquit Deus, vt per eas tentaret Israelem. Non sinet homine opprimere eos. Praeteritis aetatibus fuit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. Sed & recte intelligendum est, ne Deo magna pars gubernationis mundi & rerum humanarum detrahatur. Est enim permissio non prouidentiae & operationis diuinae in operationibus malorum cessatio, aut otiosa speculatio, qua fiat, vt actiones illae non ab alio principio, quam a creaturis agentibus pendeant: sed est gratiae diuinae subtractio, qua Deus (dum voluntatis suae decreta per creaturas rationales exequitur) aut non docet creaturam agentem, quid ipse fieri velit, aut voluntatem eius ad obedientiam ipse non flectit: nihilominus interim creaturam sic desertam & peccantem recte mouet, & quae decreuit, optime per eam exsequitur.
units.tr: Nor is the word permission to be rejected, since it is sometimes used in Scripture: "He did not permit you to touch her"; "God did not permit him to harm me"; "These are the nations which God left, to test Israel by them"; "He will not allow man to oppress them"; "In past generations he allowed all nations to walk in their own ways." But it must also be rightly understood, lest a great part of the government of the world and of human affairs be taken away from God. For permission is not a cessation of divine providence and operation in the actions of evil men, nor an idle speculation by which those actions should depend on some other principle than the acting creatures. Rather, it is a withdrawal of divine grace, by which God (while he carries out the decrees of his will through rational creatures) either does not teach the acting creature what he himself wishes to be done, or does not himself turn its will to obedience; nevertheless, in the meantime he rightly moves the creature thus abandoned and sinning, and he carries out through it what he has decreed, most excellently.

units.la: Vniuersa bona, & mala dirigit. Vniuersa, inquam, nempe praeterita ab initio mundi, praesentia & futura, in omnem vsq; aeternitatem. Recordamini impiorum, quae a seculo contigerunt, quoniam ego Deus, & non est vltra Deus, neq; est sicut ego, &c.
units.tr: He directs all good and evil things. All, I say, namely things past from the beginning of the world, present and future, to all eternity. "Remember the wicked things that have happened from the beginning of the age, for I am God, and there is no other God, nor is there anyone like me, etc."

units.la: Ad suam gloriam. Hoc est; agnitionem & celebrationem iustitiae, omnipotentiae, sapientiae, misericordiae & bonitatis diuinae.
units.tr: To his own glory. That is, to the acknowledgment and celebration of the justice, omnipotence, wisdom, mercy and goodness of God.

units.la: Et ad electorum salutem. Hoc est; ad vitam, laetitiam, iustitiam, gloriam & felicitatem aeternam Ecclesiae promouendam. Huc autem, nempe ad gloriam Dei, & electorum salutem, omnia Dei consilia & opera a Deo referri, extra controuersiam esse debet: nam in omnibus gloria Dei, & cura ecclesiae patet na conspicitur. Caeli enarrant gloriam Dei. Propter nomen meum longum faciam fauorem meum. Omnia propter seipsum fecit DEVS. Nominus, quod quod iis, qui diligunt DEVM, omnia simul conferant ad bonum. Rom. 8, 28. Neque hic peccauit, neque parentes eius, sed vt opera Dei manifesta Ioh. 9, 2. fierent in eo.
units.tr: And to the salvation of the elect. That is, to the advancement of the eternal life, joy, righteousness, glory and happiness of the Church. That all of God's counsels and works are referred by God to this end, namely the glory of God and the salvation of the elect, must be beyond controversy; for in all things the glory of God and the care of the Church are plainly seen. "The heavens declare the glory of God"; "For my name's sake I will prolong my favour"; "The Lord made all things for himself" (Prov. 16:4); that "all things work together for good for those who love God" (Rom. 8:28); "Neither this man sinned, nor his parents, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (John 9:2).

units.la: Hactenus explicata est prouidentiae diuinae definitio, ex qua jam oritur Qvæstio maximè consideranda: An omnium rerum sit prouidentia: seu, an prouidentia ad omnia se extendat? Responsio quidem ex definitione est manifesta, omnia etiam maxima & minima sub prouidentiam Dei ita cadere, vt quæ bona sunt, ex prouidentia & Deo efficiente, quæ verò mala, secundum prouidentiam & Deo permittente fiant. Verum cum à multis hæc doctrina vel ignoretur, vel impugnetur, amplius ex scriptura est declaranda & demonstranda.
units.tr: So far the definition of divine providence has been explained, and from it there now arises the question that must be considered most carefully: Is there providence of all things, or does providence extend to all things? The answer is indeed plain from the definition: all things, even the greatest and the least, fall under the providence of God in such a way that what is good comes to pass by providence and God effecting it, while what is evil comes to pass according to providence and God permitting it. But since this doctrine is either unknown or attacked by many, it must be explained and demonstrated more fully from Scripture.

units.la: Omnia igitur siue maxima, siue minima, DEI prouidentia regi, probatur primo testimoniis scripturæ sacræ, deinde rationibus.
units.tr: Therefore, that all things, whether greatest or least, are governed by the providence of God, is proved first by the testimonies of Holy Scripture, and then by arguments.

units.la: TESTIMONIA, quibus demonstratur, prouidentiam Dei ad omnia se extendere, alia sunt vniuersalia, quæ generaliter & in vniuersum omnes res & euentus prouidentiæ diuinæ subesse docent: alia particularia, quæ speciatim singula à Deo gubernari confirmant. Illa prouidentiam vniuersalem, hæc prouidentiam specialem asserunt. Particularia verò testimonia sunt vel de creaturis, vel de iis, quæ quotidiè fiunt, hoc est, de euentibus: & de creaturis, vel irrationalibus, iisque tum animatis tum inanimatis, vel rationolibus, & voluntariè agentibus, siue bene, siue male. De euentibus autem vel contingentibus, vel casualibus, vel necessariis. Quæ enim fiunt, vel sunt casualia, vel fortuita, sed nobis tantum, qui causas veras non videmus: vel contingentia, ratione causarum contingenter agentium: vel necessaria, ratione causarum necessariò agentium in natura. Deo autem nihil est casuale vel contingens, sed omnia necessaria: licet respectu bonarum & malarum actionum diuerso modo.
units.tr: The testimonies by which it is shown that the providence of God extends to all things are of two kinds: some are universal, which teach generally and in general that all things and events are subject to divine providence; others are particular, which confirm that each single thing is governed by God in particular. The former assert a universal providence, the latter a special providence. The particular testimonies concern either creatures or those things which happen every day, that is, events; and they concern creatures either irrational, whether animate or inanimate, or rational and acting voluntarily, whether well or badly. Events, moreover, are either contingent, or accidental, or necessary. For things that happen are either accidental or fortuitous, but only to us, who do not see the true causes; or contingent, by reason of causes acting contingently; or necessary, by reason of causes acting necessarily in nature. But nothing is accidental or contingent to God, and all things are necessary to him, although in a different way with respect to good and evil actions.

units.la: Typus igitur, qui sequitur, euidenter nobis ostendet, quaenam res prouidentiae diuinae proprie sint subiectae. Et is quidem valde videtur necessarius, eo quod tam inter Philosophos quam Theologos magna semper fuit controversia de arduo hoc argumento: adeo, ut extra scripturam sacram de illo, qui pronunciare multa velit, in tenebris obambulare sit necesse. Hieronymus & Damascenus negant a Deo curari res vilissimas, multo verò minus mala quaeque in mundo: sicut nec res contingentes aut fortuitas. Rationem addiderunt Aristoteles & Plinius lib. 2. cap. 7. quia scilicet indignum sit Dei maiestate, curare res sordidas, & minimi pretij, multo verò minus peccata hominum. Sed hoc est, ut loquitur Cyprianus lib. 1. cap. 1, Deo honorem non dare, cuius nutu & arbitrio regi & gubernari omnia scimus & credimus.
units.tr: The type that follows will therefore clearly show us which things are properly subject to divine providence. And this seems very necessary, because there has always been great controversy about this difficult subject both among philosophers and among theologians: so much so that, apart from Holy Scripture, whoever wishes to pronounce many things about it must necessarily wander in darkness. Jerome and Damascene deny that the most worthless things, and much less any evils in the world, are cared for by God, nor are contingent or fortuitous things. Aristotle and Pliny (Book 2, chapter 7) added the reason: namely, that it is unworthy of the majesty of God to care for sordid things of little value, and much less for the sins of men. But this, as Cyprian says (Book 1, chapter 1), is "not to give honour to God, whom we know and believe to govern and direct all things by his nod and will."

units.la: Typus rerum prouidentiae diuinae subiectarum.
units.tr: The kinds of things subject to the providence of God.

units.la: I. Vniuersa & omnia generatim: quae prouidentia dicitur vniuersalis seu generalis. 1. rationales: angeli, homines; tum boni, mali; agentes liberè & voluntarie; bene, male. 2. irrationales & brutae: animatae, inanimes. 3. fortuiti & casuales; 4. contingentes; 5. necessarij; seu boni, mali.
units.tr: I. All things and everything in general, which is called universal or general providence: (1) rational beings, angels and men, both good and evil, acting freely and willingly, rightly or wrongly; (2) irrational and brute beings, animate and inanimate; (3) fortuitous and chance events; (4) contingent things; (5) necessary things, or good and evil.

units.la: II. Singula speciatim: quae prouidentia dicitur particularis seu specialis. Hac autem dirigitur speciatim singulae creaturae: aeque tum singuli euentus, tum Providentia Dei regitur totus mundus, & in toto mundo tum.
units.tr: II. Single things in particular, which is called particular or special providence. Each creature is directed in particular, and single events likewise; the whole world is governed by the providence of God, and so is everything in the whole world.

units.la: Jam singulis his veluti capitibus testimonia quædam illustriora addenda sunt.
units.tr: Now certain more illustrious testimonies must be added to each of these headings.

units.la: 1. De vniuersali prouidentia testantur ista: Omnia efficit ex consilio voluntatis suæ. Ipse dat omnibus vitam, & halitum, & omnia. Ipse dixit, & non facit? Locutus est, & non præstabit illud? Tu fecisti cælum, terram, maria, & vniuersa, quæ sunt in eis: viuificans quoque omnia hæc. Dixit ergo, & non facit? locutus est, & non implebit? formans lucem, & creans tenebras: faciens pacem, & creans malum: Ego Iehoua faciens omnia hæc. Sapientia pertingit ab extremo ad extremum fortiter, atque omnia moderatur suaviter.
units.tr: 1. Concerning universal providence these passages bear witness: "He works all things according to the counsel of his will." "He himself gives to all life, and breath, and all things." "Has he said, and will he not do it? Has he spoken, and will he not perform it?" "You have made heaven, earth, and the seas, and all that is in them, and you give life to all these things." "Has he said, and will he not do it? Has he spoken, and will he not fulfil it? Forming the light and creating the darkness, making peace and creating evil: I, the LORD, do all these things." "Wisdom reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly."

units.la: 2. De speciali: & quidem de rationalibus creaturis præclara testimonia suppeditat historia Iosephi: Non vestro consilio, sed Dei voluntate huc missus sum. Vos cogitastis aduersum me malum: Deus autem cogitauit illud in bonum, ut faceret secundum diem hanc. Item historia Pharaonis: Quis posuit os in homine? vel quis facit surdum & mutum? vel videntem & cæcum? nonne ego Iehoua? Nunc igitur vade, & ego ero cum ore tuo, & docebo te, quid loquaris. Videatur tota historia cap.3.4.7.8.9.10.14. Dixit Iehoua ad Iosuam: Ne timeas à facie regum, cras enim hac eadem hora tradam omnes istos vulnerandos in conspectu Israelis. Iehoua præcepit Simei, ut malediceret Dauidi. Quis decipiet Achab? decipies ac prævalebis. Cor regis in manu Domini, quocunque voluerit: inclinabit illud. Deus converterat cor regis Darij ad Iudæos. Apud Esaiam Devs vocat regem Assyriorum virgam furoris sui, & addit: Cum impleuerit Dominus cuncta opera sua in monte Sion, & in Ierusalem: visitabo super fructum magnifici cordis Assur regis, & super gloriam altitudinis oculorum eius. Quis est iste, qui dicit, ut fieret Domino non jubente? Iuxta voluntatem suam facit tam in virtutibus cœli, quam in habitatoribus terræ: nec est, qui resistat manui eius, & dicat ei, quare fecisti? Herodes & Pilatus cum gentibus & populis Israel coacti sunt aduersus Filium tuum Iesum, ut facerent quæcunque manus tua & consilium tuum prius definierat facienda.
units.tr: 2. Concerning particular providence, and indeed concerning rational creatures, the story of Joseph provides notable testimonies: "It was not by your counsel, but by the will of God, that I was sent hither. You thought evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring about what is done this day." Likewise the story of Pharaoh: "Who has made man's mouth? Or who makes the deaf and the dumb, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall say." Let the whole story be read in chapters 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 14. The LORD said to Joshua: "Do not fear the face of the kings, for tomorrow at this same hour I will deliver all of them to be slain in the sight of Israel." The LORD commanded Shimei to curse David. "Who will deceive Ahab? You will deceive him and prevail." "The heart of the king is in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will." God turned the heart of King Darius towards the Jews. In Isaiah, God calls the king of the Assyrians the rod of his anger, and adds: "When the Lord has accomplished all his work on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of the haughtiness of his eyes." "Who is this who says that a thing should come to pass when the Lord has not commanded it?" "He does according to his will, both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; there is none who can resist his hand or say to him, What are you doing?" Herod and Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, were gathered together against your Son Jesus, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had decided beforehand should be done.

units.la: 3. Irrationalibus, viuentibus, & vitæ expertibus. Dominus custodit omnia ossa iusti, vnum ex his non conteretur. Qui ascendere facit nubes ab extremo terræ, fulgura cum pluuia facit, qui edu- cit ventum è thesauris suis. Qui dat iumentis escam ipsorum, & pullis coruorum invocantibus eum. Pater vester cœlestis alit volucres cœli. Quod si herbam agri Deus ita circumuestit, nonne vos multo magis, &c.
units.tr: 3. Concerning irrational creatures, both living and lacking life: "The Lord keeps all the bones of the righteous; not one of them shall be broken." "He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth; he makes lightnings with the rain; he brings the wind out of his treasuries." "He gives the beasts their food, and the young ravens that call upon him." "Your heavenly Father feeds the birds of the air." "But if God so clothes the grass of the field, will he not much more clothe you?" and so on.

units.la: 4. De casualibus & fortuitis. Qui non est insidiatus ei, sed Deus eum tradidit in manum eius: constituam tibi locum, ad quem fugiet. Nonne duo passerculi assario veneunt? at vnus ex iis non cadit humi sine Patre vestro. Vestri vero etiam capilli capitis numerati sunt omnes. Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit: sit nomen Domini benedictum. In sinum proiicitur sors, & a Iehova est omne iudicium eius.
units.tr: 4. Concerning chance and fortuitous events: "He did not lie in wait for him, but God delivered him into his hand; I will appoint you a place to which he shall flee." "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And yet not one of them falls to the ground without your Father." "But even the hairs of your head are all numbered." "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." "The lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing of it is from the LORD."

units.la: 5. De necessariis: quorum necessitas pendet vel a consilio Dei nobis per verbum patefacto: Facta sunt haec, ut impleretur scriptura, Non confringetur ullum os ipsius. Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere a mortuis tertia die. Necesse est venire scandala. Si possibile esset, seducerentur electi. Oves mea non peribunt in aeternum, neque rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea. Vel pendet ab ordine naturae diuinitus instituto, seu a causis physicis necessitate physica agentibus. Pluuia producit herba, gignit rorem, pruinam, glaciem: producit hyades suo tempore, arcturum: caeli motus regit, & per hoc efficax est in sublunaribus, &c. Tonat Deus voce sua mirabilia. Qui rigat montes de superioribus suis, ut educat panem de terra, & vinum, quod laetificat cor hominis, ut faciem nitere faciat pra oleo: de fructu operum tuorum satiabitur terra, qui germinare facit foenum pro iumentis, & herbam ad vsum hominum, & panem, qui cor hominis fulcit, &c. fecit lunam in tempora, sol novit occasum suum: ponit tenebras, & est nox, &c.
units.tr: 5. Concerning necessary things, whose necessity depends either on the counsel of God made known to us through the Word: "These things were done that the Scripture might be fulfilled: not one of his bones shall be broken." "So it is written, and so it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day." "It must needs be that offences come." "If it were possible, the elect would be led astray." "My sheep shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand." Or it depends on the order of nature instituted by God, or on physical causes acting by physical necessity: "The rain produces the grass, begets dew, frost and ice; it brings forth the Hyades in their season, and Arcturus; it governs the motions of the heavens, and through this it is effective in the sublunary things," and so on. "God thunders wondrously with his voice." "He waters the mountains from his upper chambers, that he may bring forth bread from the earth, and wine which makes glad the heart of man, and oil to make the face shine; the earth is satisfied with the fruit of your works; he makes the grass grow for the cattle and the herb for the use of man, and bread which strengthens the heart of man," and so on. "He made the moon for the seasons; the sun knows its going down; he makes darkness, and it is night," and so on.

units.la: Testimonia similia paene infinita sunt in scriptura, quae diuinam prouidentiam ad omnia & singula se extendere demonstrant: sed haec pauca sufficient. Ex his enim certo constat, omnia tam mala, quam bona, tam parua, quam magna Dei prouidentia regi: ita tamen, ut bona fiant non tantum secundum prouidentiam, sed etiam ex prouidentia, tanquam ex causa, hoc est, Deo volente, praecipiente & efficiente: mala vero, quatenus mala, non ex prouidentia, hoc est, Deo non volente, nec mandante, nec sciente vel adiuuante, sed permittente, & ad fines a se destinatos dirigente.
units.tr: Testimonies similar to these are almost endless in Scripture, and they show that divine providence extends to all things and to each single thing; but these few will suffice. For from them it is certainly clear that all things, evil and good, small and great, are governed by the providence of God. Yet good things come about not only in accordance with providence but also from providence, as from a cause; that is, with God willing, commanding and effecting them. Evil things, however, insofar as they are evil, do not come from providence; that is, God does not will them, nor command them, nor know them or help them, but permits them and directs them to the ends he has appointed.

units.la: RATIONES, quibus demonstratur, prouidentiam Dei ad omnia & singula se extendere, fere suat eadem cum illis, quae probant esse prouidentiam.
units.tr: The arguments by which it is shown that the providence of God extends to all and to each thing are nearly the same as those which prove that there is a providence at all.

units.la: 1. Sine eius voluntate nihil potest fieri, qui est omnipotens. Deo igitur simpliciter aliquid nolente, impossibile est quicquam fieri, cum sit omnipotens. Quicquid vero fit, id Deo vel simpliciter vel secundum quid volente fieri necesse est.
units.tr: 1. Nothing can happen without his will, since he is almighty. Therefore, if God in no way willed something, it would be impossible for it to come about, since he is almighty. Whatever does happen must necessarily happen with God willing it, either absolutely or in some respect.

units.la: 2. Summe sapientis gubernatoris est, ut nihil eorum, quae in potestate habet, sinat fieri sine voluntate sua & consilio: & quanto quis sapientior est, tanto latius se extendit eius gubernatio. At Dei sapientia est infinita, & omnia sunt in eius potestate. Vt quid dicis Iacob, & quid loqueris Israel? abscondita est via mea a Deo meo, iudicium meum transiit, &c. Ergo in universo mundo nihil fit, nisi quod vult ac decreuit Deus.
units.tr: 2. It is the mark of the highest and wisest governor that he allows nothing within his power to happen without his will and counsel; and the wiser someone is, the more widely his governance extends. But God's wisdom is infinite, and all things are in his power. "Why do you say, Jacob, and why do you speak, Israel? My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment passes by God," and so on. Therefore in the whole world nothing happens except what God wills and has decreed.

units.la: 3. Omnium rerum sunt certi fines, & quidem omnes boni. Omnia autem bona sunt à Deo, & Deus ea vult ac moderatur. Omnes igitur fines rerum vult ac moderatur Deus. Qui autem vult fines, is vult & media ad fines. Quare & media vult Deus, eaq; simpliciter, si bona, vel aliquo modo, si mala sint. Cum igitur omnia quae sunt & fiunt, vel fines sint, vel media, consequitur, Deum omnia velle & administrare.
units.tr: 3. All things have certain ends, and indeed all good ones. But all good things are from God, and God wills and governs them. Therefore God wills and governs all the ends of things. But whoever wills the ends also wills the means to those ends. Hence God wills the means too: simply, if they are good, and in some way, if they are evil. Since, therefore, all that is and all that happens is either an end or a means, it follows that God wills and administers all things.

units.la: 4. Est aliqua causa prima, quae non pendet ab aliis, sed à quo omnes aliae pendent. Deus est illa causa prima. Ergo à Dei nutu omnes causae secundae pendent.
units.tr: 4. There is some first cause which depends on nothing else, but on which all others depend. God is that first cause. Therefore all secondary causes depend on the nod of God.

units.la: 5. Deus omnia ab aeterno praescivit immutabiliter: quia falli aut errare in sua praescientia non potuit. Ideo praescientia Dei est certa & infallibilis omnium rerum notitia. Sic igitur nunc res omnes evenire necesse est, sicut eas futuras praescivit Deus: & quidem ideo, quia praesciit. Non enim praescientiam petiuit ex rebus creatis, sed à seipso. Ab ea igitur omnes eventus pendent & fluunt immutabiliter.
units.tr: 5. God foreknew all things from eternity, unchangeably, because he could not be deceived or err in his foreknowledge. Therefore God's foreknowledge is a certain and infallible knowledge of all things. So all things must now come to pass just as God foreknew they would be future; and indeed they do so because he foreknew them, for he did not derive his foreknowledge from created things but from himself. Therefore all events depend on it and flow from it unchangeably.

units.la: 6. Omnia bona sunt à Deo tanquam à prima causa. Omnes res positiuae in natura, ut substantiae, motus, actiones, in quantum sunt hoc, bonae sunt. Ergo sunt à Deo, Deique providentia fiunt.
units.tr: 6. All good things are from God as from the first cause. All positive things in nature, such as substances, motions and actions, are good insofar as they are what they are. Therefore they are from God and come to pass by the providence of God.

units.la: Confutatio sophismatum contra providentiam Dei.
units.tr: Refutation of the sophisms against the providence of God.

units.la: Primum sophisma de confusionibus.
units.tr: The first sophism, concerning disorder.

units.la: Confusa non reguntur à Deo: quia Deus non est author confusionis. In mundo est multiplex confusio. Ergo vel nihil, vel saltem non omnia regantur divina providentia. Respond. Verum in mundo multa sint confusa: sunt tamen & multa ordinata: ut, motus coelestes, conservatio specierum, politiae, poenae sceleratorum. Non potest igitur universaliter concludi, nihil in mundo regi à Deo. 2. De confusis tantum sequitur, confusionem non esse à Deo, quae confusio accedit malitia diabolorum & hominum. Plus igitur etiam sic est in conclusione, quam in praemissis.
units.tr: Things that are confused are not governed by God, because God is not the author of confusion. There is manifold confusion in the world. Therefore either nothing, or at least not everything, is governed by divine providence. Answer: It is true that many things in the world are confused, but there are also many that are ordered: for example, the heavenly motions, the preservation of species, civil government, and the punishment of the wicked. So it cannot be concluded universally that nothing in the world is governed by God. (2) From the premise about confused things it follows only that the confusion is not from God, since that confusion comes from the malice of devils and men. So the conclusion here goes beyond the premises.

units.la: 3. Ad maiorem. Confusa non reguntur à Deo, nempe quatenus confusa sunt. Nihilominus reguntur, quatenus in ipsa etiam confusione ordo aliquis reperitur. Atqui nihil adeo inordinatum est, vel gignitur in mundo, in quo non etiam ordo divinae sapientiae, potentiae & justitiae aliquo modo elucear, & ab ipsa scriptura nobis monstretur. Exempli causa: in parricidio Judaeorum crucifigentium Filium Dei, in venditione Josephi, in seditione Absolomi, &c. horribilis fuit confusio, quoad voluntates & actiones hominum: sed & optimus fuit ordo, quoad voluntatem & consilium Dei, tradentis Filium in mortem propter peccata. cata nostra, mittentis Iosephum in Ægyptum, punientis Dauidem & Absolomum, &c. Sic in eodem euentu confusio & ordo esse potest diuersu respectu. Sequitur ergo, confusa non esse, nec regi à Deo, quatenus confusa & peccata sunt: esse verò ac regi, quatenus cum ordine diuinæ sapientiæ & iustitiæ congruunt.
units.tr: (3) On the major premise: things that are confused are not governed by God, namely insofar as they are confused. Nevertheless they are governed insofar as some order is found even in that confusion. Yet nothing is so disordered, or arises in the world, in which the order of divine wisdom, power and justice does not in some way shine forth, and which Scripture itself does not show us. For example, in the parricide of the Jews who crucified the Son of God, in the selling of Joseph, in the rebellion of Absalom, and so on, there was a dreadful confusion as far as the wills and actions of men were concerned; but there was also the best order as far as the will and counsel of God were concerned, who delivered his Son to death for our sins, who sent Joseph into Egypt, who punished David and Absalom, and so on. Thus in the same event there can be confusion and order from different respects. It follows, therefore, that things are not confused, nor governed by God, insofar as they are confused and sinful; but they are and are governed insofar as they agree with the order of divine wisdom and justice.

units.la: Inst. Quod repugnat voluntati Dei, non regitur à Deo. Voluntas diabolorum & impiorum hominum repugnat voluntati Dei. Ergo non regitur à Deo. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini. Maior enim de voluntate Dei patefacta, & arcana simul: minor tantum de patefacta est vera.
units.tr: Objection. What is contrary to the will of God is not governed by God. The will of devils and of wicked men is contrary to the will of God. Therefore it is not governed by God. Answer. There are four terms. For the major premise concerns the will of God as revealed and also as hidden; the minor concerns only the revealed will, and only that is true.

units.la: Secundum sophisma de causa peccati.
units.tr: The second sophism, concerning the cause of sin.

units.la: Omnes actiones & motus sunt à Deo. Multæ actiones sunt peccata. Ergo peccatum est à Deo, & per consequens, dogma de vniuersali prouidentia facit Deum authorem peccati. Resp. Est fallacia accidentis. Actiones enim impiorum sunt peccata, non per se, quatenus actiones sunt, sed per accidens, propter defectum & prauitatem voluntatis malorum, non hoc spectantium, vt in actione sua voluntatem Dei exsequantur. Hic enim defectus & hæc prauitas est accidens voluntatis & actionis illius, quam Deus per vitiosam voluntatem vult fieri.
units.tr: All actions and motions are from God. Many actions are sins. Therefore sin is from God, and consequently the doctrine of universal providence makes God the author of sin. Answer. This is the fallacy of accident. For the actions of the impious are sins not in themselves, insofar as they are actions, but accidentally, on account of the defect and perversity of the wicked will, which does not aim at this, namely to carry out the will of God in its action. For this defect and this perversity is an accident of that will and action, which God wills to come about through a faulty will.

units.la: Inst. 1. Multæ actiones sunt suo genere peccata. Ergo etiam per se. Resp. Conceditur de actionibus, quatenus sunt prohibitæ à Deo & à creaturis contra voluntatem Dei perpetrantur: minimè vero, quatenus sunt actiones, quas Deus vult aut iubet fieri. Nam respectu diuinæ voluntatis eas cientis, semper sunt iustissima Dei iudicia, nec sine manifesta Dei contumelia sub nomine peccati, tanquam sub genere comprehendi possunt: eo- que antecedens est falsum.
units.tr: Objection 1. Many actions are sins by their own kind. Therefore they are sins also in themselves. Answer. It is granted concerning actions insofar as they are forbidden by God and are committed by creatures against the will of God; but by no means insofar as they are actions which God wills or commands to be done. For with respect to the divine will which brings them about, they are always the most just judgments of God, and they cannot be comprehended under the name of sin as under a genus without manifest dishonour to God. Therefore the antecedent is false.

units.la: Inst. 2. Qui vult actionem, quæ per se peccatum est, is vult peccatum. Deus vult actiones, quæ per se peccata sunt, vt venditionem Iosephi in Ægyptum, seditionem Absolomi, seditionem pseudoprophetarum, crudelitatem Assyriorum, crucifixionem Christi, &c. Ergo vult peccatum. Resp. Maior est vera de eo, qui vult actionem, quæ suæ voluntatis respectu peccatum est: seu, qui vult actionem eodem fine, quo is, qui peccat: non autem de eo, qui vult & efficit opus, quod alienæ voluntatis respectu peccatum est: seu, qui vult opus illud alio fine, coque bono, & cum natura ac lege Dei congruente. At Assyriorum & aliorum peccantium actiones, quas Deus efficaciter volebat, peccata erant, non Dei, sed voluntatis hominum peccantium respectu. Deus enim illa omnia volebat optimo fine: homines pe. pessimo. Hæc responsio sumta est ex vniuersali regula, cuius tam in Theologicis, quàm in moralibus & physicis exemplis veritas manifesta est: videlicet: Cùm eiusdem effectus plures causæ sint, alia bona, alia vitiosa: effectus ille respectu causarum bonarum bonus est, respectu vitiosarum verò vitiosus ac malus est: ac bona causa sunt per se causa boni, per accidens verò mali ac vitiosi effectus sine vitio, quod est in effectu propter causam aliquam vitiosam: & contra, mala causa sunt per se causa mali, per accidens autem boni, quod est in effectu. Vniuersaliter enim verum est, causas impulsiuas & finales facere actionum discrimina. Hinc igitur eadem actio, puta, venditio Iosephi in Ægyptum, pessimum opus fuit respectu fratrum, & simul optimum, respectu Dei, propter diuersas causas impulsiuas, & finales. Sicut autem bonum opus Dei non potest referri ad fratres: sic nec sceleratum opus fratrum potest ascribi Deo, &c.
units.tr: Objection 2. Whoever wills an action which is sinful in itself, wills sin. God wills actions which are sinful in themselves, such as the selling of Joseph into Egypt, the rebellion of Absalom, the rebellion of the false prophets, the cruelty of the Assyrians, the crucifixion of Christ, and so on. Therefore he wills sin. Answer. The major premise is true of one who wills an action which is sinful with respect to his own will, or who wills an action with the same end for which the sinner acts; but not of one who wills and effects a work which is sinful with respect to another's will, or who wills that work for another end, a good one, agreeing with the nature and law of God. But the actions of the Assyrians and of the other sinners, which God efficaciously willed, were sins with respect to the will of the sinning men, not of God. For God willed all those things for the best end; men for the worst. This answer is taken from a universal rule, whose truth is evident in theological, moral and physical examples, namely: when one and the same effect has several causes, some good and some faulty, that effect is good with respect to the good causes, but faulty and evil with respect to the faulty ones. Good causes are by themselves the cause of good, but accidentally of evil and faulty effects, without the fault which is in the effect on account of some faulty cause; and conversely, evil causes are by themselves the cause of evil, but accidentally of good, which is in the effect. For it is universally true that the impelling and final causes make the distinction of actions. Hence the same action, for example the selling of Joseph into Egypt, was the worst work with respect to the brothers, and at the same time the best with respect to God, on account of the different impelling and final causes. But just as a good work of God cannot be referred to the brothers, so neither can the wicked work of the brothers be ascribed to God, and so on.

units.la: Lvtherus de seruo arbitrio, declarat similitudine equitis, equitantis equum claudum. Eques impellens equum claudum intendit motum, & iter suum conficit: quo magis verò equum impellit, eò magis equus claudicat. Sic Deus vtens instrumentis malis intendit iusta sua iudicia. Quanto magis verò eos impellit, tanto magis illi peccant. Vt verò ibi causa claudicationis non est eques, sed equus claudus: ita hic causa peccati non est Deus, sed instrumenta peccantia.
units.tr: Luther, On the Bondage of the Will, explains by the similitude of a rider riding a lame horse. The rider who urges on a lame horse intends the movement and completes his journey; yet the more he drives the horse on, the more the horse limps. So God, using evil instruments, intends his just judgments; but the more he drives them on, the more they sin. Yet just as in that case the cause of the limping is not the rider but the lame horse, so here the cause of sin is not God but the sinning instruments.

units.la: Inst. 3. Quod non potest fieri, Deo simpliciter nolente, & tamen fit, id fit Deo volente. Peccatum, etiam quatenus peccatum, non potest fieri Deo simpliciter nolente, quia est omnipotens. Ergo fit Deo volente. Resp. Negatur consequentia: quia in maiore non est sufficiens enumeratio. Deest enim, aut permittente: quia peccatum fit Deo nec simpliciter nolente, nec simpliciter volente, sed voluntarie permittente. 2. Est ambiguitas in verbo nolle: quod aliàs significat improbare & inhibere simul; & sic Deo nolente impossibile est aliquid fieri, alioqui non esset omnipotens: aliàs significat improbare tantum, non autem inhibere, sed permittere. Sic fiunt peccata Deo nolente, hoc est, improbante, sed tamen non impediente, quia fiant.
units.tr: Objection 3. What cannot come about if God simply does not will it, and yet does come about, comes about with God willing it. Sin, even as sin, cannot come about if God simply does not will it, because he is omnipotent. Therefore it comes about with God willing it. Answer. The consequence is denied, because the enumeration in the major premise is not sufficient. For the words or permitting are missing: sin comes about neither with God simply not willing it nor with God simply willing it, but with God willing voluntarily to permit it. (2) There is an ambiguity in the word not to will, which sometimes means to disapprove and to prohibit at the same time; and in that sense, if God does not will something, it is impossible for it to happen, otherwise he would not be omnipotent. At other times it means only to disapprove, but not to prohibit, and to permit. In this sense sins come about with God not willing them, that is, disapproving, yet not hindering them from coming about.

units.la: Inst. 4. Priuatio rectitudinis creaturæ est à Deo. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini: Priuatio enim in maiore significat actiuè desertionem & subtractionem gratiæ, quæ est iustissima pœna creaturæ peccantis: ideoque à Deo: in minore significat passiuè carentiam rectitudinis debitæ inesse: quæ carentia cum à creaturis vltro attrahatur & recipiatur, inque iis contra legem Dei exsistit, peccatum est, quod à Deo nec efficitur, nec intenditur. ditur. Breuiter: Priuatio est à Deo, quatenus est pœna, & non est à Deo, quatenus est peccatum seu pugnantia cum Lege in creaturis.
units.tr: Objection 4. The privation of the rectitude of a creature is from God. Answer. There are four terms. Privation in the major premise signifies actively the desertion and withdrawal of grace, which is the most just punishment of the sinning creature; and therefore it is from God. In the minor it signifies passively the lack of the rectitude which ought to be present; and this lack, since it is drawn in and received by creatures of their own accord, and exists in them against the law of God, is sin, which is neither effected nor intended by God. In brief: privation is from God insofar as it is a punishment, and it is not from God insofar as it is sin, that is, a conflict with the Law in creatures.

units.la: Inst. 5. Peccantes reguntur à Deo. At peccantium actiones sunt peccata. Ergo peccata sunt à Deo. Resp. 1. Plus est in conclusione, quàm in præmissis. Tantum enim sequitur: ergo peccata reguntur à Deo: quod verum est, quatenus nimirum actiones & motus sunt, & ad gloriam Dei diriguntur. 2. Est fallacia accidentis in minore. Actiones enim peccata sunt, quatenus ab hominibus vitiosis fiunt contra Legem, non quatenus à Deo in creaturis cientur. Malæ ergo fiunt & sunt, non ex se, sed ex accidenti, quod accidens est prauitas creaturarum, à quibus fiunt: sicut aqua pura fit sordida, fluens per canalem immundum, vinum bonum acescit in vase acido, juxta illud: Sincerum est nisi vas quodcunq; infundis, acescit.
units.tr: Objection 5. Sinners are governed by God. But the actions of sinners are sins. Therefore sins are from God. Answer. (1) There is more in the conclusion than in the premises. For it follows only that sins are governed by God, which is true, namely insofar as they are actions and motions and are directed to the glory of God. (2) In the minor there is the fallacy of accident. For actions are sins insofar as they are done by faulty men against the Law, not insofar as they are stirred up by God in creatures. They therefore become and are evil not in themselves but accidentally, and this accident is the perversity of the creatures by whom they are done; just as pure water becomes foul when it flows through a filthy channel, and good wine turns sour in a sour vessel, according to the line: Unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour.

units.la: Sic juxta similitudinem LVTHERI prius allatam, equitatio boni equitis fit claudicatio, si equus sit claudus. In his & similibus per se bona ex accidenti depravantur: ideoq; committitur paralogismus accidentis, cum à re proceditur ad id, quod cum re concurrit ex accidenti, hoc modo: Equitatio est ab equite: equitatio est claudicatio: ergo claudicatio est ab equite. Vel: Venditio Iosephi per fratres fuit peccatum: Deus venditionem eam voluit: ergo voluit peccatum.
units.tr: Thus, according to the comparison of Luther mentioned earlier, the riding of a good horseman becomes limping if the horse is lame. In such cases things that are good in themselves are corrupted by accident, and so the fallacy of accident is committed when one proceeds from a thing to what happens to concur with it accidentally, in this way: Riding is from the rider; riding is limping; therefore limping is from the rider. Or: The selling of Joseph by his brothers was a sin; God willed that selling; therefore he willed the sin.

units.la: Inst. 6. Quæ fiunt Dei prouidentiâ, eorum Deus est author. Omnia mala fiunt Dei prouidentiâ. Ergo eorum author est Deus. Resp. De malis pœnæ concedituř totum: de malis culpæ distinguenda est maior. Quæ fiunt prouidentiâ Dei effectiuè, seu ita, vt ea tanquam ex causa efficiente fluant, eorum author & effector est Deus: non autem eorum, quæ fiunt Dei prouidentiâ tantum permissiuè, seu Deo tantum permittente, determinante & ad fines optimos dirigente, vt sunt mala culpæ. Nam mala culpæ seu peccata, quatenus talia, non habent rationem boni, sicut rationem boni habent malæ pœnæ. Itaque Deus non vult peccata, nec ea probat, nec efficit, juuat vel intendit: sed tantum fieri permittit, hoc est, non impedit, quo minus fiant: vel vt in illis puniendis justitiam suam exerceat, vel vt in iis remittendis misericordiam suam ostendat. Conclusit scriptura omnia sub peccatum, vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus. Ad hoc ipsum excitaui te, vt ostendam in te potentiam meam. Ideo in definitione est, quod mala Deus fieri permittat. Permissio autem, vt præcessit, est diuinæ gratiæ subtractio, qua Deus vel non praefacit creaturæ voluntatem suam, vt secundum eam agat, vel non flectit voluntatem creaturæ, vt obediat ipsi, vt honore ipsum assiafficiat, vt secundum voluntatem Dei reuelatam agat.Cùm fictor somniorum surrexerit inter vos, non obedias illi: quia vos tentat Dominus Deus vester. Deus incitat Dauidem, vt dicat Ioabo: Vade, numera populum & Iehudam. Postea cor ipsum Dauidem percussit, vt ageret pœnitentiam. Et tamen creaturam sic desertam nihilominus rectè monet Deus, vt iustissima sua iudicia per eam exsequatur. Non minus enim bona agit per mala instrumenta, quàm per bona. Sicut enim Dei opus non fit melius à bonitate instrumenti: sic non fit peius ex malitia instrumenti. Vult Deus actiones malas, sed quatenus sunt pœnæ malorum. Omnia enim bona sunt à Deo. Omnes pœnæ sunt bonæ. Ergo à Deo, iuxta illud: Non est malum in ciuitate, quod non fecit Dominus: intelligitur malum pœnæ. De malo verò culpæ dicit Jacobus: Nemo, cùm tentatur, (hoc est, cùm ad malum sollicitatur) dicat se à Deo tentari. Tantum igitur malum pœnæ est à Deo, sicut & castigationes, & martyria piorum, quæ ipse vult & efficit, teste Iosepho ad fratres. Nunc igitur ne dolore afficiamini, neque sit ita in oculis vestris, quod vendideritis me huc; quia propter vitam misit me Deus ante vos in Ægyptum.
units.tr: Inst. 6. Whatever happens by the providence of God, God is its author. All evils happen by the providence of God. Therefore God is their author. Answer. The whole of the conclusion is conceded for evils of punishment; the major premise must be distinguished for evils of guilt. God is the author and effecter of those things that happen by his providence effectively, that is, in such a way that they flow from him as from an efficient cause. He is not the author of those things that happen by his providence only permissively, that is, with God merely permitting, determining and directing them to the best ends, as is the case with evils of guilt. For evils of guilt, or sins, as such, do not have the character of good, whereas evils of punishment do have the character of good. Thus God does not will sins, nor does he approve, effect, help or intend them; he only allows them to happen, that is, he does not prevent them from happening, either so that he may exercise his justice in punishing them, or so that he may show his mercy in pardoning them. "Scripture has concluded all things under sin, that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers" (Gal. 3:22). "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you" (Exod. 9:16). Therefore the definition says that God permits evils to happen. Permission, as said before, is the withdrawal of divine grace, by which God either does not set before the creature his will so that it may act according to it, or does not bend the creature's will so that it obeys him, honors him, and acts according to the will of God as revealed. "If a dreamer of dreams arises among you, do not obey him, for the Lord your God tests you" (Deut. 13:3). God stirs up David to say to Joab: "Go, number the people and Judah" (2 Sam. 24:1). Afterwards he struck David's own heart, so that he would repent. And yet God rightly admonishes even a creature thus abandoned, so that through it he may carry out his most just judgments. For he works good no less through evil instruments than through good ones. Just as the work of God is not made better by the goodness of the instrument, so it is not made worse by the wickedness of the instrument. God wills evil actions, but only insofar as they are punishments of the wicked. For all good things are from God, and all punishments are good; therefore they are from God, according to the saying: "Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?" (Amos 3:6); this is to be understood of the evil of punishment. But of the evil of guilt James says: "Let no one, when he is tempted (that is, when he is enticed to evil), say that he is tempted by God" (Jas. 1:13). Therefore only the evil of punishment is from God, as also the chastisements and martyrdoms of the godly, which he wills and effects, as Joseph testifies to his brothers: "Now therefore do not be grieved, nor let it be a trouble in your eyes that you sold me here; for God sent me before you into Egypt for the preservation of life" (Gen. 45:5).

units.la: Obiect. Deus non vult mortem. Resp. Non vult mortem, quatenus est cruciatus & destructio creaturæ: sed vult eam quatenus est pœna peccati; & exsecutio sui iudicij. Non audierunt vocem patris sui, quia volebat Iehova occidere eos.
units.tr: Objection: God does not will death. Answer: He does not will death insofar as it is torment and destruction of the creature, but he wills it insofar as it is the punishment of sin and the execution of his judgment. "They did not listen to the voice of their father, because the LORD willed to kill them" (1 Sam. 2:25).

units.la: Tertium sophisma de voluntatibus contradictoriis.
units.tr: The third sophism, concerning contradictory wills.

units.la: Qui idem opus lege prohibet, & voluntate arcana vult fieri, in eo sunt voluntates contradictoriæ. At in Deo non sunt voluntates contradictoriæ. Non ergo arcana voluntate vult ea, quæ lege prohibet, vt rapinas, cædes, raptus, &c. Resp.1. Conceditur totum, quatenus hæc contra Legem fiunt à creaturis, & sunt peccata. Eatenus enim Deus nec vult, nec probat, sed tantum, quatenus sunt vel motus, vel pœnæ peccatorum. 2. Ad maiorem: Contradicit sibi, qui idem opus vult, & non vult, eodem respectu seu fine. At Deus idem opus vult & non vult diuerso respectu & fine. Vult v.g. venditionem Iosephi, quatenus est occasio euectionis Iosephi, conseruationis familiæ Jacobi, & impletionis oraculi de seruitute seminis Abrahami in Ægypto. Eandem verò non vult, sed lege prohibet, & damnat, tanquam horribile parricidium, & quatenus à fratribus ex odio admittitur. Et sic de cæteris.
units.tr: One who by law forbids a work and by a hidden will wills that same work to be done has contradictory wills in that matter. But there are not contradictory wills in God. Therefore he does not by a hidden will will those things that he forbids by law, such as robberies, murders, rapes, etc. Answer 1: The whole is conceded, insofar as these things are done by creatures against the Law and are sins. For in that respect God neither wills nor approves them, but only insofar as they are either motions or punishments of sins. 2. To the major premise: One who wills and does not will the same work in the same respect or for the same end contradicts himself. But God wills and does not will the same work in different respects and for different ends. For example, he wills the selling of Joseph insofar as it is the occasion of Joseph's exaltation, of the preservation of Jacob's family, and of the fulfilment of the oracle concerning the servitude of Abraham's seed in Egypt. But that same act he does not will, but forbids and condemns, as a horrible parricide, and insofar as it is committed by the brothers out of hatred. And so with the rest.

units.la: Quartum sophisma de libertate & contingentia.
units.tr: The fourth sophism, concerning liberty and contingency.

units.la: Quod fit immutabili Dei decreto, id non fit contingenter & liberè, sed necessariò. At multa fiunt contingenter & liberè. Ergo multa non fiunt ex immutabili Dei decreto & providentia, aut tollitur libertas & contingentia. Resp. ad maiorem: Quod fit immutabili Dei decreto, id non fit contingenter: nempe respectu causae primae, seu respectu immutabilis decreti divini. Potest tamen fieri contingenter, respectu causae secundae & proximae, contingenter vel libere agentis. Contingentia enim est ordo inter causam & effectum immutabilem: sicut necessitas est ordo inter causam & effectum necessarium: & tales sunt effectus, quales causae. Potest vero idem effectus procedere ex mutabili causa, diverso respectu: ut sunt omnia, quae Deus facit per creaturas, hoc est, quorum Deus & creaturae sunt causae. Ita respectu Dei est immutabilis ordo inter causam & effectum. At respectu creaturarum est ordo mutabilis inter causam & eundem effectum. Proinde ratione Dei est necessitas: ratione creaturarum est contingentia in eodem effectu. Non igitur absurdum est, eundem effectum dici necessarium, & contingentem, diversarum causarum respectu, hoc est, respectu causae primae immutabiliter agentis necessarium, respectu vero causae proximae mutabiliter agentis contingentem. 2. Negatur, quod in maiore dicitur, non fieri vel posse fieri libere, quod fit immutabili Dei decreto. Non enim immutabilitas, sed coactio, seu non necessitas immutabilitatis, sed necessitas coactionis tollit libertatem. Deus immutabiliter ac necessario bonus est: & tamen liberrime bonus est: diaboli immutabiliter ac necessario mali sunt: & tamen liberrima voluntate mali sunt, & mala faciunt.
units.tr: What is done by the unchangeable decree of God is not done contingently and freely, but necessarily. But many things are done contingently and freely. Therefore many things are not done by the unchangeable decree and providence of God, or else liberty and contingency are abolished. Answer to the major: What is done by the unchangeable decree of God is not done contingently, namely with respect to the first cause, that is, with respect to the unchangeable divine decree. It can, however, be done contingently with respect to the second and proximate cause, which acts contingently or freely. For contingency is an order between a cause and an effect that is unchangeable, just as necessity is an order between a cause and a necessary effect; and effects are such as their causes are. Yet the same effect can proceed from a mutable cause in a different respect. This is so with all the things God does through creatures, that is, things of which God and the creatures are both causes. Thus with respect to God there is an unchangeable order between cause and effect, but with respect to creatures there is a changeable order between cause and the same effect. Accordingly, in relation to God there is necessity; in relation to creatures there is contingency in the same effect. It is therefore not absurd to say that the same effect is both necessary and contingent with respect to different causes: necessary with respect to the first cause, which acts unchangeably, but contingent with respect to the proximate cause, which acts changeably. 2. I deny what is said in the major, that what is done by the unchangeable decree of God is not done, or cannot be done, freely. For it is not immutability but compulsion, or rather not the necessity of immutability but the necessity of compulsion, that takes away liberty. God is unchangeably and necessarily good, and yet He is most freely good; the devils are unchangeably and necessarily evil, and yet they are evil and do evil by the freest will.

units.la: Quintum sophisma de utilitate mediorum.
units.tr: The fifth sophism, concerning the usefulness of means.

units.la: Quae immutabili Dei voluntate & providentia fiunt, ad ea impedienda vel promovenda frustra adhibentur media, hoc est, consilia, praecepta, doctrinae, hortationes, promissiones, minae, labores, conatus, &c. Atqui haec media non frustra adhibentur: quia a Deo mandantur. Ergo non omnia fiunt immutabili Dei consilio & providentia. Resp. Primo, negatur maior: quia posita causa prima principali, non necesse est remoueri secundam & instrumentalem, neque contra. Ratio est, quia Deus ad fines & effectus a se decretos producendos, etiam decreuit adhibere media & causas secundas, iisque uti se velle in verbo suo & naturae ordine ostendit, & nos uti jussit. Ut igitur non frustra sol quotidie oritur & occidit, neque frustra agri conseruntur, aut pluuia rigantur, aut corpora victu reficiuntur, etiamsi Deus lucem & tenebras creat, fruges e terra educit, vita & longitudinem dierum nostrorum est: ita nec frustra docentur, & ad doctrinam conformare vitam suam student homines: etiamsi & actiones & cuenc & euentus salutares non nisi à Deo proficiscuntur. Vtendum igitur est mediis. 1. Vt Deo, qui & fines & media ad fines ordinauit, & nobis præscripsit, obtemperemus: alioqui cum nostro periculo Deum tentamus. 2. Vt bona nobis promissa consequamur. 3. Vt bonam retineamus conscientiam, si vtentes mediis euentus exspectatos non obtineamus. Deinde est etiam fallacia à dicto secundum quid. Nam etiam vbi non proficitur mediis, ad id tamen prosunt, vt impios reddant inexcusabiles. Sicut Euangelium licet à Judæis non reciperetur, non tamen prædicatum est frustra, sed in testimonium ipsis.
units.tr: Those things which are done by the unchangeable will and providence of God: the means applied to hinder or promote them are applied in vain, that is, counsels, precepts, teachings, exhortations, promises, threats, labours, endeavours, etc. But these means are not applied in vain, because they are commanded by God. Therefore not all things are done by the unchangeable counsel and providence of God. Answer. First, I deny the major: because, once the first principal cause is posited, the secondary and instrumental causes need not be removed, nor the reverse. The reason is that God, in order to produce the ends and effects He has decreed, has also decreed to employ means and secondary causes, and He has shown in His word and in the order of nature that He wills us to use them, and has commanded us to use them. Just as the sun rises and sets each day not in vain, and fields are not sown in vain, or watered by rain, or bodies refreshed with food, even though God creates light and darkness, brings fruits out of the earth, and gives life and the length of our days: so too teaching is not given in vain, and men strive to shape their lives according to doctrine, even though all saving actions, desires and events proceed only from God. Therefore the means must be used. 1. So that we may obey God, who has ordained both the ends and the means to the ends and has prescribed them to us; otherwise we tempt God to our peril. 2. So that we may obtain the good things promised to us. 3. So that we may keep a good conscience, if, using the means, we do not obtain the outcome we hope for. Next, there is also a fallacy of the argument from what is said with qualification (a dicto secundum quid). For even where nothing is gained by the means, they still serve to make the impious inexcusable. Just as the Gospel, although it was not received by the Jews, was not preached in vain, but as a testimony against them.

units.la: Sextum sophisma, de præmiis & pœnis.
units.tr: The sixth sophism, concerning rewards and punishments.

units.la: Necessaria non merentur præmia, vel pœnas. Atqui opera bona merentur præmia, mala pœnas. Ergo bona & mala non eueniunt necessariò, sed mutabiliter. Resp. 1. Conceditur totum respectu causarum secundarum & proximarum, ex quibus multæ agunt mutabiliter, eoq; effectus producunt mutabiles. 2. Negatur in minore, quod bona opera mereantur præmia apud Deum, etsi mereri possunt apud homines, vt dicitur de Abrahamo: Si justificatus est operibus, habet, quod glorietur, sed non apud Deum. 3. De malis negatur maior vniuersaliter intellecta. Ad hoc enim, vt mala opera mereantur pœnas, sufficit eorum prauitas, & mala hominum voluntas, siue sint necessaria, siue non: & ipse Aristoteles hoc argumentum tractans affirmat, non excusari ebrium, si ex ebrietate peccet, & merito reprehendi ac puniri homines propter vitia corporis vel animi, quorum ipsi sunt causa, etiamsi ea vitare aut deponere non possunt, eò quod ipsi sibi sponte ea attraxerint.
units.tr: Necessary things do not merit rewards or punishments. But good works merit rewards and evil works punishments. Therefore good and evil things do not happen necessarily, but changeably. Answer. 1. I grant the whole with respect to secondary and proximate causes, of which many act changeably and so produce changeable effects. 2. I deny in the minor that good works merit rewards before God, although they can merit them before men, as is said of Abraham: If he was justified by works, he has whereof to glory, but not before God. 3. Concerning evil things I deny the major as universally understood. For it is enough, in order that evil works merit punishments, that they are depraved and that the will of men is evil, whether these things are necessary or not. And Aristotle himself, treating this argument, affirms that a drunkard is not excused if he sins through drunkenness, and that men are rightly blamed and punished for vices of body or mind of which they themselves are the cause, even if they cannot avoid or put them off, because they have voluntarily brought them upon themselves.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXVIII.
units.tr: QUESTION XXVIII.

units.la: Quid nobis prodest hæc cognitio creationis & prouidentiæ diuinæ? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What good does this knowledge of creation and of God's providence do us? ANSWER.

units.la: Vt in aduersis patientes a, in secundis grati simus b, in futuro verò optimam in Deo fidissimo Patre spem repositam habeamus c, certò scientes, nihil esse, quod nos ab eius amore abstrahat d, quandoquidem omnes creaturæ ita sunt in eius potestate, vt sine eius arbi
units.tr: That we may be patient a in adversity, thankful b in prosperity, and may have our best hope in the future laid up in God, our most faithful Father c, knowing for certain that nothing can separate us from his love d, since all creatures are so in his power that without his will they can not only do nothing, but cannot even be moved e.

units.la: {a} Rom. 4, 2. arbitrio non modo nihil agere, sed ne moueri quidem possint e.
units.tr: {a} Rom. 4, 2. will not only do nothing, but cannot even be moved e.

units.la: a Rom. 5. verf. 3. Iac. 1, 3. Psal. 39, 10. Iob 1, 21. 22. b 1 Thess. 5, 18. Deut. 8, 10. c Psal. 55, 23. Rom. 5, 4. d Rom. 8, 38. 39. e Iob. 1, 11. & 2, 6. Prouerb. 21, 1. Actor. 17, 25.
EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: Hanc doctrinam de creatione rerum, & de prouidentia Dei, credere necesse est:
units.tr: It is necessary to believe this doctrine concerning the creation of things and the providence of God, for the following reasons.

units.la: 1. Propter gloriam Dei. Negata enim creatione & prouidentia, negantur Dei attributa. His autem negatis Deus non celebratur, sed negatur. Agnoscenda est igitur prouidentia, vt tribuatur DEO gloria omnipotentiae, sapientiae, bonitatis, & justitiae in rebus omnibus creandis, conseruandis & dirigendis.
units.tr: 1. For the glory of God. For if creation and providence are denied, the attributes of God are denied. And when these are denied, God is not celebrated but denied. Providence must therefore be acknowledged, so that glory is given to God for his omnipotence, wisdom, goodness and justice in the creating, preserving and directing of all things.

units.la: 2. Propter nostram salutem & consolationem: & quidem primò, vt simus patientes in rebus aduersis. Quicquid enim consilio & voluntate Dei nobis euenit, & nobis est salutare, illud patienter debemus ferre. At omnia, etiam mala, consilio & voluntate Dei nobis eueniunt, nobisque sunt salutaria. Ergo haec debemus patienter ferre, & in omnibus paternam Dei erga nos voluntatem considerare. Secundò, vt in rebus secundis simus Deo grati pro beneficiis acceptis. A quo enim omnia bona corporalia & spiritualia, magna & parua, accipimus, ei debemus esse grati. A Deo bonorum omnium authore, omnia bona habemus. Ergo Deo grati esse, hoc est, eius beneficia agnoscere & celebrare debemus. Gratitudo enim ex veritate & justitia constat: ideo in agnitione, celebratione, & remuneratione beneficiorum consistit. Tertiò, vt spem bonam de futuris concipiamus: hoc est, certò statuamus, quia prouidentia sua Dominus nos ex malis hactenus eripuit, omnia nobis etiam in posterum profutura ad salutem, neque vnquam Deum nos ita deserturum, vt percamus. Breuiter: Fines doctrinae de prouidentia sunt 1. Gloria Dei. 2. Patientia nostra in aduersis. 3. Gratitudo in secundis. 4. Spes de futuris.
units.tr: 2. For our salvation and consolation. And indeed, first, that we may be patient in adversity. For whatever happens to us by the counsel and will of God, and is salutary for us, we ought to bear patiently. But all things, even evils, happen to us by the counsel and will of God, and are salutary for us. Therefore we ought to bear these things patiently, and in all things to consider the fatherly will of God towards us. Second, that in prosperity we may be grateful to God for the benefits received. For we ought to be grateful to him from whom we receive all good things, bodily and spiritual, great and small. We have all good things from God, the author of all good. Therefore we ought to be grateful to God, that is, to acknowledge and celebrate his benefits. For gratitude consists of truth and justice; and so it lies in acknowledging, celebrating and repaying benefits. Third, that we may conceive good hope concerning the future: that is, that we may firmly establish that, since the Lord by his providence has so far rescued us from evils, all things will also in future turn out for our salvation, and that God will never so forsake us that we perish. In brief: the ends of the doctrine of providence are (1) the glory of God; (2) our patience in adversity; (3) gratitude in prosperity; (4) hope concerning the future.

units.la: Ex his patet, omnis religionis & pietatis fundamenta conuelli, si non statuatur prouidentia Dei: quia 1. in aduersis nunquam erimus patientes, nisi sciamus à Deo Patre nostro ea nobis immitti. 2. Nunquam erimus pro beneficiis grati, nisi agnoscamus, ea diuinitus nobis dari. 3. Nunquam habebimus spem bonam & certam de futuris, nisi faciamus voluntatem Dei praesentem, eamque de nobis & omnibus electis seruandis immutabilem tabilem esse persuasi simus. Recte igitur Augustinus: Si, inquit, providentia Dei rebus humanis non præsidet, nihil est amplius de religione satagendum.
units.tr: From these things it is plain that all the foundations of religion and piety are overturned if the providence of God is not maintained. For (1) in adversity we will never be patient unless we know that these things are sent upon us by God our Father; (2) we will never be grateful for benefits unless we acknowledge that they are given to us by divine providence; (3) we will never have good and certain hope concerning the future unless we are persuaded that God's present will is in effect, and that it is unchangeable concerning us and concerning the preservation of all the elect. Rightly therefore Augustine says: "If the providence of God does not preside over human affairs, there is nothing further to be concerned about in religion."

units.la: DE DEO FILIO.
units.tr: CONCERNING GOD THE SON.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXIX. Quare Filius Dei appellatur IESVS, hoc est, Saluator?
units.tr: QUESTION 29. Why is the Son of God called JESUS, that is, Saviour?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Quia nos saluat ab omnibus peccatis nostris {a}: nec vlla salus vel peti aliunde debet, vel alibi reperiri potest {b}.
units.tr: Because he saves us from all our sins; and no salvation ought to be sought elsewhere, nor can it be found anywhere else.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: In secunda parte symboli, quæ nunc sequitur, de mediatore agitur. Doctrina autem de Mediatore constat duabus partibus: una de mediatoris persona, altera de eius officio. De persona sua articuli duo: Et in Iesum Christum, Filium eius unigenitum, Dominum nostrum: qui conceptus est de Spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria virgine. De officio agunt quatuor articuli sequentes, usque ad tertiam symboli partem, quæ est de Spiritu sancto. Duæ autem sunt officij partes: humiliatio seu meritum, & glorificatio seu efficacia. Nam humiliatione Christus est meritus, glorificatione est efficax. De humiliatione agit articulus quartus: Passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus, descendit ad inferos. De glorificatione quintus & sextus: Tertia die resurrexit à mortuis: ascendit ad cœlos, sedet ad dexteram Dei Patris omnipotentis. Septimus de aduentu, pertinet ad consummationem glorificationis, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: The second part of the creed, which now follows, deals with the Mediator. The doctrine of the Mediator consists of two parts: one concerning the person of the Mediator, the other concerning his office. Two articles concern his person: And in Jesus Christ, his only begotten Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary. The following four articles deal with his office, up to the third part of the creed, which concerns the Holy Spirit. The office has two parts: humiliation, or merit, and glorification, or efficacy. For by humiliation Christ merited, and by glorification he is effective. The fourth article treats of humiliation: Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead and buried, descended into hell. The fifth and sixth treat of glorification: The third day he rose from the dead; he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty. The seventh, concerning his coming, belongs to the completion of glorification, when God will be all in all.

units.la: Hinc apparet summa sapientia articulos istos esse conscriptos. Sunt enim eleganter ad quæstionem de Mediatore accommodati. Prior pars officij humiliatio hos habet gradus: passus, crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus, descendit ad inferos. Ita paulatim à minoribus ad majora descendimus: ad extremam scilicet humiliationem, quæ fuit descensus ad inferos. Altera pars officij glorificatio contra paulatim ascendit à minori gloria ad maiorem, vsq; ad supremum gradum, qui est sessio ad dexteram Dei. Idem ordo in eadem sapientia fuit in prima symboli parte: & conspicitur quoq; in tertia, in qua pulcherrimo ordine recensentur beneficia Christi, quæ nobis per Spiritum sanctum applicantur, & est tanquam fructus præcedentium articulorum. Differt autem officium ab ipsis beneficiis, sicut causa & effectus, vel sicut antecedens & consequens. Beneficia sunt res partæ officio: Officium est ipsa impetratio rerum & earum collatio: sicut aliud est pecunia, aliud actus dandi pecuniam.
units.tr: From this it is clear that these articles were composed with the highest wisdom. For they are elegantly fitted to the question about the Mediator. The first part of the office, humiliation, has these stages: suffered, crucified, dead, buried, descended into hell. Thus we descend gradually from lesser things to greater, namely to the lowest humiliation, which was the descent into hell. The other part of the office, glorification, on the contrary rises gradually from lesser glory to greater, up to the highest step, which is sitting at the right hand of God. The same order is found in the same wisdom in the first part of the creed, and it is also seen in the third, in which the benefits of Christ, which are applied to us through the Holy Spirit, are recounted in a most beautiful order, and which is as it were the fruit of the preceding articles. Now the office differs from the benefits themselves as cause and effect, or as antecedent and consequent. The benefits are the things obtained by the office; the office is the very procuring of these things and their bestowal, just as money is one thing and the act of giving money is another.

units.la: Et in Iesum [scilicet credo. Repetendum est verbum: quia sicut credimus in Deum Patrem, sic etiam credimus in Filium Dei Patris; juxta dicta: Creditis in Deum, et iam in me credite. Credite mihi, quod ego sum in Patre, & Pater in me. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem misit ille. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam. Ut omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem. Hoc est certum argumentum verae deitatis Filij. Fides enim est cultus soli Deo debitus.
units.tr: And in Jesus [namely I believe. The verb must be repeated, because just as we believe in God the Father, so we also believe in the Son of God the Father; according to the sayings: You believe in God, believe also in me. Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me. I and the Father are one. This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. He who believes in the Son has eternal life. That all may honour the Son, just as they honour the Father. This is a certain proof of the true deity of the Son. For faith is worship due to God alone.

units.la: Porrò cum de nomine Iesu hic quæritur, non tantum de etymologia quæritur, quid nomen significet, sed præcipuè de officio mediatoris, quod hoc nomine significatur. Significat autem Iesus (græcè ιησους, hebraicè Iehoschuah sive Ieschuah) salvatorem seu authorem salutis: quod nomen impositum ipse Deus mediatori in novo testamento. Vera etymologia nominis est tradita ab angelo, dicente: Quia salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis ipsorum. Ab officio igitur Filius Dei appellatus est Iesus, hoc est, salvator, quia est noster Salvator, quia nos liberat a malo culpæ & pœnæ, & quidem solus, & perfectissimè nos salvos facit. Salutem autem, quam affert, est justitia & vita æterna. Hoc ex ipso nomine colligitur, quia nomen non habet sine re, sed propter officium.
units.tr: Furthermore, when the name Jesus is inquired into here, the question is not only about the etymology, what the name means, but especially about the office of the Mediator, which is signified by this name. Now Jesus (in Greek [ιησους], in Hebrew Iehoschuah or Ieschuah) signifies a saviour or author of salvation; this name was given to the Mediator by God himself in the New Testament. The true etymology of the name was given by the angel, saying: For he will save his people from their sins. The Son of God is therefore called Jesus, that is, Saviour, from his office, because he is our Saviour, because he frees us from the evil of guilt and of punishment, and indeed he alone, and makes us perfectly safe. The salvation he brings is righteousness and eternal life. This is gathered from the name itself, because the name does not exist without the reality, but on account of the office.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Etiam multi alij habuerunt hoc nomen Iesus, ut Josua dux, Jesus Pontifex, &c. Ergo ex hoc nomine nihil potest colligi. Resp.
