The glory, majesty and excellence of gifts will be for us not ordinary, but chiefly from this, that we shall condemn the enemies, that is, in condemning them we shall subscribe to the judgement of God. We shall have a kingdom, I say, not over the Church, but over all the remaining creatures. Christ alone, however, holds rule with full right both over the whole Church and over all creatures. You will sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel. Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? 3. He himself conquered the enemies by his own power; but we conquer the enemies in him and through him, that is, by his grace and help. Take courage, I have overcome the world. 4. He himself rules the Church with the sceptre of his Spirit and Word, moving hearts and restoring in us the lost image. This belongs to Christ alone. We cannot give the Holy Spirit; we are only ministers and administrators of the outward voice and rites, just as the Baptist said: I indeed baptise you with water; but he who comes after me will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. Who then is Paul? Who is Apollos? They are ministers through whom you believed, and as the Lord gave to each.

units.la: Vsus ergo huius doctrinæ ingens est: 1. Ad consolationem: quod per fidem sumus Christo insiti, tanquam membra capiti, ut perpetuò ab eo gestemur, regamur & viuificemur: & quod vocationis suæ communicatione fecit nos Deo & patri suo prophetas, sacerdotes & reges. Hæc est ineffabilis Christianorum dignitas. 2. Ad commonefactionem. Cùm enim omnes simus doctores & prophetæ Dei, ergo perpetuò eum celebremus: cum sacerdotes, ergo nos totos in hostiam viuam ei offeramus: cùm reges, ergo alacres pugnemus contra hostes, ut cum eo regnemus.
units.tr: The use of this doctrine, therefore, is great: 1. for consolation: that through faith we are grafted into Christ, as members into the head, so that we are continually borne, ruled and quickened by him; and that by sharing his calling he has made us prophets, priests and kings to God and his Father. This is the unspeakable dignity of Christians. 2. for admonition. Since we are all teachers and prophets of God, let us therefore always praise him; since we are priests, let us offer ourselves wholly to him as a living sacrifice; since we are kings, let us fight eagerly against the enemies, so that we may reign with him.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXXIII.
units.tr: QUESTION XXXIII.

units.la: Quam ob causam Christus vocatur Filius Dei unigenitus, cùm nos quoq; simus filij Dei? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Why is Christ called the only-begotten Son of God, when we too are sons of God? ANSWER.

units.la: Quia solus Christus est coæternus & naturalis æterni Patris Filius 4: nos autem propter eum ex gratia adoptati sumus b.
units.tr: Because Christ alone is the coeternal and natural Son of the eternal Father 4; but we have been adopted through him by grace b.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hic continetur locus de deitate Filij. In quæstione talis est obiectio: Qui est vnigenitus, non habet fratres. Christus habet fratres. Nam & nos sumus filij Dei. Ergo non est vnigenitus. Resp. distinctione filiationis Christi & nostræ: aliter Christus, aliter nos sumus filij Dei. Christus est Filius Dei vnigenitus, naturalis, proprius, &c. Nos sumus filij Dei propter Christum, ex gratia à Patre adoptati.
units.tr: This passage contains the doctrine of the Son's deity. The objection in the question runs thus: whoever is the only-begotten has no brothers; Christ has brothers, for we too are sons of God; therefore he is not the only-begotten. Answer: by distinguishing the sonship of Christ from ours. Christ is the only-begotten, natural, proper Son of God, and so on. We are sons of God because of Christ, adopted by the Father through grace.

units.la: Vt hæc magis fiant perspicua, paucis explicandum est: quinam, & quot modis dicantur filij: & sic deinde, quinam sint, & vocentur filij Dei.
units.tr: So that these points may become clearer, we must explain briefly who and how many kinds of sons there are, and then who they are and who are called sons of God.

units.la: Filij sunt & dicuntur, vel nati filij, vel adoptiui.
units.tr: Sons are either begotten sons or adopted sons.

units.la: Nati filij sunt, qui simul coeperunt esse, & filij esse. Et hi aut sunt nati ex parentibus aut nati per gratiam Filij.
units.tr: Begotten sons are those who began to exist and to be sons at the same moment. These are either born of parents or born through the grace of the Son.

units.la: Nati ex parentibus filij proprie dicuntur naturales, quibus essentia suorum parentum communicatur, eaque vel ex parte, vel tota. Ex parte nobis communicatur essentia & natura nostrorum parentum, ex quibus nascimur. Tota Christo à Patre secundum diuinitatem communicata est essentia diuina. Vt igitur nos sumus naturales filij parentum nostrorum: ita Christus secundum diuinitatem suam est naturalis Filius Dei, eiusdem essentiæ & naturæ cum Patre, ex cuius substantia modo inenarrabili genitus est ab æterno. Sicut Pater vitam habet in seipso, sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in seipso. Communicauit igitur ei Pater vitam, qua ipse per se viuit, & omnes creaturas viuificat, quæ vita est ipsa vna & æterna Deitas.
units.tr: Sons born of parents are properly called natural sons, to whom the essence of their parents is communicated, either in part or in whole. In part: the essence and nature of our parents, from whom we are born, is communicated to us. In whole: the divine essence was communicated to Christ by the Father according to his deity. So just as we are the natural sons of our parents, Christ according to his deity is the natural Son of God, of the same essence and nature as the Father, from whose substance he was begotten from eternity in an unspeakable manner. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself. The Father therefore communicated to him the life by which he himself lives and quickens all creatures, which life is the one and eternal Deity itself.

units.la: Nati per gratiam filij sunt, qui simul quidem coeperunt esse, & filij esse: sed quod sunt filij, id habent vel per gratiam creationis, vel per gratiam conceptionis de Spiritu sancto, & vnionis cum λόγῳ.
units.tr: Sons born through grace are those who began at the same time to exist and to be sons, but what makes them sons they have either through the grace of creation, or through the grace of conception by the Holy Spirit and union with the [λόγῳ] Word.

units.la: Per gratiam creationis filij Dei sunt angeli, Adam ante lapsum: quia Deus eos creauit, vt haberet eos pro filiis, & ij rursus Deum agnoscerent & celebrarent, vt benignum Patrem. Dicuntur autem hi nati per gratiam filij improprie quidem, sed eatenus tamen, quatenus coeperunt simul & filij esse & existere.
units.tr: Angels and Adam before the fall are sons of God by the grace of creation, because God created them so that he might have them as sons, and so that they in turn might acknowledge and praise God as a kind Father. These are called sons born through grace, improperly indeed, but only insofar as they began at once both to be sons and to exist.

units.la: Per gratiam conceptionis è Spiritu sancto, & vnionis cum λόγῳ, Filius Dei est solus Christus secundum humanam naturam: quia secundum hanc fuit filius Dei per gratiam, statim eo momento, quo coepit homo esse & nasci: idque ideo, quia virtute Spiritus sancti, solus ab omni labe purus, ex virginis substantia natus est, & personaliter cum λόγῳ vnitus. Adoptati seu adoptiui filij sunt, qui non simul coeperunt esse, & esse filij, sed qui jam erant, antequam adoptarentur, qui aliquando fuerunt non filij, qui exstiterunt, antequam essent filij. Facti autem sunt filij tantum voluntate adoptantis eos, & donantis jure filiorum, ita ut sint eo loco, ac si essent ex eo nati. Sic Adam post lapsum: & omnes electi renati sunt filij Dei adoptiui, propter Christum Filium naturalem adoptati. Antequam vero adoptarentur, erant filiij ræ.
units.tr: By the grace of conception from the Holy Spirit and union with the [λόγῳ] Word, the Son of God is Christ alone according to his human nature, because according to this nature he was the Son of God by grace from the very moment he began to be a man and to be born. This is because, by the power of the Holy Spirit, he alone, pure from all stain, was born of the substance of the virgin and was personally united with the Word. Adopted or adoptive sons are those who did not begin to exist and to be sons at the same time, but who already existed before they were adopted; they once were not sons, but existed before they were sons. They became sons only by the will of the one who adopts them and grants them the right of sons, so that they stand in the same position as if they had been born of him. So Adam after the fall, and all the elect who are reborn, are adoptive sons of God, adopted for the sake of Christ the natural Son. Before they were adopted, however, they were children of wrath.

units.la: Ex his patet manifeste, tum, quomodo nos filij Dei simus, nempe adoptione: tum, quomodo Christus Filius Dei sit vnigenitus, nempe dupliciter, 1. Secundum diuinitatem suam: quia secundum hanc genitus est ab æterno de Patris essentia. Vidimus gloriam eius quasi vnigeniti à Patre. 2. Secundum humanitatem aliquatenus, quia etiam secundum hanc tali modo est genitus, quali nunquam quisquam alius, ex virgine nimirum incorrupta, vi Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: From these points it is clear, first, how we are sons of God, namely by adoption; and second, how Christ is the Son of God, the only-begotten, namely in two ways. 1. According to his deity, because according to this he was begotten from eternity from the essence of the Father. We have seen his glory, as of the only-begotten from the Father. 2. According to his humanity, to some extent, because also according to this he was begotten in a way that no one else ever was, namely from the incorrupt virgin by the power of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Dicitur idem primogenitus secundum diuinitatem, tempore & dignitate tantum, idque propter modum genituræ miraculosum & peculiarem, & propter dona, quibus antecellit omnes. Jus primogenituræ erat, habere duas partes ex hæreditate, cum reliqui tantum haberent singuli vnam. Causa autem juris illius erat officium. Reliquis enim primogenitus præerat, & eos gubernabat. Primogenitus omnis creaturæ. Primogenitus ex mortuis, vt in omnibus primas teneat.
units.tr: The same Christ is called the firstborn according to his deity, in time and in dignity only, and this on account of the miraculous and peculiar manner of his begetting, and because of the gifts by which he surpasses all. The right of the firstborn was to have two portions of the inheritance, while the others each had only one. The reason for this right was the office: the firstborn was set over the rest and governed them. The firstborn of every creature. The firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the first place.

units.la: Filius Dei proprius dicitur, quia genitus, non adoptatus. proprio Filio non pepercit.
units.tr: He is called the proper Son of God because he was begotten, not adopted. He did not spare his own Son.

units.la: Notandæ etiam sunt formulæ rectè loquendi de filiatione Christi & nostra. Christus secundum diuinitatem dicitur Filius Dei naturalis, quia de essentia Patris ab æterno genitus. Secundum humanitatem non dicitur Filius naturalis, sed per gratiam, non quidem adoptionis, sed conceptionis de Spiritu sancto, & vnionis cum λόγῳ. Ratio illius est: quia secundum humanitatem non est genitus ex essentia Patris. Ratio huius: quia non est sanctus filius ex non filio, sed quo momento coepit esse, coepit etiam filius esse. Angeli enim dicuntur filij Dei, non naturales, sed per gratiam creationis, vt & homo ante lapsum. Renati in hac vita sunt filij gratiâ, non creationis, sed adoptionis. Habet igitur se gratia ad adoptionem, tanquam genus ad speciem. Sunt enim gratiæ tres, vel quatuor gradus, tanquam species: nempe creationis, conceptionis è Spiritu sancto, vnionis cum λόγῳ, & adoptionis, vt liquet ex prius dictis.
units.tr: We must also note the correct ways of speaking about the sonship of Christ and of ourselves. Christ according to his deity is called the natural Son of God, because he was begotten from eternity from the essence of the Father. According to his humanity he is not called a natural Son, but a son through grace, not indeed of adoption, but of conception by the Holy Spirit and union with the [λόγῳ] Word. The reason for the first is that according to his humanity he was not begotten from the essence of the Father. The reason for the second is that he was not made a son out of a non-son, but from the moment he began to exist, he also began to be a son. For angels are called sons of God, not natural sons, but through the grace of creation, as was also man before the fall. Those reborn in this life are sons by grace, not of creation, but of adoption. Thus grace stands to adoption as genus to species. There are three or four degrees of grace, as species: namely of creation, of conception by the Holy Spirit, of union with the [λόγῳ] Word, and of adoption, as is clear from what has been said before.

units.la: Typus filiorum Dei.
units.tr: The type of the sons of God.

units.la: Filij Dei sunt vel Nati Ex parentibus per generationem, qui proprie sunt naturales, quibus communicatur essentia parentum suorum Tota: vt Christo secundum diuinitatem communicatur essentia diuina Patris tota. Ex parte: vt nobis essentia parentum nostrorum communicatur tantum ex parte. Ex Deo per gratiam creationis: vt Angeli. Adam ante lapsum. conceptionis è Spiritu sancto, & vnionis cum λόγῳ: vt Christus secundum humanam naturam. Adoptati A Deo, vt Adam ante lapsum: omnes electi renati. ab hominibus, &c.
units.tr: The sons of God are either those born of parents by generation, who are properly natural, and to whom the whole essence of their parents is communicated, as the whole divine essence of the Father is communicated to Christ according to his divinity; or they are so only in part, as the essence of our parents is communicated to us only in part; or they are sons of God by the grace of creation, as the angels and Adam before the fall; or by conception from the Holy Spirit and union with the Word [λόγῳ], as Christ according to his human nature; or they are adopted by God, as Adam before the fall, and all the elect who are reborn, by men, etc.

units.la: Alius typus.
units.tr: Another type.

units.la: Filius Dei Vnus est naturalis, per æternam generationem: λόγῳ æterni Patris. Alij omnes sunt per gratiam Creationis: vt Angeli, Adam ante lapsum. Conceptionis è Spiritu sancto: Vnionis cum λόγῳ: vt Christus secundum humanitatem. Adoptionis: vt Adam post lapsum: Omnes electi renati.
units.tr: The only Son of God is natural, by the eternal generation of the eternal Father's Word [λόγῳ]. All others are sons by the grace of creation, as the angels and Adam before the fall; by conception from the Holy Spirit and union with the Word [λόγῳ], as Christ according to his humanity; or by adoption, as Adam after the fall and all the elect who are reborn.

units.la: Ex his jam clarius patet solutio obiectionis. Qui habet fratres, non est vnigenitus. Christus habet fratres. Ergo non est vnigenitus. Resp. Per distinctionem maioris : non est vnigenitus, qui habet fratres, nempe eiusdem generationis, & naturæ. At Christus habet fratres non eiusdem generationis, aut naturæ, hoc est, non genitos ex substantia Patris, sed tantum à Patre ex gratia adoptatos.
units.tr: From these things the solution of the objection is now more clearly evident. He who has brethren is not the only-begotten. Christ has brethren. Therefore he is not the only-begotten. Reply. By distinguishing the major: he is not the only-begotten who has brethren of the same generation and nature. But Christ has brethren not of the same generation or nature, that is, not begotten from the substance of the Father, but only adopted by the Father through grace.

units.la: Inst. Quomodo igitur sumus fratres Christi? Resp. Fraternitas nostra cum Christo consistit in his quatuor. 1. In similitudine naturæ humanæ: & quia nati sumus ex eodem patre Adamo. 2. In amore eius fraterna erga nos. 3. In conformitate cum ipso, quæ in perfecta justitia & beatitudine consistit. 4. In consummatione beneficiorum.
units.tr: Objection. How then are we brethren of Christ? Reply. Our brotherhood with Christ consists in these four things. 1. In the likeness of human nature, and because we were born from the same father, Adam. 2. In his brotherly love toward us. 3. In conformity to him, which consists in perfect righteousness and blessedness. 4. In the fulfilment of benefits.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Qui habet generationem dissimilem generationi aliorum filiorum, is eius respectu dicitur vnigenitus. Christus secundum humanitatem habet generationem dissimilem generationi aliorum filiorum: quia solus est conceptus de Spiritu sancto, natus ex virgine. Ergo respectu huius generationis ex virgine dicitur vnigenitus secundum humanitatem, non autem propter generationem aliquam æternam ex Patre secundum diuinitatem. Respond. Minor ludit fallacia à secundum quid, vt simpliciter: quasi Christus tantum secundum humanitatem dissimilis sit generationi aliorum fratrum: quod est falsum. Nam etiam secundum diuinitatem generatione est longè dissimillimus. Secundum hanc enim est vnigenitus, & quidem solus naturalis Patris Filius, nobis tota specie seu natura dissimilis. Secundum illam verò natus est ex matre nobis non specie vel natura humana, sed tantum miraculosæ conceptionis modo dissimilis. Etsi igitur etiam respectu huius dici potest vnigenitus Dei Filius: tamen in scriptura & in symbolo proprie dicitur vnigenitus, non secundum humanam, sed secundum diuinam naturam. Nam secundum humanam naturam habet multos fratres eiusdem naturæ: secundum diuinam vero nullos habet fratres, sed solus est Dei Patris naturalis Filius, diuinitate μονογενής. De nullo enim alio dicitur, quod Pater dederit ei vitam habere in semetipso: & quod in ipso habitet omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Ideo expresse dicitur vnigenitus à Patre, non à matre. Et ipsa vox μονογενής proprie respicit naturam, non conceptionem miraculosam, & significat solum genitum, non singulari modo genitum.
units.tr: Objection 2. He who has a generation unlike the generation of other sons is called only-begotten with respect to it. Christ according to his humanity has a generation unlike the generation of other sons, because he alone was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of a virgin. Therefore with respect to this generation from the virgin he is called only-begotten according to his humanity, and not on account of any eternal generation from the Father according to his divinity. Reply. The minor plays a fallacy of from a certain respect as if it were absolute: as if Christ were unlike the generation of the other brethren only according to his humanity, which is false. For even according to his divinity he is most utterly unlike them in generation. For according to this he is the only-begotten, and indeed the only natural Son of the Father, wholly unlike us in species or nature. But according to that other nature he was born of a mother, unlike us not in human species or nature, but only in the manner of a miraculous conception. Therefore, although he may also be called the only-begotten Son of God with respect to this, yet in Scripture and in the creed he is properly called only-begotten not according to his human but according to his divine nature. For according to his human nature he has many brethren of the same nature; but according to his divine nature he has no brethren, but is alone the natural Son of God the Father, only-begotten [μονογενής] in divinity. For it is said of no other that the Father has given him to have life in himself, and that in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Hence he is expressly called only-begotten of the Father, not of the mother. And the word only-begotten [μονογενής] properly refers to nature, not to the miraculous conception, and signifies only begotten, not begotten in a singular manner.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Omnis filius est vel naturalis, vel adoptiuus. Christus secundum humanitatem non est naturalis Dei filius: Ergo est adoptiuus. Resp. Non est sufficiens enumeratio in maiore. Potest enim quis esse filius Dei gratia sine adoptione, vt patet ex prius dictis.
units.tr: Objection 3. Every son is either natural or adopted. Christ according to his humanity is not the natural Son of God; therefore he is adopted. Reply. The enumeration in the major is not sufficient. For someone can be a son of God by grace without adoption, as is clear from what has been said above.

units.la: Jam quid est, Credo in Iesum Filium Dei vnigenitum? Resp. 1. Credo Iesum esse Filium Dei vnigenitum, hoc est, naturalem, proprium, non habentem fratres, natum de substantia Patris ab aeterno, verum Deum de vero Deo. Sed hoc non est satis. Nam etiam diaboli hoc credunt, & contremiscunt. Itaque addendum est 2. Credo, mihi, hoc est, in meam salutem eum esse Filium Dei vnigenitum: seu, credo eum ideo esse natura Filium, vt me faciat filium adoptione, mihi & omnibus electis communicet jus & dignitatem filiorum Dei, sicut dicitur: Vidimus gloriam eius, tanquam gloriam vnigeniti a Patre: & his, qui credunt in nomen eius, dedit hanc dignitatem, vt filij Dei fiant. Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco. Dilexit nos in illo dilecto.
units.tr: Now what is meant by I believe in Jesus Christ the only-begotten Son of God? Reply. 1. I believe that Jesus is the only-begotten Son of God, that is, natural, proper, having no brethren, born of the substance of the Father from eternity, true God of true God. But this is not enough. For the devils also believe this, and tremble. Therefore it must be added: 2. I believe, for me, that is, that he is the only-begotten Son of God for my salvation; or, I believe that he is by nature the Son for this purpose, that he may make me a son by adoption, and may communicate to me and to all the elect the right and dignity of the sons of God, as it is said: We have seen his glory, as the glory of the only-begotten of the Father; and to those who believe in his name he gave this dignity, that they should become sons of God. This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. He loved us in the beloved.

units.la: DE DEITATE CHRISTI.
units.tr: On the Deity of Christ.

units.la: Quoniam vero doctrina haec de vnigenito Filio Dei fundamentum est nostrae salutis, quod ab haereticis variè depravatur & impugnatur, ideo vberius hoc loco est explicanda & confirmanda. Quatuor vero de deitate filij praecipuè quaeruntur. I. An in Christo praeter corpus & animam sit & fuerit aliquod ὑφισταμένον. II. An sit persona distincta a Patre & Spiritu sancto. III. An æqualis Patri & Spiritui sancto. IV. An ὁμοούσιον vtrique.
units.tr: Since this doctrine concerning the only-begotten Son of God is the foundation of our salvation, and since it is variously distorted and attacked by heretics, it must be explained and confirmed here at greater length. Four main questions are asked about the deity of the Son: I. Whether in Christ, besides the body and soul, there is and has been some subsisting thing [ὑφισταμένον]. II. Whether he is a person distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit. III. Whether he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit. IV. Whether he is of one substance [ὁμοούσιον] with them.

units.la: Totidem igitur capita demonstranda sunt contra diversos haereticos.
units.tr: There are therefore as many points to be demonstrated against the various heretics.

units.la: 1. Quod Christus natus ex virgine etiam ante & praeter carnem sit & fuerit ὑφισταμένον.
units.tr: 1. That Christ, born of the virgin, is and has been a subsisting thing [ὑφισταμένον] even before and apart from the flesh.

units.la: 2. Quod sit persona distincta a Patre & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: 2. That he is a person distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 3. Quod sit ἴσον, æqualis vtrique.
units.tr: 3. That he is equal [ἴσον] to both, equal to them.

units.la: 4. Quod eidem sit ὁμοούσιον, consubstantialis.
units.tr: 4. That he is of one substance [ὁμοούσιον] with them, consubstantial.

units.la: Est autem duplex via colligendi argumenta pro divinitate Filij, vt & Spiritus sancti: vel juxta ordinem Bibliorum: haec est prolixior: vel secundum certas classes argumentorum: haec est breuior, & magis juuat memoriam. Ideo nos eam hic sequemur.
units.tr: There are two ways of gathering arguments for the divinity of the Son, and likewise of the Holy Spirit: either according to the order of the books of the Bible, which is the longer way, or according to certain classes of arguments, which is the shorter and better aids the memory. Therefore we shall follow the latter here.

units.la: I. Quod Filius Dei λόγος sit & fuerit ὑπostatic ante & prater carnem assumtam.
units.tr: I. That the Son of God, the λόγος, is and was a hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] before and apart from the assumed flesh.

units.la: Hæc thesis probanda est contra veteres & recentes hæreticos, Ebionem, Cerinthum, Samosatenum, Photinum, Seruetum, Socinum, & alios. Classes argumentorum, quibus probatur ὑπαρξις λόγου ante& præter carnem, possunt constitui octo vel nouem.
units.tr: This thesis must be proved against the ancient and recent heretics: Ebion, Cerinthus, Samosatenus, Photinus, Servetus, Socinus, and others. The classes of arguments by which the existence [ὕπαρξις] of the λόγος before and apart from the flesh is proved can be set up as eight or nine.

units.la: Classis I. Ad hanc pertinent ea loca scripturæ, quæ expresse ponunt in Christo duas naturas: & quibus describitur λόγος, quod sit factus homo, sit manifestatus in carne, assumserit carnem, &c. Λόγος factus est caro. Assumsit semen Abrahæ. Deus manifestatus est in carne. Omnis spiritus, qui non confitetur Iesum Christum venisse in carnem, ex Deo non est. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui de cœlo descendit, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo. Ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum. Quoniam pueri participes erant carnis & sanguinis, ipse particeps factus est eorundem consimiliter. Antequam Abraham esset, ego sum. Ergo alia natura est, quæ apparuit in carne, quæ assumsit carnem, quæ de cœlo descendit, & in hunc mundum veniens, particeps facta est carnis & sanguinis, & fuit ante Abrahamum: alia item natura, quæ assumta est, in quam venit, & in qua apparuit. Assumens enim & assumtum non sunt idem. Quia igitur λόγος assumsit naturam humanam, alius ab ea sit oportet, qui & ante eam assumtam exstiterit, nec in eam sit conuersus, sed habeat ὑπαρξιν ab assumta carne diuersam ac distinctam. Argumentum tale est: Assumens est ante assumtum. De λόγῳ seu Filio dicitur, quod assumserit carnem, factus sit caro. Ergo Filius λόγος fuit ante carnem assumtam. Maior est manifesta: minor patet ex dictis.
units.tr: Class 1. To this belong those passages of Scripture which expressly place two natures in Christ, and which describe the λόγος as having been made man, as manifested in the flesh, as having assumed flesh, and so on. "The Word was made flesh." "He assumed the seed of Abraham." "God was manifested in the flesh." "Every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God." "No one has ascended into heaven, but he who came down from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven." "For this I was born, and for this I came into the world." "Since the children were partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same." "Before Abraham was, I am." Therefore there is another nature which appeared in the flesh, which assumed flesh, which came down from heaven and, coming into this world, became a partaker of flesh and blood, and which was before Abraham; and likewise there is another nature which was assumed, into which he came, and in which he appeared. For the one who assumes and the thing assumed are not the same. Since, therefore, the λόγος assumed human nature, he must be other than that nature, and must have existed before that nature was assumed, and not have been changed into it, but must have a existence distinct and different from the assumed flesh. The argument runs thus: the assumer is before the assumed. Of the λόγος, or Son, it is said that he assumed flesh and was made flesh. Therefore the Son, the λόγος, was before the flesh was assumed. The major premise is plain; the minor is clear from what has been said.

units.la: Pertinent huc etiam ea loca, quibus λόγος, quia assumsit, discernitur à carne, quam assumsit. Filius factus ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem, declaratus Filius Dei potenter secundum spiritum sanctificationis. Ex quibus est Christus secundum carnem, Deus benedictus in secula. Christus mortificatus carne, vivificatus spiritu. Est igitur aliquid in Christo, quod non est ex semine Dauidis & ex patribus, quod non est mortificatum. Destruite templum hoc, & tribus diebus erigam illud. Est igitur alia natura, quæ destructam suscitat, nempe, λόγος, qui vocatur à Johanne μονογενὴς υἱὸς.
units.tr: Here also belong those passages in which the λόγος, because he assumed, is distinguished from the flesh which he assumed. "Made of the seed of David according to the flesh, declared to be the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of sanctification." "Of whom is Christ according to the flesh, God blessed for ever." "Christ put to death in the flesh, made alive by the Spirit." There is therefore something in Christ which is not of the seed of David and of the fathers, and which was not put to death. "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." There is therefore another nature which raises up what was destroyed, namely the λόγος, who is called by John the only-begotten Son [μονογενὴς υἱὸς].

units.la: Obiect. 1. λόγος, hoc est, iste prædicator Iesus factus est caro, hoc est, fuit homo mortalis. R. Corruptela impudens. λόγος dicitur fuisse Deus, antequam assumeret carnem, fuisse Deus, per eum omnia facta esse, in sua venisse, illuminare omnem hominem venienvenientem in hunc mundum, tandem factus esse caro, & omnes ex plenitudine eius accepisse. Ergo hic λόγος[?] fuit ante omnes homines venientes in hunc mundum, & ipse Adam, Abraham, Moses per eum sunt illuminati, acceperunt ex eius plenitudine, &c. Ego sum panis ille vitae, qui de caelo descendit. Christus per spiritum profectus temporibus Noe, spiritibus qui sunt in carcere olim im-morigeris praedicauit. Sed caro praedicatoris Jesu non descendit de caelo, nec fuit temporibus Noe.
units.tr: Objection 1. The λόγος, that is, this preacher Jesus, was made flesh, that is, was a mortal man. Answer: this is a shameless corruption. The λόγος is said to have been God before he assumed flesh; to have been God; through him all things were made; to have come to his own; to enlighten every man coming into this world; and finally to have been made flesh, and all to have received from his fullness. Therefore this λόγος was before all men coming into this world, and Adam himself, Abraham and Moses were enlightened through him and received from his fullness, and so on. "I am that bread of life, which came down from heaven." "Christ, going forth by the Spirit, in the days of Noah preached to the spirits who are in prison, who once were disobedient." But the flesh of the preacher Jesus did not come down from heaven, nor was it in the days of Noah.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Christus in novo Testamento dicitur esse homo. Ergo non aliqua est natura invisibilis in hoc homine, & sic corrumpitur scriptura: quia cum dico te esse scholasticum, non dico, scholasticum esse in te, &c. Resp. 1. Christus ab Apostolo vocatur Filius Dei secundum spiritum. Scriptura asserit hunc hominem esse Deum, in ipso habitare omnem plenitudinem Deitatis corporaliter. Christus de se ipso: Destruite, inquit, templum hoc. Et autor epistolae ad Hebraeos meminit tabernaculi naturae humanae: carnem vocat velum, nempe Deitatis. Passus est secundum carnem, λόγος factus est caro, & venit in propria. Ergo oportet in hac carne, & in hoc homine esse aliam naturam. 2. Scriptura Christo diserte tribuit pugnantes proprietates, quae uni naturae uno tempore non possunt tribui. Tribuit etiam ei naturam finitam & infinitam. Antequam Abraham esset, ego sum. Ergo necesse est hoc accipi per communicationem idiomatum de diuersis naturis.
units.tr: Objection 2. In the New Testament Christ is called a man. Therefore there is no invisible nature in this man, and so Scripture is corrupted; for when I say that you are a schoolman, I do not say that a schoolman is in you, and so on. Answer 1. Christ is called by the Apostle the Son of God according to the Spirit. Scripture asserts that this man is God, and that in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Christ speaks of himself: "Destroy this temple," he says. And the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews mentions the tabernacle of the human nature: he calls the flesh a veil, namely of the Godhead. "He suffered according to the flesh," "the Word was made flesh, and came to his own." Therefore there must be in this flesh and in this man another nature. 2. Scripture expressly attributes to Christ contrary properties, which cannot be attributed to one nature at one time. It also attributes to him a finite and an infinite nature. "Before Abraham was, I am." Therefore this must be understood by communication of properties from the different natures.

units.la: Classis secunda. Ad hanc referuntur loca scripturae, quibus vocatur Filius Dei proprius, quia est de substantia Patris genitus, non adoptatus. Qui Filio proprio non pepercit. Judaei clamant adversus Christum coram Pilato: Filium Dei se fecit, nempe proprium & naturalem: alioquin ipsi Judaei fuissent rei blasphemiae, cuius accusabant Christum, cum & ipsi se aequiparent Dei filios. Et alio loco clarius id explicatur, ubi dicuntur Judaei voluisse Christum trucidare, quod Deum dixisset Patrem suum, Deo se aequalem faciens, hoc est, Patrem sibi proprium & peculiarem. quod ex eo colligitur: quia operandi verbum, quod Deo proprium est, sibi vendicat. Colligitur ergo ex ipsorum Judaeorum verbis, Christum se appellare Filium Dei proprium & naturalem, hoc est, habentem jus filii naturâ, quod alij ex gratia per ipsum accipiunt. Quod si Christus appellasset sese filium Dei adoptiuum vel gratia tantũ, Judaei nunquam judicassent cum blasphemum. Sic enim seipsos blasphemos judicassent, quoniam se etiam filios Dei adoptiuos esse gloriabantur. Quod si calumnia fuisset Judaeorum, certè Christus eam refutasset. Non autem repulit à se, quod dicebant Judaei, immò hoc ipsum, quod dicebant, verum esse firmis rationibus ostendit. Quia igitur Christus est proprius Dei Filius: alia praeter humanam in ipso natura sit necesse est, secundum quam proprius sit Dei Filius. Nam secundum humanam naturam est ex nostro genere.
units.tr: Class 2. To this class belong the passages of Scripture in which the Son of God is called proper, because he was begotten of the substance of the Father, not adopted. "He did not spare his own Son." The Jews cried out against Christ before Pilate: "He made himself the Son of God," namely a proper and natural Son; otherwise the Jews themselves would have been guilty of the blasphemy of which they accused Christ, since they too boasted that they were sons of God. In another place this is explained more clearly, where the Jews are said to have wanted to kill Christ because he "had called God his Father, making himself equal to God," that is, claiming God as his own and peculiar Father. This is gathered from the fact that he claims for himself the verb "to work," which is proper to God. It is gathered, therefore, from the very words of the Jews, that Christ calls himself the proper and natural Son of God, "that is, having by nature the right of a son," which others receive from him through grace. But if Christ had called himself an adopted son of God, or a son only by grace, the Jews would never have judged it blasphemy. For in that case they would have judged themselves blasphemous, since they gloried that they too were adopted sons of God. And if the Jews' charge had been a calumny, Christ would surely have refuted it. Yet he did not reject what the Jews said; rather he showed by firm reasons that the very thing they said was true. Since, therefore, Christ is the proper Son of God, there must be in him some nature besides the human one, according to which he is the proper Son of God. For according to his human nature he is of our kind.

units.la: Obiect. Serveti. Dicitur Filius Dei proprius; quia a Deo est factus: sicut ecclesia Dei populus proprius appellatur. Resp. Corruptela est. Apostolus loco ante citato Filium Dei proprium opponit nobis & angelis, tanquam filiis non propriis. Angeli enim sunt filij gratia creationis, nos gratia adoptionis. Proprius autem filius dicitur, qui est de substantia patris sui propagatus. Cum itaque solus Christus dicatur proprius Dei Filius, etiam ipse solus de substantia Patris est propagatus: ac proinde solus ipse est Filius Dei naturalis, non adoptione, vel gratia, sicut nos. Qui enim gratia vel adoptione filius est, non est filius naturalis, neque proprius.
units.tr: Objection of Servetus. He is called the proper Son of God because he was made by God, just as the Church of God is called a "proper people." Answer. This is a corruption. In the passage cited above the Apostle sets the proper Son of God over against us and the angels, as sons who are not proper. For angels are sons by the grace of creation, and we by the grace of adoption. But a proper son is called one who has been propagated from the substance of his father. Since, therefore, Christ alone is called the proper Son of God, he alone has been propagated from the substance of the Father; and consequently he alone is the natural Son of God, not by adoption or grace as we are. For whoever is a son by grace or adoption is neither a natural nor a proper son.

units.la: Inst 1. Non habetur in scriptura, Christum esse Filium Dei naturalem. Ergo est figmentum hominum. Resp. 1. Habentur aequipollentia: quia dicitur filius proprius, filius unigenitus a Patre. 2. Ex argumento Apostoli ad Romanos, & Judaeorum apud Johannem necessario sequitur, ut est ostensum.
units.tr: Instance 1. It is not found in Scripture that Christ is the natural Son of God. Therefore it is a fiction of men. Answer 1. There are equivalent expressions: for he is called the proper Son, the only-begotten Son from the Father. 2. From the Apostle's argument to the Romans and from the Jews' words in John it necessarily follows, as has been shown.

units.la: Inst. 2. Potuit semper esse λόγος in Deo, sed non filius. Dictus autem est filius, respectu futurae filiationis in carne assumta. Resp. 1. Sic non esset filius Dei proprius. 2. λόγος talis filius appellatur, cui Pater dedit vitam habere in seipso. 3. Non esset discrimen personale inter Patrem & Filium: quia λόγος secundum Scripturam nulla fuit tritum. Fuisset igitur Pater sine Filio, & Pater idem qui Filius, ut voluit Sabellius.
units.tr: Instance 2. The λόγος could always have been in God, but not as Son; he was called Son with respect to the future sonship in the assumed flesh. Answer 1. In that case he would not be the proper Son of God. 2. The λόγος is called such a Son to whom the Father gave to have life in himself. 3. There would be no personal distinction between Father and Son, for according to Scripture the λόγος was never separate. Then the Father would have been without a Son, and the Father would be the same as the Son, as Sabellius wished.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Classis III. Haec continet dicta, quibus Christus vocatur Filius Dei unigenitus, μονογενής. Spectavimus gloriam eius, ut gloriam unigeniti a Patre. Ita Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, &c. Unigenitus autem est, qui non habet fratres. At Christus secundum humanam naturam habet fratres.
units.tr: Class III. This class contains the passages in which Christ is called the only-begotten Son of God, μονογενής: We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father (John 1:14); God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son (John 3:16), etc. Now an only-begotten is one who has no brothers. But Christ, according to his human nature, has brothers.

units.la: Debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri. Quam ob causam non erubescit fratres ipsos vocare. Est igitur in Christo alia natura, secundum quam est unigenitus Patris Filius, & secundum quam non habet fratres.
units.tr: He had to be made like his brothers in all things; for which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb. 2:11, 17). There is therefore in Christ another nature, according to which he is the only-begotten Son of the Father, and according to which he has no brothers.

units.la: Obiect. Dicitur unigenitus: quia solus genitus est homo Jesus ex virgine per Spiritum sanctum. Resp. Est corruptela. Nam 1. Unigenitus est, qui solus est ex Patris substantia genitus, 2. In scripturis saepe discernitur generatio λόγου ex Patre, & generatio Christi ex virgine, ut sapientia dicit: Ab initio ante colles formata, seu (ut reddit Chaldaeus paraphrastes) genita sum, Spectavimus gloriam eius, ut gloriam unigeniti a Patre. Apud Mat-
units.tr: Objection. He is called only-begotten because Jesus the man alone was born of the virgin through the Holy Spirit. Answer. This is a perversion. For (1) the only-begotten is the one who alone is begotten of the substance of the Father; (2) in the Scriptures the generation of the Word from the Father is often distinguished from the generation of Christ from the virgin, as Wisdom says: I was formed from the beginning, before the hills (Prov. 8:23), or (as the Chaldee paraphrast renders it) I was begotten; We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten from the Father. Among Mat-

units.la: Quaest. XXXIII. De Deitate Filii
units.tr: Quaest. XXXIII. De Deitate Filii

units.la: Matthæum verò legimus, Iesum, qui dicitur Christus, ex Maria esse genitum. 3. Vnigenitus opponitur angelis & hominibus, quippe qui neque per adoptionem, vt hi, neque per creationis gratiam, vt illi, sed naturâ filius est. Excipiunt. Vidimus gloriam eius, scilicet hominis Iesu. Resp. Corruptela. Relationem τοῦ λόγου non habet aliud antecedens, ad quod referatur, nisi &, vidimus gloriam eius, scilicet, verbi. Si igitur λόγος ipse vocatur caro, & est vnigenitus à Patre: certè non significat vnigenitus hoc loco generationem ex Maria, sed generationem ex Patre ab æterno.
units.tr: But we read in Matthew that Jesus, who is called Christ, was born of Mary. (3) The only-begotten is set against angels and men, since he is the Son by nature, neither by adoption as they are, nor by the grace of creation as they are. They object: "We have seen his glory," namely the glory of the man Jesus. Answer: this is a distortion. The relative of [τοῦ λόγου] has no other antecedent to which it refers than "and we have seen his glory," namely of the Word. So if the Word himself is called flesh and is the only-begotten of the Father, then surely "only-begotten" does not here signify generation from Mary, but generation from the Father from eternity.

units.la: Classis IV.
units.tr: Classis IV.

units.la: Ad hanc classem pertinent omnia testimonia scripturæ, quibus nomen Filij Dei tribuitur Christo secundum divinam naturam etiam ante assumtam carnem. vt: Quis stabiliuit omnes terminos terræ? quod nomen eius? & quod nomen filij eius? Locutus est Deus nobis per Filium, per quem & secula fecit. Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum, vt condemnet mundum. Pater Filium misit in mundum. Humana autem natura in mundo est nata. Erat ergo Filius, antequam humana natura in mundum mitteretur.
units.tr: To this class belong all the testimonies of Scripture in which the name of Son of God is given to Christ according to the divine nature, even before the flesh was assumed, as: Who has established all the bounds of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? God has spoken to us by the Son, through whom he also made the worlds. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world. The Father sent the Son into the world. But the human nature was born in the world. Therefore the Son existed before the human nature was sent into the world.

units.la: Huc referuntur & illa, quæ Filio tribuunt opera divina ante carnem assumptam, vt: Per eum (Filium) condita sunt omnia, quæ in cœlo sunt, & quæ in terra. Pater meus vsque huc operatur, & ego operor. Quacunque Pater facit, Filius similiter facit. At caro Christi nec omnia operatur, quæ Pater, nec quicquam eodem modo, quo Pater, etiam tunc, cum erat facta, nedum ab initio. Ergo secundum quod ab initio operatur omnia filius, id fuit aliud quàm caro. Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater, neque Patrem, nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit Filius revelare. Si Filius revelavit etiam iis, qui vixerunt ante naturam eius humanam: Ergo ante assumptam carnem fuit.
units.tr: To this class also belong those passages which ascribe to the Son the divine works done before the flesh was assumed, as: All things that are in heaven and that are in earth were created through him (the Son). My Father works until now, and I work. Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. But the flesh of Christ neither does all the things the Father does, nor does anything in the same way as the Father, even when it had been made, much less from the beginning. Therefore, according to that by which the Son worked all things from the beginning, he was something other than the flesh. No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. If the Son revealed the Father even to those who lived before his human nature, then he existed before the flesh was assumed.

units.la: Pertinent præterea huc testimonia, quibus nomen Dei expressè tribuitur Christo secundum naturam aliam, præter humanam. Et hæc diligenter colligenda sunt. Hoc enim valde vrgent aduersarij, non nisi secundum humanam naturam Christo Dei nomen attribui in scripturis. λόγος erat Deus. Deus manifestatus est in carne. Ad hoc manifestatus est Filius Dei, vt destruat opera diaboli. Est igitur in Christo natura, quæ ante assumtam carnem vocatur Filius Dei. Non ergo possunt hæretici dicere, Christum tunc demum appellatum fuisse Filium Dei; quando miraculose conceptus est, vel miracula operari cœpit.
units.tr: Moreover, there belong here the testimonies by which the name of God is expressly given to Christ according to another nature besides the human. These must be gathered carefully, for the adversaries press this strongly: that in the Scriptures the name of God is attributed to Christ only according to the human nature. The Word was God. God was manifested in the flesh. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil. There is therefore in Christ a nature which, before the flesh was assumed, is called the Son of God. Heretics therefore cannot say that Christ was then first called the Son of God when he was conceived miraculously, or when he began to work miracles.

units.la: Classis V.
units.tr: Classis V.

units.la: Huc refero dicta scripturæ de λόγῳ λόγος, de quo Iohannes, fuit persona ante carnem. Filius est λόγος. Ergo filius est perpersona præter & ante carnem assumptam. Ad probationem maioris pertinent omnes partes descriptionis λόγου apud Iohannem : quod fuit in principio mundi, & quidem Deus : quod per ipsum factæ sunt omnes creaturæ : quod fuit vita & lux, hoc est, author omnis vitæ & lucis in hominibus : quod inde ab initio fuit in mundo, etiam cum non agnosceretur, &c. Eadem de λόγῳ docentur 1 Io.1.&3. Ap.19. quæ omnia cum non nisi in ὑφιστάμενον viuum, intelligens & operans competere possint, euidenter confirmant, λόγῳ, de quo ista scribuntur, esse personam, & fuisse ante hominem IESUM ex virgine natum. Minor patet ex textu Iohannis : Vidimus gloriam eius (nempe λόγου incarnati) tanquam gloriam unigeniti à Patre. Item, quem dixerat λόγῳ, cum Paulo post vocat Filium unigenitum existentem in sinu Patris. Item, Iohannes dicit per λόγῳ, Paulus per Filium à Deo mundum creatum esse. Est igitur persona, quæ λόγος, & Filius Dei, etiam ante Iesum natum ex virgine subsistens, & nunc in assumta humana natura habitans personaliter.
units.tr: I refer here the sayings of Scripture about the Word [λόγος], of whom John speaks: the Word was a person before the flesh. The Son is the Word. Therefore the Son is a person, existing apart from and before the assumed flesh. All parts of John's description of the Word [λόγου] support the major premise: he who was in the beginning of the world, and indeed was God; through him all creatures were made; he was life and light, that is, the author of all life and light in men; he who from the beginning was in the world, even when he was not recognised, and so on. The same things are taught about the Word [λόγῳ] in 1 John 1 and 3, and Revelation 19, which, since they can apply only to a living, intelligent and active subsistent being, clearly confirm that the Word of whom these things are written is a person, and that he existed before Jesus the man born of the virgin. The minor premise is plain from the text of John: "We have seen his glory (namely of the incarnate Word), as the glory of the only-begotten from the Father." Likewise, the one whom he had called the Word, Paul afterwards calls "the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father." Likewise, John says that the world was made through the Word, and Paul says that it was made by God through the Son. Therefore there is a person, who is the Word and the Son of God, subsisting even before Jesus was born of the virgin, and now dwelling personally in the assumed human nature.

units.la: Classis VI. Ad hanc referuntur loca, quæ Christum testantur esse sapientiam Dei.
units.tr: Classis VI. To this class belong the passages which testify that Christ is the wisdom of God.

units.la: Sapientia Dei, per quam omnia condidit, est æterna. Filius est illa sapientia. Ergo Filius est æternus, proinde exstitit ante naturam humanam. Maior est in prouerbiis: Iehoua possedit me ab initio viæ suæ jam tum ante opera sua: cum non dum essent abyssi, genita sum. Minor probatur. 1. Ipsa sapientia dicit se genitam. Genitum vero esse, cum de natura intelligente dicitur, non est aliud, quam esse filium. 2. Christus ipse vocat se Dei sapientiam, Propterea etiam sapientia Dei dixit: Mittam ad vos prophetas, &c. 3. Paulus etiam vocat Christum Dei sapientiam: Prædicamus Christum Dei potentiam & Dei sapientiam. 4. Eadem à Salomone adscribuntur Sapientiæ, quæ alibi Sermoni & Filio tribuuntur, quòd ea fecerit propriâ efficaciâ, & quæ fusius cap.7.8.9.&10. persequitur liber Sapientiæ. Ergo Sapientia est Filius Dei.
units.tr: The wisdom of God, through which he made all things, is eternal. The Son is that wisdom. Therefore the Son is eternal, and so existed before the human nature. The major premise is in Proverbs: "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his way, even before his works of old. Before the depths were, I was brought forth." The minor premise is proved as follows. 1. Wisdom itself says that it was begotten. To be begotten, when said of an intelligent nature, is nothing other than to be a son. 2. Christ himself calls himself the wisdom of God: "Therefore also the wisdom of God said: I will send them prophets," and so on. 3. Paul also calls Christ the wisdom of God: "We preach Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." 4. The same things that are elsewhere ascribed to the Word and the Son are ascribed by Solomon to Wisdom, namely that she made things by her own efficacy; and the Book of Wisdom pursues this more fully in chapters 7, 8, 9 and 10. Therefore Wisdom is the Son of God.

units.la: Classis VII. Ad hanc referuntur testimonia scripturæ de officio Mediatoris, quod est, colligere & seruare Ecclesiam universam, indigent merito & efficacia. Vt Ecclesia plenè liberetur, indiget mediatore, non tantum propter quem, sed etiam per quem colligatur & seruetur. Hic mediator neque est Pater, neque Spiritus sanctus. Est igitur Filius Christus totius Ecclesiæ Mediator jam ab initio exsistens.
units.tr: Class VII. To this class belong the testimonies of Scripture about the office of the Mediator, which is to gather and preserve the whole Church, and which requires merit and efficacy. For the Church to be fully delivered, it needs a mediator, not only on account of whom it is gathered, but also through whom it is gathered and preserved. This mediator is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit. Therefore Christ the Son is the Mediator of the whole Church, existing already from the beginning.

units.la: Propter Christum futurum poterat in gratiam recipi vetus ecclesia: sed per ipsum non potuit, nisi exsistentiam recipi. Nam non exsistentis nulla potuit esse efficacia. Unde cuinam citur, Christum extitisse ante assumptam carnem. Non enim potest esse inter Deum & homines amicitia sine mediatore jam exsisten-
units.tr: The old Church could be received into grace on account of the Christ who was to come, but it could not be received through him unless he already existed, for there can be no efficacy from one who does not exist. Hence it follows that Christ existed before the assumed flesh. For there cannot be friendship between God and men without a mediator who already exists.

units.la: Ioh.1,14. Ioh.1,18. Ioh.1,3. Hebr.1,2. Luc.11,49. 1Cor.1,24. exsistente. At in veteri Testamento fuit amicitia inter Deum & homines, nempe credentes. Ergo aut ille, aut alius tunc fuit mediator ecclesiæ. Non alius fuit, sed ille solus: quia tantum unus mediator Dei & hominum. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem & in secula. Quod verò non possit esse amicitia inter Deum & homines sine mediatore jam exsistente, ex officio mediatoris patet. Nam mediatoris officium est, non tantum deprecatione & sacrificio nobis placare Patrem, sed omnia etiam bona impetrata sua potentia & efficacia conferre credentibus, patefacere hominibus voluntatem DEI, instituere ministerium, colligere & seruare ecclesiam, & quidem totam. Nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit Filius revelare. Ergo nec Adam Deum cognouit, nisi per Filium: & per consequens Filius tunc fuit.
units.tr: Jn 1:14; Jn 1:18; Jn 1:3; Heb. 1:2; Luke 11:49; 1 Cor. 1:24. Existing. But in the Old Testament there was friendship between God and men, namely believers. Therefore either he, or another, was then the Mediator of the Church. There was no other, but he alone, because there is only one Mediator between God and men. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. That friendship between God and men cannot exist without a mediator already existing is clear from the office of the mediator. For the office of the mediator is not only to reconcile the Father to us by intercession and sacrifice, but also to bestow on believers all good things obtained by his power and efficacy, to reveal the will of God to men, to institute the ministry, and to gather and preserve the Church, and indeed the whole Church. No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. Therefore Adam too did not know God except through the Son, and consequently the Son was then already existing.

units.la: Huc referuntur testimonia non tantum de futuro Christi merito loquentia, sed etiam de ipsius efficacia. Omnia subjecit (Pater) pedibus eius, eumq; constituit caput super omnia ipsi ecclesiæ. Superstructi super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, cuius angularis lapis est ipse Iesus Christus. Est ergo Christus fundamentum, caput, sustentator & gubernator Ecclesiæ: proinde exstitit, antequam esset ecclesia. Ego sum via, veritas, & vita, nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Ego vitam æternam do eis. In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux illa vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Utrique per ipsum habemus aditum per unum Spiritum ad Patrem. Ipse dedit alios quidem apostolos, alios verò prophetas, alios autem pastores & doctores. Petrus ait, Spiritum Christi fuisse in prophetis, & pronunciasse venturas Christi perpessiones. Moses quidem fidelis fuit in tota domo ipsius, ut famulus, ad testificanda, quæ post dicenda erant: at Christus ut Filius domui suæ præest. Christus ergo patefecit voluntatem Dei, instituit ministerium, est architectus domus suæ, eamque gubernat: quod quia ipsum inde ab initio nascentis ecclesiæ fecisse constat, non dubitandum est, quin semper fuerit. Hæc est voluntas Patris, ut quicquid mihi dederit, non perdam ex eo. Seruat igitur Ecclesiam: ideo semper fuit: quia semper Ecclesia seruata est.
units.tr: These testimonies speak not only of the future merit of Christ, but also of his present efficacy. He (the Father) has put all things under his feet, and has appointed him head over all things to the Church. Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, of which Jesus Christ himself is the cornerstone. Christ is therefore the foundation, head, sustainer and governor of the Church; therefore he existed before there was a church. I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me. I give them eternal life. In him was life, and that life was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world. Through him we both have access by one Spirit to the Father. He himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, and others as ministers and teachers. Peter says that the Spirit of Christ was in the prophets and foretold the coming sufferings of Christ. Moses indeed was faithful in all his house, as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken afterwards; but Christ as a Son is over his own house. Christ therefore revealed the will of God, instituted the ministry, is the architect of his own house, and governs it. Since it is established that he did this from the beginning of the newly born Church, there is no doubt that he has always been. This is the will of the Father, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me. He therefore preserves the Church; so he has always existed, because the Church has always been preserved.

units.la: Insigne est testimonium apud Malachiam: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, qui præparabit viam ante faciem meam: & statim veniet ad templum suum Dominator, quem vos quaeritis: Angelus testatam: id quod confirmatur hoc argumento. Cui paratur via, is est Christus. Qui promittit, is est cui paratur via. Ergo qui promittit, est Christus, Maior est manifesta. Non enim Pater, sed Chri-
units.tr: Malachi gives a notable testimony: "Behold, I send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before my face; and the Lord, whom you seek, shall suddenly come to his temple; the Angel of the covenant." This is confirmed by the following argument. He for whom the way is prepared is Christ. He who makes the promise is the one for whom the way is prepared. Therefore he who makes the promise is Christ. The major premise is plain. For it was not the Father but Christ who was awaited, and he followed John.

units.la: Ioh. 6, 39. Christus exspectabatur, & is Johannem secutus est. probatur ex textu. Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, qui praeparabit viam ante faciem meam. Fuit ergo Christus ante assumptam carnem, quia misit angelum suum Johannem. Et quidem ante assumtam carnem fuit verus Deus. Templum enim vocat suum, ad quod se dicit venturum. Nemini vero in cultum exstruitur templum, nisi Deo. Blasphemum est igitur dicere, Christum ante carnem assumptam non exstitisse. Nec obstat, quod dicit in tertia persona: Ut veniat dominator ad templum suum. Quis enim sit ille dominator, satis ostendit (nempe non Pater, sed Filius.) Ego dominator, qui promitto Johannem, quiqui sum Angelus foederis. Deinde fieri potest, ut propheta mutata persona non amplius introducat Christum, sed ipsum Patrem de Filio mittendo loquentem repraesentet.
units.tr: John 6:39. Christus exspectabatur, and he followed John. This is proved from the text: "Behold, I send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before my face." Christ therefore existed before he assumed flesh, since he sent his messenger John. Moreover, before he assumed flesh he was true God. For he calls the temple his own, to which he says he will come. But a temple is built for worship only for God. It is therefore blasphemy to say that Christ did not exist before he assumed flesh. Nor does it stand in the way that the prophet says in the third person: "That the Lord may come to his temple." For who that Lord is, is sufficiently shown (namely, not the Father but the Son): I am the Lord who promises John, who am the Angel of the covenant. Next, it may happen that the prophet, changing the person, no longer introduces Christ speaking, but represents the Father himself speaking about the Son who is sent.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Classis VIII. Haec continet testimonia de angelo, qui in veteri testamento patribus apparuit tanquam legatus Dei. Angelus, qui eripuit me de cunctis malis, benedicat pueris istis, &c. Hunc Angelum, qui & Angelus Jehovae & Jehova multis locis appellatur, ecclesia semper confessa est, fuisse Filium Dei: idque i. quia tota scriptura docet, Filium esse legatum Patris ad ecclesiam, & gerere mediatoris officium. Et mox veniet ad templum suum dominator, quem quaeritis, & angelus foederis quem expetitis. Ad Filium autem dixit: Thronus tuus Deus in seculum seculi, &c. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem in secula, &c. 2. Quia quod apud Mosen dicitur de illo angelo, cum fuisse tentatum ab Israelitis in deserto, id apud Paulum dicitur de Christo. Ex his & similibus sic licebit argumentari. Angelus legatus Patris fuit ante carnem assumptam. Angelus ille non fuit Pater, nec Spiritus sanctus, sed Filius: quia solus Filius est legatus Patris, & mediator. Ergo Filius fuit ante carnem assumptam.
units.tr: Class VIII. This class contains the testimonies about the angel who appeared to the fathers in the Old Testament as God's legate. "The Angel who has redeemed me from all evils, bless these boys," etc. The Church has always confessed that this Angel, who is also called the Angel of Jehovah and Jehovah in many places, was the Son of God. This is so (1) because all of Scripture teaches that the Son is the Father's legate to the Church and performs the office of mediator. "And soon the Lord whom you seek shall come suddenly to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire. But to the Son he said: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever," etc. "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever," etc. (2) Because what is said of that angel in Moses, when he was tempted by the Israelites in the desert, is said of Christ in Paul. From these and similar passages one may argue thus: the Angel was the Father's legate before he assumed flesh; that Angel was not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son, because only the Son is the Father's legate and mediator. Therefore the Son existed before he assumed flesh.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Classis IX. Haec postrema classe comprehenduntur loca scripturae, quibus Christus aperte dicitur verus Deus, nomine & proprietatibus. Ex quibus est Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula. Hic est verus Deus, & vita aeterna. Hic aperte homo ille Iesus Christus appellatur verus Deus. Si igitur est verus Deus, utique semper extitit. Unus enim verus Deus est ab aeterno. Deus manifestatus in carne: & hic manifeste Christus appellatur Deus.
units.tr: Class IX. In this final class are gathered the passages of Scripture in which Christ is openly called true God, by name and by properties. "Of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever." "This is the true God and eternal life." Here that man Jesus Christ is plainly called the true God. If therefore he is the true God, he has certainly always existed, for there is one true God from eternity. "God manifested in the flesh": here too Christ is clearly called God.

units.la: Ad hanc classem referre licet & illa testimonia, quae tribuunt Christo opera creationis, miraculorum, redemptionis, regenerationis, defensionis, glorificationis, item gubernationis totius mundi: ad quae requiritur infinita sapientia, omnipotentia, omniscientia & ubiquitas, cuiusmodi passim hactenus multa supra sunt citata. Ex quibus luculenter apparet, homini Christo tribui non tantum nomen, sed & proprietates veri Dei. Attributio autem proprietatum veri Dei nobis argumentum suppeditat magis firmum, quam attributio tantum nominis veri Dei seu Jehouae. Nomina enim Dei possunt aliquo modo alicubi exponi metaphoricè: sed proprietates divinae Christo attributae alio detorqueri nequeunt. Huiusmodi argumentis si nos muniamus, adversarij non poterunt consistere, sed velint nolint fateri cogentur, Christum fuisse ante assumtam carnem.
units.tr: To this class may also be referred those testimonies which ascribe to Christ the works of creation, of miracles, of redemption, of regeneration, of defence, of glorification, and likewise the government of the whole world; these require infinite wisdom, omnipotence, omniscience and omnipresence, of which many examples have been cited above throughout. From these it clearly appears that not only the name but also the properties of the true God are attributed to the man Christ. Moreover, the ascription of the properties of the true God gives us a firmer argument than the mere ascription of the name of the true God or Jehovah. For the names of God can in some way be explained figuratively in some places; but the divine properties ascribed to Christ cannot be twisted to mean something else. If we arm ourselves with arguments of this kind, our opponents will not be able to stand; whether they wish it or not, they will be compelled to confess that Christ existed before he assumed flesh.

units.la: Hac propositione constituta, quod Filius fuerit ὑφισταμένον aliquod ante carnem, quaeritur, quid fuerit? creator, an creatura? an Spiritus Dei coaeternus? an in tempore creatus? Ad hanc quaestionem respondetur ex descriptionibus λόγου & sapientiae, quae exstant apud Johannem & Salomonem. Inde enim facilè apparet, eum fuisse creatorem, coaeternam Patri personam.
units.tr: Having laid down this proposition, that the Son was some subsisting [ὑφισταμένον] being before the flesh, the question is asked: what was he? A creator or a creature? Or the co-eternal Spirit of God? Or one created in time? This question is answered from the descriptions of the Word [λόγου] and of wisdom which are found in John and Solomon. From these it is easily seen that he was the creator, a person co-eternal with the Father.

units.la: II. Quod Filius sit persona distincta, à Patre & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: II. That the Son is a distinct person from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Personam Filij à persona Patris esse distinctam, tenendum est propter Noetum, Sabellium, & horum similes: qui dixerunt, Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti esse entiam esse eiusdem personae, seu, hos tres esse unam personam, sed diversa nomina esse propter diversitatem officij.
units.tr: The distinction of the person of the Son from the person of the Father must be maintained against Noetus, Sabellius, and their like, who said that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, or that these three are one person but have different names because of their different offices.

units.la: 1 Ad probandum verò, quod Filius non tantum officio, sed persona sit distinctus à Patre, sufficit unum argumentum: Christus Filius Dei est quod nemo est suiipsius filius, sed omnis filius est patris filius: alioqui idem & filius & pater essent eodem respectu, quod est absurdum. Ergo λόγος est Filius Patris, non ipse Pater. Vel sic: tres & Spiritus sancto. Nemo suiipsius est filius. Hoc ὑφισταμένον vocatur filius. Ergo distinctum est hoc ὑφισταμένον à Patre & Spiritu sancto. Accedunt deinde alia.
units.tr: 1. To prove that the Son is distinct from the Father not only in office but in person, one argument is enough. Christ is the Son of God. No one is the son of himself, but every son is the son of a father. Otherwise the same person would be both son and father in the same respect, which is absurd. Therefore the Word [λόγος] is the Son of the Father, not the Father himself. Or put it this way: the Father and the Holy Spirit are not the Son. No one is the son of himself. This subsistence [ὑφισταμένον] is called the Son. Therefore this subsistence is distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit. Other arguments follow.

units.la: 2. Patefactio diuinitatis in tribus personis distinctis. Tres sunt, qui testificantur in coelo: Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus sanctus, & hi tres unum sunt. Et dixit Deus: Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra: non dicit: faciam. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Consolator autem ille, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, docebit vos omnia. Cum autem venerit Consolator ille, quem ego mittam vobis à Patre (Spiritus, illeveritatis, qui à Patre emanat) ille testabitur de me. Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filij, & Spiritus sancti. Spiritus sanctus descendit in specie columbae: Filius baptizatur in Jordane: Patris vox auditur è coelis: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco.
units.tr: 2. The manifestation of the divinity in three distinct persons. There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one. And God said, Let us make man in our image: he does not say, I will make. I and the Father are one. But the Comforter, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things. But when the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father (the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father), he will bear witness of me. Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove; the Son was baptized in the Jordan; the voice of the Father was heard from heaven: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

units.la: N 4 3. Aper-
units.tr: N 4 3. Aper-

units.la: 3. Aperta scripturæ testimonia, vbi dicitur, quod Pater sit alius, Filius sit alius, Spiritus sit alius. Alius est, qui testatur de me: nempe Pater clamans è cœlo: Hic est Filius meus, &c. Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius, qui misit me. Non potest Filius à semet operari, nisi viderit Patrem operantem. Ego rogabo Patrem, & alium paracletum mittet vobis.
units.tr: 3. The plain testimonies of Scripture, where it is said that the Father is one, the Son is another, and the Spirit is another. It is another who bears witness of me: namely the Father crying from heaven: This is my Son, etc. My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it. I will pray the Father, and he will send you another Comforter.

units.la: 4. Attributa distincta personarum. Pater genuit Filium, Filius est genitus. Pater mittit, Filius est missus. Pater non dicitur factus caro, sed solus Filius. Filius assumsit semen Abrahæ, non Pater. Filius factus est supplex, intercessor, sacerdos, propheta, rex, mediator, non Pater. Alius igitur est Pater, alius Filius. Pater à se per Filium: Filius non à se, nec per Patrem, sed per se à Patre. Denique Christus baptizatus est, non Pater, neque Spiritus sanctus. Est igitur Christus alius à Patre & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: 4. The distinct attributes of the persons. The Father begot the Son; the Son is begotten. The Father sends; the Son is sent. The Father is not said to have become flesh, but the Son alone. The Son took the seed of Abraham, not the Father. The Son became a suppliant, intercessor, priest, prophet, king, and mediator; not the Father. Therefore the Father is one, the Son another. The Father is from himself through the Son; the Son is not from himself, nor through the Father, but is from the Father through himself. Finally, Christ was baptized, not the Father nor the Holy Spirit. Therefore Christ is other than the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: III. Quod Filius Patri & Spiritui sancto sit æqualis Deitate.
units.tr: III. That the Son is equal in deity to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Filium esse Patri & Spiritui sancto æqualem Deitate, hoc est, non Deum factitium, aut creatum ante alias creaturas, nec Deum propter divinas qualitates aut operationes, aut Deum aliquem minorem, ut finxerunt Arius, Eunomius, Samosatenus, Servetus, & similes hæretici; sed naturâ Deum cum Patre & Spiritu sancto: probatur.
units.tr: That the Son is equal in deity to the Father and the Holy Spirit, that is, not a made-up God, nor a created God before other creatures, nor a God only by divine qualities or operations, nor some lesser god, as Arius, Eunomius, Samosatenus, Servetus, and similar heretics imagined, but by nature God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. Distertis testimoniis scripturæ: Hæc est voluntas Patris, ut omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem. Pater autem debet honorari ut verus Deus, non ut factitius. Sic igitur & Filius. Quæ Pater facit, Filius similiter facit. Sicut Pater habet vitam in se ipso, sic Filio dedit habere in se ipso. Quæ (Christus) est supra omnia Deus & λογητὸς, laudandus in secula. Hic est ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς, verus ille Deus, & vita æterna. Secundus homo ipse Dominus è cœlo. Omnia, quæ habet Pater, mea sunt. In quo habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Qui cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam, esse æqualem Deo.
units.tr: 1. By the clear testimonies of Scripture: This is the will of the Father, that all should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. But the Father ought to be honoured as the true God, not a made-up one. So also the Son. Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself. He who (Christ) is over all, God, blessed [λογητός], to be praised for ever. This is the true God [ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεός], and eternal life. The second man is the Lord himself from heaven. All that the Father has is mine. In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Who, being in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God.

units.la: 2. Est verus, proprius, & naturalis Dei Filius, vnigenitus, natus de essentia Patris. Si de essentia Dei natus: ergo ei tota & eadem communicata est. Vnica enim Dei essentia, infinita cùm sit & impartibilis, non communicatur ex parte, alioqui non esset infinita. Quia igitur Filius totam essentiam habet communicatam: ideo est Patri æqualis, & per consequens verus Deus.
units.tr: 2. He is the true, proper, and natural Son of God, the only-begotten, born of the essence of the Father. If he was born of the essence of God, then the whole and the same essence has been communicated to him. For the essence of God is one, infinite, and indivisible, and it is not communicated in part; otherwise it would not be infinite. Therefore, since the Son has the whole essence communicated to him, he is equal to the Father, and consequently true God.

units.la: 3. Scriptura Filio tribuit omnes proprietates Dei essentiales, non minus quàm Patri. Quod sit æternus. Ante colles formata sunt. sum. In principio erat sermo. Immensus. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui de cœlo descendit, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo. Ut Christus habitet per fidem in cordibus vestris. Omnipotens. Quacunque Pater facit, Filius similiter facit. Secundum efficaciam, qua potest ipse sibi subjicere omnia. Ferens omnia verbo potentiae suae. Immensae sapientiae. Vocabitur nomen eius consiliarius. Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater, neque Patrem quisquam novit, nisi Filius. &c. Καρδιογνώστης. Iesus autem non credebat se iis, eo quod ipse nosset omnes: nec opus esset, ut quisquam testaretur de homine: ipse enim sciebat, quid esset in homine. Nunc scimus, quod scis omnia. Sanctificator ecclesiae. Christus dilexit ecclesiam, & semetipsum tradidit pro ea, ut eam sanctificaret mundatam lavacro aquae per verbum. Immutabilis. Caelum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt. Veritas ipsa, & fons veritatis. Ego etsi testimonium perhiberem de me ipso, verum est testimonium meum. Ego sum via, veritas & vita. Ineffabili misericordia. Sicut & Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit semetipsum oblationem & hostiam Deo. Irascens peccatis, & ea vindicans, etiam arcana. Qui non credit Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Cadite super nos, & occultate nos ab ira sedentis super thronum & ab ira agni, quia venit dies magnus irae, & quis poterit consistere? Est ergo Filius naturâ Deus, & Patri aequalis.
units.tr: 3. Scripture ascribes to the Son all the essential properties of God, no less than to the Father. That he is eternal: Before the hills were they formed. In the beginning was the Word. He is immense: No one has ascended into heaven, but he who came down from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven. That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith. He is omnipotent: Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. By the power by which he is able to subject all things to himself. Bearing all things by the word of his power. He has immense wisdom: His name shall be called Counsellor. No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son. And so on. He is searcher of hearts [καρδιογνώστης]. But Jesus did not trust himself to them, because he knew all men, and he had no need that anyone should testify about man, for he himself knew what was in man. Now we know that you know all things. He is the sanctifier of the Church: Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for it, that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water through the word. He is unchangeable: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. He is truth itself and the fountain of truth: Even if I bear witness of myself, my testimony is true. I am the way, the truth, and the life. He has an unspeakable mercy: As Christ also loved us, and gave himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God. He is angry at sins and avenges them, even the hidden ones: He who does not believe the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. Fall on us, and hide us from the wrath of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? The Son is therefore God by nature, and equal to the Father.

units.la: 4. Eadem scriptura omnia opera divina tribuit Filio pariter & Patri. Primum universalia, quod sit creator. Per ipsum omnia facta sunt. Conservator & gubernator omnium. Qui sustinet omnia verbo suo potenti. Deinde specialia ad Ecclesiae salutem pertinentia: quod mittat prophetas, apostolos, & alios ministros Ecclesiae. Sicut misit me Pater, ita & ego mitto vos. Et ipse dedit alios quidem prophetas, alios autem apostolos, alios evangelistas, alios pastores & doctores. Instruens ministros donis necessariis. Ego dabo vobis os & spiritum, cui non poterunt contradicere, neque resistere omnes adversantes vobis. Patefaciens doctrinam. Unigenitus ille Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit nobis. Confirmans doctrinam per miracula. Illi vero egressi praedicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante, & sermonem confirmante per signa subsequentia. Instituens sacramenta.
