Why it was necessary for the hypostatic union to take place.

units.la: I. An sint duæ naturæ in Mediatore.
units.tr: I. Whether there are two natures in the Mediator.

units.la: Quod in mediatore sit natura diuina, probatum est supra. Quod sit humana, negatum olim fuit à Marcione, & hodie negatur à Svvenckfeldianis, qui nominetenus tantum, hominem Christum nunc in gloria esse, concedunt. Probandum itaque est Christum esse hominem verum, naturalem, constantem corpore & anima olim in statu humilitatis, obnoxium infirmitatibus omnibus, excepto peccato: hoc est, probanda est contra Marcionem & Svvenckfeldium non tam ipsa natura, quam veritas naturæ humanæ. Probaturigitur.
units.tr: That the Mediator has a divine nature has been proved above. That he has a human nature was denied formerly by Marcion, and today it is denied by the Schwenckfeldians, who concede only in name that Christ as man is now in glory. It must therefore be proved that Christ is a true and natural man, consisting of body and soul, who in the state of humiliation was subject to all infirmities except sin. That is, against Marcion and Schwenckfeld what must be proved is not so much the existence of the nature itself as the truth of the human nature. It is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. Scriptura testimoniis, quæ ostendunt Christum habere omnes partes naturæ humanæ, & nobis per omnia factum esse similem, solo peccato excepto. Nam & qui sanctificat, & sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes: quam ob causam non erubescit fratres ipsos vocare. Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, &c. Non enim angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahæ assumsit, unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, ut misericors esset, & fidelis pontifex in iis, quæ apud Deum agenda forent, ad expiandum peccata populi. Non habemus pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum in omnibus similiter, absque peccato. Huc pertinent testimonia, quibus post resurrectionem Dominus ipse veritatem naturæ suæ humanæ probauit: Contrectate me, & videte, quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout me conspicitis habere, &c.
units.tr: 1. From Scripture, by testimonies which show that Christ has all the parts of human nature and was made like us in every way, sin alone excepted. For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one; for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren. Since therefore the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise has become a partaker of the same, etc. For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham; wherefore he ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. To this belong the testimonies in which the Lord himself, after the resurrection, proved the truth of his human nature: Handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have, etc.

units.la: Apollinaris dixit, fuisse quidem veram Christi humanam carnem, sed pro anima habuisse vnitum λόγῳ. Hic error refutatur scripturæ his dictis: Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Contristatio non competit corpori, quod est res bruta; neque diuinitati, quæ est expers passionis. Pater, in manus tuas depono spiritum meum. Et cum hæc dixisset, exspirauit. Emisit spiritum. Spiritus animam significat, non diuinitatem: quia diuinitas nunquam desscessit. cessit à natura humana. Oportuit enim Deum suo sanguine redimere ecclesiam: est vbique, nec translatio localis ei competit. Debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri. At sine anima non fuisset fratribus suis per omnia similis: quia non fuisset verus homo.
units.tr: Apollinaris said that Christ's human flesh was indeed real, but that he had the Word [λόγῳ] joined to it in place of a soul. This error is refuted by these words of Scripture: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. Sorrow does not belong to the body, which is an insensible thing, nor to the deity, which is free from suffering. Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. And when he had said this, he gave up the ghost. The spirit signifies the soul, not the deity, because the deity never departed from the human nature. For God had to redeem the Church with his own blood; he is everywhere, and local movement does not belong to him. He ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren. But without a soul he would not have been in all things like his brethren, because he would not have been a true man.

units.la: 2. A promissionibus diuinis. Messias talis erat promissus, qui esset semen mulieris, semen Abrahami, filius Dauidis, filius virginis, &c. Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis. Ecce virgo concipiet & pariet filium. Liber generationis Iesu Christi filij Dauid, filij Abraham. Benedictus fructus ventris tui. De Filio Dei, facto ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem. Argumentum hoc firmum est: Assumsit carnem ex semine Abrahami & Dauidis, Ergo veram carnem.
units.tr: 2. From the divine promises. The Messiah was promised as one who would be the seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham, the son of David, the son of the virgin, etc. The seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Blessed is the fruit of thy womb. Concerning the Son of God, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh. This argument is firm: he took flesh from the seed of Abraham and David; therefore he took true flesh.

units.la: 3. Officium mediatoris requirebat in Christo naturam verè humanam, sumtam ex nostra natura, quæ peccauerat, & quæ erat per ipsum redimenda, &c. vt supra. Oportebat eandem naturam pati, quæ peccauerat. At nostra natura peccauit. Ergo eandem oportebat Christum assumere, non autem ex nihilo creatam, aut de cœlo demissam, &c. nec tantum assumere, sed etiam retinere, & carnem nostram manere in æternum: quia ea conditione Pater nos recipit in gratiam, si Filio suo maneamus insiti. Hæc consolatio in æternum nobis est necessaria, quod Christus sit frater noster, gestet carnem nostram. Sumus caro de carne eius, & os de ossibus eius. Hanc consolationem amitteremus, si Christus non verè assumsisset, & retineret naturam nostram: quoniam sine ea non esset frater noster.
units.tr: 3. The office of mediator required in Christ a truly human nature, taken from our nature, which had sinned and which was to be redeemed by him, etc., as above. It was necessary that the same nature which had sinned should suffer. But our nature sinned. Therefore it was necessary for Christ to assume the same nature, not one created out of nothing or sent down from heaven, etc.; and not only to assume it but also to retain it, and for our flesh to remain for ever. For the Father receives us into grace on this condition, that we remain grafted into his Son. This consolation is necessary for us for ever: that Christ is our brother and bears our flesh. We are flesh of his flesh, and bone of his bones. We would lose this consolation if Christ had not truly assumed and retained our nature, since without it he would not be our brother.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Caro Adami est peccatrix. Caro Christi non est peccatrix. Ergo caro Christi non est Adami. Resp. Ab accidente ad substantiam non valet consequentia. Caro Adami, non per se ante lapsum: sed per accidens post lapsum peccatrix est: sequitur ergo, carnem Christi tantum secundum accidens illud non esse carnem Adami: non autem, non esse secundum substantiam Adæ carnem. Itaque argumentum sic potius inuertitur: Caro Adami secundum substantiam est vera caro. Caro Christi est caro Adami secundum substantiam. Ergo caro Christi est vera caro.
units.tr: Objection 1. The flesh of Adam is sinful. The flesh of Christ is not sinful. Therefore the flesh of Christ is not of Adam. Answer. The consequence from accident to substance does not hold. The flesh of Adam was not sinful in itself before the fall, but became sinful accidentally after the fall. It follows, then, that the flesh of Christ is not the flesh of Adam only in that accident, but not that it is not Adam's flesh in substance. So the argument should rather be turned around thus: The flesh of Adam is in substance true flesh. The flesh of Christ is in substance the flesh of Adam. Therefore the flesh of Christ is true flesh.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Christus est conceptus ex Spiritu sancto. Ergo caro eius est propagata ex substantia Spiritus sancti: proinde non est creatura. Respond. vt supra: Est fallacia figuræ dictionis, Nam particula ex significat causam efficientem, non materialem.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit. Therefore his flesh was propagated from the substance of the Holy Spirit, and so it is not a creature. Answer as above: this is a fallacy of the figure of speech, for the particle of [ex] signifies the efficient cause, not the material cause.

units.la: Obj. 3. In Deo non sunt duæ naturæ. Christus est Deus. Ergo in Christo non sunt duæ naturæ. Resp. Ex puris particularibus nihil sequitur. Maior non habet dici de omni, & vera tantum est de Deo Patre, & Spiritu sancto, non de Filio incarnato, qui est Deus manifestatus in carne.
units.tr: Objection 3. In God there are not two natures. Christ is God. Therefore in Christ there are not two natures. Answer. Nothing follows from purely particular premises. The major premise cannot be stated of everything; it is true only of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, not of the incarnate Son, who is God manifested in the flesh.

units.la: Inst. 1. Deo nihil potest accedere. Filius est Deus. Ergo non potest ei accedere humana natura. Resp. ad maiorem: Deo nihil potest accedere, perfectione: potest autem copulatione: quia assumsit semen Abrahae.
units.tr: Instance 1. Nothing can be added to God. The Son is God. Therefore a human nature cannot be joined to him. Answer to the major: Nothing can be added to God in respect of perfection; but something can be added by conjunction, because he assumed the seed of Abraham.

units.la: Inst. 2. Deus inhabitat lucem inaccessam. Ergo non potest humana natura ad Deum accedere. Resp. Conceditur non posse naturam humanam accedere ad Deum, nisi Deus ipse sibi eam ex gratia admoveat, assumat & uniat.
units.tr: Instance 2. God dwells in unapproachable light. Therefore a human nature cannot approach God. Answer. It is granted that a human nature cannot approach God unless God himself, out of grace, brings it near to himself, assumes it and unites it to himself.

units.la: Inst. 3. Deo ignominiosum est esse creaturam. Resp. Deo ignominiosum est, mutari in creaturam, non autem uniri cum natura creata, sine mutatione suae essentiae.
units.tr: Instance 3. It is dishonourable for God to be a creature. Answer. It is dishonourable for God to be changed into a creature, but not to be united with a created nature without any change in his essence.

units.la: II. An Christus sit una persona, vel plures.
units.tr: II. Whether Christ is one person or several.

units.la: Duae quidem naturae in Christo sunt, sed una tantum persona. Marcion dixit duos fuisse Christos: unum crucifixum, alterum non: hunc Christum tantum descendisse super Iesum in cruce suspensum. Sed oportuit unum esse Christum: quia oportuit unum esse mediatorem merito & efficacia. Ergo & unam tantum oportuit esse personam.
units.tr: There are indeed two natures in Christ, but only one person. Marcion said that there were two Christs: one crucified, the other not crucified; this Christ, he said, had descended upon Jesus when He was hanging on the cross. But Christ had to be one, because there had to be one Mediator, in merit and in efficacy. Therefore there had to be only one person as well.

units.la: Obiect. 1. In quo sunt duae res constituentes duas integras personas, in illo etiam sunt duae personae. In Christo sunt duae res constituentes duas integras personas: λόγος enim est integra persona: item corpus & anima, &c. Ergo in Christo sunt duae personae. Resp. Negatur minoris altera pars, quod corpus & anima in λόγῳ constituant personam. Hoc falsum esse, patet ex definitione personae, quae non competit naturae humanae à λόγῳ assumtae. Non enim subsistit per se, sed sustentatur in & ab alio, nempe in & à λόγῳ. Nam tunc primum coepit esse, cum est assumta à λόγῳ, & tunc assumta est cum coepit esse: quia & nunquam exstitisset, nisi à λόγῳ assumpta esset, nec exsisteret nunc, nisi à λόγῳ sustentaretur. Est etiam pars alterius, nempe personae Mediatoris. At persona est individuum intelligens, per se subsistens, non sustentatum ab alio, nec est pars alterius. λόγος quidem persona fuit, & est, quatenus assumsit carnem: habet vero rationem naturae, quatenus unitus est carni. Unde fit, ut recte dicatur: Persona naturam assumsit: &, Natura naturam unita est. Humana enim natura in Christo est condita, ut sit pars alterius: & recte dicere possumus, humanam Christi naturam esse alterius partem: modo in partis nomine nulla intelligatur imperfectio. Tunc enim non sine periculo sic loqueremur: ideoque multi ab hac locutione abstinuerunt. Damascenus tamen alij, ea loquendi formula sæpe vtuntur, personam λόγου incarnati esse ὑπόστασιν, compositam.
units.tr: Objection 1. In whom there are two things constituting two complete persons, in him there are also two persons. In Christ there are two things constituting two complete persons: for the Word [λόγος] is a complete person; likewise body and soul, etc. Therefore there are two persons in Christ. Answer. The second part of the minor premise is denied: that body and soul, in the Word, constitute a person. That this is false is plain from the definition of person, which does not apply to the human nature assumed by the Word. For it does not subsist of itself, but is upheld in and by another, namely in and by the Word. For it began to exist at the very moment it was assumed by the Word, and it was assumed at the moment it began to exist; since it would never have existed unless it had been assumed by the Word, nor would it exist now unless it were sustained by the Word. It is also a part of another, namely of the person of the Mediator. But a person is an intelligent individual, subsisting of itself, not sustained by another, and not a part of another. The Word indeed was and is a person, insofar as He assumed flesh; but He has the character of a nature insofar as He is united to flesh. Hence it is rightly said: the Person assumed the nature, and: the nature is united to the nature. For the human nature in Christ was created so as to be a part of another; and we may rightly say that the human nature of Christ is a part of another, provided that no imperfection is understood in the name of part. For otherwise we would be speaking without danger, and therefore many have abstained from this manner of speaking. Damascene and others, however, often use this form of expression, calling the person of the incarnate Word a composite hypostasis.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Sic neque λόγος erit persona, quia & ipse est pars personæ. Quod est pars personæ, non est persona. λόγος est pars persona. Ergo λόγος non est persona. Resp. ad maiorem. Quod est pars personæ, scilicet tantum, hoc est, ita, vt non etiam sit persona: vel, quod est pars personæ, non est persona, scilicet ea ipsa, cuius, & quatenus est pars. Sic λόγος non est integra persona Mediatoris, etsi per se est integra persona secunda divinitatis.
units.tr: Objection 2. In that case the Word will not be a person either, because He too is a part of a person. What is a part of a person is not a person. The Word is a part of a person. Therefore the Word is not a person. Answer to the major. What is a part of a person is so only in part, that is, in such a way that it is not also a person; or: what is a part of a person is not a person, namely that same person of which, and insofar as, it is a part. Thus the Word is not the complete person of the Mediator, although in Himself He is a complete person of the second divinity.

units.la: Obiect. 3. DEVS & homo sunt duæ personæ. Christus est Deus & homo. Ergo sunt duæ personæ. R. Maior vera est extra vnionem. Christus verò est Deus & homo in vnione. Est ergo fallacia compositionis & divisionis. Nam Deus & homo in maiore sensu diuisò: in minore sensu composito accipiuntur.
units.tr: Objection 3. God and man are two persons. Christ is God and man. Therefore there are two persons. Answer. The major is true outside the union. But Christ is God and man in the union. There is therefore a fallacy of composition and division. For God and man are taken in the divided sense in the major, and in the composite sense in the minor.

units.la: Inst. 1. λόγος vniuit sibi corpus & animam. Ergo personam. Resp. Vniuit sibi carnem & sanguinem, non quæ per se subsisterent, sed vt subsisterent in sua ὑπόστασι.
units.tr: Objection 1 (of the instance). The Word united to Himself a body and soul. Therefore a person. Answer. He united to Himself flesh and blood, not things which would subsist of themselves, but so that they would subsist in His hypostasis.

units.la: Inst. 2. Vniuit sibi partes essentiales personæ. Ergo personam. Resp. Maior valet de partibus per se subsistentibus: Christi autem corpus & anima non subsistunt per se, nec subsistitissent extra hanc vnionem.
units.tr: Objection 2 (of the instance). He united to Himself the essential parts of a person. Therefore a person. Answer. The major holds of parts which subsist of themselves; but the body and soul of Christ do not subsist of themselves, nor would they have subsisted apart from this union.

units.la: Inst. 3. Non subsistens per se est imperfectior eo, quod subsistit per se. Natura humana Christi non subsistit per se, nostra autem per se subsistit. Ergo humana Christi natura est imperfectior nostra. Resp. Est fallacia ἀμφιβολίας in vocabulo per se. Humana natura quomodo subsistat per se. Natura humana Christi non subsistit per se: quatenus non est ipsa per se & separatim persona: quo modo per se subsistere non debuit; quia sic per se subsistens Christus non esset nobis perfectior: sed esset nudus homo, sicut nos sumus. Et tamen subsistit per se, quatenus non subsistit per accidens: sed est substantia, constituens partem integri indiuidui Mediatoris ἀνθρώπου.
units.tr: Objection 3 (of the instance). What does not subsist of itself is less perfect than what subsists of itself. The human nature of Christ does not subsist of itself, but ours does subsist of itself. Therefore the human nature of Christ is less perfect than ours. Answer. There is a fallacy of ambiguity in the word of itself. How the human nature subsists of itself. The human nature of Christ does not subsist of itself, insofar as it is not in itself and separately a person; it ought not to subsist of itself in that way, since a Christ subsisting of himself would not be more perfect for us, but would be a mere man, as we are. And yet it subsists of itself, insofar as it does not subsist by accident; but it is a substance, constituting a part of the complete individual Mediator, the God-man.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Mortuus & perpetuò viuens non sunt idem. Christus est mortuus, & perpetuò viuens. Ergo non est vna persona. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini: quia Maior intelligitur secundum idem: Minor non secundum idem, sed secundum diuersas naturas.
units.tr: Objection 4. The dead and the perpetually living are not the same. Christ is dead, and perpetually living. Therefore He is not one person. Answer. There are four terms: because the major is understood in the same respect, while the minor is not understood in the same respect, but according to different natures.

units.la: III. Qualis sit naturarum vnio: & quomodo facta.
units.tr: III. What sort of union of the natures there is, and how it was brought about.

units.la: Facta est hæc vnio duarum naturarum in vnam personam Christi, operatione Spiritus sancti, in ipsa conceptione: ita vt duæ naturæ in vna Christi persona subsistant inconfusè, inconuer-tibitibiliter, indiuulse, & inseparabiliter: vt est in symbolo Chalcedo- nensi. Vocatur vnio hypostatica: hoc est, personalis: quia duæ naturæ diuersæ, arcano modo, vnitæ sunt in vnam personam: saluis & integris manentibus vtriusque naturæ proprietatibus essentialibus. Christus igitur propter hanc vnionem dicitur, & verè est Deus & homo: secundum distinctas naturas. Deus secundum diuinam: homo secundum humanam naturam. Quod ex te nascetur sanctum, Filius Dei vocabitur. in ipso habitat tota ple- nitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Verbum caro factum est. Semen Abrahæ assumsit. Deus manifestatus est in carne.
units.tr: This union of the two natures into one person of Christ was brought about by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in the very conception itself; so that the two natures subsist in the one person of Christ unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, and inseparably, as is stated in the Chalcedonian creed. It is called the hypostatic union, that is, personal, because two different natures are joined in one person in a hidden manner, while the essential properties of each nature remain safe and whole. Therefore, on account of this union, Christ is called and truly is both God and man, according to the distinct natures: God according to the divine nature, man according to the human nature. That which shall be born of you will be called holy, the Son of God. In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. The Word was made flesh. He took hold of the seed of Abraham. God was manifested in the flesh.

units.la: IV. Quare oportuerit fieri vnionem hypostaticam.
units.tr: IV. Why the hypostatic union had to come about.

units.la: Supra sunt expositæ causæ, cur oportuerit Mediatorem esse verum & perfectè justum hominem, & simul verum Deum; quas non necesse est hic repetere. Propter eandem causas oportuit fieri vnionem hypostaticam naturarum in Mediatore, vt simul verus homo & verus Deus esset, qui justitiam & vitam amissam nobis & merèri & restituere posset.
units.tr: The causes why the Mediator had to be a true and perfectly righteous man, and at the same time true God, have been set out above, and there is no need to repeat them here. For the same causes it was necessary that a hypostatic union of the natures should take place in the Mediator, so that he might be at once a true man and a true God, able both to merit for us and to restore the righteousness and life we had lost.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXXVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 37.

units.la: Quid credis? cùm dicis: Passus est? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What do you believe when you say: He suffered? ANSWER.

units.la: Eum toto quidem vitæ suæ tempore, quo in terris egit, præcipuè verò in eius extremo, iram Dei aduersus peccarum vniuersi generis humani, corpore & anima sustinuisse a, vt sua passione tanquam vnico sacrificio propitiatorio b corpus & animam nostram ab æterna damnatione liberaret c, & nobis gratiam Dei, justitiam & vitam æternam acquireret.
units.tr: That throughout the whole of his life on earth, but especially at its end, he bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sins of the whole human race, so that by his suffering, as the one propitiatory sacrifice, he might free our body and soul from eternal damnation, and might win for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hactenus de persona Mediatoris, sequitur de officio: ac primum de humiliatione Christi, priore scilicet officij parte, ad quam pertinet articulus quartus: Passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus fixus, mortuus, & sepultus, descendit ad inferos. Passio Christi statim sequitur eius conceptionem & natiuitatem. 1. Quia in eius passione & morte tota nostra salus consistit. 2. Quia tota eius vita fuit continua passio & calamitas. Interim in historia transactae vitae ipsius ab Euangelistis descripta, multa etiam utiliter possunt ac debent obseruari. Nam. 1. ostendit, hanc personam esse Messiam promissum, cum in ea concurrant & impleantur omnia prophetarum vaticinia. 2. Est consideratio humilitatis & obedientiae, quam Patri praestitit.
units.tr: So far we have spoken of the person of the Mediator; now follows his office, and first his humiliation, the first part of the office, to which belongs the fourth article: Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried, descended into hell. The suffering of Christ immediately follows his conception and birth, for two reasons: (1) because our whole salvation consists in his passion and death; (2) because his whole life was a continual suffering and affliction. Meanwhile, in the history of his life as described by the Evangelists, many things can and should be usefully observed. For (1) it shows that this person is the promised Messiah, since in him all the prophetic predictions meet and are fulfilled; (2) it offers a consideration of the humility and obedience he showed to the Father.

units.la: Huc pertinent ea, quae sunt meditanda in passione Christi. 1. Historia congruens cum miraculis. 2. Causae fructus passionis. 3. Exemplum, quo nos Christus per passiones praecessit in gloriam.
units.tr: To this belong the things to be meditated upon in the passion of Christ: (1) the history, in harmony with the miracles; (2) the causes and fruits of the passion; (3) the example by which Christ went before us through sufferings into glory.

units.la: Plenioris vero explicationis causa considerentur hae quaestiones.
units.tr: For a fuller explanation, the following questions are to be considered.

units.la: DE PASSIONE CHRISTI.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE PASSION OF CHRIST.

units.la: I. Quid passionis nomine intelligatur; seu, quid Christus sit passus. II. An sit passus secundum utramque naturam. III. Qua passionis causa impulsiva. IV. Qua causa finales & fructus.
units.tr: I. What is meant by the name of passion, or what Christ suffered. II. Whether he suffered according to both natures. III. The impelling cause of the passion. IV. The final causes and fruits.

units.la: I. Quid nomine passionis intelligatur: seu, quid sit passus Christus.
units.tr: I. What is meant by the name of passion, or what Christ suffered.

units.la: Nomine passionis intelligitur tota humiliatio, seu obedientia totius humiliationis, omnes miseriae, infirmitates, dolores, cruciatus, ignominiae, quibus Christus ab articulo natiuitatis ad horam usque mortis, tam anima, quam corpore, nostri causa fuit obnoxius. Dolorum enim praecipua pars fuerunt cruciatus animae, in qua sensit iram Dei aduersus peccata generis humani. Principaliter tamen intelligitur actus extremus vitae eius, in quo passus est extremos animae & corporis cruciatus, propter nostra peccata. Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me dereliquisti? Vere languores nostros ipse tulit. Coniecit in eum peccata omnium nostrum. Propterea sic voluit eum Dominus conterere.
units.tr: By the name passion is meant the whole humiliation, or the obedience of the whole humiliation: all the miseries, infirmities, pains, torments, and dishonours to which Christ, from the article of his birth to the hour of his death, was subject for our sake, both in soul and in body. For the chief part of his pains were the torments of his soul, in which he felt the wrath of God against the sins of the human race. Chiefly, however, it means the final act of his life, in which he suffered the extreme torments of soul and body for our sins. "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death." "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" "Surely he hath borne our griefs." "The Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all." "Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him."

units.la: Quid igitur Christus est passus? 1. Carentiam seu priuationem summae felicitatis, laetitiae, & omnium bonorum, quibus frui debuit. 2. Omnes infirmitates naturae humanae, excepto peccato: esuriit, sitiuit, defessus est, tristitia & dolore fuit affectus; &c. 3. Extremam inopiam & pauperratem. Filius hominis non habet, vbi caput reclinet. 4. Inhonitas injurias, contumelias, calucalumnias, insidias, obtrectationes, opprobria, blasphemias, abiectionem & contemtum. Ego vermis, & non homo. Vidimus eum, & non erat illi aspectus, vel forma. 5. Tentationes diaboli. Tentatus in omnibus similiter, absque peccato. 6. Mortem corporis, & quidem contumeliosam, nempe crucis. 7. Gravissimos animæ cruciatus, sensum videlicet iræ Dei adversus peccata universi generis humani. Hinc est, quod alta voce clamat in cruce: Deus meus, Deus meus, cur dereliquisti me? quasi dicat: cur non repellis à me tantos cruciatus? Ita videmus, quæ & quanta pro nobis Christus sit passus.
units.tr: What then did Christ suffer? (1) The lack and deprivation of supreme happiness, joy, and all the good things which he ought to have enjoyed. (2) All the infirmities of human nature, apart from sin: he hungered, thirsted, grew weary, and was affected with sorrow and grief, etc. (3) Extreme poverty and want: "The Son of man hath not where to lay his head." (4) Unjust injuries, insults, slanders, snares, detractions, reproaches, blasphemies, abasement, and contempt: "I am a worm, and no man; I was seen, and he had no form or comeliness." (5) The temptations of the devil: "Tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin." (6) Death of the body, and that a shameful one, namely the cross. (7) The most grievous torments of the soul, namely the sense of God's wrath against the sins of the whole human race. Hence it is that he cries out with a loud voice on the cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?", as if to say: why dost thou not drive away from me such great torments? Thus we see what and how great things Christ suffered for us.

units.la: Sed cùm fuerit divina natura unita humanæ, qui fieri potuit, ut humana ita frangeretur, ac debilitaretur, ut erumperet in illas voces: cùm tamen alij martyres fuerint multo fortiores? Resp. Id factum est, propter diversitatem supplicij Christi, & aliorum martyrum. Laurentius jacens in craticula, non sentit horrendam iram Dei, neque adversus sua, neque adversus humani generis peccata: quorum poena tota in Filium Dei effusa erat, sicut inquit Iesaias, Christum percussum & contritum fuisse à Deo, propter peccata nostra: non, inquam, sensit Deum percutientem & iratum Laurentius, sed reconciliatum & propitium: nec sicut Christus horrores mortis & inferni expertus est, sed ingentem consolationem, quod pro confessione Euangelij pateretur; ac certus fuit, peccata sibi remissa esse per & propter Filium Dei, in quem ea Deus reiecerat, juxta dictum: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Hinc itaque factum est, ut maiori constantia & animi præsentia Laurentius fuisse in suo martyrio, quàm Christus in suo λύτρῳ videatur. Ideo autem humana Christi natura, licet unita esset divinitati, potuit sudare sanguinem in horto, & in voces illas erumpere: Deus meus, ut quid me dereliquisti? non, quod facta esset naturarum diuulsio, sed quod humanitas à divinitate ad tempus desereretur, quiescente λόγῳ, ut loquitur Irenæus, nec ferente auxilium & liberationem humanitati afflictæ, donec passio sufficiens peracta esset.
units.tr: But since the divine nature was united with the human, how could it happen that the human nature was so broken and weakened that it burst out into those words, when other martyrs were far stronger? Answer: this came about because of the difference between the punishment of Christ and that of other martyrs. Laurence, lying on the gridiron, did not feel the dreadful wrath of God, neither against his own sins nor against the sins of the human race, whose whole punishment was poured out upon the Son of God; as Isaiah says, that Christ was smitten and bruised by God for our sins. I say that Laurence did not feel God striking and angry, but reconciled and propitious; nor did he experience the horrors of death and hell as Christ did, but had great consolation, that he suffered for the confession of the Gospel; and he was certain that his sins were forgiven him through and for the sake of the Son of God, upon whom God had laid them, according to the saying: "Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins of the world." Hence it came about that Laurence seems to have shown greater constancy and presence of mind in his martyrdom than Christ in his ransom [λύτρον]. Moreover, the human nature of Christ, although united with the divinity, could sweat blood in the garden and burst out into those words: My God, why hast thou forsaken me? not because the natures were torn apart, but because the humanity was for a time deserted by the divinity, the Word being at rest (as Irenaeus says), and not bringing help and deliverance to the afflicted humanity, until the sufficient passion was completed.

units.la: Differt igitur passio Christi ab aliorum passionibus. 1. Ipsa forma. Christus enim corpore & anima sentit totalem Dei iram: alij non item. 2. Causa impulsiva. Christus patitur propter peccata, non sua, sed nostra. 3. Finis. Passio Christi est λύτρον, & sacrificium unicum propitiatorium pro nostris peccatis. Aliorum passiones non sunt λύτρων, sed vel τιμωρίαι, vel δοκιμασίαι, vel μαρτύρια.
units.tr: The passion of Christ therefore differs from the sufferings of others. (1) The very form. For Christ, in body and soul, feels the whole wrath of God; others do not. (2) The impelling cause. Christ suffers on account of sins, not his own but ours. (3) The end. The passion of Christ is a ransom [λύτρον] and the one propitiatory sacrifice for our sins. The sufferings of others are not ransoms [λύτρων], but either punishments [τιμωρίαι], or trials [δοκιμασίαι], or testimonies [μαρτύρια].

units.la: Obiect. 1. Innocens ex ordine justitiæ Dei non debet plecti pro nocentibus: quia justitiæ est plectere sontes. Christus est innoinnocens. Pugnat ergo cum regula justitiæ eius supplicium, quod innocens sustinuit pro nobis nocentibus. Resp. ad maiorem: Innocens non debet plecti pro nocentibus. 1. Nisi innocens vltrò se offerat pro nocentibus. 2. Nisi volens sic patiatur, vt præstet sufficiens λύτρον. 3. Et ipse interim non pereat in supplicio, sed emergat. 4. Possit etiam efficere, ne ij, pro quibus satisfacit, in posterum peccent. 5. Et sit eiusdem naturæ cum iis, pro quibus est satisfaciendum. Talis satisfactor si substituatur, nihil fit contra justitiam Dei. Sic enim patiendo vterq; seruatur, & patiens, & pro quo fit passio. Talis autem satisfactor est Christus. Nam & omnia hæc fecit, & non tantum est homo eiusdem naturæ vobiscum, sed etiam nos sumus eius membra. Propter hanc nostri cum capite Christo coniunctionem, supplicium eius verè fuit nostrum supplicium; unde passim dicunt Apostoli, nos omnes passos & mortuos esse in Christo. Cum enim totum corpus luit pœnam, plectuntur omnia membra. Plura de hoc argumento vide infra articulo de remissione peccatorum, quæst. 56. & aliquid etiam supra quæst. 13. de modo satisfactionis. Summa. Vt aliquis pro alio satisfaciat, debent ista concurrere 1. Sufficiens satisfactio. 2. Eaque spontanea. 3. Vt is, cui debetur, fit ea contentus. Ista concurrunt in satisfactione Christi.
units.tr: Objection 1. The innocent, by the order of God's justice, ought not to be punished for the guilty, since it belongs to justice to punish the guilty. Christ is innocent. Therefore his punishment, which the innocent bore for us the guilty, is contrary to the rule of his justice. Answer to the major premise: The innocent ought not to be punished for the guilty: (1) unless the innocent of his own accord offers himself for the guilty; (2) unless he willingly suffers in such a way as to provide a sufficient ransom [λύτρον]; (3) and unless he himself in the meantime does not perish in the punishment, but rises again; (4) and is able also to bring it about that those for whom he makes satisfaction do not sin in the future; (5) and is of the same nature as those for whom the satisfaction is to be made. If such a satisfier is substituted, nothing is done against the justice of God. For by suffering in this way both are saved, both the one who suffers and the one for whom the suffering is undergone. Such a satisfier is Christ. For he did all these things, and he is not only a man of the same nature as we are, but we are also his members. Because of this union of us with Christ the Head, his punishment was truly our punishment; hence the Apostles everywhere say that we all were crucified and died in Christ. For when the whole body pays the penalty, all the members are punished. More on this argument see below, in the article on the forgiveness of sins, question 56, and something also above in question 13 on the manner of satisfaction. Summary. For one person to satisfy for another, the following must concur: (1) a sufficient satisfaction; (2) and that a voluntary one; (3) that he to whom it is owed is content with it. These concur in the satisfaction of Christ.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Inter satisfactionem & culpam debet esse proportio. Sed inter vnius personæ passionem, & infinitorum hominum peccata, nulla est proportio. Quomodo igitur vnius Christi poteست respondere infinitorum hominum peccatis? Resp. Potest duplici causa. 1. Ob dignitatem personæ: quia est verus Deus, & homo purus. 2. Ob grauitatem supplicij: quia est passus maledictam mortem; quam nos in æternum debuissemus pati. Æquipollet igitur ipsius passio pœnæ æternæ, immò eam superat: quia Deum pati plus est, quàm omnes creaturas interire. Miraculum maximum fuit, Filium Dei clamare in cruce: Deus meus, quid me dereliquisti?
units.tr: Objection 2. There must be a proportion between a satisfaction and the guilt it pays for. But there is no proportion between the suffering of one person and the sins of infinitely many men. How then could the suffering of Christ alone correspond to the sins of infinitely many men? Answer. It can, for two reasons. (1) Because of the dignity of the person: he is true God and pure man. (2) Because of the severity of the punishment: he suffered the accursed death, which we ourselves ought to have suffered for ever. His suffering therefore equals the punishment of eternal death, or rather surpasses it, since for God to suffer is more than for all creatures to perish. It was the greatest miracle when the Son of God cried out on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

units.la: Inst. 1. Deus non potest pati & mori. Christus est passus & mortuus. Ergo non est Deus. Resp. ad maiorem: Deus, hoc est, persona, quæ tantum est Deus, non potest pati, seu, est impassibilis secundum id, secundum quod Deus est. Christus autem non tantum est Deus, sed etiam homo. Vel: concedo totum argumentum recte intellectum. Nam Christus non est Deus secundum id, quo est passus & mortuus, hoc est, secundum naturam humanam.
units.tr: Objection 1. God cannot suffer and die. Christ suffered and died. Therefore he is not God. Answer to the major premise: God, that is, the person who is only God, cannot suffer; or, he is impassible in respect of that in which he is God. But Christ is not only God but also man. Or: I grant the whole argument, rightly understood. For Christ is not God in respect of that by which he suffered and died, that is, in respect of his human nature.

units.la: Inst. 2. Si Christus non est Deus secundum quod passus est? falsum igitur, quod dicitur, Deum Ecclesiam redemisse suo sanguine. Resp. Est communicatio idiomatum, seu, locutio ex. synecdochica, vera tamen in concreto. Deus, hoc est, ea persona, quæ est Deus & homo, redemit Ecclesiam suo sanguine, quem profudit secundum humanitatem. Est autem communicatio idiomatum tribuere toti personæ, quod est alterius naturæ proprium, in concreto: quia nomen concretum significat personam, in qua est utraque natura, & eius naturæ proprietas, de qua ea prædicatur. Ideo nihil impedit, quo minus de tota persona prædicetur; quod est alterius naturæ proprium, modo illa proprietas personæ insit. De nomine vero abstracto tantum prædicantur proprietates eius naturæ, cuius sunt proprię. Hæc obiter.
units.tr: Objection 2. If Christ is not God in respect of what he suffered, then it is false to say that God redeemed the Church with his blood. Answer. This is a communication of attributes, or a figure of speech by synecdoche, yet true in the concrete. God, that is, the person who is God and man, redeemed the Church with his blood, which he shed according to his humanity. A communication of attributes consists in ascribing to the whole person what belongs to the other nature, in the concrete, because a concrete name signifies the person in whom both natures are, and the property of that nature of which the predicate is affirmed. Nothing therefore prevents something that belongs to one nature from being predicated of the whole person, provided that property really inheres in the person. But properties are predicated of an abstract name only of the nature to which they belong. So much in passing.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Temporalis & æternæ pœnæ nulla est proportio. Christus passus est tantum temporalem pœnam. Ergo non potuit satisfacere pro pœnis æternis. Resp. ad maiorem. Nulla est proportio temporalis & æternæ pœnæ, in eodem subiecto: sed potest esse in diuersis subiectis: quia supplicium temporale Filij Dei dignitate præcellit totius mundi æterno supplicio, propter causas prius explicatas.
units.tr: Objection 3. There is no proportion between temporal and eternal punishment. Christ suffered only temporal punishment. Therefore he could not make satisfaction for eternal punishments. Answer to the major premise. There is no proportion between temporal and eternal punishment in the same subject; but there can be one between different subjects, because the temporal suffering of the Son of God, by reason of his dignity, far exceeds the eternal suffering of the whole world, for the causes explained above.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Si Christus pro omnibus satisfecit, omnes debent seruari. Atqui non omnes seruantur. Ergo non perfecte satisfecit. Resp. Satisfecit pro omnibus, quoad sufficientiam λύτρου, sed non quoad applicationem. Nam legem impleuit dupliciter: 1. Iustitia sua propria. 2. Satisfactione pro omnium peccatis sufficiente & perfectissimâ. Vtraque est perfectissima legis impletio. Satisfactio autem fit nostra applicatione, quæ etiam est duplex: Prior fit à Deo, cum nos iustificat propter Filij sui meritum, & facit, vt desinamus peccare. Altera fit à nobis fide. Applicamus enim nobis meritum Christi, quando statuimus vera fide, Deum propter λύτρου Filij sui nobis remittere peccata. Sine hac applicatione satisfactio Christi licet in se sufficientissima, nulli prodest.
units.tr: Objection 4. If Christ made satisfaction for all, then all must be saved. But not all are saved. Therefore he did not satisfy perfectly. Answer. He made satisfaction for all as to the sufficiency of the ransom [λύτρου], but not as to its application. For he fulfilled the law in two ways: (1) by his own righteousness; (2) by a satisfaction for the sins of all, sufficient and most perfect. Both are the most perfect fulfilment of the law. Now the satisfaction is made ours by application, which is also twofold. The first is made by God, when he justifies us on account of the merit of his Son and causes us to cease from sinning. The second is made by us through faith. For we apply to ourselves the merit of Christ when by true faith we conclude that God, for the sake of the ransom [λύτρου] of his Son, forgives us our sins. Without this application, the satisfaction of Christ, however fully sufficient in itself, profits no one.

units.la: Obiect. 5. At etiam in lege Mosis fuerunt sacrificia propitiatoria. Resp. Non proprie expiatoria, sed typica. Christi autem sacrificium vnicum est vere & proprie expiatorium. Non enim potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. Sanguis Iesu Christi Filij Dei purgat nos ab omni peccato. Ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi.
units.tr: Objection 5. But in the law of Moses there were also propitiatory sacrifices. Answer. They were not properly expiatory but typical. The sacrifice of Christ alone is truly and properly expiatory. "For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins" (Heb. 10:4). "The blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). "He is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2).

units.la: II. An Christus sit passus secundum vtramque naturam.
units.tr: II. Whether Christ suffered according to both natures.

units.la: Non secundum vtramque naturam, neque secundum diuinitatem, sed secundum humanam naturam tantum Christus passus est anima & corpore. Diuina enim natura cum sit immutabilis, impassiimpassibilis, immortalis, & vita ipsa, pati & mori non potuit. Ita autem passus est secundum humanitatem suam, ut morte & passione sua satisfeceret pro infinitis hominum peccatis: diuina autem natura humanitatem suam sustinuit in doloribus, passioni vigorem addens, & mortuam reuocauit in vitam. Nam & Christus semel propeccatis passus fuit, justus pro injustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret, mortificatus quidem carne, vivificatus autem spiritu. Christus pro nobis passus est carne. Destruite templum hoc, & tribus diebus ego erigam illud. Mortuus sum, & ecce vivo. Habeo potestatem ponendi animam, & rursus eam assumendi. Haec dicta testantur, praeter carnem fuisse aliam naturam in Christo, quae non est passa & mortua: Sicut homo erat, ut tentaretur: sic & verbum erat, ut glorificaretur, requiescente quidem verbo, ut possit tentari, crucifigi & mori: & tamen humanitati unito, ut posset vincere, &c.
units.tr: Christ did not suffer according to both natures, nor according to the deity, but according to the human nature only, in soul and body. For the divine nature, since it is immutable, impassible, immortal, and life itself, could not suffer or die. Yet he suffered according to his humanity in such a way that by his death and passion he made satisfaction for the infinite sins of men; while the divine nature sustained his humanity in its sorrows, lending vigour to the passion, and recalled the dead humanity to life. For Christ also "once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit" (1 Pet. 3:18). "Christ suffered for us in the flesh" (1 Pet. 4:1). "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19). "I died, and behold, I am alive" (Rev. 1:18). "I have power to lay down my life, and power to take it again" (John 10:18). These sayings testify that in Christ, besides the flesh, there was another nature which did not suffer and did not die. "As he was man, he could be tempted; so also he was the Word, that he might be glorified, the Word indeed resting, so that he could be tempted, crucified, and die; and yet united to the humanity, so that he could conquer," and so on.

units.la: Obiect. Deus suo sanguine Ecclesiam acquisivit. Ergo Deitas est passa. Respond. Non sequitur: quia mutatur genus praedicationis. Deus est mortuus, dicitur per communicationem idiomatum, seu, per synecdochen. Sed Deitas est passa, dicitur sine figura. Item, a concreto ad abstractum non valet consequentia. Concretum significat subiectum habens formam. Abstractum nudam formam. Non omnia vero comperiunt formae, quae subiecto. In hac doctrina Concretum est nomen personae. Abstractum nomen naturae. Non omnia autem comperunt naturae, quae personae. Ut igitur non sequitur: Homo est compositus ex elementis, corporeus & mortalis: Ergo & anima est composita ex elementis, corporea, & mortalis: ita non sequitur; Christus Deus est passus, mortuus: Ergo Christi Deitas est passa & mortua.
units.tr: Objection. God acquired the Church with his own blood. Therefore the Deity suffered. Answer. It does not follow, because the kind of predication changes. "God died" is said by communication of attributes, or by synecdoche. But "the Deity suffered" is said without a figure. Likewise, the inference from the concrete to the abstract is not valid. The concrete signifies a subject having a form; the abstract the bare form. But not all things that belong to the form belong to the subject, and not all things that belong to the subject belong to the nature. In this doctrine the concrete is the name of the person; the abstract the name of the nature. Therefore, just as it does not follow that "man is composed of elements, corporeal and mortal, therefore the soul is composed of elements, corporeal and mortal," so it does not follow that "Christ, who is God, suffered and died, therefore the Deity of Christ suffered and died."

units.la: III. Quae causae impulsivae passionis Christi?
units.tr: III. What were the impelling causes of Christ's passion?

units.la: Causa movens Deum, ut daret Filium pro nobis, fuit 1. Amor Dei erga genus humanum. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret. 2. Misericordia Dei erga lapsos in peccatum & mortem. Ex sua misericordia servavit nos. 3. Voluntas in Deo vindicandi injustitiam diaboli, qua nos ab ipso auerterat, & imaginem Dei mutilauerat in contumeliam creatoris.
units.tr: The cause moving God to give his Son for us was: (1) the love of God toward the human race: Thus God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son. (2) The mercy of God toward those fallen into sin and death: According to his mercy he saved us. (3) The will in God to avenge the injustice of the devil, by which he turned us away from him and marred the image of God, to the insult of the Creator.

units.la: IV. Quae causae finales, & qui fructus passionis Christi?
units.tr: IV. What are the final causes, and what is the fruit, of Christ's passion?

units.la: Causae finales & fructus passionis Christi idem sunt diversa ratione. Respectu Christi patientis dicuntur causae finales: 1. Patericas spectu nostri, fructus. Sunt autem finales causae praecipuae, 1. Patesfactio amoris, bonitatis, misericordiæ & justitiæ Dei, dum punit Filium pro nobis. 2. Vt eius passio esset λύτρον sufficiens pro peccatis nostris, seu redemtio nostri. Duæ igitur sunt: gloria Dei & salus nostra. Ad priorem pertinet agnitio magnitudinis peccati: vt cogitemus, quantum malum sit peccatum, & quid mereatur. Ad posteriorem justificatio, qua Rom. 8, 30. omnia beneficia comprehenduntur, quæ Christus meritus est moriendo, & quæ confert nobis emersione ex morte. Inde scimus, mortem non esse perniciosam piis, & ideo non esse timendam.
units.tr: The final causes and the fruits of Christ's passion are the same, but viewed in different ways. With respect to Christ suffering, they are called final causes; with respect to us, fruits. The chief final causes are these: (1) the making manifest of the love, goodness, mercy and justice of God, while he punishes his Son for us; (2) that his passion might be a ransom [λύτρον] sufficient for our sins, or the redemption of us. There are therefore two: the glory of God and our salvation. To the former belongs the recognition of the greatness of sin, so that we consider how great an evil sin is and what it deserves. To the latter belongs justification, in which all the benefits are comprehended, which Christ merited by dying and which he confers on us by rising out of death (Rom. 8:30). Hence we know that death is not harmful to the godly, and therefore is not to be feared.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XXXVIII. Quid causæ fuit, cur sub judice Pilato pateretur? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: QUESTION XXXVIII. What was the reason that he suffered under the judge Pilate? ANSWER.

units.la: Vt innocens coram judice politico damnatus posset a severo Dei judicio, quod omnes manebat, eximeret .
units.tr: That the innocent one, condemned by a civil judge, might be freed from the severe judgment of God, which awaited all.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Pilati judicis fit mentio in passione Christi. 1. Quia Christus ab hoc judice consecutus est testimonium innocentiæ. 2. Vt sciamus, Christū quantumuis voce ipsius judicis innocentem pronunciatum, tamen damnatum esse, & quidem ordinario judicio. 3. Monemur de impletione miraculorum. Obliquam, obliquam ponam eam; etiam hæc non fuit; donec veniat, cui jure convenit. Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, neque legislator de pedibus eius, donec veniat Siloh. Facit igitur nomen Pilati, ad confirmationem nostri, Iesum esse exhibitum Messiam. Tunc enim sceptrum erat ablatum à Juda: quia à Romano judice damnatur Christus.
units.tr: The mention of the judge Pilate occurs in the passion of Christ. (1) Because Christ received from this judge a testimony of his innocence. (2) That we may know that Christ, although pronounced innocent by the very voice of the judge, was nevertheless condemned, and that by an ordinary judgment. (3) We are reminded of the fulfilment of prophecies. I will set aside the oblique matter; this too was not (done) until he comes, to whom it rightly belongs: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes" (Gen. 49:10). The name of Pilate therefore serves to confirm for us that Jesus was exhibited as the Messiah. For the sceptre had then been taken from Judah, since Christ was condemned by a Roman judge.

units.la: Quare autem debuit sub judice pati, & condemnari ordinarie?
units.tr: Why, however, ought he to have suffered under a judge and to have been condemned in the ordinary way?

units.la: 1. Vt sciremus, cum ab ipso Deo propter nostra peccata condemnatum esse: ac proinde judicio Dei pro nobis satisfecisse, ne nos in severo iudicio Dei condemnaremur: sicut & mortem pro nobis sustinuit, vt nos à morte liberaret. Nam judicij ordinarij præses est ipse Deus. 2. Vt consequeretur testimonium suæ innocentiæ ab ipso judice, à quo est condemnatus. Ideo non debuit Christus clam à Judæis abripi, neque per tumultum ad mortem trahi: sed legitimo ordine & judicio, facta inquisitione in omnes accusationes, voluit eum Pater 1. Examinari, ut pateret eius innocentia. 2 Damnari, ut constaret, eum innocentem antea pronunciatum, non sua, sed nostra culpa condemnatum esse: atque ita ipsius injusta damnatio esset loco justissimæ condemnationis nostræ. 3. Interfici, tum ut implerentur vaticinia, tum ut constaret, eum & à Judæis, & à gentibus interfectum, & in crucem actum esse. Hæc ergo circumstantia in passione Christi diligenter est consideranda; ut sciamus, hunc Jesum à Pilato damnatum, esse Messiam, & nos per hunc à severo Dei judicio esse exemtos.
units.tr: (1) That we might know that he was condemned by God himself on account of our sins, and so satisfied the judgment of God on our behalf, lest we be condemned in the severe judgment of God; just as he also endured death for us, that he might free us from death. For the president of the ordinary judgment is God himself. (2) That he might obtain a testimony of his innocence from the very judge by whom he was condemned. Therefore Christ ought not to have been secretly snatched away by the Jews, nor dragged to death by tumult; but by lawful order and judgment, with an inquiry made into all the accusations, the Father willed that he be (1) examined, so that his innocence might be made plain; (2) condemned, so that it might be established that he, though previously pronounced innocent, was condemned not for his own fault but for ours, and thus his unjust condemnation would take the place of our most just condemnation; (3) killed, both that the prophecies might be fulfilled and that it might be established that he was put to death and crucified both by the Jews and by the Gentiles. This circumstance in the passion of Christ is therefore to be considered carefully, so that we may know that this Jesus, condemned by Pilate, is the Messiah, and that through him we are freed from the severe judgment of God.

units.la: Jam quid est, Credere in Iesum Christum passum sub Pontio Pilato to? Est ita credere, Christum esse passum, ut non tantum fidem historicam habeas, sed etiam fiduciam in eius passione collocas. Est, inquam, credere 1. Christum esse passum, hoc est, inde à nativitatis momento omnis generis miserias sustinuisse: præcipuè vero extremo vitæ tempore sub judice Pilato acerbissimos quosque cruciatus animo & corpore perpessum esse, & horrendam Dei iram sensisse, in compensationem peccatorum totius mundi, & ad placandam Dei iram adversus peccatum. 2. Certo confidere, eum etiam pro me esse passum, hoc est, sua passione etiam pro meis peccatis satisfecisse, & meruisse mihi esse remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum sanctum, & vitam æternam.
units.tr: Now what is it to believe "in Jesus Christ, suffered under Pontius Pilate"? It is to believe in such a way that Christ suffered, that you not only have an historical faith but also place your trust in his passion. It is, I say, to believe (1) that Christ suffered, that is, that from the moment of his birth he endured miseries of every kind, but especially in the last part of his life, under the judge Pilate, he underwent the most bitter torments in soul and body and felt the dreadful wrath of God, as a compensation for the sins of the whole world and to appease the wrath of God against sin; (2) to trust with certainty that he suffered also for me, that is, that by his passion he also satisfied for my sins, and merited for me the forgiveness of sins, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life.

units.la: QUÆSTIO XXXIX.
units.tr: QUESTION XXXIX.

units.la: Estne verò quiddam amplius, quod affixus est cruci, quam si alio genere mortis affectus esset?
units.tr: Is there, however, anything more in his being fastened to the cross than if he had been afflicted with another kind of death?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Sanè amplius. Ex hac enim re sum certus, eum maledictionem, quæ mihi incumbebat, in se recepisse a. Nam mors crucis à Deo erat maledicta b.
units.tr: Certainly more so. For from this fact I am certain that he took upon himself the curse that lay upon me. For death on a cross was cursed by God.
a Gal. 3.13. b Deut. 21.23.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Mors crucis est exaggeratio supplicij Christi, & confirmatio fidei nostræ. Si enim Christus est crucifixus: ergo 1. sustinuit maledictionem, quia hæc mors signum erat maledictionis. 2. pro nobis, quia ipse in se erat justus.
units.tr: The death on the cross heightens the suffering of Christ and confirms our faith. For if Christ was crucified, then: (1) he bore the curse, because this death was a sign of the curse; (2) he bore it for us, because he himself was righteous in himself.

units.la: Voluit igitur Deus Filium suum obire tam probrosum mortis supplicium, his potissimum de causis:
units.tr: God therefore willed that his Son should undergo so shameful a kind of death, chiefly for these reasons:

units.la: 1. Vt sciremus, ipsi incubuisse maledictionem peccatis nostris debitam. Nam mors crucis fuit à Deo maledicta, juxta illud: Maledictus qui pendet in ligno.
units.tr: (1) So that we might know that the curse due to our sins fell upon him. For death on a cross was cursed by God, according to that saying: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."

units.la: 2. Vt esset exasperatio supplicij, & nos tanto magis in fide confirmaremur, certo statuentes, cum hoc supplicij genere recepisse in se reatum nostrum, & sustinuisse pro nobis maledictionem, vt nos à maledictione liberaret. Hoc docet Paulus: Christus nos redemit ab exsecratione legis, pro nobis factus exsecratio: Scriptum est enim: Exsecrabilis quisquis in ligno pendet.
units.tr: (2) So that the suffering would be made more severe, and we would be the more strongly confirmed in faith, firmly holding that, by this kind of punishment, he took our guilt upon himself and bore the curse for us, so that he might free us from the curse. Paul teaches this: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."

units.la: 3. Vt nos ad maiorem gratitudinem excitaremur, consideran-tes, quam detestabilis res sit peccatum: adeo nimirum, vt non potuerit expiari, nisi acerbissima & maximè probrosa morte vnigeniti Filij Dei.
units.tr: (3) So that we might be stirred to greater gratitude, considering how detestable a thing sin is: so much so that it could not be atoned for except by the most bitter and most shameful death of the only-begotten Son of God.

units.la: 4. Vt veritas responderet figuris. Oportuit enim veritatem respondere figuris, vt nos sciremus, typos impletos esse in Christo. Nam vetera sacrificia, quæ victimam Christi adumbrabant, imponebantur lignis, & antequam cremarentur, levaban-tur in altum à sacerdote, vt significaretur: Christum ligno crucis exaltandum esse, vt se hostiam sanctam offerret Patri. Idem adumbratum fuit in Isaaco, qui lignis imponebatur à patre sacrificandus. Denique serpens æneus de palo suspendebatur à Mose in deserto, quem typum Christus de seipso interpretatur. Sicut Moses extulit serpentem in deserto: ita tolli oportet Filium hominis. Et ego si exaltatus fuero è terra, omnes traham ad me ipsum.
units.tr: (4) So that the truth would correspond to the figures. For it was fitting that the truth should correspond to the figures, so that we might know that the types were fulfilled in Christ. For the ancient sacrifices, which foreshadowed the sacrifice of Christ, were laid upon wood, and before they were burned they were lifted up on high by the priest, to signify that Christ was to be lifted up on the wood of the cross, so that he might offer himself as a holy victim to the Father. The same was foreshadowed in Isaac, who was laid upon the wood to be sacrificed by his father. Lastly, the bronze serpent was hung by Moses on a pole in the wilderness, a type which Christ himself interprets of himself: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself."

units.la: Quid igitur est, Credere in Christum crucifixum? Est credere, Christum pro me factum esse maledictioni obnoxium, vt me ab ea liberaret.
units.tr: What, then, is "to believe in Christ crucified"? It is to believe that Christ was made subject to the curse for me, so that he might free me from it.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XL.
units.tr: QUESTION XL.

units.la: Cur necesse fuit, vt Christus ad mortem vsque se demitteret?
units.tr: Why was it necessary for Christ to humble himself even unto death?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Propterea, quod justitiæ & veritati Dei a, nullo alio pacto pro nostris peccatis potuit satisfieri, quam ipsa morte Filij Dei b.
units.tr: Because the justice and truth of God could not be satisfied for our sins in any other way than by the very death of the Son of God, (a) Gen. 2:17; (b) Rom. 8:3, 4; Heb. 2:14, 15.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATION.

units.la: Hic considerandum
units.tr: Here we must consider

units.la: DE MORTE CHRISTI.
units.tr: ON THE DEATH OF CHRIST.

units.la: I. Quomodo Christus dicatur mortuus. II. An oportuerit Christum mori. III. Pro quibus sit mortuus.
units.tr: I. In what sense Christ is said to have died. II. Whether it was fitting for Christ to die. III. For whom he died.

units.la: I. Quomodo Christus dicatur mortuus.
units.tr: I. In what sense Christ is said to have died.

units.la: Huius quæstionis explicatio necessaria est propter hereticos, qui sensum huius Articuli depravarunt. Marcion dicebat, totam dispensationem Σ λόγω in carne, & omnia, quæ Christus pro nobis subiit, fuisse tantum imaginaria, & Christum visum tantummodò ut hominem, sed non fuisse. Nestorius naturas Christi agnoscens, sed separans, nec Filium Dei, sed hominem tantummodò crucifixum & mortuum esse contendens, dicebat: Noli gloriari Iudæe; hominem, non Deum crucifixisti. Huius temporis Ubiquitarij volunt, humanitatem Christi à momento incarnationis omnibus Deitatis proprietatibus ita fuisse prædictam, ut inter eam & Deitatem hoc tantum interfit, quòd illa per accidens habeat, quæcunque hæc per se & ex se habet. Hinc Christum in morte, immo cum fœtus lateret in utero virginis, non tantum Deitate, sed etiam corpore, in cælo, & ubique fuisse, imaginantur: & hoc formam Dei vocant: vicissim omnia humanitatis idiomata, etiam passionem & mortem, fuisse appropriata Deitati: & ita Christum passum & mortuum esse secundum utramque naturam: quæ phrases in eorum libris reperiuntur. Nos verò in symbolo credimus,
units.tr: An explanation of this question is necessary because of the heretics who have distorted the sense of this article. Marcion taught that the whole dispensation of the Word [λόγῳ] in the flesh, and everything that Christ suffered for us, was merely imaginary, and that Christ was seen only as a man but was not one. Nestorius, while acknowledging the natures of Christ but separating them, contended that it was not the Son of God but only the man who was crucified and died, and said: Do not boast, O Jew; you crucified a man, not God. The Ubiquitarians of our own time hold that from the moment of the incarnation the humanity of Christ was endowed with all the properties of the Deity, so that between it and the Deity there is only this difference: that the humanity has by accident whatever the Deity has in itself and from itself. Hence they imagine that Christ, even in death, or even while the foetus lay in the womb of the Virgin, was present not only in his Deity but also in his body, in heaven and everywhere; and they call this the form of God. Conversely, they hold that all the attributes of the humanity, even the passion and death, were transferred to the Deity; and so they say that Christ suffered and died according to both natures. Such phrases are found in their books. But we, in the Creed, believe:

units.la: I. Christum verè esse mortuum: hoc est, verà diuulsione animæ à corpore factâ, & quidem locali, ita, ut anima & corpus in morte non simul essent in uno loco: nec anima esset, ubi erat corpus insepulchro: nec corpus esset, ubi erat anima in paradiso: proinde nec animam, nec corpus Christi fuisse ubique: quia secus non fuisset verè mortuus, juxta dicta: Emisit spiritum. Expiravit. Inclinato capite tradidit spiritum.
units.tr: I. That Christ truly died: that is, that his soul was truly separated from his body by a real separation, and indeed a local one, so that in death the soul and the body were not in one place together: the soul was not where the body lay in the tomb, nor was the body where the soul was in paradise. Therefore neither the soul nor the body of Christ was everywhere; for otherwise he would not have truly died, according to the words: He sent forth the spirit. He breathed his last. With head bowed he gave up the spirit.

units.la: Obiect. Expirauit, vt anima tamen maneret in corpore: sicut virtus, id est, Diuinitas egressa dicitur ex ipso, quæ tamen mansit in corpore. Resp. Est dissimilitudo. Diuinitas operabatur extra naturam humanam, vt nihilominus in ea maneret. Anima emissa ex corpore, in eo non mansit. Ratio dissimilitudinis est: quia diuinitas est actus increatus, infinitus: anima verò est actus creatus, finitus.
units.tr: Objection. He breathed his last, yet the soul remained in the body, just as power, that is, the Deity, is said to have gone forth from him, and yet remained in the body. Answer. There is a dissimilarity. The Deity worked outside the human nature, and yet remained in it nevertheless. The soul, once sent out of the body, did not remain in it. The reason for the dissimilarity is this: the Deity is an uncreated and infinite act, but the soul is a created and finite act.

units.la: II. Chri-
units.tr: II. Chri-

units.la: QVÆST. XL.
units.tr: QUESTION XL.

units.la: II. Christum esse mortuum salua manente naturarum vnio-ne personali. Licet enim anima à corpore esset verè separata: tamen λόγῳ- animam & corpus suum non deseruit, sed manuit nihilominus vtrique personaliter coniunctus, eoque illa animæ & corporis diuulsione, duæ naturæ in Christo non fuerunt ab inuicem diuulsæ.
units.tr: II. Christ died while the personal union of the natures remained intact. For although the soul was truly separated from the body, the Word did not forsake his soul and body, but nevertheless remained personally joined to both; and by that separation of soul and body the two natures in Christ were not divided from one another.

units.la: Obiect. Cur ergò clamauit: Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me deseruisti? Respond. Quia derelictus fuit subtractione auxilij & liberationis à cruce: minimè verò diuulsione Deitatis à carne. Deus enim debuit mori, vt proprio suo sanguine acquireret Ecclesiam. Naturæ igitur diuelli nec debuerunt, nec potuerunt.
units.tr: Objection. Why then did he cry out: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Answer. Because he was forsaken by the withdrawal of help and deliverance from the cross, and certainly not by the separation of the Deity from the flesh. For God had to die, so that he might acquire the Church with his own blood. Therefore the natures ought not to have been, and could not have been, divided.

units.la: III. Christum esse mortuum non Deitate, sed tantum carne: proinde non secundum vtramque naturam, sed tantum secundum humanam. Deitas enim in se, & sua essentia, est simpliciter impassibilis & immortalis. Vnde Petrus dicit: Mortificatus quidem carne: viuificatus autem spiritu. Item: Christus pro nobis est passus carne.
units.tr: III. Christ died not in his Deity but only in his flesh; therefore he died not according to both natures but only according to the human nature. For the Deity in itself, and in its essence, is simply impassible and immortal. Hence Peter says: Put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit. Likewise: Christ suffered for us in the flesh.

units.la: Ex quibus liquet, vnionem naturarum non esse vbiquitatem: & vbiquitatem carnis repugnare morti Christi. Si enim vel anima, vel caro, vel vtraque simul fuisset vbique, anima nunquam & nusquam à corpore per mortem verè fuisset separata: nec potuisset ab eo verè separari: & sic Christus verè non esset mortuus.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the union of the natures is not ubiquity, and that the ubiquity of the flesh is incompatible with the death of Christ. For if either the soul, or the flesh, or both together had been everywhere, the soul could never and nowhere have been truly separated from the body by death, nor could it have been truly separated from it; and so Christ would not truly have died.

units.la: III. An necesse fuerit Christum mori pro nobis.
units.tr: III. Whether it was necessary for Christ to die for us.

units.la: Necesse fuit, Christum, vt satisfacere pro nobis, non solùm pati, sed etiam mori pro nobis.
units.tr: It was necessary for Christ, in order to make satisfaction for us, not only to suffer but also to die for us.

units.la: I. Propter iustitiam Dei, hoc est, vt iustitiæ Dei satisfieret pro hominis peccato. Peccatum enim tantum est malum, vt ex ordine iustitiæ mereatur destructionem peccantis. Est enim læsio summi boni, quæ non nisi summo supplicio, seu vltima destructione naturæ peccantis, hoc est, morte expiari potuit: juxta dicta: Anima, quæ peccauit, morietur. Stipendium peccati mors est. Quoniam igitur Christus partes nostras in se susceperat, no-straque persona induerat, qui peccaueramus, & meriti eramus mortem, non tantum æternam, sed etiam temporalem: necesse fuit, eum pro nobis mori ac destrui. Est enim mors dissolutio animæ à corpore: quâ factâ corpus etiam ipsum dissoluitur ac destruitur: sicut domus dicitur destrui, quando partes aliæ ab aliis separantur. Etsi autem mors eius non fuit, nec esse potuit æterna duratione, (à morte siquidem enim retineri erat impossibile) fuit tamen æternæ æquivalens magnitudine pretij, propter dignitatem personæ morientis, quæ erat Filius Dei. Nam Filium Dei mori, plus fuit, quam totum mundum destrui. Filium autem Dei pro nobis mori necesse fuit, vt mors eius esset λύτρον sufficiens pro nostris peccatis. Nulla enim creatura tale suppli-cium sustinere pro nobis potuisset, quod æterno æquipolleret, & simul temporale esset: prout supra quæst. 14. 15. 16. 17. fuisse est declaratum.
units.tr: 1. On account of the justice of God, that is, so that satisfaction might be made to the justice of God for the sin of man. For sin is such an evil that, by the order of justice, it deserves the destruction of the sinner. It is an injury to the highest good, which could be expiated only by the highest punishment, or the final destruction of the sinning nature, that is, by death; according to the words: The soul that sins shall die. The wages of sin is death. Since therefore Christ had taken our part upon himself and had put on our person, we who had sinned and deserved death, not only eternal but also temporal, it was necessary for him to die and be destroyed for us. For death is the dissolution of the soul from the body; and when this happens the body too is dissolved and destroyed, just as a house is said to be destroyed when its parts are separated from one another. Although his death was not, and could not be, of eternal duration (for it was impossible for him to be held by death), it was nevertheless equivalent in magnitude of price to an eternal death, on account of the dignity of the person who died, who was the Son of God. For the death of the Son of God was more than the destruction of the whole world. And it was necessary for the Son of God to die for us, so that his death might be a sufficient ransom [λύτρον] for our sins. For no creature could have endured for us such a punishment as would be equal to an eternal one and yet temporal at the same time, as was shown above in questions 14, 15, 16, and 17.

units.la: Obiectio. Meriti sumus æternam mortem. Ergo animæ eorum, qui DEO per Christum non reconciliantur, non deberent à corporibus separari, vt patiantur æternam damnationem. Respond. Hoc non sequitur; sed tantum; oportere eorum corpora & animas post separationem morte temporali sanctam, rursus vniri, vt possint æternam pati: quod & fiet tandem.
units.tr: Objection. We deserved eternal death. Therefore the souls of those who are not reconciled to God through Christ ought not to be separated from their bodies, so that they may suffer eternal damnation. Answer. This does not follow; it only means that their bodies and souls, after separation by a temporal death, must be united again so that they may suffer eternal punishment; which will indeed happen in the end.

units.la: 2. Propter veritatem Dei: hoc est, vt veritati Dei satisfieret, qui dixerat: Quacunque die comederis de fructu hoc, morte morieris. Hanc communionem post admissum peccatum impleri oportuit.
units.tr: 2. On account of the truth of God: that is, so that satisfaction might be made to the truth of God, who had said: On whatever day you eat of this fruit, you shall surely die. This threatened communion of death had to be fulfilled after sin was committed.

units.la: Obiect. Atqui Adam post peccatum non continuo est mortuus. Resp. Reuera mox spiritualiter moriebatur æterna morte: & iam erat mortuus animâ, cum diceret: Audiui vocem tuam, & timui, quia nudus sum. Erat terror, & sensus iræ Dei, lucta cum morte, amissio omnium donorum, animi & corporis. Sed tamen accessit ἰmιxία Euangelij. Non enim expresse dixerat Deus, quod homo totus è vestigio esset moriturus: quia æternum periisset. Filius ergo Dei obtulit mitigationem, excitans hominem ad nouam vitam promissione Euangelij: sictans hominem ad nouam vitam promissione Euangelij, vt morti corporali maneret obnoxius, sed quæ ei lethalis non esset.
units.tr: Objection. Yet Adam did not die at once after the sin. Answer. In truth he was at once dying spiritually with eternal death, and already he was dead in soul when he said: I heard your voice, and I was afraid, because I was naked. There was terror, and a sense of the wrath of God, a struggle with death, the loss of all gifts, of soul and body. But there was also an admixture of the Gospel [ἐπιμιξία]. For God had not expressly said that the whole man would die on the spot, since he would have perished eternally. The Son of God therefore offered a mitigation, rousing man to new life by the promise of the Gospel, so that he would remain subject to bodily death, but a death that would not be lethal to him.

units.la: 3. Propter promissiones Patribus factas: tum verbis: Sicut ouis ad occisionem ducetur, & sicut agnus coram tondente suo obmutescet. Post hebdomadas sexaginta duas excidetur Christus, &c. tum typis & sacrificiis, quibus significauit Deus, Christum debere mori, & quidem tali morte, quæ esset sacrificium & pretium æquipollens peccatis nostris. Hoc autem nullius creaturæ opus esse potuit, sed solius Filij Dei. Ideo Filium Dei tam diram pro nobis mortem oppetere oportuit.
units.tr: 3. On account of the promises made to the Fathers: both in words: As a sheep he will be led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he will be silent. After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be cut off, etc.; and in types and sacrifices, by which God signified that Christ must die, and indeed by such a death as would be a sacrifice and a price equivalent to our sins. But this could not be the work of any creature, only of the Son of God. Therefore it was fitting that the Son of God should undergo such a dreadful death for us.

units.la: 4. Denique Christus ipse prædixerat, necesse esse, vt moreretur. Nisi ego abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos. Nisi re- uuero, partem non habes mecum. Nonne oportuit Christum hac pati?
units.tr: 4. Finally, Christ himself had foretold that it was necessary for him to die. Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. Unless I return, you have no part with me. Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things?

units.la: Tres igitur circumstantiæ in hac quæstione concurrunt. 1. Quod necesse fuit, justitiæ & veritati DEI pro peccatis nostris satisfieri. 2. Et quidem morte. 3. Et quidem morte Filij DEI.
units.tr: Three circumstances therefore come together in this question. 1. That it was necessary for satisfaction to be made to the justice and truth of God for our sins. 2. And indeed by death. 3. And indeed by the death of the Son of God.

units.la: Ex his verò triplicem doctrinam licet haurire. 1. Peccata nostra maximè fugienda esse, quippe quæ expiari non potuerunt, nisi intervenien te morte Filij Dei. 2. Nos Filio Dei debere summè gratos esse, pro tanto eius beneficio, nobis ex inenarrabili gratiâ collato. 3. Omnia peccata nostra, quot, & quantacunque ea sint, sola Christi morte expiata esse in judicio DEI.
units.tr: From these things a threefold doctrine may rightly be drawn. (1) Our sins are above all to be shunned, since they could not be expiated except by the intervening death of the Son of God. (2) We ought to be exceedingly grateful to the Son of God for so great a benefit, bestowed on us from his unspeakable grace. (3) All our sins, however many and however great they may be, are expiated by the death of Christ alone in the judgment of God.

units.la: III. An Christus sit mortuus pro omnibus hominibus.
units.tr: III. Whether Christ died for all men.

units.la: [Quæstionem hanc non recordor: neque inveni in vllis notis Mss. à D. Vrsino hic explicatam fuisse. Nondum enim nostro sæculo à quoquam agitata erat. De ea tamen quid senserit, non est obscurum ex supra-dictis, de passione Christi quæst. XXXVII. ubi ad obiectionem IV.
