And the kingdom and the power and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all powers shall serve and obey him. Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end. His kingdom shall have no end. Therefore it was necessary that human nature, the seed of David, be raised up and reign. 2. The Mediator, who is our brother and true man, had to intercede for us always and appear before God as an eternal priest. You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. It is Christ who died; yes, rather, who was also raised up; who is also at the right hand of God; who also makes intercession for us. 3. The Mediator, who is true man, had to be a mediator by merit and efficacy. For it was not enough for him to die for us; he had also to confer by his power on the Church and on all of us the benefits which he had obtained for us by dying: namely righteousness, the Holy Spirit, life and eternal glory. For both belong to the Mediator, to merit and to confer. But he could not have conferred them had he remained in death, for he would not have been. What does not exist does nothing. Therefore these benefits were also deposited in him by the divinity, so that he himself might make us partakers of them. Of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace. Nor should it seem strange that Christ confers on us the same benefits which he obtained for us from the divinity by his death. For even a man can obtain something for another and confer it. Suppose someone intercedes for you with a prince on account of a gift of a thousand crowns. The prince does this to grant the favour of the one who asks, and gives him a gift which he may pass on to you. He will obtain the gift from the prince and at the same time confer it.

units.la: Etsi verò Christus mortis suæ beneficia conferre nobis potuisset per deitatem suam, cuius potentiâ nos justificat & regenerat: tamen sicut Deus decreuit per hominem suscitare mortuos, (per hominem enim resurrectio mortuorum,) & per virum iudicare mundum : sic etiam decreuit hæc beneficia dare per hominem Iesum, vt idem esset mediator, & maneret verus Deus & homo. Propterea etiam oportebat CHRISTVM perpetuo manere nostrum fratrem, nostrumque caput : nos vice versa oportebat ipsi per veram fidem insitos esse perpetuò, & manere eius membra. Manete in me, & ego in vobis. Nam in semine
units.tr: Although Christ could have conferred the benefits of his death on us through his deity, by whose power he justifies and regenerates us, nevertheless, just as God decreed to raise the dead through a man (for the resurrection of the dead comes through a man), and to judge the world through a man, so he also decreed to give these benefits through the man Jesus, so that the same person would be Mediator and would remain true God and man. For this reason it was also necessary that Christ remain forever our brother and our head, and that we, in turn, be grafted into him perpetually by true faith and remain his members. Abide in me, and I in you. For in the seed

units.la: Dauidis fundata est salus nostra. Seruus meus Dauid pascet eos in aeternum. Atqui ipse non mansisset frater noster, neque nos fuissemus membra eius, si natura ipsius humana mansisset in morte.
units.tr: of David our salvation is founded. My servant David shall feed them for ever. Yet he would not have remained our brother, nor would we have been his members, if his human nature had remained in death.

units.la: Obiect. In veteri testamento ante incarnationem, etiam sine humana natura mediator, eadem beneficia patribus contulit, quæ nobis confert in nouo testamento: & non minus ante assumtam carnem fuit mediator, quam post eam assumtam. Ergo non fuit necesse, Christum propterea fieri hominem, & mori. Resp. Illa ne tunc quidem fecisset, nisi aliquando futurus fuisset homo, & perpetuò etiam homo mansurus. Sic neq; iam faceret, si non resurrexisset, vel si assumtam naturam non retineret in æternum. Pater authoritatem dedit Filio iudicium etiam exercendi: quatenus filius hominis est.
units.tr: Objection. In the Old Testament, before the incarnation, the Mediator, even without a human nature, conferred on the fathers the same benefits which he confers on us in the New Testament; and he was no less Mediator before he assumed flesh than after. Therefore it was not necessary for Christ to become man and die for this reason. Answer. He would not even then have done so, unless he was at some time going to be man and to remain man for ever. Likewise he would not now do so, if he had not risen or did not retain the assumed nature for ever. The Father has given the Son authority to also execute judgment, because he is the Son of man.

units.la: 5. Propter nostram salutem: idque tripliciter. 1. Propter iustificationem nostri: Traditus est propter peccata nostra, & excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri. Requirebatur autem ad iustificationem nostri resurrectio mediatoris. Primò, quia sine resurrectione satisfactio eius non fuisset perfecta, neq; supplicium finitum. Nisi autem perfecta fuisset satisfactio, & finitum fuisset supplicium eius, nos ex æterna morte non emersissemus, à qua sic oportebat mediatorem nos liberare, vt eam plane in nobis vinceret. Vt verò in nobis mortem penitus vincceret, necesse fuit, vt prius eam vincceret in seipso, atq; ita impleret re ipsa, quod prædictum erat: Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Vbi tua, ô mors, victoria? Vbi tuus, ô sepulchrum, stimulus? & ita pudefaceret hostes exprobrantes ei: Alios seruauit, seipsum seruare non potest, Medice, cura teipsum. Deinde, nisi mortem vicisset, non potuisset nobis conferre beneficia, quæ morte sua nobis erat meritus. Eiusdem autem erat, nobis mereri, & conferre, vt est dictum prius. Immò nescíremus, eum pro nobis satisfecisse, si mansisset in morte. Id enim certum fuisset argumentum, eum non satisfecisse pro peccatis, sed superatum esse à morte & mole peccatorum. Vbi enim mors, ibi peccatum. Aut si satisfecisset, & tamen mansisset in morte, hoc pugnasset cum iustitia Dei. Oportuit igitur Christum resurgere, tum ad hoc, vt pro nobis satisfaceret: tum etiam ad hoc, vt sciremus ipsum perfectè satisfecisse, & beneficia sua nobis esse promeritum: tum denique ad hoc, vt ipse eadem nobis posset applicare, hoc est, vt ipsius merito & efficacia perfectè justificaremur & salvaremur. 2. Propter regenerationem nostri. Non enim consistit justificatio siue remissio peccatorum, sine regeneratione & inchoatione nouæ vitæ. 3. Propter conservationem beneficiorum, suscitationem & glorificationem nostri. Deus vult hoc modo in æternum nos viuificare & glorificare, vt inserti massæ humanæ Filij eius perpetuò ab ea gestemur, & ex ea vitam hauriamus. Per hominem mors, per hominem quoq; resurrectio mortuorum. Nisi quis in me manserit, eiectus foras statim vt palmes arescet. His igitur de causis necesse fuit, vt Christus resurgeret, hoc est, anima eius cum suo corpore per mortem depositò rursus conjungeretur. Resurrectio enim nihil est aliud, quàm eiusdem corporis cum eadem anima coniunctio.
units.tr: 5. On account of our salvation, and this in three ways. 1. On account of our justification: he was delivered up for our sins and was raised for our justification. Now the resurrection of the Mediator was required for our justification. First, because without the resurrection his satisfaction would not have been complete, nor his punishment finished. But unless his satisfaction had been complete and his punishment finished, we would not have emerged from eternal death, from which the Mediator had to free us in such a way as to conquer it utterly in us. But in order to conquer death completely in us, it was necessary first to conquer it in himself, and so to fulfil in fact what had been foretold: Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O grave, where is your sting? and thus to put to shame the enemies who taunted him: He saved others; he cannot save himself. Physician, heal yourself. Next, unless he had conquered death, he could not have conferred on us the benefits which he had merited for us by his death. But it belongs to the same one to merit for us and to confer, as was said before. Indeed we would not have known that he had satisfied for us, had he remained in death. For that would have been a sure sign that he had not satisfied for sins, but had been overcome by death and the weight of sins. For where there is death, there is sin. Or if he had satisfied and yet remained in death, this would have been contrary to the justice of God. It was therefore necessary for Christ to rise: both so that he might make satisfaction for us; and so that we might know that he had satisfied perfectly and had merited his benefits for us; and finally so that he himself might be able to apply them to us, that is, that we might be perfectly justified and saved by his merit and efficacy. 2. On account of our regeneration. For justification, or the remission of sins, does not stand without regeneration and the beginning of a new life. 3. On account of the preservation of the benefits, and our resurrection and glorification. God wills in this way to quicken and glorify us for ever, so that, grafted into the human nature of his Son, we may be perpetually sustained by it and draw life from it. By man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead. Unless someone abides in me, he is cast out like a branch and immediately withers. For these reasons it was necessary that Christ rise, that is, that his soul, having been separated from his body by death, be joined to it again. For resurrection is nothing other than the reunion of the same body with the same soul.

units.la: IV. Qui sint fructus resurrectionis Christi.
units.tr: IV. What the fruits of Christ's resurrection are.

units.la: Diuersæ sunt quæstiones, quare Christus resurrexerit, & quosnam fructus resurrectio Christi nobis afferat. Non enim omnes causæ resurrectionis sunt eiusdem fructus: & aliter causæ, aliter fructus resurrectionis consideantur: quin & ipsa beneficia Christi per eius resurrectionem nobis collata, aliter considerantur, vt causæ resurrectionis, quatenus postulabant eum resurgere, vt ea nobis conferret: aliter vt eiusdem fructus, quatenus potentia resurrectionis suæ illa nobis confert.
units.tr: There are various questions about why Christ rose again and what fruits his resurrection brings us. The causes of the resurrection are not all the same as its fruits, and causes and fruits are considered differently. Likewise, the benefits Christ has conferred on us through his resurrection are considered in one way as causes of the resurrection, insofar as they required him to rise in order to confer them on us, and in another way as its fruits, insofar as by the power of his resurrection he confers them on us.

units.la: Duplex porrò fructus resurrectionis Christi: alter Christum spectat, alter nos. Primò per resurrectionem à mortuis ipse est declaratus Filius Dei, nempe vnigenitus & naturalis, qui sit ipse etiam Deus. Sua enim potentia reuixit, quod est solius Dei. In ipso vita erat. Pater dedit ei vitam habere in seipso, sicut habet Pater vitam in seipso. Deinde & humana Christi natura per resurrectionem ornata est donis cœlestibus, immortalitate & ea gratia, quæ decet naturam Filij Dei. Deus exseruit potentiam suam in Christo, cum excitauit eum ex mortuis, collocauit ad dexteram suam in cœlis longè supra omne imperium, ac potestatem, & potentiam, & dominium, & omne nomen, quod nominatur, non solum in hoc seculo, verum etiam in futuro: & omnia subiecit pedibus eius, eumque constituit caput super omnia ipsi ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The fruit of Christ's resurrection is twofold: one concerns Christ, the other concerns us. First, through his resurrection from the dead he himself was declared to be the Son of God, namely the only-begotten and natural Son, who is also himself God. For he was revived by his own power, which belongs to God alone. In him was life. The Father has given him to have life in himself, as the Father has life in himself. Then too the human nature of Christ was adorned through the resurrection with heavenly gifts, immortality and that grace which befits the nature of the Son of God. God put forth his power in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavens, far above every rule, authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he put all things under his feet and appointed him head over all things to the church itself.

units.la: Fructus resurrectionis Christi nos spectans est multiplex. In genere omnia beneficia mortis Christi sunt fructus resurrectionis. Resurrectio enim Christi facit, vt mors eius suum habeat effectum. Resurrectione sua Christus applicat beneficia, quæ morte nobis erat meritus: & hoc pacto eadem sunt mortis & resurrectionis beneficia, nisi quod aliter nobis sunt merita per mortem, aliter conferuntur per resurrectionem. Actum mortis non erat necesse durare per omne tempus veteris & noui Ecclesiæ. Actum verò conferendi & applicandi necesse erat perpetuò durare: proinde necesse erat, mediatorem omni tempore esse: vt beneficia, quæ semel erat promeritus, semper conferret Ecclesiæ. Conferri enim absque Mediatore non possunt: nec absque mediatore Ecclesia consistere vel ad momentum potest.
units.tr: The fruit of Christ's resurrection that concerns us is manifold. In general, all the benefits of Christ's death are fruits of the resurrection. For Christ's resurrection makes his death have its effect. By his resurrection Christ applies the benefits which by his death he had merited for us. In this way the benefits of death and of resurrection are the same, except that they were merited for us through his death and are conferred through his resurrection. The work of death did not need to last through all the time of the old and new Church. The work of conferring and applying, however, had to last continually; therefore the Mediator had to be present at all times, so that he might always confer on the Church the benefits he had once merited. For these cannot be conferred without a Mediator, and the Church cannot subsist even for a moment without a mediator.

units.la: In veteri igitur Ecclesia mediator beneficia mortis suae futurae patribus conferebat, valore & efficacia resurrectionis suae futurae: sicut nobis eadem nunc confert, efficacia resurrectionis suae jam factae.
units.tr: In the old Church, therefore, the Mediator conferred the benefits of his future death on the fathers, by the value and efficacy of his future resurrection, just as he now confers the same on us by the efficacy of his resurrection already accomplished.

units.la: RESTAT, ut in specie fructus praecipuos, quos resurrectio Christi nobis adfert, enumeremus.
units.tr: It remains for us to enumerate, in particular, the chief fruits which the resurrection of Christ brings to us.

units.la: 1. Resurrectione Christi confirmamur de merito, quod satisfactum sit perfecte pro nostris peccatis. Nam peccatum vel unicum in morte Christum detinuisset, nisi omnia expiasset. In tantum enim carcerem detrusus erat, ex quo, nisi exsoluto extremo quadrante, in aeternum non fuisset dimissus. At dimissus est; quia ex morte resurrexit. Extremum igitur quadrantem peccatorum nostrorum persoluit. Propter hoc Christi meritum habemus remissionem peccatorum, & justificamur coram Deo. Confirmamur enim de appellatione beneficiorum Christi: quae fieri non potuissent, si non resurrexisset. Nam, ut ante dictum est, oportuit eundem mediatorem hominem mereri & conferre, ideoque resurgere. Quia igitur resurrexit, certi sumus, non tantum, quod sit meritus, sed etiam quod possit conferre, & conferat justificationem credentibus. Suscitatus est enim ad justificationem nostram: hoc est, ad justitiam suam nobis conferendam & applicandam.
units.tr: 1. By the resurrection of Christ we are assured of the merit, namely that satisfaction has been made perfectly for our sins. For even one sin would have held Christ in death had he not expiated all of them. He had been thrust into prison, from which he would not have been released for ever unless the last penny had been paid. But he was released, because he rose from death. Therefore he paid the last penny of our sins. On account of this we have the remission of sins through the merit of Christ, and we are justified before God. We are confirmed also concerning the appointment of Christ's benefits, which could not have been made had he not risen. For, as was said before, the same Mediator had to merit and confer as man, and therefore had to rise. Since, then, he has risen, we are certain not only that he has merited but also that he can confer, and does confer, justification on believers. For he was raised for our justification: that is, to confer and apply his righteousness to us.

units.la: 2. Fructus resurrectionis Christi est donatio Spiritus sancti: per quem Christus nos regenerat, & excitat ad novam vitam. Oportebat eum prius a seipso depellere mortem, deinde a nobis: oportebat nos ipsi, tanquam membra capiti inseri, ut ex eo in nos gratia Spiritus sancti deflueret. Postquam igitur resurrexit, impetrat & donat nobis Spiritum sanctum, nosque sibi insertos regenerat & vivificat. Olim quidem pij etiam Spiritu sancto donati sunt & regenerati: sed parcius, quam nunc in novo Testamento: idque vi resurrectionis Christi futurae: ut dictum est supra. Nam Spiritus sanctus, cuius virtute nos regeneramur, patribus non potuit donari, nisi intuitu futurae resurrectionis Messiae, cuius exaltationi effusio Spiritus sancti erat reservata: ut docetur Joh. 7, 39. Nondum erat Spiritus sanctus: quia Christus nondum erat glorificatus.
units.tr: 2. A fruit of Christ's resurrection is the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom Christ regenerates us and rouses us to new life. He first had to drive death away from himself and then from us. We, as members, had to be grafted into the head, so that the grace of the Holy Spirit might flow from him into us. Therefore, after he rose, he obtains and gives us the Holy Spirit, and regenerates and quickens us, grafted into himself. Formerly indeed the godly too were endowed with the Holy Spirit and regenerated, but more sparingly than now under the New Testament, and that by virtue of the future resurrection of Christ, as was said above. For the Holy Spirit, by whose power we are regenerated, could not be given to the fathers except with a view to the future resurrection of the Messiah, whose exaltation the outpouring of the Spirit was reserved for, as is taught in Joh. 7, 39. The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Christ was not yet glorified.

units.la: 3. Fructus est resuscitatio corporum nostrorum. Resurrectio nostra. 1. Quia enim Christi est nobis pignus resurrectionis nostrae. Christus est caput nostrum, nos sumus eius membra. Convenit vero gloriae capitis, ut membra etiam sint gloriosa: quae si manerent in morte, esset quidem Christus, sed non esset caput rex : vel esset caput sine membris, rex sine regno : quia non est caput, nisi respectu membrorum: neque rex, nisi respectu regni. 2. Si Christus resurrexit, aboleuit peccatum: non autem suum: ergo nostrum.
units.tr: 3. A fruit is the raising up of our bodies: our resurrection. 1. For Christ is a pledge to us of our resurrection. Christ is our head, and we are his members. It befits the glory of the head that the members also be glorious. If they remained in death, Christ would indeed exist, but he would not be a head that is king; he would be a head without members, a king without a kingdom, since he is not head except with respect to members, nor king except with respect to a kingdom. 2. If Christ has risen, he has abolished sin, but not his own, since he had none; therefore he has abolished ours.

units.la: Si peccatum nostrum aboleuit, etiam mortem nostram aboleuit. Sublata enim causa tollitur effectus. Stipendium peccati mors est. Porrò si mortem aboleuit, & resurgendo perfectam pro peccatis nostris satisfactionem declarauit: vtique resurrectio eius certum est testimonium resurrectionis nostrae futurae. Satisfactione enim praestita, non possumus teneri à morte. 3. Sicut primus Adam bona accepit pro se, & pro omnibus posteris, & eadem sibi atque omnibus nobis amisit: sic Christus secundus Adam vitam & gloriam accepit pro se & pro omnibus nobis: proinde & omnia haec bona sua nobis communicauit. 4. Quia idem Spiritus habitat in nobis, qui in Christo: etiam eadem agit in nobis, quae in capite. Nam semper sibi est similis: neque agit in capite, & dormit in membris. Ergo cum sese suo spiritu excitauerit, etiam nos eodem spiritu excitabit. Si spiritus eius, qui excitauit Iesum à mortuis, habitat in vobis: viuificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra, per inhabitantem eius spiritum in vobis. 5. Ipse est frater noster. Ergo propter amorem non relinquet nos in morte: & multo magis propter gloriam & potentiam suam. Si enim seipsum excitauit mortuus: multo magis nos excitare poterit viuus. &, si potuit se excitare in humilitate moriens: multo magis poterit nos excitare ad dextram Dei gloriosè regnans. Praeter tres hos fructus resurrectionis Christi, sunt etiam alij.
units.tr: If he has abolished our sin, he has also abolished our death, for when the cause is removed the effect is removed. The wages of sin is death. Moreover, if he has abolished death, and by rising has declared his perfect satisfaction for our sins, then his resurrection is surely a certain testimony of our future resurrection. For once satisfaction has been made, we cannot be held by death. 3. As the first Adam received good things for himself and for all his posterity, and lost them for himself and for all of us, so Christ, the second Adam, received life and glory for himself and for all of us; therefore he has also communicated all these good things of his to us. 4. Because the same Spirit dwells in us as dwells in Christ, he also works in us the same things he works in the head. For he is always like himself; he does not work in the head and sleep in the members. Therefore, since he has roused himself by his Spirit, he will also rouse us by the same Spirit. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he will also quicken your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you. 5. He is our brother. Therefore, out of love, he will not leave us in death, and much more on account of his glory and power. For if he raised himself when dead, much more can he raise us while alive. And if he could raise himself while dying in humiliation, much more can he raise us, reigning gloriously at the right hand of God. Besides these three fruits of Christ's resurrection, there are others.

units.la: 4. Ex resurrectione Christi scimus, ipsum esse promissum Messiam: impletis in eo vaticiniis.
units.tr: 4. From the resurrection of Christ we know that he is the promised Messiah, the prophecies having been fulfilled in him.

units.la: 5. Ex eadem certi sumus, eum nunc partes mediatoris obire: applicare nobis beneficium redemptionis: conseruare nos perpetuo in justitia applicata: inchoare in nobis nouam vitam: & de consummatione aeternae vitae nos confirmare: quod non poterat, nisi resurgeret.
units.tr: 5. From the same we are certain that he now performs the part of Mediator: that he applies to us the benefit of redemption, preserves us continually in the righteousness applied, begins a new life in us, and confirms us concerning the consummation of eternal life. None of this could be done unless he had risen.

units.la: 6. Quia nunc viuit & regnat in perpetuum, certi sumus, eum perpetuo etiam seruaturum, & defensurum esse Ecclesiam.
units.tr: 6. Because he now lives and reigns for ever, we are certain that he will also preserve and defend the Church continually.

units.la: 7. Postremus resurrectionis Christi fructus non minimus est consummatio omnium beneficiorum Christi, & glorificatio Ecclesiae. Ideo enim Christus ex morte resurrexit, nosque à peccatis liberauit, vt regni & gloriae suae nos coharedes redderet. Primogenitus ex mortuis. Haredes quidem Dei: coharedes autem Christi. Conformabit nos sibi: quia ipse viuit, & nos viuemus per eum, eodem spiritu. Si Spiritus eius, qui excitauit Iesum à mortuis, habitat in vobis, viuificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra, per habitantem eius Spiritum in vobis. Rursus veniam, & assumam vos ad me, vt vbi ego sum, etiam vos sitis.
units.tr: 7. The last fruit of Christ's resurrection, and not the least, is the completion of all Christ's benefits and the glorification of the Church. For Christ rose from death and freed us from sins in order to make us co-heirs of his kingdom and glory. The firstborn from the dead. Heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ. He will conform us to himself, because he lives and we shall live through him by the same Spirit. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he will also quicken your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you. Again I will come and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be also.

units.la: Summa fructuum est: Quoniam Christus expiatione peccatorum nostrorum facta ex morte resurrexit: inde constat, eum esse Filium Dei declaratum: & nos iustitia sua donare: Spiritus sui virtute ad nouam vitam nos regenerare: ac tandem vitæ, felicitatis, & gloriæ suæ sempiternæ nos consortes factu- rum esse.
units.tr: The sum of the fruits is this: since Christ, having made atonement for our sins by his death, rose again, it follows that he is declared to be the Son of God, that he bestows his righteousness upon us, that by the power of his Spirit he regenerates us to a new life, and that at last he will make us partakers of his life, happiness and eternal glory.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Resurrectio Christi non potest esse testimonium vel causa resurrectionis impiorum: quia impij non sunt Christi membra. Ergo impij non resurgent. Resp. Impij etiam resurgent: non quidem propter resurrectionem Christi: sed propter aliam causam. Excitabuntur enim necessariò propter iustitiam Dei & iudicium futurum, vt accipiant in corporibus digna factis suis. Omnes enim oportet comparere coram tribunali Christi: vt vnusquisque reportet, qua in corpore fecerit, congruenter ad id, quod fecerit, bonum vel malum.
units.tr: Objection 1. The resurrection of Christ cannot be the testimony or cause of the resurrection of the wicked, because the wicked are not members of Christ. Therefore the wicked will not rise. Answer. The wicked will also rise, but not on account of Christ's resurrection; they will rise for another cause. For they will necessarily be raised on account of the justice of God and the future judgment, so that they may receive in their bodies what is worthy of their deeds. For all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil, according to what he has done.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Beneficia ista sunt mortis Christi: Ergo non resurrectionis Resp. Sunt mortis: quatenus Christus per mortem ea est meritus: & resurrectionis. 1. Declaratione: quia resurrectione Christus declarauit, ea beneficia morte sua nobis parta esse. Emergendo enim ex poenis ostendit, pro peccatis à se plenè satisfactum esse. 2. Applicatione: quia resurgens beneficia sua nobis applicat. Ex diuite pauper, & ex paupere diues est factus, vt nos paupertate illius ditesceremus.
units.tr: Objection 2. These benefits belong to the death of Christ; therefore they do not belong to his resurrection. Answer. They belong to his death, insofar as Christ merited them by his death, and to his resurrection, in two ways. 1. By declaration: because by his resurrection Christ declared that these benefits had been procured for us by his death. For by rising out of his sufferings he showed that he had made full satisfaction for sins. 2. By application: because, rising, he applies his benefits to us. From rich he became poor, and from poor he became rich, that we might be made rich by his poverty.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Ante effectum est causa. Ante iustificationem patrum & resurrectionem sanctorum in veteri Testamento non erat causa, resurrectio Christi. Ergo nec effectus. Resp. Negatur Minor. Causa quidem non fuit rei impletione: Fuit verò DEI promissione, & patrum fide: proinde etiam valore & efficacia: juxta consilium DEI. Patres enim fideles recipiebantur in gratiam, donabantur remissione peccatorum, & Spiritu sancto, cæteraque beneficia salutis accipiebant, per & propter mediatorem aliquando exhibendum, ex morte suscitandum & glorificandum.
units.tr: Objection 3. The cause comes before the effect. Before the justification of the fathers and the resurrection of the saints in the Old Testament, the resurrection of Christ was not a cause; therefore it is not an effect either. Answer. The minor premise is denied. It was not a cause by the fulfilment of the thing, but it was a cause by the promise of God and the faith of the fathers, and so also by its worth and efficacy, according to the counsel of God. For the faithful fathers were received into grace, were granted the forgiveness of sins and the Holy Spirit, and received the other benefits of salvation through and on account of the Mediator, who was to be revealed at a certain time, raised from death and glorified.

units.la: JAM quid est, Credere in CHRISTVM, qui tertia die resurexit ex mortuis? Est credere, 1. Christum verè mortuum, & animam suam ad corpus mortuum reuocasse, ac rediuiuum tertio die prodiisse. 2. Animam & corpus verum retinuisse, ab infirmitatibus tamen liberum & glorificatum. 3. Idque propria diuina potentia. 4. In hunc finem, vt nos iustitiæ, sansanctitatis, & gloriæ suæ, quam morte nobis pepererat, faceret participes.
units.tr: Now what is it to believe in Christ, who rose again from the dead on the third day? It is to believe: 1. that Christ truly died, and recalled his soul to his dead body, and came forth alive on the third day; 2. that he kept a true body and soul, yet free from infirmities and glorified; 3. and that he did this by his own divine power; 4. to this end, that he might make us partakers of the righteousness, holiness and glory which he had won for us by his death.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XLVI.
units.tr: QUESTION XLVI.

units.la: Quomodo intelligis illud? Ascendit ad cœlos. EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: How do you understand that: He ascended into heaven? EXPLANATION.

units.la: Quod aspicientibus discipulis Christus de terra in cœlum sublatus est a, atque etiamnum nostra causa ibidem est b & erit: donec redeat ad judicandum viuos & mortuos c.
units.tr: That Christ, while the disciples looked on, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and is still there for our sake, and will remain there until he returns to judge the living and the dead.
a Acts 1:9. Mark 16:19. Luke 24:51. b Heb. 9:24, and 4:14. Rom. 8:34. Col. 3:1. c Acts 1:11. Matt. 24:30.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Ascensio Christi in cœlum fuit visibilis, localis, & vera translatio corporis & animæ Christi de terra in cœlum, quod est supra omnes cœlos visibiles, ad dexteram Dei, ad lucem inaccessam, vbi nunc est, & manet: & vnde redibit ad iudicium. In hac duo itidem, vt in resurrectione, sunt consideranda: historia, & fructus. In historia rursus, 1. Quis ascenderit? Ille ipse, qui passus est, & resurrexit. 2. Secundum quid? Secundum naturam humanam. 3. Quò? Sursum in cœlum, supra hos aspectabiles cœlos. 4. Quibus auxiliis? Propria diuinitatis suæ potentia. 5. Quare? Vt esset caput nostrum, Pontifex cœlestis. 6. Quomodo? Visibiliter, assPicientibus discipulis, vera & locali elevatione corporis de terra in cœlum. 7. Quando? Quadragesimo die post resurrectionem. 8. Vbi? Bethaniæ, in monte oliuarum. 6. Quo fructu? Explicatur quæst.49. Sed omnia reuocari possunt ad hæc pauciora.
units.tr: The ascension of Christ into heaven was visible, local, and a true transfer of the body and soul of Christ from the earth into heaven, which lies above all the visible heavens, to the right hand of God, to the light unapproachable, where he now is and remains, and from where he will return to judgment. In this, as in the resurrection, two things are to be considered: the history and the fruits. In the history, again: 1. Who ascended? He himself, who suffered and rose again. 2. In respect of what? In respect of his human nature. 3. Whither? Upward into heaven, above these visible heavens. 4. By what aids? By the power of his own divinity. 5. Why? That he might be our head, our heavenly High Priest. 6. How? Visibly, while the disciples looked on, by a real and local elevation of the body from the earth into heaven. 7. When? On the fortieth day after the resurrection. 8. Where? At Bethany, on the Mount of Olives. 6. With what fruit? This is explained in question 49. But all these can be reduced to fewer heads.

units.la: DE ASSCENSIONE CHRISTI quæritur
units.tr: CONCERNING THE ASCENSION OF CHRIST, IT IS ASKED

units.la: I. De Asscensione Christi quæritur II. Quò Christus ascenderit? III. Quomodo? IV. Quare? V. Quid ascensio Christi à nostra differat? VI. Qui sint fructus ascensionis Christi?
units.tr: I. Concerning the ascension of Christ, it is asked. II. Whither did Christ ascend? III. How? IV. Why? V. How does the ascension of Christ differ from ours? VI. What are the fruits of the ascension of Christ?

units.la: I. Quò Christus ascenderit?
units.tr: I. Whither did Christ ascend?

units.la: Postquam Christus Apostolis sæpe probasset resurrectionem suam, veramq; humanitatem: die quadragesimo post resurrectionem, cum esset vnà cum ipsis in Bethania, intuentibus eis ascendit in cœlum. Cœlum autem in scriptura tripliciter significat. 1. Aerem. Intuemini volucres cœli. 2. Regionem æthe-ream. Cum video cœlos tuos, opus digitorum tuorum. Ascendit super omnes cœlos: nempe, hos visibiles. 3. Locum beatorum, qui est spacium illud immensum, lucidissimum, gloriosum, extra & supra hunc mundum, & hoc cœlum aspectabile, domicilium Dei, angelorum & beatorum hominum, in quo Deus immediatè & gloriosè sese patefacit, & communicat beatis angelis & hominibus: vbi parata est sedes nostræ beatitudinis cum Christo & sanctis spiritibus. In hoc cœlo Deus dicitur habitare: non quod cœli spacio contineatur, sed quia ibi maximè apparet, & gloriam suam communicat aspectandam & fruendam beatis angelis & hominibus. Vocatur etiam in scriptura, Nouus mundus, cœlum nouum, cœlestis Hierosolyma, paradisus, sinus Abrahæ, &c. Hoc cœlum non est vbique, sed sursum à terra & inferno separatum. Inter vos & nos magnus hiatus constitutus est, vt ij, qui volunt hinc transire ad vos, non possint, neque isthinc huc transire. Cœlum sedes mea, terra scabellum pedum meorum. In hoc cœlum raptus est Elias. De hoc cœlo aduenit Spiritus sanctus in die pentecostes. Paulus vocat tertium cœlum. Hac tertia significatione accipitur hoc loco.
units.tr: After Christ had often proved to the apostles his resurrection and his true humanity, on the fortieth day after the resurrection, while he was with them at Bethany, he ascended into heaven as they watched. Now in Scripture "heaven" has three meanings. 1. The air: Behold the birds of heaven. 2. The ethereal region: When I see your heavens, the work of your fingers. He ascended above all the heavens, namely these visible ones. 3. The place of the blessed, which is that immense, most bright and glorious space outside and above this world and this visible heaven, the dwelling of God, of the angels and of the blessed men, in which God reveals himself immediately and gloriously and imparts himself to the blessed angels and men, and where the seat of our blessedness is prepared with Christ and the holy spirits. In this heaven God is said to dwell, not because he is contained in the space of heaven, but because there he most manifestly appears and communicates his glory to be beheld and enjoyed by the blessed angels and men. In Scripture it is also called a new world, a new heaven, the heavenly Jerusalem, paradise, the bosom of Abraham, etc. This heaven is not everywhere, but is set apart on high from the earth and from hell. Between you and us a great gulf is fixed, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can they pass from there to us. Heaven is my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet. Elijah was taken up into this heaven. The Holy Spirit came down from this heaven on the day of Pentecost. Paul calls it the third heaven. It is in this third sense that the word is taken here.

units.la: In hoc igitur cœlum, nempe beatorum ascendit Christus. Confirmant hoc plurima & euidentissima testimonia scripturæ, quæ diabolus in æternum non eludet. Asspicientibus ipsis elevatus est, & nubes susceptum eum abstulit ab oculis eorum, & cum intentis in cœlum oculis, eo proficiscente, ecce duo viri astitessent intenti in cœlum oculis, eo proficiscente, ecce duo viri astiterunt eis albo vestimento, & dixerunt: Viri Galilæi, quid statis intuentes in cœlum? hic Iesus, qui sursum receptus est à vobis in cœlum, ita veniet, quemadmodum conspexistis eum proficiscentem in cœlum.
units.tr: Into this heaven, namely the heaven of the blessed, Christ ascended. Very many and most evident testimonies of Scripture confirm this, which the devil will never be able to evade. "While they looked on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him out of their sight; and while they looked steadfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel, and said: Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? This same Jesus, who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven."

units.la: In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt, hoc est, multa domicilia, in quibus manere possumus. Vado paraturus vobis locum. Sursystem receptus est. Videbatur sursum in cœlum. Videbat oculis corporalibus noua acie diuinitus instructis trans & per cœlos omnes visibiles, Christum in eadem natura humana, in qua exinanitus fuerat. Quæ sursum sunt, quærite, vbi Christus est. Ascendit longè supra omnes cœlos. Penetrauit cœlos. Excelsior cœlis factus. Ingressus est in ipsum cœlum, vt nunc appareat in conspectu DEI pro nobis. Conuersatio nostra in cœlo est: vnde Christum expectamus.
units.tr: "In my Father's house are many mansions," that is, many dwelling-places in which we may remain. "I go to prepare a place for you." He was taken up on high. He was seen to ascend into heaven. With bodily eyes, sharpened by a new power divinely given, he was seen passing through and beyond all the visible heavens, Christ in the same human nature in which he had been emptied. "Seek those things which are above, where Christ is." He ascended far above all the heavens. He passed through the heavens. He was made higher than the heavens. He entered into heaven itself, that he might now appear in the presence of God for us. "Our conversation is in heaven, from whence we look for Christ."

units.la: Obiect. At nos conuersamur in terra. Ergo cœlum est in terra.
units.tr: Objection: But we live on earth. Therefore heaven is on earth.

units.la: Resp. Conuersio nostra est in cœlo, 1. spe & certitudine. 2. inchoatione vitæ cœlestis. In hoc ergo cœlum, nempe in domicilium Dei & beatorum, Christus ascendit, & ibi nunc est, & inde veniet ad judicium, juxta testimonia scripturæ.
units.tr: Answer. Our conversation is in heaven: 1. in hope and certainty; 2. in the beginning of the heavenly life. Into this heaven, that is, into the dwelling of God and of the blessed, Christ ascended, and there he is now, and from there he will come to judgment, according to the testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: Ideo autem voluit Deus nos scire locum, in quem Christus ascendit; 1. Ut constaret, eum ascendendo non evanuisse, sed mansisse, & mansurum perpetuo verum hominem in cœlo. 2. Ut sciremus, quo convertendæ essent cogitationes & preces nostræ, & ubi eum invenire deberemus, atque ita caveretur idololatria. 3. Ut sciremus nostrum domicilium, in quod nos Christus tandem sit deducturus, & in quo cum Christo in æternum simus habituri.
units.tr: Moreover, God willed that we should know the place into which Christ ascended: 1. so that it would be established that by ascending he did not vanish, but remained, and will remain forever a true man in heaven; 2. so that we would know where our thoughts and prayers ought to be directed, and where we should seek him, and thus idolatry is guarded against; 3. so that we would know our dwelling place, into which Christ will at last lead us, and in which we are to have him with us forever.

units.la: II. Quomodo Christus ascenderit in cælum.
units.tr: II. How Christ ascended into heaven.

units.la: Christus ascendit in cœlum. 1. Secundum humanam naturam. Me non semper habebitis, &c. Contra: Qui est in cœlo, non ascendit in cœlum. Filius hominis erat in cœlo. Ergo non ascendit in cœlum. Resp. Qui est in cœlo, non ascendit in cœlum, secundum id, quo est in cœlo, nempe secundum divinitatem: secundum quam concedimus Christum non ascendisse. Ea enim jam ante in cœlo erat; & sicut, cum Christus secundum divinitatem esset in terra, non ideo migrabat e cœlo: sic cum idem est in cœlo, non ideo discedit a nobis. Cyprianus: Dominus ascendit in cœlum, non ubi verbum Dei prius non fuerat, quippe qui erat semper in cœlis, & manebat in Patre, sed ubi verbum caro factum ante non sedebat.
units.tr: Christ ascended into heaven: 1. according to his human nature. "I will not always be with you," etc. To the contrary: He who is in heaven does not ascend into heaven. The Son of man was in heaven. Therefore he did not ascend into heaven. Reply: He who is in heaven does not ascend into heaven according to that by which he is in heaven, namely his divinity. According to his divinity we grant that Christ did not ascend, for it was already in heaven before. Just as, when Christ according to his divinity was on earth, he did not for that reason leave heaven, so when he is the same in heaven, he does not for that reason depart from us. Cyprian: "The Lord ascended into heaven, not to a place where the Word of God had not previously been, for he was always in the heavens and remained in the Father, but to a place where the Word made flesh had not previously sat."

units.la: Inst. Quod descendit, etiam ascendit. Divinitas descendit. Ergo, &c. Respond. Mutatur genus prædicationis. Divinitas descendit improprie, non motu locali: sed manifestando se in carne, in qua prius non se manifestaverat. Ascensio autem fuit motus localis corporis Christi in cœlum proprie dictus: sicut sequitur.
units.tr: Objection: What has descended has also ascended. The divinity descended. Therefore, etc. Reply: The kind of predication changes. The divinity descended improperly, not by local motion, but by manifesting itself in the flesh, in which it had not previously manifested itself. The ascension, however, was a local motion of Christ's body into heaven, properly so called, as follows.

units.la: 1. Ascendit localiter & corporaliter, hoc est, vere mutavit locum: ex loco inferiori transtulit naturam suam humanam reali & propriissima translatione in locum superiorem in cœlum: quod fieri non potuisset, si corpore prius fuisset ubique. Vere mutasse locum probatur his dictis: Me non semper habetis. Nisi abiero, Consolator ille non veniet ad vos. Relinquo mundum, & vado ad Patrem. Quid si videritis Filium hominis ascendentem eo, ubi prius erat? Quæ sursum sunt, quærite, ubi Christus est ad dextram Dei. Ἀνελήφθη, sursum receptus est. Nubes abstulit eum ab oculis eorum.
units.tr: 1. He ascended locally and bodily, that is, he truly changed place. He transferred his human nature from a lower place to a higher one, in heaven, by a real and most proper translation. This could not have happened if his body had previously been everywhere. That he truly changed place is proved by these sayings: "You will not always have me." "Unless I go away, that Comforter will not come to you." "I leave the world and go to the Father." "What if you see the Son of man ascending to where he was before?" "Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God." He was taken up [anelēphthē], received up on high. "A cloud took him out of their sight."

units.la: 3. Ascendit visibiliter. Oculis enim erat conspicua corporis ejus in cœlum translatio. Ferebatur sursum, videntibus discipulis. pulis. Assumptus est, donec ipsum non amplius viderent. Tamdiu conspexerunt ascendentem, donec nube sublatus esset ex eorum conspectu.
units.tr: 3. He ascended visibly. For his translation into heaven was visible to the eyes. He was carried upward while the disciples watched. He was taken up until they no longer saw him. They gazed at him as he ascended until a cloud lifted him out of their sight.

units.la: 4. Sua ipsius potentia, virtute suæ diuinitatis, qua etiam à mortuis resurrexit. Ascendo ad Patrem meum. Vado paraturus vobis locum. Dextrá igitur Dei exaltatus.
units.tr: 4. By his own power, by the virtue of his divinity, by which he also rose from the dead. "I ascend to my Father." "I go to prepare a place for you." Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God.

units.la: 5. Quadragesimo die à resurrectione. Et quare non citius, vel statim à resurrectione? 1. Vt certam faceret resurrectionē: & veritatem carnis suæ. Quibus etiam seipsum, postquam ipse passus fuit, repræsentarat vivum, multis indubitatis signis. 2. Vt discipulos erudiret de suo regno: revocaret eis in memoriam prius dicta, alia-que adderet, atque ita non illos tantum, sed & nos de resurrectione sua, deque carnis seu humanæ suæ naturæ veritate confirmaret. Per dies quadraginta conspectus est ab iis, & dicens, qua ad regnum Dei spectant.
units.tr: 5. On the fortieth day after the resurrection. Why not sooner, or immediately after the resurrection? 1. To make the resurrection and the truth of his flesh certain: "To these he also presented himself alive after his passion, by many infallible proofs." 2. To instruct the disciples about his kingdom, to recall to their memory what had been said before, and to add other things; and thus to confirm not only them but also us concerning his resurrection and the truth of his flesh, that is, of his human nature. "Being seen by them during forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God."

units.la: 6. Non reuersurus ante judicium Ita veniet, quemadmodum vos ad spexistis eum proficiscentem in cælum. Rursus veniam, assumam vos ad me. Mortem Domini annunciate, donec veniat. Quem oportet cælo suscipi, usque ad tempora restitutionis omnium.
units.tr: 6. He will not return before the judgment. "He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." "I will come again and take you to myself." "Proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." "Whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things."

units.la: Obiect. 1. Extra cælum non est locus. Ergo ascensio in cælum non est localis translatio. Resp. ad antecedens. Extra cælum quoque beatorum nullus omnino datur locus. Extra cælum quoque æthereum nullus datur locus physicus seu Aristotelicus, qui est superficies continentis cedentis contento. Datur verò locus hyperphysicus, supernaturalis cœlestis, qui qualis sit, discemus suo tempore notitia intuitiva. Satis est jam, nos scire & credere, quod sit, juxta testimonia scripturæ. Vado, paraturus vobis LOCVM. Rursum veniam, & vos ad me assumam, vt VBI ego sum, & vos sitis, & QVO ego abeam, scitis. Pater, volo, vt VBI ego sum, & illi sint mecum, quos dedisti mihi. SVRSVM receptus est. Qua SVRSVM sunt, quærite. VBI Christus est ad dexteram Dei sedens. Conversatio nostra in cœlo est, VNDE & Seruatorem expectamus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Hæc & similia testimonia docent, cœlum, in quod Christus ascendit, & quod est supra hos aspectabiles cœlos, verè locum esse. Nam particulæ SVM, QVO, VNDE, VBI, significant locum. HVNC locum Aristoteles nec sciuit, nec credidit: quia ignorauit scripturas.
units.tr: Objection 1. There is no place outside heaven. Therefore the ascension into heaven is not a local translation. Reply to the antecedent: Outside heaven there is absolutely no place for the blessed either. Outside the ethereal heaven there is no physical or Aristotelian place, which is the surface of the containing body touching the contained. There is, however, a hyperphysical, supernatural, heavenly place. What it is like we shall learn in its own time by intuitive knowledge. It is enough for now that we know and believe that it exists, according to the testimonies of Scripture: "I go to prepare a PLACE for you. I will come again and take you to myself, so that WHERE I am, you may be also, and WHITHER I go you know." "Father, I will that WHERE I am, they also may be with me, whom you have given me." He was taken UP. "Seek the things that are ABOVE, WHERE Christ is sitting at the right hand of God." "Our conversation is in heaven, FROM WHENCE also we await our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ." These and similar testimonies teach that the heaven into which Christ ascended, which is above these visible heavens, is truly a place. For the particles SUM, QUO, UNDE, UBI signify place. Aristotle neither knew this place nor believed in it, because he was ignorant of the Scriptures.

units.la: Inst. Ergo tamen est translatus de loco in non locum. Quòd verò non est in loco, id est vbique. Christus non est in loco: quia ascendit supra cœlum visibile, extra quod non est locus. Est igitur vbique. Resp. 1. Negatur maior, vbique esse, quod non est in loco: alioqui & cœlum supremum esset vbique. Nam & cœlum supremum non est in loco, nec tamen est vbique. 2. Minor vera est de loco physico. Est enim Christus translatus in locum non physicum, & jam est in loco non physico. Sed est falsa de loco hyperphysico, supernaturali, qui continet quidem, sed non continetur: cuiusmodi locus est extra cœlum visibile, & in quo Christus nunc est secundum scripturas. 3. Per βλαφον. Christus translatus est de loco in locum: an in non locum translatus sit, nihil refert. Ergo mutavit locum. Est igitur natura humana finita, mutans locum: proinde non est vbique. Nam esse vbique, & mutare locum, sunt contradictoria. Ideo diuinitas, quæ sola est infinita & vbique, non dicitur mutare locum.
units.tr: Objection. Therefore he was nevertheless translated from place to non-place. But what is not in a place is everywhere. Christ is not in a place, because he ascended above the visible heaven, outside which there is no place. Therefore he is everywhere. Reply: 1. The major premise is denied: to be everywhere, for what is not in a place; otherwise the highest heaven would also be everywhere. For the highest heaven is not in a place either, and yet it is not everywhere. 2. The minor is true of physical place. For Christ was translated into a non-physical place and now is in a non-physical place. But it is false of hyperphysical, supernatural place, which indeed contains but is not contained. Such a place is outside the visible heaven, and it is where Christ now is according to the Scriptures. 3. By a fallacy [βλαφον]. Whether Christ was translated into non-place is irrelevant; he was translated from place to place. Therefore he changed place. Therefore his finite human nature changes place, and so it is not everywhere. For to be everywhere and to change place are contradictory. Hence the divinity, which alone is infinite and everywhere, is not said to change place.

units.la: Hic quærunt effugium Vbiquitarij, ne lædantur hoc telo. Quod mutat locum, non est vbique. Corpus Christi mutat locum. Non igitur est vbique. Maiorem huius syllogismi concedunt esse veram, terminis acceptis vno modo. Hic vero contendunt terminos accipi diversis modis: hoc est, corpus Christi esse vbique, modo maiestatis: mutare locum, modo physici corporis. Verum hoc cavillo non eludunt contradictionem. Nam diversus modus, qui contradictionem tollat, non debet coincidere cum prædicatis: alioqui fit ςατζαλαφια & petitio principij: ut si eos imitatus dicam: Aer hic est lucidus secundum modum lucis, & non est lucidus, sed tenebrosus, secundum modum tenebrarum. Item. Hic est pauper, secundum modum paupertatis: & non est pauper, sed dives, secundum modum divitiarum. Sic vero revera idem de eodem prædicatur, & negatur, nec contradictio evitatur. Nam modus paupertatis nihil aliud est, quam paupertas: & modus divitiarum nihil aliud, quam divitiæ. Similiter isti modi, quos pro concilianda contradictione confingunt, cum prædicatis revera coincidunt, & sunt id ipsum, in quo est contradictio. Nam interrogati, quid sit modus maiestatis? respondent, esse omnipotentiam & immensitatem, seu infinitatem: quid modus physici corporis? dimensitatem seu finitatem. Cum igitur dicunt: Corpus Christi est vbique, modo maiestatis: & non est vbique, sed mutavit locum, modo physici corporis: revera dicunt, corpus Christi esse vbique, secundum suam immensitatem seu infinitatem: & non esse vbique, sed mutare locum, secundum suam dimensitatem seu finitatem: & sic idem corpus Christi esse simul immensum & dimensum: infinitum & finitum, vbiq; & non ibique. Quæ manifeste sunt contradictoria.
units.tr: Here the Ubiquitarians, to avoid being wounded by this weapon, seek an escape: whatever changes place is not everywhere; the body of Christ changes place; therefore it is not everywhere. They grant that the major premise of this syllogism is true when the terms are taken in one way. But here they contend that the terms are taken in different ways: namely, that the body of Christ is everywhere in the mode of majesty, and that it changes place in the mode of a physical body. But this quibble does not get them out of the contradiction. For a different mode, if it is to remove the contradiction, must not coincide with the predicates; otherwise there is an equivocation [ςατζαλαφια] and a begging of the question. Suppose I imitate them and say: "This air is bright according to the mode of light, and it is not bright but dark according to the mode of darkness." Or: "This man is poor according to the mode of poverty, and he is not poor but rich according to the mode of riches." Thus the same thing is in truth predicated and denied of the same thing, and the contradiction is not avoided. For the mode of poverty is nothing other than poverty, and the mode of riches nothing other than riches. In the same way, those modes which they invent to reconcile the contradiction in truth coincide with the predicates and are the very thing in which the contradiction lies. For when asked what the mode of majesty is, they answer that it is omnipotence and immensity, or infinity; and what the mode of a physical body is, they answer that it is dimension, or finitude. Therefore when they say: "The body of Christ is everywhere in the mode of majesty, and it is not everywhere but changes place in the mode of a physical body," they in truth say that the body of Christ is everywhere according to its immensity or infinity, and is not everywhere but changes place according to its dimension or finitude. Thus the same body of Christ would be at once immense and dimensioned, infinite and finite, everywhere and not everywhere. These are plainly contradictory.

units.la: Sic igitur diversis suis modis contradictionem non tollunt, sed fuco verborum tantum eludunt: & manet, quod ante confirmatum est, Christum localiter verè ascendisse, & articulum hunc de locali ascensione intelligendum esse.
units.tr: So, by their various devices, they do not remove the contradiction but only evade it with a veneer of words. What was confirmed earlier still stands: Christ truly ascended locally, and this article about the local ascension must be understood in that sense.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Oppositá debent eodem modo explicari, vt retineatur oppositio. Articuli, ascendit in cœlum, & descendit ad inferos, sunt oppositi. Ergo sicut articulus de descensu figuratè accipitur de extrema humiliatione: sic articulus de ascensione figuratè debet accipi de summa maiestate, non de motu locali. Resp. ad maiorem per distinct. Oppositá sunt eodem modo explicanda, nisi explicatio pugnet cum articulis fidei, & cum aliis scripturæ locis. Hic autem pugnaret. Nam hunc articulum scriptura explicat de ascensione locali. Ita veniet, sicut vidistis eum proficiscentem in cœlum. Illum verò explicat de descensu spirituali, vt supra ostensum est. Et sic vtrumque accipere, analogia fidei postulat. 2. Minor negatur. Hi enim duo articuli non sunt oppositi. Nam ascensio ad cœlos non est summus gradus gloriæ, quemadmodum descensus ad inferos est summus gradus humiliationis: sed sessio ad dexteram Patris est summus gradus gloriæ. Itaque de his duobus articulis: Descendit ad inferos, & Sedet ad dexteram Dei, maiorem concedimus. Sessioni enim ad dexteram Dei opponitur descensus ad inferos: vnde scriptura duos hos articulos, de descensu Christi ad inferos, & de eius ad dexteram Patris sessione, figuratè interpretatur. 3. Si de maiestate, quam volunt, hoc est, de exæquatione naturarum ascensio accipiatur, omnes reliqui articuli de vera Christi humana natura penitus evertentur.
units.tr: Objection 2. Opposites must be explained in the same way, so that the opposition is preserved. The articles "he ascended into heaven" and "he descended into hell" are opposites. Therefore, just as the article about the descent is taken figuratively, of the lowest humiliation, so the article about the ascension must be taken figuratively, of the highest majesty, and not of local motion. Answer to the major premise, with a distinction: opposites are to be explained in the same way, unless the explanation conflicts with the articles of faith and with other passages of Scripture. Here it would conflict. For Scripture explains this article of the ascension as local: "So he will come, just as you saw him going into heaven" (Acts 1:11). And it explains the other article as a spiritual descent, as has been shown above. The analogy of faith requires that each be taken in its own sense. The minor premise is denied. These two articles are not opposites. For the ascension into the heavens is not the highest degree of glory, as the descent into hell is the lowest degree of humiliation; the highest degree of glory is the sitting at the right hand of the Father. So concerning these two articles, "He descended into hell" and "He sits at the right hand of God," we grant the major premise. For the descent into hell is set over against the sitting at God's right hand, and so Scripture interprets these two articles, the descent of Christ into hell and his sitting at the Father's right hand, figuratively. 3. If the ascension is taken of that majesty which they want, that is, of the equalising of the natures, then all the remaining articles concerning the true human nature of Christ would be utterly overthrown.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XLVII.
units.tr: QUESTION XLVII.

units.la: An ergo Christus non est nobiscum, vsque ad finem mundi, quemadmodum a promisit?
units.tr: Is Christ then not with us even to the end of the world, as he promised?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Christus est verus Deus & verus homo. Itaque secundum naturam humanam jam non est in b terra: at secundum diuinitatem suam, maiestatem, gratiam & spiritum, nullo vnquam tempore à nobis c abest.
units.tr: Christ is true God and true man. Therefore, according to his human nature, he is now not on earth; but according to his divinity, majesty, grace and Spirit, he is at no time absent from us.

units.la: a Matth. 28, 20. b Hebr. 8, 4. Matth. 26, 11. Ioh. 16, 28. & 17, 11, Act. 3, 21. c Ioh. 14, 18. Matth. 28, 20. Aug. tract. 50. in Ioh.
units.tr: a Matth. 28, 20. b Hebr. 8, 4. Matth. 26, 11. Ioh. 16, 28. & 17, 11, Act. 3, 21. c Ioh. 14, 18. Matth. 28, 20. Aug. tract. 50. in Ioh.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Est occupatio obiectionis vbiquitariæ. Christus promisit se nobiscum fore, vsque ad consummationem seculi. Ergo non ita ascenascendit in cœlum, quin & nunc sit in terra & vbique sua humanitate. Resp. Plus concluditur, quàm sequitur. Christus promissione sua loquitur de præsentia personæ, tribuens ei quod Deitatis proprium. Secundum eam enim, sicut ante ascensionem erat in cœlo & vbique, sic post ascensionem promisit se nobiscum perpetuò mansurum in terra & vbique. Non igitur sequitur: Christus post ascensionem est nobiscum, &c. Ergo est nobiscum secundum humanitatem. Alioqui possemus etiam ita argumentari: Christus dixit, Abeo, relinquo mundum. Me non semper habebitis vobiscum. Ergo plane non est nobiscum, ne quidem secundum diuinitatem. Sed non sequitur: quia & hic loquitur da abitu personæ, tribuens ei, quod est humanitatis proprium: per communicationem Idiomatum, propter vnionem personalem duarum naturarum: vt supra est declaratum. Hæc responsio & explicatio non est nostra, sed Augustini, vbi sic scribit: Secundum maiestatem suam, secundum prouidentiam, secundum ineffabilem gratiam impletur, quod ab eo dictum est: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, vsque ad consummationem seculi. Secundum carnem verò, quam verbum assumpsit, secundum id, quod de virgine natus est, secundum quod à Iudæis prehensus est, quod ligno confixus, quod de cruce depositus, quod linteis inuolutus, quod in sepulchro conditus, quod in resurrectione manifestatus, non semper me habebitis vobiscum. Quare? quoniam conuersatus est, secundum corporis præsentiam, quadraginta diebus cum discipulis, & eis deducentibus, videndo, non sequendo, ascendit in cœlum, & non est hic. Ibi est enim, sedet ad dexteram Dei: & hic non enim recessit præsentia maiestatis. Aliter: secundum præsentiam maiestatis semper habemus Christum: secundum præsentiam carnis, recte dictum est discipulis: me autem non semper habebitis. Habuit enim illum Ecclesia secundum præsentiam carnis, paucis diebus; modo fide tenet, oculis non videt.
units.tr: This is a refutation of the ubiquitarian objection: Christ promised to be with us until the end of the age; therefore he did not so ascend into heaven but that he is now also on earth and everywhere by his humanity. Answer: More is concluded than follows. Christ speaks in his promise of the presence of the person, ascribing to him what is proper to the Godhead. For according to that nature, just as before the ascension he was in heaven and everywhere, so after the ascension he promised that he would remain with us on earth and everywhere forever. It does not follow, therefore: Christ after the ascension is with us, etc., therefore he is with us according to his humanity. Otherwise we could also argue thus: Christ said, "I am going away, I am leaving the world. You will not always have me with you" (John 16:28; Matt. 26:11). Therefore he is plainly not with us, not even according to his divinity. But this does not follow, because there too he speaks of the departure of the person, ascribing to him what belongs to his humanity, by the communication of properties, on account of the personal union of the two natures, as was declared above. This answer and explanation is not ours but Augustine's, where he writes thus: According to his majesty, according to his providence, according to his ineffable grace, is fulfilled what was said by him: "Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age." But according to the flesh, which the Word assumed, according to that which he was born of the virgin, according to which he was seized by the Jews, that he was fastened to the wood, that he was taken down from the cross, that he was wrapped in linen cloths, that he was laid in the sepulchre, that he was manifested in the resurrection, you will not always have me with you. Why? Because he conversed, according to the presence of his body, for forty days with the disciples, and while they escorted him, they saw him, did not follow him; he ascended into heaven, and is not here. For there he is, sitting at the right hand of God; and here, indeed, the presence of his majesty has not departed. In another way: according to the presence of his majesty we always have Christ; according to the presence of his flesh, it was rightly said to the disciples: "You will not always have me." For the Church had him according to the presence of the flesh for a few days; now it holds him by faith, and does not see him with the eyes.

units.la: Christus igitur post ascensionem nobiscum mansit, & nobis adest, 1. Spiritu suo & Deitate. 2. Fide nostra & fiducia ipsum intuente. 3. Dilectione mutua, quia diligit nos, & nos ipsum, ita, vt non obliuiscatur nostri. 4. Vnione etiam cum natura ipsius humana. Est enim idem spiritus in nobis & in ipso, qui nos cum ipso copulat. 6. Spe consummationis, hoc est, spe certa veniendi ad ipsum.
units.tr: Christ, therefore, after the ascension remained with us and is present with us: 1. by his Spirit and Godhead; 2. when our faith and trust look to him; 3. by mutual love, because he loves us and we him, so that he does not forget us; 4. also by union with his human nature. For there is the same Spirit in us and in him, who joins us to him. 6. By the hope of consummation, that is, the certain hope of coming to him.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XLVIII.
units.tr: QUESTION 48.

units.la: An verò isto pacto duæ naturæ in Christo non diuelluntur, si non sit humana, vbicunq; est diuina?
units.tr: But in this way, are the two natures in Christ not torn apart, if the human nature is not wherever the divine nature is?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Minimè. Nam cùm diuinitas comprehendi non queat, & omni loco præsens sit 4: necessariò consequitur, esse eam quidem extra naturam humanam, quam assumsit b, sed nihilominus tamen esse in eadem, eique personaliter vnitam permanere.
units.tr: By no means. For since the divinity cannot be comprehended and is present in every place 4, it necessarily follows that it is indeed outside the human nature which it assumed, yet nevertheless is in that same nature and remains personally united to it.

units.la: a Ierem. 23. verf. 24. Actor. 7, 49. b Iohan. 3, 13. Coloss. 2, 9. Iohan. 3, 13. & 11, 15. Matth. 28, 6.
units.tr: a Jer. 23, verse 24. Acts 7:49. b John 3:13. Col. 2:9. John 3:13, and 11:15. Matt. 28:6.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Aliud argumentum siue instantia vbiquitariorum.
units.tr: Another argument, or instance, of the Ubiquitarians.

units.la: In Christi persona duæ naturæ inseparabili vnione conue-niunt. Ergo vbicunque est Christi diuinitas, ibi & ipsius humanitas sit oportet. Respond. Ita coniunctæ sunt hæ duæ naturæ, vt distinctæ tamen maneant earum proprietates, & nullius fiat in alteram conuersio. Fieret autem, si vtraque esset vbique, & infinita.
units.tr: In the person of Christ the two natures are united in an inseparable union. Therefore wherever the divinity of Christ is, his humanity must also be there. Answer: these two natures are so joined that their properties nevertheless remain distinct, and there is no conversion of either into the other. That would happen if each were everywhere and infinite.

units.la: Inst. 1. Duæ naturæ, quarum vna non est vbicunq; est altera, diuelluntur, nec vnitæ manent personaliter. At naturæ duæ in persona Christi manent personaliter vnitæ. Ergo necesse est humanam esse, vbicunq; est diuina; secus diuellitur vnio. Resp. Maior vera est de duabus naturis æqualibus, pariter finitis vel infinitis: falsa de inæqualibus, quarum vna finita est, altera infinita. Finita enim natura non potest esse simul in pluribus locis; infinita autem potest esse tota in finita, & tota simul extra eam: adeo vt si vel vno puncto à finita diuellerctur, vel intra finitam ita clauderetur, vt extra eam non esset, infinita non esset. Atqui naturæ in Christo sunt inæquales: humana est finita, vno tem-pore, vno tantum loco existens. Diuina verò infinita est, simul in natura humana sua assumta, & extra eam vbique existens salua vnione.
units.tr: Inst. 1. Two natures, of which one is not wherever the other is, are torn apart and do not remain personally united. But the two natures in the person of Christ remain personally united. Therefore the human nature must be wherever the divine nature is; otherwise the union is dissolved. Resp. The major premise is true of two natures that are equal, both finite or both infinite, but false of unequal natures, of which one is finite and the other infinite. For a finite nature cannot be in several places at once; but an infinite nature can be wholly within a finite one and wholly outside it at the same time. So if the infinite nature were torn from the finite one by even a single point, or were enclosed within the finite one so that it was not outside it, it would not be infinite. But the natures in Christ are unequal: the human nature is finite, existing at one time and in only one place. The divine nature, however, is infinite, at once in the human nature it assumed and existing everywhere outside it, with the union preserved.

units.la: Inst. 2. Fiet nihilominus separatio in aliquo loco, vbi natura humana non est: licet non fiat, vbi illa est.
units.tr: Inst. 2. Nevertheless a separation will occur in some place where the human nature is not, even if it does not occur where that nature is.

units.la: Resp. Nequaquam: quia diuinitas tota & eadem (quippe immensa & impartibilis) est in natura sua humana: & in eo loco, vbi ea est; & simul extra eam in omnibus locis, vbi ea per suas dimendimensiones essentialiter esse non potest: juxta Nazianzeni dictum: λόγος ἔστιν ἐν τῷ ταύτῳ τόπῳ, καὶ ἔστιν ὁπουδήποτε: sed singulari modo est in suo templo. Si verò (vt modo dictum) vel in vno puncto ab humanitate diuulsa, vel intra humanitatem clausa esset diuinitas: eo ipso infinita non esset.
units.tr: Resp. By no means: because the divinity, whole and the same (being indeed immeasurable and indivisible), is in its human nature and in the place where it is; and at the same time it is outside that nature in all places where, by its own dimensions, it cannot essentially be. According to the saying of Nazianzen: "The Word is in one and the same place, and is everywhere" [λόγος ἔστιν ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τόπῳ, καὶ ἔστιν ὁπουδήποτε]; but it is present in a singular way in its own temple. If, however, as has just been said, the divinity were torn from the humanity at even one point, or were enclosed within the humanity, then by that very fact it would not be infinite.

units.la: Inst. 3. Si natura humana non est ornata diuinis proprietatibus, nullum erit discrimen inter Christum & reliquos sanctos. Non enim datur aliud discrimen inter Christum & Petrum, nisi naturarum exæquatio. Resp. Antecedens falsum est cum ratione. Manet enim multiplex discrimen, etiam sine naturarum exæquatione.
units.tr: Inst. 3. If the human nature is not adorned with the divine properties, there will be no difference between Christ and the other saints. For there is no other difference between Christ and Peter except the equalising of the natures. Resp. The antecedent is false, and rightly so. For a manifold difference remains even without any equalising of the natures.

units.la: Inst. 4. Discrimen inter Christum & sanctos, vel est in substantia, vel in proprietatibus, & donis. Non in substantia: quia tam in sanctis, quàm in Christo habitat tota Deitas. Ergo in proprietatibus & donis. Resp. Negatur consequentia: quia non est sufficiens enumeratio. Est enim tertiū arcana & hypostatica duarum naturarum vnio: quæ in Christo est, in Petro non est. In Christo enim habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter: ita vt Christus homo sit Deus: & Deus sit homo. Sic verò deitas non habitat in Petro, & in aliis sanctis.
units.tr: Inst. 4. The difference between Christ and the saints is either in substance or in properties and gifts. Not in substance, because the whole Deity dwells in the saints just as it does in Christ. Therefore it lies in properties and gifts. Resp. The consequence is denied, because the enumeration is not sufficient. For there is a third thing, the secret and hypostatic union of the two natures, which is in Christ and is not in Peter. For in Christ dwells all the fullness of the Deity bodily, so that Christ as man is God, and God is man. But the Deity does not dwell in this way in Peter or the other saints.

units.la: Inst. 5. Atqui dicitur: Datum est ei nomen supra omne nomen. Resp. Datum est ei nomen supra omne nomen: sicut data est ipsa Deitas, vnione, non exæquatione naturarum. Sicut enim Deitas est data humanitati, sic etiam propria Deitatis ei sunt data. Deitas autem humanitati est data per vnionem, non vt humanitas sit Deitas, sed vt homo sit Deus, nempe secundum suam Deitatem. Sic propria Deitatis humanitati sunt data per vnionem, non vt humanitas sit æterna, immensa, vbique, &c. sed vt homo sit æternus, immensus, vbique, &c. nempe secundum Deitatem.
units.tr: Inst. 5. But it is said: He was given a name above every name. Resp. He was given a name above every name, just as the Deity itself was given, by union and not by equalising of the natures. For just as the Deity was given to the humanity, so also the properties of the Deity were given to it. The Deity was given to the humanity through the union, not so that the humanity should be Deity, but so that the man should be God, namely according to his Deity. Thus the properties of the Deity were given to the humanity through the union, not so that the humanity should be eternal, immeasurable, everywhere, and so on, but so that the man should be eternal, immeasurable, everywhere, and so on, namely according to the Deity.

units.la: [Coronidis loco juniores observent tres pestilentissimas herbas crescentes in horto vbiquitario.
units.tr: [As a crown, so to speak, let younger readers note three most pestilential herbs growing in the ubiquitarian garden.

units.la: I. Cum Nestorio naturas Christi diuellunt: dum pro vnione naturarum exæquationem vel operationem vnius per alteram substituunt. Possunt enim duæ res, duo spiritus, duæ naturæ exæquari, vel personæ mutuò agere, etiam sine vnione personali. Sic duo angeli proprietatibus, donis, & operationibus possunt esse æquales, neq; tamen sunt vna persona. Pater Filio per æternam generationem omnes proprietates essentiales, immò totam essentiam diuinam communicauit: idem omnia in, cum & per Filium operatur: neq; tamen est vna cum Patre persona, sed vna essentia. Deus habitat in Petro, Paulo & aliis beatis spiritibus, qui iam sunt in cœlo, idq; per ineffabilem communicationem donorum & ope-
units.tr: I. They tear apart the natures of Christ together with Nestorius, when in place of the union of the natures they substitute an equalising of them, or the operation of one by the other. For two things, two spirits, two natures can be made equal, or persons can act mutually, even without a personal union. Thus two angels can be equal in properties, gifts and operations, and yet are not one person. The Father has communicated to the Son, through eternal generation, all essential properties, indeed the whole divine essence; the same Father works all things in, with and through the Son, yet he is not one person with the Father but one essence. God dwells in Peter, Paul and the other blessed spirits who are now in heaven, and this through an ineffable communication of gifts and

units.la: Vide Apologeticum Biblicum l. 3. cap. 2. & operationum: atque habitat in illis, tanquam in suo templo; quandoquidem beati spiritus potius, quàm corpora ipsorum, sunt templa Dei, & membra Christi: & tamen Deitatis ac beatorum spirituum nulla prorsus est vnio personalis.
units.tr: See the Biblical Apologetic, book 3, chapter 2. and operations; and he dwells in them as in his own temple, since the blessed spirits, rather than their bodies, are the temples of God and members of Christ. Yet there is absolutely no personal union between the Deity and the blessed spirits.

units.la: II. Cùm Eutychete naturas confundunt, dum eas exæquant.
units.tr: II. They confound the natures together with Eutyches, when they make them equal.

units.la: III. Eripiunt nobis arma, quibus pugnandum est contra Arianos & Samosatenianos. Scripturæ enim loca probantia Deitatem Christi eneruant, trahendo ea ad exæquationem naturæ humanæ çum diuinâ.]
units.tr: III. They take from us the weapons with which we must fight against the Arians and the Samosatenians. For they weaken the passages of Scripture that prove the Deity of Christ, by drawing them toward an equalising of the human nature with the divine.]

units.la: III. Quare Christus ascenderit in cœlum.
units.tr: III. Why Christ ascended into heaven.

units.la: Christus ascendit. Primò, propter suam & Patris gloriam, 1. Regnum cœleste habere debuit. Igitur non potuit manere in terra. Qui descendit; ipse est, qui etiam ascendit longè supra omnes cœlos, vt impleret omnia. Quapropter extulit eum Deus in summam sublimitatem, vt omnis lingua confiteatur, Dominum esse Iesum Christum ad gloriam Patris. 2. Conueniebat etiam capiti, vt esset glorificatum donorum excellentia supra reliqua membra, quod in terra fieri non potuit. Deinde, propter nos, triplici causa.
units.tr: Christ ascended. First, for his own glory and the Father's: (1) he ought to have a heavenly kingdom, and therefore he could not remain on earth. He who descended is the same who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. Wherefore God exalted him to the highest place, that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of the Father. (2) It also befitted the Head that he should be glorified in the excellence of his gifts above the other members, which could not happen on earth. Next, for our sake, for a threefold reason.

units.la: 1. Vt intercederet pro nobis in cœlo. Qui est ad dextram Patris, qui etiam intercedit pro nobis. Intercedit autem pro nobis; 1. Valore sui sacrificij jam præstiti, qui tantus est, vt propter eum Pater nos debeat recipere in gratiam. 2. Voluntate sua, qua constanter vult, vt Pater nos recipiat in gratiam intuitu & recordatione sacrificij in corpore suo peracti. 3. Assensu Patris approbantis hanc voluntatem Filij, acceptantis valorem sacrificij eius tanquam λύτρον pro nostris peccatis, & vnà cum Filio in gratiam nos recipientis. Sic igitur intercedendo beneficia sua & merita nobis applicat. Ad hanc applicationem requirebatur glorificatio mediatoris, cuius partes sunt, resurrectio, ascensio & sessio ad dextram Patris.
units.tr: (1) That he might intercede for us in heaven. He who is at the right hand of the Father, who also intercedes for us. He intercedes for us: (1) by the worth of his sacrifice already offered, which is so great that for his sake the Father ought to receive us into favour; (2) by his will, by which he constantly wills that the Father receive us into favour, with regard to and in remembrance of the sacrifice accomplished in his body; (3) by the assent of the Father, approving this will of the Son and accepting the worth of his sacrifice as a ransom [λύτρον] for our sins, and together with the Son receiving us into favour. Thus by interceding he applies his benefits and merits to us. For this application the glorification of the Mediator was required, whose parts are resurrection, ascension and session at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: Obiect. Etiam in terra pro nobis intercessit. Resp. Ea intercessio fiebat respectu intercessionis futuræ. Nam hac conditione intercedebat prius, vt mediator in cœlesti sanctuario, peracto in terris sacrificio, perpetuo appareret.
