Propterea vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis. Vos non creditis, quia non estis ex ovibus meis. Omnia fecit Deus propter semetipsum; etiam impium ad diem malum.
units.tr: That there is therefore predestination in God, that is, election and reprobation, is proved by these testimonies of Scripture: "Many are called, but few are chosen." "You did not choose me, but I chose you." "I have other sheep that are not of this fold." "He chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid." "He predestined us to adopt us as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will." "I have a great people in this city." "And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed." "Whom he predestined, these he also called." Reprobation is spoken of specifically in these sayings: "God, willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction." "Jacob I loved, Esau I hated." "To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but to them it is not given." "They were long ago marked out for this judgment." "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you." "Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God." "You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep." "God made all things for himself, even the wicked for the evil day."

units.la: Obiect. 1. Promissio gratiæ est universalis. Ergo nulla est electio aliorum præ aliis. Resp. Promissio est universalis respectu credentium, hoc est, pertinet ad omnes credentes. Particularis est, respectu omnium hominum: quia ad magnam partem, quæ est infidelium, non pertinet. Revera autem adversarii negant esse universalem, cum dicunt, conversos posse deficere: quia hoc est labefactare promissionem universalem.
units.tr: Objection 1: The promise of grace is universal. Therefore there is no election of some rather than others. Answer: The promise is universal with respect to believers, that is, it pertains to all believers. It is particular with respect to all men, because it does not pertain to the great part, which is of unbelievers. Indeed, our opponents deny that it is universal, when they say that converted persons can fall away, for this is to undermine the universal promise.

units.la: Inst. Atqui dicitur, quod Deus velit omnes salvos fieri. Ergo omnes elegit. Resp. Contra. Multi sunt vocati, pauci electi. Cor populi huius pinguefactum est, dicit Dominus, ne convertantur & sanem eos. Hic dicitur, quod Deus velit aliquos non servari. Ergo hæc testimonia pugnant? Absit. Deus vult omnes salvos fieri. 1. Quatenus omnium salute lætatur. Alibi dicitur, eum lætari pœna impiorum, non quidem in quantum cruciatus est, sed in quantum est executio iustitiæ. 2. Vult omnes salvos fieri, quatenus omnes aliquo modo vocat & invitat ad pœnitentiam, sed non vult omnes salvos facere, quia non vult efficere in omnibus, ut vocationi pareant. Benefacit quidem omnibus, si forte palpent & agnoscant: omnes invitat, omnibus dicit: Probitas & obedientia mihi placet: omnes mihi eam debetis: Sed non omnibus dicit: in vobis efficiam. Efficit autem in quibus vult, hoc est, in electis, idque quia ab æterno sic ei placuit: Electio apprehendit, cæteri induraverunt. Etiam pater, quia sic placuit tibi.
units.tr: Further objection: But it is said that God wills all to be saved. Therefore he has chosen all. Answer: On the contrary: "Many are called, but few are chosen." "The heart of this people has grown fat, says the Lord, lest they should be converted and I should heal them." Here it is said that God wills some not to be saved. Do these testimonies therefore conflict? Far from it. God wills all to be saved: (1) insofar as he rejoices in the salvation of all; elsewhere it is said that he rejoices in the punishment of the wicked, not indeed as it is torment, but as it is the execution of justice. (2) He wills all to be saved insofar as he calls and invites all to repentance, but he does not will to save all, because he does not will to bring it about in all that they obey the call. He indeed does good to all, if perhaps they will be won over and acknowledge it: he invites all, and says to all: "Uprightness and obedience please me: you all owe them to me." But he does not say to all: "I will work in you." He works in those in whom he wills, that is, in the elect, and this is because it has so pleased him from eternity: "The elect obtained it, the rest were hardened. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you."

units.la: Obiect. 2. Qui dat æqualibus inæqualia, est προσωπολήψια. Respond. Per distinctionem. Προσωπολήψια est, qui dat æqualibus inæqualia. 1. Si det propter causas externas, quæ non sunt conditio, propter quam dandum vel non dandum sit æquale præmium vel pœna, hoc est, cum in iudicio negligitur causa communis utriusque partis, & spectantur alia ad causam non pertinentia, ut alterius partis divitiæ, potentia, honores, amicitia, &c. Hæc προσωπολήψια. Deus in electione non spectavit, nec spectare potuit: quia omnes homines in pari corruptione & perditionis massa invenit: ex qua elegit in Christo servandos, quos voluit, aliis in sua corruptione relictis. 2. Etiam προσωπολήψια est, qui dat æqualibus inæqualia, hoc est, si cum iure teneatur æqualibus dare æqualia, det tamen inæqualia. Deus autem elegit, quos voluit, liberrime, ex mera misericordia & gratia, nemini ad aliquid dandum obligatus. Omnes eramus peccatores & hostes, ideo iustissime poterat omnes excludere. Et si iniustitia caderet in Deum (quod absit) iustus & προσωπολήψια esset aliquid dando. Quod ergo aliquorum miseretur, aliquorum non, nulla est προσωπολήψια: sicut tu, si misericordia motus uni medico des, alteri non des eleemosynam.
units.tr: Objection 2: He who gives unequal things to equals is a respecter of persons. Answer: By distinction. A respecter of persons is one who gives unequal things to equals. (1) If he gives on account of external causes, which are not the condition on account of which an equal reward or punishment is or is not to be given, that is, when in judgment the common cause of both parties is neglected and other things are regarded that do not pertain to the cause, such as the wealth, power, honours or friendship of one party, and so on: this is respect of persons. God did not regard these in election, nor could he, because he found all men in equal corruption and the mass of perdition; out of this mass he chose in Christ those whom he willed to save, leaving the others in their corruption. (2) Respect of persons is also when one gives unequal things to equals, that is, if, when he is bound by right to give equal things to equals, he nevertheless gives unequal things. But God chose whom he willed most freely, from pure mercy and grace, being obliged to give anything to no one. We were all sinners and enemies, and therefore he could most justly have excluded all. And if injustice were to fall upon God (far be it), he would be unjust and a respecter of persons in giving anything. That he has mercy on some and not on others, therefore, is no respect of persons: just as, if you, moved by pity, give a physician something and do not give it to another, you give no alms.

units.la: {a} προσωπολήψια quis. vel vni des assem, alteri denarium, non es ideo καὶ ἐυ πο λὐτρῶς; quia neutri fuisti obligatus. Cur igitur tu homuncio Deum accusas injustitiæ, quod miseretur, quorum vult, & quorum non vult, non miseretur, cum nulli sit obligatus? An non licet mihi (inquit Dominus) quod volo, facere in meis? An oculus tuus malus est, quia ego bonus? Quis prior dedit Domino, & retribuetur ei? Hoc scire gloriæ Dei interest.
units.tr: {a} Who respects persons? If you give one a penny and another a denarius, are you not therefore a benefactor? You were obliged to neither. Why then, you mere mortal, do you accuse God of injustice, because he shows mercy to whom he wills and does not show mercy to whom he does not will, when he is obliged to no one? "Is it not lawful for me," says the Lord, "to do what I will with my own? Is your eye evil because I am good?" "Who first gave to the Lord, that he should be repaid?" It concerns the glory of God to know this.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Justum est, eum, qui accepit λὐτρον sufficiens pro omnium peccatis, omnes in gratiam recipere. Deus λὐτρον accepit sufficiens in Filio pro totius mundi peccatis. Ergo tenetur omnes recipere in gratiam. Resp. Justum est, eum recipere omnes in gratiam, qui accepit λὐτρον sufficiens pro omnibus, & applicatum omnibus. Sed hic non fit applicatio adomnes: quia dicitur: Et noluerunt venire. Multi vocati, pauci electi. Non rogo pro mundo, sed pro iis, quos dedisti mihi.
units.tr: Objection 3: It is just that he who has received a ransom sufficient for the sins of all should receive all into grace. God has received in the Son a ransom sufficient for the sins of the whole world. Therefore he is bound to receive all into grace. Answer: It is just that he should receive all into grace who has received a ransom sufficient for all and applied to all. But here there is no application to all, because it is said: "And they would not come." "Many are called, but few are chosen." "I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me."

units.la: Inst. 1. Λὐτρον sufficiens debet applicari omnibus. Christi λὐτρον est sufficiens. Ergo, &c. Maior probatur: quia infinitæ misericordiæ Dei est benefacere omnibus. Resp. 1. Negatur in hoc consistere infinitam Dei misericordiam. Non enim in numero eorum, qui seruantur, sed in modo, quo seruantur per Christum qui seruantur, consistit Dei misericordia. 2. Deus non omnibus vult hoc beneficium dare: quia etiam est summè sapiens & justus. Vult ergo simul exercere misericordiam & justitiam. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum daret: ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Volens autem ostendere iram, pertulit multa lenitate vasa iræ, adaptata ad interitum: & ut notas faceret divitias gloriæ suæ erga vasa misericordiæ, &c.
units.tr: Further objection, 1: A sufficient ransom ought to be applied to all. The ransom of Christ is sufficient. Therefore, etc. The major premise is proved because it belongs to the infinite mercy of God to do good to all. Answer: (1) It is denied that the infinite mercy of God consists in this. For the mercy of God consists not in the number of those who are saved, but in the manner in which those who are saved are saved through Christ. (2) God does not will to give this benefit to all, because he is also most wise and just. He wills therefore to exercise mercy and justice at the same time. "So God loved the world that he gave his Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." "But willing to show his wrath, he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy," etc.

units.la: Inst. 2. Qui accepit λὐτρον sufficiens pro omnibus, & non omnes seruat, est injustus: quia plus æquo accipit. At Deus non est injustus. Ergo omnes recipit in gratiam propter λὐτρον. Christi λὐτρον sufficientia non obligat ad recipiendos omnes, sed applicatio. Non autem obligauit se, quod omnibus velit applicare λὐτρον, nec fit applicatio sine fide, quam dat, quibus vult: nempe electis: nec tenetur dare omnibus.
units.tr: Further objection, 2: He who has received a ransom sufficient for all, and does not save all, is unjust, because he receives more than is fair. But God is not unjust. Therefore he receives all into grace on account of the ransom. The sufficiency of Christ's ransom does not oblige him to receive all, but its application does. Nor has he bound himself to apply the ransom to all, and no application takes place without the faith that he gives to whom he wills, namely the elect; nor is he bound to give it to all.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Qui suæ gloriæ causa aliquos affligit, est injustus. Deus non est injustus. Non ergo aliquos suæ gloriæ causa reprobat & affligit. Resp. 1. Nego maiorem universaliter sumtam. De creaturis quidem vera esse potest, quæ suam gloriam quærere non debent, sed Dei, necjus absolutum habent in omnes alios, sicut Deus, habens potestatem statuendi de suo, quod vult,
units.tr: Objection 4. He who afflicts some for the sake of his own glory is unjust. God is not unjust. Therefore he does not reprobate and afflict some for the sake of his glory. Answer 1. I deny the major premise as stated universally. It may indeed be true of creatures, who ought not to seek their own glory but God's, and who do not have absolute right over all others, as God has, who has the power to dispose of what is his as he wills,

units.la: Quæst. LIV.
units.tr: Question LIV.

units.la: vult, & faciendi vas aliud ad honorem, aliud ad dedecus pro arbitrio sine injustitia. De Deo igitur est falsa : quia Deus est summum bonum, quod quicquid facit, & cuius causa quicquid fit, injustum esse non potest. Huius autem gloria requirebat, ut non solũ misericordiam in saluandis electis, sed etiam justitiam in damnandis reprobis patefaceret. Ne autem horum damnatio videatur injusta, addenda est 2. Resp. per distinct. Injustus est, qui gloriæ suæ causa aliquos affligit, nempe innocentes, & sine ipsorum culpa. Deus vero gloriæ suæ causa reprobat, affligit, & damnat reprobos, non innocentes, sed peccatores, natura filios iræ : quia omnes, ut dictum est, ordine prius in massa perditionis inuenit, quam reprobauit. Reprobando igitur & damnando peccatores, non est injustus.
units.tr: will, and to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour at his discretion, without injustice. The premise is therefore false when applied to God, because God is the highest good, and whatever he does, and whatever is done for his sake, cannot be unjust. Moreover, his glory required that he reveal not only mercy in saving the elect but also justice in condemning the reprobate. Lest their condemnation seem unjust, a second answer must be added, by way of distinction: he is unjust who afflicts some for the sake of his own glory, namely the innocent, and without any fault of theirs. But God, for the sake of his glory, reprobates, afflicts and condemns the reprobate, not the innocent but sinners, children of wrath by nature, because, as has been said, he finds all of them in the mass of perdition prior in order to his reprobating them. Therefore in reprobating and condemning sinners, he is not unjust.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Qui destinat ad finem, destinat etiam ad media, per quæ venitur ad finem. Deus, juxta hanc doctrinam, destinat aliquos ad finem, hoc est, ad damnationem. Ergo etiam ad media: hoc est, ad peccata. Resp. Negatur minor: quod damnatio, ad quam Deus reprobos destinat, sit finis peccatorum. Finis enim proprie est, quod mouet agentem, & quod agens intendit. Peccantes vero peccatis suis non intendunt damnationem, sed impletionem suarum cupiditatum. Peccata igitur ad damnationem non habent se, ut media ad finem, sed ut causa ad effectum. Sic vero maior fit falsa vniuersaliter. Neque enim justus judex latronem destinans ad rotam, etiam destinauit ad latrocinia. Quin etiam de mediis & fine maior vniuersaliter non est vera, & requirit distinctionem : quia potest aliquis per media in se vitiosa & peccantia peruenire ad finem bonum sine injustitia: & tunc non, qui destinat media ad finem, etiam destinat ad vitia & peccata: verbi gratia. Dux belli destinat milites nequam ad pugnam & victoriam: non destinat vero ad nequitiam, quam milites interim admittunt : dux vero improbat.
units.tr: Objection 5. He who destines someone to an end also destines him to the means by which the end is reached. God, according to this doctrine, destines some to an end, that is, to damnation. Therefore he also destines them to the means, that is, to sins. Answer: The minor premise is denied, namely that the damnation to which God destines the reprobate is the end of their sins. For an end, properly speaking, is that which moves the agent and which the agent intends. But those who sin do not intend damnation by their sins; they intend the fulfilment of their desires. Sins therefore do not stand to damnation as means to an end, but as cause to effect. In this sense the major premise becomes false universally. For a just judge who destines a robber to the wheel has not thereby destined him to robberies. Indeed, even concerning means and end, the major premise is not universally true and requires a distinction: for someone can, by means that are in themselves vicious and sinful, reach a good end without injustice; and then he who destines the means to the end does not also destine them to the vices and sins. For example, a general of an army destines wicked soldiers to battle and victory; he does not, however, destine them to the wickedness which the soldiers meanwhile commit; the general disapproves of that.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Qui omnes vocat, & interim tantum aliquos vult seruare, is simulat. Deus, &c. Ergo, &c. Respond. Is simulat, qui omnes vocat, non vult autem omnes venire, nec omnes venientes seruare. Hoc vero de Deo est falsum. Dicit enim: Venientem ad me non eijciam foras. Inst. Deus scit reprobos non posse venire: ergo vocando simulat, vel illudit. Resp. Negatur. Scit quidem, eos non posse venire : sed & scit, suo vitio eos non posse: ac ne quidem velle venire. Vocando autem non simulat vel illudit: sed testatur, quid velit, & quid ipsi facere debeant. Duas enim habet causas, cur omnes vocet. 1. Ut per vocationem electos ad se trahat, & venire faciat. 2. Ut reprobos venire nolentes reddat inexcusabiles, ne in judicio excipere possint, se etiam fuisse venturos turos, si vocati fuissent. Inst. Debuit eos etiam per vocationem ad se trahere, sicut electos. Resp. Non debuit; sed miseretur, cuius vult, Rom. 9, 18.
units.tr: Objection 6. He who calls all, while meanwhile willing to save only some, is pretending. God, etc. Therefore, etc. Answer: He pretends who calls all but does not will all to come, nor to save all who come. But this is false of God. For he says: "Him that comes to me I will in no wise cast out" (John 6:37). Objection: God knows that the reprobate cannot come; therefore, by calling them, he pretends or mocks. Answer: Denied. He indeed knows they cannot come, but he also knows that they cannot, and indeed do not wish to come, through their own fault. By calling, however, he does not pretend or mock; he bears witness to what he wills and to what they ought to do. For he has two reasons why he calls all: (1) so that through the calling he may draw the elect to himself and make them come; (2) so that he may render the reprobate, who are unwilling to come, inexcusable, lest in judgment they be able to plead that they too would have come had they been called. Objection: He ought to have drawn them to himself through the calling, as he did the elect. Answer: He ought not; but "he has mercy on whom he will" (Rom. 9, 18).

units.la: Obiect. 7. Quorum salus pendet ab æterno Dei consilio, ij non possunt habere consolationem. Salus nostra, &c. Ergo, &c. Resp. Maior vera est, de consilio arcano simpliciter, nec revelato in Euangelio; falsa, de consilio arcano quidem, sed revelato nobis, 1. Per euangelium. 2. Per Spiritum sanctum, obsignantem corda nostra de gratia Dei. 3. Per fidem & effecta alia prædestinationis in nobis, juxta dicta: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Spiritus contestatur spiritui nostro, quod sumus filii Dei. Ex hoc cognoscimus, nos in eo habitare, & ipsum in nobis: quia de Spiritu suo dedit nobis. Ante hanc patefactionem verum est, quod ex arcano Dei consilio consolationem habere non possumus. Post patefactionem maior est falsa.
units.tr: Objection 7. Those whose salvation depends on God's eternal counsel cannot have consolation. Our salvation, etc. Therefore, etc. Answer: The major premise is true of the hidden counsel considered simply, as not revealed in the Gospel; it is false of the hidden counsel insofar as it has been revealed to us: (1) through the gospel; (2) through the Holy Spirit, who seals our hearts concerning the grace of God; (3) through faith and the other effects of predestination in us, according to the sayings: "Being justified by faith, we have peace" (Rom. 5:1); "The Spirit himself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Rom. 8:16). From this we know that we dwell in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit (1 John 4:13). Before this revelation it is true that we cannot have consolation from the hidden counsel of God. After the revelation the major premise is false.

units.la: Obiect. 8. Quod frustra fit, nemo debet suscipere. Reprobi frustra agunt pœnitentiam: quia impossibile est, eos servari. Resp. Est contradictio in minore. Reprobum esse, & agere pœnitentiam: quia si agerent pœnitentiam, non essent reprobi. Igitur non est periculum ab hoc absurdo.
units.tr: Objection 8. Nobody ought to undertake what is done in vain. The reprobate repent in vain, because it is impossible for them to be saved. Answer: There is a contradiction in the minor premise. To be reprobate and to repent cannot both be true, because if they repented they would not be reprobate. Therefore there is no danger from this absurdity.

units.la: II. Quid sit prædestinatio.
units.tr: II. What predestination is.

units.la: Prædestinatio differt à providentia, sicut species à genere, vel pars à toto. Providentia est consilium Dei de omnibus creaturis gubernandis. Prædestinatio de solis hominibus, ex lapso genere humano redimendis vel deserendis. Est enim PRÆDESTINATIO consilium Dei æternum, quo decreuit, ex genere humano per lapsum Adami corrupto & perdito, misericorditer aliquos in Christo eligere, & per fidem servare: reliquos in massa perditionis relinquere, & propter peccata sua punire, ad suam in illis misericordiam, in iis justitiam & potentiam declarandam. Hæc definitio prædestinationis competit, non angelis, sed solis hominibus, salvandis, & non salvandis.
units.tr: Predestination differs from providence as a species differs from its genus, or a part from its whole. Providence is God's plan for governing all creatures. Predestination concerns only human beings, whether they are to be redeemed or abandoned from the fallen human race. Predestination is God's eternal plan, by which he decided, out of the human race corrupted and lost through the fall of Adam, to choose some in Christ in mercy and to save them through faith, and to leave the rest in the mass of perdition and punish them for their sins, so as to display his mercy in the first and his justice and power in the second. This definition of predestination applies not to angels but only to human beings, those to be saved and those not to be saved.

units.la: Prædestinationis ergo partes sunt electio & reprobatio. Electio est decretum Dei, quo statuit aliquorum ex omnibus in perditionis massa jacentibus misereri in Christo, & donare eos conversione, fide, justitia & vita æterna. Reprobatio, est decretum Dei, quo statuit alios in perditione Adami relinquere, & propter peccata sua juste damnare. Utrumque esse decretum Dei, probant hæc & similia dicta. Scio, quos elegerim. Elegit nos in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Servauit nos ex proposito suo, & gratia, quæ data est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia. Cuius vult, miseretur. Consilio igitur facta est electio ab æterna. æterno: quia in Deo nihil est noui, sed omnia ab æterno decre-uit Deus, quæ in tempore facit. Si vero aliquos elegit, cæteros igitur rejecit. Nam quod ex multis eligitur, id aliis repudiatis eligitur.
units.tr: The parts of predestination, then, are election and reprobation. Election is the decree of God by which he determined to show mercy in Christ to some out of all those lying in the mass of perdition, and to grant them conversion, faith, righteousness and eternal life. Reprobation is the decree of God by which he determined to leave others in the perdition of Adam and justly condemn them for their sins. That both are decrees of God is proved by these and similar sayings: "I know whom I have chosen." "He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world." "He saved us according to his own purpose and the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before the world began." "He has mercy on whom he wills." Election was therefore made by plan and from eternity: for nothing is new in God, but God decreed from eternity everything that he does in time. And if he chose some, he therefore rejected the rest; for whatever is chosen from many is chosen by rejecting the others.

units.la: III. Quæ sint prædestinationis causæ.
units.tr: III. What are the causes of predestination.

units.la: Causa efficiens & impulsiva prædestinationis est beneplacitum DEI. Etiam Pater, quia sic placuit tibi. In nobis Deus nihil præuidere potuit, cuius gratia nos præ aliis eligeret, cùm essemus natura filij iræ, sicut & cæteri. Quicquid verò boni in nobis reperitur, id totum in nobis efficere ab æterno decreuit: & nunc efficit. Nihil enim efficit in nobis boni in tempore, quod non efficere decreuerit ab æterno. Proinde solum gratuitum & liberrimum Dei beneplacitum, seu absoluta Dei misericordia est causa efficiens & impulsiva electionis nostræ, nullo respectu alicuius boni in nobis prævisi factæ. Cuius vult, miseretur. Non vos me elegistis, &c. Prædestinauit Deus, quos adoptaret in filios per Iesum Christum in sese pro benevolo affectu voluntatis sui. Nondum nati pueri, cùm nihil fecissent boni vel mali, ut propositum Dei, quod est secundum electionem ipsius, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante, firmum maneret, dictum est ei. Maior seruiet minori. Non est volentis aut currentis, sed est miserentis Dei. Cuius vult, miseretur: quem vult, indurat. Gratias agentes Patri, qui idoneos nos fecit ad participandum sortem sanctorum in luce. Quis enim te discreuit? Quid autem habes, quod non acceperis? Qui seruauit nos, & vocauit vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex suo proposito & gratia, quæ data est nobis in Iesu Christo ante tempora secularia.
units.tr: The efficient and moving cause of predestination is the good pleasure of God: "Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in your sight." In us God could foresee nothing on account of which he would choose us before others, since we were by nature children of wrath, as the rest also were. Whatever good is found in us, God decreed from eternity to work all of it in us, and now he works it. For he does nothing good in us in time that he did not decree from eternity to do. Therefore the free and most liberal good pleasure of God alone, or the absolute mercy of God, is the efficient and moving cause of our election, made without regard to any good foreseen in us. "He has mercy on whom he wills." "You did not choose me," etc. God predestined those whom he would adopt as sons through Jesus Christ in himself, according to the kindly purpose of his will. Before the children were born, and before they had done anything good or bad, so that God's purpose according to election might stand firm, not by works but by him who calls, it was said to her: "The elder shall serve the younger." It does not depend on the will or the effort of man, but on God who shows mercy. "He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." "Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light." "For who makes you to differ?" "What do you have that you did not receive?" "He saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before the world began.

units.la: Similiter reprobationis causa efficiens est Dei beneplacitum. Nam cùm omnes natura simus filij iræ, periissemus omnes, si peccatum fuisset reprobationis causa, ut aliquibus videtur. Non igitur in hominibus fuit hæc causa, sed in Deo est voluntas liberè discernens ex massa perditionis seruandos à non seruandis, sicut dicitur: Miseretur, cuius vult, quem autem non vult, indurat. Etiam Pater, quia sic placuit tibi. Itaque de indiuiduis, cur hic sit electus, ille reprobatus, nulla alia dari potest ratio, nisi solum Dei beneplacitum.
units.tr: Likewise the efficient cause of reprobation is the good pleasure of God. For since we are all by nature children of wrath, we would all have perished if sin had been the cause of reprobation, as some think. So the cause was not in human beings, but in God there is a will that freely distinguishes between those to be saved and those not to be saved from the mass of perdition, as it is said: "He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens." "Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in your sight." Thus, concerning individuals, no other reason can be given why this one is chosen and that one reprobated, except the good pleasure of God alone.

units.la: Damnationis verò causa est omnino in ipsis hominibus, nempe peccatum, quod in reprobis Deus inuenit. Voluit enim & vult Deus in damnatione reproborum suam justitiam declarare. Non igitur quemquam in tempore damnat, aut damnationi ab æterno addixit, nisi propter peccatum: ac ne qui-dem damnationem vult, quatenus damnatio est, sed quatenus justa pœna. Non autem habet locum pœna, nisi vbi antecedit peccatum.
units.tr: The cause of condemnation, however, lies wholly in human beings themselves, namely sin, which God finds in the reprobate. For God willed and wills to display his justice in the condemnation of the reprobate. Therefore he does not condemn anyone in time, nor did he assign anyone to condemnation from eternity, except on account of sin; and he does not will condemnation as condemnation, but as a just punishment. Punishment, however, has a place only where sin goes before.

units.la: Finalis causa suprema prædestinationis est illustratio gloriæ Dei. Electionis causa finalis vltima est patefactio bonitatis & misericordiæ Dei in electis gratuito seruandis: proxima verò est electorum justificatio & salus per Christum. Vtramque hanc electionis nostræ causam Apostolus complectitur his verbis: Prædestinauit nos ad laudem gloriosæ suæ gratiæ, qua nos effecit sibi gratos in illo dilecto. Ex aduerso reprobationis causa finalis prima, est declaratio justitiæ, seueritatis, & odii aduersus peccatum in reprobis. Volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, pertulit multa lenitate vasa iræ adoptata ad interitum. Proxima, est justa reproborum damnatio propter peccata.
units.tr: The highest final cause of predestination is the illustration of the glory of God. The ultimate final cause of election is the revelation of the goodness and mercy of God in the elect, who are to be saved freely; the nearer cause is the justification and salvation of the elect through Christ. The Apostle embraces both causes of our election in these words: "He predestined us to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he has made us acceptable to himself in the Beloved." On the other side, the first final cause of reprobation is the declaration of justice, severity and hatred against sin in the reprobate. "Willing to show his wrath and make known his power, he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction." The nearer cause is the just condemnation of the reprobate on account of their sins.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Deus præcognouit bona opera nostra. Ergo propter ea nos elegit. Resp. Præcognouit bona opera nostra, non quæ ipse in nobis efficere statuit, sed quæ facturi eramus: sicut etiam personas præcognouit: hoc est, eligere & seruare in Christo statuit: alioqui nulla bona opera potuissent præcognoscere: quia ante electionem in massa perditionis, filios iræ mortuos in peccatis inuenit.
units.tr: Objection 1. God foreknew our good works; therefore he chose us on account of them. Answer. He foreknew our good works, not those which he decided to work in us, but those which we were going to do; just as he also foreknew persons, that is, he decided to choose and save them in Christ. Otherwise no good works could have been foreknown, because before election he found us as children of wrath, dead in sins, in the mass of perdition.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Quos Deus elegit in Christo, eos inuenit in Christo: ratio; quia nulli benefacit in Christo, nisi qui sit in Christo. Deus nos elegit in Christo. Ergo inuenit nos in Christo, hoc est, præuidit nos fore in Christo: nos præ aliis credituros, & futuros aliis meliores, & ideo nos elegit. Resp. Negatur maior. Ratio vera est, non de electione, sed de effectis electionis, & consummatione beneficiorum Christi, quæ nulli contingunt, nisi in Christo existenti per fidem; sicut dicitur: Nisi in me manseritis, non habebitis vitam in vobis. De electione & prima salutis causa est falsa, vt extextu liquet. Elegit enim nos ante jacta mundi fundamenta, non quia eramus futuri, sed vt essemus aliis meliores, hoc est, sancti & inculpati: non quia iam essemus in Christo, sed vt nos insereret Christo, & adoptaret in filios. Non igitur fides vel sanctitas nostra præuisa, est causa, sed effectus nostræ electionis in Christo. Elegit nos, nicht darumb, dass wir in Christo fromb wären oder seyn würden, sondern dass wir in Christo fromb würden: hoc est, non quia pii fuimus, aut futuri eramus, sed vt in Christo pii euaderemus. Elegit nos non existentes iam filios, sed adoptandos in filios. Non enim, inquit Augustinus, elegit nos ideo, quod tunc sancti essemus: immò nec ideo, quia tunc sancti futuri essemus: sed potius elegit nos ad hoc, vt in tempore gratia sancti essemus per bona opera. Sed Pelagianus veritati resistens ait: Præscieбat Deus, qui essent futuri sancti & immaculati per liberã voluntatis arbitrium: & ideo eos in sua præscientia, quales futuros esse præsciuit, elegit. Quem confutat hic Apostolus, dicens: ut essemus sancti. Qui vero hodie sic cauillantur, cum Pelagio supponunt falsum, homines ex lapsu non esse adeo corruptos, & mortuos in peccatis, quin ex se possint præuenire gratiam, vel præuenienti gratiæ cooperari, atque mereri: hoc est, negant peccatum originis.
units.tr: Objection 2. Those whom God chose in Christ, he found in Christ; the reason being that he does good to no one in Christ except one who is in Christ. "God chose us in Christ." Therefore he found us in Christ, that is, he foresaw that we would be in Christ: that we would believe before others and would be better than others, and for this reason he chose us. Answer. The major premise is denied. The true reasoning concerns not election but the effects of election and the completion of Christ's benefits, which come to no one except one existing in Christ through faith; as it is said: "Unless you abide in me, you will not have life in you." Concerning election and the first cause of salvation, the objection is false, as the context makes clear. For he chose us before the foundation of the world, not because we were going to be, but so that we would be better than others, that is, holy and blameless; not because we were already in Christ, but so that he would graft us into Christ and adopt us as sons. Therefore our foreseen faith or holiness is not the cause, but the effect, of our election in Christ. He chose us, not so that we were or would be godly in Christ, but so that we would become godly in Christ: that is, not because we were or were going to be pious, but so that we would become pious in Christ. He chose us not as sons already existing, but as those to be adopted as sons. For, says Augustine, he did not choose us because we would then be holy; nor even because we would then be going to be holy; but rather he chose us for this, that in time we might by good works be holy through grace. But the Pelagian, resisting the truth, says: God foreknew who would be holy and blameless through the free choice of the will, and therefore he chose them in his foreknowledge, as he foreknew they would be. This Apostle refutes, saying: "that we should be holy." Those who today likewise quibble, with Pelagius assume a falsehood: that human beings after the fall are not so corrupted and dead in sins that they cannot of themselves anticipate grace, or cooperate with preventing grace, and merit it. That is, they deny original sin.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Causa electionis est meritum Christi fide applicatum. Ergo non beneplacitum Dei. Resp. Etiamsi verum esset antecedens, consequentia tamen non valeret: quia posita causa secunda, non remouetur prima. Sed negatur antecedens: quia meritum Christi fide applicatum est vocatione & electione posterius: sicut ipsa fides. Non potest igitur esse electionis causa. Beneplacitum vero Dei est ordine prius his omnibus, electione, merito Christi, fide, applicatione fidei. Electio est prior reliquis, tanquam causa effectis. Deus enim nos elegit, & donauit Christo, ut ei tanquam capiti per fidem insiti seruemur: sicut dicit ipse: Pater, tui erant, quos dedisti mihi. Et Apostolus: Elegit nos in Christo, hoc est, Christi merito per fidem justificandos & seruandos.
units.tr: Objection 3. The cause of election is the merit of Christ applied by faith. Therefore it is not the good pleasure of God. Answer: Even if the antecedent were true, the consequence would not hold, because when a secondary cause is posited, the primary cause is not removed. But the antecedent is denied, since the merit of Christ applied by faith comes after calling and election, just as faith itself does. It therefore cannot be the cause of election. The good pleasure of God, however, comes before all of these in order: election, the merit of Christ, faith, and the application of faith. Election is prior to the rest, as a cause is prior to its effects. For God chose us and gave us to Christ, so that we might be preserved in him as members implanted in him as the head through faith, just as he himself says: "Father, they were yours, and you gave them to me." And the Apostle: "He chose us in Christ," that is, to be justified and preserved by the merit of Christ through faith.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Mala opera sunt causa reprobationis. Ergo bona opera sunt causa electionis. Resp. Negatur antecedens. Mala enim opera non sunt causa reprobationis: sed eorum, quæ sequuntur reprobationem: hoc est, damnationis, & ordinationis ad eam. Si enim peccata fuissent causa reprobationis, omnes fuissemus reprobati: quia omnes pariter fuimus peccatores, filij iræ, & mortui in peccatis. Ex massa vero perditionis Deus elegit vel reprobauit, quos voluit: sicut dicitur: Nondum nati pueri, cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, &c. dictum est: Maior seruiet minori. Iacob dilexi, Esau odio habui. Nonne potestatem habet figulus, ut ex eadem massa faciat vas ad honorem, & vas ad dedecus? Miseretur, cuius vult, quem vult, indurat. Bona autem opera causa electionis esse non possunt: quia ordine sunt posteriora electione, atque etiam justificatione. Non enim præcedunt justificandos, sed sequuntur justificatos: inquit Augustinus. Electio vero est causa fidei & iustificationis per fidem, & bonorum operum ex fide: ut docet Apostolus Eph.1. v.3.4.5.6.
units.tr: Objection 4. Evil works are the cause of reprobation. Therefore good works are the cause of election. Answer: The antecedent is denied. Evil works are not the cause of reprobation, but of those things which follow reprobation, that is, of damnation and of the ordaining of men to it. For if sins had been the cause of reprobation, all of us would have been reprobated, since all alike were sinners, children of wrath, and dead in sins. But God elected or reprobated out of the mass of perdition whom he willed, as it is said: "When the boys were not yet born, and had done neither good nor evil, it was said: The elder shall serve the younger. I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau. Has not the potter power over the same lump, to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour? He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." But good works cannot be the cause of election, because in order they come after election and also after justification. "For they do not precede those who are to be justified, but follow those who have been justified," says Augustine. Election, indeed, is the cause of faith and of justification through faith, and of good works that flow from faith, as the Apostle teaches, Eph. 1:3, 4, 5, 6.

units.la: IV. Quæ sint prædestinationis effecta.
units.tr: IV. What are the effects of predestination.

units.la: Electionis effectus est totum opus salutis, & omnes gradus redemptionis nostræ: videlicet 1. Missio ac donatio mediatoris Christi; & eius sacrificium. 2. Vocatio & conuersio electorum ad Christum per Spiritum sanctum & verbum. 3. Fides, iustificatio, ficatio, & regeneratio. 4. Bona opera. 5. Perseuerantia finalis in fide 6. Suscitatio electorum ad gloriam. 7. Glorificatio, & vita æterna.
units.tr: The effect of election is the whole work of salvation and all the stages of our redemption, namely: (1) the sending and gift of the Mediator Christ, and his sacrifice; (2) the calling and conversion of the elect to Christ through the Holy Spirit and the Word; (3) faith, justification, sanctification, and regeneration; (4) good works; (5) final perseverance in faith; (6) the raising of the elect to glory; (7) glorification and eternal life.

units.la: Reprobationis partim effecta, partim consequentia sunt 1. Priuatio gratiæ diuinæ, seu desertio. 2. Excæcatio & induratio. 3. Perseuerantia in infidelitate & peccatis. 4. Suscitatio ad iudicium. 5. Abiectio in æternas poenas.
units.tr: The effects and consequences of reprobation are, partly, these: (1) the privation of divine grace, or desertion; (2) blinding and hardening; (3) perseverance in unbelief and sins; (4) being raised up to judgment; (5) being cast down into eternal punishments.

units.la: Obiectio 1. Contrariarum causarum sunt contrarii effectus. Electionis effectus sunt bona opera. Ergo reprobationis effectus sunt mala opera. Resp. Ex puris particularibus nihil sequitur. Maior non semper est vera de causis voluntariis: quæ possunt dissimiliter agere, nec producere contrarios effectus, vt hoc loco est dissimilitudo: quia DEVS bona opera in electis deveruit efficere: mala vero in reprobis non efficere, sed tantum permittere. Propria autem malorum operum causa est praua diaboli & hominum voluntas.
units.tr: Objection 1. Contrary causes have contrary effects. The effects of election are good works. Therefore the effects of reprobation are evil works. Answer: Nothing follows from particular premises alone. The major premise is not always true of voluntary causes, which can act in different ways and need not produce contrary effects, as is the case here: for God is ready to produce good works in the elect, but in the reprobate he does not produce evil works, only permits them. The proper cause of evil works, however, is the perverse will of the devil and of men.

units.la: Obiect.2. Cæcitas est effectus reprobationis. Cæcitas est peccatum. Ergo peccatum est reprobationis effectum. Resp.1. Negatur minor. Non cæcitas, sed excæcatio proprie est reprobationis effectus. Cæcitas enim naturalis ordine antecessit reprobationem: quia Deus eam in reprobis inuenit: eandem vero etiam sequitur: quia DEVS in reprobis non tollit, sicut in electis, sed sæpe graviore cæcitate justo judicio punit, juxta illud: Vade, excæca cor populi huius. 2. Minor etiam debet distingui: quod cæcitas sit & peccatum, & pœna peccati. Peccatum est, in quantum voluntarie attracta, diuinæ legi repugnans. Pœna est, in quantum voluntarie cæcis à Deo justè infligitur, vel aggrauatur. Hoc sensu posteriore datur, cæcitatem esse reprobationis effectum: priore non item. Sunt igitur quatuor termini.
units.tr: Objection 2. Blindness is an effect of reprobation. Blindness is sin. Therefore sin is an effect of reprobation. Answer: 1. The minor is denied. Strictly speaking, it is not blindness but blinding that is an effect of reprobation. For natural blindness came before reprobation in order, since God found it in the reprobate; yet it also follows reprobation, since God does not remove it in the reprobate as he does in the elect, but often punishes it with a heavier blindness by his just judgment, according to the words: "Go, blind the heart of this people." 2. The minor must also be distinguished: that blindness is both sin and punishment of sin. It is sin insofar as it is voluntarily drawn in and opposed to the divine law. It is punishment insofar as it is justly inflicted or increased by God upon those who are voluntarily blind. In the latter sense it is granted that blindness is an effect of reprobation; in the former sense it is not. There are therefore four terms.

units.la: Obiect.3. Induratio est effectus reprobationis: & est peccatum. Ergo, &c. Resp.1. Minor negatur. Non enim induratio, sed duritries, hoc est, contumacia cordis impiorum est peccatum: cuius induratio est justa pœna. 2. Etiam maior potest negari vniuersaliter. Neque enim Deus omnes reprobos legitur indurare, sed tantum aliquos, malitiosa contumacia indurationis diuinæ pœnam sibi accersentes: vt Pharaonē, Cananæos, & Ægyptios, &c. Si verò induratio per se esset effectus reprobationis, Deus omnes reprobos induraret. Itaque potius est singulare consequens reprobationis, & pœna, quæ reprobationem in aliquibus sequitur; cuius pœnæ Deum esse authorem, non est negandum: cum scriptura id clarè affirmer.
units.tr: Objection 3. Hardening is an effect of reprobation, and it is sin. Therefore, etc. Answer: 1. The minor is denied. For it is not hardening but hardness, that is, the obstinacy of the hearts of the wicked, that is sin, of which hardening is the just punishment. 2. The major too may be denied universally. For it is not read that God hardens all the reprobate, but only some, who bring upon themselves the divine punishment of hardening by their malicious obstinacy, as Pharaoh, the Canaanites, the Egyptians, and so on. If hardening were in itself an effect of reprobation, God would harden all the reprobate. Hence it is rather a particular consequence of reprobation, and a punishment that follows reprobation in some; and it must not be denied that God is the author of this punishment, since Scripture clearly affirms it.

units.la: V. An praedestinatio sit mutabilis:
units.tr: V. Whether predestination is changeable:

units.la: Praedestinatio est firma & immutabilis. Id patet vel ex generali ratione, quod Deus est immutabilis, cuius decretum non pendet à vicissitudine rerum, sed haec potius à Dei decreto. Quod igitur Deus ab aeterno decreuit de electis seruandis, & reprobis damnandis, id haud dubie immutabiliter decreuit, ideoque firma & immutabilis est tum electio, tum reprobatio. Confirmant hoc scripturae testimonia: Consilium meum stabit. Deus sum, & non mutor. Haec est voluntas Patris, ut ex iis, quos dedit mihi, nullum perdam. Oues meas nemo rapiet ex manu mea. Vos non creditis; quia ex ouibus meis non estis. Firmum stat fundamentum Dei: nouit Dominus, qui sunt sui. Fundamentum Paulus vocat decretum Dei de electis saluandis: 1. Quia est fons nostrae salutis, omniumque mediorum ad salutem. 2. Propter firmitudinem: quia nunquam concutitur. Haec nos scire interest, ut habeamus firmam consolationem, & possimus credere vitam aeternam, coque omnes alios articulos fidei. Ratio est saepe repetita, & saepe meditanda: quia qui incertus est, vel dubitat de gratia futura, etiam incertus est, & dubitat de gratia praesente: quia Deus est immutabilis, nec potest eos vnquam odisse, quos semel ab aeterno amauit & elegit in Christo.
units.tr: Predestination is firm and immutable. This is clear first from the general principle that God is unchanging, and that his decree does not depend on the changes of things, but rather that things depend on his decree. So what God decreed from eternity concerning the saving of the elect and the damning of the reprobate, he certainly decreed unchangeably; therefore both election and reprobation are firm and immutable. The testimonies of Scripture confirm this: My counsel shall stand, and I am God, and I do not change. This is the will of the Father, that of those whom he has given me I should lose none. No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hand. You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. The firm foundation of God stands: the Lord knows those who are his. Paul calls God's decree concerning the saving of the elect a foundation: (1) because it is the source of our salvation and of all the means to salvation; (2) because of its firmness, since it is never shaken. It matters for us to know this, so that we may have firm comfort and may believe in eternal life, and with it all the other articles of faith. The reasoning is often repeated and often to be meditated on: whoever is uncertain, or doubts, about future grace, is also uncertain and doubts about present grace, because God is unchangeable and can never hate those whom he has once loved and chosen from eternity in Christ.

units.la: VI. Quatenus praedestinatio sit nobis nota: & an possimus ac debeamus de ea esse certi.
units.tr: VI. How far predestination is known to us, and whether we can and ought to be certain of it.

units.la: Praedestinatio nobis ignota est, nec inuestiganda à priori. Quis enim ascendit in coelum, & cognoscet mentem Domini? Cognoscitur vero ex patefactione, per verbum Dei. Ex hoc notum est, & esse debet omnibus, in genere, 1. Esse aliquos electos, aliquos reprobos, non omnes: Multi vocati, pauci electi. 2. Omnes in Christum vere credentes esse ab aeterno electos, seu ex electorum numero: Crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam aeternam. 3. Electos non posse perire, sed certo saluari. Oues meas nemo rapiet ex manu mea. In specie, an hic vel ille sit electus, nostrum non est inquirere. De nostra vero electione singuli possumus, & debemus esse certi, à posteriori, hoc est, ex effectis, & signis electionis, vera nimirum fide & conuersione nostra ad Deum. Si enim vere in Christum credimus, electi sumus. Scimus autem nos vere in Christum credere. Credens enim scit se credere. Ergo etiam scire possumus electionem nostram. Remittitur vero hic quisque ad examen fidei suae: Vosipsos tentate, an sitis in fide: vos ipsos probate: an non agnoscitis Iesum Christum in vobis esse, nisi reprobi estis? Tenemur etiam credere in Christum, credere vitam æternam. Hoc autem credere, reuera est credere nos in Christo esse ad vitam æternam electos, proinde nos esse ex numero electorum. Ergo de electione nostra certo credere debemus. Statuendum est quoque, præter me, &te, etiam alios esse electos. Tenemur enim credere articulum de ecclesia, & de communione sanctorum. Tu verò solus non es ecclesia, vel communio illa. Indiuidua tamen discernere & dicere: hic est electus, ille non, &c. tuum non est. De omnibus verò & singulis est benè sperandum, & ex charitatis regula statuendum, omnes eos esse electos, in quibus effecta electionis, fides & conuersio ad Deum apparent. Sic enim Paulus ex fide & effectis fidei Thessalonicenses iudicabat electos esse, 1 Thess. 1. uerf. 4. & 2 Thess. 2. uerf. 13. & Petrus aduenas, ad quos scribebat, 1 Petr. 1. uerf. 1.
units.tr: Predestination is unknown to us, and it is not to be investigated a priori. For who has gone up into heaven and known the mind of the Lord? It is known, however, from its disclosure through the Word of God. From this it is known, and ought to be known by all in general, (1) that some are elect and some reprobate, not all: Many are called, few are chosen. (2) That all who truly believe in Christ were chosen from eternity, or belong to the number of the elect: As many as were appointed to eternal life believed. (3) That the elect cannot perish but are certainly saved: No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hand. Whether this or that particular person is elect is not for us to inquire. But concerning our own election, each of us can and ought to be certain a posteriori, that is, from its effects and signs, namely true faith and our conversion to God. For if we truly believe in Christ, we are elect. But we know that we truly believe in Christ. For one who believes knows that he believes. Therefore we can also know our election. Each person is referred here to the examination of his own faith: Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not recognise that Jesus Christ is in you, unless you are reprobate? We are also bound to believe in Christ and to believe in eternal life. But to believe this is really to believe that we are chosen in Christ to eternal life, and therefore that we belong to the number of the elect. So we ought to believe with certainty concerning our election. It must also be held that, besides me and you, there are others who are elect. For we are bound to believe the article concerning the Church and the communion of saints. But you alone are not the Church, or that communion. Yet to distinguish individuals and say: this one is elect, that one is not, and so on, is not your business. Concerning all and each we ought to hope well, and by the rule of charity to judge that all in whom the effects of election appear, namely faith and conversion to God, are elect. For so Paul judged from the faith and the effects of faith that the Thessalonians were elect, 1 Thess. 1 verse 4, and 2 Thess. 2 verse 13, and Peter that the strangers to whom he wrote were elect, 1 Pet. 1 verse 1.

units.la: De reprobatione sua vel aliorum nemo pronunciare debet vel potest. Deus enim non vult quenquem statuere, se esse reprobum: nisi finaliter non velit credere in Christum: vult verò & iubet omnes credere Euangelio, & agere pœnitentiam. Hoc qui facturi sint, nos ignoramus: qui hodie nondum est conuersus, potest cras converti, ante finem vitæ. Sunt enim duodecim horæ diei, &c.
units.tr: No one ought or is able to pronounce concerning the reprobation of himself or of others. For God does not wish anyone to determine that he is reprobate, unless he finally refuses to believe in Christ; but he wills and commands all to believe the Gospel and to repent. We do not know who will do this: someone who has not yet been converted today can be converted tomorrow, before the end of life. For there are twelve hours of the day, etc.

units.la: VII. An electi semper sint membra Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: VII. Whether the elect are always members of the Church.

units.la: Electi non semper sunt membra Ecclesiæ, sed tum demum, quando conuertuntur, & regenerantur per Spiritum sanctum. Dicitur enim: Quicunque Spiritum Christi non habet, non est eius. Item Ecclesia dicitur sancta. Sed tum demum electi fiunt sancti, cùm conuertuntur. Nam Paulus expressè dicit: Tales eratis & vos quondam, sed abluti estis, sanctificati estis. Item: Transfulit nos in regnum Filij sui. Alii autem in Ecclesia nascuntur, manent, & moriuntur: alii non nascuntur in ea, sed vocantur, aut statim, aut sero ad visibilem & invisibilem ecclesiam, ut latro in cruce. Item: Alias oues habeo, quas oportet me adducere, inquit Christus. Sic reprobi non semper sunt alieni ab Ecclesia, sed aliquando sunt membra visibilis ecclesiæ: nunquam autem vere sunt de ecclesia: etsi pro eius membris habentur.
units.tr: The elect are not always members of the Church, but only when they are converted and regenerated by the Holy Spirit. For it is said: Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his. Likewise the Church is called holy. But the elect become holy only when they are converted. For Paul says expressly: Such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified. Likewise: He has transferred us into the kingdom of his Son. Some are born in the Church, remain in it, and die in it; others are not born in it but are called to the visible and invisible Church, either at once or late, like the thief on the cross. Likewise Christ says: I have other sheep, which I must bring. So the reprobate are not always aliens from the Church, but at times they are members of the visible Church; yet they are never truly of the Church, even though they are regarded as its members.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Omnes credentes semper sunt membra Ecclesiæ. Omnes autem electi sunt credentes: quia sunt termini convertibiles, electi, & credentes. Ergo omnes electi semper sunt membra ecclesiæ. Resp. ad minorem. Sunt termini conuertibiles, sed adhibita limitatione temporis. Omnes credentes sunt electi: & omnes electi sunt vel fiunt credentes, finaliter. Aliquan- do autem electi nondum credunt: antequam nimirum vocentur, sicut Paulus ante vocationem erat persequutor. Omnes tamen ante finem vocantur ad fidem, & ecclesiæ associantur.
units.tr: Objection 1. All believers are always members of the Church. But all the elect are believers, because the terms elect and believers are convertible. Therefore all the elect are always members of the Church. Answer to the minor premise: the terms are convertible, but with a limitation of time added. All believers are elect, and all the elect are, or finally become, believers. But sometimes the elect do not yet believe, namely before they are called, just as Paul was a persecutor before his calling. Yet all are called to faith before the end, and are joined to the Church.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Christus etiam nondum conuersos ex gentibus vocat oues suas, Ioh.10.16. Habeo alias oues, quas oportet me adducere. Ergo electi videntur etiam ante conuersionem esse membra ecclesiæ. Respon. Oues etiam tunc erant, quoad curam & consilium Dei; nondum autem quoad impletionem decreti, hoc est, oues erant prædestinatione, sed nondum vocatione ad visibilem ecclesiam. Summa. Electi non semper sunt membra ecclesiæ: sed tamen necesse est, eos in hac vita ad ecclesiam tandem adduci, etiamsi id aliquando serò vel in articulo mortis accidat. Hoc est, quod dicitur, oportere omnes electos in hac vita credere, & inchoare vitam æternam.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ also calls his sheep who are not yet converted from the Gentiles, John 10:16: I have other sheep, which I must bring. Therefore the elect seem to be members of the Church even before their conversion. Answer. They were sheep even then, as far as God's care and counsel were concerned; but not yet as far as the fulfilment of the decree is concerned. That is, they were sheep by predestination, but not yet by calling into the visible Church. Summary. The elect are not always members of the Church; but nevertheless it is necessary that they are at last brought to the Church in this life, even if this sometimes happens late, or at the point of death. This is what is meant when it is said that all the elect must believe in this life and begin eternal life.

units.la: VIII. An electi deficiant ab ecclesia.
units.tr: VIII. Whether the elect fall away from the Church.

units.la: Hæc quæstio patet ex iis, quæ de immutabilitate electionis, & perseverantia sanctorum supra sunt dicta. Electi ergo post- quam semel verè accesserunt ad ecclesiam sanctorum, deficere quidem aliquando possunt, sed nunquam discedunt ab ecclesia totaliter & finaliter. Non totaliter: quia nunquam sic deficiunt, vt fiant hostes Dei & ecclesiæ: non finaliter, quia non perseverant in apostasia, sed certo tandem redeunt ad pœnitentiam. Calamum quassatum non confringet, & linum fumigans non extinguet. Oues meas nemo rapiet è manu mea. Qui vero totaliter & finaliter ab ecclesia deficiunt, eos certum est, nunquam fuisse verè conuersos & electos: iuxta dictum: Ex nobis egressi sunt, quia ex nobis non erant. Nam si fuissent ex nobis, mansissent utique nobiscum.
units.tr: This question is clear from what has been said above about the immutability of election and the perseverance of the saints. The elect, therefore, once they have truly come to the Church of the saints, can indeed sometimes fall away, but they never leave the Church totally and finally. Not totally, because they never fall away in such a way as to become enemies of God and the Church; not finally, because they do not persist in apostasy, but certainly return at last to repentance. "A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not quench." "No one will snatch my sheep out of my hand." Those, however, who fall away from the Church totally and finally, it is certain, were never truly converted and elect, according to the saying: "They went out from us, because they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have remained with us."

units.la: Obiect. Etiam sancti sæpe deficiunt, vt Dauid, Petrus, &c. Respon. Deficiunt, sed non totaliter, nec finaliter. Vt Petrus non defecit totaliter nec finaliter. Nam retinebat in corde amorem Christi, etiam cum metu periculi eum ore negaret; idem mox agnoscebat delictum, & vere resipiscebat. Vnde Augustinus: Non defecit Petrum fides in corde, cum cessaret confessio in ore. Dauid quoque non defecit totaliter, sed à Domino per prophetam correptus, vere resipuit, & fidem non extinctam, sed ad tempus sopitam fuisse ostendit precatione: Spiritum tuum sanctum ne auferas à me. Sanctiigitur & electi nunquam prorsus deficiunt. Quo vero discrimine peccent electi & reprobi, explicatum est supra parte I. Quæst. VII.
units.tr: Objection: Even saints often fall, as David, Peter, etc. Answer: They fall, but not totally, nor finally. Thus Peter did not fall totally nor finally. For he kept in his heart the love of Christ, even when, for fear of danger, he denied him with his mouth; he soon acknowledged the offence and truly repented. Hence Augustine: "Faith did not fail Peter in his heart, when the confession ceased in his mouth." David also did not fall totally, but, rebuked by the Lord through the prophet, he truly repented, and by his prayer showed that his faith had not been extinguished but only lulled for a time: "Take not thy Holy Spirit from me." Therefore the saints and the elect never utterly fall away. By what difference the elect and the reprobate sin has been explained above in Part I, Question VII.

units.la: IX. Quis sit visus doctrinae de praedestinatione.
units.tr: IX. What the doctrine of predestination aims at.

units.la: Visus est 1. Ut Deo in solidum tribuatur salutis nostrae gloria. Quid habes, quod non accepisti? 2. Ut firmam consolationem habeamus. Hanc habebimus, ubi de iis, quae hic docentur, non dubitaverimus: immutabile esse decretum Dei de servandis electis: & quisque fidelis fide in Christum confidet, se unum esse ex electorum numero, vivum ecclesiae membrum, eoque nunquam e manibus Christi rapiendum.
units.tr: It aims, first, that the glory of our salvation be wholly ascribed to God: "What have you that you did not receive?" Second, that we may have firm comfort. We will have this if we do not doubt what is taught here: that God's decree to save the elect is unchangeable, and that every believer, trusting in Christ by faith, may be confident that he is one of the number of the elect, a living member of the Church, and therefore never to be snatched from the hands of Christ.

units.la: QVAESTIO LV. Quid sibi vult communio sanctorum? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: QUESTION 55. What is meant by the communion of saints? ANSWER.

units.la: Primum, quod universi & singuli credentes, Christi & omnium eius bonorum tanquam ipsius membra communionem habeant a. Deinde, quod singuli, quae acceperunt dona, in commune commodum, & universorum salutem, promptè & alacriter conferre debeant b.
units.tr: First, that all and each of the believers have communion in Christ and in all his benefits, as members of him a. Second, that each one ought to share promptly and eagerly whatever gifts he has received for the common good and the salvation of all b.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Sequentes articuli sunt de Christi beneficiis ecclesiae collatis & conferendis. Communio est relatio inter duos, vel plures, rem sive possessionem communem habentes. Commune relatiuum: fundamentum rei, quae communis est. Terminus possessores sive plures, sive unus, plurium vel unius rei.
units.tr: The articles that follow concern the benefits of Christ bestowed and to be bestowed upon the Church. Communion is a relation between two or more who hold a thing or possession in common. Common is relative: it is the ground of the thing that is common. The term denotes the possessors, whether one or several, of the thing of several or of one.

units.la: Communio igitur sanctorum est Christi & omnium eius beneficiorum communis possessio: & donorum, quae singulis ecclesiae membris data sunt, in salutem corporis collatio.
units.tr: The communion therefore of saints is the common possession of Christ and of all his benefits, and the bestowing for the salvation of the body of the gifts given to the individual members of the Church.

units.la: Sancti dicuntur omnes sanctificati, hoc est, segregati à mundo, absoluti à peccatis, & justificati per imputatam Christi justitiam: & regenerati per Spiritum sanctum. Et haec eratis nonnulli, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed justificati estis in nomine Domini Iesu, & per Spiritum Dei nostri. Horum communionem credimus: in quae in his potissimum consistit.
units.tr: Saints are called all who are sanctified, that is, set apart from the world, freed from sins, justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ, and regenerated by the Holy Spirit. "And such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God." We believe in the communion of these, which consists chiefly in the following.

units.la: Primo: in unione totius ecclesiae tanquam corporis, cum Christo capite, per Spiritum sanctum, in capite & membris habitanbitantem, membraq; capiti conformia reddentem; juxta dicta: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Qui manet in me, & ego in ipso, hic fert fructum multum. Per unum spiritum omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus. Qui agglutinatur Domino, unus spiritus est. Per hoc cognoscimus, nos in eo habitare, & ipsum in nobis, quod de Spiritu suo dedit nobis.
units.tr: First: in the union of the whole Church as a body with Christ its head, through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in the head and the members and makes the members conformed to the head; according to the words: "I am the vine, you are the branches. He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit." "By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body." "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." "By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit."

units.la: Ergo vanum commentum est, communionem Christi & sanctorum esse subsistentiam corporis Christi intra nostra corpora. Repugnant ei testimonia dicta, & toties in scripturis repetita capitis & membrorum comparatio. Cohærent enim membra, non mixtim subsistunt. Membra non sunt intra caput, vel contra: nec palmites intra vitem, vel contra: sed sicut differunt, nexu autem conueniente in unum corpus copulantur. Hinc etiam de communione sacramentali, hoc est, ea, quam sacramenta obsignant, recte judicatur eam esse spiritualem. Sacramenta enim non aliud obsignant, quam quod verbum promittit. Communio autem corporalis cum Christo verbo nusquam promittitur, sed spiritualis, quæ fit per spiritum Dei, in Christo, & in nobis habitantem. Accedit, quod communionem hanc perpetuo continuari oportet. Ad hoc enim Christus se communicat nobis, ut habitet & maneat in nobis. Talis proinde communio, qualis mansio. Mansio autem est spiritualis, non corporalis: quia perpetua. Spiritualis igitur etiam communio. Firmissimum est hoc argumentum, in cuius solutionem excogitata est Vbiquitas. Nam ad corporalem communionem obtinendam, affirmandum erat, Christum perpetuo in omnibus piis habitare corporaliter.
units.tr: Therefore it is an empty invention that the communion of Christ and the saints is the subsistence of the body of Christ within our bodies. The passages cited, and the comparison of head and members so often repeated in the Scriptures, are opposed to it. For members cohere; they do not subsist mixed together. The members are not within the head, or the reverse, nor are the branches within the vine, or the reverse; but they differ in their parts, and are joined together into one body by a fitting bond. Hence it is also rightly judged that the sacramental communion, that is, the communion which the sacraments seal, is spiritual. For the sacraments seal nothing other than what the word promises. Now a bodily communion with Christ is nowhere promised in the word, but a spiritual one, which takes place through the Spirit of God dwelling in Christ and in us. Moreover, this communion must be continued perpetually. For Christ imparts himself to us for this purpose, that he may dwell and abide in us. Such communion, therefore, is as the abiding is. But the abiding is spiritual, not bodily, because it is perpetual. Therefore the communion too is spiritual. This argument is most firm, and the doctrine of the Ubiquity was devised to answer it. For in order to maintain a bodily communion, it had to be affirmed that Christ dwells bodily and perpetually in all the godly.

units.la: Secundo: In unione omnium membrorum Christi inter se, per eundem Christi spiritum in omnibus habitantem. 1 Cor. 12, 13. Per unum spiritum omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus. Rom. 12,5. Ita multi unum corpus sumus in Christo.
units.tr: Second: in the union of all the members of Christ with one another, through the same Spirit of Christ dwelling in all. 1 Cor. 12:13. By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. Rom. 12:5. So we, being many, are one body in Christ.

units.la: Tertio: In communione eorundem beneficiorum Christi. Eadem omnibus sanctis reconciliatio cum Deo, redemtio, justificatio, sanctificatio, vita & salus, & reliqua beneficia omnia, ad salutem necessaria, per & propter Christum. Eph. 4,4 5. Unum est corpus, & unus spiritus: sicut & vocati estis in spem unam vocationis vestræ. Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma.
units.tr: Third: in the communion of the same benefits of Christ. To all the saints belong the same reconciliation with God, redemption, justification, sanctification, life and salvation, and all the other benefits necessary for salvation, through and on account of Christ. Eph. 4:4, 5. There is one body and one Spirit, as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism.

units.la: Quarto: In distributione donorum spiritualium: quæ conferuntur à Deo ecclesiæ, & singulis membris in salutem totius corporis: ita tamen, ut membra alia aliis in ecclesia donis antecellant. Nam varia sunt Spiritus sancti dona. Ephes. 4, 7. Sed unicuique datur gratia pro mensura donationis Christi. Vnusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem ita, alius autem ita. Discrimina donorum sunt: sed vnicuique datur declaratio ad vtilitatem. Nam huic per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alij sermo cognitionis per eundem Spiritum: alij verò fides, per eundem Spiritum, &c.
units.tr: Fourth: in the distribution of spiritual gifts, which God bestows on the Church and on the individual members for the salvation of the whole body; yet so that some members excel others in the gifts in the Church. For the gifts of the Holy Spirit are various. Eph. 4:7. "But to each one is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ." "Each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that." "There are differences of gifts, but to each is given a manifestation for the common good." For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge through the same Spirit, and to another faith through the same Spirit, etc.

units.la: Obiect. Alia aliorum sunt dona. Ergo non est communio eorundem bonorum: quod in tertia parte dicitur. Resp. Conceditur argumentū de donisparticularibus, quæ singulis membris singula & diuersa, maiora vel minora, plura vel pauciora dantur pro cuiusque vocatione: non autem de donis communibus ad salutem necessariis, qualia sunt beneficia Christi prius enumerata. De illis in quarta, de his in tertia communionis parte agitur. Hæc igitur eadem & communia sunt omnium, quoad ipsa beneficia: licet quoad participationis gradum, pergmagna etiam sit diuersitas. Non enim eum gradum fidei, sanctitatis, &c. quem Abraham, Petrus, Paulus habuerunt, omnes consequuntur.
units.tr: Objection: The gifts of one are different from those of another. Therefore there is no communion of the same goods, which is stated in the third part. Answer: The argument is granted concerning the particular gifts, which are given to individual members, each different, greater or lesser, more or fewer, according to each one's calling. But it is not granted concerning the common gifts necessary for salvation, such as the benefits of Christ listed earlier. The fourth part treats of the former, the third part of the latter. These, therefore, are the same and common to all as regards the benefits themselves, although as regards the degree of participation there is also very great diversity. For not all attain the degree of faith, holiness, etc., which Abraham, Peter and Paul had.

units.la: Quintò: In obligatione membrorum omnium, vt ea, quæ acceperunt dona, in commune commodum, & vniuersorum salutem, eum primis autem in gloriam capitis sui CHRISTI, promptè & alacriter conferant. Charitas non quærit, quæ sua sunt. Dedit alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, &c. ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerij: ad ædificationem corporis Christi. Ne sua quisque spectetis, sed vnusquisque etiam, quæ sunt aliorum.
units.tr: Fifth: in the obligation of all the members, that they share promptly and eagerly the gifts they have received for the common good and the salvation of all, and above all for the glory of their head, Christ. "Love does not seek its own." "He gave some as apostles, some as prophets, etc., for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ." "Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others."

units.la: Ex his apparet, quid sit, credere communionem sanctorum: nempe credere semper fuisse, esse, & fore aliquos verè sanctos in ecclesia visibili: eosque cum Christo & inter se habere vnam communionem: hoc est, Christo vt capiti per Spiritum sanctum vniri, ex eodem per fidem haurire iustitiam & vitam æternam, aliaq; dona tum ad salutem, tum ad vocationem singulis necessaria: & per eundem Spiritum, charitate mutua, & communi donorum vsu, in vnum corpus coalescere: me deniq; in eorum etiam numero esse, ac semper mansurum.
units.tr: From these things it is clear what it is to believe in the communion of saints: namely, to believe that there always have been, are, and will be some truly holy persons in the visible Church; and that they have one communion with Christ and with one another: that is, that they are united to Christ as head through the Holy Spirit, draw from him through faith righteousness and eternal life, and other gifts necessary for each one both for salvation and for his calling; and that through the same Spirit, by mutual love and the common use of gifts, they grow together into one body; and finally, that I too am among their number, and always shall remain so.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LVI. Quid credis de remissione peccatorum?
units.tr: QUESTION 56. What do you believe concerning the forgiveness of sins?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Deum propter satisfactionem Christi meorum peccatorum, atque illius etiam prauitatis, cum qua mihi per omnem vitam a pugnandum est, memoriam omnem b depositae, & me justitia Christi gratis donare, ne vn- quam in judicium Dei veniam.
units.tr: I believe that God, for the sake of Christ's satisfaction, has blotted out all memory of my sins and of that depravity with which I must struggle throughout my whole life, and that He grants me, as a gift and freely, the righteousness of Christ, so that I shall never come into God's judgment.

units.la: a 1 Iohan. 2. verf. 2. 1 Iohan. 1, 7. 2 Corinth. 12, 9. b Roman. 7. v. 23.24.25. Ierem. 31, 34. Mich. 7.19. Psalm. 103, 3.10.12. 2 Ioh. 3. v. 18. Iohan. 5. verf. 24.
units.tr: a 1 Iohan. 2. verf. 2. 1 Iohan. 1, 7. 2 Corinth. 12, 9. b Roman. 7. v. 23.24.25. Ierem. 31, 34. Mich. 7.19. Psalm. 103, 3.10.12. 2 Ioh. 3. v. 18. Iohan. 5. verf. 24.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hic articulus est omnibus aliis creditu difficilior. Morituris enim quidius citius persuaseris, quàm remissionem peccatorum. Et satan omnia patitur nos credere, modo hanc consolationem nobis eripiat. Consideran-dum ergo
units.tr: This article is more difficult to believe than all the others. For you could more easily persuade dying people of anything than of the forgiveness of sins. And Satan allows us to believe everything, provided he snatches this consolation from us. We must consider, therefore,

units.la: DE REMISSIONE PECCATORVM.
units.tr: ON THE REMISSION OF SINS.

units.la: I. Quid sit. II. A quo fiat. III. Propter quid fiat. IV. An congruat cum justitia Dei. V. An sit gratuita. VI. Quomodo, & quando detur.
units.tr: I. What it is. II. By whom it is granted. III. For what reason it is granted. IV. Whether it agrees with the justice of God. V. Whether it is gratuitous. VI. How and when it is given.

units.la: I. Quid sit remissio peccatorum.
units.tr: I. What the remission of sins is.

units.la: Remissio peccatorum est propositum in Deo non puniendi peccata fidelium, propter satisfactionem Christi. Vel, est condonatio poenae promeritae, & largitio, atque imputatio justitiae alienae, nempe Christi. Plenius definietur hoc modo: Est voluntas Dei, qua electis credentibus non imputat peccata, sed remittit culpam & poenam peccati: imputat verò justitiam, eosq; pro justis habet, & diligit, ac si nunquam peccassent, liberat à morte, ac donat vita aeterna, gratis, per & propter satisfactionem & intercessionem Filij mediatoris. Psal. 32, 1. Rom. 5, 7. Beati, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, &c. Remittere igitur peccata non est, peccata pro non peccatis habere, vel peccatis non offendi, & irasci, sed peccatores habere pro non peccatoribus, seu, peccatores absolvere à peccatorum reatu & culpa, & reputare pro justis, propter satisfactionem alienam, fide apprehensam & applicatam. Breviter: Deus remittit credentibus peccata: quia non vult eos in ipsis punire, eò quod puniuit in Christo Mediatore. Idem ergo sunt, habere remissionem peccatorum, &, esse justum coram Deo. Contra: Lex non tantum requirit, ut non peccemus: sed etiam, ut praestemus obedientiam: non tantum, ut omittamus mala, sed etiam, ut faciamus bona. Ergo non satis est,
units.tr: The remission of sins is God's purpose not to punish the sins of believers, on account of the satisfaction of Christ. Or, it is the pardon of the deserved punishment, and the bestowal and imputation of an alien righteousness, namely that of Christ. It may be defined more fully in this way: it is the will of God by which he does not impute sins to the elect who believe, but remits the guilt and punishment of sin; he imputes righteousness, holds them and loves them as righteous, as if they had never sinned; he frees them from death and gives them eternal life, freely, through and on account of the satisfaction and intercession of the Son as Mediator. Ps. 32:1; Rom. 5:7: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, etc. To remit sins, therefore, is not to regard sins as non-sins, or not to be offended and angered by sins, but to regard sinners as non-sinners; or, to absolve sinners from the guilt and liability of sin, and to count them as righteous, on account of another's satisfaction, apprehended and applied by faith. In brief: God forgives believers their sins, because he does not wish to punish them in themselves, since he has punished them in Christ the Mediator.
