To have the remission of sins and to be righteous before God are therefore the same thing. On the other side: the law requires not only that we do not sin, but also that we render obedience; not only that we leave off evil, but also that we do good. Therefore it is not enough

units.la: Remissio peccatorum quid. est, vt peccata sint condonata, sed etiam necessaria est perfecta legis præstatio, ad hoc, vt simus justi. Resp. Etiam omissio boni est peccatum. Qui enim potest facere bonum, & non facit, ei peccatum est, Jacobi 4,17. Sed etiam hoc peccatum nobis remittitur: quia Christus pro omnibus peccatis tam omissionis, quàm commissionis sufficientissimè satisfecit. Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato, 1 Joh. 1. vers. 7. Habemus igitur in Christo perfectam remissionem omnium peccatorum, tam omissionis, quàm commissionis: proinde etiam peccati omissæ obedientiæ, & sic perfectam justitiam: ita, vt vnicè Christi merito coram Deo justi reputemur.
units.tr: That sins be pardoned is not enough, but the perfect fulfilment of the law is also necessary, so that we may be righteous. Answer: the omission of good is also sin. For whoever knows how to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin, James 4:17. But this sin too is forgiven us, because Christ made full satisfaction for all sins, both of omission and of commission. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1:7. We have therefore in Christ the perfect remission of all sins, both of omission and of commission; and consequently also of the sin of omitted obedience, and thus perfect righteousness, so that we are reckoned righteous before God by the merit of Christ alone.

units.la: II. A quo fiat remissio.
units.tr: II. By whom the remission is granted.

units.la: Peccatorum remissio fit à solo Deo. Quis enim potest remittere peccata, nisi solus Deus? Luc. 5,21. Ego ego sum, qui deleo iniquitates tuas propter me, Esa. 43. v. 25. A Deo, inquam, Patre, Filio & Spiritu sancto. Nam in nomine trium personarum, Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti, baptizamur. Baptismus autem fit in remissionem peccatorum, vt ex Johannis baptismo constat. De Deo Patre, quod remittat peccata, petentibus & credentibus, constat ex quotidiana precatione. De Filio dicit scriptura: Vt verò sciatis Filium hominis habere potestatem remittendi peccata. De Spiritu sancto dicitur, quod offendatur & contristetur peccatis. Ergo & ipse peccata remittit. Nullius enim peccatum remittere potest, nisi in quem peccatur, & qui peccatis offenditur. Diserte etiam verbis de peccato in Spiritum sanctum, CHRISTVS apud Euangelistas loquitur. Causa autem, quod à solo DEO, Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto peccata remittantur, hæc est: quia nemo, nisi pars offensa, potest peccatum remittere. Solus autem Deus Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus peccatis nostris offenditur. Ergo solus Deus ea potest remittere: & per consequens, de hoc jure Dei nulla creatura potest quicquam largiri. Vnde David ait: Tibi soli peccavi, & malum coram te feci. Solus Dominus misereri potest, (inquit Cyprianus de lapsis) veniam peccatis, quæ in ipsum commissa sunt, solus potest largiri, qui peccata portavit.
units.tr: The remission of sins is granted by God alone. For who can forgive sins but God alone? Luke 5:21. I, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, Isa. 43:25. By God, I say, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. For we are baptized in the name of the three persons, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Baptism, moreover, is into the remission of sins, as is clear from the baptism of John. That God the Father forgives sins to those who ask and believe is clear from the daily prayer. Of the Son Scripture says: But that you may know that the Son of man has power to forgive sins. Of the Holy Spirit it is said that he is offended and grieved by sins. Therefore he too forgives sins. For no one can forgive the sin of another unless it is against him and he is offended by the sin. Christ also speaks plainly of the sin against the Holy Spirit in the Evangelists. The reason why sins are forgiven by God alone, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is this: no one except the injured party can forgive a sin. But God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit alone are offended by our sins. Therefore God alone can remit them, and consequently no creature can grant anything of this right of God. Hence David says: Against you only have I sinned, and done evil in your sight. The Lord alone can show mercy, says Cyprian in his book on the lapsed, he alone, who bore our sins, can grant pardon for sins committed against himself.

units.la: Obiect. Etiam Apostoli & Ecclesia remittunt peccata; quia dicitur: Quæcunque ligaveritis in terra, erunt ligata in cælo: & quæcunque solveritis in terra, erunt soluta in cælo. Item: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur iis: & quorum retinueritis, retenta erunt. Ergo non solus Deus remittit peccata. Resp. Apostoli remittunt peccata, quatenus internuncij sunt remissionis divinæ. Similiter Ecclesia remittit peccata, cùm ex mandato Domini agens. agentibus pœnitentiam, remissionem peccatorum denunciat. Item proximus proximo remittit peccata: quando condonat priuatas offensas. Solus autem Deus liberat nos à culpa & reatu peccati suâ authoritate: solus Deus nos abluit à peccatis sanguine Filij sui: solus denique Deus remittit omnia peccata, originale & actualia, omissionis & ignorantiæ, secundum illud: Qui sanat omnes infirmitates tuas. Nulla est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Objection: the apostles and the Church also remit sins, because it is said: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. Also: Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained. Therefore God does not alone remit sins. Answer: the apostles remit sins insofar as they are messengers of the divine remission. Likewise the Church remits sins when, acting by the command of the Lord, it announces the remission of sins to those who repent. Also, one neighbour remits sins to another when he pardons private offences. But God alone frees us from the guilt and liability of sin by his own authority; God alone cleanses us from sins by the blood of his Son; and God alone, finally, remits all sins, original and actual, of omission and of ignorance, according to that saying: Who heals all your infirmities; there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

units.la: III. Propter quid fiat remissio.
units.tr: III. On what ground remission is granted.

units.la: Deus peccata nobis remittit, 1. Ex mera misericordia & gratuito amore erga nos. 2. Propter intercessionem & satisfactionem Christi mediatoris fide applicatam. Etsi igitur deprecamur peccata, & Deus peccantibus remittit peccata, tamen remissio non fit propter preces nostras. Deprecatio enim absq; satisfactione fieri non potest: quia id esset rogare, ut Deus de iustitia sua aliquid concedat: Christus semel pro peccatis passus est, iustus pro iniustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret. Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato. Quoniam in Christo placuit Patri, ut omnis plenitudo inhabitaret, & pace per sanguinem crucis eius facta, per eum reconciliare omnia sibi. Accessistis ad novi testamenti mediatorem Iesum, & sanguinem aspersionis præstantiora loquentem, quàm loqueretur sanguis Abel. In Christo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius: remissionem peccatorum ex divite ipsius gratia.
units.tr: God forgives us our sins: (1) out of pure mercy and free love toward us; (2) on account of the intercession and satisfaction of Christ the Mediator, applied by faith. So although we pray for the forgiveness of sins, and God forgives those who sin, the remission does not happen because of our prayers. For prayer cannot be made without satisfaction, since that would amount to asking God to grant something out of his justice: Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. For it pleased the Father that in Christ all fullness should dwell, and, having made peace through the blood of his cross, through him to reconcile all things to himself. You have come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better than the blood of Abel. In Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of his grace.

units.la: IV. An remissio peccatorum congruat cum iustitia DEI.
units.tr: IV. Whether the remission of sins agrees with the justice of God.

units.la: Dei, vt pote iustissimi iudicis, est, non relinquere peccatum impunitum: eoq; illud nulla satisfactione interveniente non remittere. Non igitur fit remissio à Deo ex lenitate, quæ pugnet cum eius iustitia: quia peccatum non reliquit impunitum, sed puniuit illud pro nobis in Christo sufficientissimè. Quod igitur Deus nobis peccata remittit, nosq; iustos & non puniendos pronunciat propter satisfactionem Christi perfectissimam: hoc cum iustitia, & veritate Dei non pugnat.
units.tr: It belongs to God, as the most just judge, not to leave sin unpunished, and therefore not to remit it without any intervening satisfaction. Remission is therefore not granted by God out of a leniency that conflicts with his justice, because he has not left sin unpunished but has punished it most fully in Christ on our behalf. That God forgives us our sins, and pronounces us righteous and not liable to punishment, on account of the most perfect satisfaction of Christ, does not conflict with the justice and truth of God.

units.la: Obiect. Iustitia Dei postulat, vt qui peccat, puniatur. Ergo peccatorum remissio, quæ sit sine sufficienti pœna peccantis, pugnat cum iustitia Dei. Resp. Pugnat cum iustitia Dei peccatum non punire simpliciter, hoc est, nec in peccante, nec in alio, qui pro peccante pœnam subeat. Deus autem pro nobis puniuit Filium suum, 1 Pet.3,18. Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit: iustus pro iniustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret. Inst. Innocentem punire loco nocentis, etiam pugnat cum justitia Dei. Respond. Innocentem. 1. Qui nolit subire poenam. 2. Qui non sit eiusdem naturae cum nocente. 3. Qui non possit poenam sufficientem persoluere. 4. Qui non possit ex ea emergere. Deus enim non vult innocentem perire pro nocente. 5. Qui nocentem non possit restaurare, eumque fide donare, qua suum hoc beneficium amplectatur. Haec autem conditiones omnes sunt in Christo, ut ex testimoniis sequentibus clare liquet. Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit seipsum pro nobis oblationem ac victimam Deo, in odorem bonae fragrantiae. Animam meam pono pro ovibus. Ipse vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras. Attritus est propter scelera nostra. Disciplina pacis nostrae super eum, & livore eius sanati sumus. Iehova autem voluit eum conterere. Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, ut qui vivunt, posthac non sibi vivant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est, & resurrexit. Destruite templum hoc, & tribus diebus erigam illud. Ego pono animam meam ut eam rursus assumam. Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & semetipsum tradidit pro ea, ut eam sanctificaret. Dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum. Vide etiam supra Quaestion. XIII. & XXXII.
units.tr: Objection. The justice of God requires that whoever sins be punished. Therefore a remission of sins that takes place without a sufficient punishment of the sinner conflicts with the justice of God. Answer. It conflicts with the justice of God not to punish sin at all, that is, neither in the sinner nor in another who undergoes punishment in place of the sinner. But God punished his Son on our behalf, 1 Pet. 3:18: Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God. Further objection. To punish an innocent person in place of the guilty also conflicts with the justice of God. Answer. The innocent person must be one (1) who is unwilling to undergo punishment, (2) who is not of the same nature as the guilty, (3) who cannot pay a sufficient penalty, (4) who cannot rise again out of it (for God does not want the innocent to perish for the guilty), and (5) who cannot restore the guilty and give him to himself by faith, so that he may embrace this benefit. All these conditions, however, are found in Christ, as the following testimonies clearly show: Christ loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God, as a fragrant aroma. I lay down my life for the sheep. He was wounded for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed. But the LORD was pleased to crush him. Christ died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised. Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. I lay down my life that I may take it up again. Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her. He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works. See also above, Questions XIII and XXXII.

units.la: V. An remissio peccatorum sit gratuita.
units.tr: V. Whether the remission of sins is free.

units.la: Etsi peccata nostra nobis Deus non remittit, nisi interveniente satisfactione sufficientissima: remittit tamen gratis, quia λύτρον non postulat a nobis, sed a Christo, cui peccata nostra tantis magno constiterunt.
units.tr: Although God does not forgive our sins unless a most sufficient satisfaction intervenes, he nevertheless forgives them freely, because he does not demand a ransom [λύτρον] from us but from Christ, at whose great cost our sins came.

units.la: Obiect. Si remittit propter satisfactionem: Ergo non gratis. Respond. Immo gratis, respectu nostri, hoc est, sine satisfactione nostra, licet non sine satisfactione aliena. Inst. Etiam qui hoc pacto condonat, non condonat gratis. Est enim regula: Quod quis per alium facit, id per se facere videtur. Nos igitur ipsi soluimus, soluendo per Christum. Resp. Ita quidem est. Nihilominus Deus gratis condonat: quia gratis nobis donat & satisfactionem Christum, qui non a nobis, vel de nostro datur: & satisfactionem eius, quam non ipsi praestamus, sed gratis donatam fide accipimus. Joh.3,16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum daret: &c. Rom.8,32. Qui Filio suo proprio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, &c.
units.tr: Objection. If he forgives on account of a satisfaction, then he does not forgive freely. Answer. On the contrary, it is free on our side, that is, without any satisfaction from us, although not without satisfaction from another. Further objection. Even one who forgives in this way does not forgive freely, for there is a rule: What someone does through another, he seems to do through himself. Therefore we ourselves pay, by paying through Christ. Answer. That is indeed so. Nevertheless God forgives freely, because he freely gives us both Christ, who is not given by us or from what is ours, and the satisfaction of Christ, which we do not render ourselves but receive by faith as a gift freely bestowed. John 3:16: God so loved the world that he gave his Son, etc. Rom. 8:32: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, etc.

units.la: VI. Quibus detur peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: VI. To whom the remission of sins is given.

units.la: Datur solis & singulis electis: quia datur solis & singulis credentibus: nulli autem credunt, nisi soli electi. Reprobi nunquam quam verè credunt: ideo hi nunquam verè accipiunt remissionem peccatorum. Qui credit, habet vitam æternam. Huic testimonium dant omnes Prophetæ, remissionem peccatorum accepturum per nomen eius quemuis, qui credit in eum. Non tamen omnes electi semper habent remissionem peccatorum: quia non omnes semper credunt. Tantum illi enim habent remissionē peccatorum, qui credunt, se eam habere. Hoc autem non semper credunt omnes electi: sed tum demum, cùm conuertuntur, & fide donantur. Semper tamen habent remissionem peccatorum, quoad propositum Dei. Infantes ecclesiæ habent fidem & conuersionem inclinatione, tametsi nondum actu. Habent ergo etiam remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: It is given only to the elect, and to each of them individually, because it is given only to those who believe, and only the elect believe. The reprobate never truly believe, and so they never truly receive the remission of sins. He who believes has eternal life. All the prophets bear witness to this, that everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name. Yet not all the elect always have the remission of sins, because not all of them always believe. Only those have the remission of sins who believe that they have it. But not all the elect always believe this; they do so only when they are converted and endowed with faith. Yet they always have the remission of sins as far as God's purpose is concerned. The infants of the Church have faith and conversion by inclination, although not yet in act. Therefore they also have the remission of sins.

units.la: VII. Quomodo, & quando detur peccatorum remisso.
units.tr: VII. How and when the remission of sins is given.

units.la: Remissio peccatorum datur & habetur per solam fidem, qua per Spiritum sanctum in nobis creata & accensa nos illam accipimus. Ergo tunc datur, cum fide accipitur. Decreuit quidem Deus ab æterno electis suis in Christo condonare peccata, propter eius satisfactionem: re ipsa verò tunc demum eis peccata condonat, quando credunt in Christum, reputans eos pro iustis, & per Spiritum sanctum efficiens in ipsorum cordibus, vt sentiant condonationem illam, & in perpetuum de illa certi & confirmati maneant. Decretum igitur Dei de remittendis peccatis æternum est: sed executio & patefactio eius fit, cùm remissionem peccatorum in Euangelio oblatam fide nobis applicamus. Sic semper electos suos Deus diligit: sed hæc dilectio Dei non diffunditur in cordibus electorum ante fidem & pœnitentiam. Illi enim demum habent certum illud conscientiæ testimonium, ex Spiritus sancti dono, se à Deo diligi, eoque sibi remissa esse peccata, qui verè in Christum credunt, & resipiscunt.
units.tr: The remission of sins is given and possessed through faith alone, by which, created and kindled in us by the Holy Spirit, we receive it. Therefore it is given at the time when it is received by faith. God indeed decreed from eternity to forgive the sins of his elect in Christ, on account of his satisfaction; but in fact he forgives them then, when they believe in Christ, counting them as righteous, and by the Holy Spirit bringing it about in their hearts that they perceive that forgiveness and remain certain and confirmed in it forever. The decree of God concerning the remission of sins is therefore eternal, but its execution and manifestation take place when we apply to ourselves by faith the remission of sins offered in the Gospel. Thus God always loves his elect; but this love of God is not poured out in the hearts of the elect before faith and repentance. For they alone have that certain testimony of conscience, from the gift of the Holy Spirit, that they are loved by God and that their sins are therefore forgiven, who truly believe in Christ and repent.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 57.

units.la: Quid te consolatur resurrectio carnis? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What comfort do you take from the resurrection of the flesh? ANSWER.

units.la: Quod non tantum anima mea, postquam è corpore excesserit, è vestigio ad Christum caput assumetur a: verum verùm, quod hæc quoq; caro mea potentiâ Christi excitata, rursus animæ meæ vnietur, & gloriosò corpori Christi conformabitur b.
units.tr: That not only is my soul taken up immediately to Christ its head after it has departed from the body, but also that this my flesh, raised again by the power of Christ, will be reunited with my soul and will be made like the glorious body of Christ.
a Luke 16, vv. 22–23; Luke 23, v. 43; Philippians 1:21, 23. b Job 19:25–26; 1 John 3:2; Philippians 3:21.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: Quæstiones de Resurrectione Mortuorum huc pertinentes sunt istæ: I. An anima sit immortalis. II. Vbi sit separata à corpore. III. Quid sit resurrectio, & qui de ea sint errores. IV. Vnde constet, resurrectionem certo futuram. V. Qua & qualia corpora sint resurrectura. VI. Quomodo. VII. Quando. VIII. Cuius virtute, & per quem. IX. In quem finem futura sit resurrectio.
units.tr: The questions relevant to the resurrection of the dead are these: I. Whether the soul is immortal. II. Where it is when separated from the body. III. What the resurrection is, and what errors there are about it. IV. From what it is established that the resurrection will certainly take place. V. What and what kind of bodies will rise. VI. How. VII. When. VIII. By whose power and through whom. IX. To what end the resurrection will be.

units.la: I. An anima sit immortalis: an verò moriatur cum corpore.
units.tr: I. Whether the soul is immortal, or whether it dies together with the body.

units.la: Quæstio de immortalitate animæ non est aliena ab hoc articulo. Resurrectio enim præsupponit mortem. Quæritur ergo, an animæ moriantur, & resurgant sicut corpora? Neq; superuacanea erit huius quæstionis explicatio. Facit enim 1.ad explicationem multorum scripturæ locorum, quæ videntur animam hominis facere mortalem. 2. Ad refutandos Epicureos, & Sadducæos, qui jam olim animæ immortalitatem, & carnis resurrectionem negauerunt: sicut & illi, qui dicebant, jam factam esse resurrectionem per fidem: nec aliam esse præter illam spiritualem expectandam. Hodie etiam disputatur à nonnullis anabaptistis, an animæ post discessum à corporibus dormiant vsque ad futuram coniunctionem cum corporibus. Quin & Paulus III. Papa moriturus dixit, se jam experiturum veritatem trium quæstionum, de quibus in tota vita dubitasset. 1. An animæ immortales. 2. An sit infernus. 3. An Deus. Sæpe etiam in Psalmis & apud Salomonem occurrit hæc sententia: Homo moritur vt brutum. Non mortui laudabunt te Domine, &c.
units.tr: The question of the immortality of the soul is not foreign to this article, for the resurrection presupposes death. The question is therefore whether souls die and rise again just as bodies do. Nor will the explanation of this question be superfluous. For it serves: 1. to explain many passages of Scripture which seem to make the human soul mortal; 2. to refute the Epicureans and Sadducees, who long ago denied the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the flesh, as also those who said that the resurrection had already taken place through faith, and that no other was to be expected besides that spiritual one. Today, too, some Anabaptists dispute whether souls, after their departure from the bodies, sleep until their future reunion with the bodies. Indeed, Pope Paul III, when about to die, said that he was now going to experience the truth of three questions about which he had doubted his whole life: 1. whether souls are immortal; 2. whether there is a hell; 3. whether there is a God. Often, too, in the Psalms and in Solomon this saying occurs: Man dies like the beast. The dead will not praise you, O Lord, etc.

units.la: Ex his vt possimus nos expedire, confirmanda est animæ immortalitas euidentibus scripturæ dictis, qualia sunt: Quoniam non cum interierit ipse, sumet omnia: neque descendet cum eo gloria eius: quia anima eius in vita ipsius benedicetur. Per vitam tuam, & per vitam animæ tuæ faciam hæc. Ne timete vobis ab iis, qui trucidant cidant corpus, animam autem non possunt trucidare. Animæ justorum in manu Dei sunt. De mortuis vero quod suscitandi sint, nonne legistis, &c. Ego sum Deus Abraham, & Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacob. Non est Deus mortuorum, sed viuorum. Christus in cruce pendens, dixit latroni: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso. Corpore non potuit illic esse: quia corpus eo die mortuum iacuit in sepulchro. Ergo anima eius cum Christo collecta est in paradisum, & per consequens, anima viuit. Cupio dissolui, inquit Paulus, & esse cum Christo. Loquitur de quiete & lætitia, quia cum Christo futurus erat post mortem. Sed qui nihil sentiunt, quæ potest eorum esse lætitia aut felicitas? Proinde & illi refutantur hoc loco, qui animas dormire fingunt, eoque animarum immortalitatem negant. Per dormitionem enim intelligunt mortem. In manus tuas commendo spiritum meum. Domine Iesu suscipe spiritum meum. Ego sum resurrectio & vita: qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, viuet. Cum è corpore emigramus, ad Dominum migramus. Non igitur animæ dormiunt, sed vita immortali & gloria cœlesti fruuntur apud Dominum. In Apocalypsi animæ martyrum dicuntur clamare sub altari voce magna, dicentes: Vsquequò Domine, qui sanctus es & verax, non iudicas & vindicas sanguinem nostrum de iis, qui habitant in terris? Viuunt igitur & vigilant, non dormiunt animæ. Apud Lucam Lazarus dicitur post mortem deportatus in sinum Abrahæ: Epulo ex aduerso in infernum locum tormenti. Hæc & similia scripturæ testimonia confirmant euidentissime, non tantum in corporibus ante mortem, & post resuscitationem corporum ex morte, sed & toto intermedio spacio animas humanas extra corpora esse, viuere, sentire & intelligere: tametsi modus operationis earum extra corpora nobis sit incognitus. Denique resurrectio carnis immortalitatem animæ præsupponit: proinde hanc cum illa necessariò credimus. Nam vt idem homo resurgat, necesse est, vt eadem forma substantiali, quæ est anima, corpus informetur. Accidentalis enim formæ aliqua mutatio, non facit diuersum indiuiduum, sed idem indiuiduum est, cum eadem materia eadem forma substantiali informatur. Si autem anima moriatur, & Deus aliam creet atque corpori indat, non eadem, sed diuersa forma id informabit: proinde non erit idem indiuiduum. At erit idem, vt quæstione V. ostenditur.
units.tr: So that we may disentangle ourselves from these matters, the immortality of the soul must be confirmed by plain sayings of Scripture, such as: For when he dies he shall carry nothing away, nor shall his glory descend after him; for his soul shall be blessed in his lifetime. By your life and by the life of your soul I will do these things. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God. But concerning the dead, that they are to be raised, have you not read, etc.? I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. He is not God of the dead, but of the living. Christ, hanging on the cross, said to the thief: Today you will be with me in paradise. He could not be there in body, because his body lay dead in the sepulchre that day. Therefore his soul was received with Christ into paradise, and consequently the soul lives. I desire to depart, says Paul, and to be with Christ. He speaks of rest and joy, because he was to be with Christ after death. But those who feel nothing, what joy or happiness can they have? Accordingly, those are refuted here too who pretend that souls sleep, and so deny the immortality of souls; for by sleep they understand death. Into your hands I commend my spirit. Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, shall live. When we depart from the body, we go to the Lord. Therefore souls do not sleep, but enjoy immortal life and heavenly glory with the Lord. In the Apocalypse the souls of the martyrs are said to cry out under the altar with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, who are holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? Souls therefore live and are awake; they do not sleep. In Luke, Lazarus is said to have been carried after death into Abraham's bosom, while Dives, from the opposite side, was in the place of torment in hell. These and similar testimonies of Scripture most clearly confirm that human souls not only exist, live, feel and understand in the bodies before death and after the bodies' resurrection from death, but also throughout the whole intervening space of time they exist outside the bodies, live, feel and understand; although the manner of their operation outside the bodies is unknown to us. Finally, the resurrection of the flesh presupposes the immortality of the soul; therefore we necessarily believe the one together with the other. For that the same man may rise, it is necessary that the same body be informed by the same substantial form which is the soul. For a change in an accidental form does not make a different individual, but it is the same individual when the same matter is informed by the same substantial form. If, however, the soul were to die, and God were to create another and give it to the body, the body would be informed by a different, not the same, form; therefore it would not be the same individual. But it will be the same, as is shown in question V.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Ecclesiastes ait: Vnus interitus est hominis, & iumentorum, & æqua vtriusque conditio; sicut moritur homo, sic & illa moriuntur. Ergo anima hominis non minus, quam bruti est mortalis. Respond. 1. Est fallacia à secundum quid, vt simpliciter. Vtriusque quidem est æqualis conditio, quoad moriendi necessitatem. Homines enim non minus quàm bruta coguntur mori, & ex hac vita discedere: quia statutum est omnibus hominibus semel mori. Heb.9,29. Neque habent hic fixam sedem. Sed non est eadem causa, nec eadem conditio mortis hominis & bruti. Bruta moriuntur ob materiæ corruptibilitatem, ex qua constant: homini verò mors indicta est, atque dominatio eius propter peccatum. Animæ brutorum cum corporibus exstinguuntur, nec sentient bonum vel malum: hominum verò animæ post mortem superstites expectant judicium vitæ vel mortis æternæ: vt testimonia recitata ostendunt. 2. Negatur antecedens. Ecclesiastes enim loquitur de morte hominis non ex suo, sed ex vulgi profani sensu & opinione, quam concipit ex foris apparente similitudine euentuum, qui bonis & malis accidunt. Ei enim querelæ & judiciis humanis subjungit doctrinam de prouidentia & judicio Dei, quo bonis bona, & malis mala tandem tribuentur. Eccles.11,9. Lætare juuenis, &c. sed scito, quòd propter omnia hæc adducet te Deus in judicium.
units.tr: Objection 1. Ecclesiastes says: There is one death of man and of beasts, and the condition of both is equal; as man dies, so those also die. Therefore the soul of man is no less mortal than that of a beast. Answer 1. This is a fallacy from what is true in a certain respect to what is true absolutely. The condition of both is indeed equal as regards the necessity of dying. For men, no less than beasts, are compelled to die and depart from this life, because it is appointed for all men once to die (Heb. 9:29). Nor do they have a fixed abode here. But the cause and condition of death are not the same for man and beast. Beasts die because of the corruptibility of the matter of which they consist; but death was appointed for man, and its dominion over him is on account of sin. The souls of beasts are extinguished together with their bodies, and they will feel neither good nor evil; but the souls of men, surviving after death, await the judgment of eternal life or death, as the testimonies quoted show. 2. I deny the antecedent. For Ecclesiastes speaks of the death of man not in his own sense, but in the sense and opinion of the profane crowd, which conceives it from the outwardly apparent similarity of the events that befall good and bad men. For to those complaints and human judgments he adds the teaching about the providence and judgment of God, by which good things are at last given to the good and evil things to the evil. Eccles. 11:9: Rejoice, young man, etc.; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Non mortui laudabunt te Domine, neque omnes, qui descendunt in infernum. Resp. Non ita laudabunt Dominum, sicut nos in hac vita, qui viuimus: sed non sequitur: ergo simpliciter non laudabunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. The dead will not praise you, O Lord, nor all who go down into hell. Answer: They will not praise the Lord as we do in this life, who are alive; but it does not follow: therefore they will not praise him at all.

units.la: II. Vbi, & qua conditione viuat anima à corpore separata.
units.tr: II. Where, and in what condition, the soul lives when separated from the body.

units.la: Papistæ fingunt, animas è corporibus migrare in ignem purgatorium, vt purgentur à peccatis, aliæ tardius, aliæ citius, secundum quod ista pereuntia magis vel minus amauerunt, vt loquitur Lombardus. Contra docet scriptura, non ignem aliquem post mortem, sed sanguinem Christi in hac vita, purgare animas fidelium nostras ab omni peccato: ac defunctorum quidem animas fideles, non detrudi in locum tormentorum ad excoquendum peccata, sed colligi in sinum Abrahæ ad Christum: infideles verò illico abijci in infernum, vnde nullus patet exitus, & nunc quidem flammis infernalibus torqueri, reseruari autem grauioribus tormentis ignis æterni, quem sufflabit furor Jehouæ in Christi judicio. 2 Pet. 2, 4. Jud. 6.
units.tr: The Papists imagine that souls migrate from their bodies into the purgatorial fire, to be purged of their sins, some more slowly and some more quickly, according as they loved these perishing things more or less, as Lombard puts it. Scripture teaches the contrary: it is not some fire after death but the blood of Christ in this life that cleanses the souls of the faithful from all sin. The souls of the faithful who have died are not thrust into a place of torments to burn away their sins, but are gathered into the bosom of Abraham with Christ. The unbelieving, however, are at once cast into hell, from which there is no way out. For now they are tormented in infernal flames, and they are reserved for the heavier torments of eternal fire, which the wrath of Jehovah will kindle at the judgment of Christ. 2 Pet. 2.4. Jude 6.

units.la: De conditione animarum fidelium testantur dicta: In manus tuas commendo Spiritum meum. Domine Iesu, suscipe spiritum meum. Factum est autem, vt moreretur mendicus, & asportaretur ab angelis in sinum Abrahæ. Ergo non in purgatorium. Paulus optat migrare, & esse cum Christo. Non ergo metuit purgatorium. Fideles cupiunt migrare è corpore, & ad Dominum ire habitabitatum. Non ergo prius migrant in purgatorium, quàm ad Dominum, &c.
units.tr: The sayings testify to the condition of the souls of the faithful: "Into your hands I commend my spirit" and "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." It came about that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into the bosom of Abraham. Therefore not into purgatory. "Paul desires to depart and be with Christ." Therefore he did not fear purgatory. "The faithful desire to depart from the body and to go to the Lord to dwell." Therefore they do not first pass into purgatory before going to the Lord, and so on.

units.la: De conditione animarum infidelium loquuntur hæc dicta: Mors peccatorum pessima. Timete ab eo, qui potest corpus & animam abijcere in gehennam. Epulo mox à sepultura apud inferos in tormentis clamat: Crucior in flamma hac. Vnde ei negatur exitus in æternum. Metuit etiam quinque fratribus Epicureis: quia scit, breui post venturos in eundem tormenti locum. Non igitur animæ impiorum, migrantes è corporibus, deferuntur in purgatorium, unde pateat redemptio & exitus, sed in gehennæ ignem inexstinguibilem detruduntur.
units.tr: The condition of the souls of the unbelieving is spoken of in these sayings: "The death of sinners is most evil." "Fear him who can cast both body and soul into hell." Dives, straight after burial, cries out among the dead in torments: "I am tormented in this flame." Hence it is denied him that he should ever get out. He also fears for his five Epicurean brothers, because he knows they will shortly come to the same place of torment. Therefore the souls of the wicked, when they depart from their bodies, are not carried off into purgatory, from which there is redemption and a way out, but are thrust into the unquenchable fire of hell.

units.la: III. Quid sit resurrectio, & qui sint de ea errores.
units.tr: III. What the resurrection is, and what errors there are about it.

units.la: Resurrectio aliquando in scriptura significat spiritualem conversionem hominis: vt, Hæc est resurrectio prima. Sed in hoc articulo resurrectio carnis est restitutio substantiæ corporum nostrorum post mortem, ex eadem materia, qua nunc constant, & vivificatio eorundem vita immortali & incorruptibili per eandem animam, qua nunc viuunt, immortalem: futura à Deo per Christum in fine mundi, virtute ac potentia diuina, electorum quidem ad gloriam æternam, reproborum verò ad pœnas æternas.
units.tr: "Resurrection" sometimes in Scripture means the spiritual conversion of a man, as in "This is the first resurrection." But in this article "resurrection of the flesh" means the restoration of the substance of our bodies after death, from the same matter of which they now consist, and the quickening of the same bodies with immortal and incorruptible life through the same soul, now living and immortal, which is to be brought about by God through Christ at the end of the world, by divine virtue and power: for the elect, to eternal glory, and for the reprobate, to eternal punishment.

units.la: Resurrectio igitur seu resuscitatio carnis erit 1. Instauratio eiusdem corporis, hoc est, recollectio illius massæ seu materiæ, quæ corpus nostrum constituit, & quæ in omnia elementa fuit dissipata. 2. Vnio corporis cum eadem anima, quam prius habuit, & vivificatio per eam, & effectio immortalitatis in illa. 3. Glorificatio electorum, & abiectio reproborum sempiterna.
units.tr: The resurrection, or raising up, of the flesh will therefore be: (1) the restoration of the same body, that is, the gathering together again of that mass or matter which constituted our body and which was scattered into all the elements; (2) the union of the body with the same soul which it had before, and its quickening through the soul, and the making of it immortal; (3) the glorifying of the elect and the everlasting rejection of the reprobate.

units.la: De hac resurrectione præcipuè triplex fuit error. 1. Quidam eam prorsus negarunt, fingentes, animas cum corporibus interire: vt Sadducæi, de quibus in actis: Sadducæi dicunt, non esse resurrectionem, neq; angelum, neq; spiritum. 2. Alij concesserunt quidem animarum immortalitatem: sed interpretati sunt resurrectionem de regeneratione in hac vita. Corpora autem resurgere negarunt: etiamsi animas post mortem piorum æterna felicitate fruituras concederent. Authores huius opinionis videntur fuisse Hymenæus & Philetus, de quibus Apostolus: Aberrant, dicentes: resurrectionem iam esse factam, & subuertunt quorundam fidem. 3. Anabaptistæ hodie negant eadem numero corpora, quæ nunc habemus, resurrectura, sed Deum in secundo Christi aduentu alia conditurum conceduat. Contra hos errores credendum est scripturæ asseuerranti. ranti, mortuos certo resurrecturos esse eadem carne, qua mortui fuerunt.
units.tr: Concerning this resurrection there have been chiefly three errors. (1) Some have denied it altogether, feigning that souls perish along with bodies, as the Sadducees did, of whom Acts says: "The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit." (2) Others did indeed grant the immortality of souls, but interpreted the resurrection as regeneration in this life. They denied that bodies rise again, even while granting that the souls of the pious will enjoy eternal happiness after death. The authors of this opinion seem to have been Hymenaeus and Philetus, of whom the Apostle says: "They err, saying that the resurrection is already past, and they overthrow the faith of some." (3) The Anabaptists today deny that the same bodies in number which we now have will rise again, but they concede that God will create other bodies at the second coming of Christ. Against these errors we must believe Scripture, which assures us that the dead will certainly rise again in the same flesh in which they died.

units.la: IV. Unde constet, resurrectionem certò futuram.
units.tr: IV. How it is established that the resurrection will certainly come.

units.la: Probabiliter quidem colligi potest ex philosophia, futuram aliquando resurrectionem: sed certò futuram, non potest ex ea demonstrari. Nam in philosophia cognitio veritatis & justitiæ Dei est mutila. In sacris verò literis rationes certæ ac firmæ sunt. Ex iis igitur solis certissimè futuram esse resurrectionem demonstratur: idque primum apertis testimoniis: deinde rationibus inde desumtis.
units.tr: It can indeed be probably gathered from philosophy that there will one day be a resurrection, but it cannot be demonstrated from philosophy that it will certainly come. For in philosophy the knowledge of the truth and justice of God is maimed. In the sacred letters, however, the reasons are certain and firm. From these alone, therefore, it is most certainly demonstrated that there will be a resurrection: first from the plain testimonies, and then from the arguments drawn from them.

units.la: Testimonia, quæ certitudinem futuræ resurrectionis confirmant, evidentissima sunt tam in veteri quàm in novo testamento. to. Scio quod redemptor meus vivit, & in novissimo die de terra resurrecturus sum, & rursum circumdabor pelle mea, & in carne mea videbo Deum. Reviviscent mortui, cadavera quoque mea resurgent. Ecce ego aperiens sepulchra vestra, deducam vos è sepulchris vestris. Tandem multi ex dormientibus in pulverulenta terra expergiscentur, hi ad vitam æternam, illi ad opprobria & contemtũ æternum. Veniet hora, qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem eius, & prodibunt: qui bona fecerunt, in resurrectionem vitæ: qui verò mala egerunt, in resurrectionem condemnationis. Ego suscitabo eum in novissimo die. Si resurrectio mortuorum non est, Christus quoque non est excitatus: quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis videlicet est prædicatio nostra: insides vestra. Si credimus Iesum mortuum esse & resurrexisse, ita etiam eos, qui obdormierunt in Iesu, adducet cum eo. Et vidi mortuos magnos & pusillos, stantes in conspectu Dei, &c. Et reddidit mare mortuos, quos habebat: mors quoque & infernus reddiderunt mortuos suos, quos habebant. His testimoniis addantur argumenta ex scripturis desumta.
units.tr: The testimonies that confirm the certainty of the future resurrection are most evident in both the Old and the New Testament. "I know that my Redeemer lives, and that I shall rise from the earth at the last day, and I shall again be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God." "The dead shall live; my dead bodies shall rise again." "Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your graves." "At last many of those who sleep in the dusty earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to shame and everlasting contempt." "The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice and come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation." "I will raise him up at the last day." "If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised; and if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is vain, and your faith is vain." "If we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also will God bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus." "And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before God," and so on. "And the sea gave up the dead that were in it; death and hell gave up the dead that were in them." To these testimonies may be added the arguments drawn from Scripture.

units.la: I. Deus est Deus Abraham, Isaac & Jacob: & est Deus viuorum, non mortuorum. Atqui non esset Deus totius Abraham, neque Deus viuorum, nisi corpus Abrahami aliquando resuscitandum esset. Est Deus totius hominis, non partis. At non esset Deus totius hominis, sed tantum partis, si corpus nunquam resurgeret. Hoc argumento vtitur Christus aduersus Sadducæos.
units.tr: I. God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he is the God of the living, not of the dead. But Abraham's whole person would not be God's, nor would God be the God of the living, unless Abraham's body were one day to be raised. God is the God of the whole man, not of a part. But he would not be the God of the whole man, but only of a part, if the body never rose again. Christ uses this argument against the Sadducees.

units.la: II. Deus prδmittit vitam æternam, non tantum animæ, sed etiam corpori piorum: impiis contrà minatur æternas pœnas animæ & corporis. Has autem promissiones & minas Dei oportet impleri. Earum enim certitudo est immutabilis. Atqui qui non implebuntur, si non resurgent mortui. Quoniam igitur Deus certissimè exsequetur suo tempore, quod pius promisit. misit, & impiis est comminatus: mortui quoque resurgant ne- cesse est.
units.tr: II. God promises eternal life not only to the soul but also to the body of the pious, and on the other hand threatens the wicked with eternal punishment of soul and body. But these promises and threats of God must be fulfilled, for their certainty is unchangeable. Yet they would not be fulfilled if the dead did not rise. Since, therefore, God will most certainly carry out in his own time what he promised to the pious and threatened to the impious, the dead must also necessarily rise.

units.la: III. Præmia & pœnæ pertinent ad totum hominem: quia totus homo peccauit. Ergo corpora resurgent, piorum quidem, vt fruantur gloria & felicitate gratuita in cœlis: impiorum verò, vt luant pœnas meritis debitas in inferno.
units.tr: III. Rewards and punishments belong to the whole man, because the whole man has sinned. Therefore bodies will rise: those of the pious, so that they may enjoy glory and free happiness in heaven; but those of the impious, so that they may pay the punishments due to their merits in hell.

units.la: IV. Misericordia Dei perfecta est, & ad totum hominem extenditur: quia nos totos vult saluos fieri. Resurgent igitur & corpora nostra.
units.tr: IV. The mercy of God is perfect and extends to the whole man, because he wills to save us wholly. Therefore our bodies too will rise.

units.la: V. Iustitia Dei perfecta postulat, vt totum id, quod peccauit, in æternum puniatur. Peccarunt autem non tantum animæ, sed & corpora impiorum. Vt igitur in æternum puniantur corpora, à mortuis resurgant necesse est.
units.tr: V. The perfect justice of God requires that everything which has sinned should be punished eternally. But not only the souls of the wicked have sinned, but also their bodies. Therefore, in order that the bodies may be punished eternally, they must necessarily rise from the dead.

units.la: VI. Christus resurrexit. Ergo & nos resurgemus. Valet consequentia, 1. Quia Christus ideo resurrexit, vt nos posseт resuscitare. 2. Quia Christus est caput, nos membra. Cum igitur Christus caput nostrum resurrexerit, etiam nos eius membra resurgemus. Nam gloria capitis postulat, vt membra habeat sibi conformia. Si vero membra manerent putrida, caput non esset gloriosum. 3. Idem spiritus est in nobis, qui in Christo resuscitato: is nos cum Christo coniungit & vnit, atque eadem in nobis operatur, quæ in Christo: quia sui semper est similis. At excitauit Christum. Ergo & nos excitabit. Est argumentum Apostoli Rom. 8.11.
units.tr: VI. Christ has risen. Therefore we too shall rise. The inference holds, (1) because Christ rose so that he might be able to raise us up; (2) because Christ is the head and we are the members. Since Christ our head has risen, we his members will rise too. For the glory of the head requires that it have members conformed to it; if the members remained corrupt, the head would not be glorious. (3) The same Spirit is in us who raised Christ; he joins and unites us with Christ and works in us the same things that he works in Christ, because he is always like himself. But he raised up Christ. Therefore he will also raise us up. This is the argument of the Apostle, Rom. 8.11.

units.la: VII. Christus dicitur habiturus regnum æternum. Id autem non esset habiturus, si corpora nostra perpetuo manerent in morte. Neq; enim sufficeret, animas nostras esse æternas. Nam vt regnum Christi sit æternum, æternos habeat subditos, eosque totos, necesse est. Igitur & corpora nostra resurgent: vt Christo regi nostro toti in æternum subiecti viuamus.
units.tr: VII. Christ is said to have an everlasting kingdom. Yet he would not have it if our bodies remained in death forever. For it would not be enough that our souls are eternal. If Christ's kingdom is to be everlasting, it must have eternal subjects, and all of them. Therefore our bodies too will rise, so that we may live forever, wholly subject to Christ our King.

units.la: VIII. Christus est perfectus seruator: quia totum hominem redemit, & Deo reconciliauit. Igitur & corruptum corpus per Christum suscitabitur & resurget.
units.tr: VIII. Christ is the perfect Saviour, because he redeemed the whole man and reconciled him to God. Therefore the corrupted body too will be raised up and rise again through Christ.

units.la: IX. Christus non est infirmior ad saluandum, quam Adam ad perdendum: immo totum illud & amplius Christus moriendo restituit, quod Adam peccando perdidit. At Adam cum anima etiam corpus perdidit. Immo maiorem felicitatem Christus nobis est meritus quam habituri fuissemus, si nunquam peccassemus. Amiserat autem nobis Adam inter cætera dona etiam corporis vitam & salutem. Ergo Christus etiam nobis restituit, & per consequens corpora etiam resurgent.
units.tr: IX. Christ is no weaker to save than Adam was to destroy. Indeed, by dying, Christ restored everything that Adam lost by sinning, and more besides. But Adam, along with the soul, lost the body too. Indeed, Christ has merited for us a greater happiness than we would have had if we had never sinned. Adam, however, had forfeited for us, among his other gifts, the life and health of the body. Therefore Christ has restored these to us as well, and consequently the bodies too will rise.

units.la: X. Deus homini post lapsum legem suam promulgavit. Ergo eam vult ab homine aliquando perfecte seruari. Id autem non fit in hac vita. Ergo fiet in altera: eoque homines resurgent.
units.tr: X. After the fall, God promulgated his law to man. Therefore he wills that at some time it be perfectly kept by man. But this does not happen in this life. Therefore it will happen in the next, and by that men will rise again.

units.la: XI. Stipendium peccati mors est. Abolito igitur peccato, mors abolebitur, & vita restituetur.
units.tr: XI. The wages of sin is death. Therefore, when sin is abolished, death will be abolished too, and life will be restored.

units.la: XII. A fine, propter quem corpora sunt condita, & animæ coniuncta: videlicet, vt in ipsis quoque, sicut anima, habitet Spiritus sanctus, sintq; templa Spiritus sancti in æternum. Corpora igitur resurgent, & viuent in æternum.
units.tr: XII. The bodies were created, and joined to the souls, for an end: namely, that the Holy Spirit may dwell in them too, as in the soul, and that they may be temples of the Holy Spirit forever. Therefore the bodies will rise and live forever.

units.la: V. Quæ, & qualia corpora sint resurrectura.
units.tr: V. What kind of bodies, and of what quality, are to rise.

units.la: Resurgent non tantum humana corpora, sed etiam eadem substantia, & numero, quæ nunc gestamus: non alia à Christo creata, vt Anabaptistæ volunt. Job enim dicit: Videbo Deum in carne mea: hac pelle mea circumdabor. Et Apostolus: Quisquis recipiet in corpore suo quod fecit. Oportet hoc mortale induere immortalitatem. Ideo in ecclesiis Africanis dicebatur: Credo resurrectionem carnis huius. Et verbum resurgendi hoc ipsum satis euincit. Nihil enim potest resurgere, nisi quod cecidit. Hoc est, enim resurrectio, inquit Ambrosius, sicut verbi ipsius sono exprimitur, vt quod cecidit, resurgat, quod mortuum fuit, reuiuiscat. Euincit & Dei iustitia. Hæc est enim (inquit idem Ambrosius) series & causa iustitiæ, vt quoniam corporis animiqué communis est actus, quæ animus cogitauit, corpus effecit, vtrumque in iudicium veniat, vtrumque aut pœnæ dedatur, aut gloriæ reservetur. Postulat enim iustitia Dei, vt caro sanctorum, quæ militauit, coronetur: & caro impiorum, quæ blasphemauit, torqueatur, teste Apostolo. Quare vnicuique animæ non confusum aut extraneum corpus, sed suum, quod habuerat, reparabitur, vt consequenter possit, pro agonibus præsentis vitæ, cum anima sua caro vel pudica coronari, vel impudica puniri. Denique sicut Christus eadem carne, qua ceciderat, resurrexit: sic & nos eadem hac carne nostra resurgemus.
units.tr: Not only human bodies will rise, but also the very same substance and the same numerical bodies that we now bear, not others created by Christ, as the Anabaptists hold. For Job says: I shall see God in my flesh; I shall be clothed with this skin of mine. And the Apostle: Each one will receive in his body what he has done. This mortal must put on immortality. For this reason the churches of Africa used to say: I believe in the resurrection of this flesh. And the very word "rise again" proves this well enough. For nothing can rise again except what has fallen. For this is resurrection, says Ambrose, as the sound of the very word expresses it: that what has fallen should rise, and what was dead should come back to life. The justice of God also proves it. For this is (says the same Ambrose) the sequence and the reason of justice: since the action of body and soul is common, the body carries out what the soul has thought, so both should come to judgment, and both either be handed over to punishment or be reserved for glory. For the justice of God requires that the flesh of the saints, which fought the good fight, be crowned, and the flesh of the impious, which blasphemed, be tormented, as the Apostle testifies. Wherefore to each soul will be restored, not a confused or foreign body, but its own, which it had, so that consequently the chaste flesh may be crowned, or the unchaste flesh punished, together with its soul, for the contests of the present life. Finally, just as Christ rose again with the same flesh with which he had fallen, so also we shall rise again with this same flesh of ours.

units.la: Obj. Caro & sanguis hereditatem regni Dei non consequentur. Hæc corpora nostra sunt caro & sanguis. Non igitur possunt regnum Dei consequi, eoque non ista, sed alia corpora resurgent. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini. Caro & sanguis in dicto Apostoli significabit prauam qualitatem substantiæ adhærentem, vel substantiam respectu eius qualitatis: in minore significat ipsam substantiam corporum, de qua Anabaptistæ conclusionem suam intelligunt. Vel est fallacia accidentis: quia propter accidens negatur substantia: seu procedit a substantia vitiata ad substantiam simpliciter, hoc modo: Caro & sanguis mortalis & corruptibipribilis, vt nunc est, non consequentur regnum Dei. Ergo caro & sanguis simpliciter non consequentur. Caro igitur, nempe peccatrix & corruptibilis, non possidebit regnum Dei: ingredi-tur vero caro gloriosa & immortalis. Hoc docet Apostolus; Seminatur corpus animale, resurget corpus spirituale.
units.tr: Objection. Flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God. These bodies of ours are flesh and blood. Therefore they cannot obtain the kingdom of God, and so not these bodies but other bodies will rise. Reply. There are four terms here. In the Apostle's saying, "flesh and blood" will signify the wicked quality clinging to the substance, or the substance with respect to that quality. In the minor premise it signifies the very substance of the bodies, and it is on this that the Anabaptists base their conclusion. Or it is a fallacy of accident: because a thing is denied of the substance on account of an accident, or it proceeds from a substance that is vitiated to the substance simply, in this way: flesh and blood that is mortal and corruptible, as it now is, will not obtain the kingdom of God. Therefore flesh and blood simply will not obtain it. Thus the flesh that is sinful and corruptible, certainly, will not possess the kingdom of God; but glorious and immortal flesh will enter it. This the Apostle teaches: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.

units.la: Inst. Corpora nostra resurgent spiritualia. Ergo tunc non habebunt proprietates carnis. Resp. Spirituale corpus nominat Apostolus, non quod mutatum sit in spiritum, aut omnibus proprietatibus spiritui sit aequale, sed quod a Spiritu Dei regitur, immortale, & ab omnibus aerumnis immune: coelesti vero splendore, gloria, industria, robore, sanctitate ornatum. Sicut contra animale nominat, non quod in animam sit conversum, aut omnibus proprietatibus animae sit simile, sed quod ab anima in hac immortalitate gestatur, vivificatur & gubernatur. Hanc esse sententiam verborum Pauli probatur, 1. Quia dicit: Resurget corpus spirituale. Spiritus vero non est corpus. 2. Addit: Oportet hoc corruptibile corpus induere incorruptibilitatem. 3. Corpus Christi post resurrectionem habebat carnem & ossa: & erat maxime spirituale & gloriosum. Ergo multo magis nostra corpora spiritualia habebunt carnem & ossa. Sic etiam interpretatur Augustinus: Quod spirituale dixit corpus in resurrectione futurum, non propterea putandum est, quod non corpus, sed spiritus erit: sed spirituale corpus omni modo spiritui subditum dicit, sine aliqua corruptione ut modo. Non enim quia quod modo habemus corpus animale appellat, ideo putandum est, non illud esse corpus, sed animam. Ergo quemadmodum corpus animale nunc dicitur, quia subditum est animae: spirituale autem dici nondum potest, quia nondum spiritui plene subiectum est, quamdiu corrumpi potest: sic & tunc spirituale vocabitur, cum spiritui atque aeternitati nulla corruptione resistere poterit.
units.tr: Instance. Our bodies will rise spiritual. Therefore then they will not have the properties of flesh. Reply. The Apostle calls it a spiritual body not because it is changed into spirit, or is equal to spirit in all its properties, but because it is ruled by the Spirit of God, immortal, free from all miseries, and adorned with heavenly splendour, glory, vigour, strength and holiness. Likewise he calls the present body natural, not because it is converted into soul, or is like the soul in all its properties, but because it is carried, quickened and governed by the soul in this mortality. That this is the meaning of Paul's words is proved: first, because he says, it will rise a spiritual body, but spirit is not body. Second, he adds: This corruptible body must put on incorruptibility. Third, Christ's body after the resurrection had flesh and bones, and was most spiritual and glorious. Therefore much more will our bodies have flesh and bones and be spiritual. Augustine also interprets it thus: That he called the body future in the resurrection spiritual, is not to be thought to mean that it will not be a body but a spirit; rather he says that the spiritual body will be wholly subject to the spirit in every way, without any corruption as now. For it is not because he calls what we now have a natural body that we should think it is not a body but a soul. Just as the body is now called natural because it is subject to the soul, yet cannot yet be called spiritual because it is not yet fully subject to the spirit, as long as it can be corrupted, so then it will be called spiritual, when it can resist the spirit and eternity by no corruption.

units.la: VI. Quomodo sit futura resurrectio.
units.tr: VI. How the resurrection will take place.

units.la: Fiet manifeste & gloriose, non occulte, spectantibus omnibus angelis, hominibus & diabolis, cum magna laetitia piorum, & horrore impiorum. Veniet enim Christus de coelo cum comitatu omnium angelorum, cum hortationis clamore & voce archangeli, ac tuba Dei, cuius clangore mortui omnes excitati prodibunt e sepulchris: & omnes sistentur coram summo & justissimo judice Jesu Christo. Qui vero in adventu Domini adhuc erunt superstites, immutabuntur subito, ex mortalibus immortales effecti: eritque eis haec immutatio pro morte & suscitatione.
units.tr: It will happen openly and in glory, not in secret, with all angels, men and devils looking on: to the great joy of the godly and the horror of the wicked. For Christ will come down from heaven with the retinue of all the angels, with the shout of command and the voice of the archangel, and the trumpet of God; at its blast all the dead will be raised and will come forth from their graves, and all will be brought before the supreme and most just judge, Jesus Christ. Those who are still alive at the coming of the Lord will be changed suddenly, made immortal from mortal; and this change will serve them in place of death and resurrection.

units.la: Vide 1 Corinth.15. verf.42.43 &c. & 1 Thess.4. verf.15.16. &c.
units.tr: See 1 Corinthians 15:42-43 etc., and 1 Thessalonians 4:15-16 etc.

units.la: Pars II.
units.tr: Pars II.

units.la: VII. Quando futura sit resurrectio.
units.tr: VII. When the resurrection will take place.

units.la: Futura est resurrectio in fine mundi, die nouissimo, juxta dicta: Ego suscitabo eum in nouissimo die. Et Martha confitetur: Scio resurrecturum (Lazarum fratrem) in resurrectione, vltimo illo die. Quis autem futurus sit vltimus dies, nemo nopit, neque angeli quidem; sed solus Deus. Visus est: ne imaginemur nobis futuram suscitationem tum, cum minimè est futura, atque ita ipsi turbemus fidem nostram.
units.tr: The resurrection will take place at the end of the world, on the last day, according to the words: I will raise him up at the last day. And Martha confesses: I know that he (Lazarus, her brother) will rise again in the resurrection at the last day. But who the last day will be, no one knows, not even the angels, but God alone. The use of this is: we should not imagine that the resurrection will be at some time when it is by no means going to happen, and so disturb our own faith.

units.la: VIII. Cuius virtute, seu per quem, mortui sint resuscitandi.
units.tr: VIII. By whose power, or through whom, the dead are to be raised.

units.la: Suscitatio mortuorum fiet virtute Christi, & per Christum Mediatorem. Ego suscitabo eum in nouissimo die. De corpore hoc est intelligendum. Nam animas non resuscitabit: quia animae non moriuntur. Etquidem Christus homo nos suscitabit, voce quidem humana, virtute autem diuina. Veniet hora, qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filij hominis. Statuit Deus diem, in quo iuste iudicaturus est orbem terrarum, per eum virum, quem definijt, fide palam facta omnibus, illo a mortuis excitato. Visus est: tum, vt suscitationem ipsam possimus credere ex eo, quod suscitator sit satis potens; quia omnipotens Deus: & quod velit, quia est caput nostrum: tum, vt hac certa consolatione fruamur, CHRISTVM, cum sit caro nostra, non relicturum esse carnem suam in morte, sed nos tandem suscitaturum ad vitam aeternam, cuius causa carnem nostram assumpsit, & nos redemit.
units.tr: The raising of the dead will take place by the power of Christ and through Christ the Mediator. I will raise him up at the last day. This must be understood of the body, for he will not raise the souls, because souls do not die. Indeed, Christ as man will raise us with a human voice, but by divine power: The hour is coming in which all who are in the graves will hear the voice of the Son of Man. God has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, through that man whom he has appointed, having given assurance to all by raising him from the dead. The use of this is: first, so that we may believe the resurrection itself from the fact that the one who raises is powerful enough, since he is almighty God, and that he is willing, since he is our head; second, so that we may enjoy this sure consolation, that CHRIST, since he is our flesh, will not leave his flesh in death, but will at last raise us to eternal life, for the sake of which he took on our flesh and redeemed us.

units.la: Obiect. At Pater dicitur nos suscitaturus, & ipsum Christum suscitasse. Is qui excitauit Christum a mortuis, viuificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra, per inhabitantem eius Spiritum in vobis. Ergo non per Christum, nec virtute Christi suscitabuntur mortui. Resp. Opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indiuisa, seruato tamen ordine personarum in agendo. Vt ergo non excluditur Pater, cum suscitatio tribuitur Filio: ita nec excluditur Filius, cum suscitatio tribuitur Patri, vel Spiritui sancto. Pater igitur suscitabit nos mediatè per Filium & Spiritum sanctum: Filius suscitabit nos immediatè per Spiritum suum, vt redemtor & iudex. Exspectamus è coelo Seruatorem nostrum Iesum Christum, qui transformabit corpus nostrum humile, vt conforme fiat glorioso corpori suo, pro efficacitate, qua potest etiam subijcere sibi omnia. Sicut Pater excitat mortuos, & viuificat: ita & Filius, quos vult, viuificat. Spiritus eius, qui sanctus suscitabit nos immediatè per se. Si Spiritus eius, qui Iesum excitauit a mortuis, habitat in vobis.
units.tr: Objection. But the Father is said to raise us, and to have raised Christ himself: He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, through his Spirit dwelling in you. Therefore the dead will not be raised through Christ, nor by the power of Christ. Answer. The works of the Trinity toward the outside are undivided, yet the order of the persons in acting is preserved. Just as the Father is not excluded when the raising is attributed to the Son, so the Son is not excluded when the raising is attributed to the Father or to the Holy Spirit. The Father, then, will raise us mediately through the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son will raise us immediately through his own Spirit, as redeemer and judge. We look for our Saviour Jesus Christ from heaven, who will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body, by the power by which he is able even to subject all things to himself. As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills. His Spirit, who is holy, will raise us immediately by himself. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you.

units.la: IX. In quem finem, & ad quam conditionem mortui sint resurrecturi.
units.tr: IX. To what end, and into what condition, the dead are to rise.

units.la: Finis vltimus resuscitationis mortuorum est gloria Dei. Futura est enim resurrectio, vt Deus patefaciat, & perfectè exerceat misericordiam suam in electis glorificandis : iustitiam vero in reprobis damnandis : & ita patefaciat ineffabilem certitudinem promissionum & comminationum suarum in vtrisque. Finis proximus & subordinatus est salus & gloria electorum : poena vero & abiectio reproborum. Electi enim resurgent ad vitam aeternam : reprobi ad ignem aeternum, juxta dicta: Multi ex dormientibus in pulueru lenta terra expergiscentur, hi ad vitam aeternam: illi ad opprobria & contemtum aeternum. Prodibunt, qui bona fecerunt, in resurrectionem vitae: qui mala, in resurrectionem condemnationis. Dabo ei sedere in Throno meo. Induentur stolis albis. Fulgebunt sicut sol. Maledicti abite à me in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius, &c. Et abibunt isti in supplicium aeternum, justi vero in vitam aeternam. Atque haec erit conditio, ad quam omnes mortui resurgent.
units.tr: The ultimate end of the raising of the dead is the glory of God. For the resurrection will take place so that God may reveal and fully exercise his mercy toward the elect who are to be glorified, and his justice toward the reprobate who are to be condemned, and so reveal the unspeakable certainty of his promises and threats in both. The proximate and subordinate end is the salvation and glory of the elect, but the punishment and abasement of the reprobate. For the elect will rise to eternal life, and the reprobate to eternal fire, according to the words: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to eternal life, others to everlasting shame and contempt. Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation. I will grant him to sit on my throne. They will be clothed in white robes. They will shine like the sun. Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, etc. And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. And this will be the condition into which all the dead will rise.

units.la: Obiect. Resurrectio Christi ab Apostolo dicitur causa nostrae resurrectionis, & nostra resurrectio effectus seu beneficium resurrectionis Christi, Haec autem causa, atque hoc beneficium non pertinet ad impios. Igitur illi non resurgent. Ad quos enim non pertinet causa resurrectionis, ad eos nec ipsa resurrectio pertinere videtur. Ad impios non pertinet causa. Ergo, &c. Resp. ad maiorem: Ad quos non pertinet resurrectionis causa, scilicet nulla. Etsi autem ad impios non pertinet causa vna, resurrectio Christi, hoc est, etsi impij non resurgent ideo, quia Christus resurrexit, tamen resurgent propter aliam causam, videlicet, propter justum Dei judicium, quo destinabit eos aeternis poenis. Possunt enim eiusdem effectus, plures ac diuersae causae esse, praesertim in diuersis subiectis. Resurrectionis ergo piorum causa est Christi capitis resurrectio. Impiorum vero non resurrectio Christi, (quia non sunt membra Christi) sed justitia Dei, & minarum diuinarum veritas. Breuiter: Non sequitur: Non resurgent propter resurrectionem Christi. Ergo non resurgent, quia resurgent propter aliam causam, nimirum vt puniantur. Vnus quidem resurrectionis omnium finis est gloria Dei, sed ad hunc finem diuerso modo peruenietur.
units.tr: Objection. The resurrection of Christ is called by the Apostle the cause of our resurrection, and our resurrection is the effect or benefit of Christ's resurrection. But this cause and this benefit do not pertain to the wicked. Therefore they will not rise. For it seems that the resurrection itself does not pertain to those to whom the cause of the resurrection does not pertain. The cause does not pertain to the wicked. Therefore, etc. Answer to the major premise: To those to whom the cause of the resurrection does not pertain, namely no cause at all, the resurrection does not pertain. But although the one cause, the resurrection of Christ, does not pertain to the wicked, that is, although the wicked will not rise for this reason, because Christ rose, yet they will rise for another cause, namely the just judgment of God, by which he will appoint them to eternal punishments. For the same effect can have several and different causes, especially in different subjects. The cause of the resurrection of the godly is therefore the resurrection of Christ their head; but the cause of the resurrection of the wicked is not the resurrection of Christ (since they are not members of Christ) but the justice of God and the truth of his divine threats. In short: It does not follow: they will not rise because of the resurrection of Christ, therefore they will not rise, since they will rise for another cause, namely that they may be punished. There is indeed one end of the resurrection of all, the glory of God, but this end is reached in different ways.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LVIII.
units.tr: QUESTION 58.

units.la: Quam consolationem capis ex articulo de vita æterna? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What consolation do you draw from the article on eternal life? ANSWER.

units.la: Quod, quoniam in præsentia vitæ æternæ initia in meo corde præsentisco a futurum sit, vt post hanc vitam plena perfectaque beatitudine potiar, in qua Deum in æternum celebrem: quam quidem beatitudinem nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec vllus homo cogitatione comprehendit b.
units.tr: That, since I perceive in my heart, in the present life, the beginnings of eternal life, I shall after this life obtain full and perfect blessedness, in which I shall praise God forever. This blessedness no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no man has grasped in thought.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hic articulus in fine ponitur, 1. Quia post alios implebitur perfecte. 2. Quia est effectus aliorum omnium. Propter hunc enim omnes alij creduntur, & omnia, quæ credimus in aliis, facta sunt, vt hunc vltimum credere & consequi, hoc est, vita æterna frui possimus. Est ergo hic articulus colophon totius salutis & vitæ nostræ. Sunt autem de VITA ÆTERNA hæ potissimum quæstiones: I. Quid sit vita æterna, II. A quo detur. III. Quibus detur. IV. Quare detur. V. Quomodo detur. VI. Quando detur. VII. An & vnde in hac vita de ea possimus esse certi.
units.tr: This article is placed at the end: 1. because it is fulfilled perfectly after the others; 2. because it is the effect of all the others. For on account of this one all the others are believed, and everything we believe in the others has been done so that we may believe this last one and attain it, that is, be able to enjoy eternal life. This article is therefore the capstone of all our salvation and life. The most important questions about ETERNAL LIFE are these: I. What eternal life is. II. By whom it is given. III. To whom it is given. IV. Why it is given. V. How it is given. VI. When it is given. VII. Whether, and from what source, we can be certain of it in this life.

units.la: I. Quid sit vita æterna.
units.tr: I. What eternal life is.

units.la: Videtur inexplicabilis quæstio, quia dicitur de ea: Nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in mentem hominis venerunt, quæ parauit Deus iis, qui ipsum diligunt. Ex analogia tamen vitæ, de qua philosophi disputant, & ex scriptura, quid sit vita æterna, vtcunque intelligi potest. Vita apud philosophos varie definitur. Est enim ὁμωνύμως. In genere, quatenus Deo, angelis, animabus & plantis competit, vita est ipsum esse viuentis. Nam & spiritus viuunt, sed id non habent ex anima, verum ex essentia. In animabus vero proprie vita est esse viuentis animati, quod nihil est aliud quam præditum esse anima, seu habere in se animam viuentem. Anima enim est id, quo animal viuit, seu est vitæ forma essentialis, qua quæ prædita sunt, viuunt. Sumitur autem pro actu primo mo & secundo, hoc est, pro ipso esse, & pro actione, seu pro ipso viuere, & pro operatione viuentis. Sic igitur plenius dicitur: Vita animalis est exsistentia, seu mansio animæ in corpore animato, & operatio viuentis animalis. Vel, est animæ ἐντελέχεια, efficiens operationes animato proprias. Vel denique, est aptitudo animalis ad efficiendum operationes sibi proprias, ex vnione animæ cum corpore promanantes.
units.tr: The question seems inexplicable, since it is said of it: "Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and it has not entered the mind of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." Nevertheless, from the analogy of life, about which the philosophers dispute, and from Scripture, what eternal life is can be understood in some measure. Among the philosophers, life is defined in various ways, for the word is equivocal (ὁμωνύμως). In general, insofar as it belongs to God, angels, souls and plants, life is the very being of the living thing. For spirits also live, but they have this not from a soul but from their essence. In animals, however, life properly means the being of an animated living thing, which is nothing other than being endowed with a soul, that is, having a living soul within oneself. For the soul is that by which an animal lives; it is the essential form of life, by which those endowed with it live. It is taken, moreover, both for first act and for second act, that is, for being itself and for action, or for living itself and for the operation of what lives. So it is stated more fully thus: animal life is the existence, or abiding, of the soul in an animated body, and the operation of the living animal. Or, it is the entelechy of the soul, effecting operations proper to the animated thing. Or finally, it is the aptitude of the animal for performing operations proper to itself, which flow from the union of soul and body.

units.la: Æternum dicitur, 1. Quod principio & fine caret, vt DEvs. 2. Quod principio caret, sed finem habet, vt decreta Dei. 3. Quod principium habet, sed caret fine, vt angeli, &c. Atque hoc tertio modo vita cœlestis dicitur æterna, hoc est, principium habens, sed fine carens. Sic Vita æterna hominis nihil est aliud, quam æternum esse hominis renati & glorificati: quod esse erit, habere in se imaginem Dei perfectè instauratam, ad quam homo initio erat conditus, hoc est, perfectam sapientiam, iustitiam & felicitatem, seu veram agnitionem & dilectionem Dei cum æterna lætitia coniunctam. Ac docendi causa in his ἐνσεχνίας s includimus ipsas δυνάμεις. Nam posse Deum rectè agnoscere & diligere, non minus est de vita spirituali, quàm iptum agnoscere & diligere: siquidè animalis homo non intelligit ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Aliter sic eam describemus: Est perfecta instauratio imaginis Dei, & lætitia æterna, acquiescens in Deo, gloria cœlestis, abundantia & fruitio omnium bonorum, quæ ad statum perfectæ felicitatis requiruntur. Vel breuius: Est perfecta conformitas hominis cum Deo, in vera & perfecta Dei agnitione, dilectione, & gloria animæ & corporis consistens. Sic ad intelligendum, quid sit vita æterna, consideranda sunt hæc duo: 1. Vnio & corporis & animæ nostræ cum Deo. 2. Conformitas cum Deo, quæ ex vnione tanquam effectus ex causa profluit.
units.tr: Something is called eternal in three ways: 1. what has neither beginning nor end, as God; 2. what has no beginning but has an end, as the decrees of God; 3. what has a beginning but no end, as the angels, and so on. It is in this third sense that heavenly life is called eternal, that is, having a beginning but lacking an end. Thus the eternal life of man is nothing other than the eternal being of the man who is reborn and glorified. This being will consist in having within oneself the image of God perfectly restored, to which man was created at the beginning: that is, perfect wisdom, righteousness and happiness, or true knowledge and love of God joined with eternal joy. For the sake of teaching, we include among these the powers themselves. For to be able to know and love God rightly is no less part of spiritual life than knowing and loving him, since the natural man does not understand the things of the Spirit of God. We will describe it otherwise thus: it is the perfect restoration of the image of God, eternal joy resting in God, heavenly glory, and the abundance and enjoyment of all the good things required for the state of perfect happiness. Or, more briefly: it is the perfect conformity of man with God, consisting in true and perfect knowledge and love of God, and in the glory of soul and body. So, to understand what eternal life is, two things must be considered: 1. the union of both our body and our soul with God; 2. conformity with God, which flows from the union as an effect from its cause.

units.la: Conformitas autem est perspicua & illustris cognitio Dei, & voluntatis, atque operum eius: iustitia, perfecta lætitia in Deo acquiescens, gloria maxima, qua corpora nostra florebunt, & fulgebunt vt sol, & sufficientia omnium bonorum ad veram perfectamque felicitatem pertinentium in Deo. Hæc materiam & formam vitæ æternæ vtcunque exprimunt.
