Quod si causæ efficientes & finales addantur, forte plena erit definitio talis: Vita æterna erit inhabitatio æterna Dei in electis per Spiritum sanctum, & per eundem Spiritum immediatè accensa in mentibus eorum vera Dei, voluntatis, atque operum eius omnium cognitio: vera atque integra sapientia & iustitia: conformitas integra, cum mente & voluntate Dei: itemque lætitia in Deo secundum animam & corpus, gratis donata electis à Deo, per & propter Christum; & in hac quidem vita inchoata, in altera verò perficienda, ad Deum in omnem æternitatem celebrandum & glorificandum.
units.tr: Conformity is clear and illustrious knowledge of God, of his will and of his works; righteousness; perfect joy resting in God; the greatest glory, by which our bodies will flourish and shine like the sun; and sufficiency of all good things belonging to true and perfect happiness, found in God. These in some measure express the matter and form of eternal life. If the efficient and final causes are added, perhaps the full definition will be this: eternal life is the eternal indwelling of God in the elect through the Holy Spirit, and, by the same Spirit, the true knowledge of God, of his will and of all his works kindled immediately in their minds; true and whole wisdom and righteousness; complete conformity with the mind and will of God; likewise joy in God, in soul and body, freely given to the elect by God through and for the sake of Christ. This life is begun in the present life, but is to be perfected in the other, so that God may be celebrated and glorified to all eternity.

units.la: Huius definitionis partes omnes desumptæ sunt ex scriptura.
units.tr: All the parts of this definition are taken from Scripture.

units.la: 1. Erit inhabitatio æterna Dei in nobis per Spiritum sanctum. Ego & Pater veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Alium con- solatorem dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in æternum. 2. Erit agnitio Dei & sapientia perfecta. Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. 3. Erit justitia. Pares angelis erunt, & filii Dei, cum sint filii resurrectionis. 4. Erit lætitia in Deo. Gaudium vestrum nemo tollet à vobis. 5. Erit sufficientia omnium bonorum. Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Nec templum vidi in ea. Dominus enim Deus omnipotens templum illius est, id est, agnus. Neque urbs ista eget sole vel luna, ut luceant in ea, nam gloria Dei illuxit eam, & lucerna eius est agnus. Quæ hic habemus bona inchoata, ibi erunt omnia perfecta. Postquam adven erit, quod per- sectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur. 6. Erit sine interruptione & fine. Absterget Deus omnem lachrymam. Regni eius non erit finis. Regnum & potestas & magnitudo regni, quæ est sub ter omne cælum, detur populo sanctorum, cuius regnum est regnum sempiternum, hoc est, principio & fine carens.
units.tr: 1. There will be the eternal indwelling of God in us through the Holy Spirit. "I and the Father will come and make our abode with him. He will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you forever." 2. There will be knowledge of God and perfect wisdom. "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." 3. There will be righteousness. "They will be equal to the angels and sons of God, since they are sons of the resurrection." 4. There will be joy in God. "No one will take your joy from you." 5. There will be sufficiency of all good things. "God will be all in all." "And I saw no temple in it; for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, that is, the Lamb. Nor does that city need the sun or the moon to shine in it, for the glory of God has lit it, and its lamp is the Lamb." What we have here as good things begun will there all be perfect. "When that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be abolished." 6. It will be without interruption and without end. "God will wipe away every tear. Of his kingdom there will be no end. The kingdom and the power and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom," that is, lacking beginning and end.

units.la: Obiect. Viuere in æternum, est habere vitam æternam. Impij etiam viuent in æternum: suscitabuntur enim immortales. Ergo etiam impij habebunt vitam æternam. Resp. Ex imperfecta definitione non valet consequentia. Nam vita æterna non definitur sola præsentia perpetua animæ in corpore, seu immortalitate: sed etiam vita, gloria & felicitate cælesti ac spirituali, quam Spiritus sanctus propria sua operatione in electis efficiet. Etsi autem impij post resurrectionem erunt immortales; tamen animalis eorum vita non erit vita, sed mors æterna: quia cum ea coniuncta erit. 1. Æterna à Deo abiectio. 2. Privatio agnitionis & gratiæ Dei. 3. Perpetuus & inenarrabilis cruciatus. Vermis eorum non morietur. Illic erit fletus & stridor dentium. Ex his intelligitur, quid sit mors æterna: & quod sic dicatur; non quia semel moriendo ea defungentur reprobi, sed quia perpetuò morientur, & perpetuos cruciatus sentient sine fine.
units.tr: Objection: To live forever is to have eternal life. The impious also will live forever, for they will be raised immortal. Therefore the impious too will have eternal life. Answer: The consequence does not hold from an imperfect definition. For eternal life is not defined merely as the perpetual presence of the soul in the body, or immortality, but also as life, glory and heavenly and spiritual happiness, which the Holy Spirit will bring about in the elect by his own operation. Although the impious will be immortal after the resurrection, their animal life will not be life but eternal death, because it will be joined with: 1. eternal rejection by God; 2. deprivation of the knowledge and grace of God; 3. perpetual and unspeakable torment. "Their worm will not die. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." From these it is understood what eternal death is, and that it is so called not because the reprobate die once and are done with it, but because they will die perpetually and feel perpetual torments without end.

units.la: II. A quo detur vita æterna.
units.tr: II. From whom eternal life is given.

units.la: Solus Deus dat vitam æternam. Donum Dei est vita æterna: & quidem Deus Pater tanquam author & fons omnis vitæ dat per Filium & Spiritum sanctum; Filius per Spiritum sanctum; Spiritus sanctus per seipsum: qui ordo operationum personis diuinis est naturalis. De Patre dicitur: Sicut Pater excitat mortuos, & viuiviuificat. Sicut Pater habet vitam in seipso. De Filio: Sic & Filius, quos vult, viuificat. Sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in seipso. In ipso vita erat. Pater futuri seculi seu æternitatis. Ego vitam æternam do eis, nempe merito & efficacia. De Spiritu sancto: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum Dei. Si Spiritus eius, qui Christum excitauit a mortuis, habitat in vobis: suscitabit et-iam mortalia corpora vestra, per inhabitantem eius spiritum in vobis. Hæc testimonia obseruanda sunt; quia etiam ad Filij & Spiritus sancti Deitatem, & cum Patre ὁμοούσιον probandam faciunt.
units.tr: Only God gives eternal life. Eternal life is the gift of God: God the Father, as the author and fountain of all life, gives it through the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son gives it through the Spirit; the Holy Spirit gives it through himself. This order of operation is natural to the divine persons. Of the Father it is said: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, as the Father has life in himself. Of the Son: Even so the Son gives life to whom he will. So he has given to the Son also to have life in himself. In him was life. The Father of the age to come. I give them eternal life, namely by merit and efficacy. Of the Holy Spirit: Unless a man is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. If the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you. These testimonies are to be noted, because they also serve to prove the deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that they are homoousios [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father.

units.la: Obj. Etiam ministri euangelij dant vitam æternam. Per Euan-gelium in Iesu Christo ego vos genui. Id si feceris, teipsum seruabis, & eos, qui te audierint. Ergo non solus Deus dat vitam. Resp. Possunt eiusdē effectus plures esse causæ subordinatæ. Christus & Spiritus sanctus dant vitam propria sua potentia: ministri sunt instrumenta, per quæ Christus virtute sui spiritus agit & operatur. Sic de nobis reputet homo, vt de ministris Christi, & de dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. Quis igitur est Paulus? quis autem Apollos? nisi ministri, per quos credidistis, & vt cuique Dominus dedit: ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit, sed Deus dedit incrementum.
units.tr: Objection: The ministers of the gospel also give eternal life. "Through the gospel I have begotten you in Christ Jesus." "If you do this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you." Therefore God does not alone give life. Answer: several subordinate causes can be causes of the same effect. Christ and the Holy Spirit give life by their own power; ministers are instruments through whom Christ, by the power of his Spirit, acts and works. So a man should regard ministers in the same way as the ministers of Christ and the stewards of the mysteries of God. "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos? Only ministers, through whom you believed, and as the Lord gave to each: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase."

units.la: Inst. Etiam Christus dat vitam communicata potentia. Ergo non propria. Resp. Dat vitam potentia communicata, non per gratiam, sed per naturam siue æternam generationem. Per inuersionem igitur sequitur: Dat vitam communicata sibi potentia per æternam generationem a Patre. Ergo non dat aliena, sicut ministri ecclesiæ; sed propria potentia. Sicut Pater habet vitam in seipso: sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in seipso.
units.tr: Instance: Christ also gives life by a communicated power; therefore not by his own power. Answer: he gives life by a communicated power, but not by grace; rather by nature, that is, by eternal generation. By conversion it follows: he gives life by a power communicated to him by the Father through eternal generation. Therefore he does not give what belongs to another, as the ministers of the Church do, but gives by his own power. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself.

units.la: III. Quibus detur vita æterna.
units.tr: III. To whom eternal life is given.

units.la: Datur vita æterna omnibus & solis electis ab æterno, seu conuersis in hac vita. Ego vitam æternam do eis, nempe ouibus meis, hoc est, electis. Non rogo pro mundo, sed pro iis, quos dedisti mihi: ego custodiui eos, & nemo ex iis periit, nisi filius ille perditionis. Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis a jactis fundamentis mundi. Nemo potest ad me venire, nisi Pater traxerit eum. Quos prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit, & quos vocauit, eos etiam justificauit, quos autem justificauit, eos etiam glorificauit. Fides & pœnitentia sunt electorum propria. Hæc autem sunt principia & pars vitæ æternæ. Ergo vita æterna est electorum propria. Electio assecuta est, cæteri occaluerunt. Obseruandum hoc loco, cum quæstio est, quibus detur vita æterna, melius responderi, dari vitam æternam electis, quàm, dari conuersis. Nam conuersio & fides sunt vitæ æternæ principium. Dicere igitur, vitam æternam dari conuersis, idem est, ac si dicas, vitam dari viuentibus. Cum quaeritur, quibus detur initium vitae aeternae, etiam recte respondetur, electis. Si enim dicas, dari conuersis, principium petis, eum hoc ipsum quaeratur, quos Deus conuertat.
units.tr: Eternal life is given to all and only the elect, from eternity, or to those converted in this life. "I give eternal life to them, namely to my sheep," that is, to the elect. "I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me. I have kept them, and none of them has perished, except the son of perdition." "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." "No one can come to me unless the Father draw him." "Whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified." Faith and repentance belong properly to the elect. These are the beginnings and part of eternal life. Therefore eternal life belongs properly to the elect. The election obtained it; the rest were hardened. In this place we must observe that when the question is to whom eternal life is given, it is better to answer that it is given to the elect than that it is given to the converted. For conversion and faith are the beginning of eternal life. To say, therefore, that eternal life is given to the converted is the same as saying that life is given to the living. When it is asked to whom the beginning of eternal life is given, the correct answer is also the elect. For if you say, to the converted, you beg the question, since it is exactly what is being asked: whom God converts.

units.la: IV. Quare detur.
units.tr: IV. Why it is given.

units.la: Vita aeterna nobis datur, non propter opera nostra, siue praesentia siue praeuisa: sed ex sola gratuita Dei benevolentia erga humanum genus, & voluntate ostendendi misericordiam suam in seruandis electis, intercedente merito & satisfactione Christi mediatoris, nobis per fidem imputata, in hunc finem, vt Deus à nobis in aeternum celebretur. Donum Dei est vita aeterna in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Gratia Dei seruati sumus, non ex nobis: donum Dei est, ne quis glorietur. Nam ipsius sumus opus, conditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quae praeparauit Deus, vt in eis versaremur. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum daret, vt omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat &c. Causa igitur impulsiua vitae aeternae nobis datae, non est vllum hominis opus in nobis vel praeuisum, vel praesens. Nam ante initium vitae aeternae, hoc est, ante conuersionem omnia opera nostra merentur mortem aeternam: post eius initium, hoc est, post conuersionem, sunt eiusdem effectus. Nihil autem est sui ipsius causa. Adducitur quidem ad vitam aeternam per multa media. Sed aliud sunt media per quae, aliud est causa propter quam adducimur ad vitam aeternam a Deo. Finalis causa, propter quam datur, est, vt Dei misericordia a nobis agnoscatur & celebretur. Ad laudem gloriosae gratiae suae, qua nos gratos sibi effecit in dilecto.
units.tr: Eternal life is given to us not on account of our works, whether present or foreseen, but from the sole free goodwill of God toward the human race, and from his purpose to show his mercy in saving the elect, through the intercession of the merit and satisfaction of Christ the Mediator, imputed to us through faith, to this end: that God may be celebrated by us for ever. "The gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." "By the grace of God we have been saved, not of ourselves; it is the gift of God, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God has prepared, that we should walk in them." "So God loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish," etc. The impulsive cause of the eternal life given to us, therefore, is no work of man in us, either foreseen or present. For before the beginning of eternal life, that is, before conversion, all our works deserve eternal death; after its beginning, that is, after conversion, they are its effects. Nothing, however, is the cause of itself. We are indeed brought to eternal life through many means. But the means by which we are brought are one thing; the cause on account of which we are brought to eternal life by God is another. The final cause, on account of which it is given, is that the mercy of God may be acknowledged and celebrated by us, to the praise of the glorious grace which he has bestowed on us in the Beloved.

units.la: V. Quomodo detur.
units.tr: V. How it is given.

units.la: Vita aeterna datur nobis per fidem. Fides per doctrinam verbi, & efficaciam Spiritus sancti. Nam per verbum Spiritus sanctus efficit in nobis cognitionem Dei & voluntatis diuinae; cognitionem sequitur studium & desiderium magis magisque Deum cognoscendi, & ad voluntatis ipsius praescriptum viuendi, juxta dicta: Quo ibimus? Verba vitae aeternae habes. Ego vos in Christo Iesu genui per Euangelium. Euangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Fides est ex auditu, auditus per verbum Dei. Atque haec est ordinaria ratio dandi nobis initium vitae aeternae: nempe per ministerium verbi. Alia ratio est infantium ecclesiae: alia item conuersionis miraculosae: qualis fuit latronis in cruce, Pauli, Cornelij, &c. Hic sermo est de ordinaria via, quae propria est adultorum,
units.tr: Eternal life is given to us through faith. Faith comes through the teaching of the Word and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. For through the Word the Holy Spirit works in us the knowledge of God and of the divine will; the knowledge is followed by an eagerness and desire to know God more and more, and to live according to his will, in accordance with the sayings: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." "I begot you in Christ Jesus through the gospel." "The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes." "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God." And this is the ordinary way of giving us the beginning of eternal life, namely through the ministry of the Word. The way for the infants of the Church is different, and so too is the way of miraculous conversion, such as that of the thief on the cross, of Paul, of Cornelius, etc. Here we are speaking of the ordinary way, which is proper to adults.

units.la: VI. Quan-
units.tr: VI. When-

units.la: Quæst. LVIII.
units.tr: Question LVIII.

units.la: VI. Quando detur.
units.tr: VI. When it is given.

units.la: Principium vitæ æternæ datur in hac vita: consummatio, post hanc vitam: sed non nisi iis, qui initium hic acceperint. Nam cui hic vita æterna data non fuerit inchoatione, ei nec post hanc vitam dabitur consummatione: hoc est, qui hic non cœperit sentire in se initium vitæ æternæ, fidem scilicet & conversionem, is nunquam ibi perfectionem sempiternæ vitæ consequetur. Breviter: Quibus datur, iis datur in hac vita inchoatione: (post hanc vitam nulli inchoatione) in altera perfectione: In hoc suspiramus, expectantes, domicilio nostro, quod est è cœlo, superindui, siquidem etiam induti, non nudi reperiemur. Habenti dabitur: et autem qui non habet, etiam quod habet, adimetur.
units.tr: The beginning of eternal life is given in this life, and its completion after this life, but only to those who have received the beginning here. For whoever has not been given eternal life here by its inchoation will not be given its consummation after this life. That is, whoever has not begun here to feel in himself the beginning of eternal life, namely faith and conversion, will never attain the perfection of everlasting life there. In brief: to those to whom it is given, it is given in this life as a beginning, and in the other life as perfection; to none is it given as a beginning after this life. In this we groan, longing to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven; if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked. For to him that hath shall be given, and he that hath not, from him shall be taken away even that which he hath.

units.la: Consummationis sunt duo gradus. Vnus, quando animæ piorum à corpore solutæ mox in cœlum deferuntur. Nam morte corporali liberamur ab omni infirmitate. Alter est maior & sublimior, quando post resuscitationem corporum reddemur toti gloriosi in cœlo, & videbimus Deum sicuti est, à facie ad faciem. Qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in condemnationem non veniet, sed transfibit è morte in vitam. Nunc filij Dei sumus, sed nondum patefactum est, quod futuri sumus. Scimus autem verè, quod, cùm ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum, sicuti est.
units.tr: There are two degrees of consummation. The first is when the souls of the godly, loosed from the body, are soon carried up into heaven, for by bodily death we are freed from every infirmity. The second is greater and more sublime: when, after the resurrection of the bodies, we shall be restored wholly glorious in heaven, and shall see God as he is, face to face. He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into condemnation, but has passed from death into life. Now we are the sons of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. But we know that when he is revealed we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.

units.la: VII. An, & unde in hac vita possimus esse certi de vita æterna.
units.tr: VII. Whether, and from what source, we can be certain of eternal life in this life.

units.la: In hac vita possumus & debemus esse certi de vita æterna, vel eam non habebimus. Solis enim & omnibus credentibus vitam æternam, datur vita æterna. Credere autem vitam æternam, est certo statuere, non tantum aliquos eius fore participes, sed meque: quod notandum est contra ἐπιχῶ papisticam. Certi enim esse debemus de perseverantia finali: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Ego vitam æternam do eis. Non daret verò æternam, si daret dubiam & incertam, quæ possit abrumpi. Dona & vocatio Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα. Oves meas nemo rapiet ex manibus meis. Qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, idem perficiet, &c. Scio cui credidi: & mihi persuasum est, eum posse depositum meum in diem illum seruare. Credens scit se credere. Hæc certitudo nititur firmis rationibus. 1. Autor vitæ æternæ est verax & immutabilis, nempe Deus. 2. Electio Dei est æterna, pariterque immutabilis. Solidum stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc: novit Dominus, qui sint sui. 3. Christus in omnibus, quæ à Patre petit, exauditur. Petiit ut Pater servet, quos dedit ei. 4. Deus non vult, ut bona ad salu-
units.tr: In this life we can and ought to be certain of eternal life, or we shall not have it. For eternal life is given only to those who believe, and to all of them. To believe in eternal life is to hold firmly that not only some others will share in it, but that I myself will. This must be noted against the Papists' suspension of judgment [ἐποχή]. For we ought to be certain of final perseverance: Being justified by faith, we have peace. I give them eternal life. But he would not give eternal life if he gave a doubtful and uncertain life, one that could be cut off. The gifts and calling of God are without repentance. No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hands. He who began a good work in you will complete it, etc. I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day. The believer knows that he believes. This certainty rests on firm reasons. (1) The author of eternal life is true and unchangeable, namely God. (2) God's election is eternal and likewise unchangeable. The firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: the Lord knows those who are his. (3) Christ is heard in all the things he asks of the Father. He asked that the Father keep those whom he has given him. (4) God does not will that we ask for the good things necessary to salvation conditionally, but categorically, because he has promised them. To doubt, therefore, the perseverance and completion of eternal life is to overthrow the faith and truth of God, and to render the intercession of Christ void.

units.la: Rom. 5, 1. Ioh. 10, 28. Rom. 11, 19. Ioh. 10, 28. Phil. 1, 6. 2 Tim. 1, 12. 2 Tim. 2, 19. Ioh. 11, 42. Ioh. 17, 11, 44. salutem necessaria ase petamus cum conditione, sed categoricè: quia promisit. Dubitare igitur de perseuerantia & consummatione vitæ æternæ, est fidem & veritatem Dei euertere, & Christi intercessionem irritam habere.
units.tr: Rom. 5, 1. Ioh. 10, 28. Rom. 11, 19. Ioh. 10, 28. Phil. 1, 6. 2 Tim. 1, 12. 2 Tim. 2, 19. Ioh. 11, 42. Ioh. 17, 11, 44. We must ask for the things necessary to salvation not conditionally, but categorically, because he has promised them. Therefore to doubt the perseverance and completion of eternal life is to overthrow the faith and truth of God and to render Christ's intercession ineffective.

units.la: Vnde autem possumus esse certi? De consummatione sumus certi ex initio: Quia habenti dabitur. Dona Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα. Fidelis est Deus; ideo sicut inchoauit, sic etiam perficiet. De initio certi sumus ex vera fide, quæ resistit dubitationibus, habet propositum repugnandi diabolo, & clamat: Credo Domine, opem fer incredulitati meæ: & ex ipso sensu, idq; dupliciter. 1. Ex pace conscientiæ cum Deo, quam habemus & sentimus in cordibus nostris, justificati fide. 2. Ex vera pœnitentia, & serio proposito obediendi Deo secundum omnia mandata, quod etiam sentimus in nobis, si habemus. Fides enim non potest esse sine vera pœnitentia. Cuius domus sumus nos, siquidem fiduciam & gloriationem spei ad finem usque firmam retinuerimus.
units.tr: But from what source can we be certain? We are certain of the completion from the beginning: To him who has, more will be given. The gifts of God are without repentance. God is faithful; therefore, as he has begun, so also he will complete it. We are certain of the beginning from true faith, which resists doubts, holds the purpose of resisting the devil, and cries out: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief. We are also certain from our own feeling, and this in two ways. (1) From the peace of conscience with God, which we have and feel in our hearts, being justified by faith. (2) From true repentance and the earnest purpose of obeying God according to all his commandments, which we also feel in ourselves, if we have them. For faith cannot exist without true repentance. We are his house, provided we hold fast the confidence and the glorying of hope firm to the end.

units.la: Quæ jam dicta sunt de hoc articulo, satis declarant, quid sit credere vitam æternam, nempe certò statuere, 1. Post hanc vitam aliam vitam, in qua ecclesia glorificabitur, & Deus in æternum celebrabitur. 2. Me etiam membrum esse istius ecclesiæ, & ideo vitæ æternæ participē futurum. 3. Me etiam, quia per fidem initium eius me habere in corde meo sentio & video, consummationem eius tandem habiturum esse.
units.tr: What has now been said about this article sufficiently explains what it is to believe in eternal life, namely, to hold firmly: (1) that after this life there is another life, in which the Church will be glorified and God will be celebrated for ever; (2) that I too am a member of this Church, and therefore will be a partaker of eternal life; (3) that I too, since I feel and see in my heart the beginning of it through faith, will at last possess its completion.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LIX.
units.tr: QUESTION LIX.

units.la: At cum hæc omnia credis, quid utilitatis inde ad te redit?
units.tr: But when you believe all these things, what use does this bring you?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Quòd in Christo justus sum coram Deo, & hæres vitæ æternæ.
units.tr: That in Christ I am righteous before God, and an heir of eternal life.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LX.
units.tr: QUESTION LX.

units.la: Quomodo iustus es coram Deo?
units.tr: How are you righteous before God?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Sola fide in Iesum Christum a, adeo vt licet me mea conscientia accuset, quod aduersus omnia mandata Dei grauiter peccauerim, nec vllum eorum seruauerim rim b: ad hæc etiamnum ad omne malum propensus sim c: nihilominus tamen (modo hæc beneficia vera animi fiducia amplectar d) sine vllo meo merito e, ex mera dei misericordia f, mihi perfecta satisfactio g, justitia & sanctitas Christi h, imputetur ac donetur i, perinde ac si nec vllum ipse peccatum admisissem, nec vlla mihi labes inhæreret: immò verò quasi eam obedientiam, quam pro me Christus præstitit, ipse perfectè præstitissem k.
units.tr: By faith alone in Jesus Christ a, so that although my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all the commandments of God, and have kept none of them b, and although I am still inclined to all evil c, nevertheless (provided only that I embrace these benefits with the true confidence of the heart d), without any merit of my own e, by the sheer mercy of God f, the perfect satisfaction g, righteousness and holiness of Christ h, is imputed and granted to me i, just as if I had never committed any sin and no stain had ever clung to me; indeed, just as if I myself had perfectly performed that obedience which Christ rendered in my place k.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Doctrina de justificatione, quæ nunc sequitur, est ex præcipuis fidei nostræ capitibus, non solum, quia de præcipuis rebus agit, sed etiam, quia ab hæreticis præcipuè in controuersiam vocatur. Duæ enim sunt controuersiæ præcipuæ inter ecclesiam & hæreticos, vna de Deo, altera de justificatione hominis coram Deo. Euersa alterutra harum doctrinarum, reliquæ partes fidei nostræ facilimè ruunt, & nihil ad salutem prosunt. Quamobrem in doctrina de Deo & justificatione maximè nos aduersus hæreticos munire debemus. De Deo supra est tractatum: DE JVSTIFICATIONE hic considerandum: I. Quid sit justitia in genere. II. Quotuplex sit justitia. III. Quid justitia differat à justificatione. IV. Quares sit nostra justitia coram Deo. V. Quomodo illa fiat nostra. VI. Cur Christi justitia fiat nostra.
units.tr: The doctrine of justification, which now follows, is among the chief heads of our faith, not only because it deals with the chief matters, but also because it is especially disputed by the heretics. For there are two chief controversies between the Church and the heretics: one concerning God, the other concerning the justification of man before God. If either of these doctrines is overthrown, the remaining parts of our faith collapse very easily and profit nothing for salvation. Wherefore we ought especially to fortify ourselves against the heretics in the doctrine of God and of justification. Concerning God, it has been treated above. Concerning JUSTIFICATION, the following must be considered here: I. What righteousness is in general. II. How many kinds of righteousness there are. III. How righteousness differs from justification. IV. What our righteousness before God is. V. How that righteousness becomes ours. VI. Why Christ's righteousness becomes ours.

units.la: I. Quid sit iustitia in genere.
units.tr: I. What justice is in general.

units.la: Iustitia dicitur à jure, quod est lex, & est ἰσονομία, seu ἰσονομον quiddam, hoc est, conformitas cum lege: sicut peccatum est ἀνομία seu ἄνομον [?], hoc est, discrepantia à lege. Definitur ergo in genere, quod sit conformitas cum Deo & lege diuina: quam definitio tam generalis vix dari potest, quæ DEO simul & creaturis, eoque summis justitiæ generibus, increatæ videlicet & creatæ competat, nisi valde ὁμωνύμως. Nam increata iustitia est DEVS ipse, fons & norma omnis justitiæ. Creata iustitia est effectus increatæ seu diuinæ justitiæ in creaturis rationalibus. Iustitia igitur in vniuersum, quatenus creaturis rationalibus competit, est impletio legum, ad creaturas rationales pertinentium: seu, est conformitas creaturarum rationalium cum legibus ad ipsas pertinentibus. Denique iustitia est impletio legis: & conformitas cum lege, est ipsa iustitia. Hoc tenendum: quia oportet nos justificari per impletionem legis. Nam etiam euangelica iustitia est impletio legis, neque pugnat cum lege. Per euangelium enim lex non aboletur, sed stabilitur. Rom.3,31.
units.tr: Justice (iustitia) is so called from right (ius), which means law. It is isonomy [ἰσονομία], something equal to the law, that is, conformity with the law, just as sin is lawlessness [ἀνομία], that is, departure from the law. It is therefore defined in general as conformity with God and the divine law. Yet a definition so general can hardly be given that would fit God and creatures alike, and so the highest kinds of justice, the uncreated and the created, only in a very equivocal sense. For uncreated justice is God himself, the fountain and norm of all justice. Created justice is the effect of uncreated or divine justice in rational creatures. Justice in general, therefore, insofar as it belongs to rational creatures, is the fulfilling of the laws that pertain to them; or it is the conformity of rational creatures with the laws that pertain to them. In short, justice is the fulfilling of the law, and conformity with the law is justice itself. This must be held, because we must be justified by the fulfilling of the law. For evangelical justice too is the fulfilling of the law and does not conflict with it. Through the gospel the law is not abolished but established. Rom. 3:31.

units.la: 11. Quotuplex sit iustitia.
units.tr: II. How many kinds of justice there are.

units.la: Iustitia in genere est vel increata, vt Deus ipse iustus: vel creata, vt justitia in creaturis rationalibus. Creata, est vel Legalis vel Euangelica. Legalis est impletio legis, præstita ab eo ipso, qui per eam dicitur iustus: seu, est talis impletio legis, quæ fit propria alicuius obedientia: seu, est conformitas cum lege, quæ in eo ipso est, qui dicitur iustus. Hæc iustitia legalis fuit in nobis ante lapsum, & est in angelis, & in Christo quatenus homo est, in gradu excellentissimo, tanquam forma in subiecto. Euangelica iustitia est impletio legis, non à nobis, sed ab alio pro nobis præstita, nimirum λύτρω, illud filiis autem à Deo per fidem imputata, nimirum Dei nobis per fidem imputatum. Legalis iustitia aut per obedientiam legis, aut per pœnam præstatur. Alterutram enim lex requiriit. Qua fit per obedientiam legis, vel est vniuersalis, vel particularis. Vniuersalis est obseruatio omnium legum ad nos pertinentium: seu, est obedientia secundum omnes leges ad nos pertinentes. Nam curare leges, aut res alienas, non est justitia, sed πολυπραγμοσύνη, contra quam dicitur: contendite quieti esse, & res vestras agere. Vniuersalis rursus duplex est: perfecta & imperfecta. Perfecta est interna & externa obedientia erga omnes leges ad nos pertinentes: seu est perfecta conformitas cum lege Dei. Qui fecerit ea, viuet in eis. Et: Qui facit justitiam, justus est. Imperfecta, est conformitas tantum inchoata, & non omnia, vel omnia non eo modo faciens, quæ & quomodo lex requirit. Hæc imperfecta etiam duplex est: philosophica, & Christiana. Philosophica est notitia legis diuinæ & virtutum imperfecta, obscura & languida in mente, & qualecunque propositum in voluntate & corde faciendi recta secundum illam notitiam, & gubernatio morium & morum secundum leges. Christiana est regeneratio seu notitia Dei & legis diuinæ: imperfecta quidem, sed tamen illustrior & perfectior, quam philosophica, orta ex fide & dilectione Dei, acceensa in mentibus & cordibus renatorum, virtute SpiriSpiritus sancti per Euangelium, & coniuncta cum seria inclinatione voluntatis & cordis, ad obediendum Deo, secundum omnia ipsius mandata. Hæc proprie est electorum & renatorum in hac vita, & profluit ex fide justificante. Particularis est virtus suum cuique tribuens. Estque duplex, commutativa & distributiva. Commutativa est, quæ seruat æqualitatem in contractibus, seu in commutatione rerum & pretiorum, operarum & officiorum. Distributiva, quæ seruat proportionem in distributione officiorum, dignitatum, honorum, præmiorum & pœnarum: tribuens personis conuenientia præmia, pœnas, &c. Agricola colat agrum, Politicus gubernet rempublicam, Theologus doceat ecclesiam, bonis præmia, malis pœnæ tribuantur, cui tributum, tributum detur.
units.tr: Justice in general is either uncreated, as God himself is just, or created, as justice is in rational creatures. Created justice is either legal or evangelical. Legal justice is the fulfilling of the law performed by the very person who is called just through it; that is, it is such a fulfilling of the law as becomes a person's own obedience; or it is conformity with the law existing in the very person who is called just. This legal justice was in us before the fall, is in the angels, and is in Christ as he is man, in the most excellent degree, as a form in its subject. Evangelical justice is the fulfilling of the law performed not by us but by another on our behalf, namely by the ransom [λύτρον], and imputed by God to the sons through faith, namely the righteousness of God imputed to us through faith. Legal justice is accomplished either by obedience to the law or by punishment, for the law requires one or the other. That which is accomplished by obedience to the law is either universal or particular. Universal justice is the observance of all the laws that pertain to us; that is, it is obedience according to all the laws that pertain to us. For to meddle with the laws or with other people's affairs is not justice but meddlesomeness [πολυπραγμοσύνη], against which it is said: strive to be quiet and to attend to your own affairs. Universal justice is again twofold: perfect and imperfect. Perfect justice is inward and outward obedience to all the laws that pertain to us; that is, it is perfect conformity with the law of God. He who does these things shall live by them. And: He who does righteousness is righteous. Imperfect justice is conformity only begun, either not doing all things or not doing all things in the way and manner the law requires. This imperfect justice is also twofold: philosophical and Christian. Philosophical justice is an imperfect, obscure and feeble knowledge of the divine law and of the virtues in the mind, together with some sort of purpose in the will and heart to act rightly according to that knowledge, and the governing of manners and morals according to the laws. Christian justice is regeneration, or the knowledge of God and of the divine law: imperfect indeed, but nonetheless clearer and more perfect than the philosophical, arising from faith in and love of God, kindled in the minds and hearts of the regenerate by the power of the Holy Spirit through the gospel, and joined with a earnest inclination of will and heart to obey God in all his commands. This is properly the justice of the elect and regenerate in this life, and it flows from justifying faith. Particular justice is the virtue that gives each his own. It is twofold, commutative and distributive. Commutative justice is that which keeps equality in contracts, that is, in the exchange of goods and prices, of labours and services. Distributive justice keeps proportion in the distribution of offices, dignities, honours, rewards and punishments, assigning to persons the rewards, punishments and so on that suit them. Let the farmer tend the field, let the statesman govern the commonwealth, let the theologian teach the Church; let rewards be given to the good and punishments to the wicked; let tribute be paid to whom tribute is due.

units.la: Distinguitur etiam justitia à subjectis, in justitiam personæ & causæ. Iustitia personæ est, cùm persona est justa & conformis legi: Iustitia causæ, cùm persona habet causam justam & bonam in aliqua controuersia, siue persona sit bona, siue mala. Hac Dauid in Psalmis passim se consolatur: alias vocatur justitia bona conscientiæ.
units.tr: Justice is also distinguished according to its subjects into the justice of the person and the justice of the cause. The justice of the person is when the person is just and conformed to the law. The justice of the cause is when a person has a just and good cause in some controversy, whether the person be good or bad. David often comforts himself with this in the Psalms. It is also called the justice of a good conscience.

units.la: Typus partitionum iustitiae.
units.tr: The scheme of the divisions of righteousness.

units.la: Iustitia: in genere est conformitas cum Deo & lege divina: seu est simpletio totius legis. Et est vel Increata: quae est ipse Deus, cuius essentia est mera justitia. Creata: quae est effectus Dei in creaturis rationalibus, qua legi divinae sunt conformes. Estque vel Legalis, quae & operum; est obedientia perfecta legi ab angelis, vel hominibus praestita. Haec rursus est vel Universalis: quae est obedientia secundum omnes leges ad nos pertinentes. Eaq; est vel Particularis: quae est virtus suum cuique tribuens. Et est vel Commutativa: servans aequalitatem in contractibus, & permutatione rerum ac pretiorum. Distributiva: servans proportionem in distributione officiorum, dignitatum, praemiorum, poenarum. Evangelica: quae & fidei, est impletio legis, non a nobis, sed ab alio pro nobis praestita, hoc est, λύτρον Filj Dei nobis imputatum. Perfecta: quae est conformitas interna & externa cum lege Dei, & aliis ad nos pertinentibus. Imperfecta: quae est conformitas quidem, sed tantum inchoata. Haec rursus est vel Philosophica seu humana, quae est notitia legis divinae, imperfecta, obscura, & languida, & obedientiae externae aliqualis praestatio. Christiana: quae est notitia Dei & legis divinae imperfecta quidem, sed tamen illustris, accensa in mente a Spiritu sancto per evangelium, & conjuncta cum seria inclinatione voluntatis & cordis ad obediendum Deo secundum omnia mandata.
units.tr: Righteousness in general is conformity with God and the divine law, or the sum of the whole law. It is either Uncreated, which is God himself, whose essence is pure righteousness; or Created, which is the effect of God in rational creatures, by which they are conformed to the divine law. Created righteousness is either Legal, which is also called the righteousness of works, namely the perfect obedience rendered to the law by angels or men; or Evangelical, which is also called the righteousness of faith. Legal righteousness is in turn either Universal, which is obedience to all the laws that pertain to us, or Particular, which is the virtue that gives each his due. Particular righteousness is either Commutative, keeping equality in contracts and in the exchange of goods and prices, or Distributive, keeping proportion in the distribution of offices, dignities, rewards and punishments. Evangelical righteousness, which is also called the righteousness of faith, is the fulfilment of the law not performed by us but by another on our behalf, that is, the ransom of the Son of God imputed to us. Legal righteousness is either Perfect, which is internal and external conformity with the law of God and with the other things pertaining to us, or Imperfect, which is conformity indeed but only begun. Imperfect righteousness is in turn either Philosophical or human, which consists in an imperfect, obscure and feeble knowledge of the divine law together with some outward obedience, or Christian, which consists in an imperfect yet clear knowledge of God and the divine law, kindled in the mind by the Holy Spirit through the gospel, and joined with a serious inclination of the will and heart to obey God in all his commandments.

units.la: III. Quid, & quotuplex sit iustificatio: & quid a iustitia differat.
units.tr: III. What justification is, of how many kinds it is, and how it differs from righteousness.

units.la: Iustitia est conformitas cum lege, seu legis impletio, seu res, qua iusti sumus coram Deo. Iustificatio est iustitiæ applicatio ad aliquem. Differunt igitur iustitia & iustificatio, vt forma & applicatio formæ ad subiectum: vt albedo & dealbatio, seu albifica-tio. Diuiditur autem iustificatio, sicut iustitia. Alia est legalis, alia euangelica. Legalis iustificatio est effectio conformitatis cum Deo & lege in nobis. Hæc inchoatur in nobis, cum per Spiritum sanctum regeneramur. Euangelica iustificatio est applicatio iustitiæ euangelicæ: seu, est imputatio iustitiæ alienæ, quæ est extra nos in Christo: seu, est imputatio & applicatio iustitiæ Christi, quam pro nobis moriendo in cruce & resurgendo præstitit. Non est transfusio iustitiæ aut qualitatum in nos, sed absolutio à peccatis in iudicio Dei propter alienam iustitiam. Idem igitur sunt iustificatio, & remissio peccatorum. Iustificare enim est Deum nobis non imputare peccatum, sed nos acceptare pro iustis, & absoluere seu iustos pronunciare propter imputatam iustitiam Christi. Probatur hoc verbum sic esse accipiendum. Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis viuens, hoc est, non absoluetur, iustus pronunciabitur, nempe iustitia inhærente. Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum tecta sunt peccata. Beatus cui non imputat iniquitatem, &c. Ex hoc dicto Paulus interpretatur iustificationem de remissione peccatorum, seu de imputatione iustitiæ: vbi septies verbum imputandi reperit.
units.tr: Righteousness is conformity with the law, or the fulfilment of the law, or the state by which we are righteous before God. Justification is the application of righteousness to someone. Righteousness and justification therefore differ as a form differs from the application of the form to a subject, as whiteness differs from whitening, or the making white. Justification is divided in the same way as righteousness. One kind is legal, another evangelical. Legal justification is the bringing about of conformity with God and the law in us. This begins in us when we are regenerated by the Holy Spirit. Evangelical justification is the application of evangelical righteousness; or it is the imputation of an alien righteousness, which is outside us, in Christ; or it is the imputation and application of the righteousness of Christ, which he performed for us by dying on the cross and rising again. It is not a transfusion of righteousness or of qualities into us, but absolution from sins in the judgment of God on account of an alien righteousness. Justification and the remission of sins are therefore the same thing. For to justify means that God does not impute sin to us, but accepts us as righteous, and absolves us, or pronounces us righteous, on account of the imputed righteousness of Christ. That this word must be taken in this sense is proved thus: In thy sight shall no man living be justified, that is, no one shall be absolved or pronounced righteous on the ground of righteousness inherent in him. Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord imputeth not iniquity, etc. From this saying Paul interprets justification as the remission of sins, or the imputation of righteousness, where he finds the word imputing seven times.

units.la: Obiect. Iustus est legi conformis. Iustificare est iustum facere. Ergo iustificare est legi conformem facere. Resp. Concedo totum, est legi conformem facere, vel in se, quæ conformitas dicitur iustitia inhærens, infusa, legalis, propria: vel in alio, quæ conformitas dicitur iustitia imputata, fidei, euangelica, aliena: quia non inhæret in nobis, sed est in Christo. Hæc etiam est conformitas legis. Fides enim legem non inanem reddit, sed stabilit. Et tamen est nostra iustitia & iustificatio. Quæritur enim de iustitia, qua nos peccatores coram Deo iusti sumus in hac vita: non de ea, qua iusti erimus in altera vita, vel iusti fuissemus ante lapsum, si homo non peccasset.
units.tr: Objection: A righteous person is conformed to the law. To justify is to make righteous. Therefore to justify is to make someone conformed to the law. Reply: I grant the whole: it is to make someone conformed to the law, either in oneself, a conformity called inherent, infused, legal and proper righteousness; or in another, a conformity called imputed, faith-based, evangelical and alien righteousness, because it does not inhere in us but is in Christ. This too is conformity to the law, for faith does not make the law void but establishes it. And yet it is our righteousness and our justification. For the question concerns the righteousness by which we, as sinners, are righteous before God in this life, not the righteousness by which we shall be righteous in the other life, or would have been righteous before the fall, had man not sinned.

units.la: IV. Quæres sit iustitia nostra coram Deo in hac vita.
units.tr: IV. What is our righteousness before God in this life?

units.la: Hic potissimum dissentit doctrina ecclesiæ à ratione humana & à commentis Pharisaicis Papistarum. Hi enim rem illam, qua coram Deo sint iusti, quærunt in seipsis, & fingunt esse conso.conformitatem suam cum lege Dei, seu habitum justitiæ sibi inhærentem, partim infusum, partim actionibus & operibus bonis acquisitum. Ecclesia verò rem illam non quærit in seipsa, sed extra se in Christo. Est autem justitia nostra, qua justi sumus coram Deo in hac vita, non conformitas nostra cum lege, non bona opera, non fides ipsa: sed sola Christi satisfactio, præstita legi pro nobis, seu pœna, quam sustinuit Christus pro nobis, atque adeo tota humiliatio Christi, seu humiliationis obedientia ab initio conceptionis ad glorificationem usque, hoc est, assumtio carnis, servitutis, penuriæ, ignominiæ & infirmitatis, passionis & mortis tolerantia, &c. quæ omnia subiit pro nobis volens, ad nutum & voluntatem Patris: quicquid denique fecit & passus est, ad quod ipse, tanquam Dei filius, non fuit obligatus, tus, est satisfactio eius, quam pro nobis præstitit, & justitia, quæ nobis credentibus à Deo gratis imputatur. Ea enim satisfactio æquipollet vel impletioni legis per obedientiam, vel pœnæ æternæ propter peccata: ad quorum alterutrum nos legegamur. Non decreueram inter vos quicquam scire, nisi Christum Iesum eumque crucifixum. In ipso estis consummati. Per vnius obedientiam justi constituentur multi. Liuore eius sanati sumus. Con- iecit in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Hic calix nouum testamentum est in meo sanguine, qui pro vobis effunditur, in remissionem peccatorum. Omnes justificantur gratis, id est, eius gratia per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus, vt esset placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates. Iustificati eius sanguine seruabimur ab ira. Reconciliati per mortem Filij eius. Qui cum esset dines, factus est pauper, vt nos pauperta- te eius ditescescremus. Redemit nos ab exsecratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est exsecratio. In quo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, hoc est, remissionem peccatorum. Sanguis Iesu Christi Filij Dei purgat nos ab omni peccato. Christus quidem legem impleuit dupliciter: 1. Sanctitate naturæ humanæ. 2. Obedientia vsque ad mortem crucis. Vtraque est perfecta legis impletio: & prior quidem requirebatur propter alteram. Oportebat enim mediatorem esse per se justum & sanctum, vt posset pro nobis præstare obedientiam Patri vsque ad mortem crucis, ac satisfacere. Talis enim nobis conueniebat pontifex, qui esset, &c. Hæc verò obedientia est justitia nostra, qua Deo placemus: sanguinis effusio & mors est satisfactio, propter quam fide nobis imputatam à Deo in gratiam recipimur. Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato: nempe non solum admissionis, sed etiam omissionis. Nam effusio sanguinis, est satisfactionis complementum: ideo sola dicitur justitia nostra.
units.tr: Here the teaching of the Church differs most sharply from human reason and from the Pharisaical inventions of the Papists. For they seek that by which men are righteous before God in themselves, and they imagine it to be their own conformity with the law of God, or a habit of righteousness inhering in them, partly infused and partly acquired by good actions and works. The Church, however, does not seek that in itself but outside itself, in Christ. Our righteousness, by which we are righteous before God in this life, is not our conformity with the law, not good works, not faith itself, but the sole satisfaction of Christ, rendered to the law on our behalf, or the punishment which Christ bore for us; and so the whole humiliation of Christ, that is, his obedience of humiliation from the beginning of his conception to his glorification: his assumption of flesh, servitude, poverty, dishonour and weakness, his endurance of suffering and death, and so on. All these he undertook for us willingly, at the nod and will of the Father. In short, whatever he did and suffered, to which he himself, as the Son of God, was not bound, is his satisfaction, which he rendered for us, and his righteousness, which is freely imputed by God to us who believe. For that satisfaction is equivalent either to the fulfilment of the law through obedience, or to the eternal punishment due for sins, and we are bound to one or the other. I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. In him you are made complete. By the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. By his stripes we are healed. The Lord hath laid on him the iniquities of us all. This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you, for the remission of sins. All are justified freely, by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood. Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven. Being justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath. Reconciled by the death of his Son. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, that we through his poverty might be made rich. He redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. In whom we have redemption through his blood, that is, the forgiveness of sins. The blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanseth us from all sin. Christ indeed fulfilled the law in two ways: (1) by the holiness of his human nature; (2) by obedience even unto the death of the cross. Both are the perfect fulfilment of the law, and the former was required for the sake of the latter. For the Mediator had to be righteous and holy in himself, so that he could render obedience to the Father on our behalf, even unto the death of the cross, and make satisfaction. For such a high priest was fitting for us, one who would be holy, harmless, undefiled, etc. This obedience is our righteousness, by which we are pleasing to God; the shedding of his blood and his death is the satisfaction, on account of which we are received into favour by God, who imputes it to us through faith. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth us from all sin: that is, not only from sins of commission but also from sins of omission. For the shedding of blood is the completion of the satisfaction, and therefore it alone is called our righteousness.

units.la: Christus legem impleuit dupliciter.
units.tr: Christ fulfilled the law in two ways.

units.la: Distinguendum autem est inter has quæstiones. 1. Quomodo creatura rationalis possit esse justa coram Deo. 2. Quomodo homo peccator existens, possit haberi justus coram Deo. 3. An creaturam esse justam conformitate inhærente cum lege. Sic homo ante lapsum erat justus, & angeli in cœlo sunt justi coram Deo. De secundo, hominem peccatorem haberi justum, sola imputatione meriti Christi: & de hac quæstione proprie sermo est, cum de justificatione agitur. Per opera vero peccator justus esse vel fieri non potest: 1. quia ante justificationem opera eius sunt omnia corrupta & peccata. 2. post justificationem sunt omnia imperfecta. 3. Etiamsi essent perfecta, sicut erunt in altera vita: tamen non possemus iis satisfacere pro peccatis præteritis. Demereri de Deo, docet Christus in Evangelio, dicens: Cum omnia feceritis, dicite: servi inutiles sumus, quod debuimus fecimus. Opera autem debita non possunt esse merita: quia Mererì proprie est facere vel pati aliquid indebitum. Ac ne Christi quidem obedientia est meritum propterea, quod Deo aliquid boni inde accedat, sed propter personæ dignitatem, & innocentiam: quia filius Dei passus est pro nobis pœnam indebitam.
units.tr: We must distinguish between these questions: (1) How a rational creature can be righteous before God; (2) How a sinful man can be held righteous before God; (3) Whether a creature is righteous through conformity inhering with the law. Thus man was righteous before the fall, and the angels in heaven are righteous before God. The second question, how a sinner may be held righteous by the sole imputation of the merit of Christ, is the one with which we are properly concerned when justification is under discussion. A sinner cannot be or become righteous through works, for: (1) before justification all his works are corrupt and sinful; (2) after justification they are all imperfect; (3) even if they were perfect, as they will be in the other life, we could not make satisfaction for past sins by them. Christ teaches in the Gospel that we cannot merit anything from God, saying: When you have done all, say: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done. But debts owed cannot be merits, because to merit, properly speaking, is to do or suffer something not owed. Nor is the obedience of Christ a merit in the sense that anything good accrues to God from it, but it has merit on account of the dignity and innocence of the person, because the Son of God suffered on our behalf a punishment he did not owe.

units.la: V. Quomodo satisfactio Christi, cum sit extra nos, fiat nostra iustitia.
units.tr: V. How Christ's satisfaction, though it lies outside us, becomes our righteousness.

units.la: Cum vero absurdum videatur, nos iustificari re quapiam extra nos existente: explicandum porro est quomodo satisfactio seu obedientia Christi fiat nostra. Nisi enim fiat nostra, seu nobis applicetur, non possumus ea esse iusti. Nostra igitur fit, seu nobis applicatur dupliciter. 1. Deus ipse nobis applicat, hoc est, imputat iustitiam Christi, acceptans nos pro iustis propter illam, non secus ac si nostra esset. 2. Nos applicamus nobis, dum accipimus iustitiam Christi per fidem: hoc est, statuimus, quod Deus eam nobis donet, & propter eam nos reputet iustos, absolvens nos ab omni reatu & culpa. Duplex igitur est applicatio, respectu Dei, & respectu nostri. Respectu Dei applicatio est iustitiæ Christi ut pro nobis valeat, acceptat, & propter eam nos pro iustis habet, perinde ac si nunquam peccassemus, vel pœnam sufficientem pro peccatis nostris ipsi exsoluissemus. Respectu nostri applicatio est ipse actus credendi: quo certò confidimus, obedientiam Christi à Deo nobis imputari, & donari, &c. Utramq; applicationem necesse est concurrere. Deus enim hac lege nobis appli-
units.tr: Since it seems absurd that we should be justified by something that exists outside us, we must explain how the satisfaction or obedience of Christ becomes ours. For unless it becomes ours, or is applied to us, we cannot be justified by it. It becomes ours, or is applied to us, in two ways. (1) God himself applies it to us, that is, he imputes the righteousness of Christ and accepts us as righteous on account of it, just as if it were our own. (2) We apply it to ourselves when we receive the righteousness of Christ through faith; that is, we determine that God gives it to us and counts us righteous on account of it, absolving us from all guilt and blame. There is therefore a twofold application, with respect to God and with respect to us. With respect to God, the application of Christ's righteousness is that it avails for us; he accepts it and on account of it holds us as righteous, as if we had never sinned or had ourselves paid a sufficient penalty for our sins. With respect to us, the application is the act of believing itself, by which we firmly trust that the obedience of Christ is imputed and given to us by God, and so on. Both applications must concur. For God applies the righteousness of Christ to us by imputation in such a way that we also apply it to ourselves through faith.

units.la: Quæst. LX. De Iustificatione Fidei. cat justitiam Christi per imputationem, vt nos ipsi quoque eam nobis applicemus per fidem. Etiamsi enim aliquis alteri offerat beneficium: tamen si is, cui offertur, id non accipiat, non ipsi applicatur, nec fit ipsius beneficium. Sine nostra igitur applicatione diuina applicatio non est. Et tamen nostra etiam est a Deo. Deus enim prius nobis imputat satisfactionem Christi: posterius in nobis efficit fidem, qua illam imputatam nobis applicemus. Vnde apparet, quod applicatio diuina applicationem nostram (quae est fidei) ordine praecedat, & sit eius causa; licet non sit sine nostra. Non vos me elegistis (inquit Christus) sed ego elegi vos.
units.tr: Question LX. On the Justification of Faith. Even if someone offers a benefit to another, yet if the one to whom it is offered does not accept it, it is not applied to him and does not become his benefit. Without our application, therefore, there is no divine application. And yet it is also from God. For God first imputes to us the satisfaction of Christ, and afterwards produces in us the faith by which we apply that imputed satisfaction to ourselves. From this it is clear that the divine application precedes our application (which is faith) in order, and is its cause, although it is not without ours. You did not choose me, says Christ, but I chose you.

units.la: Ex his, quae de vtraque applicatione dicta sunt, patet 1. Non esse absurdum dicere, nos iustificari iustitia aliena. Iustitia enim, qua per fidem iusti censemur coram Deo, non est simpliciter aliena: sed fit nostra applicatione: cuius subiectum est Christus, quatenus ab eo semel fuit praestita: nos sumus terminus, quatenus nobis fide imputatur & applicatur. 2. Vocabulum imputationis esse angustius vocabulo applicationis. Illud enim dicitur de solo Deo, hoc etiam de nobis. 3. Aliter Deum nobis iustitiam Christi applicare: aliter nos. Deus applicat imputando: nos applicamus credendo & accipiendo. 4. Iustificandi verbum in ecclesia non significare legaliter, ex injusto justum facere, justitiae qualitate indita, sed euangelice, injustum in se quasi justum absoluere a reatu, necvelle punire, propter alienam satisfactionem ipsi imputatam. Sic vtitur hoc verbo scriptura, nec alia est eius significatio in omnibus linguis. Nam הצדיק justificare Hebraeis significat reum absoluere, innocentem pronunciare. Ego non justifico impium, & condemnat insontem, vterq; abominatio Iehoua. Διχαιόω etiam Graecis significat, alias κῤῥάζειν, supplicio afficere, causa in judicio cognita, vt Suidas annotat. Sic Christus: Ex verbis tuis justificaberis. Prior significatio dupliciter vsurpatur in scriptura. Vel enim significat, non condemnare, sed absoluere in judicio. Quis condemnabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Vel significat justum agnoscere, declarare, &c. Iustificata est sapientia a filiis suis. Vt justificeris in sermonibus tuis. Vtraq; tamen significatio in idem recidit. Justificare autem, pro justum facere, seu justitiae habitum infundere, apud latinos nusquam reperitur: & vt maxime reperiri posset: in scriptura tamen & ecclesia aliter accipi, restantur haec manifesta loca, quae non aliter, quam de absolutione & acceptatione gratuita peccatoris possunt intelligi. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Publicanus descendit justificatus, hoc est, absolutus a reatu, &c. tu, & acceptus Deo magis, quàm pharisæus. Ab omnibus, à quibus non potuistis per legem Mosis justificari, per hunc, quisquis credit, justificatur. Et: Annuntio vobis remissionem peccatorum, &c. Hic justificari manifestè significat absolui, & accipere remissionem peccatorum. Iustificantur gratis. Iustificans eum, qui est ex fide. Hominem justificare absque operibus. Ei, qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam. Iustificati eius sanguine. Reconciliati Deo per mortem.
units.tr: From what has been said about each application, the following is clear. (1) It is not absurd to say that we are justified by an alien righteousness. For the righteousness by which we are counted righteous before God through faith is not alien in the simple sense, but becomes ours by application. Its subject is Christ, inasmuch as it was once performed by him; we are the terminus, inasmuch as it is imputed and applied to us by faith. (2) The word imputation is narrower than the word application. The former is said of God alone, the latter also of us. (3) God applies the righteousness of Christ to us in one way, and we apply it in another: God applies it by imputing, we apply it by believing and receiving. (4) In the Church the verb to justify does not mean legally, to make a righteous person out of an unrighteous one by infusing a quality of righteousness, but evangelically, to absolve from guilt one who is unjust in himself, as if he were just, and to be unwilling to punish him, on account of another's satisfaction imputed to him. Scripture uses this word in this sense, and its meaning is no different in any language. For the Hebrew word הצדיק [hatsdiq] means to absolve the guilty and to pronounce the innocent innocent: I do not justify the wicked, and he who condemns the innocent, both are an abomination to the LORD (Prov. 17.15). The Greek δικαιόω [dikaioō] also means, in other contexts, to punish [κολάζειν], to inflict punishment after a cause has been heard in judgment, as Suidas notes. So Christ says: By your words you will be justified (Matt. 12.37). The former meaning is used in Scripture in two ways. Either it means not to condemn but to absolve in judgment: Who will condemn the elect of God? It is God who justifies (Rom. 8.33). Or it means to acknowledge or declare someone to be righteous: Wisdom is justified by her children (Matt. 11.19); that you may be justified in your words (Ps. 51.4). Yet both meanings come to the same thing. To justify in the sense of making righteous, or infusing a habit of righteousness, is found nowhere in Latin usage, and even if it could be found there, Scripture and the Church understand it otherwise, since these clear passages cannot be understood in any other way than as the absolution and gracious acceptance of a sinner. Who will accuse the elect of God? It is God who justifies. The publican went down justified, that is, absolved from guilt, and more acceptable to God than the Pharisee (Luke 18.14). By this man everyone who believes is justified from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses (Acts 13.38-39). And: I proclaim to you the forgiveness of sins, etc. Here to be justified clearly means to be absolved and to receive the forgiveness of sins. They are justified freely (Rom. 3.24). Justifying him who is of faith (Rom. 3.26). To justify a man without works. To him who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness (Rom. 4.5). Justified by his blood (Rom. 5.9). Reconciled to God through death (Rom. 5.10).

units.la: VI. Cur Christi satisfactio nostra fiat: seu, quare Deus eam nobis imputet ad iustitiam.
units.tr: VI. How Christ's satisfaction is made ours; or, why God imputes it to us for righteousness.

units.la: Iustitia Christi nobis à Deo imputatur & applicatur nullo merito nostro praeterito aut praesente, sed mera & gratuita misericordia, ut qui nos ab aeterno praedestinauit ad hanc gratiam, & gratis elegit in Christo, quibus eam suo tempore per fidem applicaret, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ [?], ut loquitur Apostolus: hoc est, secundum merum beneplacitum voluntatis suae, non propter motus nostra probitate, quam nos habituros praeviderit. Ratio: quia nihil in nobis boni esse potest, nisi prius id in nobis operetur Deus. Removenda est igitur omnis opinio meriti: quippe quae cum gratia Dei pugnat. Estq; divinae gratiae negatio. Nam misericordia & gratia Dei sola est vtriusq; applicationis causa: ipse pro immensa bonitate sua & facit, ut illud nobis applicari possimus. Causa igitur, cur haec applicatio, est in solo Deo, nequaquam verò in nobis, non aliquid in nobis praevisum, nec etiam ipsa apprehensio justitiae Christi. Omnia enim bona in nobis sunt effectus applicationis meriti Christi. Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Gratia estis servati per fidem, idque non ex vobis: Dei donum est.
units.tr: The righteousness of Christ is imputed and applied to us by God without any merit of ours, whether past or present, but by mere and free mercy: since He chose us from eternity for this grace and freely elected us in Christ, to whom He would apply it in His appointed time through faith, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ [?], as the Apostle says; that is, according to the mere good pleasure of His will, not on account of any goodness of ours which He foresaw we would have. The reason is this: nothing good can be in us unless God first works it in us. All opinion of merit must therefore be removed, since it is opposed to the grace of God, and is a denial of divine grace. For the mercy and grace of God alone is the cause of both the imputation and the application: He Himself, out of His immeasurable goodness, both makes it so that we can have this applied to us. The cause, therefore, why this application takes place lies in God alone, and in no way in us; not in anything foreseen in us, nor even in our own apprehension of the righteousness of Christ. For all good things in us are effects of the application of the merit of Christ. What do you have that you did not receive? By grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.

units.la: Christus igitur varie se habet ad iustificationem nostram. 1. Ut subiectum, in quo est nostra iustitia. 2. Ut causa adiuuans, quia impetrat. 3. Ut efficiens principalis: quia vna cum Patre justificat, & dat fidem, qua credimus. Misericordia Dei habet se ut causa impulsiua in Deo. Satisfactio Christi est causa materialis iustitiae nostrae. Fides nostra est causa instrumentalis, apprehendens & applicans nobis iustitiam Christi. Obseruandum ergo, non eodem sensu dici, nos gratia Dei, & merito Christi, & fide iustificari. Primum intelligitur de causa impulsiua in Deo: secundum de causa materiali in Christo: tertium de causa instrumentali in nobis. Misericordia seu gratia Dei iustificamur, ut causa impulsiua proegumena, qua permotus Deus nos iustificat & serat. Merito Christi iustificamur, partim ut causa materiali iustificationis, quatenus obedientia Christi nobis applicata placemus Deo. Deo, & ea, quasi veste induti, pro justis reputamur, partim vt causa impulsiva procatarctica & meritoria, quatenus propter eam nos absoluit. Fide justificamur, vt causa instrumentali, qua quasi manu iustitiam Christi nobis imputatam apprehendimus.
units.tr: Christ therefore stands in various relations to our justification. (1) As the subject, in which our righteousness is; (2) as a helping cause, because He obtains it; (3) as the principal efficient cause, because together with the Father He justifies and gives the faith by which we believe. The mercy of God stands as the moving cause in God. The satisfaction of Christ is the material cause of our righteousness. Our faith is the instrumental cause, apprehending and applying to us the righteousness of Christ. It is to be observed, therefore, that we are said to be justified by the grace of God, by the merit of Christ, and by faith, not in the same sense. The first is understood of the moving cause in God; the second of the material cause in Christ; the third of the instrumental cause in us. We are justified by the mercy or grace of God as the antecedent moving cause, by which God, moved, justifies and saves us. We are justified by the merit of Christ partly as the material cause of justification, inasmuch as, by the obedience of Christ applied to us, we please God, and, clothed as it were in that obedience, are reckoned righteous; partly as the impulsive, procatarctic and meritorious cause, inasmuch as for its sake He absolves us. We are justified by faith as the instrumental cause, by which we apprehend, as it were by a hand, the righteousness of Christ imputed to us.

units.la: Vulgo dicitur: Fide justificamur correlatiuè, siue obiectiuè: hoc est, eo justificamur, quod est correlatiuum & obiectum fidei: nempe merito Christi, ad quod refertur, seu quod fides apprehendit. Nam fides & satisfactio Christi habent se correlatiuè, vt accipiens & acceptum. Rectè autem sic loquimur: quia tunc fides correlatiuè de causa materiali justificationis intelligitur, & sensus est: meritum Christi justificat, non fides: dicitur, non apprehensum justificat, non instrumentum apprehendens. Sed justificatio etiam sine relatione rectè tribuitur fidei, vt causæ instrumentali. Fide justificamur, hoc est, per fidem, vt per medium. Vsitatè enim effectus causæ efficientis etiam tribuitur instrumento: vt, cum prædicatores dicuntur seruare se & alios, 1 Tim. 4. vers. 10.
units.tr: It is commonly said: we are justified by faith correlatively, or objectively; that is, we are justified by that which is the correlative and object of faith: namely, the merit of Christ, to which faith refers, or which faith apprehends. For faith and the satisfaction of Christ stand correlatively to each other, as the receiver and the thing received. We speak rightly in this way, because then faith is understood correlatively concerning the material cause of justification, and the sense is: the merit of Christ justifies, not faith; it is not said that the apprehended justifies, but that the apprehending instrument does not. Yet justification may also rightly be attributed to faith without any correlation, as to an instrumental cause. We are justified by faith, that is, through faith as through a means. For the effect of an efficient cause is commonly attributed also to the instrument, as when preachers are said to save themselves and others, 1 Tim. 4. verse 10.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXI.
units.tr: QUESTION LXI.

units.la: Cur sola fida te iustum esse affirmas? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Why do you affirm that you are righteous by faith alone? ANSWER.

units.la: Non quòd dignitate meæ fidei Deo placeam, sed quòd sola satisfactio, justitia, & sanctitas Christi, meæ justitia sit coram Deo a: ego verò eam non alia ratione, quam fide amplecti, & mihi applicare queam b.
units.tr: Not because I please God by the worth of my faith, but because the sole satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God a. I embrace that righteousness in no other way than by faith, and I am able to apply it to myself b.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Sola fide dicimus nos justificari: 1. Quia solo fidei obiecto justificamur, hoc est, Christi meriti, extra quod nulla est justitia nostra, vel eius pars. Gratis enim justificamur propter Christum. Nihil præter meritum Christi potest esse justitia nostra coram Deo, neque ex toto, neque ex parte: quia tantum credendo & accipiendo alienam justitiam justificamur: non faciendo, aut merendo. Excluduntur igitur omnia opera, etiam ipsa fides, quatenus virtus est, vel qualitas, vel opus. 2. Quia proprius actus fidei est apprehendere & sibi applicare justitiam Christi: immò fides nihil est aliud, quam acceptio & ap-
units.tr: We say that we are justified by faith alone: (1) because we are justified by the sole object of faith, that is, the merit of Christ, outside of which there is no righteousness of ours, or any part of it. For we are justified freely on account of Christ. Nothing besides the merit of Christ can be our righteousness before God, either wholly or in part, because we are justified only by believing and receiving another's righteousness, not by doing or deserving. Therefore all works are excluded, even faith itself, insofar as it is a virtue, a quality, or a work. (2) Because the proper act of faith is to apprehend and apply to oneself the righteousness of Christ. Indeed, faith is nothing other than the acceptance and

units.la: Sola fide justificamur. & apprehensio justitiæ alienæ, seu meriti Christi, in promissione Euangelij nobis oblati.
units.tr: the apprehension of another's righteousness, or the merit of Christ, offered to us in the promise of the Gospel.

units.la: 3. Quia sola fides est instrumentum apprehendens satisfactionem Christi. Hinc liquet, cur exclusiua sola fit retinenda, & contra pontificios urgenda: videlicet 1. Ad exprimendum id, quod Paulus dicit: Justificamur δωρεάν, χάριτι, χωρὶς ἔργων, gratis, gratia, absque operibus: & quod Christus dicit: Tantummodo crede. 2. Vt omnia opera & merita nostra, vel aliena à causa justificationis excludantur: & fides tantum correlatiuè intelligatur: Sola fide, hoc est, solo merito Christi justificamur. 3. Vt non modo omne nostrum meritum, sed etiam ipsa fides excludatur ab eo, quod fide accipitur: & sit sensus: sola fide, id est, non merendo, sed tantum accipiendo justificamur: sicut cum dicitur; hic pauper tantum accipiendo eleemosynam est seruatus, vel ditatus; excluduntur omnia opera & merita, etiam ipsa acceptio eleemosynæ, quatenus pro merito habetur. Ideo Paulus semper dicit, nos justificari τῇ πίστει, & ἐκ τῆς πίστεως, fide, & per fidem, tanquam per organum; nusquam vero ἐκ τῶν πίστεων, propter fidem, vt pontificij volunt, qui vtramque phrasin admittunt quidem, sed perperam intelligunt, ac si fides sit quidem applicatio justitiæ Christi, sed præterea etiam opus aliquod, seu meritum, quo mereamur esse justi. Quod cum natura fidei ex diametro pugnat. Nam si propter fidem essemus justi, jam fides non esset acceptio alienæ justitiæ, sed esset meritum, & causa propriæ justitiæ, nec alienam satisfactionem, qua non haberet opus, acciperet. 4. Vt intelligatur necessitas fidei ad justificationem, & sciatur, non quidem merito fidei, sed tamen non nisi fide accipiente justitiam Christi nos justificari: quia fidei actus proprius est, justitiam eam accipere. 5. Orthodoxi patres, exclusiuam sola fide sæpe urgent. Origenes: Dicit apostolus sufficere SOLIVS FIDEI justificationem, ita, vt credens quis TANTVMMODO justificetur: etiamsi nihil operis ab eo fuerit expletum. Ambrosius: Iustificati sunt gratis; qui nihil operantes, neque vicem reddentes, SOLA FIDE justificati sunt dono DEI. Ibidem: Quomodo igitur Iudæi per opera legis justificari se putent justificatione Abraham; cum videant, Abrahamum non ex operibus legis, sed SOLA FIDE justificatum? Non igitur opus est Lege, quando impius per SOLAM FIDEM justificatur apud Deum. Et ibidem sæpius exclusiuam SOLA repetitur. Idem: Quia hoc constitutum est à Deo, vt qui credit in Christum, saluus sit sine opere. SOLA FIDE gratis recipiens peccatorum remissionem. Sola igitur fide justificamur, hoc est, propter solius Christi meritum fide accipimus remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: (3) Because faith alone is the instrument that apprehends the satisfaction of Christ. Hence it is clear why the exclusive sola is to be retained and pressed against the Papists, namely: (1) to express what Paul says, "We are justified δωρεάν, χάριτι, χωρὶς ἔργων [freely, by grace, without works]," and what Christ says, "Only believe." (2) So that all our works and merits, or those foreign to the cause of justification, are excluded, and faith is understood only correlatively: "by faith alone," that is, by the sole merit of Christ we are justified. (3) So that not only all our merit but also faith itself is excluded from that which is received by faith, and the sense is: "by faith alone," that is, we are justified not by deserving but only by receiving, just as when it is said that this poor man was saved or enriched only by receiving alms; all works and merits are excluded, even the very receiving of alms, insofar as it is held to be a merit. Therefore Paul always says that we are justified τῇ πίστει and ἐκ τῆς πίστεως [by faith, and from faith], by faith and through faith, as through an organ; but never ἐκ τῶν πίστεων [on account of faith], as the Papists want.
