They admit both phrases but understand them wrongly, as if faith were indeed the application of Christ's righteousness, but also some additional work or merit by which we deserve to be righteous. This fights diametrically with the nature of faith. For if we were justified on account of faith, then faith would no longer be the acceptance of another's righteousness but would be a merit and the cause of our own righteousness, nor would it receive a foreign satisfaction, since it would then have a work of its own. (4) So that the necessity of faith for justification may be understood, and it may be known that we are justified, not indeed by the merit of faith, but yet only by faith receiving the righteousness of Christ, because it is the proper act of faith to receive that righteousness. (5) The orthodox Fathers often urge the exclusive "by faith alone." Origen: "The apostle says that justification is sufficient by FAITH ALONE, so that the one who believes is justified ONLY, even if no work has been done by him." Ambrose: "They are justified freely who, working nothing and making no return, are justified by FAITH ALONE through the gift of God." Ibidem: "How then do the Jews think they are justified by the works of the law, by the justification of Abraham, when they see that Abraham was justified not by the works of the law but by FAITH ALONE? There is no need of the Law when the ungodly is justified before God through FAITH ALONE." And in the same place the exclusive SOLA is repeated several times. Again: "Because it has been decreed by God that he who believes in Christ shall be saved without works, receiving the forgiveness of sins freely by FAITH ALONE." Therefore we are justified by faith alone, that is, by the merit of Christ alone we receive the forgiveness of sins by faith.

units.la: Cur exclusiua sola fit retinenda: ua sola sit retinenda. Rom. 3, 34. Marci 5, 36.
units.tr: Why the exclusive "sola" is to be retained. Rom. 3, 34. Mark 5, 36.

units.la: Origenes in Rom. lib. 3. cap. 3. Ambros. in Roman. 3. in cap. 3. In 1. ad Corinth. 1, 4. Hoc firmiter tenendum est, 1. Propter gloriam Dei, ne extenuetur Christi sacrificium. 2. Propter nostram consolationem, ut possimus esse certi, justitiam nostram non pendere ex operibus nostris (alioqui semper essemus incerti, & millies eam amitteremus) sed ex solo Christi sacrificio & merito.
units.tr: Origen in Rom. lib. 3. cap. 3. Ambros. in Roman. 3. in cap. 3. In 1. ad Corinth. 1, 4. This must be held firmly: (1) for the glory of God, lest the sacrifice of Christ be diminished; (2) for our consolation, so that we may be certain that our righteousness does not depend on our works (otherwise we would always be uncertain and would lose it a thousand times), but on the sacrifice and merit of Christ alone.

units.la: OBIECTIONES.
units.tr: OBJECTIONS.

units.la: Papistarum contra justitiam fidei: quòd non fide, vel non sola fide justificemur.
units.tr: Objections of the Papists against the righteousness of faith: that we are not justified by faith, or not by faith alone.

units.la: OBIECTIO I. Quod non est in scriptura, non est docendum. Solâ fide hominem justificari, non est traditum in scriptura. Ergo, &c:
units.tr: Objection I. What is not in Scripture must not be taught. That man is justified by faith alone is not handed down in Scripture. Therefore, etc.

units.la: RESPONDEO ad Maiorem. Dogma in scriptura non traditum, neque quoad verba, neque quoad sensum, non est recipiendum, At solâ fide nos justificari continetur in scriptura, quoad sensum: quando dicit, nos justificari gratis, gratiâ, sine operibus legis, sine lege, non ex nobis, non ex operibus, non ex justitia, quam fecerimus nos, sed fide: quando item dicit; Sanguis Iesu Christi mundat nos ab omni peccato. Idem enim est, sanguine seu merito Christi fide apprehenso justificari, quod sola fide justificari, tantum credendo & accipiendo, nihil merendo. Est ergo fallacia à secundum quid, ut simpliciter.
units.tr: I answer the major premise. A doctrine not handed down in Scripture, neither in words nor in sense, must not be received. But that we are justified by faith alone is contained in Scripture in sense, when it says that we are justified freely, by grace, without the works of the law, without law, not of ourselves, not by works, not by any righteousness which we have done, but by faith; likewise when it says: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. For to be justified by the blood, or merit, of Christ apprehended by faith is the same as to be justified by faith alone, by believing and receiving only, and merit nothing. So it is a fallacy of moving from a qualified statement to an unqualified one.

units.la: Obj. II. Quod non est solum, non justificat solum. Fides non est sola. Ergo non justificat sola. Resp. Si conclusio recte intelligatur, ut ex praemissis sequitur, hoc sensu: Ergo fides non justificat sola: nempe existens: datur totum argumentum. Fides enim justificans nunquam existit sola sine dilectione & bonis operibus, tanquam fructibus, &c. Si vero ex sensu Papistarum conclusio sic accipiatur. Ergo non sola justificat: hoc est, non sola habet actum justificandi, seu accipiendi justitiam Christi: tunc vel plus est in conclusione, quàm in praemissis, vel Maior est falsa. Possum enim ego solus loqui in hypocausto, etiamsi non sim solus. Potest res non esse sola, sed cum aliis coniuncta, & tamen sola habere hunc vel illum actum: ut voluntas non est sola, sed coniuncta cum parte intelligente, & tamen sola vult: anima hominis non est sola, sed coniuncta cum corpore; & tamen sola intelligit: acies cultri non est sola, sed coniuncta cum manubrio, & tamen sola secat. Est ergo, ut vulgo dicitur, fallacia compositionis & divisionis. Exclusiua enim Sola, quae in Minore cohaeret cum verbo Est, in conclusione ab eo diuellitur, & componitur cum verbo Iustificat.
units.tr: Obj. II. What is not alone does not justify alone. Faith is not alone. Therefore it does not justify alone. Answer: If the conclusion is understood correctly, as it follows from the premises, in this sense, "therefore faith does not justify alone", namely while existing, the whole argument is granted. For justifying faith never exists alone without love and good works, as their fruits, etc. But if the conclusion is taken in the sense of the Papists, "therefore it does not justify alone", that is, does not alone have the act of justifying, or of receiving the righteousness of Christ, then either there is more in the conclusion than in the premises, or the major premise is false. For I can speak alone in a hypocaust even though I am not alone. A thing may not be alone but joined with others, and yet alone have this or that act: the will is not alone but joined with the understanding, and yet alone wills; the soul of man is not alone but joined with the body, and yet alone understands; the edge of a knife is not alone but joined with the handle, and yet alone cuts. It is therefore, as is commonly said, a fallacy of composition and division. For the exclusive alone, which in the minor clings to the verb is, is in the conclusion torn away from that verb and joined to the verb justifies.

units.la: Obiect. III. Quod requiritur in justificandis, sine eo fides non justificat. Bona opera requiruntur in justificandis. Ergo sine bonis operibus fides non justificat: proinde nec sola justificat. Respond. Est eadem fallacia: propter ambiguam constructionem particulæ SINE, Quod requiritur in justificandis, sine eo fides, nempe existens, non iustificat. (quia sic non esset fides viva, sed mortua.) Etsi autem fides viva non existit sola, sed charitatem semper coniunctam habet, & per eam est efficax: sola tamen justificat: hoc est, sola habet actum justificandi, seu amplectendi, & sibi applicandi Christi meritum. Minor etiam est dextre acci-pienda. In justificandis requiruntur fides & opera: sed non eodem modo. Fides cum suo actu proprio (sine quo fides considerari nequit) requiritur tamquam necessarium medium seu instrumentum, quo meritum Christi nobis applicamus. Bona vero opera non requiruntur, ut iis apprehendamus meritum Christi, ac multo minus, ut per, vel propter ea justificemur: sed ut iis ostendamus fidem nostram, quæ sine operibus est mortua, & non nisi ex iis cognoscitur: hoc est, opera requiruntur, ut effecta fidei, & testimonium gratitudinis nostræ erga Deum. Non quicquid necesse est cohærere cum causa, id etiam propterea necessarium est ad effectum producendum. Sic bona opera licet necessario cum fide cohæreant: non tamen ad apprehensionem meriti Christi sunt necessaria.
units.tr: Obiect. III. What is required in justifying, without which faith does not justify. Good works are required in justifying. Therefore without good works faith does not justify, and so not even alone. Respond. It is the same fallacy, owing to the ambiguous construction of the particle without: "What is required in justifying, without which faith, namely existing, does not justify" (because such faith would not be living but dead). Although living faith does not exist alone, but always has love joined with it and is effective through love, yet it alone justifies: that is, it alone has the act of justifying, or of embracing and applying to itself the merit of Christ. The minor too must be rightly understood. In justifying, faith and works are required, but not in the same way. Faith, with its own proper act (without which faith cannot be considered), is required as the necessary means or instrument by which we apply the merit of Christ to ourselves. Good works, however, are not required so that we may apprehend the merit of Christ by them, much less so that we may be justified through them or on account of them; they are required so that by them we may show our faith, which without works is dead and is known only from them. That is, works are required as the effects of faith and as the testimony of our gratitude toward God. Not everything that must necessarily cohere with a cause is therefore necessary for producing the effect. So good works, although they necessarily cohere with faith, are not necessary for the apprehension of Christ's merit.

units.la: Obiect. IV. Vbi requiruntur plura, ibi non est ponenda exclusiva. In justificandis præter fidem requiruntur bona opera. Ergo non est dicendum, nos sola fide justificari. Resp. Est eadem solutio. Vbi requiruntur plura: nempe: eodem modo. In justificandis requiruntur plura, fides, & opera: sed non eodem modo. Fides ut medium apprehendens alienam iustitiam: Opera ut fidei & gratitudinis nostræ testimonium.
units.tr: Obiect. IV. Where several things are required, an exclusive word must not be placed. In justifying, besides faith, good works are required. Therefore we must not say that we are justified by faith alone. Resp. It is the same solution. Where several things are required, namely in the same way. In justifying several things are required, faith and works, but not in the same way: faith as the means apprehending another's righteousness; works as the testimony of our faith and gratitude.

units.la: Obiect. V. Qui iustificantur duabus rebus, non iustificantur una sola. Nos docemus hominem iustificari duabus rebus: fide, & merito CHRISTI. Ergo non dicendum, hominem iustificari sola fide. Respond. Rursus est eadem solutio. Non iustificatur una re sola, qui iustificatur duabus eodem modo. Nos iustificamur duabus rebus, sed diversimode: fide, ut instrumento apprehendente iustitiam; merito CHRISTI, ut causa materiali nostræ iustitiæ.
units.tr: Obiect. V. Those who are justified by two things are not justified by one thing alone. We teach that man is justified by two things: faith and the merit of Christ. Therefore it must not be said that man is justified by faith alone. Respond. Again it is the same solution. He is not justified by one thing alone who is justified by two things in the same way. We are justified by two things, but in different ways: by faith, as the instrument apprehending righteousness; by the merit of Christ, as the material cause of our righteousness.

units.la: Obiect. VI. Notitia non iustificat. Fides est notitia. Ergo fides non iustificat. Resp. Est fallacia à secundum quid. Notitia, nempe tantum, sed etiam fiducia, qua tanquam medio nobis applicamus meritum Christi. Ac multum differunt Notitia & Fiducia.
units.tr: Obiect. VI. Knowledge does not justify. Faith is knowledge. Therefore faith does not justify. Resp. It is a fallacy of moving from a qualified statement. Knowledge alone does not justify; but neither does knowledge alone, but also trust, by which, as a means, we apply to ourselves the merit of Christ. And knowledge and trust differ greatly.

units.la: Illa est in intellectu: haec vero in voluntate & corde: nec est tantum cognitio alicuius rei, sed etiam propositum faciendi vel applicandi hoc, quod cognoscimus, & in eo acquiescendi, ut de eo laetemur, & securi simus. Germanicè: Verttrawen. Itaq; credere in Deum non est tantum Deum agnoscere, sed etiam in Deo fiduciam habere. Alioqui etiam diabolus habet notitiam Dei & promissionum eius. Sed non habet fiduciam. Ideo notitia eius non est fides justificans, sed tantum historica: de qua dicit Jacobus: Daemones credunt, & contremiscunt. De tali fide damus Papistis tantum argumentum: de justificante non item.
units.tr: The one is in the intellect, but the other is in the will and the heart. Nor is it merely the knowledge of a thing, but also a purpose of doing or applying what we know, and of resting in it, so that we rejoice in it and are secure. In German: Vertrauen. Therefore to believe in God is not merely to acknowledge God, but also to have trust in God. Otherwise even the devil has knowledge of God and of His promises, but he does not have trust. So his knowledge is not justifying faith, but merely historical; of which James says: The devils believe and tremble. We grant the Papists the argument about such faith only, not about justifying faith.

units.la: Obiect.VII. Jacobus ait: Videtis igitur, ex operibus justificari hominem, non ex fide tantum. Ergo non sola fides justificat. Resp. Est duplex δικαιωσις in verbis. Primo, Jacobus non loquitur de justitia, qua coram Deo justificamur: hoc est, qua, vel propter quam à Deo justi reputamur: hoc est, justi agnoscimur, & compertimur esse justificati. Probatur 1. ex vers.18. Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis. Mihi, inquit, nempe homini. Ergo de ostensione fidei & justitia coram hominibus loquitur. 2. Ex vers.21. Abraham pater ille nonne ex operibus justificatus est cum obtulisset filium super altare? quod de justificatione coram Deo non potest intelligi. Nam historia testatur, Abrahamum multò ante oblationem filij à Deo per fidem fuisse justum reputatum. Et Paulus dicit: Abrahamum non ex operibus, sed fide iustificatum esse coram Deo. Jacobus autem non pugnat cum Paulo. Hoc igitur vult Jacobus: Abrahamum quidem fide justificatum fuisse coram Deo, sicut scriptum est: Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam: bonis vero operibus, & obedientiam erga Deum justitiam suam testificatam fecisse hominibus, & sic etiam coram hominibus justificatum: hoc est, justum fuisse agnitum & declaratum. Haec est prima δικαιωσις in verbo justificari. Altera est in vocabulo fides. Jacobus enim cum fidei justificationem derogat, non loquitur de fide vera, de qua Paulus, sed de fide solitaria, operibus destituta, seu mortua: quae est frigida notitia, absque fiducia & operibus. Id patet ex verbis: Ita quoque fides, si opera non habeat, mortua est per se: qualem fidem etiam daemonibus tribuit, qui certè fidem justificantem non habent. Et v.26. Fidem, quam negauit justificare, cadaueri mortuo comparat. Talis autem fides non est fides justificans. Denique, ne de δικαιωσει verbi justificare cum Papistis multum litigare sit necesse, est etiam alia responsio ex textu, quod Jacobus vers.18.21.24.25. per metonymiam effecti opera vocat fidem habentem opera. Vtrique enim fidei operibus vacuae seu mortuae opponit opera: hoc est, fidem operibus praeditam: qualem Abrahami fidem fuisse laudar. Est ergo sensus verborum: Videtis hominem justifi-cari operibus: hoc est, fide, operibus praedita: & non fide tantum: hoc est, & non fide solitaria, operibus vacua.
units.tr: Obiect. VII. James says: You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only. Therefore faith alone does not justify. Resp. The word justification [δικαίωσις] is used in two senses. First, James is not speaking of the righteousness by which we are justified before God, that is, by which or on account of which we are reckoned righteous by God, that is, acknowledged as righteous and shown to be justified. This is proved, first, from v. 18: Show me your faith by your works. To me, he says, that is, to a man; therefore he speaks of showing faith and righteousness before men. Second, from v. 21: Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he offered his son upon the altar? which cannot be understood of justification before God. For history testifies that Abraham had been reckoned righteous by God through faith long before he offered his son. And Paul says that Abraham was justified before God not by works but by faith. James, however, does not contradict Paul. So James means this: Abraham was indeed justified before God by faith, as it is written, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness; but by good works and obedience toward God he showed his righteousness to men, and so was justified also before men, that is, was recognized and declared to be righteous. This is the first sense of the word justify. The second is in the word faith. For when James detracts from the justification of faith, he is not speaking of true faith, of which Paul speaks, but of solitary faith, destitute of works, or dead: which is cold knowledge without trust and works. This is clear from the words: So also faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself; he attributes such faith even to the devils, who certainly do not have justifying faith. And in v. 26 he compares to a dead corpse the faith which he denied justifies. But such faith is not justifying faith. Finally, lest it be necessary to dispute at length with the Papists about the sense of the word justify [δικαιοῦν], there is also another answer from the text: in vv. 18, 21, 24, 25 James, by metonymy of the effect, calls faith that has works by the name works. For he opposes works to a faith empty of works, or dead; that is, to faith endowed with works, such as the faith of Abraham which he praises. The sense of the words is therefore: You see that a man is justified by works, that is, by faith endowed with works; and not by faith only, that is, not by solitary faith, empty of works.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXII.
units.tr: QUESTION 62.

units.la: Cur nostra bona opera non possunt esse iustitia, vel pars aliqua iustitiae coram Deo?
units.tr: Why can our good works not be righteousness, or any part of righteousness, before God?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Propterea, quod oporteat eam justitiam, quae in judicio Dei consistat, perfectè absolutam esse, & omni ex parte legi divinae congruentem a. Nostra verò etiam praestantissima quaeq; opera, in hac vita imperfecta, atq; adeo peccatis inquinata b.
units.tr: Because the righteousness that stands in God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and wholly in agreement with the divine law in every respect. a Yet even our most excellent works, in this life, are imperfect, and therefore polluted by sins. b

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hactenus vera doctrina de Justificatione fidei est explicata, & confirmata: sequitur falsa doctrina Papistarum refutanda: quòd operibus, vel partim fide, partim operibus justificemur. Argumentum huic contrarium tale est: Justitiam, quae in Dei judicio constat, oportet esse absolutè perfectam, & omni ex parte divinae legi congruentem. Nostra verò, etiam praestantissima opera in hac vita sunt imperfecta, atq; adeo peccatis inquinata. Ergo nostra etiam praestantissima opera non possunt esse justitia nostra in judicio Dei, neque ex toto, neq; ex parte. Maior patet ex lege: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in iis. Maledictus omnis, qui non permanet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis, ut ea faciat. Minor est manifesta. Multa enim facimus mala, quae debebamus omittere, & multa omittimus bona, quae debebamus facere: immò multa admiscemus mala: hoc est, bona facimus malè. Id testantur sanctorum querelae, & quotidiana precatio: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Ne ingrediaris in judicium cum servo tuo. Opera igitur imperfecta non possunt esse justitia perfecta. Haec est prima & praecipua causa, cur operibus non possumus justificari coram Deo: quia justitia nostra esset imperfecta, cum opera sint imperfecta. Accedunt huic plures aliae causae. Nam 11. etiamsi opera nostra essent perfecta, tamen sunt debita: ita ut non possimus iis delicta praeterita exsoluere: Cùm omnia feceritis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus, quod debuimus, fecimus. 111. Non sunt nostra, sed Dei, opeoperantis ea in nobis. iv. Sunt temporaria, nec habent proportionem cum bonis æternis. Inter mercedem verò & meritum oportet esse proportionem. v. Sunt effectus justificationis: ergo non causa. vi. Haberemus, de quo gloriaremur, contra illud: Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. vii. Conscientia destitueretur certa consolatione. viii. Christus frustra esset mortuus. ix. Non eadem esset salutis via in utroque testamento, si Abraham esset justificatus sola fide: nos vero justificaremur operibus, sive solis, sive cum fide. x. Christus non esset perfectus seruator: quia extra eum esset pars aliqua justitiæ & salutis nostræ in operibus nostris.
units.tr: So far the true doctrine of justification by faith has been explained and confirmed. There follows the refutation of the false doctrine of the Papists, that we are justified by works, or partly by faith and partly by works. The argument against this runs as follows. Righteousness that stands in God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and wholly in agreement with the divine law in every respect. Yet our works, even the most excellent, are imperfect in this life, and therefore polluted by sins. Therefore our most excellent works cannot be our righteousness in God's judgment, neither wholly nor in part. Major is plain from the law: He who does them shall live in them. Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them. Minor is evident. For we commit many evils that we ought to omit, and we omit many good things that we ought to do; indeed we mix many evils in, that is, we do good things badly. The complaints of the saints and their daily prayer bear witness to this: Forgive us our debts. Do not enter into judgment with your servant. Imperfect works therefore cannot be perfect righteousness. This is the first and chief reason why we cannot be justified before God by works: our righteousness would be imperfect, since the works are imperfect. Several other reasons join this one. (1) Even if our works were perfect, they are still owed, so that we cannot by them pay off past offences: When you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do. (2) They are not ours but God's, since he works them in us. (3) They are temporal, and have no proportion to eternal goods; yet there must be proportion between reward and merit. (4) They are effects of justification, therefore not its cause. (5) We would have something to glory in, contrary to: Not of works, lest anyone should boast. (6) Conscience would lack certain comfort. (7) Christ would have died in vain. (8) The way of salvation would not be the same in both covenants, if Abraham was justified by faith alone while we were justified by works, whether by works alone or by works together with faith. (9) Christ would not be the perfect Saviour, since outside him there would be some part of our righteousness and salvation in our works.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXIII.
units.tr: QUESTION 63.

units.la: Quomodo bona opera nihil promereantur, cùm Deus in præsenti & in futura vita mercedem pro his se daturum promittat?
units.tr: How do good works merit nothing, when God promises that he will give a reward for them in the present life and in the life to come?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Merces ea non datur ex merito, sed ex gratia a.
units.tr: That reward is not given on account of merit, but of grace. a

units.la: a Luc. 17. vers. 10.
QVÆSTIO LXIV.
units.tr: QUESTION 64.

units.la: An autem hæc doctrina non reddit homines securos & profanos?
units.tr: Does not this doctrine, however, make people secure and profane?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Non. Neq; enim fieri potest, quin ij, qui Christo per fidem insiti sunt, fructus proferant gratitudinis a.
units.tr: No. For it is impossible that those who have been grafted into Christ through faith should not bring forth the fruits of gratitude. a
a Matt. 7:18. John 15:5.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Est occupatio duorum argumentorum, quibus Papistæ justificationem, & merita operum stabilire solent.
units.tr: This is the argument of two reasons by which the Papists usually try to establish justification and the merit of works.

units.la: Prior Obiectio hæc est: Merces supponit meritum: ut ubi merces est, ibi sit meritum. Sunt enim merces & meritum correlativa: quorum uno posito, ponitur & alterum. Sed bonis operibus merces à Deo proponitur vita æterna. Ergo bona opera sunt meritum vitæ æternæ. Resp. Maior aliquando est vera de creaturis, quia homines de hominibus mereri possunt: sed nec semper apud homines ibi meritum esse consequitur, ubi est merces. Nam & ab hominibus præmia sæpe dantur non ex merito,
units.tr: The first objection is this: a reward presupposes merit, so wherever there is a reward there is merit. For reward and merit are correlatives: when one is posited, the other is posited too. But eternal life is proposed by God as a reward for good works. Therefore good works are the merit of eternal life. Answer: The major premise is sometimes true of creatures, since men can merit from men. But among men it does not always follow that there is merit wherever there is a reward, for rewards are often given by men not on account of merit,

units.la: De Deo autem improprie dicitur, quòd vita æterna proponatur operibus nostris vt merces. Apud Deum enim nos operibus nostris nihil, ne quidem bolum panis, ne dum vitam æternam mereri possumus: quia omnia opera nostra sunt Deo debita, teste Christo: Cùm omnia feceritis, quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Serui inutiles sumus: quæ debuimus, fecimus. Vel sic: Pro quo datur merces, id est meritum. Pro bonis operibus datur merces. Ergo bona opera sunt meritum, ex ordine justitiæ. Resp. Pro quo datur merces ex obligatione, id est meritum. Pro bonis verò operibus datur merces, non ex obligatione, sed ex gratia. Non igitur sunt merita. In mercede autem duo considerantur, obligatio & compensatio. Obligatio in operibus cessat: compensatio eorum sequitur ex gratia. Operibus igitur merces datur: non quia eis debetur, sed quia gratuita compensatio ea sequitur. Dat enim Deus operibus nostris gratuitam mercedem, non ex debito, sed 1. quia gratis dare gratis promisit. 2. Vt ostendat, ea sibi placere. 3. Vt doceat, vitam æternam tantum strenuè laborantibus & certantibus esse propositam. 4. Quia non minus certò, quàm si meriti essemus, est daturus.
units.tr: but it is improperly said of God that eternal life is proposed to our works as a reward. For before God we can merit nothing by our works, not even a morsel of bread, much less eternal life, since all our works are owed to God, as Christ witnesses: When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done. Or put it thus: for whatever is given a reward, there is merit. A reward is given for good works. Therefore good works are merit, by the order of justice. Answer: For whatever is given a reward out of obligation, there is merit. But a reward is given for good works not out of obligation but out of grace. Therefore they are not merits. In a reward, however, two things are considered: obligation and recompense. Obligation ceases in works; their recompense follows from grace. A reward is therefore given to works not because they are owed, but because a free recompense follows them. For God gives our works a free reward, not as a debt, but (1) because he freely promised to give freely; (2) to show that they please him; (3) to teach that eternal life is set before only those who labour and strive earnestly; (4) because he will give it no less surely than if we had merited it.

units.la: ALTERA Obiectio talis est: Vera doctrina de Justificatione non reddit homines securos & profanos. Doctrina de Justificatione per solam fidem, & non per opera, reddit homines securos & profanos. Non igitur est vera. Resp. Minor est calumnia Pistarum aduersus Euangelium de Justificatione fidei: & fallacia accidentis. Si enim doctrina de justitia fidei aliquos reddit securos, id fit per accidens. Per se effectus huius doctrinæ est stimulus gratitudinis erga Deum declarandæ. Fit autem hominum vitio & peruersitate, vt aliqui abutantur gratiâ ad velamen carnis & malitiæ.
units.tr: Instance 1. Even evils that happen only by accident must be avoided. Therefore, since this doctrine is an evil to men, at least by accident, it must be avoided. Answer to the major premise. Even evils that happen by accident must be avoided, unless a greater or weightier cause lies behind it, why what is an evil to some through their own fault should not be dropped, but kept and taught. There are necessary causes why this doctrine should be taught and not dropped: (1) the command and glory of God; (2) the salvation of the elect.

units.la: Inst. 1. Etiam per accidens mala sunt fugienda. Ergo cùm hæc doctrina vel per accidens hominibus sit mala, fugienda est. Resp. ad Maiorem. Fugienda sunt etiam per accidens mala, nisi maior vel grauior subsit causa, cur non omittendum, sed retinendum, & docendum sit id, quod aliquibus ipsorum vitio est malum. Causæ autem sunt necessariæ, cur docenda, & non omittenda sit hæc doctrina. 1. Mandatum, & gloria Dei. 2. Salus electorum.
units.tr: Objection 1. Even evils that are such only incidentally are to be avoided. Therefore, since this doctrine is evil for men, at least incidentally, it is to be avoided. Answer to the major premise: Even evils that are incidental are to be avoided unless some greater or weightier cause stands in the way, a cause why what is evil for some of them through their own fault should not be omitted but retained and taught. There are necessary causes why this doctrine should be taught and not omitted: (1) the command and the glory of God; (2) the salvation of the elect.

units.la: Inst. 2. Quod non potest nocere, id non est necesse cauere. Futura peccata, juxta doctrinam de Justificatione fidei, non possunt nobis nocere: quia CHRISTVS pro omnibus peccatis satisfecit, tam pro admittendis, quàm pro admissis. Ergo nihil attinet peccata futura cauere: & sic manet, quòd hæc doctrina homines faciat securos. Resp. 1. ad Maiorem per distinctionem, Non necesse est cauere, quod non potest nocere: nempe, siue caueatur, siue non. Peccata autem futura non nocent, si caueantur. 2. Minor est falsa. Peccata enim futura, nisi caueantur, maximè nocent. Nam Deum offendunt, quod est maximum daminum: nos spoliant conformitate cum Deo, & bonitate communi: etsi scientiæ: & attrahunt pœnas corporales etiam fidelibus: etsi pœnæ æternæ resipiscentibus remittantur.
units.tr: Objection 2. What cannot do harm need not be guarded against. Future sins, according to the doctrine of justification by faith, cannot harm us, because Christ has made satisfaction for all sins, both those to be committed and those already committed. Therefore there is no point in guarding against future sins, and so this doctrine makes men secure. Answer: 1. To the major premise, by a distinction: it is not necessary to guard against what cannot do harm, namely whether it is guarded against or not. But future sins do not harm if they are guarded against. 2. The minor premise is false. For future sins, unless they are guarded against, do the greatest harm. For they offend God, which is the greatest loss; they strip us of conformity with God and of the common goodness, and of knowledge; and they bring bodily punishments even upon believers, although eternal punishments are remitted to those who repent.

units.la: Huc pertinent etiam alia Papistarum argumenta, quibus justificationem, & merita operum stabiliunt, vt sunt seqq.
units.tr: To this belong also the other arguments of the Papists by which they establish justification and the merits of works, such as the following.

units.la: Obiect. III. Fide justificamur. Fides est opus. Ergo operibus justificamur. Resp. 1. Negatur consequentia: quia plus est in conclusione, quàm in præmissis: ex quibus tantum sequitur, quòd illo opere justificemur: nempe tanquam instrumento seu medio: quod potest concedi: non verò tanquam causa impulsiva, vel merito. Aliud est enim justificari fide, id est sanguine Christi, mediante fide: aliud justificari propter fidem, vel meritum fidei. 2. Mutatur genus prædicationis; quia fides in Maiore correlatiuè: in Minore proprie sumitur.
units.tr: Objection III. We are justified by faith. Faith is a work. Therefore we are justified by works. Answer: 1. The inference is denied, because the conclusion contains more than the premises. From them it follows only that we are justified by that work, namely as an instrument or means, which may be conceded, but not as an impulsive cause or merit. For it is one thing to be justified by faith, that is, by the blood of Christ through faith; it is another to be justified on account of faith or the merit of faith. 2. The kind of predication changes, because faith is taken correlatively in the major premise but properly in the minor.

units.la: Obiect. IV. Justitia nostra est id, quo formaliter sumus justi. Resp. Fides est justitia nostra. Ergo fide formaliter sumus justi. 1. Mutatur genus prædicationis. Maior proprie: Minor correlatiuè intelligitur: alioqui est falsa. Proprie enim non fides, sed fidei correlatum, meritum Christi, quod fides in promissione Euangelij intuens sibi applicat, est justitia nostra. 2. Sunt etiam quatuor termini. Maior loquitur de justitia legali: Minor de euangelica: vel, Maior est falsa. Justitia enim euangelica non est formaliter in nobis, sicut albedo in pariete, sed imputatur nobis per fidem, sicut dicitur: Credenti fides sua imputatur ad justitiam.
units.tr: Objection 4. Our righteousness is that by which we are formally righteous. Answer: Faith is our righteousness; therefore we are formally righteous by faith. 1. The kind of predication changes: the major is understood properly, the minor relatively; otherwise it is false. For properly it is not faith but the correlate of faith, the merit of Christ, which faith, looking to the promise of the Gospel, applies to itself, that is our righteousness. 2. There are also four terms. The major speaks of legal righteousness, the minor of evangelical righteousness; or else the major is false. For evangelical righteousness is not formally in us, as whiteness is in a wall, but is imputed to us through faith, as it is said: "To him who believes, his faith is imputed for righteousness."

units.la: Obiect. V. Quod imputatur nobis ad justitiam, propter id sumus justi. Fides nobis imputatur ad justitiam. Ergo propter fidem sumus justi. Resp. Iterum mutato genere prædicationis, proprio in figuratum, non valet consequentia. Maior est vera de eo, quod imputatur proprie. Minor loquitur de fide nobis imputata ad justitiam correlatiuè: quia non fides proprie, sed objectum fidei, seu meritum Christi fide apprehensum imputatur nobis ad justitiam: secus esset falsa.
units.tr: Objection 5. What is imputed to us for righteousness, on account of that we are righteous. Faith is imputed to us for righteousness. Therefore on account of faith we are righteous. Answer: Again, with the kind of predication changed from proper to figurative, the inference does not hold. The major is true of what is imputed properly. The minor speaks of faith imputed to us for righteousness relatively: for it is not faith properly, but the object of faith, or the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, that is imputed to us for righteousness; otherwise the minor would be false.

units.la: Obiectio VI. Mala opera damnant. Ergo bona opera justificant: quia contrariorum sunt contrarij effectus. Resp. Contraria non sunt paria. Mala opera sunt perfectè mala: bona sunt imperfectè bona. 2. Etiamsi bona essent perfectè bona: tamen non merentur vitam æternam: quia sunt debita. Malis operibus debetur merces ex ordine justitiæ, bonis non item: quia ad ea facienda sumus obligati. Creatura enim obligata est creatori: nec illa ex aduerso creatorem vllis operibus aut modis ad sibi benefaciendum obligare potest. Sed prior responsio sufficit: quia opera bona cum sint imperfecta in hac vita, justificare non possunt.
units.tr: Objection 6. Evil works condemn. Therefore good works justify, because contraries have contrary effects. Answer: Contraries are not equal. Evil works are wholly evil; good works are only partly good. 2. Even if good works were wholly good, they would not merit eternal life, because they are owed. Wages are due to evil works by the order of justice, but not to good works, since we are bound to do them. For the creature is bound to the Creator, and conversely the creature can bind the Creator by no works or means to do it good. But the first answer suffices: since good works, being imperfect in this life, cannot justify.

units.la: Obiect. VII. Qui facit justitiam, justus est. Qui facit bona opera, facit justitiam. Ergo bona opera justificant. Resp.1. Justus est; nempe, coram hominibus: hoc est, faciendo justitiam, seipsum aliis declarat. Coram Deo autem non faciendo justitiam, sed credendo in Filium Dei, justi sumus. Ex operibus enim legis coram Deo non justificabitur vllus viuens. 2. Johannes non docet, quomodo simus justi, sed quales sint justi, nempe facientes justitiam, seu regenerati: quasi dicat: qui est regeneratus, est vere justus, seu se justificatum ostendit.
units.tr: Objection 7. He who does righteousness is righteous. He who does good works does righteousness. Therefore good works justify. Answer: 1. He is righteous, namely before men: that is, by doing righteousness he declares himself to others. Before God, however, we are righteous not by doing righteousness but by believing in the Son of God. For "by the works of the law no living man will be justified before God." 2. John does not teach how we are righteous, but what sort of people the righteous are, namely those who do righteousness, or the regenerate: as if he said, he who is regenerate is truly righteous, or shows himself to be justified.

units.la: Obiectio VIII. CHRISTVS dicit mulieri: Remissa sunt ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multum. Ergo dilectio est causa justificationis.
units.tr: Objection 8. Christ says to the woman: "Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much." Therefore love is the cause of justification.

units.la: Resp.1. Christus argumentatur à posteriore ad prius, ab effectu ad causam. Ex eo, quod mulier Christum multum dilexit, colligit, ei multa remissa esse; sicut debitor maior creditorem multum dilexit; quia ei multum remiserat: quasi dicat quia magnus est beneficij sensus, & magna gratitudo in hac muliere, necesse est magnum ei beneficium contigisse, & multa peccata ei remissa esse. Hunc & non alium esse sensum, patet ex parabola. 2. Non quicquid est causa consequentiæ, est etiam causa consequentis, seu rei; nec particula QVIA semper significat causam, sed sæpe effectum. Non enim sequitur: Sol ortus est; quia dies est. Ergo dies est causa ortus solis. Contrarium potius est verum. Est ergo fallacia consequentis.
units.tr: Answer: 1. Christ argues from the consequent to the antecedent, from effect to cause. From the fact that the woman loved Christ much, he infers that her many sins were forgiven, just as the debtor who had been forgiven much loved the creditor much because he had forgiven him much: as if he said that because the sense of the benefit is great and the gratitude in this woman is great, it must be that a great benefit had come to her and many sins had been forgiven her. That this, and no other, is the sense is clear from the parable. 2. Not whatever is the cause of an inference is also the cause of the thing inferred; and the particle "because" does not always signify a cause, but often an effect. For it does not follow: "The sun has risen; because it is day. Therefore day is the cause of the sunrise." The opposite is rather true. It is therefore the fallacy of the consequent.

units.la: Obiect. IX. Quod non requiritur ad justificationem, non necesse est facere. Bona opera non requiruntur ad justificationem. Ergo non necesse est ea facere. Vel; si necesse est ea facere, requiruntur ergo ad justificationem. Resp. Negatur Maior; quia vnius rei possunt esse plures fines. Etsi enim bona opera non requiruntur ad justificationem, requiruntur tamen ob alias causas, vt Deo simus grati, & ipse per nos celebretur: juxta præceptum: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant bona opera vestra, & glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui in cœlis est. Plura causæ in doctrina de Gratitudine explicantur infra Quæst. LXXXVIII.
units.tr: Objection 9. What is not required for justification need not be done. Good works are not required for justification. Therefore they need not be done. Or: if they must be done, they are therefore required for justification. Answer: The major is denied; for one thing may have several ends. Although good works are not required for justification, they are required for other reasons: that we may be pleasing to God, and that he may be glorified through us, according to the precept: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." The several causes are explained in the doctrine of gratitude below, question 88.

units.la: Obiectio X. Opus Pinehæ dicitur ei imputatum fuisse ad justitiam. Ergo opera justificant. Resp. Est fallacia figuræ dictionis, ex mala interpretatione phrasis: cuius non est sensus, quòd PincPinehas per opus suum fuerit justificatus, sed quod opus Pinehas, licet videretur praeter legem & officium sacerdotis factum, tamen quasi juste ab eo factum, fuerit reputatum, & approbatum Deo.
units.tr: Objection 10. The work of Phinehas is said to have been imputed to him for righteousness. Therefore works justify. Answer: This is a fallacy of figure of speech, arising from a wrong interpretation of the phrase. Its sense is not that Phinehas was justified by his work, but that the work of Phinehas, although it seemed to have been done beyond the law and the office of the priest, was nevertheless reckoned and approved by God as having been done justly.

units.la: Obiect. XI. Decem aurei possunt esse pars in solvendo debito centum aureorum. Ergo etiam bona opera possunt esse pars aliqua justitiæ nostræ coram Deo. Resp. Est dissimilitudo in exemplis. 1. Decem aurei sunt pars integra centum aureorum; & decies multiplicati integram summam totius debiti constituunt. Opera vero nostra non sunt pars integra, sed imperfecta obedientiæ debitæ, & centies millies multiplicata nunquam possunt integram obedientiam constituere. 2. Decem aurei accepti possunt à creditore pro parte debiti: quia de solutione reliqua potest spes esse. Opera vero nostra imperfecta à Deo non acceptantur pro parte justitiæ: quia nulla potest spes esse perfectæ solutionis à nobis præstandæ. Omnis vero imperfectio à lege damnatur.
units.tr: Objection 11. Ten gold coins can be part of the payment of a debt of a hundred gold coins. Therefore good works also can be some part of our righteousness before God. Answer: There is a dissimilarity in the examples. 1. Ten gold coins are an integral part of a hundred, and when multiplied ten times they make up the whole sum of the entire debt. Our works, however, are not an integral part but an imperfect part of the obedience owed, and though multiplied a hundred thousand times they can never make up the whole obedience. 2. Ten gold coins may be accepted by the creditor as part of the debt, because hope may remain of payment of the rest. But our imperfect works are not accepted by God as part of righteousness, because no hope can remain of a perfect payment to be rendered by us. Every imperfection, however, is condemned by the law.

units.la: OBIECTIONES.
units.tr: OBJECTIONS.

units.la: Osiandri contra Iustitiam imputatam fidei.
units.tr: Osiander's objections against the imputed righteousness of faith.

units.la: Obiectio I. Justitia, quam Christus attulit, est æterna: quia Messias adducet justitiam sempiternam. Justitia imputata fidei non est ea justitia, quam attulit Christus.
units.tr: Objection I. The righteousness that Christ brought is eternal, because the Messiah will bring everlasting righteousness. The righteousness imputed to faith is not the righteousness that Christ brought.

units.la: Resp. Negatur Minor: quia justitia imputata est sempiterna, 1. Duratione & continuatione imputationis in hac vita. 2. Perfectione justitiæ inchoatæ. Utraq; enim justitia est Messiæ imputata & inchoata. Utraq; erit æterna. Nam in æternum placebimus Deo propter Christum Filium. Itaque etiam imputatio continuabitur, vel potius mutabitur in justitiam propriam. Inst. Ubi non est peccatum, ibi non habet locum remissio, & imputatio. In vita æterna non erit peccatum. Ergo, &c. Resp. Conceditur totum recte intellectum. Non erit remissio peccati, nempe præteritorum: quia sentis: erit tamen remissio peccatorum præteritorum in hac vita, semper & in omnem æternitatem durabit, hoc est, in æternum non imputabuntur nobis peccata olim remissa. Immò etiam inhærens illa conformitas nostra cum Deo, in altera vita erit effectus imputatæ justitiæ.
units.tr: Answer. The minor premise is denied, because the imputed righteousness is everlasting: (1) in the duration and continuation of its imputation in this life; (2) in the perfection of the righteousness that is begun. For both kinds of righteousness are imputed to and begun in the Messiah, and both will be eternal, since we shall please God for ever on account of Christ the Son. Thus imputation too will continue, or rather will be changed into our own righteousness. Objection. Where there is no sin, there is no place for remission or imputation. In eternal life there will be no sin. Therefore, etc. Answer. The whole argument is granted when rightly understood. There will be no remission of sin, namely of past sins, because [the author's sense is that] there will be nothing left to forgive; yet there is remission of past sins in this life, and it will last always and into all eternity, that is, the sins once forgiven will never be imputed to us in eternity. Indeed, that inherent conformity of ours with God will, in the other life, be an effect of the imputed righteousness.

units.la: Obiect. II. Iehova est justitia nostra. Ergo non justificamur justitia imputata, sed Deus ipse essentialiter habitans in nobis est nostra justitia. Resp. Fallacia figuræ dictionis. In dicto Jeremiæ est metalepsis, effectus pro causa, seu abstracti pro concreto: Iehova est justitia nostra, hoc est, justificator noster: sicut Christus dicitur nobis factus à Deo sapientia, justitia, sanctificatio & redemtio, hoc est, sapientiæ doctor, justificator, sanctificator & redemtor. Justitia, qua Deus nunc nos justificat, non est in nobis, nec est ipse Deus habitans in nobis: quia Deus sic esset accidens creaturæ. Osiander non discernit causam ab effectu, justitiam increatam à creata. Sicut non vivimus, aut sapientes sumus essentia Dei, (hoc enim perinde esset, ac si dicas, nos æque sapientes esse, ac Deus est) ita etiam non justi sumus essentia Dei. Nihil igitur magis est impium, quàm dicere, essentialem justitiam creatoris esse justitiam creaturarum. Inde enim sequeretur, nos habere ipsius Dei justitiam, immò Dei essentiam, & Deos esse.
units.tr: Objection II. Jehovah is our righteousness. Therefore we are not justified by imputed righteousness, but God himself, dwelling essentially in us, is our righteousness. Answer. This is the fallacy of figure of speech. In Jeremiah's saying there is a metalepsis, an effect put for a cause, or an abstract for a concrete: Jehovah is our righteousness, that is, our justifier, just as Christ is said to have been made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, that is, the teacher of wisdom, the justifier, the sanctifier and the redeemer. The righteousness by which God now justifies us is not in us, nor is it God himself dwelling in us, for then God would be an accident of the creature. Osiander does not distinguish cause from effect, uncreated righteousness from created. Just as we do not live or are wise by the essence of God (for that would be the same as saying that we are as wise as God is), so we are not righteous by the essence of God either. Nothing, therefore, is more impious than to say that the essential righteousness of the Creator is the righteousness of creatures. For it would follow from this that we have God's own righteousness, indeed God's own essence, and that we are gods.

units.la: DE SACRAMENTIS.
units.tr: OF THE SACRAMENTS.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXV.
units.tr: QUESTION 65.

units.la: Quoniam igitur sola fides nos Christi atque omnium eius beneficiorum participes facit: unde hæc fides proficiscitur?
units.tr: Since, then, faith alone makes us partakers of Christ and of all his benefits, from where does this faith proceed?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: A Spiritu sancto a, qui eam per prædicationem Evangelij in nostris cordibus accendit, & per usum sacramentorum confirmat b.
units.tr: From the Holy Spirit a, who kindles it in our hearts through the preaching of the Gospel, and strengthens it through the use of the sacraments b.

units.la: a Ephes. 2. vers. 8. & 6, v. 23. Ioh. 3. 5. Philip. 1, 29. b Matth. 28. vers. 19, 20. 1 Pet. 1, 22, 23.
units.tr: a Ephes. 2. vers. 8. & 6, v. 23. Ioh. 3. 5. Philip. 1, 29. b Matth. 28. vers. 19, 20. 1 Pet. 1, 22, 23.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hæc quæstio ostendit cohærentiam doctrinæ fidei & sacramentorum. Fidem enim, de qua hactenus est dictum, Spiritus sanctus ordinariè operatur in nobis per ministerium ecclesiasticum, cuius duæ sunt partes: verbum & sacramenta. Per verbum fidem accendit: per sacramenta accensam fovet, confirmat, & obsignat. Verbum enim se habet ut diploma: sacramenta ut signa diplomati annexa. Diploma est Euangelium, cui annexa sunt sacramenta, tanquam sigilla voluntatis Dei. Quicquid enim in verbo de salute nostra per Christum obtinenda promittitur, id sacramenta tanquam signa & sigilla verbo seu diplomati apposita nobis, ad succurrendum infirmitati nostræ, magis magisque confirmant. Recte igitur nunc de sacramentis, fidei signaculis Euangelio appensis sequitur.
units.tr: This question shows the connection between the teaching about faith and the teaching about the sacraments. The faith of which we have spoken so far is ordinarily worked in us by the Holy Spirit through the ecclesiastical ministry, which has two parts: the Word and the sacraments. Through the Word he kindles faith; through the sacraments he nourishes, confirms and seals the faith that has been kindled. For the Word stands like a charter, and the sacraments like seals attached to the charter. The charter is the Gospel, to which the sacraments are appended as seals of the will of God. For whatever is promised in the Word concerning the obtaining of our salvation through Christ, the sacraments, as signs and seals attached to the Word or charter, confirm more and more to us, to help our weakness. Rightly, therefore, after the sacraments, which are seals of faith appended to the Gospel, the discussion now follows.

units.la: Obiect. Dicitur, quod Spiritus sanctus & verbum efficiant idem fidem, & quod sacramenta eam foveant: An igitur hæc duo nihil inter se differunt? Resp. Multum differunt. Spiritus sansanctus efficit & confirmat in nobis fidem, vt causa efficiens: verbum & sacramenta, vt causæ instrumentales. 2. Spiritus sanctus etiam sine verbo & sacramentis potest efficere fidem: verbum & sacramenta sine Spiritu sancto nihil possunt. 3. Spiritus sanctus vbicunque habitat, est efficax: verbum & sacramenta non item.
units.tr: Objection: It is said that the Holy Spirit and the Word produce the same faith, and that the sacraments nourish it. Do these two then differ in nothing? Answer: They differ greatly. (1) The Holy Spirit produces and confirms faith in us as the efficient cause; the Word and the sacraments act as instrumental causes. (2) The Holy Spirit can produce faith even without the Word and the sacraments; the Word and the sacraments can do nothing without the Holy Spirit. (3) Wherever the Holy Spirit dwells, he is effective; the Word and the sacraments are not so.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXVI. Quid sunt sacramenta?
units.tr: QUESTION 66. What are the sacraments?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Sunt sacra & in oculos incurrentia signa & sigilla, ob eam causam à Deo instituta, vt per ea nobis promissionem Euangelij magis declaret & obsignet: quod scilicet non vniuersis tantum, verum etiam singulis credentibus, propter vnicum illud Christi sacrificium in cruce peractum, gratis donet remissionem peccatorum, & vitam æternam.
units.tr: They are holy signs and seals that strike the eyes, instituted by God for this reason: that through them He may more clearly declare and seal to us the promise of the Gospel, namely that He freely gives the forgiveness of sins and eternal life not only to all in general but also to each believer, on account of that one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Recta methodus explicandi doctrinam de sacramentis requirit, vt primum dicatur de sacramentis in genere; postea in specie de baptismo, & de cœna Domini.
units.tr: The correct method of explaining the doctrine of the sacraments requires that we first speak of sacraments in general, and afterwards, in particular, of Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

units.la: In genere de SACRAMENTIS quæritur I. Quid sint sacramenta. II. Qui sint eorum fines. III. Quid sacramenta differant à sacrificiis. IV. Quid sacramenta commune habeant cum verbo, & quid ab eo-dem differant. V. Quid discrepent sacramenta vetera & noua. VI. Quæ sint partes sacramentorum: & quid signa & res signata differant. VII. Qualis sit signorum & rerum vnio, quæ vocatur sacramentalis. IIX. Qua forma loquendi de sacramentis. IX. Quis legitimus eorum vsus. X. Quid impij in sacramentis accipiant. XI. Quot sint noui Testamenti sacramenta.
units.tr: Concerning sacraments in general, the following questions arise: (1) What the sacraments are. (2) What their ends are. (3) How sacraments differ from sacrifices. (4) What sacraments have in common with the Word, and how they differ from it. (5) How the old and new sacraments differ. (6) What the parts of the sacraments are, and how the signs differ from the thing signified. (7) What kind of union of signs and things is called sacramental. (8) The manner of speaking about the sacraments. (9) The lawful use of them. (10) What the wicked receive in the sacraments. (11) How many sacraments there are in the New Testament.

units.la: I. Quid sint sacramenta?
units.tr: I. What are the sacraments?

units.la: Hic primo nominis, deinde rei definitio consideranda est. Sacramentum latinis dicebatur pecunia, à litigantibus deposita in loco sacro, vel apud pontificem, ea conditione, vt qui sponsione vicisset, suam auferret, victus suam ærario relinqueret: vnde nata est phrasis, contendere sacramento, hoc est, litigare pecunia deposita, &c. Hæc significatio sacramenti huc non pertinet. Est quoque latinis sacramentum forma solennis iuramenti in bello, seu iuramentum militare: sic dictum à sacrando, quod eo iuramento quis consecretur & destinetur huic imperatori, & non alij, ad militandum. Hinc quidam volunt, cæremonias è Deo institutas vocari sacramenta, quod, vt milites illo sacramento militari se obligabant suo imperatori, sic nos vsu sacramentorum ceu solenni iuramento coram Deo, angelis & hominibus, nos obligemus duci nostro Christo. Quæ quidem satis concinna est metaphora: sed puto ex veteribus versionibus latinis ortum esse hoc nomen, in quibus fere vbicunque in contextu græco occurrit μυστήριον, latine redditum est sacramentum. Est autem μυστήριον à μύειν, in sacris instruo, initio: vnde Germanicum [illegible, ~6 letters], derivatur ab μύω, claudo, occludo, proprie os, vel labra: quia, vt inquit Eustathius, oportebat τὰς μυστας μύειν [?] σύμα [?] arcanæ signum, habens arcanam significationem, quod non intelligunt nisi sacris initiati. Signum intelligimus rem & actionem externam, seu cæremoniam diuinitus institutam: quæ rem interiorem & spiritualem designat. Hoc Græci vocarunt μυστήριον, Latini Theologi sacramentum, id est, signum significationem arcanam habens, quam non intelligunt, nisi initiati, & de summis capitibus Christianæ religionis edocti. Eiusmodi signa semper aliqua in ecclesia exstare voluit Deus, quibus & bona Dei voluntas erga homines testata fieret, & vicissim homines fidem suam & obedientiam erga Deum declararent. Hæc de voce sacramenti: nunc ad definitionem rei accedamus.
units.tr: Here the definition of the name must be considered first, and then that of the thing. Among the Latins, sacramentum was the money deposited by litigants in a sacred place or with the pontiff, on the condition that the one who won the wager would take back his own, and the loser would leave his to the treasury. From this comes the phrase contendere sacramento, that is, to litigate over money deposited, and so on. This meaning of sacramentum has nothing to do with our subject. Among the Latins, sacramentum is also the solemn form of oath in war, or the military oath, so called from sacrare (to consecrate), because by that oath a man is consecrated and devoted to this commander and to no other, to serve as a soldier. Hence some hold that the ceremonies instituted by God are called sacraments, because just as soldiers bound themselves to their commander by that military oath, so we, by the use of the sacraments as a solemn oath before God, angels and men, bind ourselves to lead our Christ. This is indeed a rather neat metaphor, but I think the name arose from the old Latin versions, in which almost wherever the Greek text has μυστήριον, it is rendered in Latin as sacramentum. Now μυστήριον comes from μύειν, to instruct in sacred rites, to initiate; hence the German word [illegible, about six letters] is derived from μύω, to close, shut, properly of the mouth or lips: because, as Eustathius says, the initiates had to close their lips [τὰς μυστας μύειν] ... [σύμα] a sign of a secret, having a hidden meaning, which only those initiated into the rites understand. By sign we understand an external thing and action, or a ceremony instituted by God, which designates an inner and spiritual thing. The Greeks called this μυστήριον, and Latin theologians sacramentum, that is, a sign having a hidden meaning, which only the initiated understand, and which are taught about the chief heads of the Christian religion. God willed that signs of this kind should always exist in the Church, by which both the goodwill of God toward men would be attested, and in turn men would declare their faith and obedience toward God. So much for the word sacrament; now let us come to the definition of the thing.

units.la: Sacramenta sunt ritus, seu cæremoniæ à Deo institutæ, in hunc vsum, vt sint signa fœderis, hoc est, voluntatis Dei erga nos, & obligationis ecclesiæ ad pœnitentiam & fidem: & vt sint notæ discernentes ecclesiam ab aliis gentibus & sectis. In Catechesi sic definiuntur: Sacramenta sunt sacra & in oculos incurrentia signa & sigilla, ob eam causam à Deo instituta, vt per ea nobis promissionem evangelij magis declaret & obsignet, &c. Ita sunt membra definitionis. tionis: primum ad sacramentorum genus; posteriora ad eorum differentiam pertinent. Ad genus pertinet, quod dicitur: Sunt sacra, & in oculos incurrentia signa & sigilla, id est, significantia & obsignantia res sacras, ad cultum Dei ac salutem hominum pertinentes. Signum in genere est res praeter speciem, quam ingerit sensibus aliud aliquid ex se faciens in cognitionem venire: vt definit Augustinus: vel; Signum est, per quod intellectus aliud intelligit, aliud sensus percipit. Sic verba sunt signa rerum. Signum & sigillum differunt, vt genus & species. Omne sigillum est signum, sed non contra. Signum certificat & confirmat aliquid ostendit. Signa igitur sunt duplicia: alia tantum significantia, alia etiam confirmantia: hoc est, talia, ex quibus non tantum intelligimus, quid significent, sed etiam argumentamur, & ratiocinamur de re, quam significant: ita vt non relinquamur incerti, an sit verum vel falsum, quod significant: hoc est, confirmamur de certa exhibitione, & perceptione rei significatae. Vtrumque genus in definitione coniungitur: quia vtrunque sacramentis convenit. Sacramenta enim non tantum significant, quid promittatur, sed etiam obsignant, quod promittitur in euangelio. Non sunt tantum signa figuratiua, vel admonitoria, &, vt veteres vocant, ἀποφαντικά, sed etiam signa pactionalia, res in Euangelio promissas & exhibitionem earum obsignantia fidelibus. De circumcisione dicit Deus: Vt sit signum foederis inter me & vos. Paulus declarat: Signum accepit circumcisionem, σφραγίδα, signaculum iustitiae fidei. Idem ergo praestant sacramenta, quod pignora. Significant esse tibi aliquid promissum, & idem tibi confirmant. Ideo additur in definitione: & sigilla.
units.tr: Sacraments are rites or ceremonies instituted by God for this purpose: that they may be signs of the covenant, that is, of God's will toward us, and of the Church's obligation to repentance and faith; and that they may be marks distinguishing the Church from other nations and sects. In the Catechism they are defined thus: Sacraments are holy and visible signs and seals, instituted by God for this reason, that through them He may more clearly declare and seal to us the promise of the Gospel, etc. These are the parts of the definition: the first pertains to the genus of sacraments, the later ones to their difference. What pertains to the genus is what is said: They are holy, visible signs and seals, that is, signs that signify and seal sacred things pertaining to the worship of God and the salvation of men. A sign, in general, is a thing beyond its own appearance which presents itself to the senses and, by itself producing something else, brings that other thing into knowledge; as Augustine defines it: or: a sign is that by which the intellect understands one thing while the senses perceive another. Thus words are signs of things. Sign and seal differ as genus and species: every seal is a sign, but not conversely. A sign points out and presents something; a seal certifies and confirms. Signs are therefore of two kinds: some only signify, others also confirm, that is, such that from them we not only understand what they mean but also reason and infer about the thing they signify, so that we are not left uncertain whether what they signify is true or false; that is, we are assured of the actual giving and receiving of the thing signified. Both kinds are joined in the definition, because both belong to sacraments. For sacraments not only signify what is promised, but also seal what is promised in the Gospel. They are not merely figurative or admonitory signs, or, as the ancients call them, apophantic, but also covenant signs, which seal to believers the things promised in the Gospel and their bestowal. God says of circumcision: That it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you. Paul declares: He received the sign of circumcision, [σφραγίδα], a seal of the righteousness of faith. Sacraments therefore do the same work as pledges: they signify that something is promised to you, and at the same time they confirm it to you. Hence the words and seals are added in the definition.

units.la: Haec signa & sigilla vocantur sacra, 1. Quia nobis dantur a Deo. 2. Quia ad sacrum vsum dantur. Res sacrae sunt duplices. 1. Quae nobis praestantur a Deo. 2. Quae Deo praestantur a nobis. Dicuntur signa in oculos incurrentia, hoc est, visibilia. Talia enim debent esse, vt res invisibiles significent. Si enim debent esse adminicula fidei, oportet percipi externo sensu, quo monetur sensus internus. Quod enim non vides, non est tibi signum. Qui facit signum invisibile, implicat contradictionem, & facit signum non signum. Res sunt invisibiles, non signa: alioqui signa non possent significare res, multo minus confirmare: quia incertum confirmaretur per aeque incertum. Hinc veteres sacramentum ita definiunt: Sacramentum est signum visibile invisibilis gratiae.
units.tr: These signs and seals are called holy (1) because they are given to us by God, and (2) because they are given for a holy use. Holy things are of two kinds: (1) those which God bestows on us, and (2) those which we render to God. They are called signs that strike the eyes, that is, visible. For they must be such in order to signify invisible things. If they are to be aids to faith, they must be perceived by an outward sense, by which the inner sense is admonished. For what you do not see is not a sign to you. Whoever makes an invisible sign involves a contradiction and makes a sign not a sign. The things are invisible, not the signs; otherwise the signs could not signify things, much less confirm them, since what is uncertain would be confirmed by what is equally uncertain. Hence the ancients define a sacrament thus: A sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace.

units.la: Ad differentiam sacramentorum pertinet 1. quod sunt instituta à Deo. 2. Instituta ideo, vt per ea nobis Deus declaret & obsignet propromissionem euangelij. Prior differentia est generica, quàm sacramenta communem habent cum aliis signis à Deo datis, tum vniuersalibus: vt est iris: tum particularibus, vt fuit vellus Gideonis primùm rore madens: deinde siccum: contactus linguæ Esaiæ per prunam ardentem, &c. Posterior est specifica, à fine principali sumta, qua sacramenta à reliquo signorum sacrorum genere discernuntur.
units.tr: The difference of sacraments pertains to (1) that they are instituted by God, and (2) that they are instituted so that through them God may declare and seal to us the promise of the Gospel. The first difference is generic, which sacraments share both with other signs given by God, universal ones such as the rainbow, and particular ones such as the fleece of Gideon, first wet with dew and then dry, or the touch of Isaiah's lips by a burning coal, and so on. The second is specific, taken from the principal end, by which sacraments are distinguished from the rest of the kind of holy signs.

units.la: A solo Deo instituta esse hæc signa, certum est. Sicut enim Deus solus potest pronunciare de sua voluntate, & dare nobis promissionem gratiæ: sic solus per sacramenta nobis eam promissionem potest confirmare. Solus igitur Deus habet authoritatem instituendi sacramenta. Patet etiam ex eo, quod sacramentum instituere, duo complectitur, 1. Præcipere Ecclesiæ certum ritum ac cæremoniam. 2. Huic ritui addere promissionem gratiæ Dei: quod legitimè utentibus hoc signo, dare velit significatam. Hæc autem sunt solius Dei. Nam, vt remissio peccatorum, & receptio in gratiam, est solius Dei: sic etiam eius promissio. Et vt solus Deus instituit sibi cultum publicum: sic solus confirmare nobis potest per cultum publicum, hoc est, per ministerium verbi & per sacramenta, promissionem gratiæ, de accipiendis omnibus beneficiis ad salutem necessariis, quæ per cæremonias sacramentorum significantur & confirmantur.
units.tr: That these signs were instituted by God alone is certain. For just as God alone can declare His own will and give us the promise of grace, so He alone can confirm that promise to us through sacraments. Therefore God alone has the authority to institute sacraments. This is also clear from the fact that to institute a sacrament involves two things: (1) to prescribe to the Church a certain rite and ceremony; (2) to add to this rite a promise of God's grace, that He wishes to give the signified thing to those who use this sign lawfully. But these things belong to God alone. For just as the forgiveness of sins and reception into grace belong to God alone, so does His promise of them. And just as God alone instituted public worship for Himself, so He alone can confirm to us, through public worship, that is, through the ministry of the Word and through the sacraments, the promise of grace to receive all the blessings necessary for salvation, which are signified and confirmed by the ceremonies of the sacraments.

units.la: Promissio Euangelij vocatur promissio gratiæ: quia Deus eam nobis in Euangelio principaliter promittit. Huius promissionis etiam fit mentio in definitione, vt sacramentorum differentia specifica, qua ab aliis signis diuinis discernuntur, melius intelligatur: quia etiam aliarum rerum promissiones Deus dedit hominibus & signis confirmauit. Sacramenta verò sunt signa promissionis, non cuiusvis, sed gratiæ: & non tantum ad vnam personam, sicut contactus labiorum Esaiæ, sed ad totam ecclesiam pertinentis.
units.tr: The promise of the Gospel is called the promise of grace, because God principally promises it to us in the Gospel. Mention of this promise is also made in the definition, as the specific difference of sacraments by which they are distinguished from other divine signs, so that this may be better understood. For God has also given promises about other things to human beings and confirmed them with signs. Sacraments, however, are signs of a promise, not of just any promise but of grace, and they pertain not merely to one person, like the touching of Isaiah's lips, but to the whole Church.

units.la: Eam promissionem in euangelio datam per sacramenta nobis magis declarat: nempe, per analogiam signorum cum rebus, quæ per ea significantur: sicut similitudo declarat id, cuius est similitudo, fit perspicuum, & quidem magis, quàm sine similitudine: & vt vera similitudo non intelligitur, nisi analogia similitudinis intelligatur: ita nec sacramenta, nisi analogia signorum & rerum quoties sacramenta vocat picturas.
units.tr: The sacraments declare more clearly that promise given in the Gospel: namely, through the analogy between the signs and the things they signify. Just as a likeness makes clear that whose likeness it is, and does so more than it could without the likeness, and just as a true likeness is not understood unless the analogy of the likeness is understood, so too the sacraments are not understood unless the analogy between the signs and the things is understood. For this reason they are often called pictures.

units.la: Neque tantum declarat, sed & obsignat. 1. Quia siue per verbum, siue per signa nobiscum loquatur Deus, æque est verax: ideoque de voluntate sua certos nos facit, verbo pariter & sacramentis, magis tamen sacramentis. 2. Quia sacramenta sunt signa & pignora, addita promissioni, vt testentur in fide illis vrentes, verè se participes fieri bonorum, quæ promittuntur, & obsignantur.
units.tr: Sacraments not only declare but also seal. (1) Whether God speaks with us through the word or through signs, he is equally truthful, and so he makes us certain of his will, by the word and likewise by the sacraments, yet more by the sacraments. (2) Because sacraments are signs and pledges added to the promise, so that they may testify to those who rely on them in faith that they truly become partakers of the good things that are promised, and so they are sealed to them.

units.la: II. Qui sint sacramentorum fines.
units.tr: II. What the ends of the sacraments are.

units.la: 1. Principalis finis continetur in definitione: vt sint signa fœderis, seu voluntatis Dei erga nos, hoc est, vt Deus per hæc signa testetur, se rem verbo promissam, & signis significatam, fidelibus certò conferre velle: & sic fidem nostram per ea confirmet: seu, vt per sacramenta de voluntate sua efficacius, quàm per nudum verbum, nos doceat, hortetur, atque excitet ad amplectanda bona per Christum parta, & hæc Christi beneficia iisdem sigillis nobis obsignet. Per hæc enim signa & pignora fauoris DEI erga nos Spiritus sanctus non minus, sed magis efficaciter, quam per verbum, corda nostra mouet ad fidem.
units.tr: 1. The principal end is contained in the definition: that they are signs of the covenant, or of God's will toward us. That is, that God by these signs attests that he truly wishes to give to believers the thing promised in the word and signified by the signs, and so by them he confirms our faith. Or, that by the sacraments he teaches us about his will more effectively than by the bare word, exhorts and stirs us to embrace the blessings won through Christ, and seals these benefits of Christ to us by the same seals. For by these signs and pledges of God's favour toward us, the Holy Spirit moves our hearts to faith no less, but more effectively, than by the word.

units.la: 2. Professio & testificatio nostræ gratitudinis erga Deum: seu, obligatio ad obseruandam fidem & bonam conscientiam. Obstringimur enim Deo, nos futuros eius populum, sicut ipse est noster Deus: nos in ipsum crediturós, acceptu/ acturos veram pœnitentiam.
units.tr: 2. The profession and testimony of our gratitude toward God; or, an obligation to keep faith and a good conscience. For we are bound to God, to be his people, since he is our God; to believe in him, and to undertake true repentance.

units.la: 3. Distinctio ecclesiæ ab ethnicis & omnibus aliis sectis. Vult enim Deus ecclesiam suam conspici in hoc mundo, & agnosci ex his sacris signis, vt milites agnoscuntur ex tesseris militaribus, & oues ex notis quas eis pastor inurit. Jubet Judæos circumcidi: alienos ab ecclesia arcet ab esu agni paschalis. Nunc jubet Christianos baptizari, vt eucharistia: vult suum regnum à synagogis Satanæ discerni, propter gloriam suam, & propter consolationem ac salutem nostram. Sicut enim non vult se confundi cum idolis: sic non vult confundi populum suum cum regno diaboli.
units.tr: 3. The distinction of the Church from the heathen and from all other sects. For God wills his Church to be seen in this world and recognised by these holy signs, just as soldiers are recognised by their military badges, and sheep by the marks which the shepherd brands on them. He commanded the Jews to be circumcised, and he kept aliens from the Church by excluding them from eating the Passover lamb. Now he commands Christians to be baptised, and likewise to partake of the Eucharist. He wills his kingdom to be distinguished from the synagogues of Satan, for his own glory and for our consolation and salvation. For just as he does not want himself to be confused with idols, so he does not want his people to be confused with the kingdom of the devil.

units.la: 4. Seruiunt sacramenta conseruationi & propagationi doctrinæ, quia vsum sacramentorum Deus non vult esse sine verbo & explicatione: Cùm interrogauerit te filius tuus cras, dicens, & videns hæc, respondebis ei: In manu forti eduxit nos Dominus de terra Ægypti, de domo seruitutis, &c.
units.tr: 4. The sacraments serve the preservation and propagation of doctrine, because God does not want the use of the sacraments to be without the word and explanation: When your son asks you tomorrow, saying, "What do these things mean?" you shall answer him: "By a strong hand the Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage," etc.

units.la: 5. Sunt vincula dilectionis mutuæ: quia confœderati cum Christo, capite Ecclesiæ, non debent inter se dissidere. Per vnum Spiritum nos omnes in vnum corpus baptizati sumus. Pari ratione sunt vincula publicorum congressuum in ecclesia. Cùm conuenitis ad vescendum, alius alium exspectate: quoniam vnus panis vnum corpus multi multi sumus: quia omnes de uno pane participamus. Studentes seruare unitatem spiritus per vinculum pacis. Vnum est corpus, & unus Spiritus, unus Dominus, una fides: unum baptisma, &c. Nos igitur nequE communionem Christi & sanctorum constituere, neque constitutam conseruare, neq; mortem Domini annunciare vtiliter poterimus, quamdiu de institutione & vsu sacramentorum rixosè inter nos dissensiones fouebimus. Sacramenta enim sunt pignora communionis Christianorum, cum Christo inprimis, deinde etiam inter se.
units.tr: 5. They are bonds of mutual love, because those who are united in covenant with Christ, the head of the Church, ought not to be at odds with one another. By one Spirit we were all baptised into one body. For the same reason they are bonds of public assemblies in the Church. When you come together to eat, wait for one another; for we, being many, are one bread, one body, since we all partake of one bread. Striving to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, etc. Therefore we shall not be able to establish the communion of Christ and the saints, nor preserve it once established, nor proclaim the Lord's death profitably, as long as we nurture quarrelsome disputes among ourselves about the institution and use of the sacraments. For the sacraments are pledges of communion among Christians, first with Christ and then also among themselves.

units.la: III. Quid sacramenta à sacrificiis differant.
units.tr: III. How sacraments differ from sacrifices.

units.la: Tenendum est discrimen inter sacramenta & sacrificia, vt sciamus, quid agamus, cum ad sacramenta accedimus, ne faciamus ex sacramentis sacrificia, hoc est, fingamus, opera nostra ex opere operato placere Deo, & mereri remissionem peccatorum, vt fiat in papatu. Discrimen est duplex. Vnum, in ipso genere. Sacramenta tantum sunt ceremoniae, restantes de voluntate Dei erga nos: sacrificia possunt esse & ceremoniae, & opera moralia: vt sacrificia laudis, gratitudinis, vituli labiorum, eleemosynae, &c. sunt opera moralia, quibus Deo praestamus debitam obedientiam, & honorem, absque ceremonia. Alterum in principali fine. In sacramentis Deus offert nobis sua beneficia: sacrificia sunt obedientiae nostrae erga Deum testimonia. Id patet ex definitione utriusque. Sacramentum est opus, quo Deus nobis dat aliquid: nempe signa, & res signatas. Sacrificium est opus, quo nos Deo praestamus obedientiam, vel cultum, ab eo praeceptum: Seu, est opus nostrum factum in fide, & hoc fine principali, vt Deo praestetur debita obedientia, & honor. Differunt igitur, vt dare & accipere. Sacramenta Deus nobis dat: sacrificia à nobis accipit, &c. Potest vero propter diuersos respectus idem ritus sacramentum esse & sacrificium. Sacramentum, quatenus à Deo datur: sacrificium, quatenus à piis vsurpatur, praestantibus Deo suam obedientiam, & ei gratias agentibus. Itaq; sacramentum & sacrificium saepe idem sunt subiecto: semper autem differunt ratione. Omnia igitur sacramenta, respectu nostri, etiam sunt sacrificia: sed tantum λατρευτικά, non tamen λατρευτικὸν, non pro nobis in cruce oblatum. Hinc ad obiectionem facilè respondetur. Pascha, & aliae veteris Testamenti ceremoniae, erant sacrificia & sacramenta.
