Ergo ne, quàm in praemissis; quia hoc tantum sequitur, eandem rem posse esse & sacramentum, & sacrificium, quod concedimus. Sic baptifbaptismus & cœna Domini sunt sacramenta, & sacrificia diuer-sa ratione. Sunt Sacramenta, & quidem principaliter: quia sunt opus Dei, qui aliquid in iis nobis se dare testatur. Quemadmodum enim per ministros ore suo loquitur: sic ministrorum manibus porrigit nobis sacramenta, & nos ex manibus illorum, tanquam ex Dei manibus, illa accipimus. Sacrificia verò sunt minus principaliter, quatenus sunt opus nostrum, quod Deo præstamus, hoc est, quatenus ex Dei mandato symbola sacra reuerenter accipimus, atque ita obedientiam nostram erga Deum declaramus.
units.tr: We must hold to the distinction between sacraments and sacrifices, so that we know what we are doing when we come to the sacraments, and do not make sacraments into sacrifices, that is, imagine that our works please God and merit forgiveness of sins ex opere operato, as is done in Papacy. The distinction is twofold. The first lies in the genus itself: sacraments are only ceremonies, resting on God's will toward us; sacrifices may be both ceremonies and moral works, such as sacrifices of praise, thanksgiving, the calves of the lips, alms, etc., which are moral works by which we render to God due obedience and honour, without ceremony. The second lies in the principal end. In the sacraments God offers us his benefits; sacrifices are testimonies of our obedience toward God. This is clear from the definition of each. A sacrament is a work by which God gives us something, namely the signs and the things signified. A sacrifice is a work by which we render to God obedience or worship commanded by him; or, it is our work done in faith, with this principal end, that due obedience and honour be rendered to God. They differ, therefore, as giving and receiving: God gives us sacraments; he receives sacrifices from us. Yet, because of different respects, the same rite can be both a sacrament and a sacrifice: it is a sacrament insofar as it is given by God, and a sacrifice insofar as it is used by the godly, who render their obedience to God and give thanks to him. Thus a sacrament and a sacrifice are often the same in subject, but they always differ in aspect. Therefore all sacraments, with respect to us, are also sacrifices, but only [λατρευτικά] in the sense of acts of worship, not [λατρευτικὸν], the sacrifice offered for us on the cross. Hence the objection is easily answered. The Passover and other ceremonies of the Old Testament were both sacrifices and sacraments. Does it follow from this that...? It follows only what we grant: that the same thing can be both a sacrament and a sacrifice. So baptism and the Lord's Supper are sacraments and sacrifices in different respects. They are sacraments, and indeed principally so, because they are the work of God, who testifies that he gives us something in them. For just as he speaks with his mouth through ministers, so he extends the sacraments to us by the hands of ministers, and we receive them from their hands as from the hands of God. Sacrifices, however, are less principally so, insofar as they are our work, which we render to God; that is, insofar as by God's command we reverently receive the holy symbols and so declare our obedience toward God.

units.la: IV. Quid sacramenta commune habeant cum verbo, & quid ab eodem differant.
units.tr: IV. What sacraments have in common with the Word, and how they differ from it.

units.la: De hoc videatur quæstio sequens catechetica LXVII.
units.tr: On this, see the following catechetical question, LXVII.

units.la: V. Quomodo conueniant, & differant sacramenta veteris, & noui Testamenti.
units.tr: V. How the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments agree and differ.

units.la: Conueniunt. 1. Authore: quia utraque sunt instituta à Deo. 2. Rebus significatis. Nam sacramentis utriusq; testamenti eadem res significantur, promittuntur, & offeruntur fidelibus, remissio peccatorum, & donatio Spiritus sancti, per & propter Christum Iesum Christus heri & hodie idem est, & in secula. Patres in nube & mari baptizati sunt in Mosen, & omnes eandem escam spiritualem comederunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Bibebant enim ex sequenti spirituali petra. Petra verò erat Christus. Per Christum circumcisi estis circumcisione, quæ fit sine manibus, hoc est, in baptismo eadem beneficia nos accepimus, quæ veteres in circumcisione. Pascha nostrum pro nobis immolatum, est Christus. Augustinus: In signis diuersa sunt, sed in re, qua significatur, paria sunt. Omnes eandem escam spiritualem comederunt, spiritualem utique eandem. Nam corporalem alteram: quia illi manna: nos aliud. Spiritualem verò quam nos, &c. Extra Christum igitur, qui est omnium sacramentorum, veteris & noui Testamenti res significata, nemo unquam seruatus fuit, aut hodie seruatur. Unde consequitur, patres in veteri Testamento eandem habuisse κοινωνίαν Christi, quam & nos, & hanc illis non minus per verbum & sacramenta fuisse significatam, quam nobis hodie nouo fœdere significatur. Proinde non solum idololatria est, in sacramentis quærere aliam Christum, aliam κοινωνίαν in nouo κοινωνίᾳ, quàm in verbo: sed & quærere aliam κοινωνίαν in nouo Testamenti sacramentis, quàm quæ fuit in sacramentis veteris Testamenti. Differunt vero 1. Ritibus. Alios enim ritus habuerunt vetera, alios habent noua: quia mutatio signorum facta est Christi aduentu, vt significaretur cessatio veteris, & successio noui testamenti. 2. Numero. Olim fuerunt plura & operosiora: nunc sunt pauciora & faciliora. 3. Significatione. Vetera significabant Christum venturum: noua significant exhibitum. Significatio diuersa est, quoad circumstantiam temporis diuersam. Vetera significabant tempus futurum exhibendi Christi, nostra significant tempus praeteritum Christi iam in carne manifestati. 4. Duratione. Illa debebant durare tantum vsque ad primum aduentum Messiae: nostra durabunt vsq; ad aduentum secundum Messiae, hoc est, vsque ad finem mundi. 5. Obligatione. Vetera tantum Iudaeos seu posteros Abrahae obligabant: nam qui couertebantur ex gentibus, non necesse habebant ea obseruare, vt viri religiosi. Actor. 2. 5. nostra vero totam ecclesiam omnium gentium obligant: Baptizate omnes gentes, &c. Bibite ex hoc omnes, &c. 6. Claritate. Illa erant obscuriora: quia res exhibendas adumbrabant: nostra sunt clariora: quia significant res exhibitas & impletas in Christo. Claritas autem non in signis, sed in promissionibus additis consistit.
units.tr: They agree: (1) in author, because both were instituted by God; (2) in the things signified. For the same things are signified, promised and offered to believers in the sacraments of both covenants: the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit, through and for the sake of Christ Jesus, who is the same yesterday, today and forever. Our fathers were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. "In Christ you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands" (Col. 2), that is, in baptism we receive the same benefits that the ancients received in circumcision. "Our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed for us" (1 Cor. 5). Augustine: "In the signs they differ, but in the thing signified they are equal. They all ate the same spiritual food, the same spiritual food certainly. For not the same bodily food: since they ate manna, we something else. But the spiritual food, which we also eat, etc." Therefore, outside Christ, who is the thing signified of all sacraments, both Old and New Testament, no one was ever saved, or is saved today. From this it follows that the fathers in the Old Testament had the same fellowship [κοινωνίαν] with Christ as we do, and that this was signified to them no less through the Word and the sacraments than it is now signified to us under the New Covenant. Accordingly, it is not only idolatry to seek in the sacraments a Christ other than the one in the Word, or a fellowship [κοινωνίαν] different from that in the Word [κοινωνίᾳ] under the New Covenant; it is also to seek in the sacraments of the New Testament a fellowship different from that which existed in the sacraments of the Old Testament. They differ: (1) in rites. For the old sacraments had one set of rites, and the new have another, because the change of signs was made at Christ's coming, to signify the cessation of the old covenant and the succession of the new. (2) In number. Formerly there were more and more laborious ones; now there are fewer and easier ones. (3) In signification. The old signified that Christ was to come; the new signify that he has been exhibited. The signification differs with respect to the circumstance of time: the old signified the future time when Christ would be exhibited, while ours signify the past time of Christ, now already manifested in the flesh. (4) In duration. The former were to last only until the first coming of the Messiah; ours will last until the second coming of the Messiah, that is, until the end of the world. (5) In obligation. The old bound only the Jews, or the posterity of Abraham; for those who were converted from the Gentiles did not need to observe them, as religious men (Acts 2:5). Ours, however, bind the whole Church of all nations: "Baptize all nations," etc.; "Drink of this, all of you," etc. (6) In clarity. The former were more obscure, because they only foreshadowed the things to be exhibited; ours are clearer, because they signify the things already exhibited and fulfilled in Christ. Clarity, however, consists not in the signs but in the promises attached to them.

units.la: VI. Quae sint partes sacramentorum, & quid signa & res signata differant.
units.tr: VI. What the parts of the sacraments are, and how the sign and the thing signified differ.

units.la: In omni Sacramento sunt duo: signum, & res signata. Signum est elementum, & tota actio externa. Res signata est Christus, cum suis beneficiis, seu communio Christi & beneficiorum eius. Eo-dem recidit, & simplicior est vulgata Sacramenti partitio in Elementum & Verbum: quae est Augustini. Accedit verbum ad elementum: & fit Sacramentum. Unde ad quoduis sacramentum duae essentiales partes requiruntur: elementum, & verbum. Elementum est signum externum cum tota caeremonia, Verbum est promissio gratiae, seu Euangelii, de re significata cuiusque sacramenti, quae est Christus cum suis beneficiis, & horum salutaris communio. Hanc partitionem etiam probat & sequitur Apologia Augustanae Confessionis, dicens: In sacramento duae res sunt: Externum signum: & Verbum promissionis gratia: quae est promissio noui Testamenti.
units.tr: In every sacrament there are two things: the sign and the thing signified. The sign is the element and the whole external action. The thing signified is Christ with his benefits, or the communion of Christ and of his benefits. This comes to the same thing, and the more common division of the sacrament into element and word, which is Augustine's, is simpler: the word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. Hence two essential parts are required for any sacrament: the element and the word. The element is the external sign together with the whole ceremony; the word is the promise of grace, or of the Gospel, concerning the thing signified in each sacrament, which is Christ with his benefits and the saving communion of these. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession also approves and follows this division, saying: "In a sacrament there are two things: an external sign, and a word of promise of grace, which is the promise of the New Testament."

units.la: Signa & res signata varie differunt. 1. Substantia. Signa sunt corporalia, externa: res sunt spirituales, internae. 2. Modo accipiendi. Signa visibiliter, manu, ore, membris & sensibus corporalis ab omnibus, etiam infidelibus, accipiuntur. Res, sola fide a sollis credentibus. 3. Fine seu visu. Res dantur ad salutem & vitam æternam consequendam. Signa ad confirmandam fidem promissionis de rebus acceptis, vel accipiendis. 4. Res simpliciter omnibus seruandis sunt necessariæ. Signa non simpliciter, nec omnibus, sed iis tantum, qui per ætatem, vel alioqui legitimè iis vti possunt. Non enim priuatio, sed contemtus eorum damnat. 5. Denique in diuersis sacramentis signa sunt diuersa: res perpetuò eædem in omnibus sacramentis.
units.tr: Signs and things signified differ in various ways. (1) In substance. The signs are corporeal and external; the things are spiritual and internal. (2) In the manner of receiving. The signs are received visibly, by hand, mouth, limbs and the bodily senses, by all, even unbelievers. The things are received by faith alone, and only by those who believe. (3) In end, or purpose. The things are given for attaining salvation and eternal life; the signs are given to confirm faith in the promise concerning the things received or to be received. (4) The things are absolutely necessary for all to be saved. The signs are not absolutely necessary, nor for all, but only for those who by age, or otherwise lawfully, can use them. For it is not their lack, but their contempt, that condemns. (5) Finally, in different sacraments the signs are different, but the things are always the same in all sacraments.

units.la: VII. Qualis sit signorum & rerum vnio, quæ vocatur sacramentalis.
units.tr: VII. What the union of signs and things is, which is called sacramental.

units.la: Ex partitione Sacramenti in signum & rem signatam, pata est operosa quæstio, de vnione signi & rei signatæ: quæ ex partitione sacramenti juxta Augustinum, in elementum & verbum, est breuis & facilis. Harum enim partium vnio est essentialis, quasi materiæ & formæ, ex institutione diuina dependens: & qua res signata verbo promissionis declaratur & offertur: verbum autem promissionis postulat fidem, vt res signata accipiatur. Nulla hic manet quæstio, quomodo res signata cum signis, sed potius, quomodo cum vtentibus vniatur, hoc est, ab iisdem percipiatur, nempe per fidem promissioni gratiæ signis additæ habitam. De vnione autem signorum & rerum D. Vrsinus ita tradit.
units.tr: The division of a sacrament into sign and thing signified gives rise to a laborious question about the union of the sign and the thing signified. The division of a sacrament into element and word, following Augustine, makes the matter brief and easy. The union of these parts is essential, like that of matter and form, and depends on divine institution. Through it the thing signified is declared and offered by the word of promise, and the word of promise requires faith so that the thing signified may be received. Here no question remains about how the thing signified is joined with the signs. The question is rather how it is united with those who use them, that is, how it is received by them, namely through faith in the promise of grace added to the signs. Dr Ursinus teaches the following about the union of signs and things.

units.la: Vnio in genere, est duarum vel plurium rerum coniunctio, qua fit, vt res illæ aliquo modo fiant vnum. Vnio hypostatica, est duarum naturarum copulatio in vnam personam. In sacramentis copulatio signi & rei, vocatur Vnio sacramentalis. Quæritur, qualis ea sit. Papistæ in cœna fingunt conuersionem signorum in res. Sed conuersio non est vnio. Et oportet sacramentalem vnionem talem esse, quæ omnibus sacramentis conueniat: alioqui non erit vnio sacramentalis, sed baptismalis vel cœnalis. Alij volunt esse corporalem copulationem signi & rei, quasi in vnam massam, & coexistentiam vtriusque in eodem loco. Sed huiusmodi coexistentia rei & signi, vel latentia vnius in altero, non est vnio sacramentalis: quia non conuenit omnibus sacramentis. Vnio igitur sacramentalis non est coexistentia rei & signi in eodem loco, ac multo minus transmutatio vnius in aliud: vel vtriusq; consubstantiatio: sed est vnio relatiua, consistens 1. In ἀναλογίᾳ vel similitudine signorum cum rebus signatis, de qua Augustinus: Si, inquit, sacramenta quandam similitudinem earum rerum, quarum sacramenta sunt, non haberent, omnino sacramenta non essent. 2. In coniuncta exhibitione & acceptione signorum & rerum in vsu legitimo, qui non est sine fide: vt postea dicetur. Soli fideles in vsu legitimo à ministris signa, à Christo res accipiunt, & quando ita accipiunt vtrunque, id dicitur vnio sacramentalis.
units.tr: Union, in general, is the joining of two or more things by which those things somehow become one. Hypostatic union is the joining of two natures into one person. In the sacraments, the joining of sign and thing is called sacramental union. The question is what kind of union it is. The Papists imagine in the Lord's Supper a conversion of the signs into the things. But conversion is not union, and the sacramental union must be of such a kind that it belongs to all sacraments. Otherwise it would not be a sacramental union but a baptismal or a eucharistic one. Others want a bodily joining of sign and thing, as if they were one mass, and a co-existence of both in the same place. But such co-existence of thing and sign, or the hiding of one in the other, is not sacramental union, because it does not belong to all sacraments. So sacramental union is not the co-existence of thing and sign in the same place, much less a transformation of one into the other, or a consubstantiation of both. It is a relative union, consisting (1) in the [ἀναλογίᾳ] or likeness of the signs to the things signified, of which Augustine says: "If sacraments did not have some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all." (2) In the joint offering and reception of the signs and things in lawful use, which is not without faith, as will be said later. Only believers, in lawful use, receive the signs from the ministers and the things from Christ. When both are received in this way, this is called sacramental union.

units.la: Probatur 1. Ex natura sacramenti. Sacramentum est vocabulum relatiuum: cuius fundamentum est ritus & cæremonia à Deo institura. Terminus est Christus, & communio Christi cum omnibus beneficiis. Relatio est ordinatio fundamenti ad terminum, hoc est, rituum ad rem significandam. Correlatiua sunt signum & signatum, seu res signata. Hinc manifestum est, vnionem sacramentalem nihil aliud esse, quàm relationem signi ad rem significatam. Vnde regula nascitur verissima: Durante relatione, cohærent res & signa: cessante, separantur: hoc est, manente ordine diuino inter res & signa, illæ cum his exhibentur, & obsignantur: ordinatione verò diuina cessante, nec exhibitio, nec obsignatio per signa fieri potest. 2. Ex analogia sacramentorum. Vnio sacramentalis talis est, vt conueniat omnibus sacramentis. Qualis igitur fuit vnio Christi cum veteribus sacramentis: talis etiam est cum sacramentis nostris; alioqui vel sacramenta illa non fuissent sacramenta, vel vnio illa non fuisset sacramentalis, hoc est, omnibus sacramentis conueniens. At illa non potuit esse alia quàm relatiua. Ergo & nunc est talis.
units.tr: It is proved (1) from the nature of a sacrament. A sacrament is a relative term, whose foundation is the rite and ceremony instituted by God. Its term is Christ and fellowship with Christ with all his benefits. A relation is the ordering of the foundation to the term, that is, of the rites to the thing to be signified. The correlatives are the sign and the thing signified. From this it is clear that sacramental union is nothing other than the relation of the sign to the thing signified. From this a most true rule arises: while the relation lasts, the things and signs cohere; when it ceases, they are separated. That is, while the divine order between things and signs remains, the things are offered and sealed along with the signs. But when the divine ordering ceases, neither offering nor sealing can be made through the signs. (2) From the analogy of the sacraments. Sacramental union is such that it belongs to all sacraments. Therefore, whatever the union of Christ with the old sacraments was, so it is also with our sacraments. Otherwise either those sacraments would not have been sacraments, or that union would not have been sacramental, that is, belonging to all sacraments. But that union could not have been anything other than relative. Therefore it is so now too.

units.la: VIII. De formis loquendi sacramentalibus, scripturæ & ecclesiæ vsitatis.
units.tr: VIII. On the forms of sacramental speech used in Scripture and the Church.

units.la: Formæ loquendi de sacramentis partim sunt propriæ, partim figuratæ. Propriæ sunt, 1. Quando sacramenta dicuntur signa, sigilla, pignora significantia & obsignantia, quod Deus velit dare promissa. Sic circumcisio dicitur sigillum justitiæ fidei. Circumcidetis carnem præputij vestri, vt sit signum fœderis inter me & vos: & hoc signum erit in carne tua. Sic panis est signum corporis Christi. 2. Quando signis diserte additur promissio, quod accipientes signa, accipiant res per illa significatas, vt cum dicitur: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit.
units.tr: Forms of speaking about sacraments are partly proper and partly figurative. Proper forms are (1) when sacraments are called signs, seals, and pledges that signify and seal that God wishes to give the promised things. Thus circumcision is called a seal of the righteousness of faith. "You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you; and this sign shall be in your flesh." So bread is a sign of the body of Christ. (2) When the promise is expressly added to the signs, so that those who receive the signs receive the things signified by them, as when it is said: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved."

units.la: Figuratæ locutiones sunt, 1. quando signis tribuuntur nomina rerum signatarum: vt, Agnus est transitus. Petra erat Christus. Panis est corpus Christi. 2. Vel contra, quando rebus signatis tribuuntur nomina signorum: vt Pascha nostrum est Christus. 3. Quando signis tribuuntur propria rerum: vt, Panis, quem frangimus, est communio corporis Christi: Baptismus abluit peccata, saluat, regenerat. 4. Vel contra: quando propria signorum tribuuntur rebus: vt, Hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis frangitur. Sic dicimur sanguine Christi ablui, Spiritu sancto baptizari, corpore & sanguine Christi nutriri, &c.
units.tr: Figurative expressions are (1) when the names of the things signified are given to the signs, as: "The lamb is the passover." "The rock was Christ." "The bread is the body of Christ." (2) Or conversely, when the names of the signs are given to the things signified, as: "Christ is our passover." (3) When the properties of the things are attributed to the signs, as: "The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ." "Baptism washes away sins, saves, and regenerates." (4) Or conversely, when the properties of the signs are attributed to the things: as, "This is my body which is broken for you." So we are said to be washed in the blood of Christ, to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, to be nourished with the body and blood of Christ, and so on.

units.la: Breuiter: Loeutio sacramentalis est, qua nomen aut proprietas signi imponitur significato, vel contra: per metonymiam sacramentalem: & sensus est, non quod mutetur vnum in aliud, vel quod vnum contineatur in alio: sed quod signum repraesentet, & obsignet, & in vsu legitimo reuera exhibeat, quod est significatum.
units.tr: Briefly: a sacramental expression is one in which the name or property of the sign is imposed on the thing signified, or the reverse, by sacramental metonymy. The meaning is not that one is changed into the other, or that one is contained in the other, but that the sign represents and seals, and in lawful use really offers, what it signifies.

units.la: Causa locutionum sacramentalium est analogia signi & signati: de qua Augustinus: Si sacramenta quandam similitudinem earum rerum, quarum sacramenta sunt, non haberent, omnino sacramenta non essent. Ex hac autem similitudine plerumq; etiam ipsarum rerum nomina accipiunt. Sicut igitur secundum quendam modum sacramentum corporis Christi, corpus Christi est: sacramentum sanguinis Christi, sanguis Christi: ita sacramentum fidei, fides est. Etaliquin is Christi, sanguis Christi: ita sacramentum fidei, fides est. Solent res, quae significant, eius rei, quam significant, nomine significari. Hinc dictum: Petra erat Christus: non enim dixit: Petra significat Christum: sed tanquam hoc esset, quod vtiq; per substantiam non erat, sed per significationem.
units.tr: The cause of sacramental expressions is the analogy of sign and thing signified, of which Augustine says: "If sacraments did not have some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. Indeed, from this likeness the sacraments often also take the names of the things themselves. Thus, in a certain manner, the sacrament of the body of Christ is the body of Christ, and the sacrament of the blood of Christ is the blood of Christ; so also the sacrament of faith is faith." Things that signify are commonly called by the name of the thing they signify. Hence it was said, "The rock was Christ"; for he did not say, "The rock signifies Christ," but as though it were this, which in substance it was not, but in signification it was.

units.la: IX. Quis sit legitimus sacramentorum vsus.
units.tr: IX. What is the lawful use of the sacraments?

units.la: Legitimus sacramentorum vsus est, cùm ritus à Deo instituti vsurpantur à conuersis, tanquam pignora voluntaris Dei erga ipsos. Consistit ergo in his tribus. 1. Cùm obseruantur ritus à Deo instituti sine deprauatione. Insticutio Christi pura est retinenda, quae Antichristus addidit, sunt tollenda, quae abstulit, restituenda. 2. Cùm illi vsurpant ritus, quibus eos Deus instituit. Sacramenta igitur debent vsurpare tantum domestici Christi, hoc est, Christiani, qui professione fidei & poenitentiae sunt cives Ecclesiae. Si credis toto corde, licet tibi baptizari. Iohannes baptizauit confitentes peccata sua. 3. Quando ritus in eum finem vsurpantur, in quem à Deo sunt instituti, de quo supra. Harum conditionum aliqua violata, hoc est, vel ritu, vel fine mutato, sine authoritate diuina, vel signo sine fide vsurpato: manifestum est, non amplius signum cum promissione & ordinatione diuina cohaerere. De persona dicitur: Circumcisio prodest, si legem seruec, &c. De ritus violatione: Connumerantur vobis, hoc non est coenam Domini manducare. De fine: Ingregibus & armentis suis vadent ad quaerendum Dominum, & non inuenient. Nam sacrificia non erant in hunc finem à Deo instituta, ut essent merita salutis. Non igitur licet ritus à Deo praeceptos in alios fines transferre. 1. Quia id non est obtemperare Deo. 2. Quia signis mutatis, aut in alium vsum conuersis, aut pacto non ter-uato: sponsoris consensus amittitur, sine quo nihil confirmat signum vel arrhabo. Itaque extra vsum institutum sacramenta non sunt sacramenta, sed inania spectacula. Legitimus enim vsus consistit in vera fide & pœnitentia: hanc qui non habent, vel ad sacramenta non adferunt, iis sacramenta non sunt sacramenta. Proinde insaniunt, qui infideles dicunt vnà cum signis accipere res per signa significatas.
units.tr: The lawful use of the sacraments is when converted people take up the rites instituted by God, as pledges of God's good will towards them. It therefore consists in three things: (1) when the rites instituted by God are observed without corruption. The institution of Christ must be kept pure; what Antichrist has added must be removed, and what he has taken away must be restored. (2) When those to whom God has given the rites take them up. Accordingly, only the household members of Christ, that is, Christians who by profession of faith and repentance are citizens of the Church, ought to take up the sacraments. If you believe with your whole heart, you may be baptized. John baptized those who confessed their sins. (3) When the rites are taken up for the end for which God instituted them, as was said above. If any of these conditions is violated, that is, if the rite or the end is changed without divine authority, or the sign is taken up without faith, it is clear that the sign no longer holds together with the promise and ordinance of God. Concerning the person it is said: Circumcision profits if you keep the law, etc. Concerning the violation of the rite: They are counted to you; this is not to eat the Lord's Supper. Concerning the end: With their flocks and herds they will go to seek the Lord, and they will not find him. For sacrifices were not instituted by God for this end, that they should be merits of salvation. It is therefore not lawful to transfer rites commanded by God to other ends. (1) Because this is not obeying God. (2) Because when the signs are changed, or turned to another use, or the covenant is not kept, the consent of the surety is lost, and without it the sign or pledge confirms nothing. Thus outside the instituted use the sacraments are not sacraments, but empty spectacles. For the lawful use consists in true faith and repentance; for those who do not have these, or do not bring them to the sacraments, the sacraments are not sacraments. Therefore those are mad who say that unbelievers receive, together with the signs, the things signified by the signs.

units.la: X. Quid impij in sacramentis accipiant.
units.tr: X. What the wicked receive in the sacraments.

units.la: Notandum præcipuè in sacramentis, quid, quibus, quo modo Deus offerat & communicet. Impij, etsi Deus ipsis quoque in sacramentis sua beneficia offert: tamen cum destituan-tur fide, signa quidem accipiunt, sed sine promissione & re. Nu-da igitur signa accipiunt, eaque ad judicium. Id probatur. 1. Quia beneficia Christi tantum in vsu sacramentorum legiti-mo percipiuntur. Legitimum verò vsum negligunt, qui ea sumunt indignè, sine fide & pœnitentia. Ideo Paulus dicit: Quisquis ederit panem hunc, & biberit poculum hoc indignè, reus te-nebitur corporis & sanguinis Christi. Impij autem edunt & bibunt indignè: quia profanant sacramenta. 2. Cui nihil promittitur in verbo: ei sacramenta nihil obsignant. Impiis nihil promitti-tur in verbo. Omnes enim promissiones habent annexam con-ditionem fidei & pœnitentiæ, nec res promissæ, nisi in verbo signis annexo, quod impij infidelitate respuunt, offeruntur & accipiuntur. Sacramenta igitur impiis nihil obsignant, neque conferunt. Signum diplomati appensum nihil obsignat, nisi iis, quibus etiam diploma promittit. Sic Deus beneficia sua non obsignat signis, nisi iis, quibus etiam promittit verbo. Impiis verò Deus verbo nihil promittit, quamdiu manent in sua incredulitate. 3. Fide percipimus res spirituales. Impij non habent fidem. Ergo res spirituales non percipiunt. 4. Contra-dictionem implicat, esse impium: &, accipere rem signatam sacramenti.
units.tr: Chiefly we must note in the sacraments what God offers and communicates, to whom, and in what way. The wicked, although God also offers his benefits to them in the sacraments, nevertheless, since they lack faith, do receive the signs, but without the promise and the thing. They receive therefore bare signs, and these to their judgement. This is proved: (1) Because the benefits of Christ are received only in the lawful use of the sacraments. But those neglect the lawful use who take them unworthily, without faith and repentance. So Paul says: Whoever eats this bread and drinks this cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But the wicked eat and drink unworthily, because they profane the sacraments. (2) To whom nothing is promised in the word, to him the sacraments seal nothing. Nothing is promised in the word to the wicked. For all promises have attached to them the condition of faith and repentance, and the promised things are offered and received only in the word annexed to the signs, which the wicked reject through unbelief. Therefore the sacraments seal nothing to the wicked, nor do they confer anything. A seal appended to a diploma seals nothing except for those to whom the diploma also promises. So God does not seal his benefits with signs except to those to whom he also promises them in the word. But to the wicked God promises nothing in the word, as long as they remain in their unbelief. (3) We receive spiritual things by faith. The wicked do not have faith. Therefore they do not receive spiritual things. (4) It involves a contradiction to be wicked and yet to receive the thing signified by the sacrament.

units.la: XI. Quot sint noui Testamenti signa.
units.tr: XI. How many signs are there of the New Testament?

units.la: De hoc vide quæstionem catechet. LXVIII.
units.tr: On this, see Catechism question 68.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 67.

units.la: Num vtraque igitur & verbum & sacramenta eò spectant, vt fi-dem nostram ad sacrificium Christi in cruce peractum, tanquam ad vnicum nostræ salutis fundamentum, deducant?
units.tr: Do both the word and the sacraments therefore aim at this, that they lead our faith to the sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross, as to the sole foundation of our salvation?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Ita est. Nam Spiritus sanctus docet Euangelio, & confirmat sacramentis, omnem nostram salutem positam esse in vnico sacrificio Christi pro nobis in cruce oblati a.
units.tr: It is so. For the Holy Spirit teaches in the Gospel, and confirms in the sacraments, that all our salvation rests in the one sacrifice of Christ offered for us on the cross. a

units.la: a Rom.6. verf.3. Galat.3. verf.27.
units.tr: a Rom. 6, vers. 3. Gal. 3, vers. 27.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Sacramenta quædam communia habent cum verbo: quædam à verbo diuersa. Communia cum verbo habent,
units.tr: Some sacraments have things in common with the word, and some differ from the word. They have these things in common with the word:

units.la: 1. Quod vtraque Deus constituit.
units.tr: (1) That God has established both.

units.la: 2. Vtraque Deus peragit per ministros ecclesiæ. Loquitur enim nobis in verbo per ministros: in sacramentis per eosdem nobis porrigit symbola. Res autem per symbola significatas exhibet nobis immediatè Filius Dei. Is enim dicit: Accipite Spiritum sanctum. Panis, quem ego dabo, est caro mea. Et Johannes de eo: Ego baptizo vos aquâ, ipse verò baptizabit vos Spiritu sancto & igni.
units.tr: (2) God carries out both through the ministers of the Church. For he speaks to us in the word through the ministers; in the sacraments, through the same ministers, he offers us the symbols. The things signified by the symbols, however, are given to us immediately by the Son of God. For he says: Receive the Holy Spirit. The bread which I will give is my flesh. And John, speaking of him: I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.

units.la: 3. Vtraque sunt organa Spiritus sancti ad fidem in nobis accendendam & confirmandam: & sic vtraque etiam confirmant fidem.
units.tr: (3) Both are instruments of the Holy Spirit for kindling and strengthening faith in us, and so both also confirm faith.

units.la: 4. Præcipuè commune habent, quod vtraque eàdem res nobis Dei nomine offerunt. Vtrisque enim Deus testatur voluntatem suam, vtrisque eadem beneficia, eandem gratiam eumdemque Christum nobis proponit, nec aliud repræsentat & confirmat sacramentis, quàm verbo promittit. Qui verò aliud quæruntin sacramentis, quàm in verbo est promissum, ex sacramentis idola fabricant.
units.tr: (4) Chiefly they have in common that both offer us the same thing in the name of God. For by both God testifies his will; by both he sets before us the same benefits, the same grace and the same Christ, and the sacraments represent and confirm nothing other than what the word promises. But those who seek in the sacraments something other than what has been promised in the word make idols out of the sacraments.

units.la: Differunt autem à verbo sacramenta. 1. Subiecto & natura, Nam verba significant, ex instituto hominum, quibus ita placuit res significati. Symbola significant, quam habent cum rebus significatis, secundum similitudinem, quam habent cum rebus significatis. Item, verba audimus, legimus, &c. symbola visu, tactu, percipimus. Item, verba tantum significant, symbola etiam confirmant.
units.tr: The sacraments differ from the word, however: (1) In subject and nature. For words signify by the institution of men, by which it has pleased people to signify things in this way. Symbols signify by the likeness which they have to the things signified. Likewise, we hear and read words, etc.; we perceive symbols by sight and touch. Likewise, words only signify; symbols also confirm.

units.la: 2. Obiectis. Verbum promissionis & praecepti promiscuè proponitur omnibus, tàm non renatis & alienis ab ecclesia, quàm renatis & membris ecclesiæ: illis quidem, vt regenerentur & crescere incipiant, vel reddantur inexcusabiles: his verò, vt magis credant, & confirmentur. Sacramenta tantum membris ecclesiæ profitentibus fidem & pœnitentiam porriguntur, vt fides iis confirmetur & conseruetur. Item, verbum simul vniuersis & omnibus prædicatur: sacramenta singulis dantur: vnus post alium baptizatur, vni post alium communicatur cœna.
units.tr: (2) In their objects. The word of promise and command is set forth promiscuously to all, both to the unregenerate and aliens from the Church, and to the regenerate and members of the Church: to the former so that they may be regenerated and begin to grow, or be made inexcusable; to the latter so that they may believe more and be strengthened. The sacraments are given only to members of the Church who profess faith and repentance, so that faith may be confirmed and preserved in them. Likewise, the word is preached to all at once and to everyone together; the sacraments are given to individuals: one is baptized after another, and one after another receives the Supper.

units.la: 3. Verbum est instrumentum Spiritus sancti, per quod inchoat & confirmat in nobis fidem, ideoq; verbum debet præire. Sacramenta sunt organa Spiritus sancti, per quæ fidem inchoatam confirmat: ideoq; sacramenta debent sequi. Ratio discrimi-nis est: quia sacramenta sine intellectu non mouent, nec confirmant fidem. Ignoti enim nulla cupido. Itaq; declaratio symbolorum ex verbo necessario debet præmitti. Diuersa tamen ratio est infantum ecclesiæ. In his enim fides à Spiritu sancto non inchoatur, vel confirmatur verbo, sed interna gratiæ efficacia: & quia nascuntur in ecclesia, ad eos etiam pertinet fœdus & promissio: Ero Deus tuus, & semini tuo post te.
units.tr: (3) The word is the instrument of the Holy Spirit, through which he begins and strengthens faith in us, and therefore the word ought to go before. The sacraments are organs of the Holy Spirit, through which he confirms faith already begun, and therefore the sacraments ought to follow. The reason for the difference is that sacraments do not move or confirm faith without understanding; for there is no desire for what is unknown. Therefore the explanation of the symbols from the word must necessarily be put first. The case of the infants of the Church, however, is different. For in them faith is not begun by the Holy Spirit or strengthened by the word, but by the inner efficacy of grace; and because they are born in the Church, the covenant and promise also pertain to them: I will be your God, and the God of your seed after you.

units.la: 4. Verbum adultis tantum prædicatur: Sacramenta quædam etiam infantibus præbenda sunt, vt circumcisio, & baptismus.
units.tr: (4) The word is preached only to adults; some sacraments are also to be given to infants, such as circumcision and baptism.

units.la: 5. Verbum est necessarium & sufficiens ad salutem adultis. Fides enim ex auditu, auditus per verbum Dei. Sacramenta non absolutè sunt necessaria omnibus, nec per se sine verbo ad salutem sufficiunt. Sigilla enim sine diplomate nihil valent, & verissimum est illud vulgatum Bernhardi dictum: Non privatio, sed contemptus sacramenti damnat.
units.tr: (5) The word is necessary and sufficient for salvation for adults. For faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. The sacraments are not absolutely necessary for all, nor do they by themselves, without the word, suffice for salvation. For seals without a diploma are worth nothing, and that common saying of Bernard is most true: Not the lack, but the contempt of the sacrament condemns.

units.la: 6. Verbum potest esse absque sacramentis, vt in prædicatione publica vel priuata, eaque etiam efficaci, sicut apparuit in Cornelio: Sacramenta verò absque verbo nec esse, nec efficiam habere possunt.
units.tr: (6) The word can exist without the sacraments, as in public or private preaching, and that too effectively, as appeared in Cornelius; but the sacraments can neither exist nor have effect without the word.

units.la: 7. Verbum est id, quod confirmatur signis adhibitis: Sacramenta sunt ea, quibus verbum confirmatur.
units.tr: 7. The Word is that which is confirmed by the signs added to it; the sacraments are those by which the Word is confirmed.

units.la: 8. Verbum sermone: Sacramenta gestibus voluntatem Dei declarant.
units.tr: 8. The Word declares the will of God by speech; the sacraments declare it by gestures.

units.la: Denique conuenientiam & differentiam verbi & sacramentorum Augustinus uno verbo expressit, cum dixit: Sacramentum est verbum visibile. Nam cum dicit, sacramentum esse verbum, ostendit conuenientiam sacramenti & verbi, quod idem docet. Cum addit, visibile, ostendit discrimen, quod ritu differant. Breviter: Signa gestibus, verbum sermone nobis declarat volun-
units.tr: Finally, Augustine expressed the agreement and the difference between the Word and the sacraments in one phrase, when he said: A sacrament is a visible word. For when he says that a sacrament is a word, he shows the agreement of the sacrament and the Word, which is the same teaching. When he adds visible, he shows the difference, that they differ in their form of presentation. In brief: the Word declares the will of God to us by speech, the signs by gestures.

units.la: Tract. 80. sup. Ioh. voluntatem Dei. Verbo fides inchoatur & confirmatur: sacramentis inchoata confirmatur. Verbum etiam sine sacramentis Sacramenta non sine verbo prosunt. Sine cognitione adulti non seruantur: sine sacramentis, non tamen neglectis, renasci & seruari possunt. Verbum ad omnes: sacramenta ad solos credentes pertinent.
units.tr: Tractate 80 on John. The faith is begun and confirmed by the Word; the faith begun is confirmed by the sacraments. The Word also profits without the sacraments, but the sacraments do not profit without the Word. Without the knowledge of an adult they are not kept; without the sacraments, yet not neglecting them, people can be born again and be kept. The Word pertains to all; the sacraments pertain only to believers.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXVIII.
units.tr: QVÆSTIO LXVIII.

units.la: Quot sacramenta instituit Christus in nouo fœdere? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: How many sacraments did Christ institute in the New Covenant? ANSWER.

units.la: Duo: Baptismum, & sacram Cœnam.
units.tr: Two: Baptism and the holy Supper.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: In nouo Testamento tantum duo sunt sacramenta, quorum vsus perpetuus & vniuersalis est in Ecclesia, Ambrosio & Augustino consentientibus: Baptismus, qui circumcisioni & reliquis purgationibus successit, & Cœna Domini, quam agnus paschalis & reliquaq; sacrificia præcesserunt. Hæc duo & non plura sunt sacramenta noui Testamenti, quia tantum hæ duæ cæremoniæ institutæ & mandatæ sunt à Christo, addita promissione gratiæ. Argumentum est firmum. Definitio sacramenti tantum duobus ritibus in nouo Testamento competit. Tantum ergo duo habemus sacramenta.
units.tr: In the New Testament there are only two sacraments, whose use is perpetual and universal in the Church, with Ambrose and Augustine agreeing: Baptism, which succeeded circumcision and the other purifications, and the Lord's Supper, which the paschal lamb and the other sacrifices preceded. These two, and no more, are the sacraments of the New Testament, because only these two ceremonies were instituted and commanded by Christ, with the promise of grace added. The argument is firm: the definition of a sacrament applies only to two rites in the New Testament. Therefore we have only two sacraments.

units.la: Papistæ præter hæc duo numerant alia quinque: Confirmationem, pœnitentiam, ordinem, vnctionem extremam, & matrimonium. Sed hæc non sunt sacramenta proprie dicta. Nam confirmatio & vnctio sunt quidem cæremoniæ, sed necà Christo sunt instituta toti Ecclesiæ, nec habent promissionem gratiæ. Confirmatio seu impositio manuum in Ecclesia primitiua fuit symbolum vel miraculosæ collationis Spiritus sancti, quæ citò desiit, vel vocationis ad docendi officium. Vnctionis res significata cum aliis miraculosis donis etiam desiit in Ecclesia. Pœnitentiam seu absolutionem priuatam certum est esse tantum concionem Euangelij, cum signis & appendicibus promissionis gratiæ. Ordo seu ordinatio ministrorum, testificatur quidem Dei præsentiam in ministerium, sed per illud Deus potest efficax esse, etiam personis non placentibus. Matrimonium non est cæremonia, sed opus morale & ciuile. Pontificij id inter sacramenta numerant, quia Ephes. 5, 32. vetus interp. es reddidit sacramentum. Sed potius audiendus est Paulus, quàm latinus interpres. Nemo ignorat, μυστήριον Græcis non minus latè patere, quàm arcanum Latinis. Fateantur ergo Pontificij, omnia arcana esse sacramenta: atque coniugium erit sacramentum septimum: vocatio gentium erit nonum: & pietas decimum: & fortassis plura talia erunt numeranda. Nam omnibus hisce locis μυστήριον Latinus interpres transtulit sacramentum. Paulus verò mysterij nomine vtitur ad designandam Christi & ecclesiæ, non autem mariti & vxoris coniunctionem.
units.tr: The Papists, besides these two, count five others: Confirmation, penance, orders, extreme unction, and matrimony. But these are not sacraments properly so called. For confirmation and unction are indeed ceremonies, but they were not instituted by Christ for the whole Church, and they do not have a promise of grace. Confirmation, or the laying on of hands, in the primitive Church was a sign either of the miraculous conferring of the Holy Spirit, which soon ceased, or of the calling to the office of teaching. The thing signified by unction, together with the other miraculous gifts, also ceased in the Church. It is certain that private penance or absolution is only the preaching of the Gospel, with its signs and appendages of the promise of grace. The order or ordination of ministers indeed testifies to God's presence in the ministry, but through it God can be efficacious even with persons who are not pleasing to him. Matrimony is not a ceremony but a moral and civil act. The Papists number it among the sacraments because the old translator rendered Ephesians 5:32 as sacramentum. But Paul is to be heard rather than the Latin translator. No one is unaware that μυστήριον extends no less widely among the Greeks than arcanum among the Latins. Let the Papists then confess that all secrets are sacraments: and marriage will be the seventh sacrament, the calling of the Gentiles will be the ninth, and piety the tenth, and perhaps many more such will have to be counted. For in all these places the Latin translator rendered μυστήριον as sacramentum. But Paul uses the word mystery to designate the union of Christ and the Church, not the union of husband and wife.

units.la: DE BAPTISMO.
units.tr: ON BAPTISM.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXIX.
units.tr: QUESTION 69.

units.la: Quaratione in Baptismo admoneris, & confirmaris, te vnici illius sacrificij Christi participem esse.
units.tr: In what way are you admonished and assured in Baptism that you are a partaker of that one sacrifice of Christ?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Quod Christus externum aquæ lauacrũ mandauit a: addita hac promissione b, me non minus certo ipsius sanguine & Spiritu à sordibus animæ, hoc est, ab omnibus meis peccatis lauari: quam aqua extrinsecus ablutus sum c, qua sordes corporis expurgari solent.
units.tr: Because Christ commanded the external washing with water a, and added this promise b: that I am washed from the filth of my soul, that is, from all my sins, no less surely by his blood and Spirit, than my body is cleansed of its filth when I am washed externally with water c.

units.la: a Matth. 28, 19. b Ib. Marci 16, 16. Act. 2, 38. Ioh. 1, 33. Matth. 13, 11. Rom. 6, 3.4. c 1 Pet. 3, 21. Marci 1, 4. Luc. 3, 3.
units.tr: a Matt. 28:19. b Ibid.; Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38; John 1:33; Matt. 3:11; Rom. 6:3, 4. c 1 Pet. 3:21; Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: De Baptismo quæstiones præcipuæ sunt: I. Quid sit baptismus. II. Qui sint fines baptismi, seu ad quid sit institutus. III. Quis sensus verborum institutionis. IV. Vsus legitimus baptismi. V. Qua loquendi forma de baptismo. VI. Qui sint baptizandi. VII. Cui successerit baptismus. VIII. Quomodo baptismus cum circumcisione conueniat, & quid ab ea differat.
units.tr: The chief questions concerning Baptism are these: I. What baptism is. II. What the ends of baptism are, or for what purpose it was instituted. III. What the sense of the words of institution is. IV. The lawful use of baptism. V. The form of speech used of baptism. VI. Who are to be baptized. VII. What baptism succeeded. VIII. How baptism agrees with circumcision, and how it differs from it.

units.la: Duæ priores quæstiones pertinent ad quæst. catechet. LXIX. tertia & quarta ad LXXI. quinta ad LXXI. LXXII. sexta ad LXXIII. septima & octaua explicantur in loco de circumcisione, quisequitur.
units.tr: The first two questions pertain to Catechism Question 69; the third and fourth to Question 71; the fifth to Questions 71 and 72; the sixth to Question 73. The seventh and eighth are explained in the place on circumcision, which follows.

units.la: I. Quid sit Baptismus.
units.tr: I. What Baptism is.

units.la: Βαπτισμὸς & βάπτισμα : mersio, ablutio, à verbo βαπτίζω, quod est à βάπτω, mergo, tingo, abluo, adspergo. Orientales toti in aquam mergebantur. Septentrionales in regionibus frigidioribus aqua feré adsperguntur. Sed in hoc parum est situm : modò fiat ablutio per aquam. Ablutio enim est baptismus. Fit autem ablutio utroque modo, & immergendo in aquam, & adspergendo aqua.
units.tr: Baptismos and baptisma [βαπτισμὸς, βάπτισμα]: immersion, washing, from the verb baptizō [βαπτίζω], which comes from baptō [βάπτω], to dip, dye, wash, sprinkle. The people of the East were all immersed in water. In the colder northern regions they are for the most part sprinkled with water. But little depends on this: provided that washing with water takes place. For washing is baptism. Washing is done in either way, both by dipping into water and by sprinkling with water.

units.la: Definitio talis continetur in catechesi : Baptismus est externum aquae lavacrum, à Christo mandatum, addita hac promissione, nos cum baptizamur, non minus certò ab omnibus nostris peccatis, tanquam animae sordibus, ipsius sanguine & spiritu lavari, quàm extrinsecus aquâ abluimur. Aliàs sic definitur : Baptismus est caeremonia, à Filio Dei instituta in novo Testamento, qua tingimur aqua, in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti, ad significandum, nos recipi à Deo in gratiam, propter effusum pro nobis sanguinem Christi, & regenerari ipsius Spiritu: & nos vicissim obligari ad fidem & novam obedientiam Deo praestandam. Seu : Est sacramentum novi Testamenti à Christo institutum, quo fidelibus, in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti aqua baptizatis, obsignatur omnium peccatorum remissio, & Spiritus sancti donatio, & in Christi corpus atque ecclesiam insitio, & ipsi vicissim profitentur, se haec beneficia à Deo accipere, & ei deinceps viuere velle ac debere. Vel breuius : Est institutum à Filio Dei mersio in aquam, cum pronunciatione verborum : Baptizo te in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti, vt sit testimonium, eum, qui sic mergitur, per fidem reconciliari Deo propter Christum, & sanctificari Spiritu Dei ad vitam aeternam. Dicimur in gratiam recipi propter sanguinem Christi pro nobis in cruce & morte effusum : hoc est, propter totam humanam Christi reconciliationem, fide nobis applicatam. Definitionem confirmant haec dicta : Profecti, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti, hoc est, symbolo baptismi testificantes, eos à Patre propter Filium recipi in gratiam, & sanctificari eius Spiritu. Iohannes baptizabat in deserto, praedicans baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit.
units.tr: The definition is contained in the Catechism as follows: Baptism is the external washing with water, commanded by Christ, with this promise added: that when we are baptized, we are washed from all our sins, as from the filth of the soul, no less surely by his blood and Spirit than we are washed externally with water. Otherwise it is defined thus: Baptism is a ceremony instituted by the Son of God in the New Testament, by which we are dipped in water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, to signify that we are received by God into grace, on account of the blood of Christ shed for us, and are regenerated by his Spirit; and that we in turn are bound to render faith and new obedience to God. Or: It is a sacrament of the New Testament instituted by Christ, by which to the faithful, baptized with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, the forgiveness of all sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and engrafting into the body of Christ and the Church, is sealed; and they in turn profess that they receive these benefits from God, and that they wish and ought henceforth to live to him. Or more briefly: It is a dipping into water instituted by the Son of God, with the pronouncing of the words: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that it is a testimony that he who is thus dipped is reconciled to God through faith for the sake of Christ, and sanctified by the Spirit of God to eternal life. We are said to be received into grace on account of the blood of Christ shed for us on the cross and in death; that is, on account of the whole reconciliation of man by Christ, applied to us by faith. These sayings confirm the definition: Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; that is, by the sign of baptism testifying that they are received by the Father into grace for the sake of the Son, and are sanctified by his Spirit. John baptized in the desert, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. He who believes and is baptized will be saved.

units.la: Complectitur igitur baptismus 1. Elementum seu signum, quod est aqua, & tota caeremonia. 2. Verbum mandati & promissionis. Ex mandato signum habet authoritatem confirmandi. Promissio declarat & offert res caeremonia significatas : quae sunt aspersio sanguinis Christi, seu ablutio peccatorum per sanguinem Christi.
units.tr: Baptism therefore comprises: 1. the element or sign, which is water, and the whole ceremony; 2. the word of command and promise. From the command the sign has authority to confirm; the promise declares and offers the things signified by the ceremony, which are the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, or the washing away of sins through the blood of Christ.

units.la: Partes baptismi. Christi, & mortificatio veteris, atque viuificatio noui hominis. Mandatum est. Docete, & baptizate omnes gentes. Verba promissionis sunt: Baptizate in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit, &c.
units.tr: The parts of baptism are: the mortification of the old man and the vivification of the new man, through Christ. The command is: Teach and baptize all nations. The words of promise are: Baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He who believes and is baptized will be saved, etc.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Baptismus in definitione dicitur externum aquæ lauacrum. Ergo statuitur esse nudum signum. Resp. 1. Est fallacia diuisionis: quia cum baptismus dicitur signum externum, non separatur à verbo promissionis, & re significata: in legitimo vsu. 2. Non additur particula exclusiua tantum. Sine promissione quidem baptismus esset nudum signum: & incredulis, qui promissionem fide non accipiunt, reuera tantum est externum aquæ lauacrum, vt Simoni Mago: sed accedit promissio & res signata in vsu legitimo.
units.tr: Objection 1. In the definition baptism is called an external washing with water. Therefore it is held to be a bare sign. Answer 1. This is the fallacy of division: for when baptism is called an external sign, it is not separated from the word of promise and the thing signified, in lawful use. 2. The exclusive particle only is not added. Without the promise baptism would indeed be a bare sign, and to unbelievers, who do not receive the promise by faith, it is in truth only an external washing with water, as it was to Simon Magus; but the promise and the thing signified are added in lawful use.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Etiam in veteri testamento fuerunt baptismi seu ablutiones. Ergo baptismus non est sacramentum noui testamenti proprium. Respond. Magna est dissimilitudo inter lotiones legales & baptismum nostrum. 1. Lotiones illæ non erant symbola ingressus & receptionis in ecclesiam, vt noster baptismus. 2. Baptismi illi erant instituti ad abluendam immunditiem cæremonialem, vt si quis contactu cadaueris, vel rei immundæ se polluisset, immunditiei erat cæremonialis, lotione cæremoniali purganda. Noster baptismus est institutus ad eluendam immunditiem mortalem, hoc est, peccata: ideo in scriptura appellatur ablutio peccatorum. 3. Illi significabant ablutionem per & propter Christum venturum: noster eandem obsignat per & propter Christum exhibitum. 4. Illi solos Iudæos obligabant: noster ad omnes gentes, seu ad totam ecclesiam pertinet. Denique baptismi legales per Christum sunt sublati: quia immunditiés & lex ipsa cæremonialis exhibito Christo cessauit; noster est perpetuus; quia dicitur: Baptizate omnes gentes: &, ero vobiscum omnibus diebus, vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Est ergo fallacia ὁμωνυμίας, quia nihil præter nomen ablutiones illæ cum nostro baptismo habent commune.
units.tr: Objection 2. There were also baptisms, or washings, in the Old Testament. Therefore baptism is not a sacrament proper to the New Testament. Answer. There is a great dissimilarity between the legal washings and our baptism. 1. Those washings were not symbols of entrance and admission into the Church, as our baptism is. 2. Those baptisms were instituted to wash away ceremonial uncleanness: so that if anyone had defiled himself by contact with a corpse or some unclean thing, the uncleanness was ceremonial and was to be purged by a ceremonial washing. Our baptism is instituted to wash away mortal uncleanness, that is, sins; therefore in Scripture it is called the washing away of sins. 3. Those washings signified the washing through and on account of the Christ who was to come; ours seals the same through and on account of the Christ who has been revealed. 4. Those bound only the Jews; ours pertains to all nations, or to the whole Church. Finally, the legal baptisms have been abolished through Christ, because the uncleannesses and the ceremonial law itself ceased when Christ was revealed; ours is perpetual, because it is said: Baptize all nations, and I will be with you all the days, even to the end of the world. Therefore it is a fallacy of equivocation, since those washings have nothing in common with our baptism except the name.

units.la: II. Qui sint fines Baptismi?
units.tr: II. What are the ends of Baptism?

units.la: Principalis & præcipuus finis baptismi est, vt sit confirmatio fidei, hoc est, solennis testificatio, qua Christus testatur, se nos lauate suo sanguine & spiritu; hoc est, se nobis conferre remissionem peccatorum, & Spiritum sanctum, qui nos regeneret & sanctificet ad vitam æternam. seu; vt sit obsignatio promissionis gratiæ, hoc est, iustificationis & regenerationis nostræ, ac testimonium diuinæ voluntatis, quod Deus ipse hæc dona baptizatis in præsentia det, & in posterum semper daturus sit. Ipse enim per
units.tr: The principal and chief end of baptism is that it be a confirmation of faith, that is, a solemn testimony by which Christ attests that he washes us with his blood and Spirit; that is, that he confers on us the forgiveness of sins and the Holy Spirit, who regenerates and sanctifies us to eternal life. Or; that it be a sealing of the promise of grace, that is, of our justification and regeneration, and a witness of the divine will, that God himself gives these gifts to the baptized in the present and will always give them in the future. For he himself, through the hand of the minister, baptizes us and signifies this his will to us.

units.la: Hebr. 9, 10.
units.tr: Hebr. 9, 10.

units.la: Lotiones legales, & baptismus quid differant.
units.tr: Legal washings and baptism: how they differ.

units.la: Mat. 28, 20. per manus ministri nos baptizat, & nobis hanc voluntatem suam significat.
units.tr: Mat. 28, 20. through the hand of the minister he baptizes us and signifies this his will to us.

units.la: Huius diuinæ voluntatis, de conferenda nobis salute, testimonium & confirmationem esse baptismum, patet 1. Ex formula baptismi: quia baptizamur in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti, hoc est, Deo Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto assignamur, & eius proprij esse asserimus. 2. Ex promissione annexa: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Deus igitur hoc ritu testatur, se velle credentes & baptizatos seruare. 3. Ex aliis scripturæ locis. Cui nunc correspondens baptismus nos quoque seruat. Exsurge, baptizare, & ablue peccata tua, invocato nomine Domini. An ignoratis, nos quotquot baptizati sumus in Christum Iesum, in mortem eius esse baptizatos? Sepulti igitur sumus cum eo per baptismum, &c. In quo etiam circumcisi estis circumcisione, quæ fit sine manibus, corpore peccati carnis exuto in circumcisione Christi, consepulti cum eo per baptismum, &c. Ex misericordia sua seruauit nos per lauacrum regenerationis, & renouationem Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: That baptism is a testimony and confirmation of this divine will, concerning the bestowal of salvation upon us, is clear: (1) from the formula of baptism, because we are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; that is, we are assigned to God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and we are declared to be their own. (2) From the promise attached to it: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16). God therefore testifies by this rite that he wishes to save those who believe and are baptized. (3) From other passages of Scripture, to which baptism, corresponding to them, also saves us: "Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord" (Acts 22:16). "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism," etc. "In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, having put off the body of the flesh in the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in baptism," etc. "According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit" (Titus 3:5).

units.la: Ex hoc sine apparet, quare baptismus non reiteretur: quia nimirum est sacramentum receptionis in gratiam, & in fœdus Dei, quod agentibus pœnitentiam semper manet ratum. Ergo post lapsus non est opus nouo baptismo, sed tantum pœnitentia. Item, quia regeneratio semel tantum fit. Semel tantum nascimur, & semel tantum renascimur. Qui enim semel est verè insitus Christo, non eijcitur foras. Eum, qui venit ad me, non eijciam foras. Proinde satis est, baptismum, regenerationis sacramentum, semel duntaxat accipi, maximè cùm regeneratio & salus non pendeat à baptismo, alioqui toties oporteret nos rebaptizari, quoties peccamus. His accedit, quod baptismus noster circumcisioni successit. Circumcisio autem semel tantum fiebat.
units.tr: From this it is clear why baptism is not repeated: namely, because it is a sacrament of reception into grace and into the covenant of God, which always remains valid for those who repent. Therefore after a fall there is no need of a new baptism, but only of repentance. Likewise, because regeneration happens only once. We are born only once, and we are reborn only once. For he who has truly been grafted into Christ once is not cast out: "Him who comes to me I will not cast out" (John 6:37). Hence it is enough that baptism, the sacrament of regeneration, be received only once, especially since regeneration and salvation do not depend on baptism; otherwise we would have to be rebaptized as often as we sin. To this is added that our baptism succeeded circumcision, and circumcision was performed only once.

units.la: Apparet etiam, baptismum Johannis reipsa eundem esse cum nostro baptismo. Johannes enim prædicabat baptismum pœnitentiæ, in remissionem peccatorum, vt crederent in Christum Iesum, qui venturus erat post eum. Talis etiam est noster, nisi quod nunc non baptizamur in Christum venturum, sed in Christum exhibitum. Ergo baptismus Johannis & Apostolorum idem est, quoad essentiam: tantum differunt, quoad circumstantiam significandi: quod Johannes baptizabat in nomen Christi passuri & resuscitandi: Apostoli baptizarunt in nomen Christi passi & resuscitati: alioqui dicendum esset, baptismum nostrum non esse eundem cum baptismo Christi. Christus enim à Johanne est baptizatus. Obiect. Johannes dicit: Ego baptizo aqua. aquâ. Ergo fuit tantum aquæ baptismus. Resp. Johannes distinguit ministerium suum ab efficacia Christi in baptismo: alioqui rursus sequeretur, Christum tantum fuisse baptizatum aquâ, & nos etiam tantum baptizari aqua, vel non habere eundem baptismum cum Christo.
units.tr: It also appears that the baptism of John is in fact the same as our baptism. For John preached the baptism of repentance, for the remission of sins, that they might believe in Christ Jesus, who was to come after him. Ours is of the same kind, except that now we are not baptized into Christ who is to come, but into Christ who has been revealed. Therefore the baptism of John and of the Apostles is the same in essence; they differ only in the circumstance of what is signified: John baptized into the name of Christ who was to suffer and rise again; the Apostles baptized into the name of Christ who has suffered and risen again. Otherwise it would have to be said that our baptism is not the same as the baptism of Christ. For Christ was baptized by John. Objection. John says: "I baptize with water." Therefore it was only a baptism of water. Reply. John distinguishes his ministry from the efficacy of Christ in baptism; otherwise it would again follow that Christ was baptized only with water, and that we too are baptized only with water, or else that we do not have the same baptism as Christ.

units.la: Secundus finis, est testificatio officij nostri erga Deum, seu obligatio nostri & ecclesiæ ad gratitudinem, hoc est, ad fidem ac poenitentiam. Ad fidem: vt hunc solum Deum, qui est æternus Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, & Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, in cuius nomen baptizamur, agnoscamus pro vero Deo, & eum solum colamus, & beneficia oblata fide amplectamur. Ad poenitentiam: vt per omnem vitam hoc ritu admoniti, nos sanguine Filij Dei ablutos, & Spiritu eius renatos esse, gratitudinis ergo in vitæ novitate ambulemus: secundū dicta: Iohannes praedicabat baptismum poenitentiæ. Hæc eratis nonnulli, sed abluti estis, &c. Qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo adhuc vivemus in eo? An ignoratis, quotquot baptizati sumus in Christum Iesum, in mortem eius esse baptizatos? Sepulti ergo sumus cum eo per baptismum in mortem, vt sicut excitatus est Christus ex mortuis, in gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus. Baptizari in mortem Christi, est baptizari, 1. Vt simus participes omnium beneficiorum mortis Christi, non secus atq; si ipsi mortui essemus. 2. Vt moriamur etiam nos, hoc est, virtute mortis Christi concupiscentias carnis mortificemus, & cum Christo in vitam novam resurgamus. Nam in baptismo Deus promittit nobis mortificationem, & ad eandem nos obligat.
units.tr: The second end is the testimony of our duty toward God, or the obligation of ourselves and of the Church to gratitude, that is, to faith and repentance. To faith: that we may acknowledge this one God, who is the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, into whose name we are baptized, as the true God, and worship him alone, and embrace with faith the benefits offered to us. To repentance: that, admonished by this rite throughout our whole life, knowing that we have been washed by the blood of the Son of God and reborn by his Spirit, we may walk in newness of life out of gratitude, according to the words: "John preached the baptism of repentance" (Mark 1:4). "Such were some of you, but you were washed," etc. (1 Cor. 6:11). "We who have died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so also we might walk in newness of life" (Rom. 6:2–4). To be baptized into the death of Christ means to be baptized: (1) so that we may share in all the benefits of the death of Christ, just as if we ourselves had died; (2) so that we too may die, that is, by the power of Christ's death we may mortify the lusts of the flesh and rise with Christ into a new life. For in baptism God promises us mortification, and binds us to it.

units.la: Tertius, vt sit symbolum ingressus & receptionis in Ecclesiam: quia Deus omnes Ecclesiæ suæ cives vult hoc modo recipi: non baptizatos verò, cum baptizari possent, non vult censeri in Ecclesia.
units.tr: The third end is that it be a sign of entrance and reception into the Church, because God wills that all the citizens of his Church be received in this way; but those who could be baptized and were not baptized he does not will to be counted in the Church.

units.la: Huc pertinent omnia exempla eorum, qui facti sunt Christiani, vt Eunuchus, Cornelius commentariensis Philippicus, Lydia purpuraria, Paulus, &c. quamprimum facti essent Christiani, statim eucharistia baptizati fuerunt: ideo & cœna tum datur baptizatis. Ij enim soli recepti sunt in Ecclesiam.
units.tr: To this belong all the examples of those who became Christians, such as the eunuch, Cornelius the Philippian centurion, Lydia the seller of purple, Paul, etc. As soon as they became Christians, they were baptized at once, and the Lord's Supper was then given to the baptized, for only these were received into the Church.

units.la: De hoc sine loquuntur dicta: Profecti, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos, &c. Verbum μαθητεύσατε, quo CHRISTVS vtitur, proprie est, discipulos facite, baptizantes & docentes eos servare, &c. Sic declaratur à Johanne: Pharisæi audiuerunt, Christum plures discipulos facere & baptizare, quàm Iohannem. Confirmat etiam hunc finem substitutio baptismi in locum circumcisionis, quæ olim fuit sacramentum receptionis in cœtum Judæorum.
units.tr: To this the words speak: "Go, teach all nations, baptizing them, etc." (Matt. 28:19). The verb μαθητεύσατε [mathēteusate], which Christ uses, properly means "make disciples, baptizing and teaching them to observe, etc." So it is explained by John: "The Pharisees heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John" (John 4:1). This end is also confirmed by the substitution of baptism in the place of circumcision, which was formerly the sacrament of reception into the assembly of the Jews.

units.la: QuanQuartus. Vt sit nota discernens ecclesiam ab omnibus aliis gentibus, & sectis in mundo. Hic finis consequitur ad proximum. Qui enim publico sacramento in ecclesiam recipiuntur: eo ipso discernuntur, & hac quasi tessera dignoscuntur à reliqua hominum colluuie. Profecti docete omnes gentes baptizantes eos, & c. quasi dicat: colligite mihi ecclesiam per verbum, & quos feceritis mihi discipulos, toto corde credentes, eos omnes & solos baptizate, & mihi à reliquis separate.
units.tr: Fourth. That it be a mark distinguishing the Church from all other nations and sects in the world. This end follows from the one before. For those who are received into the Church by a public sacrament are thereby distinguished, and by this token, as it were, are set apart from the rest of the filth of mankind. "Go, teach all nations, baptizing them, etc." is as if he said: gather for me a Church through the Word, and baptize all and only those whom you have made my disciples, believing with their whole heart, and separate them from the rest for me.

units.la: Quintus est significatio immersionis in crucem: & consolatio de conseruatione & liberatione ecclesiæ ex ea: baptizatos videlicet mergi in afflictiones, sed & certò ex illis emergere. Hinc afflictiones vocantur baptisma: Potestis eodem baptismate baptizari, quo ego baptizor? Liberationem ex cruce declarat baptismi cæremonia. Nam immergimur quidem, sed non submergimur, aut suffocamur. Huius finis respectu baptismus diluuio comparatur. Vt enim in diluuio Noah cum suis arcæ inclusus, non sine molestiis & difficultatibus maximis seruatus est, reliquis omnibus extra arcam pereuntibus: ita in ecclesia, qui Christo adhærent, etsi premuntur calamitatibus, tamen certo tandem liberantur, reliquis extra ecclesiam, peccatorum & pœnarum diluuio absorptis. Huc etiam pertinet Pauli locus, vbi transitum maris rubri baptismo confert: Omnes in Mose baptizati sunt in nube & mari, &c.
units.tr: Fifth is the signification of immersion into the cross, and the consolation concerning the preservation and deliverance of the Church from it: namely, that the baptized are plunged into afflictions, but certainly emerge from them. Hence afflictions are called a baptism: "Can you be baptized with the same baptism with which I am baptized?" (Mark 10:38). The ceremony of baptism declares deliverance from the cross. For we are indeed immersed, but not submerged or suffocated. With respect to this end baptism is compared to the flood. For as in the flood Noah, shut up with his family in the ark, was preserved, not without troubles and very great difficulties, while all the others outside the ark perished, so in the Church those who cling to Christ, though they are pressed by calamities, are nevertheless certainly delivered in the end, while the rest outside the Church are swallowed up in the flood of sins and punishments. To this also belongs the passage of Paul where he compares the crossing of the Red Sea to baptism: "All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, etc." (1 Cor. 10:2).

units.la: Sextus. Vt significet ecclesiæ vnitatem, & sit confirmatio articuli: Credo ecclesiam catholicam, communionem sanctorum. Per vnum Spiritum nos omnes baptizati sumus. Vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma. Potest tamen hic finis comprehendi sub quarto: quia dum baptismus ecclesiæ membra discernit ab aliis, eadem ei conjungit, & vnit inter se.
units.tr: Sixth. So that it may signify the unity of the Church, and serve as confirmation of the article: "I believe the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints." By one Spirit we were all baptized. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. Yet this end may also be comprehended under the fourth, since while baptism distinguishes the members of the Church from others, it also joins them to her and unites them with one another.

units.la: Septimus. Vt sit medium conseruationis & propagationis doctrinæ de promissione gratuitæ salutis propter Christi mortem: & vt baptizati habeant occasionem discendi doctrinam de authoritate, significatione, & vsu baptismi.
units.tr: Seventh. That it may be a means of preserving and propagating the doctrine of the promise of free salvation through the death of Christ; and that the baptized may have occasion to learn the doctrine concerning the authority, meaning, and use of baptism.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXX.
units.tr: QUESTION 70.

units.la: Quid est sanguine & Spiritu Christi ablui?
units.tr: What does it mean to be washed by the blood and Spirit of Christ?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Est non tantum accipere à Deo remissionem peccatorum, gratis, propter sanguinem Christi, quem is pro nobis in suo sacrificio in cruce profudit a: sed etiam per SpiriSpiritum sanctum renouari, & ipso sanctificante membrum Christi fieri, quo magis peccatis moriamur, & sancte inculpateque viuamus{b}.
units.tr: It means not only to receive from God, freely and on account of the blood of Christ, which he poured out for us in his sacrifice on the cross, the forgiveness of sins a; it also means to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and, through his sanctifying, to become a member of Christ, so that we die more and more to sin and live holy and blameless lives {b}.

units.la: {a} Hebr. 12. verf.24. 1 Petri 1.v.2. Apoc.1.v.5. & cap.22. verf.14. Zach.13,1. Ezech. 36,25. {b} Iohan.1, 33. & 3,5. 1 Cor.6,11. & 12,13. Rom.6,4. Coloss.2.verf.12.
EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Duplex ablutio est in baptismo. Vna externa: quæ fit aqua, Altera interna: quæ fit sanguine & Spiritu Christi. Interna significatur & signatur per externam, & in vsu legitimo semper est cum ea coniuncta. Hæc etiam ablutio duplex est, ablutio sanguinis, & ablutio spiritus. Utraque fit simul, & hac quæstione declaratur. Ablutio sanguinis est condonatio peccatorum, seu justificatio propter effusum sanguinem Christi. Ablutio spiritus est renouatio per Spiritum sanctum. Ablui igitur sanguine Christi, est justificari gratis, propter sanguinem Christi in cruce pro nobis effusum. Ablui Spiritu Christi est regenerari per Spiritum sanctum: quæ regeneratio est mutatio inclinationum malarum in bonas, facta virtute Spiritus sancti in voluntate & corde, ut habeamus odium peccati, & propositum viuendi secundum voluntatem Dei.
units.tr: There are two washings in baptism. One is external, done with water. The other is internal, done with the blood and Spirit of Christ. The internal washing is signified and sealed by the external one, and when baptism is rightly used the two are always joined. This washing is also twofold: a washing by blood and a washing by Spirit. Both happen at the same time, and this question explains them. The washing by blood is the forgiveness of sins, or justification, on account of the blood of Christ that was poured out. The washing by Spirit is renewal through the Holy Spirit. So to be washed by the blood of Christ is to be justified freely, on account of the blood of Christ shed for us on the cross. To be washed by the Spirit of Christ is to be regenerated by the Holy Spirit. This regeneration is the change of evil inclinations into good ones, brought about by the power of the Holy Spirit in the will and heart, so that we hate sin and purpose to live according to the will of God.

units.la: Duplicem hanc ablutionem à peccatis baptismo significari, patet ex dictis: Iohannes prædicabat baptismum resipiscentiæ ad remissionem peccatorum.
