Neque metusiastæ suam sententiam habent ex verbis Christi simpliciter acceptis, quod ex pane fiat corpus Christi, vel, quod panis mutetur in corpus Christi: sed est ipsorum glossa & commentum. Non enim Christus dixit, panem factum esse, vel fieri, vel futurum esse corpus suum, sed simpliciter dixit, panem esse corpus suum. Vnde nulla effici potest mutatio, dummodo verba Christi simpliciter accipiantur. Falso igitur utrique persuadent populo, quod simpliciter proprietati verborum Christi insistant, cùm multipliciter & longissimè ab ea recedant.
units.tr: The Papists invent a change (μεταρρύθμισιν, as they say) at the consecration, or a conversion of the bread into the body of Christ, the accidents alone remaining; and they call this transubstantiation. Others contend for a co-existence (συνουσία) or coexistence of the body in or with the bread. The Lutherans and the Synusiasts alike boast that they take Christ's words simply, but neither makes good what they profess. For the simplicity and propriety of the words is such that nothing must be added to them for their right understanding, nor taken away, and nothing in the letter is to be altered. But those who say that the body of Christ is present with, in, or under the bread, add to Christ's words and depart from simplicity. For if what Christ said must be retained simply, and what he did not say must not be admitted, then surely one must not say: "The bread is at once bread and the body of Christ." Christ did not say this; much less: "The body of Christ is in, with, or under the bread." Nor must one add what they add of their own: "really, substantially, corporeally." For Christ uttered those bare words about the bread: "This is my body." Nor do the Lutherans have their opinion from Christ's words taken simply, that the body of Christ is made from the bread, or that the bread is changed into the body of Christ; it is their own gloss and invention. For Christ did not say that the bread has become, or is becoming, or will be his body, but simply said that the bread is his body. Hence no change can be produced, provided Christ's words are taken simply. Both, therefore, falsely persuade the people that they cling to the simple propriety of Christ's words, when in many ways and very far they depart from it.

units.la: Nos verò simpliciter sine additione & mutatione verba Christi retinemus, quod panis sit corpus Christi, & quidem vērum ac visibile illud, quod pro nobis est traditum. Quia autem hæc verba secundum τὸ ῥητὸν accepta haberent sensum repugnantem fidei Christianæ (si enim panis esset corpus Christi proprie, sequeretur, panem esse pro nobis crucifixum) ideo dicimus, in verbis Christi esse conueniente ἀλληγορία quærendam, videlicet appellari corpus Christi, quia est symbolum corporis Christi: poculum seu vinum in poculo appellari sanguinem Christi, quia est symbolum sanguinis Christi: poculum item vocari novum testamentum, quia est symbolum novi testamenti: sicut baptismus vocatur ablutio peccatorum, & lauacrum regenerationis, quia est symbolum utriusque, quæ proprie sit sanguine & Spiritu Christi. Verus igitur sensus, & vera interpretatio verborum Christi est: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur, id est, hic panis à me fractus, & vobis datus est symbolum corporis mei pro vobis in mortem traditi, & certum sigillum vestræ mecum coniunctionis; ita, vt qui crediderit, & panem hunc ederit, is verè & realiter pascatur corpore meo, pro ipso in mortem tradito. Signo igitur tribuitur nomen rei significatæ, per metonymiam sacramentalem: idque tum propter analogiam
units.tr: We, however, retain Christ's words simply, without addition or change: that the bread is the body of Christ, and indeed that true and visible body which was delivered for us. But because these words, taken according to the literal sense (τὸ ῥητὸν), would have a meaning repugnant to the Christian faith (for if the bread were properly the body of Christ, it would follow that the bread was crucified for us), therefore we say that in the words of Christ a fitting allegory (ἀλληγορία) must be sought: namely, that the body of Christ is called the body because it is the symbol of the body of Christ; the cup, or the wine in the cup, is called the blood of Christ, because it is the symbol of the blood of Christ; the cup likewise is called the new testament, because it is the symbol of the new testament; just as baptism is called the washing away of sins and the bath of regeneration, because it is the symbol of both, which are properly effected by the blood and Spirit of Christ. The true sense and true interpretation of Christ's words, therefore, is: "This is my body, which is given for you," that is, this bread broken by me and given to you is a symbol of my body delivered for you to death, and a sure seal of your communion with me; so that whoever believes and eats this bread is truly and really fed with my body, delivered to death for him. The name of the thing signified is therefore given to the sign, by sacramental metonymy; and this both on account of the analogy between sign and thing signified, and on account of the conjunction of the thing signified with the sign in lawful use.

units.la: Interpretatio orthoxa verbi Christi. logiam signi & rei signatae, tum propter coniunctionem rei signatae cum signo in usu legitimo.
units.tr: Orthodox interpretation of Christ's word.

units.la: In hac sententia indaganda non sequimur philosophiam, aut rationem humanam, ut nos traducunt adversarij, sed adhibemus eas normas, secundum quas omnium sanorum consensione de quauis scripturae interpretatione est judicandum, nempe, secundum analogiam seu regulam fidei, secundum naturam materiae subiectae, & secundum testimonia scripturae idem dicentia.
units.tr: In investigating this sense we do not follow philosophy or human reason, as our opponents malign us, but we use those norms by which, with the agreement of all sound men, any interpretation of Scripture is to be judged: namely, the analogy or rule of faith, the nature of the subject matter, and the testimonies of Scripture saying the same thing.

units.la: Nam trium istarum regularum adminiculo in scripturis indagari solet genuina sententia, quotiescunque a scripto ad sententiam transfire necessitas cogit.
units.tr: For by the aid of these three rules the genuine sense is usually sought in the Scriptures, whenever necessity compels us to pass from the letter to the sense.

units.la: I. Ut nulla interpretatio recipiatur non congruens cum regula fidei, seu pugnans cum aliquo fidei articulo, vel decalogi praecepto, vel expresso scripturae testimonio: quia Spiritus veritatis non pugnat secum.
units.tr: I. That no interpretation is to be received which is not congruent with the rule of faith, or which conflicts with any article of faith, or with a precept of the Decalogue, or with an express testimony of Scripture, because the Spirit of truth does not contradict himself.

units.la: II. Ut analogia congruat cum natura subiectae rei, de qua loquuntur verba, quorum analogia quaeritur. Verbi causa, cum hic quaeritur de coena, quae est sacramentum, videndum est, quomodo Scriptura alibi de sacramentis, & de ipsa coena loquatur.
units.tr: II. That the analogy agree with the nature of the thing subject to which the words refer, whose analogy is sought. For example, when the question concerns the Supper, which is a sacrament, we must consider how Scripture speaks elsewhere of sacraments and of the Supper itself.

units.la: III. Ut considerentur loca similia, quibus vel manifestum & in confesso est, vel ostendi potest, aliis verbis de eadem re eandem tradi doctrinam, quae loco controverso continetur. Si enim de loci alicuius clarioris vel non controversi sententia constet, etiam de controverso loco certi erimus, quandoquidem idem ubique docetur.
units.tr: III. That similar passages be considered, in which either it is manifest and admitted, or can be shown, that the same doctrine concerning the same matter is delivered in other words, which is contained in the disputed passage. For if the sense of some clearer or uncontroversial passage is established, we shall also be certain about the disputed passage, since the same thing is taught everywhere.

units.la: Cum his regulis congruens analogia verborum coenae procul dubio est vera, aliae non congruentes non sunt verae, sed falsae. Atqui nostra illa sententia, quae non nostra est, sed ipsius Christi & Apostolorum, totiusque orthodoxae antiquitatis, ad normas illas omnino congruit. Quare sine dubio est verissima, & Evangelicae veritati maxime consentanea. Accedamus autem ad argumenta, quibus veram esse confirmemus. Ea sunt quadruplicia.
units.tr: With these rules, a congruent analogy of the words of the Supper is without doubt true, and other non-congruent analogies are not true but false. But that our opinion, which is not ours but that of Christ himself and of the Apostles and of all orthodox antiquity, agrees entirely with those norms. Therefore it is beyond doubt most true, and most consonant with evangelical truth. Let us now come to the arguments by which we confirm that it is true. They are fourfold.

units.la: I. Quaedam sumuntur ex ipso contextu & circumstantia institutionis coenae Domini.
units.tr: I. Some are drawn from the very context and circumstances of the institution of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: II. Quaedam ex natura rei subiectae, intelligendo locutionem ut res patitur, hoc est, ex natura omnium sacramentorum.
units.tr: II. Some from the nature of the subject matter, understanding the figure of speech as the thing admits, that is, from the nature of all sacraments.

units.la: III. Quaedam ex analogia articulorum fidei, seu ex collatione partium doctrinae Christianae.
units.tr: III. Some from the analogy of the articles of faith, or from the comparison of the parts of Christian doctrine.

units.la: IV. Quaedam denique ex aliis similibus locis scripturae, quibus eadem res verbis non controversis proponitur.
units.tr: IV. Some finally from other similar passages of Scripture, in which the same matter is set forth in words not in dispute.

units.la: I. Genus argumentorum, quae sumuntur ex contextu & circumstantiis institutionis coenae Domini.
units.tr: I. The kind of arguments drawn from the context and circumstances of the institution of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: 1. Humana Christi natura in prima coena corporali locatione sedit suo loco ad mensam, & nunc est in coelo. Ergo tunc non erat, nec jam est simul corporaliter in pane, vel ad locum panis.
units.tr: 1. In the first Supper Christ's human nature sat in its own place at the table, by bodily location, and now it is in heaven. Therefore then it was not, and now it is not, bodily present together in the bread or in the place of the bread.

units.la: 2. Christus in prima coena non accepit in manus, nec fregit suum corpus, sed panem. Panis ergo proprie & realiter non est ipsum corpus Christi.
units.tr: 2. In the first Supper Christ did not take his own body into his hands and break it, but bread. Therefore the bread is not properly and really the body of Christ itself.

units.la: 3. Corpus Christi est natum ex virgine: panis e farina pistus. Non est igitur realiter corpus Christi.
units.tr: 3. The body of Christ was born of the Virgin; the bread was baked from flour. Therefore it is not really the body of Christ.

units.la: 4. Christus de pane visibili fracto dixit: Hoc est corpus meum: & de poculo visibili distributo: Hoc poculum est novum testamentum in meo sanguine. Non ergo retinetur τὸ ῥῆμα, cum Papistae dicunt: sub speciebus panis & vini continetur corpus meum; & ubiquitarij: in hoc, cum hoc, sub hoc pane est corpus meum: ac multo minus, cum utrique dicunt: corpus meum invisibile, contentum sub hac specie, vel sub hoc pane, est corpus meum. Utrique enim non modo a litera ad glossam manifeste discedunt, sed etiam verba Christi priore glossa foede pervertunt, quasi scriptum sit: corpus meum est sub hoc: posteriore ineptam τραγῳδίαν Christo affingunt, quasi dixerit: corpus meum est corpus meum.
units.tr: 4. Christ said of the visible bread, when he broke it, "This is my body," and of the visible cup, when he handed it round, "This cup is the new testament in my blood." Therefore the words are not retained [τὸ ῥῆμα] as the Papists say, "My body is contained under the species of bread and wine," nor as the ubiquitarians say, "My body is in, with, or under this bread." Much less is the meaning kept when both say, "My body, invisible and contained under this species or under this bread, is my body." For both not only depart plainly from the letter to the gloss, but also pervert the words of Christ shamefully: in the former gloss they make it as though it were written, "My body is under this," and in the latter they attribute to Christ a foolish tragedy [τραγῳδίαν], as though he had said, "My body is my body."

units.la: 5. Corpus Christi, quod in coena manducamus, est pro nobis traditum & crucifixum. Panis non est pro nobis traditus & crucifixus. Panis igitur proprie & realiter non est corpus Christi.
units.tr: 5. The body of Christ, which we eat in the Supper, has been delivered and crucified for us. The bread has not been delivered and crucified for us. Therefore the bread is not properly and really the body of Christ.

units.la: 6. Quomodo poculum est novum testamentum, eo modo panis est corpus Christi. Poculum est novum testamentum sacramentaliter, ut supra est declaratum, & praeterea hac ratione ostenditur, quod novum testamentum proprie non ore bibitur, sed corde creditur: poculum vero ore bibitur. Ergo proprie non potest esse novum testamentum. Eodem igitur modo panis est corpus Christi, nempe sacramentaliter.
units.tr: 6. In the way that the cup is the new testament, in that same way the bread is the body of Christ. The cup is the new testament sacramentally, as has been explained above. Moreover this is shown by the following reasoning: the new testament is not properly drunk with the mouth but believed with the heart, whereas the cup is drunk with the mouth. Therefore it cannot properly be the new testament. In the same way, then, the bread is the body of Christ, namely sacramentally.

units.la: 7. Si panis proprie est corpus, poculum sanguis Christi: necesse est in prima coena sanguinem fuisse separatum a corpore Christi, & nunc utrumque separatum nobis exhiberi, sicut symbola non sunt separata. At neque in prima coena sanguis tum erat extra corpus, neque tunc corpus Christi nobis exhibetur exsangue. Nam Christus tunc nondum erat mortuus, & nunc non moritur amplius. Non igitur proprie, sed sacramentaliter panis est corpus, poculum sanguis Christi.
units.tr: 7. If the bread is properly the body, and the cup the blood of Christ, then it is necessary that in the first Supper the blood was separated from the body of Christ, and that now both are offered to us separately, just as the signs are not separated. But in the first Supper the blood was not then outside the body, nor is the body of Christ now offered to us bloodless. For Christ was not yet dead then, and now he does not die any more. Therefore the bread is the body, and the cup the blood of Christ, not properly but sacramentally.

units.la: 8. Quod Christus ipse comedit & bibit, id non fuit proprie ipsius corpus & sanguis: alioqui seipsum comedisset & bibisset. Comedit autem de pane illo, & de poculo illo bibit: Non bibam posthac de genimine vitis huius. Chrysostomus: Ipse quoque bibit ex eo, ne auditis verbis illis dicerent: quid? igitur sanguinem bibimus? & carnem comedimus? ac ideo perturbarentur. Nam & quando prius de his verba fecit, multi solummodo propter verba scandalum passi sunt. Ne igitur id tunc quoque accideret, primus ipse hoc fecit, ut tranquillo animo ad communionem mysteriorum adduceret. Panis igitur & poculum non sunt proprie corpus & sanguis Christi, sed sacramentaliter.
units.tr: 8. What Christ himself ate and drank was not properly his own body and blood; otherwise he would have eaten and drunk himself. But he ate of that bread and drank of that cup: "I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine" (Matt. 26). Chrysostom: "He himself also drank of it, lest, when they had heard those words, they should say, 'What then? Do we drink blood and eat flesh?' and so be troubled. For when he spoke of these things before, many were offended by the words alone. So that this should not happen then too, he did it first himself, so that he might bring them to the communion of the mysteries with a calm mind." Therefore the bread and the cup are not properly the body and blood of Christ, but sacramentally.

units.la: 9. Recordatio non est corporaliter praesentium, sed absentium. Christus hoc sacramentum instituit in sui recordationem. Non igitur corporaliter est praesens in pane vel in sacramento.
units.tr: 9. Remembrance is not of those who are bodily present, but of those who are absent. Christ instituted this sacrament in remembrance of himself. Therefore he is not bodily present in the bread or in the sacrament.

units.la: 10. Aut non est Christus suo corpore substantialiter in pane, vel panis specie, aut coena non est amplius celebranda. Apostolus enim jubet nos de hoc pane edere, & de hoc poculo bibere, & mortem Domini annunciare, donec veniat. At sine dubio celebratio coenae nondum est intermittenda, sed debet ad finem mundi usque continuari. Christus igitur nondum venit, nec adest corporaliter in pane, vel specie panis.
units.tr: 10. Either Christ is not in the bread, or under the species of bread, substantially with his body, or the Supper is no longer to be celebrated. For the Apostle bids us eat of this bread and drink of this cup, and proclaim the Lord's death until he comes. But without doubt the celebration of the Supper is not yet to be discontinued, but ought to be carried on until the end of the world. Therefore Christ has not yet come, nor is he present bodily in the bread or the species of bread.

units.la: 11. Denique, quomodo in prima coena panis fuit corpus Christi, & discipuli corpus Christi manducarunt, eo modo, & non alio, etiam nunc panis est corpus Christi, & nos corpus Christi manducamus. Nostra enim coena non est alia coena, quam fuit coena discipulorum. At in prima coena panis non fuit naturaliter corpus Christi, nec discipuli corpus Christi oraliter manducarunt in pane, vel in specie panis. Christus enim corporaliter & visibiliter accubuit discipulis, nec in tota actione ullam mutationem est passus. Ergo neque nunc panis naturaliter est corpus Christi, nec corpus Christi oraliter manducamus in pane, vel specie panis.
units.tr: 11. Finally, just as in the first Supper the bread was the body of Christ, and the disciples ate the body of Christ, in that way and in no other, so now too the bread is the body of Christ, and we eat the body of Christ. For our Supper is not a different Supper from the Supper of the disciples. But in the first Supper the bread was not naturally the body of Christ, nor did the disciples eat the body of Christ orally in the bread, or in the species of bread. For Christ reclined with the disciples bodily and visibly, and in the whole action suffered no change. Therefore neither now is the bread naturally the body of Christ, nor do we eat the body of Christ orally in the bread, or in the species of bread.

units.la: II. Genus argumentorum, quae sumuntur ex natura sacramentorum.
units.tr: II. The kinds of argument drawn from the nature of the sacraments.

units.la: 1. Ipsa loquendi forma firmum argumentum suppeditat; panis est corpus Christi. Atqui panis non est sua substantia corpus Christi (ideo enim confecta est transubstantiatio.) Ergo est locutio figurata & sacramentalis, hoc est, talis, quae sacramentis est usitata, & explicata supra in institutione coenae.
units.tr: 1. The very form of the words provides a firm argument: "Bread is the body of Christ." But bread is not, in its substance, the body of Christ (for that is why transubstantiation was devised). Therefore the expression is figurative and sacramental, that is, of the kind customary in the sacraments, as explained above in the institution of the Supper.

units.la: 2. In omnibus sacramentis, quando symbolis nomina, vel propria rerum signatarum, tribuuntur, significatur non praesentia tia rerum corporalis in signis, sed similitudo rerum cum signis, & obsignatio earum per signa, & coniunctio earum cum signis in vsu legitimo. In coena Christus symbolis (pani & vino) tribuit nomina rerum signatarum corporis & sanguinis sui, hoc est corpus meum; hoc est sanguis meus. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 2. In all the sacraments, when the names or proper terms of the things signified are attributed to the signs, what is indicated is not the bodily presence of the things in the signs, but the likeness of the things to the signs, their sealing by the signs, and their conjunction with the signs in lawful use. In the Supper, Christ attributes to the elements (bread and wine) the names of the things signified, his body and blood: this is my body; this is my blood. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 3. Natura omnium sacramentorum est, vt symbola corporaliter, res significatæ spiritualiter intelligantur, & sumantur, & vt res visibiles non sint res significatæ, sed rerum significatarum symbola & pignora. Coena est sacramentum. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 3. The nature of all sacraments is that the elements are understood and received bodily, and the things signified spiritually, and that the visible things are not the things signified but the symbols and pledges of the things signified. The Supper is a sacrament. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 4. Phrases sacramentales sunt sacramentaliter intelligendæ. Verba coenæ: hoc est corpus meum, hoc est sanguis meus, sunt phrases sacramentales. Loquuntur enim de sacramento, & symbolis tribuunt nomina rerum signatarum. Sacramentaliter ergo, seu, per metonymiam sacramentalem sunt intelligenda.
units.tr: 4. Sacramental phrases are to be understood sacramentally. The words of the Supper, "this is my body, this is my blood," are sacramental phrases. For they speak of a sacrament, and attribute to the symbols the names of the things signified. They are therefore to be understood sacramentally, or by a sacramental metonymy.

units.la: Obiect. In verbis coenæ nulla metonymia est expressa. Non igitur talis interpretatio eis affingi debet. Resp. Negatur antecedens. Nam ipse Christus declarationem sacramentalem adjunxit, dicens: hoc facite, id est, hunc panem edite, & hoc poculum bibite, in mei recordationem: hoc est, vt eò admoneamini & confirmemini, corpus & sanguinem meum pro vobis esse traditum, & fusum, & dari vobis in cibum ac potum vitæ æternæ. Item: hoc poculum est nouum testamentum in meo sanguine: id est, sigillum noui testamenti, seu promissionis gratiæ jam impletæ per meum sanguinem.
units.tr: Objection: In the words of the Supper no metonymy is expressed; such an interpretation therefore ought not to be imposed on them. Answer: The antecedent is denied. For Christ himself added the sacramental explanation, saying: "Do this," that is, eat this bread and drink this cup, "in remembrance of me": namely, so that by this you may be reminded and confirmed that my body and blood were given up for you, and shed, and are given to you as food and drink of eternal life. Likewise: "This cup is the new testament in my blood": that is, the seal of the new covenant, or of the promise of grace now fulfilled through my blood.

units.la: 5. Quæ res non est in euangelio promissa, ea non potest per coenam obsignari. Sacramenta enim nihil aliud significant, exhibent, confirmant, obsignant, quàm quod verbum euangelij promittit: ideo dicuntur promissiones visibiles, & visibilia verba. In euangelio nulla promittitur manducatio corporalis, vel oralis, immò disertè damnatur & refutatur à Christo in euangelio, idque duplici argumento. 1. Quod corpus suum paulo post esset ascensurus in coelum, & procul remoturus ab oculis Judæorum. 2. Quod manducatio suæ carnis nihil prodesset. Nec facit ibi distinctionem oralis manducationis crassæ & subtilis, sed simpliciter reijcit omnem manducationem suæ carnis, quæ oris corporis fiat. Non est igitur fingenda in coena manducatio oralis, aut corporalis: quæ euangelio est contraria.
units.tr: 5. A thing that is not promised in the gospel cannot be sealed through the Supper. For sacraments signify, exhibit, confirm and seal nothing other than what the word of the gospel promises; therefore they are called "visible promises" and "visible words." No bodily or oral eating is promised in the gospel; on the contrary, it is plainly condemned and rejected by Christ in the gospel, and for two reasons. First, because he was soon to ascend into heaven and to be removed far from the eyes of the Jews. Second, because eating his flesh would profit nothing. Nor does he there make a distinction between a crude and a subtle oral eating, but simply rejects every eating of his flesh that is done with the mouth of the body. Therefore an oral or bodily eating is not to be invented in the Supper; it is contrary to the gospel.

units.la: 6. Imaginatio de præsentia & manducatione corporali carnis Christi sub pane, toto genere diuersa est à ratione formali sacramenti: Ergo est repudianda. Antecedens probatur: quia nec est signum, nec signatum: quibus duobus omne sacramentum constat. Signum non est; quia non incurrit in sensus, nec habet. haberet quod significaret. Nec potest dici res signata, quia scri-ptura de essentiali transfusione & commixtione realr carnis Christi cum nostris corporibus nusquam concionatur: nec vlla talis esse potest, nisi Eutychianorum & Schwenckfeldij deliria recipiamus. Nam sacramenta tantum de illis bonis testantur, & ea tantū obsignant, quæ in promissione euangelij continentur. Item; quia dicitur, posse fieri etiam absq; fide, & esse communis piis & impiis. Res vero signatæ sacramentorum sola fide, & a sopiis & impiis percipiuntur. Item; quia, si esset res signata, nemo sine ea seruatus esset, aut seruaretur. Nam res omnium sacramentorum sunt eædem, & dantur omnibus saluandis, quia sunt beneficia Messiæ in promissione euangelij comprehensa, quæ sunt eadem omnium, & sine quibus nemo saluatur. Nullus igitur locus substantiali præsentiæ & orali manducationi corporis Christi sub pane vel specie panis in sacramento relinquitur, & nihil reuera est, nisi inane nomen & idolum in mundo.
units.tr: 6. The imagining of a bodily presence and eating of the flesh of Christ under the bread is wholly different in kind from the formal nature of a sacrament; therefore it is to be rejected. The antecedent is proved thus: it is neither a sign nor a thing signified, and every sacrament consists of these two. It is not a sign, because it does not fall under the senses, nor does it have anything that it could signify. Nor can it be called the thing signified, because Scripture nowhere speaks of an essential transfusion and real mixing of the flesh of Christ with our bodies; and no such thing can exist unless we accept the fancies of Eutyches and Schwenckfeld. For sacraments bear witness only to those good things and seal only those things that are contained in the promise of the gospel. Likewise: because it is said that it can take place even without faith, and is common to the godly and the ungodly; whereas the things signified in the sacraments are received by faith alone, and not by the ungodly. Likewise: because, if it were the thing signified, no one would be or could be saved without it. For the things of all the sacraments are the same, and are given to all who are to be saved, because they are the benefits of the Messiah comprehended in the promise of the gospel, which are the same for all and without which no one is saved. Therefore no place is left in the sacrament for a substantial presence and oral eating of the body of Christ under the bread or the form of bread, and in truth it is nothing but an empty name and an idol in the world.

units.la: Obiectio. Corporalis manducatio est symbolum spirituale. Ergo corpus manducationis, & singularis confirmatio fidei. Ergo corpus Christi quoque est sacramentum, res vero significata est invisibilis gratia. Resp. Negatur antecedens. 1. Quia caro Christi sub pane est invisibilis. Non potest igitur aliud invisibile significare, aut fidem confirmare. Sacramenta enim seu signa debent esse visibilia, adeo ut sacramentum (inquit Erasmus) dici non mereatur, quod signo externo non peragitur. In hunc enim vsum à Deo adhibentur, vt efficaciter velut externis sensibus demonstret, quod verbo promittit: & per Spiritum sanctum in cordibus nostris efficitur, vt sint assspectabilia testimonia & pignora adhibitæ & applicatæ promissionis gratiæ. Item: Hincillud Augustini: Sacramentum est visibile verbum. Item: Signum est res praeter speciem, quam ingerit sensibus, aliud aliquid ex se faciens in cognitionem venire. Item: Signacula quidem rerum diuinarum sunt visibilia, sedres ipsæ invisibiles. Et illud Prosperi: Sacrificium ecclesiæ in duobus consistit: visibili elementorum specie: & invisibili Domini nostri Iesu Christi carne & sanguine: sacramento, & re sacramenti, id est, corpore Christi. Nulla igitur res siue actio invisibilis rationem vel appellationem sacramenti tueri potest. Per consequens, qui volunt Christi carnem in, sub, vel cum pane sacramentum esse: visibilem nobis eam, eiusque sensibilem manducationem ostendant in coena, ne à veteribus dissentire videantur. 2. Inter signum seu sacramentum, & signatum, seu rem sacramenti, oportet esse analogiam. Nisi enim sacramenta (inquit Augustinus) haberent aliquam similitudinem earum rerum quarum sunt sacramenta. menta, utique sacramenta non essent. Jam si caro Christi quoque sacramentum est, res vero sacramenti invisibilis gratia: quæ tandem erit inter hæc duo sacramentalis analogia & similitudo? Cum autem nulla esse possit, efficitur carnem Christi sacramentum dici non debere, utpote quæ tam sit res ipsa sacramenti, quam æterna salus, visibili pane tanquam symbolo analogicè significata. Sacramentalis igitur, quæ ore naturali fiat, manducatio, corpus Christi per se consideratum physico aliquo respectu non attingit. Ori enim externa duntaxat symbola in sua propria natura obiiciuntur. Augustinus quærens, quomodo panis fit corpus Christi, & vinum sanguis: Ista, inquit, ideo dicuntur sacramenta, quia in illis aliud videtur, aliud intelligitur. Quod videtur, speciem habet corporalem: quod intelligitur, fructum habet spiritualem, &c.
units.tr: Objection. Bodily eating is a spiritual symbol; therefore it is the body of eating, and a singular confirmation of faith. Therefore the body of Christ also is a sacrament, and the thing signified is invisible grace. Answer. The antecedent is denied. First, because the flesh of Christ under the bread is invisible; it cannot therefore signify another invisible thing or confirm faith. For sacraments, or signs, ought to be visible, so much so that (as Erasmus says) a thing that is not performed by an external sign does not deserve to be called a sacrament. For God employs them for this purpose: that, as it were through the external senses, he may effectively demonstrate what he promises in the word, and that, through the Holy Spirit, it may be brought about in our hearts that they become visible witnesses and pledges of the promise of grace that is applied and made ours. Likewise, hence that saying of Augustine: a sacrament is a visible word. Likewise: a sign is a thing, apart from the appearance it presents to the senses, that causes something else to come to knowledge from itself. Likewise: the seals of divine things are indeed visible, but the things themselves are invisible. And that saying of Prosper: The sacrifice of the Church consists of two things: the visible appearance of the elements, and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. No invisible thing or action, therefore, can maintain the character or the name of a sacrament. Consequently, those who want the flesh of Christ to be a sacrament "in," "under," or "with" the bread should show us that flesh visibly, and its sensible eating in the Supper, lest they seem to dissent from the ancients. Second, there must be an analogy between the sign or sacrament and the thing signified, or the sacrament of the sacrament. For unless sacraments (says Augustine) had some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would certainly not be sacraments. Now if the flesh of Christ is also a sacrament, and the thing of the sacrament is invisible grace, what sacramental analogy and likeness will there finally be between these two? But since none can exist, it follows that the flesh of Christ ought not to be called a sacrament, since it is as much the very thing of the sacrament as eternal salvation, analogically signified by the visible bread as a symbol. The sacramental eating, therefore, which is done with the natural mouth, does not reach the body of Christ considered in itself by any physical relation. For only the external symbols are presented to the mouth in their own nature. Augustine, asking how bread becomes the body of Christ and wine the blood: These things, he says, are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit, etc.

units.la: 7. Communio Christi, quæ in verbo promittitur, & sacramentis obsignatur, non est corporalis, sed spiritualis. At communio Christi, quæ fit in cœna, est eadem illa, quæ in verbo promittitur, & aliis sacramentis obsignatur. Ergo non est corporalis communio in cœna, sed spiritualis. Maior est manifesta. Nam in evangelio nulla alia docetur communio, quam spiritualis, quæ fit per fidem. Minor etiam patet: quia in omnibus promissionibus evangelij eadem beneficia nobis promittuntur, quæ in sacramentis. Sacramenta enim sunt verbum visibile: quia idem promittunt, quod verbum per signa visibilia, & sunt προσεῖς, promissiones eiusdem gratiæ.
units.tr: 7. The communion of Christ, which is promised in the word and sealed by the sacraments, is not bodily but spiritual. But the communion of Christ that takes place in the Supper is that same communion which is promised in the word and sealed by the other sacraments. Therefore the communion in the Supper is not bodily but spiritual. The major premise is manifest: for in the gospel no communion is taught other than spiritual, which takes place through faith. The minor premise is also plain, because in all the promises of the gospel the same benefits are promised to us that are in the sacraments. For sacraments are a visible word, because they promise the same thing that the word promises through visible signs, and they are promises [ὑποσχέσεις] of the same grace.

units.la: 8. Omnium sacramentorum veteris & novi testamenti est eadem significatio, & eadem Christi communio. At omnium aliorum sacramentorum est significatio, vel communio tantum spiritualis. Ergo nec in cœna est alia. Minor est in confesso. Maior explicitur ab Apostolo: Per unum spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus: Omnes in Mose baptizati sunt in nube & in mari: & omnes eandem escam spiritualem ederunt.
units.tr: 8. Every sacrament of the Old and New Testament has the same meaning and the same communion with Christ. But every other sacrament has only a spiritual meaning or communion. Therefore the Supper has no other either. The minor premise is admitted. The major premise is taught by the Apostle: By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body; All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food.

units.la: Obiect. Non est omnium sacramentorum eadem res significata. Nam in baptismo res est ablutio per sanguinem Christi: in cœna est corpus & sanguis Christi. Resp. Res non est diversa, quia idem est sanguine Christi ablui, & sanguinem Christi bibere, ut supra ostensum est. Modus autem significandi unam & eandem rem, est diversus, propter diversa signa, quæ ad unam illam & eandem rem diversam habent analogiam. Sicut ergo in baptismo, item in circumcisione, & paschate significatur, & promittitur res spiritualis, non corporalis: ita & hic in cœna.
units.tr: Objection: The thing signified is not the same in all the sacraments. For in baptism the thing is washing by the blood of Christ, but in the Supper it is the body and blood of Christ. Answer: The thing is not different, because to be washed in the blood of Christ and to drink the blood of Christ are the same, as has been shown above. But the manner of signifying one and the same thing is different, on account of the different signs, which bear a different analogy to that one and the same thing. Just as, therefore, a spiritual thing, and not a bodily one, is signified and promised in baptism, and likewise in circumcision and the Passover, so it is here in the Supper.

units.la: III. Genus argamentorum ex analogia articulorum fidei.
units.tr: III. Kind of arguments drawn from the analogy of the articles of faith.

units.la: 1. Firma sumuntur argumenta ex articulo de veritate naturæ humanæ Christi. Λόγῳ assumpsit naturam verè humanam, nobis per omnia similem, excepto peccato, & eandem propter consolationem & salutem nostram in omnem æternitatem retinet. Natura verò humana nec est infinita, nec potest simul in pluribus locis, aut pariter visibilis & invisibilis, & insensibilis esse. Solius enim immensæ deitatis est, essentia sua in pluribus, & omnibus simul locis præsentem esse, juxta dictum: Nonne ego sum, qui cœlum & terram impleo? & hoc attributo Deus ab omnibus creaturis discernitur. Simul verò visibilis & invisibilis, finita & infinita esse, ne deitas quidem potest, sed perpetuò manet substantia sua invisibilis, incomprehensibilis, & infinita, alioqui non esset immutabilis. Non igitur fingendum est, cùm diceret Christus, hoc est corpus meum, corpus eius tunc simul visibile sedisse ad mensam, & invisibile fuisse in pane: vel nunc simul visibiliter in cœlo versari, & invisibiliter pane comprehendi.
units.tr: 1. Firm arguments are drawn from the article concerning the truth of Christ's human nature. The Word (Logos) assumed a truly human nature, in all things like ours except sin, and keeps that same nature for ever, for our comfort and salvation. But human nature is neither infinite, nor can it at the same time be in several places, or be equally visible and invisible, and insensible. For it belongs only to the immense deity to be present in its essence in several places and in all places at once, according to the saying: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" and by this attribute God is distinguished from all creatures. But neither can even the deity be at once visible and invisible, finite and infinite; rather its invisible, incomprehensible and infinite substance remains forever the same, otherwise it would not be unchangeable. Therefore we must not imagine that, when Christ said "This is my body," his body was at that time sitting at the table visibly and at the same time invisibly in the bread; or that now it is visibly present in heaven and at the same time invisibly contained in the bread.

units.la: 2. Ex articulo ascensionis. Christus verè ascendit, hoc est, sublatus est suo corpore visibiliter & localiter sursum in cœlum, ita ut ipsius corpus non manserit, necjam sit in terra: vel in pane. Vel sic: Christi corpus est finitum, utpote verum corpus. Est autem jam in cœlo. Ergo non est in pane. Minor patet ex articulo ascensionis in cœlum: Aspicientibus ipsis elevatus est. Quaerite quæ sursum sunt, ubi Christus est, &c. Maior etiam patet. Si enim verum corpus Christi est infinitum, est etiam invisibile & insensibile. Ergo quod videbatur, patiebatur, & agebat in terra, non erat verum Christi corpus, sed apparens: & sic omnia quæ de Christo in articulis fidei dicuntur, non fuissent verè gesta, sed tantum fuissent visa fieri: ac proinde nos adhuc essemus in morte.
units.tr: 2. From the article of the ascension. Christ truly ascended, that is, he was taken up with his body visibly and locally upward into heaven, so that his body has not remained, nor is now, on earth or in the bread. Or thus: the body of Christ is finite, being a true body. But it is now in heaven. Therefore it is not in the bread. The minor premise is evident from the article of the ascension into heaven: While they looked on, he was lifted up; Seek those things which are above, where Christ is, etc. The major premise is also evident. For if the true body of Christ is infinite, it is also invisible and insensible. Therefore what was seen, suffered and did things on earth was not the true body of Christ but an apparent one; and thus all that is said of Christ in the articles of faith would not have been truly done, but only have seemed to be done; and consequently we would still be in death.

units.la: Hic verò duo sunt notanda. 1. Argumento ascensionis non tolli corpus Christi ex cœna, ut quidam calumniantur, sed tantum ex pane. Distantia enim cœli & terræ tantum obstat, ne corpus Christi in cœlo exsistens, simul sit in pane: non obstat vero, ne sit in cœna præsens: & per fidem spiritualiter manducetur. Nam fides nostra in verbo promissionis panis & vino annexæ, corpus Christi & sanguinem, omniaq; eius beneficia præsentissima sibi intuetur & amplectitur. 2. Argumentum ascensionis, non quidem solum, sed coniunctum cum priore de veritate naturæ humanæ, euertere corporalem præsentiam Christi in pane.
units.tr: Two things must be noted here. 1. The argument from the ascension does not remove the body of Christ from the Supper, as some slander, but only from the bread. For the distance between heaven and earth stands only in the way of the body of Christ, existing in heaven, being at the same time in the bread; it does not stand in the way of its being present in the Supper and being eaten spiritually through faith. For our faith, resting on the promise attached to the bread and wine, beholds and embraces the body and blood of Christ and all his benefits as most truly present to it. 2. The argument from the ascension, not alone but joined with the earlier one about the truth of the human nature, overthrows the bodily presence of Christ in the bread.

units.la: Si enim natura humana Christi esset ubique, vel multipræsens: non obstaret eius ascensio, quin simul in cœlo & in pane esset. Sed cum natura humana sit finita, non multipræsens, nec ubique: firmissimum est argumentum ab ascensione ductum: & sicut in prima cœna valebat consequentia, ex proprietate naturæ humanæ; corpus Christi ad mensam sedet: ergo non est in pane, vel in ore discipulorum: ita nunc valet, ex veritate ascensionis; corpus Christi est in cœlo: ergo non est in pane, aut in terris.
units.tr: For if the human nature of Christ were everywhere, or present in many places, its ascension would not prevent it from being in heaven and in the bread at once. But since the human nature is finite, not present in many places, nor everywhere, the argument drawn from the ascension is most firm; and just as at the first Supper the inference held, from the property of human nature: the body of Christ sits at the table, therefore it is not in the bread or in the mouths of the disciples; so now it holds, from the truth of the ascension: the body of Christ is in heaven, therefore it is not in the bread, or on earth.

units.la: Obiect. Tantum humana ratio judicat corporalem præsentiam in pane pugnare cum his articulis fidei. Ergo reuera non pugnat. Resp. Negatur antecedens. Non sola ratio, sed etiam fides Christiana, & verbum Dei docet, corpus Christi esse verè humanum & finitum corpus, nec simul exsistere in omnibus aut pluribus locis, & jam, postquam ascendit in cœlum, non esse in terra, sed in cœlo, donec inde redeat ad judicandum vivos & mortuos. Non igitur tantum humanæ rationi, sed etiam verbo Dei, præsentia corporis Christi in cœlo simul & in pane, repugnat. Illud quidem est extra controversiam, rationem humanam in rebus divinis contra verbum Dei non esse audiendam, sed verbo subijciendam. Interim ne in divinis quidem simpliciter est exuenda, vel abijcienda ratio, quasi brutum sensum ad verbum Dei afferre oporteat: sed ratione est rectè vtendum ad discernendum verum à falso. Ideo enim ratio à Deo nobis tributa est, vt contradictorias opiniones mentis lumine discernamus: & quid verbo Dei sit consentaneum, quid et repugnet, certò intelligentes: illud amplectamur, hoc repudium & impium, nihil omnium hæreticorum sententis tam erit impurum & monstrosum, quod ex scriptura sacra refutari possit. Semper enim hæretici & impostores excipient, suas opiniones non pugnare cum verbo Dei, sed tantum rationi humanæ hoc ita videri.
units.tr: Objection. Human reason alone judges that a bodily presence in the bread conflicts with these articles of faith. Therefore in truth it does not conflict. Answer. The antecedent is denied. Not reason alone, but also the Christian faith and the Word of God teach that the body of Christ is a truly human and finite body, that it does not exist at the same time in all or many places, and that, since it ascended into heaven, it is not on earth but in heaven, until it returns from there to judge the living and the dead. Therefore it is not only human reason but also the Word of God that opposes the presence of Christ's body in heaven and at the same time in the bread. It is indeed beyond dispute that human reason is not to be heard in divine matters against the Word of God, but is to be subjected to the Word. Yet in divine matters reason is not simply to be stripped off or cast aside, as if we had to bring a brutish sense to the Word of God; rather reason is to be rightly used to distinguish truth from falsehood. For reason has been given to us by God so that we may discern by the light of the mind contradictory opinions, and, understanding with certainty what agrees with the Word of God and what conflicts with it, embrace the one and reject the other as impious. No opinion of any heretic is so impure and monstrous that it cannot be refuted from holy Scripture. For heretics and impostors always object that their opinions do not conflict with the Word of God, but only seem so to human reason.

units.la: Inst. Scriptura tribuit corpori Christi multas proprietates, & prærogatiuas ἀπαθείας, quæ incorpora nostra non cadunt: vt, inambulare aquis, transformari, ferri sursum in cœlum, penetrare saxum & fores clausas, viriri deitati personaliter, fieri victimam pro peccatis, &c. Ergo non est absurdum, eidem tribuere præsentiam in cœlo simul & in pane, & ipsam vbiquitatem. Resp. In antecedente miscentur falsa veris. Nam penetratio corporis Christi per saxum & fores clausas, non est expressa scripturis, ideo negatur. Reliquæ prærogatiuæ sunt quidem expressæ, sed non tollunt veritatem naturæ humanæ. Nam etiam Petrus inambulauit aquis, & nos etiam transformabimur, feremur sursum, &c. Sed vbiquitas aut multipræsentia carnis CHRISTI nusquam in scripturis est expressa, nec patitur carnem CHRISTI esse creaturam, nedum verum corpus. Nam substantia simul in diuersis locis vel vbique esse, solius immensæ Deitatis proprium: omnis vero creatura est finita, & finitate sua à creatore discernitur. Finitum autem non potest simul plurib[us] locis esse, quam vno. Hinc scriptura, & veteris ecclesiæ doctores, præsentiam in pluribus locis, tanquam certum verææ & vnicæ diuinitatis argumentum proferunt: vt Christus ipse de se loquens: Filius hominis, qui est in cælo. Didymus: Ipse Spiritus sanctus, si vnus de creaturis esset, saltem circumscriptam haberet substantiam, sicut vniuersa, quæ facta sunt. Nam etsi non circumscriban-tur loco inuisibiles creaturæ: tamen proprietatem substantiæ finiuntur. Spiritus autem sanctus, cum in pluribus sit, non habet substantiam circumscriptam. Tertullianus: Si homo tantummodo Christus, quo-modo adest, vbicunque inuocatur: cum hæc hominis natura non sit, sed Dei, vt adesse omni loco possit? Admittunt igitur aduersarii fallaci-am non causæ, dum finguntur, prærogatiuas illas esse causam mul-tipræsentiæ & vbiquitatis, quæ eius causa non sunt: vel argu-mentantur à disparibus. Nam prærogatiuarum illarum, & vbi-quitatis, diuersissima est ratio.
units.tr: Objection. Scripture attributes to the body of Christ many properties and prerogatives of impassibility [ἀπαθείας] which do not fall upon our bodies: such as walking on water, being transformed, being carried up into heaven, penetrating a rock and closed doors, being united personally with the deity, being made a sacrifice for sins, etc. Therefore it is not absurd to ascribe to it also presence in heaven and in the bread at once, and ubiquity itself. Answer. In the antecedent falsehoods are mixed with truths. For the penetration of Christ's body through a rock and closed doors is not expressed in the Scriptures, and so it is denied. The remaining prerogatives are indeed expressed, but they do not remove the truth of the human nature. For Peter also walked on the waters, and we too shall be transformed, shall be carried up, etc. But the ubiquity or multipresence of the flesh of Christ is nowhere expressed in the Scriptures, and it does not allow the flesh of Christ to be a creature, much less a true body. For to be in many places or everywhere at once in substance is proper to the immense Deity alone; but every creature is finite, and is distinguished from the Creator by its finitude. Now what is finite cannot be in many places at once any more than in one. Hence the Scripture and the teachers of the ancient Church put forward presence in many places as a sure argument of true and only divinity: as Christ himself, speaking of himself: The Son of man, who is in heaven [John 3:13]. Didymus: If the Holy Spirit were one of the creatures, he would at least have a circumscribed substance, like all things that have been made. For although invisible creatures are not circumscribed by place, yet they are limited in the property of their substance. But the Holy Spirit, since he is in many places, does not have a circumscribed substance. Tertullian: If Christ were only a man, how is he present wherever he is invoked, since this nature of man is not divine, so that it could be present in every place? Our opponents therefore admit a fallacy of the cause, while they pretend that those prerogatives are the cause of multipresence and ubiquity, when they are not its cause; or else they argue from unlike things. For the reason of those prerogatives and of ubiquity is most widely different.

units.la: 3. Ex articulo de communione sanctorum. Talis nunc est com-munio sanctorum cum Christo, qualis fuit ab initio, & qualis semper futura est, tam vtentium sacramentis, quam necessitate exclusorum ab eis. Est enim vna tantum communio sanctorum, qua omnes sumus vnum corpus cum Christo. At communio sanctorum cum Christo semper fuit spiritualis, vt docet Apostolus: Qui agglutinatur Domino, vnus spiritus est. Per hoc cognoscimus enim in nobis habitare, & nos in ipso, quod de spiritu suo dedit nobis. Ipse vitis est, nos palmites: ipse caput, nos membra: ipse sponsus, nos cum tota Ecclesia sumus Christi sponsa. Vel sic. Omnes sancti habent eandem Christi communionem tam in veteri, quam in nouo testamento: tam qui possunt accedere cœnam, quam qui non possunt. 1. Cor. 10. Ephes. 4.1. Rom. 8. Neque nos Christum aliter possumus manducare, quam discipuli in prima cœna Christum manducarunt. At illi spiritualiter. Ergo & nos.
units.tr: 3. From the article on the communion of saints. The communion of the saints with Christ is now what it was from the beginning and what it will always be, both for those who use the sacraments and for those who are shut out from them by necessity. For there is only one communion of the saints, by which we are all one body with Christ. But the communion of the saints with Christ has always been spiritual, as the Apostle teaches: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." "By this we know that we dwell in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit." "He is the vine, we are the branches; he the head, we the members; he the bridegroom, and we, with the whole Church, are Christ's bride." Or put it this way. All the saints have the same communion with Christ, under the Old Testament as under the New, both those who can come to the Supper and those who cannot. (1 Cor. 10; Eph. 4; Rom. 8.) Nor can we eat Christ in any other way than the disciples ate Christ at the first supper. But they ate him spiritually. Therefore so do we.

units.la: Ex eodem articulo. Talis est manducatio Christi, qualis manducatio ipsius in nobis. Hæc autem spiritualis est. Ergo & manducatio est spiritualis. Maior patet: quia ideo manducatur, vt maneat in nobis, & nos in ipso, non vt manducatus moriatur. Qui edit carnem meam, & bibit sanguinem, in me manet, & ego in eo. Minor probatur: quia eadem est Christi manducatio in nobis, quæ & partis. Si quis
units.tr: From the same article. The eating of Christ is of the same kind as his indwelling in us. But this indwelling is spiritual. Therefore the eating is also spiritual. The major premise is plain, because Christ is eaten so that he may remain in us and we in him, not so that, once eaten, he may die. "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him." The minor premise is proved as follows: the eating of Christ, in us, is the same as his part in us. If anyone

units.la: Ioh. 6, 56. Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit, & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. At quomodo pater in nobis manet & habitat? certe per Spiritum sanctum. Ergo sic etiam Christus apud nos manet, & in nobis habitat. Huc pertinent dicta: Per hoc cognoscimus eum habitare in nobis, & nos in ipso, quia de spiritu suo dedit nobis. Vt Christus inhabitet per fidem in cordibus vestris. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites: qui manet in me, &c.{note side="right"}Ioh. 14, 15.{/note}
units.tr: John 6:56. "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." But how does the Father remain and dwell in us? Certainly through the Holy Spirit. Therefore in the same way Christ also remains with us and dwells in us. To this belong the words: "By this we know that he dwells in us, and we in him, because he has given us of his Spirit"; "that Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts" (Eph. 3:17); "I am the vine, you are the branches: he who abides in me," etc. (John 15:5). [Note: John 14:15.]

units.la: 4. Ex articulo de remissione peccatorum. Si Christus corporaliter est in pane, & manu ministri porrigitur, remissio peccatorum petenda est a Deo propter id, quod est in pane, & quod minister habet in manu; siue simul cum eo maneat panis, siue non. Nam in vsu coenae remissio peccatorum propter Christum vel maxime peti debet. Communicantes igitur sic oportebat precari: Oro te pater coelestis, vt sis mihi propitius propter hunc filium tuum, qui est in hoc pane, & quem minister habet in manu, & quem ego ore meocoedo. At qui haec est ipsa illa horrenda idololatria, quae in missa Papistica exercetur, quae haud dubie tam est detestabilis Deo, vt satius sit mille mortes oppetere, quam semel eam committere. Nam Euangelium nos docet remissionem peccatorum petere a Deo, non propter Christum, qui est in pane, qui manibus gestatur, aut ore comeditur: sed propter Christum, qui passus & mortuus est pro nobis; qui nunc est in coelo ad dexteram patris & interpellat pro nobis. Sic igitur hinc argumentamur. Quod horrendam missae idololatriam stabilit, id est fugiendum. Praesentia corporalis, & manducatio oralis Christi in pane, stabilit horrendam missae idololatriam. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 4. From the article on the forgiveness of sins. If Christ is bodily in the bread, and is held out by the minister's hand, forgiveness of sins is to be sought from God on account of what is in the bread and what the minister holds in his hand, whether or not the bread remains alongside him. For in the use of the Supper forgiveness of sins is above all to be asked for on account of Christ. So those who communicate ought to pray in this way: "I pray you, heavenly Father, that you be merciful to me on account of this your Son, who is in this bread, whom the minister holds in his hand, and whom I confess with my mouth." But this is that very horrible idolatry which is practised in the Papistical mass, which is without doubt so detestable to God that it is better to face a thousand deaths than to commit it even once. For the Gospel teaches us to seek forgiveness of sins from God not on account of Christ who is in the bread, who is carried in the hands or eaten with the mouth, but on account of Christ who suffered and died for us, who now is in heaven at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us. So we argue as follows. What establishes the horrible idolatry of the mass is to be shunned. Bodily presence and oral eating of Christ in the bread establish the horrible idolatry of the mass. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 5. Accedunt huc argumenta de sacrificio, & adoratione Christi. Vbicunque constat Christum adesse corporaliter, siue visibili siue inuisibili modo: ibi est adorandus; mentibus videlicet & gestibus eo conuersis. At in coena Christus non est sic adorandus, mentibus videlicet & gestibus ad panem, vel ad locum panis conuersis. Ergo non est corporaliter in pane, vel in loco panis. Maior per se patet. Minor probatur; quia in novo testamento post Christi ascensionem in coelum non licet adorationem alligare certo loco aut rei, sine expresso mandato & promissione Dei, absque manifesta idololatria. Omnis enim adoratio alligata certo loco, aut rei in terris, per Christum est sublata & prohibita: Venit hora, quando neque in monte hoc, neque Hierosolymis adorabitis patrem. Vos adoratis, quod nescitis: nos adoramus, quod scimus: quia salus ex Iudaeis est. Sed venit hora & nunc est, cum veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu & veritate. Etenim pater tales{note side="right"}Ioh. 4, 21.{/note} tales quærit, qui ipsum adorent. Deus est spiritus: & qui adorant eum, oportet, ut spiritu & veritate adorent. Deinde, si adorandus esset Christus in cœna, mentibus & gestibus ad panem directis: tota illa oblatio per manus sacrificulorum staret, qua offerunt Patri Filium ad impetrandam remissionem peccatorum: & sic iteranda esset Christi crucifixio.
units.tr: 5. Arguments about the sacrifice and the adoration of Christ also belong here. Wherever it is certain that Christ is present bodily, whether in a visible or an invisible manner, there he is to be adored, with minds and gestures turned towards him. But in the Supper Christ is not to be adored in this way, that is, with minds and gestures turned towards the bread or towards the place of the bread. Therefore he is not bodily in the bread, or in the place of the bread. The major premise is evident in itself. The minor is proved as follows: in the New Testament, after Christ's ascension into heaven, it is not permitted to tie adoration to a certain place or thing without an express command and promise of God, and without manifest idolatry. For all adoration tied to a certain place or thing on earth has been abolished and forbidden through Christ: "The hour comes when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:21ff.). Next, if Christ were to be adored in the Supper, with minds and gestures directed to the bread, then that whole offering by the hands of the sacrificing priests, by which they offer the Son to the Father to obtain forgiveness of sins, would stand; and so the crucifixion of Christ would have to be repeated.

units.la: Obiect. Christus non jussit se in pane offerri, vel adorari, sed manducari. Non igitur præsentia corporali stabilitur oblatio, vel adoratio Papistica. Resp. 1. Petunt principium, dicentes, Christum jussisse se in pane manducari, id enim nusquam est scriptum. 2. Tergiversantur. De Christo adorando habemus mandatum universale: Ipse est Dominus Deus tuus, & adorabis eum. Et adorent eum omnes angeli Dei. Huic mandato universali sine exceptione, aut præcepti singularis exspectatione, omnes obtemperare, & Christum in pane adorare cogeremur, non minus, quàm si præsentem oculis intueremur, si certò constaret eum in pane invisibiliter latere. Sic Thomas non exspectat mandatum speciale, sed rectè facit, adorationem convertens ad locum, ubi stantem videt Christum, dicens: Dominus meus, & Deus meus. Stante igitur opinione de præsentia corporali, stat Papistica adoratio & oblatio, & tota missa pontificia. Nam obtelationem Christi in missa, ne ipsi quidem Pontificij intelligi volunt de mactatione aliqua, sed de ostensione CHRISTI corporaliter præsentis, & de petitione atque impetratione remissionis propter eum, quem sacrifici manibus tenent, & patri ostendunt.
units.tr: Objection. Christ did not command himself to be offered or adored in the bread, but to be eaten. Therefore the Papistical offering or adoration is not established by bodily presence. Answer. 1. They beg the question, saying that Christ commanded himself to be eaten in the bread; for this is written nowhere. 2. They evade the point. We have a universal command about adoring Christ: "He is the Lord your God, and you shall worship him." "And let all the angels of God worship him." We would all be bound to obey this universal command without exception, and without waiting for a particular precept, and to adore Christ in the bread, no less than if we saw him present before our eyes, if it were certain that he lay hidden invisibly in the bread. So Thomas did not wait for a special command, but rightly turned his adoration to the place where he saw Christ standing, saying: "My Lord and my God." So, while the opinion of bodily presence stands, the Papistical adoration and offering stand, and the whole papal mass stands. For even the Papists themselves do not wish the offering of Christ in the mass to be understood as any kind of slaughter, but as the showing of Christ bodily present, and as the petition for and obtaining of forgiveness on account of him whom they hold in the sacrificing hands and show to the Father.

units.la: IV. Genus argumentorum ex similibus scripturæ locis similem vel eandem doctrinam continentibus, verbis non controversis.
units.tr: IV. The kind of argument drawn from similar passages of Scripture that contain a similar or the same doctrine, in words not in dispute.

units.la: 1. Similium phrasium similis est sententia & interpretatio. Omnes istæ phrases pro similibus habentur, nempe pro sacramentalibus, in quibus nomina vel propria effecta rerum significatarum tribuuntur signis: Circumcisio est fœdus Dei. Agnus est transitus Iehovæ. Sabbathum est fœdus Dei. Sacrificia Levitica sunt expiatio peccatorum. Sanguis victimarum est sanguis fœderis. Operculum arcæ est propitiatorium. Petra erat Christus. Panis est corpus Christi. Poculum est novum testamentum. Baptismus abluit peccata: est lavacrum regenerationis: fecit nos salvos &c. Ergo similis omnium interpretatio. Sic autem Deus ipse quasdam ex his interpretatur: Circumcisio est signum fœderis. Agnus est signum & memoriale transitus. Sabbathum est signum fœderis. Merito igitur nos etiam reliquas sic interpretamur: Sacrificia significant expiationem peccatorum per missam. Sanguis victimarum est sacramentum, confirmans foedus, seu, est signum sanguinis Christi, quo sancitum est foedus. Operculum significat ἱλαστήριον. Petra significabat Christum. Panis est sacramentum corporis Christi. Poculum est sacramentum, obsignans nouum foedus. Baptismus est sacramentum ablutionis peccatorum, regenerationis, & salutis nostrae.
units.tr: 1. Similar phrases have a similar meaning and interpretation. All these phrases are to be taken as alike, namely as sacramental, in which the names or the effects of the things signified are given to the signs: Circumcision is the covenant of God. The lamb is the Passover of the LORD. The Sabbath is the covenant of God. The Levitical sacrifices are the atonement for sins. The blood of the victims is the blood of the covenant. The mercy seat is the propitiatory. The rock was Christ. The bread is the body of Christ. The cup is the new testament. Baptism washes away sins; it is the washing of regeneration; it has saved us, etc. Therefore all of them are to be interpreted alike. God himself interprets some of them in this way: Circumcision is the sign of the covenant. The lamb is the sign and memorial of the Passover. The Sabbath is the sign of the covenant. Rightly, then, we also interpret the rest in this way: The sacrifices signify the atonement for sins through the Mass. The blood of the victims is a sacrament confirming the covenant, or it is the sign of the blood of Christ, by which the covenant was ratified. The mercy seat signifies [hilasterion]. The rock signified Christ. The bread is the sacrament of the body of Christ. The cup is a sacrament sealing the new covenant. Baptism is the sacrament of the cleansing of sins, of regeneration, and of our salvation.

units.la: 2. Sicut poculum est nouum testamentum, sic etiam est sanguis Christi. Maior patet, quia verba Lucae & Pauli, Hoc est sanguis meus noui testamenti, haud dubiè sunt eiusdem sententiae. Minor prius est probata, & non potest aliter accipi. Testamentum enim non est res vel caeremonia externa, sed est gratuita reconciliatio cum Deo propter Christi sanguinem in Euangelio promissa. Poculum igitur vel est res ipsa promissa, vel est sigillum promissionis. At non est promissio, nec ipsa res promissa. Ergo est sigillum promissionis.
units.tr: 2. Just as the cup is the new testament, so also is the blood of Christ. The major premise is plain, because the words of Luke and Paul, This is my blood of the new testament, undoubtedly have the same sense. The minor premise has already been proved, and it cannot be taken in any other way. For a testament is not a thing or an outward ceremony, but is the free reconciliation with God, promised in the Gospel on account of the blood of Christ. The cup, therefore, is either the thing itself that is promised, or it is the seal of the promise. But it is not the promise, nor is it the thing promised. Therefore it is the seal of the promise.

units.la: 3. Ex loco: Panis, quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi? Sicut panis est communio corporis Christi, sic etiam est corpus Christi. Ratio: quia verborum Pauli & Christi est idem sensus. Paulus enim verba Christi interpretatur. At panis est communio corporis Christi sacramentaliter, hoc est, est sacramentum, vel signum spiritualis communionis nostrae cum corpore Christi. Nam proprie, & ad literam, panis non potest dici communio. Ergo panis etiam est corpus Christi sacramentaliter, hoc est, est sacramentum vel signum corporis Christi. Quod autem communio, seu communicatio corporis Christi sit spiritualis, probatur. 1. Paulus loquitur de tali communione, qua vnus panis vnum corpus multi sumus. Atqui vnum corpus multi sumus spiritualiter. 2. Communio Christi, de qua loquitur, non potest consistere cum communione daemoniorum. Non potestis (inquit) poculum Domini bibere, & poculum daemoniorum: non potestis mensae Domini participes esse, & mensae daemoniorum: argumentum est, non ab indecoro, ut aliqui fingunt, sed ab impossibili, sicut illud Christi: Non potestis Deo seruire, & mammonae. Quae concordia Christi cum Belial? quae pars fideli cum infideli? 3. Haec plicatur in scriptura: Communio nostra est cum Patre & cum Filio eius Iesu Christo. Si dixerimus, nos communionem habere cum eo, & in tenebris incedimus, mentimur, nec sincerè agimus: sin autem in luce ambulamus, sicut ipse est in luce: communionem habemus mutuam,
units.tr: 3. From the passage: The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? Just as the bread is the communion of the body of Christ, so also it is the body of Christ. The reason: because the words of Paul and of Christ have the same sense, for Paul interprets the words of Christ. But the bread is the communion of the body of Christ sacramentally, that is, it is a sacrament or sign of our spiritual communion with the body of Christ. For properly and literally, bread cannot be called communion. Therefore bread is also the body of Christ sacramentally, that is, it is a sacrament or sign of the body of Christ. That the communion, or communication, of the body of Christ is spiritual, is proved as follows. (1) Paul speaks of that communion by which we, being many, are one bread, one body. But we, being many, are one body spiritually. (2) The communion of Christ of which he speaks cannot exist together with the communion of demons. You cannot (he says) drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. The argument is not from what is unseemly, as some pretend, but from what is impossible, like that saying of Christ: You cannot serve God and mammon. What agreement has Christ with Belial? What share has a believer with an unbeliever? (3) This is made plain in Scripture: Our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie and do not act truly; but if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another,

units.la: Luc.22,20. Act.21,16. Tit.3,5. 1 Pet.3,21. Genes.17,11. Ex.12,13,14. Exod.13,9. Exod.31,17. 1 Cor.10,16. 1 Cor.10,20. Matt.6,24. 2 Cor.6,15. 1 Io.1,3,6,7. tuam, & sanguis Iesu Christi Filij eius purgat nos ab omni peccato. Neque aliam, quam spiritualem communionem sanctorum cum Christo, & inuicem, credimus in symbolo. 4. Denique de spirituali κοινωνία verba Pauli interpretatur Chrysostomus: Quare non dixit μέθεξιν? vt aliquid excellentius indicet, summam putá vnionem. Et mox: Quid appello κοινωνίαν? Idem ipsum corpus sumus. Quid nam est panis? Corpus Christi. Quid autem fiunt qui accipiunt corpus Christi? Non multa, sed vnum corpus. Nam quemadmodum panis ex multis granis vnitur, sic inuicem cum Christo conjungimur.
units.tr: Luke 22:20. Acts 21:16. Titus 3:5. 1 Pet. 3:21. Gen. 17:11. Ex. 12:13, 14. Ex. 13:9. Ex. 31:17. 1 Cor. 10:16. 1 Cor. 10:20. Matt. 6:24. 2 Cor. 6:15. 1 John 1:3, 6, 7. and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. Nor do we believe in the creed any communion other than the spiritual communion of the saints with Christ and with one another. (4) Finally, Chrysostom interprets Paul's words about spiritual koinonia in this way: Why did he not say [methexin]? So that he might indicate something more excellent, namely the highest union. And soon after: What do I call [koinonia]? We are the same body. What is the bread? The body of Christ. And what do those who receive the body of Christ become? Not many, but one body. For just as the bread is united from many grains, so we are joined together with Christ.

units.la: 4. Ex verbis Christi: Quid igitur si conspexeritis Filium hominis ascendentem eò, vbi prius erat? spiritus est, qui viuificat: caro non prodest quicquam: verba, quae ego loquor vobis, spiritus & vita sunt. His verbis Christus oralem esum carnis suae expresse reijcit, & duplici argumento refutat, vt supra ostensum est: contra vero confirmat manducationem spiritualem. Non igitur fingendus est in coena corporalis esus corporis Christi: cum talis esus in Euangelio sit expresse damnatus.
units.tr: 4. From the words of Christ: What then if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing; the words that I speak to you are spirit and life. By these words Christ expressly rejects the oral eating of his flesh, and refutes it with a twofold argument, as has been shown above; on the contrary, he confirms spiritual eating. Therefore a corporal eating of the body of Christ in the Supper must not be imagined, since such eating has been expressly condemned in the Gospel.

units.la: Obiect. Caput sextum Johannis non pertinet ad coenam. Ergo nihil facit contra oralem manducationem corporis Christi in coena institutam. Resp. Est fallacia a secundum quid. Non pertinet ad caeremoniam coenae. Hinc non sequitur: Ergo simpliciter non pertinet ad coenam. Pertinet enim ad promissionem coenae, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: quia haec promissio est ex concione Johannis sexto desumpta, & symbolis panis & vini annexa, atqi confirmata. Non igitur potest de alio esu corporis Christi intelligi in coena, quam de quo sonat in concione Johannis 6. hoc est, de spirituali. Oralis enim manducatio concione Joh. 6. damnatur.
units.tr: Objection. The sixth chapter of John does not pertain to the Supper. Therefore it does nothing against the oral eating of the body of Christ instituted in the Supper. Answer. This is the fallacy of secundum quid (in a certain respect). It does not pertain to the ceremony of the Supper. But it does not follow from this that it simply does not pertain to the Supper. For it pertains to the promise of the Supper, This is my body, which is given for you, because this promise is taken from the sermon of John chapter 6, and is joined to and confirmed by the signs of bread and wine. Therefore it cannot be understood of a different eating of the body of Christ in the Supper from that which is spoken of in the sermon of John 6, that is, of a spiritual eating. For oral eating is condemned in the sermon of John 6.

units.la: Inst. Non oralis, sed Capernaitica damnatur. Resp. Oralis est Capernaitica. Ergo damnatur. Capernaitica enim non est tam cruenta laniatio carnis Christi, & inter dentes commansio, vt praetenditur, sed simpliciter esus oralis. Neque enim dicunt Capernaitae: Quomodo potest hic nobis carnem suam dare ad vorandum, dentibus terendum, laniandum? &c. sed simpliciter dicunt; ad manducandum, nempe ore. Nec Christus ab orali manducatione crassa eos revocat ad oralem manducationem subtilem, sed orali manducationi cuicunque carnis suae opponit assensionem suam in coelum paulo post futuram, qua corpus suum ab ore ipsorum longissime întremoturus, & manducationem spiritualem, quae fiat spiritu ex fide, eos docet.
units.tr: Instance. It is not oral eating that is condemned, but Capernaitic eating. Answer. Oral eating is Capernaitic. Therefore it is condemned. For Capernaitic eating is not the bloody mangling of the flesh of Christ and chewing between the teeth, as is alleged; it is simply oral eating. For the Capernaites do not say: How can this man give us his flesh to eat, to be ground by the teeth, torn to pieces, etc.; they simply say: to eat, namely with the mouth. Nor does Christ call them back from crude oral eating to a subtle oral eating; instead, against any oral eating of his flesh he sets his own ascension into heaven, which was to take place shortly after, by which he would remove his body far from their mouths, and he teaches them a spiritual eating, which is done by the Spirit through faith.

units.la: 5. Ex eodem c. 6. Joh. Manducare carnem Christi, & bibere sanguinem Christi, est in Christum credere, in Christo manere, & ipsum manentem in se habere: quod patet: quia utrique, nempe manducationi carnis suæ, & fidei in se, eundem effectum vitæ æternæ tribuit. In cœna sancitur eadem hæc manducatio. Non potest enim alia promissio, præter hanc, in toto Euangelio ostendi, cuius obsignandæ causa cœna sit instituta. Ergo etiam in cœna manducare corpus Christi, & bibere sanguinem Christi est in Christum credere, in Christo manere, & ipsum manentem in se habere.
units.tr: 5. From the same sixth chapter of John: to eat the flesh of Christ and to drink the blood of Christ is to believe in Christ, to abide in Christ, and to have him abiding in oneself. This is plain, because he attributes the same effect of eternal life to both, namely to eating his flesh and to faith in him. In the Supper this same eating is sealed. For no other promise can be shown in the whole Gospel, besides this one, for the sealing of which the Supper was instituted. Therefore also in the Supper, to eat the body of Christ and to drink the blood of Christ is to believe in Christ, to abide in Christ, and to have him abiding in oneself.

units.la: 6. Ex loco 1 Corinth. 12. 13. Per unum spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, sive Iudæi, sive Græci, sive serui, sive liberi: & una potatione omnes potati sumus in unum spiritum. Hinc geminum argumentum petitur. 1. Qualis potatio, talis manducatio spiritualis. 2. Manducatio corporis & bibitio sanguinis Christi, est communis omnibus fidelibus, etiam patribus veteris Testamenti. Omnes enim in unum spiritum una potatione potati sumus. Manducatio oralis non est communis omnibus fideli-bus. Nam patres ante Christum natum non potuerunt carnem Christi oraliter manducare: & hodie infantes, & multi adulti, facultatem vtendi cœna non habentes, non possunt eam manducare oraliter.
units.tr: 6. From 1 Corinthians 12:13: By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free; and we were all made to drink into one Spirit by one drinking. From this a twofold argument is drawn. (1) Such as the drinking is, so is the spiritual eating. (2) The eating of the body and the drinking of the blood of Christ are common to all the faithful, including the fathers of the Old Testament. For we were all made to drink into one Spirit by one drinking. Oral eating is not common to all the faithful. For the fathers before the birth of Christ could not eat the flesh of Christ orally; and today infants, and many adults who do not have the opportunity of using the Supper, cannot eat it orally.

units.la: Oralis igitur manducatio carnis Christi, non est vera illa manducatio, quam Euangelium promittit, & quam cœna obsignat.
units.tr: The oral eating of Christ's flesh, therefore, is not that true eating which the Gospel promises and which the Supper seals.

units.la: Testimonia patrum.
units.tr: Testimonies of the Fathers

units.la: His argumentis ex S. scriptura, & fidei nostræ fundamento depromtis, addantur testimonia patrum, & doctorum purioris Ecclesiæ, quos non est obscurum monumenta eorum perlustranti-bus, eandem nobiscum doctrinam de sacra cœna tradere. Ex multis tantum quædam illustriora proferemus.
units.tr: To these arguments, drawn from Holy Scripture and the foundation of our faith, let us add the testimonies of the Fathers and the teachers of the purer Church, who, as anyone who reads their writings will see, hand down the same doctrine concerning the holy Supper as we do. We will cite only some of the more notable from among many.

units.la: Irenæus. Panis terrenus accepta vocatione verbo Dei, non amplius est communis panis, sed efficitur eucharistia, quæ constat ex duabus, terrena & cœlesti.
units.tr: Irenaeus. The earthly bread, after receiving the calling of God's Word, is no longer common bread, but becomes the eucharist, which consists of two things, an earthly and a heavenly.

units.la: Tertullianus. Acceptum panem & distributum discipulis, corpus suum illum fecit: Hoc est corpus meum dicendo, id est, figura corporis mei.
units.tr: Tertullian. He took the bread and distributed it to the disciples, and made it his body, saying, "This is my body," that is, the figure of my body.

units.la: Clemens Alexandrinus. Hoc est bibere Iesu sanguinem, esse participem incorruptionis Domini.
units.tr: Clement of Alexandria. To drink the blood of Jesus is to partake of the incorruptibility of the Lord.
