units.la: Cyprianus. Nec potest videri sanguis eius, quo redemti & iustifi-cati sumus, esse in calice, quando vinum desit calici, quo Christi sanguis ostenditur, qui scripturarum omnium sacramento & testimonio prædicatur. Idem: Hæc quoties agimus, non dentes ad merden-dum acuimus, sed fide sincera panem sanctum frangimus, & partimur. dum quod diuinum & humanum est, distinguimus & separamus, itemq; simul separata jungentes, vnum Deum & hominem fatemur: sed & nos ipsi corpus eius effecti, sacramento & re sacramenti capiti nostro connectimur, & vnimur.
units.tr: Cyprian. Nor can his blood, by which we have been redeemed and justified, seem to be in the cup when there is no wine in the cup, by which the blood of Christ is shown, which is proclaimed by the sacrament and testimony of all the Scriptures. Again: Whenever we do these things, we do not sharpen our teeth for chewing, but with sincere faith we break and share the holy bread; and while we distinguish and separate what is divine and what is human, and again, joining together what has been separated, we confess one God and man. Moreover, we ourselves, having been made his body, are joined and united to our Head by the sacrament and by the reality of the sacrament.

units.la: Cano. Concilij Niceni. In diuina mensa rursus etiam hic non proposito pani & vino pueriliter adhaeramus, sed sublata in altum mente per fidem, consideremus proponi in sacra illa mensa agnum Dei tollentem peccata mundi, qui sine mactatione à sacerdotibus sacrificatur: & pretiosum eius corpus & sanguinem vere accipientes nos, credamus hoc esse nostra resurrectionis SYMBOLA. Nam ideo etiam non multum, sed parum accipimus, vt cognoscamus, quod non ad saturitatem, sed ad sanctificationem accipiatur.
units.tr: Canon of the Council of Nicaea. At the divine table, here too, we should not cling childishly to the bread and wine set before us, but with our mind lifted up on high through faith, let us consider that the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, is set forth on that holy table, and is offered in sacrifice without slaughter by the priests; and, truly receiving his precious body and blood, let us believe that this is the pledge of our resurrection SYMBOLS. For this reason we receive not much but little, so that we may know that it is received not for satiety but for sanctification.

units.la: Basilius. Apposuimus ANTITYPA sancti corporis & sanguinis tui.
units.tr: Basil. We have set before you the ANTITYPES of your holy body and blood.

units.la: Hilarius. Haec accepta atq; hausta id efficiunt, vt nos in Christo, & Christus in nobis sit.
units.tr: Hilary. These things, when received and drunk, bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ is in us.

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus. ANTITYPA pretiosi sanguinis & corporis Christi.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen. ANTITYPES of the precious blood and body of Christ.

units.la: Ambrosius. Quia morte Domini liberati sumus, huius rei memores, in edendo & potando carnem & sanguinem Domini, quae pro nobis oblata sunt, SIGNIFICAMVS. Idem. Haec oblatio est FIGVRA CORPORIS ET SANGVINIS Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Ambrose. Because we have been freed by the death of the Lord, mindful of this, in eating and drinking the flesh and blood of the Lord, which were offered for us, WE SIGNIFY. Again: This offering is the FIGURE OF THE BODY AND BLOOD of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Augustinus. Non dubitauit Dominus dicere: Hoc est corpus meum, cum daret signum sui corporis. Idem. Dominus Iudam adhibuit ad convivium, in quo corporis & sanguinis sui FIGVRAM discipulis suis commendauit & tradidit. Item. Si sacramenta quandam similitudinem earum rerum, quarum sacramenta sunt, non haberent, omnino sacramenta non essent. Ex hac autem similitudine plerunq; etiam ipsarum rerum nomina accipiunt. Sicut ergo secundum quendam modum sacramentum corporis Christi, corpus Christi est: sacramentum sanguinis Christi, sanguis Christi est: ita sacramentum fidei fides est. Item. Sic ut ergo caelestis panis, qui caro Christi est, Svo modo vocatur corpus Christi, cum revera sit SACRAMENTVM CORPORIS CHRISTI, illius videlicet, quod visibile, palpabile, mortale in cruce positum est: vocatur q; ipsa immolatio carnis, qua sacerdotis manibus fit, CHRISTI passio, mors, crucifixio, NON REI VERITATE, SED SIGNIFICANTIS MYSTERIO: sic sacramentum fidei, quo baptismus intelligitur, fides est. Item. Ista, fratres, ideo dicuntur sacramenta, quod in eis aliud videtur, aliud intelligitur. Quod videtur, speciem habet corporalem; quod intelligitur, fructum habet spiritualem.
units.tr: Augustine. The Lord did not hesitate to say, "This is my body," when he gave the sign of his body. Again: The Lord admitted Judas to the feast, in which he commended and handed to his disciples the FIGURE of his body and blood. Likewise: If sacraments did not have a certain likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness, they often receive even the names of the things themselves. Therefore, just as in a certain way the sacrament of the body of Christ is the body of Christ, and the sacrament of the blood of Christ is the blood of Christ, so the sacrament of faith is faith. Likewise: So, then, the heavenly bread, which is the flesh of Christ, is called in one way the body of Christ, although it is really THE SACRAMENT OF THE BODY OF CHRIST, namely of that body which was visible, tangible, mortal, and placed on the cross; and the very immolation of the flesh, which is performed by the hands of the priest, is called THE PASSION, DEATH, AND CRUCIFIXION OF CHRIST, NOT IN THE REALITY OF THE THING, but in the mystery of signifying: so the sacrament of faith, by which baptism is understood, is faith. Likewise: These things, brothers, are therefore called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

units.la: Chrysostomus. Hic est sanguis meus, qui effunditur in remissionem peccatorum: quod dicebat, vt ostenderet, passionem & crucem sterium esse, & discipulos consolaretur. Theodoretus. Seruator certè noster nomina commutauit, & corpori quidem idem, quod erat symboli ac signi, nomen imposuit: symbolo autem, quod erat corporis. Causa mutationis manifesta est iis, qui sunt diuinis mysteriis initiati. Volebat enim eos, qui sunt diuinorum mysteriorum participes, non attendere naturam eorum, quae videntur, sed propter nominum mutationem, mutationi, quae fit ex gratia, credere. Qui enim quod natura est corpus, triticum & panem appellauit, & vitem seipsum rursus nominauit, is symbola, quae videntur, appellatione corporis & sanguinis honorauit, non naturam quidem mutans, sed naturam gratiam adijciens. Celebre etiam est dictum Macarij monachi: ἄγεος ἡ οἱν Θ, αὐ πιτυπον τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῆ ἡ αἷμα ὡς ἐν ἀλλοίᾳ ωσφίειτα· ἡ ἢ μεταλαμβάνοντες ἐκ τ φανομένων ἄρτε, πνευματικῶς τῶ σωμα ἐ κυριου ἰδίαυ. Reliqua breuitatis causa praetereuntur.
units.tr: Chrysostom. "This is my blood, which is poured out for the forgiveness of sins." He said this to show that the passion and the cross were a mystery, and to comfort the disciples. Theodoret. Our Saviour, certainly, changed the names: to the body he gave the very name that belonged to the symbol and sign, and to the symbol he gave the name that belonged to the body. The reason for the change is plain to those who have been initiated into the divine mysteries. For he wished those who are partakers of the divine mysteries not to attend to the nature of the things that are seen, but, on account of the change of names, to believe in the change that is made by grace. For he who called what is by nature a body wheat and bread, and who again called himself a vine, has honoured the symbols that are seen with the names of body and blood, not indeed changing their nature, but adding grace to nature. There is also a well-known saying of the monk Macarius: [ἄγεος ἡ οἱν Θ, αὐ πιτυπον τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῆ ἡ αἷμα ὡς ἐν ἀλλοίᾳ ωσφίειτα· ἡ ἢ μεταλαμβάνοντες ἐκ τ φανομένων ἄρτε, πνευματικῶς τῶ σωμα ἐ κυριου ἰδίαυ.] The rest is passed over for the sake of brevity.

units.la: D. Davidis Parei Consideratio Transsubstantiationis & Consubstantiationis.
units.tr: D. Davidis Parei Consideratio Transsubstantiationis & Consubstantiationis.

units.la: Iam facile est intelligere, quid de Transsubstantiatione & Consubstantiatione sentiendum sit. Quid vero Papistae per illam, & Lutherani per hanc proprie intelligant, & statuant, planius patebit ex sequentibus.
units.tr: Now it is easy to see what should be thought about transubstantiation and consubstantiation. What the Papists properly mean by the first, and the Lutherans by the second, and what they maintain, will be made clearer from what follows.

units.la: DE TRANSSVBSTANTIATIONE.
units.tr: CONCERNING TRANSUBSTANTIATION.

units.la: Papistae docent, vi consecrationis, hoc est, prolationis verborum super elementa panis & vini: Hoc est enim corpus meum: Hic est enim calix mei sanguinis noui testamenti: panem & vinum substantialiter converti in corpus & sanguinem Christi, remanentibus tantum speciebus, seu accidentibus panis, & vini, figura, colore, sapore, & pondere, &c. Vocant igitur haec verba consecratoria, operatoria, & effectiva conversionis: & dicunt, in vltimo instanti prolationis syllabae VM, confectam esse conversionem: & tunc non amplius esse panem & vinum, sed subspecies panis & vini substantialiter adesse & contineri corpus & sanguinem Christi, & oraliter ab omnibus manducari ac bibi in eucharistia.
units.tr: The Papists teach that, by the power of consecration, that is, by the utterance of the words over the elements of bread and wine, "This is my body," "This is the cup of my blood of the new testament," the bread and wine are substantially converted into the body and blood of Christ, with only the appearances, or accidents, of bread and wine remaining: the figure, colour, taste, weight, and so on. They therefore call these words of consecration operative and effective of the conversion, and they say that the conversion is completed at the last instant of the utterance of the syllable VM. From then on there is no longer bread and wine, but beneath the appearances of bread and wine the body and blood of Christ are substantially present and contained, and are eaten and drunk orally by all in the Eucharist.

units.la: De modo conversionis non inter omnes convenit. Alij dicunt, substantiam panis & vini per modum transsubstantiationis converti in substantiam corporis & sanguinis Christi, ita vt illa essentialiter fiat ista, speciebus tantum externis remanentibus, & vocant, conversionem substantialem. Alij volunt, substantiam panis & vini non converti, sed per annihilationem euanescere, & in eius locum succedere substantiam corporis & sanguinis
units.tr: There is no agreement among all of them about the mode of the conversion. Some say that the substance of bread and wine is converted by way of transubstantiation into the substance of the body and blood of Christ, so that the former becomes essentially the latter, with only the outward appearances remaining; and they call this a substantial conversion. Others hold that the substance of bread and wine is not converted, but vanishes by annihilation, and that in its place there succeeds the substance of the body and blood of Christ,

units.la: Dialog. I. Christi, ita vt sub accidentib. illis, sub quibus prius erat substantia panis & vini, post consecrationē sit substantia corporis & sanguinis Christi, & vocant conuersionē formalem. Vtramq; Lombardus exponit l. 4. dist. sed priorem solam probare videtur. Vtramq; tamen conuersionem vocant Transsubstantiationem. Pronomen igitur hoc volunt demonstrare substantiam vagam, sed indeterminatam, in generali, vt loquuntur, sine quanto & quali, sub illis accidentibus contentam, ita vt non demonstret panem, nec corpus Christi, sed aliquid contentum sub speciebus, quod ante consecrationem fuerat panis, sed vi verborum caepit esse corpus Christi, vt sensus verborum sit: hoc est corpus meum, id est, quod continetur sub hoc, seu his speciebus, est corpus meum.
units.tr: Dialogue I. so that under those accidents beneath which the substance of bread and wine was before, after the consecration there is the substance of the body and blood of Christ; and they call this a formal conversion. Lombard expounds both in book 4, distinction 10, but seems to prove only the former. Yet they call both conversions transubstantiation. They therefore want the pronoun this to point to a vague but indeterminate substance, in general, as they put it, without quantity or quality, contained under those accidents; so that it points neither to the bread nor to the body of Christ, but to something contained under the appearances, which before the consecration had been bread, but by the power of the words has begun to be the body of Christ. The sense of the words would then be: This is my body, that is, what is contained under this, or these, appearances, is my body.

units.la: De accidentibus varie disputant, vbi fundentur, an in corpore Christi, an in aere, an in materia prima, an in superficie extensa, an in nihilo. Et communis opinio est, quod existant sine subiecto. Haec est scholasticorum, & omnium papistarum doctrina, cuius, vt apparet, duo praecipue sunt capita: vnum, de transsubstantiatione, alterum, de manducatione orali. Sed vtrunque est falsum & impium commentum, a verbis Christi alienum. Ac posterius quidem de orali manducatione sub speciebus, iisdem argumentis euertitur, quibus spiritualis manducatio prius est confirmata: transsubstantiatio vero sic refutatur.
units.tr: They dispute variously about the accidents, where they are founded: whether in the body of Christ, or in the air, or in prime matter, or in an extended surface, or in nothing. And the common opinion is that they exist without a subject. This is the doctrine of the schoolmen and of all the Papists, of which, as is evident, there are chiefly two heads: one concerning transubstantiation, the other concerning oral manducation. But both are a false and impious invention, alien to the words of Christ. The latter, concerning oral eating under the appearances, is overthrown by the same arguments by which spiritual eating was confirmed earlier; transubstantiation, however, is refuted as follows.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CONTRA TRANSSVBSTANTIATIONEM Papistarum.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE TRANSUBSTANTIATION OF THE PAPISTS.

units.la: I. Quod in Eucharistia est corpus Christi, id non annihilatur, aut transmutatur: sed manet: alioquin corpus Christi non maneret, nec adesset in Eucharistia. Panis Eucharistiae est corpus Christi. Panis igitur in Eucharistia manet, nec annihilatur, aut transmutatur. Maior patet. Minor liquet ex verbis Lucae & Pauli de poculo: Hoc poculum est nouum Testamentum. Panis, quem frangimus, est communio corporis Christi. Probatur etiam ex verbis, hoc modo: Quod Christus fregit, id dixit esse suum corpus. Fregit autem panem, non substantiam vagam, nec tantum accidentia panis. Ergo panem dixit esse corpus suum. Probatur & sic: Hoc, aut demonstrat panem, aut sola accidentia panis, aut substantiam vagam. Non substantiam vagam, sed corpus Christi, aut substantiam vagam: quia Christus non dedit, nec fregit substantiam vagam, sed panem. Non corpus Christi visibile, aut inuisibile: quia visibile discipulis assidebat & loquebatur: inuisibile Christus nullum habuit: & ipsi papistae fatentur, corpus Christi nondum adesse sub specie panis, cum sacerdos incipit pronunciare particulam . hoc, sed demum adesse post mutationem factam: mutationem autem fieri in vltimo instanti consecrationis, quo profertur vltima syllaba, vm,, in his verbis: hoc est enim corpus meum. Non dez niq; sola accidentia panis, quia Christus non fregit nudaaccidentia. Nihil igitur aliud, quam panem monstrat particula hoc: nec aliud sonant verba Christi, hoc est corpus meum, quàm, hic panis est corpus meum.
units.tr: I. What is the body of Christ in the Eucharist is not annihilated or transmuted, but remains; otherwise the body of Christ would not remain, nor be present in the Eucharist. The bread of the Eucharist is the body of Christ. Therefore the bread in the Eucharist remains, and is neither annihilated nor transmuted. The major premise is plain. The minor is clear from the words of Luke and Paul about the cup: This cup is the new testament. The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ. It is also proved from the words in this way: what Christ broke, he called his body. But he broke bread, not a vague substance, nor the bare accidents of bread. Therefore he called the bread his body. It is proved also thus: this either points out the bread, or the bare accidents of bread, or a vague substance. Not a vague substance, but the body of Christ, or a vague substance: because Christ neither gave nor broke a vague substance, but bread. Not the visible or invisible body of Christ: because the visible body sat beside the disciples and spoke; Christ had no invisible body; and the Papists themselves confess that the body of Christ is not yet present under the appearance of bread when the priest begins to pronounce the particle this, but is present only after the change has been made; and the change is made at the last instant of the consecration, when the last syllable, VM, is uttered in the words "This is my body." Nor is it the bare accidents of bread, because Christ did not break bare accidents. Therefore the particle this points to nothing but the bread, and the words of Christ, This is my body, say no other thing than This bread is my body.

units.la: 2. Christus fregit panem. Corpus suum non fregit. Ergo panis non est realiter corpus Christi.
units.tr: 2. Christ broke the bread. He did not break his body. Therefore the bread is not really the body of Christ.

units.la: 3. Corpus Christi est traditum pro nobis. Panis non est traditus pro nobis. Ergo panis non est realiter corpus Christi.
units.tr: 3. The body of Christ was given up for us. The bread was not given up for us. Therefore the bread is not really the body of Christ.

units.la: 4. Christus non dicit, sicut transsubstantiatores: sub his speciebus est corpus meum: vel, corpus meum continetur sub his speciebus. Ergo transsubstantiatores non retinent verba Christi, sed pervertunt.
units.tr: 4. Christ does not say, as the transubstantiators do: Under these appearances is my body, or My body is contained under these appearances. Therefore the transubstantiators do not retain the words of Christ, but pervert them.

units.la: 5. Christus non dixit hoc fiat: sed: hoc est corpus meum. Ergo verba Christi non conuertunt panem in substantiam corporis Christi, sed tantum docent, panem in hoc vsu esse corpus Christi, nempe, sacramentaliter.
units.tr: 5. Christ did not say Let this be done, but This is my body. Therefore the words of Christ do not convert the bread into the substance of the body of Christ, but only teach that the bread in this use is the body of Christ, namely sacramentally.

units.la: 6. Paulus id quod foris datur & sumitur, expresse nominat panem ante & post esum. Ergo panis nec annnihilatur, nec mutatur in substantiam corporis, sed manet panis.
units.tr: 6. Paul expressly calls what is given and taken outwardly bread, both before and after eating. Therefore the bread is neither annihilated nor changed into the substance of the body, but remains bread.

units.la: 7. In omni sacramento duo sunt: signum & res signata, seu, vt Irenæus loquitur, res terrena, & res cœlestis, sine quibus sacramentum constare non potest. At transsubstantiatio tollit signum seu rem terrenam, nempe panem & vinum, ex eucharistia. Ergo totam rationem sacramenti tollit.
units.tr: 7. In every sacrament there are two things: the sign and the thing signified, or, as Irenaeus puts it, the earthly thing and the heavenly thing, without which a sacrament cannot exist. But transubstantiation removes from the Eucharist the sign, or earthly thing, namely the bread and wine. Therefore it removes the whole nature of the sacrament.

units.la: 8. Spectrum panis & vini non potest confirmare fidem rerum cœlestium, sed eam ludificabitur, tanquam res vana, quæ non est id, quod esse videtur. At signum in eucharistia debet confirmare fidem rerum cœlestium, tam certo nimirum nospasci corpore & sanguine Domini, quam certo percipimus panem & vinum: sacramenta enim sunt instituta ad confirmandam fidem per visibilia signa. Facessat ergo transsubstantiatio, quæ signum in spectrum transformat.
units.tr: 8. The appearance of bread and wine cannot confirm faith in heavenly things, but will mock it, as an empty thing which is not what it seems to be. But the sign in the Eucharist ought to confirm faith in heavenly things, that is, we are as surely fed by the body and blood of the Lord as we surely perceive the bread and wine; for sacraments were instituted to confirm faith through visible signs. Let transubstantiation, then, which turns the sign into an appearance, be done away with.

units.la: 9. Transsubstantiatio tollit analogiam signi & rei signatæ, de qua Augustinus: quod corpus sic pascit animam, sicut panis nutrit corpus: & sicut panis triticeus est vna massa ex multis granis coœta; sic multi fiunt vnus panis, & vnum corpus, qui de vno pane participant. Hanc enim analogiam sola accidentia panis & vini sustinere non possunt; quia accidentia non nutriunt: nec potes dicere; quemadmodum accidentia panis & vini nutriunt corpus ad hanc vitam; ita Christi corpus animam meam nutritad vitam æternam. Erit enim collatio rei veræ & falsæ. Analogia igitur signi & rei manifestè satis transsubstantiationem refellit.
units.tr: 9. Transubstantiation removes the analogy of sign and thing signified, of which Augustine speaks: that the body is fed in the same way that the soul is fed, just as bread nourishes the body; and just as the wheaten loaf is one mass gathered from many grains, so many become one bread and one body, who partake of the one bread. The bare accidents of bread and wine cannot sustain this analogy, because accidents do not nourish; nor can you say: as the accidents of bread and wine nourish the body to this life, so the body of Christ nourishes my soul to eternal life. For there would be a comparison of a true thing with a false one. Therefore the analogy of sign and thing clearly enough refutes transubstantiation.

units.la: DE CONSVBSTANTIATIONE LVTHERANORVM.
units.tr: On the Consubstantiation of the Lutherans.

units.la: Papistæ finxerunt, duo magna miracula fieri in eucharistia vi consecrationis, conuersionem substantiarum, & subsistentiam accidentium sine subiecto: quarum illam cum analogia totius fidei Christianæ, hanc etiam cum sana philosophia pugnare, manifestum est. Vis vero illa consecrationis nihil est, nisi magicum commentum diaboli, & humanæ rationis.
units.tr: The Papists have invented two great miracles that take place in the Eucharist by the power of consecration: the conversion of substances, and the subsistence of accidents without a subject. It is plain that the first clashes with the whole analogy of the Christian faith, and the second with sound philosophy. That power of consecration is nothing but a magical fiction of the devil and of human reason.

units.la: Hoc igitur jam olim doctores aliqui intelligentes, ut evitarent tam absurda miracula, pro transsubstantiatione finxerunt consubstantiationem, hoc est, coexistentiam duarum substantiarum in eodem loco, seu præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi, non sub speciebus panis & vini, sed sub ipso pane & vino.
units.tr: Some teachers, perceiving this long ago and wishing to avoid such absurd miracles, therefore invented consubstantiation in place of transubstantiation. That is, they taught the coexistence of two substances in one place, or the presence of the body and blood of Christ not under the appearances of bread and wine, but in the bread and wine themselves.

units.la: Hi igitur voluerunt symbola non transsubstantiari, sed consubstantiari, hoc est, panem & vinum manere, sed cum, in, & sub pane & vino substantialiter esse & oraliter manducari & bibi corpus & sanguinem Christi.
units.tr: These men therefore wanted the symbols not to be transubstantiated but to be consubstantiated. That is, they held that the bread and wine remain, but that the body and blood of Christ are substantially present with, in, and under the bread and wine, and are eaten and drunk orally.

units.la: Hanc opinionem testatur Lombardus ante sua tempora jam à nonnullis defensam fuisse: sed eam vocat miram.
units.tr: Lombard testifies that this opinion had already been defended by some before his time, but he calls it strange.

units.la: Guitmundus eam tribuit Berengario post palinodiam: & vocat impanationem.
units.tr: Guitmund attributes it to Berengar after his recantation, and calls it impanation.

units.la: Alij asscribunt cuidam Walramo, aduersus quem exstant duo opuscula Anselmi.
units.tr: Others ascribe it to a certain Walram, against whom two little works of Anselm exist.

units.la: Alij Ruperto abbati Tuitiensi, qui non multo post Guitmundum vixit, circa annum Domini 1114.
units.tr: Others ascribe it to Rupert, abbot of Tuy, who lived not long after Guitmund, around the year of the Lord 1114.

units.la: Petrus de Alliaco Cardinalis Cameracensis testatur, se consubstantiationem potius, quàm transsubstantiationem amplecti velle, nisi contra statuisset ecclesia Romana. Vixit is circa annum Domini 1416.
units.tr: Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, testifies that he would rather embrace consubstantiation than transubstantiation, were it not that the Roman Church had decreed otherwise. He lived around the year of the Lord 1416.

units.la: Tandem Lvtherus authoritatem Cardinalis Cameracensis secutus, vt ipse testatur, primò quidem statuit, non esse articulum fidei, vtrum maneat substantia panis cum corpore Domini: sed vtrumque posse teneri absque hæresi. Postea probabilius ei est visum, panem manere, & sub, in, cum pane, esse corpus Christi. Tandem pro necessario articulo fidei defendit contra Papistas & Helveticas ecclesias. Atq; hæc nunc est vulgata opinio eorum, qui se vocant Lvtheranos. Verba igitur Christi: Hoc est corpus meum, interpretantur per ista: In hoc, cum hoc, sub hoc pane est corpus meum. Nec minus, quàm Papistæ interim gloriantur, se retinere nere literam sine tropo. Et quidem quoties cum Papistis pugnant, particula τοῦτο, hoc, eis panem solū demonstrat: & panis ipse est corpus Christi. Quoties vero in Sacramentarios (quos ita criminantur) stylum stringunt, particula τοῦτο, hoc, non panem solum, sed panem cum corpore inuisibiliter intus latente, ipsis demonstrat, & sensus est: Hoc est corpus meum, id est, hic panis, & corpus meum in pane latens, est corpus meum. Illustrant hanc glossam similibus, vt aiunt, vulgo vsitatis: Christum, cum dicit, hoc est corpus meum, perinde loqui, atque cum rusticus de auena in sacco dicit: hoc est auena, saccum demonstrans: vel mercator de pecunia in loculis: hoc est pecunia, crumenam exhibens; vel mater de infante in cunis: hoc est infans meus, cunas ostendens: vel caupo de vino: hoc est vinum Rhenanum, cyathum porrigens. Hæc ex libris & disputationibus eorum nota sunt.
units.tr: Finally Luther, following the authority of the Cardinal of Cambrai, as he himself testifies, at first held that it is not an article of faith whether the substance of the bread remains with the body of the Lord, but that either view may be held without heresy. Afterwards it seemed more probable to him that the bread remains and that the body of Christ is under, in, and with the bread. Finally he defended it as a necessary article of faith against the Papists and the Helvetic churches. And this is now the common opinion of those who call themselves Lutherans. They therefore interpret the words of Christ, This is my body, by these: In this, with this, under this bread is my body. And they boast no less than the Papists that they retain the letter without a trope. Indeed, whenever they fight with the Papists, the particle τοῦτο [this] points to the bread alone, and the bread itself is the body of Christ. But whenever they take up the pen against those whom they accuse of being Sacramentarians, the particle τοῦτο, this, points to them not the bread alone but the bread together with the body lying invisibly hidden within it, and the sense is: This is my body, that is, this bread, and my body lying hidden in the bread, is my body. They illustrate this gloss with similar examples, as they say, commonly used: when Christ says this is my body, he speaks just as a peasant who points at a sack says of the oats in it, this is oats; or a merchant, pointing at a purse, says of the money in it, this is money; or a mother, pointing at the cradle, says of the infant in it, this is my child; or a tavern-keeper, offering a cup, says of the wine, this is Rhenish wine. These things are known from their books and disputations.

units.la: Sed bonis istis viris accidit, quod Poeta dicit: Stulti dum vitant vitia, in contraria currunt. Nam pro absurdo miraculo subsistentiæ accidentium sine subiecto, finxerunt aliud absurdius de penetratione duorum corporum: & longius, quam papistæ, à verbis Christi recesserunt, siue litera spectetur, siue sententia. Littera est, hoc, id est, hic panis est corpus meum: sententia est: panis illa visibilis fractus & distributus, est verum & essentiale corpus meum pro vobis traditum: non essentiali conuersione, vt papistæ volunt, (panis enim non est à λόγῳ assumtus, nec pro nobis traditus) sed mysticè, seu sacramentali metonymia: vt Christus ipse, & Paulus, & orthodoxa antiquitas interpretatur. Ab hac litera & sententia verborum Christi, glossa consubstantiatorum toto cœlo abest. Sicut enim non est verum, papistas retinere τὸ ἐστιν, cum pro verbis Christi; hoc est corpus meum: hanc Seraphicam glossam supponunt, hæres seu substantia vaga, contenta sub his speciebus, est corpus meum: sic multo minus est verum, consubstantiatores litera & sensus verborum retinere, cum pro verbis Christi, hæc sua nobis afferunt: in, cum, sub pane est corpus meum, vel panis & corpus in pane inuisibiliter latens, est corpus meum. Nam nec solus panis, nec panis cum corpore intus latente, proprie & sine tropo est corpus Christi: sicut nec crumena vacua, vel nummis plena, proprie & sine tropo est pecunia. Locutiones vero adhibent ab eo, quod illustrare volunt, nimis alienas. In illis enim phrasibus prius constat, rem esse in eo, quod monstrant; puta, auenam in sacco, nummos in crumena, infantem in cunis, vinum in cyatho &c. Corpus autem Christi esse in pane, nondum illi monstrarunt, nec in æternum demonstrabunt. A nobis vero pernegatur: quia symbolum fidei Christianæ cum tota scriptura plane contra testatur, Christum suo corpore nunc non esse in terra, vel in pane latere, sed in coelo gloriosè regnare, donec inds redeat adjudicium. Est ergo aperta petitio principij, qua consubstantiatores hic niituntur.
units.tr: But it has happened to these good men what the poet says: Fools, while they avoid vices, run into their opposites. For in place of the absurd miracle of accidents subsisting without a subject, they have invented another more absurd, concerning the penetration of two bodies; and they have departed further from the words of Christ than the Papists have, whether the letter or the sense is considered. The letter is this, that is, this bread is my body; the sense is: that visible bread, broken and distributed, is my true and essential body given for you. This is not by an essential conversion, as the Papists want (for the bread is not assumed from the Word [λόγῳ], nor was it given for us), but mystically, or by sacramental metonymy, as Christ himself, and Paul, and orthodox antiquity interpret it. The gloss of the consubstantiators is wholly remote from this letter and sense of Christ's words. For just as it is not true that the Papists retain the is [τὸ ἐστιν], since, in place of the words of Christ, this is my body, they substitute that seraphic gloss, a substance or a wandering essence, contained under these appearances, is my body; so it is much less true that the consubstantiators retain the letter and sense of the words when, in place of the words of Christ, they offer us their own: in, with, under the bread is my body, or the bread and the body invisibly lying in the bread is my body. For neither the bread alone, nor the bread with the body lying hidden within it, is properly and without a trope the body of Christ; just as an empty purse, or one full of coins, is not properly and without a trope money. Moreover, the comparisons they use are far too unlike what they wish to illustrate. In those phrases it is already established that the thing is in what is pointed at: for example, oats in the sack, coins in the purse, the infant in the cradle, wine in the cup, and so on. But that the body of Christ is in the bread they have not yet shown, nor will they ever show it. We, on the other hand, flatly deny it, because the creed of the Christian faith, together with the whole of Scripture, plainly testifies that Christ is now not on earth in his body, nor hidden in the bread, but reigns gloriously in heaven until he returns to judge. The consubstantiators here therefore rely on a plain begging of the question.

units.la: DE SCHISMATE CONSVBSTANTIATORVM LVTHERANORVM.
units.tr: ON THE SCHISM OF THE LUTHERAN CONSUBSTANTIATORS.

units.la: LVTHERVS initio pro fundamento sententiæ suæ posuit solam Christi verba, Hoc est Corpus meum: postea verò in certamine contra Aduersarios Anno 1527.1528. confugit ad Vbiquitatem: tandemque pro uno fundamento quatuor sibi statuit. 1. Vnionem personalem naturarum in Christo. 2. Dexteram Dei, ubique existentem. 3. Veritatem Dei, qui mentiri non potest. 4. Triplicem corporis Christi modum essendi alicubi. Verum ab his etiam tandem depulsus, rursus se ad verba Christi recepit, & disputationem de Vbiquitate carnis Christi missam fieri voluit. Nihilominus postea quidam eius discipuli, in verbis Christi pro consubstantiatione non satis præsidij inuenientes, Vbiquitatem rursus in arenam protraxerunt, quam etiam hucusque proram & puppim suæ causæ statuunt: aliis interim Vbiquitatem rejicientibus.
units.tr: Luther at first laid down, as the foundation of his opinion, the words of Christ alone, "This is my body." Later, however, in the controversy against his opponents in the years 1527 and 1528, he took refuge in Ubiquity; and at length he set up four foundations in place of one: (1) the personal union of the natures in Christ; (2) the right hand of God, existing everywhere; (3) the truth of God, who cannot lie; (4) the threefold mode of Christ's body's being somewhere. But being driven from these also in the end, he returned again to the words of Christ, and wished the dispute about the ubiquity of Christ's flesh to be dropped. Nevertheless, afterwards some of his disciples, finding not enough support for consubstantiation in the words of Christ, dragged Ubiquity back into the arena again, and to this day they make it the prow and the stern of their cause, while others in the meantime reject Ubiquity.

units.la: HINC natum est consubstantiatorum schisma, & triplex secta. Alij volunt esse Lutheranj simplices, qui ex solis Christi verbis consubstantiationem & manducationem oralem defendunt. Alij sunt Lutherani multipræsentiarij, qui propter omnipotentiam diuinam carni realiter communicatam, corpus Christi non quidem ubique, sed in multis simul locis & hostiis Coenæ Dominicæ præsens esse statuunt. Alij denique sunt Lutherani omnipræsentiarij, seu Vbiquitarij, qui ad propugnandam corporis Christi præsentiam in pane, clypeum Vbiquitatis arripientes docent, corpus Christi vi vnionis cum λόγῳ ubique exsistente, ubique esse: proinde etiam in pane Eucharistiæ præsens adesse, etiam ante & extra vsum coenæ: ritum & consecrationem vero efficere, vt in hoc pane comedatur, in alio non item.
units.tr: From this arose the schism of the consubstantiators and a threefold sect. Some wish to be called plain Lutherans, who defend consubstantiation and oral manducation from the words of Christ alone. Others are Lutheran multipresentiaries, who, on account of the divine omnipotence really communicated to the flesh, hold that the body of Christ is present not indeed everywhere, but in many places at once and in the hosts of the Lord's Supper. Finally, others are Lutheran omnipresentiaries, or Ubiquitarians, who, seizing the shield of Ubiquity to defend the presence of Christ's body in the bread, teach that the body of Christ, by virtue of its union with the Word existing everywhere, is everywhere; and therefore is also present in the bread of the Eucharist, even before and outside the use of the supper; but that the rite and the consecration make it so that it is eaten in this bread and not in another.

units.la: EX HIS juniores intelligunt, consubstantiationis hodie duo præcipuè fundamenta esse: Vbiquitatem Christi, & verba Christi: vel potius vnum tantum, Vbiquitatem solam. Hanc enim ideo excogitarunt Vbiquitarij: quia in verbis Christi nimis ruinosum fundamentum opinionis suæ esse tandem obseruarunt: quandoquidem per glossam suam non solum à litera, sed etiam à naturali constructione & sensu verborum manifestè recedunt, Pro litera enim hoc, seu hic panis est corpus meum, supponunt; In hoc, vel, in hoc pane est corpus meum. Constructio naturalis verborum borum est: Hoc, vel hic panis est corpus meum: Constructio verò glossæ est: Corpus meum est in hoc, vel, in hoc pane. Sensus literalis & verus verborum est: quid sit panis Eucharistia: nempe, corpus Christi visibile pro nobis crucifixum. Sensus glossæ literalis, sed falsus est: Ubi sit corpus Christi invisibile pro nobis non crucifixum: nempe, in pane. Sic verbis Domini penitus deiecti, ad solam Vbiquitatem confugere coguntur. Vbiquitatis verò tum infirmitas, tum falsitas supra in explicatione Articulorum fidei de personali unione, deq; ascensione in cœlum, & sessione ad dextram Dei, satis ostensa fiat, atque discussa.
units.tr: From these things the younger men understand that there are today two principal foundations of consubstantiation: the ubiquity of Christ and the words of Christ; or rather, only one, ubiquity alone. For the Ubiquitarians devised this because they at length observed that the words of Christ were too ruinous a foundation for their opinion; since by their gloss they clearly depart not only from the letter but also from the natural construction and sense of the words. For, in support of the letter, they supply "this," or "this bread is my body," and read "in this," or "in this bread is my body." The natural construction of these words is: "This," or "this bread is my body." But the construction of the gloss is: "My body is in this," or "in this bread." The literal and true sense of the words is: what the bread of the Eucharist is, namely, the visible body of Christ crucified for us. The literal but false sense of the gloss is: where the invisible body of Christ, not crucified for us, is, namely, in the bread. Thus, utterly cast down from the words of the Lord, they are forced to take refuge in ubiquity alone. But the weakness and falsity of ubiquity has been sufficiently shown and examined above, in the explanation of the articles of faith concerning the personal union, and concerning the ascension into heaven and the session at the right hand of God.

units.la: Hucusque D. Paræi consideratio Transsubstantiationis & Consubstantiationis.
units.tr: Thus far the consideration of Transsubstantiation and Consubstantiation by D. Paraeus.

units.la: OBIECTIONVM
units.tr: Objections

units.la: Pro Consubstantiatione refutatio.
units.tr: Refutation of the arguments for consubstantiation.

units.la: Obiect.1. Vsitatissima locutio est, cum duæ res coniunctæ, altera apparens, altera non apparens, simul dantur, ut ea sola nominetur, quæ non apparet: ut de loculis pecunia plenis dicitur: Hoc est pecunia: de cantharo vini: Hoc est vinum, &c. Christus eodem modo duas res coniunctas, panem & corpus suum porrigens, eam saltem quæ non apparebat in pane nominavit, dicens: Hoc est Corpus meum. Ergo locutio Christi est vsitatissima & propria, nec indiget vlla explicatione.
units.tr: Objection 1. It is a very common way of speaking that when two things are joined together, one visible and the other not visible, and both are given at once, only the one that is not visible is named. Thus of purses full of money we say This is money, and of a cup of wine This is wine, etc. In the same way Christ, offering two joined things, bread and his body, named at least the one that was not visible in the bread, saying This is my body. Therefore Christ's way of speaking is very common and proper, and needs no explanation.

units.la: Resp.1. ad Maiorem. Est locutio vsitatissima, &c. nimirum, quando rem non apparentem, quæ nominatur, in altera apparente contineri certò constat: sicut constat, pecuniam contineri in loculis, vinum cantharo: secus nec vsitatè, nec perspicuè, nec verè, sed falsò dicitur de crumena vacua: hoc est pecunia: de cantharo vacuo: hoc est vinum, &c. Atqui nondum constat, neque hactenus probarunt Consubstantiatores, corpus Christi delitui esse in pane, cum de pane diceret Christus: Hoc est corpus meum: sicut constare oportet, pecuniam repositam esse in crumena, vel contineri in vase, quando dicitur: hac est pecunia: hoc est vinum.
units.tr: Answer to the major premise. It is a very common way of speaking, etc., namely when it is certain that the thing named, which is not visible, is contained in the other thing, which is visible. Thus it is certain that money is contained in a purse, and wine in a cup. Otherwise it is said neither commonly, nor clearly, nor truly, but falsely: of an empty purse, this is money; of an empty cup, this is wine, etc. But it is not yet established, and the Consubstantiationists have not so far proved, that the body of Christ lies hidden in the bread, when Christ said of the bread, This is my body. It would have to be established that money is put away in a purse, or contained in a vessel, when one says this is money or this is wine.

units.la: Nos contra asserimus ex historia, corpus Christi in prima cœna non delituisse in pane, sed mensæ visibiliter accubuisse: & nunc in cœlo esse, donec inde redeat ad judicium. Est ergo aperta petitio principii. 2. Minor falsa est. Christus enim non corpus suum invisibile, sed panem visibilem de mensa acceptum & fractum, manu sua discipulis porrigens dixit: Accipite, edite, hoc, seu, hic panis, est corpus meum: qui sensus particulæ, hoc, est manifestus, & supra probatus ex verbis de poculo: hoc poculum est novum Testamentum: & verbis Pauli: Panis, quem frangimus, est communio corporis poris Christi. Adde, quod panis & corpus Christi simul, neq; proprie, neq; figuratè sunt, & verè dici possunt corpus Christi: & affingeretur Christo inanis Tautologia : panis & corpus meum est corpus meum. Rursus igitur est petitio principij. 3. Consequentia negatur: quia plus est in conclusione, quàm in premissis, quando concludunt, locutionem esse vsitatissimam & propriam. Hæc duo enim minimè idem valent: quia potest locutio aliqua esse vsitatissima, & tamen non esse propria, sed figurata, quales sunt omnes illæ locutiones de pecunia, vino, infante, arena, &c. Quis enim ita insanit, vt credat, loculos vel vacuos, vel pecunia refertos esse pecuniam propriè? Sic vsitata quidem, & discipulis notissima erat locutio sacramentalis de Paschate: Vbi vis, paremus tibi Pascha? Et tamen discipuli ita loquentes non propriè, sed figuratè loquebantur, signo tribuentes nomen rei significatæ, Agnum vocantes Pascha, hoc est, transitum, quem significabat, metonymia sacramentali. Tantum ergo sequitur: verba Christi fuisse vsitata, & discipulis perspicua: non autem fuisse propria, ad literam, & sine tropo sacramentali intellecta.
units.tr: We on the contrary assert from history that the body of Christ in the first Supper did not lie hidden in the bread, but reclined visibly at the table, and is now in heaven until he returns from there to judgment. Therefore it is a plain begging of the question. 2. The minor is false. For Christ did not, offering his invisible body, but offering visible bread taken from the table and broken, give it to the disciples with his own hand, saying Take, eat, this, or, this bread is my body. The sense of the particle this is plain, and was proved above from the words about the cup, this cup is the new testament, and from Paul's words, The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ. Add that bread and the body of Christ together are not one thing, either properly or figuratively, and could truly be called the body of Christ only if an empty tautology were ascribed to Christ: bread and my body is my body. Again, therefore, it is a begging of the question. 3. The consequence is denied, because there is more in the conclusion than in the premises, when they conclude that the way of speaking is very common and proper. These two things are by no means equivalent, because a way of speaking can be very common and yet not proper but figurative. Such are all those ways of speaking about money, wine, infant, sand, etc. For who is so mad as to believe that empty purses, or purses full of money, are properly money? So too the sacramental way of speaking about the Passover was common and well known to the disciples: Where do you want us to prepare the Passover for you? Yet the disciples, speaking thus, did not speak properly but figuratively, giving the name of the thing signified to the sign, and calling the lamb Passover, that is, passing over (transitum), which it signified, by a sacramental metonymy. Therefore only this follows: that the words of Christ were common and plain to the disciples. It does not follow that they were proper, understood literally and without a sacramental trope.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Christus dixit: Hoc est corpus meum: est autem verax. Ergo ei credendum est, sepositò philosophico acumine: & per consequens, verba eius simpliciter, vt sonant, sunt intelligenda. Resp. 1. Est fallacia non causæ. Veritas enim Christi facit quidem, vt verba eius sint verissima, quibus sepositò acumine philosophico sit credendum: non facit autem, vt sint propriè ad literam intelligenda. Nam etiam qui verax est, potest loqui figuratè: sicut Christus non minus erat verax, cùm diceret figuratè: Ego sum lux mundi: Ego sum ostium ouilis: Ego sum vitis vera, vos estis palmites: Pater meus est agricola: Ego sum via, veritas & vita: Ego sum pastor bonus: &c. quàm cùm diceret propriè: Ego sum Iesus, quem quaeritis: Ego vos elegi: Pater meus dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus, &c. Verax igitur est Christus, & verà sunt eius verba, etiam quando metonymia sacramentali diceret de pane: Hoc est corpus meum: pro, est sacramentum, seu sacrum signum corporis mei. Procul verò è scholis explodendi sunt illi inepti Logici, qui figuratas locutiones esse mendacia dicere non verentur. 2. Per ἐνάντιον. Christus est verax. Ergo panem vocans corpus suum, non dixit, corpus suum esse in pane, quod discipuli videbant esse extra panem, & mensæ secum accumbere. Item. Verba sunt accipienda simpliciter: Ergo non est eis affingenda glossa, pugnans cum litera, quod corpus Christi sit in pane, vel panis sit corporis Christi latibulum.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ said This is my body, and he is truthful. Therefore he is to be believed, setting aside philosophical subtlety, and consequently his words are to be understood simply as they sound. Answer 1. This is the fallacy of non-cause. Christ's truthfulness does indeed make his words most true, and they are to be believed, setting aside philosophical subtlety. But it does not make them to be understood properly and literally. For even one who is truthful can speak figuratively. Christ was no less truthful when he said figuratively, I am the light of the world; I am the door of the sheep; I am the true vine, you are the branches; my Father is the husbandman; I am the way, the truth and the life; I am the good shepherd, etc., than when he spoke properly, I am Jesus whom you seek; I have chosen you; my Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask, etc. Christ therefore is truthful, and his words are true, even when by sacramental metonymy he said of the bread, This is my body, that is, it is a sacrament, or holy sign, of my body. Those foolish logicians, who do not hesitate to say that figurative expressions are lies, should be driven far away from the schools. 2. By the contrary [ἐνάντιον]. Christ is truthful. Therefore, in calling the bread his body, he did not say that his body is in the bread, when the disciples saw that it was outside the bread and reclining at the table with them. Likewise: the words are to be taken simply. Therefore no gloss that contradicts the letter is to be added to them, that the body of Christ is in the bread, or that the bread is a hiding place for the body of Christ.

units.la: Obj. 3. Christus est omnipotens. Ergo potest efficere, vt corpus suum sit corporaliter in pane. Resp. A posse ad incsse non valet let consequentia. Nam non est quæstio, quid Christus possit, sed quid velit. Nusquam promisit, se corpore suo præsentem fore in pane, vel in loco panis: sed contra promisit, se corpore suo ascensurum in cælum, & relicturum esse mundum. Nihil igitur derogatur omnipotentiæ Christi.
units.tr: Objection 3. Christ is omnipotent. Therefore he can bring it about that his body is present corporeally in the bread. Answer. The consequence from what he can do to what he does does not hold. For the question is not what Christ can do, but what he wills. Nowhere did he promise that he would be present with his body in the bread, or in the place of the bread. On the contrary, he promised that he would ascend into heaven with his body and leave the world. Nothing therefore is taken from the omnipotence of Christ.

units.la: Inst. Panis est in loco cœnæ præsens: & est corpus Christi. Ergo corpus Christi est in loco cœnæ præsens. Resp. Mutato genere prædicationis non valet consequentia. Minor enim est figurata, etiam aduersariorum confessione. Nam Iacobus Andreæ in Disputatione Maulbrunnensi, cùm aliter elabi non posset, expressè confitebatur, hanc esse figuratam: Panis est corpus Christi. Si autem panis est corpus Christi, falsa erit glossa, quod in pane sit corpus Christi.
units.tr: Instance. Bread is present in the place of the supper, and it is the body of Christ. Therefore the body of Christ is present in the place of the supper. Answer. The consequence does not hold when the kind of predication is changed. For the minor is figurative, even by the confession of our opponents. James Andreae, in the Maulbronn Disputation, when he could not otherwise slip away, expressly admitted that this is figurative: Bread is the body of Christ. But if bread is the body of Christ, then the gloss that the body of Christ is in the bread is false.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Verba Christi non sunt mutanda. Christus dixit: Hoc est corpus meum. Ergo non debet loco verbi est, poni verbum significat. Resp. 1. Concedimus totum. Non enim pro est ponimus significat, nec verba Christi mutamus: sed ut sunt ab eo pronunciata, retinemus: dicimus vero, hanc esse genuinam eorum sententiam, quod panis sit corpus Christi sacramentaliter: hoc est, sacramentum, siue sacrum signum corporis Christi: seu quod significet corpus Christi: quia Christus ipse sic interpretatur, addens: Hoc facite in mei memoriam. Et Paulus: Hoc poculum est nouum testamentum in meo sanguine. Et Tertullianus: Panem acceptum & distributum discipulis, corpus suum illum fecit: Hoc est corpus meum, dicendo, hoc est, figura corporis mei. Et Ambrosius: Hæc oblatio est figura corporis & sanguinis Domini. Et Augustinus: Non dubitauit Dominus dicere: Hoc est corpus meum, cum daret signum sui corporis. 2. Retorquemus argumentum. Verba Christi non sunt mutanda: Ergo facessat glossa Transubstantiatorum: sub his speciebus continetur corpus meum: & Transubstantiatorum: In hoc pane est corpus meum. 3. Denique verba Christi non sunt mutanda: nempe, in alium sensum, quam Christus voluit: sæpe tamen sunt mutanda, id est, recte interpretanda: vt cum dixit: Erue oculum, &c. Auferenti tunicam da & pallium. Verba enim sunt intelligenda pro rerum natura, & ex mente loquentis.
units.tr: Objection 4. The words of Christ are not to be changed. Christ said This is my body. Therefore the verb signifies should not be put in place of the verb is. Answer 1. We grant the whole. For we do not put signifies for is, nor do we change the words of Christ. We keep them as he pronounced them. We say, however, that this is their genuine meaning: that the bread is the body of Christ sacramentally, that is, a sacrament or holy sign of the body of Christ, or that it signifies the body of Christ. Christ himself interprets it so, adding Do this in remembrance of me. So too Paul: This cup is the new testament in my blood. And Tertullian: Having taken the bread and distributed it to the disciples, he made it his body, saying, This is my body, that is, the figure of my body. And Ambrose: This oblation is a figure of the body and blood of the Lord. And Augustine: The Lord did not hesitate to say, This is my body, when he gave the sign of his body. 2. We turn the argument back. The words of Christ are not to be changed. Therefore let the gloss of the Transubstantiationists go away: under these species my body is contained; and their other gloss, in this bread is my body. 3. Finally, the words of Christ are not to be changed, that is, into another sense than the one Christ willed. Yet they are often to be changed, that is, rightly interpreted, as when he said Pluck out the eye, etc., and to the one who takes your coat, give also your cloak. For words are to be understood according to the nature of things and the mind of the speaker.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Verba testamentorum sunt intelligenda proprie, ne detur occasio litigandi de voluntate testatoris. Cœna est nouum Testamentum. Ergo, &c. Resp. ad Maiorem. Verba Testamentorum sunt intelligenda proprie: nempe ea, quæ proprie sunt dicta: figuratè verò, quæ sunt dicta figuratè. Si dicant, Omnia, negatur Maior. Satis est, Testamentorum verba & phrases esse claras & perspicuas: etsi sæpe non sunt proprie, sed
units.tr: Objection 5. The words of wills are to be understood properly, lest occasion be given for dispute about the intention of the testator. The Supper is the New Testament. Therefore, etc. Answer to the major premise. The words of wills are to be understood properly, namely those that are said properly; but those that are said figuratively are to be understood figuratively. If they say all, the major premise is denied. It is enough that the words and phrases of a testament are clear and plain, even though they are often not proper, but

units.la: Protocol. Lat. pag. 160.
units.tr: Protocol. Lat. p. 160.

units.la: Lib. 4. contr. Marc. Lib. 2. de sacram. c. 4. Contr. Ad. im. c. 12. sed figuratæ. Cum enim de testatoris mente & voluntate constat, frustra disputatur de litera. Sic Deus in veteri Testamento locutus est figuratè de circumcisione: est fœdus meum: de Agno: est transitus: de sacrificiis: sunt expiatio peccatorum: & Christus in novo Testamento figuratè dixit de pane: est corpus meum pro vobis traditum: & de poculo: est novum Testamentum in meo sanguine: duplici figura vinum vocans poculum per synecdochen, & poculum vocans novum Testamentum, hoc est, reconciliationem generis humani cum Deo, per metonymiam.
units.tr: Book 4 against Marcion. Book 2 on the sacraments, ch. 4. Against Adimantus, ch. 12. But the words are figurative. For once the mind and will of the testator is established, it is pointless to dispute about the letter. So God spoke figuratively in the Old Testament about circumcision: it is my covenant; about the lamb: it is the Passover; about the sacrifices: they are the expiation of sins. And Christ in the New Testament spoke figuratively about the bread: this is my body given for you; and about the cup: this is the new covenant in my blood. Here he used a double figure: calling the wine the cup by synecdoche, and calling the cup the new covenant, that is, the reconciliation of the human race with God, by metonymy.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Manducatio panis est oralis. Manducatio corporis Christi est etiam manducatio panis. Ergo manducatio corporis Christi est etiam oralis. Resp. Minor vel figurata, vel falsa est. Figurata est sic intellecta: Manducatio corporis Christi est res manducatione panis significata. Sic nihil sequitur, mutato genere prædicationis. Proprie verò intellecta est falsa. Manducatio enim panis est externa, visibilis, corporalis: manducatio corporis Christi est interna, invisibilis, spiritualis. Proprie igitur una manducatio esse non possunt: sed differunt, ut signum & res signata. Panis enim & eius manducatio est signum: corpus Christi, & eius manducatio est res signata. Sicut igitur res signata est signum, vel contra, non proprie, sed figurate: sic manducatio corporis Christi est manducatio panis, non proprie, sed figurate. Mutato igitur genere prædicationis nihil sequitur.
units.tr: Objection 6. The eating of bread is oral. The eating of the body of Christ is also the eating of bread. Therefore the eating of the body of Christ is also oral. Answer. The minor premise is either figurative or false. Figurative it is, if understood thus: the eating of the body of Christ is the thing signified by the eating of bread. In that case nothing follows, since the mode of predication has changed. But properly understood it is false. For the eating of bread is external, visible and bodily; the eating of the body of Christ is internal, invisible and spiritual. Properly, therefore, these cannot be one eating; they differ as sign and thing signified. For the bread and its eating are the sign; the body of Christ and its eating are the thing signified. Just as the thing signified is called the sign, or the reverse, not properly but figuratively, so the eating of the body of Christ is the eating of bread not properly but figuratively. Therefore, with the mode of predication changed, nothing follows.

units.la: Obiectio 7. Quod nos nutrit & viuificat, id necesse est ore intra nos recipi. Corpus & sanguis Christi nos nutriunt & viuificant. Necesse est igitur, ea ore intra nos recipi, manducari ac bibi. Resp. Ex puris particularibus nihil sequitur: quia Maior non est vniuersaliter vera. Non enim ex solo pane vivit homo. Distinguenda igitur Maior: Quod nos nutrit, & viuificat naturaliter: hoc est, per contactum & accretionem physicam, sicut cibus & potus naturalis, qui utique nos non nutrit, nisi ore intra nos sumptus accrescat substantiæ corporis nostri. De animæ verò nutritione, quæ spiritualis est, aliter est loquendum. Christi corpus & sanguis nos nutriunt & viuificant, ita ut ore intra nos recepta, accrescant substantiæ nostræ, efficiantque in nobis qualitates, sicuti alimenta naturaliter, vel pharmaca intra corpus sumta efficere solent: sed nutriunt & viuificant nos spiritualiter, modo ab illa nutritione naturali longè diverso. Pro diverso igitur nutritionis modo etiam perceptionis modus, seu esus corporis Christi diversus est. Modus ille, quo corpus & sanguis Christi nos nutriunt atque viuificant, consistit in tribus. 1. In ratione meriti. Quia enim corpus Christi pro nobis est in mortem traditum, & sanguis Christi pro nobis effusus in remissionem peccatorum: iccirco nos vitâ æternâ donamur: & hoc modo corpus & sanguis Christi nos nutriunt & viuificant suo merito, seu, vt meritum vitæ. 2. In applicatione meriti per fidem. Viuificamur enim, dum corporis & sanguinis Christi meritum vera fide nobis applicamus, seu, dum propter illud nos vitam æternam habere credimus, firmiterque confidimus. Fides verò hæc nititur Christo pendente in cruce, non autem corporaliter intra nos recepto, vel habitante. 3. In vnione cum Christo per Spiritum eius. Viuificamur enim, dum Spiritus Christi in nobis & in Christo habitans, nos cum eo vnit per fidem, & eandem in nobis atque in Christo vitam operatur. Nam DEo non placemus, nisi Christo insiti simus. Ea enim lege Deus propter Christi merita vult nos recipere in gratiam, & peccata nobis remittere: quidem Christo per fidem & Spiritum eius insiti simus, ac maneamus. Atque hoc est corpus & sanguinem Christi manducare & bibere: hoc est, corpore & sanguine Christi nutriri & viuificari. Non igitur requiritur illapsus vel ingressus aliquis corporis & sanguinis Christi in corpora nostra, ad hoc, vt corpore & sanguine Christi pascamur & viuificemur.
units.tr: Objection 7. What nourishes and quickens us must necessarily be received within us by the mouth. The body and blood of Christ nourish and quicken us. It is necessary, therefore, that they be received within us by the mouth, eaten and drunk. Answer. Nothing follows from particular premises alone, since the major premise is not universally true. For man does not live by bread alone. The major premise must therefore be distinguished: what nourishes and quickens us naturally, that is, by contact and physical accretion, as natural food and drink do, which of course do not nourish us unless, taken into us by the mouth, they add to the substance of our body. But concerning the nourishment of the soul, which is spiritual, we must speak otherwise. The body and blood of Christ nourish and quicken us, not in such a way that, received within us by the mouth, they add to our substance and produce qualities in us, as foods or medicines taken into the body usually do; but they nourish and quicken us spiritually, by a mode far different from that natural nourishment. Therefore, according to the different mode of nourishment, the mode of reception, or the eating of the body of Christ, is also different. That mode by which the body and blood of Christ nourish and quicken us consists in three things. (1) In the ground of merit. For since the body of Christ was delivered up to death for us, and the blood of Christ was shed for us for the remission of sins, we are therefore given eternal life; and in this way the body and blood of Christ nourish and quicken us by their merit, or, as the merit of life. (2) In the application of merit through faith. For we are quickened when, by true faith, we apply to ourselves the merit of the body and blood of Christ, or, when we believe and firmly trust that we have eternal life on account of it. But this faith rests on Christ hanging on the cross, not on his body received or dwelling corporally within us. (3) In union with Christ through his Spirit. For we are quickened when the Spirit of Christ, dwelling in us and in Christ, joins us to him through faith and works the same life in us as in Christ. For we cannot please God unless we are grafted into Christ. For on this condition God, for the merits of Christ, is willing to receive us into grace and to remit our sins: namely, if we are grafted into Christ through faith and his Spirit, and remain so. And this is to eat and drink the body and blood of Christ: that is, to be nourished and quickened by the body and blood of Christ. Therefore no entry or insertion of the body and blood of Christ into our bodies is required, in order that we be fed and quickened by the body and blood of Christ.

units.la: Inst. Non tantum animæ, sed & corpora nostra pascuntur corpore & sanguine Christi ad immortalitatem. Ergo non tantum animas, sed etiam corpora oportet manducare & bibere. Corpora autem nostra manducant & bibunt oraliter, &c. Resp. Maior omissa est falsa vniuersaliter. Quicquid pascitur corpore Christi, id manducat illud, &c. An enim crus tuum, vel cubitus tuus ideo comedit, quia nutritur cibo, quem per os intumà natura est ad hoc factum, vt per id nutrimentum vniuerso corpori suggeratur. Sic non necesse est corpora nostra ore manducare corpus Christi, vt eo pascamur ad immortalitatem: satis est os fidei cibum spiritualem accipere, vt spirituale nutrimentum ac vita in totum hominem transfundantur.
units.tr: Inference. Not only our souls but also our bodies are fed by the body and blood of Christ unto immortality. Therefore not only our souls but also our bodies must eat and drink. Our bodies, however, eat and drink orally, etc. Answer. The major premise, as omitted, is false universally: whatever is fed by the body of Christ, eats it, etc. For do you eat with your leg or your elbow because they are nourished by food which nature has made to be taken in through the mouth, so that this nourishment may be conveyed to the whole body? Likewise, it is not necessary for our bodies to eat the body of Christ orally, in order that we be fed unto immortality by it. It is enough that the mouth of faith receive the spiritual food, so that spiritual nourishment and life may be poured into the whole man.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXXIX.
units.tr: QUESTION 79.

units.la: Cur ergo Christus panem appellat suum corpus, calicem verò suum sanguinem, seu nouum fœdus per suum sanguinem: Paulus item panem & vinum communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi?
units.tr: Why then does Christ call bread his body, and the cup his blood, or the new covenant through his blood? Why does Paul likewise call the bread and wine the communion of the body and blood of Christ?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Christus non sine graui causa ita loquitur: videlicet, non solum, vt nos doceat, quemadmodum panis & vinum corporis vitam sustentant: sic etiam crucifixum suum corpus, & effusum suum sanguinem vere esse animæ nostræ cibum ac potum, quo ad vitam æternam nutriatur a: Verum multò magis, vt hoc visibili signo ac pignore nobis certum faciat, nos non minus vere corporis & sanguinis sui, per operationem Spiritus sancti, participes esse, quam sacra ista symbola in eius memoriam, ore corporis percipimus b. Tum etiam, quod eius passio & obedientia, tam certò nostra sit, quàm si ipsimet pro nostris peccatis pœnas dedissemus, & Deo satisfecissemus.
units.tr: Christ does not speak thus without weighty cause. He wishes, first, not only to teach us that just as bread and wine sustain the life of the body, so also his crucified body and poured-out blood are truly the food and drink of our soul, by which it is nourished to eternal life a. Much more, he wishes by this visible sign and pledge to make certain for us that we are no less truly partakers of his body and blood, through the working of the Holy Spirit, than we receive these sacred symbols with the mouth of the body in remembrance of him b. Then also, his passion and obedience are as surely ours as if we ourselves had paid the penalties for our sins and satisfied God.

units.la: a Ioh. 6, 55. b 1 Corinth. 10, 16.
EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Cùm neque μετουσία, neque συνουσία verbis Christi significetur: quæritur, cur ergo panis dicatur corpus Christi, calix sanguis Christi, hoc est: cur nomina rerum signatarum tribuantur signis.
units.tr: Since the words of Christ signify neither participation [μετουσία] nor communion [συνουσία], the question is why bread is called the body of Christ and the cup the blood of Christ; that is, why the names of the things signified are given to the signs.

units.la: Duæ sunt causæ, propter quas Christus sic loquitur. 1. Propter similitudinem seu analogiam, quam inter se habent signum & res signata, panis & corpus Christi. 2. Propter certitudinem, seu confirmationem coniunctæ exhibitionis signi & rei signatæ in vero visu.
units.tr: There are two causes for which Christ speaks thus. (1) On account of the likeness or analogy which the sign and the thing signified have with each other, namely bread and the body of Christ. (2) On account of the certainty, or confirmation, of the conjoined exhibition of the sign and the thing signified in a true showing.

units.la: Analogia panis & corporis Christi in his præcipuè consistit: 1. Vt panis & vinum nutriunt corpus ad hanc vitam: ita corpus & sanguis Christi nutriunt animam ad vitam æternam. 2. Vt panis non deglutitur integer, sed manducatur fractus; ita corpus Christi percipitur mactatū in crucem. 4. 4. Vt panis & vinum sine appetitu non prosunt vescenti, sed oportet afferre famem & sitim ad mensam: ita corpus & sanguis Christi non prosunt, nisi esurientibus & sitientibus justitiam.
units.tr: The analogy between bread and the body of Christ consists chiefly in this: (1) as bread and wine nourish the body for this life, so the body and blood of Christ nourish the soul to eternal life; (2) as bread is not swallowed whole but eaten broken, so the body of Christ is received as slain on the cross; (3) as bread and wine do not profit the one who eats them without appetite, but hunger and thirst must be brought to the table, so the body and blood of Christ profit only those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

units.la: 5. Vt ex multis granis fit vnus panis, & ex multis acinis vnum vinum: sic nos per haec symbola multi efficimur vnum corpus, & in vnum corpus coalescimus cum Christo, & inter nos certitudo seu obsignatio fidei similiter causa est cur de signis dicatur, quod est rei significatae proprium. Testantur enim signa, sacrificium Christi peractum esse in nostram salutem, tam vere, quam vere habemus signa: immo nos pasci crucifixo corpore, & effuso sanguine Christi tam vere, quam vere sacra symbola corporis & sanguinis Christi percipimus.
units.tr: 5. As many grains make one loaf, and many grapes one wine, so through these symbols we, many, are made one body and grow together into one body with Christ and with one another. The certainty, or sealing, of faith is likewise the reason why the thing signified is named from the signs, which is the proper character of the thing signified. For the signs testify that Christ's sacrifice has been completed for our salvation, as truly as we truly have the signs; indeed, that we are fed on the crucified body and poured-out blood of Christ as truly as we truly receive the sacred symbols of the body and blood of Christ.

units.la: QVAESTIO LXXX. Quid interest inter coenam Domini, & Missam Papisticam?
units.tr: QUESTION 80. What is the difference between the Lord's Supper and the Papistical Mass?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Coena Domini nobis testatur, nos perfectam remissionem omnium nostrorum peccatorum habere, propter vnicum illud Christi sacrificium, quod ipsemet se-mel in cruce peregit a. Tum etiam nos per Spiritum sanctum inseri Christo b, quia jam secundum naturam suam humanam, tantum in coelis est, ad dexteram Patris c, ibi-que vult a nobis adorari d.
units.tr: The Lord's Supper testifies to us that we have perfect remission of all our sins, on account of that one sacrifice of Christ which he himself offered once for all on the cross a. It also testifies that we are engrafted into Christ through the Holy Spirit b, since he now, according to his human nature, is only in heaven, at the right hand of the Father c, and there wishes to be adored by us d.

units.la: In Missa autem negatur, vivos & mortuos habere remissionem peccatorum, propter vnicam CHRISTI passionem, nisi etiamnum quotidie Christus pro ipsis a sacrificulis offeratur. Tum etiam docetur, Christum corporaliter sub speciebus panis & vini esse, ideoque in illis adorandum esse e. Atque ita ipsum Missae fundamentum, nihil aliud est, quam abnegatio unici illius sacrificij & passionis Iesu Christi, & execranda idolo-latria.
units.tr: In the Mass, however, it is denied that the living and the dead have remission of sins on account of the one passion of Christ, unless Christ is still offered every day for them by the sacrificing priests. It is also taught that Christ is bodily present under the species of bread and wine, and therefore is to be adored in them e. And so the very foundation of the Mass is nothing other than the denial of that unique sacrifice and passion of Jesus Christ, and execrable idolatry.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Necessaria est hæc quæstio, propter errores & horribiles abusus, qui per Missam irrepserunt in Ecclesiam. Alias quæritur, cur Missa sit abolenda? Sed hic ista quæstio continetur: quia discrimina, seu antitheses cœnæ Domini & Missæ sunt totidem causæ, cur Missa sit abolenda. Cùm enim habeat multa pugnantia cum cœna Domini, non debet cum ea confundi, nec eius loco in Ecclesia obtrudi, nec à piis magistratibus iu Ecclesia ferri, sed aboleri.
units.tr: This question is necessary because of the errors and dreadful abuses that have crept into the Church through the Mass. Otherwise the question is asked, why the Mass should be abolished. Here, however, that question is contained within this one: the differences, or antitheses, between the Lord's Supper and the Mass are so many reasons why the Mass should be abolished. For since it has many things that conflict with the Lord's Supper, it must not be confused with it, nor be thrust into the Church in its place, nor be retained in the Church by pious magistrates, but must be abolished.

units.la: Missam aliqui deducunt ab Hebraeo מסה quod significat tributum, seu oblationem spontaneam, à מסה tribuo, quod à quapersona pendi consuevit. Vox construeta habetur Deut.16. v.10. Missah nidhath jadecha, hoc est, oblationem spontaneam manus tua. Sic autem appellatur ea oblatio, quasi annum tributum, quod tamen spontaneum erat. Alij interpretantur sufficientiam, nimirum ut daretur, quod satis esset: & fortasse verius: quia Deut.15,8. Dominus præcipit Israelitis, ut manuum suam pauperi aperiant, & ei mutuent, quod sufficit. Id Chaldaeus paraphrastes interpretatur Missach. Hinc illi Missam dictam esse putant, quasi tributum & oblatio spontanea, quæ passim Deo in Ecclesia pro viuis & mortuis offeratur. Sed id non est verisimile. Constat quidem, Ecclesiam Latinorum voces nonnullas ab Hebraeis mutuatam esse, ut sathan, osianna, sabbaoth, halleluiah, paschah, &c. sed hæc & similes voces, ad latinam Ecclesiam non venerunt, nisi per Græcam: ideo in nouo Testamento Græce conscripto, etiam reperiuntur, neq; nos vllas Hebraeas voces habemus ad nostram Ecclesiam deriuatas, quas Ecclesia Græca prius non habuerit. Si quoq; patres Græcos excutiamus, nunquam ab eis vox Missæ vsurpata reperietur. Ideo Missæ nomen ab Hebraeis deductum non opinor.
units.tr: Some derive Missam from the Hebrew מסה, which means a tribute or a voluntary offering, from מסה, to pay, which is customarily required from a person. The construct form occurs in Deut. 16:10, Missah nidhath jadecha [מִשַּׂאַת נִדְבַת יָדְךָ], that is, a voluntary offering of your hand. That offering is so called as if it were an annual tribute, though it was voluntary. Others interpret it as sufficiency, namely what is given so that it is enough; and perhaps this is more accurate, because in Deut. 15:8 the Lord commands the Israelites to open their hand to the poor and lend to him what is sufficient. The Chaldee paraphrast translates this as Missach. From this they think the Mass was so named, as if it were a tribute and a voluntary offering, which is offered everywhere to God in the Church for the living and the dead. But this is not likely. It is certain indeed that the Latin Church borrowed some words from the Hebrews, such as sathan, osianna, sabbaoth, halleluiah, paschah, etc. But these and similar words came into the Latin Church only through the Greek. Therefore they are also found in the New Testament, which was written in Greek, and we have no Hebrew words derived for our Church that the Greek Church did not have first. Moreover, if we search the Greek Fathers, the word Mass will never be found used by them. So I do not think that the name Mass is derived from the Hebrews.

units.la: Missæ igitur nomen, quod vtique latinum est, sumrum videtur ex patribus, qui remissam dixerunt pro remissione, vt Tertullianus: Diximus, inquit, de remissa peccatorum. Et Cyprianus: Qui remissam peccatorum erat daturus, lauacro regenerationis defunctos non dedignatus. Idem: Qui blasphemat Spiritum sanctum, remissam peccatorum non habet. Vt ergo dixerunt remissam pro missione, sic missam pro missione dixisse videntur. A mittendo igitur nomen habet. Sed hic rursus variant. Alij enim volunt missam, quasi missionem, ab antiqua consuetudine actuum Ecclesiasticorum, quæ a Græcis Ecclesiis ad Latinas defluxit, quod finitis concionibus & lectionibus, ante consecrationis mysterium diaconus foras mittebat, hoc est, exire jubebat catechumenos. chumenos, energumenos, & excommunicatos, alta voce clamans: Si quis è catechumenis remansit, exeat: atq; ita Missa vocitatur dicta, quasi Missio: quia scilicet erat postrema pars actionum sacrarum. Alij Missam, quasi dimissam, vel dimissionem dictam putant, à formula dimittendi coetus ecclesiasticos: quia finitis precibus & ritibus clamabat diaconus: Ite, missa est. Alij à missis eleemosynis seu collectis, quae in λἰτυργιαῖς sacra mittebantur, & dicebatur: Ite, missa est, scilicet collecta & eleemosyna, quae mittebatur, & dabatur pauperibus. Summa. Quod in Ecclesia post missionem sive catechumenorum sive eleemosynarum agebatur, missam appellarunt. Lombardus aliter, Missa (inquit) dicitur, eo quod coelestis nuncius ad consecrandum vivificum corpus adveniat, juxta dictum sacerdotis dicentis: Omnipotens Deus, jube haec perferri per manus sancti Angeli tui in sublime altare tuum, &c. Idcirco nisi angelus venerit, Missa nequaquam jure vocari potest. Videte ineptias! Idem. Missa dicitur, vel quia missa est hostia, cuius commemoratio fit in illo officio: unde dicitur: Ite, missa est, sequimini hostiam, quae missa est ad coelestia, tendentes post eam: vel quia missus coelestis venit ad consecrandum dominicum corpus, per quem ad altare coeleste defertur hostia: unde dicitur: Ite, missa est.
units.tr: The name Mass, which is certainly Latin, therefore seems to have been taken from the Fathers, who used remissam for remissione, as Tertullian does: We have spoken, he says, of the remission of sins. And Cyprian: He who was about to give remission of sins did not disdain those who had died by the bath of regeneration. Again: He who blasphemes the Holy Spirit does not have remission of sins. So just as they used remissam for remissione, so they seem to have used missam for missione. Therefore it has its name from sending. But here again they differ. For some want missam, as if it were missionem (dismissal), to come from an ancient custom of ecclesiastical acts, which passed down from the Greek Churches to the Latin, namely that when the sermons and readings were finished, before the mystery of consecration, the deacon sent out, that is, ordered out, the catechumens, energumens, and excommunicated, calling out in a loud voice: If anyone of the catechumens remains, let him go out. And thus the Mass is called Missa, as if Missio, because clearly it was the last part of the sacred actions. Others think the Mass was called missa, as if dimissam or dimissionem, from the formula for dismissing the ecclesiastical assemblies, because when the prayers and rites were finished the deacon cried out: Go, it is the dismissal. Others derive it from the missis (alms or collections) that were sent in the sacred λειτουργίαις [leitourgiais], and it was said: Go, it is the dismissal, namely the collection and alms that were sent and given to the poor. In sum: what was done in the Church after the dismissal, whether of the catechumens or of the alms, they called the Mass.
