Ad bona opera homines sunt cogendi, suo scilicet ordine, ita vt præcedat coactio ad opera moralia, sequatur deinde coactio ad ceremonialia. Et sic intelligi debet, quod ait Christus: Compelle eos intrare.
units.tr: Objection 3. Men are to be compelled to good works. The use of the sacraments is a good work. Therefore no one is to be kept from it, but all are rather to be compelled to it. Answer: 1. The minor premise is not true unless it is understood of the use made by the faithful; but when the sacraments are taken up by unbelievers, their use is not a good work but an abuse and profanation of the sacraments. Therefore Christ dissuades the impious from this good work when he says: "Leave your gift at the altar and go," etc. 2. The major premise must be distinguished. Men are to be compelled to good works, in their proper order, so that compulsion to moral works comes first and then compulsion to ceremonial ones. And this is how we must understand what Christ says: "Compel them to come in."

units.la: Si sic obiiciunt: Bona opera non sunt prohibenda. Vsus sacramentorum est bonum opus. Ergo nō est prohibendus; concedi-mus. mus totum. Non enim prohibemus vsum, sed abusum. Inst.1. Deus voluit omnes accedere ad pascha celebrandum. Resp. O-mnes non sceleratos, sed eos, qui erant membra populi, & debe-bant tolerari in societate politica: de contumacibus erat man-datum, vt tollerentur. Inst.2. At nihilominus multa comitantur & fiunt mala. Resp. Fiunt ab impoenitentibus, & sequi nolenti-bus, non a monentibus. Beati autem, qui esuriunt & sitiunt justi-tiam, hoc est, qui cupiunt fieri bona. Si non fiant, ipsorum non est culpa. Non autem debemus facere mala, aut omittere bona, quae Deus jubet, vt bonum inde sequatur. Nos nostrum faciamus officium, euentum Deo committamus. Si non fiant, bonam ta-men conscientiam retineamus.
units.tr: If they object thus: good works are not to be forbidden; the use of the sacraments is a good work; therefore it is not to be forbidden. We grant the whole argument. For we do not forbid the use, but the abuse. Further objection 1. God willed that all should come to celebrate the Passover. Answer: Not all the wicked, but those who were members of the people and had to be tolerated in political society; the command concerned the obstinate, that they should be tolerated. Further objection 2. Nevertheless many evils accompany and occur. Answer: They are done by the unrepentant, and by those unwilling to follow, not by those who admonish. "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness," that is, who desire to become good. If they do not become so, the fault is not theirs. But we ought not to do evil, or omit the good things God commands, in order that good may follow from it. Let us do our duty and commit the outcome to God. If they do not come about, let us nonetheless keep a good conscience.

units.la: Obiect.5. Prophetae, Apostoli & Johannes neminem exclue-runt, immo Johannes baptizabat progeniem viperarum. Ergo neque nostri ministri debent excludere. Resp. ad antecedens. De Johanne negatur. Etsi ex progenie viperarum erant, quos baptí-zabat, tamen non amplius erant viperae, cum baptizarentur. Baptizabat enim confitentes peccata sua: praedicabat eis baptis-mum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum, & exigebat a ba-ptizatis, vt agerent fructus poenitentiâ dignos. Prophetae etiamsi non potuerunt excludere a sacrificiis & sacramentis impios: tamen scelera & abusum sacrificiorum damnarunt, & saepe lon-gas habuerunt conciones contra Ecclesiam, quae illos admitte-bat ad sacrificia. Apostolos vsos esse exclusione, Pauli exem-plo constat: quia jussit incestuosum tradi Satanae, & ex Eccle-sia eijci.
units.tr: Objection 5. The prophets, the apostles and John excluded no one; indeed John baptized a brood of vipers. Therefore neither should our ministers exclude. Answer to the antecedent: This is denied concerning John. Although those he baptized were of the brood of vipers, they were no longer vipers when they were baptized. For he baptized those confessing their sins; he preached to them the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, and required of those baptized that they bring forth fruits worthy of repentance. The prophets, even if they could not exclude the impious from sacrifices and sacraments, nevertheless condemned their crimes and the abuse of the sacrifices, and often delivered long sermons against the Church which admitted them to the sacrifices. That the apostles used exclusion is clear from the example of Paul, since he ordered the incestuous man to be delivered to Satan and cast out of the Church.

units.la: Inst. Johannes profitentes fidem & poenitentiam admittebat solus, & impoenitentes reijciebat solus. Ergo vni ministro licebit vel admittere profitentes doctrinam & poenitentiam, vel contumaces eijcere vel excludere, quod supra fuit negatum: aut exemplum Baptistae nihil probat. Resp. Est dissimilitudo in exem-plis. Johannes erat praeditus authoritate prophetica & apostoli-ca, quam ministri non habent. Deinde agebatur tunc de collec-tione novae Ecclesiae, non de exclusione eorum, qui fuerunt in Ecclesia, & ab ea defecerant.
units.tr: Objection. John admitted alone those professing faith and repentance, and alone rejected the unrepentant. Therefore it will be lawful for a single minister either to admit those professing doctrine and repentance, or to cast out or exclude the obstinate, which was denied above; or else the example of the Baptist proves nothing. Answer: There is a dissimilarity in the examples. John was endowed with prophetic and apostolic authority, which ministers do not have. Furthermore, at that time the gathering of the new Church was in question, not the exclusion of those who had been in the Church and had fallen away from it.

units.la: APPENDIX DE EXCOMMUNICATIONE.
units.tr: APPENDIX ON EXCOMMUNICATION.

units.la: Solutiones breves sophismatum, quibus in publica disputatione Heidelbergae habita, praeside D. Petro Boquino, respondente pro gradu Doctorali M. Georgio Witthero Anglo, anno anno 1568. die 10. Iunÿ, disciplinam ecclesiasticam oppugnare quidam conati sunt: exceptâ ex ore Doct. Vrsini in disputationis repetitione postridie privatim in Collegio Sapientia instituta.
units.tr: Brief solutions of the sophisms with which certain men have tried to attack church discipline in a public disputation held at Heidelberg in the year 1568, on 10 June, under the presidency of D. Peter Boquin, with M. George Witther, an Englishman, responding for the doctoral degree; also taken from the lips of Dr. Ursinus, privately in the College of Sapientia, in the repetition of the disputation the following day.

units.la: Theses de disciplina ecclesiastica propositæ erant duæ istæ:
units.tr: The two theses on ecclesiastical discipline that were proposed were these:

units.la: XII. Ad sinceram verbi divini praedicationem, & legitimam sacramentorum administrationem, oportet in Ecclesia gubernationis vigere officium.
units.tr: XII. For the sincere preaching of the divine Word and the lawful administration of the sacraments, there must be a function of government flourishing in the Church.

units.la: XIII. Officium autem hoc voco, ut ministri cum presbyteris quosvis peccantes (etiam principes) arguendi, increpandi, excommunicandi, reliquaq; ad disciplinam ecclesiasticam pertinentia peragendi facultatem & habeant & exerceant.
units.tr: XIII. I call this function the power, which ministers together with the elders have and exercise, to rebuke, admonish and excommunicate any sinners whatever (even princes), and to carry out the other things that pertain to ecclesiastical discipline.

units.la: Obj. 1. Vbi recte debent administrari verbum & sacramenta, ibi debet vigere officium disciplinæ. Sic in primitiva Ecclesia & hodie in multis ecclesiis bene constitutis non viget officiū disciplinæ. Ergo in iis non recte administrata sunt, nec administrantur verbū & sacramenta. Atqui hoc est absurdum. Ergo & illud. Resp. ad maiorem per distinctionem. Recte administrari sacramenta, est ambiguum. Potest intelligi de administratione secundum πρῶτον, hoc est, tali, quæ prorsus congruat cum præscripto Domini. Potest etiam intelligi de administratione non secundum Ecclesiæ. In toto mundo sacramenta non administrantur recte secundum primam significationem: secundū alteram verò non item. Etsi enim subinde fiunt aliqui næui, qui propter imbecillitatem humanam subito corrigi nequeunt: tamen administratio defectus agnosci & deplorari. Beati enim, qui esuriunt & sitiunt justitiam. Hæc nisi concedantur, nulla erit ecclesia pura in mundo. Hæc solutio sufficeret. Sed minor etiam negatur. Nam in primitiva Ecclesia fuit officium disciplinæ, ut in Corinthiaca multis næuis laborante: & mansit etiam in male constituta Ecclesia, sed cum magno abusu, ut in Papistica. Inst. contra negationem minoris. In nostris & Helveticis Ecclesiis bene constitutis non viget excommunicatio. Ergo stat minor. Resp. ad antecedens. Quod in aliquibus non viget, male fit. Nihilominus infringitur minor: quia etiam in istis Ecclesiis recte administratur verbum & sacramenta, secundum alteram significationem. Modo addamus illud: Beati qui esuriunt & sitiunt justitiam. Cæterum in prima Ecclesia aliquot centum annis post Christum, disciplinam viguisse, patet ex hoc dicto Chrysostomi: Si quis flagitiosus veniet ad mensam Domini, ne porrigas illi corpus & sanguinem Domini. Si nolet cedere, indica mihi: sanguinem potius fundam, quàm illum admisero.
units.tr: Objection 1. Where the Word and the sacraments ought to be rightly administered, there the office of discipline ought to flourish. In the primitive Church, and today in many well-constituted churches, the office of discipline does not flourish. Therefore in these the Word and sacraments are not rightly administered, nor are they administered. But this is absurd. Therefore the former is too. Answer: I distinguish the major premise. That the sacraments are rightly administered is ambiguous. It can be understood of administration according to the first [πρῶτον] sense, that is, administration that wholly agrees with the Lord's prescription. It can also be understood of administration not according to the Church's (ideal). Throughout the whole world the sacraments are not rightly administered in the first sense, but in the other sense they are. For although from time to time some blemishes occur, which because of human weakness cannot be corrected at once, yet the defect is to be acknowledged and lamented in the administration. "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness." If these points are not conceded, there will be no pure church in the world. This solution would suffice. But the minor premise is also denied. For in the primitive Church there was the office of discipline, as in the Corinthian church, which laboured under many blemishes; and it remained even in a badly constituted church, but with great abuse, as in the Papist church. Objection against the denial of the minor premise: in our churches and the Helvetic churches, which are well constituted, excommunication does not flourish. Therefore the minor stands. Answer to the antecedent: that it does not flourish in some places is an evil. Nevertheless the minor premise is refuted, because in these churches too the Word and sacraments are rightly administered, in the second sense. Only let us add that saying: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness." Moreover, that discipline flourished in the primitive Church for some hundred years after Christ is clear from this saying of Chrysostom: "If any scandalous person comes to the Lord's table, do not give him the body and blood of the Lord. If he will not withdraw, tell me: I would sooner shed my own blood than admit him."

units.la: Obiect. 1. Doctrina carens verbo Dei, & exemplis probatis, non est Ecclesiæ obtrudenda. Hæc doctrina de excommunicatione caret verbo Dei & exemplis probatis. Ergo non debet obtrudi Ecclesiæ. Resp. Negatur minor. Verbum exstat Matth.18. Dic Ecclesiæ: si Ecclesiam non audierit sit tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus. Exemplum verò 1 Cor.5. huiusmodi homo tradatur Satanæ ad interitum carnis. Et 1,20. Quos tradidi Satanæ.
units.tr: Objection 1. Doctrine lacking the Word of God and approved examples is not to be imposed on the Church. This doctrine of excommunication lacks the Word of God and approved examples. Therefore it must not be imposed on the Church. Answer. The minor premise is denied. The Word is in Matthew 18: "Tell it to the Church; if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector." The example is in 1 Corinthians 5: "such a man is to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh," and 1 Corinthians 5:20: "whom I have delivered to Satan."

units.la: Contra Verbum.
units.tr: Against the Word.

units.la: Inst. 1. Matth.18. Nulla fit mentio presbyterij, neque excommunicationis. Ergo hoc verbum nihil probat. Resp. Negatur antecedens, quia etsi non habeantur verba formalia: tamen sententia continetur. Presbyterium enim continetur ibi, Dic Ecclesiæ: excommunicatio ibi, sit tibi velut Ethnicus, & publicanus.
units.tr: Objection 1. Matthew 18. There is no mention of the presbytery or of excommunication. Therefore this text proves nothing. Answer. The antecedent is denied, because although the formal words are not found, the sense is contained there. For the presbytery is contained in "Tell it to the Church," and excommunication in "let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector."

units.la: Inst. 2. Ecclesia non est presbyterium. Jubet autem Christus indicationem fieri apud Ecclesiam, & admonitionem per Ecclesiam. Ergo non fit mentio presbyterij. Resp. Negatur maior. quamuis etiam potest concedi totum argumentum, videlicet, quod Christus non intelligat presbyterium, sed proprie sumat vocabulum Ecclesiæ ante Christum Judaicæ. post Christum Christianæ. Sed in Ecclesiæ jurisdictione oportet esse ordinem, oportet esse aliquos ab Ecclesia constitutos: qui actiones dirigant: alioqui esset ἀταξία. Nec potest observari id, quod Christus jubet sine circumstantiarum determinatione. Itaque sub Ecclesia continetur presbyterium, & per consequens intelligitur de synedrio.
units.tr: Objection 2. The Church is not the presbytery. But Christ commands that the matter be reported before the Church, and that admonition be given through the Church. Therefore there is no mention of the presbytery. Answer. The major premise is denied, although the whole argument may also be conceded, namely that Christ does not mean the presbytery, but takes the word "Church" properly: before Christ, the Jewish Church; after Christ, the Christian Church. But in the jurisdiction of the Church there must be order, there must be some appointed by the Church who direct the proceedings; otherwise there would be disorder [ἀταξία]. Nor can what Christ commands be observed without determining the circumstances. So the presbytery is contained under the Church, and consequently it is understood of the synedrion.

units.la: Inst. 3. Verum quidem est, non posse fieri indicationem apud totam Ecclesiam, sed apud aliquod synedrium, quod tamen sit politicum, ut sit sensus: dic Ecclesiæ, id est, senatui vibis. Resp. Jam fatentur, non posse indicationem fieri apud totam Ecclesiasticum, sed apud aliquod synedrium, non tamen Ecclesiasticum, sed politicum. Quæstio igitur est, an intelligendum sit de synedrio politico. Hoc ipsi debent probare. Probant. Synedrium illud fuit politicum. Christus jubet indicare apud synedrion. Ergo apud politicum. Resp. Negatur maior. Illi probant. Synedrion, quod dabat Paulo potestatem interficiendi Christianos, afficiebat pœnis corporalibus. Ergo erat politicum. Respond. ad maiorem: Quod afficit pœnis corporalibus, nempe jure. Pontifices afficiebant, sed injuriâ: quia non habebant jus, sed rapiebant ad se. Sic etiam de Stephani morte. Est enim per tumultum interfectus: & sacerdotibus quidem volentibus, sed malè.
units.tr: Objection 3. It is true that the matter cannot be reported before the whole Church, but before some synedrion, which however is civil, so that the sense is: "tell the Church," that is, the senate of the city. Answer. They now admit that the matter cannot be reported before the whole ecclesiastical body, but before some synedrion, yet not an ecclesiastical one but a civil one. The question therefore is whether it must be understood of a civil synedrion. This they themselves must prove. They try to prove it. That synedrion was civil. Christ commands that the matter be reported before the synedrion. Therefore before a civil body. Answer. The major premise is denied. They prove it. The synedrion which gave Paul power to kill Christians inflicted bodily punishments. Therefore it was civil. Answer to the major premise: that it inflicts bodily punishments, namely by right. The priests did inflict them, but by injustice, because they had no right and seized it for themselves. So also in the case of Stephen's death: he was killed by a tumult, and by the priests indeed willingly, but wrongly.

units.la: Inst. 4. Ex Augustino. Judæi mentiebantur, cùm dicerent: Non licet nobis interficere quenquam. Resp. Augustini verba sic habent: An non interficiebant, quem interficiendum offerebant? Sed intelligendum est: eos dixisse, non sibi licere interficere quenquam propter diei festi sanctitatem, quem celebrare jam cœperant. Itane obduruistis falsi Israelitæ? itane omnem sensum nimia malitia amisistis, ut ideo vos à sanguine innocentis impollutos esse credatis, quia cum fundendum alteri tradidistis? Non igitur dicit Augustinus, eos fuisse mentitos, sed tantum, eos nihilominus fecisse, quod sibi non licere clamabant.
units.tr: Objection 4. From Augustine. The Jews lied when they said: "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death." Answer. Augustine's words run thus: "Were they not killing him whom they were offering for execution? But it must be understood that they said it was not lawful for them to kill anyone because of the holiness of the feast day, which they had now begun to celebrate. Have you grown so hard, you false Israelites? Have you lost all sense through excessive malice, so that you believe yourselves undefiled by the blood of the innocent, because you handed him over to be slain by another?" Augustine therefore does not say that they lied, but only that they nevertheless did what they cried out was not lawful for them.

units.la: Inst. 5. Ex Chrysostomo. Non licet nobis: scilicet propter vicinitatem festi. Resp. Non est verum, bona venia Chrysostomi: quia historiæ testantur, jurisdictionem civilem & leges ipsis fuisse ereptas ab Herode magno: & Josephus scribit, totum synedrium ab eo fuisse trucidatum unà cum Hyrcano, uno excepto Samea. Hoc igitur Judæi volunt dicere ad Pilatum: Tu habes jus gladij, nobis non licet interficere quenquam: quod & ipse Pilatus confirmat: Nescis me potestatem habere te crucifigendi, & potestatem habere te absoluendi?
units.tr: Objection 5. From Chrysostom. "It is not lawful for us": namely, because of the nearness of the feast. Answer. This is not true, with all due respect to Chrysostom, because histories testify that civil jurisdiction and laws were taken from them by Herod the Great; and Josephus writes that the whole synedrion was slaughtered by him together with Hyrcanus, with the single exception of Samaias. The Jews therefore wish to say this to Pilate: "You have the right of the sword; it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death"; which Pilate himself confirms: "Do you not know that I have power to crucify you, and power to release you?"

units.la: Inst. 6. Sed ipse dixit: Sumite vos eum, & secundum legem vestram judicate. Resp. Intelligit legem Mosis, quasi dicat: Si est blasphemus, obruatur lapidibus, me concedente.
units.tr: Objection 6. But he himself said: "Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law." Answer. He means the law of Moses, as if to say: "If he is a blasphemer, let him be stoned, with my permission."

units.la: Inst. 7. Josephus scribit, Judæis fuisse leges concessas à Claudio. Resp. Ergo prius eas non habuerunt. Deinde concessit eis leges Ecclesiasticas, hoc est, αὐτονομίαν religionis: Volo (inquit) inconcussa esse jura eorum à Caij insania, eisque jus esse persevearandi in patriis ritibus.
units.tr: Objection 7. Josephus writes that laws were granted to the Jews by Claudius. Answer. Then they did not have them before. Moreover, he granted them ecclesiastical laws, that is, self-government [αὐτονομίαν] in religion: "I wish (he says) their rights to remain unshaken by the madness of Caius, and that it be their right to persevere in their ancestral rites."

units.la: Inst. 8. Jus gladij fuit eis ademtum ab Herode magno. Ergo prius habuerunt, & synedrium erat politicum tunc, cum Christus juberet synedrio indicari. Ergo jussit indicari senatui politico. Nullum enim aliud synedrium erat, quod non erat politicum. Nam tria erant synedria in Judæa: 1. Synedrium maius, quod erat totius regni senatus, ut in Gallia Parlamentum. 2. Synedrium minus, quod erat urbis Hierosolymæ senatus. 3. Triumviratus. Hæc omnia erant politica, &c. Resp. 1. per muersionem. Si Judæi jus politicum amiserunt sub Herode magno: non igitur id habuerunt tempore Christi. Nam constat, Herodem magnû prius fuisse mortuum, quàm Christus inciperet docere.
units.tr: Objection 8. The right of the sword was taken from them by Herod the Great. Therefore they had it before, and the synedrion was civil at that time, when Christ commanded the matter to be reported to the synedrion. Therefore he ordered it to be reported to the civil senate. For there was no other synedrion which was not civil. For there were three synedria in Judea: 1. The greater synedrion, which was the senate of the whole kingdom, as the Parlement in France. 2. The lesser synedrion, which was the senate of the city of Jerusalem. 3. The triumvirate. All these were civil, etc. Answer. 1. By inversion. If the Jews lost civil right under Herod the Great, then they did not have it at the time of Christ. For it is established that Herod the Great had died before Christ began to teach.

units.la: 2. Ad argumentum: Synedrium erat politicum. Resp. ad maiorem: Erat politicum, sed non tantum: habebat etiam potestatem ecclesiasticam, quia tractabat simul causas religionis, constabat ex Pharisæis, & aliis legum peritis seu scribis, hoc est, ex Theologis, & Jurisconsultis. Idem in populo Judaico erant Theologi & Jurecoonsulti. Nam habebant leges morales & forenses. Synedrium igitur minus, de quo Christus loquitur, non fuit merè politicum, sed simul ecclesiasticum. Jam est quæstio, an jubeat synedrio indicari ut politico, an vero ut ecclesiastico? Resp. Ut ecclesiastico. Probatur ex textu. 1. Quia jubet contumacem habere pro Ethnico & publicano, hoc est, pro alieno à regno Dei. Declarare vero aliquem publicanum & alienum à regno Dei non est magistratus politici, sed ecclesiastici: quia publicanus potest esse membrum civitatis, sed non ecclesiæ Christi. 2. Christus addit: Amen dico vobis, quicquid ligaveritis in terris, &c. & respondet illi, qui posset objicere: quid mea refert, etiamsi ecclesia me habeat pro nebulone & publicano? tamen ego nihilominus suaviter bibam vinum, Davon werde ich nicht mager/ hoc est, inde ego non macescam. Huic igitur respondet: non erit irritum judicium Ecclesiæ: quia ego ero exsecutor illius. Supra quidem Matth. 16. Dabo tibi claves regni cœlorum, loquitur de communi authoritate ministerij: sed hic nominatim loquitur de authoritate Ecclesiæ in hac causa. Ligare igitur & soluere non est magistratus politici, sed ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 2. To the argument that the Sanhedrin was political: Reply to the major premise: it was political, but not only that. It also had ecclesiastical power, because it dealt at the same time with causes of religion. It consisted of Pharisees and other experts in the law, that is, scribes, who were both theologians and jurists. Among the Jewish people the theologians and jurists were the same men, since they had both moral and civil laws. The lesser Sanhedrin of which Christ speaks was therefore not merely political but also ecclesiastical. The question now is whether he orders that a matter be referred to the Sanhedrin as a political body or as an ecclesiastical one. Reply: as an ecclesiastical one. This is proved from the text. 1. He bids us regard the contumacious person as a heathen and a tax-collector, that is, as foreign to the kingdom of God. To declare someone a tax-collector and a stranger to the kingdom of God belongs not to the political magistrate but to the ecclesiastical one, because a tax-collector can be a member of the state but not of the Church of Christ. 2. Christ adds: Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth, etc. He answers the one who might object, "What does it matter to me if the Church holds me for a scoundrel and a tax-collector? Yet I will drink my wine pleasantly all the same. Davon werde ich nicht mager," that is, therefore I shall not grow lean. To this he replies that the judgment of the Church will not be void, because he himself will carry it out. Indeed, in Matthew 16, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, speaks of the common authority of the ministry, but here he speaks by name of the authority of the Church in this matter. To bind and to loose therefore belongs not to the political magistrate but to the Church.

units.la: Hactenus de priore membro, sub nomine Ecclesiæ fieri mentionem excommunicationis presbyterij: nunc de altero, etiam fieri mentionem per æquipollentiam, ibi: Sit tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus.
units.tr: So far concerning the first member, in which mention of excommunication is made under the name of the Church of the eldership. Now concerning the second, in which mention of excommunication is also made by equivalence: Let him be to you as a heathen and a tax-collector.

units.la: Inst. 1. Haberi pro Ethnico & publicano, & esse excommunicatum, non sunt idem. Ergo excommunicatio non continetur ibi per æquipollentiam. Resp. Negatur antecedens. Probant. Sit tibi ut Ethnicus: non loquitur de judicio publico Ecclesiæ, sed de privato singulorum. Ergo non à tota Ecclesia illico est excommunicatus, qui habetur pro Ethnico à privatis. Resp. Quem singuli habent pro Ethnico, eum tota Ecclesia habet pro tali. Ergo loquitur de judicio ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Objection 1: To be regarded as a heathen and a tax-collector and to be excommunicated are not the same thing. Therefore excommunication is not contained there by equivalence. Reply: The antecedent is denied. Proof: "Let him be to you as a heathen" does not speak of the public judgment of the Church but of the private judgment of individuals. Therefore he who is regarded as a heathen by private persons is not at once excommunicated by the whole Church. Reply: Whom individuals regard as a heathen, the whole Church regards as such. Therefore it speaks of the judgment of the Church.

units.la: Inst. 2. Non habetur in textu: Quem Ecclesia habet pro Ethnico. Ergo eo, sed, qui Ecclesiam non audit, eum tu habeas pro Ethnico. Resp. Non habes eum pro Ethnico, ex judicio Ecclesiæ, sed ex tuo. Bene: ideo habeo, quia non audit Ecclesiam. Verum non audire Ecclesiam, & esse publicanum, hoc est, alienum ab Ecclesia, an pon sunt idem? Sed addo alterum minus disputabile. Non dicit tantum privatis singulis, sed toti Ecclesiæ. Nam tibi & Ecclesiæ æquiæquipollent. Ratio: cùm Christus jubet aliquem à me haberi pro Ethnico, an jubet eum interea ab Ecclesia haberi pro Christiano? Minimè: quia vellet contradictoria, siue contraria judicia de eodem homine simul fieri. Pro publicano igitur haberi ab uno, est, pro tali haberi ab omnibus, & à tota Ecclesia, ac, si non fieret illa denunciatio in specie, nullus posset haberi pro publicano. Ab Ecclesia autem haberi pro publicano, est excommunicari, & esse extra κοινωνίαν Ecclesiæ. Stat igitur etiam posterius membrum, fieri ibi mentionem excommunicationis, & eam Ecclesiæ mandari.
units.tr: Objection 2: The text does not say, "Whom the Church regards as a heathen, let him be so regarded by you," but, "Whoever does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen." Reply: You do not regard him as a heathen by the judgment of the Church but by your own. Well, I regard him so because he does not hear the Church. But are not not hearing the Church and being a tax-collector, that is, alien to the Church, the same thing? I add another point, less open to dispute. He does not speak only to individual persons but to the whole Church, for to you and to the Church are equivalent. The reason is this: when Christ bids that someone be regarded by me as a heathen, does he at the same time bid that he be regarded by the Church as a Christian? Certainly not, since he would then want contradictory or contrary judgments about the same man to be made at once. To be regarded as a tax-collector by one is therefore to be regarded as such by all, and by the whole Church. Without that declaration made in particular, no one could be regarded as a tax-collector. But to be regarded as a tax-collector by the Church is to be excommunicated and to be outside the fellowship [κοινωνίαν] of the Church. So the latter member also stands: mention of excommunication is made there, and it is committed to the Church.

units.la: Inst. 3. Scelerati possunt haberi pro Ethnicis & publicanis sine excommunicatione. Et publicanus & excommunicatus non sunt idem. Resp. Negatur antecedens: quia habere aliquem extra κοινωνίαν ecclesiæ, & excommunicare, sunt idem.
units.tr: Objection 3: The wicked can be regarded as heathens and tax-collectors without excommunication, and a tax-collector and an excommunicate are not the same. Reply: The antecedent is denied, because to hold someone outside the fellowship of the Church and to excommunicate him are the same.

units.la: Inst. 4. Sed possumus aliquem habere pro publicano, hoc est, sentire de eo in animo, quod sit talis, sine excommunicatione. Resp. Christus non loquitur de cogitationibus, sed de actionibus Ecclesiæ. Si quis Ecclesiam non audit, oportet te illud scire: & ut possis cum habere pro Ethnico & publicano, oportet scire, non quid Ecclesia de illo sentiat in animo, sed quid de eo publice statuat. Deinde Paulus vetat cum sceleratis capere cibum & potum: Cum eiusmodi ne edatis quidem. Conuictus autem cum scelerato non potest vitari, ex occulta cogitatione: sed ex publico judicio Ecclesiæ. Ergo non est tantum cogitatio in animo. Tertiò, ibidem: Tollite ipsum sceleratum ex vobis ipsis: hoc est, declarate eum non esse membrum Ecclesiæ. Ergo habere pro publicano, non est tantum cogitare in animo, sed etiam pronunciare & excommunicare.
units.tr: Objection 4: But we can regard someone as a tax-collector, that is, think in our minds that he is such, without excommunication. Reply: Christ does not speak of thoughts but of the actions of the Church. If anyone does not hear the Church, you must know this; and in order that you may regard him as a heathen and a tax-collector, you must know not what the Church thinks of him in its mind but what it publicly decides about him. Next, Paul forbids taking food and drink with the wicked: Not even to eat with such a one (1 Cor. 5). But living together with a wicked person cannot be avoided by a secret thought; it can only be avoided by the public judgment of the Church. Therefore it is not merely a thought in the mind. Thirdly, in the same place: Take away the wicked person from among yourselves, that is, declare him not to be a member of the Church. Therefore to regard someone as a tax-collector is not merely to think it in the mind, but also to pronounce it and to excommunicate.

units.la: Contra exempla excommunicationis apostolicæ. 1 Cor. 5. 2 Thess. 3, 1. 1 Tim. 1. &c.
units.tr: Against the examples of apostolic excommunication: 1 Cor. 5; 2 Thess. 3:1; 1 Tim. 1, etc.

units.la: Qui hodie improbant disciplinam ecclesiæ, exemplum Pauli dupliciter eluduntur. Alij simpliciter negant apostolum loqui de excommunicatione, cùm dicit: Qui talia fecit, tradatur Satanæ: quia tradere Satanæ non sit excommunicare, sed miraculosa poena è medio tollere, ministerio Satanæ, vel saltem imprecationibus & diris devouere, & Satanæ excruciandum tradere: ita vt nihilominus Ecclesiæ membrum maneat. Alij concedunt, Paulum loqui de excommunicatione: sed negant, exemplum pertinere ad nos: quia nunc sint Christiani magistratus, disciplinæ custodes, quibus Ecclesia Apostolorum tempore fuerit destituta. Respond. Sed contra priores sonant verba Apostoli:
units.tr: Those who today reject the discipline of the Church get round the example of Paul in two ways. Some simply deny that the Apostle is speaking of excommunication when he says: Let him who has done such a thing be delivered to Satan. They argue that to deliver to Satan is not to excommunicate but to remove the man from the midst by a miraculous punishment, through the ministry of Satan, or at least to devote him to curses and imprecations and hand him over to Satan to be tormented, so that he nevertheless remains a member of the Church. Others grant that Paul is speaking of excommunication, but deny that the example applies to us, because Christian magistrates now guard discipline, whereas the Church in the time of the Apostles lacked them. Reply. But the words of the Apostle are against the first group:

units.la: Tollite vos malum è medio Ecclesiae: cùm tali nec famite cibum. Hæc non possunt intelligi de supplicio capitali miraculoso, quale erat Ananiae & Sapphirae, sed sonant de ordinario officio & judicio Ecclesiae. 1. Quia dicit: Tollite vos: & reprehendit eos, quod non sustulerint: Et vos inflati estis, ac non potius luxistis, ut toleretur è medio vestri, qui facinus hoc patravit? At non omnes habebant donum Petri: injuria igitur eos reprehenderet, propter non edictum miraculum. 2. Quia requirit consensum Ecclesiae. Congregatis vobis, & meo spiritu. Tali vero solemnitate ad miraculum non erat opus. 3. Quia vult eum tradi satanae ad interitum carnis, ut spiritus salvus sit in die Domini Iesu, hoc est, ita vult tractari, ut nihilominus in hac vita maneat & resipiscat, dometur eius caro vera contritione, mortificetur vetus, & vivificetur novus homo. Ergo non vult eum interfici. 4. Loquitur de separatione, & exclusione ex Ecclesia, cum inquit: Expurgate vetus fermentum. Ne commisceamini cum scortatoribus. Ne edatis cum eo. Haec omnia loquuntur de separatione, non de supplicio capitali. 5. Collatio locorum scripturae docet, eos, qui negant doctrinam Christianam, ore vel vita, non esse habendos pro Christianis. Ambrosius dicit hunc incestuosum, cognito flagitio, pellendum fuisse de coetu fraternitatis, hoc est, de Ecclesia. Qui vero eiecti sunt ex Ecclesia, merito dicuntur traditi satanae: quia versantur in regno satanae, quamdiu non resipiscunt.
units.tr: "Take the evil away from among yourselves," and "not even to eat with such a man." These things cannot be understood of a miraculous capital punishment, such as that of Ananias and Sapphira, but they refer to the ordinary office and judgment of the Church. (1) Because he says, "Take away" and rebukes them because they did not remove him: "And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he who did this deed might be taken away from among you?" But not all had Peter's gift; it would therefore be unjust to rebuke them for failing to perform a miracle. (2) Because he requires the consent of the Church: "When you are gathered together, and my spirit is present." Such a solemn assembly was not needed for a miracle. (3) Because he wants him delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus; that is, he wants him so treated that he nevertheless remains in this life and repents, his flesh is subdued by true contrition, the old man is mortified and the new man quickened. Therefore he does not want him killed. (4) He speaks of separation and exclusion from the Church, when he says: "Purge out the old leaven. Do not associate with fornicators. Do not eat with such a one." All these things speak of separation, not of capital punishment. (5) A comparison of passages of Scripture teaches that those who deny Christian doctrine, by word or by life, are not to be regarded as Christians. Ambrose says that this incestuous man, once his crime was known, had to be expelled from the fellowship of the brothers, that is, from the Church. Those who are cast out of the Church are rightly said to be delivered to Satan, because they remain in the kingdom of Satan as long as they do not repent.

units.la: Posteriores illi admittunt fallaciam non causae, cum dicunt Paulum ideo voluisse incestum excommunicari: quia tunc non fuerit Christianus magistratus. Longe enim aliae rationes Paulus adducit, etiam nunc durantes. 1. Mandatum Christi: Vobis cum spiritu meo in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi congregatis, hoc est, authoritate & mandato Christi: Dic Ecclesiae: sit tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus. 2. Ut excommunicatus resipiscat & salvus fiat: Tradatur satanae ad interitum carnis, ut spiritus salvus fiat in die Domini nostri Iesu. 3. Ne reliqui inficiantur. An nescitis paululo fermenti fermentari totam massam? 4. Quia pascha nostrum immolatum est Christus: ut viuamus in azymis syncaeritatis & veritatis, simus nova conspersio, eiiciamus vetus fermentum malitiae & nequitiae, vel saltem ex professo non feramus, si totum eijcere non possimus.
units.tr: The latter group admit a fallacy about the cause when they say that Paul wanted the incest to be excommunicated because at that time there was no Christian magistrate. Paul adduces quite different reasons, which still hold today. (1) The command of Christ: "When you are gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with my spirit," that is, by the authority and command of Christ: "Tell the Church: let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector." (2) That the excommunicated man may repent and be saved: "Let him be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus." (3) That the rest may not be infected: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" (4) Because our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed; so that we may live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and be a new batch, and cast out the old leaven of malice and wickedness, or at least not tolerate it openly if we cannot cast out all of it.

units.la: Hæ sunt causæ, cur Paulus mandet incestum tolli ex ecclesia. Nusquam vero legitur, ecclesiam ideo sceleratos excommunicasse, quod careret Christiano magistratu. Nam officia ecclesiae & magistratus semper fuerunt, & manent distincta. Certum est igitur, Apostolum loqui de excommunicatione, cùm dicit: Tradite eum satanae, tollite malum è vobis: & præcipere de ecclesiae ordiordinario officio contra flagitiosos: siue tum accesserit miracu- lum, siue non.
units.tr: These are the reasons why Paul commands that the incestuous man be removed from the Church. Nowhere is it read that the Church excommunicated wicked men because it lacked a Christian magistrate. For the offices of the Church and of the magistrate have always been, and remain, distinct. It is therefore certain that the Apostle is speaking of excommunication when he says, "Deliver him to Satan, take away the evil from among you," and that he is commanding the ordinary office of the Church against flagitious persons, whether or not a miracle accompanied it.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Nathan non excommunicauit Dauidem adulterum. Ergo neq; Paulus excommunicauit hunc incestuosum. R. Da- uid post primam admonitionē resipuit: ergo non debuit excom- municari. Paulus etiam loquitur cum conditione pœnitentiæ, Tollite: si scilicet non agat, vel non jam egerit pœnitentiam: qua interueniente, jubet eum recipi. Hanc conditionem necesse est subintelligere: quia Christus voluit præire gradus admoni- tionum, & Deus quocunque tempore pœnitentiam agentes in gratiam recipit. Latro in cruce non excommunicatur, sed recipi- tur à Christo, agens pœnitentiam. Si septuagies septies peccauerit in te frater, remittes ei. Non igitur peccantes, sed pertinaces sunt ex- communicandi, qualis Dauid non erat.
units.tr: Objection 1. Nathan did not excommunicate the adulterer David. Therefore neither did Paul excommunicate this incestuous man. Reply. David repented after the first admonition; therefore he ought not to have been excommunicated. Paul also speaks under the condition of repentance: "Take away," that is, if he does not repent, or has not yet repented; and when repentance intervenes, he orders him to be received. This condition must be understood, because Christ wished the steps of admonition to come first, and God receives into grace those who repent at whatever time. The thief on the cross was not excommunicated but received by Christ, since he repented. "If your brother sins against you seventy times seven, you shall forgive him." Therefore it is not those who sin but the obstinate who are to be excommunicated, and David was not of that kind.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Christus neminem excommunicauit. Ergo nec Paulus fecit: nec Ecclesia quemquam excommunicare debet. Resp. Non valet consequentia, à negatione facti, ad negationem juris. Tale argumentum est: Christus neminem baptizauit: ergo nec Paulus debuit: nec ecclesia debet quenquam baptizare. Sic neminem excommunicauit: jussit verò excommunicari con- tumaces: sit tibi velut Ethnicus. Relinque munus tuum ad altare, &c. Philippus dicit eunucho: Licet tibi baptizari, si credis toto corde. Ergo non baptizasset eum, si non credidisset.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ excommunicated no one. Therefore neither did Paul, nor ought the Church to excommunicate anyone. Reply. The inference from a negation of fact to a negation of right is not valid. It is like this argument: Christ baptized no one; therefore neither ought Paul to have baptized, nor ought the Church to baptize anyone. Likewise, Christ excommunicated no one, but he commanded the obstinate to be excommunicated: "Let him be to you as a Gentile. Leave your gift there before the altar, etc." Philip says to the eunuch: "You may be baptized, if you believe with all your heart." Therefore he would not have baptized him if he had not believed.

units.la: Obi. 3. Paulus dicit: οὐχ ἐπενθήσατε, ἵνα ἐξαρθῇ ἐκ μέσου ὑμῶν: hoc est, non luxistis, ut tolleretur è medio vestri. Ergo debuerunt orare, ut Deus eum tolleret miraculosè per satanam. Resp. Fallacia figuræ dictionis. οὐχ ἐπενθήσατε significat, non fuistis anxij de scandalo illo tollendo, quod debuit à vobis tolli: à vobis, inquam, quia in fine dicit, ἐξάρατε, tollite vos eum. ἐξαρθῇ igitur significat tollendum fuisse per ecclesiam, non per satanam. Inst. Paulus de se utitur hoc verbo, κῇ πενθῶ ποιεῖς: Et lugeam multos eorum, qui ante peccauerunt, nec resipuerunt: &c. Hic lugere non significat anxium esse de tollendo scandalo. Ergo necibi. Resp. ex textu. Ibidem dixit: Si venero, non parcam. Hanc luctus causam exponit, quod cogatur seuerius animaduertere in contumaces, hoc est, eos tandem ex Ecclesia eijcere.
units.tr: Objection 3. Paul says: "οὐχ ἐπενθήσατε, ἵνα ἐξαρθῇ ἐκ μέσου ὑμῶν" [you did not mourn, that he might be taken away from among you]. Therefore they ought to have prayed that God would remove him miraculously through Satan. Reply. This is a fallacy of the figure of speech. "οὐχ ἐπενθήσατε" means: you were not anxious about removing that scandal, which ought to have been removed by you; by you, I say, because at the end he says "ἐξάρατε, tollite vos eum" [remove, take him away yourselves]. "ἐξαρθῇ" therefore means that he was to be removed by the Church, not by Satan. Objection further. Paul uses this verb of himself: "καὶ πενθήσω πολλούς" [and I shall mourn over many]: "And I shall mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented," etc. Here "to mourn" does not mean to be anxious about removing a scandal. Therefore neither there. Reply. From the text itself. In the same place he said: "If I come, I will not spare." He explains the cause of his grief: that he is forced to deal more severely with the obstinate, that is, finally to cast them out of the Church.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Paulus seipsum explicat, quod non præceperit Co- rinthiis excommunicationem incestuosi, cum dicit: Sufficit eiusmodi homini ἐπιτιμία ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων, hoc est, objurgatio à pluribus profecta. Ergo habere pro Ethnico & publicano, & tollere è me- dio, tantum est ἐπιτιμᾶν. Resp. Est fallacia consequentis: quia ex uno exemplo non constituitur regula. Non sequitur: hic tan- tum
units.tr: Objection 4. Paul explains himself, that he did not command the Corinthians to excommunicate the incestuous man, when he says: "Sufficient for such a man is the ἐπιτιμία [rebuke] of the majority," that is, a reproof issued by many. Therefore to regard him as a Gentile and a tax collector, and to remove him from the midst, is only "ἐπιτιμᾶν" [to rebuke]. Reply. This is the fallacy of the consequent, because a rule is not established from a single example. It does not follow: here only rebuke was needed, because he repented; therefore rebuke is always all that is needed.

units.la: 1 Cor. 5.2. Matt. 18,17. Act. 8,37. 2 Cor. 12,21. 2 Cor. 13,2. 2 Cor. 2,6. Matt. 18,21. tum opus fuit ἐπιλυμία, quia resipuit: ergo semper tantum opus est ἐπιλυμία.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 5.2. Matt. 18,17. Act. 8,37. 2 Cor. 12,21. 2 Cor. 13,2. 2 Cor. 2,6. Matt. 18,21. Rebuke was needed, then, because he repented; therefore rebuke is always all that is needed.

units.la: Inst. Quod isti fecerunt, Paulus jussit. Sed hi tantum reprehenderunt. Ergo Paulus tantum jussit ἐπιλυμᾶν, dum jussit è medio tollere, satanæ tradere. Resp. ad maiorem. Paulus jussit reprehendere, sed non tantum: quia jussit etiam eijcere, nisi resipiscet. Si autem resipisceret, dixit, satis esse ἐπιλυμᾶν. Non igitur sequitur. Illi tantū reprehenderunt. Ergo Paulus tantum jussit reprehendere. Hæc est vera solutio. Sed etiam est alia: ἐπιλυμᾶν hic non tantum est improbare factum, aut objurgare, sed etiam excommunicare: quia excommunicatio tantum fit verbo. Sic accipi non tantum potest, sed etiam oportet.
units.tr: Objection. What these men did, Paul commanded. But they only rebuked. Therefore Paul only commanded rebuke, when he commanded that he be removed from the midst and delivered to Satan. Reply to the major. Paul commanded rebuke, but not only rebuke, because he also commanded that he be cast out unless he repented. If, however, he did repent, he said that rebuke was sufficient. It does not therefore follow that they only rebuked, and so Paul only commanded rebuke. This is the true solution. But there is also another: here "ἐπιτιμᾶν" [to rebuke] means not merely to disapprove of the deed or to reprove, but also to excommunicate, since excommunication is effected by word alone. It can be understood thus, and indeed must be.

units.la: 1. Quia dicit: ὥστε τύναυ, πον μᾶλλον ὑμᾶς χαρίσασθαι: ut è diverso magis condonare debeatis. Ergo jam fuit excommunicatus, & nondum receptus, sed recipiendus, nec tantum objurgatus, sed etiam ejectus.
units.tr: 1. Because he says: "so that on the contrary you ought rather to forgive him." Therefore he had already been excommunicated and not yet received, but was to be received; and he had not merely been rebuked but also cast out.

units.la: 2. Υ̓ ωὸ ̓ πωλὶ ὁ ωμ ὶ ἀ pluribus. Hinc confirmatur, quod Christus ecclesiam dicat ecclesiæ primores, non confusam plebeculam. Fuit enim ἐπιλυμία facta ab ecclesiæ presbyteris & primoribus, ut cognoscerem vos obedire.
units.tr: 2. [Greek text illegible in the scan] … many. From this it is confirmed that Christ calls the chief men of the church, not the confused common crowd, the church. For the censure [ἐπιτιμία] was imposed by the elders and chief men of the church, so that I might know that you obey.

units.la: 3. Nam in hoc (inquit) etiam scripsi, ut cognoscerem vos obedire. Laudat igitur, quod sint obsecuti.
units.tr: 3. For in this (he says) I also wrote, so that I might know that you obey. He therefore praises them for having complied.

units.la: 4. Παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς χαρίσασθαι ὧν ἀγαπᾶτε: hoc est, precor, ut vos ratam faciatis in illū charitatem. χαρίσασθαι, est publica voce decernere condonationem. Ergo ante ipsi nondum erat condonatum. Sic sumitur Gal.3,15. κύρωσις ἀνθρωπίνη διαθήκη, publica authoritate sancitum testamentum. Vult igitur publico testimonio declarari dilectionē erga ipsum. Ergo χαρίσασθαι, condonare, erat, excommunicatum in gratiam recipere: idq; sæpius repetit. Fuit autem interuallū aliquod inter scriptionē posterioris & prioris epistolæ ad Corinthios. Fuit igitur excommunicatus. In prima epistola dicit se audiuisse quosdam sceleratos versari in grege ecclesiæ illos jubet excōmunicari. Verisimile est hic Corinthios obtemperasse, excōmunicando illos, & rescripsisse Paulo, quod obtemperauerint: quia in secunda, cap.2. laudat eorū obedientiam. Ad epistolam autem Corinthiorū respondet Paulus secunda epistola, & jubet incestum recipi, si resipiscat. Deniq; ante resipiscentia vetat, ne commisceantur cum illo incesto. Ergo fuit ejectus.
units.tr: 4. "I beg you to forgive [χαρίσασθαι] those whom you love." That is: I pray that you would ratify your love towards him. To forgive [χαρίσασθαι] is to decree a pardon by public voice. Therefore it had not yet been pardoned by them. It is used in this sense at Gal. 3:15: "a human covenant [κύρωσις ἀνθρωπίνη διαθήκη]," a testament ratified by public authority. He wishes, then, that his love towards the man be declared by public testimony. Therefore to forgive [χαρίσασθαι] means to receive back into favour one who has been excommunicated, and he repeats this often. There was, moreover, some interval between the writing of the later and the earlier letter to the Corinthians. He had therefore been excommunicated. In the first letter he says that he has heard that certain wicked men are living within the flock of the church, and he orders them to be excommunicated. It is likely that the Corinthians here obeyed, excommunicating them, and wrote back to Paul that they had obeyed; for in the second letter, chapter 2, he praises their obedience. Paul answers the Corinthians' letter in a second letter, and orders the incestuous man to be received back if he repents. Finally, before repentance, he forbids them to mix with that incestuous man. Therefore he had been expelled.

units.la: Obiect.5. Excommunicatio non requirit excusationem. Ergo non jusserat Paulus excusat se, quod jusserat eum tradi satanæ. Ergo non jusserat maior: quia excommunicari, sed aliquid gravius. Resp. Negatur maior: quia exclusio ex ecclesia, & regno Christi, cum sit grauissima pœna, multo maiorem requirit excusationem, quam quoduis supplicium corporale.
units.tr: Objection 5. Excommunication does not require an excuse. Therefore Paul did not need to excuse himself for ordering that the man be handed over to Satan. Therefore he did not order excommunication, but something more severe. Answer. The major premise is denied: exclusion from the church and the kingdom of Christ, since it is the gravest punishment, requires a far greater excuse than any bodily punishment whatever.

units.la: Quæst. LXXXV.
units.tr: Question 85.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Ministri non possunt excludere ex regno Dei, Ergo Paulus non iubet eos hoc facere. Resp. ad antecedens. Non possunt suaauthoritate: sed possunt, nomine Christi, iuxta præceptum apostoli: Vobis cum spiritu meo in nomine Domini Iesu congregatis. Deinde, non possunt eiicere, sed possunt, & debent eiectionem denunciare iis, quos Deus se eiicere in verbo suo significat. Excommunicare enim nihil est aliud, quam eiectionem, quæ fit à Deo, denunciando contumacibus, diuino iudicio subscribere. Hoc vero Ecclesia facere non tantum potest, sed etiam debet. Ideo Paulus reprehendit Corinthios, quod incestum non excommunicassent, sed expectassent, donec monerentur. Ergo reprehendit eos, quod aberrassent à regula, hoc est, quod non fecissent officium ecclesiæ cognitum & ordinarium, iuxta mandatum vniuersale, &c.
units.tr: Objection 6. Ministers cannot exclude anyone from the kingdom of God. Therefore Paul does not order them to do this. Answer to the antecedent. They cannot do so by their own authority, but they can, in the name of Christ, according to the apostle's precept: "When you are gathered together, with my spirit, in the name of the Lord Jesus." Further, they cannot cast out, but they can and ought to declare the casting out to those whom God signifies in his word that he casts out. For to excommunicate is nothing other than to declare, to the obstinate, the expulsion that is effected by God, and so to assent to the divine judgment. This the Church not only can do but is also bound to do. Therefore Paul rebukes the Corinthians because they had not excommunicated the incestuous man but had waited until he was admonished. Therefore he rebukes them for having departed from the rule, that is, for not having performed the known and ordinary duty of the church, according to the universal command, etc.

units.la: Obiect. 7. ὅς ἀλέθρῳ σαρκὸς, ad interitum carnis iubet incestum tradi satanæ. ὁ ἀλέθρος vero in scriptura perpetuo significat interneccionem. Ergo & hoc loco notatur miraculosa corporis interitio per satanam vt saluetur anima. Resp. Ex circumstantiis patet hoc loco significare mortificationem veteris hominis. Antithesis enim carnis & spiritus, & phrasis ipsa Paulo est vtdi Satanæ, vt mortificetur caro: & seruetur Spiritus, hoc est, vt conuerratur in hac vita, & saluus esse possit in vita æterna. Non igitur vult eum tolli ex hac vita per miraculum. Inst. Atqui Satanæ nemo tradi potest ad conuersionem seu mortificationem veteris hominis. Resp. Verum est per se: at per accidens, hoc est, per Dei misericordiam fit, vt electi in ipsis castigationibus corrigantur, Eadem vero ratione nos ipsorum interpretationem negabimus; quia satan neminem occidit, vt anima eius saluetur.
units.tr: Objection 7. He orders the incestuous man to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh [εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός]. But the destruction [ὁ ὄλεθρος] in Scripture always means slaughter. Therefore in this passage too is noted a miraculous destruction of the body by Satan, so that the soul may be saved. Answer. From the circumstances it is clear that here it signifies the mortification of the old man. For the antithesis of flesh and spirit, and the very phrase itself, show that Paul means: deliver him to Satan, that the flesh may be mortified and the spirit saved, that is, that he may be converted in this life and be able to be saved in eternal life. He does not therefore wish him to be taken from this life by a miracle. Objection. But no one can be handed over to Satan for the conversion or mortification of the old man. Answer. This is true in itself; but by accident, that is, by God's mercy, it comes about that the elect are corrected by these very chastisements. By the same reasoning, however, we shall deny their interpretation, since Satan kills no one so that his soul may be saved.

units.la: Obiect. 8. Si voluisset eum excommunicari, clarius id significassent. Respond. Non tantum claritas, sed etiam vis & δείνωσις oram Corinthii intelligebant, quid vellet; alioqui iniuste eos reprehenderet.
units.tr: Objection 8. If he had wished him to be excommunicated, they would have signified it more clearly. Answer. It was not only the clarity but also the force and emphasis of the expression that made the Corinthians understand what he wished; otherwise he would have rebuked them unjustly.

units.la: Obiect. 9. Frater non est excommunicandus. Paulus vult eum, quem iusserat notari per epistolam, habere pro fratre. Ergo non vult eum excommunicari. Maior probatur. Contraria no possunt simul poni. At sunt contraria: habere pro fratre, & excommunicare enim est non habere pro fratre. Ergo idem habebitur pro fratre, & pro non fratre, quod est absurdum. Respond. 1. Negatur minor prosyllogismi, quod sint contraria. Amplius est, habere pro fratre, quia sunt gradus fraternitatis. Non ergo valet contrarietas. Nam omnes homines sunt fratres proximi, etiam Christiani & Turcæ. Interim Christiani, etiamsi Turcas habeant pro fratribus & proximis, & salutem eorum expetant, tamen non habent eos pro fratribus, hoc est, pro Christianis. Si igitur Turcas; multo magis illos debent habere pro fratribus, & studere eorum saluti, qui prius fuerunt fratres, hoc est, Christiani. 2. Est fallacia secundum quid. Habere pro fratre, nempe dilectione, studio & spe eum servandi, non autem numerone interfilios Dei & membra Ecclesiæ, priusquam resipiscat. 3. Non dicit: habete eum pro fratre: sed, monete eum ut fratrem: hoc est, ut eum, qui fuit frater, & qui resipiscens rursus debet fieri frater. Non enim omnino arcentur à spe salutis, qui excommunicantur, sed ut redeant ad se, & rursus includantur. Utitur vero Paulus hac phrasi: quia dilectionem & spem emendationis vult esse regulam objurgationum. Frater enim monet fratrem amicè & bono fine.
units.tr: Objection 9. A brother is not to be excommunicated. Paul wishes the man whom he had ordered to be marked by letter to be regarded as a brother. Therefore he does not wish him to be excommunicated. The major is proved. Contraries cannot be affirmed together. But they are contraries: to regard as a brother, and to excommunicate, for to excommunicate is not to regard as a brother. Therefore the same man would be regarded both as a brother and as not a brother, which is absurd. Answer. 1. The minor of the prosyllogism is denied, that they are contraries. Moreover, to regard as a brother admits of degrees, for there are degrees of brotherhood. Therefore the contrariety does not hold. For all men are near brothers, Christians and Turks alike. Yet Christians, even though they regard Turks as brothers and neighbours and desire their salvation, nevertheless do not regard them as brothers in the sense of being Christians. If therefore they must regard Turks thus, much more ought they to regard as brothers, and to study the salvation of, those who were formerly brothers, that is, Christians. 2. It is a fallacy of the qualified sense. To regard as a brother, namely with love, zeal and hope of saving him, is not the same as numbering him among the sons of God and the members of the Church before he repents. 3. He does not say: regard him as a brother; but: admonish him as a brother, that is, as one who was a brother and who, when he repents, ought again to become a brother. For those who are excommunicated are not wholly shut out from the hope of salvation, but are excluded so that they may return to themselves and be received again. Paul uses this expression because he wishes love and the hope of amendment to be the rule of rebukes. For a brother admonishes a brother in a friendly way and for a good end.

units.la: Obj. 10. Quod fecit Paulus, non est nobis imitandum. Paulus excommunicavit Hymenæum & Alexandrum sine consensu Ecclesiæ. Ergo nemo est excommunicandus. Maior probatur: quia fecit authoritate apostolica: & minor: quia dicit: Tradidi satanæ Hymenæum & Alexandrum. Nostri autem ministri & pastores Ecclesiæ id non possunt. Ergo oportet Paulum peculiari aliqua ratione id fecisse. Resp. Conceditur totum: non debemus imitari, si fecit solus: non autem sequitur: ergo non licet excommunicare. Est enim plus in conclusione. Quod licuit Paulo apostolica authoritate, id licet Ecclesiæ ministris ordinario officio. Deinde etiam minor potest negari: quia in textu tantum dicitur, quid Paulus fecerit, non quomodo, solus, an cum aliis id fecerit.
units.tr: Objection 10. What Paul did is not for us to imitate. Paul excommunicated Hymenaeus and Alexander without the consent of the Church. Therefore no one is to be excommunicated. The major is proved: because he did it by apostolic authority; and the minor: because he says: "I have delivered to Satan Hymenaeus and Alexander." But our ministers and pastors of the Church cannot do this. Therefore Paul must have done it for some peculiar reason. Answer. The whole is conceded: we ought not to imitate him if he acted alone; but it does not follow: therefore it is not lawful to excommunicate. For there is more in the conclusion. What was lawful for Paul by apostolic authority is lawful for the ministers of the Church in the ordinary discharge of their office. Further, the minor can also be denied, because the text says only what Paul did, not how he did it, whether alone or with others.

units.la: TERTIA PARS. DE GRATITUDINE.
units.tr: THIRD PART. CONCERNING GRATITUDE.

units.la: Post locum de miseria hominis, & de liberatione eius per Christum, etiam doctrina de gratitudine est necessaria. 1. Propter gloriam Dei: quia praecipuus finis nostrae redemtionis est gratitudo, hoc est, agnitio & celebratio beneficiorum Christi. 2. Propter consolationem nostram, quae in gratuita liberatione consistit. Liberatio autem non pertinet, nisi ad eos, qui se Deo gratos praestare student. 3. Ut Deo legitimum cultum praestare possimus. Deus enim omnem ἐπλοφρονειαν damnat. Ergo de vera gratitudine, quae est cultus Deo debitus, ex verbo Dei docendum est. 4. Ut sciamus, omnia bona opera nostra esse gratitudinem, & non meritum.
units.tr: After the section on the misery of man and his deliverance through Christ, the doctrine of gratitude is also necessary. (1) For the glory of God, because the chief end of our redemption is gratitude, that is, the acknowledgment and celebration of Christ's benefits. (2) For our comfort, which consists in free deliverance. Deliverance, however, belongs only to those who strive to show themselves grateful to God. (3) So that we may render God lawful worship. For God condemns every kind of levity [ἐπλοφρονειαν]. Therefore the true gratitude, which is the worship due to God, must be taught from the Word of God. (4) So that we may know that all our good works are gratitude and not merit.

units.la: Est autem gratitudo in genere, virtus, agnoscens & profitens, a quo & quanta beneficia acceperis, & studium praestandi beneficiis mutua officia, honesta & possibilia. Complectitur veritatem: quia agnoscit, & praedicat beneficia accepta: justitiam: quia studet referre gratiam aequalem benemeritis.
units.tr: Gratitude in general is a virtue that acknowledges and professes from whom and how great benefits one has received, and that strives to repay the benefactors with mutual duties that are honourable and possible. It embraces truth, because it acknowledges and proclaims the benefits received, and justice, because it strives to return favour equal to the good deeds.

units.la: Christiana igitur gratitudo, quae hic docetur, est agnitio & professio gratuitae redemtionis per Christum a peccato & morte, & studium vitandi peccata, omnemque Dei offensam & vitam instituendi ex ipsius voluntate, omnia etiam bona ab ipso solo ex vera fide petendi, expectandi, accipiendi, & pro acceptis gratias agendi.
units.tr: Christian gratitude, therefore, which is taught here, is the acknowledgment and profession of the free redemption through Christ from sin and death, and the zeal to avoid sins and every offence against God, and to order one's life according to his will; and also to seek, expect and receive all good things from him alone by true faith, and to give thanks for what has been received.

units.la: Huius gratitudinis etiam sunt duae partes: veritas & justitia. Veritas agnoscit, & profitetur beneficium gratuitae redemtionis, & pro eo Deo gratias agit. Justitia offert Deo εὐάρεστον: Deus autem non postulat a nobis aliam, quam verum sui cultum seu obedientiam, & bona opera. Ad veritatem ergo pertinet doctrina de precatione: ad justitiam doctrina de bonis operibus. Horum autem fons est conversio hominis ad Deum. Tantum enim renatorum opera sunt bona, & placent Deo. Norma bonorum operum est lex Dei. Hic igitur simul de conversione hominis ad Deum & de lege Dei tractatur. Sic ad partem de gratitudine quatuor praecipue loci communes pertinent: de conversione, de bonis operibus, de lege Dei, & de precatione. Horum locorum ordo & cohærentia etiam sic colligitur. Ex varia & multiplici doctrina partis vtriusq; præcedentis didicimus, nos à peccato & morte, hoc est, ab omnibus malis pœnæ & culpæ, nullo nostro merito, sed mera Dei gratia per & propter Christum redemtos esse. Inde consequitur, nos pro hoc summo beneficio ad gratitudinem erga Deum obligari. Cæterum non possumus nos Deo gratos probare, nisi simus vere conuersi. Quicquid enim fit à non conuersis, fit sine fide, proindepeccatum & abominatio est coram Deo. Primùm igitur de conuersione hominis disendum est. Sequitur locus de bonis operibus. Absq; his enim vera conuersio nequit consistere, & iis nos gratitudinem nostram erga Deum præcipuè declaramus. Postea subiungitur doctrina de lege Dei, ex qua opera bona cognoscuntur. Nam opera vere bona, quibus Deus recte colitur, & quibus gratitudo nostra declaratur, ea demum sunt, quæ ex fide, ad legis diuinæ præscriptũ hoc fine fiunt, vt Deus colatur & glorificetur. Quia verò Deus principaliter à nobis vult coli ac celebrari vera inuocatio ne ac precibus, ad gratitudinem etiam requiritur precatio. Ergo ad extremum doctrina de precatione subijcitur.
units.tr: This gratitude has two parts: truth and justice. Truth acknowledges and professes the benefit of free redemption, and gives thanks to God for it. Justice offers to God what is pleasing [εὐάρεστον]; God, however, requires from us nothing other than the true worship of himself, or obedience, and good works. To truth therefore belongs the doctrine of prayer; to justice the doctrine of good works. The source of these is the conversion of man to God, for only the works of the regenerate are good and pleasing to God. The norm of good works is the law of God. Here, therefore, the conversion of man to God and the law of God are treated together. Thus four principal commonplaces belong to the part on gratitude: concerning conversion, concerning good works, concerning the law of God, and concerning prayer. The order and coherence of these topics may also be gathered as follows. From the varied and manifold doctrine of both preceding parts we have learned that we have been redeemed from sin and death, that is, from all evils of punishment and guilt, by no merit of our own but by the mere grace of God, through and on account of Christ. From this it follows that we are bound to gratitude toward God for this supreme benefit. Moreover, we cannot prove ourselves pleasing to God unless we are truly converted. For whatever is done by the unconverted is done without faith, and therefore is sin and an abomination before God. Therefore concerning the conversion of man must first be taught. Next follows the locus concerning good works, for without these true conversion cannot exist, and by these above all we declare our gratitude toward God. Afterwards is added the doctrine concerning the law of God, by which good works are known. For those works which are truly good, by which God is rightly worshipped and by which our gratitude is declared, are those which are done from faith, according to the prescription of the divine law, with this end: that God may be worshipped and glorified. Since, however, God chiefly wills to be worshipped and celebrated by us through true invocation and prayers, prayer is also required for gratitude. Lastly, therefore, the doctrine concerning prayer is subjoined.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXXXVI.
units.tr: QUESTION LXXXVI.

units.la: Cum ab omnibus peccatis & miseriis, sine vllo nostro merito, sola Dei misericordia, propter Christum, liberati simus: quid est, cur bona opera faciamus?
units.tr: Since we have been freed from all sins and miseries, without any merit of our own, by the sole mercy of God on account of Christ, why do we do good works?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Quia postquam nos Christus suo sanguine redemit, renouat nos quoque suo Spiritu ad imaginem sui: vt tantis beneficiis affecti, in omni vita nos erga DEVM gratos declaremus a, & ipse per nos celebretur b. Deinde, vt nos quoque ex fructibus de sua quisque fide certi simus c. Postremo, vt vitæ nostræ integritate alios Christo lucrifaciamus d.
units.tr: Because after Christ has redeemed us by his blood, he also renews us by his Spirit to his own image, so that, being affected by such great benefits, we may show ourselves grateful to God in all our life a, and that he may be celebrated through us b. Next, so that each of us may also be certain of his own faith from its fruits c. Lastly, so that by the integrity of our life we may win others to Christ d.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quæstio de causis impulsiuis bonorum operum est primo loco, & ante quæstionem de conuersione posita: non quod bona opera præcedant conuersionem, sed quia per eam sequentia cum præcedentibus commodè connectuntur. Nam ex doctrina de gratuita satisfactione, humana ratio sic argumentatur. Pro quo alius satisfecit, is non tenetur ipse satisfacere. Pro nobis satisfecit Christus. Ergo non opus est, vt nos bona opera faciatum sequitur: Ergo non tenemur ipsi satisfacere: atq; id conceditur. 1. Propter justitiam Dei, quæ non exigit duas solutiones. 2. Propter salutem nostram, quæ alioqui nulla esset. Tenemur tamen ad obedientiam, & ad bona opera propter causas, quæ hac quæstione explicantur.
units.tr: The question about the impelling causes of good works comes first, and is placed before the question about conversion. This is not because good works precede conversion, but because by this order what follows is conveniently connected with what goes before. For from the doctrine of gratuitous satisfaction, human reason argues in this way: whoever has satisfied on behalf of another is not bound to satisfy himself. Christ has satisfied on our behalf. Therefore we need not do good works. It follows that we are not bound to satisfy ourselves; and this is granted: (1) because of the justice of God, which does not demand two payments; (2) because of our salvation, which otherwise would be lost. Nevertheless, we are bound to obedience and to good works, for the reasons that are explained in this question.

units.la: 1. Quia bona opera sunt effectus renouationis nostræ per Spiritum sanctum, quæ cum gratuita justificatione perpetuò cohæret. Quos enim vocauit, hos & justificauit, & glorificauit. Tales fuistis, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, &c. Ergo non facientes bona opera declarant, se nec renatos esse Spiritu Dei, nec sanguine Christi redemtos.
units.tr: 1. Because good works are the effects of our renewal through the Holy Spirit, which is always joined with gratuitous justification. "Whom he called, these he also justified, and glorified." "Such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified," etc. Therefore those who do not perform good works show that they have neither been born again of the Spirit of God nor been redeemed by the blood of Christ.

units.la: 2. Vt gratitudinem nostram ergaDeum pro redemtionis beneficio declaremus. Sistite membra vestra arma justitiæ Deo. Sistite corpora vestra hostiam viuam, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem illum cultum vestrum, &c.
units.tr: 2. So that we may declare our gratitude to God for the benefit of redemption. "Present your members as weapons of righteousness to God." "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service," etc.

units.la: 3. Vt Deus per nos celebretur. Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant bona opera vestra, & glorificetur Pater vester, qui in cœlis est: Item: Vt ex bonis operibus, quæ spectarint, glorificent Deum in die visitationis.
units.tr: 3. So that God may be glorified through us. "Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven." Likewise: "that they may glorify God in the day of visitation, from the good works which they have observed."

units.la: 4. Quia sunt fructus fidei, ex quibus de nostra, & aliorum fide judicatur. Studete vocationem & electionem vestram firmam efficere: vbi quædam exemplaria addunt, (per bona opera.) Omnis arbor bona fert fructus bonos: non potest arbor bona fructus malos ferre. Fides est per charitatem efficax. Fructus Spiritus est charitas, gaudium, pax, benignitas, fides, mansuetudo, temperantia.
units.tr: 4. Because they are the fruits of faith, by which our faith and that of others is judged. "Be diligent to make your calling and election sure," where some copies add "through good works." "Every good tree bears good fruit; a good tree cannot bear evil fruit." "Faith working through love." "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, kindness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control."

units.la: 5. Vt proximum Christo lucrifaciamus. Et tu conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Vxores subiectæ sint viris suis, vt etiam, si qui non obediunt sermoni, per vxorum conuersationem absque sermone lucrifiant. Nempe igitur ea, quæ ad pacem faciunt, sectemur: & quæ ad mutuam ædificationem.
units.tr: 5. So that we may gain our neighbour for Christ. "And when you have turned, strengthen your brothers." "Let wives be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives." Let us therefore pursue what promotes peace, and what promotes mutual edification.

units.la: Hæc causæ concionibus paræneticis ad populũ diligenter explicandæ, & urgendæ sunt: huc pertinet totum caput 6. & pars capitis 8. usq; ad v. 16. Epistolæ ad Romanos.
units.tr: These causes are to be carefully explained and urged in hortatory sermons to the people; to this belongs the whole sixth chapter and part of the eighth chapter, to verse 16, of the Epistle to the Romans.

units.la: Pro declaratione primæ causæ notandū, non dari beneficium justificationis sine beneficio regenerationis. 1. Quia Christus vtrumq; est meritus: remissionem peccatorum, & inhabitationem Dei in nobis per Spiritum sanctum. Spiritus autem sanctus cessario conuunt harcant. nunquam est otiosus, sed semper efficax, & homines, in quibus habitat, Deo efficit conformes. 2. Quia fide purificantur corda. Quibus enim fide applicatum est Christi meritum, in iis accenditur Dei amor, & studium Deo grata faciendi. 3. Quia Deus nemini dat beneficium justificationis, nisi qui etiam gratitudinem praestet. Gratitudinem vero nemo praestat, nisi qui beneficium regenerationis accipit. Neutrum ergo ab altero potest separari.
units.tr: To explain the first cause, it should be noted that the benefit of justification is not given without the benefit of regeneration. (1) Because Christ merited both: the forgiveness of sins and the indwelling of God in us through the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is never idle but always effective, and makes the men in whom he dwells conformed to God. (2) Because hearts are purified by faith. For in those to whom the merit of Christ is applied by faith, the love of God and the desire to please God are kindled. (3) Because God gives the benefit of justification to no one who does not also show gratitude. But no one shows gratitude unless he has received the benefit of regeneration. Therefore neither can be separated from the other.

units.la: Est etiam notandum discrimen primae & secundae causae, Prima ostendit, quid CHRISTVS virtute mortis suae in nobis efficiat. Secunda, ad quid nos pro beneficiis acceptis obligemur.
units.tr: It should also be noted that there is a distinction between the first and the second cause. The first shows what Christ, by the power of his death, effects in us; the second shows to what we are obliged for the benefits received.

units.la: QVÆSTIO LXXXVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 87.

units.la: Non possunt igitur illi servari, qui ingrati, & in peccatis secure perseistentes, à sua pravitate ad Deum non convertuntur? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Can those then not be saved who are ungrateful and, persisting securely in their sins, are not converted from their wickedness to God? ANSWER.

units.la: Nullo modo. Nam ut scriptura testatur, nec impudici, nec idololatrae, nec adulteri, nec fures, nec avari, nec ebriosi, nec conviciatores, nec raptores, hereditatem regni DEI consequentur.
units.tr: By no means. For, as Scripture testifies, neither the impure, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATION.

units.la: Est πρῶτα ὡς prioris quaestionis. Cum bona opera sint fructus nostrae regenerationis, & gratitudo Deo debita, & argumenta verae fidei, quam habentes soli servantur: sequitur e contrario, mala opera esse fructus carnis, ingratitudinem erga Deum, & argumenta infidelitatis, in qua perseverantes servari non possunt. Ergo quicunque a malis operibus ad Deum non convertuntur, sed in peccatis perseverant, in aeternum damnantur, juxta dicta: Ne erratis, neque fornicatores, neque maechi, neque molles, &c. regni Dei hereditatem possidebunt. Qua praedico vobis, sicut praedixi, eos videlicet, qui hoc agunt regni Dei non fore haeredes. Nam hoc nostis, nullum scortatorem, aut impurum, aut avarum, qui est idololatra, habere hereditatem in regno Christi & Dei. Propter hoc enim venit ira Dei super filios contumacia. Qui non diligit fratrem, manet in morte.
units.tr: This follows from the previous question. Since good works are the fruits of our regeneration, the gratitude owed to God, and the evidence of true faith, which only those who possess it are saved, it follows conversely that evil works are the fruits of the flesh, ingratitude towards God, and the evidence of unbelief, in which those who persist cannot be saved. Therefore whoever is not converted from evil works to God, but persists in sins, is condemned for ever, according to the saying: "Do not err; neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, etc., shall possess the inheritance of the kingdom of God." "Which I tell you beforehand, as I have also said before, that those who do such things shall not be heirs of the kingdom of God. For you know this, that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person, who is an idolater, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience." "He who does not love his brother abides in death."

units.la: 1 Cor. 6, 9. Galat. 5, 21. Ephes. 5, 5. 6. 1 Ioh. 3, 14. Observandum est simul, hic contineri aliam causam bonorum operum, ab effectu contrarij: quia bona opera non habentes, sed perseverantes in peccatis, non possunt seruari, vtpote vera fide & conuersione destituti.
units.tr: Galat. 5, 21. Ephes. 5, 5. 6. 1 Ioh. 3, 14. It should be noted at the same time that another cause of good works is contained here, from the contrary effect: because those who do not have good works, but persist in sins, cannot be saved, being destitute of true faith and conversion.

units.la: QVAESTIO LXXXVIII.
units.tr: QUESTION 88.

units.la: Quibus partibus constat conuersio hominis ad Deum?
units.tr: What parts make up the conversion of man to God?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Mortificatione veteris a, & viuificatione noui hominis.
units.tr: The mortification of the old man a, and the vivification of the new man.

units.la: QVAESTIO LXXXIX.
units.tr: QUESTION 89.

units.la: Quid est mortificatio veteris hominis?
units.tr: What is the mortification of the old man?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vere & ex animo dolere, quod peccatis tuis Deum offenderis, eaq; magis ac magis b odisse & fugere.
