units.tr: To grieve truly and from the heart that by your sins you have offended God, and to hate and flee them more and more b.

units.la: QVAESTIO XC.
units.tr: QUESTION 90.

units.la: Quid est viuificatio noui hominis?
units.tr: What is the vivification of the new man?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vera c laetitia in Deo per Christum, & seriu ac promptum studium instituendi vitam ex voluntate DEI, omniaque d bona opera exercendi.
units.tr: True joy in God through Christ, and an earnest and ready zeal to order one's life according to the will of God, and to practise all good works.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATION.

units.la: Sequitur doctrina de Conversione hominis ad Deum, de qua praecipuè tenendum: I. An conuersio sit necessaria. II. Quid sit. III. Quae eius partes. IV. Qua causa. V. Qui effectus. VI. An sit perfecta in hac vita. VII. Quid conuersio piorum à pœnitentia impiorum differat.
units.tr: There follows the doctrine of the conversion of man to God, on which the following points are chiefly to be held: I. Whether conversion is necessary. II. What it is. III. What its parts are. IV. By what cause. V. What its effects are. VI. Whether it is perfect in this life. VII. How the conversion of the godly differs from the repentance of the ungodly.

units.la: I. An sit necessaria conuersio hominis ad DEVM.
units.tr: I. Whether the conversion of man to God is necessary.

units.la: Conuersio hominis in hac vita adeo est necessaria, vt sine ea nemo salutem æternam post hanc vitam consequatur, secun-dum dicta: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum cœlorum. Nisi resipueritis, omnes similiter peribitis. Talia facientes, regnum Dei non possidebunt. Superinduemur: siquidem induti, & non nudi reperiemur. Pertinet huc exemplum fatuarum virginum, quæ excluduntur à nuptiis, non habentes lampadas ardentes, oleo instructas. Et præceptum Christi: Sint lumbi ve- stri præcincti, & lucerna vestra accensa. Estote parati: quia qua hora non putatis, Filius hominis veniet. Item: Veniet dominus eius serui die, qua non exspectat, & qua hora non nouit, & separabit eum, par-temq; cum infidis ei assignabit. Huc referri potest præclara sen-tentia Cypriani contra Demetrianum, sub finem: Quando isthinc excessum fuerit, nullus jam locus pœnitentiæ est, nullus satisfactionis effectus. Hic vita aut amittitur, aut tenetur: hic saluti æterna culeu Dei & fructu fidei prouidetur. Nec quisquam aut peccatis retardetur, aut armis, quo minus veniat ad consequendam salutem. In isto adhuc mundo manenti nulla pœnitentia sera est, &c. Ex his patet, quàm sit necessaria conuersio: & quod in hortatione ad resipiscen-tiam fundamentum sit jaciendum de necessitate conuersionis in omnibus saluandis.
units.tr: Conversion of man in this life is so necessary that without it no one obtains eternal salvation after this life, according to the words: "Unless a man is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven." "Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish." "Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God." "Let us put on the armour; for if we are clothed, we shall not be found naked." To this belongs the example of the foolish virgins, who were shut out from the marriage feast, not having burning lamps furnished with oil. And the precept of Christ: "Let your loins be girded and your lamp burning. Be ready, for at an hour you do not expect, the Son of man will come." Likewise: "The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not look for him, and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and assign him his portion with the unfaithful." To this may be referred the excellent saying of Cyprian against Demetrianus, towards the end: "When one has departed from here, there is no longer any place for repentance, no effect of satisfaction. Here life is either lost or kept; here eternal salvation is provided for by God's grace and the fruit of faith. Nor should anyone be hindered by sins or by arms from coming to obtain salvation. For a person still remaining in this world, no repentance is too late," etc. From these things it is clear how necessary conversion is, and that in the exhortation to repentance the foundation must be laid concerning the necessity of conversion for all who are to be saved.

units.la: II. Quid sit conuersio hominis ad Deum.
units.tr: II. What the conversion of man to God is.

units.la: Hebræis vocatur Theschubah, Græcis μετάνοια & μεταμέλεια. Aliqui volunt sic differre: quod μετάνοια tantum de pœnitentia piorum: μεταμέλεια etiam de pœnitentia impiorum dicatur. De Iuda dicitur, μεταμεληθεὶς ὁ Ἰούδας. De Esau dicitur: quod locum μετανοίας non inuenerit. De Deo dicitur: χαρίσματα τοῦ Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα, hoc est, eiusmodi, vt eorum ipsum pœnitere non possit. Septuaginta de Deo promiscuè vsurpant vtrumque: Pœnitet me (μεταμέλομαι) quod constituí Saul in regem. Sanctus Israel non aget pœnitentiam, οὐ μεταμεληθήσεται. Discrimen ergo vel exile, vel nullum est: nisi quod μετάνοια proprie mutationem mentis, μεταμέλεια mutationem voluntatis aut consilij significat. In conuersione autem fit mutatio vtriusque partis.
units.tr: In Hebrew it is called Theschubah; in Greek metanoia and metameleia. Some hold that they differ in this way: metanoia is used only of the repentance of the godly, while metameleia is also used of the repentance of the ungodly. Of Judas it is said that he repented [μεταμεληθεὶς ὁ Ἰούδας]. Of Esau it is said that he found no place for repentance [μετανοίας]. Of God it is said that the gifts of God are without repentance [ἀμεταμέλητα], that is, of such a kind that God cannot repent of them. The Septuagint use both words indiscriminately of God: "I repent [μεταμέλομαι] that I set up Saul as king"; "The Holy One of Israel will not repent [οὐ μεταμεληθήσεται]." The difference, then, is either slight or none, except that metanoia properly signifies a change of mind, and metameleia a change of will or purpose. In conversion, however, both are changed.

units.la: Latini varias habent appellationes. Vocant enim regenerationem, renouationem, resipiscentiam, conuersionem, pœnitentiam. Ex his resiresipiscentia videtur proprie respondere vocabulo μετάνοια. Sic enim resipiscentia est à resipisco, hoc est, post factum sapere incipio: sic μετανοέω est à μετανοέω, quod est post factum sapio, sententiam retracto, & consilium muto. Poenitentia dicitur, vel à poenitet, vel à poena, quod dolor in poenitentia sit quasi poena: vel, ut Erasmus putat, à pone tenendo, quasi poenitere sit posterius consilium tenere, seu intelligere post factum. Undequaque sit poenitentiae nomen, obscurius est nomine conversionis. Nam poenitentia non complectitur totum terminum, videlicet à quo, & ad quem, sed tantum significat dolorē post peccatum. Conversio autem totum complectitur: quia poenitentiae addit mutationem ex fide, quam inchoatio novae obedientiae sequitur. Deinde latius patet nomen poenitentiae, quàm conversionis. Nam conversio tantum dicitur de iis, qui soli ad Deum convertuntur: sic etiam μετάνοια & resipiscentia tantum de piis usurpatur: quia tribus his nominibus nova piorum vita significatur. Poenitentia verò etiam dicitur de impiis, de Saule & Juda, quem quidem sui sceleris poenituit, sed non est conversus: quia impij dolentes, non convertuntur aut corriguntur. Haec de appellationibus. Jam quid sit conversio, videamus.
units.tr: The Latins have various names for it. They call it regeneration, renewal, repentance (resipiscentia), conversion, and penitence (poenitentia). Of these, resipiscentia seems to correspond most properly to the Greek word μετάνοια. For resipiscentia comes from resipisco, that is, I begin to be wise after the deed; and μετανοέω [metanoeo] comes from μετά and νοέω, meaning to think after the deed, to retract one's opinion and change one's purpose. Poenitentia is derived either from poenitet or from poena, because the grief in penitence is as it were a punishment; or, as Erasmus thinks, from pone tenendo, as if poenitere meant to hold a later purpose, or to understand after the deed. Yet, however the word poenitentia is derived, it is less clear than the word conversio. For poenitentia does not embrace the whole process, namely the terminus from which and the terminus to which, but signifies only the grief after sin. Conversio, however, embraces the whole, because it adds to penitence the change that comes from faith, which is followed by the beginning of new obedience. Furthermore, the word poenitentia has a wider application than conversio. For conversio is said only of those who are turned to God alone; likewise μετάνοια and resipiscentia are used only of the godly, because these three words signify the new life of the godly. Poenitentia, however, is also said of the ungodly, of Saul and Judas, who indeed repented of their wickedness but were not converted, because the ungodly who grieve are not converted or corrected. So much for the names. Now let us see what conversion is.

units.la: Definitio partialis ex quaest. 88. peti potest, quod sit mortificatio veteris, & vivificatio novi hominis. Definitur plenius hoc modo Conversio ad Deum est mutatio mentis & voluntatis pravae in bonam, à Spiritu sancto per praedicationem Legis & Evangelij in electis excitata, quam consequitur studium bonorum operum, & vitae conformatio ad omnia Dei mandata. Confirmatur dictis scripturae: Si converteritimini, converteritimini usque ad me. Lauate, mundi estote. Sed ablute estis, sed sanctificati estis per nomen Domini Iesu, & per Spiritum Dei nostri. Desiste à malo, & fac bonum. Integra definitio ponitur Actorum cap. 26. vers. 18. Mitto te ad aperiendum oculos, ut se convertant à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Satanae ad Deum, ut remissionem peccatorum ac sortem inter sanctificatos accipiant per fidem, quae est in me. Et vers. 20. Annunciavi, ut resipiscerent & converterent se ad Deum: opera facientes digna iis, qui resipuissent.
units.tr: A partial definition may be taken from question 88, namely that it is the mortification of the old man and the quickening of the new man. A fuller definition is this: Conversio ad Deum is the change of a corrupt mind and will into a good one, stirred up in the elect by the Holy Spirit through the preaching of the Law and the Gospel, which is followed by zeal for good works and the conforming of life to all God's commandments. It is confirmed by the words of Scripture: "If you turn, turn to me." "Wash, be clean." But "you were washed, you were sanctified, in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God." "Cease from evil and do good." A complete definition is given in Acts 26:18: "I send you to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a lot among the sanctified through faith that is in me." And verse 20: "I preached that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of those who repent."

units.la: III. Quibus partibus conversio constet.
units.tr: III. Of what parts conversion consists.

units.la: Partes conversionis sunt duae: mortificatio veteris hominis, & vivificatio novi hominis. Ita melius loquimur cum Apostolo, quam cum iis, qui contritionem & fidem partes conversionis constituunt. Per contritionem intelligunt mortificationem: per fidem intelligunt laetitiam, sequente studium justitiae & novam obedientiam: quae quidem sunt effectus fidei, sed non ipsa fides. & contritio conversionem praecedit, nec est ipsa conversio, aut pars illius, sed tantum praeparatio ad conversionem, & quidem in solis electis, non in aliis. Vetus homo, qui mortificatur, est peccator tantum, hoc est, natura hominis corrupta, novus homo, qui viuificatur, est, qui incipit cessare à peccatis, hoc est, natura hominis regenerata. Mortificatio veteris hominis, seu carnis, est abnegatio & abolitio prauitatis naturae in nobis, & continet 1. agnitionem peccati & irae Dei. 2. Dolorem propter peccatum, & propter offensum Deum. 3. Detestationem ac fugam peccati. De ea loquuntur dicta: Si spiritu actiones corporis mortificaueritis. Lacerate corda vestra, & non vestes. Venite, reuertemur ad Dominum: quia ipse lacerauit nos, & ipse sanabit nos. Hinc apparet, valde impropriè tribui mortificationem, nedum conversionem, im-piis, in quibus non est odium, vel fuga peccati: nec dolor propter peccatum: quae omnia mortificatio complectitur. Agnitio peccati praecedit dolorem, quia affectus cordis sequuntur cognitionem. Dolor sequitur agnitionem peccati, in impiis quidem ex sensu praesentis, & ex metu futuri mali, temporalium nempe & aeternarum poenarum: & hic dolor de impiis proprie nec pars est conversionis, nec praeparatio ad eam, sed potius fuga & auersio à Deo: & aditus ad desperationem: ut patet in Caino, Saule, Juda, &c. Vocatur contritio non salutaris, & dolor mundi efficiens mortem, seu dolor non secundum Deum. In piis vero dolor nascitur ex offensione Dei, quam serio agnoscunt & deplorant, & est coniunctus cum odio ac detestatione peccati admissi, & cum fuga seu auersione à peccato praesenti & futuro. Hic dolor est pars conversionis, vel certè praeparatio ad eam, & vocatur contritio salutaris, & tristitia secundum Deum, efficiens resipiscentiam ad salutem. Differunt vero subiectis: Agnitio peccati est in mente, dolor in corde, fuga in voluntate, auerso voluntatis & cordis malo ad bonum: juxta illud Psalmi: Desiste à malo, & fac bonum.
units.tr: Conversion has two parts: mortification of the old man and quickening of the new man. We speak thus more fittingly with the Apostle than do those who make contrition and faith the parts of conversion. By contrition they mean mortification; by faith they mean joy, followed by zeal for righteousness and new obedience. These are indeed effects of faith, but they are not faith itself. And contrition precedes conversion; it is not conversion itself or a part of it, but only a preparation for conversion, and that only in the elect, not in others. The old man, who is mortified, is the sinner only, that is, human nature corrupted. The new man, who is quickened, is one who begins to cease from sins, that is, human nature regenerated. The mortification of the old man, or of the flesh, is the denial and abolition of the depravity of nature in us, and it contains (1) the recognition of sin and of God's wrath; (2) sorrow on account of sin and because God has been offended; (3) detestation and flight of sin. The passages speak of this: "If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body." "Rend your hearts, and not your garments." "Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has torn us, and he will heal us." From this it is clear that mortification, and still less conversion, is very improperly ascribed to the ungodly, in whom there is no hatred or flight of sin, nor sorrow for sin, all of which mortification embraces. The recognition of sin precedes sorrow, because the affections of the heart follow knowledge. Sorrow follows the recognition of sin; in the ungodly, indeed, it arises from a sense of present evil and from fear of future evil, namely temporal and eternal punishments. This sorrow in the ungodly is properly neither a part of conversion nor a preparation for it, but rather a flight and aversion from God, and an approach to despair, as is evident in Cain, Saul, Judas, and others. It is called unsaving contrition, and the sorrow of the world that works death, or sorrow not according to God. In the godly, however, sorrow arises from offence to God, which they seriously acknowledge and deplore; it is joined with hatred and detestation of the sin committed, and with flight or aversion from present and future sin. This sorrow is a part of conversion, or at least a preparation for it, and it is called saving contrition, and sorrow according to God, producing repentance unto salvation. The parts differ in their subjects: the recognition of sin is in the mind, the sorrow in the heart, the flight in the will, the turning of the will and heart from evil to good; according to the words of the Psalm: "Cease from evil, and do good."

units.la: Vocatur in scriptura mortificatio. 1. Quia sicut mortuus non potest edere actiones hominis viui: sic natura praua, abolita eius corruptione, non amplius exercet suas actiones, hoc est, non amplius actualia peccata producit, represso peccato originali. Qui enim mortuus est, liber est à peccato. 2. Quia haec mortificatio non fit absque dolore & luctâ. Nam caro concupiscit adversus spiritum: & ob hanc causam mortificatio etiam appellatur crucifixio carnis. Qui sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt cum affectibus & concupiscentiis suis. 3. Quia est fuga peccati, seu, cessatio à peccato. Nec simpliciter vocatur mortificatio, sed mortificatio ficatio veteris hominis, quia per eam non substantia hominis, sed peccatum in homine destruitur. Additur etiam, veteris hominis, ad discernendum piorum & impiorum poenitentiam. In illis enim non homo, sed vetus homo: in his non vetus homo, sed homo destruitur.
units.tr: In Scripture it is called mortification. (1) Because, just as a dead man cannot perform the actions of a living man, so a corrupt nature, once its corruption is abolished, no longer exercises its actions, that is, no longer produces actual sins, the original sin being held in check. For he who is dead is free from sin. (2) Because this mortification does not happen without pain and struggle. For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and for this reason mortification is also called the crucifixion of the flesh: "Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts." (3) Because it is a flight from sin, or a ceasing from sin. It is not simply called mortification, but mortification of the old man, because through it not the substance of the man but the sin in the man is destroyed. The words of the old man are added also to distinguish the repentance of the godly from that of the ungodly. For in the godly it is not the man but the old man that is destroyed; in the ungodly it is not the old man but the man himself that is destroyed.

units.la: Vivificatio noui hominis est vera laetitia in Deo per Christum: & serium ac promptum studium instituendi vitam ex voluntate Dei, omniaque bona opera exercendi. Complectitur tria mortificationi contraria. 1. Agnitionem misericordiae Dei, & applicationem eius per fidem in Christo. 2. Laetitiam inde ortam de Deo placato per Christum, & de obedientia inchoata & perficienda. 3. Ardens studium nouae obedientiae, & serium propositum non amplius peccandi, sed gratitudinem Deo per totam vitam praestandi, & amorem eius retinendi, quod studiū est ipsa noua obedientia, iuxta dicta: Iustificati fide pacem habemus erga Deo per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Regnum Dei est iustitia, & pax, & gaudium per Spiritum sanctum. Qui habito in excelsis, & in contritis & humilibus spiritu, vt refocillem spiritum humilium, & cor contritorum. Ita etiam vos colligite, vos ipsos mortuos esse peccato, viuere autem per Iesum Christum dominum nostrum. Viuo autem non amplius ego, sed viuit in me Christus, & vitam, quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem filij Dei, qui dilexit & tradidit semetipsum pro me.
units.tr: The quickening of the new man is true joy in God through Christ, and a earnest and ready zeal for ordering life according to the will of God, and for performing all good works. It embraces three things opposed to mortification: (1) the recognition of God's mercy and its application through faith in Christ; (2) the joy arising from this, that God is reconciled through Christ, and from the new obedience begun and to be perfected; (3) an ardent zeal for new obedience, and a earnest resolve no longer to sin but to render gratitude to God throughout life and to keep his love; this zeal is itself the new obedience, according to the words: "Justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." "The kingdom of God is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit." "For thus says he who is high and lofty, who dwells in the holy place, and with the contrite and humble of spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble and the heart of the contrite." "So also you must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord." "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

units.la: Vocatur vivificatio haec pars conuersionis. 1. Quia sicut homo viuus agit actiones hominis viui: sic vivificatio est accensio noua lucis in mente, & generatio nouarum qualitatum & motionum in voluntate & corde, ex quibus noua vita & nouae operationes sequuntur. 2. Quia est laetitia in Deo per Christum, quae est res suauissima. Additur, per Christum: quia non possumus laetari in Deo, nisi placato. Non autem placatur nobis Deus, nisi per Christum. Non ergo possumus laetari in Deo, nisi per Christum.
units.tr: This part of conversion is called vivification. First, because just as a living man performs the actions of a living man, so vivification is the kindling of a new light in the mind and the generation of new qualities and motions in the will and heart, from which a new life and new operations follow. Second, because there is joy in God through Christ, which is a most sweet thing. The words "through Christ" are added because we cannot rejoice in God unless He is reconciled to us, and God is not reconciled to us except through Christ. Therefore we cannot rejoice in God except through Christ.

units.la: Vtraque conuersionis pars manat ex fide. Ratio est: quia nemo potest odisse peccatum, & ad Deum accedere, nisi Deum diligat. Nemo autem diligit Deum, nisi praeditus fide. Quod ergo in neutra parte fit expressa mentio fidei, factum est, non quod fides excludatur, sed quia in tota doctrina de conuersione & gratitudine praesupponitur, sicut causa praesupponitur a suo effectu.
units.tr: Both parts of conversion flow from faith. The reason is this: no one can hate sin and draw near to God unless he loves God, and no one loves God unless he is endowed with faith. That faith is not expressly mentioned in either part is not because faith is excluded, but because it is presupposed throughout the whole doctrine of conversion and gratitude, just as a cause is presupposed by its effect.

units.la: Obiect. Fides parit laetitiam. Ergo non parit dolorem & mortificationem. Resp. Non est absurdum, eandem causam producere diuersos effectus, diuersa causatione, & diuerso respectu. Fides parit dolorem non per se, sed per accidens, quod est peccatum, tum, quo Deum tam benignum patrem offendimus. Lætitiam operatur per se: quia facit nos certos de paterna Dei voluntate erga nos per & propter Christum.Inst. Præcedit enim fidem: quia à lege fit initium prædicationis pœnitentiæ. Prædicatio legis præcedit ante fidem. Resp. Concedo, esse aliquem, sed non talem, qui dicatio legis operatur dolorem & iram. Ergo est dolor aliquis fit pars conuersionis. Nam dolor impiorum, qui est ante fidem, & sine fide, est potius auersio à Deo, quam conuersio ad Deum: quæ cum sint contraria, non possunt, neque in toto, neque in parte convenire. In electis vero dolor ille est quædam παρασκευή, præparatio ad conversionem, vt modo est dictum.
units.tr: Objection. Faith produces joy; therefore it does not produce sorrow and mortification. Answer. It is not absurd for the same cause to produce different effects, by different causation and in different respects. Faith produces sorrow not directly but accidentally, namely in that sin, by which we offend so kind a Father. It produces joy directly, because it makes us certain of God's fatherly will towards us through and for the sake of Christ. Further objection. For the preaching of repentance begins from the law, and the preaching of the law comes before faith. Answer. I grant that there is some such preaching, but not such that the preaching of the law works sorrow and wrath. Therefore there is some sorrow which becomes part of conversion. For the sorrow of the wicked, which comes before faith and without faith, is rather aversion from God than conversion to God; and since these are contrary, they can agree neither in the whole nor in a part. In the elect, however, that sorrow is a certain preparation for conversion, as has just been said.

units.la: IV. Quæ sint conuersionis causæ.
units.tr: IV. What the causes of conversion are.

units.la: Causa efficiens principalis conuersionis nostræ est Spiritus sanctus seu Deus ipse. Hinc sancti petunt se à Deo converti, & reduci: Conuerte me, & convertar: quia tu domine es Deus meus. Conuerte nos domine ad te. Hunc Deus dextera sua exaltatum constituit principem & seruatorem, vt det resipiscentiam Israeli, & remissionem peccatorum. Egregium est deitatis Christi argumentum: quia resipiscentiam & remissionem peccatorum dare est solius Dei. Nempe etiam gentibus Deus resipiscentiam dedit ad vitam. Ecquando det eis Deus resipiscentiam ad agnitionem veritatis, & resipiscant à Diaboli laqueis, &c.
units.tr: The principal efficient cause of our conversion is the Holy Spirit, or God Himself. Hence the saints pray to be converted and brought back by God: "Convert me, and I shall be converted, for you, Lord, are my God." "Turn us, O Lord, unto you." God has exalted this One at His right hand as Prince and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. This is an outstanding proof of the deity of Christ, because to give repentance and forgiveness of sins belongs to God alone. Indeed God also gave repentance to the Gentiles unto life. Would that God might give them repentance unto the knowledge of the truth, that they might recover from the snares of the devil, etc.

units.la: Instrumentales causæ mediæ, sunt. 1. Lex. 2. Euangelium. Post doctrinam Euangelii rursus doctrina legis. Præcedit enim concio legis, præparans nos ad concionem Euangelii: quia lege non est agnitio peccati, eoque nec dolor de peccato. Euangelii concio legem debet sequi, erigens corda contrita fiducia misericordiæ Dei per Christum. Sine hac enim concione non est fides, & sine fide non est dilectio Dei: proinde neque conuersio ad Deum. Concionem Euangelij rursus sequitur concio legis, vt ea sit norma gratitudinis, & vitæ nostræ. Lex igitur præcedit, vt excitet agnitionem & dolorem peccati: sequitur vt conuersis sit regula vitæ. Hinc Prophetæ primo accusant peccata, minantur pœnas, hortantur ad resipiscentiam, postea consolantur & promittunt veniam resipiscentibus: ad extremum rursus hortantur, & officia pietatis præscribunt. Tales quoque fuerunt conciones Iohannis Baptistæ. Sic igitur concio pœnitentiæ complectitur Legem & Euangelium: etsi in efficienda conuersione distinctæ sunt vtriusque partes.
units.tr: The instrumental means causes are: (1) the law; (2) the gospel. After the doctrine of the gospel comes again the doctrine of the law. For the preaching of the law comes first, preparing us for the preaching of the gospel, since through the law comes the knowledge of sin, and so also sorrow for sin. The preaching of the gospel ought to follow the law, raising up contrite hearts by trust in the mercy of God through Christ. For without this preaching there is no faith, and without faith no love of God, and consequently no conversion to God. Again the preaching of the gospel is followed by the preaching of the law, so that it may be the rule of gratitude and of our life. The law therefore comes first, to stir up the knowledge and sorrow of sin; it follows, so that it may be a rule of life for the converted. Hence the prophets first accuse sins, threaten punishments, and exhort to repentance; afterwards they comfort and promise pardon to the penitent; at last they exhort again and prescribe the duties of godliness. Such also were the sermons of John the Baptist. Thus the sermon of repentance embraces both law and gospel, although in bringing about conversion the two parts are distinct.

units.la: Causa instrumentalis proxima & interna conuersionis est fides. Sine fide enim non est dilectio Dei : & nisi simus persuasi de voluntate Dei erga nos, quod nobis velit mittere peccata, per & propter Christum, nunquam inchoabitur in nobis conuersio, neque quoad mortificationem, neque quoad viuificationem : quia fide purificantur corda: sine fide non possumus amare Deum, nec habere veram lætitiam in Deo. Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Ex fide tanquam ex fonte omnia bona opera, proinde & conuersionem promanare oportet. Quicquid enim non est ex fide, peccatum est. Ergo conuersio non est vera, nisi ex fide, seu præ-lucente fide fiat.
units.tr: The proximate and internal instrumental cause of conversion is faith. For without faith there is no love of God; and unless we are persuaded of God's will towards us, that He wishes to remit our sins through and for the sake of Christ, conversion will never begin in us, either as to mortification or as to vivification, because hearts are purified by faith; without faith we cannot love God nor have true joy in God. Justified by faith, we have peace. All good works, and therefore conversion too, must flow from faith as from a fountain. For whatever is not of faith is sin. Therefore conversion is not true unless it comes from faith, or takes place with faith shining before it.

units.la: Adiuuantes causæ conuersionis sunt: crux, δοκιμασία, castigationes nostræ, & aliorum. Item beneficia, pœnæ & exempla aliorum, &c. Castigasti me, & castigatus sum, vt vitulus. Bonum est mihi, Domine, quod humiliasti me, vt cognoscerem vias tuas. Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant bona opera, &c.
units.tr: The helping causes of conversion are: the cross, testing (δοκιμασία), our own chastisements and those of others. Likewise benefits, punishments and the examples of others, etc. You have chastened me, and I was chastened, like a calf. It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me, that I might learn your ways. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, etc.

units.la: Subiectum, seu materia in qua, est mens, voluntas, cor, & omnes affectus hominis, in quibus fit mutatio per conuersionem. Forma conuersionis est ipsa conuersio, & conuersionis accidentia, videlicet 1. In mente & intellectu rectum judicium de Deo: deque eius voluntate & operibus. 2. In voluntate serium ac promtum studium vitandi lapsus, & offensiones Dei: ac positum obediendi Deo, secundum omnia eius mandata. 3. In corde noui ac boni motus & affectus cum lege Dei congruentes. 4. In actionibus externis, & tota vita rectitudo, & obedientia inchoata secundum legem Dei.
units.tr: The subject, or the matter in which, is the mind, will, heart, and all the affections of man, in which change takes place through conversion. The form of conversion is conversion itself, and the accidents of conversion, namely: (1) in the mind and understanding, a right judgment about God, and about His will and works; (2) in the will, a serious and ready zeal to avoid lapses and offences against God, and a settled purpose to obey God in all His commands; (3) in the heart, new and good motions and affections agreeing with the law of God; (4) in outward actions and the whole of life, uprightness and obedience begun according to the law of God.

units.la: Obiectum, est 1. peccatum seu inobedientia, tanquam terminus à quo. 2. Iustitia seu noua obedientia, tanquam terminus ad quem. Finis conuersionis præcipuus est gloria Dei: proximus & subordinatus, est bonum nostrum, hoc est, beatitudo nostra & fruitio æternæ vitæ. Minus principalis est conuersio aliorum: Et tu conuersus confirma fratres. Sic luceat lux vestra, vt videant bona opera vestra, & glorificent Patrem, &c.
units.tr: The object is (1) sin or disobedience, as the terminus from which; (2) righteousness or new obedience, as the terminus to which. The chief end of conversion is the glory of God; the nearer and subordinate end is our good, that is, our blessedness and the enjoyment of eternal life. The conversion of others is a less principal end: And you, when converted, strengthen your brethren. So let your light shine, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father, etc.

units.la: [Huc pertinent quæstiones de Pelagianismo: an homo sine gratia Spiritus sancti possit seipsum convertere: & an possit se ad gratiam præparare & applicare per liberum arbitrium. Priorem Pelagius defendebat contra scripturam: Converte me, & convertar. Deus dat velle & perficere. Non potest arbor mala bonos fructus ferre. Posteriorem Scholastici & Pontificij hodie tuentur, contra eadem scripturæ dicta, & contra illud: Nemo potest ad me venire, nisi Pater traxerit eum. Thomas Aquinas tribuit libero arbitrio præparationem, sed non conuersionem. Præparationem verò pingit fuco, quod sit quidem ad gratiam habitualem conuersionis, sed tamen per auxilium gratuitum Dei interius monentis. Vide sum. Theolog. partis prima parte secunda, quaest.109. ad 6.]
units.tr: [To this belong the questions about Pelagianism: whether man can convert himself without the grace of the Holy Spirit, and whether he can prepare and apply himself to grace by free will. Pelagius defended the former against Scripture: Convert me, and I shall be converted. God gives to will and to perform. A bad tree cannot bear good fruit. The latter the Scholastics and Papists today maintain, against the same sayings of Scripture and against that word: No one can come to me unless the Father draws him. Thomas Aquinas attributes preparation, but not conversion, to free will. This preparation he colours with a pretence, saying that it is indeed directed towards habitual grace of conversion, yet only through the free help of God inwardly admonishing. See the Summa of Theology, first part of the second part, question 109, article 6.]

units.la: V. Qui sint conuersionis effectus.
units.tr: V. What the effects of conversion are.

units.la: Effectus conuersionis sunt: 1. Verus & ardens amor DEI & proximi. 2. Setium studium obediendi Deo, sine exceptione secundum omnia eius mandata. 3. Omnia bona opera, seu ipsa obedientia nova. 4. Denique studium conuertendi, & in salutis viam dirigendi etiam alios. Summa. Fructus veræ poenitentiæ sunt officia pietatis erga DEVM, & charitatis erga proximum.
units.tr: The effects of conversion are: (1) a true and burning love of God and of neighbour; (2) a sincere zeal to obey God, without exception, in all his commandments; (3) all good works, or in other words, the new obedience itself; (4) finally, zeal to convert others too and to direct them into the way of salvation. Summary. The fruits of true repentance are the duties of piety towards God and of charity towards one's neighbour.

units.la: VI. An sit conuersio perfecta in hac vita.
units.tr: VI. Whether conversion is complete in this life.

units.la: Conuersio nostra ad Deum nunquam perficitur in hac vita, sed est in perpetuo motu, donec in cœlesti vita perfectionem consequetur. Ex parte cognoscimus. Testantur idem querelæ & preces Sanctorum. Ab occultis meis munda me. Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit, &c. Remitte nobis peccata. Lucta item carnis & spiritus in conuersis, de qua Rom.8. Galat.5. Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, &c. Hortationes item Prophetarum & Apostolorum, vt conuersi magis conuertantur. Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc: qui sanctus est, sanctificetur adhuc. Demonstratur etiam ratione euidentissima. Nec mortificatio carnis, nec viuificatio spiritus in hac vita est absoluta in sanctis. Ergo nec tota conuersio. De mortificatione constat: quia sancti non modo perpetuò luctantur cum dubitationibus, & concupiscentia carnis, sed in luctu etiam sæpe ad tempus succumbunt, sæpe peccant, labuntur, & Deum offendunt: licet peccata sua non defendant, sed deplorent, ac vitare studeant. De viuificationis imperfectione eadem lucta testatur: & certè cùm cognitio tantum sit ex parte, renouatio voluntatis & cordis etiam talis erit. Voluntas enim sequitur cognitionem.
units.tr: Our conversion to God is never completed in this life, but is in constant motion until it attains perfection in the heavenly life. We know in part. The complaints and prayers of the saints testify to the same thing: Cleanse me from my secret faults. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me, etc. Forgive us our sins. So too is the struggle of flesh and spirit in the converted, of which Romans 8 and Galatians 5 speak: The flesh lusts against the spirit, etc. So too are the exhortations of the Prophets and Apostles that the converted should be converted more and more: He who is righteous, let him be justified still; he who is holy, let him be sanctified still. It is also shown by the most evident reasoning: the mortification of the flesh and the quickening of the spirit are not complete in the saints in this life. Therefore neither is the whole conversion. That mortification is incomplete is clear, because the saints not only struggle continually with doubts and the lust of the flesh, but in the struggle often succumb for a time, often sin, slip and offend God, although they do not defend their sins but lament them and strive to avoid them. The same struggle bears witness to the imperfection of the quickening: and certainly, since knowledge is only in part, the renewal of the will and heart will be of the same kind. For the will follows knowledge.

units.la: Duæ autem euidentes causæ sunt, cur voluntas in conuersis imperfectè ad bonum feratur in hac vita. 1. Quia in hac vita renouatio naturæ nunquam fit perfecta, neque quoad agnitionem Dei, neq; quoad inclinationes ad obediendum Deo, quod vel Pauli querela satis confirmat: Scio quod non habitat in me, hoc est, in carne mea bonum. 2. Quod conuersi non semper à Spiritu sancto reguntur, sed interdum à Deo vel examinandi, vel castigandi, vel humiliandi ipsos causa, ad tempus deseruntur, sed tamen men ad pœnitentiam reuocantur, vt non pereant: Credo, Do- mine, sed opem fer incredulitati meæ.
units.tr: There are, however, two evident causes why the will of the converted is carried towards good only imperfectly in this life. (1) Because in this life the renewal of nature is never made perfect, neither as regards the knowledge of God nor as regards the inclinations to obey God; Paul's complaint sufficiently confirms this: I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good thing. (2) Because the converted are not always governed by the Holy Spirit, but are sometimes left for a time by God, either to test them, or to chastise them, or to humble them; yet they are recalled to repentance so that they do not perish: I believe, Lord, but help my unbelief.

units.la: Cur autem Deus in hac vita conuersionem non perficiat, cum possit: causæ hæ sunt: 1. Vt sancti humilientur, exerceantur in fide, patientia, precibus, & lucta aduersus carnem, nec superbiant opinione perfectionis, sed quotidie orent: Ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruo tuo. Remitte nobis peccata. 2. Vt ad perfectionem magis ac magis contendant, eamque ardentius desiderent. 3. Vt contemto hoc mundo, ad vitam cœlestem magis aspirent ac properent: vtpote cui intelligunt perfectionem suam esse reseruatam: Superna curate, non terrena. Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Mortificate igitur membra vestra terrestria. Nondum patefactum est, quod erimus: scimus autem fore, vt cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei simus.
units.tr: Why God does not complete conversion in this life, although he is able to, the causes are these: (1) that the saints may be humbled, exercised in faith, patience, prayer, and the struggle against the flesh, and that they may not be puffed up with the opinion of perfection but pray every day: Enter not into judgment with your servant. Forgive us our sins. (2) That they may strive more and more towards perfection and desire it more ardently. (3) That, having despised this world, they may aspire and hasten more towards the heavenly life, since they understand that their perfection is reserved there: Seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth. Your life is hidden with Christ in God. Mortify therefore your earthly members. It has not yet been revealed what we shall be; but we know that when he is revealed we shall be like him.

units.la: [De hac imperfectione præclarè Calvinus: Atque hæc quidem (inquit) instauratio non vno momento, vel die, vel anno impletur, sed per continuos, immo & lentos interdum profectus abolet Deus in electis carnis corruptelas: repurgat eos sordibus, sibique in templa consecrat, sensus eorum omnes ad veram puritatem renouans, quo se tota vita exerceant in poenitentia: sciantque huic militiæ nullum nisi in morte esse finem. Legantur & sequentes paragraphi vsq; ad decimum quintum, quibus disputatio de reliquiis peccatorum in sanctis contra catharos & anabaptistas, erudite explicatur.]
units.tr: [Calvin speaks admirably of this imperfection: "This restoration," he says, "is not accomplished in one moment, or one day, or one year, but God abolishes the corruptions of the flesh in the elect by continual and sometimes slow advances; he cleanses them from their filth and consecrates them as his own temples, renewing all their senses to true purity, so that their whole life may be spent in repentance, and they may know that this warfare has no end except in death." The following paragraphs, down to the fifteenth, should also be read, in which the disputation about the remnants of sin in the saints, against the Cathari and the Anabaptists, is learnedly explained.]

units.la: VII. Quid conuersio piorum, & pœnitentia impiorum differat.
units.tr: VII. How the conversion of the godly differs from the repentance of the ungodly.

units.la: Nomen pœnitentiæ tam impiis, quàm piis tribuitur: quia aliquid habent commune: videlicet agnitionem peccati, & dolorem post peccatum. Sed in cæteris magnum discrimen est. 1. In causa impulsiua pœnitentiæ seu doloris. Impij dolent, non propter offensum Deum, sed tantum propter paratum sibi supplicium, & venturum cruciatum, absque quo si esset, de peccato nunquam dolerent. Ita Cain dolebat tantum propter poenam: Maior est iniquitas mea (hoc est, iniquitatis meæ poena) quàm vt eam ferre possim. Ecce eicis me hodie à facie terræ, &c. Pij verò doluerunt quidem & ipsi poenam, sed præcipuè dolent propter ipsum peccatum, & propter offensum Deum. Ita Dauid: Tibi soli peccaui: & malum coram te feci. Peccatum meum contra me est semper. Sic in Petro dolor est propter Christum offensum: in Juda tantum propter cruciatum sibi paratum, non propter ipsum peccatum. Hoc discrimen versiculi Horatiani exprimunt: Oderunt peccare boni, virtutis amore. Tu nihil admittes in te formidine poenæ. Horat. lib. 2. epist. 16.
units.tr: The name of repentance is given both to the ungodly and to the godly, because they have something in common, namely, the acknowledgment of sin and sorrow after sin. But in other respects there is a great difference. (1) In the impelling cause of repentance or sorrow. The ungodly grieve not because God has been offended, but only because of the punishment prepared for them and the torment that is coming; if there were no such punishment, they would never grieve over sin. So Cain grieved only on account of the punishment: My iniquity is greater (that is, the punishment of my iniquity) than I can bear. Behold, you cast me out this day from the face of the earth, etc. But the godly indeed grieve over their punishment too, yet they grieve chiefly over the sin itself and because God has been offended. So David: Against you only have I sinned, and done evil in your sight. My sin is always before me. So in Peter the sorrow is over Christ who was offended; in Judas only over the torment prepared for him, not over the sin itself. The verses of Horace express this difference: The good shun sin for love of virtue. You, through fear of punishment, will admit nothing into yourself. Horace, Epistles, book 2, letter 16.

units.la: 2. In causa efficiente. Impij agunt pœnitentiam ex diffidentia & desperatione, ita vt ruant magis in desperationem, fremitum, atque odium aduersus Deum. Pij vero resipiscunt ex fide seu fiducia misericordiæ Dei, & gratuitæ reconciliationis per & propter Christum.
units.tr: (2) In the efficient cause. The ungodly perform repentance out of distrust and despair, so that they rush all the more into despair, rage, and hatred against God. The godly, however, repent out of faith, or trust in the mercy of God and in the free reconciliation through and for the sake of Christ.

units.la: 3. In ipsa forma. Piorum pœnitentia est conuersio à diabolo, à peccatis, & à natura veteri ad Deum: quia non tantum dolent, sed etiam se erigunt fiducia Mediatoris, confidunt Deo, lætantur in Deo, & in eo acquiescunt cum Davide: Asperges me hyssopo, Domine, & mundabor. Impiorum pœnitentia est auersio à Deo ad ipsum diabolum, odium, fuga, fremitus aduersus Deum, & initium desperationis.
units.tr: (3) In the form itself. The repentance of the godly is a conversion from the devil, from sins, and from the old nature to God; for they not only grieve, but also raise themselves up by trust in the Mediator, they rely upon God, rejoice in God, and rest in him with David: Purge me with hyssop, Lord, and I shall be clean. The repentance of the ungodly is an aversion from God to the devil himself, hatred, flight, and rage against God, and the beginning of despair.

units.la: 4. In effectu. Resipiscentiam piorum sequitur noua obedientia: quanto magis resipiscunt, tanto magis vetus homo in ipsis emoritur, & studium iustitiæ augetur. Impiorum pœnitentiam non sequitur noua obedientia, sed pergunt illi in peccatis, & redeunt ad vomitum, licet aliquandiu pœnitentiam simulent, vt Achab. Mortificantur quidem ipsi, ac destruuntur, sed naturæ vetustas, hoc est, peccatum, in ipsis non mortificatur: immò quanto magis agunt pœnitentiam, tanto magis in ipsis crescit odium, fremitus, & fuga Dei, auersio à Deo, & accessus ad diabolum.
units.tr: (4) In the effect. The repentance of the godly is followed by new obedience; the more they repent, the more the old man dies in them, and the zeal for righteousness increases. The repentance of the ungodly is not followed by new obedience, but they persist in their sins and return to their vomit, although for a while they feign repentance, as Ahab did. They indeed are mortified and destroyed, but the old nature, that is, sin, is not mortified in them; indeed, the more they perform repentance, the more in them there grows hatred, rage, and flight from God, aversion from God, and approach to the devil.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XCI. Quæ sunt bona opera? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: QUESTION 91. What are good works? ANSWER.

units.la: Tantum ea, quæ ex vera fide a, secundum legem Dei fiunt b, & ad eius solius gloriam referuntur c: Non ea autem, quæ à nobis opinione recti conficta, aut ab hominibus tradita sunt d.
units.tr: Only those works which are done from true faith, according to the law of God, and are referred to his alone for his glory. Not those which we have devised by our own opinion of what is right, or which have been handed down by men.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: In doctrina de BONIS OPERIBVS præcipuè quæritur: I. Quid sint bona opera. II. Quomodo possint fieri. III. An sanctorum opera sint pura seu perfectè bona. IV. Quo-
units.tr: In the doctrine of GOOD WORKS the following are chiefly asked: I. What good works are. II. How they can be done. III. Whether the works of the saints are pure, or perfectly good. IV. How-

units.la: Quaest. XCI. DE BONIS OPERIBVS.
units.tr: Question 91. CONCERNING GOOD WORKS.

units.la: IV. Quomodo, dum sunt imperfectè bona, placeant Deo. V. Cur sint facienda. VI. An sint meritoria coram Deo.
units.tr: IV. How, although they are only imperfectly good, they please God. V. Why they are to be done. VI. Whether they are meritorious before God.

units.la: I. Quid sint bona opera.
units.tr: I. What good works are.

units.la: Bona opera sunt, quæ fiunt secundum legem Dei, ex vera fide, &ad solius Dei gloriam referuntur. Tria hic consideranda sunt: 1. Conditiones bonorum operum. 2. Discrimen operum renatorum & non renatorum. 3. Quatenus opera moralia impiorum sint peccata.
units.tr: Good works are those which are done according to the law of God, from true faith, and are referred to the glory of God alone. Three things are to be considered here: 1. the conditions of good works; 2. the difference between the works of the regenerate and of the unregenerate; 3. in what way the moral works of the ungodly are sins.

units.la: Primo igitur, vt opus aliquod sit bonum, & Deo placeat, requiruntur tres conditiones.
units.tr: First, then, three conditions are required for a work to be good and pleasing to God.

units.la: 1. Vt sit mandatum à Deo. Nulla enim creatura habet jus instituendi cultum Dei. Bona autem opera (loquimur de bono morali) & cultus Dei sunt idem. Bonum morale à bono naturali plurimum differt. Omnes actus, quatenus sunt actus, etiam malorum, sunt bonum naturale, seu boni naturaliter, hoc est, quiddam à Deo conditū in natura. Sed non omnes sunt bonum morale, seu boni moraliter, hoc est, cum justitia Dei congruentes. Excluditur hac conditione omnis εὐλογ[?] & commentum de bona intentione, cùm homines mala faciunt, vt eueniant bona, vel cum ipsi confingunt opera, quæ Deo pro cultu obtrudunt, non quidem per se mala, sed tamen non præcepta à Deo. Nam ad cultum Dei non sufficit, aliquod opus non esse malum, vel non prohibitum, sed oportet esse à Deo præceptum, secundum dicta: Obedientia melior est sacrificiis. In præceptis meis ambulabitis. Frustra me colunt mandatis hominum. At (inquis) opera adiaphora non sunt præcepta à Deo: & multa tamen adiaphora placent Deo. Respond. Placent non per se, sed per accidens, quatenus in genere dilectionis continentur, & quatenus iis vitantur scandala, & salus proximi juuatur. Eatenus enim sunt à Deo præcepta, licet non in specie, tamen in genere.
units.tr: 1. That it be commanded by God. For no creature has the right to institute the worship of God. Good works (we are speaking of moral good) and the worship of God are one and the same. Moral good differs greatly from natural good. All acts, insofar as they are acts, even of evil people, are natural good, or good in a natural sense, that is, something created by God in nature. But not all are moral good, or good in a moral sense, that is, agreeing with the justice of God. By this condition is excluded all will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκία] and the invention about a good intention, when men do evil so that good may come of it, or when they devise works which they force upon God as worship, works not evil in themselves but not commanded by God. For to the worship of God it is not enough that a work is not evil or not forbidden; it must be commanded by God, according to the sayings: Obedience is better than sacrifices. You shall walk in my precepts. In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. But (you say) indifferent works are not commanded by God, and yet many indifferent things please God. Answer: they please not in themselves but by accident, insofar as they are included in the general category of love, and insofar as by them offences are avoided and the salvation of the neighbour is helped. Thus they are commanded by God, not in particular indeed, but in general.

units.la: 2. Vt fiat ex vera fide, nitente merito & intercessione Mediatoris, ex qua sis certus, personam & opus placere Deo, propter Mediatorem. Nam ex vera fide aliquid facere, est 1. statuere, quod persona placeat Deo, propter satisfactionem Christi. 2. Quod etiam obedientia placeat Deo, tum quia eius imperfectio etiam acceptetur propter Christi satisfactionem, propter quam persona placet Deo. Sine fide autem fieri non potest, vt quis Deo placeat: nec sufficit fides, qua scias, DEVM hoc velle, & hoc opus esse à Deo mandatum. Sic enim etiam impij scientes & facientes, quod Deus vult, ex fide agerent. Sed longius fides vera extenditur: quia & fidem historicam in se comprehendit, & (quod praecipuum est) promissiones euangelij ad se applicat. De hac vera fide dicitur: Quicquid non fit ex fide, peccatum est. Impossibile est sine fide placere Deo. Et ratio utriusque dicti non est obscura: quia sine fide non est dilectio Dei, & per consequens, nec dilectio proximi. Omne autem opus, quod non ex dilectione Dei proficiscitur, est hypocrisis, immo contumelia & contemtus Dei. Qui enim audet aliquid facere, sive Deo placeat, sive non, contemnit Deum, & afficit eum contumelia. Nec sine fide est bona conscientia: quod autem non fit bona conscientia, non potest Deo placere.
units.tr: 2. That it be done from true faith, resting on the merit and intercession of the Mediator, by which you may be certain that the person and the work please God on account of the Mediator. For to do something from true faith is 1. to hold that the person pleases God on account of the satisfaction of Christ; 2. also that obedience pleases God, both because its imperfection is accepted on account of Christ's satisfaction, on account of which the person pleases God. Now without faith it is not possible for anyone to please God; nor is that faith sufficient by which you know that God wills this and that this work is commanded by God. For in that way even the ungodly, knowing and doing what God wills, would act from faith. But true faith extends further: for it comprehends within itself historical faith and, what is chief, applies to itself the promises of the gospel. Of this true faith it is said: Whatever is not of faith is sin. It is impossible to please God without faith. And the reason for both sayings is not obscure: because without faith there is no love of God, and consequently no love of the neighbour either. Moreover every work that does not proceed from love of God is hypocrisy, indeed an insult and contempt of God. For whoever dares to do something, whether it pleases God or not, despises God and offers him an insult. Nor is there a good conscience without faith; and what is not done with a good conscience cannot please God.

units.la: 3. Ut referatur principaliter ad honorem & gloriam solius Dei. Honor complectitur amorem, reverentiam, obedientiam, gratitudinem. Ergo ad honorem Dei aliquid facere, est id facere, ut testemur amorem nostrum, & reverentiam nostram, & obedientiam nostram erga Deum, idque gratitudinis causa, pro beneficiis acceptis. Huc principaliter oportet referri opera, ut sint bona, & Deo placeant: ad Dei videlicet gloriam: non ad gloriam, vel utilitatem nostram: alioqui non fiunt ex Dei amore, sed ex φιλαυτία vel φιλοδοξία, & sunt mera hypocrisis. Quare, si igitur aliquid facimus, Deus est respiciendus: nec est curandum, quid homines dicant, laudent, vituperent: modo sciamus placere Deo, quod fecimus, juxta illud Apostoli: Omnia ad Dei gloriam facite. Veram interim gloriam apud homines possumus etiam legitime & secundario expetere & consequi, juxta illud: Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona vestra, &c.
units.tr: 3. That it be referred principally to the honour and glory of God alone. Honour embraces love, reverence, obedience, gratitude. Therefore to do something to the honour of God is to do it so that we bear witness to our love, our reverence and our obedience towards God, and that for the sake of gratitude for benefits received. Works must be referred principally to this, if they are to be good and please God: namely to the glory of God, not to our own glory or advantage; otherwise they are not done from love of God but from self-love [φιλαυτία] or love of glory [φιλοδοξία], and they are mere hypocrisy. Wherefore, if we do anything, God is to be regarded, nor is it to be cared what men say, praise or blame, provided we know that what we have done pleases God, according to the saying of the Apostle: Do all things to the glory of God. Meanwhile we may also lawfully and in a secondary sense seek and obtain true glory among men, according to the saying: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, etc.

units.la: Breviter: Requiritur fides in bonis operibus: quia nisi certo statuamus, ea Deo placere, fiunt cum Dei contemtu. Requiritur mandatum, quia fides respicit verbum. Proinde cum praeter verbum nulla sit fides: nulla etiam bona opera praeter illud esse possunt. Denique requiritur, ut fiant ad gloriam Dei, quia si fiant studio propriae gloriae, aut utilitatis, non possunt Deo placere.
units.tr: Briefly: faith is required in good works, because unless we firmly hold that they please God, they are done with contempt of God. A command is required, because faith looks to the Word; therefore, since there is no faith apart from the Word, no good works can exist apart from it either. Finally, it is required that they be done to the glory of God, because if they are done for the sake of one's own glory or advantage, they cannot please God.

units.la: Excluduntur his conditionibus omnia opera. 1. Quae pugnant cum lege, & voluntate Dei in lege patefacta, ut sunt peccata per se. 2. Quae quidem non pugnant cum lege, nec per se mala, nec bona sunt, sed adiaphora, per accidens tamen possunt fieri mala, accedente opinione cultus, vel scandalo. Opera enim cum lege non pugnantia, & non a Deo, sed ab hominibus praecepta, per accidens fiunt mala & peccata, cum fiunt opinione cultus Dei, aut cum scandalo proximi. Haec in duas priores conditiones impingunt. 3. Quae sunt per se bona, & praecepta a Deo, per accidens autem fiunt peccata, dum illegitime, nec modo, nec fine debito, hoc est, non ex fide, nec hoc fine principali fiunt, vt Deus celebretur. Hæc in duas posteriores conditiones peccant.
units.tr: By these conditions all works are excluded: 1. those which fight against the law and the will of God revealed in the law, as are sins in themselves; 2. those which indeed do not fight against the law, and are not evil in themselves, nor good, but indifferent, yet may by accident become evil, when a notion of worship or an offence is added. For works not contrary to the law, and commanded not by God but by men, become evil and sins by accident when they are done with the opinion of worshipping God, or with offence to the neighbour. These strike against the first two conditions. 3. Those which are good in themselves and commanded by God, but by accident become sins, when they are done unlawfully, neither in the right manner, nor with the due end, that is, not from faith, nor with this chief aim, that God may be honoured. These offend against the two last conditions.

units.la: Secundo. Differunt igitur opera renatorum & non renatorum: quod opera renatorum fiunt ad conditiones dictas. Opera bona non renatorum, etsi sunt à Deo mandata: tamen 1. non fiunt ex fide: 2. nec sunt coniuncta cum interna obedientia, sed fiunt simulate, & sunt mera hypocrisis: 3. sicut non promanant ex recta causa, hoc est, ex fide; sic non referuntur ad legitimum finem, hoc est, ad gloriam Dei. Ergo bona opera dici non merentur.
units.tr: Second. The works of the regenerate and of the unregenerate therefore differ, in that the works of the regenerate are done under the conditions stated. The good works of the unregenerate, although they are commanded by God, nevertheless: 1. are not done from faith; 2. are not joined with inner obedience, but are done feignedly, and are mere hypocrisy; 3. just as they do not spring from a right cause, that is, from faith, so they are not referred to a lawful end, that is, to the glory of God. Therefore they do not deserve to be called good works.

units.la: Tertiò. Hæc inter opera piorum & impiorum differentia confirmat, etiam ipsa impiorum opera moralia esse peccata, non quidem talia, qualia sunt, quæ sua natura cum lege divina pugnant. Hæc enim per se & suo genere sunt peccata: illa tantum per accidens, propter defectum, quod neque ex fide, neque ad Dei gloriam fiunt. Non igitur valet consequentia: Bona opera non renatorum & Ethnicorum sunt peccata: Ergo sunt fugienda: quia est fallacia accidentis, vt supra in doctrina de peccato est explicatum.
units.tr: Third. This difference between the works of the godly and of the ungodly confirms that even the moral works of the ungodly are sins; not indeed of the kind which by their nature fight against the divine law. For these are sins in themselves and by their kind; the others only by accident, on account of the defect that they are done neither from faith nor to the glory of God. Therefore the inference is not valid: The good works of the unregenerate and of the heathen are sins; therefore they are to be avoided, because it is a fallacy of accident, as was explained above in the doctrine of sin.

units.la: Typus bonorum operum.
units.tr: The type of good works.

units.la: Opera bona aliqua: vere bona, quæ juxta definitionem fiunt ex Dei mandato ex fide ad Dei gloriam perfecta, vt angelorum & hominum ante lapsum, & in vita cœlesti imperfecta, vt renatorum in hac vita apparenter bona, quæ sunt mandata quidem à Deo, & suo genere bona, sed mala per accidens, vt pote non facta eo modo, & fine, quo debebant. mandata ab hominibus religionis causa: vt traditiones, consilia, præcepta Pharisæorum & papistarum. Matth. 15. Frustra me colunt, &c.
units.tr: Some good works are truly good: those done according to the definition, by God's command, from faith, and perfected to God's glory, as those of the angels and of men before the fall, and imperfect in the heavenly life. Those of the regenerate in this life are apparently good: they are indeed commanded by God and good in their kind, but evil by accident, since they are not done in the manner and for the end they ought to be. Works commanded by men for the sake of religion are such as traditions, counsels and precepts of the Pharisees and Papists. Matt. 15: "In vain do they worship me," etc.

units.la: II. Quomodo bona opera fieri possint: seu, quomodo sint possibilia.
units.tr: II. How good works can be done, or how they are possible.

units.la: Haec quaestio explicanda est propter Pelagianos, qui bona opera etiam non renatis tribuebant: & propter semipelagianos, qui fingunt praeparatoria opera liberi arbitrij, &c. Possibilia igitur sunt bona opera per gratiam Spiritus sancti, & quidem solis renatis, quorum cor vere est regeneratum à Spiritu sancto per fidem Euangelij, idq; non tantum prima conversione, sed etiam continua gubernatione Spiritus sancti, efficientis in eis agnitionem peccati, fidem & novae obedientiae studium, indies etiam dona in ipsis augentis & confirmantis. Cui etiam subscribit Hieronymus, inquiens: Anathema sit, qui dicit legem possibilem sine gratia Spiritus sancti. Sine gratia enim & continua gubernatione Spiritus sancti etiam sanctissimi nihil nisi peccare possunt, ut videre est in Davide, Petro & aliis. Sine regeneratione vero ne quidem inchoari potest pars ulla boni operis: quia natura sumus mali, & mortui in peccatis: Omnes justitiae nostrae velut pannus menstruatae: quo dicto Esaias comprehendit seipsum & sanctissimos quosque. Si in sanctis coram Deo nihil reperitur nisi peccatum, quid erit in non-renatis? Quid boni hi praestare valeant, docet Paulus Rom. cap.1.&2. Docent etiam haec dicta: Non potest arbor fructus bonos ferre. Si Aethiops potest mutare pellem suam, & pardus maculas suas: etiam vos potestis bene agere, assueti male facere. Sine me nihil potestis facere. Deus est, qui efficit in nobis, ut velimus, & ut perficiamus pro gratuita sua voluntate, & omnia nostra opera sunt σχυσαλα. At Christi justitia non imputatur nobis ante conversionem. Impossibile est ergo, nos, vel opera nostra ante conversionem placere Deo. Fides est causa bonorum operum. Fides est à Deo: Ergo & opera effectus fidei sunt à Deo, nec esse esse possunt ante fidem & conversionem: alioqui effectus esset prior sua causa.
units.tr: This question must be explained because of the Pelagians, who attributed good works even to the unregenerate, and because of the semi-Pelagians, who invent preparatory works of free will, etc. Good works are therefore possible through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and indeed only for the regenerate, whose heart has truly been regenerated by the Holy Spirit through faith in the Gospel. This is so not only by the first conversion but also by the continual governance of the Holy Spirit, who works in them the knowledge of sin, faith and a zeal for new obedience, and who daily increases and confirms the gifts in them. Jerome also agrees with this, saying: "Let him be anathema who says that the law is possible without the grace of the Holy Spirit." For without grace and the continual governance of the Holy Spirit, even the most holy can do nothing but sin, as is seen in David, Peter and others. Without regeneration indeed not even the smallest part of a good work can begin, because we are evil by nature and dead in sins: "All our righteousnesses are like a polluted rag"; in which saying Isaiah includes himself and all the most holy. If nothing is found in the saints before God but sin, what will be found in the unregenerate? What such men can accomplish is taught by Paul, Rom. 1 and 2. These sayings also teach this: "A tree cannot bring forth good fruit." "If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots, then you also can do good, you who are accustomed to do evil." "Without me you can do nothing." "God is he who works in us both to will and to perform, according to his good pleasure," and all our works are "filthy rags" [σχυσαλα]. But the righteousness of Christ is not imputed to us before conversion. It is impossible, therefore, for us, or our works, before conversion to please God. Faith is the cause of good works. Faith is from God; therefore the works also, as effects of faith, are from God, and they cannot be before faith and conversion, otherwise the effect would be prior to its cause.

units.la: Quaeritur. An nulla sint opera praeparatoria? Resp. Si opera praeparatoria vocantur, quae sunt occasio poenitentiae, seu quibus Deus vtitur ad efficiendam in nobis resipiscentiam, qualia sunt: externa honesta disciplina, & vita secundum legem, auditio, lectio, meditatio verbi: item etiam crux & res adversae: potest contedi, quod sint aliqua. Si autem praeparatoria intelliguntur opera ante conversionem secundum legem facta, quibus tanquam bono hominum conatu Deus alliciatur, ad veram conversionem & alia beneficia ipsis danda, negatur, quod sint aliqua: quia juxta regulam Pauli: Quicquid ex fide non est, peccatum est. Papistae talia opera vocant merita congrui, q. d. ex se quidem imperfecta, & nihil merentia, tamen propter quæ sit congruum misericordiæ Dei, dare hominibus conuersionem & vitam æternam. Sed mi-seretur Deus, quorum vult: non eorum, qui merentur. Nemo enim de Deo aliquid meretur, nisi plagas. Cum omnia feceritis, dicite: serui inutiles sumus, quæ debuimus, fecimus.
units.tr: It is asked: are there no preparatory works? Answer: If those are called preparatory works which are an occasion of repentance, or which God uses to bring about repentance in us, such as: outward honest discipline, a life according to the law, hearing, reading, meditation on the Word, "likewise also the cross and adverse circumstances," it may be granted that there are some. But if preparatory works are understood to be works done before conversion according to the law, by which God is, as it were, enticed by a good human endeavour to true conversion and to other benefits to be given to them, this is denied that there are any; because according to the rule of Paul: "Whatever is not of faith is sin." The Papists call such works "merits of congruity," as if to say: in themselves indeed imperfect and deserving nothing, yet on account of which it is fitting for the mercy of God to give men conversion and eternal life. "But God has mercy on whom he wills," not on those who merit it. For no one merits anything from God except stripes. "When you have done all, say: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do."

units.la: III. An opera renatorum sint perfectè bona.
units.tr: III. Whether the works of the regenerate are perfectly good.

units.la: Opera sanctorum non sunt perfectè bona in hac vita: 1. Quia etiam sancti multa faciunt mala per se peccata, propter quæ rei sunt coram Deo, & digni, vt abijciantur in pœnas æternas. Petrus ter abnegat Christum, Dauid committit adulterium, interficit Yriam, conatur scelus tegere, numerat populum, &c. Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus. 2. Quia multa operata bona, quæ facere deberent secundum legem. 3. Quia etiam bona, quæ faciunt, non sunt tam perfectè bona & pura, atque requirit legis ἀκριβεία, sed semper sunt coniuncta cum næuis, & inquinata peccatis. In optimis eorum operibus nunquam est ea rectitudinis perfectio, quæ esse debebat. Ratio ex loco de conuersione intelligitur. Fides enim, regeneratio, dilectio Dei & proximi, vnde bona opera proficiscuntur, manent in nobis imperfecta in hac vita. Ex causa igitur imperfecta non possunt sequi perfecti effectus: Video aliam legem in membris meis, rebellantem legi mentis meæ. Hæc est causa, cur opera pia non possint consistere in judicio Dei: Ne ingrediaris in judicium cum seruo tuo, quia coram te non justificabitur vllus viuens. Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus. Cum igitur omnia sint imperfecta, agnoscamus & deploremus næuos, & imbecillitatem nostram, atque ad perfectionem tanto magis contendamus.
units.tr: The works of the saints are not perfectly good in this life: 1. Because even the saints do many things that are evil in themselves and sins, on account of which they are guilty before God and deserving to be cast into eternal punishments. Peter denies Christ three times; David commits adultery, kills Uriah, tries to cover the crime, numbers the people, etc. "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things." 2. Because they leave undone many good works which they ought to do according to the law. 3. Because even the good works they do are not so perfectly good and pure, as the strict exactness [ἀκριβεία] of the law requires, but are always joined with blemishes and polluted by sins. In their best works there is never that perfection of rectitude which ought to be there. The reason is understood from the place on conversion. For faith, regeneration, and the love of God and neighbour, from which good works proceed, remain in us imperfect in this life. From an imperfect cause therefore perfect effects cannot follow: "I see another law in my members, rebelling against the law of my mind." This is the reason why pious works cannot stand in the judgment of God: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no living man will be justified." "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things." Since therefore all things are imperfect, let us acknowledge and lament our blemishes and our weakness, and strive all the more for perfection.

units.la: Hinc etiam liquet, impium esse commentum monachorum de operibus supererogatoriis, quæ fingunt esse opera indebita Deo & legi, quando homines plus præstant, quam debeant: quod Deus manet debitor illorum. Blasphemum dogma: Cum omnia feceritis, dicite, serui inutiles sumus, quod debuimus, Luc.17,10. fecimus.
units.tr: Hence it also is clear that the monks' invention about "supererogatory" works is impious, which they feign to be works not owed to God and the law, when men do more than they ought, so that God remains their debtor. It is a blasphemous doctrine: "When you have done all, say: we are unprofitable servants, we have done what we ought to do," Luke 17:10.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Si quid supererogaueris, &c. Ergo sunt aliqua opera supererogationis. Respond. In parabola non debent ex omnibus circumstantiis extrui dogmata: quia simile non est idem. Samaritanus dicit: Si quid supererogaueris, non Deo, sed huic ægroto. Obiect. 2. Consilium do vobis. Ergo sunt quaedam consilia de operibus indebitis. Resp. Do consilium; nempe, de commoditate ad hanc vitam: non de meritis vitae aeternae.
units.tr: Objection 1: "If you spend anything beyond, etc." Therefore there are some works of supererogation. Answer: Doctrines ought not to be built from all the circumstances of a parable, because a likeness is not the same thing. The Samaritan says: "If you spend anything beyond this, I will repay you, not to God but to this sick man." Objection 2: "I give you counsel." Therefore there are certain counsels about works that are not owed. Answer: I give counsel, namely about what is advantageous for this life, not about the merits of eternal life.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Si vis perfectus esse, vende, quae habes. Ergo sunt aliqua consilia de perfectione. Resp. Est mandatum speciale, quo super-bus adolescens vocatur ad humilitatem & dilectionem proximi, & ad officium apostolatus in Judaea. Neque Christus requiritab eo supererogationem, sed perfectionem, & quidem ideo requirit, ut quantum ab ea absit, intelligat.
units.tr: Objection 3: "If you wish to be perfect, sell what you have." Therefore there are some counsels about perfection. Answer: It is a special command, by which the proud young man is called to humility and love of his neighbour, and to the office of the apostleship in Judea. Nor does Christ require of him supererogation, but perfection; and he requires it indeed so that he may understand how far he is from it.

units.la: IV. Quomodo opera nostra, cum sint imperfecte bona, placeant Deo.
units.tr: IV. How our works, although they are imperfectly good, are pleasing to God.

units.la: Si opera nostra non placerent Deo, frustra fierent. Sciendum igitur est, quomodo placeant. Cum in se sint imperfecta, & multis modis contaminata, in se non possunt Deo placere, propter summum αξιόρεως, quod in Deo est. Placent tamen ei in Christo mediatore, per fidem, hoc est, propter meritum, & satisfactionem Christi, fide nobis imputatam, & propter intercessionem eius apud Patrem pro nobis. Sic enim nos ipsi placemus Deo, non in nobis, sed in Filio: sic & opera nostra in se imperfecta Deo placent, propter justitiam Filij: quia quicquid in eis imperfectum est, aut impurum, tegitur, ne in conspectum Dei veniat. Oportet prius placere personam, postea opera placent, alioqui etiam optima opera non placent, cum persona est sine fide, sed sunt abominatio: quia nihil sunt, nisi hypocrisis. Et sicut persona placet, sic etiam placent opera. Placet autem persona propter mediatorem, hoc est, imputatione meriti & justitiae Christi, cum ea quasi veste est indutae coram Deo. Propter quod inde & opera personae sic placent Deo propter Mediatorem. Deus justitiam nostram & opera nostra imperfecta, qualia in se sunt, non examinat secundum rigorem legis, secundum quem illa potius damnaret: sed respicit ea in Filio suo. Hinc dicitur Deus respexisse ad Abelem, & sacrificium eius, nempe in Filio, in quem Abel credidit. Obtulit enim per fidem. Hinc etiam Christus dicitur Pontifex, per quem opera nostra offeruntur Deo. Dicitur & Altare, cui preces & opera nostra impositae placent Deo, quae aliàs foeterent in conspectu Dei. Defectus ergo & omnis imperfectio nostra nostrorum operum tegitur, & veluti sarcitur perfectione satisfactionis Christi in judicio Dei. Ideo dicit Paulus: Ut comperiar in eo, non habens meam justitiam, quae ex lege, sed eam, quae est ex fide Christi.
units.tr: If our works did not please God, they would be done in vain. It must therefore be understood how they please him. In themselves they are imperfect and stained in many ways, so they cannot please God in themselves, on account of the supreme majesty [αξιόρεως] that is in God. Yet they do please him in Christ the Mediator, through faith; that is, on account of the merit and satisfaction of Christ, imputed to us by faith, and on account of his intercession for us before the Father. For in the same way we ourselves please God, not in ourselves but in the Son. So also our works, imperfect in themselves, please God on account of the righteousness of the Son, because whatever is imperfect or impure in them is covered so that it does not come into the sight of God. The person must first please, and then the works please; otherwise even the best works do not please, when the person is without faith, but they are an abomination, because they are nothing but hypocrisy. As the person pleases, so the works also please. The person pleases on account of the Mediator, that is, by the imputation of the merit and righteousness of Christ, with which the person is clothed before God as with a garment. For this reason the works of the person also please God in this way, on account of the Mediator. God does not examine our righteousness and our imperfect works as they are in themselves, according to the strictness of the law, by which he would rather condemn them; but he regards them in his Son. Hence God is said to have looked upon Abel and his sacrifice, namely in the Son, in whom Abel believed, for he offered by faith. Hence also Christ is called the High Priest through whom our works are offered to God. He is also called the Altar, on which our prayers and works, when laid upon him, please God, which otherwise would stink in the sight of God. Therefore the defects and all the imperfection of our works are covered, and as it were made good, by the perfection of the satisfaction of Christ in the judgment of God. So Paul says: "That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ" (Phil. 3:9).

units.la: V. Cur facienda sint bona opera: & an sint necessaria?
units.tr: V. Why good works are to be done, and whether they are necessary?

units.la: Supra ad quæst. 68. aliquot causæ impulsivæ bonorum operum explicatæ, quæ huc pertinent: nempe, regeneratio necessaria rio cohærens cum iustificatione: gratitudo pro redemtione: celebratio Dei: confirmatio nostræ fidei, electionis: & bonum exemplum, quo alii Christo lucrifiant. Hæ causæ possunt latissimè deduci, revocatæ ad tres classes, si dicamus, bona opera esse facienda, Dei, nostri, & proximi causa.
units.tr: Above, at question 68, several impelling causes of good works were explained, which pertain to this point: namely, regeneration, which is necessarily joined with justification; gratitude for redemption; the glorifying of God; the confirmation of our faith and election; and a good example, by which others are gained for Christ. These causes can be set out at length, if they are brought back to three classes, saying that good works are to be done for the sake of God, of ourselves, and of our neighbour.

units.la: Dei causa sunt facienda 1. Vt illustretur gloria patris nostri cœlestis, seu propter gloriam Dei. Nam illustratio gloriæ Dei est præcipuus finis, in quem Deus mandat, & à nobis vult fieri bona opera, vt & nos iis Deum celebremus, & alii ea videntes eundem glorificent: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant bona vestra, & glorificent patrem vestrum in cœlis.
units.tr: For the sake of God, works are to be done: (1) That the glory of our heavenly Father may be made manifest, that is, on account of the glory of God. For the manifestation of the glory of God is the chief end for which God commands good works and wills that they be done by us, so that both we may thereby praise God and others, seeing them, may glorify him likewise: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

units.la: 2. Vt præstetur Deo obedientia debita, seu, propter mandatum Dei. Requiritenim Deus initium obedientiæ in hac vita, perfectionem in altera. Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, &c. Hoc est præceptum meum, vt diligatis alij alios. Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra. Liberati à peccatis servi facti estis Deo. Sistite membra arma iustitiæ.
