units.tr: (2) That the obedience owed to God may be rendered, that is, on account of the command of God. For God requires the beginning of obedience in this life and its perfection in the next: Let your light so shine before men, etc. This is my commandment, that you love one another. This is the will of God, your sanctification. Being freed from sin, you have become servants of God. Present your members as weapons of righteousness.

units.la: 3. Vt simus Deo grati, seu, propter gratitudinem, quam Deo debemus. Iustum est enim, vt qui nos redemit, & à quo summa beneficia accepimus, eum amemus, colamus, reueream ur, & notum aniorem & gratitudinem obedientia nostra & bonis operibus declaremus. Deus officia nostra meretur suis beneficiis; nos non meremur eius beneficia nostris officiis; ideo pro his gratitudinem ei debemus, quæ obedientia & bonis operibus declaratur. Precor vos fratres, per miserationes Dei, vt sistatis corpora vestra hostiam viuam, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem illum cultum vestrum. Offerentes spirituales hostias acceptas Deo per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: (3) That we may be pleasing to God, that is, on account of the gratitude which we owe to God. For it is right that we should love, honour, revere and worship him who redeemed us and from whom we have received the greatest benefits, and that we should declare our known love and gratitude by our obedience and good works. God deserves our services by his benefits; we do not deserve his benefits by our services; therefore we owe him gratitude for these, which is shown by obedience and good works: I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service; offering spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

units.la: Nostri causa, 1. Vt bonis operibus testemur fidem nostram, & de ea ex iis certi simus. Arbor enim bona non potest nisi bonos fructus ferre. Repleti fructibus iustitiæ, qui sunt in vobis, per Iesum Christum, ad gloriam & laudem Dei. Fides sine operibus est mortua. Ex operibus ergo agnoscimus, nos habere veram fidem: quia effectus non est sine sua causa, & causam ex proprio effectu cognoscere oportet. Si ergo bona opera & nouam obedientiam in nobis non sentimus, sumus hypocritæ, nec habemus veram fidem, sed malam conscientiam. Fides vera enim (quæ nunquam fructibus omnibus suis caret) sola velut arbor fructifera profert bona
units.tr: For our own sake, (1) That by good works we may bear witness to our faith, and be assured of it from them: For a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit. Being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are in you through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God. Faith without works is dead. From the works, therefore, we recognise that we have true faith, because an effect is not without its cause, and it is necessary to know the cause from its own effect. If, therefore, we do not perceive good works and new obedience in ourselves, we are hypocrites, and do not have true faith, but an evil conscience. For true faith (which never lacks all its fruits) alone, like a fruitful tree, brings forth good

units.la: opera, obedientiam, resipiscentiam, & hæc fidem veram discer-nunt ab historica, temporali, & ab ipsa hypocrisi.
units.tr: works, obedience and repentance, and these distinguish true faith from historical and temporary faith, and from hypocrisy itself.

units.la: 2. Vt ũmus certi de remissione peccatorum nobis per Christum impetrata, nos esse propter Christum justificatos. Justificatio & regeneratio sunt coniuncta beneficia, quæ sic inter se cohærent, vt nunquam possint separari. Christus enim vtrumque simul nobis impetrauit, nempe peccatorum remissionem & Spiritum sanctum: qui per fidem studium bonorum operum ac nouam obedientiam in nobis excitet.
units.tr: (2) That we may be certain of the forgiveness of sins obtained for us through Christ, and that we have been justified through Christ. Justification and regeneration are joined benefits, which so cohere with one another that they can never be separated. For Christ obtained both for us at once: namely, the forgiveness of sins and the Holy Spirit, who by faith stirs up in us zeal for good works and new obedience.

units.la: 3. Vt certissimus de nostra electione & salute: Studete vocationem vestram, & electionem firmam efficere. Hæc causa proueniit ex præcedente. Solos enim justificatos propter meritum Filij sui Deus ex mera sua misericordia ab æterno elegit: Quos prædestinauit, hos & vocauit, & justificauit. De electione igitur sumus certi ex justificatione. Justificationem verò (quæ nunquam datur electis sine sanctificatione) nos esse consecutos in Christo, cognoscimus ex fide: fidem ex fructibus fidei, hoc est, bonis operibus, noua obedientia, & vera resipiscentia.
units.tr: (3) That we may be most certain of our election and salvation: Be diligent to make your calling and election sure. This cause arises from the preceding one. For God, from his mere mercy, from eternity elected only those justified on account of the merit of his Son: Whom he predestined, these he also called, and justified. Therefore we are certain of our election from our justification. But that justification, which is never given to the elect without sanctification, we know we have obtained in Christ from faith; and we know faith from the fruits of faith, that is, from good works, new obedience and true repentance.

units.la: 4. Vt bonis operibus fides nostra exerceatur, alatur, corroboretur, & prouehatur. Nam qui indulgent prauis cupiditatibus contra conscientiam, in iis non potest esse fides, eoque nec bona conscientia, nec fiducia in Deo placato & benevolo. Sensum enim fauoris erga nos diuini, & pacatam conscientiam tantum ex fide obtinemus: Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Suscipiendum: Rom. 8, 13. 2 Tim. 1, 6. ta donum, quod in te est, &c.
units.tr: (4) That our faith may be exercised, nourished, strengthened and advanced by good works. For those who indulge wicked desires against their conscience cannot have faith in them, and therefore neither a good conscience nor trust in a God who is reconciled and well-disposed. For we obtain the sense of divine favour towards us, and a peaceful conscience, only from faith: If you live according to the flesh, you will die. Rom. 8:13. 2 Tim. 1:6. Stir up the gift of God that is in you, etc.

units.la: 5. Vt bonis operibus ornemus & cohonestemus vitam, profesionem, & vocationem nostram: Precor, vt ambuletis ita, vt dignum est vocatione: qua vocati estis.
units.tr: (5) That we may adorn and grace our life, profession and calling with good works: I beseech you that you walk worthy of the calling with which you have been called.

units.la: 6. Vt vitemus poenas temporales & æternas: Quoniam enim arbor non fert fructus bonos, exciditur, & in ignem conjicitur. Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Propter iniquitates corripit filios hominum.
units.tr: (6) That we may avoid temporal and eternal punishments: For since the tree does not bring forth good fruit, it is cut down and cast into the fire. If you live according to the flesh, you will die. For the iniquities of the sons of men he chastises.

units.la: 7. Vt à Deo consequamur præmia spiritualia & corporalia, quæ ex promissione comitantur bona opera in hac & futura vita: Pietas ad omnia est vtilis, habens promissionem huius & futuræ vitæ. Nisi enim Deus vellet spem præmiorum, & metum pœnarum esse causas impulsiuas bonorum operum, non vteretur iis argumentis in promissionibus & comminationibus suis.
units.tr: (7) That from God we may obtain spiritual and bodily rewards, which in this life and the future are attached to good works by promise: Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. For if God did not wish the hope of rewards and the fear of punishments to be impelling causes of good works, he would not use such arguments in his promises and threats.

units.la: Denique proximi causa debent fieri bona opera. 1. Vt simus vtiles proximo, & cum piis officiis atque exemplis ædificemus: Hæc omnia propter vos, vt gratia illa copiosissima pluribus gratias agentibus, redundet in gloriam Dei, &c. Permanere in carne magis necessarium est propter vos. 2.
units.tr: Finally, good works ought to be done for our neighbour's sake. (1) That we may be useful to our neighbour, and build him up with pious offices and examples: All these things are for your sakes, so that the abundant grace may, through the many who give thanks, redound to the glory of God, etc. To remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake. (2)

units.la: 2. Vt per nos vitentur scandala. Væ enim homini, per quem veniunt scandala. Nomen Dei blasphematur propter vos inter gentes.
units.tr: 2. That through us scandals may be avoided. For woe to the man through whom scandals come. Because of you the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles.

units.la: 3. Vt lucrifacìamus infideles: Et tu conuersus aliquando, confirma fratres tuos.
units.tr: 3. That we may win unbelievers: And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.

units.la: Quæstio hic mota est, Vtrum bona opera sint necessaria ad salutem? Aliqui simpliciter defenderunt, alii contra contenderunt, bona opera esse perniciosa ad salutem. Vtraque locutio est ambigua & scandalosa, maximè posterior: quia videtur non modo bonorum operum studium, sed etiam fiduciam, damnare. Posterior ergo est reiicienda: prior sic declaranda: quod sint necessaria ad salutem, non tanquam causa ad effectum, vel tanquam meritum ad mercedem: sed tanquam pars ipsius salutis, vel tanquam antecedens ad consequens, vel tanquam medium, sine quo ad finem non peruenitur. Dici quidem potest eadem ratione necessaria ad iustitiam, vel ad iustificationem, vel in iustificatione, tanquam consequens iustificationis, cum qua regeneratio inseparabiliter est coniuncta: sed ego his loquendi formis non vterer. 1. quia sunt ambiguæ. 2. quia pariunt contentiones, & præbent aduersariis ansam calumniandi. 3. quia iis non vtitur Scriptura, cum qua nobis est loquendum. Tutius dicitur, bona opera esse necessaria in iustificatis, & in saluandis. In iustificandis esse necessaria, ambiguè dicitur: quia intelligi potest, quasi requirantur ante iustificationem, & sint causa iustificationis. Recte vero Augustinus: Bona opera non præcedunt iustificatos, sed sequuntur iustificatos. Hinc patet responsio ad obiectionem: Quod non habentes, non possunt saluari, id est necessarium ad salutem. Non habentes bona opera non possunt saluari, vt dicitur quæst.87. Ergo bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem. Respond. ad maiorem per distinctionem. Est necessarium antecedens salutem, nempe, vel vt pars salutis, vel vt quiddam necessario antecedens, vt causa, vel vt meritum salutis. Secundum hanc declarationem maioris, conclusio intellecta conceditur. Sunt enim bona opera necessaria ad salutem, vel potius in saluandis (sic enim præstat loqui vitandæ ambiguitatis causa) tanquam pars ipsius salutis: aut tanquam antecedens salutis: non autem tanquam causa, vel meritum eius.
units.tr: The question has been raised here, Whether good works are necessary to salvation? Some have defended it without qualification, and others have argued against it, that good works are harmful to salvation. Both expressions are ambiguous and open to offence, the latter especially, because it seems to condemn not only the pursuit of good works but also confidence in them. The latter must therefore be rejected, and the former explained thus: that they are necessary to salvation, not as a cause is to its effect, or as merit is to its reward, but as a part of salvation itself, or as an antecedent to a consequent, or as a means without which the end is not reached. It may indeed be said, on the same reasoning, that they are necessary to righteousness, or to justification, or in justification, as a consequence of justification, with which regeneration is inseparably joined; but I would not use these forms of speech. First, because they are ambiguous. Second, because they produce disputes and give our opponents an occasion for slander. Third, because Scripture does not use them, and we must speak in Scripture's language. It is safer to say that good works are necessary in the justified and in those who are to be saved. To say that they are necessary in those who are to be justified is ambiguous, because it may be understood as if they were required before justification and were its cause. Augustine rightly says: Good works do not precede the justified, but follow the justified. From this the answer to the objection is plain: that those who do not have them cannot be saved, which means that they are necessary to salvation. Those who do not have good works cannot be saved, as is said in question 87. Therefore good works are necessary to salvation. I answer the major premise by a distinction. That which is necessary may precede salvation either as a part of salvation, or as something necessarily antecedent, like a cause, or like the merit of salvation. According to this explanation of the major premise, the conclusion, understood in this sense, is granted. For good works are necessary to salvation, or rather in those who are to be saved (for it is better to speak so, to avoid ambiguity), as a part of salvation itself, or as an antecedent of salvation, but not as its cause or merit.

units.la: VI. An bona opera sint meritoria coram Deo.
units.tr: VI. Whether good works are meritorious before God.

units.la: Ex quinta quæstione oritur sexta, sicut quarta ex tertia. Cum enim audiunt homines, nos consequi præmia à Deo bonis operibus, statim concludunt, nos iis aliquid meriri. Sciendū est igitur, bona opera esse quidem necessaria, & facienda etiam pro-pter præmia consequentia, sed tamen non esse meritoria, hoc est, nihil mereri à Deo: ne minimam quidem particulam bono-rum spiritualium vel corporalium. Rationes verissimæ & evi-dentissimæ sunt.
units.tr: The sixth question arises from the fifth, as the fourth arises from the third. For when men hear that we obtain rewards from God by good works, they at once conclude that we merit something by them. It must be known, therefore, that good works are indeed necessary, and are to be done also for the rewards that follow, but they are nevertheless not meritorious, that is, they merit nothing from God, not even the smallest part of spiritual or bodily good things. There are very true and very evident reasons for this.

units.la: 1. Opera nostra sunt imperfecta, tam partibus, quàm gradi-bus. Partibus, quoniam multa bona omittimus, quæ lex præcipit; multa mala facimus, quæ prohibet, & semper bonis mala ad-miscemus, scriptura & experientia teste: Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, spiritus adversus carnem: hæc autem inter se opposita sunt, ut non quæcunque volueritis, ea faciatis. Imperfecta autem opera non modo nihil merentur, sed etiam damnantur in judicio Dei: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, &c. Gradibus etiam imperfecta sunt: quia præstantissima sanctorum opera sunt immunda & vitiosa in Dei conspectu, eò quod non fiunt à per-sectè renatis, neque ex tanto Dei & proximi amore, quantus in lege requiritur: Facti sumus, ut immundi omnes nos, & quasi pannus menstruatæ universa justitia. Hoc Propheta dicit etiam de suis bonis operibus. Paulus idem de suis pronunciat: Duco omnia damnum esse propter eminentiam Christi Iesu Domini nostri, propter quem omnibus istis meipsum multavi, eaque duco esse σκύβαλα, hoc est, stercora, ut Christum lucrifaciam. Sic judicant sancti de sua justitia & suis meritis.
units.tr: 1. Our works are imperfect, both in their parts and in their degrees. In their parts, because we leave out many good things that the law commands, and do many evil things that it forbids, and always mix evil with good, as Scripture and experience bear witness: The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. Imperfect works not only merit nothing, but are also condemned in the judgment of God: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things, etc. They are imperfect also in their degrees, because the most excellent works of the saints are unclean and faulty in the sight of God, since they are not done by those who are perfectly reborn, nor from that great love of God and neighbour which the law requires: We have all become like unclean things, and all our righteousness is like a polluted cloth. The prophet says this also of his own good works. Paul pronounces the same of his: I count all things loss for the excellence of Christ Jesus our Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all these things, and I count them as dung [σκύβαλα], that is, dung, so that I may win Christ. So the saints judge of their own righteousness and their own merits.

units.la: 2. Nulla creatura faciens præstantissima opera, potest quic-quam mereri de Deo, aut Deum sibi obligare ad aliquid dandum ex debito, & secundum ordinem justitiæ Dei. Huius rationem reddit Apostolus: Quis prius dedit ei, & retribuet ei? An non licet mihi facere de meo, quod volo? Non magis meremur conservationem, quàm creationem: sed utrumque fecit & facit liberrima voluntate & gratuito beneficio. A nobis nihil accipit beneficij, nihil nos creatori nostro conferre possumus. Ubi verò non est beneficium, ibi nec meritum. Meritum enim præsupponit beneficium acceptum.
units.tr: 2. No creature, however excellent its works, can merit anything from God, or bind God to give anything as a debt, and according to the order of God's justice. The Apostle gives the reason for this: Who first gave to him, and will be repaid by him? Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is mine? We no more merit preservation than creation, but God did and does both by his most free will and by his gratuitous kindness. We receive nothing of benefit from ourselves, and we can confer nothing on our Creator. Where there is no benefit, there is no merit either, for merit presupposes a benefit received.

units.la: 3. Opera nostra sunt debita. Omnes enim creaturæ debent creatori cultum & gratitudinem, adeò ut si nunquam peccare-mus, tamen non possemus Deo satis præstare cultum & gratitu-dinem debitam: Cùm omnia feceritis, dicite: servi inutiles sumus: fecimus, quod debuimus.
units.tr: 3. Our works are owed. For all creatures owe their Creator worship and gratitude, so that even if we had never sinned, we still could not render to God the worship and gratitude that is due: When you have done all things, say: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.

units.la: 4. Si quæ bona opera facimus, ea non sunt nostra, sed Dei, per quem operantis: Deus enim est, qui efficit velle & perficere, pro gratuita sua voluntate. Quid habes, quod non acceperis? Sumus natura filij iræ, mortui in peccatis: arbores malæ, quæ bonos fructus non faciunt. Deus verò gratis nos fecit arbores bonas, & fructus bonos in nobis operatur, sicut dicitur: Ipsius factura sumus, creati in Christo Iesu ad bona opera, quæ præparavit, ut in illis ambulemus. Si quid ergo boni præstamus, id est Dei donum, non nostrum meritum. Impudens fuerit, qui cum centum florenos dono acceperit à diuite, putet se mereri mille alios, centum illos accipiendo, cum ipse potius hoc accepto dono obligetur diuiti, non diues ipsi.
units.tr: 4. If we do any good works, they are not ours but God's, by whom they are wrought: For it is God who works in us both to will and to do, according to his gracious good pleasure. What do you have that you have not received? We are by nature children of wrath, dead in sins; bad trees, which do not bear good fruit. But God has freely made us good trees, and works good fruit in us, as it is said: We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which he prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. If therefore we perform anything good, it is the gift of God, not our merit. A man would be shameless who, having received a hundred florins as a gift from a rich man, thought he deserved a thousand others because he had received those hundred; for by receiving that gift he is rather bound to the rich man, not the rich man to him.

units.la: 5. Nulla est proportio inter opera nostra, tam imperfecta, & inter summa beneficia, quæ nobis Pater in Filio suo gratis donat.
units.tr: 5. There is no proportion between our works, so imperfect, and the very great benefits which the Father freely gives us in his Son.

units.la: 6. Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. At si meremur operibus nostris remissionem peccatorum, habemus, de quo glorie-mur in nobis, nec Deo gloriam tribuamus, sicut dicitur: Si Abraham justificatus est operibus, habet, de quo glorietur, at non apud Deum.
units.tr: 6. He who glories, let him glory in the Lord. But if we merit the forgiveness of sins by our works, we have something in ourselves to glory in, and we do not give the glory to God, as it is said: If Abraham was justified by works, he has something to glory in, but not before God.

units.la: 7. Justi sumus, antequam faciamus bona opera. Nondum nati pueris, cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, ut propositum Dei, quod est secundum ipsius electionem, id est, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante, firmum maneret, dictum est ei: Maior serviet minori, &c. Non igitur bona opera facientes demum justificamur coram Deo, sed ea facimus jam justificati.
units.tr: 7. We are righteous before we do good works. When the children were not yet born, and had done neither good nor evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not by works but by him who calls, it was said to her: The elder shall serve the younger, etc. Therefore we are not justified before God only when we do good works, but we do those works already justified.

units.la: 8. Opinio meriti & justificationis per opera labefactat consolationem Christianam, turbat conscientias, & cogit homines de salute dubitare & desperare. Audientes enim vocem legis: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus: & suam imperfectionem considerantes, convincuntur in conscientiis, quod nunquam omnia præstiterint: ideo coguntur perpetuò incerti fluctuare, & maledictionem horrescere. Sed fides conscientiis dat firmam consolationem: quia nititur promissione, quæ est certa. Ex fide est hæreditas, ut sit per gratiam, & ut sit firma promisso toti semini.
units.tr: 8. The opinion of merit and of justification by works undermines Christian comfort, troubles consciences, and compels men to doubt and despair of salvation. For those who hear the voice of the law, Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things, and who consider their own imperfection, are convicted in conscience that they have never performed everything; therefore they are constantly forced to waver in uncertainty and to shrink from the curse. But faith gives firm comfort to consciences, because it rests on a promise, which is sure. The inheritance is of faith, so that it may be by grace, and so that the promise may be firm to all the seed.

units.la: 9. Si ex operibus esset justitia, irrita fieret promissio, & Christus frustra esset mortuus.
units.tr: 9. If righteousness were of works, the promise would be void, and Christ would have died in vain.

units.la: 10. Si admitteretur opinio de meritis operum, non esset eadem ratio salutis: aliter Abraham, aliter Iacob in cruce justificatus fuisset: nos item aliter justificaremur. Atqui unica est via ad salutem: Ego sum via, veritas & vita. Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Unus est Mediator DEI & hominum. Unus est Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma. Iesus Christus heri & hodie, & in secula. Non est aliud nomen sub cœlo, in quo oportet nos salvos fieri.
units.tr: 10. If the opinion about the merits of works were admitted, there would not be one and the same way of salvation: Abraham would have been justified in one way, Jacob in another, and we would be justified in yet another. But there is only one way to salvation: I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. There is one Mediator between God and men. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever. There is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved.

units.la: 11. Christus non largiretur nobis omnem salutem, coque non esset perfectus seruator; si à nobis aliquid ad justitiam nostram stam merito eius addendum esset. Tantum enim de merito eius detraheretur, quantum de nostro accederet. Atqui est perfectus seruator noster, teste Apostolo: Non est in vllo alio salus, In quo habemus redemptionem in sanguine eius, hoc est, remissionem peccatorum. Gratia estis seruati per fidem, idque non ex vobis: Dei donum est, ne quis glorietur. Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato.
units.tr: 11. If Christ did not bestow all salvation on us, he would not be a perfect Saviour, and it would follow that something must be added to his merit from our own righteousness. For as much as would be taken from his merit would be added from ours. But he is our perfect Saviour, as the Apostle witnesses: There is no salvation in any other. In whom we have redemption through his blood, that is, the forgiveness of sins. By grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, lest anyone should boast. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin.

units.la: Obiect. Merces praesupponit meritum. Deus vocat praemia & mercedem illa bona, quae promittit & dat facientibus bona opera. Ergo bona opera praesupponunt meritum, & sunt meritoria coram Deo. Resp. Maior aliquando valet inter creaturas, sed nunquam apud Deum; quia de Deo nulla creatura mereri potest, eo quod Deus nulli quicquam debet. Vocat tamen praemia & mercedem bona, quae largitur pro bonis operibus, sed gratuitam: quia ea gratis compensat, non ex debito. Nihil ei ex nobis accedit commodi, neque operibus nostris ipse incommodiget. Immo nobis potius ex bonis nostris operibus commodum accedit, quia sunt conformatio nostri cum Deo, & beneficium Dei, quo ipsi nos obligamur Deo ad gratitudinem, non Deus nobis. Non minus igitur absurdum est dicere, nos bonis operibus de Deo mereri salutem, quam si quis diceret: Tu dedisti mihi centum florenos: Ergo & debes mihi dare mille florenos. Mandat tamen ea nobis Deus, & facientibus promittit compensationem gratuitam, sicut pater promittit praemia filiis, &c.
units.tr: Objection: A reward presupposes merit. God calls the good things that he promises and gives to those who do good works both rewards and wages. Therefore good works presuppose merit and are meritorious before God. Answer: A greater reward sometimes holds good among creatures, but never before God, because no creature can merit anything from God, since God owes nothing to anyone. Yet God calls the good things that he bestows for good works rewards and wages, but they are free gifts, because he repays them freely and not as a debt. No advantage comes to him from us, and he does not stand in need of our works. Rather, some advantage comes to us from our good works, because they are the conforming of ourselves to God and a benefit of God, by which we are bound to God in gratitude, not God to us. It is therefore no less absurd to say that we merit salvation from God by good works than if someone were to say: You gave me a hundred florins; therefore you owe me a thousand florins in return. Nevertheless, God commands these things to us, and promises a free recompense to those who do them, just as a father promises rewards to his children, and so on.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XCII.
units.tr: QUESTION XCII.

units.la: Quæ est lex Dei?
units.tr: What is the law of God?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Loquutus est Deus omnia verba haec 4. Exod. 20, 1. & Deut. 5, 6.
units.tr: God spoke all these words, four in number. Exod. 20:1; Deut. 5:6.

units.la: Primum præceptum.
units.tr: The first commandment.

units.la: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te ex Ægypto, domo seruitutis. Non habebis Deos alienos in conspectu meo.
units.tr: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me.

units.la: Secundum.
units.tr: The second.

units.la: Ne sculpas tibi simulacrum, nec vllam imaginem effingas eorum, quae aut supra sunt in coelo, aut infra in terra, aut in aquis sub terra; neque incurues te illis, neque colas ea. Ego enim sum Dominus Deus tuus, fortis, zelotes, vindicans peccata patrum in filiis, idq; in tertia & quarta progenie eorum, qui oderunt me: & misericordia vtens in millesimam eorum, qui diligunt me, & obseruant præcepta mea.
units.tr: You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of those things that are in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth; you shall not bow down to them, nor serve them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

units.la: Tertium.
units.tr: The third.

units.la: Ne vsurpes nomen Domini Dei tui temerè. Neque enim Dominus dimittet eum impunitum, qui nomen eius vanè vsurpauerit.
units.tr: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. For the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.

units.la: Quartum.
units.tr: The fourth.

units.la: Memento, vt diem sabbati sanctifices. Sex diebus operaberis, & facies omne opus tuum. At septima die sabbatum erit Domino Deo tuo. Non facies vllum opus, nec tu, nec filius tuus, nec filia tua, nec seruus tuus, nec ancilla tua, nec jumentum tuum, nec aduena, qui est intra portas tuas. Nam sex diebus fecit Deus coelum, terram, mare, & quæcunque in iis sunt, & requiescit die septimo: ideoque benedixit diei sabbati, & sanctificauit eum.
units.tr: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labour, and do all your work. But the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God. In it you shall not do any work, neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your cattle, nor the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days God made heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day; therefore he blessed the sabbath day and sanctified it.

units.la: Quintum.
units.tr: The fifth.

units.la: Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam, vt diu viuas in terra, quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi.
units.tr: Honour your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the Lord your God gives you.

units.la: Sextum.
units.tr: The sixth.

units.la: Non occides.
units.tr: You shall not kill.

units.la: Septimum.
units.tr: The seventh.

units.la: Non committes adulterium.
units.tr: You shall not commit adultery.

units.la: Octauum.
units.tr: The eighth.

units.la: Non furaberis.
units.tr: You shall not steal.

units.la: Nonum.
units.tr: The ninth.

units.la: Non dices contra proximum tuum falsum testimonium.
units.tr: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.

units.la: Decimum.
units.tr: The tenth.

units.la: Non concupisces domum proximi tui, nec concupisces uxorem proximi tui, nec seruum eius, nec ancillam, nec bouem, nec asinum, nec quicquam eorum, quæ sunt proximi tui.
units.tr: You shall not covet your neighbour's house, nor covet your neighbour's wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that belongs to your neighbour.

units.la: Pars III. EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: Part III. EXPOSITION.

units.la: Sequitur doctrina de Lege Dei, quæ est norma bonorum operum. De ea præcipuè quæstiones sunt: I. Quid sit lex in genere. II. Quæ sint legis divinæ partes, sive species. III. Quatenus lex sit abrogata per Christum, & quatenus non. IV. Quid lex moralis ab evangelio differat. V. Quomodo decalogus dividatur. VI. Quæ sit vera sententia decalogi & singulorum præceptorum. VII. Quatenus lex possit servari à renatis. VIII. Quis sit usus legis.
units.tr: Next comes the doctrine of God's Law, which is the rule of good works. The main questions about it are: I. What law is in general. II. What the parts, or kinds, of divine law are. III. How far the law has been abrogated through Christ, and how far it has not. IV. How the moral law differs from the gospel. V. How the Decalogue is divided. VI. What the true meaning of the Decalogue and of its individual precepts is. VII. How far the law can be kept by the regenerate. VIII. What the use of the law is.

units.la: Ex his quatuor prioribus huc pertinent: quinta ad quæstionem catechet. XCIII. sexta ad XCIV. & seqq. septima ad CXIV. octava ad CXV.
units.tr: Of these, the first four belong here. The fifth belongs to Catechism question 93, the sixth to question 94 and following, the seventh to question 114, and the eighth to question 115.

units.la: I. Quid sit Lex in genere.
units.tr: I. What law is in general.

units.la: Lex dicitur à legendo, id est, publicando: vel à legendo, id est, deligendo. Cum priore etymo convenit vox Hebræa <bl>תורה</bl> Thorah, id est, doctrina, quia leges ideo publicantur, ut omnes eas legant & discant. Hinc est, quod ignorantia legis aut juris non excusat: immò qui ignorant leges ad se pertinentes, eo ipso peccant. Cum altero convenit vox Græca νόμος, lex, à νέμω, distribuo: quia lex singulis officia distribuit.
units.tr: Lex is said to come from legendo, that is, publishing, or from legendo, that is, choosing. The Hebrew word Thorah [תורה], that is, teaching, agrees with the first derivation, because laws are published so that everyone may read and learn them. Hence ignorance of the law or of right does not excuse; indeed, those who do not know the laws that concern them sin by that very fact. The Greek word νόμος, law, agrees with the second, from νέμω, I distribute, because law distributes duties to individuals.

units.la: Est autem lex in genere, sententia præcipiens honesta, obligans naturam rationalem ad obedientiam, cum promissione præmij, & comminatione pœnæ, si violetur. Est sententia præcipiens honesta (alioqui non est lex) obligans creaturam rationalem (lex enim non est illis lata, qui non obligantur ad obedientiam) cum promissione præmij. Lex gratis promittit bona præstantibus obedientiam: quia nulla obedientia potest esse meritoria apud Deum.
units.tr: Law in general is a statement prescribing what is honourable, binding a rational nature to obedience, with a promise of reward and a threat of punishment if it is violated. It is a statement prescribing what is honourable (otherwise it is not law), binding a rational creature (for a law is not given to those who are not bound to obedience), with a promise of reward. The law promises good things freely to those who render obedience, because no obedience can be meritorious before God.

units.la: Obiect. Etiam Evangelium promittit bona gratis: ergo lex ab evangelio non differt. Resp. Aliter lex, aliter evangelium promittit gratis. Lex promittit vitam gratis, hoc est, non ex debito, vel merito: sed tamen cum pacto perfectæ obedientiæ nostræ. Evangelium promittit gratis, hoc est, nullo merito vel debito, nec cum conditione perfectæ obedientiæ nostræ: sed cum sola fide in Christum.
units.tr: Objection: the gospel also promises good things freely; therefore the law does not differ from the gospel. Answer: the law and the gospel promise freely in different ways. The law promises life freely, that is, not from debt or merit, but nevertheless on the condition of our perfect obedience. The gospel promises freely, that is, without any merit or debt, and not on the condition of our perfect obedience, but on faith alone in Christ.

units.la: II. Quæ sint partes sive species legis: & quæ sint horum discrimina.
units.tr: II. What the parts, or kinds, of law are, and what the differences between them are.

units.la: Leges aliæ sunt divinæ, aliæ humanæ. Humanæ, quæ ab hominibus sanciuntur, & certos homines obligant ad certas actiones exterexternas, de quibus neq; præceptio, neq; prohibitio diuina est expressa, cum promissione præmiorum, & comminatione pœnarum corporalium. Hæ sunt aut politicæ, aut ecclesiasticæ. Politicæ, quales sunt leges positiuæ, quæ à magistratibus, vel à tota communitate feruntur, de certo ordine actionum seruando in politia, in contractibus, judicijs, pœnis, &c. Ecclesiasticæ siue cæremoniales sunt, quæ ecclesiæ consensu feruntur de ordine actionum in ministerio ecclesiæ: & sunt determinationes circumstantiarum seruientes legi diuinæ.
units.tr: Some laws are divine, others human. Human laws are those enacted by men, which bind certain people to certain external actions about which no divine command or prohibition has been expressly given, with a promise of rewards and a threat of bodily punishments. These are either political or ecclesiastical. Political laws are positive laws, enacted by magistrates or by the whole community, concerning the due order of actions to be observed in the state, in contracts, in judgments, in punishments, and so on. Ecclesiastical, or ceremonial, laws are those enacted by the consent of the Church concerning the order of actions in the ministry of the Church; they are determinations of circumstances serving the divine law.

units.la: Diuinæ leges, quæ à Deo sancitæ sunt, partim ad angelos, partim ad omnes homines, partim ad aliquos homines pertinent, & hos non ad externas tantum actiones obligant, sed etiam internas qualitates, actiones & motus requirunt, nec tantum corporalia & temporalia, sed etiam spiritualia & æterna præmia & pœnas proponunt, & sunt fines legum humanarum. Diuinæ leges aliæ sunt æternæ & immutabiles, aliæ mutabiles quidem, sed non nisi à Deo ipso, à quo sunt latæ, mutari possunt.
units.tr: Divine laws, which have been sanctioned by God, pertain partly to angels, partly to all men, and partly to certain men. They bind not only to external actions but also require internal qualities, actions and motions, and they propose not only bodily and temporal rewards and punishments but also spiritual and eternal ones; these are the ends of human laws. Divine laws are some eternal and unchangeable, others indeed changeable, but able to be changed only by God himself, by whom they were given.

units.la: Communiter dicuntur legis diuinæ esse tres species seu partes: moralis, cæremonialis & forensis.
units.tr: It is commonly said that there are three kinds, or parts, of divine law: moral, ceremonial and forensic.

units.la: Lex moralis est doctrina congruens cum æterna & immota sapientia, & regula justitiæ in Deo, discernens recta & non recta, natura nota, & insita creaturis rationalibus in creatione, & postea sæpe repetita & declarata voce diuina, docens quid sit Deus, & qualis sit: obligans omnes creaturas rationales ad perfectam obedientiam, & conformitatem cum illa regula interiram & externam, & promittens fauorem Dei, & vitam æternam omnibus perfectam obedientiam præstantibus, & denuncians pœnas æternas omnibus, qui non perfectè illi conformes sunt: nisi fiat remissio peccatorum, & reconciliatio propter Filium Dei mediatorem.
units.tr: The moral law is a doctrine agreeing with the eternal and unchanging wisdom and the rule of justice in God, distinguishing right from wrong; it is known by nature, implanted in rational creatures at their creation, and afterwards often repeated and declared by the divine voice. It teaches what God is and what kind of being he is; it binds all rational creatures to perfect obedience and to conformity with that rule, inwardly and outwardly; it promises God's favour and eternal life to all who render perfect obedience, and it announces eternal punishments to all who are not perfectly conformed to it, unless there is forgiveness of sins and reconciliation through the Son of God, the Mediator.

units.la: Congruens cum æterna & immota sapientia.] Est lex æterna, ab initio vsque ad finem mundi manens eadem. Et ideo creati eramus, ideo etiam redemti sumus per Christum, & regenerati per Spiritum sanctum, vt hanc legem in hac & æterna vita seruemus, hoc est, vt Deum & proximum ex toto corde amemus. Nouam doctrinam non scribo vobis, sed doctrinam veterem, quam videlicet habuistis jam inde à principio.
units.tr: Agreeing with the eternal and unchanging wisdom. This law is eternal, remaining the same from the beginning to the end of the world. For this reason we were created, for this reason also we have been redeemed through Christ and regenerated through the Holy Spirit, so that we may keep this law in this life and in eternal life, that is, so that we may love God and our neighbour with all our heart. I am not writing a new doctrine to you, but the old doctrine, which you have had from the beginning.

units.la: Postea sæpe repetita.] Deus repetiuit legem naturæ mentibus nostris impressam. 1. Quia per lapsum erat obscurata. 2. Multa etiam erant obliterata, & amissa. 3. Ne reliquiæ in mentibus hominum putarentur esse tantum opinio, & tandem penitus extinguerentur.
units.tr: Often repeated afterwards. God has repeated the law of nature, impressed on our minds, for three reasons: (1) because it had been obscured by the Fall; (2) because many things had also been blotted out and lost; (3) lest the remnants in men's minds should be thought to be mere opinion, and at last be utterly extinguished.

units.la: Cæremoniales leges sunt leges à Deo latæ per Mosen de cæremoniis, hoc est, de actionibus, siue gestibus externis solennibus: seu cum earundem circumstantiarum obseruatione peragendis in cultu Dei publico: obligantes populum Judaicum, vsque ad aduentum Messiæ, vt discernerent eum populum ab aliis gentibus, & essent signa, symbola, typi, seu vmbræ resũ spiritualium in nouo testamento per Christũ implendarum. Cæremonis vocantur actiones externæ, solennes, sæpe eodem modo & iisdem circumstantiis repetendæ, institutæ à Deo, vel ab hominibus, vt adhibeantur in externo Dei cultu, ordinis & decori ve significationis causa. Latæ à Deo cæremoniæ, sunt cultus Dei: ab hominibus institutæ non sunt cultus Dei: sed, si bonæ sint, cultui diuino seruiunt.
units.tr: Ceremonial laws are the laws given by God through Moses concerning ceremonies, that is, concerning solemn external actions or gestures, or concerning their performance with the observance of their circumstances in the public worship of God. They obliged the Jewish people until the coming of the Messiah, so that they might distinguish that people from other nations, and be signs, symbols, types, or shadows of spiritual realities to be fulfilled in the New Testament through Christ. Ceremonies are called external, solemn actions, often to be repeated in the same way and with the same circumstances, instituted either by God or by men, to be used in the external worship of God for the sake of order, decency or signification. Ceremonies given by God are the worship of God; those instituted by men are not the worship of God, but if they are good they serve divine worship.

units.la: Forenses seu iudiciales leges erant leges de ordine politico, seu de gubernatione ciuili, & externæ disciplinæ defensione, secundum vtramque tabulam decalogi, hoc est, de ordine & officiis magistratuum, iudiciorum, contractuum, pœnarum, distinctione dominiorum, &c. latæ à Deo per Mosen populo Judaico, ad constitutionem, & conseruationem politiæ Judaicæ, obligantes omnes posteros Abrahami, discernentes eos à reliquo genere humano vsq; ad aduentum Messiæ: idque vt essent neruus conseruationis & gubernationis politiæ Mosaicæ, vsq; ad exhibitum Messiam, & certæ notæ, quibus populus iste discerneretur ab omnibus aliis, & simul contineretur honesta disciplina, atque ordine decoro: & vt essent typi ordinis in regno Christi futuri, hoc est, spiritualis gubernationis Messiæ.
units.tr: Forensic, or judicial, laws were laws concerning the political order, or civil government, and the defence of external discipline, according to both tables of the Decalogue; that is, concerning the order and duties of magistrates, judgments, contracts, punishments, the distinction of property, and so on. They were given by God through Moses to the Jewish people for the constitution and preservation of the Jewish commonwealth, binding all the posterity of Abraham and distinguishing them from the rest of the human race until the coming of the Messiah. This was so that they might be the sinew of the preservation and government of the Mosaic state until the Messiah was revealed, and a certain mark by which that people would be distinguished from all others, and at the same time so that honest discipline and decent order would be maintained; and so that they would be types of the order of the future kingdom of Christ, that is, of the spiritual government of the Messiah.

units.la: Moralis lex est fons omnium aliarum legum bonarum, quæ quidem dignæ sunt legum nomine, & plane congruit cum decalogo, atque etiam necessaria consequentia ex eo deducitur, ad eo, vt qui illum violat, etiam hanc violet. Cæremoniales verò & forenses leges, siue diuinæ sint, siue humanæ, modo sint bonæ, congruunt quidem cum decalogo, sed necessaria consequentia ex eo non deducuntur, sicut moralis: subseruiunt verò ei tanquam determinationes quædam circumstantiarum. Hinc optimè perspicitur discrimen harum legum. Aliud enim est necessariò sequi ex decalogo, aliud cum eo congruere, & eius obseruationi seruire. Est tamen discrimen hoc varium, quia non est eadem gubernatio ecclesiæ & politiæ: necest idem harum legum omnium finis: nec denique eodem modo omnes hæ leges abrogantur.
units.tr: The moral law is the source of all other good laws, which truly deserve the name of laws; it agrees plainly with the Decalogue, and is even deduced from it by necessary consequence, so that whoever violates it also violates this. Ceremonial and forensic laws, whether divine or human, provided they are good, indeed agree with the Decalogue, but they are not deduced from it by necessary consequence as the moral law is; rather, they serve it as certain determinations of circumstances. From this the difference between these laws is most clearly seen. For it is one thing to follow necessarily from the Decalogue, and another to agree with it and serve its observance. Yet this difference varies, because the government of the Church and of the state is not the same, the end of all these laws is not the same, and, finally, all these laws are not abrogated in the same way.

units.la: Præcipua verò harum legum discrimina consistunt in obligatione, patefactione, duratione, & vsu. Morales leges sunt natura notæ, quæ obligant omnes homnes, & sunt perpetuæ: alia vero non item. Morales requirunt internam & externam obedientiam: alia tantum externam. Morales sunt generales ad homines quoslibet pertinentes: alia sunt speciales, non pertinentes ad quoslibet. Morales sunt aliarum fines: alia moralibus subserviunt. Morales multarum aliarum typi sunt: alia sunt typi moralium. Denique morales non ceduntaliis: alia vero cedunt moralibus.
units.tr: The principal differences among these laws lie in obligation, disclosure, duration, and use. Moral laws are known by nature, bind all human beings, and are perpetual; the others are not. Moral laws require inward and outward obedience; the others require only outward obedience. Moral laws are general, pertaining to all people; the others are special and do not pertain to everyone. Moral laws are the ends of the others; the others serve the moral laws. Moral laws are the types of many others; the others are types of moral laws. Finally, moral laws do not give way to the others; the others give way to moral laws.

units.la: Obiter notandum, quid lex moralis, naturalis, & decalogus differant. Decalogus est summa legum moralium, quæ in tota scriptura veteris & noui Testamenti sunt sparsæ. Lex moralis idem erant in natura integra. In natura corrupta legis naturalis pars bona obfuscata est per peccatum, & tantum particula eius de obedientia Dei post lapsum mansit reliqua in mente humana: qua de causa Deus integram legis suæ sententiam in Ecclesia repetiuit, & declarauit in decalogo. Decalogus igitur est renouatio & instauratio legis naturæ: Lex verò naturæ tantum est pars decalogi. Hæc distinctio partium legis diuinæ retinenda est, cum propter ipsum discrimen istarum legum, quo neglecto non recte earum vis & sententia intelligitur, tum vt de abrogatione & vsu legis recte iudicari ac docei possit.
units.tr: It is worth noting in passing how the moral law, the natural law, and the Decalogue differ. The Decalogue is the sum of the moral laws, which are scattered throughout the whole of Scripture, Old and New Testament. The moral law was the same in nature when it was whole. In corrupted nature, the good part of the natural law was obscured by sin, and only a small remnant of its obedience to God remained in the human mind after the fall. For this reason God restated the full sense of his law in the Church and set it forth in the Decalogue. The Decalogue is therefore the renewal and restoration of the natural law, and the natural law is only a part of the Decalogue. This distinction between the parts of the divine law must be retained, both because of the very difference between these laws, without which their force and meaning are not rightly understood, and so that a correct judgment and teaching about the abrogation and use of the law can be given.

units.la: III. Quatenus Lex sit abrogata per Christum, & quatenus non.
units.tr: III. How far the Law has been abrogated by Christ, and how far not.

units.la: Vsitata & vera responsio est: lex Mosaica cæremonialis & forensis abrogata est, quod ad obedientiam moralis, quod ad maledictionem, sed non quod ad obedientiam attinet.
units.tr: The customary and true answer is this: the Mosaic ceremonial and forensic law has been abrogated as regards the obligation of moral obedience and as regards the curse, but not as regards obedience itself.

units.la: Cæremoniales & forenses leges Christi aduentu sic abrogatas esse, vt neminem jam obligent ad obedientiam; & nostri temporis respectu rationem legum non habeant, probatur: 1. Quia abrogationem istam etiam Prophetæ in veteri Testamento docuerunt: Christus roborauit fœdus multis hebdomade vna: & dimidia hebdomade cessare faciet sacrificium & oblationem. Tu es sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech. 2. Christus & Apostoli in nouo Testamento hanc abrogationem diserte exposuerunt: Actor.7,8. Hebr. 7, 11.12.13.18. & cap. 8, 8.9.10.11.12.13. Pro multis testimoniis est decretum synodi Apostolicæ: Visum est Spiritui sancto & nobis, ne quid amplius vobis oneris imponeremus, quàm hæc necessaria. 3. Causis mutatis mutantur & leges exillis pendentes. Causæ legum cæremonialium & forensium erant: vna, vt hac formâ cultus & politiæ populus Iudaicus, ex quo erat nasciturus Messias, discerneretur ab aliis gentibus vsque ad eius aduentum: altera, vt essent typi Messiæ & beneficiorum eius. Hæ causæ exhibito Christo cessarunt. Nam discretionem Judæorum & gentium sublatam esse, testatur Apostolus: Ipse vtraque fecit vnum, &c. In Christo neque circumcisio quicquam valet, neque præputium, sed noua creatura. Et rituum significationem impletam esse, per Christum docetur passim: Hoc declarante Spiritu sancto, nondum patefactam fuisse viam ad sacrarium. Lex & Prophetæ vsque ad Iohannem. Ne quis vos damnet ob cibum & potum.
units.tr: That the ceremonial and forensic laws were so abrogated by the coming of Christ that they no longer bind anyone to obedience, and that in our time they have no authority as laws, is proved as follows. (1) Because the prophets of the Old Testament also taught this abrogation: Christ "shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and oblation to cease" (Dan. 9); "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek" (Ps. 110). (2) Christ and the apostles set out this abrogation plainly in the New Testament: Acts 7:8; Heb. 7:11, 12, 13, 18; and Heb. 8:8–13. In addition to many testimonies there is the decree of the apostolic synod: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things" (Acts 15). (3) When the causes change, the laws that depend on them change too. The causes of the ceremonial and forensic laws were, first, that by this form of worship and polity the Jewish people, from whom the Messiah was to be born, might be distinguished from the other nations until his coming; and second, that they might be types of the Messiah and of his benefits. These causes ceased when Christ was revealed. For the Apostle testifies that the distinction between Jews and Gentiles has been removed: "He himself made both one, etc. In Christ neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation." And it is taught everywhere that the meaning of the rites has been fulfilled through Christ: "The Holy Spirit signifying this, that the way into the sanctuary was not yet made manifest. The Law and the Prophets until John. Let no one condemn you for food or drink."

units.la: Iudæi obijciunt: 1. Cultus Mosaicus ex mandato, regnum Judaicum ex promissione Dei perpetuò durare debuit. Circumcisio pactum perpetuum. Pascha observandum statuto perpetuo. Hæc requies mea in seculum. Sabbathum pactum perpetuum. Thronus tuus vsque in seculum. Ergo cultus & politia Mosaica non fuit abroganda per Christum. Resp. Est gemina fallacia, à dicto secundum quid, vt simpliciter. Primò, maior loquitur de absoluta perpetuitate, minor de restricta: quandoquidem in dictis perpetuitas promittitur cæremoniarum & regni non infinita, sed vsque ad Christum, qui post Mosen erat audiendus. Nam particula עלם passim in scriptura non æternitatem, sed perpetuationem longi, definiti tamen temporis significat. Siceruitoeim seculum: hoc est, vsque ad annum jubilæum, vt liquet ex collatione eius legis, cum lege jubilæi, Leuit.25,40. Deinde, vt in minore absoluram quoq; perpetuitatem promitti concedatur: sed duntaxat ea tamen non est ipsorum typorum & vmbrarum: sed perpetua Ecclesia perpetuò sit duratura, etiamsi typi & symbola perChristi rerum significatarum siue spiritualium, quod harum veritas in stum aboleantur. Sic enim circumcisionis significatio etiamnum durat, & in regno Christi perpetuum est sabbathum, & perpetuum erit in vita æterna. Denique regnum Dauidis in Christi throno est æternum.
units.tr: The Jews object: (1) The Mosaic worship, by God's command, and the Jewish kingdom, by God's promise, ought to last for ever. "Circumcision is an everlasting covenant. The Passover is to be observed as a perpetual statute. This is my rest for ever. The sabbath is an everlasting covenant. Your throne for ever and ever." Therefore the Mosaic worship and polity were not to be abolished by Christ. Answer. This is a double fallacy, an argument from a statement made in a qualified sense to one made absolutely. First, the major premise speaks of absolute perpetuity, while the minor speaks of a limited perpetuity. For in these passages the perpetuity promised to the ceremonies and the kingdom is not unlimited, but lasts until Christ, who was to be heard after Moses. For the particle עלם in Scripture generally signifies not eternity but the continuance of a long yet defined period of time. Thus "for ever" (usque in seculum) means until the year of jubilee, as is clear from comparing that law with the law of the jubilee, Lev. 25:40. Second, even if it is granted that an absolute perpetuity is promised in the lesser sense, it does not apply to the types and shadows themselves but to the things they signified, that is, the spiritual things, whose truth is not abolished by Christ. Thus the meaning of circumcision still endures, the sabbath is perpetual in the kingdom of Christ, and it will be perpetual in eternal life. Finally, the kingdom of David is eternal in the throne of Christ.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Cultus, quem Ezechiel cap.40. vsque ad finem suæ prophetiæ describit, pertinet ad regnum Messiæ, & in eo observandus. At cultus ille est merè typicus & cæremonialis. Ergo cultus typicus & cæremonialis etiam in regno Messiæ est observandus: proinde per Messiam non debuit aboleri, sed instauran Judaica religio & politia. Resp. Maior non est simpliciter vera, quia Propheta vaticinatur quidem de regno Messiæ, sed non tantum. Simul enim describit cultus cæremonialis instaurationem in Judæa post reditum ex Babylone futuram, & duraturam vsque ad Messiam. Minor etiam negatur. Non enim tantum typorum instauratio promittitur, sed sub typica descriptione præcipuè promittitur spiritualis magnificentia ecclesiæ in regno Messiæ, in hac quidem vita inchoanda, in altera verò perficienda: id
units.tr: Objection. (2) The worship that Ezekiel describes in chapter 40, down to the end of his prophecy, belongs to the kingdom of the Messiah and is to be observed in it. But that worship is purely typical and ceremonial. Therefore typical and ceremonial worship is to be observed also in the kingdom of the Messiah, and so the Jewish religion and polity ought to be restored, not abolished by the Messiah. Answer. The major premise is not simply true, because the prophet does indeed prophesy about the kingdom of the Messiah, but not only that. At the same time he describes the restoration of ceremonial worship in Judea that was to take place after the return from Babylon and was to last until the Messiah. The minor is also denied. For it is not only a restoration of types that is promised, but under the typical description what is chiefly promised is the spiritual splendour of the Church in the kingdom of the Messiah, to be begun in this life and perfected in the next.

units.la: Sub typica descriptione promittit spi. rituale condi tione ecclesiæ id quod euidentibus argumentis probari potest. 1. Esdræ historia docet, hanc instautationem non fuisse impletam ante Christi aduentum. Sed nec potest eius aduentum tam splendidè Ecclesiæ conditionem in his terris futuram, vt somniant Judæi, credere nos sinunt alia Prophetarum oracula de aduentu & regno Messiæ humili & contemto in hoc mundo. Quare vel significata, hoc est, de Ecclesia, vel concedendum, nunquam necimpletam, nec implendam esse hanc prophetiam, quod est absurdum. 2. Promissio, qua futurum negat Propheta, vt dominus Israelis & reges eorum vltra polluant sanctum nomen eius, spiritualem omnino sensum postulat de perfectione futuræ vitæ. Solent enim Prophetæ exordium regni Christi cum eiusdem complemento connectere. 3. Aquæ ex templo profluentes, non ponssunt de elementaribus aquis accipi, sed significant dona Spiritus sancti copiosè effundenda cœlitus in regno Christi. 4. Denique nos Christiani interpretem habemus Johannem in Apocalypsi cap. 21. & 22. vbi Hierosolyma spiritualis ac cœlestis, hoc est, Ecclesia noui Testamenti glorificata, verbis quasi ex illa Ezechielis hypotyposi desumtis, describitur. Quare hæc prophetia ad probandam cæremoniarum obseruationem in regno Messiæ nihil facit.
units.tr: Under a typical description he promises the spiritual condition of the Church, and this can be proved by clear arguments. (1) The history of Ezra teaches that this restoration was not fulfilled before the coming of Christ. Nor can we believe, as the Jews dream, that at his coming the condition of the Church on this earth would be so splendid, since other oracles of the prophets about the coming and kingdom of the Messiah, which were humble and despised in this world, do not allow it. Therefore either the things signified, that is the Church, must be understood, or it must be conceded that this prophecy has never been fulfilled and is not to be fulfilled, which is absurd. (2) The promise, in which the prophet says that the Lord of Israel and their kings will no longer defile his holy name, requires a wholly spiritual sense, referring to the perfection of the life to come. For the prophets usually join the beginning of Christ's kingdom to its completion. (3) The waters flowing out of the temple cannot be taken as elemental waters; they signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are to be poured out copiously from heaven in the kingdom of Christ. (4) Finally, we Christians have John as our interpreter in Revelation 21 and 22, where the spiritual and heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the glorified Church of the New Testament, is described in words taken, as it were, from that sketch of Ezekiel. Therefore this prophecy does nothing to prove that ceremonial observance is to continue in the kingdom of the Messiah.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Optima & justissima politiæ forma semper est retinenda. Judaicæ politiæ forma fuit optima & justissima, vt pote à Deo ipso constituta. Ergo est retinenda. Resp. Est fallacia à dicto secundum quid, vt simpliciter. Maior simpliciter: minor secundum quid est vera. Judaicæ politiæ forma fuit optima, non absolutè, sed illo tempore, & illo loco, & in illa gente. In ea enim multa fuerunt ad illius gentis, regionis, temporis, & cultus cæremonialis rationem accommodata, quorum obseruatio neque justa, neque vtilis futura esset, quia causæ, cur illæ leges tunc ferrentur Judæis, sublatæ aut mutatæ sunt: vt de libello repudij, de ducendis viduis cognatorum, &c. Neque Deus ideo eam politiam instituit, vt omnes gentes & ætates ad eam alligaret, sed tantum, vt populum suum hac disciplina ab aliis populis ad tempus sejungeret. Instant. Licet Christianis vti legibus Atticis, Romanis, &c. Multo magis Mosaicis. Resp. Concedatur, modo fiat absque opinione necessitatis, hoc est, non ideo obseruentur leges Moßs, quia Moses præcepit populo judaico, sed quia rationes probabiles sunt, quare nunc etiam sic agatur: & si rationes mutentur, eas mutanda libertas retinetur. Hactenus de abrogatione legum cæremonialium & forensium.
units.tr: Objection. (3) The best and most just form of polity is always to be retained. The form of the Jewish polity was the best and most just, since it was instituted by God himself. Therefore it is to be retained. Answer. This is a fallacy of an argument from a statement made in a qualified sense to one made absolutely. The major is true absolutely, the minor only in a qualified sense. The form of the Jewish polity was the best not absolutely, but at that time, in that place, and for that people. For it contained many things adapted to the character of that nation, region, and time, and to its ceremonial worship, the observance of which would be neither just nor useful, because the causes for which those laws were given to the Jews have been removed or changed, as with the bill of divorce, the marriage of widows to their kinsmen, and so on. Nor did God establish that polity in order to bind all nations and ages to it, but only to set his people apart from other peoples for a time by this discipline. Objection renewed. It is lawful for Christians to use the laws of Athens, of Rome, and so on; much more the Mosaic laws. Answer. This may be granted, provided it is done without any belief in necessity; that is, the laws of Moses are not observed because Moses commanded them to the Jewish people, but because there are probable reasons why it is still right to act in this way; and if the reasons change, the freedom to change them is retained. So far concerning the abrogation of the ceremonial and forensic laws.

units.la: Lex moralis per Christum secundum aliquid est abrogata, & secundum aliquid non. Abrogata est credentibus dupliciter. 1. Quoad maledictionem, ne possit justificatos fide in Christum damnare, propter imputatum eis Christi meritum: seu quoad justificationem, quia judicium de nobis non fertur secundum legem, sed secundum Euangelium. Judicium enim legis nos damnaret & perderet: quia vox legis est: Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo vllus viuens. Sed euangelij vox est: Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet vitam æternam. Hæc abrogatio legis prima & præcipua pars est libertatis Christianæ, de qua dicitur: Non est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. 2. Quoad coactionem. Lex enim non amplius extorquet obedientiam tanquam tyrannus aut herus seruum nequam cogens ad obedientiam: quia Christus obedientiam spontaneam Spiritu suo in nobis inchoat, vt voluntarie legi obtemperemus. De hac parte libertatis Christianæ dicit Apostolus: Peccatum vobis non dominabitur. Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia: quod quid sit, toto 7. capite explicat. Lex iusto non est posita, sed legis contemtoribus, &c. Ad uersus eos, qui sunt eiusmodi, non est lex.
units.tr: The moral law has been abrogated through Christ in one respect but not in another. It has been abrogated for believers in two ways. 1. As to its curse, so that it cannot condemn those justified by faith in Christ, since Christ's merit is imputed to them; or as to justification, because judgment about us is not passed according to the law but according to the Gospel. For the judgment of the law would condemn and destroy us, because the voice of the law is: No living man will be justified in your sight. But the voice of the Gospel is: Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life. This abrogation of the law is the first and chief part of Christian liberty, of which it is said: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. You are not under the law, but under grace. 2. As to compulsion. For the law no longer extorts obedience like a tyrant or master compelling an unworthy slave to obey, because Christ, by his Spirit, begins a willing obedience in us, so that we obey the law freely. Of this part of Christian liberty the Apostle speaks: Sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the law, but under grace; and he explains what this means throughout the seventh chapter. The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for lawbreakers, etc. For those of this kind there is no law.

units.la: Obiect. Lex & Prophetæ usq; ad Iohannem. Si ergo tunc demum lex abrogata fuit, quoad condemnationem, cum Christus apparuit in carne, sequitur fideles fuisse sub condemnatione, qui ante aduentum Christi vixerunt. Resp. Lex fuit abrogata, quoad condemnationem, tam in veteri testamento credentibus, quam his, qui sunt in nouo: illis in veteri, quoad efficaciam: his in nouo, quoad impletionem & exhibitionem.
units.tr: Objection. "The Law and the Prophets were until John." If, then, the law was abrogated as to condemnation only when Christ appeared in the flesh, it follows that the faithful who lived before Christ's coming were under condemnation. Answer. The law was abrogated as to condemnation both for believers under the Old Testament and for those under the New: for the former in its efficacy, for the latter in its fulfilment and exhibition.

units.la: Non autem abrogata est lex moralis seu decalogus, quantum ad obedientiam, sed Deus perpetuò, non minus nunc, quam olim, requirit tam à renatis, quam à non renatis, vt legi suæ obedientiam præstent. Probatur 1. A fine, propter quem Christus nos à peccatis & maledictione legis liberauit. Is fuit, vt nos à peccatis & maledictione liberatos templa Dei facerent, non autem, vt nos in peccatis & inimicitia cum Deo perseueraremus. 2. Quanto plura & maiora sunt Dei erga nos beneficia, tanto magis obligamur illi ad obedientiam, & gratitudinem præstandam. At in Christo obtinemus plura & maiora beneficia, quam omnibus aliis Deus præstat. Nam ad creationis & sustentationis communia beneficia addit etiam justificationis & regenerationis gratiam. Magis ergo quam antea & quam alij ad obedientiam legis obligamur. 3. Ad testimonium scripturæ: Ne existimate me venisse, vt dissoluam legem & Prophetas, non veni, vt dissoluam, sed vt impleam. Hoc de tota lege, præcipuè verò de morali dicitur, quam Christus quatuor modis impleuit.
units.tr: The moral law, or the Decalogue, however, has not been abrogated as to obedience; rather God perpetually requires obedience to his law, now no less than formerly, both from the regenerate and from the unregenerate. This is proved: 1. From the end for which Christ freed us from sins and from the curse of the law. That end was that we, freed from sins and from the curse, should become temples of God, not that we should persevere in sins and in enmity with God. 2. The greater and more numerous God's benefits to us are, the more we are bound to him to render obedience and gratitude. But in Christ we obtain more and greater benefits than God bestows on all others. For to the common benefits of creation and preservation he adds also the grace of justification and regeneration. Therefore we are bound to obey the law more than before and more than others. 3. By the testimony of Scripture: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law and the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfil. This is said of the whole law, but especially of the moral law, which Christ fulfilled in four ways.

units.la: 1. Propria justitia & conformitate cum lege. Oportebat enim eum in se legi conformem, & perfectè justum esse secundum utramq; naturam, vt posset pro nobis satisfacere, sicut dicitur: Talis nobis conueniebat pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, &c.
units.tr: 1. By his own righteousness and conformity to the law. For it was necessary that he himself should conform to the law and be perfectly righteous according to both natures, so that he could make satisfaction for us, as it is said: Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, etc.

units.la: 2. Per solutione pœnæ sufficientis pro nostris peccatis. Cum enim legis impotentia nihil posset in carne, Deus suo ipsius Filio misso confor- mato carni peccato obnoxio, idque pro peccato, condemnauit peccatum in carne.
units.tr: 2. By paying a penalty sufficient for our sins. For since the law was powerless, being weakened by the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and that as a sin offering, condemned sin in the flesh.

units.la: 3. Implet legem in nobis suo spiritu, reformans nos per eum ad imaginem Dei: Vetus ille homo cum Christo crucifixus est, vt eneruetur corpus peccati, ne posthac nos seruiamus peccato. Si Spiritus eius, qui excitauit Christum à mortuis, habitat in vobis, viuificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra, per inhabitantem eius spiritum in vobis.
units.tr: 3. He fulfils the law in us by his Spirit, reforming us through him to the image of God: Our old man was crucified with Christ, so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, that we should no longer serve sin. If the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.

units.la: 4. Implet docendo & repurgando legem à corruptelis pharisæorum, vt videre est in concione montana, & alibi. Sic itaq; docet & restituit obedientiam legis in nobis, non abolet legem, quantum ad obedientiam attinet.
units.tr: 4. He fulfils the law by teaching and purifying it from the corruptions of the Pharisees, as can be seen in the Sermon on the Mount and elsewhere. Thus he teaches and restores obedience to the law in us; he does not abolish the law as far as obedience is concerned.

units.la: Idem confirmat Paulus: Legem igitur inanem reddimus per fidem? immò legem stabilimus.
units.tr: Paul confirms the same: Do we then make void the law through faith? Certainly not; rather we establish the law.

units.la: Stabilitur verò lex per fidem tripliciter. 1. Confessione & approbatione judicij legis aduersus nos, quod non præstemus debitam legi obedientiam, proinde fimus rei damnationis: sine, quia fide nobis applicamus satisfactionem Christi, æquipollentem pœnæ æternæ, quam lex nobis non præstantibus obedientiam irrogabat. Qua satisfactione fit, vt justificemur non quidem ex lege, nec tamen contra legem: sed cum lege, cui pro nobis Christus sua obedientia satisfecit. 3. Noua obedientia, earum in vita æterna. Breuiter idem sic dicitur: Lex stabilitur per fidem, tum quia justitia fidei docet, nos in nobis non esse justos, justificari autem non nisi intercedente perfecta satisfactione, quam lex postulat, tum quia per fidem fit obedientiæ legis instauratio in nobis.
units.tr: The law is established by faith in three ways. (1) By confessing and approving the judgment of the law against us, that we do not render the obedience due to the law and so are liable to condemnation; (2) because by faith we apply to ourselves the satisfaction of Christ, equivalent to the eternal punishment which the law imposed on us for failing to render obedience. By this satisfaction we are justified, not indeed from the law, nor yet against the law, but together with the law, to which Christ has made satisfaction for us by his obedience. (3) By new obedience, whose fruit is in eternal life. Briefly, the same is stated thus: the law is established by faith, both because the righteousness of faith teaches that we are not righteous in ourselves, and that we are justified only through the intervention of the perfect satisfaction which the law demands, and both because through faith the restoration of obedience to the law takes place in us.

units.la: Summa igitur doctrinæ de abrogatione legis hæc est: Leges Mosaicæ cæremoniales & forenses, penitus abrogatæ sunt Christi aduentu, quoad obligationem & obedientiam: Lex verò moralis non quod ad obedientiam, sed tantum quod ad maledictionem & coactionem attinet. Obiectiones Antinomorum, Libertinorum, & similium, qui contendunt, legem moralem ad Christianos nihil pertinere, neque in Ecclesia Christi docendam esse, requirantur infra quaestione 115. de usu legis.
units.tr: The sum of the doctrine concerning the abrogation of the law, therefore, is this: the Mosaic ceremonial and judicial laws have been wholly abrogated by Christ's coming, as to obligation and obedience; but the moral law is abrogated not as to obedience but only as to its curse and compulsion. The objections of the Antinomians, the Libertines and others like them, who maintain that the moral law has nothing to do with Christians and is not to be taught in the Church of Christ, are to be sought below in question 115, concerning the use of the law.

units.la: V. Quid lex moralis ab Euangelio differat.
units.tr: V. How the moral law differs from the Gospel.

units.la: Declaratio huius quaestionis multis modis est necessaria, ut ex discriminibus intelligi potest. Nascitur vero potissimum ex definitione legis vbi dicitur, quod lex praemia promittat praestantibus integram obedientiam: promittat autem gratis, quia nulla obedientia potest esse meritoria apud DEVM. Sed & Euangelium promittit gratis vitam aeternam. Videtur ergo Lex ab Euangelio non differre. Sed magnum est discrimen.
units.tr: The explanation of this question is necessary in many ways, as can be understood from the differences. It arises chiefly from the definition of the law, where it is said that the law promises rewards to those who render complete obedience; and it promises them freely, because no obedience can be meritorious before God. But the Gospel also promises eternal life freely. The law therefore seems not to differ from the Gospel. Yet the difference is great.

units.la: Differunt 1. Modo patefactionis. Lex est naturâ nota: Euangelium post lapsum hominis diuinitus est revelatum. 2. Subiectio seu doctrina. Lex proponit justitiam Dei nudam: Euangelium coniunctam cum misericordia. Item Lex docet, quales nos esse oporteat, vt seruemur: Euangelium etiam docet, quomodo tales efficiamur, quales Lex requirit, nempe in Christo per fidem. 3. Conditionibus & promissionibus. Lex promittit vitam aeternam & omnia bona, cum conditione propriae & perfectae iustitiae atque obedientiae in nobis. Euangelium eadem promittit cum conditione fidei nostrae in Christum, qua obedientiam alienam pro nobis praestitam, Christi videlicet, amplectimur: seu, Euangelium docet, nos gratis saluari per fidem in Christum. Cum fide autem indissolubili nexu coniuncta est conditio nouae obedientiae. 4. Effectus. Lex iram operatur, & ministerium mortis, Rom. 4. 2 Cor.3. Euangelium est ministerium vitae & spiritus, ibidem.
units.tr: They differ: (1) in the mode of revelation: the law is known by nature, whereas the Gospel was revealed by God after the fall of man; (2) in the subject matter or teaching: the law sets forth the justice of God bare, whereas the Gospel sets it forth joined with mercy; likewise, the law teaches what we ought to be in order to be saved, whereas the Gospel also teaches how we are made such as the law requires, namely in Christ through faith; (3) in the conditions and promises: the law promises eternal life and all good things on the condition of our own perfect righteousness and obedience, whereas the Gospel promises the same on the condition of our faith in Christ, by which we embrace the obedience of another rendered for us, namely Christ's; or, the Gospel teaches that we are saved freely through faith in Christ. Yet the condition of new obedience is joined with faith by an indissoluble bond; (4) in their effects: the law works wrath and is the ministry of death (Rom. 4; 2 Cor. 3), whereas the Gospel is the ministry of life and of the Spirit (ibid.).

units.la: QVAESTIO XCIII.
units.tr: QUESTION 93.

units.la: Quomodo diuiduntur haec praecepta? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: How are these precepts divided? ANSWER.

units.la: In duas tabulas 4, quarum prior quatuor praeceptis tradit, quo pacto nos erga Deum geramus: posteriori sex praeceptis, quae officia proximo debeamus b.
units.tr: Into two tables: the first, which consists of four precepts, teaches how we ought to conduct ourselves toward God; the second, of six precepts, teaches what duties we owe to our neighbour.

units.la: a Deut. 4, 13. Exod. 34, 28. Deut. 10, 32. b Matth. 22, 37.
units.tr: a Deut. 4:13. Exod. 34:28. Deut. 10:4. b Matt. 22:37.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: Quæstio de diuisione decalogi necessaria & vtilis est. 1. quia Deus ipse certum numerum tabularum & præceptorum decalogi expressit. 2. quia Christus summam totius legis in duo mandatorum genera distribuit, ta, seu in duo mandata, 3. quia recta diuisio decalogi facit ad intellectum præceptorum: admonet enim de gradibus obedientiæ vtriusque tabulæ, ac docet cultum primæ tabulæ esse præcipuum.
units.tr: The question about the division of the Decalogue is both necessary and useful. (1) Because God himself set out the exact number of the tables and precepts of the Decalogue. (2) Because Christ distributed the sum of the whole law into two kinds of commandments, that is, into two commandments. (3) Because a correct division of the Decalogue helps us to understand the precepts: it reminds us of the degrees of obedience in each table, and it teaches that the worship of the first table is the more important.

units.la: Cæterum triplici ratione decalogus diuiditur.
units.tr: Moreover, the Decalogue is divided in three ways.

units.la: I. Diuiditur in duas tabulas à Mose & Christo, quarum prior complectitur officia erga Deum immediate: posterior erga Deum mediate. seu: prior tradit quo pacto nos erga Deum geramus, posterior quæ officia proximo debeamus. Hæc diuisio nititur expresso Dei verbo: Dola tibi duas tabulas lapideas. Item eo, quod Christus & Paulus referunt totam legem ad dilectionem Dei & proximi: Diliges dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota cogitatione tua. Istud est primum & maximum mandatum. Secundum autem est simile huic: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Distinctio hæc prodest: 1. Vt sententiam totius legis & perfectionem obedientiæ melius intelligamus. 2.
