Vt regulam vulgatam obseruemus, præcepta secundæ tabulæ cedere præceptis primæ in eodem genere cultus; hoc est, dilectionem & gloriam Dei anteponendam esse dilectioni & saluti omnium creaturarum, iuxta illud: Oportet Deo magis obedire, quam hominibus.
units.tr: I. The Decalogue is divided by Moses and Christ into two tables. The first embraces the duties owed to God immediately; the second, the duties owed to God mediately. In other words, the first teaches how we should conduct ourselves towards God, and the second what duties we owe to our neighbour. This division rests on the express word of God: Hew thee two tables of stone. It also rests on the fact that Christ and Paul refer the whole law to the love of God and of neighbour: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. This distinction is useful: (1) so that we may better understand the sense of the whole law and the perfection of obedience; (2) so that we may observe the common rule that the precepts of the second table yield to those of the first within the same kind of worship, that is, that the love and glory of God must be placed before the love and welfare of all creatures, according to that saying: We ought to obey God rather than men.

units.la: II. Diuiditur decalogus in decem præcepta seu decem verba, quorum quatuor primæ, sex secundæ tabulæ tribuuntur. Numerauit autem Deus decem præcepta seu leges, non quod hoc numero magis quam alio fuerit delectatus, sed propter ipsarum rerum totidem summas & argumenta. Nam omnia quæ Deo & proximo debemus, decem legibus comprehenduntur, vt nihil sit omissum, nihil superfluum. Sic quatuor primæ tabulæ præcepta continent omnia, quæ Deo debemus immediate, & sex secundæ tabulæ complectuntur omnia ea, quæ ad hanc vitam feliciter degendam pertinent.
units.tr: II. The Decalogue is divided into ten precepts, or ten words. Of these, four are assigned to the first table and six to the second. God numbered the ten precepts or laws not because he took greater delight in this number than in any other, but because of the same number of heads and subjects in the matters themselves. For everything we owe to God and to our neighbour is comprehended in the ten laws, so that nothing is omitted and nothing is superfluous. Thus the four precepts of the first table contain everything we owe to God immediately, and the six of the second table embrace everything that pertains to living this life well.

units.la: Est tamen de enumeratione præceptorum dissensio. Ab aliis enim tria, ab aliis quinque, ab aliis quatuor præcepta primæ tabulæ numerantur. Sed rectam esse distinctionem eam qua quatuor præcepta primæ tabulæ sic attribuuntur, vt primum sit de non habendis diis alienis; secundum de nõ faciendis sculptilibus; tertium de nomine Dei temere non vsurpando; quartum de sabbatho sanctificando, sex reliqua ad tabulam secundam referuntur: hæ rationes ostendunt.
units.tr: There is, however, disagreement about the numbering of the precepts. Some count three precepts in the first table, some five, and some four. But the correct distinction is the one by which the four precepts of the first table are assigned as follows: the first concerns not having other gods; the second concerns not making graven images; the third concerns not taking the name of God in vain; the fourth concerns sanctifying the sabbath; the remaining six refer to the second table. These reasons show this.

units.la: 1. Distincta sunt præcepta, quæ distinguuntur sententiis. Cum enim Deus ipse decalogum in decem verba distribuerit, haud dubie præcepta sensu inter se differre voluit. Ergo diuersa sunt, quæ sensu differunt: non diuersa, sed vnum præceptum sunt, quæ sensu non differunt. Præceptum de non habendis diis alienis, & de non faciendis sculptilibus, sententiis differunt. Illud enim verat aliud numen præter solum verum Deum coli: hoc verat solum verum Deum aliter coli, quàm ipse præcepit. Contra præceptum de concupiscentia, quod aliqui in nonum, & decimum diuiduunt, sensu vnum esse, tum ipsimet testantur, quoties in explicationibus suis nonum suum & decimum coniungunt: tum vero Paulus docet, cum de concupiscentia, tanquam de vno præcepto dicit: Non nouissem, concupiscentiam esse peccatum, nisi lex dixisset: Non concupisces. Illa igitur duo diuersa, hæc vnum præceptum de concupiscentia prohibet: eadem ratione distrahi deberet in plura, & tot præcepta fierent, quot species rerum non concupiscendarum enumerantur.
units.tr: (1) Precepts are distinct when they are distinguished by their meaning. Since God himself divided the Decalogue into ten words, he undoubtedly wanted the precepts to differ from one another in sense. So those things which differ in sense are different; those which do not differ in sense are not different but form one precept. The precept about not having other gods and the one about not making graven images differ in meaning. The former forbids that any god besides the one true God be worshipped; the latter forbids that the one true God be worshipped in a way other than he himself has commanded. On the other hand, that the precept about coveting, which some divide into the ninth and tenth, is one in sense, is attested by those very people themselves, whenever in their explanations they join their ninth and tenth. Indeed Paul teaches this when, speaking of coveting as of one precept, he says: I had not known sin to be coveting, unless the law had said: You shall not covet. That law, therefore, forbids coveting in one precept, not in two. By the same reasoning it ought to be split into several, and there would be as many precepts as there are kinds of things enumerated as not to be coveted.

units.la: 2. Haud dubiè præcepta diuersa sunt, non eadem, quæ diuersis periodis & versibus: non diuersa, sed vnum præceptum sunt, quæ vno versu à Mose pronuntur. Præcepti de non habendis diis alienis, & de non faciendis idolis, Moses versiculis distinxit. Distincta igitur sunt præcepta. Contra, præcepti, de concupiscentia domus & vxoris, periodis non distinxit, sed vno versiculo comprehendit. Vnum igitur est de concupiscentia præceptum.
units.tr: (2) Precepts are certainly different when they are not the same and are set out in different sentences and verses; they are not different but form one precept when they are pronounced in one verse by Moses. Moses marked off the precept about not having other gods and the one about not making idols by separate verses. So these precepts are distinct. On the other hand, the precept about coveting a house and a wife he did not divide into separate sentences, but comprised in a single verse. Therefore the precept about coveting is one.

units.la: 3. Moses haud dubiè eundem præceptorum ordinem in Exodo & Deuteronomio retinuit. Iam autem verba decimi præcepti de concupiscentia domus & vxoris non eodem, sed diuerso ordine posuit. Nam in Exodo præcedunt hæc verba: Non concupisces vxorem proximi tui: sequuntur hæc: Non concupisces domum proximi tui. In Deuteronomio præcedunt hæc: Non concupisces domum proximi tui: sequuntur illa: Non concupisces vxorem proximi tui. Sunt igitur hæc vnius præcepti partes: alioqui non poterit dari nonum præceptum, & dicendum erit, Moisen in altero loco nonum præceptum cum decimo confudisse, & partem decimi in locum noni substituisse, cuius absurditatis non est insimulandus. Hac igitur verborum transpositione satis per Mosen Deus declarat, se velle vnum duntaxat esse præceptum, quæcunque vna periodo coniunctim comprehensa in decimo præcepto leguntur.
units.tr: (3) Moses undoubtedly kept the same order of the precepts in Exodus and in Deuteronomy. Yet he did not place the words of the tenth precept about coveting a house and a wife in the same order in both places, but in a different order. For in Exodus the following words come first: You shall not covet your neighbour's wife; then follow these: You shall not covet your neighbour's house. In Deuteronomy the following come first: You shall not covet your neighbour's house; then those follow: You shall not covet your neighbour's wife. These are therefore parts of one precept. Otherwise there could be no ninth precept, and it would have to be said that Moses in the second passage confused the ninth precept with the tenth and substituted part of the tenth in place of the ninth, and Moses cannot be charged with such an absurdity. By this transposition of words, then, God sufficiently declares through Moses that he wishes whatever is read together, comprehended in one sentence in the tenth precept, to be one precept only.

units.la: 4. Authoritas admodum locuples est, qua hæc præceptorum distinctio confirmatur. Sic enim primum & secundum distinguunt, decimum coniungunt veteres Iudæorum scriptores: Iosephus lib.3.antiq.Iud. Philo in expos. decalogi. Sic & Christianorum Græci scriptores: Athanasius in synopsi script. lib. 2. Origenes lib. 3. super Exod.hom.8. Gregorius Nazianzenus in carm. Chrysostomus siue author operis imperfecti in Matth.hom.49. Zonaras tomo primo histor. Nicephorus historia Eccles. Et scriptores Latini: Hieronymus in cap.6. ad Ephes. Ambrosius in eundem locum ad Ephes. Sulpitius Seuerus lib.1. historia sacra. Augustinus lib.1. quaestionum veteris & noui Testamenti quaest.7. & lib.2. quaest. super Exod. cap.17. Fuit ergo haec distinctio decalogi, tanquam rectior, iam olim in Ecclesiis Græcis & Latinis recepta. Ergo à nobis restitutio est facta, non immutatio decalogi.
units.tr: (4) The authority in support of this distinction of the precepts is very weighty. The Jewish writers Josephus (book 3 of the Jewish Antiquities) and Philo (in his exposition of the Decalogue) thus distinguish the first and second and join the tenth. Likewise the Greek Christian writers: Athanasius in the Synopsis of Scripture, book 2; Origen, book 3 on Exodus, homily 8; Gregory Nazianzen in his poem; Chrysostom or the author of the unfinished work on Matthew, homily 49; Zonaras, volume 1 of his Histories; Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History. And the Latin writers: Jerome on Ephesians, chapter 6; Ambrose on the same passage in Ephesians; Sulpicius Severus, book 1 of Sacred History; Augustine, book 1 of Questions on the Old and New Testament, question 7, and book 2, question 17 on Exodus. This division of the Decalogue, therefore, as the more correct, was long ago received in the Greek and Latin Churches. Thus it is our restoration, not an alteration, of the Decalogue.

units.la: Nec refert, quod Iosephus, Philo & aliqui Græci quinq; praecepta vtriusque tabulæ tribuunt. Nam in hoc nihilominus conueniunt omnes, verba de vno Deo colendo, & de non habendis simulacris, esse duo distincta praecepta: de concupiscentia verò non duo, sed vnum.
units.tr: Nor does it matter that Josephus, Philo and some Greeks assign five precepts to each table. For in this they all nonetheless agree: that the words about worshipping the one God and about not having images are two distinct precepts, but the words about coveting are not two but one.

units.la: Reperitur quidem & altera diuisio, qua tantum tria praecepta in prima, septem in secunda tabula numerantur, apud Augustin. epist.119.ad Ian.c.11, & quaest.sup.Exod.c.7. Sed infirma est trinitatis allegoria, qua Augustinus pro ratione vtitur.
units.tr: There is indeed another division, in which only three precepts are counted in the first table and seven in the second, found in Augustine, letter 119 to Januarius, chapter 11, and in the Questions on Exodus, chapter 7. But the allegory of the Trinity, which Augustine uses as his reason, is weak.

units.la: Obseruandum verò, si modo doctrina & sententia decalogi de vero Deo, & vero cultu Dei integra retineatur, de verborum numeratione non odiose pugnandum esse.
units.tr: It should be observed, however, that if only the teaching and meaning of the Decalogue about the true God and the true worship of God are kept intact, we should not contend bitterly over the numbering of the words.

units.la: III. Diuiditur decalogus secundum materiam subiectam, seu secundū res, quæ iubentur aut prohibentur in decalogo, in cultum Dei immediatum & mediatum. Generaliter in decalogo praecipitur cultus Dei: contrarium diuino cultui vetatur. Cultus Dei est vel immediatus, cum opera moralia immediatè Deo praestantur: vel mediatus, cum opera moralia proximo praestantur propter Deum. Immediatus in prima tabula continetur, & est vel internus, vel externus. Internus in eo consistit, partim vt verum Deum colamus, ifq; sancitur in primo praecepto: partim vt modo legitimo intus & foris eum colamus, & hic in secundo praecepto docetur. Externus est aut priuatus, aut publicus. Priuatus continet opera moralia singulorum priuata, quae ab vnoquoque semper praestari debent, quantum ad confessionem linguae & operum dei Deo: & hic in tertio praecepto traditur. Publicus consistit in sanctificatione sabbathi, & traditur in quarto praecepto. Mediatus Dei cultus, qui in officiis erga homines vel proximos consistit, in secunda tabula continetur, estq; similiter externus, & internus. Externus consistit partim in officiis superiorū erga inferiores, & contra; de quib. officiis, vt de ordine etiam politico sub iis comprehenso, agitur in quinto praecepto: partim in officiis proximorū erga proximos, quæ in reliquis præceptis stabiliuntur: eaq; sunt vel conseruatio vitæ & salutis suæ & alienæ, quæ in sexto: vel conseruatio castitatis vel coniugiorum, quæ in septimo: vel conseruatio rerum seu possessionum, quæ in octauo: vel conseruatio veritatis, quæ in nono præcepto exigitur. Mediatus cultus interinus, seu interna officia cultus mediati sunt affectionum omnium erga proximum rectitudo: quæ includenda est omnibus præceptis præcedentibus, & in decimo præcepto adjungitur.
units.tr: III. The Decalogue is divided according to the subject matter, or according to the things that are commanded or forbidden in the Decalogue, into immediate and mediate worship of God. In general, the Decalogue prescribes the worship of God and forbids whatever is contrary to divine worship. The worship of God is either immediate, when moral works are rendered directly to God, or mediate, when moral works are rendered to our neighbour for God's sake. Immediate worship is contained in the first table, and is either internal or external. Internal worship consists partly in worshipping the true God, which is laid down in the first precept, and partly in worshipping him inwardly and outwardly in a lawful manner, which is taught in the second precept. External worship is either private or public. Private worship comprises the private moral works of individuals, which each person must always render, as to the confession of God with the tongue and the works done to God; this is handed down in the third precept. Public worship consists in sanctifying the sabbath, and is handed down in the fourth precept. Mediate worship of God, which consists in duties towards men or neighbours, is contained in the second table, and is likewise external and internal. External mediate worship consists partly in duties of superiors towards inferiors, and the reverse; these duties, together with the political order comprised under them, are treated in the fifth precept; partly in the duties of neighbours towards neighbours, which are established in the remaining precepts. These are either the preservation of one's own life and health and that of others, which is in the sixth precept; or the preservation of chastity and of marriages, which is in the seventh; or the preservation of goods or possessions, which is in the eighth; or the preservation of truth, which is required in the ninth precept. Internal mediate worship, that is, the inward duties of mediate worship, is the rectitude of all affections towards one's neighbour; this must be included in all the preceding precepts, and is added in the tenth precept.

units.la: Hinc ad obiectionem facilis est responsio. Officia erga proximum non sunt cultus Dei. Secunda tabula præcipit officia erga proximum. Resp. Ergo secundæ tabulæ obedientia non est cultus Dei. Maior tantum est vera de cultu Dei immediato, de quo etiam datur conclusio. Obedientia enim secundæ tabulæ non est cultus Dei immediatus, vt obedientia primæ, est tamen cultus Dei mediatus, hoc est, qui Deo præstatur in proximo, seu mediante proximo. Nam officia dilectionis proximi ex dilectione Dei proficisci debent, & sic præstita placent Deo, & fiunt ipsi Deo non minus, quàm obedientia primæ tabulæ. Respectu igitur Dei, propter quem fiunt, dicuntur & sunt cultus Dei: respectu verò proximi, cui immediatè fiunt, dicuntur officia. Differt autem cultus utriusque tabulæ obiectis. Prima tantum immediatum obiectum habet, Deum. Secunda immediatum obiectum habet proximum: & simul mediatum, Deum.
units.tr: Hence the answer to the objection is easy. The duties towards one's neighbour are not the worship of God. The second table commands duties towards one's neighbour. Answer: therefore obedience to the second table is not the worship of God. The major premise is true only of the immediate worship of God, and a conclusion is given about it as well. For obedience to the second table is not immediate worship of God, as obedience to the first table is; yet it is mediate worship of God, that is, worship which is rendered to God in the neighbour, or through the neighbour. For the duties of love towards the neighbour ought to proceed from the love of God, and so, when performed, they please God and are done to God himself no less than the obedience of the first table. Therefore with respect to God, on whose account they are done, they are called and are the worship of God; but with respect to the neighbour, to whom they are done immediately, they are called duties. Moreover, the worship of each table differs in its objects. The first has only one immediate object, God. The second has an immediate object, the neighbour, and at the same time a mediate object, God.

units.la: Typus tertiæ divisionis Decalogi.
units.tr: A summary of the third division of the Decalogue.

units.la: In decalogo præcipitur cultus Dei immediatus erga Deum, isque vel internus: de colendo vno vero Deo, vt in præcepto I. de recta verum Deum cognoscendi ratione, vt in II. externus, qui est vel privatus: vt in III. | publicus: vt in IV. mediatus erga proximum propter Deum: isque vel externus, qui consistit in officiis superiorum erga inferiores: & contra: vt in V. conservatione vitæ & salutis proximi: vt in VI. castitatis: vt in VII. rerum & possessionum: vt in VIII. veritatis: vt in IX. internus, qui est moderatio & rectitudo cuiuspiam, ne quis expetat aut cogitet aliquid contra præcepta priora omnia: vt in X.
units.tr: In the Decalogue there is commanded (1) immediate worship of God, directed towards God, and this is either internal, as in the first commandment, concerning the worship of the one true God and the right way of knowing the true God; or external, as in the second; and external worship is either private, as in the third, or public, as in the fourth. (2) Mediate worship, directed towards the neighbour for the sake of God, and this is either external, which consists in the duties of superiors towards inferiors and conversely, as in the fifth; in the preservation of the life and safety of one's neighbour, as in the sixth; of chastity, as in the seventh; of goods and possessions, as in the eighth; and of truth, as in the ninth. (3) Internal worship, which is the moderation and rectitude of a person's heart, so that no one desires or thinks anything contrary to all the preceding commandments, as in the tenth.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XCIV. Quid postulat DEVS in primo præcepto?
units.tr: QUESTION 94. What does God require in the first commandment?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vt, quam mihi chara est salus animæ meæ, tam studiose vitem & fugiam omnem idololatriam a, magiam, incantationem, superstitionem b, inuocationem sanctorum, aut cæterarum creaturarum c: vnicum autem & verum Deum recte agnoscam d, ipsi soli fidam e, summa humilitate f & patientia me illi subijciam g, ab eo solo omnia bona expectem h, deniq; intimo cordis affectu ipsum amem i, reuerear, k venerer l, adeo vt omnibus potius creaturis renunciem, quam vt vel minimum contra eius voluntatem committam m.
units.tr: That, as dear to me as the salvation of my soul is, I may earnestly avoid and flee from all idolatry a, magic, incantation, superstition b, invocation of the saints or of other creatures c; that I may rightly acknowledge the one and true God d, trust in him alone e, submit myself to him with the utmost humility f and patience g, expect all good things from him alone h, and finally love i, reverence k and worship l him with the inmost affection of my heart, so that I would renounce all creatures rather than commit the smallest thing against his will m.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XCV. Quid est idololatria?
units.tr: QUESTION 95. What is idolatry?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Est loco vnius Dei, aut præter vnum illum & verum Deum, qui se in suo verbo patefecit, aliud quippiam fingere aut habere, in quo spem reponas a.
units.tr: It is to make up or hold something else in place of the one God, or alongside that one true God who has revealed himself in his word, something in which you place your hope a.

units.la: a Ephes. 5, 5.1 Paral. 16,26. Philip. 3, 19. Galat. 4, 8. Ephes. 2, 12. 1 Ioh. 2,3. Ioh. 9. Ioh. 5,23.
units.tr: a Ephes. 5, 5. 1 Paral. 16,26. Philip. 3, 19. Galat. 4, 8. Ephes. 2, 12. 1 Ioh. 2,3. Ioh. 9. Ioh. 5,23.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Antequam de sententia singulorum præceptorum in specie dicatur, tenendæ sunt regulæ quædam generales, ad totius decalogi, & singulorum præceptorum intelligentiam necessariæ.
units.tr: Before the meaning of the individual precepts is set out one by one, certain general rules must be kept, which are necessary for understanding the whole Decalogue and each precept.

units.la: I. Decalogus est intelligendus secundum interpretationem scripturæ, hoc est, secundum declarationem Prophetarum, Christi & Apostolorum: non autem secundum judicium humanum autphilosophicum tantum. Coniungenda est explicatio passim sparsa in scripturis: non autem hærendum in breuibus illis præceptis. Nec philosophia moralis sufficit ad interpretationem, cum ea non contineat nisi particulam legis. Atque hoc est vnum & magnum discrimen philosophiæ & doctrinæ, quæ in Ecclesia traditur.
units.tr: I. The Decalogue must be understood according to the interpretation of Scripture, that is, according to the declaration of the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles, and not according to human or merely philosophical judgment. The explanation scattered throughout the Scriptures must be joined to it, and one must not cling to those brief precepts alone. Nor is moral philosophy sufficient for interpretation, since it contains only a part of the law. This is the one great difference between philosophy and the doctrine handed down in the Church.

units.la: II. Decalogus postulat in omnibus præceptis obedientiam interuam & externam, in mente, voluntate, corde & actionibus omnibus, perfectam, non tantum partibus, sed & gradibus, hoc est, vt non tantum omnibus officiis sed etiam omnibus officiorum gradibus perfectissimè DEO obtemperemus: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus. Lex spiritualis est. Qui irascitur fratri suo temerè, tenetur judicio, &c.
units.tr: II. The Decalogue requires inward and outward obedience in all its precepts, in mind, will, heart and all actions, and perfect obedience not only in parts but in degrees; that is, we must obey God most perfectly not only in all duties but in all degrees of each duty. "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things" (Gal. 3, 10). The law is spiritual (Rom. 7, 14). "Whoever is angry with his brother without cause is liable to judgment," etc. (Matt. 5, 22).

units.la: III. Primum præceptum debet includi in reliquis omnibus, hoc est, obedientia primi præcepti debet esse causa impulsiva & finalis obedientiæ reliquorum præceptorum omnium, alioquin non est cultus Dei, sed hypocrisis quicquid agimus: omnia siquidem, quæ præcipiuntur reliquis præceptis, facienda sunt ex dilectione Dei, & propter eam, hoc est, ideo quia Deum super omnia amamus, & vt ipsum celebremus.
units.tr: III. The first precept must be included in all the rest; that is, obedience to the first precept must be the impelling and final cause of obedience to all the other precepts. Otherwise, whatever we do is not the worship of God but hypocrisy. For everything commanded in the other precepts is to be done out of love for God and for his sake; that is, because we love God above all things, and so that we may praise him.

units.la: IV. Vt recte judicemus de sententia cuiusque præcepti, ante omnia scopum seu finem eius considerare oportet. Finis enim legis ostendit eius sententiam, & ex fine, quem Deus in quolibet præcepto intendit seu consequi voluit, de mediis ad illum consequendum recte & facile judicabimus. Regula hæc etiam in humanarum legum interpretatione valet, & eius plenior declaratio est in locis Theolog. D. Vrsini.
units.tr: IV. To judge rightly of the meaning of each precept, we must first of all consider its scope or end. For the end of a law shows its meaning, and from the end that God intends or wishes to attain in any precept, we will judge rightly and easily of the means of attaining it. This rule also holds in the interpretation of human laws, and a fuller explanation of it is found in the Theological Places of D. Ursinus.

units.la: V. Propter diuersos fines & respectus eadem virtus seu idem opus in diuersis præceptis præcipi potest: quia fines faciunt actionum discrimina, & eadem virtus potest diuersis scopis inseruire. Vt fortitudo est virtus sexti præcepti, & simul quinti, quia etiam requiritur in magistratu suscepturo defensionem aliorum. Tenenda est hæc regula, ne nos strictra nimium torqueamus in distinguendis & collocandis virtutibus.
units.tr: V. Because of different ends and respects, the same virtue or the same work can be commanded in different precepts, since ends make the distinction of actions, and one virtue can serve different purposes. Thus fortitude is a virtue of the sixth precept and also of the fifth, since it is required also in the magistrate who is to undertake the defence of others. This rule must be kept, so that we do not stretch the boundaries too tightly in distinguishing and assigning the virtues.

units.la: VI. In præceptis affirmatiuis negatiua: & in negatiuis affirmatiua continentur. Quod enim præcipitur, eius contrarium prohibetur: & quod prohibetur, eius contrarium præcipitur. Sic igitur in præceptione virtutum, semper prohibitio vitiorum includiincluditur, & vicissim. Vbi enim bonum aliquod mandatur, ibi malum in specie oppositum prohibetur, propterea quod bonum illud præstari non potest, nisi oppositum malum omittatur. Per malum autem non tantum actio mali, sed etiam omissio boni intelligitur.
units.tr: VI. Negative precepts are contained in affirmative ones, and affirmative in negative ones. For what is commanded, its contrary is forbidden; and what is forbidden, its contrary is commanded. So in the command of virtues the prohibition of the corresponding vices is always included, and conversely. For where some good is commanded, the evil opposed to it is forbidden, because that good cannot be performed unless the opposing evil is avoided. By evil, moreover, is understood not only the doing of evil but also the omission of good.

units.la: VII. Cauendum ne nimis angustè præcepta accipiamus. Semper igitur in genere etiam species omnes : in specie præcipua etiam cognatæ species ac totum genus : in effectu etiam causa, in relatiuo etiam correlatiuum intelligendum est. Ita cum homicidium vel adulterium prohibetur, omnis injusta læsio, & omnes vagæ libidines damnantur : cum præcipitur castitas, simul præcipitur temperantia, quæ est mater castitatis : cum præcipitur subiectio, simul præcipitur correlatiuum eius, nempe magistratus.
units.tr: VII. Care must be taken not to take the precepts too narrowly. Therefore, in the genus, all the species must always be understood; in a principal species, also the kindred species and the whole genus; in the effect, also the cause; in the relative, also the correlative. Thus when homicide or adultery is forbidden, every unjust injury and all wandering lusts are condemned; when chastity is commanded, temperance, which is the mother of chastity, is commanded at the same time; when subjection is commanded, its correlative, namely the magistrate, is commanded at the same time.

units.la: VIII. Præcepta secundæ tabulæ cedunt præceptis primæ tabulæ : & cæremonialia moralibus.
units.tr: VIII. The precepts of the second table yield to the precepts of the first table, and the ceremonial precepts yield to the moral.

units.la: Obiect. Secundum mandatum est simile primo. Ergo secunda tabula non cedit primæ. Respond. Fallacia à dicto secundum quid, vt simpliciter. Secundum est simile primo, non simpliciter, sed, sicut supra est explicatum, 1. In eodem genere cultus moralis, qui perpetuo anteponendus est cæremoniali. Cæremoniæ enim etiam officiis charitatis secundæ tabulæ cedere debent. 2. In eodem genere pœna æterna, quæ propter utriusque tabulæ violationem æquè infligitur. 3. In coherentia necessaria dilectionis Dei & proximi, tanquam causæ & effectus, qua fit, vt neutra sine altera præstari possit. Non enim amatur Deus, nisi & ametur proximus, nec verè amatur proximus, quin & ametur Deus. Si quis dixerit, diligo Deum, & fratrem suum oderit, mendax est. Qui enim non diligit fratrem suum, quem videt, Deum, quem non videt, quomodo potest diligere?
units.tr: Objection. The second commandment is like the first. Therefore the second table does not yield to the first. Answer. This is a fallacy of moving from what is said with a qualification to what is said without one. The second is like the first not absolutely, but, as explained above: 1. In the same kind of moral worship, which must always be placed before the ceremonial. For ceremonies must also yield to the duties of charity in the second table. 2. In the same kind of eternal punishment, which is equally inflicted for the violation of either table. 3. In the necessary connection of love of God and of neighbour, as cause and effect, whereby neither can be performed without the other. For God is not loved unless the neighbour is loved too, nor is the neighbour truly loved without God being loved as well. "If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?"

units.la: Atque hic est scopus Christi Matth.22. Pharisæi enim æquabant cæremonias diuinas & superstitiones suas obedientiæ secundæ tabulæ, quem errorem Christus corrigens dicit, secundam tabulam esse similem primæ tabulæ, hoc est, sicut obedientia primæ est moralis, spiritualis & principalis, sic etiam esse obedientiam secundæ, & sicut cæremoniæ cedunt primæ, sic etiam cedere secundæ.
units.tr: And this is Christ's purpose in Matthew 22. For the Pharisees made their divine ceremonies and their superstitions equal to obedience to the second table. Correcting this error, Christ says that the second table is like the first; that is, just as obedience to the first is moral, spiritual and principal, so too is obedience to the second, and just as the ceremonies yield to the first, so they also yield to the second.

units.la: Interim magna etiam est dissimilitudo inter præcepta primæ & secundæ tabulæ, 1. In obiectis. Primæ enim tabulæ obiectum est ipse Deus, secundæ proximus. Quanto igitur Deus maior est proximo, tanto maior est obedientia primæ tabulæ obedientiâ secundæ : & quanto proximus inferior est Deo, tanto magis obedientia secundæ tabulæ cedit obedientiæ primæ. 2. In ordine seu consequentia. Nam obedientia primæ tabulæ est maximè principalis: obedientia secundæ est minus principalis, & principali subseruiens. Nam ideo debemus diligere proximum, vt diligamus Deum: & illa obedientia est huius causa: hæc ex illa proficiscitur, non contra. Sic Christus: Qui non odit patrem & matrem, & suam ipsius animam propter me, non potest esse discipulus meus. Propter hanc duplicem & maximam dissimilitudinem rectè præcepta secundæ tabulæ cedunt præceptis primæ tabulæ.
units.tr: Yet there is also a great dissimilarity between the precepts of the first and second tables. 1. In the objects. For the object of the first table is God himself, and of the second the neighbour. The greater God is than the neighbour, the greater obedience to the first table is than obedience to the second; and the more inferior the neighbour is to God, the more obedience to the second table yields to obedience to the first. 2. In order or sequence. For obedience to the first table is the most principal; obedience to the second is less principal and serves the principal. For we ought to love our neighbour so that we may love God; that obedience is the cause of this one, and this one proceeds from that, not the reverse. So Christ: "Whoever does not hate father and mother, and even his own soul, for my sake, cannot be my disciple." On account of this double and greatest dissimilarity, the precepts of the second table rightly yield to the precepts of the first.

units.la: Inst. Officia dilectionis erga proximum non cedunt cæremoniis primæ tabulæ iuxta illud: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium, Officia dilectionis erga proximum sunt obedientia secundæ tabulæ. Ergo obedientia secundæ tabulæ non cedit obedientiæ primæ tabulæ. Resp. Plus est in conclusione, quàm in præmissis. Tantum sequitur: ergo officia secundæ tabulæ non cedunt cæremoniis primæ tabulæ: quod est verum, neq; euertit regulam. Ea enim de moralibus, non de cæremonialibus intelliguntur. Si igitur necessitas & salus proximi omissionē cęremoniæ postulat: hæc potius omittenda est, quàm illa negligenda. Et sic intelligendum est dictum: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium. Hactenus regulæ generales de recta interpretatione decalogi, sequitur de sententia singulorum præceptorum in specie.
units.tr: Objection. The duties of love toward the neighbour do not yield to the ceremonies of the first table, according to that saying: "I desire mercy, not sacrifice," The duties of love toward the neighbour are obedience of the second table. Therefore obedience of the second table does not yield to obedience of the first. Answer. There is more in the conclusion than in the premises. It follows only that the duties of the second table do not yield to the ceremonies of the first table, which is true and does not overturn the rule. For those sayings are to be understood of moral matters, not ceremonial ones. If therefore the necessity and welfare of the neighbour demand the omission of a ceremony, that should rather be omitted than the duty neglected. And so the saying must be understood: "I desire mercy, not sacrifice." So far the general rules for the right interpretation of the Decalogue; what follows concerns the meaning of the individual precepts.

units.la: PRIMI PRÆCEPTI sunt duæ partes: Præceptum & Præfatio. Præfationis verba sunt: Ego sum Iehoua Deus tuus, qui eduxi te è terra Ægypti, domo seruitutis. Præfatio hæc pertinet ad totum decalogum, qui describit & discernit Deum legislatorem ab omnibus creaturis, legumlatoribus & fictitiis numinibus, & continet tres rationes, cur & primi & sequentium præceptorum obedientia erga ipsum præstanda sit. 1. Dicit, se esse Iehouam, quo se verum Deum discernit ab omnibus creaturis, vt se summum iusque imperandi habere ostendat. Ego, inquit, quem videlicet audis loquentem & ferentem tibi leges. Sum Iehoua, hoc est, verus Deus à se & per se existens, & aliis rebus omnibus dans esse, coqi authoritatem omnibus imperandi summam habens, creator omnium, æternus, omnipotens, author & conseruator omnium bonorum. Ergo mihi obedias. 2. Dicit, se esse DEVM populi sui, vt promissione beneficentiæ nos ad obseruantiam magis alliciat. Est quidem Deus omnium creaturarum Deus, creatione, conseruatione & gubernatione: sed ecclesiæ Deus est peculiari, & communicatione sui. Deus enim protectione singulari, & communicatione sui. Deus enim prıè illorum est Deus, quos præ cæteris diligit: unde Dauid felicem prædicat eam gentem, quæ Deum habet pro Deo. Beata gens, cuius est Deus Iehoua: populus, quem elegit in hæreditatem sibi. Deus
units.tr: The FIRST PRECEPT has two parts: the precept and the preface. The words of the preface are: "I am Jehovah your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." This preface pertains to the whole Decalogue; it describes and distinguishes God the lawgiver from all creatures, from human lawgivers and from fictitious deities, and it contains three reasons why obedience is to be rendered to him, both to the first precept and to those that follow. 1. He says that he is Jehovah, by which he distinguishes himself as the true God from all creatures, to show that he has the highest authority and right to command. "I," he says, whom you hear speaking and giving you laws. I am Jehovah, that is, the true God, existing from himself and through himself, giving being to all other things, having supreme authority to command all, creator of all, eternal, almighty, author and preserver of all good things. Therefore obey me. 2. He says that he is the GOD of his people, so that by the promise of his beneficence he may draw us more readily to observance. He is indeed the God of all creatures, by creation, preservation and government; but he is the God of the Church in a peculiar way, by special protection and by communicating himself. For God is especially the God of those whom he loves above others; whence David pronounces happy the nation that has God for its God: "Blessed is the nation whose God is Jehovah, the people whom he has chosen for his own inheritance." God

units.la: Psal.33,12. Decalogi præfatio continet tres rationes obedientiæ. Deus ergo est Deus noster, quando eum agnoscimus talem, qualem se in verbo nobis patefecit, nempe, qui ad salutem nostram omnem suam potentiam, iustitiam, sapientiam & misericordiam conferat, & qui nos singulari amore prosequatur in filio.
units.tr: Psal. 33,12. The preface to the Decalogue contains three reasons for obedience. God is therefore our God when we acknowledge him as he has revealed himself to us in the Word: one who devotes all his power, justice, wisdom and mercy to our salvation, and who pursues us with singular love in the Son.

units.la: 3. Addit: qui eduxi te ex Ægypto: ut commemoratione recentis & insignis beneficij eos ad gratitudinem & obedientiam obligatos esse ostendat, & admoneat, quasi dicat: Ego sum is, qui me tibi patefeci, & te mihi tanto beneficio singulariter obstrinxi. Pertinet hoc etiam ad nos, quia mentione unius illustris liberationis, synecdochice omnes ecclesiæ liberationes complectitur, & cumprimis eam, quæ per Christum est facta, cuius illa liberatio fuit typus. His igitur epithetis Deus se opponit & creaturis omnibus, & idolis, sibi uni omnem obedientiam, honorem, & cultum vendicans.
units.tr: 3. He adds: who brought you out of Egypt, so that by recalling a recent and remarkable benefit he may show that they are bound to gratitude and obedience, and admonish them, as if to say: I am the one who revealed myself to you, and I have bound you to myself uniquely by so great a benefit. This also pertains to us, because by mention of one illustrious deliverance it embraces, by synecdoche, all the deliverances of the Church, and above all that which was made through Christ, of which that deliverance was a type. By these epithets, therefore, God sets himself against all creatures and idols, claiming for himself alone all obedience, honour and worship.

units.la: Nonnulli ex hac præfatione fecerant primum præceptum, & secundum ex sequentibus: non habebis Deos alienos in conspectu meo. Sed manifestum est, hæc verba: Ego sum Iehova Deus tuus, &c. non esse verba præcipientis, sed tantum aliquid de se commemorantis. Sequentia vero: non habebis, &c. habent formam præceptionis.
units.tr: Some had made the first commandment out of this preface, and the second out of what follows: "You shall have no other gods before me." But it is evident that the words "I am Jehovah your God, etc." are not words of command but only a recalling of something about himself. The following words, "You shall not have, etc.", have the form of a command.

units.la: Præceptum igitur est: non habebis Deos alienos in conspectu meo. Finis huius præcepti est, ut solum verum Deum in ecclesia patefactum agnoscamus, eiq; debitum honorem mente, voluntate & corde tribuamus. Porro hoc præceptum ita negatiuum est, ut contineat in se affirmatiuum: non habebis Deos alienos: sed me Iehovam illum in ecclesia patefactum solum habebis Deum. Est autem habere Deum, agnoscere quod sit Deus, quod sit unus, quod sit talis, qualem se in Ecclesia patefecit, & quod etiam erga nos sit talis: proinde ipsi soli fidere, summa humilitate & patientia, timore ac reverentia se illi subiicere: ipsum amare, & ab eo solo omnia bona exspectare. In hoc consistit obedientia huius præcepti, cuius partes sunt virtutes, quæ mox sequuntur. Deus alienus est res omnis, cui proprია attributa & opera veri Dei tribuuntur, cum tamen illa non habeat, neq; ei conveniant. Habere Deos alienos, est non habere verum Deum, hoc est, aut nullum, aut plures, aut alium, quam patefactum Deum habere: aut Deum non agnoscere talem, qualem se patefecit, aut non fidere Deo, nec se Deo bona sperare, ipsum non amare aut reuereri. Huius impietatis partes sunt vitia virtutibus, quæ mox sequentur, opposita. Co-ram me, vel in conspectu meo, quasi dicat: non tantum in conspectu hominum gestibus vel verbis, sed nec tantum intus in arcano tcrecessu cordis tui: quia coram facie mea nihil est occultum, sed mihi cordium & renum scrutatori omnia patent, & prorsus sunt manifesta.
units.tr: The commandment, therefore, is: you shall have no other gods before me. The purpose of this commandment is that we acknowledge the only true God, revealed in the Church, and render him the honour due with mind, will and heart. Moreover, this commandment is negative in such a way that it contains an affirmative within it: you shall not have other gods; but you shall have me, Jehovah, revealed in the Church, as your only God. To have God is to acknowledge that he is God, that he is one, that he is such as he has revealed himself in the Church, and that he is such towards us as well; hence to trust in him alone, to submit oneself to him with the utmost humility and patience, with fear and reverence, to love him, and to expect all good things from him alone. In this consists the obedience of this commandment, whose parts are the virtues that immediately follow. An other god is any thing to which the proper attributes and works of the true God are ascribed, although it has neither those attributes nor those works, nor do they belong to it. To have other gods is not to have the true God, that is, to have either none, or several, or another than the God revealed; or not to acknowledge God as he has revealed himself, or not to trust in God, nor to hope for good things from him, nor to love or revere him. The parts of this impiety are the vices opposed to the virtues that immediately follow. "Before me" (coram me, in conspectu meo) is as if he said: not only in the sight of men by gestures or words, but not even only inwardly in the hidden recesses of your heart; for nothing is hidden before my face, but all things lie open and wholly manifest to me, the searcher of hearts and reins.

units.la: Facilima ratio explicandi singula praecepta est, distributio obedientiae cuiusque praecepti in suas virtutes tanquam partes, adiunctis deinde vitiis, quae virtutibus iisdem sunt opposita. Partes igitur obedientiae primi huius praecepti sunt virtutes sequentes: agnitio Dei, fides, spes, dilectio Dei, timor Dei, humilitas & patientia. Hae virtutes praecipiuntur, & harum contraria vitia prohibentur.
units.tr: The easiest way to explain the individual commandments is to distribute the obedience due to each commandment into its virtues as parts, and then to add the vices opposed to those same virtues. The parts of obedience to this first commandment are therefore the following virtues: knowledge of God, faith, hope, love of God, fear of God, humility and patience. These virtues are enjoined, and their contrary vices are forbidden.

units.la: I. AGNITIO DEI, est ita sentire de Deo, sicut se verbo & operibus patefecit, & ea cognitione ad fiduciam, dilectionem, timorem, & cultum illius veri Dei moveri & excitari. De hac dicitur: Quomodo credent, de quo non audierunt? Haec est vita aeterna, ut te solum cognoscant esse verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum.
units.tr: I. THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD is to think of God as he has revealed himself by word and works, and by that knowledge to be moved and stirred to trust, love, fear and worship that true God. Of this it is said: "How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? This is eternal life, that they know you to be the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent."

units.la: Extrema seu vitia huic virtuti repugnantia sunt plura.
units.tr: The extremes, or vices opposed to this virtue, are several.

units.la: 1. Ignorantia veri Dei, & voluntatis eius, quae est, non scire de Deo, aut de illis dubitare, quae ex creatoris beneficio, & patefactionibus divinis scire debemus. Estque vel innata insciitia eorum, quae propter naturae pravitatem ignoramus, aut intelligere non possumus, vel affectata ignoratio eorum, quae conscientia dictat esse inquirenda, nec tamen serio discendi ac Deo obtemperandi studio inquiruntur. De utraque dicitur: Non est, qui intelligat, non est, qui inquirat Deum. Animalis homo non intelligit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei.
units.tr: 1. Ignorance of the true God and of his will, which is not to know about God, or to doubt those things which we ought to know from the Creator's benefit and from divine revelations. This is either the innate ignorance of those things which, on account of the depravity of nature, we do not know or cannot understand; or the affected ignorance of those things which conscience dictates should be sought, yet which are not sought with earnest zeal for learning and for obeying God. Of both it is said: "There is none who understands, there is none who seeks God." "The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God."

units.la: 2. Errores & falsae opiniones de Deo: ut cum alij fingunt, nullum esse Deum: alij plures deos comminiscuntur, ut olim Ethnici, Manichaei, &c. aut si non profitentur, tamen reipsa plures faciunt, dum solius Dei propria creaturis tribuunt, ut qui angelos vel homines demortuos invocant in papatu. Invocatio enim tribuit ei, qui invocatur, infinitam sapientiam & potentiam. Unde Paulus eos, qui invocant creaturas, dicit mutare gloriam inuisibilis Dei in effigiatam imaginem hominis mortalis, & volucrum, quadrupedum, & reptilium: item mutare veritatem Dei in mendacium, dum colunt & serviunt rebus creatis praeterito creatore. Ideo angelus à Johanne non vult adorari, & hanc affert rationem: Quia conservus tuus sum, & vnus ex fratribus tuis, qui habent testimonium Iesu: Deum adora, &c. Pari modo falsas de Deo opiniones fingunt, & à vero Deo aberrant, qui Deum quidem vnum agnoscunt, sed non verum, qui se in Evangelio patefecit: ut Philosophi saniores, & Mahumetani. Item, qui verum quidem Deum se agnoscere profitentur, sed tamen à vero Deo aberrant, & eius loco colunt idolum, quod sibi fingunt, quia alium hunc Deum imaginantur, quam ipse in verbo se esse ostendit: vt Iudæi, Samosatenici, Ariani, & pneumatomachi, &c. Qui non honorat filium, non honorat patrem. Quisquis negat filium, is nec patrem habet.
units.tr: 2. Errors and false opinions about God: as when some pretend that there is no God, others invent several gods, as the heathen of old, the Manichaeans, etc.; or if they do not profess this, yet in fact they make several, while they ascribe to creatures what belongs to God alone, as do those who invoke angels or dead men in the papacy. For invocation ascribes to the one invoked infinite wisdom and power. Hence Paul says that those who invoke creatures change the glory of the invisible God into the image of mortal man, and of birds, four-footed beasts and reptiles; likewise they change the truth of God into a lie, while they worship and serve created things and pass over the Creator. Therefore the angel in John did not want to be worshipped, and gives this reason: "Because I am your fellow servant, and one of your brethren who have the testimony of Jesus: worship God, etc." In the same way those go astray from the true God and form false opinions about him who acknowledge a God, but not the true one, who revealed himself in the Gospel: such as the more sober philosophers and the Mahumetans. Likewise those who profess to acknowledge the true God, yet stray from him and in his place worship an idol they fashion for themselves, because they imagine this God to be other than he shows himself to be in his Word: such as the Jews, the Samosatenes, the Arians and the Pneumatomachians, etc. "He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father. Whoever denies the Son, he does not have the Father either."

units.la: 3. Magia, quæ inprimis pugnat cum agnitione Dei. Est enim fœdus seu pactum cum diabolo Dei hoste, adhibitis certis verbis aut cæremoniis initum, vt hoc vel illud facientes aut dicentes, accipiant à diabolo promissa, eaque quæ à solo Deo sunt petenda & accipienda: vt nimirum diaboli ope cognoscant aut efficiant res non necessarias, vel ad explendas malas cupiditates, vel ad ostentationem, vel ad vitæ commoditatem, spectantes. Magus est vox Persica, significans philosophum vel doctorem. Sed homines videntes suam ignorantiam, accersiuerunt operam diaboli: inde nomen hæsit in vituperio, & Magia vsurpari cœpit pro eo, quod nos vocamus Zauberey.
units.tr: 3. Magic, which above all fights against the knowledge of God. For it is a pact or covenant with the devil, the enemy of God, entered into by means of certain words or ceremonies, so that by doing or saying this or that they may receive from the devil the things promised, which are to be sought and received from God alone: namely, that by the devil's help they may know or bring about unnecessary things, either to satisfy evil desires, or for display, or for the comforts of life. Magus is a Persian word, meaning philosopher or teacher. But men, seeing their own ignorance, sought the devil's work; thence the name stuck in disgrace, and Magic began to be used for what we call witchcraft.

units.la: Ad magiam pertinent incantationes. quæ sunt vsurpatio verborum & cæremoniarum ex pacto cum diabolo, quibus dictis vel factis diabolus efficiat, quod incantatores volunt. In ipsis verbis & cæremoniis nulla inest efficacia, sed diabolus ipse promissa perficit, hoc fine, vt homines à Deo ad ipsum deficiant, & ipsum pro Deo colant. Damnantur autem non solum ipsi magi & incantatores, sed etiam qui horum opera vtuntur, seu magicolæ. De vtrisque enim dicit Deus in lege: Vir siue mulier, in quibus fuerit python, vel ariolorum spiritus, moriendo morietur. Non inuenietur in medio tui magus & incantator, congregans congregationem, consulens pythonem, ariolos, & qui seiscitatur à mortuis. Abominationi enim est Iehoua quisquis facit hæc, &c.
units.tr: To magic belong incantations, which are the use of words and ceremonies under a pact with the devil, by which, when they are said or done, the devil brings about what the enchanters want. There is no efficacy in the words and ceremonies themselves; the devil himself performs what is promised, with this aim: that men may fall away from God to him and worship him in God's place. And condemned are not only the magicians and enchanters themselves, but also those who make use of their work, the magic-users. For God speaks of both in the law: a man or woman in whom there is a python or a spirit of divination shall surely die. There shall not be found among you a magician or enchanter, one who gathers a gathering, one who consults a python, diviners, or one who inquires of the dead. For whoever does these things is an abomination to Jehovah, etc.

units.la: 4. Superstitio, quæ est, certis rebus vel obseruationibus gentium aut verborum tribuere effectus, qui neque rationibus physicis aut politicis, neque verbo Dei niituntur, & vel non sequntur, vel à diabolo & aliis causis fiunt, quam existimatur. Etsi autem non est pactum cum diabolo: est tamen idololatria. Comprehenduntur sub hoc vitio etiam auguria, obseruationes somniorum, diuinationes, signa & prædictiones ariolorum, quæ omnia disertis verbis in scriptura damnantur.
units.tr: 4. Superstition is ascribing effects to certain things, observances of the heathen, or words, which rest neither on physical or political reasons nor on the Word of God, and which either do not follow, or come about from the devil or from other causes than is thought. Although there is no pact with the devil, it is nevertheless idolatry. Under this vice are also included augury, observation of dreams, divinations, signs and predictions of soothsayers, all of which are condemned in express words in Scripture.

units.la: 5. Omnis fiducia in creaturis collata, quæ veræ agnitioni Dei manifestè repugnat, quandoquidem qui eam ad creaturas transfert, reuera plures Deos fingit. Vnde Deus in verbo suo simpliciter damnat omnes, qui vel in hominibus, vel in opibus & diuitiis, vel in vllis rebus creatis fiduciam collocant. Et sic huius vitii nomine etiam auaritia damnatur.
units.tr: 5. Every trust placed in creatures clearly contradicts the true knowledge of God, since whoever transfers trust to creatures in fact invents several gods. Hence God in his Word simply condemns all who place their trust in men, or in wealth and riches, or in any created things. And so under the name of this vice covetousness is also condemned.

units.la: 6. Idololatria, quæ quæstione xcv. definitur. Sunt autem duæ species idololatriæ. Vna cum professione colitur alius, quam verus Deus: seu, cum colitur pro Deo id, quod non est Deus. Hæc est apertior & crassior, & proprie pertinet ad hoc primum præceptum. Altera cum non professione colitur alius Deus, sed erratur in modo cultus, hoc est, cum verus quidem Deus colitur, sed alio modo, quam quo se in secundo præcepto, & passim in verbo suo coli præcepit. Hæc subtilior est, & à secundo præcepto damnatur. Qui enim Deum colunt ad statuas, etiamsi negent, sc colere alium præter verum Deum, tamen nihilominus sunt idololatræ. Fingunt enim talem Deum, qui velit coli ad statuas: proinde mutant voluntatem Dei. Mutata autem voluntate Dei, mutatur ipse Deus.
units.tr: 6. Idolatry, which is defined in question 95. There are two kinds of idolatry. In the first, another than the true God is worshipped openly, or that which is not God is worshipped as God. This is the more obvious and gross kind, and properly pertains to this first commandment. In the second, another God is not openly worshipped, but there is error in the mode of worship: that is, the true God is indeed worshipped, but in a way other than that which he commands in the second commandment and throughout his Word. This kind is subtler, and is condemned by the second commandment. For those who worship God by means of images, even if they deny that they worship any other than the true God, are nevertheless idolaters. For they feign a God who wishes to be worshipped by images; thus they change the will of God. But when the will of God is changed, God himself is changed.

units.la: 7. Contemtus Dei, qui est, cognita quidem de Deo habere, quæ sunt vera, sed iis ad ipsum diligendum & colendum non permoueri: seu, est agnoscere quidem unum verum Deum in Ecclesia patefactum, sed tamen hac agnitione ad Dei amorem, cultum, timorem & fiduciam non excitari. Neque enim notitia veri Dei sufficit, sed accedere oportet permotionem illam, alioqui etiam diaboli & gentes veram Dei agnitionem haberent, quod Apostolus negat: Sunt inexcusabiles propterea, quod cum Deum cognouerint, tamen vt Deum non glorificauerunt, neque gratias ei egerunt, &c.
units.tr: 7. Contempt of God, which is to have indeed true knowledge of God, but not to be moved by it to love and worship him; or, it is to acknowledge indeed the one true God revealed in the Church, but not to be stirred by this knowledge to love, worship, fear and trust in God. For knowledge of the true God is not enough; that emotion must accompany it, otherwise even the devils and the Gentiles would have true knowledge of God, which the Apostle denies: "They are therefore inexcusable, because when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor gave thanks to him, etc." (Rom. 1.)

units.la: II. FIDES est certa persuasio, qua assentimur omni verbo Dei nobis tradito, & quasi statuimus, promissionem gratuitæ misericordiæ Dei propter Christum ad nos pertinere; & fiducia accipiens hoc beneficium Dei, & in eo acquiescens, accensa in mentibus, voluntatibus & cordibus electorum à Spiritu sancto, per verbum Dei, & in illis efficiens lætitiam in Deo, inuocationem Dei, & obedientiam, secundum omnia Dei præcepta: Credite in Dominum Deum vestrum, & securi eritis.
units.tr: II. Faith is a certain persuasion by which we assent to every word of God delivered to us, and as it were establish that the promise of God's free mercy on account of Christ pertains to us; and trust, receiving this benefit of God and resting in it, kindled in the minds, wills and hearts of the elect by the Holy Spirit through the Word of God, and producing in them joy in God, invocation of God, and obedience to all God's commands: "Believe in the Lord your God, and you shall be secure." (2 Chron. 20.)

units.la: In defectu fidei repugnat 1. Incredulitas, quæ auditis & cognitis sententiis de Deo non assentitur. 2. Dubitatio, quæ neque assentitur firmiter doctrinæ de Deo, neque omnino repugnat, sed fluctuans nunc in unam, nunc in alteram partem languidè inclinat. 3. Diffidentia, quæ notitiam de Deo & promissiones diuinas ad se non applicat, ac metu defectionis diuinæ ab officio recedit, & quærit præsidia extra Deum. De his omnibus dictum est: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem eum facit, quia non credit testimonio, quo testificatus est Deus de Filio suo, &c. 4. Fides hypocritica, & defectio à fide, quæ est assentiri doctrinæ Ecclesiæ, eiusque cognitione lætari ad tempus, sed sine applicatione & fiducia promissionis gratiæ diuinæ, & sine regeneratione: ac propterea ratiotationibus, vel aliis causis vinci, & illum assensum ac professionem pietatis rursus abijcere: Qui in petrosa semen excepit, est qui sermonem audit, & eum statim in gaudio accipit: non habet autem radicem in se: sed temporarius est, ortaque oppressione vel persecutione propter sermonem, statim offenditur. Ad tempus credunt, & tempore tentationis deficiunt. Etiam Simon credidit, &c.
units.tr: Opposed to faith in defect are: (1) unbelief, which does not assent to the statements about God when they are heard and known; (2) doubt, which neither assents firmly to the doctrine concerning God nor wholly opposes it, but wavers now to one side, now to the other, and leans weakly; (3) diffidence, which does not apply the knowledge of God and the divine promises to oneself, and out of fear that God will fail withdraws from duty and seeks aids outside God. Of all these it is said: "He who does not believe God makes him a liar, because he does not believe the testimony by which God has testified concerning his Son, etc." (1 John 5.) (4) Hypocritical faith and falling away from faith, which is to assent to the doctrine of the Church, and to rejoice for a time in knowing it, but without applying and trusting the promise of divine grace, and without regeneration; and therefore it is overcome by arguments or other causes, and casts off again that assent and profession of piety: "He who received the seed on stony ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself, but is temporary, and when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, he is immediately offended. They believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away." Simon also believed, etc.

units.la: In excessu fidei repugnat 1. Tentatio Dei, quæ est, ex incredulitate, aut diffidentia, aut contemtu Dei, & fiducia aut studio propriæ sapientiæ, justitiæ, potentiæ aut gloriæ, discedere à verbo & ordine divino, atque ita experimentum capere divinæ veritatis aut potentiæ, ac Deum contumaciter & superbè ad iram provocare: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Neque tentemus Christum, sicut quidam eorum tentarunt, & à serpentibus perierunt. An ad iram Dominum provocabimus? an validiores eo sumus? 2. Securitas carnalis, quæ est, sine cogitatione de Deo & ipsius voluntate, & de infirmitate sua, & de periculis suis, & sine aguitione ac deploratione peccatorum suorum, & sine timore Dei viuere, & tamen immunitatem ab ira Dei, & à pœnis sibi polliceri. De his prædicitur: Sicut erant dies Noæ, ita erit & adventus Filij hominis: sicut enim diebus, qui præcesserunt diluuium, edebant, bibebant, uxores ducebant, & nuptum dabant, ad eum usque diem, quo ingressus est Noa in arcam, nec cognouerunt diluuium, usque dum venisset, & diluisset omnes: ita erit & adventus Filij hominis.
units.tr: Opposed to excess of faith are: (1) tempting God, which arises from unbelief, diffidence, or contempt of God, and from trust in or zeal for one's own wisdom, righteousness, power or glory; it departs from the Word and divine order, and so tests the truth or power of God, and stubbornly and proudly provokes God to anger: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." "Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted and perished by serpents." "Shall we provoke the Lord to anger? Are we stronger than he?" (1 Cor. 10.) (2) Carnal security, which is to live without thought of God and his will, of one's own weakness and one's dangers, and without acknowledgment and lamentation of one's sins, and without fear of God, yet to promise oneself immunity from God's wrath and punishments. Of such people it is foretold: "As the days of Noah were, so will the coming of the Son of man be; for as in the days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying wives and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and they did not know of the flood until it came and swept them all away: so will the coming of the Son of man be." (Matt. 24.)

units.la: III. Spes est expectatio certa vitæ æternæ propter Christum gratis dandæ, & mitigationis præsentium malorum, & liberationis ab aliis, juxta consilium & voluntatem Dei. De hac dicitur: Integrè sperate in eam, quæ ad vos defertur, gratiam, in patefactione Iesu Christi. Spes non confundit.
units.tr: III. Hope is a certain expectation of eternal life, to be given freely on account of Christ, together with the alleviation of present evils and deliverance from others, according to the counsel and will of God. Of this it is said: "Hope perfectly in the grace that is brought to you in the revelation of Jesus Christ. Hope does not disappoint."

units.la: Oritur autem spes ex fide: qui certus de præsenti Dei erga se voluntate, certus est etiam de futura, cum Deus non mutetur. Dona enim & vocatio Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα. Differunt verò spes & fides: quod fides amplectitur præsentia Dei beneficia, & voluntatem eius erga nos. Spes amplectitur præsentis & perpetuæ voluntatis divinæ effectus futuros. Sicut dicitur: Fides est rerum sperandarum fiducia, & demonstratio rerum non apparentium. Spe salui facti sumus: spes autem, quæ videtur, non est spes, &c.
units.tr: Hope arises from faith: whoever is certain of God's present will toward himself is certain also of his future will, since God does not change. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance [ἀμεταμέλητα]. Hope and faith differ, however, in that faith embraces God's present benefits and his will toward us, while hope embraces the future effects of his present and perpetual will. As it is said: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. We were saved by hope; but hope that is seen is not hope, etc."

units.la: Spei repugnat in defectu, 1. Desperatio: quæ est, peccata sua maiora æstimare, quam meritum Filij Dei, & misericordiam Dei in Filio mediatore oblatam repudiare, ideoque non expectare beneficia credentibus promissa, sed horribili sensu iræ metu futuræ abiectionis in pœnas æternas cruciari, & Deum, tanquam crudelem tyrannum, exhorrescere atque odisse: ut
units.tr: Opposed to hope in defect is (1) despair, which is to judge one's sins greater than the merit of the Son of God, and to reject the mercy of God offered in the Son as Mediator, and so not to expect the benefits promised to believers, but to be tormented by a horrible sense of God's anger and the fear of future rejection into eternal punishments, and to dread and hate God as a cruel tyrant, as

units.la: Cain exclamat: Maior est iniquitas mea, quam vt remittatur. Ab hac dehortatur nos Paulus: Ne doleatis, sicut ceteri, qui spem non habent. Vbi auctum est peccatum, ibi superabundauit gratia. 2. Dubitaito de futuris beneficiis expressis in verbo, aut de vita aeterna, de defensione ac liberatione in tentationibus, deque perseuerantia finali.
units.tr: Cain cries out: "My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven." From this Paul dissuades us: "Do not grieve as the others do, who have no hope." "Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more." (2) Doubt about the future benefits expressed in the Word, or about eternal life, or about defence and deliverance in temptations, and about final perseverance.

units.la: In excessu repugnat spei, Securitas spiritualis: quae paulo ante definita. Sicut autem haec passim in verbo Dei damnantur, ita securitas spiritualis commendatur, & in omnibus piis requiritur, quae nimirum nos aduersus omnes conscientiae pauores de gratia Dei confirmat, & nihil est aliud, nisi fides & spes coniuncta cum vera resipiscentia, quae non metuit defectionem, aut abiectionem a Deo, propter certitudinem de immutabili Dei voluntate & fauore erga se. De hac dicitur: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, quomodo non omnia etiam cum eo nobis gratificabitur?
units.tr: Opposed to hope in excess is spiritual security, which was defined a little above. As these are condemned throughout God's Word, so spiritual security is commended and required in all the godly, for it confirms us against all fears of conscience concerning God's grace, and is nothing other than faith and hope joined with true repentance, which does not fear falling away or rejection by God, on account of the certainty of God's unchangeable will and favour toward oneself. Of this it is said: "If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?"

units.la: IV. DILECTIO DEI est Deum agnoscere summe bonum, & summe beneficum, & misericordem non solum in se, sed etiam erga nos, & propterea cum summe amare, & coniunctionem atque conformitatem cum ipso, & voluntatis ipsius executionem magis expetere, quam omnes alias res, & promptum esse ad omnia, quae amamus, in gratiam ipsius amittenda. Seu, est, ex agnitione infinitae bonitatis Dei eum sic amare, vt malimus omnia amittere, quam ipsius communione carere, aut eum vllain re offendere. Duo enim complectitur vera dilectio. 1. Studium salutis & conseruationis eius rei, quae amatur. 2. Velle ei vniri, seu eam sibi coniungi. De hac dicitur: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo, &c. Si quis venit ad me, & non edit patrem suum, & matrem suam, & uxorem, atque adeo etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Dilectioni repugnat in defectu, 1. Abiectio amoris Dei, seu contemtus & odium Dei, quod est, propter naturae auersionem a Deo & justitia Dei, & propter inclinationem ad peccandum fugere Deum accusantem & punientem peccata, eique irasci. De hoc peccato dicitur: Intelligentia carnis inimicitia est aduersus Deum. Legi enim Dei non subditur: nam ne potest quidem. 2. Amor sui aut creaturarum inordinatus, qui est suas cupiditates, aut voluptates, aut vitam, aut gloriam, aut alias res anteferre Deo, & ipsius voluntati & gloriae, ac malle ipsum negligere & offendere, quam res illas, quas amamus, amittere. Qui amat patrem aut matrem supra me, non est me dignus. 3. Simulatio amoris DEI. In excessu dilectione (nisi superstitione) peccari vix potest: quia nunquam tam valde diligimus Deum, vel proximum, quam debemus.
units.tr: IV. THE LOVE OF GOD is to acknowledge God as the highest good, the highest benefactor, and merciful not only in himself but also toward us; and therefore to love him above all things, to desire union and conformity with him and the carrying out of his will more than all other things, and to be ready to lose everything we love for his sake. Or, it is to love God, from the recognition of his infinite goodness, in such a way that we would rather lose everything than go without his fellowship or offend him in anything. True love embraces two things: 1. zeal for the safety and preservation of the thing loved; 2. the will to be united with it, or joined to it. Of this it is said: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc. If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, and his mother, and his wife, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Opposed to love, by way of defect, are: 1. the rejection of the love of God, that is, contempt and hatred of God, which arises from the nature's aversion to God and the justice of God, and from an inclination to sin, to flee from God who accuses and punishes sins, and to be angry with him. Of this sin it is said: The wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can be. 2. Inordinate love of self or of creatures, which is to prefer one's own desires, pleasures, life, glory, or other things to God, and to his will and glory, and to choose to neglect and offend him rather than lose those things we love. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. 3. Pretence of love for God. In excess, love (unless it becomes superstition) can hardly go wrong, because we never love God or our neighbour as much as we ought.

units.la: V. Timor Dei est agnoscere iram Dei immensam aduersus peccatum, & potentiam eius ad puniendum, & pro summo malo ducere offensionem Dei, & alienationem ab ipso, ac propterea summè odisse ac detestari peccatum, & ad quaevis alia mala ferenda potius paratum esse, quam Deum in re vlla offendere velle. Seu: est ex agnitione sapientiae, potentiae, iustitiae & iuris Dei, quod habet in omnes creaturas, & ex subiectione erga eum, nolle ipsum offendere. De hac dicitur: Timebis tibi à Deo tuo: Ego Iehova. Quis non timebit te ô Rex gentium? Tuum est enim decus inter omnes gentium sapientes, & in universis regnis illorum nullus est similis tui.
units.tr: V. The FEAR OF GOD is to acknowledge God's immense wrath against sin and his power to punish it, to regard offence against God and estrangement from him as the greatest evil, and therefore to hate and detest sin above all things, and to be readier to endure any other evil than to be willing to offend God in any matter. Or: it is, from the recognition of the wisdom, power, justice and right of God, which he has over all creatures, and from submission to him, to be unwilling to offend him. Of this it is said: You shall fear the Lord your God: I am Jehovah. Who shall not fear you, O King of the nations? For among all the wise of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, there is none like you.

units.la: Obiect. Summum bonum non potest timeri: quia timor est fuga mali. Deus est summum bonum. Non ergo potest timeri. Resp. ad maiorem. Non potest timeri summum bonum, nempe, quatenus tale est: sed hoc respectu, quatenus etiam est aliud quid. Sic Deus timetur, non quatenus est summum bonum, (sic enim diligitur) sed quatenus etiam est iustus, & potens ad puniendum: seu timetur respectu mali destructionis & poenae, quod potest infligere.
units.tr: Objection: The highest good cannot be feared, because fear is the flight from evil. God is the highest good. Therefore he cannot be feared. Reply to the major: the highest good cannot be feared as such, that is, insofar as it is the highest good; but it can be feared in this respect, insofar as it is also something else. Thus God is feared not as the highest good (for so he is loved), but insofar as he is also just and able to punish; that is, he is feared with respect to the evil of destruction and punishment which he can inflict.

units.la: Timor & dilectio Dei differunt. Nam 1. Dilectio persequitur bonum, videlicet Deum & coniunctionem cum eo: Timor auersatur malum, videlicet offensam & iram Dei, & auulsionem ab ipso: seu, dilectio est, nolle priuari summo bono: timor est, cauere summi boni offensam. 2. Dilectio oritur ex agnitione bonitatis Dei: timor ex agnitione potentiae, iustitiae & iuris, quod habet in omnes creaturas.
units.tr: The fear and love of God differ. For 1. love pursues a good, namely God and union with him; fear shrinks from an evil, namely the offence and wrath of God and separation from him. That is, love is unwillingness to be deprived of the highest good; fear is caution lest we offend the highest good. 2. Love arises from the recognition of God's goodness; fear from the recognition of his power, justice and right over all creatures.

units.la: Differt etiam timor Dei, qui erat in natura hominis integra, ab eo, qui nunc est in renatis in hac vita. Timor Dei in natura integra, qualis nunc est, & erit in beatis angelis & hominibus in vita aeterna, est auersatio summa peccati & poenarum peccati, sed sine dolore: quia neque peccatum in ipsis est, neque poena peccati, & certi sunt nunquam fore, vt peccent, aut puniantur: Praecipitabit mortem in sempiternum, & auferet Deus omnem lachrymam ab omni facie. Timor Dei in renatis in hac vita, est agnitio peccati & irae Dei, & dolor serius propter offensionem Dei & calamitates, quas propter peccatum nos & alij sustinemus, & metus futurorum peccatorum & poenarum: & ardens studium effugiendi haec mala, propter agnitionem misericordiae Dei, nobis per Christum praestitae. De hoc dicitur: Neque tu times Deum? Timete eum, qui potest potest corpus & animam perdere in gehenna. Hic timor vsitatè vocatur filialis, quia talis est, qualis filiorum erga parentes, qui dolent propter iram & offensionem patris, & metuunt, ne porro offendant eum, & puniantur: & tamen de amore & animo patris erga se perpetuò persuasi sunt: ideoque amant eum, & propter hunc amorem illius, quem offenderunt, acrius dolent, vt de Petro dicitur: Egressus flevit amare.
units.tr: The fear of God which existed in man's integral nature also differs from that which is now in the regenerate in this life. The fear of God in integral nature, such as it now is and will be in the blessed angels and men in eternal life, is a supreme aversion to sin and to the punishments of sin, but without grief, because there is neither sin in them nor punishment for sin, and they are certain that they will never sin or be punished: He will swallow up death for ever, and the Lord God will wipe away tears from every face. The fear of God in the regenerate in this life is the recognition of sin and of God's wrath, and a grave sorrow on account of the offence against God and the calamities which we and others suffer because of sin, and the dread of future sins and punishments, together with an ardent zeal to escape these evils, from the recognition of God's mercy bestowed on us through Christ. Of this it is said: Do you not fear God? Fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell. This fear is commonly called filial, because it is like the fear of children toward their parents, who grieve at their father's anger and offence and dread lest they offend him further and be punished; and yet they are always persuaded of their father's love and goodwill toward them, and so they love him, and because of this love they grieve all the more sharply at having offended him. Thus it is said of Peter: He went out and wept bitterly.

units.la: A timore filiali multum differt timor servilis, qualis est servorum erga heros, & est fugere poenas, sine fide & sine desiderio aut studio mutandi vitam, cum desperatione, & fuga Dei, & aversione ab ipso. 1. Filialis provenit ex fiducia & dilectione Dei. Servilis oritur ex agnitione & accusatione peccati, & sensu judicij atq; irae Dei. 2. Filialis principaliter aversatur offensionem Dei siue peccatum, sed non ipsum Deum. Servilis est fuga & odium ipsius non peccati, sed poenarum & judicij divini, ac proinde ipsius Dei. 3. Filialis coniunctus est cum certitudine salutis & vitae aeternae. Servilis est metus & exspectatio aeternae damnationis & abiectionis à Deo, tanto maior, quanto maior est dubitatio vel desperatio de gratia & misericordia Dei. Hic timor est in diabolo & impiis, estque initium aeternae mortis, quod impij sentiunt in hac vita: Vocem tuam audiui, & timui. Daemones credunt & cortremiscunt.
units.tr: Far different from filial fear is servile fear, which is the fear of slaves toward a master, and is the flight from punishments without faith and without desire or zeal to change one's life, with despair and flight from God and aversion from him. 1. Filial fear arises from trust in and love of God; servile fear arises from the recognition and accusation of sin, and from the sense of God's judgment and wrath. 2. Filial fear is chiefly averse to the offence of God, or sin, but not to God himself; servile fear is a flight from and hatred of not sin but punishment and divine judgment, and therefore of God himself. 3. Filial fear is joined with certainty of salvation and eternal life; servile fear is the dread and expectation of eternal damnation and of rejection by God, the greater as doubt or despair about the grace and mercy of God is greater. This fear is in the devil and the wicked, and it is the beginning of eternal death, which the wicked feel even in this life: I heard your voice, and I was afraid. The demons believe and tremble.

units.la: Notandum, saepe in scriptura, dilectionem, & timorem Dei sumi pro cultu Dei, seu obedientia universali erga omnia Dei mandata: Per hoc cognoscimus, nos diligere filios Dei, cum nos Deum diligimus, & mandata eius seruamus. Finis mandati est charitas ex corde puro, & conscientia bona, & fide non simulata. Initium sapientiae timor Domini.&c. Ratio est quia dilectio & timor Dei, cum ex fide & spe nascantur, sunt causae totius obedientiae. Qui enim vere diligunt & timent Deum, nolunt eum vlla re offendere, & studeant omnia ipsi grata facere.
units.tr: It should be noted that in Scripture the love and fear of God are often taken for the worship of God, or universal obedience to all God's commands: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and keep his commandments. The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, etc. The reason is that the love and fear of God, since they spring from faith and hope, are the causes of all obedience. For those who truly love and fear God are unwilling to offend him in anything, and strive to do all things pleasing to him.
