units.la: Timori Dei repugnat in defectu prophanitas & securitas carnalis: contemtus Dei. In excessu timor servilis & desperatio, de quibus prius dictum est.
units.tr: Opposed to the fear of God, by way of defect, are profanity and carnal security, which is contempt of God. In excess are servile fear and despair, of which we have spoken before.

units.la: VI. HVMILITAS seu ταπεινοφροσύνη, est, agnoscere, quod bona omnia, quae in nobis sunt, & per nos fiunt, non ex dignitate aut facultate aliqua nostra, sed ex gratuita Dei bonitate existant, atque ita ex agnitione maiestatis divinae & nostrae infirmitatis ac indignitatis se Deo subijcere, ipsi soli tribuere gloriam omnium bonorum, quae in nobis sunt, ideoque vere Deum timere, & agnoscere ac deplorare suos defectus ac vitia, non appetere locum altiorem, nec donis, sed solo Dei auxilio confisum intra vocationem suam se continere, non despicere alios prae se, nec impedire eos in suo officio faciendo, sed agnoscere, aliis etiam esse aut fieri posse organa Dei salutaria, ideoque locum & honorem suum libenter ipsis tribuere, & ipsis cedere, non tribuere sibi vel tentare maiora viribus suis, nec affectare excellentiam supra alios, sed contentum esse donis & loco a Deo sibi concessis, & omnia dona & studia sua conferre ad gloriam Dei, & salutem proximorum, etiam inferiorum & indignorum, nec fremere aduersus Deum, si frustremur spe, aut contemnamur, sed Deo sapientiae & justitiae laudem in omnibus tribuere. De hac virtute dicitur: Quis te discreuit? quid autem habes, quod non accepisti? quod si etiam accepisti, quid gloriaris, ut qui non acceperis? Deus superbis resistit, humilibus dat gratiam. Humiliamini igitur sub potente manu Dei, &c. Quisquis se deiecerit, ut puerulus iste, is est maximus in regno coelorum. Nihil gerite per contentionem, aut per inane gloriam, sed ex modestia quisque alium se praestantiorem existimet.
units.tr: VI. HUMILITY, or ταπεινοφροσύνη, is to acknowledge that all the good things which are in us and done through us exist not by any dignity or ability of our own but by the free goodness of God; and so, from the recognition of divine majesty and of our own weakness and unworthiness, to subject oneself to God, to ascribe to him alone the glory of all the good things that are in us, and therefore truly to fear God, to acknowledge and lament one's own defects and faults; not to seek a higher place, nor to trust in gifts but in God's help alone, and to keep oneself within one's calling; not to despise others in comparison with oneself, nor to hinder them in doing their duty, but to recognise that others also are, or can become, saving instruments of God, and therefore willingly to give them one's place and honour and yield to them; not to claim for oneself or attempt things beyond one's strength, nor to aspire to excellence above others, but to be content with the gifts and place given by God, and to direct all one's gifts and efforts to the glory of God and the salvation of neighbours, even the lowly and unworthy; and not to rage against God if we are disappointed in hope or despised, but to ascribe to God the praise of wisdom and justice in all things. Of this virtue it is said: Who makes you to differ? And what have you that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you glory, as if you had not received it? God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, etc. Whoever humbles himself like this little child, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Do nothing through contention or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem others better than himself.

units.la: Humilitati opposita est in defectu Superbia vel arrogantia: quae est, dona sua non Deo, sed propriae dignitati aut facultati accepta ferre, ideoque se suaque dona admirari, non vere timere Deum, nec agnoscere & deplorare suos defectus, & subinde alteriorem locum appetere, ac non Deo, sed suis donis confisum sibi tribuere etiam quae non habet, tentare maiora viribus, & aliena avocatione, alios prae se contemnere, ac deprimere, nulli cedere, sed velle supra alios ire & eminere, & dona sua & consilia principaliter ad suam gloriam referre, Deo atque hominibus irasci, & contra Deum fremere, cum impediuntur cupiditates & consilia, accusare etiam Deum erroris aut injustitiae, si ipsius consilia cum judiciis & affectibus humanis non congruant. Breuius: Superbia. Est se suaque dona admirari, ea sibi tribuere, aliena tentare, & aduersus Deum fremere, si impediantur cupiditates. De hoc vitio dicitur: Deus superbis resistit. Abominatio coram Deo omne cor superbum.
units.tr: Opposed to humility, by way of defect, is pride or arrogance: which is to ascribe one's gifts not to God but to one's own worth or ability, and therefore to admire oneself and one's gifts, not truly to fear God, nor to acknowledge and lament one's failings; to seek a higher place again and again; to trust in one's own gifts rather than in God and so attribute to oneself even what one does not have; to attempt things beyond one's strength; by a diversion of attention, to despise and belittle others in comparison with oneself; to yield to no one but to want to go above and stand out over others; to refer one's gifts and plans chiefly to one's own glory; to be angry at God and men and to rage against God when one's desires and plans are thwarted; and even to accuse God of error or injustice if his counsels do not agree with human judgements and feelings. More briefly: Pride is to admire oneself and one's gifts, to claim them for oneself, to attempt what belongs to others, and to rage against God when one's desires are thwarted. Of this vice it is said: God resists the proud. Every proud heart is an abomination before the Lord.

units.la: In excessu eidem repugnat Simulatio modestiae seu humanitatis laudem venari negatione eorum, quae in animo sibi tribuit, seu vere, seu fallo, & recusatione eorum, quae expetit, & consequi clam conatur: Cum jejunatis, ne sitis ut hypocritae tetrici: obscurant enim facies suas, ut appareant hominibus jejunare. Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam. Aristoteles appellat βαυνγπαυούγους, fictum fastidium, & colaborantes vocat βαυνγπαυούγους, ficte fastidientes. Alij reddunt gloriosos veteratores. Verba sunt Ethic. lib. 4. cap. 7. Οἱ δὲ, ἢ τε μι- ἀφρονη ... hoc est: Qui autem & parua & manifesta dissimulant, versipelles
units.tr: Opposed to this vice in excess is feigned modesty, or the hunting after a reputation for humility by denying what one secretly claims for oneself, whether truly or falsely, and by refusing what one desires and secretly strives to obtain: When you fast, do not be like gloomy hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward. Aristotle calls this [εἰρωνείαν], feigned disdain, and calls those who practise it [εἴρωνας], feigned disdainers. Others render them boastful pretenders. These are the words of the Ethics, book 4, chapter 7: [Οἱ δὲ ... ] that is: those who dissemble even small and obvious things.

units.la: Cor. 4,7. 1 Pet. 5,5.6. Marc. 10,15. Phil. 2,3. 1 Pet 5,5. Prov. 16,5. Matth. 6,16. pelles dicuntur, & passim contemnuntur, ac interdum arrogantia est, qualis est Lacedæmoniorum vestitus. Simulata igitur humilitas est duplex superbia.
units.tr: Cor. 4,7. 1 Pet. 5,5.6. Marc. 10,15. Phil. 2,3. 1 Pet 5,5. Prov. 16,5. Matth. 6,16. Such crafty dissemblers are called shifty fellows and are everywhere despised, and sometimes their pretence is itself arrogance, as was the dress of the Spartans. Feigned humility is therefore a double pride.

units.la: VII. PATIENTIA est, ex agnitione diuinæ sapientiæ, prouidentiæ, justitiæ & bonitatis obedire Deo in perferendis aduersis, quæ Deus iubet ferre, neq; propter dolorem fremere contra Deum, aut facere aliquid contra eius mandata, sed in dolore sperare, et ab ipso liberationem duciam & spem diuini auxilij retinere, & ab ipso liberationem petere, & hac agnitione & fiducia diuinæ voluntatis dolorem moderari. Seu breuius: Est ex agnitione maiestatis diuinæ & fiducia auxilij Dei & liberationis, obedire Deo, in ferendis malis, quæ ipse nobis immittit, sicut dicitur: Sile Domino, & spera in eo. Expecta Dominum, & custodi viam eius, & exaltabit te.
units.tr: VII. PATIENCE is, from the recognition of divine wisdom, providence, justice and goodness, to obey God in bearing the adversities which God commands us to bear, neither to rage against God on account of the pain, nor to do anything contrary to his commands, but in suffering to hope, to hold on to the expectation and hope of divine help, and to seek deliverance from him, and by this recognition and trust in the divine will to moderate one's pain. Or more briefly: It is, from the recognition of the majesty of God and trust in the help and deliverance of God, to obey God in bearing the evils which he sends upon us, as it is said: Be silent before the Lord and hope in him. Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you.

units.la: Humilitas & patientia pertinent ad primum præceptum, non solum, quia sunt partes obedientiæ internæ, quam immediatè erga se Deus postulat: sed etiam quia ex vera Dei agnitione, fiducia, dilectione & timore, tanquam effectus necessarij consequuntur.
units.tr: Humility and patience belong to the first commandment, not only because they are parts of the inward obedience which God requires of us immediately, but also because they follow as necessary effects from true knowledge of God, trust, love and fear.

units.la: Patientiæ contraria est in defectu, impatientia, quæ est ex ignoratione & diffidentia diuinæ sapientiæ, prouidentiæ, justitiæ & bonitatis, nolle obedire in perferendis aduersis, quæ ipse iubet perferre, ac propter dolorem fremere contra Deum, aut facere aliquid contra eius mandata, nec petere aut expectare à Deo auxilium & liberationem, nec agnitione & fiducia diuinæ voluntatis dolorem moderari, sed ei indulgere, & eo fractum impelli vel sollicitari ad desperationem. Exempla sunt Saul & Judas: item multi affectus in querelis Jobi, quibus etiam pij sæpe concutiuntur.
units.tr: The opposite of patience, by way of defect, is impatience, which arises from ignorance of and distrust in divine wisdom, providence, justice and goodness: to be unwilling to obey in bearing the adversities which God himself commands us to bear, to rage against God on account of the pain, or to do something against his commands, to seek or expect no help and deliverance from God, and not to moderate the pain by recognition and trust in the divine will, but to indulge in it and, being broken by it, to be driven or goaded into despair. Examples are Saul and Judas; likewise the many emotions in the complaints of Job, by which even the godly are often shaken.

units.la: In excessu ei repugnat Temeritas, quæ est, ex stultitia ignorante, aut non considerante pericula, vel vocatione suam & voluntatem Dei, aut ex fiducia sui adire pericula sine necessitate: Qui amat periculum, peribit in eo.
units.tr: Opposed to this in excess is rashness, which arises from foolishness that ignores or does not consider the dangers, or one's calling and the will of God, or from confidence in oneself to face dangers without necessity: He who loves danger will perish in it.

units.la: Notandum, sæpe in hoc & in aliis præceptis eadem vitia pluribus ac diuersis virtutibus opponi. Sic enim cum fide, spe, timore Dei pugnat securitas carnalis: cum spe, dilectione Dei, &c. cum vera agnitione tate & patientia pugnat tentatio Dei, &c. Idem in aliorum Dei & fide maximè pugnat idololatria. Idem in aliorum præceptorum virtutibus & vitiis ysu venit, & obseruari debet.
units.tr: It should be noted that in this and the other commandments the same vices are often set against several different and diverse virtues. Thus carnal security is opposed both to faith, hope and the fear of God; despair is opposed to hope and love of God, etc.; the tempting of God is opposed to true knowledge of God, etc.; and idolatry above all is opposed to faith in God. The same happens with the virtues and vices of the other commandments, and it must be observed.

units.la: Quaestio XCVI. Quid postulat secundum praeceptum?
units.tr: Question 96. What does the second commandment require?

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Ne Deum vlla imagine aut figura exprimamus: a neque vlla alia ratione eum colamus, quàm quâ se in suo verbo coli praecepit b.
units.tr: We must not represent God by any image or figure, nor worship him in any way other than that in which he has commanded himself to be worshipped in his Word.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Duo continentur secundo praecepto: praeceptum, & hortatio ad obedientiam. Praecepti finis est, vt verus ille Deus, qui se in primo praecepto solum coli praecepit, rectè colatur, eo nimirum cultu, quo justum est eum coli a creaturis intelligentibus, quod ipsi placet, non autem cultu ab hominib. cogitato aut conficto: seu, vt legitimus veri Dei cultus incorruptus conseruetur, nec superstitiosis cultibus vlla ratione misceatur vel violetur. Praecipitur igitur verus veri Dei cultus, & regula sancitur, vt in nec cultui diuinitus instituto quicquam addamus, aut eundem vel minimam in parte mutilemus: quod & aliis locis disertè nobis a Domino injungitur. Est autem verus Dei cultus omne opus internum vel externum mandatum à Deo, factum in fide, statuente, quod persona & opus placeat Deo, propter mediatorem, hoc principali fine, vt Deus glorificetur. Et verè Deum colere est praecipit.
units.tr: Two things are contained in the second commandment: the command itself and the exhortation to obedience. The aim of the command is that the true God, who has commanded that he alone be worshipped in the first commandment, may be worshipped rightly, namely with that worship by which it is right for him to be worshipped by intelligent creatures, and which pleases him, and not with worship devised or invented by men. Or, to put it another way, the lawful worship of the true God is to be kept pure, and is not to be mixed or corrupted in any way with superstitious worship. The command therefore enjoins the true worship of the true God, and lays down the rule that we must add nothing to the worship divinely instituted, nor diminish it in the least part; the Lord enjoins this in plain terms in other places too. The true worship of God is every inward or outward work commanded by God, done in faith, trusting that the person and the work are pleasing to God for the sake of the Mediator, with this chief end, that God may be glorified. And to worship God truly is what the command requires.

units.la: Contra prohibetur omnis <bl>ἀθελοθρησκία</bl>, hoc est, cultus fictitius, vt non tantum creaturas & statuas pro Deo non habeamus aut veneremur, sed nec ipsum verum Deum vlla imagine aut figura exprimamus, nec eum ad statuas, aut per eas vel vllo alio cultus genere, quod ipse non praecepit, colamus. Cum enim Deus damnet speciem falsorum cultuum praecipuam, crassissimam, & maximè conspicuam, videlicet, cultum fui ad statuas: manifestum est, eum etiam species alias falsorum cultum damnare, cum haec sit fons aliarum omnium. Prohibet enim crassissimam speciem, non vt alias excludat, sed quia est fons omnium aliarum. Omnes igitur cultus, qui non à Deo, sed ab hominibus sunt instituti, & in quibus eadem prohibitionis causa reperitur, hac crassissima specie nominata prohibentur.
units.tr: On the other hand, every <bl>ἀθελοθρησκία</bl> is forbidden, that is, fictitious worship (more correctly, self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκία]). So we must not only not regard or venerate creatures and statues as God, but we must not represent the true God himself by any image or figure, nor worship him through statues, or by any other kind of worship which he has not commanded. For since God condemns the chief, grossest and most conspicuous kind of false worship, namely worship of himself by means of statues, it is clear that he also condemns the other kinds of false worship, since this is the source of all the rest. He forbids the grossest kind not in order to exclude the others, but because it is the source of all of them. Therefore all forms of worship which have been instituted not by God but by men, and in which the same cause for prohibition is found, are forbidden under this named grossest kind.

units.la: Proinde huic secundo præcepto contraria sunt ea, quæ vero cultui diuino aduersantur.
units.tr: Accordingly, those things which oppose the true divine worship are contrary to this second commandment.

units.la: 1. Idololatria, quæ est cultus numinis fictitius aut superstitiosus. Sunt autem (vt prius est dictum) idololatriæ duæ species præcipuæ. Prima crassior, cum fictitium numen colitur, hoc est, cum loco veri Dei aut præter illum alicui rei, fictæ vel existenti, honor seu cultus tribuitur, qui soli vero Deo competit. Hæc species in primo præcepto prohibetur, & aliqua ex parte in terratio. Altera est subtilior, cum verus Deus coli fingitur, sed erratur in genere cultus, hoc est, cum vero Deo cultus fingitur præstari aliquo opere, quod ipse non præcepit. Hæc species idolatriæ hoc præcepto proprie damnatur, & nominatur ἐθελοθρησκεία humana: vnde superstitiosi dicuntur, quicunque cultum DEI suis commentis adulterant. Damnatur passim in scriptura: Frustra me colunt mandatis hominum. Videte, ne quis sit, qui vos depraedetur per philosophiam & inanem deceptionem, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum. Ne quis vos damnet ob cibum & potum, &c. quæ omnia ipso vsu perempt, præscripta ex mandatis & doctrinis hominum, quæ rationem quidem habent sapientiæ & in submissione animi, & in eo, quod corperi non parcunt: non tamen vllius sunt pretij: cum ad ea spectent, quibus sarcitur caro.
units.tr: 1. Idolatry, which is the worship of a fictitious or superstitious deity. There are, as was said before, two chief kinds of idolatry. The first is the grosser, when a fictitious deity is worshipped, that is, when honour or worship which belongs to the true God alone is given, in place of him or beside him, to some thing, whether imagined or existing. This kind is forbidden in the first commandment, and in part also in the third. The other is the subtler, when the true God is worshipped in pretence, but there is an error in the manner of worship, that is, when worship is supposed to be rendered to the true God by some work which he has not commanded. This kind of idolatry is properly condemned by this commandment, and is called human self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία]. Hence those who corrupt the worship of God with their own inventions are called superstitious. It is condemned everywhere in Scripture: In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men (Matt. 15:9). See that no one take you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ (Col. 2:8). Let no one judge you in respect of food or drink (Col. 2:16), etc. All these things perish in the very using, being prescribed by the commandments and doctrines of men, which indeed have a appearance of wisdom, in self-imposed worship and humility of mind, and in not sparing the body; yet they have no value at all, since they serve only to satisfy the flesh.

units.la: Hinc patet responsio ad Obiect. In primo præcepto prohibetur idololatria. In hoc etiam. Ergo coincidunt. Resp. In primo alia idololatria prohibetur, qua alius Deus colitur, in secundo item alia, qua verus Deus alia, quam debet, ratione colitur. Instant. Sed tamen semper est idololatria, & semper alius Deus colitur. Resp. Reuera semper est idolum: sed non semper intentione & professione hominum. Ideo qui peccant contra secundum præceptum, peccant etiam contra primum, quia qui Deum aliter colunt, atque vult coli, illi fingunt Deum aliter effectum atque est, hoc est, alium Deum. Ita non Deum, sed cerebri sui commentum, quod sic affectum esse sibi persuadent, colunt.
units.tr: From this the answer to the objection is plain. Objection: Idolatry is forbidden in the first commandment; it is forbidden in this one too; therefore the two coincide. Answer: In the first commandment one kind of idolatry is forbidden, by which another god is worshipped; in the second another kind, by which the true God is worshipped in a way other than he ought to be. Objection persists: But it is still always idolatry, and always another god is worshipped. Answer: Indeed it is always an idol, but not always so in the intention and profession of men. Therefore those who sin against the second commandment also sin against the first, because those who worship God otherwise than he wishes to be worshipped invent a God who is different from what he is, that is, another God. Thus they worship not God, but a figment of their own brain, which they persuade themselves is such as they imagine.

units.la: 2. Hypocrisis, quæ est simulatio veræ pietatis, & cultus Dei, faciens externa opera a DEO præcepta, moralia vel cæremonialia, sine vera fide & conuersione seu obedientia interna. Hoc vitium depingitur & damnatur his verbis apud Esaiam: Propterea, quod appropinquat populus iste ore suo, & labiis suis honorat me, cor autem suum longè facit à me: & timuerunt me mandatis hominum. hominum : propterea ecce ego addam, ut mira faciam in populo isto, &c.
units.tr: 2. Hypocrisy, which is the pretence of true piety and of the worship of God, performing outward works commanded by God, whether moral or ceremonial, without true faith and conversion, or inward obedience. This vice is portrayed and condemned in these words of Isaiah: Because this people draws near with its mouth and honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me, and they fear me by the commandments of men; therefore, behold, I will add to do marvellous things among this people, etc. (Isa. 29:13, 14).

units.la: 3. Profanitas, quæ est totius religionis & cultus Dei interni & externi, aut partis alicuius contemtus, aut voluntaria omissio: ideoq; non tantū cum hoc præcepto pugnat profanitas, sed cum toto Dei cultu in prima & secunda tabula.
units.tr: 3. Profanity, which is the contempt, or voluntary neglect, of the whole religion and worship of God, inward or outward, or of some part of it. Therefore profanity conflicts not only with this commandment but with the whole worship of God in the first and second tables.

units.la: Pro tuenda superstitione obiciunt. Dicta illa contra ἐθελοθρη-σκίαν citata, tantum loqui de cæremoniis Mosaicis, & de impiis hominum mandatis, quod non sint cultus Dei: non autem de iis præceptis humanis, quæ ab ecclesiia vel episcopis sanciuntur, nec aliquid jubent verbo Dei repugnans. Resp. Falsum hoc esse ostendunt declarationes locis illis additæ, quæ reijciunt etiam illas leges humanas, quibus aliquid cultus diuini gratia præci-pitur, quod à Deo mandatum non est, etiamsi sit res suo genere non impia, necà Deo prohibita. Sic Christus propter opinio-nem cultus, reijcit traditionem Judæorum per se non impiam, delotione manuum: Non quod ingreditur in os, polluit hominem, sed quod egreditur ex homine, hoc polluit hominem. Væ vobis scribæ & pharisæi hypocritæ, quoniam purgatis exteriorem poculi patinaq; par-tem, intus autem sunt plena rapina & intemperantia. Talia sunt cæ-libatus, & discrimina ciborum ac dierum, de quibus Paulus dis-putat, & quæ doctrinas dæmoniorum vocat, tametsi ea per se licita piis esse, alibi doceat. Quare etiam ea, quæ per se sunt adia-phora, hoc est, à Deo nec mandata, nec prohibita, si præcipian-tur, & fiant tanquam cultus Dei, hoc est, ita ut eorum præsta-tione Deus honore, omissione vero contumelia afficiatur, illis & similibus scripturæ dictis damnari manifestum est.
units.tr: In defence of superstition they object that the sayings cited above against self-devised worship speak only of the Mosaic ceremonies, and of the impious commandments of men, which are not the worship of God; but not of those human precepts which are enacted by the Church or by bishops, and which command nothing contrary to the Word of God. Answer: That this is false is shown by the explanations added to those passages, which reject also those human laws by which something is commanded for the sake of divine worship, which God has not commanded, even though the thing in its kind is not impious and is not forbidden by God. Thus Christ, on account of the opinion of worship, rejects the tradition of the Jews, which in itself was not impious, concerning the washing of hands: Not what goes into the mouth defiles a man, but what comes out of a man, this defiles a man. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but within they are full of robbery and intemperance (Matt. 15:11; Matt. 23:25). Such are celibacy, and the distinctions of foods and days, about which Paul disputes, and which he calls doctrines of demons, although elsewhere he teaches that these things are in themselves lawful for the godly. Therefore it is manifest that those things which are in themselves indifferent, that is, neither commanded nor forbidden by God, if they are enjoined and done as worship of God, that is, so that by their performance God is honoured and by their omission he is dishonoured, are condemned by these and similar sayings of Scripture.

units.la: Sunt igitur opera adiaphora à cultibus Dei diligenter discer-nenda: 1. Quia fingere alium Dei cultum, est aliam Dei voluntatem, proinde & alium Deum fingere. Illud ergo facientes, ut olim Aaron & Jeroboam, non minus accusantur idololatriæ, quam qui ex professo alium Deum, præter Jehouam, in ecclesia pate-factum colunt. 2. Quia confusis cultibus, confunditur verus Deus cum idolis, quæ humanitus excogitatis cultibus honoran-tur. 3. Quia quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Qui autem ali-quid Dei colendi causa facit, nesciente vel dubitante conscien-tia, an Deus hoc modo coli velit, is non agit ex fide: quia igno-rat, an hoc suum opus placeat Deo, an vero displiceat, & DEUM contemnit eo, quod facere aliquid audet, etiamsi Deo displiceat.
units.tr: Indifferent works must therefore be carefully distinguished from the worship of God. 1. Because to devise another worship of God is to devise another will of God, and therefore another God. Those who do this, like Aaron and Jeroboam of old, are accused of idolatry no less than those who openly worship another God besides Jehovah in the Church. 2. Because by confusing worships, the true God is confused with idols, which are honoured with worships devised by men. 3. Because whatever is not of faith is sin (Rom. 14:23). Moreover, whoever does something for the sake of worshipping God, while his conscience is ignorant or doubtful whether God wishes to be worshipped in this way, does not act from faith, because he does not know whether this work of his pleases God or displeases him; and he despises God by daring to do something which may displease God.

units.la: Quoniam vero defensores cultuum humanorum etiam quæ-dam dicta proferunt, quibus scriptura jubet præceptis hominum parere, & inde concludunt, ea vim divinorum præceptorum, & cultus diuini rationem habere, ideo necesse est, quaedam hoc loco de praeceptis humanis, & eorum discriminibus explicare.
units.tr: But since defenders of human worship also bring forward certain sayings, in which Scripture commands obedience to the precepts of men, and from these conclude that such precepts have the force of divine commands and the character of divine worship, it is therefore necessary, at this point, to explain certain things about human precepts and the distinctions among them.

units.la: DE PRÆCEPTIS HVMANIS, ET TRADITIONVM ECCLESIASTICARVM AVTHORITATE.
units.tr: On Human Precepts, and the Authority of Ecclesiastical Traditions.

units.la: Quatuor sunt genera eorum, quae homines praecipiunt.
units.tr: There are four kinds of things that men prescribe.

units.la: I. Sunt PRÆCEPTA DIVINA, quæ vult quidem Deus, vt homines proponant aliis obseruanda: verum non suo, sed ipsius Dei nomine, nempe tanquam ministri & internuncij, non tanquam authores. Sic ministri ecclesiæ vniuersam doctrinam coelestem proponunt ecclesiæ, parentes liberis, præceptores discipulis, magistratus decalogi præcepta subditis. Horum præceptorum obedientia est & nominatur cultus Dei, qui sunt præcepta non humana, sed diuina, quibus obedire necesse est, etiamsi nullius creaturæ authoritas, aut iussio accederet, immò etiamsi omnes creaturæ contrarium præciperent. De his præceptis loquuntur dicta: Custodi, fili mi, præcepta patris tui. Qui superbierit, nolens obedire sacerdotis imperio, ex decreto iudicis morietur. Si ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus, & velut publicanus. Et similia multa, vt Luc.10,17. 1 Thess.4,2.8. Exod.16,8. Matth.23, 2.3. Heb.13,17. 1 Cor.4,21. 2 Cor.13,10. 2 Thess.1,4. Quæ omnia obedire iubent hominibus, tanquam ministris Dei in iis, quae sunt ministerii: non autem concedunt potestatem cuiquam nos Dei cultus suo arbitratu instituendi, iuxta dicta: Ne addas verbis eius, ne forte increpet te. Quemadmodum te sum precatus, vt aenuncies quibusdam, ne diuersam doctrinam doceant. Item 1 Tim.6. v.2.3.4.7. 1 Tim.3,16.17.
units.tr: I. There are DIVINE PRECEPTS, which God indeed wills that men should set before others to be observed, but not in their own name, rather in the name of God himself, namely as ministers and messengers, not as authors. Thus the ministers of the Church set forth the whole heavenly doctrine to the Church, parents to their children, teachers to their pupils, and magistrates the precepts of the Decalogue to their subjects. Obedience to these precepts is, and is called, the worship of God. These are precepts not of men but of God, and they must be obeyed even if no authority or command of any creature were added, indeed even if all creatures commanded the contrary. The following sayings speak of these precepts: Keep, my son, the precepts of your father. Whoever is proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest shall die by the decree of the judge. If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican. And many similar passages, such as Luke 10:17; 1 Thess. 4:2, 8; Exod. 16:8; Matt. 23:2, 3; Heb. 13:17; 1 Cor. 4:21; 2 Cor. 13:10; 2 Thess. 1:4. All these passages bid men to obey them as ministers of God in those things which belong to the ministry. But they do not grant to anyone the power of establishing the worship of God at his own pleasure, according to the saying: Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you. Just as I have asked you to charge certain people that they should not teach a different doctrine. Likewise 1 Tim. 6:2, 3, 4, 7; 1 Tim. 3:16, 17.

units.la: II. Sunt præcepta humana politica, quæ sunt determinationes circumstantiarum necessariæ & vtiles ad seruanda præcepta moralia secundæ tabulæ. Tales sunt leges positiuæ magistratuum, parentum, præceptorum, dominorum, & omnium, qui aliis præsunt in vita externa. Harum legum obedientia etiam est cultus Dei, quantum ad genus attinet, quia genus hoc est morale, & à Deo præceptum, videlicet obedientia erga magistratum, & alios, qui præsunt: quantum verò ad speciem facti siue circumstantias attinet, non est quidem cultus Dei, quia cultus Dei sunt illa deorum opera, quæ propter Dei mandatum facere necesse est, etiamsi nullius creaturæ mandatum aut respectus accedat: hæc autem, nisi à gubernatoribus præcepta essent, fieri aut omitti sine vlla Dei offensione possent. Veruntamen obligat conscientias, hoc est, necessariò præstatur, nec sine offensione Dei negligitur, propter ipsum mandatum magistratuum, etiam extra casum scandali. Verbi causa, gestare & non gestare arma, non est cultus
units.tr: II. There are human political precepts, which are determinations of circumstances necessary and useful for keeping the moral precepts of the second table. Such are the positive laws of magistrates, parents, teachers, masters, and of all who preside over others in external life. Obedience to these laws is also the worship of God as far as the kind is concerned, because this kind is moral and commanded by God, namely obedience toward the magistrate and others who preside. But as far as the particular act or its circumstances are concerned, it is not indeed the worship of God, because the worship of God consists in those works of piety which must be done on account of God's command, even if no command or regard of any creature were added. These works, however, unless they had been prescribed by the governors, could be done or omitted without any offence to God. Nevertheless they bind consciences; that is, they must be performed, and are not neglected without offence to God, on account of the very command of the magistrates, even apart from the case of scandal. For example, to bear arms or not to bear arms is not the worship of God. Divine precepts proposed by men. But when a command or prohibition of the magistrate is added, the obedience then rendered is the worship of God, and he who acts against it sins against God, even if the act could remain hidden and offend no one. For the kind itself, namely obedience toward the magistrate, which is the worship of God, is then violated. Nevertheless the actions themselves are not, in themselves and properly, the worship of God, but only incidentally, on account of the command of the magistrate; had that command not intervened, obedience would not be violated. To this belong the sayings: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. Whoever opposes the power resists the ordinance of God. Remind them to submit themselves to rulers. Likewise Eph. 6:1; Col. 3:22, 23.

units.la: Præcepta divina ab hominibus proposita. cultus Dei: sed accedente magistratus præcepto vel interdicto, obedientia, quæ tunc præstatur, est cultus Dei, & peccat in eum, qui contra facit, etiamsi latere possit, & neminem homi-num offendat: quia genus, videlicet, obedientia erga magistra-tum, quæ est cultus Dei, tunc violatur. Actiones tamen ipsæ per se & proprie non sunt cultus Dei, sed per accidens, propter man-datum magistratus, quod nisi interveniret, obedientia non vio-laretur. Huc pertinent dicta: Omnis anima potestatibus superemi-nentibus subiecta esto. Quisquis opponit se potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit. Suggere ipsis, ut sese subijciant principatibus. Item Eph. 6, 1. Coloss. 3. v. 22. 23.
units.tr: III. There are ecclesiastical or ceremonial human precepts, which are determinations of necessary or useful circumstances for keeping the moral precepts of the first table. Of this kind are the time, place, form and order of sermons, prayers and ecclesiastical readings, fasts, the manner of proceeding in the election of ministers, in gathering and distributing alms, and similar matters, concerning which God has commanded nothing in particular. The genus of these laws, like that of the political ones, is moral (provided they are rightly and usefully enacted), and therefore is the worship of God. But the ceremonies themselves which are prescribed here are not only not the worship of God, but they also do not bind consciences, nor is their observance necessary apart from the case of scandal. Thus the assemblies of the Church for hearing the Word of God, public and private prayers, not disturbing the useful order of sermons in the church, not harming a neighbour by scandal, etc., are the worship of God. But it is not the worship of God to meet on this or that day or hour, to recite prayers in this or that form of words, standing or kneeling, to read or expound this or that part of the sacred text on this or that day, or to eat or abstain from meat, etc.

units.la: III. Sunt præcepta hominum ecclesiastica seu cæremonialia, quæ sunt determinationes circumstantiarum necessariarum vel utiles ad seruanda præcepta moralia primæ tabulæ: cuius generis sunt, tempus, locus, forma & series concionum, precum, lectionum ecclesiasticarum, jejunia, modus procedendi in electione ministrorum, in colligendis & distribuendis eleemosynis, & similia, de quibus in specie nihil est à Deo præceptum. Harum etiam legum genus, ut politicarum est morale (si modo recte & vtiliter sint latæ) ac proinde cultus Dei est: ipsæ verò cæremoniæ, quæ hic præcipiuntur, non modo cultus Dei non sunt: sed etiam conscientias non obligant: neque extra casum scandali necessaria est earum obseruatio. Sic cultus Dei sunt congressus ecclesiæ ad audiendum verbum Dei, preces publicæ & priuatæ, non turbare ordinem concionum vtilem in ecclesia, scandalo non lædere proximum, &c. Sic non est cultus Dei, hoc vel illo die aut hora conuenire; preces hac vel illa sermonis forma, stando vel genibus flexis recitare, hoc vel illo die, hanc vel illam sacri textus partem legere, aut inrer-pietari in ecclesia, vesci aut non vesci carnibus, &c.
units.tr: III. There are ecclesiastical or ceremonial human precepts, which are determinations of the circumstances that are necessary or useful for keeping the moral precepts of the first table. Of this kind are the time, place, form and order of sermons, prayers and ecclesiastical readings, fasts, the procedure in choosing ministers, in collecting and distributing alms, and similar matters, on which God has commanded nothing in particular. The kind of law that these belong to is moral, as with civil laws, provided they are made rightly and usefully, and so they are worship of God. The ceremonies themselves, however, which are prescribed here, are not only not worship of God, but also do not bind the conscience, and their observance is not necessary apart from the case of scandal. Thus the assembling of the Church to hear the Word of God, public and private prayers, not disturbing the useful order of sermons in the Church, not injuring a neighbour by scandal, etc., are worship of God. Thus it is not worship of God to meet on this or that day or hour; to recite prayers in this or that form of words, standing or kneeling; to read or expound this or that part of the sacred text in the church; to eat or abstain from meat, etc.

units.la: Obiect. Edicta magistratus obligant conscientias. Ergo etiam traditiones ecclesiasticæ. Resp. Est dissimilitudo in exemplis. Deus magistratui dedit authoritatem condendi leges politicas, eamque hoc vinculo muniuit, ut minetur iram suam leges illas violantibus: ecclesiæ vero vel ministris ecclesiæ talem authoritatem non dedit, sed tantum, ut leges eorum & constitutiones bonæ seruentur ex regula charitatis, hoc est, studio vitandi scandala, non autem ex necessitate obediendi propter conscientiam. Discrimen hoc expresse docetur in scriptura: Scitis principes gentium in eos dominari, &c. vos autem non sic. Neque ut dominantes in cleris. Nemo vos damnet ob cibum vel potum, aut respectum diei festi. In libertate, qua Christus vos liberauit, persistite. Causæ huius discriminis sunt manifestæ. 1. Quia ingens discrimen est inter magistratum politicum, cuius est imperare subditis, & coercere non obtemperantes vi corporali: & inter ministros Ecclesiæ, quibus imperium tale non est concessum, sed mandatum officium docendi homines de voluntate Dei. 2. Quia violatione legum ecclesiasticarum sine scandalo non violatur prima tabula decalogi, cui seruire debent: at violatione legum politicarum, etiam extra scandalum, violatur secunda tabula, quia vel reipublicæ aliquid detrahitur, & societas politica lædi-tur, vel aliquid eam lædendi occasio præbetur.
units.tr: Objection: The edicts of the magistrate bind the conscience; therefore so do ecclesiastical traditions. Answer: There is a difference between the examples. God gave the magistrate authority to make civil laws and fortified it with this bond, that he threatens his wrath on those who break those laws. But he did not give such authority to the Church or to its ministers; he gave only that their good laws and constitutions be kept out of the rule of charity, that is, from the zeal to avoid scandals, and not from necessity of obeying for conscience' sake. This distinction is expressly taught in Scripture: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, etc.; but it shall not be so among you. Neither as being lords over God's heritage. Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a holy day. Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made you free. The causes of this distinction are plain. 1. Because there is a great difference between the civil magistrate, whose task is to command subjects and to restrain the disobedient by physical force, and the ministers of the Church, to whom such power has not been granted, but the duty of teaching men the will of God has been entrusted. 2. Because by violating ecclesiastical laws, without scandal, the first table of the Decalogue, which they ought to serve, is not violated; but by violating civil laws, even apart from scandal, the second table is violated, because either something is taken away from the commonwealth and political society is harmed, or an occasion is given for harming it.

units.la: Inst. Maiori siue digniori officio debetur maior obedientia. Ergo ecclesiasticæ constitutiones ministrorum non minus, sed magis obligant conscientias, quàm leges ciuiles. Resp. ad maiorem: Debetur digniori officio maior obedientia in iis, quæ sunt ipsius officij propria. Magistratus verò politici officium est prium, condere leges propter ipsum mandatum observandas: ministerij ecclesiastici proprium est, ordinare cæremonialia, quæ seruentur, non propter mandatum Dei, nec propter mandatum hominum, sed propter vitanda scandala.
units.tr: Objection: A greater obedience is owed to a greater or more worthy office. Therefore the constitutions of ministers bind the conscience not less, but more, than civil laws. Answer to the major premise: a greater obedience is owed to a more worthy office in those matters which belong to that office itself. But it is the proper office of the civil magistrate to make laws which are to be observed on account of the command itself. It is the proper task of the ecclesiastical ministry to ordain ceremonies, which are kept not on account of God's command, nor on account of men's command, but in order to avoid scandals.

units.la: IV. Sunt præcepta humana cum præceptis diuinis pugnantia. His obtemperare Deus prohibet, siue à magistratu politico, siue ab ecclesia & ministris ecclesiæ præcipiantur, juxta dicta: Oportet Deo magis obedire quàm hominibus. Quare transgredimini mandatum Dei propter traditionem?
units.tr: IV. There are human precepts that conflict with divine precepts. God forbids obeying these, whether they are commanded by the civil magistrate or by the Church and its ministers, according to the saying: We ought to obey God rather than men. And: Why do you also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?

units.la: Hinc facilè respondetur ad Obiect. 1. Jubet Deus obedire præceptis hominum. Resp. 1. Bonis & non pugnantibus cum verbo Dei. 2. A se præceptis per homines, vt sibi præstetur cultus. 3. Præceptis politicis ex hominum authoritate pendentibus, non quidem cultus diuini causa, sed tamen propter conscientiam. 4. Ecclesiasticis siue cæremonialibus, neque cultus, neque conscientiæ, sed scandali vitandi causa.
units.tr: From this the objection, that God commands obedience to the precepts of men, is easily answered. Answer: (1) to good precepts which do not conflict with the Word of God; (2) to precepts that men impose on their own account, so that worship is paid to themselves; (3) to political precepts which depend on the authority of men, not indeed for the sake of divine worship, but nevertheless on account of conscience; (4) to ecclesiastical or ceremonial precepts, which are neither worship nor matters of conscience, but are for the sake of avoiding scandal.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Quæ instinctu Spiritus sancti præcipit ecclesia, sunt præcepta diuina & cultus Dei. Bonas & vtiles constitutiones ecclesia facit, gubernante ipsius consilia Spiritu sancto. Ergo bonæ constitutiones ecclesiæ, obligant conscientias, & earum obseruatio est cultus Dei. Resp. ad maiorem. Sunt cultus Dei, quæ nomine & authoritate Spiritus sancti præcipit, non retinens libertatem de illis deliberandi, aut ea mutandi, aut extra scandalum omittendi: non autem sunt cultus Dei, quæ authoritate & nomine suo consulit, statuit, & præcipit ecclesia, etiam in his etiam eligendis & constituendis ductu Spiritus sancti regatur. Dictat enim Spiritus sanctus ecclesiæ vtrumque, & quod ea, quæ vitandi scandali fit vtile ad vitanda scandala, & quod ea, quæ vitandi scandali causa præcipiuntur, neq; cultus Dei sint, neq; extra casum scandali sint obseruatu necessaria, vt patet ex dictis: Hoc autem dico ex concessione, non ex imperio. Hoc autem dico ad vestrum commodum, vt non laqueum vobis iniiciam, sed vt decenter adhaereatis Domino absque vlla distractione. Sic Paulus vetat vesci idolothytis cum scandalo: extra id vero liberum relinquit. Sic apostoli in synodo instinctu Spiritus sancti praecipiunt abstinentiam a suffocato & sanguine: & tamen relinquunt ecclesiae libertatem omittendi praeceptum scandalo cessante.
units.tr: Objection 2. What the Church prescribes by the impulse of the Holy Spirit are divine precepts and worship of God. The Church makes good and useful constitutions, the Holy Spirit governing its counsels. Therefore the good constitutions of the Church bind the conscience, and their observance is worship of God. Answer to the major premise. Those are worship of God which are prescribed in the name and by the authority of the Holy Spirit, without retaining liberty to deliberate about them, to change them, or to omit them outside the case of scandal. Those are not worship of God which the Church advises, decides and prescribes by its own authority and in its own name, even though in choosing and establishing these things it is guided by the impulse of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit dictates to the Church both that those things which are useful for avoiding scandal are to be done, and that those things which are prescribed for the sake of avoiding scandal are neither worship of God nor necessary to observe outside the case of scandal, as is clear from what has been said: But I say this by way of concession, not of command. And I say this for your own good, that I may not cast a snare upon you, but that you may cleave to the Lord decently and without distraction. Thus Paul forbids eating food sacrificed to idols where there is scandal, but beyond that he leaves it free. Thus the apostles in the synod, by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, enjoin abstinence from what is strangled and from blood; yet they leave the Church the liberty to omit the precept when the scandal has ceased.

units.la: Obiect.3. Quae ad Dei gloriam fiunt: iis colitur Deus. Sed determinata ab ecclesia fiunt ad gloriam Dei. Ergo haec etiam sunt cultus Dei. Resp. ad maiorem: quae ad Dei gloriam fiunt, nempe per se, hoc est, quae ab ipso Deo praecepta sunt, in hunc finem vt obedientiam nostram erga ipsum his operibus declaremus: non autem, quae per accidens serviunt gloriae Dei, hoc est, quae iis praestandis, quae a Deo sunt praecepta, aliquando serviunt, propter accidentales causas, quae si non concurrant, Deus honore affici potest tam a facientibus ea, quam ab omittentibus, modo fiant vel omittantur ex fide.
units.tr: Objection 3. Those things done for God's glory are the things by which God is worshipped. But things determined by the Church are done for God's glory. Therefore these also are worship of God. Answer to the major premise: Those things done for God's glory per se, that is, those which God himself has commanded, so that by these works we declare our obedience to him, are worship. But things that serve God's glory only per accidens are not. These are the things that sometimes serve God's glory when the things God has commanded are performed, because of accidental causes. If those causes do not concur, God can be honoured equally by those who do such things and by those who omit them, provided they are done or omitted from faith.

units.la: Obiect.4. Quidam sancti coluerunt Deum absque mandato Dei, vt Samuel sacrificans Ramathae: Elias sacrificans in Carmelo: Manoah sacrificans Zarae. Ergo quaedam opera a Deo non mandata sunt cultus Dei. Resp. His exemplis nequaquam stabiliri potest ἐθελοθρησκεία. Nam 1. quod ad sacrificia attinet, erant cultus Dei, quia erant opera a Deo mandata. 2. quod ad loca, ea ante aedificatum templum erant libera, nec in circumstantia locorum cultus Dei erat positus. 3. quod ad personas, Samuel & Elias habebant extraordinariam sacrificandi potestatem, quia erant prophetae. Manoah pater Simsonis vel ipse non sacrificauit, sed sacrificium angelo, quem putabat prophetam esse, offerendum tradidit, vel ipse ab angelo iussus obtulit, atque ita nihil praeter legem divinam egit.
units.tr: Objection 4. Some saints worshipped God without a command from God, as Samuel sacrificing at Ramah, Elijah sacrificing on Carmel, and Manoah sacrificing at Zorah. Therefore some works not commanded by God are worship of God. Answer: These examples can by no means establish self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία]. For (1) as regards the sacrifices, they were worship of God because they were works commanded by God. (2) As regards the places, these were free before the temple was built, and the worship of God was not tied to the circumstances of place. (3) As regards the persons, Samuel and Elijah had an extraordinary power of sacrificing because they were prophets. Manoah, the father of Samson, either did not sacrifice himself but handed the sacrifice over to be offered to the angel, whom he believed to be a prophet, or he offered it himself because the angel commanded him. In either case he did nothing beyond the divine law.

units.la: Obiect.5. Quicquid fit ex fide & Deo placet, est cultus Dei. Haec opera sponte ab hominibus suscepta fiunt ex fide, & placent Deo. Ergo sunt cultus Dei. Resp. Maior est particularis. Neque enim ad cultum Dei definiendum sufficit, vt aliquid placeat Deo, cum etiam adiaphorae actiones possint fieri ex fide, & Deo placere, licet aliter, quam cultus Dei proprie dictus. Hic enim sic placet Deo, vt eius oppositum ei displiceat, ac proinde non possit fieri ex fide. Adiaphora autem sic probantur Deo, vt eorum opposita non improbentur, ac proinde vtraque, fieri possint ex fide, quae opus & personam Deo placere statuat. Hactenus de praecepto. Restat hortatio explicanda. Sed prius doctrina de imaginibus ad praeceptum pertinens est expedienda, quae duabus quaestionibus catechet. continetur.
units.tr: Objection 5. Whatever is done from faith and pleases God is worship of God. These works, undertaken voluntarily by men, are done from faith and please God. Therefore they are worship of God. Answer: The major premise is only particular, not universal. For it is not enough for defining the worship of God that something pleases God, since even adiaphora actions can be done from faith and please God, though in a different way from what is properly called the worship of God. For the latter pleases God in such a way that its opposite displeases him, and therefore it cannot be done without faith. Adiaphora, however, are so approved by God that their opposites are not disapproved, and therefore both can be done from faith, which holds that the work and the person please God. So much concerning the precept. It remains to explain the exhortation. But first the doctrine of images, which belongs to the precept, must be set out, and it is contained in two catechism questions.

units.la: Mm 5 Quast.
units.tr: Mm 5 Quast.

units.la: QVÆSTIO XCVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 97.

units.la: An nulla ergo prorsus fingenda sunt imagines aut simulacra?
units.tr: Therefore, should absolutely no images or statues be made?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Deus nec vlla ratione effingi debet, nec potest a. Creaturas autem, etsi exprimere quidem licet: vetat tamen Deus earum imagines fingi aut haberi, quo vel ipsas, vel Deum per ipsas colamus, aut honoremus b.
units.tr: God ought not to be represented in any way, and He cannot be a. Creatures, indeed, may be portrayed, but God forbids that their images be made or kept, so that we do not worship or honour them, or God through them b.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Obseruandum est, in verbis secundi præcepti duas esse partes. Prior vetat simulacra & imagines fieri & haberi: Non facies tibi sculptile, nec vllam imaginem, &c. Posterior vetat simulacra & imagines diuino honore coli: Non incuruabis te illis, nec coles ea. In priore quæritur, an omnes statuæ & imagines: &, si non omnes, quæ igitur & quatenus sint licitæ, vel non. In altera quæritur, an adoratio ad statuas sit simpliciter prohibita, nec vlla ratione possit defendi.
units.tr: It must be observed that the words of the second commandment have two parts. The first forbids making and keeping images and likenesses: Thou shalt not make thee any graven image, or any likeness, etc. The second forbids that images and likenesses be worshipped with divine honour: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them. In the first part the question is whether all statues and images are forbidden, and if not all, which are lawful and to what extent, or not. In the second part the question is whether adoration directed to statues is absolutely prohibited and can in no way be defended.

units.la: DE IMAGINIBVS ET STATVIS IN TEMPLIS CHRISTIANORVM.
units.tr: DE IMAGINIBVS ET STATVIS IN TEMPLIS CHRISTIANORVM.

units.la: Quæstiones præcipuæ explicandæ: I. An & quatenus imagines templorum hoc præcepto prohibentur. II. An adoratio ad statuas possit defendi. III. Quare imagines & statuæ in templis Christianorum sint abolenda. IV. Quomodo & à quibus sint imagines tollendæ.
units.tr: The principal questions to be explained are: I. Whether and to what extent images in temples are forbidden by this precept. II. Whether the worship directed to statues can be defended. III. Why images and statues are to be abolished in the temples of Christians. IV. How and by whom images are to be removed.

units.la: Duæ priores huc pertinent: duæ posteriores ad sequentem quæstionem XCVIII.
units.tr: The first two belong here; the last two belong to the following question, XCVIII.

units.la: I. An omnes statuæ & imagines sint prohibitæ.
units.tr: I. Whether all statues and images are forbidden.

units.la: Hebræis vsitatæ sunt voces zelem & themunah, imago: & Pesel, sculptile, & Hhezebh, idolum vel simulacrum, à Hhazabh, turbare, dolore afficere, ab effectu: quia idolum conscientias turbat & cruciat. Græci vocant εἰκόνα, imaginem, & εἴδωλον, speciem, vel imunculam, quam homines sibi ad numen repræsentandum aut colendum effingunt, siue sit solida statua, siue nuda imago. Latinis
units.tr: The Hebrews used the words zelem and themunah for image; Pesel for a carved thing; and Hhezebh for an idol or likeness. The last is from Hhazabh, to trouble or to afflict with pain, named from its effect, because an idol troubles and torments consciences. The Greeks call it eikona [εἰκόνα], image, and eidolon [εἴδωλον], a form or little likeness, which men fashion for themselves to represent or worship a deity, whether it is a solid statue or a bare picture. Among the Latins

units.la: Quæst. XCVII.
units.tr: Question XCVII.

units.la: Latinis imago est species repræsentata vel picta: statua species solida, sculpta vel fusa: simulacrum, idem. Idolum Græco Latinum factum, idem significat. Sophistæ discrimen commenti sunt, vt cultum statuarum defenderent. Volunt enim simulacrum significare imaginem rei verè existentis, idolum imaginem rei fictitiæ. Itaque idolorum quidem cultum prohiberi, non autem simulacrorum. Sed ineptam esse distinctionem patet. 1. Ex ipso etymo, quo simulacrum & idolum non magis differunt, quàm panis & εἴδωλον. Prius enim latinum, posterius græcum est vocabulum eiusdem rei. Sicut enim εἴδωλον formula est à formando, sic simulacrum est similitudo, à similando, teste Lactantio. 2. Interpretes scripturæ promiscuè vtraque voce vtuntur. Nam vocem Hebraam Hhezebh Septuaginta vbiq; reddiderunt εἴδωλον, Latini simulacrum. Sic illud: Cauete vobis ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων: Latinus reddidit: fugite simulacra. 3. Promiscuus vsus vtriusque vocis apud bonos authores occurrit. Cicero atomos vocat imagines & idola. Euripides vmbram Polydori, & vmbram Achillis vocat εἴδωλα. Homerus animam matris, Elpenoris, Herculis, & omnes animas defunctorum, res vtique non fictas, sed verè existentes (licet in fabula apud inferos repræsentatas) εἴδωλον & εἴδωλα appellat. Juxta Sophistas autem simulacrum diaboli, rei vtiq; verè existentis, quod hodie à Mexicanis coli dicitur, non esse idolum, quo nihil absurdius. Idolum ergo non tantum est imago rei fictitiæ, sed etiam veræ. Contra simulacrum vsurpatur pro imagine rei fictitiæ. Plinius idolum Cereris numinis fictitii vocat simulacrum: Vitruuius imaginem siue idolum Dianæ vocat simulacrum. Fictitia est ergo sophistarum distinctio inter idolum & simulacrum. Hæc de appellationibus.
units.tr: among the Latins an image is a represented or painted likeness; a statua is a solid likeness, carved or cast; simulacrum means the same. Idolum, a Greek word made Latin, means the same thing. The sophists invented a distinction in order to defend the worship of statues. For they want simulacrum to signify the image of a thing that really exists, and idolum the image of a fictitious thing. So the worship of idols, they say, is forbidden, but not the worship of simulacra. But the distinction is plainly foolish. 1. From the etymology itself: simulacrum and idolum differ no more than panis and eidolon [εἴδωλον] do. For the Latin word is the earlier and the Greek the later name for the same thing. Just as eidolon is a form from forming, so simulacrum is similitudo, a likeness, from similando, according to Lactantius. 2. The interpreters of Scripture use both words interchangeably. The Seventy everywhere render the Hebrew Hhezebh by eidolon, and the Latins by simulacrum. So that verse, "Take heed to yourselves from the idols [ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων]," the Latin translator rendered "flee simulacra." 3. The interchangeable use of both words occurs among good authors. Cicero calls atoms images and idola. Euripides calls the shade of Polydorus and the shade of Achilles eidola [εἴδωλα]. Homer calls the soul of his mother, of Elpenor, of Hercules, and all the souls of the dead, things surely not fictitious but truly existing (though in the fable they are represented in the underworld), eidolon and eidola. Yet according to the sophists, the simulacrum of the devil, a thing truly existing, which is said today to be worshipped by the Mexicans, is not an idolum, and nothing could be more absurd. An idolum therefore is not only the image of a fictitious thing but also of a real one. On the contrary, simulacrum is used for the image of a fictitious thing. Pliny calls the idol of the goddess Ceres, a fictitious deity, a simulacrum; Vitruvius calls the image or idol of Diana a simulacrum. The sophists' distinction between idolum and simulacrum is therefore fictitious. So much for the names.

units.la: Jam ad quæstionem Resp. non simpliciter hic prohiberi simulacra, statuas, imagines fieri vel habere: quia ars pictoria, sculptoria, fusoria, textoria, inter eximia & vitæ humanæ vtilia Dei dona atq; ornamenta recensetur; & Deus ipse in tabernaculo imagines quasdam fingi, & Salomon in solio suo leones, in templo palmas & Cherubim jussu Dei sculpi curauit. Nec obscura est ratio: quia scriptura & pictura ad memoriam rei gestæ, ad ornatum & ad oblectationem vitæ liberalem pertinent. Vetat ergo lex non vsum imaginū, sed abusum; qui est, cum vel ad repræsentandum, vel ad colendū Deum, aut creaturas, sculpturæ & picturæ fiunt. Proinde nec simpliciter omnes imagines vel statuæ, sed tantum aliquæ tanquam illicitæ prohibentur: videlicet. Primò omnes imagines vel statuæ Dei, hoc est, quæ ad repræsentandum aut colendum Deum effinguntur, simpliciter hic damnantur. Id patet, 1. Ex fine præcepti, qui est cultus diuini incorrupti conseruatio.
units.tr: Now to the question. The answer is that images, statues and simulacra are not simply forbidden here to be made or kept, because the arts of painting, sculpture, casting and weaving are counted among the excellent gifts and ornaments of God, useful for human life. God himself ordered certain images to be fashioned in the tabernacle, and by God's command Solomon had lions made for his throne and palms and cherubim carved in the temple. Nor is the reason obscure: writing and painting serve to remember deeds, to adorn life, and to give it honest delight. The law therefore forbids not the use of images but the abuse, which occurs when sculptures and paintings are made to represent or to worship God or creatures. Accordingly, not all images or statues are forbidden, but only some as unlawful, namely: First, all images or statues of God, that is, those fashioned to represent or to worship God, are simply condemned here. This is clear, 1. From the purpose of the precept, which is the preservation of the pure worship of God.

units.la: 2. Ex natura Dei: Deus est incorporeus & infinitus: Impossibile est igitur, eum corporea & finita imagine exprimi aut repræsentari, sine diuinæ maiestatis diminutione, juxta dicta: Quis mensus est pugillo suo aquas, & cœlos palmo direxit? Cui igitur assimilabitis me, & æquabor illi, dicit sanctus? Mutarunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in effigiem mortalis hominis, & volucrum & quadrupedum & reptilium. 3. Ex Dei interdicto: Cauete diligenter animabus vestris: non enim vidistis vllam imaginem die quo loquutus est Iehoua ad vos in Horeb è medio ignis; Ne forte corrumpamini & faciatis vobis sculptile, aut imaginē vllius simulacri, effigiem masculi & fœmina, effigiem cuiuscunq; animalis, &c. 4. Ex causa huius interdicti; quia hæc simulacra non modo nihil prosunt, sed etiam multum nocent hominibus. Sunt enim eis occasio & causa idolatriæ & pœnarum. Breuiter: Deus sculpi non debet, quia nec vult, nec potest, nec prodest. Memorabile est, quod Plutarchus de Numa in vita eius his verbis scriptum reliquit: Numa Romanis vsu effigiei alicuius diuûm, quæ hominis aut animalis formam haberet, interdixit. Neque priscis illis temporibus fuit apud illos vel picta vlla imago Dei, vel fi&ta; sed primis centum atque septuaginta annis, etsi templa ædificassent, atque sacras casas struxissent, nullum tamen omnino simulacrum efformauere: neq; nempe eo, quod & nefas esset præstantiora deterioribus adsimulare: neq; Deum aliter quàm mente attingi posse censerent. Damascenus scribit conari Deum effingere, rem esse insipientem & impiam: licet is alias imaginum cultum non obscurè defendat; Ideo cum aliis imaginum patronis damnatur septima synodo à Constantino & filio eius Leone celebrata, quæ decreuit, ne Christus pingeretur, aut fingeretur, etiam quoad naturam humanam: quia exprimi non posset arte nisi eius humanitas: & qui talia faciunt, videantur vel Nestorianum vel Eutychianum errorem stabilire. Secundo: Illicitæ sunt imagines & statuæ creaturarum, quæ in templis, in compitis, vel alibi ad cultum Dei, vel ad ornatum periculosum ponuntur. Non incurvabis te illis, &c. Filioli, fugite idola. 1 Ioh. 5,21. Licitæ verò imagines creaturarũ esse possunt, quæ extra temp-la, citra periculum & speciem idololatriæ, superstitionis aut scandali, ad vsum politicum, hoc est, historicũ aut symbolicum, vel ad honestum ornatum fiunt: cuiusmodi imagines erant leones in throno Salomonis, imago Cæsaris in numismate, &c. Obiect. 1. Non facies simulacrum. Ergo Deus prohibet artem sculptoriam. R. Prohibet abusum. Is autem est: 1. Si Deum velimus sculpere. 2. Si ad statuas cultum Dei alligemus.
units.tr: 2. From the nature of God: God is incorporeal and infinite. It is therefore impossible that he be expressed or represented by a corporeal and finite image without diminishing the divine majesty, according to the words: "Who has measured the waters in his fist, and marked out the heavens with a span? To whom then will you liken me, that I should be equal to him? says the Holy One." "They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of mortal man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things." 3. From God's prohibition: "Take diligent heed to your souls, for you saw no image on the day when the LORD spoke to you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire; lest perhaps you be corrupted and make for yourselves a carved image, or the likeness of any figure, the form of male or female, the form of any animal, etc." 4. From the cause of this prohibition: such images not only profit nothing but also harm men greatly, for they are an occasion and cause of idolatry and of punishments. In brief: God ought not to be carved, because he neither wills it, nor can it be done, nor is it of any use. It is worth remembering what Plutarch wrote about Numa in his life, in these words: "Numa forbade the Romans the use of an image of any of the gods that had the form of a man or an animal. In those early times there was among them no painted or fashioned image of God; but for the first hundred and seventy years, although they built temples and erected sacred shrines, they made no image of him at all, since it was wrong to liken better things to worse, and they thought God could be grasped only by the mind." Damascene writes that to attempt to fashion God is a foolish and impious thing, although elsewhere he defends the worship of images not obscurely. Therefore he is condemned, along with the other defenders of images, by the seventh synod, held under Constantine and his son Leo, which decreed that Christ should not be painted or fashioned, even in his human nature, because his humanity could not be expressed by art, and those who do such things seem to establish either the Nestorian or the Eutychian error. Second: images and statues of creatures are unlawful when they are placed in temples, at crossroads, or elsewhere for the worship of God or for dangerous ornament. "You shall not bow down to them, etc." "Little children, flee from idols." 1 John 5:21. Images of creatures can, however, be lawful when they are made outside temples, without danger and without any appearance of idolatry, superstition or offence, for political use, that is, historical or symbolic, or for honest ornament. Of this kind were the lions on Solomon's throne, the image of Caesar on a coin, and so on. Objection 1: "You shall not make a likeness." Therefore God forbids the art of sculpture. Answer: he forbids the abuse. That abuse is: 1. if we wish to carve God; 2. if we tie the worship of God to statues.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Ipsa scriptura sacra Deo tribuit humana membra, & sic ipsius naturam & proprietatis significat. Ergo etiam nobis licet Deum per simulacra repræsentare. Resp. Est dissimilitudo inter illas metaphoras verborum & simulacra : quia illis in verbo Dei addita est declaratio, quæ errorem prohibet: neque iis verbis alligari solet cultus Dei. His autem nec declaratio adjuncta est, & facilimè ab hominibus cultus & adoratio eis affingitur. Illis igitur metaphoris Deus ipse de se vsus est per ἀνθρωπομόρφειαν, ad succurrendum nostræ infirmitati, & nobis de se loquentibus vti permisit: picturis autem & statuis nec ipse se repræsentauit, nec nos ad se repræsentandum vti voluit, sed grauiter vetuit. Vnde sequitur quidem, licere nobis exemplo scripturæ Deo humana membra per ἀνθρωπομόρφειαν tribuere: non sequitur autem, licere nobis Deum per colores vel sculpturas humanis membris efformare.
units.tr: Objection 2: Scripture itself attributes human members to God, and so signifies his nature and properties. Therefore we too may represent God by likenesses. Answer: there is a dissimilarity between those figures of speech and images. In God's word a declaration is added to those metaphors which prevents error, and worship is not usually bound to those words. But to images no declaration is added, and worship and adoration are very easily ascribed to them by men. God himself therefore used those metaphors about himself by anthropomorphism [ἀνθρωπομόρφειαν], to help our weakness, and he permitted us to use them when speaking of him. But as to pictures and statues, he neither represented himself by them nor wished us to represent him by them, but gravely forbade it. Whence it follows indeed that, by the example of Scripture, we may attribute human members to God by anthropomorphism; but it does not follow that we may form God by colours or sculptures in human members.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Deus olim in specie humana videndum se præbuit. Ergo nobis eadem signa licet imitari. Resp. Deus quidem certis rationibus id fecit: at nobis istius rei imitationem interdixit. Nec obscura est prohibitionis ratio. Deo enim licet se manifestare, quocunque modo ipsi placet. Nulli autem creaturæ licet Deum signo, quo ipse non jussit, repræsentare. Est igitur dissimilitudo in exemplis. Præterea, species illæ habebant promissionem præsentiæ & exauditionis Dei ad illas: quod de simulacris illas imitantibus dici non potest sine manifesta idololatria. Denique species illæ tantisper manebant, donec illis Deus ad patefactionem sui vti volebat, ideoque ad idololatriam rapi non poterant, neque legimus, à quoquam vnquam, nisi à defectoribus Christianis, Deum tali specie effigiatum fuisse. Statuæ verò & picturæ, quas homines ad patefactiones diuinas repræsentandas faciunt, neque ad patefactiones Dei, neque ad repræsentationem patefactionum à Deo sunt ordinatæ; proinde sunt obiectum & occasio idololatriæ.
units.tr: Objection 3. God once showed himself to be seen in human form. Therefore we may imitate those same signs. Answer. God indeed did this for certain reasons, but he forbade us to imitate it. The reason for the prohibition is not obscure. God may reveal himself in whatever way pleases him, but no creature may represent God by a sign that God has not commanded. There is therefore a dissimilarity between the examples. Moreover, those appearances carried a promise of God's presence and of his hearing of those who prayed to him, which cannot be said of images that imitate them without manifest idolatry. Finally, those appearances lasted only as long as God wished them for revealing himself, and so they could not be turned into idolatry. We read of no one, except apostate Christians, having been given a likeness of God in such a form. Statues and pictures, however, which men make to represent the divine revelations, are ordained neither for the revelations of God nor for representing the revelations made by God. Therefore they are the object and occasion of idolatry.

units.la: Typus distinctionis imaginum.
units.tr: A summary of the distinction of images.

units.la: Imaginum aliæ sunt naturales, vt meteoricæ & physicæ aliæ. artificiales : quales sunt sculptiles fusiles. pictæ. Hæ distinguuntur materia, obiectis, finib. : suntq; vel Dei, quæ simpliciter damnátur hoc præcepto, & passim, idque quia maiestatem Dei imminuunt, & ex Deo idolum faciunt. creaturarum: licita, quæ extra templa & periculum idolatriæ, vsum politicum vel honestum ornatumhabent. Illicita, quæ in templis ad cultum Dei vel ornatum periculosum ponūtur.
units.tr: Some images are natural, such as meteoric and physical ones; others are artificial, such as carved, cast and painted ones. These are distinguished by their matter, their objects and their ends. Some are of God, and these are condemned simply and everywhere by this precept, because they diminish the majesty of God and make an idol out of God. Others are of creatures: lawful ones, which stand outside temples and the danger of idolatry and have a civil or honest use or ornament; and unlawful ones, which are placed in temples for the worship of God or for a dangerous ornament.

units.la: II. An omnis adoratio ad statuas sit prohibita, nec possit vlla ratione defendi.
units.tr: II. Whether all adoration directed at statues is forbidden and cannot be defended by any reasoning.

units.la: De hac quæstione ex secunda parte præcepti respondetur, quæ simpliciter vetat, non tantum qui ad creaturas, sed etiam quiad cultum siue honorem diuinum imaginibus & statuis exhibere verum Deum referatur: Non eis incuruabis te, nec coles ea.
units.tr: This question is answered from the second part of the precept, which simply forbids not only that images and statues be given worship that is referred to creatures, but also that they be given the worship or honour due to the true God: You shall not bow down to them, nor serve them.

units.la: Obiect.1. Non veneramur statuas (inquiunt cultores idolorum in papatu) sed Deum, cuius illæ sunt signa, juxta versiculos, qui tribuuntur synodo Nicenæ II. Hoc Deus est, quod imago docet: non est Deus ipsa. Hanc videas, sed mente colas, quod cernis in ipsa.
units.tr: Objection 1. The worshippers of idols in the papacy say: "We do not venerate statues, but God, of whom they are signs," according to the verses which are attributed to the Second Council of Nicaea: "This is what God teaches through the image; it is not God itself. You may look at this, but worship in the mind what you see in it."

units.la: Et illos Thomæ:
units.tr: And those of Thomas:

units.la: Effigiem Christi dum transis, semper honora: Non tamen effigiem, sed quem designat, adora.
units.tr: "As you pass by the likeness of Christ, always honour it; yet adore not the likeness, but him whom it designates."

units.la: Resp.1. Negatur statuas esse signa Dei: quia per eas Deus vere significari non potest, cum sit immensus: & vt maximè possset, tamen non debet, quia prohibuit: & quia signa Deo, per quæ significetur, statuere, in nullius creaturæ potestate, sed in solius Dei arbitrio est positum. 2. Est fallacia non causa. Idololatriæ causa & forma est, non tantum statuarum, sed ipsius etiam Dei adoratio, quæ præter, vel contra eius verbum ad statuas vel alias creaturas exercetur: id quod vituli Aaronis & Ieroboami satis confirmant. Etsi enim & hi dicerent: Ecce dij tui Israel, qui eduxerunt te de terra Ægypti: Cras erit solemnitas Iehovæ: tamen cul-tus illos vt horribilem idololatriam Deus est detestatus, & grauiter puniuit. Non igitur Deus, sed diabolus colitur in idolis, vtut nomen Dei idololatræ prætexant: sicut Paulus de gentibus dicit: Quæ immolant (idolis,) dæmoniis immolant, non Deo: quamuis & ipsi nomen Dei suis cultibus prætexerent.
units.tr: Answer 1. It is denied that statues are signs of God, because God cannot truly be signified by them, since he is immense. And even if he could be signified in this way, he ought not to be, because he has forbidden it; and because it is not in the power of any creature to appoint signs by which God may be signified, but this lies only in God's own decision. 2. It is the fallacy of not the cause. The cause and form of idolatry is not only the statues but the worship of God itself, which is offered to statues or other creatures apart from, or contrary to, his word. The calves of Aaron and of Jeroboam confirm this well enough. For although these men also said: "Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt" and "Tomorrow there will be a festival to Jehovah," nevertheless God detested those cults as horrible idolatry and punished them severely. Therefore it is not God but the devil who is worshipped in idols, however much the idolaters pretend the name of God, as Paul says of the Gentiles: "What they sacrifice to idols they sacrifice to demons, not to God." Yet even they pretended the name of God in their rites.

units.la: Obiect.1. Honor signi est rei signatæ honor. Imagines sunt signa Dei. Ergo honor imaginib. exhibitus exhibetur etiam Deo. Resp. Rursus neganda est minor, vel maior distinguenda, honorem signi ad rem signatam pertinere, quando signum reuera est signum, hoc est, ab eo institutum, qui instituendi potestatem habet, & quando is honor signo habetur, quem ei legitimus author signi haberi iussit. Honoris enim regula non est voluntas honorantis, sed honorandi. Quare cum Deus vtrumque vetuerit, & statuas sibi fieri, & se ad statuas sibi vel creaturis factas honorari; non honore, sed contumelia afficitur, cum honor ad statuas ipsi inuito obtruditur.
units.tr: Objection 1. The honour of a sign is the honour of the thing signified. Images are signs of God. Therefore the honour shown to images is shown also to God. Answer. Again, the minor premise must be denied, or the major distinguished: the honour of a sign pertains to the thing signified when the sign is really a sign, that is, instituted by one who has the power to institute it, and when that honour is paid to the sign which the lawful author of the sign has commanded to be paid to it. For the rule of honour is not the will of the one who honours, but of the one who is to be honoured. Therefore, since God has forbidden both that statues be made for himself and that he be honoured through statues made for himself or for creatures, he is not honoured but insulted when honour is forced upon statues against his will.

units.la: Inst. Contumelia illata signo etiam sine mandato Dei facto, redundat in Deum. Ergo etiam honor tali signo Dei delatus, ipsi Deo defertur. Respond. Negatur consequentia, quia contraria contrariis tunc recte tribuuntur, cum contrarietas prædicatorum pendet ex eo ipso, secundum quod opponuntur subiecta, non autem, cum pendet ex alio aliquo: vt hic Dei contumelia sequitur quidem ad contumeliam signi, siue legitimi, siue illegitimi, quæcunq; ab ipsius mandato discedendi. Sed honor Dei non sequitur ad honorem signi, nisi & signum & honor signi à Deo sit ordinatus, quia ad honorem Dei non sufficit intentio ipsum honorandi, sed requiritur etiam modus ab ipso præscriptus.
units.tr: Objection. An insult offered to a sign, even one made without God's command, reflects upon God. Therefore the honour paid to such a sign of God is also paid to God himself. Answer. The inference is denied, because contraries are rightly attributed to contraries only when the contrariety of the predicates depends on the very thing according to which the subjects are opposed, and not when it depends on something else. Thus an insult to God does indeed follow from an insult to a sign, whether lawful or unlawful, whenever that sign departs from his command. But the honour of God does not follow from the honour of a sign unless both the sign and the honour of the sign have been ordained by God, because for honouring God it is not enough to intend to honour him; the manner prescribed by him is also required.

units.la: Obiect.2. Monumentis præstantium aut bene meritorum hominum licet honorem habere. Ergo multo magis statuis angeli & sanctorum. Respon.1.ad antecedens: licet monumentis præstantium virorum honorem habere, nempe eum, qui sir gratia & honorifica eorum memoria, & rerum illarum, quas tanquam monumenta sui reliquerunt, in eum vsum, in quem recte consulerunt, collatio, vel earum, si necessitas mutationem postulet, sine voluntate aut studio ipsos afficiendi contumelia, corruptio aut destructio. Minime autem honore eis deferre licet diuidiuinum, qualis est: quem idolis isti deferunt, siue λατρείας siue δουλείας nomine eum pallient. 2. Illa etiam monumenta talia esse debent, quæ in idololatriam tracta non fuerint: alioqui non honor illis habendus, sed omnino abolenda sunt, exemplo serpentis æneî, quem Ezechias confregit, cum in idololatriam abiisset, etsi prius tanquam diuini beneficij in deserto præstiti monumentum, asseruatus fuerat.
units.tr: Objection 2. It is lawful to show honour to the monuments of outstanding or well-deserving men. Therefore much more to statues of angels and saints.
