Est autem allegoriam illam, qua Christus cogitationes, cruciatus, & statum impiorum in pœnis exprimere voluerit, partes parabolæ ostendunt. 2. Etsi hæc ita gesta essent: tamen nihil prohibant: cum ex sermone Epulonis eas preces accepisse, non autem cogitationes eius arcanas inspexisse, & Epuloni supplicanti respondisse quidem, sed nihil gratificatus esse dicatur Abraham.
units.tr: Objection 7. The soul of Dives saw Abraham in heaven from hell and invoked him, and Abraham heard him, and Dives knew the state of his five brothers in this life. Therefore the saints living in heaven know the state and the prayers of those who live on earth, and they are to be invoked. Answer: Doctrines cannot be established from allegories and parables. The parts of the parable show what the allegory was meant to express: Christ wished to portray the thoughts, torments and state of the wicked in punishment. (2) Even if these things happened just so, nothing prevents it, since it is said that Dives received those prayers from his speech, not that Abraham looked into his secret thoughts; and Abraham is said to have answered the suppliant Dives but to have granted him nothing.

units.la: Obiect. 8. Christus secundum humanam naturam cognoscit omnia. Ergo & sancti. Resp. Est dissimilitudo in exemplis. Mens humana Christi intelligit ac scit: aures atque oculi etiam ipsius corporales audiunt & vident omnia, quæcunque secundum naturam humanam vult mente vel sensibus externis percipere, propter vnionem personalem, id est, reuelante natura diuina, & propter officium mediatoris. Omnia vero sic etiam reuelari angelis & sanctis, quæ reuelantur intellectui humano Christi ab ipsius diuinitate, e scriptura non potest probari.
units.tr: Objection 8. Christ knows all things according to his human nature. Therefore so do the saints. Answer: There is a dissimilarity in the examples. The human mind of Christ understands and knows, and his ears and eyes, even his bodily ones, hear and see all things which, according to his human nature, he wishes to perceive by the mind or by the external senses. This is on account of the personal union, that is, the divine nature revealing, and on account of the office of mediator. But that all the things which are revealed to the human intellect of Christ by his divinity are likewise revealed to angels and saints cannot be proved from Scripture.

units.la: Obiect. 9. In speculo Trinitatis relucent omnium rerum imagines. Sancti angeli & beati homines intuentur speculum diuinitatis, iuxta illud: Angeli in cœlis semper vident faciem patris mei, qui est in cœlis. Ergo vident omnia in speculo divinitatis, quæ nos agimus, patimur, &c. Resp. 1. Maior incerta est, neque ex scriptura probatur. 2. Nec est firma minor. Nam Deum nemo vidit unquam. 3. Etsi angeli & sancti in cœlo illustri cognitione fruantur, tamen non est fingendum, eos omnia naturaliter perspicere, quæcunque in Deo sunt. Sic enim ipsorum sapientia esset infinita, hoc est, æqualis divinæ sapientiæ; quod absurdum, & scripturæ testimoniis est contrarium, cum angeli etiam dicantur ignorare diem judicij. Constat autem, Deum vnicuique tam in cœlo, quam in terra pro sua Œšνια patefacere, quantum vult.
units.tr: Objection 9. The images of all things shine forth in the mirror of the Trinity. The holy angels and the blessed men gaze upon the mirror of the divinity, according to that saying: The angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. Therefore they see in the mirror of the divinity all that we do, suffer, and so on. Answer: (1) The major premise is uncertain and is not proved from Scripture. (2) The minor is not firm either, for no one has ever seen God. (3) Even if the angels and saints in heaven enjoy a clear knowledge, we must not imagine that they naturally perceive all things that are in God. For then their wisdom would be infinite, that is, equal to the divine wisdom, which is absurd and contrary to the testimonies of Scripture, since the angels are also said to be ignorant of the day of judgment. It is certain, however, that God reveals to each one, both in heaven and on earth, as much as he wishes, according to his economy [οἰκονομίαν].

units.la: Obiect. 10. Tanta est amicitia sanctorum cum Deo & Christo, vt negare illis non possit patefactionem eorum, quæ petimus. R. A causa non sufficiente ad effectum, non valet consequentia. Consistit enim hæc amicitia, quantumuis Deus sanctis non omnia pro libito, sed ea duntaxat patefaciat, quæ ipsos scire gloriæ suæ, & felicitatis eorum interest.
units.tr: Objection 10. The friendship of the saints with God and Christ is so great that he cannot deny them the disclosure of what we ask. Answer. The consequence does not hold from an insufficient cause to the effect. For this friendship remains even though God does not disclose everything to the saints at their pleasure, but only those things which it is in the interest of his glory and of their happiness that they should know.

units.la: Obiect. 11. Christus est mediator redemptionis: sancti sunt mediatores intercessionis. Ergo nihil derogatur Christo, si sancti, vt intercessores & deprecatores invocentur. Resp. Distinctio hæc negatur: quia scriptura docet, Christum solum & vnicum mediatorem non tantum semel nos moriendo redemisse, sed etiam semper apparere pro nobis, & intercedere in conspectu Patris. Est igitur ipse solus tam intercessionis, quàm redemptionis mediator.
units.tr: Objection 11. Christ is the mediator of redemption; the saints are mediators of intercession. Therefore nothing is taken from Christ if the saints are invoked as intercessors and advocates. Answer. This distinction is denied, because Scripture teaches that Christ, the only and sole mediator, not only redeemed us once by dying but also always appears on our behalf and intercedes in the sight of the Father. He is therefore the sole mediator both of intercession and of redemption.

units.la: Obiect. 12. Christus est solus mediator virtute meriti & intercessionis propriæ: sancti vero sunt mediatores & intercessores virtute meriti & intercessionis Christi, hoc est, intercessio eorum pro nobis valet apud Deum propter Christi meritum & intercessionem: ergo non transfertur ad ipsos, quod est Christi proprium. Resp. Christo æquè sunt injurij, qui hoc objiciunt. Non enim in antecedente est sufficiens enumeratio earum rationum, quibus Christi honor ad alios transfertur; quandoquidem non solum qui propria, sed etiam, qui Christi virtute nobis apud Deum merieri dicuntur bona, propter solius Christi meritum promissa, in Christi locum substituuntur. Deinde, si placent exaudiuntur preces sanctorum, virtute meriti & intercessionis Christi, non possunt utique placere, & nobis aliquid impetrare propter suam sanctitatem & meritum: sicuti tradunt Papistæ: siquidem qui ipse indiget mediatore & intercessore, is non potest aliorum esse intercessor, etsi pro aliis orare possit. Destruunt igitur aduersarij suam ipsorum doctrinam. Obiect. 13. Orantes pro nobis in vita cœlesti, sunt invocandi. Sancti pro nobis orant in vita cœlesti. Ergo sunt invocandi. Resp. Fallacia non causæ: quia precatio alicuius pro altero non est sufficiens causa, propter quam sit invocandus alius, qui pro nobis litantis ecclesiæ in terra, & vota ipsorum exaudiri secundum consilium Dei: sed sanctos intelligere mala singulorum, & preces exaudire, concedi non potest.
units.tr: Objection 12. Christ is the only mediator by virtue of his own merit and intercession; the saints, however, are mediators and intercessors by virtue of the merit and intercession of Christ, that is, their intercession for us avails with God because of the merit and intercession of Christ. Therefore what is proper to Christ is not transferred to them. Answer. Those who raise this objection do an injury to Christ no less than the others. For the enumeration of the grounds on which the honour of Christ is transferred to others is not complete in the antecedent, since those who are said to obtain good things for us with God, not only by their own merit but also by the virtue of Christ, and goods promised on account of Christ's merit alone, are substituted in the place of Christ. Moreover, if the prayers of the saints are heard because they are pleasing, by virtue of the merit and intercession of Christ, then they certainly cannot be pleasing and obtain something for us on account of their own holiness and merit, as the Papists teach. For he who himself needs a mediator and intercessor cannot be an intercessor for others, even though he may be able to pray for others. Thus the adversaries destroy their own doctrine. Objection 13. Those who pray for us in the heavenly life are to be invoked. The saints pray for us in the heavenly life. Therefore they are to be invoked. Answer: This is a fallacy of the non-cause, because one person's prayer for another is not a sufficient cause why the other should be invoked, who prays for us... but it cannot be conceded that the saints understand the evils of individuals and hear their prayers, the Church on earth sacrificing and its vows being heard according to the counsel of God.

units.la: Obj. 14. Si steterint Moses & Samuel coram me, non est anima mea ad populum hunc. Ergo sancti stant coram Deo, & orant pro nobis. Resp. 1. Etiam toto concesso, tamen non sequitur, ideo esse invocandos, ut est ostensum. 2. Est prosopopœia introducens mortuos precantes, tanquam adhuc viventes, quasi dicat, si Moses & Samuel adhuc viuerent, & orarent pro isto populo impio, sicut viventes orarunt pro sui temporis populo, & exauditi fuerunt: non impetrarent ei gratiam & veniam. Similis locus est apud Ezechielem, similiter explicandus.
units.tr: Objection 14. If Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people. Therefore the saints stand before God and pray for us. Answer: (1) Even granting the whole, it does not follow that they are therefore to be invoked, as has been shown. (2) It is a prosopopoeia, introducing the dead as praying as though still living, as if he said: if Moses and Samuel were still living and prayed for this impious people, as the living prayed for the people of their own time and were heard, they would not obtain grace and pardon for them. A similar passage is in Ezekiel, and it is to be explained in the same way.

units.la: Obiect. 15. Dominus ait per Esaiam: Protegam civitatem hanc, ut seruem eam propter me, & propter Dauidem seruum meum. Ergo propter merita & intercessionem Dauidis & aliorum sanctorum post mortem Deus benefacit hominibus in terra. Resp. Non respectu meriti Dauidis, sed respectu promissionis de Messia ex Dauidis posteritate nascituro, promittitur urbis protectio & liberatio. Inst. Liberatio urbis ab obsidione Assyriorum etiam sine beneficio Messiæ fieri potuit. Ergo non promittitur propter Messiam, sed propter merita Dauidis. Resp. Errant, quicunque putant, Christi beneficium tantum ad eas res pertinere, aut promissiones, sine quibus præstitis, non potuisset seruari promissio Dauidi facta. Omnia enim beneficia Dei, tam corporalia, quàm spiritualia, tam ante, quam post Messiam exhibitum, tam sine quibus poterat, quam sine quibus non poterat promissio de ipso exhibendo impleri, præstantur Ecclesiæ propter Christum. Quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei, in Christo sunt etiam & amen.
units.tr: Objection 15. The Lord says through Isaiah: I will protect this city to save it for my own sake and for David my servant. Therefore God does good to men on earth on account of the merits and intercession of David and of other saints after death. Answer: The protection and deliverance of the city are promised not with respect to David's merit, but with respect to the promise of the Messiah, who was to be born from David's posterity. Objection: The deliverance of the city from the siege of the Assyrians could also have happened without the benefit of the Messiah. Therefore it is promised not on account of the Messiah but on account of the merits of David. Answer: They err who think that the benefit of Christ pertains only to those things, or those promises, without which the promise made to David could not have been kept. For all the benefits of God, both bodily and spiritual, both before and after the Messiah was exhibited, both those without which it could be and those without which the promise of his coming could not be fulfilled, are granted to the Church on account of Christ. For however many the promises of God are, in Christ they are also yes and amen.

units.la: Obiect. 16. Jacob dicit de filiis Joseph: Invocetur nomen meum super eos, nomina quoque patrum meorum Abraham, Isaac. Ergo sanctos licet invocare. Resp. Fallacia est figuræ dictionis: quia phrasis Hebraica non significat adorationem, sed adoptionem filiorum Josephi: & est sensus: vocentur nomine meo, seu denominentur à me, hoc est, dicantur mei filij, non nepotes. Similis phrasis est apud Esaiam: Septem mulieres dicent uni viro: Tantummodo vocetur nomen tuum super nos: (id est, dicamur uxores tuæ: abs te deminemur) aufer opprobrium nostrum.
units.tr: Objection 16. Jacob says of the sons of Joseph: let my name be invoked upon them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Therefore it is lawful to invoke the saints. Answer: This is a fallacy of figure of speech, for the Hebrew phrase signifies not adoration but the adoption of Joseph's sons. The sense is: let them be called by my name, or be named after me, that is, let them be called my sons, not grandsons. A similar phrase is in Isaiah: seven women shall say to one man: only let your name be called upon us (that is, let us be called your wives, let us be named after you); take away our reproach.

units.la: Obiect. 17. Eliphas dicit Jobo: Voca quaso, an sit, qui respondeat tibi, & ad quem sanctorum respicies? Ergo Jobus jubetur implorare opem alicuius sancti. Resp. Locus aperte aduersatur angelorum invocationi. Dicit enim angelus adeo antecellere hominibus puritate, vt nec quidem respondeant, vel appareant hominibus vocati.
units.tr: Objection 17. Eliphaz says to Job: Call, I pray you, if there is anyone who will answer you, and to which of the saints will you turn? Therefore Job is bidden to implore the help of some saint. Answer: The passage plainly contradicts the invocation of angels. For the angel is said to surpass men so much in purity that they do not even answer or appear to men who call upon them.

units.la: Obiect. 18. Christus dicit: Quatenus id fecistis vni ex his fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Ergo invocatio sanctorum est honor, qui ipsi Christo exhibetur. Resp. Christus non loquitur de invocatione sanctorum post mortem: sed de officiis dilectionis, afflictis membris suis in hac vita exhibitis. Locus igitur nihil facit ad rem.
units.tr: Objection 18. Christ says: Inasmuch as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me. Therefore the invocation of saints is an honour paid to Christ himself. Answer: Christ is not speaking of the invocation of saints after death, but of the offices of love shown to his afflicted members in this life. The passage therefore has nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: Obiectio 19. Respondit angelus Jehouae, & dixit: Jehova exercituum, quousque tu non misereris Ierusalem, & urbium Iuda, quas spreuisti his septuaginta annis? Ergo angeli orant in specie pro necessitatibus hominum, eoque sunt invocandi. Resp. 1. Exloco Zachariae non potest ostendi, quod angeli omnium necessitates intelligant. Calamitates autem Judaeorum non tantum angelis, sed etiam hominibus erant in conspectu. 2. Negatur consequentia ab angelis ad sanctos mortuos. Angelis enim mandata est cura Ecclesiae in hac vita. Itaque in terris vident nostras necessitates, quas non vident sancti, quibus hoc officium non est commissum. 3. Ab angelorum precibus ad ipsorum invocationem non valet consequentia: vt supra ostensum.
units.tr: Objection 19. The angel of Jehovah answered and said: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have despised these seventy years? Therefore the angels intercede in particular for the needs of men, and so they are to be invoked. Answer: 1. From the passage in Zechariah it cannot be shown that the angels know all men's needs. The calamities of the Jews were in view not only of the angels but also of men. 2. The inference from angels to dead saints is denied. For the care of the Church in this life has been committed to the angels. Thus they see our needs on earth, which the saints do not see, since this office has not been entrusted to them. 3. The inference from the prayers of angels to the invocation of them is not valid, as was shown above.

units.la: Obiectio 20. Judas Maccabaeus in somnio vidit Oniam Pontificem & Jeremiam Prophetam orantes pro populo. Ergo sancti mortui orant pro nobis, & sunt invocandi. Resp. Liber apocryphus nihil probat: & rursus negatur consequentia a precibus sanctorum ad invocationem ipsorum: quando quidem non omnis, qui orat pro nobis, continuo a nobis est invocandus.
units.tr: Objection 20. Judas Maccabeus saw in a dream Onias the high priest and Jeremiah the prophet praying for the people. Therefore dead saints pray for us, and are to be invoked. Answer: The apocryphal book proves nothing. And again the inference from the prayers of saints to the invocation of them is denied, since not everyone who prays for us must at once be invoked by us.

units.la: Obiectio 21. Baruch dicit: Audi quaso preces mortuorum Israel. Respond. Ergo sancti pro nobis precantur, & sunt invocandi. Baruch est apocryphus, & est fallacia figurae dictionis. Mortui enim Israelitae dicuntur non defuncti, sed viuentes, & invocantes DEVM in hac vita, sed propter calamitates mortuis similes.
units.tr: Objection 21. Baruch says: Hear, I pray you, the prayers of the dead of Israel. Answer: Therefore the saints pray for us and are to be invoked. Baruch is apocryphal, and this is a fallacy of figure of speech. For the dead of Israel are not called the departed, but the living, who call upon God in this life, yet are like the dead because of their calamities.

units.la: Obiect. 22. Non licet sine intercessione ad principem irrumpere. Ergo multo minus in Dei conspectu venire. Resp. Concedilur totum. Neq; enim sine mediatore Christo ad Deum cuiquam accessus patet, sicut ipse dicit: Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Praeclare vero respondet Ambrosius in expositione epistolae ad Romanos, sic scribens: Solent quidam misera uti excusatione, dicentes, per justos posse iri ad Deum, sicut per comites pervenitur ad regem. Age: nunquid tam demens est aliquis, & salutis suae immemor, ut honorificentiam regis vindicet comiti, cum hac de re, si qui etiam tractare fuerint inventi, jure ut rei damnentur maiestatis? & isti non putant reos, qui honorem nominis Dei deferunt creaturae, & relicto Domino adorant conservos, quasi sit aliquid plus quod serviatur Deo. Nam & ideo ad regem per tribunos & comites itur, quia homo utique rex, & nescit, quibus debeat rempublicam credere. Ad Deum autem, quem utique non latet (omnium enim merita novit) promerendum, sufragatore non est opus, sed mente devota. v bicunq; enim talis locutus fuerit, nihil respondebit, &c. Et Chrysostomus: Mulier Chananaea non rogat Iacobum, non obsecrat Iohannem, neq; pergit ad Petrum, nec intendit Apostolorum chorum, non quaesiuit mediatorem; sed pro omnibus illis poenitentiam accepit comitem, quae inducati locum implevit, & sic ad summum fontem perrexit.
units.tr: Objection 22. It is not permitted to break in upon a prince without an intercessor. Therefore much less may one come into the presence of God. Answer: The whole is conceded. For no access to God is open to anyone without Christ as mediator, as he himself says: No one comes to the Father except through me. Ambrose answers admirably in his exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, writing thus: Some are wont to use a wretched excuse, saying that one can approach God through the righteous, just as one comes to a king through companions. Come now, is anyone so foolish, and so forgetful of his own salvation, as to claim for a companion the honour due to the king? In this matter, if any were found even to discuss it, they would rightly be condemned as guilty of treason. And they do not think those guilty who transfer to a creature the honour of the name of God, and, forsaking the Lord, worship fellow servants, as if there were something more to be served in God. For people go to the king through tribunes and companions because a man, being a king, does not know to whom he ought to entrust the commonwealth. But to win the favour of God, who certainly is not hidden from anyone (for he knows the merits of all), there is no need of a go-between, but of a devout mind. Whoever speaks in this way will receive no answer, etc. And Chrysostom: The Canaanite woman does not ask James, does not entreat John, does not go on to Peter, nor direct her attention to the company of the apostles; she did not seek a mediator. But instead of all those she took repentance as her companion, which fulfilled the place of an introducer, and so went on to the highest fountain.

units.la: Hactenus de sexta virtute, quae fuit invocatio Dei.
units.tr: Thus far concerning the sixth virtue, which was the invocation of God.

units.la: VII. Jurațio legitima, quae est species invocationis Dei, qua petitur, ut Deus sit testis animi jurantis, quod non velit in ea te, de qua jurat, fallere, & puniat jurantem, si iciens fallat: sancita à Deo, ut sit vinculum veritatis inter homines, & testimonium, quod Deus sit author & defensor veritatis.
units.tr: VII. Lawful swearing, which is a kind of invocation of God, by which it is asked that God be witness to the mind of the one swearing, that he does not wish to deceive in the matter about which he swears, and that he punish the one swearing if he deceives knowingly. It was ordained by God so that there might be a bond of truth among men, and a testimony that God is the author and defender of truth.

units.la: Huic contraria est: 1. Juramenti legitimi recusatio, quando quis detrectat juramentum, quod gloria Dei, & salus proximi postulat. Omnis controversia finis est jusjurandum, ad confirmationem adhibitum.
units.tr: Contrary to this are: 1. Refusal of lawful oath, when someone declines an oath which the glory of God and the welfare of a neighbour demand. An oath given for confirmation is the end of every controversy.

units.la: 2. Perjurium: quando quis sciens & volens per juramentum fallit, vel legitimum non servat. Peierare enim est vel rem falsam jurare, puta, te non esse reum caedis, cum interfeceris: vel rem licite juratam non praestare.
units.tr: 2. Perjury: when someone knowingly and willingly deceives by an oath, or does not keep a lawful oath. For to perjure is either to swear to a false thing, for example that you are not guilty of murder when you have committed it, or not to perform a thing lawfully sworn to.

units.la: 3. Juramentum idololatricum: quod non per solum verum Deum juratur.
units.tr: 3. Idolatrous oath: one that is sworn not by the only true God.

units.la: 4. Juramentum de re illicita: quale erat juramentum Herodis.
units.tr: 4. Oath concerning an unlawful matter: such as was the oath of Herod.

units.la: 5. Juramentum temerarium: ex levitate, hoc est, nulla necessaria, aut nulla gravi de causa datum. Et de hoc loquuntur dicta juramentum prohibentia. Matth. 5. & 23. & Jac. 5.
units.tr: 5. Rash oath: given out of levity, that is, given for no necessary or grave reason. It is of this that the sayings forbidding oaths speak: Matt. 5, 23 and James 5.

units.la: Sed doctrina de juramento duabus quaestionibus sequentibus fusius explicatur.
units.tr: But the doctrine of oaths is explained more fully in the two following questions.

units.la: Hom. 16. & variis in Matth. locis.
units.tr: Hom. 16, and in various places on Matthew.

units.la: Iuramenti legitimum.
units.tr: Lawful oath.

units.la: Hebr. 6, 16.
Peierare.
units.tr: To perjure.

units.la: Matt. 14, 9.
units.tr: Matt. 14, 9.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CI.
units.tr: QUESTION 101.

units.la: Potestne quis etiam pie per nomen Dei iurare?
units.tr: Can anyone also swear piously by the name of God?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Potest; cum vel magistratus id exigit, vel alioqui necessitas hoc pacto fidem firmari, & veritatem stabiliri postulat: quo & gloria Dei illustretur, & aliorum saluti consulatur. Nam eius generis iusiurandum verbo Dei sancitur a, ideoque etiam à sanctis in veteri & nouo foedere recte est vsurpatum b.
units.tr: Yes, he can: when the magistrate demands it, or when otherwise necessity requires that faith be confirmed in this way and truth be established, so that the glory of God may be illustrated and the salvation of others be promoted. For an oath of this kind is sanctioned by the Word of God a, and therefore it has also been rightly used by the saints under the old and the new covenant b.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CII.
units.tr: QUESTION 102.

units.la: Estne licitum, iurare per sanctos, & alias creaturas?
units.tr: Is it lawful to swear by the saints and other creatures?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Non. Nam legitimum iuramentum est invocatio Dei a, qua petitur, vt is tanquam vnicus cordium inspector, testimonium det veritati b, & iurantem puniat, si sciens fallat c: Porrò hic honos nulli creaturae conuenit d.
units.tr: No. For a lawful oath is an invocation of God, by which it is sought that He, as the only inspector of hearts, should bear witness to the truth and punish the one swearing if he swears falsely knowingly. Moreover, this honour belongs to no creature.

units.la: a b c 2 Corinth. 1. verf. 13. d Matth. 4, 10. 1 Reg. 8, 39. Genes. 17, 1. Deut. 31. verf. 35.
units.tr: a b c 2 Corinthians 1, verse 23. d Matthew 4:10. 1 Kings 8:39. Genesis 17:1. Deuteronomy 31, verse 35.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: His duabus quaestionibus fusius explicatur doctrina de iuramento.
units.tr: The doctrine of the oath is explained more fully in these two questions.

units.la: DE IVRAMENTO.
units.tr: ON OATHS.

units.la: De iuramento praecipuè quaeritur: I. Quid sit iuramentum. II. Per quem sit iurandum. III. Liceatne Christiano iurare. IV. De quibus rebus sit jurandum.
units.tr: Concerning oaths, the following is chiefly asked: (I) what an oath is; (II) by whom one ought to swear; (III) whether it is lawful for a Christian to swear; (IV) about what matters one ought to swear.

units.la: V. An omnia juramenta sint seruanda.
units.tr: (V) Whether all oaths are to be kept.

units.la: Tria postrema ad quæstionem CI. pertinent, duo priora ad quæstionem CII.
units.tr: The last three belong to question CI, and the first two to question CII.

units.la: I. Quid sit iuramentum.
units.tr: I. What an oath is.

units.la: Iuramentum sæpe pro toto cultu Dei in scriptura vsurpatur, vt: Per nomen eius jurabis. In die illa erunt quinque ciuitates in terra Ægypti, loquentes lingua Canaan, & jurantes per Iehouam exercituum. Mihi curuabitur omne genu: per me jurabit omnis lingua. Et de cultu noui Testamenti: Qui jurabit in terra, jurabit in Deo verace. Si jurauerit per nomen meum, ædificabuntur in medio populi mei, &c. Causa est, quia per quem juramus, eum profitemur, nos pro Deo habere. Proprie vero juramentum est inuocatio Dei, qua petitur, vt is tanquam vnicus cordium inspector, testimonium det veritati, & jurantem puniat, si sciens fallat. Sic definit catechesis: & desumta est definitio ex formula juramenti, qua vtitur Apostolus: Ego vero testem innuoco DEVM in animam meam, me idcirco nondum venisse Corinthum, vt vobis parcam.
units.tr: Oath is often used in Scripture for the whole worship of God, as in: "You shall swear by his name." "In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the LORD of hosts." "To me every knee shall bow; by me every tongue shall swear." And of the worship of the New Testament: "He who swears in the land shall swear by the true God." "If he swears by my name, they shall be built up in the midst of my people," etc. The reason is that by whomever we swear, we profess that we hold him to be God. Properly, however, an oath is an invocation of God, by which it is asked that he, as the one and only searcher of hearts, give testimony to the truth and punish the one swearing if he deceives knowingly. The catechism defines it thus, and the definition is taken from the formula of oath that the Apostle uses: "But I call God as witness against my soul," that I had not yet come to Corinth so as to spare you.

units.la: Testimonium det. Nempe seruando jurantem & benefaciendo ei, si recte juret: puniendo autem, & destruendo eum, si sciens mentiatur. Sancitum enim est juramentum à Deo, vt sit vinculum veritatis inter homines, & testimonium, quod Deus sit author & defensor veritatis.
units.tr: He gives testimony. Namely, by preserving the one swearing and blessing him if he swears rightly, but by punishing and destroying him if he lies knowingly. For the oath has been established by God so that it may be a bond of truth among men, and a testimony that God is the author and defender of truth.

units.la: II. Per quem sit iurandum.
units.tr: II. By whom one ought to swear.

units.la: Per nomen solius veri Dei est jurandum. 1. Quia Deus sic præcepit, vt per se solum juretur: sicut solus ipse timendus est & colendus: Iehouam Deum tuum timebis, illum coles, illi adhærebis, & per nomen eius jurabis. 2. Deus diserte vetat, ne per nomen aliud juremus: Per nomen exterorum Deorum non jurabis. 3. Deus sibi soli inuocationis cultum vult tribui: & damnat eos, qui in juramentis creaturas cum DEO conjungunt. Est autem juramentum inuocationis Dei species, vt ex definitione patet. 4. Juramentum tribuit ei, per quem juratur, inspectionem cordium, omniscientiam, omnipræsentiam, &c. Et quidem requiritur, quia in juramentis agitur non de rebus manifestis, de quibus constat, sed arcanis, incertis, & de quibus, an homines fallant, potest judicare tantum is, qui est cordium inspector. Solus autem Deus est ψευδογνώστης, omniscius, omnipræsens. Hinc probatur, Christum esse verum Deum, & per eum etiam jurandum
units.tr: One must swear only by the name of the one true God. (1) Because God has so commanded, that he alone be sworn by, just as he alone is to be feared and worshipped: "You shall fear the LORD your God, you shall serve him, you shall cleave to him, and you shall swear by his name." (2) God expressly forbids us to swear by any other name: "You shall not swear by the name of other gods." (3) God wills that the worship of invocation be given to himself alone, and he condemns those who in their oaths join creatures with God. An oath, however, is a kind of invocation of God, as is clear from the definition. (4) By an oath the one by whom we swear is attributed the inspection of hearts, omniscience, omnipresence, and so on. And indeed this is required, because in oaths the matter is not about things that are manifest and known, but about hidden and uncertain things, and as to whether men are lying, only he who is the searcher of hearts can judge. Now God alone is the omniscient one [ψευδογνώστης], omniscient and omnipresent. From this it is proved that Christ is true God, and that one must also swear by him. For he knows all things and understands what is in man. So also the Holy Spirit searches all things.

units.la: Deut.10,20; Esa.18,19; Esa.45,23; Ier.12,16; 1 Cor.1,23; Deu.10,20; Exod.23,13. dum esse. Ipse enim scit omnia, & novit, quid sit in homine. Sic etiam Spiritus sanctus scrutatur omnia. 5. Per quem juratur, ei defertur executio poenae & omnipotentia. qua nimirum defendat veritatem, & puniat perjuros. At solus Deus est omnipotens, & poenae executor. Nolite metuere eos, qui trucidant corpus, animam autem non possunt trucidare: sed timete potius eum, qui potest & corpus & animam perdere in gehenna. Homines autem non possunt exsecutores esse perjurii, quia falso jurantes effugiunt hominum judicia: vel quia homines non sunt κατέχει ut videant, an fallant jurantes nec ne, perjuri sunt potentiores, quam ut ab hominibus ad poenam trahi possint. Jurandum igitur est non nisi per nomen solius Dei.
units.tr: Deut. 10:20; Isa. 18:19; Isa. 45:23; Jer. 12:16; 1 Cor. 1:23; Deut. 10:20; Exod. 23:13. (5) By whomever one swears, the execution of punishment and omnipotence are attributed to him, namely that he may defend the truth and punish perjurers. But God alone is omnipotent and the executor of punishment: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell." Men, however, cannot be the executors of perjury, because those who swear falsely escape human judgments; or, because men are not able [κατέχει] to see whether those swearing are lying or not, and perjurers are too powerful to be dragged to punishment by men. Therefore one must swear only by the name of God alone.

units.la: Hinc sequitur, juramenta per sanctos, & alias creaturas esse idololatrica, & a Deo prohibita.
units.tr: From this it follows that oaths by saints and other creatures are idolatrous and forbidden by God.

units.la: Obiect. Atqui Josephus juravit per salutem, seu vitam Pharaonis. Ergo etiam per homines & creaturas licet jurare. Resp. Atqui concedunt, Josephum peccasse juratem Ethnicorum more, qui per reges solebant jurare: ut celaret fratres, quis esset. Sed possumus aliter respondere, & dicere, verba eius non fuisse juramentum proprie, sed vehementem duntaxat asseverationem, ut sit sententia: quam vere vivit & salvus est Pharao, aut ego eum saltem volo, tam vere hac dico. Eadem est ratio similium asseverationum; ut Hannae: Vivit anima tua (scilicet) Heli. Abneri: vivit anima tua rex (Saul) sinovi. Dauidis: Vivit Iehova & vivit anima tua (Dauidis.) anima tua. Jonathae: vivit Iehova & vivit anima tua. Sunt enim hae locutiones non proprie juramenta, sed asseverationes; euidentiae seu vehementiae causa adhibitae, cum collatione alicuius rei certae & manifestae: ut sententia earum sit, ea, quae asseverantur, tam esse certa, quam est certum, eum, quem nominat asseverans, viuere.
units.tr: Objection. But Joseph swore by the health, or life, of Pharaoh. Therefore it is lawful to swear also by men and creatures. Answer. They concede that Joseph sinned by swearing in the manner of the Gentiles, who used to swear by kings, in order to hide from his brothers who he was. But we can also answer otherwise, and say that his words were not properly an oath, but only a vehement asseveration, so that the meaning is: "As surely as Pharaoh lives and is safe, or as surely as I wish him to be, so surely I say these things." The same is the case with similar asseverations, such as Hannah's: "As your soul lives," (namely, Eli). Abner's: "As your soul lives, O king" (Saul), "I am..."; David's: "As the LORD lives and as your soul lives" (David's soul); Jonathan's: "As the LORD lives and as your soul lives." For these expressions are not properly oaths but asseverations, used for the sake of emphasis and vehemence, with the comparison of some certain and manifest thing, so that their meaning is that what is asserted is as certain as it is certain that the one whom the speaker names is alive.

units.la: III. Liceatne Christianis iurare.
units.tr: III. Whether Christians may swear.

units.la: Quod liceat pie per nomen Dei jurare, magistratu id exigente, vel alioqui necessitate flagitante, quatuor argumentis hic probatur.
units.tr: That it is lawful to swear piously by the name of God, when the magistrate requires it or necessity otherwise demands it, is proved here by four arguments.

units.la: 1. Ut gloria Dei illustretur. Veritas enim & patefactio eius est Deo gloriosa.
units.tr: 1. So that the glory of God may be displayed. For the truth and its disclosure are glorious to God.

units.la: 2. Ut aliorum saluti consulatur: quia salus nostra in veritate, praesertim in illa coelesti consistit.
units.tr: 2. So that the salvation of others may be cared for, since our salvation consists in the truth, especially that heavenly truth.

units.la: 3. Quia legitimum jusjurandum verbo Dei sancitur.
units.tr: 3. Because lawful oath-taking is sanctioned by the Word of God.

units.la: 4. Quia a sanctis recte est usurpatum. Anabaptistae excipiunt, olim quidem in veteri testamento sub lege patribus licuisse, in novo autem testamento nobis prohibitum. tum esse jurare. Ideo rationibus superioribus etiam addendæ sunt hæ, quibus diuersum probatur.
units.tr: 4. Because it has been rightly practised by the saints. The Anabaptists object that, although it was once permitted to the fathers under the law of the Old Testament, it is forbidden to us under the New Testament. Therefore the following arguments, which prove the contrary, must be added to the above.

units.la: 5. Christus dicit: Non veni soluere legem, sed implere. Loquitur autem de lege morali, ad quam juramentum pertinet. Non ergo sublatum est à Christo jusjurandum.
units.tr: 5. Christ says: I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfil it. He is speaking, however, of the moral law, to which the oath belongs. Therefore the oath has not been abolished by Christ.

units.la: 6. Cultus Dei moralis est perpetuus. Juramentum legitimum est cultus moralis; quia est inuocatio Dei. Est ergo perpetuum.
units.tr: 6. The moral worship of God is perpetual. A lawful oath is moral worship, because it is an invocation of God. Therefore it is perpetual.

units.la: 7. Prophetæ describentes cultum nouæ ecclesiæ, vocant juramentum per nomen Dei. Qui jurabit in terra, jurabit in vero Deo. Ergo licet nouæ ecclesiæ jurare per nomen veri Dei.
units.tr: 7. The prophets, describing the worship of the new Church, call swearing by the name of God: He who swears in the land shall swear by the true God. Therefore it is lawful for the new Church to swear by the name of the true God.

units.la: 8. A fine juramenti. Confirmatio fidei & veritatis & decisio litium reipublicæ & ecclesiæ est vtilis, licita, necessaria, Deoque gloriosa. Juramentum est confirmatio fidei & veritatis & decisio litium. Omnis controuersia finis est jusjurandi ad confirmationem adhibitum. Ergo jusjurandum Christianis non tantum est licitum, sed etiam necessarium.
units.tr: 8. From the end of the oath. The confirmation of faith and truth, and the settling of disputes, is useful, lawful, necessary to the commonwealth and the Church, and glorious to God. An oath is the confirmation of faith and truth and the settling of disputes. Every controversy ends in an oath employed for confirmation. Therefore the oath is not only lawful but even necessary for Christians.

units.la: 9. Ab exemplis Christi & sanctorum in nouo Testamento. Christus ipse non semel, sed sæpissimè vsus est jurandi formula ad confirmationem suæ doctrinæ: Amen, amen dico vobis &c. Et Paulus: Testis est mihi Deus, cui seruio spiritu meo in euangelio Filij eius, &c. Ego verò testem Deum invoco in animam meam, me idcirco non dum venisse. Veritatem dico per Christum, non mentior, attestante mihi simul conscientia mea per Spiritum sanctum. Testis est mihi Deus, quàm propense amem vos. Vos testes estis, & Deus, quomodo sancte & inculpatè vobiscum, qui creditis, vixerimus. Hæc & similia argumenta & exempla demonstrant, etiam in nouo fœdere legitimè jurare Christianis concessum esse.
units.tr: 9. From the examples of Christ and the saints in the New Testament. Christ himself did not once only, but very often, use the form of swearing to confirm his teaching: Verily, verily I say unto you, etc. And Paul: God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, etc. But I call God as witness upon my soul, that it was for this reason that I have not yet come. I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness along with the Holy Spirit. God is my witness how much I love you. You are witnesses, and God too, how holily and blamelessly we have lived among you who believe. These and similar arguments and examples show that it has been granted to Christians in the New Covenant also to swear lawfully.

units.la: Objiciunt Anabaptistæ dictum Christi: Ego verò dico vobis, ne juretis omnino, neque per cœlum, quia thronus Dei est, neque per terram, quia scabellum est pedum eius: neque per Hierosolymam, quia urbs est magni regis: neque per caput tuum jures, quia non potes vnum capillum album vel nigrum facere. Esto autem sermo vester, etiam, etiam, non, non: quod supra hoc redundat, à malo est. Et Jacobi: Ante omnia fra- tres mei ne jurate, neque per cœlum, neque per terram, neque aliud vllum jusjurandum: sit autem vestrum est est: & non non, ne in condemnatio-nem incidatis. R. Verum his dictis non prohiberi omnia, sed tantum temeraria, & non necessaria juramenta, perspicuum est, tum ex aliorum locorum & exemplorum veteris ac noui testamenti collatione, tum præcipuè ex scopo Christi, qui veram legis sententiam, à corruptelis ibi vindicans, & hypocrisin pharisæorum taxans docet, tertio præcepto decalogi damnari non tantum perjuria, sed etiam juramenta non necessaria, & temeraria. eaque non tantum directa, in quibus nomen Dei exprimitur: sed etiam indirecta, in quibus creaturis nominatis Dei nomen dissimulatum intelligitur: cuiusmodi vulgo in quotidiano sermone tunc erant vsitata. Hypocritæ enim obliquas jurandi formulas per templum, per altare, per cœlum, &c. excusabant, quasi sic jurantes nomen Dei non profanarent, modo Deum non nominarent, nec fierent perjuri, etiamsi fidem indirecta jurandi formula darent: tamen fallerent. Christus verè ostendit, etiam tunc iurari per nomen Dei, cum cœlum & terram nominatur, quia nulla est pars mundi, vel creatura, cui non insculpserit Deus nomen & notam gloriæ suæ. Et cum per cœlum & terram juratur, ipsius opificis intuitu, non in creaturis subsistit jurisjurandi religio: sed Deus ipse solus aduocatur in testem, productis in medium gloriæ eius symbolis. Neque enim Deus hæret in verbis, sed mentem jurantis spectat, nec tam in syllabis, quàm in sententiis honor & contumelia nominis diuini consistit: quemadmodum Christus hoc ipsum disertis verbis docet Matthæi 23. quæ cum hoc loco nunc explicato conferenda sunt. Eadem est Jacobi mens & sententia.
units.tr: The Anabaptists object the saying of Christ: But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God, nor by the earth, for it is his footstool, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King, nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no; whatever is more than this is of evil. And the saying of James: Above all, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any other oath; but let your yes be yes, and your no, no, lest you fall into condemnation. A: That these words do not forbid all oaths, but only rash and unnecessary ones, is plain both from the comparison of other passages and examples of the Old and New Testaments, and especially from the purpose of Christ, who, vindicating the true sense of the law from its corruptions and rebuking the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, teaches that by the third precept of the Decalogue not only perjuries are condemned, but also unnecessary and rash oaths: and these not only direct oaths, in which the name of God is expressed, but also indirect ones, in which, by naming creatures, the name of God is understood to be concealed; such oaths were then commonly in use in everyday speech. For the hypocrites excused their oblique forms of swearing, by the temple, by the altar, by heaven, etc., as if those swearing in this way did not profane the name of God, provided they did not name God and did not become perjurers, even though they gave their pledge by an indirect form of oath; yet they deceived. Christ truly shows that God's name is sworn by even when heaven and earth are named, because there is no part of the world or creature in which God has not engraved his name and the mark of his glory. And when one swears by heaven and earth, the sanctity of the oath does not rest in the creatures out of regard for their Maker, but God himself alone is called as witness, the symbols of his glory being brought forward. For God does not cling to words but looks to the mind of the one swearing, and honour and dishonour of the divine name consist not so much in syllables as in meanings, as Christ himself teaches this very thing in plain words in Matthew 23, which passage must be compared with the one now explained. The mind and meaning of James is the same.

units.la: Inst. 1. Christus dicit: Ne juretis omnino; & Jacobus: Neque aliud vllum juramentum. Ergo omne juramentum Christianis prohiberur. Resp. Fallacia est compositionis. Particula omnino non refertur ad verbum jurandi, sed ad varias formulas temerarij juramenti, quas Pharisæi fingebant esse licitas: quasi dicat; falsò vel temerè ne juretis omnino, neque directè, neque indirectè. Sic Jacobus: Nullum aliud juramentum juretis, nempe temerarium, vel falsum, cuius aliquot speciebus enumeratis, similes omnes prohiberi indicat. Alioqui Christus ipse contra suum præceptum peccasset, cum hic dicit: Sermo vester sit, est est, non non: & tamen alibi sæpe in sermone & doctrina sua grauissima hac asseueratione vtitur: Amen amen dico vobis. Jacobus damnaret Paulum, qui jure jurando inuocauit Deum testem in animam suam. Et Spiritus sanctus secum pugnaret, per Jacobum damnans, per alium Apostolum commendans jusjurandum, tanquam remedium vtile & necessarium societati humanæ sinien-dis litibus & controuersiis, sine quibus vita humana in ista fragilitate esse non potest.
units.tr: Objection 1. Christ says: Do not swear at all; and James: nor any other oath. Therefore every oath is forbidden to Christians. Answer. This is the fallacy of composition. The particle at all does not refer to the verb of swearing, but to the various forms of rash swearing which the Pharisees were pretending were lawful; as if he said: do not swear falsely or rashly at all, neither directly nor indirectly. So James: do not swear any other oath, namely a rash or false one; having listed some kinds of it, he indicates that all similar ones are forbidden. Otherwise Christ himself would have sinned against his own precept, when he says: Let your speech be yes, yes, no, no; and yet elsewhere he often uses this most solemn asseveration in his speech and teaching: Verily, verily I say unto you. James would condemn Paul, who, by an oath, called God as witness upon his soul. And the Holy Spirit would be at odds with himself, condemning oath-taking through James and commending it through another apostle, as a useful and necessary remedy for human society to settle disputes and controversies, without which human life cannot exist in this frailty.

units.la: Inst. 2. Concessiones & exempla juramenti in scriptura pertinent ad juramenta publica, hoc est, quæ publico nomine exiguntur vel dantur. Saltem ergo priuata juramenta, quæ priuati priuatis præstant, omnino sunt prohibita. Resp. 1. Negatur antecedens: quia restrictio illa non modo non reperitur in concessionibus & exemplis scripturæ, sed ne quidem locum habet, quod
units.tr: Objection 2. The concessions and examples of oaths in Scripture pertain to public oaths, that is, those demanded or given in a public capacity. At least, then, private oaths, which private persons make to private persons, are entirely forbidden. Answer 1. The antecedent is denied: for that restriction is not only not found in the concessions and examples of Scripture, but does not even hold, as the inspection of the passages shows.

units.la: Matth. 23, 16. 27. quod inspectio locorum ostendit. 2. Exempla priuati juramenti manifesta sunt Jacobi & Labanis, Booz, Abdiæ, Abigaelis, & Dauidis. 3. Idem probatur ex fine juramenti. Finis enim juramenti, scilicet confirmatio fidei & veritatis, ac decisio litium, ad omnes Christianos, etiam priuatos spectat: proinde ipsum quoque juramentum, quo fidem & veritatem confirmamus.
units.tr: Matthew 23:16, 27. 2. Examples of private oaths are plain: those of Jacob and Laban, Boaz, Obadiah, Abigail, and David. 3. The same is proved from the end of the oath. For the end of the oath, namely the confirmation of faith and truth and the settling of disputes, concerns all Christians, even private persons; therefore the oath itself, by which we confirm faith and truth, does too.

units.la: IV. De quibus rebus sit iurandum, seu quae iuramenta sint licita, quaeillicita.
units.tr: IV. On what things one should swear, or which oaths are lawful and which unlawful.

units.la: Juramenta licita tantum ea sunt, quae non pugnant cum verbo Dei, & quae præstantur de rebus veris, certò cognitis, licitis, possibilibus & gravibus, necessariis, utilibus, dignis tali ac tanta confirmatione, hoc est, confirmationem per juramentum propter gloriam Dei, aut salutem proximi postulantibus. De his igitur solis est jurandum
units.tr: Lawful oaths are only those which do not conflict with the Word of God, and which are made about things that are true, certainly known, lawful, possible, weighty, necessary, useful, worthy, and which are confirmed with such an oath, that is, with confirmation by oath sought for the glory of God or the salvation of a neighbour. Only about these, therefore, is one to swear.

units.la: Illicita verò sunt, quae cum verbo Dei pugnant, & fiunt de rebus vel falsis, vel incertis, vel illicitis, vel impossibilibus, vel levibus aut futilibus. De talibus igitur non est jurandum. Qui enim jurat de rebus falsis, facit Deum testem mendacij: qui de incertis, jurat mala conscientia, & cum Dei contemtu, cum audeat eum testem facere eius, quod nescit, an sit veritas vel mendacium: & qui sic jurat, ei perinde est, sive veritatis, sive mendacij testem Deum constituat: & simul petit, ut Deus vel testimonium det mendacio, vel si non velit haberi testis mendacij, ipse jurantem puniat. Qui de illicitis jurat, facit Deum fautorem & approbatorem illius, quod lege prohibuit, atque ita facit Deum sibi contradicentem: quia petit, ut Deus ipsum puniat, si faciat, quod præcipit, vel si non faciat, quod prohibuit. Præterea qui sic jurat, aut habet propositum faciendi contra Dei mandatum, aut si non jurat serio, allegat Deum testem mendacij. Qui jurat de impossibilibus, is vel insanit, vel Deum & homines ludificat, cum non possit habere serium propositum faciendi id, quod nec vult, nec potest. Denique qui leviter jurat, non præstat reverentiam Deo, & qui facile jurat, facile peierat. Principalis causa juramenti debet esse 1. gloria Dei, 2. salus proximi privata & publica.
units.tr: Unlawful oaths, however, are those which conflict with the Word of God and which are made about things that are either false, or uncertain, or unlawful, or impossible, or trivial and frivolous. One must not swear about such things. For he who swears about false things makes God a witness of a lie. He who swears about uncertain things swears with a bad conscience and in contempt of God, since he dares to make him a witness of something he does not know to be truth or lie; and he who swears thus is indifferent whether he makes God a witness of truth or of lie, and at the same time asks that God either give testimony to the lie or, if he does not wish to be held a witness of a lie, punish the one who swears. He who swears about unlawful things makes God a supporter and approver of what he has forbidden by law, and so makes God contradict himself, because he asks that God punish him if he does what God commands, or if he does not do what God has forbidden. Moreover, he who swears thus either intends to act against God's command, or, if he does not swear in earnest, cites God as a witness of a lie. He who swears about impossible things is either mad or mocks God and men, since he cannot have a serious intention of doing what he neither wills nor is able to do. Finally, he who swears lightly does not show reverence to God, and he who swears easily perjures himself easily. The principal cause of an oath ought to be (1) the glory of God, and (2) the private and public salvation of the neighbour.

units.la: Obiect. De incertis non est jurandum. Futura contingentia, qualia sunt ea, quae facturos se promittunt homines, sunt incerta. Ergo de futuris seu præstandis à nobis non est jurandum. Resp. In futuris non juratur, nec est jurandum de eventu, qui non est in nostra potestate; sed de voluntate nostra præsenti, id quod justum & licitum est, sive nunc, sive inposterum faciendi, & de obliobligatione ad id faciendum præsenti & futura, de qua vnusquisq; certus esse potest & debet. Et sic iurarunt Abraham, Isaac, Abimelech, Dauid, Ionathan, Booz, &c. Obligantes se ad officia in posterum præstanda.
units.tr: Objection: one must not swear about uncertain things. Future contingent things, such as those which men promise they will do, are uncertain. Therefore one must not swear about future things, or about things to be performed by us. Reply: one does not swear about the future, nor should one swear about the outcome, which is not in our power; rather one swears about our present will, that we will do what is just and lawful, whether now or hereafter, and about our obligation to do it, present and future, of which each person can and ought to be certain. And so Abraham, Isaac, Abimelech, David, Jonathan, Boaz, and others swore, binding themselves to duties to be performed afterwards.

units.la: V. An omnia iuramenta sint seruanda.
units.tr: V. Whether all oaths are to be kept.

units.la: Iuramenta recte concepta de rebus licitis, veris, certis, grauibus & possibilibus necessario sunt seruanda. Si enim cognoueris, & testatus fueris, te iuste obligari ad seruanda ea, quæ iurasti, & Deum testem appellasti, si sciens & volens fidem fallis, obligationem iustam violas, & redderis periurus. Iuramenta autem de rebus illicitis facta siue per errorem, siue per infirmitatem contra conscientiam non sunt seruanda, sed retractanda & corrigenda poenitentiam agendo, & a malo proposito desistendo, non autem in eo perseuerando, & male iuratum exsequendo. Contemtus in oculis Iehovae, reprobus, qui iurauit in malum, & non mutat. Nam qui seruat iuramentum illicitum, bis peccat: semel male iurando, & iterum male iuratum seruando: iuxta regulam, quod male iuratur, peius seruatur. Quæ enim Deus prohibet, ea nec iurata vult seruari, & quæ vetat promittere vel iurare, ea tanto magis facere prohibet, quanto est gravius facere, quam promittere. Qui igitur seruat id, quod male iurauit, peccatum peccato cumulat: vt Herodes interficiens Iohannem Baptistam, prætextu iurisiurandi. Sic seruantes vota monastica, quibus iurarunt idololatriam & impium cœlibatum, bis peccant: quia male iurarunt, & male iuratum peius seruant.
units.tr: Oaths rightly framed about lawful, true, certain, weighty and possible things must necessarily be kept. For if you have known and affirmed that you are justly bound to keep what you have sworn, and have called God as witness, and then knowingly and willingly break your word, you violate a just obligation and make yourself a perjurer. Oaths, however, made about unlawful things, whether through error or through weakness against conscience, are not to be kept, but are to be retracted and corrected, by repenting and desisting from the evil purpose, not by persevering in it and carrying out what was wrongly sworn. Contemptible in the eyes of Jehovah is the reprobate who has sworn to evil and does not change. For he who keeps an unlawful oath sins twice: once by swearing wickedly, and again by keeping what was wrongly sworn, according to the rule, what is wrongly sworn is worse kept. For what God forbids, he does not wish to be kept even when sworn; and what he forbids us to promise or swear, he forbids us to do all the more, as doing is graver than promising. Whoever keeps what he has wrongly sworn therefore heaps sin upon sin, as Herod did in killing John the Baptist on the pretext of his oath. So those who keep monastic vows, by which they swore to idolatry and impious celibacy, sin twice: because they swore wrongly, and they keep what was wrongly sworn all the worse.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Qui iurat se facturum aliquid, quod potest, nec seruat, is Deum constituit testem mendacii. At qui iurat se facturum eadem, iurat quod potest. Ergo qui iurat se facturum eadem, nec facit, constituit Deum testem mendacii. Non debet autem Deus constitui testis mendacii. Ergo iurata cædes debet perfici. Resp. ad maiorem, quæ vera est, de re possibili licita, de possibili illicita est falsa. Illicitum enim non seruatu minime facit Deum testem mendacii, quandoquidem mali retractatio bona est, vt retractatio iuramenti Dauidis, quo iurauerat se Nabalem perditurum cum familia, &c.
units.tr: Objection 1. He who swears that he will do something he is able to do, and does not keep it, makes God a witness of a lie. But he who swears that he will do the same murder swears to something he is able to do. Therefore he who swears that he will do the same, and does not do it, makes God a witness of a lie. But God must not be made a witness of a lie. Therefore sworn murder ought to be carried out. Reply to the major premise: it is true of a possible lawful thing; of a possible unlawful thing it is false. For not keeping an unlawful oath by no means makes God a witness of a lie, since retracting evil is good, as in the retraction of David's oath, by which he had sworn that he would destroy Nabal with his household, and so on.

units.la: Obj. 2. Seruatum est Gibeonitis iurametum illicitum de pace contra mandatum Domini. Licet igitur iusiurandum de rebus illicitis seruare. Resp. 1. Negatur fuisse illicitum. Mandato enim Dei non excludebantur à pace, si qui ex gentib. quas Deus deleri iusserat, pacem peterent, & ad religionem Israeliticam accederent, quod fecerunt Gibeonitæ. 2. Est fallacia non causæ. Israelitæ seruarunt hoc iuramentum, non quod astringerentur (decepti enim jurauerant) sed 1. propter scandalum vitandum, quo deformari poterat nomen DEI apud Ethnicos, si non seruassent: 2. quia etiam sine juramento pacem petentes, & religionem accipientes licitum ac justum erat seruare.
units.tr: Objection 2. The oath of peace given to the Gibeonites, which was unlawful and against the command of the Lord, was kept. Therefore it is lawful to keep an oath about unlawful things. Reply: (1) It is denied that it was unlawful. For by God's command they were not excluded from peace if any of the peoples whom God had ordered to be destroyed sought peace and came over to the Israelite religion, as the Gibeonites did. (2) It is a fallacy of non-cause. The Israelites kept this oath not because they were bound by it (for they had sworn being deceived), but (1) to avoid scandal, by which the name of God could have been disfigured among the heathen had they not kept it; (2) because even without an oath, it was lawful and just for those seeking peace and receiving the religion to be kept.

units.la: Ex his, quæ de seruando legitimo juramento dicta sunt, facile respondetur ad quæstionem: An juramenta extorta sint seruanda? Sun seruanda, si non continent aliquid, quod sit illicitum, aut si habent conditiones supra positas, etiamsi sint nobis inutilia aut detrimentosa. Ad impia vero juranda nemo debet adigi, nec extorqueri quidem debent illis tormentis impia juramenta, sed potius est moriendum. Si quæ tamen impia juramenta facta sint ex metu, vel infirmitate contra conscientiam, illa non obligant, & sunt retractanda, quia quod impium est actu, est & impium juratu: neq; peccatum peccato est cumulandum. Extorta autem juramenta, sed non impia, de rebus licitis & possibilibus, etiamsi difficilibus aut damnosis, sunt seruanda. Si vero post impossibilitas accedit, non obligant. Si non accedit, seruanda sunt, vt grauius malum euitetur, quia minus malum tenen dis lege diuina eligere. Si justum est facere, quod coactus promisisti, justum est etiam juramento teid facturum promittere. Nam quod facere licet, hoc licet etiam promittere juramento præstandum, vt, in latronem incidens, cogitur juramento promittere summam pecuniæ, & insuper silentium, pro vitæ redemtione. Hic non tantum licet, sed etiam debet (si possit præstare) latroni vtrumque: jurare, & juratum seruare, vt vitam redimat. Quod enim licet jurare, etiam licet facere: & contra.
units.tr: From what has been said about keeping a lawful oath, the question is easily answered: Are extorted oaths to be kept? They are to be kept if they contain nothing unlawful, or if they have the conditions laid down above, even if they prove useless or harmful to us. But no one ought to be compelled to swear to impious things, nor should impious oaths be extorted even by torments; rather one ought to die. If impious oaths have nonetheless been made from fear or weakness against conscience, they do not bind and are to be retracted, because what is impious in deed is impious in swearing too, and sin must not be heaped on sin. Extorted oaths, however, if not impious, about lawful and possible things, are to be kept, even if they are difficult or damaging. If impossibility supervenes afterwards, they do not bind. If it does not supervene, they are to be kept, so that a greater evil may be avoided, because under divine law it is right to choose the lesser evil. If it is just to do what you were forced to promise, it is also just to promise with an oath that you will do it. For what it is lawful to do, it is also lawful to promise on oath. Thus, when someone falls in with a robber and is forced to promise by oath a sum of money, and besides silence, in exchange for his life, here it is not only lawful but one ought (if one is able to perform it) to give the robber both: to swear, and to keep the sworn promise, so as to redeem one's life. For what it is lawful to swear, it is also lawful to do, and conversely.

units.la: Obiect. Quod est damnosum reipublicæ, non est iurandum, iuratum, non est seruandum. Jurare latroni silentium, est damnosum reipublicæ. Ergo latroni silentium non est iurandum, iuratum non est seruandum. Resp 1. ad maiorem: quod damnosum est reipublicæ, non est promittendum, si possimus id facere sine periculo vitæ nostræ: deinde si eo temporis articulo, quo quis in tali vitæ discrimine constitutus est, non propriæ saluti potius sit consulendum, quam tale indicium faciendum. 2. Negatur minor, quia reipublicæ potius est vtile, silentium latroni promittere, promissumq; seruare. Ipse enim, qui silentium latroni iuramento promisit, hac ratione seruatur. Interest autem reipublicæ, vt ciuis seruetur. Quod si latroni necem minitanti silentium non iuraret, nec sibi, nec reipublicæ consuleret. Silentium igitur latroni iureiurando promittere, cum sit minus malum reipublicæ, quam ciuem trucidari, potius est eligendum.
units.tr: Objection. What is harmful to the commonwealth must not be sworn to, and what has been sworn must not be kept. To swear silence to a robber is harmful to the commonwealth. Therefore silence must not be sworn to a robber, and what has been sworn need not be kept. Reply: (1) to the major premise: what is harmful to the commonwealth must not be promised, if we can avoid it without danger to our life; further, if at that moment when someone is placed in such peril of life, one ought rather to consult one's own safety than make such a disclosure. (2) The minor is denied, because it is rather useful to the commonwealth to promise silence to a robber and to keep the promise. For he who has promised silence to a robber by oath is preserved by this means, and it is in the interest of the commonwealth that a citizen be preserved. But if he did not swear silence to a robber threatening death, he would consult neither himself nor the commonwealth. Therefore to promise silence to a robber by oath, since it is a lesser evil for the commonwealth than for a citizen to be slaughtered, is rather to be chosen.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CIII. Quid præcipit Deus in quarto præcepto?
units.tr: QUESTION 103. What does God command in the fourth commandment?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Primùm, vt ministerium Euangelij, & scholæ, con-seruentur a: vtque ego cum aliis, tùm præcipuè festis diebus, studiosè cœtus diuinos frequentem b, verbum DEI diligenter audiam c, vtar sacramentis d, precibus publicis meas quoque preces adjungam e, pro facultatibus aliquid conferam in pauperes f. Deinde, vt in omni vita à prauis actionibus vacem, Domino concedens, vt per Spiritum sanctum in me suum opus faciat, atque ita sempiternum illud sabbatum in hac vita exordiar g.
units.tr: First, that the ministry of the Gospel and the schools be preserveda; and that I, together with others, but especially on festival days, diligently attend the assemblies for worshipb, hear the Word of God carefullyc, make use of the sacramentsd, join my own prayers to the public prayerse, and contribute something from my means to the poorf. Then, that I refrain from wicked actions throughout my whole life, granting to the Lord that through the Holy Spirit he may do his work in me, and so begin in this life that everlasting Sabbathg.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Quarti præcepti duæ sunt partes: præceptum, & ratio præcepti. Præceptum est: Memento vt diem sabbati sanctifices: & in eo non facies vllum opus, &c. Huius rursus duæ sunt partes. Vna moralis & perpetua, vt sanctificetur sabbathum: altera cæremonialis, & temporaria, vt sanctificetur septimus dies.
units.tr: The fourth commandment has two parts: the precept and the reason of the precept. The precept is: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy; and in it you shall do no manner of work, etc. This in turn has two parts. One is moral and perpetual, that the sabbath be kept holy; the other is ceremonial and temporary, that the seventh day be kept holy.

units.la: Priorem partem esse moralem & perpetuam, patet ex fine, & ex causis præcepti perpetuis. Finis præcepti est publica Dei celebratio in ecclesia, & conseruatio ministerij ecclesiastici perpetua. Vult enim Deus omnibus temporibus esse aliquod publicum ecclesiæ ministerium, & congressus fidelium, in quibus sonet vera doctrina de Deo: 1. vt ipse publicè in mundo celebretur: 2. vt pietas & fides electorum publicis exercitiis excitetur & alatur: 3. vt homines sese mutuo in fide ædificent, & alij alios ad pietatem provocent: 4. vt consensus in doctrina ecclesiæ & cultu Dei seruetur: 5. vt denique ecclesia in mundo discernatur. Hæc causa, & à reliqua hominum multitudine discernatur, sed ad omnia ecclesiæ tempora pertineant: sequitur, Deum semper velle ministerium ecclesiæ conseruari, & vsum eius frequentari, proproinde genus huius præcepti, seu partem eius moralem, ab initio mundi vsque ad finem omnes homines obligare, vt aliquod tempus tribuant concionibus & precationibus publicis, & administrationi sacramentorum.
units.tr: That the former part is moral and perpetual is clear from the end and from the causes of the precept, which are perpetual. The end of the precept is the public celebration of God in the Church and the lasting preservation of the ecclesiastical ministry. For God wills that at all times there should be some public ministry of the Church and assemblies of the faithful, in which the true doctrine concerning God is proclaimed: (1) so that he may be publicly celebrated in the world; (2) so that the piety and faith of the elect may be stirred up and nourished by public exercises; (3) so that people may build one another up in the faith, and encourage one another to godliness; (4) so that agreement in the doctrine and worship of God may be maintained in the Church; (5) and finally, so that the Church may be distinguished in the world from the rest of humankind. Since these causes pertain to all the times of the Church, it follows that God always wills the ministry of the Church to be preserved and its use to be frequented. Therefore the kind of this precept, or its moral part, binds all people from the beginning of the world to its end, so that they set aside some time for sermons, public prayers, and the administration of the sacraments.

units.la: Alteram partem esse cæremonialem, non perpetuam, patet: quia sabbatum septimi diei, à Deo in legis promulgatione destinatum erat obseruationi cultus Mosaici, seu cæremoniarum Leuiticarum, ac datum Iudæis in sacramentum, hoc est typum sanctificationis ecclesiæ per Messiam venturum, sicut dicitur: Sabbatum meum custodietis, quia signum est inter me & vos, vt sciatis, quod ego sum Iehoua, sanctificans vos. Sabbata mea dedi eis, vt essent in signum inter me, & ipsos, vt sciant, quod sim Iehoua qui sanctifico ipsos. Per aduentum igitur Messiæ, vna cum alijs cæremoniis ac typis, etiam sabbatum septimi diei est impletum, & abrogatum. Hæc breuiter de præcepto.
units.tr: That the other part is ceremonial and not perpetual is clear, because the sabbath of the seventh day was appointed by God at the promulgation of the law for the observance of the Mosaic worship, that is, of the Levitical ceremonies, and was given to the Jews as a sacrament, that is, as a type of the sanctification of the Church to come through the Messiah, as it is said: You shall keep my sabbaths, for it is a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you. I gave them my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them. Therefore, with the coming of the Messiah, together with the other ceremonies and types, the sabbath of the seventh day was also fulfilled and abrogated. This is a brief account of the precept.

units.la: Ratio præcepti est: Nam sex diebus fecit Deus & cælum & terram, &c. Sumta est ab exemplo Dei quiescentis die septimo à creatione, post sex dierum operationem. Pertinet ergo proprie ad circumstantiam septimi diei, seu ad partem præcepti cæremonialem. Imitatio tamen quietis, ad quam nos Deus invitat, non tantum cæremonialis, ad Iudæos spectans, sed etiam moralis seu spiritualis per cæremonialem significata, ad omnes homines pertinens.
units.tr: The reason of the precept is: For in six days God made heaven and earth, etc. It is taken from the example of God resting on the seventh day from creation, after six days of working. It therefore pertains properly to the circumstance of the seventh day, or to the ceremonial part of the precept. The imitation of this rest, however, to which God invites us, pertains not only to the ceremonial part, which concerns the Jews, but also to the moral or spiritual part, which is signified through the ceremonial, and pertains to all people.

units.la: Cæterum, vt præceptum cum ratione plenius intelligatur, verba vtriusque paucis consideranda sunt. Postea locos huc pertinentes, de sabbato, de ministerio ecclesiastico, & de cæremoniis compendiosè explicabimus.
units.tr: Moreover, so that the precept may be understood more fully together with its reason, the words of each part must be considered briefly. Afterwards we shall explain briefly the topics pertaining to this, concerning the sabbath, the ecclesiastical ministry, and the ceremonies.

units.la: Memento vt diem sabbati sanctifices.] Quid, & quotuplex sit sabbatum, postea dicetur. Cum emphasi quasi de re seuerissime præcepta dicit: memento vt sanctifices, quasi dicat, magna cura & religione obserues. Est ergo seuerissimum præceptum, cuius violationem Deus olim etiam morte plecti voluit.
units.tr: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.] What the sabbath is, and of how many kinds, will be said later. With emphasis, as if speaking of a matter most strictly commanded, he says: Remember to keep it holy, as if to say: observe it with great care and reverence. This is therefore a most strict precept, the violation of which God once wished to be punished even by death.

units.la: Causa tam seueri præcepti erant. 1. Quia violatio sabbati erat totius cultus diuini violatio. Neglectus enim ministerij ecclesiastici doctrinam & cultum Dei facilime corrumpit. 2. Quia tam seuera sabbati typici exactione, magnitudinem & necessitatem rei significatæ, hoc est, sabbati spiritualis, Deus indicare voluit. 3. Quia sabbatum externum subseruire vult inchoando & perficiendo in nobis sabbato spirituali.
units.tr: The reasons for so strict a precept were these. (1) Because the violation of the sabbath was a violation of the whole divine worship. For neglect of the ecclesiastical ministry very easily corrupts the doctrine and worship of God. (2) Because by so strict an exaction of the typical sabbath God wished to indicate the greatness and necessity of the thing signified, that is, of the spiritual sabbath. (3) Because the external sabbath is meant to serve the beginning and perfecting of the spiritual sabbath in us.

units.la: Sanctifices] Sanctificare sabbatum non est otio ignauo diem conterere, sed vitare peccata, & opera sancta sabbato peragere. Aliter Deus, aliter homines sabbatū sanctificare dicuntur, Deus sabbatum sanctificat, quia illud cultui diuino destinat: homines illud sanctificant, quando illud in vsum à Deo destinatum referunt.
units.tr: To keep it holy.] To keep the sabbath holy is not to waste the day in idle sloth, but to avoid sins and to carry on holy works on the sabbath. God and humans are said to sanctify the sabbath in different ways: God sanctifies the sabbath because he sets it apart for divine worship; humans sanctify it when they restore it to the use appointed by God.

units.la: Sex diebus operaberis.] Sex dies laboribus, septimum cultui divino attribuit: non quod velit aliis diebus cultum Dei & rerum diuinarum meditationem omitti, sed 1. vt sabbato non priuatus tantum, vt aliis temporibus, sed etiam publicus in ecclesia cultus Deo tribuatur. 2. Vt cultui diuino tam priuato, quam publico tunc cedant labores alij, quos pro sua vocatione aliis diebus quisque exercet.
units.tr: Six days you shall labour.] He assigns six days to labours and the seventh to the divine worship; not that he wishes the worship of God and the meditation on divine things to be omitted on the other days, but (1) so that on the sabbath worship is rendered to God not only privately, as at other times, but also publicly in the Church; (2) so that other labours, which each person performs on other days according to his calling, give way to divine worship, both private and public.

units.la: Non facies vllum opus.] Prohibet sabbato opera non quæuis, sed seruilia, hoc est, impedientia cultum Dei & vsum ministerij: quæ declaratio expressè est addita alibi: Nullũ opus seruile facitote, &c. Opera vero, quæ sabbati vsum non impediunt, sed potius illustrant & confirmant, qualia sunt opera ad cultum Dei, siue ad cæremonias sacras, siue ad dilectionem proximi, & ad suæ, vel alienæ vitæ necessitatem sic pertinentia, vt in tempus aliud reijci non possint, non modo sabbato non prohibet, sed maximè obseruationem eorum requirit Deus.
units.tr: You shall do no manner of work.] He forbids on the sabbath not every kind of work, but servile work, that is, work that hinders the worship of God and the use of the ministry. This clarification is expressly added elsewhere: You shall do no servile work, etc. But works that do not hinder the use of the sabbath, but rather adorn and confirm it, such as works pertaining to the worship of God, whether to the sacred ceremonies or to love of neighbour, and to the necessity of one's own or another's life, in such a way that they cannot be put off to another time, God not only does not forbid on the sabbath, but especially requires their performance.

units.la: Nec tu, nec filius tuus, nec filia tua.] Liberos & familiam vult à laboribus cessare duabus de causis. 1. Principaliter, vt hi quoque à parentibus & heris in cultu Dei educentur, & instituantur, & ad vsum ministerij ecclesiæ admittantur. Nam & hos Deus vult esse ecclesiæ suæ membra. 2. Quia dilectionem & beneficentiam erga proximum præsertim sabbato vult exerceri & conspici in ecclesia.
units.tr: Neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter.] He wills children and household to cease from labours for two reasons. (1) Principally, so that these too may be brought up and instructed by parents and masters in the worship of God, and admitted to the use of the ministry of the Church. For God wills these also to be members of his Church. (2) Because he wills love and beneficence towards the neighbour to be exercised and seen in the Church, especially on the sabbath.

units.la: Neque aduena, qui est intra portas tuas] Aduenas jubet labores intermittere, conuersos quidem ad religionem veram, tanquam ecclesiæ domesticos: infideles autem non propter ipsos, sed propter Israelitas, ne suo exemplo scandalum præberent ecclesiæ: neue ipsorum libertas occasio esset Judæis per illos faciendi sabbato labores, quos per se facere ipsis non licebat, atque ita fraus legi diuinæ fieret.
units.tr: Nor the stranger who is within your gates.] He commands strangers also to cease from labour: those indeed who have turned to the true religion, as members of the household of the Church; but unbelievers not for their own sake, but for the sake of the Israelites, lest by their example they should give offence to the Church, and lest their freedom should become an occasion for the Jews to do on the sabbath the labours which it was not lawful for them to do themselves, and thus a fraud be committed against the divine law.

units.la: Hinc ad tres quæstiones patet responsio. 1. An etiam aliæ gentes ad cæremonias Judaicas obligatæ fuerint, si inter Judæos versantur. 2. An alieni ab ecclesia ad religionem cogi possint, aut debeant. 3. An sacramenta, inter quæ erat sabbatum, communia esse debeant infidelibus cum ecclesia.
units.tr: From this the answer to three questions is plain. (1) Whether other nations also were bound to the Jewish ceremonies, if they dwelt among the Jews. (2) Whether aliens from the Church can or ought to be compelled to religion. (3) Whether the sacraments, among which was the sabbath, ought to be common to unbelievers with the Church.

units.la: Ad primam & secundam respondetur, neque ad omnes cæremonias, neq; ad religionem Judaicam fuisse obligatos, aut coactos peregrinos, in populo Judaico degentes: sed rantum ad externam disciplinam, quæ erat necessaria, ad vitanda scandala ecclesiæ, in qua versabantur. Debet enim magistratus esse custos discidisciplinæ secundum vtramq; rabulam decalogi apud suos subditos, & prohibere manifesta idola & blasphemias: à peregrinis autem & hospitibus, quatenus potest, etiam, ne scandala manifestationem, erat peculiaris ratio sabbati, quod non per Mosen deo præceptum erat, proinde vsq: ad Messiam omnes obligabat: etsi sic obsoleuerat hoc præceptum apud alias gentes, vt illud inter præcipua opprobria ponerent, quibus deridebant, & exagitabant Iudæos, sabbatarios eos appellantes, quod sabbatum nimis religiose colerent.
units.tr: To the first and second it is answered that sojourners living among the Jewish people were bound and compelled neither to all the ceremonies nor to the Jewish religion, but only to the external discipline, which was necessary for avoiding scandals to the Church among which they lived. For the magistrate ought to be the guardian of discipline, according to both tables of the decalogue, among his own subjects, and to prohibit manifest idolatries and blasphemies; but from strangers and guests, as far as he can, he should also prevent public scandals.
