God added this promise to this precept (1) so that he might invite us more strongly to its observance by a singular benefit, as a reward set before us; (2) so that he might bear witness how much he values the honour of parents, and how severely he wills those punished who do not render their parents the honour that is theirs; (3) and finally, how necessary the obedience of this precept is, since obedience towards parents is the preparation for and the impelling cause of obedience to the whole rest of the law. Paul, citing this promise, says that this is the first commandment with a promise, namely a special promise of a benefit which God pledges to those who render this obedience. The benefit which he promises is long life upon the earth.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Prima tabula etiam habet promissionem adiunctam. Ergo & praeceptum non est primum, habens promissionem. Resp. Hoc praeceptum habet speciale promissionem: prima tabula generalem.
units.tr: Objection 1. The first table also has a promise attached. Therefore this precept is not the first having a promise. Reply. This precept has a special promise; the first table a general one.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Atqui longaevitas propter miserias huius vitae non videtur esse beneficium. Ergo est inutilis promissio. Resp. ad antecedens. Fit per accidens, ut non videatur beneficium longaevitas, quae per se revera magnum est, licet coniuncta sit nostro vitio cum miseriis.
units.tr: Objection 2. But long life, because of the miseries of this life, does not seem to be a benefit. Therefore the promise is useless. Reply to the antecedent. It happens by accident that long life does not seem a benefit, although in itself it is truly a great good, even though, through our fault, it is joined with miseries.

units.la: Inst. 1. Bonum cum magnis malis coniunctum, potius est deprecandum, quam optandum. Longaevitas coniuncta est magnis malis. Ergo propter haec accidentia potius deprecanda quam optanda videtur longaevitas. Resp. ad maiorem. Bonum est deprecandum, si mala coniuncta sint ipso maiora. Piis autem promittitur cum longaevitate mitigatio calamitatum, & fruitio diuturna divinae benedictionis etiam in hac vita. Tum etiam celebratio Dei diuturna in hac vita tantum bonum est, ut calamitates huius vitae cum eo conferri non debeant.
units.tr: Instance 1. A good joined with great evils is rather to be prayed against than desired. Long life is joined with great evils. Therefore, because of these accidents, long life seems rather to be prayed against than desired. Reply to the major. A good is to be prayed against if the evils joined to it are greater than it. But to the godly is promised, along with long life, the mitigation of calamities and the lasting enjoyment of divine blessing even in this life. Moreover, the long celebration of God in this life is so great a good that the calamities of this life ought not to be compared with it.

units.la: Inst. 2. Etiam impii & inobedientes sunt longaevi. Ergo longaevitas non est beneficium piorum proprium. Resp. 1. Exempla pauca non cuertunt regulam. Plerique enim inobedientes male & cito pereunt. Oculum qui subsannat patrem, effodiant corui torrentis. Qui maledicit patri & matri suae, huius lucerna exstinguetur in medis tenebris. Piis bona corporalia dantur ad ipsorum salutem: impiis partim ut reddantur inexcusabiles, partim ut his pij & electi qui ipsis admixti sunt, fruantur.
units.tr: Instance 2. The impious and disobedient also live long. Therefore long life is not a benefit peculiar to the godly. Reply 1. A few examples do not overturn the rule. For most disobedient persons perish miserably and early. The eye that mocks a father, let the ravens of the valley pick it out. He who curses his father and mother, his lamp shall be put out in the midst of darkness. To the godly, bodily goods are given for their salvation; to the impious, partly so that they may be made inexcusable, partly so that the godly and elect who are mixed among them may enjoy them.

units.la: Inst. 3. Multi obedientes & pij liberi cito moriuntur. Ergo promissio non est universalis. Resp. 1. Rursus pauca exempla contrariam non cuertunt regulam. Plerique enim pij sunt longaevi. 2. Promissiones bonorum corporalium intelliguntur cum exceptione castigationis & crucis. 3. Translatio matura in caelestem vitam piis est amplissima longaevitatis terrenae compensatio.
units.tr: Inst. 3. Many obedient and pious children also die young. Therefore the promise is not universal. Answer: 1. Again, a few examples do not overturn the rule, for most pious people live long. 2. The promises of bodily goods are to be understood with the exception of chastisement and the cross. 3. For the pious, early translation to heavenly life is a far greater compensation for a shorter earthly life.

units.la: Partes obedientiae huius praecepti sunt triplices. 1. Aliae sunt virtutes superiorum propriae. 2. Aliae inferiorum propriae. 3. Aliae communes utrisque.
units.tr: The parts of obedience to this commandment are threefold. 1. Some belong to the virtues of superiors. 2. Some belong to the virtues of inferiors. 3. Some are common to both.

units.la: Virtutes superiorum propriae, secundum officia distinctae.
units.tr: The virtues proper to superiors, distinguished according to their offices.

units.la: I. Parentum officia sunt:
units.tr: I. The duties of parents are:

units.la: 1. Alere ac nutrire liberos.
units.tr: 1. To feed and nourish their children.

units.la: 2. Defendere eos contra injurias.
units.tr: 2. To defend them against injuries.

units.la: 3. Instituere eos, vel instituendos aliis tradere.
units.tr: 3. To instruct them, or to hand them over to others to be instructed.

units.la: 4. Regere eos disciplina domestica. Eadem tutoribus conueniunt, qui parentibus succedunt.
units.tr: 4. To govern them by domestic discipline. The same duties fall to guardians, who succeed parents.

units.la: Peccata igitur cum officio parentum pugnantia sunt:
units.tr: The sins contrary to the duty of parents are therefore these:

units.la: 1. Non quaerere aut suppeditare alimenta necessaria liberis, vel eos educare in luxu.
units.tr: 1. Not to seek out or supply the necessary food for children, or to bring them up in luxury.

units.la: 2. Non tueri eos contra injurias, aut non assuefacere ad patientiam & mansuetudinem, aut peccare zelo imprudenti propter leves & nullas injurias liberis illatas.
units.tr: 2. Not to protect them against injuries, or not to accustom them to patience and gentleness, or to sin through imprudent zeal over slight or imaginary injuries done to the children.

units.la: 3. Non erudire, aut non curare eos erudiri pro sua & liberorum facultate, aut malis praeceptis vel exemplis eos corrumpere.
units.tr: 3. Not to teach them, or not to take care that they are taught according to their own means and their children's abilities, or to corrupt them by bad precepts or examples.

units.la: 4. Educare eos in otio & licentia peccatorum: non castigare pro necessitate: vel praeter officium, aut peccati modum in eos saevire, & nimia austeritate eos alienare.
units.tr: 4. To bring them up in idleness and in licence to sin; not to punish when necessity requires it; or to rage against them beyond the duty of the office or the measure of the fault; or to alienate them by excessive severity.

units.la: II. Praeceptorum seu doctorum est:
units.tr: II. The duty of teachers is:

units.la: 1. Docere seu instituere fideliter discipulos, quia sunt parentum in instituendo loco.
units.tr: 1. To teach, or to instruct their pupils faithfully, since teachers stand in the place of parents in instruction.

units.la: 2. Regere eos disciplina scholastica.
units.tr: 2. To govern them by school discipline.

units.la: Peccata praeceptorum sunt eadem, quae & parentum in institutione ac disciplina.
units.tr: The sins of teachers are the same as those of parents in instruction and discipline.

units.la: III. Magistratuum officia ad haec capita revocari possunt.
units.tr: III. The duties of magistrates can be traced back to these heads.

units.la: 1. Mandare disciplinam secundum utramque tabulam decalogi.
units.tr: 1. To enjoin discipline according to both tables of the decalogue.

units.la: 2. Exsequi decalogi praecepta, defendendo servantes, coercendo ac puniendo violantes disciplinam.
units.tr: 2. To carry out the precepts of the decalogue, defending those who keep them and restraining and punishing those who violate the discipline.

units.la: 3. Condere aliquas leges positivas ad conseruandum ordinem politicum. Sunt autem positivae leges, determinationes circumstantiarum, ad ordinem & decorum reipublicae conseruandum necessariae, & seruientes observationi decalogi in politia.
units.tr: 3. To enact certain positive laws for preserving political order. Positive laws are determinations of circumstances necessary for keeping the order and decorum of the commonwealth, and serving the observance of the decalogue in the state.

units.la: 4. Exequi etiam istas suas leges.
units.tr: 4. To enforce these laws of their own making.

units.la: Magistratus officio opponuntur duo extrema:
units.tr: Two extremes are opposed to the office of magistrate:

units.la: 1. Ignavia, quae est vel non requirere a subditis disciplinam totius decalogi, vel non ordinare, quae ad conseruationem & decorum societatis civilis requiruntur: vel non defendere innocentes contra injurias, vel non coercere, aut nimis leviter punire contra leges positivas peccantes. 2. Tyrannis, quæ est vel iniusta præcipere subditis, vel non peccantes punire, vel atrocius, quam pro delicti modo punire.
units.tr: 1. Sloth, which is either not to require of subjects discipline under the whole decalogue, or not to ordain what is required for the preservation and decorum of civil society; or not to defend the innocent against injuries; or not to restrain, or to punish too lightly, those who offend against positive laws. 2. Tyranny, which is either to command subjects unjust things, or to punish those who do not offend, or to punish more savagely than the measure of the offence allows.

units.la: IV. Herorum seu dominorum est:
units.tr: IV. The duty of masters is:

units.la: 1. Mandare familiæ justa & possibilia: seu præcipere justas & licitas operas, non illicitas, non impossibiles, non nimis gra-ues, aut non necessarias.
units.tr: 1. To command the household what is just and possible; that is, to prescribe just and lawful tasks, not unlawful, impossible, excessively burdensome, or unnecessary ones.

units.la: 2. Suppeditare alimenta, & dare mercedem pro labore.
units.tr: 2. To supply food and to give wages for labour.

units.la: 3 Regere disciplina œconomica. Cibaria, & virga, & onus asino: panis & disciplina seruo.
units.tr: 3. To govern by household discipline. "Fodder and the rod and a burden for the donkey; bread and discipline for the servant."

units.la: Peccata dominorum sunt:
units.tr: The sins of masters are:

units.la: 1. Condere familiæ otium ignauum & licentiam.
units.tr: 1. To allow idle sloth and licence in the household.

units.la: 2. Imperare iniusta, vel onera nimis grauia.
units.tr: 2. To command unjust things, or burdens that are too heavy.

units.la: 3. Alimenta & mercedem fraudulenter dare.
units.tr: 3. To give food and wages fraudulently.

units.la: 4. Nimia asperitate familiam exacerbare.
units.tr: 4. To provoke the household by excessive harshness.

units.la: V. Seniorum autem & aliorum, qui prudentia & authoritate præstant, officium est: alios exemplo vitæ, & consiliis, & monitionibus regere & juuare.
units.tr: V. The duty of elders and of others who excel in prudence and authority is to guide and help others by the example of their life, and by counsels and admonitions.

units.la: Peccant isti contra conscientiam suam.
units.tr: These people sin against their own conscience:

units.la: 1. Stultitia & consiliorum prauitate.
units.tr: 1. through folly and perverse counsels.

units.la: 2. Morum leuitate & malis exemplis.
units.tr: 2. through levity of conduct and bad examples.

units.la: 3. Neglectu juniorum, aut aliorum inferiorum, quos peccare vident, nec consilio & authoritate, cum possint, corrigunt.
units.tr: 3. through neglect of the young, or of other inferiors whom they see sinning, and whom they do not correct by counsel and authority when they are able to do so.

units.la: Virtutes inferiorum propriæ.
units.tr: The proper virtues of inferiors.

units.la: Officia inferiorum proprio nomine honoris exprimuntur. Honor autem complectitur 1. Reuerentiam seu agnitionem, & approbationem ordinis diuini in officio & gradu superiorum, eiusque approbationis declarationem externam. 2. Amorem enim non amamus, eos non possumus reuereri. 3.Obedientiam in iis, quæ secundum officii sui rationem seniores jubent, & quidem voluntariam, sicut filij lætantur grata facientes parentibus. 4. Gratitudinem erga superiores seu ἀντιπαλαγίαν. 5. Ἐπιείκεια erga eosdem, quæ est tolerare vitia vel infirmitates parentum & superiorum, quæ sine nominis diuini contumelia tolerari possunt, aut quæ cum lege diuina non pugnant. Ex his facile colligitur, quæ officia inferioribus mandata, & ipsorum officiis conuenientia ipsi singulis ordinibus debeant.
units.tr: The duties of inferiors are expressed by the proper name of honour. Honour, moreover, embraces: 1. reverence, that is, acknowledgement and approval of the divine order in the office and rank of superiors, and the outward declaration of that approval; 2. love, for we cannot revere those whom we do not love; 3. obedience in those things which superiors command according to the reason of their office, and that obedience should be willing, as children gladly do what pleases their parents; 4. gratitude towards superiors, or repayment [ἀντιπαλαγία]; 5. gentleness [Ἐπιείκεια] towards the same, which is to tolerate the vices or infirmities of parents and superiors that can be tolerated without insult to the divine name, or that do not conflict with the divine law. From these points it is easily gathered which duties are enjoined on inferiors, and which befit the duties of each rank.

units.la: Peccant vero inferiores contra honorem superioribus debitum, vel non habentes eos eo loco, quo diuinitus constituti sunt: vel plus quam hominibus conuenit, eis tribuentes: vel odio eos prosequentes, præsertim propter ipsorum officium: vel recusantes obedientiam erga justa & legitima mandata: vel obsequentes in speciem aut injusta & impia praecipientibus: vel laedentes eos injuriis, aut non juvantes, quibus possunt officiis: vel gratificantes assentatorie & injuste: vel exagitantes ipsorum infirmitates: vel per adulationem laudantes errata aut vitia: vel deniq; non monentes eos suo loco de vitiis enormibus & periculosis cum debita reuerentia.
units.tr: But inferiors sin against the honour owed to superiors when they do not hold them in the place where God has set them; or when they give them more than befits men; or when they pursue them with hatred, especially on account of their office; or when they refuse obedience to just and lawful commands; or when they comply in appearance with those who command unjust and impious things; or when they injure them with insults, or do not help them with the services they can give; or when they flatter and unjustly indulge them; or when they expose their infirmities; or when they praise their errors or vices through flattery; or finally, when they do not warn them, in their proper place and with due reverence, about enormous and dangerous vices.

units.la: Virtutes superioribus & inferioribus communes.
units.tr: Virtues common to superiors and inferiors.

units.la: Communia omnium officia seu virtutes, quae omnibus hominum gradibus hic praecipiuntur, & quibus oppositia vitia damnantur, sunt:
units.tr: The duties or virtues common to all ranks of men, which are enjoined here, and the vices opposed to them, which are condemned, are these:

units.la: I. Justitia universalis, quae est obedientia secundum omnes leges ad nos pertinentes, propter vniuscuiusque vocationem. Eam hic praecipi manifestum est, quia superiores hanc postulare debent ab inferioribus, & eos exemplo suo ad obtemperandum provocare: & inferiores omnibus justis imperiis jubentur obedire.
units.tr: I. Universal justice, which is obedience to all the laws that apply to us, according to each person's calling. That this is enjoined here is plain, because superiors ought to require it of inferiors and by their own example urge them to obey, and inferiors are commanded to obey all just commands.

units.la: Huic repugnat, 1. Omnes neglectus officij, quod justae leges a singulis requirunt, sive superioribus sive inferioribus. 2. Omnis contumacia, inobedientia & seditio. 3. Simulatio officij & hypocrisis sive ὑποκρισις.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) every neglect of duty that just laws require of each person, whether superiors or inferiors; (2) all contumacy, disobedience and sedition; (3) the pretence of duty and hypocrisy, or hypocrisis.

units.la: II. Justitia particularis distributiva, quae est virtus sercum proportionem in distribuendis officiis, praemiis vel poenis: seu est virtus suum cuiq; tribuens. Summa, vniuscuiusq; officium aut honor, aut praemium illi competens: Reddite omnibus quod debetis, cui tributum debetis, tributum, cui vectigal, vectigal, cui honorem, honorem, cui timorem, timorem.
units.tr: II. Distributive particular justice, which is the virtue of observing proportion in distributing offices, rewards or punishments; or it is the virtue that gives each person his own. In short, each person's duty, or the honour or reward that suits him: Render to all what you owe: tribute to whom tribute is owed, custom to whom custom, honour to whom honour, fear to whom fear.

units.la: Cum hac pugnat error, temeritas & ἀξιωματικὴ in distribuendis officiis, vel deferendis honoribus, vel tribuendis praemiis.
units.tr: Error, rashness and axiōmatikē in distributing offices, bestowing honours or granting rewards are contrary to this.

units.la: III. Sedulitas seu diligentia, seu fidelitas, quae est, partes officij sui proprias rectè intelligere, eas juxta mandatum Dei facere libenter, assiduè, & cum conatu rectè faciendi, omissis alienis à sua vocatione & non necessariis, hoc fine principali, ut Deo grata & hominibus salutaria faciamus. Contendatis quieti esse & res vestras agere. Qui praeest, cum diligentia praesit. Servite ut servi Christi, facientes ex animo, quae Deus vult. Quodcunq; potest facere manus tua, instanter operare. Dicitur sedulitas à sedendo. Eius est non tantum intelligere partes officij sui, sed etiam non intellectas inquirere. Qui enim nescit, nec tamen inquirit, nihilominus
units.tr: III. Diligence, or carefulness, or faithfulness, which is to understand rightly the parts of one's own office, to perform them gladly, constantly and with an effort to do them rightly according to God's command, leaving aside what belongs to others or is not needed for one's calling, with this chief aim, that we do what is pleasing to God and beneficial to men. Make it your ambition to be quiet and to attend to your own affairs. He who rules, let him rule with diligence. Serve as servants of Christ, doing from the heart what God wills. Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might. Diligence (sedulitas) is so called from sitting (sedendo). It consists not only in understanding the parts of one's office but also in inquiring into those parts not yet understood. For he who does not know, and yet does not inquire, nevertheless

units.la: Exod.18.19. Rom.13,7. 1Thess.4,11. Rom.12,8. Ephes.6,6. Eccles.9,10. nus reddet rationem officij neglecti: quia ignorantia affectata non excusabit.
units.tr: Exod. 18:19. Rom. 13:7. 1 Thess. 4:11. Rom. 12:8. Eph. 6:6. Eccles. 9:10. will render an account of the duty neglected, because wilful ignorance will not excuse him.

units.la: Huic contraria est 1. Negligentia seu ignavia, quae vel non inquirit officij sui partes, vel eas volens omittit, aut non libenter aut non integrè, aut non assiduè facit. 2. Simulatio diligentia, quae officium principaliter suae gloriae vel commoditatis causa facit. 3. Curiositas, quae ingerit se officiis alienis.
units.tr: Contrary to this are: (1) negligence or sloth, which either does not inquire into the parts of its office, or, though knowing them, deliberately omits them, or performs them unwillingly, incompletely or inconstantly; (2) pretended diligence, which does its office chiefly for the sake of its own glory or advantage; (3) curiosity, which thrusts itself into the offices of others.

units.la: IV. AMOR erga sanguine junctos, vt parentes, liberos, cognatos, &c. qui vocatur storgé. Cum enim jubet Deus honorari parentes, etiam vult illos diligi, & quidem vt parentes: & cum vt parentes esse vult, etiam vult ab ipsis amari liberos, & quidem vt liberos.
units.tr: IV. Love toward those joined by blood, such as parents, children, relatives, and so on, which is called storgē. For when God commands that parents be honoured, he also wills that they be loved, and indeed as parents; and when he wills that they be parents, he also wills that children be loved by them, and indeed as children.

units.la: Huic repugnat 1. Atgeia, quae vel odit, vel non amat sanguine junctos, nec est solicita de eorum salute. 2. Indilligentia, quae propter amorem ad ipsorum peccata perniciosa ipsis vel aliis conniuet, aut ipsis gratificatur in rebus à Deo prohibitis.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) atgeia, which either hates or does not love those joined by blood, and is not concerned for their salvation; (2) indiligentia, which, out of affection, overlooks their ruinous sins, either in them or in others, or indulges them in things forbidden by God.

units.la: V. GRATITVDO, quae est virtus ex veritate & justitia constans, agnoscens, à quo, qualia & quanta beneficia acceperimus, & studium seu voluntatem habens praestandi mutua officia honesta, & possibilia. Qui reddit malum pro bono, de domo eius non recedet malum.
units.tr: V. GRATITUDE, which is a virtue arising from truth and justice, that acknowledges from whom, what kind and how great benefits we have received, and that has the zeal or will to render mutual honest and possible services. Whoever repays evil for good, evil will not depart from his house.

units.la: Huic aduersatur 1. Ingratitudo, quae vel non agnoscit, vel non profitetur authorem, & magnitudinem beneficij accepti: vel non studet praestare mutua officia. 2. Gratificatio pro beneficiis illicita.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) ingratitude, which either does not acknowledge or confess the giver and the greatness of the benefit received, or does not strive to render mutual services; (2) the unlawful repaying of benefits.

units.la: VI. GRAVITAS, quae est virtus ex agnitione officij seu gravitatis, seruans conuenientiam personae, & constantiam in dictis, gestibus & factis, vt tueamur honestam existimationem vel authoritatem, ne officium contumelia afficiatur. Quia enim Deus vult honorari superiores, vult etiam vt ipsi honorem suum tueantur. Gloria verò, quae est approbatio nostrae & alienae conscientiae rectè judicantis, cum sit virtus ad gloriam Dei & salutem hominum necessaria, dum modo fines hi spectentur, omnino est appetenda. Melius est nomen bonum, quàm diuitiae multa. Opus suum probet vnusquisque, & tunc in semetipso gloriationem habebit, & non in alio. Per omnia temetipsum praebens exemplar bonorum operum, in doctrina integritatem, gravitatem.
units.tr: VI. SERIOUSNESS (gravitas), which is a virtue arising from the recognition of one's office or dignity, that keeps the fitness of one's person and constancy in words, gestures and deeds, so that we may preserve an honest esteem and authority, lest the office be disgraced. For since God wills that superiors be honoured, he also wills that they guard their own honour. Glory, moreover, which is the approval of our own and others' consciences judging rightly, since it is a virtue necessary for the glory of God and the salvation of men, is altogether to be sought, provided these ends are kept in view. A good name is better than great riches. Let each one test his own work, and then he will have his boasting in himself and not in another. In all things present yourself as a pattern of good works, showing integrity and seriousness in teaching.

units.la: Huic repugnat 1. Leuitas, non seruans in dictis & factis, aut gestibus decorum personae aut constantiam, aut non habens studium retinendi famam & existimationem honestam. 2. Fastus seu ambitio, quae est propter officium aut dona sua sese efferre ostentare, & alios contemnere & negligere, & quærere loca al-tiora & applausus hominum, non studio gloriæ Dei, & salutis proximorum, sed cupiditate supra alios eminendi.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) levity, which does not keep the propriety of one's person or constancy in words, deeds or gestures, or has no zeal to keep a good name and honest esteem; (2) haughtiness or ambition, which is to puff oneself up and show off because of one's office or gifts, to despise and neglect others, and to seek higher places and the applause of men, not from zeal for God's glory and the salvation of neighbours, but from the desire to stand out above others.

units.la: VII. Modestia est virtus grauitati cognata, quæ ex agnitio-ne propriæ imbecillitatis, & consideratione loci atq; officij, quo sumus collocati à Deo, seruat conuenientiam in opinionibus & sermone de nobis, & in factis ac gestu, hoc sine, ne plus, quam oporteat, nobis tribuamus, aut reuerentiam aliis debitam viole-mus: ne in vestitu, gestu, sermone & vita plus splendoris osten-d mus, quam opus est: ne nos aliis præferamus, aut eos opprima-mus: sed pro nostris viribus & modulo nos geramus, cum agni-tione donorum Dei in aliis, & nostrorum defectuum. Modestia affinis est grauitas. Grauitas enim non coniuncta cum modestia degenerat in ambitionē & fastum. Si quis videtur sibi esse aliquid, cum nihil sit, hunc suus ipsius animus fallit. Humilitas & modestia differunt: quod hæc est erga homines, agnoscens sua vitia, & dona in aliis: humilitas est erga Deum.
units.tr: VII. Modesty is a virtue akin to seriousness, which, arising from the recognition of one's own weakness and from consideration of the place and office in which God has set us, keeps fitness in opinions and speech about ourselves, and in deeds and bearing, to this end: that we not attribute to ourselves more than is fitting, nor violate the reverence due to others; that in dress, bearing, speech and life we show no more splendour than is needed; that we do not put ourselves before others or oppress them; but that we conduct ourselves according to our powers and measure, acknowledging the gifts of God in others and our own defects. Seriousness is closely related to modesty, for seriousness not joined with modesty degenerates into ambition and haughtiness. If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, his own mind deceives him. Humility and modesty differ in this: the latter is toward men, acknowledging one's own faults and the gifts in others; humility is toward God.

units.la: Cum modestia pugnat: Immodestia, quæ in dictis, factis aut gestibus transgreditur conuenientiam personæ suæ, aut eorum, quibus cum versamur. 2. Arrogantia, quæ in opinione aut sermone tribuit sibi maiora veris, aut admiratur, aut sine necessitate, aut vltra modum prædicat, & ostentat sua dona. 3. Simulatio modestiæ, quæ est in admiratione sui seipsum extenuare, aut honores & officia detrectare, quæ quis expetit, vt laudationem sui vel opinionem modestiæ venetur.
units.tr: Opposed to modesty are: (1) immodesty, which in words, deeds or bearing oversteps the fitness of one's person, or of those among whom we live. (2) Arrogance, which in opinion or speech ascribes to itself more than is true, boasts without need or beyond measure, and displays its gifts. (3) Pretended modesty, which in a show of self-depreciation refuses honours and offices that one actually desires, hunting for praise of oneself or a reputation for modesty.

units.la: VIII. Æquitas siue ἐπιείκεια est virtus, propter causam probabilem leniens rigorem strictì juris, in puniendis vel ran-dis aliorum erratis: patienter ferens aliquos defectus, non enormiter lædentes salutem proximorum, publicam & priua-tam, & huiusmodi vitia aliorum regens, & corrigere studeas. Subditi estote cum omni timore Domini, non solum bonis & æquis, sed etiam prauis.
units.tr: VIII. Equity, or epieikeia, is a virtue which, for a probable reason, softens the rigour of strict law in punishing or pardoning the faults of others; which patiently bears certain defects that do not gravely harm the salvation of neighbours, public or private, and which seeks to govern and correct such faults in others. Be subject to every human authority, not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward.

units.la: Huic aduersatur, 1. Rigor immodicus in censura peccantium, præsertim ex infirmitate, sine enormi læsione salutis suæ, vel alienæ. 2. Lenitas non puniens, aut non reprehendens suo loco vitia enormia. 3. Assentatio, quæ gratiæ aut commodorum suorum studio laudat non laudanda, vel tribuit ali-cui maiora, quam conueniat.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) excessive severity in censuring sinners, especially from weakness, without grave injury to one's own or another's salvation; (2) leniency that does not punish or rebuke grave vices in their proper place; (3) flattery, which, for the sake of favour or its own advantage, praises what should not be praised, or ascribes to someone more than is fitting.

units.la: Galat. 6, 3.
QVÆSTIO CV.
units.tr: QUESTION 105.

units.la: Quid flagitat Deus in sexto præcepto?
units.tr: What does God require in the sixth commandment?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vt proximum neque cogitatione, neq; verbis, neque gestibus, nedum factis, vel per me, vel per alium contumelia afficiam, aut oderim, aut lædam, aut a occidam: sed omnem b vindictæ cupiditatem abijciam. Ad hæc ne meipsum lædam, aut sciens in aliquod c periculum conijciam. Quocirca etiam, ne cædes fierent, magistratum d gladio armauit.
units.tr: That I neither insult nor hate my neighbour, nor harm or kill him, whether by thought, by words, by gestures, much less by deeds, either in person or through another. a Instead, I will cast off every b desire for revenge. Furthermore, I will not harm myself, nor knowingly expose myself to any c danger. For this reason also, to prevent murders, God d armed the magistrate with the sword.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CVI.
units.tr: QUESTION 106.

units.la: Atqui hoc præceptum solam cædem prohibere videtur?
units.tr: But does this commandment seem to forbid only murder?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: At cædem prohibendo docet Deus, se radicem & originem cædis a, iram scilicet b, inuidiam c, odium, & vindictæ cupiditatem, atque ea omnia prod cæde ducere.
units.tr: In forbidding murder, God teaches that he forbids also its root and origin, namely anger, envy, hatred and the desire for revenge, and that all of these lead to murder. a b c

units.la: a Proverb.14,30. Rom.3,29. b 1 Iohan.2,11. c Iacobi 1,20. Galat.5,19. d 1 Ioh.3,15.
units.tr: a Prov. 14:30. Rom. 3:29. b 1 John 2:11. c James 1:20. Gal. 5:19. d 1 John 3:15.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 107.

units.la: An verò id satis est, nos neminem eo, quo dictum est modo, occidere?
units.tr: But is it enough for us not to kill anyone in the way that has been stated?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Non est satis: dum enim Deus iram, inuidiam, odium damnat, postulat vt proximum æque ac nos ipsos a diligamus, & vt b humilitate, lenitate, mansuetudine c, patientia, & misericordia, erga eum vtamur, quodque ei damno esse possit, quantum in nobis est e, auertamus. Ad summam, ita animo affecti simus, vt ne inimicis quidem f benefacere dubitemus.
units.tr: It is not enough. For when God condemns anger, envy and hatred, he requires that we love our neighbour as ourselves, a and that we use towards him b humility, gentleness, meekness, c patience and mercy, and that we turn away, as far as lies in us, from whatever could do him harm. e In short, we should be so disposed in mind that we do not hesitate to do good even to our enemies. f

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Scopus seu finis sexti praecepti est conseruatio vitae, & incolumitatis corporum, atque adeo salutis tum nostrae, tum aliorum. Praecipiuntur igitur omnia, quae ad incolumitatem vitae nostrae & aliorum pertinent. Contra prohibentur omnia, quae ad destructionem eius spectant, hoc est, omnis injusta laesio, & laesionis cupiditas, & huius cupiditatis significatio. Nominatur in prohibitione homicidium, non quod hoc solum Deus prohibeat, sed vt vna cum effectu proprias causas tollat, & peccata cohaerentia nomine homicidij complectens, eorum gravitate significata, nos ab illis eo efficacius absterreat, juxta regulam: Praecepta aut prohibita specie aliqua praecipua, etiam cognata & species sive totum genus praecipitur aut prohibetur.
units.tr: The aim or purpose of the sixth commandment is the preservation of life and the safety of bodies, and thus the well-being both of ourselves and of others. Therefore everything is commanded that pertains to the safety of our own life and that of others. On the other hand, everything is forbidden that tends to its destruction, that is, every unjust injury, the desire to injure, and the outward expression of that desire. The prohibition names homicide, not because God forbids this alone, but so that, together with the effect, he may remove its proper causes; and by embracing under the name of homicide the sins connected with it, he may, by signifying their gravity, the more effectively deter us from them, according to the rule: When some chief precept or prohibition is given in a particular kind, cognate kinds and the whole genus are also commanded or forbidden.

units.la: Hic probandum est 1. quod etiam interna homicidia hoc praecepto prohibeantur. 2. Quod laesio nostri etiam prohibeatur. 3. Quod defensio praecipiatur.
units.tr: Here we must prove: 1. that even internal homicides are forbidden by this commandment; 2. that injury to ourselves is also forbidden; 3. that defence is commanded.

units.la: 1. Interna etiam homicidia prohiberi hoc praecepto probatur. 1. Ex regula: Cum praecipitur aut prohibetur effectus, etiam causa praecipi aut prohiberi intelligitur. 2. Ex scopo. Non vult Deus, vt laedamus. 3. Ex interpretatione Christi. Qui temere irascitur fratri suo, reus est judicij. Itaque cum externa caede prohibetur omnis injusta laesio proximi, & omnes huius laesionis causae, occasiones vel significationes, vt ira, invidia, odium & vindictae cupiditas.
units.tr: 1. That internal homicides are forbidden by this commandment is proved as follows. (1) From the rule: When an effect is commanded or forbidden, the cause is also understood to be commanded or forbidden. (2) From the aim: God does not wish us to injure. (3) From the interpretation of Christ: "Whoever is angry with his brother without cause is liable to judgment." Therefore, along with outward murder, every unjust injury to a neighbour is forbidden, and all the causes, occasions or signs of such injury, such as anger, envy, hatred and the desire for revenge.

units.la: II. Non autem aliorum, sed etiam nostrae ipsorum vitae laesio aut neglectus prohibetur: quia causa, cur Deus jubeat nos alienae vitae rationem habere, eadem sunt etiam in nobis ipsis, videlicet 1. Imago Dei, quae per nos non debet destrui, neque in nobis, neque in aliis. 2. Similitudo naturae, & origo ex primis parentibus. Sicut enim non laedendus est proximus, quia est caro nostra; sic neque nosipsi, quia nemo unquam carnem suam odio habuit. 3. Magnitudo precij, quo Christus & alios, & nos redemit. 4. Membrorum Christi coniunctio. Hae causae cum in nobis ipsis quoq; reperiantur: sequitur hac lege etiam singulis suae cuiusq; vitae & corporis laesionem ac neglectum prohiberi.
units.tr: II. Not only the injury or neglect of the life of others, but also of our own life, is forbidden. For the reasons why God commands us to care for another's life are the same in ourselves, namely: (1) the image of God, which must not be destroyed by us, neither in ourselves nor in others; (2) the likeness of nature and origin from our first parents. For just as the neighbour must not be harmed because he is our flesh, so neither must we ourselves, since no one has ever hated his own flesh; (3) the greatness of the price by which Christ redeemed both others and us; (4) the union of the members of Christ. Since these reasons are also found in ourselves, it follows by this same law that the injury and neglect of each person's own life and body is likewise forbidden.

units.la: III. Defensio proximi praecipitur. Cum enim lex non tantum jubeat peccata cavere, sed etiam eorum contraria facere: manifestum festum est, Deum non tantum hic prohibere, ne laedamus vitam & salutem cuiusquam, sed etiam praecipere, ut quatenus fieri potest eam defendamus & foveamus. Praeceptum igitur negativum: Non occides: includit affirmatiuum; vitam proximi conser-vabis.
units.tr: III. The defence of the neighbour is commanded. For since the law not only commands us to avoid sins but also to do the opposites of them, it is quite plain that God here forbids not only that we injure the life and safety of anyone, but also commands that we defend and cherish it, as far as it can be done. Thus the negative precept, You shall not kill, includes the affirmative: You shall preserve your neighbour's life.

units.la: Summa praecepti est, ut neque nostram, neque alterius vitam aut salutem corporis externo opere laedamus, sive id fiat vi, sive dolo, sive negligentia: neue affectu aut voluntate laesionem eius expetamus, aut nos expetere gestu vel verbis significemus: contra vero, vitam proximi & nostram seruemus, & omnibus benefaciamus. Igitur, non occides, significat, 1. neque te, neque alios desiderabis occidere. Quod enim a nobis fieri non vult Deus, id neque expeti aut desiderari concedit. 2. neque significabis desiderium vel te vel alios occidendi. Nam cuius appetitionem Deus prohibet, eius etiam significationem verbis aut gestu seu vultu factam prohibet. 3. neque desiderium istud exsequeris. Nam cuius appetitionem & significationem Deus vetat, eius executionem multo magis vetat utique. Antithesis ergo est: Te & alios iuuabis. 1. desiderio. 2. significatione. 3. executione. Hinc oriuntur omnes huius praecepti virtutes, & similiter vitia cum iisdem pugnantia. Vitia, quae prohibentur, ad destructionem: virtutes, quae praecipiuntur, ad conseruationem vitae & salutis hominum spectant.
units.tr: The sum of the precept is that we should injure neither our own nor another's life or bodily safety by any outward act, whether this is done by force, by deceit or by negligence; nor should we desire its injury in our affection or will, or signal by gesture or words that we desire it. On the contrary, we should preserve both our neighbour's life and our own, and do good to all. Therefore, you shall not kill means: (1) you will not desire to kill either yourself or others, for what God does not want us to do, he does not allow us to wish for or desire; (2) you will not signify by word or gesture or look any desire to kill either yourself or others, for God forbids the signifying of what he forbids us to desire; (3) you will not carry out that desire, for what God forbids us to desire and to signify, he forbids far more to be carried out. The antithesis, then, is: You shall help yourself and others: (1) in desire, (2) in signification, (3) in execution. From this arise all the virtues of this commandment, and likewise the vices contrary to them. The vices that are forbidden look to destruction; the virtues that are commanded look to the preservation of human life and safety.

units.la: Conseruatur autem vita hominum vel non laedendo, vel iuuando. Unde duo genera virtutum huius praecepti constituuntur: aliae non laedentes hominum salutem, aliae eandem iuuantes. Non laedentes sunt triplices. Nam non laedimus aut non laedo, seu non irritati: aut irritati: aut utroque modo. In primo modo versatur Iustitia particularis neminem laedens. In secundo, Mansuetudo & ἐπιείκεια. In tertio, φιλανθρωπία. Iuuantes salutem hominis rursus sunt duplices. Nam iuuamus aut depellendo mala, aut benefaciendo. In primo modo versatur, Iustitia commutatiua puniens, Fortitudo, & Nemesis. In altero, Humanitas, Misericordia & Amicitia.
units.tr: The life of men is preserved either by not injuring or by helping. Hence two kinds of virtues of this commandment are established: some do not harm human safety, others help to preserve it. Those that do not harm are threefold. For we either do not injure, and are not provoked; or we do injure, being provoked; or we do so in both ways. In the first manner belongs particular justice, which harms no one. In the second, meekness and equity [ἐπιείκεια, epieikeia]. In the third, philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία, philanthropia]. Those that help human safety are in turn twofold, for we help either by warding off evils or by doing good. In the first manner belong punitive commutative justice, fortitude, and Nemesis. In the second, humanity, mercy and friendship.

units.la: Virtutes non laedentes hominum salutem.
units.tr: Virtues that do not harm human well-being.

units.la: I. Iustitia particularis neminem laedens ea est, quae neq; studio, neq; negligentia laedit cuiusquam vitam aut corpus, a quo nos laesi non sumus, nisi Deo iubente. Seu, est virtus cauens omnes laesiones salutis nostrae vel proximi, quae vel vio-lentia, vel fraude, vel negligentia fiunt. Haec in verbis praecepti exprimitur: Non occides.
units.tr: I. Particular justice, which harms no one, is the virtue that neither by design nor by carelessness injures the life or body of anyone from whom we have not been harmed, unless God commands it. Or, it is the virtue guarding against every injury to our own or our neighbour's well-being, whether done by violence, by fraud, or by negligence. This is expressed in the words of the precept: Thou shalt not kill.

units.la: Virtutes duplices huius praecepti.
units.tr: There are two kinds of virtue under this precept.

units.la: Non laedentes.
units.tr: Not harming.

units.la: Iuuantes. Cum hac pugnat, & hoc precepto damnatur 1. Omnis lasio nostrae vel alienae virtae aut corporis, sive studio, sive per negligentiam praeter leges facta. 2. Lenitudo, qua laedendi non laeduntur ab iis, quorum id est officij.
units.tr: Helping. Opposed to this, and condemned by this precept, are: (1) every injury done to our own or another's life or body, whether by design or through negligence, contrary to the laws; (2) laxity, by which those whose duty it is to prevent harm do not prevent it.

units.la: II. MANSVETVDO seu placabilitas, seu ignoscentia, est virtus moderatrix irae, quae nec propter nullam, nec propter leuem causam irascitur, nec vbi legitima irae causa est, personae laedentis destructionem optat, sed propter contumeliam Dei, vel injustitiam & detrimentu proximi indignatur, & nullius quantumuis magnae iniuriae vindicandae cupiditate in animo admittit, sed etiam inimicorum, & male meritorum salute optat ex animo, & ei tuendae pro nostra facultate & ipsorum necessitate studet. Seu est virtus moderatrix irae, quae cauet omnem iram injustam, & justam etiam sic moderatur, vt non egrediatur limites a Deo praescriptos, nec ardeat cupiditate vindictae, sed condonet offensas etiam graues, etiam inimicis: ne ira feratur in personas, sed vitia, vt etiam eorum, qui grauissime peccarunt, salutem optemus. Beati mites, quoniam ipsi haereditatis jure terram possidebunt.
units.tr: II. MEEKNESS or placability, or forgiveness, is the virtue that moderates anger. It is not angry without cause or for a slight cause, and where there is a lawful cause for anger it does not wish the destruction of the person who has done the wrong. Rather, it is indignant at the dishonour done to God, or at injustice and loss suffered by a neighbour. It does not admit into the mind any desire for revenge, however great the injury, but sincerely wishes well even to enemies and to those who have deserved ill of us, and strives, as far as our means allow and their need requires, to help them. Or, it is the virtue moderating anger, which guards against all unjust anger, and so moderates even just anger that it does not go beyond the limits prescribed by God, nor burns with desire for vengeance, but pardons offences, even grave ones, even from enemies. Anger is not to be directed against persons but against sins, so that we wish salvation even for those who have sinned most gravely. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.

units.la: Huic contraria est 1. Lenitas, quae est, non indignari propter atroces injurias, nec coercere ac punire, aut in his prohibendis nimis remissum esse. 2. Iracundia, & omnis ira iniusta vel immoderata. 3. Vindicta cupiditas & simultas.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) leniency, which is not being indignant at atrocious injuries, and not restraining and punishing them, or being too lax in preventing them; (2) irascibility, and every unjust or immoderate anger; (3) a desire for revenge and enmity.

units.la: III. Επιείκεια est virtus mansuetudini cognata, stricti juris (quod poenas peccatis aequat) moderatrix propter causam probabilem: vt cum propter factum, aut officiu vel propter salutem publicam, aut priuatam eorum, qui peccant, aut propter scandalum vitandum, aliquid remittitur de nostro jure, in puniendis peccatis, vel persequendis injuriis. Moderatio vestra sit nota omnibus hominibus, &c.
units.tr: III. Ἐπιείκεια [epieikeia] is a virtue akin to meekness. It moderates strict law (which matches penalties to sins) for a probable reason: when, on account of the deed or the office, or for the public good, or the private good of those who sin, or to avoid scandal, something is remitted from our right in punishing sins or pursuing wrongs. Let your moderation be known unto all men.

units.la: Huic aduersatur 1. Crudelitas & seueritas iniusta, seu rigor immedicus. 2. Nimia lenitas, quae est non moueri iis rebus, quibus ex officio oportebat moueri, vt Deus iubet, &c. 3. Ωμότης.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) cruelty and unjust severity, or immoderate rigour; (2) excessive leniency, which is not being moved by those things by which one ought to be moved in one's office, as God commands; (3) Ὠμότης [ōmotēs], savagery.

units.la: IV. Φιλησυχία, studium pacis & concordiae, est diligentia cauendi causas offensionum, & occasiones discordiarum, contentionum & odiorum non necessarias, & offensos nobis vel aliis reconciliandi, & pacis retinendae causa non detrectare molestias, & toleratiam, circa contumeliam Dei, & atrocem nostrae vel alienae salutis laesionem. Breuiter: Est virtus cauens omnes defensiones & occasiones irarum & discordiarum, & ortas studens tollere, arripiens occasiones.
units.tr: IV. Φιλησυχία [philēsychia], the study of peace and concord, is the diligence to avoid the causes of offence and the unnecessary occasions of discord, strife and hatred, to reconcile those who are offended with us or with others, and, for the sake of keeping peace, not to shrink from troubles and from patient endurance, provided that God's honour and the grave injury to our own or another's salvation are not at stake. In brief: it is the virtue guarding against all provocations and occasions of anger and discord, and eagerly seeking to remove them when they arise, seizing opportunities for peace.

units.la: Huic opposita est 1. Turbulentia, praebens vel arripiens occasiones turbarum: ad quam pertinet libido contendendi, obtrectandi, calumniandi, susurrandi, &c. Damnantur ergo omnes contentiones obsi obtrectatores, calumniatores, susurrones. 2. Lentitas. 3. Gratificatio iniusta.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) turbulence, which offers or seizes occasions of disturbance, to which belongs the lust for contending, slandering, calumniating, whispering, and so on. So all quarrelsome, slanderous, calumnious and whispering persons are condemned. (2) Sluggishness. (3) Unjust flattery.

units.la: Virtutes iuuantes hominum salutem.
units.tr: Virtues that help human well-being.

units.la: V. Justitia commutativa puniens est, quae seruat aequalitatem peccati & poenae, pro ratione circumstantiarum in iudicio politico, ad tuendam gloriam Dei, & societatē generis humani necessaria. Seu, est virtus seruans aequalitatem peccatorum & poenarum, infligens vel aequales, vel propter probabilem causam minores. Cum enim Deus vetet laedi societatem, & magistratum velit esse vindicē disciplinae secundum totum decalogum: vult etiam iustis poenis coerceri atrociter hunc ordinem violantes. Ac nisi haec iustitia seruetur, non potest consistere humana forma tua pro anima ipsius, & populus tuus pro populo ipsius. Pertinet igitur haec iustitia ad hoc praeceptum.
units.tr: V. Punitive commutative justice is the virtue that keeps the balance between sin and punishment, according to the circumstances, in the civil judgement, necessary for upholding God's glory and the fellowship of the human race. Or, it is the virtue that keeps the balance between sins and punishments, inflicting either equal penalties or, for a probable reason, lesser ones. For since God forbids the fellowship to be harmed, and wishes the magistrate to be the avenger of discipline according to the whole decalogue, he also wills that those who atrociously violate this order be restrained by just penalties. And unless this justice is maintained, human society cannot stand: a life for his life, and a people for his people. This justice therefore belongs to this precept.

units.la: Obiect. Dicitur: Non occides. Ergo prorsus non est occidendum, & per consequens, haec iustitia hic non praecipitur, ut quae seruari non potest, nisi multi occidantur. Resp. 1. Non occides. nempe tu priuatus, tuo arbitrio & libidine, me non iubente, faciente exceptionem ab hac lege. Hoc vero non tollit officium magistratus. Est enim minister Dei, & gladium a Deo accep-tum non gerit frustra. Cum ergo magistratus occidit facinorosos, non homines occidunt, sed Deus ipse occidit. 2. Per inuersionem: ideo sunt occidendi aliqui, ne humana societas a latronibus occidatur.
units.tr: Objection. It is said: Thou shalt not kill. Therefore no one at all is to be killed, and consequently this justice is not commanded here, since it cannot be maintained unless many are killed. Answer. (1) Thou shalt not kill, that is, you as a private person, by your own judgement and lust, without my command, make no exception to this law. But this does not take away the office of the magistrate: for he is the minister of God, and does not bear the sword in vain. Therefore, when the magistrate puts criminals to death, it is not men who kill them, but God himself who kills. (2) By inversion: some are to be killed so that human society is not killed by robbers.

units.la: Cum iustitia seuera pugnat Iniustitia, quae aut prorsus non punit, aut punit iniuste, vt. crudelitas & rigor nimius aut calumnia iuris stricti. 2. vindicta priuata. 3. lenitas. 4. ...
units.tr: Opposed to severe justice is injustice, which either does not punish at all or punishes unjustly, as cruelty and excessive rigour, or the chicanery of strict law. (2) Private vengeance. (3) Leniency. (4) ...

units.la: VI. Fortitudo est virtus, quae subit pericula secundum rationem, propter gloriam Dei, & salutem ecclesiae ac reipublicae, & propter defensionē & conseruationem vitae & salutis propriae vel alienae, contra atroces iniurias. Oritur autem fortitudo sanctorum ex fide, & spe, & dilectione Dei ac proximi. Heroica fortitudo est singulare donum Dei, vt in Iosua, Samsone, Gedeone, Dauide, &c. Bellica fortitudo est propugnatrix iustitiae, & susceptio defensionis iustae nostri & aliorum, etsi non sit sine periculo. Bellum, est vel defensio necessaria contra exercentes latrocinia seu crudelitatem in subditos, vel poena iusta propter atroces iniurias, quae manu armata suscipitur ab ordinaria potestate.
units.tr: VI. Fortitude is the virtue that undergoes dangers according to right reason, for the glory of God, the salvation of the Church and the commonwealth, and for the defence and preservation of one's own or another's life and well-being against atrocious injuries. Moreover, the fortitude of the saints arises from faith, hope and love of God and neighbour. Heroic fortitude is a singular gift of God, as in Joshua, Samson, Gideon, David, and others. Military fortitude is the defender of justice, and the undertaking of a just defence of ourselves and others, even if it is not without danger. War is either a necessary defence against those who practise robbery or cruelty against their subjects, or a just punishment for atrocious injuries, undertaken by lawful authority under arms.

units.la: Huic repugnat timiditas refugiens pericula necessaria, & temeritas subiens pericula non necessaria.
units.tr: Opposed to this are timidity, which shrinks from necessary dangers, and rashness, which runs into unnecessary dangers.

units.la: VII. Nemesis siue zelus est amore justitiae & proximi indignari propter atrocem injuriam, innocentibus illatam, & pro facultate sua eam depellere aut vindicare, juxta mandatum Dei. Seu, est virtus juste irascens & indignans propter contumeliam Dei, & atrocem injuriam: qua vel Deus, vel proximus afficitur.
units.tr: VII. Nemesis, or zeal, is being indignant, out of love of justice and of neighbour, at an atrocious injury done to the innocent, and, according to God's command, to drive it off or avenge it as far as one's means allow. Or, it is the virtue that justly is angry and indignant at the dishonour done to God and at atrocious injury, by which either God or a neighbour is afflicted.

units.la: Cum zelo seu nemesi pugnat lenitas, & ira injusta.
units.tr: Opposed to zeal or Nemesis are leniency, and unjust anger.

units.la: VIII. Humanitas seu φιλανθρωπία seu dilectio proximi in specie & proprie dicta, est veram benevolentiam praestare erga homines, quam alios erga nos praestare vellemus, & eam sermone, gestu & officiis convenientibus significare. Seu, est in animo, voluntate & corde, benevolentia erga alios, & eius declaratio gestu, sermone & officiis possibilibus. Dilectio sit minime simulata.
units.tr: VIII. Humanity, or φιλανθρωπία [philanthrōpia], or love of neighbour in the specific and proper sense, is to show true goodwill towards human beings, such as we would wish others to show us, and to express it by suitable words, gestures and services. Or, it is goodwill towards others in the mind, will and heart, and its declaration by gesture, speech and possible services. Let love be without hypocrisy.

units.la: Huic opponitur 1. Inhumanitas seu morositas, quae propria humanitatis omittit, vel facit contraria. 2. Malevolentia seu invidia, quae est dolor de alterius bono, & studium illud ad se pertrahendi, vel saltem ab altero avertendi: mir nicht dir nicht. 3. Amor sui cum neglectu proximi & horum significatio. 4. Gratificatio injusta.
units.tr: Opposed to this are: (1) inhumanity or moroseness, which omits or does the opposite of what humanity requires; (2) malevolence or envy, which is grief at another's good and the effort to draw it to oneself, or at least to turn it away from the other: neither mine nor yours; (3) self-love with neglect of the neighbour and the display of this; (4) unjust flattery.

units.la: IX. Misericordia est dolere propter calamitatem innocentium, aut ex infirmitate lapsorum, & eam lenire conari. Seu est virtus, quae compatitur calamitatibus justorum, vel eorum, qui ex ignorantia aut infirmitate peccarunt, & studet eas tollere aut lenire, quantum justitia permittit, nec gaudet calamitatibus etiam hostium. Beati misericordes: quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur.
units.tr: IX. Mercy is to grieve at the calamity of the innocent, or at the weakness of those who have fallen, and to try to soften it. Or it is the virtue which has compassion for the calamities of the righteous, or of those who have sinned through ignorance or weakness, and strives to remove or lessen them, as far as justice permits, and does not rejoice even in the calamities of enemies. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

units.la: Cum misericordia pugnat ἐπιχαιρεκακία, ἀπάθεια & lenitas.
units.tr: Opposed to mercy are ἐπιχαιρεκακία [epichairekakia], ἀπάθεια [apatheia] and leniency.

units.la: X. Amicitia species humanitatis, est vera & mutua benevolentia, mutua virtutis in illis agnitione, vel honestis officiis excitata, praestans mutua officia honesta & possibilia: Vir amicus praestat se amicum illis. Est enim amicus magis coniunctus quam frater.
units.tr: X. Friendship, a species of humanity, is true and mutual goodwill, aroused by mutual recognition of virtue in one another or by honourable services, rendering mutual honourable and possible services. A friend shows himself friendly to those who are his friends. For a friend is more closely joined than a brother.

units.la: Extrema amicitiae sunt 1. Inimicitia. 2. Neglectus amicorum, 3. Lenitas in contrahendis & dissoluendis amicitiis. 4. Simulatio amicitiae. 5. Adulatio. 6. Gratificatio injusta.
units.tr: The extremes of friendship are: (1) enmity; (2) neglect of friends; (3) laxity in forming and dissolving friendships; (4) pretended friendship; (5) flattery; (6) unjust indulgence. ## Type of the sixth precept

units.la: Typus sexti præcepti.

Sexto præcepto: Non occides: prohibetur omnis læsio iniusta vitæ nostræ, vel proximi. Lædítur autem vel nocendo, quod fit vel externa vi: vt cæde. (bus. obtrectationi- injuriis qbusuis. interno affectu: vt ira. odio. (dictæ, cupiditate vindeserendo & non iuuando pro virili, quod est neglectus officiorum, quæ ad conseruationem vitæ requiruntur. præcipitur conseruatio vitæ nostræ & alienæ. non lædendo. Non lædere debent vel non irritati, quod est iustitiæ. irritati, quod est mansuetudinis & [?]ἐπιεικείας. vtroq; modo, quod est [?]φιλησυχίας. Conseruatur autem vel iuuando: iuuatur autem proximus vel iniuriarum depulsione, quod facit iustitia commutatiua in puniendo, fortitudo, & Nemesis. beneficiorum exhibitione, vt fit humanitate seu beneuolentia, misericordia, amicitia.
units.tr: In the sixth precept, "You shall not kill," every unjust injury to our own life or to our neighbour's life is forbidden. Our neighbour is injured either by harming him or by failing to help him. Harm is done by external force, as in slaughter, or by wounding, or by injuries of any kind, or by slander and detraction; or it is done by an inner disposition, such as anger, hatred or desire for revenge. Failing to help him, as far as one can, is the neglect of the duties required for preserving life. What is commanded is the preservation of our own life and of another's, and this is done by not harming. Those who are not provoked must not harm, which belongs to justice. Those who are provoked must not harm, which belongs to gentleness and equity [ἐπιείκεια]. In either case the disposition is one of peacefulness [φιλησυχία]. Preservation, however, is also achieved by helping. A neighbour is helped by the warding off of injuries, which is the work of commutative justice in punishing, of fortitude, and of Nemesis; or by the bestowing of benefits, which is done through kindness or benevolence, mercy and friendship.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CVIII. Quæ est sententia septimi præcepti?
units.tr: QUESTION 108. What is the meaning of the seventh commandment?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Deum omnem turpitudinem exsecrati: ideoq; nos eam penitus odisse & detestari debere: contraq; temperanter, modestè & castè, siue in sacro coniugio, siue in vita cœlibe viuere oportere.
units.tr: God condemns all impurity, and therefore we ought to hate and utterly detest it; on the contrary, we ought to live temperately, modestly and chastely, whether in holy wedlock or in celibate life.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CIX. Nihilne amplius prohibet Deus hoc præcepto, quam adulterium, & id genus turpitudines?
units.tr: QUESTION 109. Does God forbid anything else by this commandment besides adultery and such-like filthiness?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Cum corpus & animus noster templa sint Spiritus sancti: vult Deus, vt vtrumq; pure sancteq; possideamus. Ideoq; facta, gestus, sermones, cogitationes, cupiditates fœdas, & quicquid hominem ad ista allicit, in vniuersum prohibet.
units.tr: Since our body and soul are temples of the Holy Spirit, God wills that we possess both in purity and holiness. He therefore forbids in general all foul deeds, gestures, words, thoughts and lusts, and whatever entices a person to them.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Sancit hoc præcepto Deus conservationem castitatis & conjugii, atque adeo coniugium ipsum. Quod enim prohibet, eius contrarium sancit, & vult conseruari. Prohibet vero adulterium, quod est violatio fidei coniugalis. Nominato adulterio tanquam specie omnium, quæ castitati repugnant, crassissima, simul prohibet & damnat omnes vagas libidines in coniugio & extra illud, seu omnia alia peccata & vitia castitati contraria, eorumque causas, occasiones, effectus, antecedentia, consequentia, &c. Ex aduerso præcipit virtutes ad castitatem pertinentes. Rationes hæ sunt: 1. Ex una specie reliqua cognata intelliguntur. Ergo prohibito adulterio tanquam libidinis specie crassissima, etiam prohiberi intelliguntur aliæ libidinum species. 2. Vbi causa damnatur, ibi & effectus damnatur, & concies. contra. Cum igitur hic damnetur adulterium, etiam adulterij antecedentia & consequentia damnantur. 3. Scopus praecepti est conservatio castitatis in genere humano, & munitio conjugii. Quicquid ergo facit ad castitatem conseruandam, & munien-dum conjugium, hac lege praecipitur, & contrarium prohibe-tur. Virtutes igitur septimi praecepti praecipue sunt tres: castitas, verecundia & temperantia.
units.tr: By this commandment God enjoins the preservation of chastity and of marriage, and so marriage itself. For what he forbids, he enjoins the contrary of, and wills to be preserved. He forbids adultery, which is the violation of marital faith. By naming adultery, the grossest form of all that is opposed to chastity, he at the same time forbids and condemns all wandering lusts, both within marriage and outside it, or all other sins and vices contrary to chastity, together with their causes, occasions, effects, antecedents, consequences, and so on. On the other side, he commands the virtues that pertain to chastity. The reasons are these: (1) From one species the other related kinds are understood. Therefore, when adultery is forbidden as the grossest species of lust, the other species of lust are understood to be forbidden as well. (2) Where a cause is condemned, its effect is condemned too, and conversely. Since adultery is condemned here, the antecedents and consequences of adultery are condemned as well. (3) The aim of the commandment is the preservation of chastity in the human race and the protection of marriage. Whatever contributes to preserving chastity and protecting marriage is therefore commanded by this law, and the contrary is forbidden. The virtues of the seventh commandment are therefore chiefly three: chastity, modesty and temperance.

units.la: I. CASTITAS
units.tr: I. CHASTITY

units.la: in genere est virtus seruans munditiam animi & corporis cum voluntate Dei congruentem, & vitans omnes libidines à Deo prohibitas, omnes concubitus illicitos, & commixtionem corporum inordinatam, & omnes earum cupiditates, occasiones, causas, effectus, suspiciones, &c. tam in conjugio quam in vita coelibe. Castitatem dici volunt à graeco ἁγνός, id est ornamentum totius hominis, & omnium alia-rum virtutum. Nomen igitur καθ' ἐξοχὴν huic virtuti est imaginem Dei, iuxta illud:
units.tr: Chastity in general is the virtue that keeps the purity of soul and body agreeing with the will of God, and that avoids all lusts forbidden by God, all unlawful intercourse, disorderly mixing of bodies, and all the desires, occasions, causes, effects, suspicions, and so on, both in marriage and in the single life. They say that castitas (chastity) is named from the Greek ἁγνός [hagnos], that is, the ornament of the whole person and of all other virtues. The name chastity is therefore given to this virtue par excellence [kath' exochēn], since God himself is chaste, and his image is in us, according to the saying:

units.la: Mens est casta Deus, casta vult mente vocari:
units.tr: God is chaste; he wishes to be called chaste in mind:

units.la: Et castas iussit pondus habere preces.
units.tr: And he has ordained that chaste prayers have weight.

units.la: Est autem duplex, coelebs & coniugalis. Castitas coelebs est virtus vitans omnes vagas libidines extra conjugium. Castitas duplex. coniugalis est in coniugio seruare ordinem mirando Dei consilio instituturum.
units.tr: Chastity is of two kinds, single and married. Single chastity is the virtue that avoids all wandering lusts outside marriage. Married chastity is keeping, within marriage, the order that God in his wisdom instituted.

units.la: Causa castitatis sunt 1. Mandatum Dei: Haec est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis à fornicatione, & sciat unusquisque vestrum vas suum possidere cum sanctificatione & honore. Sectamini pacem & castitatem, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum. 2. Conser-uatio imaginis Dei. 3. Studium cauendi deformationem imagi-nis Dei & coniunctionis inter Christum & ecclesiam, de qua apostolus: Fugite fornicationem: an ignoratis corpora vestra esse membra Christi? Num igitur tollens membra Christi faciam scorti membra? absit. 4. Praemia & poenae.
units.tr: The causes of chastity are (1) the command of God: "This is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication, and that each one of you know how to possess his vessel in holiness and honour. Follow peace and chastity, without which no one will see the Lord." (2) The preservation of the image of God. (3) The zeal to avoid disfiguring the image of God and the union between Christ and the Church, of which the apostle says: "Flee fornication. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? God forbid." (4) Rewards and punishments.

units.la: Pugnantia cum castitate sunt: castitas simulata, & coelibatus impurus, scortatio, concubinatus, incestus, adulteria, & omnes vagae ac nefariae libidines, harum causae, occasiones & effectus.
units.tr: Things contrary to chastity are: pretended chastity and impure celibacy, whoredom, concubinage, incest, adulteries, and all wandering and wicked lusts, with their causes, occasions and effects.

units.la: Omnes vero libidinum species referri possunt ad tria genera. Primi generis sunt, quae sunt παρὰ φύσιν, & a diabolo, quae nisi tantum, quia eam corrumpunt & priuant conformitate cum Deo, sed etiam quia haec natura nostra depravata ab iis abhorret: cu-ius generis sunt, quae recensentur ab apostolo ad Rom. c. 1. vt confusiones specierum & sexuum, item sexus foeminei abusus. Haec scelera & horrenda flagitia à magistratu extraordinariis supplisuppliciis sunt punienda. Incestus habet magnam partem pugnantiæ cum nostra natura, licet incestuum exempla exstent apud primos parentes: sed ea fiebant ex necessitate vel dispensatione diuina. Itaque erat vt exceptio à regula.
units.tr: All kinds of lust can be referred to three classes. Those of the first class are those that are para physin [παρὰ φύσιν], contrary to nature, and from the devil, which not only corrupt us and deprive us of conformity with God, but also because our nature, depraved as it is, shrinks from them. Of this class are those listed by the apostle in Romans 1: confusions of kinds and sexes, and likewise the abuse of the female sex. These crimes and horrible shameful deeds must be punished by the magistrate with extraordinary punishments. Incest has a great share of contradiction to our nature, although instances of incest exist among the first parents; but these came about from necessity or divine dispensation, and so were an exception to the rule.

units.la: Secundi generis sunt, quæ sunt ab hac natura nostra prava, vt fcortationes inter liberos à coniugio: adulteria inter coniugatas personas vtrinque: consuetudines coniugatorum cum aliis non coniugatis. Si coniugatus cum non coniugatis rem habet, est adulterium simplex. Si coniugatus cum altera coniugata consuetudinem habet, est adulterium duplex. Violat enim suum & alterius coniugium. Scortatio est commixtio non coniugarum. Incestus & adulteria magistratus ex officio seuerè punire debet. Nam sunt multo atrociores furtis. Adulteriis Deus capitale iudicium constituit. Scortationem etsi capitaliter puniendam non constituerit Deus: tamen cum sæpe dicat: Non sit scortum inter vos: eam suo modo puniendam significat. Sunt & aliæ libidines, quæ ab hac vitiosa nostra natura commiscuntur, quibus indulgemus aut delectamur, nec eas vitare studemus, quæ licet non puniantur in foro politico: coniunctæ tamen sunt cum mala conscientia, & puniuntur à Deo.
units.tr: Those of the second class are those that arise from this our corrupt nature, such as fornication between unmarried persons, adultery between married persons on either side, and the relations of married people with others who are not married. If a married man has to do with an unmarried woman, it is simple adultery. If a married man has a relationship with another married woman, it is double adultery, for he violates both his own marriage and hers. Fornication is the mixing of unmarried persons. The magistrate ought, as part of his office, to punish incest and adultery severely, for they are far more atrocious than theft. God has laid down capital judgment for adulteries. Although God has not decreed that fornication be punished capitally, yet since he so often says, "Let there be no whoredom among you," he indicates that it is to be punished in its own way. There are also other lusts that mingle with this vicious nature of ours, which we indulge or take pleasure in, and do not strive to avoid. Although these are not punished in the civil court, they are nonetheless joined with a guilty conscience and are punished by God.

units.la: Tertij generis sunt inclinationes prauæ, quibus tamen non indulgent boni viri, sed resistunt, & auferunt iis occasiones: & his non turbatur conscientia, quia inuocatur Deus, & peritur gratia resistendi, & in cordibus est testimonium deremissione peccatorum. Atque istorum peccatorum post lapsum remedium est institutum coniugium. Itaque contra istas inclinationes dicendum est: Præstat nubere, quàm uri: quamuis Paulus iis verbis non probet coniugia immatura, noxia reipublicæ, ante justam ætatem inita, aut inhonesta, hoc est, contra bonos mores.
units.tr: Those of the third class are wicked inclinations, which good people do not indulge but resist, removing their occasions. Conscience is not disturbed by these, because God is called upon, the grace of resisting is sought, and there is in the heart the testimony of the forgiveness of sins. Marriage was instituted after the fall as the remedy for these sins. Therefore against such inclinations it must be said: "It is better to marry than to burn." Yet Paul does not by these words approve marriages that are premature, harmful to the commonwealth, entered before the proper age, or dishonourable, that is, contrary to good morals.

units.la: II. VERECVNDIA est virtus abhorrens ab omni turpitudine, coniuncta cum pudore, dolore, & contristatione, vel ob præteritam turpitudinem, vel ob metum futuræ, & habens propositum fugiendi non ipsam tantum turpitudinem, sed & omnes eius occasiones, argumenta & signa. Græcis vocatur αἰδὼς, pudor, quam Aristoteles in Ethicis dicit esse φόβος, metum turpitudinis. Requiritur ad castitatem tanquam adiumentum, & causa, & effectus, & consequens, & signum castitatis.
units.tr: II. MODESTY is the virtue that shrinks from all filthiness, joined with shame, grief and sorrow, either for past filthiness or for fear of future filthiness, and that has the purpose of fleeing not only filthiness itself but also all its occasions, arguments and signs. In Greek it is called aidōs [αἰδὼς], shame, which Aristotle in his Ethics says is phobos [φόβος], fear of disgrace. It is required for chastity as its aid, cause, effect, consequence and sign.

units.la: Extrema pugnantia cum verecundia sunt I. Impudentia, ἀναισχυντία, quæ non curat turpitudinem. 2. Stupor seu rusticus pudor & peruersus, cum quem eius pudet, cuius non debebat, velut rei honestæ, quæ non acquirit pudo-rem. 3. Obscœnitas & scurrilitas.
units.tr: The extremes opposed to modesty are: (1) Impudence [ἀναισχυντία, anaischyntia], which does not care about filthiness; (2) Stupidity, or a rustic and perverse shame, when a person is ashamed of what he should not be ashamed of, as of an honourable thing, and does not acquire shame where it is due; (3) Obscenity and buffoonery.

units.la: III. TEMPERANTIA est virtus seruans modum naturæ, honestati & rectæ rationi, ordini item personarum, locorum & temporum conuenientem, in rebus ad corpus pertinentibus, ac in cibo & potu, & horum appetitionibus. Hæc mater & nutricula est omnium aliarum virtutum, & castitatis causa est, sine qua non. Sine temperantia enim non possumus esse casti. Cauete, ne quando grauentur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate, & curis huius vitæ. Et ne inebriemini vino, in quo est ἀσωτία, id est, luxus & dissolutio. Vt interdiu compositè ambulemus, non in commessationibus & ebrietatibus, non cubilibus ac proteruiis, non lite & inuidia: sed induimini Domino Iesu Christo, & carnis curam non habete ad explendas cupiditates.
units.tr: III. TEMPERANCE is the virtue that keeps the measure of nature, suited to honesty and right reason, and likewise to the order of persons, places and times, in matters pertaining to the body, and in food and drink and the appetites for them. This is the mother and nurse of all the other virtues, and it is the indispensable cause of chastity, for without temperance we cannot be chaste. "Take heed that your hearts are not weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the cares of this life. And do not be drunk with wine, in which is asōtia [ἀσωτία], that is, debauchery and dissipation. Let us walk becomingly as in the day, not in revelling and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfil its lusts."

units.la: Extrema temperantiæ sunt 1. Intemperantia in cibo & potu, ingurgitationes, voracitas seu ingluuies, ebrietas, crapula, quæ proprie significat non ipsam ingurgitationem, sed posttridianam nauseam & vertiginem capitis, à κραιπάλη, caput quatio. 2. Luxuria, quæ est nimia profusio & superfluitas in cibis, vestitu, supellectile, &c. Temperantia nocens, seu abstinentia nimia & hypocritica, non conueniens naturæ, vt temperantia eremitarum: item jejunia superstitiosa.
units.tr: The extremes of temperance are: (1) Intemperance in food and drink: gluttony, voracity or greediness, drunkenness, crapula [from kraipalē, κραιπάλη], which properly means not the gorging itself but the nausea and dizziness of the head the day after, from caput quatio, I shake the head. (2) Luxury, which is excessive lavishness and superfluity in food, clothing, household goods, and so on. Harmful temperance, or excessive and hypocritical abstinence, not suited to nature, such as the temperance of the hermits; likewise superstitious fasts.

units.la: DE CONIVGIO.
units.tr: ON MARRIAGE.

units.la: Quoniam hoc præcepto coniugium sancitur, de eo præcipuè consideretur: I. II. Quid sit coniugium. III. Qua coniugij instituti causa. IV. Qua coniugia sint legitima. V. An coniugium sit ἀδιάφορον. VI. Qua officia coniugum. Qua sint coniugio contraria.
units.tr: Since marriage is established by this precept, it is to be considered chiefly under these heads: I. II. What marriage is. III. For what cause marriage was instituted. IV. Which marriages are lawful. V. Whether marriage is indifferent [ἀδιάφορον]. VI. What are the duties of spouses, and what things are contrary to marriage.

units.la: I. Quid sit coniugium.
units.tr: I. What marriage is.

units.la: Coniugium est legitima & indissolubilis coniunctio vnius maris & vnius fœminæ, instituta à Deo, ad generis humani propagationem, vt agnoscamus, cum esse castum, & execrari omnes libidines, & ex genere humano legitimè propagato sibi colligere velle æternam ecclesiam, à qua rectè agnoscatur & colatur, vtque inter coniuges sit societas laborum, curarum & precum.
units.tr: Marriage is a lawful and indissoluble union of one man and one woman, instituted by God for the propagation of the human race, so that we may acknowledge that it is chaste and reject all lusts, and that from the human race lawfully propagated we may gather for ourselves the eternal Church, by which God may rightly be acknowledged and worshipped; and so that between the spouses there may be a fellowship of labours, cares and prayers.

units.la: II. Quae sint causae instituti coniugij.
units.tr: II. What are the causes for which marriage was instituted.

units.la: Author coniugij est ipse DEVS. Coniugium enim non est inuentum humanum, sed ordinatio diuina ante lapsum hominis sancita in paradiso. Causae seu fines coniugij ex definitione intelliguntur. 1. Vt sit medium legitimae propagationis generis humani. 2. Collectio ecclesiae. 3. Imago coniunctionis inter Deum & ecclesiam. 4. Vt vitentur vagae libidines. 5. Vt sit societas laborum & inuocationis inter coniuges. Arctior est ista societas reliquis omnibus, eoque vota coniugum sunt ardentiora. Ardentius enim eos juuamus precibus, quibus arctius juncti sumus, vt parentes ardentius orant pro liberis, quam liberi pro parentibus: quia, vt vulgo dicitur, amor descendit, non ascendit.
units.tr: God himself is the author of marriage. For marriage is not a human invention but a divine ordinance, established in Paradise before the fall of man. The causes or ends of marriage are understood from its definition: (1) that it may be the means of the lawful propagation of the human race; (2) the gathering of the Church; (3) an image of the union between God and the Church; (4) that wandering lusts may be avoided; (5) that there may be a fellowship of labours and of invocation between the spouses. This fellowship is closer than all the others, and so the vows of spouses are more ardent. For we help one another more ardently with prayers by whom we are more closely joined, just as parents pray more ardently for their children than children for their parents, because, as is commonly said, love descends, it does not ascend.

units.la: III. Quae coniugia sint legitima.
units.tr: III. Which marriages are lawful.

units.la: Vt coniugium sit legitima coniunctio, requiruntur haec: 1. Vt contrahatur inter personas ad coniugium idoneas. 2. Vt contrahatur vtriusque partis consensu. 3. Accedat consensus parentum, vel qui sunt parentum loco, & quorum consensus requiritur per leges. 4. Ne committatur error in personis. 5. Incontractu seruentur honestae conditiones, decorum & modus legitimus. 6. Matrimonium contrahatur tantum inter duas personas. Erunt duo in carne vna. Patres quidem plures habuerunt vxores: sed legibus, non exemplis est judicandum. 7. Matrimonia contrahantur in Domino, hoc est, inter fideles, & cum inuocatione Dei. 8. Ne contrahantur inter personas prohibitas, seu in gradibus cognationis prohibitis à Deo vel legibus honestis.
