units.tr: For a marriage to be a lawful union, the following are required: (1) that it be contracted between persons fit for marriage; (2) that it be contracted with the consent of both parties; (3) that the consent of the parents be added, or of those who stand in the place of parents, whose consent is required by law; (4) that no error be committed about the persons; (5) that in the contract honourable conditions, propriety and lawful measure be observed; (6) that marriage be contracted only between two persons. They shall be two in one flesh. The Fathers indeed had several wives, but matters are to be judged by laws, not by examples; (7) that marriages be contracted in the Lord, that is, between believers, and with the invocation of God; (8) that they not be contracted between persons who are forbidden, that is, within degrees of kinship forbidden by God or by honest laws.

units.la: Cognatio seu propinquitas, est vel consanguinitas vel affinitas. Consanguinitas, est inter personas ab eadem stirpe ortas, & sanguine, cognatione proprius iunctas. Affinitas, est cognatio, ex coniugio orta inter vnum coniugem & alterius coniugis consanguineos. Discernuntur autem Stirps est persona, à qua aliae sunt deriuatae. Linea est series consanguineorum ab vna stirpe deducta. Gradus est distantia agnatorum & cognatorum à stirpe inter se. De gradibus est regula communis: Quot sunt personae à stipite seu stirpe, tot sunt gradus. Lege diuina gradus secundus, legibus politicis laudatis etiam tertius prohibetur. Linea est aut ascendentium, aut descendentium, aut collateralium. Ascendentes sunt omnes maiores. Descendentes sunt omnes posteri. Collaterales qui non sunt alij ex aliis, sed ex isdem. Col-
units.tr: Kinship or relationship is either by blood or by marriage. Kinship by blood is between persons born of the same stock and joined more closely by blood and kinship. Kinship by marriage is the relationship arising from marriage between one spouse and the blood relatives of the other spouse. They are distinguished thus: stock is the person from whom others are derived; line is the series of blood relatives drawn from one stock; degree is the distance of agnates and cognates from the stock and from one another. There is a common rule about degrees: as many persons as there are from the stock or root, so many are the degrees. By divine law the second degree is forbidden, and by the civil laws praised above the third is forbidden too. The line is either of ascendants, or of descendants, or collateral. Ascendants are all forebears. Descendants are all posterity. Collaterals are those who are not descended one from another but from the same stock. The collateral line

units.la: Fines coniugij.
units.tr: The ends of marriage.

units.la: Genef. 2, 24. Matth. 19, 5.

Gradus cognationis. lateralium linea est æqualis, aut inæqualis. Æqualis, quando æqualis est distantia à communi stipite. Inæqualis, quando inæqualis est distantia. Prohibitiones graduum sunt à Deo Leuit.18. expressæ. Ac morales & naturales illas esse probatur, 1. Quia gentes graduum illorum violatione dicuntur admisisse abominationes, & propter has deletæ esse. Gentes verò non habuerunt leges cæremoniales, vel politicas Mosis. 2. Quia propter violationem harum legum, hoc est, propter vagas libidines & nuptias incestas Deus mundum diluvio puniuit. 3. Ex scopo, quia finis, hoc est, prohibitio incestus propter reverentiam sanguinis facta, est universalis, perpetua & moralis. 4. Paulus acerrimè reprehendit & excommunicari jubet incestum, qui uxorem patris duxerat, & baptista dicit Herodi: Non licet tibi habere fratris uxorem.
units.tr: Degrees of kinship. The collateral line is either equal or unequal. Equal, when the distance from the common stock is equal; unequal, when the distance is unequal. The prohibitions of degrees are expressed by God in Lev. 18. And that these are moral and natural prohibitions is proved: (1) because the nations are said to have committed abominations by violating those degrees, and to have been destroyed on account of them; but the nations did not have the ceremonial or civil laws of Moses; (2) because on account of the violation of these laws, that is, on account of wandering lusts and incestuous marriages, God punished the world with the flood; (3) from the purpose, because the end, that is, the prohibition of incest made out of reverence for blood, is universal, perpetual and moral; (4) Paul most sharply rebukes the incestuous man who had taken his father's wife and orders him to be excommunicated, and the Baptist says to Herod: It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife.

units.la: IV. An coniugium sit adiaphorum.
units.tr: Whether marriage is indifferent.

units.la: Coniugium à Deo concessum est omnibus, qui ad id sunt idonei. Adiaphorum verò seu indifferens, hoc est, nec mandatum à Deo, nec prohibitum, sed liberum est iis, qui habent continentiæ donum. Reliquis hoc donum non habentibus, non modo concessum, sed & mandatum est, ut nubant in Domino. Proinde his non est adiaphorum, sed necessarium. Bonum est viro mulierem non attingere, sed propter fornicationem suam quisque uxorem habeat. Cœlibibus & viduis dico: bonum eis est, si manserint, ut ego. Quod si se non continent, matrimonium contrahant. Nam melius est matrimonium contrahere, quàm uri. Est verò justum tempus & decorum seruandum in nuptiis primis vel secundis contrahendis, nec frena sunt laxanda flammis cupiditatum, sed precibus & laborum sedulitate restingui debent, quantum fieri potest: & ut conscientia non debet violari, sic neque honestas. [Cuius quanta olim in Romanis legibus ratio habita fuerit, testatur Plutarchus in Numa, sic scribens: Mulieres à morte mariti decem menses viduæ permanebant. Quod si quæ intra decimum mensem nupsisset: eam leges Numæ vaccam pragnantem immolare jubebant, &c.]
units.tr: Marriage is granted by God to all who are fit for it. But it is not indifferent, that is, neither commanded nor forbidden by God, but is free for those who have the gift of continence. For those who do not have this gift, marriage is not only granted but also commanded, that they marry in the Lord. Therefore for them it is not indifferent but necessary. It is good for a man not to touch a woman, but because of fornication let each man have his own wife. To the unmarried and widows I say: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. A proper and seemly time is, however, to be observed in contracting first or second marriages, and the reins are not to be loosened for the flames of desires, but they ought to be quenched, as far as possible, by prayers and diligence in labour; and just as conscience must not be violated, neither must decency. [How much regard was once paid to this in Roman laws, Plutarch bears witness in his Life of Numa, writing thus: Women remained widows for ten months after the death of their husband. But if any had married within the tenth month, the laws of Numa ordered her to sacrifice a pregnant cow, etc.]

units.la: V. Quæ sint officia coniugum?
units.tr: V. What are the duties of spouses?

units.la: Officia communia & mutua coniugum sunt 1. Amor mutuus. 2. Fides coniugalis, ut solus solam, & sola solum constanter diligat. 3. Communio bonorum, & in malis συμπάθεια. 4. Susceptio & educatio sobolis. 5. Επιεικεια seu tolerantia defectuum, cum studio sanandi. Mariti officium est 1. coniugem & sobolem nutrire. 2. gubernare. 3. defendere coniugem & sobolem. Vxoris est 1. adjuuare maritum in paranda & conseruanda re familiari. 2. obedientia & reuerentia erga maritum. Quando haec negliguntur, in vsum legitimum coniugij grauissime peccatur.
units.tr: The common and mutual duties of spouses are: (1) mutual love; (2) marital fidelity, so that the one spouse constantly loves only the other, and the other only the one; (3) sharing of goods, and fellow-feeling [συμπάθεια] in misfortunes; (4) the receiving and bringing up of offspring; (5) gentleness [ἐπιείκεια], or tolerance of faults, together with diligence in curing them. The duty of the husband is: (1) to nourish his wife and children; (2) to govern; (3) to defend wife and children. The duty of the wife is: (1) to help her husband in acquiring and preserving the household property; (2) obedience and reverence towards her husband. When these are neglected, the lawful use of marriage is most gravely sinned against.

units.la: VI. Quae sint coniugio contraria.
units.tr: VI. What things are contrary to marriage?

units.la: Coniugio contraria sunt, quae & castitati. 1. Scortationes & adulteria, quibus fides & castitas coniugalis ab altero vel utroque coniuge rumpitur. Item, incestus, illicita & illegitima copulatio, abusus coniugij. 2. Diuortia temeraria, Romanis & Judaeis olim & hodie barbaris visitata, videlicet extra casum adulterij, vel desertionis. Persona vero deserta, vel ad desertionem sollicitata, non facit diuortium. 3. Prohibitio & vsurpatio coniugij.
units.tr: Those things are contrary to marriage which are also contrary to chastity: (1) whoredoms and adulteries, by which the faithfulness and chastity of marriage are broken by one or both spouses; likewise incest, unlawful and illegitimate union, and the abuse of marriage. (2) Rash divorces, which were practised by the Romans and Jews of old and by barbarians today, namely outside the case of adultery or desertion. A person who has been deserted, or who has been enticed into desertion, does not make a divorce. (3) The forbidding and the usurping of marriage.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CX.
units.tr: QUAESTIO CX.

units.la: Quid vetat Deus in octauo præcepto? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What does God forbid in the eighth commandment? ANSWER.

units.la: Non solum ea furta & rapinas , quas magistratus punit: sed furti nomine comprehendit, quicquid est malarum artium & aucupiorum, quibus aliena captamus, & ad nos viaut specie recti transferre studemus: qualia sunt, iniquum pondus, iniusta vlna, inæqualis mensura , fucosa merx, fallax moneta, vsura, aut alia quaeuis ratio, aut modus rem faciendi à DEO interdictus. His adde omnem auaritiam , & abmultiplicem diuinorum donorum profusionem & abusum .
units.tr: Not only those thefts and robberies which the magistrate punishes, but under the name of theft he comprehends whatever is of evil arts and snares, by which we seek to catch what belongs to others and to transfer it to ourselves under the appearance of right. Such are: a false weight, an unjust measure, an uneven yardstick, a deceptive ware, false money, usury, or any other method or manner of getting a thing that God forbids. To these add all covetousness, and the manifold waste and abuse of God's gifts.

units.la: a 1 Corinth. 6. verf.10. b 1 Corinth. 5, 10. Esa. 33. v.1. c Luc. 3. verf.14. 1 Thess. 4, 6. d Prouerb. 11, 1. & 16, 11. Ezech. 45. v. 9, 10. Deut. 25, 15. c Psalm. 15, 5. Luc. 6. verf. 35. f 1 Cor. 6. v.10. g Prouerb. 5, 16. & 21, 20.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXI. Quæ sunt ea, quæ Deus hic iubet?
units.tr: QUAESTIO CXI. What are those things which God commands here?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vt commoda & utilitates proximi, quantum possim, & adjuvem, & augeam: cum eo sic agam, ut mecum agi cuperem a, sedulo & fideliter opus faciam, ut aliorum quoque egestati subvenire queam b.
units.tr: That I help and increase the advantages and profits of my neighbour, as far as I can, and that I deal with him as I would wish to be dealt with a, working diligently and faithfully, so that I may also be able to help the need of others b.

units.la: a Matth. 7. verf.12. b Ephes. 4. verf.28.
units.tr: a Matt. 7. verse 12. b Eph. 4. verse 28.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Sancitur hoc præcepto distinctio dominiorum, seu proprie rerum possessio. Finis præcepti est conservatio rerum seu possessionum, quas Deus singulis elargitur, ad vitæ sustentationem. Si enim non debemus furari, oportet, ut singuli res suas possideant. Prohibet ergo Deus omnes fraudes, malas artes & aucupia, quibus res proximi lædunturu, minuuntur, & dominia confunduntur. Contra sancit omnes virtutes, quibus res proximi conservantur & juvantur.
units.tr: This commandment sanctions the distinction of ownership, or the proper possession of goods. The purpose of the commandment is the preservation of the goods or possessions which God bestows on each person for the sustenance of life. For if we ought not to steal, it is necessary that each person should possess his own goods. God therefore forbids all frauds, evil arts and snares, by which the goods of a neighbour are harmed, diminished, and ownership confused. On the other hand, he enjoins all virtues by which the goods of a neighbour are preserved and helped.

units.la: Non furtum facies.] Hoc est, non concupisces, vel tentabis per fraudem ad te trahere bona proximi. Ergo defendas, conserves, augeas ea, & des, quod est proximi. Nominat autem furtum velut crassissimam fraudis speciem, ut in ea reliquarum omnium turpitudo intelligatur.
units.tr: You shall not steal.] That is, you shall not covet, or attempt by fraud to draw to yourself the goods of your neighbour. Therefore you should defend, preserve, and increase his goods, and give him what is his. But he names theft as the grossest kind of fraud, so that in it the baseness of all the rest may be understood.

units.la: Virtutes octavi præcepti.
units.tr: The virtues of the eighth commandment.

units.la: I: JUSTITIA COMMUTATIVA, quæ est virtus in acquisitione bonorum, non appetens res alienas, & servans æqualitatem arithmeticam in contractibus & communi vita, in acquisitione & commutatione rerum secundum justas leges: ut justitia commutativa est, cum servatur æqualitas inter mercem & pretium, mercedem & laborem, &c. De dominiis & divisione rerum præcipit Imperator lib. 2. tit. 1. Inst. quod quædam naturali jure sunt communes omnium, ut aer, aqua profluens, mare, littora maris. Quædam publica, ut flumina, portus, riparum usus, &c. quædam universitatis, quæ sunt in civitatibus, ut theatra, stadia, &c. quædam nullius: ut res sacræ & religiosæ & sanctæ: pleraque singulorum, quæ ex variis causis cuique acquiruntur. Itaque res, quæ ad alium dominum transferuntur, sunt nullius, aut aliquius. Quæ sunt nullius, fiunt illorum, qui eas acquirunt. Quæ sunt aliorum, transferuntur vel vi & inuito domino: ut per captivitatem in bello: vel volente domino, vt per hæreditatem & contractum. Per hæreditatem, vel cum testamento, vel sine eo. Contractus est consensus inter aliquos de translatione, communicatione, vel commutatione rerum secundum justas & honestas leges. Contractus omnes continentur sub justitia commutatiua: sunt autem decem contractuum species. 1. Emtio & venditio, ein Kauff und Verkauff/ quando res à venditore transfertur ad emtorem, ita vt emptor det justum & æquiualens pretium. Ea fit alias cum pacto de reuendendo, alias sine eo. Huc pertinet emtio redituum, quæ non magis est vsura, quam elocatio fundi, pro certa pecunia quotannis reddenda. 2. Mutuatio, leihen / oder borgen / est contractus, in quo vsus alicuius transfertur ad alium, ita vt reddatur æquualens. Datur aliquid in mutatione, non vt reddatur idem indiuiduum, sed simile vel æquipollens. 3. Commodatio, leihen/ quando vsus rei ad certum tempus conceditur alicui, vt sine pretio idem indiuiduum integrum & incorruptum reddatur. 4. Donatio, Schenckung / quando res à justo domino, qui jus habet illam donandi, ex libera voluntate transfertur ad alium sine compensatione. At (inquis) justitia postulat, vt æqualia dentur pro æqualibus. Hoc non fit in donatione. Ergo hæc cum justitia pugnat. Resp. Maior vera est, si res darentur hoc animo, vt fiat compensatio. 5. Permutatio, ein Wechsel, quando à legitimis & volentibus dominis res permutatur, aut res datur pro æquiualente. 6. Locatio & elocatio, Vermiethung/ est contractus, quo alicuius rei vsus sine dominio, à legitimis dominis ad alios transfertur, ad certum tempus pro certo pretio, ita vt eadem res incorrupta reddatur. 7. Oppignoratio, Verpfändung / quando res ad alium transfertur, vt sit ei obligata vsu trantisper, donec alia res, quæ ei debetur, ipsi persoluatur: vel quando res traditur alicui ea conditione, vt si intra certum tempus non redimatur, alter habeat jus ea vtendi pro voluntate. 8. Depositum, ein Beylag / quando nec vsus, nec dominium, sed tantum custodia rei alicui committitur. 9. Societas, Gesellschafft/ est contractus, in quo alius pecuniam, alius operarum, qui vna negotiantur, in quo alius pecuniam, alius operam, seu laborem confert ea conditione, vt vnicuique pars lucri & damni cedat, & neuter vel solus lucrum capiat, vel solus damnum sentiat. 10. Ἐμφύτευσις, Erbbestandnüß/ est contractus, quo vsus vel dominium vtile fundi à domino transfertur ad conalonum, vt eum colat, & obligatus sit domino ad certam aliquam seruitutem præstandam.
units.tr: I. COMMUTATIVE JUSTICE, which is the virtue in acquiring goods, not desiring the goods of others, and keeping arithmetical equality in contracts and in common life, in acquiring and exchanging things according to just laws. Thus commutative justice exists when equality is kept between goods and price, wages and labour, etc. The Emperor, in book 2, title 1 of the Institutes, lays down rules about ownership and the division of things: that some things are by natural law common to all, such as air, running water, the sea, and the seashores; some are public, such as rivers, harbours, the use of banks, etc.; some belong to a community, such as theatres and stadiums in cities; some belong to no one, such as sacred, religious, and holy things; and most belong to individuals, who acquire them by various causes. Therefore things that are transferred to another owner either belong to no one or belong to someone. Those that belong to no one become the property of those who acquire them. Those that belong to others are transferred either by force and against the owner's will, as by capture in war, or with the owner's willing consent, as by inheritance or contract. Inheritance is by will or without one. A contract is an agreement between parties about the transfer, sharing, or exchange of things according to just and honourable laws. All contracts fall under commutative justice, and there are ten kinds of contract. 1. Buying and selling, ein Kauff und Verkauff, when a thing is transferred from the seller to the buyer, the buyer giving a just and equivalent price. This happens sometimes with an agreement of resale, sometimes without it. To this belongs the purchase of rents, which is no more usury than the letting of a field for a certain sum to be paid yearly. 2. Loan for consumption, leihen oder borgen, is a contract in which the use of something is transferred to another, on condition that an equivalent be returned. In a loan something is given not so that the same individual thing is returned, but a like or equivalent thing. 3. Loan for use, commodatum, leihen, when the use of a thing is granted to someone for a set time, on condition that without payment the same individual thing is returned whole and uncorrupted. 4. Gift, Schenckung, when a thing is transferred freely by its rightful owner, who has the right to give it, to another without any compensation. But (you say) justice requires that equal things be given for equal things, and this does not happen in a gift; therefore it fights against justice. Answer: The major premise is true, if things were given with the intention that compensation should follow. 5. Exchange, ein Wechsel, when things are exchanged by lawful and willing owners, or a thing is given in return for an equivalent. 6. Letting and hiring, Vermiethung, is a contract by which the use of a thing, without ownership, is transferred from its lawful owners to others for a certain time at a certain price, on condition that the same thing is returned uncorrupted. 7. Pledge, Verpfändung, when a thing is transferred to another so that it stands bound to him in its use until another thing owed to him is paid to him; or when a thing is handed over to someone on the condition that, if it is not redeemed within a certain time, the other may have the right to use it as he pleases. 8. Deposit, ein Beylag, when neither use nor ownership, but only the custody of a thing, is entrusted to someone. 9. Partnership, Gesellschafft, is a contract in which one person contributes money and another his labour or work, those who do business together, on the condition that each party shares in the gain and loss, and that neither takes the gain alone or bears the loss alone. 10. Emphyteusis [Ἐμφύτευσις], Erbbestandnüß, is a contract by which the use or useful ownership of a field is transferred by the owner to a tenant, so that he may cultivate it, and be bound to the owner to render a certain service.

units.la: Pugnat cum justitia commutatiua omnis injusta rerum translatio, quæ fit vel vi, vt rapinæ, vel fraude, vt furta. Furtum est abla-tio rei alienæ, inscio & inuito domino, animo eum priuandi. Furti plurimæ sunt species in omni vita, publica & priuata. 1. Peculatus, est furtum admissum in re ad rempublicam spectantes. 2. Sacrilegium, est ablatio rei sacræ. 3. Stellionatus, sunt fraudes & imposituræ in contractibus, præstigiæ, & corruptelæ contractuum, injusti contractus, &c. 4. Vsura est lucrum, quod accipitur solius mutationis causa. Excluduntur ab vsura contractus justi, emtio, contractus de reddendis redditibus, compensatio damni justa, societas, &c. Multæ sunt quæstiones de vsuris, de quibus judicari debet ex dicto: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris.
units.tr: Every unjust transfer of goods is contrary to commutative justice, whether it is made by force, as robberies, or by fraud, as thefts. Theft is the taking away of another's thing, without the knowledge and against the will of the owner, with the intention of depriving him of it. There are very many kinds of theft in all of life, public and private. 1. Peculation is theft committed in matters concerning the commonwealth. 2. Sacrilege is the taking away of a sacred thing. 3. Stellionate consists of frauds and deceptions in contracts, tricks, and corruptions of contracts, unjust contracts, etc. 4. Usury is the gain that is received solely for the sake of a loan. Just contracts are excluded from usury: buying, contracts for paying rents, a just compensation for loss, partnership, etc. There are many questions about usury, which ought to be judged by the rule: What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.

units.la: II. Αὐτάρκεια, est virtus, qua sumus contenti rebus nostris præsentibus, & juste acquisitis: placidè ferimus paupertatem, aliaque incommoda, nec appetimus aliena aut non necessaria bona.
units.tr: II. Self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] is the virtue by which we are content with our present possessions, justly acquired; we bear poverty and other hardships calmly, and do not desire the goods of others or goods we do not need.

units.la: Extrema, in defectu: Auaritia & furtum. In excessu: Αὐθάδεια, sive recusatio, quando quis simulat se ea accipere nolle, quæ accipere posset, & maxime cuperet. Item inhumanitas, quæ est nihil accipere velle.
units.tr: The extremes: in defect, covetousness and theft. In excess, authadeia [αὐθάδεια], or refusal, when someone pretends that he does not want to receive things which he could receive and would most desire. Likewise inhumanity, which is to wish to receive nothing.

units.la: III. FIDELITAS est virtus, quæ cauet, & auertere studet alterius detrimenta, & libenter ac diligenter vocationis suæ partibus defungitur, vt & nobis & nostris necessaria suppetant, & aliis etiam suppeditare possimus hoc fine principali, vt Deus celebretur.
units.tr: III. FAITHFULNESS is the virtue which takes care, and strives to avert the harm of another, and willingly and diligently performs the parts of its calling, so that what is necessary may be available to us and our own, and so that we may also be able to supply others, with this chief end, that God may be glorified.

units.la: Extrema huius sunt 1. Infidelitas, non cauens damnum proximi, nec diligenter faciens officium. 2. Negligentia & ignauia, quæ tantum frui vult alienis commodis, nec vult conferre aliquid in societatem communem. Qui non facit labores, quos potest & debet, facit furtum.
units.tr: The extremes of this virtue are: (1) unfaithfulness, which takes no care to avoid harm to a neighbour and does not diligently perform its duty; (2) negligence and sloth, which wants only to enjoy the advantages of others and is unwilling to contribute anything to the common fellowship. Whoever does not perform the labours that he can and ought to perform, commits theft.

units.la: Obiect. Fidelitatis in quinto præcepto facta est mentio. Non ergo huc pertinet. Resp. Non est absurdum, vnam & eandem virtutem poni in diuersis præceptis, propter diuersos fines & respectus. Fines enim actionum & virtutum faciunt discrimina. Ponitur in hoc præcepto fidelitas, quatenus studium est cauendi aliorum incommoda, & faciendi opus ac labores, quibus acquiramus nobis victum & amictum, & res necessarias: in quinto præcepto fidelitas ponitur, quatenus est obedientia in officio faciendo.
units.tr: Objection: Faithfulness is mentioned under the fifth commandment. Therefore it does not belong here. Answer: It is not absurd for one and the same virtue to be placed under different precepts, on account of different ends and respects. For the ends of actions and virtues make the distinctions. Faithfulness is placed in this precept insofar as it is an earnest care to avoid harming others and to do the work and labours by which we acquire food and clothing and the things necessary for life; in the fifth precept faithfulness is placed insofar as it is obedience in performing one's duty.

units.la: IV. LIBERALITAS est virtus, quæ largitur indigentibus secundum rectam rationem, seu quæ communicat aliis facultates suas sine obligatione ciuili, seu jure diuino & naturali, sed pietatis & dilectionis causa, liberali pectore, pro facultate sua, & alterius necessitate, sciens nimirum, vbi, quibus, quando & quantum possit largiri, & seruat mediocritatem inter profusionem & sordes.
units.tr: IV. LIBERALITY is the virtue which bestows on the needy according to right reason; or, which shares its resources with others without civil obligation, or obligation by divine and natural law, but for the sake of piety and love, with a generous heart, according to its means and the other's need, knowing, namely, where, to whom, when and how much it can give, and keeping the mean between extravagance and meanness.

units.la: Obiectiones contra distinctionem dominiorum.
units.tr: Objections against the distinction of ownership.

units.la: Obi.1. Apostolis bona omnia fuerunt communia. Ergo nobis debent omnia esse communia. Resp.1. Est dissimilitudo in exemplis. Nam κοινωνία facultatum apostolis fuit facilis & necessaria. Facilis, quia erant pauci. Necessaria, quia periculum erat, si non venderent, per vim illis priuarentur. Nunc neq; facilitas illa est, neq; necessitas. Apostoli igitur adducti causis probabilibus communionem rerum tunc induxerunt, quæ causæ nunc non sunt. 2. Fecerunt id non intercedente lege, sed liberè. Nonne si seruasses, manebat tibi, & venundatum in tua erat potestate? Voluntaria igitur erat illa bonorum communio: ad quam nemo cogebatur. 3. Erat consuetudo particularis. Nam aliæ ecclesiæ eam non observabant. Colligebantur enim in Macedonia & Achaia eleemosynæ, quæ mittebantur Hierosolymam. 4. Erat temporaria. Nam postea mutatis causis desiit.
units.tr: Objection 1: All goods were held in common by the apostles. Therefore all things ought to be held in common by us. Answer 1: There is a dissimilarity in the examples. For the fellowship of goods [κοινωνία] among the apostles was easy and necessary. Easy, because there were few of them. Necessary, because there was danger that, if they did not sell, they would be deprived of their goods by force. Now neither that ease nor that necessity exists. The apostles, therefore, moved by probable causes, then introduced the communion of goods, which causes do not exist now. 2. They did this not by any intervening law, but freely: "Did not your property remain yours, and after it was sold, was it not in your power?" That communion of goods, therefore, was voluntary, and no one was compelled to it. 3. It was a particular custom. For the other churches did not observe it. For alms were collected in Macedonia and Achaia, which were sent to Jerusalem. 4. It was temporary. For afterwards, when the causes changed, it ceased.

units.la: Obj.2. Naturalia sunt immutabilia. Communio bonorum est naturalis. Ergo est immutabilis, eoq; & hodie seruanda. Resp. ad maiorem, Naturalia sunt immutabilia, scilicet morali lege, non autem naturali & ciuili vrilitate.
units.tr: Objection 2: Things natural are unchangeable. The communion of goods is natural. Therefore it is unchangeable, and so is to be observed even today. Answer to the major: Things natural are unchangeable, namely by the moral law, but not by natural and civil usefulness.

units.la: Obj.3. Christus dicit adolescenti: Si vis perfectus esse, abi, vende quæ habes, & da pauperibus. Resp.1. Est dissimilitudo in exemplis: quia vocatio discipuli erat specialis, ad apostolatum pertinens. 2. Volebat Christus significare, quam procul abesset à perfectione legis, de qua gloriabatur. 3. Non dicit: Confer in commune, in fiscum: sed, da pauperibus.
units.tr: Objection 3: Christ says to the young man: "If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor." Answer 1: There is a dissimilarity in the examples, because the calling of this disciple was special, pertaining to the apostleship. 2. Christ wished to signify how far he was from the perfection of the law, in which he boasted. 3. He does not say: "Contribute to a common fund, to the treasury," but: "Give to the poor."

units.la: Obiect.4. Omnia sunt Christi. Ergo & Christianorum. Omnia vestra sunt. Resp. Omnia sunt nostra, quoad jus ad rem, sed non quoad jus in re. Omnia nobis debentur, sed nihil debemus rapere ante tempus.
units.tr: Objection 4: All things are Christ's. Therefore they are also Christians'. "All things are yours." Answer: All things are ours as to the right to the thing, but not as to the right in the thing. All things are owed to us, but we ought not to seize anything before the time.

units.la: Obiect.5. Amicorum omnia sunt communia. Resp. Non dominio & possessione, sed vsu & delectatione secundum honestas leges, seu, quoad vsum & officia honestatis, vtilitatis, ac necessitatis secundum rectam rationem. Debemus enim ab amicis petere vellemus. Non autem communia sunt omnia amicorum, quoad possessionem & dominium: siquidem vnicuiq; manet suarum rerum possessio ac dominium distinctum. Hæc rerum possessio seu distinctio dominiorum sancitur (vt diximus) hoc præcepto: quia si non debemus furari, oportet vt res nostras possideamus: idque propterea, 1. Vt nos & nostros honestè alamus. 2. Vt ad conseruationem ecclesiæ aliquid conferamus. 3. Vt reipublicæ pro modo facultatum iuvemus. 4. Vt amicis & pauperibus benefaciamus.
units.tr: Objection 5: All things of friends are common. Answer: Not in ownership and possession, but in use and enjoyment, according to honest laws; or, as to the use and the duties of honesty, usefulness and necessity, according to right reason. For we ought to ask of friends what we would wish to ask. But all things of friends are not common as to possession and ownership, since to each one there remains the possession and distinct ownership of his own things. This possession of things, or distinction of ownership, is sanctioned (as we have said) by this precept: for if we ought not to steal, it is necessary that we possess our own things; and this is so for the following reasons: 1. That we may support ourselves and ours honourably. 2. That we may contribute something to the maintenance of the church. 3. That we may help the commonwealth according to the measure of our means. 4. That we may do good to friends and the poor.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXII. Quid exigit nonum præceptum?
units.tr: QUESTION CXII. What does the ninth commandment require?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Ne aduersus quempiam dicam falsum testimonium , nullius verba calumnier , nulli obtrectem, aut conuicium faciam , neminem temerè, vel indicta causa condemnem : Verum omnis generis mendacia, fraudes, vt opera diaboli propria , nisi in me grauissimam iram Dei concitare velim, omni cura fugiam : In judiciis cæterisque negotiis veritatem sequar, & id, quod reseit, libere & constanter profitear : Ad hæc famam aliorum & existimationem, quantum queam, defendam & augeam .
units.tr: I will not bear false witness against anyone, nor slander anyone's words, nor backbite or revile anyone, nor condemn anyone rashly or without a hearing. I will avoid every kind of lie and fraud with all care, as the proper works of the devil, unless I wish to provoke the most grievous wrath of God against myself. In judgments and in other dealings I will follow the truth, and I will freely and steadfastly profess what I know. Moreover, as far as I can, I will defend and increase the good name and reputation of others.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Scopus seu finis noni præcepti est sanctio & conseruatio veritatis inter homines. Prohibetur igitur falsum testimonium, & cum eo omnes cognatæ species, quarum genus est mendacium: Non dicas falsum testimonium contra proximum tuum, vel de proximo tuo. Hoc negatiuo præcepto continetur affirmatiuum, Dicas veritatem de proximo tuo, hoc est, sis verax, sis amans discendæ & cognoscendæ veritatis. Virtutum igitur caput & quasi genus, quæ hic sanciuntur, est veritas, vel potius veracitas in sermone, in sententiis, in judiciis, in pactis & in doctrina. Sumitur enim veritas hic pro congruentia notitiæ vel sermonis cum re, de qua est sermo. Verum est ipse sermo congruens cum re. Contra vitiorum, quæ hic damnantur, genus est mendacium in iisdem.
units.tr: The aim or purpose of the ninth commandment is the maintenance and preservation of truth among men. What is forbidden, therefore, is false witness, and with it all related kinds, of which the genus is lying: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour, or concerning your neighbour." Included in this negative precept is the affirmative, "Speak the truth concerning your neighbour"; that is, be truthful, and be a lover of learning and of knowing the truth. The head and, as it were, the genus of the virtues enjoined here is truth, or rather truthfulness, in speech, in opinions, in judgments, in covenants, and in teaching. For here truth is taken to mean the agreement of knowledge or speech with the thing about which one speaks. True is the speech itself agreeing with the thing. On the other hand, the genus of the vices condemned here is lying in the same matters.

units.la: Virtutes noni præcepti.
units.tr: The virtues of the ninth commandment.

units.la: I. VERITAS seu veracitas est firma βεβαίως in voluntate, qua constanter amplectimur veras sententias, & easdem pro ratione officij nostri & circumstantiarum profitemur ac defendimus, seruamus pacta, & in sermone ac gestu vitamus insidiosas occultationes ad Dei gloriam & proximi salutem. Facit iste finis, ut diadiabolus non sit verax, etiamsi verum dicat aliquando. Nam verax est, qui veritatem dicit & amat, eique studet propter gloriam Dei & proximi salutem. De hac virtute etiam disputat Aristoteles in Ethicis breuiter, sed erudite. Veritatem in factis refert ad justitiam. Veracem proprie vocat eum, qui cum nihil interfit, tamen verax est in oratione & vita, & qui talis est in ipso habitu. Unde iterum liquet, diabolum & homines mendaces, non esse veraces, licet aliquando verum dicant.
units.tr: I. TRUTH, or truthfulness, is a firm [βεβαίως, bebaiōs] disposition of the will, by which we constantly embrace true opinions, profess and defend them as our office and circumstances require, keep our covenants, and in speech and gesture avoid deceitful concealments, for the glory of God and the salvation of our neighbour. This aim makes the devil not truthful, even if he sometimes says what is true. For he is truthful who speaks and loves the truth and strives for it for the glory of God and the salvation of his neighbour. Aristotle also discusses this virtue briefly but learnedly in the Ethics. He refers truth in deeds to justice. He calls truthful, strictly speaking, the one who, though nothing depends on it, is truthful in speech and in life, and who is such in his very character. Hence it is again clear that the devil and men who lie are not truthful, even when they sometimes say what is true.

units.la: Nomine veritatis complectimur etiam [?] virtus, qua, quantum tempus, locus & necessitas postulat, veritatem libere atq; intrepide profitemur, nec absterremur metu periculorum. Confessio veritatis praecipitur in hoc & in tertio praecepto, quomodo saepe eadem virtus ad obedientiam diuersorum praeceptorum requiritur: sed aliter in illo, aliter in hoc praecepto sancitur. Ibi, quatenus est celebratio Dei immediata: hic, quatenus fallere nolumus proximum, sed conseruatam cuiusque famam & salutem.
units.tr: Under the name of truth we also include [?] virtue, by which, as time, place and necessity require, we freely and fearlessly profess the truth, and are not deterred by fear of dangers. The confession of truth is enjoined both in this commandment and in the third, and in the same way the same virtue is required for obedience to different precepts; but it is enjoined in one way in the third and in another way in this. In the third it is enjoined insofar as it is the immediate worship of God; here it is enjoined insofar as we do not wish to deceive our neighbour, but to preserve each person's reputation and welfare.

units.la: Cum veritate pugnat in defectu 1. Mendacium, ad quod pertinet omnes fraudes, simulationes, medacia officiosa, calumniae, obtrectationes, maledicentia, quae mendacii species etiam cum candore pugnant: Item negligentia in cognoscendis sententiis veris, & ignorantia voluntaria, quae est mendaciu in mente. 2. Vanitas sive leuitas, quae est facilitas ad mentiendum. Vanus est qui multum, saepe & facile mentitur, idq; sine pudore. Mendax est qui habet studium mentiendi. Mendacium est aliter loqui vel gestibus declarare, quam sentias, & res se habeat. Est enim mentiri quasi aduersus mentem ire. Omne mendacium, quod diserte veritatem dissimulat, damnatur: nec excusantur mendacia, quae vocantur officiosa, quia non sunt facienda mala, vt eveniant bona. Et recte Lactantius in Epit. dicit: Nunquam mentiendum est, quia mendacium semper nocet, aut fallit. Veritas tamen per aliquam figurā dicta, non est mendacium, siue intelligatis, apud quem agitur, siue non. Hoc obseruandum est, ne simus nimis rigidi in examinandis sanctorum factis, nec excusemus, quae non necesse est excusari. Defendi solent mendacia officiosa exemplo obstetricum Ægyptiarum, quae mentiebantur regi, & a Deo benedicebantur. Sed non ideo benefecit eis Deus, quod mentitae essent, sed quia timuerunt Dominum, & non occiderunt infantulos Israeliticos.
units.tr: Opposed to truth by deficiency are: 1. Lying, to which belong all frauds, pretences, officious lies, calumnies, detractions, slanders, which are kinds of lying and also clash with candour; likewise negligence in learning true opinions, and wilful ignorance, which is a lie in the mind. 2. Vanity, or levity, which is readiness to lie. He is vain who lies much, often and easily, and without shame. He is a liar who has a habit of lying. To lie is to speak, or to show by gestures, otherwise than one thinks and as the matter stands. For to lie is, as it were, to go against the mind. Every lie that openly dissembles the truth is condemned; nor are those lies excused which are called officious, on the ground that evil is not to be done so that good may come of it. And Lactantius rightly says in the Epitome: "One must never lie, because a lie always either harms or deceives." A statement expressed through some figure of speech, however, is not a lie, whether or not the person to whom it is addressed understands it. This must be observed, so that we are not too rigid in judging the deeds of the saints, nor excuse what does not need excusing. Officious lies are commonly defended by the example of the Egyptian midwives, who lied to the king and were blessed by God. But God did not bless them because they lied, but because they feared the Lord and did not kill the Israelite infants.

units.la: Obiect. Quod nemini nocet & alicui prodest, id est faciendum. Mendacium officiosum est tale. Ergo, &c. Resp. Negatur minor: quia quod Deus prohibet, semper nocet: & si prodest, fit per accidens, propter Dei bonitatem. Vide Augustinum lib. de mendacio ad Consentium.
units.tr: Objection. What harms no one and benefits someone is to be done. An officious lie is such. Therefore, etc. Answer. The minor premise is denied: for what God forbids always does harm; and if it does benefit, this happens by accident, through the goodness of God. See Augustine's book On Lying, to Consentius.

units.la: In excessu pugnat 1.Intempestiua veritatis professio, quæ est margaritas objcere porcis, & sanctum dare canibus, vt ait Christus: quibus verbis omnino prohibet non necessariam & intempestiuam veritatis professionem: quia, Intempestiuè qui monet, illo nocet. 2. Curiositas, quæ est inquirere non necessaria, aut impossibilia. Aristoteli extrema veracitatis sunt ἀλαζονεία, arrogantia seu vanitas: εἰρωνεία dissimulatio, & βωμολοχία, simulatum fastidium. Hæc de veritate, virtute præcepti huius principali. Præcipiuntur & aliæ virtutes, quæ veritati ancillantur, & sunt quasi quædam eius appendices.
units.tr: Opposed by excess is 1. untimely profession of truth, which is "to cast pearls before swine, and to give what is holy to dogs," as Christ says; by these words he altogether forbids an unnecessary and untimely profession of truth, since "he who admonishes out of season does harm to him." 2. Curiosity, which is to inquire into things that are unnecessary or impossible. For Aristotle the extremes of truthfulness are [ἀλαζονεία, alazoneia], arrogance or boastfulness; [εἰρωνεία, eirōneia], dissimulation; and [βωμολοχία, bōmolochia], feigned disgust. This is what concerns truth, the principal virtue of this commandment. Other virtues are also enjoined, which serve truth and are, as it were, its appendages.

units.la: II. CANDOR est virtus, quæ recte dicta vel facta recte accipit, ambigua in meliorem partem interpretatur, quatenus causæ probabiles sunt: non facile suspiciones concipit, nec iis, quantumuis causas probabiles habentibus, indulget, nullas ex iis actiones instituit, neque inde aliquid decernit aut statuit: seu, est virtus vicina veritati, propter probabilem rationem approbans alienas voluntates, & non habens maleuolentiam, quædam etiam ambigua flectens in meliorem partem, ac bonum quidem sperans, sed rationes, men vt de rebus mutabilibus cogitans, posse mutari voluntates, & posse hominem errare de aliena voluntate, cum non penitus afficiantur latebræ humani pectoris.
units.tr: II. CANDOUR is the virtue which takes rightly what has been rightly said or done, interprets ambiguous things in the better part, insofar as there are probable grounds for doing so; does not readily form suspicions, nor indulge them even when they have probable grounds; does not undertake any actions on their basis, nor decide or settle anything from them. Or, it is a virtue akin to truth, approving the wills of others on reasonable grounds, and not harbouring ill will, bending even ambiguous things toward the better part, and hoping for good, yet mindful, as one who thinks about changeable things, that wills can change, and that a person can be mistaken about another's will, since the hidden recesses of the human heart are not fully laid open.

units.la: Pugnat cum candore in defectu calumnia & suspicacitas. Calumnia est non tantum innocentes falso criminari, sed etiam mediocriter dicta in malam partem interpretari, aut falsum etiam aspergere & affingere. Suspicacitas est recte vel ambiguè dicta siniftre accipere, & mala suspicari de bonis, vel sine ratione, aut etiam veris suspicionibus nimium indulgere. Suspiciones licet habere, nisi velimus esse stulti & bardi. Cauete ab hominibus: estote prudentes sicut serpentes, & simplices sicut columba. Sed aliud est habere suspiciones, aliud, suspicionibus indulgere. Est autem suspicio opinio mali de aliquo, propter probabilé causam, siue veram siue apparentem. Estq; duplex, mala & bona. 1.Mala est, quando proficiscitur ex causa vel prorsus falsa, vel non sufficiente: vt cum fingitur aliqua causa, quæ nulla est, seu, cum proximus est innocens. Bona verò, cum ex causa sufficiente suspicamur. 2.Mala est, quando ex suspicione aliquid certi statuitur. Bona, quando res, cum sint probabiles rationes in vtramque partem, in dubio relinquitur. 3. Mala est, quando ex suspicione consilium capitur de alicui nocendo. Bona contra. 4. Mala est, quando ex suspicione oritur odium. Bona contra.
units.tr: Opposed to candour by deficiency are calumny and suspiciousness. Calumny is not only to accuse the innocent falsely, but also to interpret moderately spoken words in a bad sense, or even to sprinkle and invent falsehoods. Suspiciousness is to take rightly or ambiguously spoken words in a sinister sense, and to suspect bad things of good people, without reason, or to indulge excessively even in well-grounded suspicions. "One may have suspicions, unless we wish to be foolish and dull. Beware of men: be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." But it is one thing to have suspicions, another to indulge them. Now suspicion is an opinion of evil about someone, on account of a probable cause, whether true or apparent. And it is twofold, bad and good. 1. It is bad when it arises from a cause that is either altogether false or insufficient, as when some cause is invented that does not exist, or when the neighbour is innocent. It is good when we suspect on a sufficient cause. 2. It is bad when something certain is decided on the basis of suspicion. It is good when, since there are probable reasons on both sides, the matter is left in doubt. 3. It is bad when a plan to harm someone is formed on the basis of suspicion. The reverse is good. 4. It is bad when hatred arises from suspicion. The reverse is good.

units.la: In excessu candori aduersatur stulta credulitas, & adulatio. Stulta credulitas, est temere quid interpretari, vel alicui assentiri, sine iusta vel probabili causa: vel quando sunt rationes manifestæ aut staæ aut probabiles, tamen credere contrariū de aliquo. Adulatio, vel assentatio est probare vel laudare non laudanda, vt aucupemur bona vel gratiam alicuius. Candor est adiumentum siue species veritatis. Ergo hic vna cum veritate præcipitur.
units.tr: In excess, candour is opposed by foolish credulity, and flattery. Foolish credulity, which is to interpret something rashly or to assent to someone without a just or probable cause, or to believe something contrary about a person even when the reasons are plain, firm or probable. Flattery, or assentation, is to approve or praise what is not worthy of praise, in order to catch someone's goods or favour. Candour is the helper, or the appearance, of truth. Therefore it is commanded here together with truth.

units.la: III. SIMPLICITAS est perspicua veritas sine ambagibus, vel, est virtus, quæ vera, recta & explicata in actibus, & communi vita, proprie & perspicuè dicit & facit. Simplicitate & candore veritas temperatur.
units.tr: III. SIMPLICITY is clear truth without circumlocution, or it is the virtue which, in actions and in common life, speaks and does what is true, straight and plain, openly and clearly. Truth is tempered by simplicity and candour.

units.la: Extrema eius sunt: simulatio simplicitatis & διπλόης in mo-ribus & sermone.
units.tr: Its extremes are the pretence of simplicity and double-dealing [διπλόης] in conduct and speech.

units.la: IV. CONSTANTIA est virtus à veritate agnita non discedens, nec mutans consilium sine necessaria & probabili causa, sed constanter dicens & faciens vera, justa & necessaria. Seu, est virtus in inuenta, agnita & approbata veritate perseuerans & similiter eam profitens ac defendens. Constantia requiritur ad veritatis conseruationem. Ergo hic etiam præcipitur.
units.tr: IV. CONSTANCY is the virtue that does not depart from truth once recognised, nor changes its purpose without a necessary and probable cause, but speaks and does what is true, just and necessary, constantly. Or, it is the virtue of persevering in truth once found, recognised and approved, and likewise professing and defending it. Constancy is required for the preservation of truth. Therefore it too is commanded here.

units.la: Extrema eius sunt: in defectu, Inconstantia seu levitas quæ est præter rationem mutare veras sententias. In excessu verò, Pertinacia seu ωὐθάδεια, seu rigor Stoicus, perseverans in falsis opinionibus, aut inutilibus actionibus, etiamsi de errore convincatur. Vitium ex confidentia ingenij, vel ex superbia atque ostentatione ortum, cedere nolens de sententia, etiam quam firmis rationibus videt esse falsam.
units.tr: Extremes of it: in defect, inconstancy or levity, which is changing true opinions contrary to reason. In excess, obstinacy or [αὐθάδεια], or Stoic rigour, persisting in false opinions or useless actions even when one is convicted of error. It is a vice arising from confidence in one's own wit, or from pride and ostentation, being unwilling to give up an opinion even when one sees, on firm grounds, that it is false.

units.la: V. DOCILITAS est virtus inquirens rationes verarum sententiarum, facile credens ac cedens meliora docentibus, aut ostentibus, idque propter certam rationem, & promptam faciens voluntatem ad acquiescendum veris & probabilibus rationibus, & ad relinquendum ea, quæ prius falsa pro veris amplectebatur.
units.tr: V. DOCILITY is the virtue of seeking the reasons for true opinions, readily believing and yielding to those who teach or show better things, and this for a sure reason; it makes the will ready to assent to true and probable reasons, and to abandon what one had previously embraced as true but which was false.

units.la: Extrema sunt eadem, quæ & constantiæ, ad quam docilitas etiam requiritur. Nam constantia sine docilitate in pertinaciam, & docilitas sine constantia in levitatem degenerat.
units.tr: Extremes are the same as those of constancy, to which docility is also required. For constancy without docility degenerates into obstinacy, and docility without constancy into levity.

units.la: Hactenus enumeratæ virtutes optimè cohærentinter se: Nam oportet veritatem temperari candore & simplicitate, percipi & agnosci docilitate, conseruari constantia. Atq; ideo præcedentes virtutes requiruntur, vt fit veritas. Tres verò sequentes requiruntur, vt vtiliter sit veritas in mundo.
units.tr: The virtues listed so far cohere well with one another. For truth must be tempered by candour and simplicity, perceived and recognised by docility, and preserved by constancy. Therefore the preceding virtues are required so that there may be truth, and the three that follow are required so that truth may be useful in the world.

units.la: VI. TACITVRNITAS est virtus reticens arcana & non necessariam loquacitatem; seu, est modus profitendi veritatem eiusmodi, quo reticentur arcana, siue vera, siue falsa, vitantur sermones non necessarij & inutiles, maximè verò intempestiui, periculosi & scandalosi. Extrema sunt in defectu garrulitas, futilitas & proditio. Garrulitas seu loquacitas est intempestiue & immodice & stolide loqui. Futilitas nihil potest reticere, sed omnia etiam arcana effutit. Proditio est indicare facta aut consilia honesta, ita vt lędantur illi, quibus videtur aut debet amicus esse qui indicat: non defendere vel non curare periculum alterius, cum quis debeat ac possit: indicare etiam non digna indicatione, quorum tamen indicatio non cetei, cui indicatur: etiam necessario indicanda animo seu fine non bono indicare: deniq; indicare perjurij aut mendacij interuentu. In excessu sunt morositas & reticentia. Morositas est nimiū silentium, wann man einem die Wort muß abkauffen: hoc est, cum quasi pretio emenda sunt verba. Reticentia est dissimulare veritatem, vbi erat profitenda, hoc est, vbi gloria Dei, & salus proximi, vel nostra, vel aliorum causa, vel dilectio amicorum requirit, vt loquamur.
units.tr: VI. TACITURNITY is the virtue that keeps secrets and avoids unnecessary talk. Or, it is a manner of professing truth by which secrets, whether true or false, are kept back, and unnecessary and useless speeches are avoided, especially those that are untimely, dangerous or scandalous. Extremes are, in defect, garrulity, frivolity and betrayal. Garrulity or loquacity is speaking untimely, immoderately and foolishly. Frivolity cannot keep anything back, but blurts out everything, even secrets. Betrayal is disclosing honourable deeds or plans so that those are harmed to whom the discloser seems, or ought, to be a friend; not defending, or not caring for, another's danger when one ought and is able to; also disclosing things not worth disclosing, whose disclosure is not pleasing to the person to whom it is made; also disclosing with a bad mind or purpose even things that must necessarily be disclosed; and finally disclosing through the intervention of perjury or lying. In excess are morosity and reticence. Morosity is excessive silence, when one must buy words from someone as if at a price. Reticence is concealing truth where it ought to be professed, that is, where the glory of God, the salvation of a neighbour, our own or others' good, or love of friends requires us to speak.

units.la: VII. COMITAS seu affabilitas est virtus libenter & cum significatione benevolentiæ audiens, respondens, loquens, vbi opus est, propter causam necessariam vel probabilem: seu, est virtus facile admittens congressus aliorum, & colloquiis, sermone & gestibus beneuolentiam significans: seu, est virtus consistens in audiendo & respondendo, cum aliqua significatione benevolentiæ.
units.tr: VII. COURTESY, or affability, is the virtue of listening, answering and speaking gladly, and with a sign of goodwill, where need arises, for a necessary or probable reason. Or, it is the virtue of readily admitting the company and conversation of others, showing goodwill in speech and gesture. Or, it is the virtue consisting in listening and replying with some sign of goodwill.

units.la: Extrema sunt eadem, quæ & taciturnitatis, leuitas & morositas: item assentatio & comitas simulata: vide Aristotelem in ethicis. Taciturnitas sine comitate fit morositas: & comitas sine taciturnitate fit garrulitas & futilitas. Sunt igitur taciturnitas & comitas cognatæ virtutes.
units.tr: Extremes are the same as those of taciturnity: levity and morosity; likewise assentation and feigned courtesy. See Aristotle in the Ethics. Taciturnity without courtesy becomes morosity, and courtesy without taciturnity becomes garrulity and frivolity. Therefore taciturnity and courtesy are kindred virtues.

units.la: VIII. VRBANITAS veritatis seu veri sermonis condimentum, est veritas figuratè dicta ad alios taxandos, monendos, vel delectandos, seruatis circumstantiis personarum, loci & temporis: seu, est facultas dicendi veritatem cum quadam venustate, ad docendum, consolandum, exhilarandum, vel taxandum alios sine acerbitate.
units.tr: VIII. URBANITY, the seasoning of true and honest speech, is truth told figuratively in order to rebuke, admonish or delight others, observing the circumstances of persons, place and time. Or, it is the ability to speak the truth with a certain charm, so as to teach, console, cheer or rebuke others without harshness.

units.la: Extrema eius sunt in excessu scurrilitas, dicacitas & obtrectatio. Scurrilitas est obscœna jocatio, præsertim in rebus seriis. Scurra, qui sic jocatur, dicitur ἀπὸ τῆς σκώρ, stercus, quoniam putida & stercora loquitur. Dicacitas est vitium jocandi acerbè, aliosq; præsertim miseros, deridendi atq; exagitandi. Obtrectatio est, quæ falsa crimina de aliis spargit, ambigue dicta male interpretatur, cum vindictæ cupiditate, studio nocendi aut conciliandi inuidiam. In defectu urbanitati repugnat, ἀνοσία seu stoliditas & insulsitas. Insulsitas est ἀνοσία est affectatio urbanitatis intempestiua. Insulsitas est affectatio urbanitatis inepta.
units.tr: Its extremes in excess are buffoonery, scoffing and detraction. Buffoonery is obscene joking, especially about serious matters. A buffoon who jokes in this way is so called from σκώρ [σκῶρ], dung, because he speaks filthy things and dung. Scoffing is the vice of joking bitterly, and of mocking and harassing others, especially the wretched. Detraction is spreading false charges about others, wickedly interpreting ambiguous words, with a desire for revenge, a purpose of harm, or a wish to stir up ill will. In defect, opposed to urbanity, is boorishness [ἀγροικία], or stupidity and insipidity. Insipidity is an untimely and inept affectation of urbanity.

units.la: Lib. 4. Eth. cap. 4.
units.tr: Lib. 4. Eth. cap. 4.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXIII. Quid prohibet decimum præceptum?
units.tr: Question 113. What does the tenth commandment forbid?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Ne vel minima cupiditate, aut cogitatione, aduersus vllum DEI præceptum corda nostra vnquam sollicitentur: sed vt perpetuo, & ex animo omne peccatum detestemur, contraque omni justitia delectemur.
units.tr: That our hearts are never troubled, even by the slightest lust or thought, against any command of God; but that we always, and from the heart, detest every sin and take delight in all righteousness.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Præceptum de concupiscentia esse vnum, non duo, manifestum est.
units.tr: That there is one precept on concupiscence, not two, is evident.

units.la: 1. Ex diuersitate recitationis apud Mosen. Exod.20,17. & Deut.5,21.
units.tr: 1. From the difference in the recital in Moses, Exod.20,17. and Deut.5,21.

units.la: 2. Ex coniunctione in vnum versiculum apud Mosen vtroque loco.
units.tr: 2. From the joining of it into one verse in Moses in both places.

units.la: 3. Ex interpretatione Pauli, qui totum contextum Mosis vno præcepto complectitur: Concupiscentiam non nouissem, nisi lex diceret: Non concupisces.
units.tr: 3. From the interpretation of Paul, who embraces the whole context of Moses in one precept: I had not known concupiscence, unless the law had said, You shall not covet.

units.la: 4. Ex eo, quod Pontificij, & alij, concupiscentiam domus & vxoris, in suis explicationibus solent coniungere: quia nimirum vident, eadem ratione vxoris & domus & omnium aliarum rerum proximi concupiscentiam prohiberi. Unde sequitur, vel vnum tantum esse præceptum de concupiscentia, vel tot esse præcepta numeranda, quot res concupiscibiles proximi prohibentur.
units.tr: 4. From the fact that the Papists and others customarily join the coveting of a house and of a wife in their explanations, because they clearly see that by the same reasoning the coveting of the neighbour's wife, house and all his other goods is forbidden. Hence it follows either that there is only one precept on coveting, or that as many precepts must be counted as there are things of the neighbour that may be coveted.

units.la: 5. Ex authoritate veterum tum Judæorum tum Christianorum interpretum, quorum nomina supra in distributione decalogi sunt recitata.
units.tr: 5. From the authority of the old interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, whose names were recited above in the division of the Decalogue.

units.la: Scopus seu finis decimi præcepti est, affectuum omnium erga Deum & proximum & res eius, rectitudo, & obedientia interna, quæ in omnibus etiam aliis præceptis includenda. Ergo dicat quis, hoc præceptum abundat, quia nihil noui postulat. Resp. Non abundat, quia additum est hoc præceptum superioribus, tanquam regula & declaratio vniuersalis, juxta quam accipi debet obedientia interna omnium aliorum præceptorum: quia de toto genere loquitur. Præcipitur itaque in hoc præcepto Iustitia originalis erga Deum & proximum, quæ est vera agnitio Dei in mente, & in voluntate inclinatio ad obediendum voluntati D e i agnitæ. Prohibetur concupiscentia, quæ est inclinatio praua vel affectus inordinatus, appetens ea, quæ D e v s prohibuit. Proprie tamen præcipitur justitia originalis erga proximum, quæ est inclinatio & desiderium præstandi proximo omnia debita officia, & salutem eius tuendi. Prohibentur eius duo extrema. 1. Peccatum originale erga proximum, quod nominatur concupiscentia: quæ est desiderium eorum, quæ noceant proximo. 2. Amor proximi inordinatus, cum in eius gratiam Deum negligimus.
units.tr: The scope or end of the tenth precept is the rectitude and inward obedience of all affections towards God, the neighbour and his goods, which is also to be included in all the other precepts. So let someone say: this precept is superfluous, because it demands nothing new. Answer. It is not superfluous, because this precept is added to the earlier ones as a universal rule and declaration, according to which the inward obedience to all the other precepts must be understood, since it speaks of the whole genus. Therefore, in this precept, original righteousness towards God and the neighbour is commanded, which is the true knowledge of God in the mind and an inclination of the will to obey the will of God as known. Concupiscence is forbidden, which is a depraved inclination or disordered affection, longing for those things which God has prohibited. Yet properly, original righteousness towards the neighbour is commanded, which is the inclination and desire to render to the neighbour all due duties and to preserve his welfare. Its two extremes are forbidden: 1. Original sin towards the neighbour, which is named concupiscence, namely the desire for those things which may harm the neighbour. 2. Inordinate love of the neighbour, when for his sake we neglect God.

units.la: Aliqui concupiscentiam & peccatū originale pro eodem habent. Differunt tamen vt effectus & causa: vel certe vt pars & totum. Concupiscentia enim est propensio ad ea, quæ prohibita sunt lege. Peccatum originale est reatus totius generis humani, & priuatio agnitionis Dei ac voluntatis diuinæ.
units.tr: Some hold concupiscence and original sin to be the same. Yet they differ as effect and cause, or at least as part and whole. For concupiscence is a propensity towards those things which are forbidden by the law. Original sin is the guilt of the whole human race and the privation of the knowledge of God and of the divine will.

units.la: Obseruandum hoc loco, non tantum prauas inclinationes esse peccata, sed & cogitationem mali peccatū esse, quatenus ei conjuncta est aliqua inclinatio & propensio ad malum prosequendum: seu cum desiderio id faciendi. Concupiscentia vero, quia sit mala, & peccatum, licet nobiscum nascatur, non potest vel debet esse dubium: cum lege prohibeatur. Nam an aliquid sit peccatum, non est judicandum ex natura, sed ex lege. Quicquid enim huic aduersatur, est peccatum: siue nobiscum nascatur, siue non.
units.tr: It must be observed here that not only depraved inclinations are sins, but also the thought of evil is a sin, insofar as some inclination and propensity to pursue evil is joined to it, or the desire of doing it. Concupiscence, however, since it is evil and sin, though it is born with us, cannot and ought not to be doubted, since it is forbidden by the law. For whether something is sin is not to be judged from nature but from the law. Whatever is opposed to this is sin, whether it is born with us or not.

units.la: Pelagiani negarunt, concupiscentiam esse peccatum. Contra lex dicit: Non concupisces. Et Paulus: Peccatum non cognoui, nisi lex dixisset: Non concupisces. Damnati sunt Pelagiani in multis synodis contra Pelagij & Cœlestij errores congregatis, circa annum Domini 420. & deinceps: Mileuitana, Carthaginensi V, Palæstina in Oriente, &c.
units.tr: The Pelagians denied that concupiscence is sin. Against them the law says: You shall not covet. And Paul: I had not known sin, unless the law had said, You shall not covet. The Pelagians were condemned in many synods gathered against the errors of Pelagius and Caelestius, around the year of the Lord 420 and afterwards: Milevis, the Fifth Council of Carthage, Palestine in the East, etc.

units.la: Argumenta præcipua Pelagianorum.
units.tr: The principal arguments of the Pelagians.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Naturalia non sunt peccata. Concupiscentia est naturalis. Ergo non est peccatum. Resp. 1. Est fallacia accidentis in minore. Nam concupiscentia inordinata ante lapsum non fuit: sed post lapsum naturæ accessit. Naturalis est ergo non per se, sed per accidens, quatenus nunc post lapsum nobiscum nascitur: est naturalis, hoc est, accidens malum, inseparabiliter adhærens naturæ per se bonæ. 2. Sunt quatuor termini, ex ὁμωνυμία vocabuli naturale. Nam in maiore significat rem bonam à Deo conditam in natura, appetitum videlicet ante lapsum, qui non erat voluntati Dei contrarius. In minore significat appetitum inorinordinatum seu accidens, quod non habemus ex creatione, sed quod per lapsum nobis attraximus.
units.tr: Objection 1. Natural things are not sins. Concupiscence is natural. Therefore it is not sin. Answer 1. This is the fallacy of accident in the minor premise. For concupiscence in disorder did not exist before the fall, but came upon nature after the fall. It is natural, therefore, not in itself but by accident, insofar as now after the fall it is born with us: it is natural, that is, an evil accident inseparably adhering to a nature good in itself. 2. There are four terms, owing to the equivocation [ὁμωνυμία] of the word natural. For in the major premise it signifies a good thing created by God in nature, namely the appetite before the fall, which was not contrary to the will of God. In the minor it signifies a disordered appetite or accident, which we have not from creation but have drawn upon ourselves through the fall.

units.la: Inst. Appetitus seu inclinatio ad appetendum conseruantia, & ad fugiendum destruentia naturam, etiam in natura corrupta non est peccatum: quia res est à Deo condita, & motus per se bonus. Talis est concupiscentia. Ergo concupiscentia non est peccatum. Resp. ad maiorem. Appetitiones & motus naturae sunt boni per se, quatenus sunt motus, non quatenus sunt motus inordinati, & feruntur in obiecta a Deo prohibita, cuiusmodi sunt motus seu appetitus omnes naturae corruptae, qui vel non feruntur in obiecta, quae oportet, vel non feruntur eo modo & fine, quo oportet: ideoque omnes sunt vitiosi & peccata. Non potest arbor mala bonos fructus ferre. Appetere fructum arboris erat naturale: sed appetere contra mandatum Dei, erat motus suo genere vitiosus & peccatum, &c.
units.tr: Instance. An appetite or inclination to seek what preserves nature and to flee what destroys it, even in corrupt nature, is not sin, because the thing is created by God and the motion is good in itself. Such is concupiscence. Therefore concupiscence is not sin. Answer to the major. The appetites and motions of nature are good in themselves insofar as they are motions, not insofar as they are disordered motions and are directed towards objects forbidden by God. Such are all the motions or appetites of corrupt nature, which either are not directed towards the objects they ought to be, or are not directed in the manner and to the end they ought to be; therefore all of them are faulty and sins. A bad tree cannot bear good fruit. To desire the fruit of the tree was natural; but to desire it against the command of God was a motion faulty in its kind and a sin, etc.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Quod non est in nostra potestate, ut sit vel non sit in nobis, non est peccatum. Concupiscentia sic est in nobis, ut non sit in nostra potestate eam exuere, &c. Ergo non est peccatum. Resp. Maior falsa est. Peccatum enim non libertate aut necessitate naturae nostrae, sed voluntate & lege Dei aestimatur. Quicquid cum hac pugnat, peccatum est, sive possit, sive non possit ab hominibus vitari. Neque Deus postulans a nobis impossibilia facit nobis iniuriam: quia praecepit, dum possibilia erant, & ipse facultatem praestandi nobis dederat. Iam licet nos hanc facultatem amiserimus: Deus tamen non amisit suum ius postulandi, quod apud nos depositum. Vide supra quaest. Catech. 9.
units.tr: Objection 2. What is not in our power, whether it is or is not in us, is not sin. Concupiscence is in us in such a way that it is not in our power to put it off, etc. Therefore it is not sin. Answer. The major is false. For sin is judged not by the freedom or necessity of our nature but by the will and law of God. Whatever fights against this is sin, whether or not men can avoid it. Nor does God, in demanding impossible things from us, do us wrong: for he commanded when things were possible, and he himself had given us the ability to perform them. Now, although we have lost this ability, God has not lost his right to demand, which is held in trust with us. See above, question 9 of the Catechism.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Peccatum facit homines obnoxios aeternae irae Dei. Concupiscentia renatos non facit obnoxius irae Dei. Nulla enim est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Ergo concupiscentia saltem in renatis non est peccatum. Resp. Est fallacia accidentis in minore. Concupiscentia enim renatos non damnat per accidens, hoc est, ex gratia Dei, non imputantis eam credentibus. Non autem hoc fit ideo, quasi concupiscentia non sit peccatum. Nam & alia peccata non damnant renatos, non quod non sint peccata, sed quia eis remissa sunt propter Christum.
units.tr: Objection 3. Sin makes men liable to the eternal wrath of God. Concupiscence does not make the regenerate liable to the wrath of God. For there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. Therefore concupiscence, at least in the regenerate, is not sin. Answer. It is the fallacy of accident in the minor premise. For concupiscence does not condemn the regenerate by accident, that is, by the grace of God, who does not impute it to believers. This is not because concupiscence is not sin. For other sins also do not condemn the regenerate, not because they are not sins, but because they have been forgiven them for Christ's sake.

units.la: Obiect. 4. In baptismo tollitur peccatum originale. Ergo concupiscentia in baptizatis non est peccatum. Resp. ad antecedens: Peccatum originale, tollitur in baptismo non simpliciter, sed quoad reatū. Manet vero in baptizatis prauitas & inclinatio ad peccandum. Et hoc est, quod Scholastici dicunt: Formale tollitur, & materiale manet. Inst. Vbi tollitur formale peccati, ibi res ipsa tollitur: quia forma dat esse rei, &c. In baptismo tollitur formale peccati originis. Ergo tollitur ipsum peccatum. Resp. Est fallacia a secundum quid: Tollitur peccati formale non simpliciter, sed quoad reatum. Peccati enim duplex est formale. 1. Pugnantia cum lege & inclinatio ad peccatum. 2. Reatus seu ordinatio ad poenam. Reatus tollitur, sed inclinatio manet: Video aliam legem in membris meis repugnantem legi mentis meae.
units.tr: Objection 4. In baptism original sin is removed. Therefore concupiscence in the baptized is not sin. Answer to the antecedent: Original sin is removed in baptism not absolutely but as to guilt. Depravity and inclination to sin, however, remain in the baptized. And this is what the Scholastics mean: The formal element is removed, and the material remains. Instance. Where the formal element of sin is removed, the thing itself is removed, because form gives being to the thing, etc. In baptism the formal element of original sin is removed. Therefore sin itself is removed. Answer. This is the fallacy of "in a certain respect." The formal element of sin is removed not absolutely but as to guilt. For the formal element of sin is twofold: 1. Conflict with the law and inclination to sin. 2. Guilt, or the ordination to punishment. The guilt is removed, but the inclination remains: I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXIV.
units.tr: QUESTION 114.

units.la: Possuntne autem illi, qui ad Deum conuersi sunt, haec praecepta perfecte seruare?
units.tr: Can those who have been converted to God keep these precepts perfectly?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Minimè. Verum etiam sanctissimi quique, quandiu viuunt, habent tantum exigua initia huius obedientiae: sic tamen, vt serio ac non simulato studio, non secundum aliqua tantùm, sed secundùm omnia Dei praecepta viuere incipiant b.
units.tr: By no means. Indeed, even the most holy people, as long as they live, have only small beginnings of this obedience. Yet they begin to live, with earnest and unfeigned zeal, not in certain respects only but according to all of God's precepts b.

units.la: a Iohan. 1. v. 8. Rom. 7,14.15. Eccles. 7.21. 1 Corinth. 13,9. b Rom. 7,22. Psalm. 1. vers. 2.
EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Quæstio est: Quomodo lex sit possibilis, & an perfecte seruari possit à renatis? Quæ quæstio vt rectè intelligatur, distinguenda est hominis natura, in integram, lapsam, & rursus integram.
units.tr: The question is: how is the law possible, and can it be kept perfectly by the regenerate? So that this question may be rightly understood, human nature must be distinguished into the state of integrity, the fallen state, and the restored state.

units.la: Natura integra possibilis erat integra totius legis obedientia secundum omnes partes & gradus, sicut angelis. Erat enim homo conditus ad imaginem Dei in perfecta sanctitate & iustitia. Natura post lapsum corrupta, adeo impossibilis est legis implemento, vt obedientiam Deo placentem ne quidem inchoare possit, secundum dicta: Omne figmentum cordis humani prauum a iuuentute. Si potest Æthiops mutare pellem suam, & pardus maculas suas, etiam vos potestis bene agere, cum sitis mali. Non potest arbor mala bonos fructus ferre. Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Cum esseris mortui in peccatis. Non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum quicquam, &c.
units.tr: Nature in its integrity was able to render complete obedience to the whole law, in all its parts and degrees, as the angels did. For man was created in the image of God, in perfect holiness and righteousness. Nature corrupted after the fall is so unable to fulfil the law that it cannot even begin an obedience pleasing to God, according to the sayings: Every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart is evil from his youth. Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then may you also do good, who are accustomed to do evil. A corrupt tree cannot bear good fruit. Whatever is not of faith is sin. You were dead in your trespasses and sins. We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything, etc.

units.la: Renatis lex fit possibilis dupliciter: Imputatione & inchoatione. Quoad imputationem, sit eis possibilis perfecte in Christo, in quo perfecte legi satisfecerunt & satisfaciunt: quia perfecta Christi obedientia eis per fidem imputatur: vt supra explicatum. tum fuit: In ipso estis consummati. Quoad inchoationem, lex fit eis possibilis etiam in seipsis; sed imperfecte: quia inchoant & praestant initium verae & perfectae obedientiae internae & externae, secundum omnia DEI mandata. Haec est enim charitas: ut mandata eius seruemus: & mandata eius grania non sunt. Sine hac inchoatione qui gloriatur se nouisse & amare DEVM, mendax est.
units.tr: The law becomes possible for the regenerate in two ways: by imputation and by inchoation. As to imputation, it is possible for them perfectly in Christ, in whom they have perfectly satisfied and do satisfy the law, because the perfect obedience of Christ is imputed to them through faith, as explained above: In him you are made complete. As to inchoation, the law becomes possible for them also in themselves, but imperfectly, because they begin and render the beginning of a true and perfect obedience, both internal and external, according to all the commandments of God. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not grievous. Without this beginning, whoever boasts that he knows and loves God is a liar.

units.la: Manet tamen renatis in hac vita lex impossibilis, quoad perfectam legis obedientiam internam & externam in seipsis. Nam omnes coguntur clamare cum Dauide: Ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruo tuo, quia in conspectu tuo non iustificabitur (nempe operibus legis) omnis viuens. Psal.143. v.2. 1. Quia non implent legem perfecte: sed multa agunt contra legem. 2. Quia etiam quae agunt secundum legem, sunt imperfecta. Nam in renatis sunt & manent multa peccata: ut, peccatum originale, & multa actualia, ignorantiae, omissionis, infirmitatis, quae tamen peccata ipsi in se agnoscunt, deplorant & deprecantur: ideo per Christum eis non imputantur. Et facti sumus, ut immundus omnes nos: & quasi pannus menstruata universa iustitia nostra. Peccata quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me.
units.tr: Nevertheless, for the regenerate in this life the law remains impossible as to perfect obedience, internal and external, in themselves. For all are compelled to cry out with David: Enter not into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no living man shall be justified (namely by the works of the law). Ps. 143:2. First, because they do not keep the law perfectly, but do many things contrary to it. Second, because even the things they do in accordance with the law are imperfect. For in the regenerate there are, and remain, many sins: original sin, and many actual sins of ignorance, omission and infirmity, which nevertheless they themselves acknowledge, lament and pray against in themselves; therefore these sins are not imputed to them through Christ. We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteousness is like a filthy garment. Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults.

units.la: Est tamen discrimen magnum inter renatos, & non renatos, cum peccant. 1. In Deo manet propositum seruandi electos. 2. Certa est renatorum finalis poenitentia. 3. Etiam in ipsis peccatis renati aliquod semen fidei & conuersionis retinent, quod non deficiant, & pereant. De impiis vero nec tale in Deo est propositum, nec certa est finalis eorum conuersio, nec deniq; initium aliquod verae obedientiae habent, sed tota voluntate peccant, & ruunt aduersus Deum, ac tandem pereunt, nisi conuertantur.
units.tr: There is nevertheless a great difference between the regenerate and the unregenerate when they sin. First, in God there remains the purpose of preserving the elect. Second, the final repentance of the regenerate is certain. Third, even in their sins the regenerate retain some seed of faith and conversion, which does not fail and perish. But in the impious there is no such purpose in God, their final conversion is not certain, and they have no beginning of true obedience at all; they sin with their whole will, rush against God, and at last perish, unless they are converted.

units.la: Contra imperfectionem operum in renatis.
units.tr: Against the imperfection of works in the regenerate.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Opera Spiritus sancti non possunt esse imperfecta. Bona opera renatorum sunt opera Spiritus sancti. Ergo necesse est ea esse perfecta, etiam in se considerata. Resp.
