Est fallacia a secundum quid ut simpliciter. Quae opera sunt Spiritus sancti renatorum sunt Spiritus sancti non simpliciter, sed ita, ut simul sint ipsorum opera. Hinc tantum sequitur, opera sanctorum esse pura, quatenus a Spiritu sancto suggeruntur & fiunt: non autem quatenus sunt etiam hominum multis defectibus ac naevis adhuc laborantium opera.
units.tr: Objection 1. The works of the Holy Spirit cannot be imperfect. The good works of the regenerate are works of the Holy Spirit. Therefore they must be perfect, even when considered in themselves. Answer: this is the fallacy of "in a certain respect" taken as "absolutely". The works that are of the Holy Spirit in the regenerate are the Holy Spirit's not absolutely, but in such a way that they are at the same time their own works. From this it follows only that the works of the saints are pure, insofar as they are suggested and performed by the Holy Spirit; not insofar as they are also the works of men who are still struggling with many defects and blemishes.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Qui sunt conformes imagini Christi, eorum opera non possunt esse imperfecta. Sancti in hac vita sunt conformes ChriChristo per nouitatem. Ergo sanctorum opera non possunt esse imperfecta. Resp. Est eadem fallacia. Maior loquitur de perfectè conformibus imagini Christi, cum sancti, de quibus est in minore, tantum sint Christo conformes ex parte, quandiu hic viuunt. Qualis enim cognitio est, talis etiam dilectio, & conformitas cum Christo in sanctis. Sed ex parte hic cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: inquit Apostolus.
units.tr: Objection 2. Those who are conformed to the image of Christ cannot have imperfect works. The saints in this life are conformed to Christ in newness. Therefore the works of the saints cannot be imperfect. Answer. It is the same fallacy. The major premise speaks of those perfectly conformed to the image of Christ, whereas the saints of whom the minor premise speaks are conformed to Christ only in part, as long as they live here. For as knowledge is, so also love and conformity to Christ are in the saints. But we know in part and we prophesy in part, as the Apostle says.

units.la: Obiect. 3. In sanctis nulla est condemnatio. Ergo opera eorum sunt perfectè bona, etiam in se considerata. Resp. Est fallacia non causæ. Non enim operum perfectio, sed Christi satisfactio renatis per fidem imputata, est causa, cur sanctis nulla sit condemnatio. Tantum ergo sequitur disiunctiuè, opera renatorum, vel in se, vel respectu imputatæ perfectionis Christi perfecta esse, & non damnari vt impura in iudicio Dei.
units.tr: Objection 3. In the saints there is no condemnation. Therefore their works are perfectly good, even when considered in themselves. Answer. It is the fallacy of a non-cause. For it is not the perfection of works but the satisfaction of Christ, imputed to the regenerate through faith, that is the cause why there is no condemnation for the saints. It follows only disjunctively that the works of the regenerate are either perfect in themselves or perfect with respect to the imputed perfection of Christ, and are not condemned as impure at the judgment of God.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Seueritas iustitiæ diuinæ non reddit bona secundum opera non perfectè bona. Christus in iudicio Dei reddet vnicuique, & sic etiam sanctis, secundum opera sua. Ergo opera sanctorum sic sunt perfecta, vt per se consistant in iudicio Dei. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini: quia maior de legali, minor de euangelica retributione operum intelligitur, hoc est, iustitia Dei non reddit bona, secundū opera imperfecta, si legaliter, seu ex pacto integræ obedientiæ legis iudicer. Christus verò sanctorum opera compensans, non iudicabit legaliter, seu ex pacto operum perfectorum, sed ex pacto fidei, seu iustitiæ suæ per fidem ipsis imputatæ & applicatæ: & tamen iudicabit secundum opera eorum, vt secundum argumenta siue testimonia fidei, ex qua profecta fuerunt, & quam fuisse in ipsis, tanquam effectus opera ostendent.
units.tr: Objection 4. The severity of divine justice does not reward good works that are not perfectly good. Christ at the judgment of God will render to each one, and so also to the saints, according to their works. Therefore the works of the saints are so perfect that they stand on their own before the judgment of God. Answer. There are four terms here, because the major premise is understood of legal, and the minor of evangelical, retribution of works. That is, the justice of God does not reward imperfect works if it judges them legally, that is, by the covenant of perfect obedience to the law. But Christ, who compensates for the works of the saints, will not judge legally, that is, by the covenant of perfect works, but by the covenant of faith, that is, by his righteousness imputed and applied to them through faith. Yet he will judge according to their works, as according to the evidence or testimony of the faith from which they proceeded, and which, as effects, show that it was in them.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Scriptura sanctorum operibus perfectionem tribuit. Confitebor tibi Domine in toto corde meo. Noah erat vir justus & perfectus in generationibus suis. Ambulaui coram te corde perfecto. Cor Asa erat perfectum omnibus diebus ipsius. Similia de perfectione etiam alibi passim occurrunt. Ergo, &c. Resp. Hæc & similia dicta loquuntur de perfectione partium, non graduum obedientiæ in sanctis, & de sinceritate oppositâ hypocrisi & simulationi pietatis. Sancti enim perfectionem gradum, quem lex requirit, nunquam hic consequuntur. Habent verò initium integræ obedientiæ & subiectionis erga Deum, secundum omnia eius mandata. Nec tamen propter hoc initium inchoatæ obedientiæ suæ, sed propter imputatam ipsis perfectam iustitiam Christi placent Deo, & perfecti sunt coram Deo in se quidem perfectione partium, hoc est, inchoatione omnium partium veræ pietatis: in Christo vero. verò etiam perfectione graduum, hoc est, imputatione perfectæ justitiæ eius per fidem; sicut dicitur: In ipso estis consummati; Christus est nobis factus à Deo sapientia, justitia, sanctificatio, & redemtio.
units.tr: Objection 5. Scripture attributes perfection to the works of the saints. I will praise you, O Lord, with my whole heart. Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations. I have walked before you with a perfect heart. The heart of Asa was perfect all his days. Similar statements about perfection occur everywhere else as well. Therefore, etc. Answer. These and similar sayings speak of the perfection of parts, not of degrees of obedience in the saints, and of sincerity as opposed to hypocrisy and feigned piety. For the saints never attain here the degree of perfection which the law requires. But they have the beginning of complete obedience and submission to God, according to all his commandments. Yet it is not on account of this beginning of their begun obedience, but on account of the perfect righteousness of Christ imputed to them, that they please God, and they are perfect before God: in themselves indeed with the perfection of parts, that is, the beginning of all the parts of true godliness; but in Christ with the perfection of degrees also, that is, by the imputation through faith of his perfect righteousness, as it is said: In him you are made complete; Christ has been made by God to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.

units.la: Inst. Etiam perfectio graduum sanctis tribuitur in scriptura: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Intelligentia perfecti sitis. & alibi passim. Ergo, &c. Resp. In his locis perfecti vocantur, non qui sunt absolute conformes legi, sed qui aliis infirmis plus habent lucis ac certitudinis, & promptitudinis exercitio confirmatæ, ad obtemperandum Deo, & ad repugnandum carnalibus desideriis, & ad ferendam crucem. Sic enim hæc perfectio alibi declaratur. Ut nè simus amplius pueri, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quovis vento doctrinæ. Non quod jam apprehenderim, aut perfectus sim, &c. Nam velle adest mihi, sed ut, quod bonum est, perficiam, non assequor. Proinde hæc perfectio relatiua est, respectum habens, non ad legem divinam, sed ad infirmos.
units.tr: Objection. Perfection of degree is also attributed to the saints in Scripture: We speak wisdom among the perfect. Be perfect in understanding. And elsewhere throughout. Therefore, etc. Answer. In these passages those are called perfect who are not absolutely conformed to the law, but who have more light and certainty than the weak, and who are strengthened by the practice of readiness to obey God, to resist carnal desires and to bear the cross. For this perfection is explained elsewhere in this way: That we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro and carried about by every wind of doctrine. Not that I have already attained, or am already perfect, etc. For the willing is present with me, but how to perform what is good I do not find. Therefore this perfection is relative, having regard not to the divine law but to the weak.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Dauid dicit: A lege tua non declinaui. Custodiui legem tuam. Fecisti justitiam & judicium. Iudica me secundum justitiam tuam, &c. Ergo renati bona sua opera in judicio Dei allegare possunt, tanquam legi perfectè conformia. Resp. Hæc & similia dicta vindicant sanctis in hac vita non conformitatem cum lege, (alioqui repugnarent dictis prius recitatis de imperfectione sanctorum) sed justitiam bonæ conscientiæ, sine qua fides non potest consistere, sicut neque bona conscientia sine fide haberi potest, sicut dicitur: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem & bonam conscientiam, quam repulsa nonnulli fidei naufragium fecerunt. Sancti enim non extimescunt tribunal Dei, & conscientia recte actorum se consolantur, non sane quod eam judicio Dei opponant, aut nullius peccati sibi sint conscii, (hæc enim considerantes clamant: Domine, ne in judicium venias cum servo tuo. Si iniquitates observaueris, Domine, quis consistet?) sed quia serium, & non hypocriticum studium habent obediendi Deo, & certò sciunt, peccata sua tecta & abluta esse sanguine Christi, & inchoatam obedientiam suam Deo propter Christum placere, & præmiis secundum promissionem Euangelij gratuito ab eo ornari.
units.tr: Objection 6. David says: I have not declined from your law. I have kept your law. You have done justice and judgment. Judge me according to your justice, etc. Therefore the reborn can plead their good works before the judgment of God, as being perfectly conformable to the law. Answer. Such sayings as these claim for the saints in this life not conformity with the law (otherwise they would contradict the passages cited earlier about the imperfection of the saints), but the righteousness of a good conscience, without which faith cannot stand, just as a good conscience cannot be had without faith. Thus it is said: Fight the good fight, holding faith and a good conscience, which some, having thrust away, have made shipwreck of faith. The saints do not dread the tribunal of God, and they take comfort in the consciousness of having acted rightly. They do not do this because they set their conscience over against the judgment of God, or because they are conscious of no sin at all (for when they consider these things they cry out: Lord, enter not into judgment with your servant. If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand?), but because they have a earnest and not a hypocritical zeal to obey God, and because they know for certain that their sins are covered and washed away by the blood of Christ, that their obedience, though begun, is pleasing to God for Christ's sake, and that by his gracious promise of the Gospel he adorns it with rewards.

units.la: Obiect. 7. Quisquis natus est ex Deo, peccatum non committit, quoniam semen ipsius in eo manet: nec potest peccare, quia ex Deo natus est. Ergo nova obedientia in renatis perfecta est, & absque peccato esse, (hoc enim etiam Johanni non est ἀναμάρτητον, sine peccato esse, (hoc enim etiam docuerat cap. 1. & 2.) sed non sanctissimos nondum cadere docuerat cap. 1. & 2.) sed non habehabere peccatum regnans, vel in eo perseuerare. Hoc enim in sanctis fidem & pietatem veram excuteret.
units.tr: Objection 7. Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; nor can he sin, because he is born of God. Therefore the new obedience in the reborn is perfect and free from sin (for this is not what John taught in chapters 1 and 2, where he taught that even the holiest still fall). Rather, the meaning is that they do not have sin reigning in them, nor persist in it. For such a thing would overthrow true faith and godliness in the saints. [ἀναμάρτητον]

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXV.
units.tr: QUESTION 115.

units.la: Cur igitur vult Deus legem suam adeo exactè & seuerè praedicari, cum nemo sit in hac vita, qui eam seruare possit?
units.tr: Why then does God will that his law be preached so strictly and severely, when no one in this life is able to keep it?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Primùm, vt in omni vita magis magisque a agnoscamus, quanta sit naturæ ad peccandum propensio, tanto que auidius remissionem peccatorum, & justitiam in Christo b expetamus. Deinde, vt hoc perpetuò agamus, illud semper meditemur, & gratiam Spiritus sancti à Patre imploremus, quo indies magis ac magis ad imaginem Dei renouemur, donec aliquando tandem, postquam ex hac vita decesserimus, propositam nobis perfectionem læti assequamur. a Rom. 3, 20. 1 Ioh. 1, 9. Psal. 32, 5. b Matth. 5, 6. Rom. 7, 24. 1 Corinth. 9, 24. Phil. 3, 12. 13. 14.
units.tr: First, so that in every life we may recognise more and more how great is the natural inclination to sin, and so eagerly seek the forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ. a Second, so that we may constantly act on this, always meditate on it, and implore from the Father the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which we are renewed day by day more and more into the image of God, until at last, after we have departed from this life, we joyfully attain the perfection set before us. a Rom. 3:20. 1 John 1:9. Ps. 32:5. b Matt. 5:6. Rom. 7:24. 1 Cor. 9:24. Phil. 3:12, 13, 14.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Cum de Vsu legis diuinæ quæritur, discrimina partium eius in conspectu haberi debent. Cæremonialium legum Mosaicarum vsus erat: Itaque lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christum, vt ex fide justificaremur.
units.tr: When the use of the divine law is under discussion, the distinctions between its parts must be kept in view. Therefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. The use of the ceremonial laws of Moses was:

units.la: 1. Pædagogia in Christum, & ipsum regnum.
units.tr: 1. To be a schooling in Christ, and a foreshadowing of his kingdom itself.

units.la: 2. Distinctio ecclesiæ Iudaicæ ab aliis gentibus.
units.tr: 2. To distinguish the Jewish Church from the other nations.

units.la: 3. Exercitium pietatis, & testificatio obedientiæ erga legem moralem.
units.tr: 3. To exercise piety and bear witness to obedience towards the moral law.

units.la: 4. Confirmatio Dei. Erant enim quædam ex iis sacramenta, hoc est signa fœderis, & sigilla gratiæ: vt circumcisio & agnus paschalis.
units.tr: 4. To confirm God's covenant. For some of them were sacraments, that is, signs of the covenant and seals of grace, such as circumcision and the Passover lamb.

units.la: Politicarum legum vsus fuit:
units.tr: The use of the civil laws was:

units.la: 1. Vt essent nervi politiæ Mosaicæ.
units.tr: 1. To be the sinews of the Mosaic commonwealth.

units.la: 2. Vt essent typi gubernationis ecclesiæ in regno Christi, quandoquidem principes & reges populi non minus, quàm sacerdotes sustinebant typum Christi pontificis & regis ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 2. To be types of the government of the Church in the kingdom of Christ, since the princes and kings of the people bore the type of Christ, the priest and king of the Church, no less than the priests did.

units.la: Hi vsus vnà cum legibus ipsis cessarunt, postquam cæremoniæ Christi aduentu impletæ & abrogatæ sunt, & politia Mosaica à Romanis euersa est.
units.tr: These uses ceased together with the laws themselves, once the ceremonies were fulfilled and abrogated at the coming of Christ, and the Mosaic polity was overthrown by the Romans.

units.la: Vsus legis moralis diuersi sunt secundum quatuor status hominis.
units.tr: The uses of the moral law differ according to the four states of man.

units.la: I. In natura integra, per peccatum nondum depravata, qualis fuit ante lapsum, erant duo vsus legis diuinæ præcipui.
units.tr: I. In the integral nature, not yet depraved by sin, such as it was before the fall, there were two chief uses of the divine law.

units.la: 1. Integra hominis conformatio cum Deo. Fulgebat enim in mente hominis non lapsi integra legis notitia, eaq; efficiebat omnium inclinationum & actionum rectitudinem seu conformitatem cum voluntate Dei.
units.tr: 1. The complete conformity of man with God. For in the mind of unfallen man there shone a complete knowledge of the law, and this brought about the rectitude, or conformity with the will of God, of all his inclinations and actions.

units.la: 2. Bona conscientia, seu fiducia beneuolentiæ DEI, & spes certa vitæ æternæ. Lex enim ex ordine iustitiæ diuinæ promittit vitam perfecte eam præstantibus. Qui fecerit ea homo, vivet in eis.
units.tr: 2. A good conscience, that is, confidence in the goodwill of God and a sure hope of eternal life. For the law, by the order of divine justice, promises life to those who perfectly perform it: The man who does these things shall live by them.

units.la: II. In natura corrupta, & nondum renata per Spiritum sanctum duo etiam sunt legis vsus.
units.tr: II. In corrupt nature, and not yet regenerated by the Holy Spirit, there are also two uses of the law.

units.la: 1. Conseruatio disciplinæ in ecclesia & extra eam. Lex enim insculpta diuinitus singulorum mentibus, & sonans voce doctorum & magistratus frenat & coercet etiam non renatos, vt vitentnt manifesta scelera, quæ pugnant cum iudicio rectæ rationis etiam in non renatis, & quæ remoueri oportet ante regenerationem. Gentes, quæ legem non habent, naturâ, quæ legis sunt, faciunt, & legem non habentes, sibi ipsis sunt lex, vt qui ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, vna testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus.
units.tr: 1. The preservation of discipline within the Church and outside it. For the law, divinely engraved on the minds of individuals and sounding from the voice of teachers and the magistrate, restrains and curbs even the unregenerate, so that they avoid manifest crimes which are contrary to the judgment of right reason even in the unregenerate, and which must be removed before regeneration. The Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires; having no law, they are a law to themselves, since they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another.

units.la: 2. Agnitio peccati. Lex enim accusat, convincit, & damnat omnes non renatos, quod sint iniusti coram Deo, & rei æternæ damnationis. Scimus autem, quæcunque lex dicit, iis, qui in lege sunt, dicere, vt omne os obturetur, & obnoxius fiat totus mundus condemnationi Dei. Propterea ex operibus legis nulla caro iustificabitur in conspectu eius. Per legem enim agnitio peccati. Peccatum non cognoui, nisi per legem. Nam etiam cupiditatem non nossem, nisi lex dixisset: Non concupisces. Hic vsus, hoc est, agnitio peccati & iudicij diuersus peccatum, per se parit odium Dei & incrementum peccati in non renatis, ac si sint reprobi, præcipitat eos in desperationem, sicut dicitur: Lex iram operatur. Peccatum occasione sumpta genuit in me omnem cupiditatem per illud mandatum, &c. Per accidens vero in electis est præparatio ad conuersionem, Deo nimirum hoc medio cogente eos agnoscere suam iniustitiam, desperare de seipsis, & quærere iustitiam ac vitam in Christo mediatore per fidem. Si data fuisset lex, quæ posset viuificare, verè ex lege iustitia esset. lege esset justitia. Sed conclusit scriptura omnia sub peccatum, ut promissio ex fide Iesu daretur credentibus.
units.tr: 2. The recognition of sin. For the law accuses, convicts and condemns all the unregenerate, in that they are unrighteous before God and liable to eternal damnation. We know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to the condemnation of God. Therefore by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified in his sight. For through the law comes the knowledge of sin. I had not known sin but by the law; for I had not known lust, unless the law had said, Thou shalt not covet. This use, that is, the recognition of sin and the judgment that sin deserves, of itself produces hatred of God and an increase of sin in the unregenerate, and if they are reprobate it casts them into despair, as it is said: The law works wrath. Sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence, etc. Incidentally, however, in the elect it is a preparation for conversion, since God by this means compels them to acknowledge their unrighteousness, to despair of themselves, and to seek righteousness and life in Christ the mediator through faith. If there had been a law given which could give life, verily righteousness should have been by the law. But the Scripture has concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.

units.la: III. In natura per Christum instaurata, seu in renatis, usus legis sunt plures.
units.tr: III. Where nature has been restored by Christ, or in the regenerate, the uses of the law are several.

units.la: 1. Conservatio disciplinae. Etsi enim hic usus principaliter ad non renatos pertinet, ut prius est dictum, qui non amore Dei & justitiae, sed tantum metu poenae & ignominiae a peccatis abstinent, juxta illud:
units.tr: 1. The preservation of discipline. Although this use chiefly concerns the unregenerate, as was said before, who abstain from sins not out of love for God and righteousness, but only from fear of punishment and disgrace, according to the saying:

units.la: Oderunt peccare mali formidine poenae: quia propter infirmitatem & tamen etiam in piis habet locum: quia propter infirmitatem & prauitatem carnis, utile & necesse est, etiam piis proponi minas legis, & poenarum exempla, ut in officio contineantur. Nam Deus etiam sanctis si in atrocia scelera ruant, atroces poenas minatur: Si auerterit se justus a justitia sua, & fecerit iniquitatem, morietur propter illam.
units.tr: The wicked hate to sin for fear of punishment. Yet because of weakness it also has a place in the godly. Because of the weakness and perversity of the flesh, it is useful and necessary that even the godly be set before the threats of the law and examples of punishment, so that they may be kept in their duty. For God threatens even his saints with grievous punishments if they fall into atrocious crimes: If the righteous man turn away from his righteousness and commit iniquity, he shall die for it.

units.la: 2. Agnitio peccati. Hic quoque usus etsi praecipue ad non renatos spectet: tamen ad renatos etiam pertinet. Nam lex etiam renatis est speculum, quo videant defectus & imperfectionem naturae suae, ipsosque ad veram in conspectu Dei humilitatem erudit, ut in vera conversione & fide indies proficiant, & crescente renovatione crescat & invocatio, qua petant magis ac magis Deo ac legi eius conformari. Delector lege Dei, quoad interiorem hominem: sed video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meae, &c. Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? De utroque hoc usu legis, nempe custodia disciplinae, & agnitione peccati, intelligendum est Pauli dictum: Lex est paedagogus noster ad Christum: idque tam in non renatis electis, quam in renatis. Nam illis est praeparatio ad conversionem, his vero est conversionis incrementum, cum fides in cordibus accendi aut consistere non possit, nisi vitentur lapsus contra conscientiam: Nemo vos seducat, qui committit peccatum, ex diabolo est.
units.tr: 2. The knowledge of sin. Although this use chiefly concerns the unregenerate, it also pertains to the regenerate. For the law is a mirror to the regenerate also, in which they see the defects and imperfection of their nature, and it teaches them true humility before the face of God, so that they may make progress in true conversion and faith day by day, and as renewal grows, prayer grows too, by which they seek more and more to be conformed to God and to his law. I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, etc. O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death? The saying of Paul, The law is our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, must be understood of both these uses of the law, namely the keeping of discipline and the knowledge of sin, and this holds for the elect who are unregenerate as well as for the regenerate. For to the former it is a preparation for conversion, but to the latter it is an increase of conversion, since faith cannot be kindled in hearts or remain there unless sins against conscience are avoided: Let no one deceive you; he who commits sin is of the devil.

units.la: 3. Norma cultus divini, & vitae Christianae. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum Domine, & lumen semitis meis. Indam legem meam mentibus eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam eam, ut in statutis meis ambulent, &c. Hic usus proprius est renatorum. Etsi enim non renatis etiam est regula actionum ante conversionem: non tamen eis est regula cultus & gratitudinis erga Deum, ut renatis.
units.tr: 3. The rule of divine worship and of the Christian life. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, O Lord, and a light unto my paths. I will put my law in their minds, and write it in their hearts, that they may walk in my statutes, etc. This use is proper to the regenerate. For although the law is also a rule of actions for the unregenerate before conversion, it is not a rule of worship and of gratitude towards God for them, as it is for the regenerate.

units.la: 4. Declaratio legis tradita ecclesiae, docet, quod sit Deus, & qualis sit.
units.tr: 4. The declaration of the law delivered to the Church teaches what God is and what kind of being he is.

units.la: 5. Vox legis in ecclesia sonans, euidens testimonium est, monstrans, quae sit vera ecclesia, & quae vera religio in mundo. Nam in sola ecclesia lex integra, & rectè intellecta traditur. Omnes verò aliæ sectæ manifestorum errorum ac flagitiorum approbatione, variis modis eam corrumpunt.
units.tr: 5. The voice of the law sounding in the Church is clear testimony, showing which is the true Church and which is the true religion in the world. For the whole law, rightly understood, is delivered only in the Church. All other sects, by approving manifest errors and wickednesses, corrupt it in various ways.

units.la: 6. Est commonefactio de imagine Dei in homine, seu testimonium de præstantia naturæ humanæ ante lapsum, & justitiæ originalis in Adamo amissæ, & beneficij in Christo recuperati.
units.tr: 6. It is a reminder of the image of God in man, or a testimony to the excellence of human nature before the fall, and of the original righteousness lost in Adam and the benefit recovered in Christ.

units.la: 7. Est testimonium de futura vita æterna, in qua demum legem perfectè implebimus. Est enim lex lata, vt ab hominibus seruetur. At non seruatur in hac vita. Restat ergo vita alia, in qua seruetur.
units.tr: 7. There is testimony concerning the future eternal life, in which at last we shall fully keep the law. For the law is given so that men may keep it. But it is not kept in this life. Another life therefore remains, in which it will be kept.

units.la: IV. In natura perfectè instaurata & glorificata post hanc vitam etsi concio legis & totum ministerium cessabit: manebit tamen notitia legis, & fulgebit perfecta eius obedientia, & cum Deo conformitas in electis. Erunt ergo tunc iidem vsus, qui prius in natura integra fuerunt ante lapsum.
units.tr: In nature perfectly restored and glorified after this life, the preaching of the law and the whole ministry will cease, yet the knowledge of the law will remain, its perfect obedience will shine forth, and the elect will be in conformity with God. There will therefore be the same uses then as there were in whole nature before the fall.

units.la: Argumenta Antinomorum, Libertinorum, & similium fanaticorum quod decalogus non sit docendus in Ecclesia Christiana.
units.tr: Arguments of the Antinomians, Libertines, and similar fanatics that the Decalogue should not be taught in the Christian Church.

units.la: Obiect.1. Quod non potest seruari, inutiliter docetur. Lex non potest seruari. Inutiliter ergo docetur in Ecclesia Christiana. Resp.1. Est fallacia non causæ. Nam impossibilitas obedientiæ percepta legis in hac infirmitate naturæ, non est sufficiens causa, cur inutilis judicari debeat concio legis in ecclesia, cum possint esse, & revera sint aliæ causæ, cur non modo vtile, sed etiam necessarium sit legem docere. Ostensum est enim multos esse vsus legis etiam in renatis. Non igitur sublato vno fine seu vsu, etiam reliquos tolli necesse est. Si seruari perfectè non potest, saltem docenda ideo est, vt imperfectionem illam, & defectus agnoscamus, vt tanto avidius remissionem peccatorum & justitiam in Christo expectamus: tantoque alacrius ad metam & perfectionem propositam nobis in Christo contendamus. 2. Est etiam fallacia à secundum quid. Legem enim aliquatenus seruari posse ante renatis, paulo ante est demonstratum. Quare minor simpliciter intellecta, est falsa.
units.tr: Objection 1. What cannot be kept is taught to no purpose. The law cannot be kept. Therefore it is taught to no purpose in the Christian Church. Answer 1. This is the fallacy of a false cause. For the impossibility of obedience, as perceived in the law given our weak nature, is not a sufficient reason for judging the preaching of the law in the church useless. There can be, and indeed there are, other reasons why it is not only useful but necessary to teach the law. For it has been shown that the law has many uses, even in the regenerate. So when one end or use is removed, the others do not necessarily go with it. If it cannot be kept perfectly, it must still be taught, so that we may recognise that imperfection and those defects, and so that we may the more eagerly look for forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ, and strive the more zealously toward the goal and perfection set before us in Christ. 2. It is also the fallacy of a qualified statement (a secundum quid). For it was demonstrated a little earlier that the law can be kept to some extent by the regenerate. So the minor premise, taken absolutely, is false.

units.la: Obiect.2. Qui præcipit impossibilia, inutilia præcipit. Deus in lege præcipit impossibilia. Præcipit ergo inutilia: proinde lex est inutilis. Resp. Idem fere argumentum cum priore, ac responsio est ad maiorem: Inutilia præcipit, qui præcipit impossibilia: scilicet 1. si sint impossibilia simpliciter. 2. si semper sint impossibilia. 3. si non alij sunt vsus istius præceptionis, quam vt perfectè fiant quæ præcipræcipiuntur. Fines autem plures esse, propter quos Deus legem præcipiat, & doceri velit in ecclesia, prius ostensum est. Rursus ergo fallacia est non causæ vt causæ.
units.tr: Objection 2. He who commands impossibilities commands useless things. God in the law commands impossibilities. Therefore he commands useless things, and so the law is useless. Answer: this is almost the same argument as the former, and the answer is to the major premise. He commands useless things who commands impossibilities: namely, 1. if they are impossible absolutely; 2. if they are always impossible; 3. if that command has no other use than that the things commanded be done perfectly. But that God has several ends for which he commands the law and wishes it taught in the church has been shown before. Again, then, this is the fallacy of taking a non-cause as a cause.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Quod Deus nobis in hac vita non vult dare, & nos consequi non possumus, id non debemus expetere. Perfectam legis impletionem Deus in hac vita nobis non vult dare. Frustra ergo eam expetimus, & ad eam annitimur per legis doctrinam. Resp. ad maiorem. Non debemus expetere, quod nobis Deus non vult dare, scilicet nisi ipse iubeat illud expetere, & sint graues expetendi causæ. Iubet autem Deus nos expetere in hac vita, ac desiderare perfectam legis impletionem: idque 1. Quia in desiderantibus vult illam tandem efficere, & nobis post hanc vitam dare, si vere & ex animo hic desideremus. 2. Vt iam proficiamus in pietate, & studium conformandi vitam ad legis diuinæ præscriptum indies magis ac magis accendatur in nobis & confirmetur. 3. Vt hoc desiderio legis implendæ nos in pœnitentia atque obedientia exerceat.
units.tr: Objection 3. What God does not wish to give us in this life, and what we cannot attain, we ought not to seek. God does not wish to give us the perfect fulfilment of the law in this life. Therefore we seek it in vain, and strive for it through the teaching of the law. Answer to the major. We ought not to seek what God does not wish to give us, namely unless he himself bids us seek it and there are weighty reasons for seeking it. But God bids us seek and desire in this life the perfect fulfilment of the law, and he does so for these reasons: 1. Because he wishes to bring it about in those who desire it, and to give it to us after this life, if we desire it here truly and from the heart. 2. So that we may now advance in godliness, and the zeal to shape our life according to the prescript of the divine law may be kindled and strengthened in us more and more each day. 3. So that by this desire to fulfil the law he may train us in repentance and obedience.

units.la: Obj. 4. Christus non est legislator. Ergo nec ministri eius debent docere legem. Resp. ad antecedens. Non est legislator Christus, quod principale officium mediatoris attinet: fuit vero & est legislator, 1. quatenus vt mediator fuit legis repurgator & instaurator, non quidem principaliter, sed vt principales mediatoris partes, videlicet reconciliationem, & saluationem generis humani efficere posset. De ministris euangelij, est eadem responsio: siquidem illi non aliam, quam Christus tradidit doctrinam, ecclesiæ proponere debent.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Christ is not a lawgiver. Therefore neither should his ministers teach the law. Answer to the antecedent. Christ is not a lawgiver in respect of the principal office of mediator; but he was and is a lawgiver: 1. insofar as, as mediator, he was the restorer and renewer of the law, not principally, but so that he might accomplish the chief parts of the mediator's work, namely the reconciliation and salvation of the human race. The answer is the same concerning the ministers of the gospel: for they ought to set before the church no other doctrine than the one Christ handed down.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Qui legi per pœnam satisfecit, non obligatur ad obedientiam, ex regula: Lex obligat aut ad obedientiam, aut ad pœnam, non simul ad utrumque. At nos per Christi pœnam satisfecimus legi. Non ergo obligamur amplius ad obedientiam legi præstandam. Resp. per distinctionem maioris. 1. Qui satisfecit per pœnam, non obligatur ad obedientiam, nempe eandem illam, propter cuius omissionem pœnas luit: obligatur vero denuo ad obedientiam legi præstandam, vel certe ad nouam pœnam. 2. Qui per pœnam non suam, sed alienam legi satisfecit, & in gratiam à Deo sine sua satisfactione receptus est, is etiamsi non ad satisfactionem pro peccatis: tamen ad gratitudinem redemtori præstandam lege obligatur. Postquam ergo Christus morte sua pro peccatis nostris satisfecit, nos quidem non ad præteriti, sed tamen ad futuri temporis obedientiam præstandam obligamur, idque gratitudinis ergo, pro liberationis beneficio nobis exhibito. Qui mortuus est, liber est à peccato. Vno pro omnibus mortuo, omnes sunt mortui: & pro omnibus mortuus est, vt qui viuunt, posthac non sibi viuant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est, & resurrexit.
units.tr: Objection 5. He who has satisfied the law by punishment is not bound to obedience, by the rule: The law binds either to obedience or to punishment, not to both at once. But we have satisfied the law through Christ's punishment. Therefore we are no longer bound to render obedience to the law. Answer, by distinguishing the major. 1. He who has satisfied by punishment is not bound to that same obedience whose omission he has paid for; but he is bound again to render obedience to the law, or at least to a new punishment. 2. He who has satisfied the law not by his own but by another's punishment, and has been received into favour by God without any satisfaction of his own, is bound by the law to render gratitude to his Redeemer, even if not to satisfaction for sins. Therefore, since Christ by his death satisfied for our sins, we are bound not to obedience for past time but to obedience for future time, and that out of gratitude for the benefit of liberation shown to us. He who has died is free from sin. One died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Christiani non reguntur lege, sed spiritu regenerationis, iuxta dictum: Iusto non est lex posita. Ergo non est docenda inter Christianos. Resp. ad antecedens. Pii non reguntur, hoc est, non coguntur lege & metu poenæ ad disciplinam sicut impii: sed tamen reguntur, hoc est, docentur lege, qui cultus Deo placeant: & Spiritus sanctus vtitur doctrina legis ad flectendos ipsos ad veram & spontaneam obedientiam. Manet ergo doctrina, atque etiam obligatio legis, etsi condemnatio & coactio tollatur. Nam ad hoc ipsum obligamur, vt sit quam maxime spontanea obedientia. Debitores sumus non carni, vt secundum carnem viuamus, sed spiritui. Iusto autem non est lex posita, nempe condemnans eum.
units.tr: Objection 6. Christians are not governed by the law but by the spirit of regeneration, according to the saying: "The law is not laid down for the righteous." Therefore it is not to be taught among Christians. Answer to the antecedent: the godly are not governed, that is, not compelled by the law and fear of punishment as the ungodly are; but they are governed, that is, taught by the law, what worship pleases God; and the Holy Spirit uses the teaching of the law to bend them to true and willing obedience. The doctrine therefore remains, and also the obligation of the law, even though condemnation and coercion are removed. For we are obliged to this very thing, that our obedience be as willing as possible. "We are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh, but to the Spirit." "But the law is not laid down for the righteous," namely to condemn him.

units.la: Obiect. 7. Non sumus sub lege, sed sub gratia. Ergo lex non obligat. Resp. Est fallacia figuræ dictionis: quia non esse sub lege, non est, non teneri obedientia legis, sed liberatum esse à maledictione & coactione legis: sicut sub gratia esse, est gratia Christi iustificatum & regeneratum esse. Inst. Qui tenentur legem præstare, nec præstant, sunt damnationi obnoxii. Nos vero non sumus obnoxii damnationi. Nulla enim est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Ergo non tenemur præstare legem.
units.tr: Objection 7. "We are not under the law but under grace." Therefore the law does not bind. Answer. This is a fallacy of ambiguous wording, because not to be under the law is not to be free from the duty of obeying the law, but to be freed from the curse and compulsion of the law; just as to be under grace is to be justified and regenerated by the grace of Christ. Instance. Those who are bound to fulfil the law, and do not, are liable to condemnation. But we are not liable to condemnation. For there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Therefore we are not bound to fulfil the law.

units.la: Resp. ad maiorem, quæ vera est, 1. si deberet legem præstare in seipso: nos autem tenemur præstare & præstamus legem in Christo. 2. Etiamsi præstare deberet in seipso, nempe semper, seu omni tempore perfecte: nos tamen in hac vita in nobis ipsis non tenemur perfecte legem præstare, sed tantum inchoare obedientiam eius secundum omnia præcepta. In vita demum perfecta ad perfectionem obligabimur.
units.tr: Answer to the major, which is true: 1. if he were bound to fulfil the law in himself; but we are bound to fulfil the law in Christ, and we do fulfil it. 2. Even if he were bound to fulfil it in himself, namely always, or perfectly at all times, yet we in this life are not bound to fulfil the law perfectly in ourselves, but only to begin its obedience according to all its precepts. In the perfect life we shall be bound to perfection.

units.la: Obiect. 8. Lex est litera occidens, & ministerium condemnationis. Christianis nulla est condemnatio. Ergo ad Christianos lex non pertinet. Resp. 1. Est fallacia accidentis. Lex enim est litera occidens, non per se, sed vitio hominum; qui quanto magis vident dissimilitudinem inter se & legem; tanto magis desperant de salute, & occiduntur. 2. Lex sola sine euangelio, est litera, hoc est, doctrina tantum docens, postulans obedientiam, denuncians iram Dei & mortem non obtemperantibus, non efficiens obedientiam spiritualem, quam requirit. Sed cum euangelio, quod est spiritus, coniuncta, ipsa quoq; incipit fieri spiritus, hoc est, efficax esse in piis: quia renati sponte obedire legi incipiunt. Lex igitur est litera. 1. sola sine euangelio. 2 respectu naturæ non renatæ. Contra euangelium est spiritus, hoc est ministerium, per quod datur Spiritus sanctus efficiens spiritualem obedientiam. non quod omnes, qui audiunt, accipiant Spiritum sanctum, & regenerentur, sed quia per id accipitur fides, qua corda viuificantur, vt legi obedire incipiant. Non ergo hinc sequitur, legem non amplius esse in ecclesia docendam. Dicit enim Christus, se venisse ad legem non soluendam, sed implendam. Et Paulus, per fidem (inquit) stabilimus legem. Impleuit vero legem Christus dupliciter, faciendo & patiendo: dum nimirum fuit in se justus, nec violauit vlla in parte legem, & pro nobis partim fecit ea, quæ non tenebatur, partim pœnam sustinuit. In nobis itidem dupliciter doctrina & spiritu, vt supra de abrogatione legis plenius est declaratum.
units.tr: Objection 8. "The law is the letter that kills, and the ministry of condemnation." No condemnation is for Christians. Therefore the law does not pertain to Christians. Answer 1. This is the fallacy of accident. For the law is the letter that kills, not in itself, but through the fault of men, who, the more they see their unlikeness to the law, the more they despair of salvation and are killed. 2. The law alone, without the gospel, is letter: that is, a doctrine that only teaches, demands obedience, threatens God's wrath and death to those who do not obey, and does not produce the spiritual obedience it requires. But joined with the gospel, which is spirit, it too begins to become spirit, that is, to be effective in the godly, because the regenerate begin to obey the law willingly. The law is therefore letter: 1. when alone, without the gospel; 2. with respect to unregenerate nature. On the other hand, "the gospel is spirit," that is, the ministry through which the Holy Spirit is given, effecting spiritual obedience. This is not because all who hear receive the Holy Spirit and are regenerated, but because through it faith is received, by which hearts are quickened to begin to obey the law. It does not follow from this that the law is no longer to be taught in the church. For Christ says that he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5). And Paul: "through faith, we establish the law" (Rom. 3). Christ fulfilled the law in two ways, by doing and by suffering: namely, while he was righteous in himself and violated no part of the law, and for us partly did those things which he was not bound to do, and partly endured the penalty. In us likewise, in two ways, by doctrine and by the Spirit, as has been more fully explained above concerning the abrogation of the law.

units.la: Obiect.9. Quod auget peccata, non est docendum in ecclesia. Lex auget peccatum. Ergo non est docenda. R.1. Est fallacia accidentis in minore. Lex auget peccatum ex accidenti, propter prauitatem hominum, idque dupliciter. Primò, quia natura hominum est deprauata, & auersa à Deo, vt quod sciunt Deo placere, non faciant: contra, quod sciunt ab eo prohiberi, id expectent, & summa voluntate perpetrent. Deinde, quia iram operatur, quanto homines, quanto magis ex lege agnoscunt sua peccata & pœnas, quas sunt meriti, tanto magis fremunt aduersus Deũ, auertantur eum, & ruunt in desperationem. Per se vero lex efficit justitiam, conformitatem cum Deo, amorem Dei, &c. Lex etiam per se auget peccatum, sed aliter accepto vocabulo augendi, hoc est, ostendit nobis, & facit, vt agnoscamus magnitudinem & multitudinem peccatorum, non autem ita auget peccatum, vt quod in se minus est, maius & grauius fiat. Sic ambiguum est medium, & quatuor terminis sunt in argumento.
units.tr: Objection 9. What increases sin should not be taught in the Church. The law increases sin. Therefore it should not be taught. Answer: this is the fallacy of accident in the minor premise. The law increases sin accidentally, on account of the perversity of men, and this in two ways. First, because human nature is corrupt and turned away from God, so that they do not do what they know pleases God, but on the contrary they long for what they know is forbidden by him, and commit it with the utmost eagerness. Second, because the law works wrath: the more men recognise from the law their sins and the punishments they deserve, the more they rage against God, turn away from him, and fall into despair. In itself, however, the law produces righteousness, conformity to God, the love of God, and so on. The law also increases sin in itself, but in a different sense of the word "increase": that is, it shows us, and causes us to recognise, the greatness and number of our sins; it does not so increase sin that what is in itself smaller becomes greater and more grievous. Thus the middle term is ambiguous, and there are four terms in the argument.

units.la: Obiect.10. Lex non est necessaria ad salutem. Ergo non debet doceri in ecclesia. Resp. Est fallacia à dicto secundum quid, vt simpliciter. Etsi doctrina legis non est necessaria, vt per eius obedientiam seruemur; est tamen necessaria propter alios vsus, vt prius est declaratum.
units.tr: Objection 10. The law is not necessary for salvation. Therefore it should not be taught in the Church. Answer: this is the fallacy of arguing from what is said in a qualified sense to what is said absolutely. Although the teaching of the law is not necessary for us to be saved by obeying it, it is nevertheless necessary for its other uses, as has been explained above.

units.la: Obiect. 11. Omnia habemus in Christo, juxta dicta: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus. In ipso sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ ac cognitionis abscondite. In ipso estis consummati.
units.tr: Objection 11. We have all things in Christ, according to the sayings: "Of his fulness have all we received." "In him are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." "In him you are made complete."

units.la: Ergo non est retrogrediendum à Christo ad Mosen, nec est opus lege in ecclesia Christi. Resp. Est fallacia consequentis à positione totius ad negationem partis. Tota sapientia & scientia seu doctrina nobis à Christo tradita, est sufficiens & necessaria ecclesiæ. Pars verò illius doctrinæ etiam est lex moralis, quia Christus non tantum fidem, sed pœnitentiam in nomine suo prædicari jussit. In perfecta igitur sapientia non excluditur, sed potius includitur legis doctrina.
units.tr: Therefore we must not go back from Christ to Moses, and there is no need for the law in the Church of Christ. Answer: this is the fallacy of inferring the denial of a part from the affirmation of the whole. The whole wisdom, knowledge and teaching delivered to us by Christ is sufficient and necessary for the Church. Part of that teaching, however, is also the moral law, since Christ commanded that not only faith but repentance be preached in his name. Therefore the teaching of the law is not excluded from perfect wisdom but rather included in it.

units.la: DE PRECATIONE.
units.tr: ON PRAYER.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXVI.
units.tr: QUESTION CXVI.

units.la: Quare Christianis necessaria est precatio?
units.tr: Why is prayer necessary for Christians?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Quia præcipua pars est eius, quam Deus à nobis postulat a, gratitudinis. Tum quia illis tantum suam gratiam & Spiritum sanctum Deus largitur, qui veris gemitibus continenter hæc ab eo petunt, & pro iis ipsi gratias b agunt.
units.tr: Because it is the chief part of the gratitude a that God requires of us. Also because God bestows his grace and the Holy Spirit only on those who continually ask for these things from him with true sighs, and give thanks to him for them b.

units.la: a Psal. 50, 40. b Matth. 7, 7. Luc. 11, 9. Matth. 13, 12.
units.tr: a Ps. 50:15. b Matt. 7:7; Luke 11:9; Matt. 13:12.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Multæ de Precatione quæri possunt: sed præcipuæ quæstiones sunt quatuor: I. II. Quid sit precatio. III. Quare sit necessaria. IV. Qua ad eam requirantur. V. De formula precationis.
units.tr: Many questions can be asked about prayer, but the principal ones are four: I. II. What prayer is. III. Why it is necessary. IV. What is required for it. V. On the form of prayer.

units.la: Duæ priores huc pertinent: tertia ad quæst. CXVII. quarta ad CXVIII.
units.tr: The first two belong here; the third is taken up in Question CXVII, and the fourth in Question CXVIII.

units.la: I. Quid sit precatio, & quas habeat species.
units.tr: I. What prayer is, and what kinds it has.

units.la: Precatio est invocatio veri Dei, profecta ex agnitione ac sensu indigentiæ nostræ, & desiderio beneficentiæ divinæ, in vera cordis conversione, & fiducia promissionis gratiæ, propter Christum mediatorem petens à Deo bona necessaria, corporalia ac spiritualia, vel pro his acceptis ei gratias agens. Genus est invocatio seu adoratio. Adoratio sæpe sumitur pro toto cultu. Quem enim adoramus, eum pro vero Deo habemus. Precatio est species seu pars invocationis: Est enim invocare Deum, à vero Deo cum animo tum corpori necessaria petere, & pro acceptis gratias agere. Hoc ponitur pro ipso genere. Species precationis sunt duæ: petitio & gratiarum actio. Petitio est precatio petens à Deo bona tum animi tum corporis necessaria. Gratiarum actio est precatio agnoscens & celebrans beneficia à Deo accepta, & obligans se ad gratitudinem Deo placentem. Gratitudo in genere, est agnitio & professio, quale & quantum sit beneficium acceptum, & obligatio ad mutua, honesta, possibilia officia. Complectitur itaque precatio veritatem & justitiam.
units.tr: Prayer is the invocation of the true God, arising from knowledge and a sense of our need and a desire for the divine goodness, in a true conversion of heart and trust in the promise of grace, asking of God for the good things we need, both bodily and spiritual, on account of Christ the Mediator, or giving thanks to him for those already received. The genus is invocation or worship. Worship is often taken for the whole of religious service, for whom we worship, we hold to be the true God. Prayer is a species or part of invocation: to invoke God is to ask of the true God what we need both in soul and in body, and to give thanks for what we have received. Here the word stands for the genus itself. There are two species of prayer: request and thanksgiving. Request is prayer asking God for the good things needed both of soul and of body. Thanksgiving is prayer acknowledging and celebrating the benefits received from God, and binding oneself to a gratitude that pleases God. Gratitude in general is the acknowledgement and profession of what kind and how great a benefit has been received, and an obligation to mutual, honourable and possible duties. Prayer therefore embraces truth and justice.

units.la: Precationis quatuor species recitantur à Paulo. 1. δεήσεις, deprecationes malorum. 2. ἐντεύξεις, bonorum petitiones. 3. προσευχαί, intercessiones pro aliis. 4. εὐχαριστίαι, gratiarum actiones pro acceptis bonis & depulsis malis. Hæc distinctio est sumta à fine.
units.tr: Paul lists four kinds of prayer: 1. δεήσεις [deēseis], supplications against evils; 2. ἐντεύξεις [enteuxeis], petitions for good things; 3. προσευχαί [proseuchai], intercessions for others; 4. εὐχαριστίαι [eucharistiai], thanksgivings for good things received and evils averted. This division is taken from the end in view.

units.la: Distinguitur etiam precatio ex circumstantiis personæ & loci, in privatam & publicam. Privata est colloquium fidelis animi cum Deo, petentis seorsum sibi vel aliis certa bona, vel pro acceptis gratias agens. Hæc verbis & locis non est alligata. Sæpe enim cor anxium pro verbis tantum suspiria & gemitus fundit, & Apostolus jubet viros precari quovis loco & puras manus attollere. Publica est, quæ à tota ecclesia in cœtu ad Deum concipitur certis verbis ministro præeunte, ut in congressibus publicis fieri debet. Ad hanc lingua requiritur. Ideo Christus dixit: Cum precamini, dicite, Pater noster, &c. Ad hoc enim lingua præcipuè est condita, ut Deus per eam celebretur: & ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Denique alij etiam ad Deum celebrandum sunt invitandi.
units.tr: Prayer is also distinguished, according to the circumstances of person and place, into private and public. Private prayer is the conversation of a faithful soul with God, asking for certain goods for oneself or others when alone, or giving thanks for what has been received. This is not bound to words or places: often an anxious heart pours out only sighs and groans without words, and the Apostle bids men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands. Public prayer is that which is offered to God by the whole Church assembled, in set words, with the minister leading, as should be done in public gatherings. Speech is required for this; therefore Christ said: When you pray, say, Our Father, etc. For speech was chiefly made for this purpose, that God may be praised by it, and out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Finally, others also must be invited to praise God.

units.la: II. Quare Christianis precatio sit necessaria.
units.tr: II. Why prayer is necessary for Christians.

units.la: Causæ, cur precatio sit necessaria, sunt hæ: 1. Mandatum Dei: quia Deus præcepit, ut se invocemus, & hoc modo principaliter vult à nobis coli & celebrari. Invoca me in die tribulationis, & ego eripiam te. Petite, & dabitur vobis. Cum precamini, dicite: Pater noster, &c. 2. Necessitas & indigentia nostra. Nam bona nobis ad salutem necessaria non consequimur à Deo, nisi ea ab ipso petamus. Solis enim petentibus ea promisit. Unde liquet precationem nobis tam esse necessariam, quàm mendico est necessaria mendicatio eleemosynæ.
units.tr: The reasons why prayer is necessary are these: 1. The command of God: because God has commanded that we call upon him, and in this way he chiefly wills to be worshipped and praised by us. Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. Ask, and it will be given you. When you pray, say: Our Father, etc. 2. Our necessity and need. For we do not obtain from God the good things necessary for salvation unless we ask for them from him. He has promised them only to those who ask. Hence it is clear that prayer is as necessary to us as begging is to a beggar who needs alms.

units.la: Quod verò de necessitate precationis dicitur, idem de necessitate gratiarum actionis intelligendum est. Nam sine gratiarum actione data amittimus, & danda necessaria non accipimus. Ac necessitas utriusque facile patebit, sive effectus, sive causam fidei atque adeo ipsam fidem consideremus. In nemine fides accenditur vel augetur, qui eam non desiderat & petit. Nemo fidem habet, qui pro ea non agit gratias: qui vera fide sunt prædití, illi gratiam divinam gustant: qui gratiam divinam degustarunt, illi pro ea Domino sese gratos præbent, eamque magis ac magis expetunt. Charitas DEI diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Hic ipse etiam Spiritus sanctus precibus impetratur. Nulli enim datur, nisi qui eum desiderat & petit.
units.tr: What is said about the necessity of prayer should be understood equally of the necessity of thanksgiving. For without thanksgiving we lose what has been given, and we do not receive what must be given. The necessity of both will be easily seen, whether we consider the effects or the cause of faith, and indeed faith itself. Faith is not kindled or increased in anyone who does not desire and ask for it. No one has faith who does not give thanks for it; those who have been endowed with true faith taste the divine grace; those who have tasted the divine grace show themselves grateful to the Lord for it and seek it more and more. The love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. This same Holy Spirit is also obtained by prayers. For he is given to no one except those who desire and ask for him.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Atqui etiam impios videmus accipere multa dona Spiritus sancti, qui tamen no petunt. Ergo non tantum petentes accipiunt. Resp. Multa quidem dona impij accipiunt, sed non principalia, nec propria electorum, qualia sunt fides, pœnitentia & conuersio, remissio peccatorum, regeneratio. Deinde, quæ accipiunt impij dona, non sunt eis salutaria: sed in perniciem cedunt. Inst. Infantes non petunt: & tamen accipiunt Spiritum sanctum. Ergo, &c. Resp. Spiritus sanctus non datur nisi petentibus eum, scilicet adultis, qui possunt eum petere. Sed & infantes eum petunt, suo modo, potentia videlicet, hoc est, inclinationem habent ad eum petendum: sicut credunt suo modo, hoc est, inclinationem habent ad fidem. Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem tuam.
units.tr: Objection 1. Yet we see that even the ungodly receive many gifts of the Holy Spirit, though they do not ask. Therefore not only those who ask receive. Answer. The ungodly do indeed receive many gifts, but not the principal ones, nor those proper to the elect, such as faith, repentance and conversion, forgiveness of sins, regeneration. Further, the gifts the ungodly receive are not salutary for them, but turn to their destruction. Instance. Infants do not ask, and yet they receive the Holy Spirit. Therefore, etc. Answer. The Holy Spirit is given only to those who ask for him, that is, to adults, who can ask. But infants also ask for him in their own way, namely potentially: that is, they have an inclination to ask for him, just as they believe in their own way, that is, they have an inclination to faith. Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise.

units.la: Obiect 2. Effectus non est prior sua causa. Preces sunt effectus Spiritus sancti: siquidem nemo potest Spiritum sanctum petere, qui ipsum non habet, & ipse solus efficit preces in nobis. Non igitur precibus accipitur Spiritus sanctus, sed est in nobis ante preces, & per consequens non demum datur petentibus. Resp. Effectus non est prior sua causa, scilicet ordine & natura, tamen potest esse simul. Sic Spiritus sanctus & eius petitio sunt simul tempore in nobis, etsi non simul natura. Est enim Spiritus sanctus in nobis natura ante preces: quia tum demum incipimus eum desiderare & à Deo petere, cum nobis datur. Tempore autem simul est cum precibus. Simul atque enim datur, incipimus desiderare eius præsentiam: & simul ac desideratur & petitur, etiam datur: hoc est, eodem momento Deus efficit in nobis desiderium Spiritus sancti, & dat Spiritum sanctum. Et quidem desiderium efficit mandando, ut petamus, & efficiens desiderium simul dat eum petentibus. Neque enim ita in nobis Deus agit, ut cum radius ex sole descendit in dolium: hoc est, sine sensu nostro. Hoc igitur donum tale est, quod simul datur, accipitur & petitur. Potest etiam distingui inter initium & incrementum, quia hoc petere non possumus, nisi illud prius habeamus. Nemo enim desiderat incrementa spiritus, nisi qui habet eius initium. Sed prior solutio sufficit. Quod enim à Christo dicitur: Quanto magis Pater vester cœlestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus, non tantum de incremento, sed etiam de initio donorum intelligi debet.
units.tr: Objection 2. An effect is not prior to its cause. Prayers are an effect of the Holy Spirit, since no one can ask for the Holy Spirit who does not already have him, and he alone produces prayers in us. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not received by prayers, but is in us before prayers, and consequently is not given at last to those who ask. Answer. An effect is not prior to its cause in order and nature, yet it can be simultaneous with it. So the Holy Spirit and our asking for him are simultaneous in us in time, though not simultaneous in nature. For the Holy Spirit is in us before prayer in nature, because we begin to desire him and ask for him from God only when he has been given to us. But in time he is simultaneous with prayer. For as soon as he is given, we begin to desire his presence; and as soon as he is desired and asked for, he is also given: that is, in the same moment God produces in us the desire for the Holy Spirit and gives the Holy Spirit. God produces the desire by commanding us to ask, and by producing the desire he at the same time gives him to those who ask. For God does not act in us as a ray descends from the sun into a cask, that is, without our perception. This gift, then, is such that it is given, received and asked for at the same time. One may also distinguish between beginning and increase, since we cannot ask for the increase unless we already have the beginning. For no one desires increase of the Spirit unless he has his beginning. But the former answer is sufficient. For what Christ says: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask, should be understood not only of the increase but also of the beginning of the gifts.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXVII. Qua ad eam precationem requiruntur, quæ Deo placeat, quaque ab ipso exaudiatur?
units.tr: QUESTION 117. What is required in prayer for it to please God and be heard by him?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Vt à solo vero Deo, qui se in verbo suo patefecit a, omnia, quæ à se peti jussit b, vero cordis affectu petamus c, ex intimo nostræ indigentiæ ac miseriæ sensu d, nos in conspectu diuinæ Maiestatis, supplices abijciamus e, huic firmo fundamento innitamur f, nos à DEO, quanquam indignos, propter CHRISTVM tamen certo exaudiri g, quemadmodum nobis in suo verbo promisit h.
units.tr: We must pray to the one true God, who has revealed himself in his word a, for all the things he has commanded us to ask b, with a sincere affection of heart c, out of a deep sense of our need and misery d. We must humbly cast ourselves down in the sight of the divine majesty e, relying on this firm foundation f: that although we are unworthy, we will certainly be heard by God for Christ's sake g, as he has promised us in his word h.

a Rev. 2:9. John 4:22. b Rom. 8:26. 1 John 5:14. James 1:5. c John 4:14. Ps. 145:18. d 2 Chron. 20:12. e Ps. 2:11, and 34:19. Isa. 66:2. f Rom. 10:14. James 1:6. g John 14:13, and 16:23. Dan. 9:17. h Matt. 7:8. Ps. 27:8.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXVIII. Quæ sunt ea, quæ à se peti iubet?
units.tr: QUESTION 118. What are the things he commands us to ask for?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Omnia tum animæ tum corpori necessaria a, quæ Dominus noster Iesus Christus, ea precatione, quam nos ipse docuit, complexus est.
units.tr: All things necessary both for the soul and for the body, which our Lord Jesus Christ included in the prayer that he himself taught us.

units.la: a Iacob.1,17. Matth. 6,33.
units.tr: a James 1:17. Matt. 6:33.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Conditiones bonæ precationis sunt:
units.tr: The conditions of good prayer are these:

units.la: 1. Directio ad verum Deum, seu, vt inuocetur verus Deus patefactus in ecclesia, per verbum propheticum & apostolicum, & per opera creationis, conseruationis & redemptionis ecclesiæ. Is autem verus Deus est æternus Pater, & Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Sicut accepimus, (inquit Basilius) ita baptizati sumus, & sicut baptizati sumus, ita credimus, & sicut credimus, ita adoramus Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: 1. Direction to the true God, that is, that the true God be called upon, as he has been made known in the Church through the prophetic and apostolic word, and through his works of creation, preservation and redemption of the Church. This true God is the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. As we have received, (says Basil) so we have been baptized, and as we have been baptized, so we believe, and as we believe, so we worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 2. Cogitatio mandati diuini. Nam sine Dei mandato dubitamus de exauditione. Meos verò incuens in Dei mandatum, certo statuit [?] fluit, preces suas Deo acceptas esse, quia cultus, quem Deus in verbo suo à nobis exigit, non potest non ei gratus esse. Precantes igitur ita cogitare debemus: Invoco: quia mandasti.
units.tr: 2. Consideration of the divine command. For without God's command we doubt that we will be heard. But one who relies on God's command firmly holds that his prayers are acceptable to God, because the worship which God requires of us in his word cannot but be pleasing to him. Those who pray should therefore think: I call upon you, because you have commanded it.

units.la: 3. Cogitatio rerum petendarum.
units.tr: 3. Consideration of the things to be asked for.

units.la: Non vult Deus nos dirigere ad affectus vagos & incertos, quid velimus petere. Putaret enim princeps se derideri, si tu venias supplex nescicns quid petas. Sic Deus vult, ut cogitemus res petendas: alioqui non est precatio, sed derisio Dei. Nescimus autem quid petamus. Ideo praescripta est à Christo precationis formula, qua summa genera rerum petendarum continentur. Petendae sunt (ut has summatim comprehendam) res tum certae, tum approbatae à Deo & promissae. Haec autem sunt duplices: spirituales & corporales. Utrasque vult titio earum fit exercitium fidei, & confirmet nostram fiduciam de obtinendis rebus spiritualibus. Causa est, quia nemo potest expectare à Deo bona, nisi ipsum habeat placatum. 2. Ut cogitemus de eius providentia, scientes ne minima quidem ista fortuito contingere.
units.tr: God does not want us to be directed to vague and uncertain feelings about what we wish to ask. For a prince would think himself mocked if you came to him as a suppliant without knowing what you were asking for. So God wills that we think about the things to be asked for; otherwise it is not prayer but mockery of God. But we do not know what to ask for. Therefore Christ has prescribed a form of prayer, which contains the chief kinds of things to be asked. (To sum these up briefly) the things to be asked are those that are both certain and approved and promised by God. These are of two kinds: spiritual and bodily. God wills that we ask for both, so that the exercise of faith may be carried out in them and our confidence in obtaining spiritual things may be strengthened. The reason is that no one can expect good things from God unless he has him reconciled. 2. So that we may think about his providence, knowing that even the smallest of these things does not happen by chance.

units.la: 4. Verum desiderium.
units.tr: 4. True desire.

units.la: Deus simulatam aut hypocriticam esse precationem, nec in ore natam, sed in corde. Vult nos vero cordis affectu ac desiderio precari. Non enim verba oris, sed gemitus cordis sunt vera precatio, sicut dicebat Mosi: Quid clamas ad me? nihil tamen Moses loquebatur. Ideo loco generis in definitione constituendum est desiderium ardens.
units.tr: God does not want prayer to be feigned or hypocritical, not born on the lips but in the heart. He wills that we pray with an affection and desire of the heart. For it is not the words of the mouth but the groanings of the heart that are true prayer, as God said to Moses: Why do you cry out to me? Yet Moses said nothing at all. Therefore a burning desire must be placed in the definition as the genus.

units.la: 5. Agnitio & sensus indigentiae nostrae.
units.tr: 5. Acknowledgment and feeling of our need.

units.la: Hic debet esse fons, ex quo nascatur desiderium. Nam quo putas te magnopere non indigere, id scrio non petis: Deo autem omnes indigemus, iuxta illud: Ἰχθὺς ... nes homines indigent Deo: orate, nam omnes homines indigent Deo.
units.tr: This must be the source from which desire arises. For you do not ask for what you think you do not greatly need. But we all lack God, according to that saying: "All men lack God: pray, for all men lack God."

units.la: 6. Vera humilitas, & agnitio nostrae indignitatis accedat.
units.tr: 6. True humility and acknowledgment of our unworthiness must be present.

units.la: Abiiciamus nos supplices coram divina maiestate. Supplicem fieri manifeste significat, sicut auff quaedam vel ira. Deus nihil nobis debet, & omnes sumus homines superbos, qualis erat pharisaeus. Quare ad precationem requiritur vera humiliatio, poenitentia, & conversio. Nam promissiones divinae tantum ad conversos pertinent: sine conversione nemo potest orare ex fide: sine fide nemo certus est de exauditione, neque accipit quae petit. Peccatores vero Deus non exaudit.
units.tr: Let us cast ourselves down as suppliants before the divine majesty. To become a suppliant clearly signifies this, just as those who are suppliant are often moved by some fear or anger. God owes us nothing, and we are all proud men, like the Pharisee. Therefore true humbling, repentance and conversion are required for prayer. For the divine promises pertain only to the converted: no one can pray from faith without conversion; without faith no one is certain of being heard, nor does he receive what he asks for. God does not hear sinners.

units.la: 7. Agnitio & fiducia mediatoris.
units.tr: 7. Acknowledgment and confidence in the mediator.

units.la: Ut statuamus nos & nostras preces placere Deo, non propter nostram dignitatem, sed propter mediatorem Christum. Sic Daniel petit se exaudiri propter Dominum: & Christus jubet nos orare Patrem in nomine suo. In altari Christo ponenda sunt preces nostra. Sic erunt DEO acceptæ.
units.tr: We must hold that we and our prayers please God, not because of our own worth, but because of the mediator Christ. So Daniel asked to be heard for the Lord's sake; and Christ bids us pray to the Father in his name. Our prayers are to be placed on the altar of Christ. So they will be acceptable to God.

units.la: 8. Fiducia certa exauditionis. In præcedenti requiritur fides, qua statuimus, nos esse justos coram Deo, & eum nobis esse placatum in Christo: hic fides exauditionis, quæ non consistit sine illa. Quia estis filij, ideo emisit DEVS Spiritum Filij sui in corda vestra, clamantem Abba Pater. Nam qui accedit ad DEVM, hunc oportet credere, Deum esse, & præmia largiri iis, qui ipsum requirunt.
units.tr: 8. Confident faith of being heard. In the preceding condition faith is required, by which we hold that we are righteous before God and that he is reconciled to us in Christ; here is the faith of being heard, which cannot exist without that. Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. For whoever comes to God must believe that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

units.la: Sed hic in fiducia exauditionis observandum discrimen rerum petendarum. Alia dona sunt necessaria ad salutem, ut spiritualia: alia corporalia, sine quibus possumus salvari: illa sunt simpliciter petenda, cum fiducia, quod simus illa accepturi, sicut petimus, hoc est in specie. Hæc sunt petenda cum conditione voluntatis Dei, & cum tali fiducia, quod illa sit nobis daturus, si serviant ipsius gloriæ, & nobis sint utilia: vel quod sit daturus alia meliora, vel hoc, vel alio tempore. Imitabimur in his petentes leprosum dicentem: Domine, si vis, potes me mundare. Neque enim electi se aliter exaudiri cupiunt: quandoquidem sæpe petimus, quæ forte nocitura magis, quam profutura nobis essent, si exaudiremur.
units.tr: But here, in confidence of being heard, the difference between the things to be asked must be observed. Some gifts are necessary for salvation, such as spiritual ones; others are bodily, without which we can be saved. The former are to be asked for simply, with confidence that we shall receive them just as we ask, that is, in kind. The latter are to be asked with the condition of God's will, and with such confidence that he will give them to us if they serve his glory and are useful to us; or that he will give other and better things, either this or at another time. In this we shall imitate the leper who said: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. For the elect do not desire to be heard otherwise, since we often ask for things which, if we were heard, might harm us more than benefit us.

units.la: Obiect. Qui dubitanter petit, non petit ex fide, nec exauditur. Corporalia dubitanter petimus, quia cum conditione: Ergo non ex fide. Resp. Maior aut est particularis, aut falsa. Naturam enim fidei non postulat, ut simus certi de omnibus beneficiis corporalibus, sed tamen de spiritualibus ad salutem necessariis, ut remissione peccatorum, & vita æterna. In corporalibus salutaris est, si fides subjiciat se verbo Dei, & petat atque expectet salutaria. Deinde & minor potest negari. Etsi enim cum conditione petimus bona corporalia, tamen de iis impetrandis non dubitamus, sed credimus, nos bona corporalia, quæ petimus à Deo, consecuturos, modo nobis sint salutaria, nec volumus exaudiri, si sint noxia futura. Ergo nihilominus ex fide petimus, dum subjicimus nos verbo & voluntati Dei, & secundum eam petimus exaudiri. Nam fides se subjicit omni verbo & voluntati Dei. Voluntas autem Dei hæc est, ut petamus simpliciter, corporalia conditionaliter, & statuamus nos accepturos, illa quidem in specie, hæc vero, quatenus gloriæ Dei & saluti nostræ conducunt. Sic igitur orantes, non dubitamus de exauditione.
units.tr: Objection. One who asks doubtfully does not ask from faith, nor is he heard. We ask for bodily things doubtfully, because we ask with a condition. Therefore not from faith. Reply. The major premise is either particular or false. For faith does not require that we be certain about all bodily benefits, but it does require certainty about spiritual things necessary for salvation, such as forgiveness of sins and eternal life. In bodily things it is salutary if faith submits itself to the word of God, and asks for and expects what is good for us. Furthermore, the minor premise can be denied. For although we ask for good bodily things with a condition, yet we do not doubt about obtaining them; rather we believe that we shall obtain the bodily goods we ask from God, provided they are good for us, and we do not wish to be heard if they would be harmful. Therefore we nonetheless pray from faith, while we submit ourselves to the word and will of God, and according to it ask to be heard. For faith submits itself to every word and will of God. The will of God, however, is this: that we ask simply for spiritual things and conditionally for bodily things, and that we hold that we shall receive the former in kind, and the latter insofar as they serve God's glory and our salvation. So, praying in this way, we do not doubt of being heard.

units.la: 9. Agnitio & cogitatio promissionis divinæ. Deus promisit se exauditurum eos, qui his conditionibus eum invocant. Invocare in dietribulationis, & ego exaudiam te. Antequam clament, ego exaudiam: adhuc illis loquentibus, ego audiam. Sine hac promissione non est fides, sine fide petitio est inanis. Nisi promissionibus dininis adhibeamus fidem, & de iis inter orandum cogitemus, nihil illæ nobis prosunt, nec possumus bona conscientia quicquam petere. Fiducia verò diuinæ promissionis pariit certitudinem exauditionis & salutis: atque hæc certitudo accendit in nobis studium invocationis.
units.tr: 9. Acknowledgment and consideration of the divine promise. God has promised that he will hear those who call upon him under these conditions. Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear. Without this promise there is no faith, and without faith a petition is empty. Unless we apply faith to the divine promises and think about them while we pray, they do us no good, nor can we ask for anything with a good conscience. But confidence in the divine promise brings forth certainty of being heard and of salvation, and this certainty kindles in us zeal for calling upon him.

units.la: Ex his conditionibus bonæ precationis apparet facile, quantum differat piorum & impiorum precatio. Pij omnes has conditiones in sua precatione servare studeat. Impij contra vel omnes eas negligunt, vel una & altera servata errant in reliquis. Alij mox in limine impingunt, errantes in cognitione essentiæ & voluntatis divinæ, & sic primam conditionem violant. Alij errant in rebus petendis, dum petunt res malas aut incertas, aut non approbatas: alij has petunt hypocriticè: alij non ex sensu indigentiæ: alij non fiducia mediatoris: alij perseverantes in sceleribus putant se exaudiendos: alij res ad salutem necessarias cum diffidentia: alij denique, petunt non cogitantes de promissione divina, & ideo non ex fide.
units.tr: From these conditions of good prayer it is easy to see how greatly the prayer of the godly differs from that of the ungodly. All the godly take care to observe these conditions in their prayer. The ungodly, on the other hand, either neglect them all, or observe one or two of them and go wrong in the rest. Some stumble at the very threshold, going astray in their knowledge of the essence and will of God, and so violate the first condition. Some go wrong in what they ask for, since they ask for things that are evil, uncertain, or not approved; some ask hypocritically; some without any sense of need; some without trust in the Mediator; some, persisting in their sins, suppose that they will be heard; some ask for things necessary to salvation with distrust; and finally some ask without thinking of the divine promise, and so not from faith.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXIX. Quæ est illa precatio?
units.tr: QUESTION 119. What is that prayer?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis. Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Veniat regnum tuum. Fiat voluntas tua, quemadmodum in cœlo, sic etiam in terra. Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Et remitte nobis debita nostra: sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Et ne inducas nos in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo. Quia tuum est regnum, & potentia, & gloria, in secula. Amen.
units.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread.
