Nihil enim ad nos attinet scrutari, quae Deus decreuit: cum habeamus regulam praescriptam hanc, ut petamus, scilicet cum conditione voluntatis diuinae, & petere, quod nos Deus iubet, ergo nos subijcere voluntati diuinae, & petere, quod nos Deus iubet.
units.tr: Objection. Impossible things are not to be asked for. That the will of God be done on earth as in heaven, or that we perform our duty on earth as the angels do in heaven, is impossible; indeed, to ask it is to ask against the decree of God. Therefore it is not to be asked, since God will never grant it in its fullness. It is one thing not to be able to attain the perfection, and another not to desire it. I deny the minor premise, in which there is the fallacy of treating a non-cause as a cause. For we do not ask that the perfection of our obedience toward God be completed in this life, but that its beginning, continuation and growth be made here, and that then, increased by continual growth after this life, it may at last be brought to completion and perfected; and so then we will do the will of God no less than it is always done by the angels in heaven. When therefore we pray that the will of God be done on earth as in heaven, as does not signify the degree but the kind of obedience, namely its beginning. To ask for this and to obtain it from God is not against the decree of God. As for the perfection, it is also our duty to ask at every moment that we be wholly freed from sin. For God wills us to desire this, even though he is unwilling to grant it to us in this life. For it is no concern of ours to inquire into what God has decreed, since we have this prescribed rule: that we ask, namely under the condition of the divine will, and that we ask what God commands us to ask, that is, that we submit ourselves to the divine will and ask what God bids us ask.

units.la: Sancta & aurea admonitio de voluntate Dei. jubet petere, siue id Deus decreuerit, siue non. Deus vult parentes nostros mori, & tamen non vult nos eorum mortem petere aut optare. Deus vult ecclesiam esse sub cruce, & tamen non vult nos crucem eius velle, sed petere liberationem: & si affligatur, patienter ferre. Contra Deus non vult nobis in hac vita praestare liberationem à peccatis perfectam: & tamen vult nos eam optare, & singulis momentis petere, vt omnino liberemur. Sunt igitur aliqua petenda, quae Deus non vult efficere, & contra quaedam, quae Deus vult efficere, non sunt petenda, sed patienter toleranda, si fiant. Nec tamen hinc sequitur, nos petere contra voluntatem Dei, quia in precibus semper nos voluntati diuinae subijcimus.
units.tr: A holy and golden admonition concerning the will of God: he bids us ask whether or not God has decreed it. God wills that our parents die, and yet he does not will that we ask for or desire their death. God wills the Church to be under the cross, and yet he does not will that we desire its cross, but that we ask for deliverance; and if it is afflicted, that we bear it patiently. On the other hand, God does not will to grant us perfect deliverance from sins in this life, and yet he wills that we desire it and ask at every moment that we be wholly freed. There are therefore some things to be asked which God does not will to bring about, and conversely some things which God wills to bring about are not to be asked, but patiently endured if they happen. Nor does it follow from this that we ask against the will of God, because in our prayers we always submit ourselves to the divine will.

units.la: QVAESTIO CXXV.
units.tr: Question 125.

units.la: Quae est quarta petitio. RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What is the fourth petition? Answer.

units.la: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie: hoc est; Sup-pedita nobis omnia, quae sunt ad hanc vitam necessaria{a}, vt per ea agnoscamus, te vnicum fontem esse, ex quo omnia bona emanant{b}, ac nisi tu benedicas, omne donum nobis infelicia & noxia esse{c}. Quapropter da, vt fiduciam nostram ab omnibus creaturis auersam, in te solo collocemus{d}.
units.tr: Give us this day our daily bread: that is, supply us with all things that are necessary for this life, so that through them we may acknowledge you as the only fountain from which all good things flow, and that, unless you bless us, every gift becomes unhappy and harmful to us. Therefore grant that we may turn our trust away from all creatures and place it in you alone.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: [Videtur haec petitio de pane quotidiano postponenda sequenti de remissione peccatorum: siquidem praestantiora beneficia prius, viliora posterius videntur petenda. Sed Christus infirmitatis nostrae rationem habens, petitionem de pane quotidiano medio loco posuit, vt precationem petitionibus rerum spiritualium, tanquam praecipuorum bonorum, incipiamus & vt impetratio bonorum corporalium fiduciam spiritualium magis nobis confirmet.] Petimus verò hac petitione BONA CORPORALIA, de quibus tenendæ sunt hæ quæstiones: I. Cur bona corporalia sint petenda. II. Quomodo sint petenda. III. Quare bona corporalia cõplexus sit Christus nomine panis. IV. Quare nostrum vocet. V. Cur quotidianum. VI. Cur hodie dandum. VII. An liceat petere divitias. VIII. An liceat quid reponere in posterum.
units.tr: [It seems that this petition about daily bread should be placed after the following one, on the forgiveness of sins, since the greater benefits seem to be asked for first and the lesser afterwards. But Christ, taking account of our weakness, placed the petition for daily bread in the middle, so that we might begin our prayer with petitions for spiritual things, as the chief goods, and so that the obtaining of bodily goods might confirm our trust in spiritual ones more firmly.] By this petition, however, we ask for BODILY GOODS, concerning which these questions must be considered: I. Why bodily goods are to be asked for. II. How they are to be asked for. III. Why Christ comprised bodily goods under the name of bread. IV. Why he calls it ours. V. Why daily. VI. Why it is to be given today. VII. Whether it is lawful to ask for riches. VIII. Whether it is lawful to lay something aside for the future.

units.la: I. Cur bona corporalia nobis sint petenda.
units.tr: I. Why bodily goods are to be asked for by us.

units.la: Bona corporalia non minus quàm spiritualia sunt à DEO petenda.
units.tr: Bodily goods are to be asked for from God no less than spiritual goods.

units.la: 1. Propter mandatum Dei, quod nobis sufficere deberet, etiamsi nulla esset alia causa. Habemus autem Dei mandatum generale & speciale. Generaliter Christus dicit: Petite, & accipietis. Speciale mandatum præponit huic precum formulæ: Vos igitur itaprecamini: quo mandato etiam jubet, ut panem seu bona corporalia petamus à Deo. Quod verò dicit: Ne cureitis, quid edatis: Item, cætera adjicientur vobis: eo non prohibet petitionē panis quotidiani, vel curam vocationis, sed diffidentiam.
units.tr: 1. On account of God's command, which ought to be enough for us even if there were no other reason. We have a command of God both general and special. In general Christ says: Ask, and you shall receive. He places a special command before this form of prayer: Pray then in this way. By this command he also bids us ask God for bread, or bodily goods. But when he says: Do not be anxious what you shall eat; likewise, all these other things shall be added to you, he does not forbid the petition for daily bread, or the care of one's calling, but distrust.

units.la: 2. Propter promissionem: Quia Deus promisit, se nobis daturum vitæ necessaria, & quidem ideo promisit, ut petamus, & de impetrandis necessariis simus securi spiritualiter, non carnaliter: Pater vester cœlestis scit, quibus indigeatis.
units.tr: 2. On account of the promise: because God has promised that he will give us the necessities of life, and indeed he promised this so that we might ask, and be spiritually, not carnally, secure about obtaining what is necessary: Your heavenly Father knows what you need.

units.la: 3. Propter gloriam DEI, ut petitio etiam corporalium sit agnitio & professio providentiæ divinæ, præsertim erga ecclesiam. Vult enim Deus sibi hanc laudem tribui, quod ipse sit fons omnium bonorum: ne putemus, ea nobis fortuito contigisse.
units.tr: 3. On account of God's glory, so that the petition for bodily things too may be an acknowledgment and profession of divine providence, especially toward the Church. For God wills that this praise be ascribed to himself, that he is the fountain of all good things, lest we think these came to us by chance.

units.la: 4. Propter nostram consolationem: ut sint nobis signa paternæ ipsius erga nos benevolentiæ: quia salutaria bona tantum promittuntur, & dantur filiis Dei. Ergo cum nobis dantur, statuere debemus, nos esse ex numero eorum, quibus illa Deus se datu-rum promisit.
units.tr: 4. On account of our consolation: so that they may be for us signs of his fatherly goodwill toward us, because only saving goods are promised, and they are given to the children of God. Therefore, when these are given to us, we ought to conclude that we are among those to whom God promised to give them.

units.la: 5. Ut petitio & exspectatio horum bonorum sit nobis exercitium fiduciæ & spei: non enim possumus nobis polliceri corporalia, nisi certi simus de spiritualibus, & de Dei voluntate erga nos, quod simus in gratia.
units.tr: 5. So that the petition for these goods and the expectation of them may be for us an exercise of trust and hope. For we cannot promise ourselves bodily things unless we are certain about spiritual things, and about God's will toward us, that we are in grace.

units.la: 6. Propter necessitatem nostram, ut possimus facere voluntatem Dei in terra, quod sine pane quotidiano facere hic non possumus: Non mortui laudabunt te Domine. 7. Denique propter hanc etiam consolationem, vt sciamus ecclesiam semper seruandam in terris, quia Deus semper eam exaudiet, & dabit panem quotidianum, juxta promissionem.
units.tr: 6. On account of our need, so that we may do the will of God on earth, which we cannot do here without daily bread: The dead do not praise you, O Lord. 7. Finally, on account of this consolation too, so that we may know that the Church is always to be preserved on earth, because God will always hear her and will give daily bread, according to his promise.

units.la: II. Quomodo petenda sint bona corporalia.
units.tr: II. How bodily goods are to be asked for.

units.la: Corporalia non minus quam alia bona in euangelio promissa petenda sunt.
units.tr: Bodily goods, no less than the other goods promised in the gospel, are to be asked for.

units.la: 1. Fiducia promissionis gratia, seu ex fide. Aliter enim non exaudimur: nec bona sunt nobis salutaria: & Deus potest respondere, nos non esse ex illis, quibus ea ipse promisit.
units.tr: 1. With trust in the promise by grace, or from faith. For otherwise we are not heard, nor are the goods salutary for us, and God can reply that we are not among those to whom he promised them.

units.la: 2. Cum conditione voluntatis Dei, vt Deus det ea quae petimus, si velit, & quatenus nouit, ea nobis expedire, & gloriae suae seruire: quia haec bona promisit, non determinatis circumstantiis. Non enim determinauit in verbo, quae bona corporalia nobis dare velit. De spiritualibus autem promisit expresse, se spiritualia daturum omni petenti.
units.tr: 2. With the condition of God's will, so that God gives what we ask, if he wills, and insofar as he knows it to be expedient for us and to serve his glory; because he promised these goods without fixed circumstances. For he has not determined in the Word which bodily goods he is willing to give us. But concerning spiritual goods he promised expressly that he would give spiritual things to every one who asks.

units.la: 3. Cum fide exauditionis, vt credamus Deum nobis tantum esse daturum, quantum sufficit.
units.tr: 3. With faith in being heard, so that we believe God will give us only as much as is sufficient.

units.la: 4. In hunc finem, vt seruiamus Deo & proximo, non in luxum aut ostentationem nostram.
units.tr: 4. To this end, that we may serve God and our neighbour, not for our luxury or display.

units.la: Qui sic non petunt, non exaudiuntur: licet accipiant quod petunt, non tamen vere exaudiuntur a Deo: quia quae accipiunt, non sunt ipsis salutaria.
units.tr: Those who do not ask in this way are not heard: although they receive what they ask, they are not truly heard by God, because what they receive is not salutary for them.

units.la: Causa vero, cur Deus hanc determinationem addiderit bonis corporalibus, quod daturus sit ea, prout singulorum salus postulat: & ipsius gloriae illustratio: duplex est. 1. Quia nos saepe nescimus, quid petamus, & quid nobis expediat: ipse autem scit. In spiritualibus autem non possumus errare, quia illa simpliciter nobis prosunt, & in iis ipse modum & viam petendi determinauit. 2. Vt nos discamus iis contenti esse, quae ab eo accepimus, & semper ipsius consilio voluntatem nostram subijciamus.
units.tr: The reason, however, why God has added this qualification to bodily goods, that he will give them as the salvation of each person requires and as the illustration of his own glory, is twofold. 1. Because we often do not know what we should ask, and what is expedient for us, but he knows. In spiritual things, however, we cannot go wrong, because those things benefit us simply, and in them he himself has determined the manner and way of asking. 2. So that we may learn to be content with what we have received from him, and always to subject our will to his counsel.

units.la: III. Quare bona corporalia complexus sit Christus nomine panis.
units.tr: III. Why Christ included all bodily goods under the name of bread.

units.la: Panis nomine per synecdochen Hebraeis vsitatam complexus est Christus omnia bona corporalia, ad hanc vitam necessaria, vt sunt, omnia alimenta, victus, amictus, bona valetudo, pax politica, &c. Hoc patet ex scopo petitionis. Panem enim petimus propter necessitatem. Atqui alia multa praeter panem sunt necessaria. Ergo nomine panis etiam illa petimus. Atq; haec synecdoche Hebraica saepius occurrit in Bibliis. In sudore vultus tui, vescéris pane tuo. Qui edit panem meum, sustulit calcaneum. Neque tantum necessaria ad vitam panis nomine Christus comprehendit, sed etiam salutarem eorum vsum. Nam panis sine vsu salutari lapis est.
units.tr: By the figure of speech synecdoche, which is common among the Hebrews, Christ under the name bread includes all bodily goods necessary for this life: all food, clothing, good health, civil peace, and so on. This is clear from the aim of the petition. We ask for bread out of necessity. But many things besides bread are necessary. Therefore we also ask for those things under the name of bread. This Hebrew synecdoche occurs often in the Bible: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread (Gen. 3.19); He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me (John 13.18). Christ includes under the name of bread not only what is necessary for life but also the wholesome use of these things. For bread without a wholesome use is a stone.

units.la: Ideo autem hæc omnia panis nomine Christus comprehendit, 1. Vt frenum iniiciat cupiditatibus nostris, ac doceat, tantum panem esse petendum, hoc est, tantum necessaria ad vitam sustentandam & serviendum Deo & proximo in nostra vocatione, tum communitum propria. 2. Vt doceat, non tantum ipsa necessaria, sed & salutarem eorum vsum a DEO petendum esse. Nihil enim prosunt, si non sint panis, & quidem salutaris.
units.tr: Christ includes all these things under the name bread for two reasons. (1) To put a bridle on our desires, and to teach that we should ask only for bread, that is, only for what is necessary to sustain life, and to serve God and our neighbour in our calling, and to support our own household. (2) To teach that we should ask God not only for the necessities themselves but also for their wholesome use. For they profit nothing unless they are bread, and indeed wholesome bread.

units.la: Redditur autem panis salutaris, 1. Si fide eum peramus & accipiamus, hoc est, eo animo, modo, ac fine, quo Deus flagitat, nempe, si non in creaturis hæreamus, sed ad Deum authorem & largitorem bonorum omnium, fideli mente penetremus. 2. Si petamus, vt ipsi det pani impetrato vim nutriendi & conseruandi corpora nostra, hoc est, si non modo ipsum panem, sed etiam benedictionem à Deo petamus. Nisi enim ipse benedicat, omnes nostræ curæ & labores sunt inanes, ipsaque adeo Dei dona nobis sunt inutilia vel noxia, juxta comminationem: Frangam baculum panis.
units.tr: Bread becomes wholesome bread (1) if we seek and receive it by faith, that is, with the attitude, manner and purpose that God requires, namely, if we do not cling to creatures but with a faithful mind look up to God as the author and giver of all good things. (2) If we ask that God would give the bread we have obtained the power to nourish and preserve our bodies, that is, if we ask not only for the bread itself but also for God's blessing on it. For unless he blesses it, all our cares and labours are in vain, and God's gifts themselves are useless or harmful to us, according to the threat: I will break the staff of bread (Lev. 26.26).

units.la: Ex his nunc liquet, quidnam petamus, cum panem petimus, nempe: 1. Non magnas opes, sed res necessarias. 2. Vt ex sint nobis panis, hoc est, sint nobis salutares, Dei benedictione, quæ si non accedat, panis non est panis, sed vertitur in lapidem, vel vertatur in lapidem, is lapidenum. Nam qui donat panem, vt vertatur in lapidem, non panem donat. Talia sunt bona impiorum, quæ vel accipiunt à Deo, vel rapiunt.
units.tr: From these points it is now clear what we ask for when we ask for bread: (1) not great riches, but things necessary; (2) that the bread may be wholesome for us, that is, may do us good, through God's blessing. Without that blessing bread is not bread but is turned into a stone, or is turned into stone, and so becomes a stone. For the one who gives bread that is turned into a stone is not giving bread. Such are the goods of the wicked, which they either receive from God or seize for themselves.

units.la: IV. Quare Christus panem vocet nostrum.
units.tr: IV. Why Christ calls it our bread.

units.la: Jubet nos Christus petere panem nostrum, non meum, tuum, alienum: 1. Vt petamus, quæ dantur nobis à Deo. Noster enim est panis, qui nobis est necessarius ad sustentationem vitæ, & qui fit noster, quando à Deo nobis datur. Itaque: Da nobis panem à te (Deus) deputatum nem nostrum, significat: Da nobis panem à te (Deus) deputatum nobis, quem tu vis esse nostrum. Vnicuique suam portionem Deus tanquam paterfamilias distribuit, quam perimus nobis dari. 2. Vt petamus res necessarias justo labore, genere vitæ Deo placente, honestoque & communi societati seruiente, à nobis acquisitas, hoc est, quas per ordinaria media, & legitimis rationibus accipiamus: porrigente eas nobis cœlitus Dei manu: Qui furatur, ne furetur amplius, sed potius non laborat, non manducet. Qui furatur, ne furetur amplius, sed potius laboret operando manibus, quod bonum sit. 3. Vt possimus eis vti bona conna conscientia, & cum gratiarum actione. Deus enim vult nos esse certos, quod datis his bonis, etiam concedat nobis potestatem fruendi illis, nec vult nos vti suis donis tanquam raptores, sed liberè, & cum gratiarum actione.
units.tr: Christ bids us ask for our bread, not mine, yours, or another's. (1) So that we may ask for what is given to us by God. For the bread is ours which is necessary to us for sustaining life, and which becomes ours when it is given to us by God. Thus Give us this day our bread means: give us, O God, the bread that you have assigned to us, which you wish to be ours. God, as the father of the household, distributes to each his portion, which we pray may be given to us. (2) So that we may ask for necessities that we have acquired by just labour, by a way of life pleasing to God, and serving honest and common society; that is, goods that we receive through ordinary means and by lawful methods, the hand of God reaching them down to us from heaven: Let him who steals steal no more, but rather let him labour, working with his hands what is good (Eph. 4.28). (3) So that we may use these goods with a good conscience and with thanksgiving. For God wishes us to be sure that, having given us these goods, he also grants us the power to enjoy them, and he does not wish us to use his gifts like robbers, but freely and with thanksgiving.

units.la: V. Cur panem vocet Quotidianum.
units.tr: V. Why he calls it daily bread.

units.la: Panem, quem petere debemus à Deo, Christus vocat quotidianum, 1. Quia vult nos quotidie petere, quantum in singulos dies nobis sufficiat. 2. Quia vult inijcere frenum nostris cupiditatibus insanis & infinitis. Pater vester scit, quibus indigetis. Melius est modicum justo, quàm divitiæ impiorum multæ. Timenti Dominum non deerit vllum bonum, scilicet vtile & necessarium. Ergo da nobis panem quotidianum, id est, da nobis panem sufficientem, da nobis tantum rerum ad vitam nobis necessariarum, quantum vnicuique nostrum ad seruiendum tibi & proximo in sua vocatione quotidie opus fuerit.
units.tr: Christ calls the bread which we ought to ask from God daily: (1) because he wills us to ask every day for as much as is enough for us each day; (2) because he wills to put a bridle on our wild and boundless desires. Your heavenly Father knows what you need (Matt. 6.32). Better is a little with righteousness than great riches of the wicked (Ps. 37.16). Those who fear the Lord shall lack no good thing (Ps. 34.10), that is, nothing useful and necessary. Therefore give us daily bread, that is, give us bread sufficient for us; give us as much of the things necessary to life as each of us needs every day to serve you and our neighbour in his calling.

units.la: VI. Cur Christus addat Hodie.
units.tr: VI. Why Christ adds today.

units.la: Addit Christus particulam hodie, 1. Vt occurrat diffidentiæ & auaritiæ nostræ, & ab hoc vtroque vitio nos abstrahat. 2. Vt ex ipso solo pendeamus, sicut heri, sic hodie, & cras, & semper exspectemus vitæ necessaria ex Dei manibus: atque sciamus, illa non parari nostris manibus, aut nostra diligentia, atque etiam accepta non prodesse corpori, nisi accedat Dei benedictio. 3. Vt exercitium fidei & precum perpetuo in nobis continuetur. Quamdiu enim dicitur hodie, tam diu vult continuari precationem, vt præcepto illi: Semper orate, obedientiam præstemus.
units.tr: Christ adds the word today: (1) so that he may meet our distrust and greed, and draw us away from both of these vices; (2) so that we may depend on him alone, and, as yesterday, so today and tomorrow and always, look for the necessities of life from the hands of God; and so that we may know that these things are not procured by our hands or by our own diligence, and that even when received they do not benefit the body unless God's blessing is added. (3) So that the exercise of faith and prayer may be kept up continually in us. For as long as it is said today, so long is prayer to be continued, that we may render obedience to the precept: Pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5.17).

units.la: VII. An liceat petere diuitias.
units.tr: VII. Whether it is lawful to ask for riches.

units.la: Hæc quæstio vnà cum proximè sequente oritur ex præcedentibus. Cum enim jubemur petere panem duntaxat quotidianum, & quidem hodie: videtur prima fronte non licere vel diuitias petere, vel in crastinum quid reponere. Cæterum diuitias petere licet, si sublata ambiguitate intelligamus diuitiarum nomine res ad sustentandam vitam necessarias. Quo modo & ab Epicuro definiuntur diuitiæ, quod sint paupertas, ad legem naturæ accommodata. Quæ definitio bona est. Verè enim divites censendi sunt, quibus ad vitam sustentandam necessaria suppetunt, quique his contenti viuunt. Sic si accipiatur diuitiarum nomen, petendæ sunt à Deo diuitiæ, quia petere debemus res necessarias naturæ, loco, & officio, ad quod à Deo sumus vocati. Ratio autem est: quia res hæ necessariæ, seu diuidiuitiæ, sunt panis quotidianus, quem petere debemus. Aliter vero etiam definiuntur diuitiæ, quod sint abundantia & copia suprares necessarias. Sic Crassus (cognominatus diues) dicebat neminem esse diuitè, nisi qui posset alere exercitum annuum. Hoc sensu diuitiæ nequaquam sunt à Deo petendæ. Hoc enim non esset panem quotidianū petere. Et Salomon in persona omnium piorum dicit: Diuitias aut paupertatē ne dederis mihi: quibus verbis Spiritus sanctus per Salomonem nos docet, diuitias, hoc est, abundantiam supra res necessarias etiam deprecari. Hoc spectat & illud Pauli: Qui volunt ditescere, incidunt in tentationem & laqueum, & cupiditates multas amentes & damnosas, quæ demergunt hominem in exitium & interitum. Et Christus has diuitias vocat spinas, quæ sine periculo tractari non possunt. Contra vero: Quod si tamen aliquid nobis Deus dederit præter ea, quæ sunt necessaria, eo recte vtamur, aut in vsus necessarios asseruemus. Jubet enim Christus etiam, colligere fragmenta. Et illustre est exemplum Josephi, monito oraculi colligentis & asseruantis annonam in futuros annos caritatis. Sic hic 1. videndum, ne in opibus collocemus fiduciam: Diuitiæ si proueniant, ne apponatis cor. 2. Vitandus luxus & omnis abusus. 3. Cogitandum nos esse œconomos Dei, qui nobis diuitias bene collocandas commiserit, & opus administrationis imposuerit, cui nos aliquando rationem dispensationis & administrationis nostræ reddituri simus.
units.tr: This question, together with the one that immediately follows, arises from what has gone before. For since we are bidden to ask only for daily bread, and indeed for today, it seems at first sight that it is not lawful either to ask for riches or to lay anything up for tomorrow. Yet it is lawful to ask for riches, provided that, the ambiguity being removed, we understand by "riches" the things necessary for sustaining life. In this sense riches are also defined by Epicurus, as "poverty adjusted to the law of nature." That definition is good. For those are truly to be counted rich to whom the things necessary for sustaining life are sufficient, and who live content with these. So if the word "riches" is taken in this sense, riches are to be asked of God, because we ought to ask for the things necessary to our nature, our place, and the duty to which we have been called by God. The reason is that these necessary things, or riches, are the daily bread which we ought to ask for. But riches are also defined otherwise, as "abundance and plenty beyond what is necessary." In this sense Crassus (surnamed the Rich) used to say that no one is rich unless he can support an annual army. In this sense riches are by no means to be asked of God; for to ask for this would not be to ask for daily bread. And Solomon, speaking in the person of all the godly, says: "Give me neither riches nor poverty" (Prov. 30); by these words the Holy Spirit teaches us through Solomon that we should also pray against riches, that is, abundance beyond necessary things. Paul's words also bear on this: "Those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and many foolish and harmful desires, which drown a man in destruction and ruin" (1 Tim. 6). And Christ calls such riches "thorns," which cannot be handled without danger. On the other hand: "But if God has given us anything beyond what is necessary, let us use it rightly, or set it aside for necessary uses." For Christ also commands us to "gather up the fragments" (John 6). And the example of Joseph is famous, who, warned by an oracle, gathered and stored up grain for the future years of famine. So here (1) we must take care not to place our trust in wealth: "If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them" (Ps. 62). (2) Luxury and every abuse must be avoided. (3) We must remember that we are stewards of God, who has entrusted us with riches to be well employed, and has laid upon us the task of administration, to which we shall one day have to render an account of our stewardship and administration.

units.la: III. An liceat aliquid reponere in futurum.
units.tr: III. Whether it is lawful to lay something up for the future.

units.la: Licet aliquid reponere in futurum, juxta mandatum: Colligite fragmenta, ne quid pereat. Hoc enim includitur in particula nam jubemur juuare rempublicam, cum opus est, & pauperib. aliquid conferre. Ergo aliquid est reponendum, vnde hoc faciamus, & quidem de nostro. Huc pertinent omnia præcepta de parsimonia & frugalitate, quæ versantur in custodiendis & vtiliter collocandis rebus bene partis in vsum suum & suorum, & vitant sumptus ac largitiones, omnemq; luxum & profusionem donorum Dei. Docet quoque apostolus officij parentum esse, aliquid colligere liberis: Non debent filij parentibus thesauros conderere, sed parentes filiis.
units.tr: It is lawful to lay something up for the future, in accordance with the command: "Gather up the fragments, that nothing be lost" (John 6). For this is included in the particle "for," since we are bidden to help the commonwealth when there is need and to contribute something to the poor. Therefore something must be laid by, from which we may do this, and indeed from our own means. To this belong all the precepts about thrift and frugality, which concern keeping and usefully investing the goods rightly acquired for our own use and that of our households, and which avoid expense and extravagance, and all luxury and waste of God's gifts. The apostle also teaches that it is the duty of parents to lay up something for their children: "Children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children" (2 Cor. 12).

units.la: Tria tamen hic obseruanda: 1. Vt ea, quæ reponuntur, sint juste parta, justo & honesto labore acquisita. 2. Ne in his reponatur fiducia. 3. Vt conferantur in vsus legitimos ac necessarios nostros & aliorum, nempe ad honestam sustentationem vitæ nostræ & familiæ, atq; amicorum: ad conseruationem ecclesiæ & reipublicæ: denique ad sublevationem pauperum, & egenorum frafratrum. Huc pertinet illud Dauidis: Ne confidatis in injuria, neq; in rapina, ne fiatis vani: diuitiæ si proueniant, ne apponatis cor. Et illud Pauli: Qui furabatur, ne furetur amplius, sed potius laboret operando, quod bonum sit, vt possit impertiri, cui opus fuerit.
units.tr: Yet three things are to be observed here: (1) that what is laid up be justly gained, acquired by just and honest labour; (2) that trust not be placed in it; (3) that it be applied to our own and others' lawful and necessary uses, namely for the honest support of our life, our household and our friends; for the maintenance of the Church and the commonwealth; and finally for the relief of the poor and needy brethren. To this belongs the saying of David: "Do not trust in oppression, nor vainly hope in robbery; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them" (Ps. 62). And Paul's: "Let him who stole steal no more, but rather let him labour, working what is good, that he may have something to share with him who has need" (Eph. 4).

units.la: Jam facile respondetur ad obiectiones contra hanc petitionem.
units.tr: Now objections against this petition are easily answered.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Quod nostrum est, non necesse est petere. Panis quotidianus est noster. Non igitur necesse est eum à Deo petere. Resp. Sunt quatuor termini ex ambiguitate vocis nostrum, quæ in maiore significat rem, quam habemus in nostra potestate: in minore rem, quæ nostra fit Dei dono, seu quæ precibus à Deo impetratur, vt supra est declaratum.
units.tr: Objection 1. What is ours need not be asked for. Daily bread is ours. Therefore it is not necessary to ask for it from God. Answer. There is a fourfold equivocation in the word "ours," which in the major premise means a thing that we have in our power, but in the minor a thing that becomes ours by the gift of God, or that is obtained from God by prayer, as has been explained above.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Quod non paratur laboribus, sed precibus, de eo non necesse est laborare. Panis quotidianus non paratur laboribus, sed precibus. Ergo non est laborandum, sed tantum orandum. Resp. Fallacia à dicto secundum quid, vt simpliciter. Quæ non parantur laboribus simpliciter, neq; vt causis, neq; vt mediis necessariis, de iis videtur frustra laborari. Sed ad paranda bona corporalia, etsi labores nostri non sunt necessarii, vt causæ efficientes totales vel principales: sunt tamen necessarij, vt media à Deo ordinata, secundum dicta: In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo. Qui non laborat, non manducet. Dat Deus omnia gratis, sed non sine labore & precibus, juxta versiculum: Dat Deus omne bonum, sed non per cornua taurum. Et notum illud Hesiodi: τῆς δ' ἀρετῆς ἱδρῶτα θεοὶ προπάροιθεν ἔθηκαν Ἀθανάτοι, hoc est, Virtutem posuere Dij non ante laborem.
units.tr: Objection 2. What is not procured by labour but by prayer, about that there is no need to labour. Daily bread is not procured by labour but by prayer. Therefore we are not to labour, but only to pray. Answer. This is a fallacy from a saying taken with qualification as if it were unqualified. Things that are not procured by labour absolutely, neither as causes nor as necessary means, are seen to be sought in vain by labour. But for procuring bodily goods, although our labours are not necessary as total or principal efficient causes, they are nevertheless necessary as means ordained by God, according to the words: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread" (Gen. 3), and "He who does not work shall not eat" (2 Thess. 3). God gives all things freely, yet not without labour and prayer, according to the little verse: "God gives every good thing, but not through the horns of a bull." And there is the well-known line of Hesiod: "Before virtue the immortal gods placed sweat" (ἀρετῆς ἱδρῶτα θεοὶ προπάροιθεν ἔθηκαν), that is, the gods placed virtue behind labour.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Christus jubet petere panem quotidianum, & hodiernum, non crastinum. Ergo non licet aliquid reponere in crastinum, sed est viuendum in diem. Quorsum igitur Paulus jubet parentes thesaurizare liberis? Resp. Est fallacia non causæ: jubet Christus petere panem quotidianum & hodiernum, hoc est, necessarium in singulos dies, hodie, cras, & quamdiu viuimus: minime vero id, quasi non velit nos laborare pro crastino, vel aliquid in crastinum reponere, aut jam data bona in crastinum sufficientia abijcere: sed vult abesse diffidentiam, avaritiam, injustam acquisitionem & inobedientiam. Non vult sibi præscribi a nobis, quid dare debeat. Mandat quidem alio loco, ne simus solliciti de crastino: sed ibi vetat nos cogitare de crastino cum diffidentia, quasi cras Deus nihil sit daturus, vel cum proposito cras non orandi, non autem de labore & precibus.
units.tr: Objection 3. Christ bids us ask for daily and today's bread, not tomorrow's. Therefore it is not lawful to lay anything up for tomorrow, but we must live from day to day. Why then does Paul bid parents lay up treasure for their children? Answer. This is a fallacy of the non-cause. Christ bids us ask for daily and today's bread, that is, what is necessary for each day, today, tomorrow, and as long as we live; by no means as if he were unwilling for us to labour for tomorrow, or to lay something up for tomorrow, or to throw away goods already given that suffice for tomorrow. Rather he wills that distrust, avarice, unjust acquisition and disobedience be absent. He does not wish us to prescribe to him what he ought to give. He indeed commands elsewhere, "Do not be anxious about tomorrow" (Matt. 6); but there he forbids us to think about tomorrow with distrust, as if God were going to give nothing tomorrow, or with the purpose of not praying tomorrow; not, however, forbidding labour and prayer.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXXVI. Quæ est quinta petitio?
units.tr: QUESTION 126. What is the fifth petition?

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris: hoc est; Nobis miserrimis peccatoribus omnia peccata nostra, atq; eam etiam prauitatem, quæ in nobis etiamnum hærer, propter Christi sanguinem ne imputes testimonium gratiæ tuæ, quemadmodum nos quoque hoc tuæ gratiæ testimonium in cordibus nostris sentimus, quod firmiter nobis propositum habemus, omnibus, qui nos offenderunt, ex animo ignoscere b.
units.tr: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors: that is, to us most wretched sinners, forgive all our sins, and also that perversity which still clings to us, and for the sake of Christ's blood do not impute it. Grant us the testimony of your grace, just as we also feel this testimony of your grace in our hearts, in that we firmly purpose to forgive from the heart all who have offended us b.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: De ordine & argumento quintæ petitionis recte & piè Cyprianus admonet his verbis: Post subsidium cibi petitur & venia delicti, ut qui à Deo pascitur, in Deo viuat: nec tantum præsenti & temporali vitæ, sed & æternæ consulitur, ad quam venire potest, si peccata donentur. Est autem hæc petitio (ut idem Cyprianus dicit) inde genua confessio ecclesiæ, qua agnoscit & deplorat peccata sua, & simul consolatio, quod acceptura sit remissionem peccatorum, juxta promissionem Christi. Item, obligatio ad mutuam ignoscentiam erga proximum. Vult ergo Christus hac petitione, 1. ut agnoscamus peccatum: 2. ut sitiamus remissionem peccatorum, quia illis ea tantum datur, qui eam desiderant, & qui non concul-cant sanguinem Filij Dei. 3. Vt exerceatur fides nostra: quoniam petitio hæc fluit ex fide, & rursus etiam fidem confirmat. Fides enim causa est precationis, precatio autem causa fidei, quod ad incrementum attinet.
units.tr: Cyprian rightly and piously instructs us about the order and subject of the fifth petition in these words: After the support of food, forgiveness of sin is asked, so that he who is fed by God may live in God; and provision is made not only for present and temporal life but also for eternal life, to which he can come if sins are forgiven. This petition is (as the same Cyprian says) a confession of the Church, by which it acknowledges and laments its sins; and at the same time a consolation, that it will receive forgiveness of sins according to the promise of Christ. It is also an obligation to mutual forgiveness towards our neighbour. Christ therefore wills by this petition: (1) that we acknowledge sin; (2) that we thirst for forgiveness of sins, since it is given only to those who desire it, and who do not trample underfoot the blood of the Son of God; (3) that our faith be exercised, since this petition flows from faith and in turn also confirms faith. For faith is the cause of prayer, and prayer is the cause of faith, as far as growth is concerned.

units.la: Quæstiones præcipuæ ponderandæ: I. Quid Christus intelligat per debita. II. Quid sit remittere debita. III. Quare petenda sit peccatorum remissio. IV. Quid sibi velit adiectio: Sicut & nos, &c.
units.tr: The chief questions to be weighed are: I. What Christ means by debts. II. What it is to remit debts. III. Why the forgiveness of sins is to be asked. IV. What the addition, "as we also forgive," &c., means.

units.la: I. Quid Christus vocet debita.
units.tr: I. What Christ calls debts.

units.la: Debita vocat omnia peccata nostra, originale & actualia, ignorantiæ, omissionis, & facti, sicut ipse interpretatur apud Lucam: Dimitte nobis peccata nostra, siquidem & ipsi dimittimus omni debenti nobis. Vocat autem debita, quia nos faciunt debitores Deo, tum obedientiæ neglectæ, tum poenæ luendæ. Cum enim peccamus, non tribuimus Deo, quod ipsi debemus: Quamdiu autem hoc ei non tribuimus, tamdiu manemus debitores, & obligamur ad satisfactionem per poenam:Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, vt faciat ea.
units.tr: He calls debts all our sins, original and actual, of ignorance, of omission, and of commission, as he himself explains in Luke: "Forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who is indebted to us." He calls them debts because they make us debtors to God, both for neglected obedience and for punishment to be paid. For when we sin, we do not render to God what we owe him; and as long as we do not render it, we remain debtors and are bound to satisfaction through punishment: Cursed is everyone who does not abide in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.

units.la: Ab hoc reatu in æternum non possemus liberari, nisi Deus peccata remitteret.
units.tr: We could never be freed from this guilt for eternity unless God forgave sins.

units.la: II. Quid sit remittere debita seu remissio peccatorum.
units.tr: II. What it is to remit debts, or the remission of sins.

units.la: Remittere dicitur creditor debitori, quando nec debitum ab eo requirit, sed ex tabulis expungit, ac si esset persolutum, nec cum plectit: vt videre est in parabola regis remittentis seruo supplici debitum 10000. talentorum. Sic Deus nobis remittit debita, dum peccata nobis non imputat, nec propter ea nos vult punire, ideo quia ea puniuit in filio mediatore. Remissio igitur peccatorum est, Deum nobis non imputare vllum peccatum, sed nos recipere in gratiam, iustos pronunciare, & habere pro filiis, mera & gratuita misericordia, propter Christi satisfactionem pro nobis ab ipso præstitam, nobis imputatam, & à nobis fide apprehensam: atque ideo nos nolle propter peccatum punire, sed nos donare iustitia & vita æterna: quia remissio peccati tollit poenam peccati. Peccatum enim & poena sunt correlatiua: Posito peccato, ponitur poena: & sublato peccato tollitur poena.
units.tr: To remit is said of a creditor toward a debtor when he neither demands the debt from him but strikes it from the records, as if it had been paid, nor punishes him with it; as can be seen in the parable of the king remitting to the servant who pleaded the debt of ten thousand talents. So God remits our debts when he does not impute our sins to us, nor wishes to punish us on account of them, because he has punished them in the Son as mediator. The remission of sins, therefore, is God's not imputing any sin to us, but receiving us into grace, pronouncing us righteous, and regarding us as sons, by pure and free mercy, on account of the satisfaction of Christ made for us by himself, imputed to us, and apprehended by us through faith; and thus his unwillingness to punish us for sin, but his bestowing on us righteousness and eternal life: because the remission of sin takes away the punishment of sin. For sin and punishment are correlatives: when sin is posited, punishment is posited; and when sin is taken away, punishment is taken away.

units.la: Obiect. Remittere peccata, est non imputare, nec velle in nobis punire peccata. At hoc pugnat cum iustitia Dei. Ergo petimus, vt Deus inuertat ordinem iustitiæ suæ. Resp. Nego consequentiam: quia remittere peccata sic demum pugnat cum iustitia Dei, si remissio fiat absq; omni satisfactione. Nos autem petimus remissionem peccatorum propter satisfactionem Christi. Non ergo remittuntur nobis peccata cum violatione iustitiæ diuinæ: quia remittuntur cum compensatione. Inst. 1. Si cum compensatione: ergo non gratis peccata nobis remittit Deus. Resp. Cum compensatione, eoque non gratis, respectu Christi: gratis vero respectu nostri, quia non accipit satisfactionem à nobis, sed à Christo. Inst. 2. Ergo tamen non gratis: quia meriti sumus in Christo. Resp. Meritum illud non est nostrum, sed Christi: quia & gratis à patre nobis donatur, & nobis meretur, nullo nostro merito intercedente, & meritum eius nobis imputatur ex gratia. Itaque gratis propter illud peccata nobis remittuntur: vnde recte inseritur, propter Christi satisfactionem non imputari nobis peccata. Non enim petimus, vt Deus agat contra suam iustitiam, & in sua mente non habeat nos pro peccapeccatoribus, se vt nobis iustitiam alienam Christi imputer, qua peccata nostra tegantur. Summa: Deus remittit peccata gratis. 1. Quia à nobis non exigit satisfactionem. 2. Quia gratis dat Filium, ipse sibi in eo satisfaciens. 3. Quia gratis donat & imputat satisfactionem Filij credentibus.
units.tr: Objection. To remit sins is not to impute them, nor to wish to punish them in us. But this conflicts with the justice of God. Therefore we ask that God overturn the order of his justice. Answer. I deny the consequence: for remitting sins conflicts with the justice of God only if the remission is made without any satisfaction. But we ask for the remission of sins on account of the satisfaction of Christ. Sins are therefore not remitted to us with a violation of divine justice, because they are remitted with compensation. Objection 2. If with compensation, then God does not forgive our sins freely. Answer. With compensation, and therefore not freely, with respect to Christ; but freely with respect to us, because he does not receive satisfaction from us, but from Christ. Objection 2. Yet not freely, because we are deserving in Christ. Answer. That merit is not ours but Christ's: for it is both given to us freely by the Father and merits for us, with no merit of ours intervening, and his merit is imputed to us out of grace. Thus sins are remitted to us freely on account of it; whence it is rightly concluded that sins are not imputed to us on account of the satisfaction of Christ. For we do not ask that God act against his own justice, and in his mind not hold us as sinners, so that he impute to us the alien righteousness of Christ by which our sins are covered. Summary: God remits sins freely. (1) Because he does not require satisfaction from us. (2) Because he gives his Son freely, satisfying himself in him. (3) Because he freely bestows and imputes the satisfaction of the Son to believers.

units.la: III. Cur petenda sit nobis peccatorum remissio.
units.tr: III. Why the forgiveness of sins is to be asked for by us.

units.la: Petenda est nobis remissio peccatorum: 1. Propter nostram salutem, vt seruemur. Nam sine remissione peccatorū non possumus seruari. Hoc autem beneficium Deus non dat, nisi petentibus. 2. Vt admoneamur de reliquiis peccatorum hærentibus etiam in sanctissimis, idq; vt perpetuo crescat pœnitentia. Quoniā etiam quotidie remissio peccatorum petenda est. 3. Vt possimus petere & accipere reliqua bona præcedentia: quia sine remissione peccatorū reliqua bona vel non dantur, vel in exitium dantur. Ideo impij sæpe quidem illa accipiunt, sed non salutaria ipsis: quia cedunt in ipsorum damnationem.
units.tr: We ought to ask for the forgiveness of sins: (1) for our own salvation, so that we may be preserved, for we cannot be preserved without the remission of sins; God does not grant this benefit except to those who ask. (2) So that we may be reminded of the remnants of sin that cling even to the most holy, and so that our repentance may grow constantly; for the remission of sins is to be asked for every day. (3) So that we may be able to ask for and receive the other good things that precede it, because without the remission of sins the other good things are either not given or are given to our ruin. Hence the wicked often indeed receive those things, but they are not salutary for them, because they turn to their own condemnation.

units.la: Obiect. Quod habemus, non necesse est petere. Pij habent remissionem peccatorum. Ergo non necesse habent eam petere. Resp. Est fallacia à dicto secundum quid, vt simpliciter: Habent quidem remissionem peccatorum, verum non quoad continuationem. Continuari enim debet remissio, quia peccata quotidie continuantur etiam in renatis. Ergo etiam continuari debet remissionis petitio. Et Deus eam petentibus continuat, quia peccati petant filij à Patre. Etsi igitur peccata nobis Deus remittit propter Christum, nihilominus vult, vt eorum petamus veniam, & quæ admisimus, & quæ admissuri sumus.
units.tr: Objection. What we have, we need not ask for. The godly have the remission of sins; therefore they do not need to ask for it. Answer. This is a fallacy of an assertion made in a qualified sense being treated as if it were absolute. They do indeed have the remission of sins, but not as to its continuance. For the remission must be continued, because sins continue daily even in the regenerate; therefore the petition for forgiveness must also be continued. And God continues it for those who ask, since the children ask it of the Father. Therefore, although God forgives us our sins for Christ's sake, he nevertheless wills that we ask for their pardon, both for those we have committed and for those we are yet to commit.

units.la: IV. Quomodo nobis remittantur peccata, seu, quid sibi velit adiectio: Sicut & nos remittimus.
units.tr: IV. How our sins are forgiven us, or, what the addition "as we also forgive" means.

units.la: Nobis ita remittuntur peccata, sicut & nos debitoribus nostris remittimus. Hoc Christus adjecit: 1. Vt ipsa forma precationis nos cogat ad Deum accedere, & remissionē ab eo petere in vera fide, & pœnitentia, cuius signum est dilectio proximi. 2. Propter nostram consolationem: vt simus certi de remissione peccatorū nostrorum: cum ipsi etiam aliis remittamus: ac possimus statuere, nos Deo placere, etsi multæ peccatorum reliquiæ in nobis adhuc hæreant. 3. In nostrum judicium, si petentes nobis remitti, non aliis nos remittamus.
units.tr: Our sins are forgiven us in the same way as we forgive our debtors. Christ added this for the following reasons: (1) so that the very form of the prayer may compel us to approach God and to seek forgiveness from him in true faith and repentance, of which the sign is love of neighbour; (2) for our consolation, so that we may be certain of the forgiveness of our sins, since we ourselves also forgive others, and so that we may judge that we please God, even though many remnants of sin still cling to us; (3) for our judgment, so that if we ask to be forgiven, we do not fail to forgive others.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Qui non remittit, ei non remittetur. Nos non remittimus. Ergo neque nobis remittetur. Resp. ad maiorem. Qui non remittit, nempe simpliciter, hoc est, nec perfecte, nec vere. Nos per-
units.tr: Objection 1. He who does not forgive will not be forgiven. We do not forgive; therefore neither will we be forgiven. Answer to the major premise. He who does not forgive, namely absolutely, that is, neither perfectly nor truly. We however...

units.la: Quaest. CXXVI. De Quinta Petitione.
units.tr: Question 126. On the Fifth Petition.

units.la: perfecte quidem non remittimus, prout nostra fert infirmitas. Modo tamen vere & sincere remittamus, Deus nobis vere & perfecte remittet.
units.tr: Indeed we do not forgive perfectly, as our weakness bears; yet if we forgive truly and sincerely, God will forgive us truly and perfectly.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Christus jubet nos petere, ut Deus nobis remittat peccata, sicut nos remittimus. At nos non perfecte remittimus. Ergo petimus, ut etiam Deus nobis non perfecte remittat. Hoc vero est perditionem petere, quia Deus etiam minima peccata damnat. Resp. Est fallacia figurae dictionis. Particula sicut in hac petitione non significat gradum, vel aequalitatem, sed speciem, veritatem, & sinceritate remissionis nostrae & Dei, ut Deus tam vere nobis remittat, quam vere & certo nos proximo ex animo remittimus: seu (ut brevius dicam) non fit collatio remissionis juxta gradus, sed juxta veritatem & voluntatem remissionis, ut sit sensus: tam perfecte Deus peccata nobis remittit, quam vere & certo nos proximo remittere parati sumus.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ bids us ask that God forgive us our sins, as we forgive. But we do not forgive perfectly. Therefore we ask that God also forgive us imperfectly. Yet this is to ask for destruction, since God condemns even the smallest sins. Answer: This is the fallacy of the figure of speech (figura dictionis). The particle as in this petition does not signify degree or equality, but the kind, the truth and the sincerity of our forgiveness and of God's, so that God forgives us as truly as we truly and certainly forgive our neighbour from the heart. Or, to put it more briefly, the comparison is not of forgiveness according to degrees, but according to the truth and will of forgiving; the sense is: God forgives our sins as perfectly as we are ready to forgive our neighbour truly and certainly.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Christus apud Lucam jubet nos precari: Remitte nobis peccata nostra: quia & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Ergo remissio nostra est causa remissionis divinae. Resp. Est fallacia non causae. Nostra remissio non allegatur ut causa efficiens vel meritoria, sed ut argumentum & testimonium remissionis divinae. Causa enim vel meritum esse non potest. 1. Quia est imperfecta. 2. Etiamsi perfecta esset, tamen non mereremur remittendo, quia remittere debemus. Inst. Ergo tamen aequalitas remissionis notatur. Resp. Non aequalitas, sed similitudo speciei.
units.tr: Objection 3. Christ, in Luke, bids us pray: Forgive us our sins, for we also forgive our debtors. Therefore our forgiveness is the cause of divine forgiveness. Answer: This is the fallacy of non-cause. Our forgiveness is not adduced as an efficient or meritorious cause, but as a sign and testimony of divine forgiveness. For it cannot be a cause or merit: (1) because it is imperfect; (2) even if it were perfect, we would not merit anything by forgiving, because we are bound to forgive. Objection: Yet equality of forgiveness is then indicated. Answer: Not equality, but similarity of kind.

units.la: Obj. 4. Qui habet memoriam injuriarum, & est cupidus vindictae, non vere remittit. Nos omnes habemus memoriam injuriarum, & sumus cupidi vindictae. Ergo non vere remittimus. Ad maiorem. Qui habet memoriam injuriarum, videlicet cum voluntate eas vindicandi, & sine repugnantia: is non vere remittit. Etsi vero nos omnem memoriam offensarum aegre, aut vix, possumus deponere: tamen modo non obsequamur affectibus, sed resistamus reliquiis peccatorum, quae nobis adhuc adhaerent, nec iis assentiamur: nil impedit, quo minus vere & ex animo aliis remittamus, illud etiam consequamur, cuius causa haec particula sicut addita fuit a Christo, & recte petimus. Recte enim petimus, cum dem & poenitentiam petimus, quam praxis petitionis huius confirmat. Fides confirmatur petitione hac, quia cum proximo vere remittimus, possumus certo statuere, nobis etiam peccata esse remissa, & sic habemus bonam conscientiam: ac sumus certi de exauditione, juxta promissionem Christi: Si remiseritis hominibus offensas ipsorum, remittet etiam vobis Pater ille caelestis. Poenitentia vera similiter in nobis augetur hac petitione: quia ad eam exstimulamur conditione adiecta: sicut & nos &c. Si enim nobis remitremitti volumus, aliis remittamus necesse est. Vtraq; causa continetur verbis Christi: Ni remiseritis hominibus offensas ipsorum, remittet etiam vobis Pater ille cœlestis, q. d. inde certo statuere poteritis à Patre vestro cœlesti vos exauditos esse: quibus verbis comprehensa est confirmatio fidei: sequens antithesis addit stimulum pœnitentiæ: Si autem non remiseritis hominibus ipsorum offensas, nec Pater vester remittet vobis offensas vestras.
units.tr: Objection 4. He who keeps the memory of injuries and is eager for revenge does not truly forgive. We all keep the memory of injuries and are eager for revenge. Therefore we do not truly forgive. To the major premise: he who keeps the memory of injuries, namely with the will to avenge them and without resistance, does not truly forgive. Although we can put aside the memory of offences only with difficulty, or scarcely at all, yet provided we do not yield to our passions but resist the remnants of sin which still cling to us, and do not assent to them, nothing hinders us from forgiving others truly and from the heart, and also from obtaining that for whose sake Christ added this particle as; and we pray rightly. For we pray rightly when we ask for faith and repentance, as the practice of this petition confirms. Faith is strengthened by this petition, because when we truly forgive our neighbour, we can determine with certainty that our own sins are forgiven too, and so we have a good conscience; and we are certain of being heard, according to the promise of Christ: If you forgive men their offences, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. True repentance is likewise increased in us by this petition, because we are stirred to it by the added condition: as we also &c. For if we wish to be forgiven, we must of necessity forgive others. Both reasons are contained in the words of Christ: If you forgive men their offences, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, that is, you may thence determine with certainty that you are heard by your heavenly Father; in these words the confirmation of faith is comprised. The following antithesis adds a goad to repentance: But if you do not forgive men their offences, neither will your Father forgive you your offences.

units.la: Obj. 5. Paulus non remisit Alexandro, quia dicit: Alexander faber nobis fecit multa mala, reddat ei Dominus secundum facta ipsius: & tamen consecutus est remissionem. Ergo remissio nostra non est necessaria. Resp. Remissio triplex est, vindictæ, pœnæ, & judicij de aliquo. 1. Vindictam omnes homines debent remittere. De hac loquitur precatio, & hanc Paulus remisit Alexandro. 2. Pœnam, vt non possunt omnes infligere, sic nec omnes possunt remittere, & ne magistratus quidem, cuius eam est infligere, potest remittere, nisi ob graves causas. Magistratui enim Deus mandavit executionem justitiæ & legis. Hanc etiam Paulus, quantum ad se, Alexandro remisit: vult tamen eum à Deo puniri, sub conditione, si perseveret in peccato. 3. Iudicium de aliis non semper est remittendum. Deus enim prohibens mendacium, non vult, vt de nebulonibus judicemus, quod sint viri boni vel honesti: sed vult nos discernere bonos à malis. Idem præcipit Christus: Ne date quod sanctum est canibus, nec margaritas porcis. Idem: Estote prudentes vt serpentes, & simplices sicut columbæ. Non ergo peccatum Paulus, retinens judicium de Alexandro, vt de homine malo, donec non resipuit.
units.tr: Objection 5. Paul did not forgive Alexander, because he says: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil; the Lord will reward him according to his works; and yet he obtained forgiveness. Therefore our forgiveness is not necessary. Answer: Forgiveness is threefold: of revenge, of punishment, and of judgement concerning someone. (1) All men ought to forgive revenge. It is of this that the prayer speaks, and this Paul forgave Alexander. (2) As not all men can inflict punishment, so not all can remit it; nor can even the magistrate, whose task it is to inflict it, remit it except for serious causes. For God has entrusted to the magistrate the execution of justice and law. Paul too, so far as he himself was concerned, forgave Alexander this; yet he wishes him to be punished by God, on condition that he persists in sin. (3) Judgement about others is not always to be remitted. For God, forbidding lying, does not want us to judge scoundrels to be good or honest men, but wants us to distinguish the good from the evil. Christ likewise commands: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor pearls to swine. Likewise: Be wise as serpents, and simple as doves. Paul therefore did not sin in retaining his judgement of Alexander as a wicked man, so long as he did not repent.

units.la: QVÆSTIO CXXVII.
units.tr: QUESTION 127.

units.la: Qua est sexta petitio? RESPONSIO.
units.tr: What is the sixth petition? ANSWER.

units.la: Ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo: hoc est; Quoniam ipsi natura adeo debiles & infirmi sumus, vt ne momento quidem subsistere possimus a: infensissimi autem hostes nostri, Satan b, mundus c, ac noster caro, d, nos continenter oppugnant: tu nos sustentes & spiritus tui robore firmes, ne in hoc spirituali certamine succumbamus e, sed tantisper illis fortiter resistamus, donec integram tandem victoriam obtineamus f.
units.tr: Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. That is: since we are by nature so weak and frail that we cannot stand even for a moment, while our most bitter enemies, Satan a, the world b, and our flesh c, assail us without ceasing, may you sustain us and strengthen us by the power of your Spirit, so that we do not succumb in this spiritual struggle, but resist them bravely for as long as it takes, until at last we obtain complete victory.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hic aliqui vnam, aliqui duas petitiones faciunt. Sed non est Tentatio certandum, modo nihil de doctrina decedat. Potius tamen duæ duplex sunt partes vnius petitionis. Ne inducas in tentationem; est petitio liberationis à malo futuro: sed libera nos à malo, est petitio liberationis à malo præsenti.
units.tr: Some make one petition here, and some make two. But the matter need not be contested, provided nothing is taken away from the doctrine. Still, the two are rather two parts of one petition. Lead us not into temptation is a petition for deliverance from future evil; but deliver us from evil is a petition for deliverance from present evil.

units.la: Consideranda vero hic: I. Quid sit tentatio. II. Quid sit inducere in tentationem. III. Quid sit liberare à malo. IV. Cur necessaria sit hæc petitio.
units.tr: Here we must consider: I. What temptation is. II. What it is to lead into temptation. III. What it is to deliver from evil. IV. Why this petition is necessary.

units.la: I. Quid sit Tentatio.
units.tr: I. What temptation is.

units.la: Duæ sunt species tentationis: Alia est Dei, alia diaboli. Tentatio Dei, seu qua Deus tentat, est exploratio fidei, pietatis, pœnitentiæ & obedientiæ nostræ, quæ fit à Deo per impedimenta quæcunque nostræ salutis, velut per omnia mala, diabolum, carnem, cupiditates, mundum, afflictiones, calamitates, diabolum, &c. vt patefiat nobis & aliis nostra fides, patientia, spes, & constantia, &c. Sic Deus dicitur tentasse Abrahamum, Iosephū, Iobum, Dauidem. Domine proba sti me. Sic dicitur tentare populum suum per falsos prophetas, & nos probare per crucem. Tentatio diaboli, seu qua diabolus & caro nostra, atq; etiam impij nos tentant, est quæuis sollicitatio ad peccandum, quæ & ipsa peccatum est. Sic diabolus tentabat Iobum, vt eum à Deo auocaret, quem ante amârat & coluerat: quamuis res aliter cesserit: & Dauidem impellens eum ad numerandum Israelem.
units.tr: There are two kinds of temptation: one is God's, the other is the devil's. The temptation of God, or the way God tempts, is the testing of our faith, piety, repentance and obedience, which God carries out through whatever hindrances there are to our salvation, such as all evils, the devil, the flesh, lusts, the world, afflictions, calamities, and so on, so that our faith, patience, hope and constancy may be made manifest both to us and to others. Thus God is said to have tempted Abraham, Joseph, Job and David. Prove me, O Lord. Thus he is said to tempt his people through false prophets, and to prove us through the cross. The temptation of the devil, or the way the devil, our flesh, and also the wicked tempt us, is any enticement to sin, and this is itself sin. Thus the devil tempted Job, to turn him away from God, whom he had earlier loved and worshipped, although the outcome was otherwise; and he moved David to number Israel.

units.la: Object. Atqui Deus neminem tentat: Vnusquisque cum tentatur, non dicat se à Deo tentari, sed tentatur à sua concupiscentia. Resp. Deus neminem tentat, sollicitando ad peccatum, tentat autem nos explorando. Diabolus, mundus, caro nostra nos tentat abstrahendo à Deo, & sollicitando ad malum. Sic Deus neminem tentat. Dicitur vero Abrahamum, Iobum, Dauidem tentasse, id est, explorasse fidem & constantiam eorum per afflictiones & crucem. Sic etiam explorat nostram fidem, spem, patientiam, dilectionem, inuocationem, constantiam, an velimus etiam cum colere in afflictionibus.
units.tr: Objection: But God tempts no one: Let no one who is tempted say that he is tempted by God, but each is tempted by his own concupiscence. Reply: God tempts no one by enticing him to sin, but he does tempt us by testing us. The devil, the world and our flesh tempt us by drawing us away from God and enticing us to evil. So God tempts no one. Yet he is said to have tempted Abraham, Job and David, that is, to have tested their faith and constancy through afflictions and the cross. In the same way he also tests our faith, hope, patience, love, invocation and constancy, and whether we are willing to worship him even in afflictions.

units.la: II. Quid sit inducere in tentationem.
units.tr: II. What it is to lead into temptation.

units.la: In tentationem Dei nos inducere, est Deum voluntate & judicio justissimo nos explorare. Inducere nos in tentationem diaboli, est, Deum permittere, vt à diabolo sollicitemur. Vtrumque hic depredeprecamur, nostri videlicet explorationem, & sollicitationem ad peccandum.
units.tr: To lead us into God's temptation is for God, by his will and most just judgment, to test us. To lead us into the devil's temptation is for God to permit us to be enticed by the devil. Here we pray against both: namely, against his testing us, and against being enticed to sin.

units.la: Petimus igitur: 1. Ne Deus nos tentet etiam explorandi causa: aut si tentet, suggerat nobis vires. 2. Ne sinat diabolum, vel mundum, vel carnem nostram nos sollicitare ad peccandum: aut si sinat, ipse nobis adsit, ne in peccata prolabamur. Est ergo sensus: Ne inducas nos in tentationem: hoc est: Ne nos tentes, supra id, quod possumus ferre: nec sinas diabolum ita nos tentare, ut vel peccemus, vel prorsus deficiamus.
units.tr: We therefore pray: (1) that God would not tempt us, even for the sake of testing; or, if he does tempt us, that he would supply us with strength; (2) that he would not allow the devil, the world or our flesh to entice us to sin; or, if he allows it, that he himself would be with us, so that we do not slide into sins. The sense, then, is: Lead us not into temptation: that is, do not tempt us beyond what we can bear, and do not allow the devil to tempt us in such a way that we either sin or utterly fail.

units.la: Obiect. Tentationes quae sunt bonae respectu Dei, sunt malae respectu diaboli; & nihilominus in has nos inducit Deus: ergo Deus est causa peccati. Resp. Fallacia est accidentis. Sunt peccata respectu diaboli: quia illis nos vult allicere ad peccata: respectu Dei non sunt peccata, quia sunt explorationes, castigationes, martyria. Harum Deus est author: quia hactenus tentationes immittit. In quantum vero sunt sollicitationes ad malum: Deus eas non vult, nec probat vel efficit, sed permittit.
units.tr: Objection. Temptations which are good with respect to God are bad with respect to the devil; and nevertheless God leads us into these. Therefore God is the cause of sin. Reply. This is the fallacy of accident. They are sins with respect to the devil, because he wishes to entice us to sin by them; with respect to God they are not sins, because they are tests, chastisements and martyrdoms. God is the author of these, since he sends temptations. But insofar as they are enticements to evil, God does not will them, nor approve or effect them, but permits them.

units.la: III. Quid sit: Libera nos à malo.
units.tr: III. What is meant by: Deliver us from evil.

units.la: Mali nomine aliqui hic intelligunt diabolum, aliqui peccatū, aliqui mortem. Sed optime comprehenduntur omnia mala aulpæ & poenæ, sive ea sint praesentia, sive futura, ipseque adeo diabolus omnium malorum author & architectus, qui vocatur ὁ πονηρὸς, per excellentiam. Scribo vobis adolescentes, quoniam νικήκατε τὸν πονηρόν malum illum vicistis. Quod supra haec redundat à malo est. Cyprianus intelligit de malis, hoc est, de cunctis aduersis, quae contra nos molitur inimicus, à quibus non potest esse firma tutela, nisi Deus nos liberet.
units.tr: By the word evil some here understand the devil, some sin, some death. But all evils of guilt and of punishment, whether present or future, are very well comprehended, and the devil himself, the author and architect of all evils, who is called ὁ πονηρὸς [ho ponēros], the evil one, par excellence. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one [νικήκατε τὸν πονηρόν]. What goes beyond these is of evil. Cyprian understands it of evils, that is, of all the adversities which the enemy devises against us, against which there can be no secure protection unless God delivers us.

units.la: Cum ergo petimus, ut nos Deus liberet à malo, petimus 1. Ut nihil mali nobis immittat, sed nos custodiat ab omnibus malis praesentibus & futuris, tum culpae tum poenae. 2. Ut si immittat mala, ea mitiget in hac vita, atque in salutem nostram convertat, ut sint nobis salutaria. 3. Ut tandem in altera vita plene ac perfecte nos liberet, & abstergat ab oculis nostris omnē lacrymam.
units.tr: When therefore we pray that God would deliver us from evil, we pray: 1. That he would send us no evil, but keep us from all evils present and future, both of guilt and of punishment. 2. That if he does send evils, he would soften them in this life and turn them to our salvation, so that they may be profitable to us. 3. That at last, in the other life, he would fully and perfectly deliver us, and wipe every tear from our eyes.

units.la: IV. Cur necessaria sit haec petitio.
units.tr: IV. Why this petition is necessary.

units.la: Necessaria haec est petitio: 1. Propter multitudinem & potentiam hostium, magnitudinem malorum, & nostram infirmitatem. 2. Propter praecedentem petitionem, ut illam possimus obtinere, quia non remittuntur nobis peccata, nisi persistamus in fide & poenitentia. Si igitur volumus, ut peccata Deus nobis remittat, oportet nos in fide & poenitentia perstare. Non persistemus autem: si supra vires tentemur, si ruamus in peccata, si denique deficiamus à Deo ipso.
units.tr: This petition is necessary: (1) on account of the number and power of our enemies, the greatness of the evils, and our own weakness; (2) on account of the preceding petition, so that we may obtain it, since our sins are not forgiven us unless we persist in faith and repentance. If therefore we want God to forgive us our sins, we must persist in faith and repentance. Yet we will not persist if we are tempted beyond our strength, if we fall into sins, and, finally, if we fall away from God himself.

units.la: Quaest. CXXVII. De Sexta Petitione.
units.tr: Question 127. On the Sixth Petition.

units.la: Obiect.1. Res bonæ & nobis vtiles non sunt deprecandæ. Tentationes Dei, vt examina per morbos, paupertatem, falsos prophetas, &c. sunt res bonæ & nobis vtiles. Ergo non sunt deprecandæ. Resp. ad maiorem: Res bonæ, vel vtiles non sunt deprecandæ, scilicet quæ per se sunt vtiles vel bonæ. At examina, afflictiones, cruces, & reliquæ tentationes tantum prosunt per accidens, propter accedentem misericordiam Dei: sine qua afflictiones non modo non sunt vtiles, sed etiam sunt pars mortis, & præsentissimus ad mortem temporalem & æternam aditus. Quatenus igitur afflictiones sunt malæ per se, & destruentes naturam, eatenus eas deprecamur. Quatenus vero nobis, qui credimus, diuina benignitate sunt salutares: eatenus eas non deprecamur. Seu, bonum illud, quod concurrit cum afflictionibus & crucej non deprecamur: sed ipsam crucem & afflictiones, quæ per se sunt malæ, quia destruunt naturam. Sic & mortem, vt per se malam deprecamur: quia & Christus eam deprecatus est: Transeat à me calix iste. Quatenus erat cruciatus & destructio. Immo eatenus nec Pater eam voluit. Quatenus verò erat ἀντ pro peccatis electorum, eatenus eam volebat & Christus & Pater: Verùmtamen non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat.
units.tr: Objection 1. Good things and things useful to us should not be prayed against. Temptations sent by God, such as trials through sickness, poverty, false prophets, etc., are good and useful to us. Therefore they should not be prayed against. Answer to the major premise: Good or useful things should not be prayed against, namely those that are good or useful in themselves. But trials, afflictions, crosses and other temptations profit us only incidentally, through the mercy of God that accompanies them. Without that mercy afflictions are not only unprofitable but are also a part of death and the most direct approach to temporal and eternal death. So far as afflictions are evil in themselves and destroy our nature, we pray against them. So far as, by the kindness of God, they are salutary to us who believe, we do not pray against them. Or: we do not pray against the good that accompanies afflictions and crosses, but against the cross and afflictions themselves, which are evil in themselves because they destroy our nature. So too we pray against death, as evil in itself, because Christ also prayed against it: Let this cup pass from me, so far as it was torment and destruction. Indeed, so far as it was this, neither did the Father will it. But so far as it was a ransom [ἀντί] for the sins of the elect, so far both Christ and the Father willed it: Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.

units.la: Obiect.2. Quæ Deus vult, ea recusare non licet. Vult autem Deus nostras tentationes. Ergo non licet eas recusare. Resp. ad maiorem: Quæ Deus vult, ea recusare non licet, scilicet, quatenus ea Deus vult, seu, quæ Deus vult simpliciter. Tentationes autem Deus vult non simpliciter, nec quatenus sunt destructio, sed tantum quatenus sunt vel exercitia fidei, & invocationis, vel ὑπομονῆς, vel δοκιμασίας constantiæ nostræ. Hactenus nos etiam debemus illas velle, non aurè simpliciter. Quod vero non oportet nos simpliciter velle tentationes, hinc patet: quia ferre illas est patientiæ: quod non esset, sed potius officij nostri, si simpliciter deberemus eas velle, nec eas deprecari nobis liceret. Non vult ergo Deus, nos velle mala quatenus mala, verum quatenus mala sunt nobis bona, vult, ea nos patienter ferre.
units.tr: Objection 2. What God wills, it is not lawful to refuse. But God wills our temptations. Therefore it is not lawful to refuse them. Answer to the major premise: What God wills, it is not lawful to refuse, namely in so far as God wills it, or what God wills absolutely. But God does not will temptations absolutely, nor as destruction, but only as they are either exercises of faith and prayer, or of endurance [ὑπομονῆς] and proving [δοκιμασίας] of our constancy. So far we too ought to will them, but not absolutely. That we ought not to will temptations absolutely is clear from this: to bear them belongs to patience. That would not be so, but would rather be a duty of ours, if we were bound to will them absolutely, and it would not be lawful for us to pray against them. God therefore does not will us to will evils as evils; but since, as evils, they are good for us, he wills that we bear them patiently.

units.la: Obiect.3. Quod nunquam impetratur, id frustra petitur. Vt in hac vita non inducamur in tentationem, nunquam impetramus. Omnes enim qui volunt piè viuere in Christo Iesu, patientur persecutiones. Ergo frustra hoc petimus. Resp. Est fallacia non causæ vt causæ. Petimus enim, ne introducamur in tentationem, non quia simus planè hic liberandi. Sed 1. Quia à multis liberamur, quibus periremus, nisi peteremus liberationem. Hæc esset sufficiens causa. 2. Vt illa etiam, in quæ incidimus mala, sint nobis salutaria. Petentibus autem in genere liberationem, vult Deus hæc duo date valde magna. Propter tamen peccati reliquias, vult esse imperfectum beneficium etiam petentibus nobis, quia pe-tere nos vult cum conditione voluntatis suae, & cum inducia, quod in altera vita integre id simus consecuturi.
units.tr: Objection 3. What is never obtained is prayed for in vain. We never obtain that we not be led into temptation in this life. For all who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecutions. Therefore we pray for this in vain. Answer: This is the fallacy of taking a non-cause for a cause. For we pray that we not be led into temptation, not because we are to be wholly delivered from them here. But (1) because we are delivered from many dangers by which we would perish, were we not to pray for deliverance; this alone would be a sufficient reason. (2) So that even the evils into which we fall may be salutary to us. When we ask in general for deliverance, God wills to grant us these two very great things. Yet, on account of the remnants of sin, the benefit remains imperfect even for us who pray, because God wills us to pray with the condition of his will, and with a delay, since in the other life we shall obtain it entirely.

units.la: Visus huius petitionis 1. Est confessio propriae infirmitatis in sustinendis tentationibus etiam minimis, ne se quis insolenter exollat, ut Petrus cum Christo mori volens; neq; confessionis aut passionis gloriam suam ducat: cum Dominus, ipse humilitatem doceat, inquiens: Vigilate & orate, ne incidatis in tentationem. Qui sibi videtur stare, videat, ne cadat. 2. Est concio de arrumnis praesentis vitae, ne simus securi: nec mundum amemus. 3. Est confessio providentiae Dei, quia (ut Cyprianus scribit) ostenditur nihil adversus nos diabolum posse, nisi Deus ante permiserit, ut omnis timor noster atque observatio ad Deum convertatur: cum in tentationibus nostris nihil malo liceat, nisi potestas ei a Deo concedatur. Datur autem potestas adversus nos malo, secundum peccata nostra, sicut dicitur: Quis dedit in direptionem Iacob, &c. Nonne Deus, cui peccaverunt, & noluerunt ambulare in viis eius? Et quidem potestas ei datur dupliciter, vel ad poenam, cum delinquimus, vel ad gloriam, cum probamur, &c. Haec Cyprianus.
units.tr: The purpose of this petition is, (1) a confession of our own weakness in bearing temptations, even the smallest, so that no one may insolently exalt himself, as Peter did when he wanted to die with Christ; nor may anyone count the glory of confession or suffering his own, since the Lord himself teaches humility, saying: Watch and pray, that you do not enter into temptation. Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. (2) A sermon on the troubles of the present life, so that we may not be secure, nor love the world. (3) A confession of the providence of God, because (as Cyprian writes) it is shown that the devil can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it, so that all our fear and attention may be turned toward God; since in our temptations the evil one is allowed to do nothing unless power is granted him by God. Now power is given to the evil one against us according to our sins, as it is said: Who gave Jacob up for plunder, etc.? Was it not the Lord, against whom they have sinned, and who would not walk in his ways? And indeed power is given to him in two ways: either for punishment, when we offend, or for glory, when we are proved, etc. So Cyprian.

units.la: Nunc observandus est ordo, & cohaerentia omnium harum petitionum 1. Iussit nos Dominus petere veram Dei agnitionem & professionem, quae est causa reliquorum beneficiorum. 2. Ut nos gubernet spiritu suo, atque ita nos in ea agnitione perpetuo conservet ac confirmet. 3. Ut quisque per eam officium in sua vocatione faciat & exsequatur. 4. Ut det nobis ea, quibus possit unusquisque officium suum facere, nempe bona corporalia. Cum prioribus fidebemus esse in vocatione nostra, oportet nos vivere & habere necessaria ad vitam, ergo cohaeret etiam petitio quarta. Nam sicut bona spiritualia & corporalium pertinent, 5. Subiunxit petitioni bonorum spiritualium & corporalium commodam objectionem de indignitate nostra: ut possis nobis dare bona spiritualia & corporalia, remitte nobis debita nostra.
