units.tr: We dealt with the saying in Matthew 5:39 above, in Aphorism X. In Matthew 26:52 Christ took the sword from his disciples and from other private persons, because it is not due to apostles, bishops, ministers, and other subjects. He did not take it away from Caesar, to whom God had previously given the sword, but rather confirmed it to him, since he said: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's." And through the Apostle: "He is God's minister, and does not bear the sword in vain."

units.la: Verum quoque est, nouum Testamentum charitatem suadere, non sanguinem, quoad ecclesiasticam & ciuilem consociationem. Nonnunquam tamen contra domesticos, & externos hostes sanguinem & gladium gerendum præcipit, ad conseruationem Reipublicæ, Ecclesiæ & communis tranquillitatis ac pacis ergo. Deus namque talem vltionem expressè mandauit etiam in nouo Testamento: atque iccirco obedientia est pars cultus diuini. Talis quoque vltio cedit in defensionem piorum, eoque charitati non est contraria, sed maximè consentanea.
units.tr: It is also true that the New Testament urges love and not bloodshed, as far as ecclesiastical and civil fellowship is concerned. Yet at times it also commands that the sword and bloodshed be used against domestic and foreign enemies, for the preservation of the commonwealth, the Church, and common tranquillity and peace. For God expressly commanded such vengeance even in the New Testament, and therefore obedience is a part of divine worship. Such vengeance also serves the defence of the godly, and so it is not contrary to love but most consistent with it.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Atqui, regerunt iidem: In nouo Testamento neque testimoniis, neque exemplis probari potest, Christianis licere bellum gerere.
units.tr: But, the same people reply, neither by testimonies nor by examples in the New Testament can it be proved that Christians may wage war.

units.la: RESPONDETVR: Primò; Nouum Testamentum defensionem subditorum minimè tollit: quæ quidem interdum non aliter nisi bello & armis per magistratum potest obtineri. Deinde; de bellis Apostoli nihil literis mandarunt: quia non erant missi, vt constituerent nouam in mundo Rempublicam, sed vt in veteri politia cuiusque loci (vbi suum cuique jus reliquerunt: sicuti patet ex Paulo Rom.13. & alibi) nouam Christo colligerent Ecclesiam. Denique Johannes Baptista Christi præcursor militibus interrogantibus: Et nos quid faciemus? non respondit: Deserite militiam; sed: Neminem concutite, neque dolo opprimite, & contenti estote stipendiis vestris. Atqui in bello stipendia militibus pendebantur. Bellum igitur non improbauit Johannes. Proinde falsum est, in nouo Testamento neque testimonia, neque exempla reperiri, in quibus belli fiat mentio.
units.tr: We answer: first, the New Testament does not at all remove the defence of subjects, which at times cannot be secured by the magistrate except through war and arms. Second, the writers of the New Testament committed nothing to writing about wars, because the apostles were not sent to establish a new commonwealth in the world, but to gather a new Church for Christ within the existing political order of each place, where they left to each his own right (as is clear from Paul, Rom. 13, and elsewhere). Finally, when soldiers asked John the Baptist, Christ's forerunner, "And what shall we do?", he did not answer, "Desert the army," but: "Do violence to no one, neither accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages" (Luke 3:14). Yet soldiers were paid wages in war. John therefore did not disapprove of war. Hence it is false that neither testimonies nor examples are found in the New Testament in which war is mentioned.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Quibus de causis, & quomodo legitimè bellum debeat geri, nunc jam non disputamus. Christiani Principes, & Magistratus id sibi propositum habeant, cogitantes, omne legitimum bellum non nisi pacis recuperandæ causa suscipi debere, bellique hanc esse rationem & indolem, vt multa damna secum inferat, nec vllum tam juste fieri posse, quin injustitiæ multũ ei sit admixtum: adeò vt longe satius sit arma abijcere, bella non necessaria auersari, justa verò non ante suscipere, quam omnia pacis media fuerint tentata: non solum, quia teste Poeta, ------ Pax optima rerum, Quas homini nouisse datum est: pax vna triumphis Innumeris potior:
units.tr: For what reasons, and how, war may lawfully be waged, we do not now go on to discuss. Let Christian princes and magistrates keep this aim before them, considering that every lawful war ought to be undertaken only for the sake of recovering peace; that war has this character and nature, that it brings many losses with it; and that no war can be waged so justly that much injustice is not mixed with it. Thus it is far better to lay down arms, to avoid unnecessary wars, and not to undertake even just wars until all means of peace have been tried. This is so not only because, as the poet says: "Peace is the best of things, which it has been granted to man to know; peace alone is better than countless triumphs."

units.la: sed multo magis, quia verbum Dei dicit: Si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuite.
units.tr: but much more because the word of God says: "If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all men" (Rom. 12:18).

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Secvndo loco, quod attinet ad Leges, quibus Christianus magistratus in gubernatione sua tenetur, recte antiqui dixerunt: Leges esse animam Reipublicæ: & Magistratum esse viuam legem: innuentes, quod quemadmodum absque legibus nulla consistit Respublica, ita absque magistratu leges vigorem suum habere non possint. Non quæritur autem nunc de legibus in genere: quid, quotuplices, quæ optimæ sint: sed quales illæ esse debeant, secundum quas magistratus Rempublicam debet administrare.
units.tr: In the second place, as regards the laws by which a Christian magistrate is bound in his government, the ancients rightly said that laws are the soul of the commonwealth, and that the magistrate is a living law, implying that just as no commonwealth can exist without laws, so laws cannot have their force without a magistrate. But the question now is not about laws in general: what they are, how many kinds there are, and which are best. The question is what sort of laws they ought to be, in accordance with which the magistrate ought to administer the commonwealth.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Quæ quidem quæstio non ideo superuacanea videri debet, quod multi homines imperiti fuerint, qui non dubitarint contendere, Christianos per omnia esse adstrictos ad leges Mosaicas, neque meliores posse leges forenses condi, quam Mosaicas, à Deo ipso præscriptas populo Israelitico. Quæ præpostera opinio multas turbas dedit in Ecclesia & Republica, tempore tumultuum Munsterianorum.
units.tr: This question ought not to seem superfluous merely because there have been many unlearned men who did not hesitate to contend that Christians are bound in all things to the laws of Moses, and that no better civil laws can be framed than the Mosaic ones, prescribed by God himself to the Israelite people. This preposterous opinion caused many disturbances in the Church and commonwealth at the time of the Münster tumults.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Sciendum igitur, nullam utique legem esse meliorem ac praestantiore ipsius Dei lege, quæ merito omnibus aliis præferatur: hoc tamen discrimine, ut illud fiat ad Dei voluntatem ac mentem in verbo suo patefactam. Discrimen hoc sumtum est ex triplici fine & scopo legis Mosaicæ.
units.tr: We must therefore recognise that there is certainly no law better or more excellent than God's own law, which rightly is preferred to all others; with this distinction, however, that it is so understood in accordance with the will and mind of God made known in his word. This distinction is taken from the threefold end and purpose of the Mosaic law.

units.la: Nam finis Unus spectat omnium promiscuè hominum mores, virtutes ac vitia: quæ ex lege naturæ singulis hominibus vel præcipiuntur, vel prohibentur. Et sic Deus legem suam in Decalogo comprehensam ab omnibus omnino hominibus voluit seruari.
units.tr: For the first end regards the morals, virtues and vices of all men without distinction, which are either commanded or forbidden to individuals by the law of nature. And so God wished his law, comprehended in the Decalogue, to be kept by absolutely all men.

units.la: Alter finis & scopus legis Mosaicæ fuit gubernare sacerdotium Leuiticum per certos ritus & cæremonias, quæ fuerunt typus sacerdotij Jesu Christi. Huius sacerdotij Aaronici leges Deus voluit durare ac vigere non nisi ad tempora Christi exhibiti, actum rursum abrogari. Has leges cæremoniales qui in nouum Testamentum velit introducere, eum Jesu Christi adventum in carnem simul abnegare, & Judaismum introducere necesse foret.
units.tr: The second end and purpose of the Mosaic law was to govern the Levitical priesthood by certain rites and ceremonies, which were a type of the priesthood of Jesus Christ. God willed that the laws of this Aaronic priesthood should endure and have force only until the time of Christ's appearance, and then be abrogated again. Whoever wished to introduce these ceremonial laws into the New Testament would at the same time deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, and it would be necessary to introduce Judaism.

units.la: Tertius legis finis & scopus politiam Judaicam spectat: in qua Deus populum Israeliticum certis legibus discernere voluit ab omnibus aliis populis: eò quod ex tribu Juda nasciturus esset Messias Salvator mundi. Hæc lex de voluntate Dei tamdiu durare debuit, quoad populorum obseruaretur discrimen. Hoc vero discrimen cessauit tum, quando Christus est natus, & ex duobus populis, Judæis ac gentibus, unum fecit populum, nempe fideles Christianos: uti testatur Paulus Ephes. 2, 14. Iccirco Christus discipulis & apostolis suis mandauit, ut non uni duntaxat populo, sed omnibus creaturis in universo mundo annunciarent Euangelium. Hanc quoque legem ciuilem si quis Christianis
units.tr: The third end of the law concerns the Jewish polity, in which God willed to distinguish the Israelite people by certain laws from all other peoples, because the Messiah, the Saviour of the world, was to be born from the tribe of Judah. This law was to last by God's will only so long as the distinction between the peoples was observed. But this distinction ceased when Christ was born and made one people out of two, Jews and Gentiles, namely faithful Christians, as Paul testifies (Eph. 2:14). For this reason Christ commanded his disciples and apostles to announce the gospel not to one people only, but to all creatures in the whole world. If anyone wished to impose this civil law on Christians

units.la: ctianis stianis vt absolutè necessariam vellet obtrudere: quid quæso aliud ageret, quam vt negaret, Christum venisse in carnem pro redemtione populi sui?
units.tr: Christians as absolutely necessary, what, I ask, would he be doing other than denying that Christ came in the flesh to redeem his people?

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Ex his liquet, Legem Dei cæremonialem & forensem Judæis olim optimam quidem fuisse legem vsque ad Christum: vtramque tamen hodie, Deo sic decernente, esse per Christum abrogatam: adeo quidem, vt & ipsi Judæi neutram hodie vel velint, vel possint seruare. Omnibus igitur populis, penes quos est Ecclesia Christi, ea est concessa libertas, vt Rempublicam vitatis & positiuis suis legibus gubernent. Legem verò moralem, quæ est <bl>ἐχνπ</bl> imago legis naturalis & communis æquitatis, Deus minimè abrogauit: quin potius illa ex præscripto Dei obligat omnes pariter homines, tam Judæos, quam gentes, siue Christianos.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the ceremonial and forensic law of God was indeed the best law for the Jews until Christ. Both are now abrogated through Christ, God so decreeing, so that even the Jews themselves neither wish nor are able to keep either of them today. Therefore all peoples among whom the Church of Christ is have been granted the liberty to govern their commonwealth by their own laws of life and their positive laws. But God by no means abrogated the moral law, which is the image [εἰκών] of the natural law and of common equity. Rather, by God's prescription it binds all people alike, Jews as well as Gentiles, or Christians.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Summa huc redit.
units.tr: The sum of this comes to the following.

units.la: I. Christiani Principis & Magistratus officium est, secundum legem moralem Dei, in Decalogi duabus Tabulis descriptam, ceu normam vnicam ac certissimam omnis æquitatis, & justitiæ, subditos suos gubernare, à qua regula ne latum quidem vnguem in politia sua administranda discedere debet.
units.tr: I. It is the duty of a Christian prince and magistrate to govern his subjects according to the moral law of God, described in the two Tables of the Decalogue, as the sole and most certain rule of all equity and justice; and from this rule he ought not to depart even by a hair's breadth in administering his commonwealth.

units.la: II. Quandoquidem ciuiles causæ (absq; quibus societas humana non consistit) de judiciis, præfecturis, emtionibus & venditionibus, aliisq; contractibus: de hereditatibus item, pœnis ac supplicüs, & id genus aliis statutis, in lege Dei expresse non sancitur, sed magistratui Christiano de iis jus ferendi liberum relinquitur: possunt vtique particulares illæ leges pro cuiusq; religionis aut prouinciæ, populi, aut ciuitatis consuetudine & prilegiis à pio quouis magistratu sanciri ac promulgari, habita tamen ratione communis & naturalis æquitatis. Inter omnes vero leges ciuiles omnium aliorum populorum æquissimæ illæ semper habitæ fuerunt, vtpote juri diuino ac naturali cumma-xime consentaneæ, quæ à Romanis olim sunt latæ: quas & ipsi Christiani Imperatores, Reges, Principes, ac subditi passim approbarunt, atq; retinuerunt: immò & Paulus apostolus, etiam tum, cum adhuc inter Judæos versaretur, illis ipsis legibus se lubens subjecit; & ad illos sæpius prouocauit in Actis: Ego, inquit, natus sum ciuis Romanus. Et: Ad tribunal Cæsaris sto, vbi me oportet judicari: Cæsarem appello. Petrus item Apostolus cohortatus est Christianos, vt legibus Romanorum se subijcerent, atque ob-remtemperarent. Approbauit itaque Romanorum Rempublicam, & eiusdem leges ciuiles, quas à Magistratu ciuili Christiano observari voluit.
units.tr: II. Since civil matters (without which human society cannot exist), concerning judgements, offices, buying and selling, and other contracts, likewise inheritances, penalties and punishments, and other statutes of this kind, are not expressly sanctioned in the law of God, but freedom to enact laws concerning them is left to the Christian magistrate, it is certainly possible for such particular laws to be enacted and promulgated by any pious magistrate according to the custom and privileges of his religion, province, people or city, provided that regard is had to common and natural equity. Among all civil laws, however, those of the Romans, which were enacted long ago, have always been regarded as the most equitable of all peoples' laws, as being most consonant with divine and natural right; and these the Christian emperors, kings, princes and subjects themselves everywhere approved and retained. Indeed the apostle Paul, even while he was still living among the Jews, willingly submitted himself to those very laws, and appealed to them frequently in the Acts: "I," he says, "am a Roman citizen." And: "I stand at Caesar's tribunal, where I must be judged; I appeal to Caesar." The apostle Peter likewise exhorted Christians to submit to the laws of the Romans and to obey them. Thus he approved the Roman commonwealth and its civil laws, which he wished to be observed by the Christian civil magistrate.

units.la: III. Denique cum neque in lege Dei morali leges forenses sint expressæ, sed Christianorum principum, subditorumque arbitrio relictæ: neque in legibus scriptis Romanorum (quæ fermè ab omnibus Christianis Rebuspublicis approbatæ sunt) viuuscuiusque populi, nationis, loci, ciuitatis, casus omnes expresse sint comprehensi: nec insuper iura municipalia, siue consuetudines ac sanctiones particulares sublatæ: Principes ac magistratus Christiani sedulo prouidebunt, certis quoq; legibus positiuis res illas adiaphoras, de quibus à Deo nihil vel præceptum vel prohibitum legimus, determinare. Exempli gratia: An opus his vel illis muniis? Num vectigal maius vel minus imponendum subditis? An arma sint gerenda ciuibus? & id genus alia. Quas leges positiuas nominant Iurisconsulti: quod iuri naturali, iuri item diuino sint consentaneæ, latæ pro communi bono Reipublicæ promouendo: eoque ab subditis omni iure seruandæ: neque citra conscientiæ violationem spernendæ; quemadmodum scriptum est: Necesse est subiici, non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam.
units.tr: III. Finally, since neither are forensic laws expressed in the moral law of God, but are left to the judgement of Christian princes and subjects; nor are all the cases of each people, nation, place, city expressly comprehended in the written laws of the Romans (which have been approved by almost all Christian commonwealths); nor, moreover, have municipal rights, or customs and particular sanctions, been abolished: Christian princes and magistrates will diligently take care to determine by certain positive laws those indifferent matters, about which we read nothing commanded or forbidden by God. For example: Is labour to be owed for these or those public works? Is a greater or lesser tax to be imposed on subjects? Are citizens to bear arms? And other matters of this kind. Jurists call these positive laws, because they are consonant with natural right and likewise with divine right, enacted for the promotion of the common good of the commonwealth; and therefore they are to be observed by subjects by every right, and are not to be spurned without violation of conscience; as it is written: "It is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience' sake."

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Ius & officium subditorum consistit in tribus. Primo; vt debito honore ac reuerentia prosequantur magistratum: obdignitatem scilicet eam, quam à Deo accepit. Honor ille non externis gestibus proprie exhibetur magistratui; quem sic quoque reuerentur homines improbi, pro malo necessario magistratum habentes: sed potissimum magistratus debito honore afficiuntur, quando subditi in magistratu agnoscunt ordinationem diuinam: quod sit vicarius & minister Dei; cui Deus ipse transtulerit suam potestatem regendi subditos secundum voluntatem Dei. Hinc dependet reuerentia & amor: timor item, & alia obsequia magistratui præstanda. Quem quidem honorem Deus in lege præcepit. Honora patrem & matrem. Magistratus enim est Pater populi: vti Iosepho acclamabat populus Gen. 41. 43. Et Sapiens ait: Mi fili, time Iehouam, & Regem. Et Paulus: Reddite timorem, cui timor debetur: Et honorem, cui honor debetur. Et Petrus: Deum timete, Regem honorate.
units.tr: The right and duty of subjects consists in three things. First: that they show due honour and reverence to the magistrate, on account of the dignity which he has received from God. This honour is not properly paid to the magistrate by outward gestures; wicked men too pay such reverence, regarding the magistrate as a necessary evil; but magistrates are rightly honoured especially when subjects recognise in the magistrate the ordinance of God: that he is the vicar and minister of God, to whom God himself has transferred his power of ruling subjects according to God's will. From this depend reverence and love, likewise fear, and the other obediences to be rendered to the magistrate. God indeed commanded this honour in the law: "Honour your father and mother." For the magistrate is the father of the people, as the people acclaimed Joseph, Gen. 41:43. And the wise man says: "My son, fear Jehovah and the king." And Paul: "Render fear to whom fear is due, and honour to whom honour is due." And Peter: "Fear God, honour the king."

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Huic honori succedit Subiectio. vt nimirum pii subditi magistratui suo in omnibus rebus iustis præstent obedientiam in Domino. Quæ quidem obedientia rursum in tribus consistit.
units.tr: To this honour succeeds subjection: namely, that pious subjects render obedience to their magistrate in all just matters, in the Lord. This obedience in turn consists of three things.

units.la: I. Vt subditi pareant omnibus præceptis ac mandatis magi-stratus.
units.tr: I. That subjects obey all the precepts and commands of the magistrate.

units.la: II. Vt pendant debita tributa, & vectigalia.
units.tr: II. That they pay the due taxes and tolls.

units.la: III. Vt ciuilia onera sine murmure ferant; quæ faciunt ad conseruationem Reipublicæ, & defensionem patriæ. De his Paulus inquit: suggere ipsis, vt sese subiiciant principatibus ac potestatibus: vt obtemperent: vt ad omne opus bonum sint parati.
units.tr: III. That they bear civil burdens without murmuring, which contribute to the preservation of the commonwealth and the defence of the fatherland. Of these Paul says: "Remind them to submit themselves to principalities and powers, to obey, to be ready for every good work."

units.la: Et; Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subiecta esto. Vbi notandum, quod ait: Potestatibus supereminentibus. Subditi enim magistratui peregrino & alieno non sunt subiecti, sed suo: quemadmodum magistratus non alienis, sed suis subditis imperare potest.
units.tr: And: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers." Where it should be noted that he says "higher powers." For subjects are not subject to a foreign and alien magistrate, but to their own; just as a magistrate can command not alien subjects, but his own.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Rationes Apostoli, quibus subiectionem hanc subditis commendat, præcipuæ sex sunt.
units.tr: The Apostle's reasons, by which he commends this subjection to subjects, are chiefly six.

units.la: I. A mandato Dei. Deus sic ordinauit, vt magistratus præsint subditis: & subditi suis magistratibus obtemperent. Atqui ordinationi diuinæ non licet resistere.
units.tr: I. From the command of God. God so ordained that magistrates should preside over subjects, and that subjects should obey their magistrates. But it is not lawful to resist the divine ordinance.

units.la: II. Ab effectu contrario turpi & pernitioso. Iniquum est, creaturam resistere creatori. Atqui resistere magistratui est ipsi Deo resistere. Est enim ex ordinatione Dei minister & vicarius.
units.tr: II. From the contrary effect, which is base and pernicious. It is unjust for a creature to resist its Creator. But to resist the magistrate is to resist God himself, for by God's ordinance the magistrate is his minister and vicar.

units.la: III. Ab effectu itidem pernitioso. Contemtus & inobedientia magistratus affert vltionem & pœnam. Debet enim magistratus terrori esse malis. Stultum vero est, se temere in pœnam concurrere.
units.tr: III. Again from a pernicious effect. Contempt and disobedience of the magistrate bring vengeance and punishment. For the magistrate ought to be a terror to evildoers. It is foolish, moreover, to rush rashly into punishment.

units.la: IV. Ab effectu vtili. Obedire magistratui & legibus, cedit laudi. Magistratus enim à Deo datus est subditis in bonum.
units.tr: IV. From a useful effect. To obey the magistrate and the laws is a matter of praise. For the magistrate has been given by God to subjects for their good.

units.la: V. A causa impulsiua proegumena: & eiusdem fine. Inobedientes si non extimescunt pœnam magistratus: conscientiam tamen suam inuiolatam præstare debent: quam certè inobedientia turpiter violant, Deique iram temporalem & æternam in se provocant.
units.tr: V. From the impelling cause that goes before, and from its end. Even if disobedient persons do not fear the magistrate's punishment, they ought nonetheless to keep their conscience inviolate; and disobedience certainly violates it shamefully, and provokes God's wrath upon themselves, both temporal and eternal.

units.la: VI. A connexis. Cui debetur tributum, eidem & obedientia denegari non potest. Subditi igitur Magistratui iure tributa solentes, obedientiam quoque debitam illi præstabunt.
units.tr: VI. From things connected with it. To whom tribute is owed, to the same obedience also cannot be denied. Subjects, therefore, who rightly pay tribute to the magistrate will also render to him the obedience due.

units.la: His argumentis Paulinis subditi in omnibus Ecclesiis & Reipublicis ad obsequium debitum Magistratui præstandum omni studio adigi debent.
units.tr: By these Pauline arguments, subjects in all churches and commonwealths ought to be driven with every effort to render due obedience to the magistrate.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Requiritur præterea à subditis Tolerantia in perferendis iniuriis siue infirmitatibus magistratuum: itemq; Deprecatio pro illis apud Deum. âpud Deum. Nam quia magistratui onus incumbit non mi-nus laboriosum, quam periculosum, sub quo fatiscere sæpè & extrema quæq; sustinere necessum est: adeo, ut vix nonnun-quam illi detur respirandi locus aut tempus; iccirco non mirum est, si humanis quoq; affectibus interdum abripiantur: vrpote superbia, ambitione, intemperantia, voluptatibus, socor-dia, obliuione, securitate, iracundia, furore: & id genus passi-onibus, quibus præcæteris cò magis obnoxii esse solent, quò maioribus etiam vrgentur molestiis & assultibus. Piorum igi-tur subditorum tunc erit officium, infirmitates illas toleranter perferre: non minus atque liberos parentum suorum næuos pa-tienter ferre æquum est.
units.tr: Subjects are also required to show tolerance toward the injuries and weaknesses of magistrates, and likewise to offer intercession for them before God. For the magistrate bears a burden no less laborious than dangerous, under which he must often faint and endure the utmost extremities, so that sometimes he scarcely gets a place or time to breathe. It is therefore no wonder if he is sometimes carried away by human passions: such as pride, ambition, intemperance, love of pleasures, carelessness, forgetfulness, complacency, anger, and rage, and passions of that kind, to which those who are pressed by the greater troubles and assaults are wont to be more exposed than others. It will therefore be the duty of pious subjects to bear those weaknesses patiently, just as it is fitting to bear patiently the blemishes of their parents, as children do.

units.la: Quin imò pro felici illorum salute & incolumitate Deum in-uocare decet, ex præscripto Apostoli. Adhortor ante omnia, ut fiant deprecationes, preces, postulationes, gratiarum actiones, pro quibusuis hominibus, pro Regibus, & quibusuis in eminentia consti-tutis: ut tranquillam & quietam vitam degamus cum omni pietate & honestate. Nam hoc bonum est, & acceptum coram Seruatore nostro Deo.
units.tr: Indeed, it is proper to call upon God for the happy welfare and safety of the magistrates, according to the Apostle's prescription: "I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings, and for all who are placed in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour." (1 Tim. 2.)

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: In consideratione dicti Paulini superius alligati tres moueri solent quæstiones: ad quas breuiter & succincte respondebimus.
units.tr: In considering the above-cited passage of Paul, three questions are usually raised, to which we shall reply briefly and concisely.

units.la: Vna, ex parte subditorum: An Papa, Episcopi, & cæteri Eccle-siastici contineantur quoq; sub nomine potestatum superemineniium.
units.tr: The first, on the part of the subjects: Whether the Pope, bishops, and other ecclesiastics are also included under the name of "higher powers."

units.la: Altera, vt & Tertia, ex parte magistratus: An magistratus illi, qui vitam degunt sceleratam, honore digni sint: quales fuerunt, Ne-ro, Caligula, aliiq;, qui idololatriæ addicti.
units.tr: The second, or third, on the part of the magistrate: Whether those magistrates who lead wicked lives are worthy of honour, such as Nero, Caligula, and others who were given over to idolatry.

units.la: Item: An illi Magistratui obedientia sit præstanda, qui subditos suos variis iniuriis & oneribus premit, atq; ita personam Tyranni in-duit: ea sæpè pracipiens, quæ impingunt in bonos mores, & honestatem contra Deum, & verbum eius.
units.tr: Likewise: Whether obedience is to be rendered to a magistrate who oppresses his subjects with various injuries and burdens, and thus assumes the person of a tyrant, often commanding things that strike against good morals and honesty, and against God and his Word.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Ad Primam Quæstionem RESPONDETUR: Episcopos, Ministros, & Pastores, etsi ratione doctrinæ & officii sui, immediatè Deo sunt subiecti; nihilominus tamen quoad vocationem ipsam, Ministerium scilicet Ecclesiasticum, & in illo obeundo diligentiam: immo verò multo magis quoad vires ac vitam, facultates, gubernationem & possessiones suas, ex generali mandato Apostoli, non minus magistratui, & eiusdem iurisdictioni ac potestati subditos esse, quam omnes alios Christianos. Hinc in veteri Testamento Sacerdotes ac Levitas in officio suo ad ou-tum tum Regum omnia fecisse legimus: vt patet ex historia Dauidis, Salomonis, Iosaphati, Ioas, Hiskiæ & Iosiæ. In nouo testamento inquit Christus: Date Cæsari, quæ sunt Cæsaris. Ipsemet quoque Christus tributum pro se & Petro exsoluit. Apostolus insuper sine limitatione ait: Omnis anima subiecta esto potestatibus superemi-nentibus. Idem de Episcopis Romanis fatetur Papa Gregorius l.1.ep.xxxi. Et Chrysostomus Episcopus Constantinopolitanus dictum Pauli: Omnis anima subiecta esto, sic explicat: Id præcipitur, inquit, non tantum sæcularibus hominibus, sed omnibus sacerdotibus ac monachis, sive sit Apostolus, sive Euangelista, sive Propheta, sive quis emersit. Hæc enim subiectio nihil impedit pietatem.
units.tr: To the first question the answer is this: bishops, ministers and pastors, although in respect of the teaching and duty of their office they are subject immediately to God, are nonetheless, as to their calling itself (namely the ecclesiastical ministry), and their diligence in discharging it, and still much more as to their persons and lives, their property, their administration and their possessions, subject to the magistrate and his jurisdiction and power no less than all other Christians, by the general command of the Apostle. Hence we read that in the Old Testament the priests and Levites did everything in their office at the nod of the kings, as is clear from the history of David, Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Hezekiah and Josiah. In the New Testament Christ says: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. Christ himself also paid the tax for himself and Peter. Moreover the Apostle says without qualification: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. Pope Gregory says the same of the Roman bishops, book 1, letter 31. And Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, explains the saying of Paul, Let every soul be subject, thus: "This is commanded," he says, "not only of secular men, but of all priests and monks, whether he be an Apostle, or an Evangelist, or a Prophet, or whoever he may be." For this subjection hinders piety in no way.

units.la: S.Bernhardus sic quoq; scribit ad Henricum Archiepiscopum Senonensem, qui Regi negabat obsequium. Omnis anima potestatibus subdita sit. Si OMNIS; & vestra. Quis vos excipit ab vniuersitate? Si quis tentat excipere, conatur decipere. Aliud Christus mandauit, ac fecit. Date Cæsari, ait, quæ sunt Cæsaris, & Deo, quæ sunt Dei. Quod ore dixit, facto præstitit. Creator Cæsaris non cunctatus est Cæsari dare tributum. Vobis exemplum reliquit, vt similiter faciatis.
units.tr: St Bernard also writes in this way to Henry, Archbishop of Sens, who was refusing obedience to the King: Let every soul be subject to the powers. If EVERY soul, then yours too. Who excepts you from the universal rule? If anyone tries to except you, he is trying to deceive. Christ commanded otherwise, and acted otherwise. "Render to Caesar," he says, "the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." What he said with his mouth he performed in deed. The Creator of Caesar did not hesitate to give tribute to Caesar. He has left you an example, that you should do likewise.

units.la: Juris Cæsarei sanctio est: Omnes secundum leges viuant: etiamsi ad diuinam domum pertineant. l. Omnes. C. de leg. & Const. princip.
units.tr: A sanction of the imperial law is this: Let all live according to the laws, even if they belong to the house of God. Code, On Laws and Constitutions of the Prince, the law Omnes.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Huic mandato & exemplo Christi se Papa Romanus subdu-xit; negando Cæsari tributum & obedientiam: nec se tantum, verum etiam vniuersum clerum Ecclesiasticum: qui cum rasa sua turba tertiam pæne partem Christianorum constituit. Nec vero se tantum & Clericos suos ex potestate Cæsaris eximit, sed & omnes suas ditiones, vrbes, bona, reditus, decimas, tributa, vectigalia, & innumeros alios census, qui antea ad Cæsarem pertinebant, nunc autem omnium sæcularium principum reditus duplo superant, quasi è manu Cæsaris violenter eripuit. Nec hoc solum: sed, quod amplius est, ipsum Cæsarem, omnesq; Reges, Principes, & sæcularem quemcunq; magistratum Christianum suis pedibus subjecit, adeoque nefarie sententiam dicti Apostolici inuertit hoc modo:
units.tr: The Roman Pope has withdrawn himself from this command and example of Christ, refusing tribute and obedience to Caesar: not only himself, but the whole ecclesiastical clergy as well, who with their shaven crowd make up nearly a third of the Christians. Nor does he merely exempt himself and his clergy from the power of Caesar, but he has also, as if he had violently snatched them from Caesar's hand, taken all his dominions, cities, goods, revenues, tithes, tributes, duties, and countless other incomes which formerly belonged to Caesar, and which now exceed twice over the revenues of all secular princes. Nor is this all: but, what is more, he has put Caesar himself, and all kings, princes, and any other Christian magistrate, under his feet, and so wickedly turned the meaning of the Apostle's saying upside down in this way:

units.la: Quod Imperator debet jurare fidelitatem Papæ, Quod Imperator debet pendere ex Papæ judicio: non Papa ex Imperatoris, Quod Imperator debet pontifici caput inclinare: assendenti equum stapedam tenere.
units.tr: That the Emperor must swear fealty to the Pope; that the Emperor must depend on the Pope's judgment, not the Pope on the Emperor's; that the Emperor must bow his head to the pontiff, and hold the stirrup for him when he mounts his horse.

units.la: Quod Papa potest Imperatorem excommunicare: immo deponere.
units.tr: That the Pope can excommunicate the Emperor, and indeed depose him.

units.la: Hic; hic, inquam, vigilandum fuerit Christianis Imperatoribus, Regibus ac Principibus: an cum Christi Vicario, & Petri successuccessore: an vero potius cum Christi, Pauli, & Petri jurato hoste rem habeant. Petrus namque omnibus Ecclesiasticis pa-riter & saecularibus Christianis hoc mandatum reliquit. 1 Pet. 2. verf. 13. 14. Subiecti estote cuiuis humanae ordinationi propter Dominum: sive Regi, ut qui supereminet: sive Praesidibus, ut qui per eum mittantur, tum ad ultionem maleficorum, tum ad laudem recte agentium.
units.tr: Here, here, I say, Christian emperors, kings and princes ought to be watchful: whether they are dealing with Christ's Vicar and the successor of Peter, or rather with the sworn enemy of Christ, and of Paul and Peter. For Peter left this command alike to all Christians, both ecclesiastical and secular. 1 Pet. 2, verses 13-14: Be subject to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake: whether to the king, as supreme, or to governors, as sent by him, both for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of those who do right.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Ad alteram quaestionem breuis ac solida haec est RESPONSIO. Subditi non tam personam, quam officium magistratus debent respicere. Nero Caesar homo erat flagitiosissimus, praestitutae nequitiae & impietatis: eoque potius poena dignus, quam honore: uti referunt Historici. At vero quia Caesar fuit, Apostoli, Petrus & Paulus monent Christianos Regem honorare. Honorandus igitur propter ordinationem Dei: ut & omnes alij, qui hanc ordinationem diuinam administrant, & potestatem in nos habent, tametsi flagitiosissimi sint, & blasphemi: ob dignitatem scilicet officij, quod sustinent: vitia autem eorum, & naevi Dei vindictae merito relinquuntur.
units.tr: To the second question, this is a brief and sound answer: subjects ought to regard not so much the person as the office of the magistrate. Nero Caesar was a most wicked man, bent on set purposes of wickedness and impiety, and therefore deserved punishment rather than honour, as the historians report. Yet because he was Caesar, the apostles Peter and Paul bid Christians honour the king. He is to be honoured, then, on account of God's ordinance, and so are all others who administer this divine ordinance and hold power over us, even if they are most wicked and blasphemous; namely, on account of the dignity of the office they bear. Their vices and blemishes, however, are rightly left to the vengeance of God.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Ad tertiam quaestionem ex verbo Dei distincte RESPONDERI debet. Pharao Rex Aegypti tyrannide exercuit in populum Israeliticum, intolerabilia onera illi imponendo: Honorandus nihilominus fuit a populo, donec Deus ab hoc jugo illum liberavit. Nebucadnezar erat crudelissimus tyrannus & latro, gravissimeque affligens populum Judaicum: eundem tamen sic affatus est Daniel: Deus potentiam, fortitudinem & gloriam tibi dedit. Jeremias hortatur Judaeos captivos ad obedientiam & deprecationem pro civitate Babel, quantumuis idololatrica. Obtemperandum itaque non bono tantum magistratui, sed & tyrannis: imo vero quaeuis potius injuriae sunt perferendae, quam vel resistendum illorum potestati, aut ordinationi divinae: & regula Petri: Subditi estote cum omni timore Domini, non solum bonis & aequis, sed etiam pravis. Cogitantes scilicet, omnes potestates, tam bonas, quam malas, a Deo nobis esse praepositas. Bonae quidem, ut in illis nobis suam gratiam & misericordiam declaret. Tyranni vero, ut in his gravissimam Dei iram aduersus peccata nostra agnoscamus. Quocirca nulli subdito aut privato (extra legitimam defensionem) licet Tyrannum invadere, etiam data occasione: quemadmodum Dauid poterat quidem Saulem interficere: quem tamen dimisit: quia extrema nondum vrgebat necessitas. Non extendam, inquit, manum meam in Dominum meum: quia unctus Iehova est. Novit quippe Deus Tyrannos vel ordinaria cuiusq; regni potentia, vel alia quauis ratione miraculosa trahere ad poenam.
units.tr: To the third question an answer must be given distinctly from the Word of God. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, exercised tyranny over the people of Israel, laying intolerable burdens upon them; nevertheless he was to be honoured by the people until God freed them from this yoke. Nebuchadnezzar was a most cruel tyrant and robber, grievously afflicting the Jewish people; yet Daniel addressed him thus: God has given you power, strength and glory. Jeremiah exhorts the Jewish captives to obedience and to prayer for the city of Babylon, however idolatrous it was. Therefore obedience is owed not only to a good magistrate but also to tyrants. Indeed, any injuries are rather to be endured than either resisting their power or the divine ordinance; and the rule of Peter applies: Be subject with all fear to the Lord, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the perverse. For we should consider that all powers, good and bad alike, have been set over us by God: the good so that in them he may declare his grace and mercy toward us, and the tyrants so that in them we may recognise the most grievous wrath of God against our sins. Wherefore no subject or private person (apart from lawful self-defence) may attack a tyrant, even when an opportunity is given, just as David could indeed have killed Saul, yet spared him, because the extreme necessity did not yet press upon him. I will not stretch out my hand, he says, against my lord, because he is the anointed of Jehovah. God knows how to bring tyrants to punishment either by the ordinary power of each kingdom or by some other miraculous means.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Quanquam obedientia haec certos quoq; habet limites. Vbi enim Tyranni subditos suos ad manifestā idololatriam, vel sceelus aliquod patrandū contra expressum Dei verbum cogere cupiunt, ibi tum sacrae literae praecipiunt, tyrannicis istis edictis nequaquam esse obtemperandum, sed juxta cuiusq; conditionem suae vocationis resistendū, ac quiduis potius tolerandum. Cum enim Nebucadnezar idolum suum sub poena fornacis ignis ardentis dentis ab omnibus vellet adorari, tres socij Danielis intrepide id recusabant, dicentes Regi: Non oportet nos super hac re respondere tibi. Ecce Deus noster, quem colimus, potest eruere nos de fornace ignis ardentis, & de manu tua, ō Rex, eruet nos. Quod si non eruat nos, notum sit tibi, ō Rex, quod Deum tuum non adoramus, & statuam quam erexisti, non colemus.
units.tr: Yet this obedience also has certain limits. For when tyrants desire to compel their subjects to manifest idolatry, or to commit some crime contrary to the express Word of God, then the holy Scriptures command that such tyrannical edicts by no means be obeyed, but that one should resist according to each person's condition and calling, and rather endure anything at all. When Nebuchadnezzar wished to be adored by all under penalty of the burning fiery furnace, the three companions of Daniel fearlessly refused, saying to the king: We have no need to answer you in this matter. Behold, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if he does not deliver us, be it known to you, O king, that we do not worship your god, nor will we worship the image which you have set up.

units.la: Dario Regi se solum, non autem Deum, adorari praecipienti non obtemperauit Daniel: & obid in speluncam leonum conjectus fuit. Zedekias rex impius prophetae Ieremiae interdixit, ne Dei mandatum populo indicaret, vt in manus Chaldaeorum se se dederet: sed caproptér in carcerem est coniectus. Petrus & Iohannes Apostoli magistratui prohibenti in nomine Iesu praedicari Euangelium, respondent: An justum sit apud Deum, vobis potius auscultare, quàm Deo, vos judicate.
units.tr: Daniel did not obey King Darius when he ordered that he be worshipped alone, and not God; and he was cast into the den of lions. The impious king Zedekiah forbade the prophet Jeremiah to declare God's command to the people, that they should surrender themselves into the hands of the Chaldeans; but for this he was thrown into prison. When the magistrate forbade Peter and John, the apostles, to preach the Gospel in the name of Jesus, they answered: Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Rectè itaq; dici solet: Magistratui obtemperandum vsq; ad aras. Et Hieronymus inquit: Iudicibus obediendum est in iis, quae sunt vera: non autem in iis, quae Religioni sunt contraria. Idq; ob eam causam: quia summa foret iniquitas, Regi in hoc mundo ita velle seruire, vt ignominia afficiatur Rex in caelo. Hinc Thomas rectè ait: Omnis potestas humana sub potestate Dei ordinatur, & nulli potestati humanae est contra Deum obediendum: secundum illud Act.4,19. Oportet obedire magis Deo, quàm hominibus. Sic Chrysost. in Matt.c.22.v.22. Si Caesar sibi velit sumere, quae Dei sunt: praecipere impia: non erit tributum Caesaris: sed seruitium diaboli.
units.tr: Thus it is rightly said: Obey the magistrate even unto the altars. And Jerome says: Judges are to be obeyed in those things which are true, but not in those which are contrary to religion. And this for the reason that it would be the greatest iniquity to wish so to serve the king of this world that the King in heaven is dishonoured. Hence Thomas rightly says: Every human power is ordered under the power of God, and no human power is to be obeyed against God, according to that word, Acts 4:19: We ought to obey God rather than men. So Chrysostom on Matthew 22:22: If Caesar wishes to take to himself what belongs to God, and commands impious things, it will not be Caesar's tribute but the service of the devil.

units.la: ATQVE haec est doctrina Orthodoxa de Magistratu & potestate ciuili: de subditorū itē debito officio erga magistratum: quae quidem ex verbo Dei, & scriptorib. ecclesiasticis in omnibus Ecclesiis & Scholis Euangelicorum Principum, tam in Imperio Romano, quàm extra illud palam tradi solet.
units.tr: AND this is the orthodox doctrine concerning the magistrate and civil power, and likewise concerning the due duty of subjects toward the magistrate, which is commonly taught openly, from the Word of God and from ecclesiastical writers, in all the Churches and Schools of the evangelical princes, both within the Roman Empire and beyond it.

units.la: FINIS
units.tr: THE END

units.la: Aphorismorum doctrina Ecclesiarum reformatarum.
units.tr: Aphorisms of the doctrine of the Reformed Churches.

units.la: D. DAVIDIS PAREI THEMA SÆCVLARE DE CAVSIS; CENtum abhinc annis, immenso DEI beneficio, ex euangelicis Germaniæ Ecclesiis eliminati, semperque fugiendi PAPATVS ROMANI.
units.tr: D. DAVID PAREUS' SECULAR THESIS ON THE CAUSES, BY WHICH A HUNDRED YEARS AGO, THROUGH THE IMMENSE BENEFIT OF GOD, THE ROMAN PAPACY WAS EXPELLED FROM THE EVANGELICAL CHURCHES OF GERMANY AND IS TO BE FOREVER SHUNNED.

units.la: Solemni disquisitioni propositum
units.tr: Proposed for solemn disputation.

units.la: In inclyta Academia Archi-Palat. Heidelbergensi.
units.tr: In the renowned Academy of the Archpalatinate at Heidelberg.

units.la: RESPONDENTE ANDREA PRAGAI Hungaro.
units.tr: With Andreas Pragai, a Hungarian, responding.

units.la: Kall. Nouemb. Anno ∞ IDC XVII. [?]
units.tr: On the Kalends of November, in the year 1617.

units.la: Eiusdemque Assertio
units.tr: And its defence by the same.

units.la: Aduersus stolidos sarcasmos MAXIMILIANI SANDÆI Societatis Iesu Presbyteri Herbipolensis.
units.tr: Against the foolish sarcasms of Maximilian Sandaeus, priest of the Society of Jesus, of Würzburg.

units.la: QVOD Maximilianus quidam Iesuita Conzio-Sandæus, siue Sandæo-Conzius THEMA SÆCVLARE de causis centum ab hinc annis ex euangelicis Ecclesiis eliminati, semperque fugiendi PAPATVS ROM. Anno superiore Kall. Nouembr. Heidelbergæ authoritate publica Præside D. DAVIDE PAREO, S. Theologiæ Professore: respondente AN-DREA PRAGAI Hungaro S. Th. Candidato propositum, atqj vul-gatum: ausus est nuper Satyrica lasciuia exagitare, mendacijs-que conscindere: nihil quidem ille à secta sua alienum fecit, cui a primis incunabilis staturum est, rem Anti-Christi Romani, cuiusquemodi etiam mendacijs restitutum ire: doctrinam vero Euangelij Christi calumniis & sophistica deprimere: neque ab his expectandum aliud fuit, qui cum Sacrosanctum SERVAtoris nostri IESV nomen mentiri ausint, quid mirum, si mendacia omnia alia? Verum quia Satyrica sua mendacia nobis inscribere, atque obtrudere non dubitauit: nostri nos officij esse duximus, non quidem compellationē eius prorsus contemnere: neque
units.tr: That a certain Jesuit, Maximilian Conzio-Sandaeus (or Sandaeo-Conzius), has lately dared, in a spirit of satirical wantonness, to attack and tear apart the THEME OF THE AGE, on the causes of the one hundred years since the Churches of the Gospel were driven out of Rome's reach, and of the PAPACY OF ROME that must always be fled. This theme was proposed and published with public authority at Heidelberg on the Kalends of November of the previous year, under the presidency of Dr David Pareus, Professor of Theology, with Andreas Pragai, a Hungarian candidate of theology, answering. He has, in doing so, done nothing foreign to his own sect, which from its earliest cradle has been bound to defend the cause of the Roman Antichrist, and to do so with lies as well. It was to be expected of men who have dared to lie about the most holy name of our Saviour Jesus that they would lie about everything else; yet what is so surprising about that? But since he has not hesitated to inscribe his satirical lies upon us and to force them on us, we have judged it our duty neither to despise his address altogether

units.la: neq; etiam stulto secundum stultitiam suam respondere: optimum verò visum nobis est, ipsum THEMA SÆCVLARE, cum breui assertione eorum, quæ mendaciis, vel sophistica depravauari vidimus, denuò integrum euulgare. Vnde candidi lectores facilimè judicabunt, causas Themate sæculari demonstratas, àspissa illa mendaciorum, conuitiorum & calumniarum COMPAGE, insciti æ, malignitatis & impudentiæ Sandæo-Conzianæ incredibilis nexu colligatâ, nequaquam dissolutas, vel labefactatas esse.
units.tr: nor to answer the fool according to his folly. It has seemed best to us to publish the THEME OF THE AGE again, whole, together with a brief statement of those points which we have seen to have been distorted by lies or sophistry. From this, candid readers will easily judge that the causes demonstrated in the Theme of the Age have not been dissolved or weakened by that thick structure of lies, insults and calumnies, bound together with the incredible network of ignorance, malice and impudence of Sandaeo-Conzius.

units.la: Apostaticam synagogam, idololatricam profanitatem, tyrannicam crudelitatē fugiendam, & eliminandam esse, fingit se non negare: saltem autem negare, aliquid huius esse in Papatu: nimirum, vt seruulus ille Terentianus heri scelus excusans: Quis, inquit, homo pro mæcho vnquam vidit in domo meretricia compre-hendi quemquam? Exspectabisne dum Bestia se Bestiam, Mulierem se Meretricē magnam profiteatur, vel adorantes eam, hoc quod faciunt, non inficientur? Nihil ad hos veterum Christianorum contumuliæ: quod asinarij, sarmentitij, semissij dicti. Non magis illæ ad Papatum, quam laudes virginis ad Bacchidem. Erant illæ Christianorum innocentiæ totidem insignia. Istos SEORTVM Antiseptico lli ciuitati incubans non adorare: tyrannidisque Christianæ administros non esse, idolis non sacrificare, orbis Christianus tunc credet, quando id facere cessabunt. Nimis denudata est fornicatio vestra: discooperuit Deus lumine verbi sui turpitudinem pollutionis vestræ: vt ei obtegendæ frustra SYNAGOGAM PROTESTANTICAM crepet Sandæo-conzius: fucandæ frustra SCHEMA rancidis deciesque protritis nænis calumniisque conflatum obijciat Conzio-Sandæus. Omnia partim palam falsa, partim calumniosa, vel friuola & ridicula, vel mendacitatis, insciti æ, impudentiæque Jesuiticæ sunt documenta, ad forum declinandum exquisita, in quo rei conuenti est prius interrogatis respondere, quam reconueniat. Iste verò ex ducentis amplius positionibus vix quartam partem saltuatim arrosit, vel potius vt Lycisca lunam allatrauit: quam si maximè largiremur, causæ nihilominus inuictæ consisterent. Hoc ostendere nunc satis erit. Corybanticum verò SCHEMA, quod iste SYNAGOGAM PROTESTANTICAM, verius JESVITICAM mendaciorum, calumniarum, nugarum SENTINAM indigetaret, (cùm sordes eius nihil ad nos) authoribus potius suis jure postliminij redonabitur.
units.tr: He pretends not to deny that the apostate synagogue, idolatrous profanity and tyrannical cruelty must be shunned and eliminated; or at least he denies that any of this exists in the Papacy. Just like that slave in Terence, excusing yesterday's crime, he says: "Who ever saw a man caught for adultery in a brothel?" Shall we wait until the Beast declares itself a Beast and the Great Harlot declares herself a harlot, or until those who worship her no longer deny what they do? The insults the old Christians received do not touch these men: that they were called asses, faggot-men, half-men. Those names apply no more to the Papacy than praises of a virgin apply to Bacchis. They were marks of Christian innocence. The Christian world will believe that these men, who brood over the Antiseptic city, do not worship, that they are not servants of Christian tyranny, and that they do not sacrifice to idols, only when they cease to do so. Your fornication is too openly exposed; God has uncovered by the light of his Word the filth of your pollution. In vain does Sandaeo-Conzius shout about a PROTESTANT SYNAGOGUE to cover it, and in vain does Conzio-Sandaeus throw at us a SCHEME concocted from rancid, oft-rubbed trifles and calumnies to hide it. Everything here is partly plainly false, partly calumnious, or else frivolous and ridiculous, and all of it is evidence of Jesuit mendacity, ignorance and impudence, contrived to evade the court, in which the accused must answer questions before he may counter-question. Out of more than two hundred propositions, he has gnawed at barely a quarter of them here and there, or rather, like a bitch, he has barked at the moon. Even if we were to grant him much more, the causes would nonetheless stand unconquered. It will be enough to show this now. As for the Corybantic SCHEME, which he would call the PROTESTANT SYNAGOGUE, though more truly it is the JESUIT cesspool of lies, calumnies and trifles (since its filth is nothing to us), it will rather be returned to its authors by the right of postliminy.

units.la: THEMA SÆCVLARE, de causis centum abhinc annis, immenso DEI beneficio ex Euangelicis Ecclesiis eliminati, semperque fugiendi Papatus Romani,
units.tr: SECULAR THEME: on the causes which, a hundred years ago, by the immense benefit of God, were removed from the Evangelical Churches, and on the Roman Papacy, which must always be fled from,

units.la: Aduersus.
units.tr: Against.

units.la: Tergiuersationes, strophas, & calumnias MAXIMILIANI SANDÆI Iesuitæ breuiter assertum.
units.tr: The evasions, twists and calumnies of Maximilian Sandaeus the Jesuit, briefly refuted.

units.la: I. QVICVNQVE vult saluus esse, ante omnia necesse est, vt fugiat PAPATVM ROMANVM.
units.tr: I. Whoever wishes to be saved must above all flee the Roman Papacy.

units.la: II. Est enim PAPATVS ROMANVS totius Religionis Christianæ sub nomine Christi euersio: cum qua nulla salus consistere potest.
units.tr: II. For the Roman Papacy is the overthrow of the whole Christian religion under the name of Christ, and no salvation can stand with it.

units.la: III. RELIGIO Christiana in fide & obedientia Euangelij: Obedientia in cultu & disciplina consistit.
units.tr: III. The Christian religion consists in the faith and obedience of the Gospel; obedience consists in worship and discipline.

units.la: IV. Papatus Rom. fidem in Apostasiam, cultum in Idololatriam: disciplinam in Tyrannidem conuertit.
units.tr: IV. The Roman Papacy turns faith into apostasy, worship into idolatry, and discipline into tyranny.

units.la: V. Sic causæ plurimæ diuinitus olim eliminati semperqj fugiendi Papatus Rom. ab aliis passim fusius expositæ ad tres breuissime reuocantur: damnabile à fide Apostasiam: horribilem pro cultu DEI, idololatriam: Anti-Christianam pro disciplina Euangelica tyrannidem.
units.tr: V. Thus the many causes, removed by God long ago and the Roman Papacy, which must always be fled from, which others have set out at length in many places, are very briefly reduced to three: a damnable apostasy from the faith; a horrible idolatry in place of the worship of God; and an Antichristian tyranny in place of evangelical discipline.

units.la: I. Papatus Romani damnabilis Apostasia à fide, quæ creditur, & qua creditur.
units.tr: I. The damnable apostasy of the Roman Papacy from the faith which is believed, and by which it is believed.

units.la: VI. De APOSTASIA Papatus Rom. à fide non trahimus historiam præteritam, sed præsentem.
units.tr: VI. Concerning the apostasy of the Roman Papacy from the faith, we do not draw on past history but on the present.

units.la: VII. PRIMO conuellere principium fidei-quæ creditur, in quod fides Christiana vltimo resoluitur, est à fide deficere, fidem & salutem euertere.
units.tr: VII. FIRST, to overthrow the principle of the faith which is believed (the principle into which the Christian faith is finally resolved) is to fall away from the faith and to subvert faith and salvation.

units.la: VIII. Principium fidei-quæ creditur, fidem Christianam vltimo terminans, est SCRIPTVRA diuina, Prophetarum & Apostolorum libris comprehensa, & quidem sola.
units.tr: VIII. The principle of the faith which is believed, which finally bounds the Christian faith, is the divine SCRIPTURE, contained in the books of the Prophets and Apostles, and that alone.

units.la: IX. Tota enim scriptura diuinitus inspirata est, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in justitia: vt perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus. 2 Tim.2,16.
units.tr: IX. For all Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. 2 Tim.2,16.

units.la: X. Hoc principium fidei-quæ creditur Papatus Romanus non vno modo, sed variè jam pridem conuulsit, hodieque conuellit.
units.tr: X. The Roman Papacy has shaken this principle of the faith which is believed not in one way only but in various ways for some time now, and still shakes it today.

units.la: XI. Scripturis sacris NIHIL DIVINITATIS inesse docet, nisi quantum accipit ab Ecclesia.
units.tr: XI. It teaches that there is NO DIVINITY in the holy Scriptures beyond what they receive from the Church.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: DECEM has positiones munsitando comprobauit Jesuita. Nulla igitur assertione indigent. Obiter verò in iis observandum, distinctionem fidei-quæ creditur, & qua-creditur exstare apud Augustinum lib.12.de Trin.cap.2.atqj etiam tradi à Lombardo lib.3. distinct.23. C. Ad XI. exclamat: Mentitur Pareus: Quid si mentiatur Jesuita? Pareus verum scripsit ex ANDRADIO Lusitano Doctore, Synodi Tridentinæ authentico Defensore, cuius lib.11. Defensionis pag.257. hæc sunt verba: Neque enim in libris ipsis, quibus sacra mysteria conscripta sunt, QVICQVAM INSIT DIVINITATIS, quæ nos ad credendum, quæ illis continentur, religione aliqua constringat: sed Ecclesiæ, quæ codices illos sacros esse docet, & antiquorum Patrum fidem & pietatem commendat, TANTA EST VIS & amplitudo, vt illis nemo sine gravissima impietatis nota possit repugnare. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The Jesuit has proved these ten propositions by mumbling, so they need no assertion. In passing, however, it should be noted that the distinction between the faith which is believed and the faith by which one believes is found in Augustine, On the Trinity, book 12, chapter 2, and is also handed down by Lombard, book 3, distinction 23. On the eleventh he exclaims: Pareus lies. What if the Jesuit is lying? Pareus wrote the truth, taken from Andradius, the Portuguese doctor and authentic defender of the Council of Trent, whose book 11 of the Defence, page 257, contains these words: For in the very books in which the sacred mysteries are written there is NO DIVINITY ANY WHERE that binds us by any religious obligation to believe what is contained in them; but the Church, which teaches that those codices are sacred and commends the faith and piety of the ancient Fathers, has such FORCE AND AMPLITUDE that no one can oppose them without the gravest mark of impiety. So he writes.

units.la: Non loquitur vero de librorum characteribus, chartis, vel membranis, quarum fides & authoritas penes librarios est, sed de libris siue scripturis ipsis sacris, de quarum authoritate disputatur. De his vtrumque positionis caput affirmat. I. Quod NIHIL DIVINITATIS eis insit: quia NEQVE QVICQVAM est NIHIL. II. Nisi quantum accipit ab Ecclesia: quia hoc vult aduersatiua: sed Ecclesiæ TANTA VIS EST. Scriptores alios breuitatis causa omittimus. Judicet Orbis Christianus de Jesuitiæ audacia, & numquid hæc sola positio assumtioni asserendæ non sit futuris esse possit?
units.tr: He does not speak of the letters of the books, or the paper and parchment, whose trustworthiness and authority rest with the printers, but of the sacred writings themselves, whose authority is in dispute. Of these he affirms both parts of the position: I. that there is NOTHING OF DIVINITY in them, because NOT ANYTHING is NOTHING. II. Except as much as it receives from the Church, for this is what the adversative means: but to the Church THERE IS SO MUCH FORCE. We omit other writers for the sake of brevity. Let the Christian world judge the Jesuit's audacity, and whether this single position may not be enough to be asserted hereafter.

units.la: XII. Neque pro authenticis eas habet, NISI authoritate Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: XII. Nor does he hold them to be authentic UNLESS by the authority of the Church.

units.la: XIII. Immò DEO non credit, NISI propter Ecclesiam.
units.tr: XIII. Indeed, he does not believe God UNLESS on account of the Church.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: Hie clypeum cum hasta abijcit Jesuita : quia nimis nouit, Papatum hic teneri. Vtramque enim positionem falsam, impiam, effutiuerunt hactenus tum alij Scriptores triarij juxta & manipulares, tum priorem quidem JOH. ECKIVS in Enchirid. his verbis : Scriptura non est authentica sine authoritate Ecclesia. Hocin margine vocat Achillem pro Catholicis. Et mox : Ita igitur patet, Ecclesiam antiquiorem scriptura : neque Scripturam authenticam esse, NISI Ecclesiae authoritate. Posteriorem vero STAPLETONVS contra Witackerum lib. de Auth. Script. cap.10.§.3. his verbis:Non credimus Deo, nisi propter Ecclesiam. Hoc vero nonne est Deum cum verbo suo Papae & Ecclesiae pedibus blasphemesubijcere?
units.tr: Here the Jesuit throws away both shield and spear, because he knows too well that the Papacy is being defended here. For both positions have hitherto been put forward, false and impious, by other writers, by the heavy-armed triarii and the common maniples alike: the first indeed by John Eck in the Enchiridion in these words: Scripture is not authentic without the authority of the Church. In the margin he calls this Achilles for the Catholics. And soon after: Thus it is plain that the Church is older than Scripture, and that Scripture is not authentic EXCEPT by the authority of the Church. The latter is put forward by Stapleton against Whitaker, in his book on the authority of Scripture, chapter 10, §3, in these words: We do not believe God except on account of the Church. Is this not to subject God and his word, blasphemously, to the feet of the Pope and the Church?

units.la: Neque eluditur tam immanis blasphemia Jesuitae cauillis: Scripturam quoad se, habere suam [?] ab ipsamet sua [?] , cuius author sit prima veritas, non PAPA: & Ecclesiam, vt columnam & stabilimentum veritatis, ad fidem scripturae tamen aliquid conferre. Nam hoc posterius nunquam, quod sciamus, fuit in quaestione: Vtrum Ecclesia ad fidem scripturae aliquid conferat? Sed illud potius Sophistarum assertum: Vtrum Deo & scripturis non credamus, nisi propter Ecclesiam? Illud vero prius etsi vere dicitur: tamen non vere creditur in Papatu. Nam ipsam internam [?] detrahunt scripturae, vt modo patuit ex Andradio, negante, libris sacris QVICQAAM inesse DIVINITATIS: & manet ex illorum mente, scripturam sacram non esse [?], neque in se, neque nobis, NISI propter Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Nor is so monstrous a blasphemy excused by the Jesuit's quibbles: that Scripture, as far as itself is concerned, has its own [?] from its very own [?], whose author is the first truth, not the Pope; and that the Church, as the pillar and stay of truth, nevertheless contributes something to the faith of Scripture. For this latter was never, so far as we know, the question: Does the Church contribute anything to the faith of Scripture? The question was rather that assertion of the Sophists: Should we not believe God and the Scriptures except on account of the Church? The former, although it is truly said, is not truly believed in the Papacy. For they strip Scripture of its inner [?], as has just been shown from Andradius, who denies that the sacred books have ANY DIVINITY in them; and it remains in their mind that Scripture is not [?], neither in itself nor for us, EXCEPT on account of the Church.

units.la: XIV. Diuinam scripturarum authoritatem à Papae arbitrio suspendit: quia in Papa tanquam in Ecclesiae totius capite authoritas illa residet.
units.tr: XIV. He makes the divine authority of the Scriptures depend on the will of the Pope, because that authority resides in the Pope as in the head of the whole Church.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: Hic vt prius aliquam speciem negaret, posterius dolo mussitauit: quo addito prius necessario consequi videbat. Si enim in Pontifice Romano tanquam in totius Ecclesiae capite omnis authoritas Ecclesiae residet: in authoritate vero Ecclesiae residet authoritas scripturarum, vt duae positiones praecedentes habent: in Pontifice Romano omnem quoque scripturarum authoritatem residere, ab eiusque arbitrio pendere necesse est. Residere vero in vno Pontifice Romano, tanquam in capite totius Ecclesiae hanc authoritatem, est de stylo communi apud Canonistas stas & Scholasticos, qui Papam extollunt supra Concilia: & Iesuita probati commatis Gregorius de Valentia aperte scribit, in Pontifice Romano, tanquam in capite totius Ecclesiæ, authoritatem illam residere. Manet igitur positio: & assumptionis probatio.
units.tr: Here, as before, he denied some aspect of the matter, and afterwards muttered it craftily; once this addition was made, he saw that the earlier point would necessarily follow. For if all authority of the Church resides in the Roman Pontiff as in the head of the whole Church, and if the authority of the Scriptures resides in the authority of the Church, as the two preceding propositions hold, then it is necessary that all authority of the Scriptures also resides in the Roman Pontiff and depends on his will. That this authority resides in the one Roman Pontiff as in the head of the whole Church is the common style among the Canonists and Schoolmen, who exalt the Pope above the Councils; and the Jesuit of approved note, Gregory of Valentia, writes plainly that this authority resides in the Roman Pontiff as in the head of the whole Church. The proposition therefore stands, and so does the proof of the assumption.

units.la: XV. Et quia Papa solus vel cum prælatis est Ecclesia, ideo Papa & Prælati scripturis credunt, propter seipsos: laicos volunt credere scripturis propter Papam & Prælatos.
units.tr: XV. And because the Pope alone, or with the prelates, is the Church, therefore the Pope and the prelates believe the Scriptures for their own sake; the laymen they wish to believe the Scriptures for the sake of the Pope and the prelates.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: Essent sane stolidi Iesuitæ, si palam ita loquerentur. Sed æquè stolidè id negant, positis, quæ ponunt: Scripturis, immò Deo, non credi, nisi propter Ecclesiam: &, Papam cum prælatis esse Ecclesiam. Hinc enim tam necesse est poni utrumque, Papam & Ecclesiam. Prælatos credere scripturis, & Deo propter seipsos: quia non credunt, nisi propter Ecclesiam, quæ sunt ipsi: Laicos credere propter Papam & Prælatos: quia credunt propter Ecclesiam, quæ est Papa & Prælati: quam necesse est poni, esse quatuor Euangelistas, posito, quod Euangelistæ sint bis duo. Rursus igitur non Pareus ponendo, sed Iesuita negando hanc Thesin, mentitur, & manet assumtio.
units.tr: The Jesuits would indeed be fools if they spoke so openly. Yet they deny it just as foolishly, given what they lay down: that Scripture, and indeed God, is believed only on account of the Church; and that the Pope with the prelates is the Church. From this it is necessary to posit both, the Pope and the Church: the prelates believe the Scriptures and God for their own sake, because they believe only on account of the Church, which they themselves are; the laymen believe on account of the Pope and the prelates, because they believe on account of the Church, which is the Pope and the prelates. It is necessary to posit this, just as it is necessary to hold that there are four Evangelists, granted that the Evangelists are twice two. Thus again it is not Pareus who posits this, but the Jesuit who, by denying this thesis, lies; and the assumption stands.

units.la: XVI. Sic Papæ, Prælatorum, laicorum fides de scripturis stat super testimonio humano, hoc est, super arena, & est nulla.
units.tr: XVI. Thus the faith of the Pope, of the prelates and of the laymen concerning the Scriptures rests on human testimony, that is, on sand, and is nothing.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: Esse hoc consectarium prioris, nemo non videt. Si enim fides Papæ & Prælatorum, qui nec dij, nec angeli, sed homines sunt, stat super ipsismet: & fides Laicorū stat super Papa & Prælatis: certè non potest stare, nisi super fundamento seu testimonio humano. Super hoc autem fidem in diuinis stare, quid est, nisi stare super arena, hoc est, esse instabilem, mobilem in horas, incertam, nullam? in diuinis enim fides incerta est nulla, cùm, Bellarmino teste, fidem veram oportear esse certissimam. Nec prodest fucus VALENTIANI Iesuitæ, authoritatem Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Papæ & Prælatorum, non esse pure humanam, nec pure diuinam, sed humano-diuinam, vel diuino-humanam. Talis enim authoritas Prophetarum quidem erat & Apostolorum, quos immediatè vocatos, & illuminatos diuinitus, licet homines essent, tamen ὁμιλεῖν[?] loqui & scribere constabat in Ecclesia. Parem verò authoritatem Papæ & Prælatis dabimus, si vel pariter se afflatos diuinitus loqui & scribere docuerint, verbum diuinitus afflatorum, hoc est, scripturam sacram protulerint. Secus decreta eorum manent testimonium humanum, & arena.
units.tr: That this is a consequence of the former point, no one fails to see. For if the faith of the Pope and of the prelates, who are neither gods nor angels but men, rests upon themselves, and the faith of the laity rests upon the Pope and the prelates, then surely it cannot rest except upon a foundation or testimony that is human. But to rest faith in divine matters upon this is nothing other than to rest upon sand, that is, to be unstable, changeable from hour to hour, uncertain, and so nothing. For faith in divine things that is uncertain is nothing, since, by the witness of Bellarmine, true faith ought to be most certain. Nor does the trickery of the Jesuit Valentian help, who says that the authority of the Church, that is, of the Pope and the prelates, is not purely human nor purely divine, but human-divine or divine-human. For such was indeed the authority of the Prophets and Apostles, who, being called immediately and enlightened by God, though they were men, were nonetheless known to speak and write in the Church. We will grant the Pope and the prelates equal authority if they show that they likewise speak and write as men inspired by God, that is, if they put forth the word of those inspired by God, the sacred Scripture. Otherwise their decrees remain human testimony, and sand.

units.la: XVII. Scripturas in iis, quæ ad fidem, cultum & mores pertinent, tantæ obscuritatis arguunt, vt à nemine nisi ex Papæ interpretatione intelligi possint.
units.tr: XVII. They argue that the Scriptures, in those matters which pertain to faith, worship and morals, are of such obscurity that they can be understood by no one except through the Pope's interpretation.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: Prius membrum est styli vulgati in Papatu: & prolixè à Bel-larmino defenditur, scripturam sacram, tum quoad res, quæ di-cuntur, tum quoad modum, quo dicuntur, esse OBSCVRISSI-MAM: quo nihil salsius: DEO & sanctis eius Prophetis & Apostolis contumeliosius: cum verbum Dei & Prophetarum, multoque magis Apostolorum, prædicetur lucerna pedibus nostris, & lumen semitis nostris, splendens in obscuro loco. Hoc igitur quidem mussitauit Iesuita: posterius vero absque fronte negat. Quasi non idem sit styli communis in Papatu: Interpretem scripturæ, verique sensus judicem neminem esse, nisi Ecclesiam, hoc est, Papam sine, vel cum Concilio: in Papa vero vt in capite totius Ecclesiæ, omnem interpretationis authoritatem residere. Quod nonne est, scripturam à nemine, nisi ex Papæ interpretatione intelligi posse? Videatur Bellarm. lib.3. de verb. cap.3. vbi scripturæ sensum ab vno judice Pontifice pe-tendum contendit.
units.tr: The first part is the prevailing style in Papacy, and Bellarmine defends it at length: that Holy Scripture, both as to the things said and as to the manner in which they are said, is most OBSCURE. Nothing could be more false, or more insulting to God and to his holy Prophets and Apostles, since the word of God and of the Prophets, and much more of the Apostles, is proclaimed as a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths, shining in a dark place. The Jesuit has indeed muttered this; but the latter part he denies without shame. As if it were not the same common style in Papacy: that no one is the interpreter of Scripture and judge of its true sense except the Church, that is, the Pope with or without a Council; and that in the Pope, as in the head of the whole Church, all authority of interpretation resides. Is this not to say that Scripture can be understood by no one except through the Pope's interpretation? See Bellarmine, book 3 on the Word, chapter 3, where he contends that the sense of Scripture must be sought from one judge, the Pope.

units.la: XVIII. Papam omnium de fide quæstionum Iudicem supremum facit: in quo fidem vltimatè sisti oporteat, etiam in iis, quæ cum Papa Euangelici habent controuersa.
units.tr: XVIII. He makes the Pope the supreme judge of all questions of faith, in whom our faith must ultimately be placed, even in those matters which the Evangelicals have in controversy with the Papists.

units.la: ASSERTIO.
units.tr: ASSERTION.

units.la: Cum tria sint positionis membra, primum, & tertium, vtpote lippis & tonsoribus notum, silentio absorbet Iesuita. Facit se Papa omnium de fide quæstionum judicem supremum. Quo iure? Quæstio de fide est, num sit Deus? num trinus, & vnus? num creator mundi? num Christus [illegible, ~3 letters] ? num mortuus pro nobis? num resurrexerit? num superi vel inferi sint? &c.
units.tr: Since the proposition has three parts, the first and the third, as is known even to men with sore eyes and to barbers, the Jesuit swallows up in silence. The Pope makes himself the supreme judge of all questions of faith. By what right? A question of faith is: Is there a God? Is he triune and one? Is he the creator of the world? Did Christ [illegible, about three letters]? Did he die for us? Did he rise again? Are there heavenly and infernal powers? And so on.

units.la: Veniet ergo de his Christianus cum Judæo, Turca, vel Atheo ad Iudicem supremum Pontificem Romanum? Quæ maior inania? Quæstio est: Num Pontifex Rom. sit caput Ecclesiæ: num Prorex Christi: num Monarcha Christianismi, Imperatorum & Regum Dominus? num supremus Interpres, censor & judex scripturarum, omniumque de fide quæstionum? num potius sit homo perditionis, sedens in templo Dei, ut Deus, bestia, mulier meretrix, sedens in civitate magna super septem montes, Antichristus denique? Venient ergo de his litigaturi Euangelici cum Iesuitis ad Iudicem supremum Potificem Romanum? Quid stultius? iniquius?
units.tr: Will therefore a Christian, with a Jew, a Turk, or an Atheist, come to the supreme judge, the Roman Pontiff, about these things? What greater absurdities! The question is: Is the Roman Pontiff the head of the Church? The vicegerent of Christ? The monarch of Christendom, lord of Emperors and Kings? The supreme interpreter, censor and judge of the Scriptures and of all questions of faith? Or is he rather the man of sin, sitting in the temple of God as if he were God, the beast, the harlot woman sitting on the great city built on seven hills, in short the Antichrist? Will therefore the Evangelicals who contend with the Jesuits come to the supreme judge, the Roman Pontiff? What could be more foolish, or more unjust?

units.la: Medium Iesuita vocat mendacium: In Papam fidem nostram ultimatè sisti debere. Profecto mendacium est, quod dicit. Non tamen mendacium, Papatum hoc docere: nisi & prius mendacium sit, Pontificem esse omnium de fide quæstionum SVPREMVM IVDICEM. Hic enim non est, nisi in quo fides omnium quæstionum ultimate sistitur, siue ut clarius dicamus, à quo ad superiorem non datur appellatio. At datur à Pontifice Romano ad scripturas sacras, ad DEVM, tanquam ad superiorem, appellatio: &, fatente Iesuita, in hanc primam veritatem propter se creditam resoluitur fides Catholica. Stat igitur omnibus suis membris hæc positio & assumtionis probatio.
units.tr: The Jesuit calls the middle term a lie: "Our faith must ultimately be placed in the Pope." Certainly what he says is a lie. Yet it is not a lie that Papacy teaches this, unless it is first a lie that the Pope is the SUPREME JUDGE of all questions of faith. For this is the case only where the faith of all questions is ultimately placed, or, to speak more plainly, from which there is no appeal to a higher authority. But an appeal is allowed from the Roman Pontiff to the Scriptures, to God, as to a higher authority; and, as the Jesuit admits, the Catholic faith is resolved into this first truth, believed for its own sake. This proposition therefore stands in all its parts, and so does the proof of the assumption.

units.la: Quis porro sit supremus fidei, interpretationum, & controversiarum de fide judex, si Papa Romanus non est? Et, sitne scriptura sacra sola, an cum traditionibus, fidei, & controversiarum norma? Et possitne scriptura sola simul & norma esse, & judicis officium sustinere? quæ Iesuita non humano ore, sed canino rictu (ut verba suaei reponamus) oblatrat. De his integri exstant Euangelicorum libri: nec sunt de Thematis sæcularis argumento.
units.tr: Moreover, who will be the supreme judge of faith, of interpretations and of controversies of faith, if the Roman Pontiff is not? And is Holy Scripture alone, or together with traditions, the rule of faith and of controversies? And can Scripture alone be both the rule and sustain the office of judge? These things the Jesuit barks not with a human mouth but with a dog's snarl, to use his own words. Full books of the Evangelicals on these matters exist; and they are not within the subject of this Secular Theme.

units.la: XI X. Scripturas imperfectionis accusat: quia neque ad fidem pietatemque colendam, neque ad salutem consequendam sufficiant, nisi traditionibus supleantur.
units.tr: XIX. He accuses the Scriptures of imperfection: because they suffice neither for cultivating faith and piety nor for obtaining salvation, unless they are supplemented by traditions.
