Nulla enim creatura perfectionem assequi potest creatoris, cum omnis creatura à non esse procedat ad esse. Non esse autem perfectioni creatoris & Dei simpliciter repugnat.
units.tr: In Greek, ὁ θεὸς ὁ τέλειος, the same as in 1 John 5:20, "the true God" ([θεὸς] God), who is none other than the one and eternal God by nature, who calls himself God of sufficiency or perfection [El Shaddai, אל שדי] Gen. 17:1. Therefore he is not called God equivocally, on account of the excellence of his gifts and office, as angels are called gods (Ps. 97:7), or as men who are princes (Ps. 82:6). That was the blasphemy of Samosatenus, and formerly of Photinus; today the Servetians and Socinians assert that Christ began from Mary and that she was merely a man. Nor is he a made-up or created God before all things, [ἐκ τῶν μὴ ὄντων] out of things that are not, as Arius raved. For no creature can attain the perfection of the Creator, since every creature proceeds from not-being to being. But not-being is simply incompatible with the perfection of the Creator and of God.

units.la: Verus & integer homo, constans anima rationali, & corpore humano: quod dicitur tum contra Marcionis & Manichæi hæresin, asseuerantium, Christum nouissimis temporibus venisse, ad animas, non ad corpora, liberandas: nec fuisse in carne vera, sed simulatam speciem carnis ludificandis humanis sensibus præbuisse: tum contra Apollinaris Syri errorem, asserentis, Filium DEI carnem sine anima suscepisse, proanima ipsum verbum in eo fuisse: Augustin. de hæres. 46,55. Vtrosque diserte refutauit Christus ipse: priores quidem, eum ex morte rediuiuus se ostendens discipulis conspectu eius territis, quasi spectrum viderent, dixit: Quid turbati estis? Videte manus meas, & pedes meos. Nam ego ipse sum. Contrectate me & videte. Nam Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout conspicitis me habere. Luc. 24. versf. 39. Posteriorem vero, cum in horto inter mortis angores & metum exclamauit: Vndiquaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. Matth. 26,38. Verbum vero nec tristitiæ passionem in se subire, nec mortem horrere potuit. Quod natura hominis assumta συμπαθῶς non perse, sed in persona verbi subsistit, perfectionem hominis adeo non diminuit, vt magis etiam perficiat. Humanam enim ἀνθρώπων esse, seu persistere, est quidem perfectio ψιλὸν ἀνθρώπων, nudum hominem redderet. Esse vero συμπαθῶς τῷ λόγῳ, ἀνθρώπῳ seu in persona Dei verbi subsistere, est perfectio ἀνθρώπου, Dei hominis, seu hominis assumti in Deum, vt loquitur Athanasius Articulo sequenti.
units.tr: A true and whole man, consisting of a rational soul and a human body. This is said against the heresy of Marcion and Manichaeus, who asserted that Christ came in the last times to free souls, not bodies, and that he was not in true flesh but presented a feigned appearance of flesh to deceive human senses; and also against the error of Apollinaris of Syria, who asserted that the Son of God took on flesh without a soul, the Word itself being in place of the soul. Augustine, On Heresies, 46, 55. Christ himself expressly refuted both. Against the first, when he showed himself to his disciples after rising from the dead, and they were terrified at the sight of him, as if they saw a spirit, he said: "Why are you troubled? See my hands and my feet, for it is I myself. Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have" (Luke 24:39). Against the second, when in the garden, amid the anguish and fear of death, he cried out: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death" (Matt. 26:38). But the Word could neither undergo the passion of sorrow in itself nor dread death. Because the assumed human nature [συμπαθῶς] subsists not by itself but in the person of the Word, it does not diminish the perfection of the man at all, but rather makes it more perfect. For to exist as a man, or to persist as a man, is indeed a perfection, but it would make him a [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον] bare man. To subsist [συμπαθῶς τῷ λόγῳ] in union with the Word, that is, in the person of the Word of God, is the perfection of the [ἀνθρώπου θεοῦ] God-man, or of the man assumed into God, as Athanasius puts it in the following article.

units.la: Christum esse Filium Dei, & Deum, hæretici dicti non negabant olim, hodieq; non negant: ludebant verò & ludunt æquiuocatione, Deum propter dotes & operationes diuinas factitium, vel ante res alias creatum, Patre minorem asseferentes. Contrà assertores fidei Christianæ, in quibus non postremus fuit Athanasius, Filium Dei Deum Patri æqualem & consubstantialem esse, euidentibus scripturæ testimoniis atque argumentis demonstrarunt. Sufficiunt hic pauca. Pariter in nomen Filij atq; Patris, & Spiritus sancti tanquam in nomen vnius veri Dei baptismo inauthoramur. Ipsi Judæi agnoscebant
units.tr: Heretics formerly did not deny, and today do not deny, that Christ is the Son of God and God; but they played with words, asserting that he is God made by divine gifts and works, or created before other things, and less than the Father. Against them, the defenders of the Christian faith, of whom Athanasius was not the least, demonstrated from clear testimonies and arguments of Scripture that the Son of God is God, equal and consubstantial with the Father. A few points suffice here. We are baptized into the name of the Son and of the Father and of the Holy Spirit as into the name of the one true God. The Jews themselves acknowledged

units.la: scebant [illegible, ~3 letters]ebant Christum, dicendo Joh. 5, 17. Pater meus usque adhuc operatur, & ego operor: Deum appellare Patrem suum proprium, & ipsum facere aequalem Deo: quod Christus adeo non negabat vel improbabat, ut toto deinceps capite, insignibus documentis ab aequalitate & identitate operationum & operum, potentiae & authoritatis, honoris & cultus sui atq; Patris confirmaret. Quaecunq; inquit, Pater facit, Filius similiter facit. Sicut Pater excitat mortuos & vivificat, ita & Filius, quos vult, vivificat, &c. Pater omne judicium dedit Filio, ut omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem. Sicut Pater habet vitam in seipso, sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in seipso &c. Plurib. non est opus. Sufficit fidei nostrae firmandae, haereticis redarguendis sola ipsius Christi de se testificatio. Si enim (ait ipse Jo. 8, 14.) testor de meipso: testimonium meum verum est. Testatur vero de seipso, Deum esse Patrem suum proprium, seq; esse aequalem Deo Patri. Verum igitur est eius de se testimonium: detestandus contra haereticorum magis, quam Judaeorum malitiosus stupor, fidem testimonio eius derogantium. Secundum divinitatem.] Non secundum humanitatem: secus homo verus non esset. Falsum vero Schwenckfeldij effatum humanitate Christi per omnia esse exaequatam Deo: seu Christum aequalem esse Deo etiam secundum humanitatem. 17. Minor Patre.] Et hoc testatur Christus de se, dicens: Pater meus maior me est, Joh. 14, 28. nempe incarnationis meae ratione, qua homo, sum minor Patre. Quod quia Arius ad Divinitatis inaequalitatem traxit, haeresin Anomoeorum inuexit. Cyrill. l. 2. Thes. c 3. In quantum natura Deus est, aequalis genitori Filius est, in quantum autem homo factus est, & ut homo crucifixus & mortuus, minor. Chalcedonensis definitio postea contra Eutychen sic declarauit. Consubstantialis Patri secundum Deitatem: consubstantialis nobis secundum humanitatem: per omnia similis nobis sine sorde peccati, Hebr. 2, 17. & 4. 15. ARTICULUS VI. SYMBOLI XII. 18. Qui licet Deus sit & homo, non duo tamen, sed unus est Christus. 19. Unus autem non conversione Divinitatis in carnem: 20. sed assumtione humanitatis in Deum: unus omnino, 21. non conversione substantiae, 22. sed unitate personae. 23. Nam sicut anima rationalis & caro unus est homo, ita Deus & homo unus Christus est. Declaratio. 18. Qui licet Deus.] Hactenus de veritate duarum naturarum Filij Dei incarnati: nunc de earundem unione, seu de personae univnitate. Articulus initio habet prolepsin: Cum Deus & homo sint duo diuersa ὑφιστάμενα: Christus igitur si Deus & homo est, non vnus erit, sed duo. Immò vnus Christus Deus & homo, non duo, propter naturarum vnionem. Sunt quidem Deus & homo diuersa ὑφιστάμενα, absq; vnione personali. Christus verò Deus & homo est in vnitate personæ. Incurrit in hanc partem articuli hæresis, quam centum post Athanasium annis Nestorius Constantinopolitanæ ecclesiæ Patriarcha inuexit: Ephesinum verò Concilium damnauit.
units.tr: (the garbled text here seems to continue the same point) that Christ, by calling God his own Father, made himself equal to God, as John 5:17 says: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." Christ did not deny or disapprove of this; rather, throughout the rest of that chapter, he confirmed it with clear proofs of the equality and identity of his works and operations, of power and authority, of honour and worship, between himself and the Father. "Whatever the Father does," he says, "the Son likewise does. As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son too gives life to whom he will, etc. The Father has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself, etc." More is not needed. For the strengthening of our faith and the refutation of heretics, Christ's own testimony about himself is enough. "If I testify of myself," he says (John 8:14), "my testimony is true." He testifies of himself that God is his own Father and that he is equal to God the Father. Therefore his testimony about himself is true, and the malicious stupidity of heretics, who detract from his testimony, is more to be detested than that of the Jews. According to the divinity. Not according to the humanity; otherwise he would not be a true man. The saying of Schwenckfeld, that by his humanity Christ is made equal to God in all things, or that Christ is equal to God even according to the humanity, is false.

units.la: 19. Vnus non conuersione. Ratio vnitatis non est conuersio dininitatis in carne, quam hęresin ducentis post Athanasium annis commentus fuit Eutyches, monachus Constantinopolitanus: qui verba Johannis: Verbum caro factum est, de conuersione verbi in carnem, quomodo aqua dicitur fuisse facta vinum, hoc est, conuersa in vinū, Joh.2,8. interpretabatur: post incarnationem non duas, sed vnam tantum naturam, carnem ex verbo factam asserens. Merito autem Concilij Chalcedonensis authoritate repressus fuit. Quomodo enim diuinitas verteretur in carnem, natura increata mutaretur in creaturam, cum sit mutationis expers? Nec Deus ergo, nec homo verè esset Christus: quia diuinitatem simul cum humanitate amisisset.
units.tr: 19. One not by conversion. The ground of the union is not a conversion of the deity into the flesh. Eutyches, a monk of Constantinople, devised this heresy about two hundred years after Athanasius. He read the words of John, The Word was made flesh, as a conversion of the Word into flesh, in the way that the water is said to have been made wine, that is, changed into wine (John 2:8). He asserted that after the incarnation there was not two natures but only one, the flesh made from the Word. He was rightly repressed by the authority of the Council of Chalcedon. For how could the deity be turned into flesh? The uncreated nature would be changed into a creature, though it is incapable of change. Then Christ would be neither true God nor true man, since he would have lost his deity together with his humanity.

units.la: 20. Sed assumtione humanitatis in Deum. Græcè εἰς θεότητα, Deitatem: non vtiq; absolutè, sed in vnam Deitatis ὑπόστασιν, hoc est, in personam λόγος. Hæc sola enim, non Pater, aut Spiritus sanctus carnem humanam assumsit in vnitatem suæ ὑποστάσεως: vide nota 8. & 1. De hac assumtione Apostolus Heb.2,14. Factus est particeps carnis & sanguinis. Et v.16. Non angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahæ assumsit, hoc est, vniuit sibi personaliter, vt loquuntur scholæ, vt vna esset verbi & carnis ὑπόστασις. Ratio igitur vnitatis personæ Christi non est conuersio verbi in carnem, sed vnio hypostatica Verbi cum carne.
units.tr: 20. But by the assumption of the humanity into God. In Greek, into Deity [εἰς θεότητα]: not absolutely, but into the one hypostasis of the Deity [ὑπόστασιν], that is, into the person [λόγος, Word]. For this Person alone, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, assumed human flesh into the unity of his [ὑποστάσεως] hypostasis. See note 8 and 1. The Apostle speaks of this assumption in Heb. 2:14: He took part of flesh and blood. And in v. 16: He did not assume angels, but he assumed the seed of Abraham, that is, he united it to himself personally, as the schools say, so that there would be one hypostasis of the Word and the flesh. The ground of the unity of Christ's person is therefore not a conversion of the Word into flesh, but the hypostatic union of the Word with the flesh.

units.la: 21. Non confusione substantia. h. e. non naturæ, & naturalium proprietatum vtriusq; commixtione in aliquod tertium, qualis confusio est aquæ & mellis in mulso: quæ hæresis postea Monophysitarum fuit, ex Eutychetis orta delirio, aduersus quam Damascenus l.3.orth.fid.c.3. prolixe disputat.
units.tr: 21. Not by confusion of substance. That is, not by a mixing of the natures and their natural properties, of both together, into some third thing, such as the confusion of water and honey in mead. This heresy later belonged to the Monophysites, arising from the madness of Eutyches, against which Damascene disputes at length in Orthodox Faith 3.3.

units.la: 22. Sed vnitate personæ. Nempe θεὸς ἄνθρωπος Dei hominis, seu verbi incarnati: distinctis & salvis manentibus verbi & carnis naturis, earumq; proprietatibus essentialibus: prout post Athanasium, Synodus Chalcedonensis Act. xx. clarius explicauit his verbis: Dominum Iesum Christum in duabus naturis inconfuse, immutabiliter, indiuise, inseparabiliter omnes agnoscimus, minime quam duarum naturarum diuersitate euacuata propter vnionem: salua magis proprietate utriusque. vtriusque natura in vnam personam conuenientibus: non in duas diuisum aut segregatum, sed vnum eundemque vnigenitum, Filium, Deum, verbum, Iesum Christum.
units.tr: 22. But by unity of person. That is, God-man [θεὸς ἄνθρωπος] of God and man, or of the incarnate Word, the natures of the Word and of the flesh remaining distinct and safe, with their essential properties. After Athanasius, the Council of Chalcedon, Act 20, explained this more clearly in these words: We all acknowledge the Lord Jesus Christ in two natures, unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably; the difference of the two natures is by no means taken away because of the union, but rather the property of each nature is preserved, and they come together into one person and one hypostasis, not divided or separated into two persons, but one and the same only-begotten Son, God, Word, Jesus Christ.

units.la: 23. Nam sicut anima rationalis.] Modus vnionis Verbi & carnis declaratur simili, quo etiam ante Athanasium vsus legitur Iustinus Martyr antiquissimus scriptor in Expositione fidei: cuius operæ pretium est verba adscribere, vt in quantum conueniat, intelligatur: Nec est, inquit, cur quisquam ex me huius vnitionis modum scisscitetur. Non pudebit enim fateri ignorantiam. Immo gloriabor potius, quod credam arcana, quibus initiatus sum, quæ nec ratio, nec mens valet percipere. Sunt, qui hanc vnitionem qualem anima cum corpore intelligant, atq; ita doceant: atq; conuenit exemplū, si non omnino, saltem ex parte. Quemadmodum enim homo, cum sit vnus, habet in se duas diuersas naturas, & alia sui parte consulit, alia consultum exsequitur, animo decernens navis structuram, manibus verò opus decretum conficiens: Sic Filius vnus cum sit natura gemina, juxta alteram patrat miracula, juxta alteram humilia quoq; in se recipit. Quatenus enim ex Patre & Deus, facit prodigia; quatenus è virgine & homo crucem, passionem & similia ultro pertulit naturaliter. Hactenus si quis conferat, similitudo quadrat egregiè. E diuerso, si totum cum toto comparat, tollet differentiam. Homo etsi constet ex anima & corpore, non tamen idem est cum eis, sed diuersum: vt homo constet ex copula corporis cum anima: & existat tertium quiddam aliud. At Christus non ex Deitate humanitateq; Christus factus est, cum non sit diuersus ab his duobus, sed vtrunq; & homo & Deus. Item anima cum corpore nunquam non afficitur: quod quidem de Deitate Christi orthodoxus nemo, modo sana mentis sit, ausit dicere aut cogitare. Itaq; hominis exemplum partim recipiendum, partim fugiendum.
units.tr: 23. For just as the rational soul. The manner of the union of the Word and the flesh is explained by a likeness. Justin Martyr, a very ancient writer, is said to have used this likeness even before Athanasius, in his Exposition of the Faith. It is worth quoting his words, so that it may be understood how far the comparison holds: Nor is there reason, he says, for anyone to ask me about the manner of this union. For I shall not be ashamed to confess ignorance. Indeed I shall rather glory that I believe the mysteries into which I have been initiated, which neither reason nor mind is able to perceive. There are those who understand this union in the way the soul is united with the body, and so teach. The comparison fits, if not entirely, at least in part. For just as man, being one, has in himself two different natures, and one part of him deliberates while another part carries out what has been deliberated, the mind deciding on the structure of a ship and the hands making the decided work: so the Son, being one, though of a twofold nature, performs miracles according to one nature, and according to the other he takes humble things upon himself. For insofar as he is God from the Father, he works wonders; insofar as he is man from the virgin, he willingly endured the cross, the passion and similar things according to his nature. So far, if anyone compares, the likeness fits admirably. On the other hand, if one compares the whole with the whole, it removes the difference. Man, though he consists of soul and body, is not the same as them, but something different, so that man consists of the joining of body with soul, and there exists a third thing. But Christ was not made from the deity and the humanity, since he is not different from these two, but both man and God. Likewise the soul is never affected apart from the body; no orthodox person, provided he is of sound mind, would dare to say or think this of the deity of Christ. So the example of man is partly to be received and partly to be avoided.

units.la: Ex quibus intelligitur, similitudinem in duobus conuenire in totidem verò discrepare.
units.tr: From these things it is understood that the likeness agrees in two respects, but differs in as many.

units.la: Conuenit primo, quod sicut anima rationalis cum corpore humano copulatur in vnam personam Ἑνωθρώπῳ [?] hominis: sic eius Verbum cum natura humana copulatur in vnam personam τᾶς Θεοῦ [?] Dei hominis, idq; ἀρρήτως ineffabili modo.
units.tr: It agrees first, in that just as the rational soul is joined with the human body into one person [Ἑνωθρώπῳ ?] of man, so his Word is joined with the human nature into one person [τᾶς Θεοῦ ?] of the God-man, and this [ἀρρήτως] in an ineffable manner.

units.la: Deinde: quod sicut vnio animæ cum corpore fit, salvis vtriusq; naturæ proprietatibus essentialibus. Manet enim anima in vnione inuisibilis, spiritualis, immortalis, rationalis, impartibilis; corpus visibile, tangibile, mortale, expers rationis, partibile: fit quoq; vnio absq; transfusione proprietatum essentialium vnius naturæ in alteram: anima non fit visibilis, corporea, mortalis, irrationalis, partibilis propter vnionem cum corpore: corpus non fit inuisibile, spirituale, immortale, rationale, impartibile, propter vnionem cum anima: fit tamen vnio cum communione proprietatum essentialium animæ & corporis in personam homines realiter transeunte, cuiusque naturæ respectu: vt homo realiter sit immortalis, rationalis, secundum animum: sit & realiter mortalis, expers rationis, secundum corpus. Sic vnio Dei verbi cum carne facta est saluis vtriusq; naturæ proprietatibus essentialibus. Manet Deus verbum in vnione æternum, increatum, simplicissimum, infinitum, omnipræsens, omnipotens, omniscium, impassibile, immortale, &c. Caro in tempore creata, composita, finita loco, potentia, scientia, passibilis, mortalis, &c. facta quoque est vnio absque transfusione proprietatum essentialium Verbum Dei Verbi in carnem, vel carnis in Deum Verbum. Verbum non est factum temporarium, creatum, compositum, finitum loco, potentia, scientia, passibile, mortale, propter vnionem cum carne: Caro non est facta æterna, increata, incomposita, infinita, omnipræsens, omnipotens, omniscia, impassibilis, immortalis, propter vnionem cum Verbo: facta tamen est vnio cum communione proprietatum essentialium Verbi & carnis, in persona Christi θεανθρώπου seu Verbi incarnati realiter transeunte, cuiusque naturæ respectu: (quem Damascenus πόπον αλλοίωσις vocat, lib. 3. Orthod. fid. cap. 4.) vt Christus modum alternationis vocat, lib. 3. Orthod. fid. cap. 4.) vt Christus Deus realiter fit homo, in tempore creatus & natus, compositus, finitus loco, potentia, scientia, fueritq; passibilis, mortalis, passus, mortuus secundum carnem assumtam: Christus homo realiter sit Deus, æternus, increatus, simplicissimus, infinitus, omnipræsens, omnipotens, omniscius, &c. secundum diuinitatem assumentem.
units.tr: Second, just as the union of the soul with the body takes place with the essential properties of each nature preserved. For the soul remains in the union invisible, spiritual, immortal, rational, indivisible; the body visible, tangible, mortal, without reason, divisible. The union is also made without any transfusion of the essential properties of one nature into the other: the soul does not become visible, corporeal, mortal, irrational, divisible because of the union with the body; the body does not become invisible, spiritual, immortal, rational, indivisible because of the union with the soul. Yet a union takes place, with a real communion of the essential properties of soul and body in the one person of man, each nature retaining its own character, so that man is really immortal and rational according to the mind, and really mortal and without reason according to the body. So the union of God the Word with the flesh has come about with the essential properties of each nature preserved. God the Word remains in the union eternal, uncreated, most simple, infinite, omnipresent, omnipotent, omniscient, impassible, immortal, and so on. The flesh, created in time, composite, finite in place, in power and knowledge, passible, mortal, and so on. The union also takes place without any transfusion of the essential properties of the Word of God into the flesh, or of the flesh into God the Word. The Word has not become temporal, created, composite, finite in place, in power, in knowledge, passible, mortal, because of the union with the flesh; the flesh has not become eternal, uncreated, uncompounded, infinite, omnipresent, omnipotent, omniscient, impassible, immortal, because of the union with the Word. Yet a union has been made, with a real communion of the essential properties of the Word and the flesh in the person of Christ, the God-man, or the incarnate Word, each nature retaining its own character. (Damascene calls this [τρόπον ἀλλοίωσις, mode of alternation], in Orthodox Faith 3.4.) Thus Christ as God really became man, created and born in time, composite, finite in place, in power and knowledge, and was passible, mortal, and suffered and died according to the flesh he assumed. Christ as man really is God, eternal, uncreated, most simple, infinite, omnipresent, omnipotent, omniscient, and so on, according to the deity that assumed.

units.la: Non conuenit verò similitudo: primo, quod in homine ex vnione animæ rationalis & corporis fit aliquid tertium specie diuersum, homo, tanquam ex materia & forma, quarum neutra est homo. In Christo non sic: quia Verbum assumens carnem, olim ante & post incarnationem erat Deus & persona eadem, olim nuda, postea carne vestita. Deinde, quod animo quidem homines in se recipit passiones corporis, cum quo tristatur & lætatur: Verbum verò DEVS est omnis affectionis & passionis expers.
units.tr: The likeness, however, does not agree in these respects. First, that in man, from the union of the rational soul and the body, there comes about something third, different in kind, namely man, as from matter and form, neither of which is man. It is not so in Christ, because the Word that assumed the flesh was before and after the incarnation the same God and the same person, formerly unclothed, afterwards clothed with flesh. Second, that men indeed receive into themselves the sufferings of the body in their mind, grieving and rejoicing with it; but the Word is God, free from every affection and passion.

units.la: ARTICVLVS V. SYMBOLI XIII.
units.tr: ARTICLE V OF THE CREED XIII.

units.la: 24. Qui passus est propter nostram salutem: 25. descendit ad inferos: 26. tertia die resurrexit à mortuis: 27. Ascendit ad cœlos: 28. sedet ad dextram Dei Patris omnipotentis: 29. inde venturus est judicare viuos & mortuos.
units.tr: 24. Who suffered for our salvation: 25. descended into hell: 26. on the third day rose again from the dead: 27. ascended into heaven: 28. sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty: 29. from thence he will come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Declaration.

units.la: 24. Qui passus est.] Fuit incarnationis mysterium: sequitur de officio Filij Dei incarnati, verbis fere ex symbolo Apostolico succincte repetitis. Hæc verò sunt, propter quæ Filium Dei incarnatum credimus, & sine quorum fiducia Filius Dei incarnatus frustra creditur. Quia enim Filius Dei noster factus erat ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἔγγυος sponsor in judicio Dei, debuit in carne nostra pro nobis opperire morte maledictam, ut maledictioni legis nostro loco satisfaceret, nobisque morte sua justitiam & vitam amissam repararet. Passus igitur est mortem crucis, pro salute nostra reparanda.
units.tr: 24. Who suffered.] This is the mystery of the incarnation; there follows what belongs to the office of the incarnate Son of God, repeated briefly in nearly the words of the Apostles' Creed. These are the things for the sake of which we believe the Son of God to have been made flesh, and without trust in which the incarnate Son of God is believed in vain. For since the Son of God had become our surety [ἔγγυος], our sponsor [sponsor] in the judgment of God, he had to submit in our flesh, on our behalf, to the death accursed by the law, so that he might satisfy the curse of the law in our place, and by his death restore to us the righteousness and life we had lost. He therefore suffered the death of the cross, to win back our salvation.

units.la: 25. Descendit ad inferos.] Ut nos à terroribus inferni liberaret: non utique descensu corporali, vel animali, post mortem, in loca inferni: talem enim descensum scriptura evidenter refellit. Luc. 23,43.53. Sed luctâ spirituali cum angoribus inferni (quam scriptura descensum ad inferos vocare solet. 1 Sam. 2,6. Ps.16,18. Psal.116,3.) ante mortem, in horto, & cruce: Matth.26,38. Luc.22.v.44.
units.tr: 25. Descended into hell.] So that he might free us from the terrors of hell: not indeed by a bodily or soul-descent after death into the places of hell, for Scripture plainly refutes such a descent (Luke 23:43, 53). Rather, it was by a spiritual struggle with the anguish of hell (which Scripture is wont to call a descent into the depths: 1 Sam. 2:6; Ps. 16:18; Ps. 116:3) before death, in the garden and on the cross: Matt. 26:38; Luke 22:44.

units.la: 26. Tertia die resurrexit.] Propter justificationem nostram, Rom.4,25. Hic articulus est basis consolationis & spei Christianæ. Si enim Christus non est excitatus ex mortuis, inanis est prædicatio Euangelij, inanis fides nostra, & sumus adhuc in peccatis nostris. 1 Corinth.15,17.
units.tr: 26. On the third day rose again.] On account of our justification, Rom. 4:25. This article is the basis of Christian comfort and hope. For if Christ has not been raised from the dead, our preaching of the Gospel is empty, our faith is empty, and we are still in our sins: 1 Cor. 15:17.

units.la: 27. Ascendit ad cœlos.] Semper quidem divinitate nobiscum est. Sed nisi corporaliter abiisset à nobis, semper eius corpus carnaliter videremus, & nunquam spiritualiter crederemus: qua fide & justificati sumus. Augustin.ser.60 de verbo Domini.
units.tr: 27. Ascended into heaven.] He is indeed always with us in his divinity. But unless he had departed from us bodily, we would always see his body in the flesh and never believe spiritually, and it is by this faith that we are justified. Augustine, Sermon 60 on the Words of the Lord.

units.la: 28. Sedet ad dextram Dei Patris.] Juxta promissionem Ps.110,1. Sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum: quod Apostolus interpretatur 1 Cor.15,25. Oportet eum regnare, donec subjecerit omnes inimicos pedibus eius. Et Eph.1,2. Collocavit eum super omne imperium & potestatem, &c. & omnia subjecit pedibus eius, eumq; constituit caput super omnia ipsi Ecclesiæ. Gloria igitur sessionis Christi ad dextram Patris est regnum Mediatoris exaltati in sua carne: non verò carnis diffusio, vel ubiquitas, quæ repugnat ei, quod sequitur.
units.tr: 28. Sits at the right hand of God the Father.] According to the promise of Ps. 110:1: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool; which the Apostle interprets, 1 Cor. 15:25: He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. And Eph. 1:20-22: He set him above every rule and authority, etc., and put all things under his feet, and appointed him head over all things for the Church. The glory of Christ's sitting at the right hand of the Father is therefore the kingly rule of the exalted Mediator in his flesh; it is not a diffusion of the flesh or its ubiquity, which contradicts what follows.

units.la: 29. Inde venturus est judicare.] Phil.3,20. 2 Tim.4,1. Judicaturus est vivos & mortuos in illustri illo suo adventu in regno suo. Augustin. epist.57. ad Dardan. Noli itaq; dubitare, ibi nunc esse hominem Christum Iesum, unde venturus est: memoriterq; recolęq; & fideliter tene Christianam confessionem, quoniam resurrexit à mortuis, ascendit in cœlum, sedet ad dextram Patris, NEC ALIUNDE, QUAM INDE venventurus est ad vivos mortuosq; judicandos. Et sic venturus est, illa angelica voce testante, quemadmodum ire visus est in cœlum, id est, in eadem carnis forma atque substantia, cui profecto immortalitatem dedit, naturam non abstulit. Secundum hanc formam non est putandus ubique diffusus. Cavendum est enim, ne ita divinitatem adstruamus hominis, ut veritatem corporis auferamus, &c.
units.tr: 29. From thence he will come to judge.] Phil. 3:20; 2 Tim. 4:1. He will judge the living and the dead at his glorious coming in his kingdom. Augustine, Letter 57 to Dardanus: Do not therefore doubt that the man Christ Jesus is now there, whence he will come; remember and keep steadfastly and faithfully the Christian confession, that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from no other place than from there will come to judge the living and the dead. And so he will come, as the angelic voice bears witness, just as he was seen to go into heaven, that is, in the same form and substance of flesh, to which indeed he gave immortality but did not take away its nature. According to this form he is not to be thought of as diffused everywhere. For care must be taken lest we so assert the divinity of the man that we take away the truth of the body, etc.

units.la: ARTICVLVS VI. SYMBOLI XIV.
units.tr: ARTICLE VI OF THE CREED XIV.

units.la: 30. Ad cuius aduentum omnes homines resurgent 31. cum corporibus suis, 32. & reddituri sunt de factis propriis ratione. 33. Et qui bona egerunt, ibunt in vitam æternam: qui vero mala, in ignem æternum.
units.tr: 30. At whose coming all men shall rise again 31. with their own bodies, 32. and shall give account of their own deeds. 33. And those who have done good will go into eternal life; but those who have done evil, into eternal fire.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Declaration.

units.la: 30. Ad cuius aduentum.] Sic docetur 1 Thess. 4, 16. cum voce Archangeli ac tuba Dei descendet de cœlo: & qui mortui fuerint in Christo, resurgent primum, &c. 1 Cor. 15, 52. Momento & ictu oculi ad ultimam tubam mortui suscitabuntur incorrupti.
units.tr: 30. At whose coming.] This is taught in 1 Thess. 4:16: with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, the Lord himself will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first, etc. 1 Cor. 15:52: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will be raised incorruptible.

units.la: 31. Cum corporibus suis.] Oportet enim hoc corruptibile induere incorruptibilitatem: & hoc mortale induere immortalitatem. 1 Corinth. 15. vers. 53.
units.tr: 31. With their own bodies.] For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality: 1 Cor. 15:53.

units.la: 32. Et reddituri sunt.] Sic scriptum est Matth. 12, 36. Dico vobis, quodcunq; verbum otiosum locuti fuerint homines, ae eo reddituri sunt rationem in die judicij. Omnes enim nos comparere oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut unusquisque reportet, qua in corpore fecerit, contrugenter ad id, quod fecerit bonum vel malum, 2 Cor. 6, 10. Iudicati sunt mortui ex iis, quae scripta erant in libris, secundum opera ipsorum, Apoc. 20. vers. 12.
units.tr: 32. And shall give account.] So it is written in Matt. 12:36: I tell you, that men shall give account on the day of judgment for every idle word they have spoken. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil: 2 Cor. 5:10. The dead were judged out of those things written in the books, according to their works: Rev. 20:12.

units.la: 33. Et qui bona egerunt.] Sicut prophetavit Daniel cap. 12. v. 2: Multi dormientium in terra pulueris expergiscentur: hi ad vitam aeternam: & illi ad opprobrium & ad contemtum sempiternum. Et Christus Ioh. 5, 28. Veniet hora, qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem eius: & prodibunt, qui bona fecerint, in resurrectionem vitae: qui vero mala egerint, in resurrectionem condemnationis.
units.tr: 33. And those who have done good.] As Daniel prophesied, Dan. 12:2: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and others to shame and everlasting contempt. And Christ, John 5:28-29: The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of condemnation.

units.la: ARTICVLVS VII. SYMBOLI XV.
units.tr: ARTICLE VII OF THE CREED XV.

units.la: CONFITEMVR dominum nostrum Iesum Christum ante secula quidem ex patre, per Spiritum sanctum vero nouissimis temporibus ex virgine secundum carnem natum, vna duntaxat persona, ex coelesti diuinitate & humana carne conflata, subsistentem. Totum Deum & totum hominem. Totū Deum etiam cum corpore, sed non secundum corpus Deum. Totū hominem etiam cum diuinitate, sed non secundum diuinitatē homine. Totū rursum adorabilē etiam cum corpore, sed nō secundum corpus adorabilem. Totum adorantem etiā cum diuinitate, sed non secundum diuinitatē, adorantē. Totum increatū etiam cum corpore, sed non secundum corpus, increatum. Totū formatum etiam cum diuinitate, sed non secundum diuinitatē formatum. Totum Deo ὁμοούσιον, etiam cum corpore, sed non secundum corpus ὁμοούσιον: quemadmodum neq; secundū diuinitatem quoq; hominibus coessentialis est: est autē nobis secundum carnē ὁμοούσιος, etiā in diuinitate existens. Etenim cū illum secundum Spiritum Deo consubstantialem dicimus, non dicimus hominibus secundū Spiritum coessentiale. Contra autem cum illum secundum carnē hominibus consubstantialē prædicamus, non prædicamus illum secundum carnē Deo coessentialem. Vt enim secundum Spiritum nobis ὁμοούσιος non est; (Nam secundum hunc Deo ὁμοούσιος est:) ita vicissim Deo secundum carnem coessentialis non est: secundum hanc autem nobis consubstantialis est. Quemadmodum autem hæc distincta, & inter se secreta pronunciamus, non ad inducendam vnius indiuisæ personæ diuisionem, sed ad denotandam naturarum & proprietatum verbi & carnis distinctionem, & inconfusibilitatem: ita illa, quæ ad indiuisæ vnionis compositionisque rationem faciunt, vnita prædicamus & veneramur.
units.tr: We confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was indeed born of the Father before all ages, but in the last times was born of the Virgin according to the flesh, subsisting as one person, compounded of heavenly divinity and human flesh. Whole God and whole man. Whole God even with the body, but not God according to the body. Whole man even with the divinity, but not man according to the divinity. Whole again, adorable even with the body, but not adorable according to the body. Whole worshipper even with the divinity, but not worshipper according to the divinity. Whole uncreated even with the body, but not uncreated according to the body. Whole formed even with the divinity, but not formed according to the divinity. Whole consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with God, even with the body, but not consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with God according to the body; just as he is not co-essential with men according to the divinity either. Yet he is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with us according to the flesh, existing also in the divinity. For when we say that he is consubstantial with God according to the Spirit, we do not say that he is co-essential with men according to the Spirit. Conversely, when we proclaim that he is consubstantial with men according to the flesh, we do not proclaim that he is co-essential with God according to the flesh. For just as he is not consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with us according to the Spirit (for according to this he is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with God), so in turn he is not co-essential with God according to the flesh; but according to the flesh he is consubstantial with us. Moreover, as we declare these things distinct and separate from one another, not to introduce a division of the one undivided person, but to denote the distinction and unconfusedness of the natures and properties of the Word and of the flesh, so we proclaim and venerate as united those things which pertain to the manner of the undivided union and composition.

units.la: Vigilius lib. 4. aduersus Eutychen.
units.tr: Vigilius, book 4, against Eutyches.

units.la: Si verbi & carnis vna natura est, quomodo, cum verbum vbique sit, non vbique inueniatur & caro? Namque quando in terra fuit, non erat vtique in coelo: & nunc, quia in coelo est, nō est vtique in terra, & in tantum non est, vt secundum ipsam Christum expectemus venturum de coelo, quē secundum verbum nobiscum esse credimus in terra. Igitur secundum vos, aut verbum cum carne suo loco continetur, aut caro cū verbo vbique est, quando vna natura contrarium quid & diuersum non recipit in seipsa. Diuersum est autem & longe dissimile, circumscribi loco, & vbique esse: & quia Verbum vbiq; est, caro autem vbique non est, apparet, vnum eundemque Christum vtriusque esse naturæ: & esse quidem vbiq; secundum naturam diuinitatis suæ, & loco contineri secundum naturam humanitatis suæ: creatum esse, & initium non habere: morti subjacere, & mori non posse: quorum vnum illi est ex natura verbi, qua Deus est: aliud ex natura carnis, qua idem Deus homo est. Igitur vnus Dei filius, idemque hominis factus filius, habet initium ex natura carnis suæ, & non habet initium ex natura diuinitatis suæ: creatus est per naturam carnis suæ, & non est creatus per naturam diuinitatis suæ: circumscriptus loco est per naturam carnis suæ, & non loco capitur per naturam diuinitatis suæ: minor est etiam angelis per naturam carnis suæ, & æqualis est Patri secundum naturam diuinitatis suæ: mortuus est natura carnis suæ, & non est mortuus natura diuinitatis suæ. HÆC EST FIDES & confessio catholica, quam apostoli tradiderunt, martyres roborauerunt, & fideles hucusque custodiunt. Unde impiissime & Eutychianæ hæreses veneno infectus, Leonem audes reprehendere, dum ex diuersitate gestorum vnius Domini Christi, veritatem edoceat vtriusque naturæ: vt quod ille ad demonstrationem vtramque protulit naturarum, professionem calumnieris duarum esse personarum.
units.tr: If the nature of the Word and of the flesh is one, how, since the Word is everywhere, is the flesh not found everywhere also? For when he was on earth, he was certainly not in heaven; and now, since he is in heaven, he is certainly not on earth, and he is so far from being on earth that we await him coming from heaven according to Christ himself, whom we believe to be with us on earth according to the Word. Therefore, according to you, either the Word is contained in place together with the flesh, or the flesh is everywhere together with the Word, since one nature does not receive in itself things contrary and diverse. But to be circumscribed by place and to be everywhere are different and utterly dissimilar. And because the Word is everywhere, but the flesh is not everywhere, it is evident that one and the same Christ is of both natures: that he is everywhere according to the nature of his divinity, but is contained in place according to the nature of his humanity; that he was created and has no beginning; that he is subject to death and cannot die. Of these, the one belongs to him from the nature of the Word, by which he is God; the other from the nature of the flesh, by which the same is God-man. Therefore the one Son of God, who has also become the Son of man, has a beginning according to the nature of his flesh and has no beginning according to the nature of his divinity; he was created according to the nature of his flesh and was not created according to the nature of his divinity; he is circumscribed in place according to the nature of his flesh and is not contained in place according to the nature of his divinity; he is also less than the angels according to the nature of his flesh and equal to the Father according to the nature of his divinity; he died according to the nature of his flesh and did not die according to the nature of his divinity. THIS IS THE CATHOLIC FAITH and confession, which the apostles delivered, the martyrs strengthened, and the faithful have kept until now. Whence you, infected with the poison of the most impious Eutychian heresy, dare to reprehend Leo, while from the diversity of the deeds of the one Lord Christ he teaches the truth of both natures; so that you calumniate his profession of two persons, because he brought forward those things to demonstrate both natures.

units.la: An Deus omnes homines sub conditione seruata legis vno fine condiderit in Adamo ad salutem?
units.tr: Whether God, under the condition of the law being kept, created all men in Adam for one end, namely salvation?

units.la: VIDEO hic, inquit Dn. Mosses, authores, si non reuera, in speciem tamen pugnare. Dn. Calvinus l. 3. Inst. cap. 21. §. 5. dicit, homines non omnes pari conditione creari. Doctor Vrsinus Quæst. 6. catech. asserit, Deum creauisse hominem, vt cum eo beatus in æternum viueret. Hæc si ita sunt; videtur lapsus hominis non cadere sub providentiam diuinam: & Deus vide-tur non assequutus finem suum, quem in creatione intendebat. Piscator contra Adream Schasmannum Propos. 29. dicit, Deum crea-
units.tr: I see here, says Mr. Moses, that the authors, if not really, at least in appearance, contradict one another. Mr. Calvin, Institutes book 3, chapter 21, section 5, says that men are not all created on the same condition. Doctor Ursinus, in Question 6 of the Catechism, asserts that God created man so that he might live blessed with him forever. If these things are so, it seems that the fall of man does not fall under divine providence, and God seems not to have attained the end which he intended in creation. Piscator, against Adrian Schasmannus, Proposition 29, says that God created

units.la: Pertinet ad explic. Cat. Quæst. VI. creauisse hominem in vno, sed non in vno fine. Et quæst. 37. ad hoc argumentū Schafmauni: Imago Dei erat concreata, & propaganda sanctitas ac iustitia, propter quam homo & Deo placebat, & integra voluntati obsequendo, aterni gaudii particeps erat futurus: respondet Piscator: falsum est, sanctitatem illam concreatam fuisse propagandam: quia verum est, ex decreto Dei fuisse amittendam, antequam primi parentes liberos gignerent. Nam si ne pilus quidem de capite nostro cadit absq; voluntate Patris: quanto minus sanctitas illa amissa fuit absq; illius voluntate, & providentia?
units.tr: (this belongs to the explanation of the Catechism, Question 6) that he created man for one purpose, but not for one end. And in Question 37, in reply to Schasmannus's argument: The image of God was concreated, and the holiness and righteousness to be propagated, on account of which man was pleasing to God, and, remaining whole in obeying the will, was going to partake of eternal joy, Piscator responds: It is false that that holiness was concreated to be propagated; for it is true that by the decree of God it was to be lost before the first parents begat children. For if not even a hair falls from our head without the Father's will, how much less was that holiness lost without his will and providence?

units.la: Responsio D. Parei.
units.tr: Response of Dr. Parey.

units.la: Quæris, D. Moses; An Deus omnes homines sub conditione servatæ legis vno fine condiderit in Adamo ad salutem? & de hac Quæstione ostendis authorum discrepantes sententias. Si dixero, me quæstionem libenter ignorare, non mentiar. Est siquidem ex arcanæ mentis diuinæ adyto petita: plus acuminis requirens, quam ædificationis habens. Dicam tamen, quid sentiendum censeam.
units.tr: You ask, Dr. Moses, whether God, under the condition of the law being kept, created all men in Adam, with one end, for salvation; and on this question you set out the differing opinions of authors. If I said that I am glad to leave the question unexplored, I would not be lying. It is drawn from the inner sanctuary of the divine mind, demands more sharpness than it offers edification. Still, I will say what I think ought to be held.

units.la: Si à priori consideres, affirmo, omnes vno fine conditos in Adamo, vt ramos in stipite: sed cum conditione: si Adam in Imagine Dei [quæ initiū & pars erat salutis] ipse staret, eamq; ad posteros propagaret: seu, in ea ipse omnes homines procrearet. Verum quia hæc conditio neque in consilio Dei erat posita, neq; in euentu ponenda: à posteriori cogimur negare, nisi Deum vel excidisse suo fine, vel consilium mutasse credere velimus: quandoquidem plurimos salutem non consequi res loquitur. Sed enim, ad præcidendas omnes argutias, sic stato.
units.tr: If you consider the matter a priori, I affirm that all were created in Adam with one end, as branches are in a trunk, but with a condition: namely, if Adam himself stood in the image of God, which was the beginning and part of salvation, and passed it on to his posterity, or if he himself were to beget all men in that image. But since this condition was neither placed in the counsel of God nor set to be fulfilled in the event, we are compelled, a posteriori, to deny it, unless we wish to believe either that God missed his end or that he changed his counsel, since the outcome shows that very many do not obtain salvation. But, to cut off all subtleties, I put it this way.

units.la: Adamus dupliciter consideradus est. Semel ante lapsum, vt stipes humani generis in potentia, verum nunquam in actū ventura. Deus enim [prout euentu docemur] non modo creauerat hominem mutabiliter bonum: qui tentatus rectitudinem suam ante generationem amittere posset: sed etiam decreuerat permittere, cum tentari, labi, & rectitudinem suam amittere, antequam generaret. Quo posito, nullos omnino in hoc statu homines procreaturus erat. Frustra igitur quæritur: An Deus in eo tū omnes ad salutem creauerit, quos ex eo tunc non procreare decreuerat, idque ob causas in multiformi eius sapientia reconditas. Deinde vero post lapsum, vt stipes generis humani in actu: quando non solum per naturam, sed etiam per Dei dispositionē homo actualiter procreaturus erat genus humanū: sed tale, qualis ipse tunc erat, prauum, & maledictioni obnoxiū. Ethuc iam pertinet præsens Quæstio, sicut & totum prædeprædestinationis circa electionem & reprobationem decretum. In procliui autem ex scriptura & experientia ipsa est responsio à posteriori: quod sicut non omnes homines ex Adamo lapso prognati ad vnum finem tendunt, sed alij ad vitam, alij ad mortem: sic non omnes ad vnum finem ex Adamo lapso procreentur: ac proinde (nisi Deum vel à procreatione hominis penitus submouere, vel otiosum circa eam fingere, aut intentione sua falli conuere, vel cedere placeat) à Deo non omnes ad vnum finem procreari vel in Adamo lapso creatos dici posse: sed vnumquemque ad eum finem, ad quem vel per naturæ prauitatem tendere permittitur: hoc est, ad mortem: vel per gratiæ beneficium in Christo dirigitur: hoc est, ad salutem. Hoc enim diuortium, quod statim inter Adami, Noæ, Abrahami, Isaaci, &c. filios natura corruptos apparuit, haud dubie Deus, non otiose vidit aut prævidit, sed quia ipsemet per gratiam in tempore fecit, juxta illud: Iacob dilexi: Esau odio habui. Et: Antequam nati essent pueri, cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, vt propositum Dei secundum electionem eius, &c. maneret: sic ab ab æterno decreuit. Vides quæstionem proxime cum doctrina de electione cohærere; de qua proinde, ne sim prolixior, plura non addam.
units.tr: Adam must be considered in two ways. First, before the fall, as the trunk of the human race in potency, yet one that was never to come into act. For God, as the outcome teaches us, had not only created man good in a changeable way, so that being tempted he could lose his uprightness before he begat children, but had also decreed to permit him to be tempted, to fall, and to lose his uprightness before he begot anyone. Given this, he was going to beget no men at all in that state. It is vain, therefore, to ask whether God then created all unto salvation in him, when he had then decided not to beget those very people, and that for causes hidden in his manifold wisdom. Second, after the fall, as the trunk of the human race in act: when man was actually going to beget the human race, not only by nature but also by God's disposition; but such as he then was, depraved and liable to the curse. To this the present question belongs, as does the whole decree of predestination concerning election and reprobation. Now the answer, a posteriori, is readily given from Scripture and from experience itself: just as not all men born of fallen Adam tend to one end, but some to life and others to death, so not all are begotten from fallen Adam for one end. Therefore (unless we wish to remove God entirely from the begetting of man, or imagine him idle in it, or grant that he is deceived in his intention), not all can be said to have been created by God for one end, or to have been created in fallen Adam; rather each is directed to that end to which he is permitted to tend through the depravity of nature, that is, to death, or is directed through the benefit of grace in Christ, that is, to salvation. For this divergence, which at once appeared among the sons of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and the rest, corrupted by nature, God undoubtedly saw and foresaw not idly, but because he himself effects it through grace in time, according to that saying: "Jacob I loved, Esau I hated." And: "Before the boys were born, when they had done nothing good or bad, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand," and so forth; thus he decreed from eternity. You see that the question coheres closely with the doctrine of election; so, lest I be too long, I will add no more on that.

units.la: Rectè igitur Caluinus dicit, homines non omnes pari conditione creari, nempe post lapsum, quantum ad finem, non quantum ad statum, quo sane omnes nascuntur pares: quia omnes filij iræ.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, Calvin says that men are not all created on equal terms, namely after the fall, as to their end but not as to their state, in which indeed all are born equal, since all are children of wrath.

units.la: De fine enim diuerso dicitur, quantum ad electos: Constituit nos ad salutem, &c. 1 Thess. 5, 9. quantum ad reliquos: Impium fecit ad diem malum. Vrsinus vero dicens, Deum creauisse hominem, vt cum eo beatus in æternum viueret, intelligi debet conditionaliter, quatenus homo in integritate persisteret. Finis igitur fuit conditionalis, ponendus non in Adamo, sed in Christo: si, quod futurum erat, Adam excidisset: & sic Schaffmannus quoque intelligendus est, sanctitatem Adamo concreatam fuisse propagandam in omnes: nempe, si Adam non prius, quàm omnes generaret, eam amitteret. Conditionaliter ergo verum dicit: sed absolutè falsum: quod ait Piscator.
units.tr: For the end is spoken of differently: as to the elect, "God has appointed us to salvation," 1 Thess. 5, 9; as to the rest, "He made the wicked for the evil day." But when Ursinus says that God created man "that he might live blessedly with him for ever," this must be understood conditionally, insofar as man would persist in integrity. The end, therefore, was conditional, and is to be located not in Adam but in Christ, if Adam had fallen away, which was going to happen. So too Schaffmann must be understood, when he says that the holiness created with Adam was to be propagated to all, namely if Adam did not lose it before he begat all. Therefore he speaks truly in a conditional sense, but what Piscator says is false absolutely.

units.la: Hæc pauca, mi Dn. Moses, de quæstione magna: vt fusius cogitandi materiam habeas: quamquam hic te, & nos omnes conuenit juxta Apostoli regulam, Rom. 12, 3: μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν.
units.tr: These few things, my dear Dr. Moses, on a great question, so that you may have more material for thought at greater length. Yet here it becomes you and all of us, according to the rule of the Apostle, Rom. 12, 3, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think so as to be sober-minded [μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν].

units.la: In THESES D. ÆGIDII HVNNII DE VNIONE HYPOSTATICA, Witteberg. Anno 1592. a.d. 8. Kalend. Iunij disputatas, ANIMADVERSIONES PRO ASSERenda Orthodoxa doctrina de Persona JESU CHRISTI: ad normam sacræ Scripturæ, & consensum piæ Antiquitatis.
units.tr: Animadversions in Support of the Orthodox Doctrine concerning the Person of Jesus Christ, according to the Rule of Holy Scripture and the Agreement of Pious Antiquity, Against the Theses of Dr. Ægidius Hunnius on the Hypostatic Union, Defended at Wittenberg on 8 Kalends of June (24 May), 1592

units.la: ARGVMENTVM THESIVM Hunnianarum DE VNIONE HYPOSTATICA.
units.tr: Summary of the Hunnian Theses on the Hypostatic Union

units.la: Fronte mel apparet: tegitur sed ventre venenum: Melleq; sub cauda toxica mixta iacent.
units.tr: Honey appears on the forehead; but poison is hidden in the belly, and venom lies mixed beneath the tail.

units.la: Theses Hunnianæ, in fronte & cauda mel insidiosum: in ventre apertum fel habent. Frontem porrigunt ad thesin ferè xvii. quousque orthodoxè satis (insidias si excipias) contra veteres hæreticos astruunt: Christum esse personam πρόσωπον, duabus constantem naturis, veris & integris, divina & humana: ac Filium DEI λόγον carnem factum, non conversione Deitatis in carnem, sed assumptione humanitatis in DEVM: quibus qui non facile & ex corde subscribit, orthodoxus est nemo.
units.tr: The Hunnian theses have honey, a treacherous honey, in their front and their tail, but an open gall in their belly. The front extends to about the seventeenth thesis. Up to that point they assert, fairly orthodoxly (if you set aside the snares), against the ancient heretics, that Christ is one person [πρόσωπον, prosōpon], consisting of two natures, true and whole, divine and human, and that the Son of God, the Word [λόγος, logos], was made flesh not by a conversion of the Deity into flesh but by the assumption of humanity into God. Anyone who does not readily and from the heart subscribe to these is orthodox in name only.

units.la: Venter felle tumet ubiquitario, thesibus proximis ad xxxix. usque. Nam hypotheses quasdam de modo ac vi unionis, tanquam futuræ disputationis de reali idiomatum communicatione deque carnis omnipræsentia, fundamenta sternit, ac mira sophistica pingit: sed falsas eas omnes: Nempe, quod λόγος totus carnem totam sic assumpserit, ut sicut caro nusquam est extra λόγον, sic λόγος nusquam sit extra carnem: hoc est, extra carnis dimensiones. Quod unio talis sit immanentia totius plenitudinis Deitatis in carne, ut extra carnem Deitas λόγος nusquam sit: Quod denique caro in illocali hypostasi & λόγος omnem localitatem altissimè transcenderit, & illocalem exsistendi modum verè sortiatur, hoc est, in unione sit illocalis. Interim definitionem & formam unionis hypostaticæ, quam tanquam caput totius disputationis primo loco expositam tam merito oportuit, (vt titulus non mentiretur) astuæ dissimulat: ne videlicet ob manifestam differentiæ specificæ falsitatem, causa ante tempus laboraret.
units.tr: The belly swells with ubiquitarian gall, from the next theses up to the thirty-ninth. For in certain hypotheses concerning the mode and force of the union, laid down as groundwork for a future disputation on the real communication of attributes and on the omnipresence of the flesh, he lays foundations and paints them with wondrous sophistry. But all of them are false. Namely: that the Word as a whole has so assumed the whole flesh that, just as the flesh is nowhere outside the Word, so the Word is nowhere outside the flesh, that is, outside the dimensions of the flesh; that the union is such an indwelling of the whole fullness of the Deity in the flesh that the Deity of the Word is nowhere outside the flesh; and finally that the flesh, in the illocal hypostasis, has altogether transcended all locality in the Word and truly obtains an illocal mode of existence, that is, that in the union it is illocal. Meanwhile he conceals, with cunning, the definition and form of the hypostatic union, which he ought rightly to have set out first, as the head of the whole disputation (so that the title would not be a lie). He does this so that, because of the manifest falsity of the specific difference, the cause should not be in trouble before its time.

units.la: Canda rursus mel ostentat, sed aculeum occultat. Deducit enim ϰοεἱσμασ quatuor. I. Quòd vnio ϰοινωνία vera & solida sit describenda. II. Quòd ϰαταχρησις λόγυ sit communicata, & collata carni ineffabiliter. III. Quòd etiam persona λόγυ Deitas, seu omnis plenitudo Deitatis sit communicata humanitati. IV. Quòd denique sub hac plenitudine omnis Deitatis infallibiliter maiestas proprietatum verbi intelligatur. Quibus quidem sanè, hoc est, de vera vnione naturarum ac proprietatum ϰοινωνία in concreto intelectis, nemo etiam orthodoxus contradicit. Sed quod tum ista, antecedentia feré omnia nihil sint, nisi vbiquitatis insidiosa ϰενωσφύσια, etiam leviter oculati videre possunt, & hoc breui examine ostenditur.
units.tr: Again he displays honey on the tail, but hides the sting. For he draws out four heads [κεφάλαια, kephalaia]: first, that the union is to be described as a true and solid communion [κοινωνία, koinōnia]; second, that the attribute [κατάχρησις, katachrēsis] of the Word is communicated and conferred on the flesh in an unspeakable way; third, that also the person of the Word, the Deity, or the whole fullness of the Deity, is communicated to the humanity; fourth, that finally under this fullness of the whole Deity the majesty of the properties of the Word is infallibly understood. Certainly no orthodox person objects to these, that is, when the true union of the natures and the communion of the properties is understood in the concrete. But that these points, and nearly all that goes before them, are nothing but the insidious kenōseis [κενώσεις] of ubiquity, even those who see only slightly can perceive, and this is shown by the brief examination that follows.

units.la: THESES HVNNIANÆ DE VNIONE.
units.tr: THESES HVNNIANÆ DE VNIONE.

units.la: I. Iesus Christus, in cuius vera notitia perpetuæ salutis cardo vertitur, est Deus, & Homo: persona scilicet duabus naturis, diuina & humana, constans.
units.tr: I. Jesus Christ, in whose true knowledge the hinge of everlasting salvation turns, is God and man: that is, a person consisting of two natures, the divine and the human.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Sic sane loquuntur patres nonnulli, & Scholastici fere omnes: personam Christi constare, confici, constitui, componi, fieri, ex duabus naturis, diuina & humana, siue ex tribus substantiis, Deitate, anima & corpore. Sed ita explicant, vt neq; confusionem naturarum, neq; imperfectionem personæ ante incarnationem, neq; quaternitatem personarum diuinitatis statuant. Pluribus enim modis aliquid vnum ex duobus vel trib. constare docent. Vno modo, cum ex duobus vel pluribus integris perfectis remanentibus vnum quid conficitur: vt in iis, quorū forma est componentibus vnum quid conficitur: vt in iis, quorū forma est compositio, vel ordo, vel figura. Sic aceruus tritici constat ex multis granis: ciuitas ex multis ciuibus. Altero modo, cum aliquid vnum fit ex perfectis non remanentibus, sed transmutatis: sicut ex elementis fit corpus mixtum, ex aqua & melle fit mulsum. Tertio modo, cum aliquid tertium specie diuersum fit ex duobus non permixtis, sed imperfectis, tanquam ex materia & forma: sicut ex anima rationali & corpore fit homo. Nullo horū modorum persona Christi ex duabus naturis constare, vel componi proprie dicitur. Neq; enim vnio hypostatica est naturarum confusio, vel ordinata tantum juxta se dispositio: qualis fere erat Nestorii. storiana ιτερώσεως: neque permixtio, (nam improprie μίξις, quidam veteres appellant) neque compositio materiæ & formæ in unum tertium, quod neutrum sit: λόγος enim non est forma carnis, nec caro materia est λόγος: neq; λόγος demum per assumtionem carnis factus est persona, vel persona alia: quod etiam thesis 8. & 12. fatentur. Quarto vero modo improprie & laxè constare ex pluribus, dicitur, in quo simul plura ponuntur. Atque hoc demum sensu personam Christi constare seu compositam esse ex duabus naturis dicunt, quatenus nimirum compositio largè est simul-positio plurium. Sic enim vnionem hypostaticam compositionem vocari aiunt. Quare cauendi erroris causa tutius ferè loquuntur, ac dicunt, personam Christi subsistere in duabus naturis: quam phrasin & Orthodoxi vt magis propriam, libentius retinent: quanquam de verbis cum nemine, qui de re recte sentiat, litigandum censemus.
units.tr: Some of the Fathers, and almost all the Scholastics, speak in this way: that the person of Christ consists, is made up, is constituted, is composed, or comes to be from two natures, the divine and the human, or from three substances, Deity, soul and body. But they explain it so as to establish neither a confusion of natures, nor an imperfection of the person before the incarnation, nor a quaternity of persons in the Godhead. For they teach that something one consists of two or three things in several ways. In one way, when one thing is made from two or more wholes that remain whole and perfect, as in those things whose form is composition, order or figure: thus a heap of wheat consists of many grains, and a city of many citizens. In another way, when something one is made from perfect things that do not remain but are changed: as a mixed body is made from the elements, and mead from water and honey. In a third way, when something third, different in kind, is made from two things not mixed but incomplete, as matter and form: as a man is made from a rational soul and a body. In none of these ways is the person of Christ properly said to consist or be composed of two natures. For the hypostatic union is neither a confusion of natures, nor merely an orderly arrangement of them side by side (such as was the view of Nestorius [ἑτερώσεως]), nor a mixture (for some of the ancients call it improperly [μίξις]), nor a composition of matter and form into a third thing that is neither of the two: for the Word [λόγος] is not the form of the flesh, nor is the flesh the matter of the Word; nor, finally, did the Word by the assumption of flesh become a person, or another person, as thesis 8 and 12 also acknowledge. In a fourth way, however, one speaks improperly and loosely of consisting of several things, where several things are placed together at once. And it is in this sense alone that they say the person of Christ consists, or is composed, of two natures, since composition in the broad sense is the placing together of several things. For they say that the hypostatic union is called a composition in this way. Therefore, to avoid error, they generally speak more safely and say that the person of Christ subsists in two natures: an expression which the Orthodox also keep more willingly as more proper; although we think that one should not quarrel over words with anyone who thinks rightly about the matter.

units.la: II. Diuina natura, vt & Dei vocabulum, hic non absolutè accipitur, (sic enim incarnata foret tota Trinitas) sed relatè intelligitur persona secunda, Filius vnigenitus, qui in sinu Patris, & cum Patre vnum est: Johannis 1. & 10. Imago Dei inconspicui. Colost. 1. ἀπαύγασμα gloriæ Patris, & character substantiæ ipsius. Hebr. 1. Deus λόγος. Johan. 1. Deus fortis, Esaiæ 9. Deus super omnia benedictus in secula, Rom. 9.
units.tr: II. The divine nature, like the word God, is not taken here absolutely (for in that case the whole Trinity would have been incarnate), but is understood relatively, as the second person, the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father and one with the Father: John 1 and 10. The image of the invisible God, Colossians 1. [ἀπαύγασμα] of the Father's glory, and the express image [χαρακτήρ] of his substance, Hebrews 1. God the Word [λόγος], John 1. The mighty God, Isaiah 9. God, blessed over all for ever, Romans 9.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Damascenus & veteres dicunt, Diuinam naturam assumsisse carnem in vna sui ipsius ὑπόστασιν, seu in ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου. Rectè igitur dicitur, diuinam naturam in Christo non absolutè, vt natura, sed relatè, vt persona est, intelligi. Ideo Thomas & Scholastici malunt dicere: persona λόγου naturam, quam natura naturam assumsit: vel saltem natura naturam mediatè, persona naturam immediatè assumsit: quoniam, vt loquuntur, vnio terminatur immediatè in persona, mediatè in natura diuina.
units.tr: Damascene and the ancients say that the divine nature assumed flesh into its own single hypostasis, or into the hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] of the Word [τοῦ λόγου]. It is therefore rightly said that the divine nature in Christ is understood not absolutely, as nature, but relatively, as it is the person. For this reason Thomas and the Scholastics prefer to say: the person of the Word assumed the nature which the nature assumed; or at least, the nature assumed the nature mediately, and the person assumed the nature immediately, since, as they put it, the union terminates immediately in the person and mediately in the divine nature.

units.la: III. Porrò humanitas in Christo non est persona ipsa subsistens: sed natura propria quidem personalitate carens, personæ autem verbi, vi vnionis, plenè capax & particeps.
units.tr: III. Furthermore, the humanity in Christ is not itself a subsisting person, but a nature which indeed lacks its own personality, yet, by virtue of the union, is fully capable of and a partaker in the personality of the Word.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Rectè dicitur, humanitatem carere propria personalitate. Est enim personalitas subsistentia seu vis subsistendi per se sine alio & extra aliud suppositum sustentans naturæ rationalis: quam quam vim humanitas nec habuit, nec habet. Sed nouè, impropriè, & insidiosè dicitur, vt vnionis carnem personæ verbi plenè particeps & participem esse. Nouè, quia neque Scriptura, neque Ecclesia sic loquitur, carnem personæ capacem esse. Improprie, quia caro neque continet vel claudit personam verbi, sicut locus locati dicitur capax: neque ipsa fit persona, vel personalitate informatur, sicut subiectum est capax formæ. Insidiose denique, quia Sophista hanc phrasin substernit reali communicationi Idiomatum in naturis: nempe vt dicat, carnem pari modo Deitatis & omnipræsentiæ capacem atque participem esse, quo pertonalitatis dicit capacem atque participem: atque ideo non sua, sed verbi Deitate & immensitate Deum & omnipræsentem esse, sicut non sua, sed verbi personalitate subsistit. Orthodoxi verò fatentur quidem cum Damasceno, hypostasin verbi per vnionem vtrinque naturæ communem esse, vt humanitas eadem nunc, qua & Diuinitas hypostasi in Christo subsistat. Sed negant, carnem ita capacem & participem factam esse personæ, vt sit ipsa persona: sicut etiam negant, ita factam esse participem Deitatis & omnipræsentiæ, vt sit ipsa Deitas, vel Deus: omnipræsentia vel omnipræsens, &c. Nec dant aliter participem dici posse personæ, Deitatis & omnipræsentiæ, quam vnione, quæ facit, non vt humanitas, sed vt homo sit persona, sit Deus, sit omnipræsens: quo sensu etiam Apostolus dicit Filium Dei participem factum carnis & sanguinis puerorum, nempe assumtione seminis Abrahami in suam hypostasin, seu hypostatica vnione, qua factum est, non vt Deitas Filij, sed vt Deus Filius sit caro & sanguis, hoc est, verus homo. Hoc demùm sensu etiam congruè dicetur, carnem, seu humanitatem Christi esse participem personæ, Deitatis & omnipræsentiæ: nempe vnione cum persona diuina, omnipræsente: quæ vnio facit, non vt humanitas Christi, sed vt homo- Christus sit persona, sit Deus, sit omnipræsens.
units.tr: It is rightly said that the humanity lacks its own personality. For personality is subsistence, or the power of subsisting in itself without another and outside another supporting suppositum, of a rational nature; and this power the humanity neither had nor has. But it is said in a novel, improper and insidious way that the flesh is fully capable of and a partaker in the personality of the Word through the union. It is novel, because neither Scripture nor the Church speaks in this way, that the flesh is capable of the person. It is improper, because the flesh neither contains nor encloses the person of the Word, as a place is said to be capable of what is placed in it; nor does it itself become a person, or get informed with personality, as a subject is capable of a form. Finally it is insidious, because the sophist slips this phrase under the real communication of the properties in the natures: namely, to say that the flesh is equally capable of and a partaker in the Deity and the omnipresence, just as it is capable of and a partaker in the personality; and therefore that it is God and omnipresent not by its own Deity and immensity but by that of the Word, just as it subsists not by its own but by the personality of the Word. The Orthodox, however, do confess with Damascene that the hypostasis of the Word is common to both natures through the union, so that the humanity now subsists in the hypostasis of Christ in the same way as the Deity does. But they deny that the flesh has been made so capable of and a partaker in the person that it is itself the person; just as they also deny that it has been made a partaker in the Deity and the omnipresence so that it is itself Deity, or God, or omnipresence, or omnipresent, and so on. Nor do they grant that it can be called a partaker of the person, the Deity and the omnipresence in any other way than by the union, which makes not the humanity but the man, the Christ, to be the person, to be God, to be omnipresent. In this sense the Apostle also says that the Son of God became a partaker of flesh and blood of the children, namely by the assumption of the seed of Abraham into his own hypostasis, or by the hypostatic union, by which it came about that not the Deity of the Son but the Son of God himself is flesh and blood, that is, a true man. Only in this sense will it also rightly be said that the flesh or humanity of Christ is a partaker of the person, the Deity and the omnipresence: namely, by its union with the divine, omnipresent person; which union makes not the humanity of Christ but the God-man Christ to be the person, to be God, to be omnipresent.

units.la: IV. Hæc in Scriptura dicitur Caro: qua voce non sola massa corporea notatur, sed plena integraq; humanitas, vero corpore & anima rationali constans.
units.tr: IV. In Scripture this is called flesh, a word that denotes not merely a bodily mass but the whole and complete humanity, consisting of a true body and a rational soul.

units.la: V. Particeps enim factus est Filius Dei carnis & sanguinis, sicut & nos: nimirum per omnia similis factus fratribus suis, absque peccato.
units.tr: V. For the Son of God became a partaker of flesh and blood, as we are: namely, made like unto his brethren in all things, apart from sin.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANNOTATION.

units.la: Recte dicit, Carnis voce integram humanitatem vero corpore & anima constantem notari: modo addatur: cum veris triusq; proprietatibus, quin & infirmitatibus omnibus, excepto peccato.
units.tr: He rightly says that the word flesh denotes the whole humanity, consisting of a true body and soul, provided it is added: together with the true properties of both, and indeed all infirmities, except sin.

units.la: Caro an & quomodo sit capax persona. Hoc dicere incipit infra Thesi 44. Hebr.2. peccato. Sin autem fratribus similis est factus per omnia: vtique & localitate & circumscriptione similis est factus: idque in vnione & in λόγῳ. Nam extra vnionem, & extra λόγῳ caro nec est, nec substitit vnquam. Falsum proinde, quod Thesi xxxvi. asserit, carnem vi vnionis in illocali λόγῳ omnem localitatem altissimè transcendisse: & illocalem exsistendi modum sortitam esse.
units.tr: Whether the flesh is capable of the person, and how. He begins to say this below, in Thesis 44. Heb. 2, apart from sin. But if he was made like his brethren in all things, then surely he was made like them also in locality and circumscription, and that in the union and in the Word [λόγῳ]. For apart from the union, and apart from the Word [λόγῳ], the flesh neither exists nor has ever subsisted. Therefore it is false what he asserts in Thesis 36, that the flesh, by virtue of the union, has in the non-local Word altogether transcended all locality and has obtained a non-local mode of existence.

units.la: VI. Itaque corporis non phantasma, sed corpus solidum ac verum λόγῳ assumsit, quod carne constat & ossibus, Lucæ 24. carne & sanguine, Johan. 16. quod etiam in gloria verum manet corpus, beatorum glorificatis corporibus substantiæ & qualitatum ratione conforme, Philip. 3.
units.tr: VI. Therefore the Word assumed not a phantasm of a body but a solid and true body, which consists of flesh and bones (Luke 24), flesh and blood (John 16). This true body also remains in glory, conforming in substance and quality to the glorified bodies of the blessed (Phil. 3).

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Hæc sola Thesis sequentia χεηστφύμε fortissimè elidit.
units.tr: This thesis alone strongly refutes the following points.

units.la: I. Si enim λόγῳ assumsit non corporis phantasma, sed corpus solidum, ac verum, vtique & corpus quantum, & dimensum, visibile, ac locale assumsit. Neque enim est verum corpus, sed phantasma, quod non est quantum: neque est solidum, quod dimensiones non habet. Dimensiones vero non habet, quod est inuisibile & illocale: ἀφίαξος χαὶ ἡ ἀπειρόγραπτος φύσις: inquit Theodoretus. Jam quale corpus λόγῳ assumsit, tale etiam corpus assumptum est in λόγῳ. Ergo falsum est: quod corpus Christi in λόγῳ illocali illocalem exsistendi modum sortiatur, hoc est, fiat, & sit illocale.
units.tr: I. For if the Word assumed not a phantasm of a body but a solid and true body, then it assumed a body that is quantified, dimensioned, visible and local. A phantasm, which is not quantified, is not a true body, and what has no dimensions is not solid. Indeed, what has no dimensions is invisible and non-local: "uncircumscribable and indescribable nature [ἀπερίγραπτος καὶ ἀπειρόγραπτος φύσις]," says Theodoret. Now, whatever kind of body the Word assumed, that same kind of body was assumed into the Word. Therefore it is false that the body of Christ, within the Word, acquires an illocal mode of existence, that is, becomes and is illocal.

units.la: II. Si corpus à λόγῳ assumtum constat carne & ossibus, Lucæ 24. carne & sanguine, Heb. 2. vtique corpus illud, quod fingitur in crustulo panis, vel sub panis accidentibus latere, & oraliter manducari, non est solidum ac verum illud corpus à λόγῳ assumtum: quia carnem & ossa non habet.
units.tr: II. If the body assumed by the Word consists of flesh and bones (Luke 24) and of flesh and blood (Heb. 2), then surely that body which is imagined to lie hidden in a crumb of bread, or under the accidents of bread, and is eaten orally, is not that solid and true body assumed by the Word, because it does not have flesh and bones.

units.la: III. Si etiam in gloria manet tale corpus, solidum nimirum ac verum, carne dimensa, & ossibus dimensis constans; vtique etiam in gloria veri corporis definitionem retinet: à qua definitione trina dimensio, & propter hanc circumscriptio & localitas non magis potest separari, quàm rationalitas ab homine.
units.tr: III. If also such a body remains in glory, namely solid and true, consisting of dimensioned flesh and dimensioned bones, then surely it also retains in glory the definition of a true body. From this definition a threefold dimension cannot be separated, and on account of it circumscription and locality cannot be separated any more than rationality can be separated from man.

units.la: IV. Si substantiæ & qualitatum ratione glorificatis beatorum corporibus conforme est: non ergo est illocale, immensum, aut vbiquitarium. Nostra enim corpora nec illocalia erunt, nec vbiquitaria: sed habebunt suum VBI, testante Christo Joh. 17, 24. Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo, vt VBI ego sum, & illi sint mecum.
units.tr: IV. If the bodies of the blessed are made glorious in conformity with the nature and qualities of substance, then they are not illocal, immense, or ubiquitous. For our bodies will be neither illocal nor ubiquitous, but will have their own WHERE, as Christ attests in John 17:24: "Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me."

units.la: k
units.tr: k

units.la: Joh.14,2.3. Vado paraturus vobis locum, & vbi abiero, & parauero vobis locum, rursum veniam, & assumam vos ad me: vt VBI ego sum, & vos sitis.
units.tr: John 14:2–3: I go to prepare a place for you; and when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.

units.la: Nec est, quod cauilletur, in se ratione substantiæ tale esse: in λόγῳ autem ratione vnionis non tale. Nam cum esse suum non in se, sed in assumente λόγῳ habeat, semperque habuerit: vti-que tale est & manet etiam in λόγῳ & in vnione, quale est assum-tum.
