Nec vlla ratio vnionis vera esse potest, quæ rationem sub-stantiæ carnis destruat. Ea autem, quam iste fingit, vnionis ratio substantiæ rationem certa contradictione destrueret, quia faceret locale non-locale, dimensum non-dimensum, quantum non-quantum, corpus non-corpus, proinde & substantiam non-substantiam.
units.tr: Nor is there any quibble that such a body is so in itself by reason of its substance, but not so in the Word by reason of the union. For since it has its being not in itself but in the assuming Word, and has always had it, it surely is and remains in the Word and in the union such as it was when assumed. Nor can any account of the union be true which destroys the account of the substance of the flesh. Indeed, the account of the union that this man invents would destroy the account of substance by a plain contradiction, for it would make the local non-local, the dimensioned non-dimensioned, the quantified non-quantified, the body non-body, and therefore the substance non-substance.

units.la: VII. Sed & animam assumsit, juxta illud, Tristis est anima mea vsq; ad mortem. Matth.26. quam etiam efflauit in cruce, Matth. 27. animam videlicet intelligentem, quæ etiam post mortem esset superstes, & quæ sapientia proficere tempore humiliationis poterat, Luc.2.
units.tr: VII. But he also assumed a soul, according to that saying, My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt. 26), which he also breathed out on the cross (Matt. 27): a rational soul, that is, which would also survive after death, and which could advance in wisdom during the time of his humiliation (Luke 2).

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Hæc Thesis recte opponitur I. Errori Appollinaris, fingentis λόγῳ assumsisse carnem sine anima: sed ipsum fuisse vice animæ. Vide Ambros. de Incarnat. lib.1. cap.7.
units.tr: This thesis is rightly set against I. the error of Apollinaris, who imagined that the Word assumed flesh without a soul, but that the Word itself took the place of the soul. See Ambrose, On the Incarnation, book 1, chapter 7.

units.la: II. Figmento papistico de tali perfectione animæ Christi, qua ab ipsa sui creatione ita fuerit repleta scientiâ & gratiâ, vt nihil potuerit proficere, aut discere, quod antea nesciret. Vide Bellar. de Christo lib. 4.cap.1.2.3.4.
units.tr: II. The Papistical fiction of such a perfection of the soul of Christ, that from the very moment of its creation it was so filled with knowledge and grace that it could make no progress and learn nothing it did not already know. See Bellarmine, On Christ, book 4, chapters 1–4.

units.la: III. Delirio Vbiquitariorum, & huius Doctoris, de Vbiquitate, & omnisciētia humanitatis Christi, inde à conceptionis & vnionis articulo. Si enim Christus vere animam efflauit in cruce: vere vtiq; facta est corporis & animæ localis separatio in morte. Igitur nec corpus, nec anima tunc fuit vbique vllo modo. Aut si tunc corpus vel anima aliquo modo fuit vbiqi, & aliquo modo non facta est vera vtriusq; separatio: nec Christus aliquo modo verè animam efflauit: hoc est, non est reuera mortuus: quod est falsum. Nihilominus tunc, hoc est, in illa separatione animæ à corpore, non est separata humanitas à λόγῳ, sed ἀδιαίρετως mansit naturarum vnio etiam in morte. Non etiam tunc Christus verè fuit homo, licet mortuus secundum corpus, viuens verò secundum animam. Sequitur ergo irrefragabiliter:
units.tr: III. The delirium of the Ubiquitarians, and of this teacher, concerning ubiquity and the omniscience of Christ's humanity from the very article of conception and union. For if Christ truly breathed out his soul on the cross, then surely a true separation of body and soul, local in place, took place in death. Therefore neither the body nor the soul was then anywhere in any way. Or if then the body or the soul was in some way everywhere, and in some way no true separation of both took place, then Christ did not in any way truly breathe out his soul; that is, he did not really die, which is false. Nevertheless, then, that is, in that separation of the soul from the body, the humanity was not separated from the Word, but the union of the natures remained indivisible even in death. Nor was Christ then truly a man, although dead according to the body and living according to the soul. It therefore follows irrefutably:

units.la: I. Vbiquitate corporis vel animæ, vel vtriusque posita negari veram Christi mortem.
units.tr: I. If the ubiquity of the body, or of the soul, or of both, is posited, the true death of Christ is denied.

units.la: II. Vbiquitatem neq; esse vnionis hypostaticæ formam, siue differentiā specificam, quod in Colloquio Maulbrunnensi dixit, & contendit Smidlinus: neq; eius effectū aut consequens: quod postea Smidlini sententiam corrigens, commentus est Chemnitius. Fuit enim vnio salua non tantum in morte, sed in toto statu humilitatis, absq; vbiquitatis aliorumue Idiomatū diuinorum realī transfusione in carnem, sine qua Vbiquitarij vociferantur, Christum non magis relinqui Deum, quàm Petrum.
units.tr: II. Ubiquity is not the form of the hypostatic union, or its specific difference, as Smidlin said at the Colloquy of Maulbronn and contended; nor is it its effect or consequence, as Chemnitz later invented while correcting Smidlin's opinion. For the union was preserved not only in death but throughout the whole state of humiliation, without any real transfusion of the divine attributes into the flesh, without which the Ubiquitarians cry out that Christ would be no more forsaken by God than Peter would be.

units.la: E quibus omnibus liquet, vbiquitatem hac Thesi rursum sibi manus inferre. Illocalé enim existendi modū, quomodo habuit corpus mortuum in cruce pendens, & in sepulchro jacens, nec tamen à λόγῳ separatum? Sed & anima, quam λόγῳ assumsit, si sapientiā proficere tempore humiliationis poterat, Luc.2. vtiq; inde ab vtero omnisciā non fuit, etiam in λόγῳ subsistens.
units.tr: From all of this it is clear that ubiquity, by this thesis, again lays hands on itself. For what illocal mode of existence did the dead body have, hanging on the cross and lying in the sepulchre, and yet not separated from the Word? But also the soul, which the Word assumed, if it could advance in wisdom during the time of humiliation (Luke 2), was surely not omniscient from the womb, even while subsisting in the Word.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Hæc natura Christi humana non quidem ad integritatem personæ ἐξ λόγος, qua simpliciter λόγῳ est; requiritur. Est enim ὁ λόγῳ persona αὐτόπλης & seipsa vndiquaque completa, inde ab æterna sua ex Patre generatione.
units.tr: This human nature of Christ is not indeed required for the integrity of the person of the Word, who is simply the Word from the Word [ἐκ λόγου], which is the Word simply. For the Word is a self-sufficient person [αὐτοτελής], wholly complete in himself, from his eternal generation from the Father.

units.la: IX. Pertinet verò ad integritatem λόγυ incarnati seu Christi, quatenus Christus est: cuius persona post incarnationem σωῳτικος est: vt scriptores Ecclesiastici testantur.
units.tr: IX. But it does pertain to the integrity of the incarnate Word, or of Christ, insofar as he is Christ, whose person after the incarnation is composite [σύνθετος], as the ecclesiastical writers testify.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: In Thesi 9. latent quædam insidiæ. Dicit carnem pertinere ad integritatem λόγος incarnati, vt postea concludat, etiam carnem vbique esse, cum integer λόγῳ incarnatus sit vbique. Astutè vero dicit, pertinere ad integritatem λόγος incarnati: non autem ad integritatem persona λόγυ incarnati, ne aliam personam λόγῳ incarnatum, hoc est, quaternitatē statuere videatur. Eodē spectat, quod personam λόγος incarnati seu Christi σωῳτικος esse dicit. Orthodoxi verò licet has locutiones non simpliciter repudient (nam etiam ipsi absq; metu cavillationis aliquando sic loquuntur) tamen rectè intelligendas esse monent, eo videlicet sensu, quo à scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, ad quorū testimonium advarsarius provocat, vsurpatę legūtur: ne hypostasis verbi nondū incarnati vel imperfecta, vel alia ab hypostasi verbi incarnati esse statuatur, vnde necessariò quaternitas sequeretur. Tenēdū ergo, quod rectè fatetur aduersarius th.8. λόγος esse personā ἀυτόπλης, i.e. seipsa perfecta, completam & integram. Tenendū est quoq;, quod idem fatetur Thesi 12. non alium Filium à Patre ab æterno genitum, alium à Maria in tempore conceptum & natum esse, sed eundem. His enim positis, manifestum est, λόγον, & λόγῳ incarnatum, non duas diversas personas, sed vnam eandemque numero hypostasin esse, neque differre πρὸ εἶναι, sed tantum πρὸ λόγῳ: sicut exempli causa Petrus nudus, & Petrus veste indutus, vna eademque persona est: à seipsa autem non subiecto, sed sola ratione differens.
units.tr: In Thesis 9 there lie hidden some snares. He says that the flesh pertains to the integrity of the incarnate Word, in order afterwards to conclude that the flesh is also everywhere, since the whole incarnate Word is everywhere. But he cleverly says that it pertains to the integrity of the incarnate Word, and not to the integrity of the person of the incarnate Word, lest he seem to posit another person of the incarnate Word, that is, a quaternity. To the same end belongs his saying that the person of the incarnate Word, or of Christ, is composite. Orthodox writers, however, while they do not simply reject these expressions (for they too sometimes speak thus without fear of cavilling), nevertheless warn that they are to be rightly understood, namely in that sense in which they are found used by the ecclesiastical writers, to whose testimony the adversary appeals: lest the hypostasis of the Word not yet incarnate be held to be imperfect, or other than the hypostasis of the incarnate Word, from which a quaternity would necessarily follow. It must therefore be held what the adversary rightly confesses in Thesis 8, that the Word is a person autotelic, that is, perfect, complete and entire in itself. It must also be held what the same man confesses in Thesis 12, that the Son begotten of the Father from eternity is not one Son and the one conceived and born of Mary in time another, but the same. For these points being granted, it is plain that the Word and the Word incarnate are not two diverse persons, but one and the same hypostasis in number, and differ not in what they are but only in their mode of being: just as, for example, Peter naked and Peter clothed are one and the same person, differing from himself not in subject but only in aspect.

units.la: Hinc porrò sequitur manifeste, nihil ad integritatem λόγῳ incarnati pertinere proprie dici posse, quin idem ad integritatem personæ λόγῳ pertinere dicatur. At hoc dicere, esset perfectionem λόγῳ negare & compositionem in Deitate ponere.
units.tr: From this it follows plainly that nothing can properly be said to pertain to the integrity of the incarnate Word without the same being said to pertain to the integrity of the person of the Word. But to say this would be to deny the perfection of the Word and to posit composition in the Deity.

units.la: Carnem igitur ad integritatem personæ λόγῳ incarnati pertinere eo accipiendum est modo, quo etiam persona σωμάτων à scriptoribus appellatur, nempe, non proprie, sed improprie. Supra enim ad thesin 1. ostensum est, personam λόγῳ incarnati σύνθετον esse, hoc est, constare, constitui, confici, componi, fieri ex duabus naturis, non sicut aceruus ex multis granis, mixtum ex elementis, animal ex corpore & anima componitur, qui modi compositionis sunt proprij, neque in Christi personam competere possunt, quin multa sequantur absurda, vt Thomas professe ostendit: sed laxa compositionis significatione, qua promiscue positione plurium quovis modo in vno sumitur. Sic enim vnio hypostatica vocari potest compositio, nempe, quod per eam ὑπόστασιν Filij Dei, vna prius subsistens natura, nunc subsistat duabus, in se interim perfecta manens, & simplex: non autem, quod persona λόγῳ incarnati conflata sit ex duabus naturis, vel ex persona & natura, quarum neutra sit illa persona, sicut homo ex anima rationali & corpore conflatur, quorum neutrum est homo.
units.tr: The flesh, therefore, pertaining to the integrity of the person of the incarnate Word, must be understood in the same way in which the person of Christ is also called composite by the writers: not properly but improperly. For above, at Thesis 1, it was shown that the person of the incarnate Word is composite, that is, consists, is constituted, made up, compounded, and comes to be from two natures; not as a heap is made up of many grains, a mixture of elements, or an animal is compounded of body and soul, which are proper modes of composition and cannot apply to the person of Christ without many absurdities following, as Thomas has shown; but in the loose sense of composition, in which it is taken indiscriminately for the placing of several things together in some way in one. For in this sense the hypostatic union may be called a composition, namely because through it the hypostasis of the Son of God, which before subsisted in one nature alone, now subsists in two, remaining meanwhile perfect and simple in itself; not because the person of the incarnate Word is compounded of two natures, or of a person and a nature, neither of which is that person, as a man is compounded of a rational soul and a body, neither of which is the man.

units.la: Pari ratione caro ad integritatem ὑπαρξεως verbi increati pertinere dici potest, non vt pars integrans aut complens personam non integram: sed vt natura assumta in ὑπαρξει verbi, in qua integrum & totum corporaliter inhabitet, tanquam in suo templo, seq; quasi vestitum habiru aut velo spectandum & palpabile exiltens, dum exhibeat, ipsum in se inaspectabile & impalpabile existens. Sic enim de inhabitatione ista λόγῳ in carne assumta ipsam scripturam loqui videmus Ioh. 2, 21. Phil. 2, 8. Heb. 10, 20. Et orthodoxos patres: ex quibus Augustinus: Verbum, inquit, factum est caro, id est homo, non tamen in hoc, quod factum est, conuersum vel mutatum, sed carne, vt carnalibus carnaliter appareret, indutum. Nec aliter loquitur aduersarius ipse, cum dixit Thesi 18. totum λόγῳ carne vestitum & indutum.
units.tr: By the same reasoning the flesh may be said to pertain to the integrity of the existence of the uncreated Word, not as a part integrating or completing a person who was not whole, but as a nature assumed into the existence of the Word, in which the whole Word dwells bodily as in its own temple, and, while it exhibits itself as clothed in flesh as in a garment or veil, visible and palpable, it itself remains invisible and impalpable. For so we see Scripture itself speak of this indwelling of the Word in the assumed flesh: John 2:21; Phil. 2:8; Heb. 10:20. And the orthodox Fathers likewise: among them Augustine: The Word, he says, was made flesh, that is, man, not however by being changed or converted into what it became, but clothed in flesh, so that it might appear carnally to the carnal. Nor does the adversary himself speak otherwise when he says in Thesis 18 that the whole Word is clothed and wrapped in flesh.

units.la: Absit tamen cogitatio, quasi caro accidentaliter tantum per <bl>Λόγῳ</bl> modum externi habitus <bl>Λόγῳ</bl> superuenerit & coniuncta fit, sicut homini vestitus accidentaliter & mutabiliter forinsecus adhæret, quæ, teste Lombardo, quorundam fuisse videtur opinio. Nam in intimam & penitissimam <bl>ἕνωσιν</bl> sic assumta est caro, vt vnio eius cum <bl>Λόγῳ</bl> sit verè hypostatica, hoc est, eandem ipsa habeat cum <bl>Λόγῳ</bl> subsistentiam.
units.tr: Yet let no thought arise as if the flesh had come to the Word merely accidentally, by way of an external garment, and were joined to it, as clothing adheres to a man accidentally and changeably from without; which, as Lombard testifies, seems to have been the opinion of some. For the flesh is assumed into so intimate and innermost union that its union with the Word is truly hypostatic, that is, it has the same subsistence with the Word.

units.la: His obseruatis ab insidiis nihil erit periculi. Nam facilè erit ex distinctione, dextraq; explicatione φαντασμάτων destruere, quicquid inde pro omnipræsentia carnis aduersarius postea construet. Integra enim & tota persona Λόγου incarnati est Deus, est immensa, est omnipræsens: quin & æterna, ex Patre genita, illocalis, &c. licet caro in eam personâ assumta non sit vel fiat Deus, immensa, omnipræsens: ac multo minus æterna, ex Patre genita, illocalis, &c. Neque enim, inquit Augustinus, est consequens, vt quod in Deo est, ita sit vbique, vt Deus.
units.tr: With these points observed there will be no danger from the snares. For from the distinction and right explanation of the phantasms it will easily be possible to overthrow whatever the adversary afterwards builds from this for the omnipresence of the flesh. For the whole and entire person of the incarnate Word is God, is immense, is omnipresent; indeed eternal, begotten of the Father, not located in place, and so on; although the flesh assumed into that person is not made, or becomes, God, immense, omnipresent, and much less eternal, begotten of the Father, not located in place, and so on. For, says Augustine, it does not follow that what is in God is everywhere in the same way as God is.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Constat ergo jam persona Saluatoris non natura duntaxat vna, sed duabus, vt immutabiliter & inconfusè, sic indiuise & insegregabiliter copulatis, & in hypostasin vnam (juxta Chalcedonensem canonem) concurrentibus.
units.tr: It is established, then, that the person of the Saviour is not one nature only but two, joined together immutably and unconfusedly, and likewise indivisibly and inseparably, and coming together into one hypostasis (according to the canon of Chalcedon).

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Persona Saluatoris constat duabus naturis, non compositione vnius tertij ex partibus integralibus, vel etiam essentialibus, vt ex materia & forma, quod tacitè fingit hic Doctor, sed eo, quo ad primam & nonam thesin, declaratum est modo. Secus enim quaternitas daretur. Verba Canonis Chalcedonensis sic sonant: Filium Dei in duabus naturis ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως, manifestatum esse, haud quaquam differentia naturarum propter vnionem sublata, sed potius vtriusque naturæ proprietate seruata, in vnam personam, & in vnam hypostasin concurrentis. Huic Canoni certè repugnat aduersarij figmentum, quod Theodoretus, fi.36. sequitur, humanitatem, respectu vnionis, in illocali Λόγῳ omnem localitatem altissimè transcendisse, & illocalem existendi modum sortitam esse. Sic enim vtriusque naturæ proprietates minimè seruatæ, sed confusæ essent. Perdidisset enim caro in illocali Λόγῳ suam localitatem, proinde & circumscriptionem, dimensiones, quantitatem, substantiam. Neque vero vllo respectu simul localis & illocalis fingi potest. Impossibile est enim vnam & eandemnaturam simul contrariarum proprietatum vel affectionum susceptricem esse, vt cum Theodoreto Damasceno passim docet.
units.tr: The person of the Saviour consists of two natures, not by the composition of one third thing from integral or even essential parts, such as matter and form, which this teacher tacitly imagines, but in the way already declared under the first and ninth theses. Otherwise there would be a quaternity. The words of the Council of Chalcedon run thus: The Son of God is made manifest in two natures, unconfusedly [ἀσυγχύτως], unchangeably [ἀτρέπτως], indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως], inseparably [ἀχωρίστως], the difference of the natures by no means being taken away because of the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring into one person and one hypostasis. The opponent's fiction certainly contradicts this canon, that Theodoret, fi.36., follows, namely that the humanity, with respect to the union, so far transcended all locality in the non-local Word [Λόγῳ] that it obtained a non-local mode of existence. For in that case the properties of each nature would not be preserved but confused. For the flesh would have lost its locality in the non-local Word, and therefore also its circumscription, dimensions, quantity and substance. Nor indeed can anything be imagined that is at once local and non-local in any respect. For it is impossible that one and the same nature should be capable of receiving contrary properties or affections at the same time, as Theodoret and John of Damascus teach throughout.

units.la: XI. Hinc vnus tantum est Dominus Jesus Christus, toto genere diuersis, vnus tantummodo Filius: in aeterna sua generatione ἀμήτωρ: in temporali nativitate ἀπάτωρ
units.tr: XI. Hence there is only one Lord Jesus Christ, altogether different in kind, only one Son: in his eternal generation without mother [ἀμήτωρ], in his temporal birth without father [ἀπάτωρ].

units.la: XII. Neq; alium Filium Pater ab aeterno genuit, alium Maria mater in tempore concepit & peperit: sed vnum illum Dei & hominis Filium.
units.tr: XII. Nor did the Father beget one Son from eternity and Mary the mother conceive and bear another in time; but that one Son of God and man.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Sicut non alium filium genuit Pater ab aeterno, alium peperit mater in tempore, sed eundem: sic non alia, sed eadem essentia & numero persona est λόγου ante incarnationem, & post eam: quoniam secunda persona Trinitatis nec mutata est per incarnationem, nec multiplicata, nec perfectior facta. Recte igitur moniti sunt juniores, dextre capiendam esse phrasin aduersarij, carnem pertinere ad integritatem λόγῳ incarnati; & personam λόγῳ incarnati σωζόμενον, seu compositam esse. Nam valde ἀνυλόγῳ incarnati ... quis dixerit, personam λόγου esse partem personæ λόγου incarnati: quia persona non est facta pars personæ, nec suæ, nec alterius. Si enim suæ, totum esset pars suiipsius: si alterius, non esset idem Filius ex Patre genitus, & ex matre natus: ac necessariò sequeretur personarum multiplicatio & quaternitas. Recte igitur etiam Augustinus: Christus, inquit, una persona est geminæ substantiæ, quia Deus & homo est. Nec tamen Deus vel homo pars huius personæ dici potest: alioqui Filius Dei Deus antequam suscipere formam serui, non erat totus, & creuit, cum homo diuinitati eius accessit.
units.tr: Just as the Father did not beget one son from eternity and the mother bear another in time, but the same Son, so the person of the Word is not another but the same, in essence and in number, before the incarnation and after it; for the second person of the Trinity was neither changed by the incarnation, nor multiplied, nor made more perfect. Therefore the younger men were rightly warned that the opponent's phrase must be understood properly, that the flesh belongs to the integrity of the incarnate Word, and that the person of the incarnate Word is preserved or composed. For who would say, ... that the person of the Word is a part of the person of the incarnate Word, since a person is not made a part of a person, neither of its own nor of another's? For if of its own, the whole would be a part of itself; if of another's, it would not be the same Son begotten of the Father and born of the mother, and a multiplication of persons and a quaternity would necessarily follow. Augustine rightly says: Christ, he says, is one person of two substances, because he is God and man. Yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person; otherwise the Son of God, being God, before he took on the form of a servant, was not whole, and grew when the man was added to his divinity.

units.la: XIII. Quemadmodum Gabriel ait: Quod ex te nascetur sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei. Unde Mariam Elisabetha Spiritu sancto plena, Matrem Domini appellat.
units.tr: XIII. As Gabriel says: That which shall be born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God. Hence Elizabeth, full of the Holy Spirit, calls Mary the Mother of the Lord.

units.la: XIV. Ob hanc personæ seu ὑποστάσεως identitatem Verbum prædicatur factum caro. Joh. 1. Germen Dauidis, Iehoua. Jerem. 23. Filius hominis, Filius Dei viui. Matth. 16. secundus homo, ipse Dominus de cœlo. 1 Corinth. cap. 15. & postremus Adam in Spiritum viuificantem factus memoratur. Ibidem.
units.tr: XIV. Because of this identity of person or hypostasis, the Word is said to have been made flesh. John 1. The Branch of David, Jehovah, Jer. 23. The Son of man, the Son of the living God, Matt. 16. The second man, the Lord himself from heaven, 1 Cor. 15, and the last Adam is recorded as made a life-giving Spirit. Ibid.

units.la: XV. Vnus autem est Christus, non conuersione deitatis in carnem, sed assumtione humanitatis in Deum.
units.tr: XV. Now Christ is one, not by the conversion of the deity into flesh, but by the assumption of the humanity into God.

units.la: XVI. Quamobrem ne phrasis Euangelistæ (Verbum caro factum est) de aliqua Verbi in carnem mutatione sonare videatur, Spiritus sanctus æquipollentibus eam explanat, asserens, Deum manifestatum esse in carne: Jesum Christum in carne venisse: Filium Dei carnis & sanguinis participem factum, & assumsisse semen Abrahæ: & in Christo habitare omnem plenitudinem Deitatis σωματικῶς. 1 Tim. 3. 1 Joh. 4. Hebr. 2. Coloss. 2.
units.tr: XVI. Therefore, lest the phrase of the Evangelist (The Word was made flesh) seem to suggest some change of the Word into flesh, the Holy Spirit explains it by equivalent expressions, asserting that God was manifested in the flesh, that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, that the Son of God was made a partaker of flesh and blood and took on the seed of Abraham, and that all the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ bodily [σωματικῶς]. 1 Tim. 3; 1 John 4; Heb. 2; Col. 2.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Hæc recte omnia: modo phrasi Athanasij Thesi 15. assumtio humanitatis in Deum non torqueatur contra Athanasij mentem, quasi vel humanitatis mutationem in Deum, vel exæquationem cum Deo, vel transfusionem idiomatum Deitatis in eam, qua ipsa sit facta Deus, significet. Nam quicquid creatum est, ait idem Athanasius, Deus esse non potest. Assumtio igitur humanitatis in Deum intelligatur de eius unione hypostatica cum Deo, seu λόγῳ, salvis utriusque proprietatibus; juxta declarationem Synodi Chalcedonensis, &c. & Augustini in libro de fide ad Petrum: Formam ergo servi, hoc est, naturam servi, in suam Deus ille accepit personam, &c.
units.tr: All these things are right; provided only that the phrase of Athanasius in thesis 15, the assumption of the humanity into God, is not twisted against Athanasius' meaning, as if it signified either a change of the humanity into God, or an equalising with God, or a transfusion of the properties of the Deity into it, by which it would itself have become God. For whatever is created, says the same Athanasius, cannot be God. Therefore the assumption of the humanity into God is to be understood of its hypostatic union with God, or the Word, the properties of each being preserved; according to the declaration of the Council of Chalcedon, etc., and of Augustine in his book on faith to Peter: That God therefore took the form of a servant, that is, the nature of a servant, into his own person, etc.

units.la: XVII. Cæterum non ita ὁ λόγος est caro factus, ut aliqua eius particula sit assumtæ carni consociata. Λόγος enim, spiritualis naturæ cum sit, in partes non secatur aut dividitur.
units.tr: XVII. Moreover, the Word did not become flesh in such a way that some particle of it was joined to the flesh assumed. For the Word, since it is of a spiritual nature, is not cut or divided into parts.

units.la: XVIII. Sed totus λόγος tota plenitudine suæ Deitatis unitus est carni, totus (ut patres orthodoxi tradunt) carne vestitus, indutus, ὁλικῶς incarnatus, inhumanatus, & incorporatus est.
units.tr: XVIII. But the whole Word, with the whole fullness of its Deity, is united to the flesh; wholly (as the orthodox Fathers teach) clothed with flesh, put on, wholly incarnated, made man, and embodied.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Etiam hæc recte. Neque enim fieri, vel fingi potest carnis cum λόγῳ ἀδιαιρέτῳ partialis unio. Totus ergo λόγος totam carnem assumsit; & cum tota carne totus λόγος unitus est personaliter.
units.tr: This too is correct. For a partial union of flesh with the Word [λόγος] cannot be made or imagined, since the Word is indivisible. Therefore the whole Word took on the whole flesh, and the whole Word is personally united with the whole flesh.

units.la: Quo sensu λόγος dicatur carne vestitus, indutus, &c. ad Thesin nonam est explicatum: nempe non per modum externi habitus secundum accidens, sed per modum intimæ unionis secundum substantiam. Hinc vero patet, λόγον non mutatum in carnem, susceptione hominis: sicut nec membra veste induta mutanmutantur, vt Augustinus loquitur: nec proprie satis dici, carnem pertinere ad integritatem personæ λόγου incarnati: hoc est, esse eius partem integralem, sicut tres pedes pertinent ad integritatem tripodis: sed potius, carnem pertinere ad personam λόγου incarnati, vt naturam à λόγῳ in vnitatem personæ assumptam, in qua se manifestaret mundo: vt Augustinus ait: Verbum est factum caro, hoc est, carne indutum, vt carnalibus carnaliter appareret.
units.tr: The sense in which the Word is said to be clothed or put on with flesh, and so on, was explained at the ninth thesis: namely, not by way of an external garment, which is accidental, but by way of an inward union, which is substantial. From this it is clear that the Word was not changed into flesh by the assumption of a man, just as the limbs are not changed when a garment is put on them, as Augustine puts it. Nor is it quite right to say that the flesh belongs to the integrity of the incarnate Word's person, that is, that it is an integral part of it, as three feet belong to the integrity of a tripod. Rather, the flesh belongs to the person of the incarnate Word as a nature taken by the Word into the unity of the person, in which he might show himself to the world. As Augustine says: The Word was made flesh, that is, clothed with flesh, so that he might appear in a fleshly way to fleshly people.

units.la: Sed nec ὁλικῶς incarnationem λόγῳ ἀμερίστως factam esse quisquam negat vel ambigit: si id intelligatur citra immensi λόγου intra carnis dimensiones inclusionem: citra item carnis finitæ cum infinito λόγῳ vbiquitariam diffusionem.
units.tr: But no one denies or doubts that the incarnation was wholly, and yet without division, accomplished by the Word, if this is understood without the enclosing of the immense Word within the dimensions of the flesh, and likewise without the ubiquitarian diffusion of the finite flesh with the infinite Word.

units.la: XIX. Quæ vnio cum sit totalis, ineptè confertur cum exemplis partialium vnionum, puta, Solis aliquam sui orbis partem contingentis: gemmæ annuli sui parti inclusæ: Antverpiæ ad Oceani partem sitæ.
units.tr: XIX. Since this union is total, it is absurdly compared with examples of partial unions: for instance, the sun touching one part of its orbit; a gem enclosed in one part of its ring; Antwerp situated on a part of the ocean.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Fatendum est, arcanam hanc & mirandam naturæ immensæ cum dimensa vnionem, nulla similitudine satis exprimi posse. Ac licet varias tam veteres quàm recentes Theologi adhibeant, de omnibus tamen verum est, quod Damascenus monet, omnia similia in multis esse dissimilia: & impossibile esse de Deitate & incarnatione exempla, quæ per omnia sint similia, invenire. Similia solis, & annuli, atque etiam Oceani, itemque animæ & corporis vsi sunt Iustinus, Cyrillus, Athanasius: Ferri igniti Basilius: ligni & cauterij igniti Athanasius: carbonis igniti Cyrillus: gladij igniti Damascenus: corporis solaris & luminis Iustinus & Athanasius. At nullum istorum rei per omnia est simile. Exemplis partialium vnionum nostros iste Theologos pungit. At parum candidè. Iis enim alicubi sunt vsi minime ad rem ipsam declarandam, à qua fatemur exempla rerum finitarum longissime abesse: sed ad sophisticam vbiquitariorum traducendam. Verbi causa, cum Iacobus Andreæ Maulbrunnæ Vbiquitatem ineptè sic demonstraret; Dextra Dei est vbique. Humanitas Christi sedet ad dextram Dei. Ergo humanitas est vbique. Nostri vitiosum argumentum esse, & quatuor laborare terminis simili plane, si formam spectes, syllogismo ostendebant: Oceanus ambit vniuersum orbem. Antverpia sita est ad Oceanum. Ergo Antverpia ambit totum orbem. Hoc modo non rem cum re, sed vitium cum vitio conferebant. Vterque enim syllogismus eodem vitio laborat. Non ergo inepte facta est haec ostensio. Nec certe melius demonstrat D. Hunnius carnis illocalitatem in λόγῳ, infra Thesi 36. Haec enim summa: λόγος est illocalis. Caro assumta est in λόγῳ. Ergo caro est illocalis. Quid ni ergo, hunc quoq; disputatorem ad quatuor Oceani & Antuerpiae terminos remittimus? Nam ut diversi sunt termini, Oceanum esse: & ad Oceanum situm esse: sic diversi sunt, λόγος esse, & in λόγῳ esse: ut & in Vulcania demonstratione diversi erant, dextram Dei esse, & ad dextram Dei sedere.
units.tr: We must confess that this secret and wonderful union of the immense nature with the measured one cannot be expressed adequately by any likeness. And although theologians, both ancient and recent, use various comparisons, it is nonetheless true of all of them what Damascene warns: all similes are dissimilar in many respects; and that it is impossible to find examples about the Deity and the incarnation that are similar in every respect. Justin, Cyril and Athanasius used likenesses of the sun, the ring, and also the ocean, and likewise of the soul and body. Basil used a piece of iron heated in the fire; Athanasius a log of wood and a cautery heated in the fire; Cyril a coal in the fire; Damascene a sword in the fire; Justin and Athanasius a solar body and light. But none of these is in every respect like the thing. Our opponents here stab at us with examples of partial unions, and that not very fairly. For these examples are used in places not to explain the matter itself, from which we admit that examples taken from finite things are very far removed, but to lead the ubiquitarians into a sophism. For instance, when James Andreae at Maulbronn absurdly tried to prove ubiquity in this way: The right hand of God is everywhere. The humanity of Christ sits at the right hand of God. Therefore the humanity is everywhere. Our side showed that this is a faulty argument, and that, if you look at its form, it suffers from four terms, in the same way as this syllogism: The ocean surrounds the whole world. Antwerp is situated on the ocean. Therefore Antwerp surrounds the whole world. In this way they were not comparing thing with thing, but fault with fault. For both syllogisms suffer from the same fault. So this demonstration was not absurdly made. Nor does Dr Hunnius prove the non-locality of the flesh in the Word any better, below at thesis 36. For his argument runs: the Word is non-local; the flesh was assumed in the Word; therefore the flesh is non-local. Why not, then, send this disputant back as well to the four terms of the ocean and Antwerp? For just as "to be the ocean" and "to be situated on the ocean" are different terms, so "to be the Word" and "to be in the Word" are different, just as in the ubiquitarian demonstration "to be the right hand of God" and "to sit at the right hand of God" were different.

units.la: XX. Conuenientior ad declarationem mysterij huius est similitudo vnionis animæ & corporis, qua vsus in symbolo suo est Athanasius, & hunc secutus Cyrillus in epistola synodica, dicens: Verbum in assumta natura talem sibi inhabitationem fecit, qualem & anima hominis habere creditur ad proprium corpus.
units.tr: XX. A likeness more suitable for explaining this mystery is the union of soul and body, which Athanasius uses in his creed, and Cyril, following him, in his synodical letter, saying: The Word made for himself, in the assumed nature, such an indwelling as the human soul is believed to have in its own body.

units.la: Smidlinus in colloquio Maulbrun. pag. 43. non recipit.
units.tr: Smidlinus, in the Maulbronn colloquy, p. 43, does not accept it.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: De hoc simili sic Iustinus: Nonnulli, inquit, vnionem eam velut anima cum corpore, mente complexi ita prodiderunt: & congruens est exemplum: tametsi non ex omni parte, aliquatenus tamen. Item. Hominis exemplum aliquatenus recipiendum est, quadamtenus autem fugiendum. Et ita sane. In hoc enim conuenit, quod sicut anima rationalis & corpus vniuntur in vnam personam, & vna hypostasi subsistunt duæ naturæ essentiis & proprietatibus distinctæ, & concurrentes in operationibus homini propriis, vnaquaque agente cum alterius communione, quod suum est proprium: sic, inquit Hieronymus, constat, vnum eundemque Christum Deum & hominem esse, & secundum vtramque formam operatum, humanitatis scilicet ac diuinitatis: & per hoc duas exercuisse operationes. Operata est enim vtraque forma vel natura cum alterius communione, quod proprium habuit: verbo siquidem operante quod verbi est: & carne exsequente, quod carnis erat, &c. Sed in multis simile non conuenit. Nam in homine fit duarum naturarum finitarum vnio. In Christo finitæ cum infinita. In homine vtraq; natura clauditur iisdem terminis. In Christo diuinitas angustiis carnis non terminatur. In homine vnio est compositio materiæ & formæ. In Christo caro non est materia Deitatis, nec Deitas forma est carnis. In homine resultat ex compositione tertium, quod neutrum duorum est. In Christo λόγῳ persona eadem est ante vnionem nuda & simplex, post vnio-
units.tr: Justin speaks of this likeness as follows: Some, he says, have expressed that union in this way, as the soul with the body, and the example is apt, though not in every part, but still to some extent. Again: The example of man must be accepted to some extent, but to some extent it must be avoided. And rightly so. For it agrees in this respect: just as the rational soul and the body are united into one person, and subsist in one hypostasis as two natures distinct in their essences and properties, and concur in the operations proper to a man, each acting in communion with the other in what is proper to it; so, says Jerome, it is established that one and the same Christ is God and man, and has acted according to each form, namely of humanity and of divinity, and by this has carried out two operations. For each form or nature acted in communion with the other in what was proper to it: the Word indeed doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belonged to the flesh, and so on. But in many respects the likeness does not hold. For in a man the union is of two finite natures. In Christ it is of the finite with the infinite. In a man both natures are enclosed within the same limits. In Christ the divinity is not bounded by the narrowness of the flesh. In a man the union is a composition of matter and form. In Christ the flesh is not the matter of the Deity, nor is the Deity the form of the flesh. In a man a third thing results from the composition, which is neither of the two. In Christ the person of the Word is the same before the union, bare and simple, and after the union

units.la: In exp. symboli, p. 301.
units.tr: In the exposition of the creed, p. 301.

units.la: Quatenus simile anima & corporis conueniat.
units.tr: How far the likeness of soul and body agrees.

units.la: Ad Paulam & Eustoch.
units.tr: To Paula and Eustochium.

units.la: Quatenus simile anima & corporis non conueniat.
units.tr: How far the likeness of soul and body does not agree.

units.la: vnionem carne vestita & quademtenus composita. In homine vnio solubilis est per mortem : Christus naturam assumtam in æternū non deponet. Deniq; huc facit, quod Thomas annotat: In homine duplex vnitas constituitur, natura, & persona. Natura, quatenus anima vnitur corpori formaliter perficiens ipsum, vt ex duobus fiat vna natura, sicut ex actu & potentia, ex materia & forma: & quantum ad hoc, non attenditur similitudo, quia natura diuina non potest esse corporis forma. Persona, quatenus ex iis constituitur vnus aliquis subsistens anima & corpore: & sic attenditur similitudo. Vnus enim Christus subsistit in natura diuina & humana.
units.tr: union clothed with flesh and in a certain way composite. In a man the union is dissoluble by death; Christ will never lay aside the assumed nature. Finally, what Thomas notes is also relevant here: In a man a twofold unity is constituted, of nature and of person. Of nature, insofar as the soul is united to the body, formally perfecting it, so that from the two there comes about one nature, as from act and potency, from matter and form; and as far as this goes, the likeness is not to the point, because the divine nature cannot be the form of a body. Of person, insofar as from these there is constituted one subsisting being of soul and body; and in this respect the likeness holds. For one Christ subsists in the divine and the human nature.

units.la: XXI. Proinde sicut anima substantia sua non est extra corpus, tota quippe suo corpori vnita, sic totus incarnatus λόγος extra suam carnem nec est, nec quæri aut inueniri potest. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XXI. Therefore, just as the soul by its substance is not outside the body, since it is wholly united to its body, so the whole incarnate Word [λόγος] is neither outside his flesh, nor can he be sought or found outside it. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Per manifestam fallaciam à dicto secundū quid, vt simpliciter, ex simili falsum concludit. Sic enim colligit Hunnius: Simile homines est conuenientius aliis. Ergo per omnia conuenit, & par est anima ac deitatis ratio, vt sicut illa corporis definitur terminis, sic ista extra carnē nusquam subsistat. Quis hic imposturam non palpet? Comparationē facit quasi parium, animæ & λόγᵴ: quæ sunt maximē imparia. Anima enim spiritus finitus cum sit, extra corpus, in quo est, esse nequit, quandiu ei est colligata: licet sit tota in toto, & in quauis parte tota. At deitas λόγου spiritus est minimè finitus, sed immensus & purißimus per simplicißimā suam immensitatem, & tota in carne finita, & tota eademq; simul extra carnē finitam, & extra omnia subsistens. Quis enim dixerit, deitatē λόγου ibi tantum fuisse, puta in vtero matris, in templo, in prætorio, in cruce, in sepulcro &c. vbi caro eius circumscripta fuisse commemoratur, abfuisse alibi, vbi caro non fuit? Quis negauerit, cœlum & terram implεsse: Romæ, Athenis, & vbiq; extra Judeam simul fuisse, cum corpus vnitissimum ei permanens intra solius Judeæ limites versaretur? Certe qui contrarium affirmat, vel deitatem corporis angustiis conclusam & circumscriptam, vel corpus cum deitate vbique diffusum fingit, hoc est, vt breuissime dicam, vel deitatem finitam, vel corpus infinitum facit. Hæc ergo est vna ex falsis illis hypothesibus, quas hic sophista vbiquitati carnis substernit. Sophisticè verò etiam conjungit, λόγῳ nec esse, nec quæri aut inueniri posse extra carnem suam: quæ neq; sententiam, neq; veritatē eandem habent. Nam quærendum non esse λόγῳ λόγον extra carnem suam, orthodoxi fatentur: quia in sola carne tanquam in templo suo vult fide ac precibus quæri & adorari: & hinc adeo cōtra Vbiquitarios conficiunt, carne λόγου in crusta Eucharistica haud latere, quia ab ipsismet ad eam non adoratur, nec adorari debet. Verū ideo alibi essentiali immensitate suâ, quam cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto habet communem, non esse, pernegant. Sic enim λόγος in carne finitâ inclusus terminaretur, aut cum λόγῳ immenso caro immensa ubique statueretur: quorum utrumque falsum. Necaliter loquuntur & sentiunt Orthodoxi Patres. Athanas. de incarnatione verbi: Λόγος est in corpore & extra omnia. Ibidem: Extra omnia subsistit. Ibid. Eodem momento, cum esset in humano corpore, extra universa existebat. Hieron. ad Marcell. Qui infinitus erat, etiam in filio hominis totus erat. Aug. lib. 2. de Incarn. In corpore totus & ubique totus aderat Filius Dei.
units.tr: This is a plain fallacy: from a statement made in a qualified sense (secundum quid) he concludes falsely as though it were unqualified, from a likeness. Hunnius reasons thus: "Man is more like other men. Therefore in all respects the case is alike, and the reasoning about the soul and about the Deity is equal, so that just as the soul is bounded by the limits of the body, so the Deity nowhere subsists outside the flesh." Who does not see the trickery here? He makes a comparison as though between equals, the soul and the Word, which are most unequal. For the soul, being a finite spirit, cannot exist outside the body in which it is, as long as it is joined to it, although it is wholly in the whole body and wholly in every part. But the Deity of the Word is a spirit by no means finite, but immense and most pure through his most simple immensity; he is wholly in the finite flesh, and wholly at the same time outside the finite flesh, and subsists outside all things. For who would say that the Deity of the Word was only there, namely in the womb of the mother, in the temple, in the praetorium, on the cross, in the tomb, and so on, where his flesh is recorded as circumscribed, and was absent elsewhere where the flesh was not? Who would deny that he filled heaven and earth, and was at the same time at Rome, at Athens, and everywhere outside Judea, while his body, most closely united to him, remained within the bounds of Judea alone? Certainly whoever asserts the contrary either imagines the Deity shut up and circumscribed by the narrowness of the body, or imagines the body diffused everywhere along with the Deity; that is, to put it very briefly, he makes either the Deity finite or the body infinite. This, then, is one of the false hypotheses which this sophist lays down as the basis for the ubiquity of the flesh. But he also sophistically joins the claim that the Word neither is, nor can be sought or found, outside his flesh; these statements have neither the same meaning nor the same truth. For the orthodox admit that the Word is not to be sought outside his own flesh, because he wills to be sought and adored in the flesh alone, as in his own temple, by faith and prayers; and for this reason they argue against the Ubiquitarians that the flesh of the Word is not hidden in the Eucharistic bread, because it is not, and ought not to be, adored by them. But they deny that he is elsewhere, by his essential immensity, which he has in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For in that case the Word, enclosed in finite flesh, would be bounded, or else the immense flesh would be posited everywhere together with the immense Word; both of which are false. The orthodox Fathers do not speak or think otherwise. Athanasius, On the Incarnation of the Word: "The Word is in the body and outside all things." Likewise: "He subsists outside all things." And again: "At the same moment, when he was in the human body, he existed outside all things." Jerome, to Marcellinus: "He who was infinite was also wholly in the Son of man." Augustine, Book 2 On the Incarnation: "In the body the Son of God was wholly present, and wholly everywhere."

units.la: XXII. Errant igitur, & vnionem admirandam hanc ad vnius duntaxat loci angustias redigunt, qui somniant vno & solo eo loco vbi natura Christi humana visibiliter commoratur, esse λόγον in carne, præter hunc locum autem in innumeris locis reliquis extra illam subsistere. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XXII. Those therefore err, and reduce this admirable union to the narrowness of a single place alone, who dream that the Word is in the flesh only in that one place where the human nature of Christ dwells visibly, and that apart from this place he subsists outside the flesh in countless other places. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Damnat erroris, non nostram, sed sacræ scripturæ, & piæ vetustatis doctrinam, atque sermonem. Scriptura enim vno consensu restatur, humanam Christi naturam vno semper loco fuisse definitam visibiliter, nunquam duobus aut pluribus simul inuisibiliter immenso; interim λόγῳ & in carne sua, & alibi, vbi caro non esset, præsentiam suam declarante, salua perpetuo vnione manente. Patres vero diserte etiā scribunt, sic fuisse λόγον in carne, vt intra angustias eas minime clausus, simul extra eā & omnia alia subsisteret. Quod dicit, non modo admirandam vnionē ad vnius duntaxat loci angustias redigi; sophisticū est, ac falsum. Neq; enim si caro vno loco clauditur, ideo & vnio in has angustias redigenda est: quia ad loci angustias redigi, & in loco esse, idioma est carnis, non vnionis. Idiomata vero naturarū vnionem nec faciunt, nec afficiunt: alioqui pari ratione catillari quis posset, vnionem corpoream, visibilem, mortuam esse, quia caro corporea, visibilis, mortua est: vel æternam, immensam, & Deū esse, quia λόγος æternus, immensus & Deus est.
units.tr: He condemns as error not our doctrine but that of Holy Scripture and of pious antiquity, and their language. For Scripture uniformly testifies that the human nature of Christ has always been visibly limited to one place, and never invisibly to two or more places at once, while the Word, declaring his presence both in his flesh and elsewhere where the flesh is not, keeps the union unbroken forever. The Fathers, moreover, expressly write also that the Word was in the flesh in such a way that, by no means shut up within those limits, he subsisted at the same time outside it and in all other things. What he says, that the admirable union is reduced merely to the narrowness of one place, is sophistical and false. For even if the flesh is enclosed in one place, the union is not therefore reduced to those limits; for to be reduced to the limits of a place and to be in a place is a property of the flesh, not of the union. Properties of the natures neither make nor alter the union; otherwise by the same reasoning one might sneer that the union is corporeal, visible and mortal, because the flesh is corporeal, visible and mortal; or that it is eternal, immense and God, because the Word is eternal, immense and God.

units.la: Etsi autem neque caro vbique cum λόγῳ diffunditur, nec λόγῳ angustiis carnis circumscribitur: tamen nusquam caro non vnita λόγῳ, inque λόγῳ subsistens: & nusquam est λόγος, non vnitus carni, inque carne sua subsistens. Vbicunque ergo est caro, ibi vnio: & vbicunque est λόγος, ibi vnio: non propter diffusionem carnis, sed propter simplicissimam immensitatem λόγος, qua sic est in carne, vt carne tamen non contineatur, sed vbique simul extra eam omnia repleat, & sic est extra carnem vt vbique tamen in ea subsistat: idque non aliqua tantum sui parte, sed totus: nec alius & alius, sed idem. Neque enim alia pars λόγου in carne, alia extra carnem fingi debet, sed totus in carne, totus extra carnem subsistit, quia immensus & impartibilis. Neque alius λόγος in cœlo, alius in terris, sed idem vbique est in carne, seu incarnatus, quia simplicissimus, licet interim caro veritate essentiæ & in uno loco vbi vult, maneat.
units.tr: Although the flesh is not diffused everywhere with the Word, nor is the Word circumscribed by the narrowness of the flesh, yet the flesh is nowhere not united to the Word, nor does it subsist apart from the Word; and the Word is nowhere not united to the flesh, nor does he subsist apart from his own flesh. Wherever the flesh is, there is the union; and wherever the Word is, there is the union. This is not because of any diffusion of the flesh, but because of the most simple immensity of the Word, by which he is so in the flesh that he is nevertheless not contained by the flesh, but at the same time fills all things everywhere outside it; and so he is outside the flesh that he nevertheless subsists everywhere within it. And this is so not by some part of himself only, but wholly; not one Word here and another there, but the same everywhere. For a different part of the Word should not be imagined in the flesh and a different part outside the flesh, but he subsists wholly in the flesh and wholly outside the flesh, because he is immense and impartible. Nor is there one Word in heaven and another on earth, but the same is everywhere in the flesh, or incarnate, because he is most simple, although meanwhile the flesh, in the truth of its essence, remains in one place where he wills.

units.la: Non itaque somniamus in uno tantum loco λόγον esse in carne, in reliquis infinitis locis extra carnem, ac proinde extra vnionem. Nam vbique est in sua carne arcano & indissolubili nexu eam gestans, ac movens: nunquam vero ac nusquam eam deserens, vel ab ea distans. In loco autem uno vel infinitis proprie nusquam est: cum in loco ea tantum sint proprie, quæ sunt dimensa. Immensus vero Deus λόγος neque corporaliter neque intellectualem habet locum, nisi metaphorice, cum ibi esse dicitur, vbi eius manifesta fit operatio: teste Damasceno lib. 1. c. 16. Summa. Vbique est & manet carni suæ vnitus λόγος, etiam extra eam existens, quia nusquam ab ea abesse potest, cum sit immensus, vbique totus idem, absque extensione aut multiplicatione: etsi interim carnis essentia nō nisi vno sitloco.
units.tr: We therefore do not dream that the Word is in the flesh in only one place, and in the countless other places outside the flesh, and therefore outside the union. For he is everywhere in his own flesh, bearing and moving it by a secret and indissoluble bond; yet he never and nowhere forsakes it or stands apart from it. But he is properly nowhere in one place or in countless places, since those things alone are properly in a place which have extension. The immense God the Word has neither a corporeal nor an intellectual place, except metaphorically, when he is said to be where his manifest operation is; so Damascene teaches, Book 1, chapter 16 of the Summa. The Word is everywhere, and remains united to his flesh, even existing outside it, because he can never be absent from it, since he is immense, wholly the same everywhere, without extension or multiplication; although meanwhile the essence of the flesh is only in one place.

units.la: Quod si minus hæc capit, vel probat, Vbiquitarius Doctor, pergat suum λόγον dimensum & extensum somniare, qui non vbique totus, sed alibi alia sui parte existat, vel etiam totus alibi absit. Nos vero cum Athanasio credimus, summæ hoc admirationis esse, quod λόγος à nemine contentus, ipse tamen omnia contineat, & cum in corpore adsit, alibi ramen non desit, sed extra omnia subsistat, in omni rerum natura, ac multo magis in carne sua præsentissimus. Hæc adoranda mysteria sunt, non ad crassam rationis acie exigenda.
units.tr: But if the Ubiquitarian doctor does not grasp or prove these things, let him go on dreaming that his Word is measured and extended, existing not wholly everywhere but in one place by one part of himself and in another place by another part, or else wholly absent from some places. We, however, with Athanasius, believe that it is a matter of the highest wonder that the Word, contained by no one, nevertheless contains all things, and that while he is present in the body, he is not absent elsewhere, but subsists outside all things, in every nature of things, and much more present in his own flesh. These are mysteries to be adored, not to be measured by the keen edge of human reason.

units.la: XXIII. At vero, quia ex Apostoli definitione personalis vnio tota vertitur & consistit in illa corporali inhabitatione & immanentia omnis plenitudinis Deitatis in carne: per immotā consequentiā infertur, quod vbi in carne non habitat, sed extra illam fingitur, ibi nec vnitus cum ea dici possit.
units.tr: XXIII. But because, from the Apostle's definition, the personal union wholly turns upon and consists in that bodily indwelling and inhabitation of all the fullness of the Deity in the flesh, it follows by a firm consequence that where he does not dwell in the flesh, but is imagined outside it, there he cannot be said to be united with it.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Probat λόγον extra carnem nusquam esse, primo ex definitione vnionis Paulina, vt ait: Deinde per contrapositionem. Ex definitione sic videtur colligere: Quod immanet in carne, non est extra eam. λόγος immanet in carne: Quia vnio est corporalis inhabitatio & immanentia λόγου in carne. Non est ergo extra carnem.
units.tr: He proves that the Logos is nowhere outside the flesh. First, from the Pauline definition of union, as he puts it; then by contraposition. From the definition he seems to draw this conclusion: what dwells in the flesh is not outside it. The Logos dwells in the flesh, because the union is the bodily indwelling and immanence of the Logos in the flesh. Therefore the Logos is not outside the flesh.

units.la: Respond. Si contenderet λόγος extra carnem nusquam sic esse, quin simul sit in carne: totum daremus. Sed cum negét simpliciter, vspiam extra carnem esse, vt cum eo carnem vbique diffundat, ad Maiorem respondemus per distinctionem: Id non esse extra carnem posse, quod sic immanet carni, vt dimensionibus eius claudatur. At λόγος hoc modo in carne immanere, & talem immanentiam esse illam, qua Apostolus vnionem indicat potius, quam definit, corporalem inhabitationem omnis plenitudinis Deitatis in carne, negamus: & aduersarius paullo post ipse negat.
units.tr: Reply: if he contended that the Logos is not outside the flesh anywhere without also being in the flesh, we would grant the whole point. But since he simply denies that the Logos is anywhere outside the flesh, so that he may spread the flesh everywhere with it, we answer the major premise by distinction: what dwells in the flesh in such a way that it is enclosed by the flesh's dimensions cannot be outside the flesh. But we deny that the Logos dwells in the flesh in this way, or that this is the immanence by which the Apostle indicates the union rather than defines it, namely the bodily indwelling of all the fullness of the Godhead in the flesh. The adversary himself denies it a little later.

units.la: Non enim sic inhabitat, vt carnis finibus circumscribatur λόγος, neque sic immanet, vt extra eam nusquam sit, sicut anima in corpore existens nusquam est extra corpus, sed vt ab ea nusquam absit aut separetur. Inhabitatio igitur non est λόγου in carne inclusio, sed arcana copulatio cum carne in vnam hypostasin.
units.tr: For the Logos does not so dwell that it is circumscribed by the limits of the flesh, nor so inhere that it is nowhere outside it, as a soul existing in a body is nowhere outside the body. Rather, it is never absent from the flesh nor separated from it. Therefore the indwelling is not an enclosing of the Logos in the flesh, but a hidden joining with the flesh into one hypostasis.

units.la: Quod vnionem vocat Immanentiam, non habet ex Apostolo, sed ex Damasceno, qui vocat περιχώρησιν (quod alii permeationem, alii immeationem, alii immanentiam seu immansionem reddunt) minime intelligens mixtionem Eutychianam naturarum vel circumscriptionem verbi in carne, aut diffusionem carnis cum verbo, sed mutuam, penitissimam atque indissolubilem vnionem vtriusque in vnam hypostasin, salvis naturis & proprietatibus: quod ex Damasceno est notius, quam vt ostendi debeat.
units.tr: The term he calls Immanence he does not have from the Apostle but from Damascene, who calls it perichōrēsis [περιχώρησιν] (which some render permeation, others immeation, others immanence or immansion). Damascene did not mean by it a Eutychian mixing of the natures, nor a circumscription of the Word within the flesh, nor a diffusion of the flesh with the Word, but a mutual, most intimate and indissoluble union of both into one hypostasis, the natures and their properties remaining safe. This is better known from Damascene than it needs to be shown.

units.la: Per contrapositionem vero ex definitione sic colligit: Vbi λόγος est vnitus carni, ibi in carne habitat, & sic immanet, vt extra eam nusquam sit. Ergo vbi in carne non habitat, sed extra illam esse fingitur, ibi nec vnitus cum ea dici potest: quod cum sit absurdum, (fieret enim alicubi Nestoriana separatio) absurdum quoque fuerit, λόγον alicubi extra carnem esse.
units.tr: By contraposition, he draws this conclusion from the definition: where the Logos is united to the flesh, there it dwells in the flesh and so inheres that it is nowhere outside it. Therefore, where it does not dwell in the flesh but is imagined to be outside it, there it cannot be said to be united with the flesh. Since this is absurd (for a Nestorian separation would then occur somewhere), it would also be absurd for the Logos to be outside the flesh anywhere.

units.la: Sed primo τὸ ποῦ, λόγῳ & vnioni improprie tribui, prius est dictum. Falsum deinde est, quod in conuertente propositione sumit de immanentia tali, qua λόγος nusquam sit extra carnem. Id enim cum sit in quæstione, principium petit. Denique ignorationem Elenchi admittit in conuersa, hæc duo: λόγον inhabitare in carne: & λόγον esse extra carnem, fingens esse pu-guantia, quæ non sunt, propter simplicissimam immensitatem λόγ§ λόγος, vt satis ostensum est. Aduersarij argumentatio directè sic erit: Vbi λόγος est vnitus carni, ibi non est extra carnem: quia vnio est immanentia. Sed vbique est vnitus carni. Nusquam ergo est extra carnem. Sed Minor eandem illam ignorationem Elenchi habet, & falsa definitione nititur. Neq; enim damus, vnionem esse immanentiam talem, qualem fingit. Proinde Maiorem negamus. Vbicunque enim λόγος est, totus in carne habitat, totus extra angustias carnis immensitate essentiæ suæ cœlum ac terram replet.
units.tr: But first, what has already been said: the "where" (τὸ ποῦ) is improperly ascribed to the Logos and to the union. Next, what he assumes in the converted proposition is false, namely that such an immanence exists that the Logos is nowhere outside the flesh. Since this is the very point in question, he begs the question. Finally, in the converse he commits the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi, treating two things as opposed when they are not: that the Logos dwells in the flesh, and that the Logos is outside the flesh. The Logos's utterly simple immensity, as has been sufficiently shown, makes them compatible. The adversary's argument, stated directly, would run: where the Logos is united to the flesh, it is not outside the flesh, because union is immanence. But it is united to the flesh everywhere. Therefore it is nowhere outside the flesh. But the minor premise has the same fallacy of ignoratio elenchi and rests on a false definition. For we do not grant that union is immanence of the kind he imagines. Therefore we deny the major premise. For wherever the Logos is, it dwells wholly in the flesh, and yet, by the immensity of its essence, it fills heaven and earth, wholly outside the narrow confines of the flesh.

units.la: XXIV. Præsertim quia secundum hanc opinionem statuendum foret, totum λόγον (cum in partes diuiduus non sit) tota sua hypostasi, totaq; Deitatis plenitudine in locis innumerabilibus extra suam humanitatem constistere: quod vt è esset, intimam illam planeq; indistantem vnionem locorum spaciis distrahere. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XXIV. Especially because, on this opinion, it would have to be held that the whole Logos (since it cannot be divided into parts) subsists with its whole hypostasis and the whole fullness of the Godhead in countless places outside its humanity. For this to be so, the intimate and utterly undistant union would have to be pulled apart by the spaces of places. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Repetis eandem cantilenam. Constituere totum λόγον tota sua hypostasi, totaque Deitatis plenitudine innumerabilibus in locis extra suam carnem, est indistantem naturarum vnionem distrahere. At hoc facere est impium. Ergo & illud. Rursus negatur Maior. Manet enim indistans vnio, etiam cum totus λόγος extra carnis angustias omnia alia replet, quia per simplicissimam immensitatem suam, neque totus, neque dimidius (indiuiduus cum sit) a carne sua discedit, neque abest, neque diuellitur, neque separatur vllis locorum spaciis, sed totus sic intra eam subsistit, vt simul totus extra eam vbique sit præsens: cum non alius, sed idem & integer λόγος sit intra carnē, qui extra eam existit. Ac valde ineptum est hoc argumentum de diuulsione naturarum. Fluit enim ex falsa imaginatione, quod λόγος extra carnem existens, non maneat vnitus carni: id quod salsissimum est, atq; impossibile. Si enim à carne sua alicubi abesset, vtique immensus non esset: & si tantum parte aliqua in carne maneret, vtique diuiduus existeret. Proinde fingere distantiam vllam inter naturas, est reuerà λόγου dimensum fingere, id quod sequens aduersarij purgatio satis etiam ostendit.
units.tr: You repeat the same old refrain: To place the whole Logos, with its whole hypostasis and the whole fullness of the Godhead, in countless places outside its flesh is to tear apart the undistant union of the natures. But to do this is impious. Therefore so is that. Again the major premise is denied. For the union remains undistant even when the whole Logos fills all other things outside the narrow confines of the flesh. By its most simple immensity, being indivisible, it departs from its flesh neither wholly nor by half, nor is it absent, torn away, or separated by any spaces of places. Rather it so subsists wholly within the flesh that it is at the same time wholly present everywhere outside it, since it is not one Logos within the flesh and another outside it, but the same and entire Logos. It is very absurd to argue from a tearing apart of the natures. For this argument flows from a false imagination, namely that the Logos existing outside the flesh does not remain united to the flesh. This is most false and impossible. For if it were absent from its flesh anywhere, it would certainly not be immense; and if it remained in the flesh only by some part, it would certainly be divisible. Therefore to imagine any distance between the natures is really to imagine the Logos measured, as the adversary's own subsequent explanation also sufficiently shows.

units.la: Quidam orthodoxi nodum soluunt distinctione hypostaseos & Deitatis λόγος: illam fatentes nusquam esse extra suam carnem, cum sit vna vtriusque hypostasis: hanc verò totam intra & extra carnem existere statuentes, cum essentia verbi sit simpliciter infinita. Verum ne aduersarij cauillentur, sic hypostasin non æque, ac essentiam λόγου infinitam statui, relinquatur (sane in me-
units.tr: Some orthodox writers untie this knot by distinguishing between the hypostasis of the Logos and its Godhead. They confess that the hypostasis is nowhere outside its own flesh, since there is one hypostasis of both; but they hold that the Godhead exists wholly within and outside the flesh, since the essence of the Word is simply infinite. But lest the adversaries carp, let it be left aside here (for the moment) that this distinction does not make the hypostasis infinite in the same way as the essence of the Logos.

units.la: Fundamentum cauilli de diuisione naturarum unde oriatur. in medio ea distinctio. Scimus hypostasin & naturam diuinam λόγῳ subiecto non differre, sed tantum ratione. Vtraque ergo cum pari ratione sit immensa simplicissimaque, pari quoque ratione vtraque tota in carne sua subsistere, & tota extra carnis angustias cum Patre & Spiritu sancto coelum ac terram replere, recte ac necessario dicitur.
units.tr: The ground of the quibble about the division of the natures, and where it arises. We know that the hypostasis and the divine nature do not differ in the Logos as subject, but only in our way of conceiving them. Since both are immense and most simple by the same reasoning, it is rightly and necessarily said that both are wholly in their flesh, and by the same reasoning both wholly fill heaven and earth with the Father and the Holy Spirit, outside the narrow confines of the flesh.

units.la: XXV. Interim ex nostra doctrina non sequitur eiusmodi aliqua inclusio τ λόγῳ in assumtam naturam, quæ personam Verbi ab infinitate sua deiectam, finitam efficiat: sed hæc potius, qua de sermone nobis est, perpetua immanentia, inhabitatio & incarnatio, hinc infertur, quæ finitam humanitatem in infinitam Filij Dei hypostasin attollit, & consequenter efficit, vt ὁ λόγος à sua carne nusquam absit, nusquam ab ea distet, nusquam extra illam subsistat, sed ἀδιαστάτως (vt Damascenus loquitur) cum ea supra vniuersam creati mundi localitatem maneat ineffabiliter ac præsentissime vnitus. ANIMADVERSIO. Hîc sentit sibi aquam hærere: hoc est, ex immanentia sua necessario sequi inclusionem & finitatem λόγῳ. Itaq; sequi negat sed frustra. Sic enim concluditur: Quod sic immanet in carne finita, vt extra eam nusquam sit: id necesse est claudi dimensionibus carnis, & finitum esse, sicut caro finita est. λόγος sic immanet in carne. Clauditur ergo dimensionibus carnis finitis: quod est absurdum. Maior veritissima. Minor aduersarij est absurda. Sequitur ergo conclusio absurda. Ait: Perpetuam imminentiam potius ex sua doctrina inferri. Atqui principium est petere, immanentiam inferre ex immanentia. Ait: Immanentiam attollere finitam humanitatem in infinitam Filij Dei hypostasin. Hanc περιπλοκίαν si de vnione carnis cum infinita carnis hypostasi intelligerer, salutis eius proprietatibus, Orthodoxi sane non abijcerent. Sed veritatis oratio simplex, mendacij perplexa: qualis & hæc est. Non n. de vnione accipit, quod dicit, sed de vbiquitaria illa carnis cum λόγῳ diffusione, quam orthodoxi simpliciter inficiantur. Nam finitate & dimensiones suas caro non magis quam ipsam naturâ exuere potest, nec quidem in ipsa vnione. Finita v.manens, si in infinitate attollitur, h.e. infinita redditur: vtriq; simul finita & infinita, quanta, & non-quanta, caro, & non-caro, hoc est, Vtopica chimæra, fingitur.
units.tr: XXV. Meanwhile, our doctrine does not imply any such enclosing of the Logos in the assumed nature, which would cast the person of the Word down from its infinity and make it finite. Rather, from the perpetual immanence, indwelling and incarnation that we are speaking of, there follows the lifting up of the finite humanity into the infinite hypostasis of the Son of God. And consequently the Logos is nowhere absent from its flesh, nowhere distant from it, nowhere subsists outside it. Rather, it remains without distance [ἀδιαστάτως], as Damascene puts it, with the flesh above the whole locality of the created world, ineffably and most presently united. ANIMADVERSIO. Here he feels that he is stuck: that is, that enclosing and finiteness of the Logos necessarily follow from its immanence. So he denies that it follows, but in vain. For the argument runs thus: what so inheres in a finite flesh that it is nowhere outside it must necessarily be enclosed by the dimensions of the flesh and be finite, as the finite flesh is. The Logos so inheres in the flesh. Therefore it is enclosed by the finite dimensions of the flesh, which is absurd. The major premise is entirely true; the adversary's minor premise is absurd. Therefore the conclusion is absurd. He says that the perpetual immanence is rather inferred from his doctrine. But to infer immanence from immanence is to beg the question. He says that immanence lifts the finite humanity into the infinite hypostasis of the Son of God. If he meant this entanglement [περιπλοκίαν] of the union of the flesh with the infinite hypostasis, Orthodox writers would certainly not reject it, as far as its properties go. But the speech of truth is simple, and the speech of falsehood is tangled, and this is of that kind. For he does not speak of the union, but of that ubiquitarian diffusion of the flesh with the Logos, which the orthodox simply deny. For the flesh can no more strip off its finiteness and dimensions, any more than its nature, not even in the union itself. A finite flesh that remains finite, if it is lifted up into infinity, that is, is made infinite, would be pretended to be at once finite and infinite, quantified and unquantified, flesh and non-flesh: a utopian chimera.

units.la: Ait : Immanentiam efficere, vt ὁ λόγος à carne sua nus-quam absit, nusquam ab ea distet. Immò non immanentia ea, quam fingit, sed simplicissima immensitas eius id efficit. Per hanc enim fit, vt totus idem sit in carne sua & extra omnes vbique ὁ λόγος.
units.tr: He says that immanence makes the Word [ὁ λόγος] never absent from his flesh and never distant from it. Nay, it is not the immanence he imagines but his most simple immensity that brings this about. For through this it comes about that the Word is wholly the same in his flesh and outside it, everywhere in all.

units.la: Ait: Immanentiam efficere, vt λόγος extra carnem nusquam subsistat, sed ἀδιαστάτως ei vnitus maneat. At rursus falsum esse-ctum tribuit causæ non veræ, & ignorationem elenchi admittit. Neq; enim inhabitatio λόγου in carne (quam ipse immanentiam ambigua voce appellare mauult) est eius inclusio vel definitio intra carnem, hoc est, intra dimensiones carnis: neque hæc duo, extra carnem esse, & ἀδιαστάτως carni vnitum manere, se mutuo tollunt, vt modo ostensum fuit: imò nisi de λόγῳ vtrunq; simul sit verum, neque immensus, neque Deus erit.
units.tr: He says that immanence makes it so that the Word never subsists outside the flesh but remains united to it inseparably [ἀδιαστάτως]. But again he assigns a false effect to a cause that is not true, and he commits a fallacy of missing the point. For the indwelling of the Word in the flesh (which he would rather call immanence, in an ambiguous word) is not its enclosure or definition within the flesh, that is, within the dimensions of the flesh. Nor do these two statements, being outside the flesh and remaining inseparably united to it, cancel each other, as has just been shown. Indeed, unless both are true of the Word at once, he will be neither immense nor God.

units.la: Quod denique ait, carnem supra omnem mundi creati lo-calitatem manere vnitam λόγῳ seu λόγῳ carni: vel inanis est περιφλογία, vel falsa sententia, carnem per vnionem factam esse illocalem, quia λόγος illocalis: de qua postea ad Thesin XXXVI. dicetur.
units.tr: Finally, what he says, that the flesh remains united to the Word, or the Word to the flesh, beyond all locality of the created world, is either empty verbiage [περιφλογία] or a false opinion: that the flesh has become non-local through the union because the Word is non-local. This will be discussed later, at Thesis XXXVI.

units.la: XXVI. Neutiquam verò sequitur, si post incarnationem ὁ λόγος non sit extra naturam personaliter assumptam, vt propterea neque extra illum locum, in quo natura Christi humana per essentiæ conditionem versatur, vllibi esse credendus sit.
units.tr: XXVI. Nor does it follow at all that, if after the incarnation the Word is not outside the nature personally assumed, he is therefore to be believed nowhere outside that place in which Christ's human nature dwells by the condition of its essence.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: CRITICAL REMARK.

units.la: Hic alium declinat scopulum, quod data immanentia, quam fingit, λόγος nusquam erit extra locum naturæ assumptæ: proinde statuetur finitus. Negat & hoc sequi: sed frustra. Sic enim conuincitur: Quod non est extra naturam finitam, certo loco exsistentè: id neq; est extra locum illum, in quo natura finita exsistit. λόγος nusquam est extra naturam suam assumptam finitam, certo loco, vbicunque sit, exsistentem. Ergo nec est vsquam extra locum illum: fingitur proinde finitus λόγος. Minor est aduersarij. Maioris ratio manifesta ac firma est: quod licet aliud sit locus, aliud natura in loco exsistens: tamen natura assumta, ipsa essentiæ conditione (vt rectè fatetur aduersarius) non est absque loco, nec extra locum cum versatur, & locus est ei æqualis. Quicquid ergo non est extra naturam assumtam, vt contentum seu locatum: id neque est extra continens seu locum eius: quia contentum & continens locatum & locus sunt æqualia.
units.tr: Here he avoids another rock. Granted the immanence he imagines, the Word will nowhere be outside the place of the assumed nature; therefore he will be declared finite. He denies that this follows, but in vain. For it is proved thus: what is not outside a finite nature existing in a certain place is not outside the place in which that finite nature exists. The Word is nowhere outside his assumed finite nature, which exists in a certain place wherever it is. Therefore he is nowhere outside that place. Thus a finite Word is imagined. The minor premise is the opponent's own. The ground of the major premise is clear and firm: although place is one thing and a nature existing in a place is another, nevertheless the assumed nature, by the very condition of its essence (as the opponent rightly confesses), is not without place, nor outside place when it dwells there, and the place is equal to it. Whatever therefore is not outside the assumed nature as contained or located is not outside its container or place either, since the contained and the container, the located and the place, are equal.

units.la: XXVII. Longe enim alia ratio est ipsius humanitatis, alia loci, qui naturaliter eam ambit aut continet.
units.tr: XXVII. For the humanity itself has a quite different relation from that of the place which naturally surrounds or contains it.

units.la: XXVIII. Etenim humanitas ipsa quidem in hypostasin vnigeniti Verbi per vnionem est euecta & translata: locus autem ambiens extra eam hypostasin Verbi manet perpetuò.
units.tr: XXVIII. For the humanity is indeed raised up and transferred into the hypostasis of the only-begotten Word by the union, whereas the place surrounding it remains outside that hypostasis of the Word for ever.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: CRITICAL REMARK.

units.la: Nimis friuola hæc est elusio maioris. Etsi enim in hoc impar humanitatis & loci est ratio, quod illa assumta, hic non assumtus est à λόγῳ[?]: manet tamen hoc, quod extremitatibus sunt simul, & æqualia: unde necessariò fit, vt quicquid non est extra vnum, id neque sit extra alterum. Tantum ergo probat Sophista, humanitatem non esse locum: minimè verò euenit verissimum axioma: Quicquid non est extra locatum, id neque est extra locum locati.
units.tr: This evasion of the major premise is far too trifling. For although the difference between humanity and place lies in this, that the former is assumed and the latter is not assumed by the Word [λόγος], still this remains: the extremes are together and equal. Whence it necessarily follows that whatever is not outside the one is not outside the other either. So the sophist proves only that humanity is not a place; but the most true axiom is not overturned: whatever is not outside the located thing is not outside the place of the located thing.

units.la: XXIX. Quid mirum igitur, si λόγῳ[?] sit extra locum humanitatis, extra substantiam verò humanitatis minimè? Siquidem & ipsa caro, quantumuis in loco, cum vult, existens & apparens: tamen vi vnionis supra localitatem in ipsa Filij Dei persona subsistit, hoc certè respectu eundem istum locum, in quo alias commoratur, ineffabiliter transcendens.
units.tr: XXIX. What wonder then if the Word is outside the place of the humanity, but certainly not outside the substance of the humanity? For the flesh itself, however much it exists and appears in a place when it wills, nevertheless by force of the union subsists in the person of the Son of God above localness, ineffably transcending, in this respect, that very place in which it otherwise dwells.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: CRITICAL REMARK.
