units.la: Immò maximè mirum. Mirum enim est & absurdum, fingere aliquid extra continens, quod non sit simul extra contentum: extra locum, quod non sit simul extra locatum. Verbi causa, extra mœnia urbis, quod non sit simul extra curiam urbis: extra Wittebergam, quod non sit simul extra palatium Hunnij nuper dono acceptum Wittebergæ contra arcem, &c.
units.tr: Nay, it is most wonderful indeed. For it is wonderful and absurd to imagine something outside the container which is not at the same time outside the contained, or outside the place which is not at the same time outside the located thing. For example: outside the walls of the city, which is not at the same time outside the city's court; or outside Wittenberg, which is not at the same time outside the palace of Hunnius, recently given to Wittenberg opposite the citadel, etc.

units.la: Caro Christi non solum voluntate, sed ipsius essentiæ conditione (teste Thesi 26.) in loco versatur. Ergo non tantum in loco est, quando vult, sed quamdiu naturam retinet, necessariò in loco existit: siue is sit physicus, vt fuit in his terris, siue cœlestis, vt nunc est in gloria.
units.tr: The flesh of Christ dwells in a place not only by will but by the condition of its very essence (as Thesis 26 bears witness). Therefore it is not in a place only when it wills; as long as it retains its nature, it necessarily exists in a place, whether that place is physical, as it was on this earth, or heavenly, as it now is in glory.

units.la: Carnem vi vnionis subsistere supra localitatem, & transcendere locum, in quo commoratur: rursus & falsum est, & contradictionem implicat. Falsum: quia carnē λόγῳ[?] vnitam seu in ipsa vnione nobis per omnia similem esse absque peccato, ipse aduersarius supra Th. 5. & 6. est fassus. Ergo in ipsa vnione etiam localitate nobis
units.tr: That the flesh, by force of the union, subsists above localness and transcends the place in which it dwells: this again is both false and implies a contradiction. It is false, because the adversary himself, above at Theses 5 and 6, has confessed that the flesh united to the Word, or in the union itself, is like us in all things without sin. Therefore, in the union itself, it is also like us in localness.

units.la: {1} [signature-like mark at the foot centre; not clearly a gathering signature] nobis est similis. Contradictoria vero sunt: carnem essentiæ conditione commorari in loco: & eandem simul locum essentia sua transcendere, hoc est, in loco non commorari, quacunq; tandem vi id fiat. Nam κενοφυΐαν de diuersa essentiæ & vnionis ratione in respectu contradictionem minimè tollit, cum hæc ipsa ratio fiue respectus se implicet, ac nihil nisi inanis sit fumus, vt supra ad Thesin. vi. est demonstratum.
units.tr: Yet they are contradictory: that the flesh dwells in a place by the condition of its essence, and that the same flesh at the same time transcends place by its essence, that is, does not dwell in place, however that is done. For the talk of a "kind of empty show" [κενοφυΐαν] concerning a different relation of essence and union does not remove the contradiction at all, since this very relation or respect contradicts itself and is nothing but empty smoke, as was demonstrated above at Thesis VI.

units.la: XXX. Dilucidior euadet res, si vis Apostolicæ vocis, qua Filium Dei semen Abrahæ seu natura humanam ex Abrahæ posteritate assumsisse docet, attendatur. Heb. 2.
units.tr: XXX. The matter will become clearer if we attend to the force of the apostolic words by which the Son of God is taught to have assumed the seed of Abraham, that is, human nature from the posterity of Abraham. Heb. 2.

units.la: XXXI. Hic enim consideranda veniunt diuinæ huius assumptionis termini, vt loquuntur Scholastici, unde videlicet λόγος illam assumserit, & quo assumserit.
units.tr: XXXI. Here the terms of this divine assumption come into consideration, as the Scholastics say: namely, whence the Word assumed it, and to what he assumed it.

units.la: XXXII. Assumsit autem carnem suam ex substantia Mariæ virginis, quæ quia suû ab Abrahamo ortû trahit, rectè Apostolus assumtum id Abrahæ semen appellat.
units.tr: XXXII. He assumed his flesh from the substance of the Virgin Mary, who, since she draws her descent from Abraham, the Apostle rightly calls the assumed seed of Abraham.

units.la: XXXIII. Assumsit vero λόγος massam illam ex virgine sumtam, non huc vel illuc, in hunc vel istum locum.
units.tr: XXXIII. The Word assumed that mass taken from the virgin not here or there, not into this or that place.

units.la: XXXIV. Quanquam enim Filius Dei carnem suam tempore exinanitionis localitati, vt suum opus in terris exigeret, subiectam esse voluit: & quanquam adhuc, quando & vbi vult, in loco visibiliter apparere potest: tamen non locus aliquis, sed illocalis unigeniti Verbi hypostasis est diuinissimæ huius assumptionis terminus, in quem per vnionem caro Saluatoris est translata.
units.tr: XXXIV. For although the Son of God willed his flesh, in the time of his humiliation, to be subject to locality so that he might carry out his work on earth, and although even now he can appear visibly in a place when and where he wills, nevertheless the terminus of this most divine assumption is not some place but the non-local hypostasis of the only-begotten Word, into which the flesh of the Saviour has been transferred by the union.

units.la: XXXV. Quod D. Athanasius in symbolo erudita breuitate complexus est, cum hypostaticam vnionem definit assumtionem humanitatis in Deum.
units.tr: XXXV. This St Athanasius summed up with learned brevity in the creed, when he defines the hypostatic union as the assumption of humanity into God.

units.la: XXXVI. In Deum igitur Deique hypostasin (apud quam omnis cogitatio loci & localitatis desinit) reali assumtione translata Christi humanitas, &, vt Damascenus orthodoxè scribit, ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λόγῳ (in ipsomet verbo) suam ὑπαρξιν, & existentiam habens, hoc personalis vnionis respectu omnem localitatem altissimè transcendit, & in λόγῳ illocalem existendi modum vere sortitur.
units.tr: XXXVI. Thus the humanity of Christ, transferred by real assumption into God and into the hypostasis of God (where every thought of place and localness ceases), and, as Damascene writes orthodoxly, having its existence [ὑπαρξιν] in the Word itself [ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λόγῳ], in respect of this personal union altogether transcends all localness and truly obtains a non-local mode of existing in the Word.

units.la: XXXVII. Proinde vt grauissimis verbis Dn. D. Chemnitius tunitij concludam: ita toti plenitudini Deitatis Filij Dei personaliter vnita est assumta natura, vt λόγῳ intra arcanum, arctissimum, intimum, profundissimum & praesentissimum complexum, non alicubi particulæ alicuius, sed totius plenitudinis diuinæ naturæ suæ, quæ supra & extra omnem locum est secum, intra se, apud se, & penes se, personaliter vnitam atque præsentissimam semper habeat, & in illa plenitudine vnitæ Deitatis assumta natura sua ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀδιαστάτως, juxta Damascenum, indiuiduam seu inseparabilem & indisiunctam, seu locorum interuallo indistantem habeat immanentiam.
units.tr: XXXVII. Therefore, to conclude with the weighty words of Dr Chemnitz: the assumed nature is so united personally to the whole fullness of the Deity of the Son of God that the Word always holds it, and has it with himself, within himself, and in his own keeping, in a secret, most close, most intimate, most profound and most present embrace. He holds it united and most present, not in some particle of his nature but in the whole fullness of his divine nature, which is above and beyond all place. And in that fullness of the united Deity the assumed nature has an indivisible and inseparable [ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀδιαστάτως, according to Damascene] and undisjoined indwelling, not distant from it by any interval of place.

units.la: XXXVIII. Eadem sententia fusissime pertractata extat in confessione vtraque Diui Lutheri, & allegatione verborū Lutheri approbat eam formula Concordiæ, quam in his regionibus publicè receptam esse constat. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The same opinion is treated at great length in both confessions of the blessed Luther, and the formula of Concord approves it by quoting Luther's words, a formula which is known to be publicly received in these regions. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Quis hic non exclamet? Quo teneam vultus mutantem Protea nodo? Quis sophistam hic comprehendat? Hic nimirum imperiti ad tam itupendas ὑεγλολογίας ore & naso attoniti obrigescunt. Massam humanam, ait, non esse assumtam huc vel illuc: non in hunc vel istum locum, non locum aliquem, sed illocalem Filij Dei hypostasin esse assumtionis Terminum ad quem: carnem Saluatoris in assumtionis Terminum esse translatam, omnem localitatem altissime transcendisse, in λόγῳ illocalem existendi modum sortiri: λόγον habere assumtam naturam intra complexum totius plenitudinis suæ diuinæ naturæ: secum: intra se: apud se: penes se: naturam humanam in plenitudine vnitæ Deitatis habere indisiunctam suam immanentiam. Quis malum sic lotus est vnquam in Ecclesia? Sepiæ hoc atramentum, & inanis præstigiarum fumus est, quo infuscatur simplex doctrina de Filio Dei, & stolidus fascinatur mundus, vt viuus videnfq; non videat, nec palpet tam crassa mendacia. Nouus & insidiosus plane est hic sermo: alienus ab ἀνανεύσεως sanorum verborum Scripturæ & piæ Antiquitatis de hoc mysterio: quo Sophista satis, nisi fallor, testatum facit, nouum ac monstrosum esse doctrinæ genus, quod profert. Qui enim noua dogmata parturiunt, etiam nouum plerunq; sermonem confingunt.
units.tr: Who would not cry out at this? By what knot can I hold Proteus as he changes his face? Who can seize this sophist? Here, no doubt, the unlearned are struck dumb, open-mouthed and wide-eyed, at such astonishing theologies [ὑεγλολογίας]. He says that the human mass was not assumed here or there, not into this or that place, nor into any place at all, but that the unlocalised hypostasis of the Son of God is the terminus to which the assumption was made. He says that the flesh of the Saviour was transferred into the terminus of the assumption, that it rose far above all localisation, and that in the Logos it obtains an unlocalised mode of existing. He says that the Logos has the assumed nature within the whole fullness of his divine nature, with him, within himself, in his presence and at his side, and that the human nature has its inseparable immanence in the fullness of the united Deity. Has anyone ever been so bemired in error in the Church? This is the ink of the cuttlefish and the empty smoke of conjuring tricks, by which the simple doctrine of the Son of God is darkened and the foolish world is bewitched, so that people with eyes see and do not see, and cannot feel such gross lies. This way of speaking is plainly new and deceitful. It is far from the wording of sound words of Scripture and of pious antiquity on this mystery, and by it the sophist makes it clear enough, unless I am mistaken, that the kind of doctrine he puts forward is new and monstrous. For those who give birth to new dogmas also commonly coin new language.

units.la: Ad rem. Aliam falsam hypothesin machinatur his Thesibus Sophista, quam Vbiquitati carnis substernat: Carnem Saluatoris in vnione seu λόγῳ illocalem factam esse. Hanc ex voce apostolica ASSVMTIONIS extundere conatur: aspersis quibusdam Scholasticorum terminis.
units.tr: To the matter. In these theses the sophist contrives another false hypothesis, which he lays as the foundation for the ubiquity of the flesh: that the flesh of the Saviour, in the union or in the Logos, has been made unlocalised. He tries to beat this out of the apostolic word ASSUMPTION, sprinkling on it certain terms of the Scholastics.

units.la: Sed & Scripturæ vocem & Scholasticorum phrasin malitiose deprauat. Nam Assumtio seminis Abrahami Paulo nequaquam significat euectionem & translationem naturæ humanæ in illocalis: sed vnio-ne calitatem Filij Dei, qua ipsa etiam fit facta illocalis: sed vnio-nem indiuiduam hypostaticam cum Filio Dei, salua manente natura veritq; proprietatibus eius: quia caro assumta non extra vnionem, sed in vnione, non extra λόγον, sed in λόγῳ, ante gloriam & in gloria, fit Filij Dei caro: & Filius Dei fit frater noster, caro de carne nostra, os de ossibus nostris: in qua κοινωνία carnis nostræ cum Filio Dei omnis consolatio, & salus Christiana consistit. Sic ipse Apostolus assumtionem hanc explicat verbis præcedentibus: Filius Dei particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis pue-rorum συγκοινωνῶ.
units.tr: But he also maliciously distorts both the word of Scripture and the phrasing of the Scholastics. For the assumption of the seed of Abraham by no means signifies to Paul the lifting up and transfer of the human nature into the unlocalised. It signifies the union with the heavenly nature of the Son of God, by which the flesh itself is also made unlocalised; it signifies the inseparable hypostatic union with the Son of God, the nature and its properties remaining intact. For the flesh assumed is made the flesh of the Son of God not outside the union but within it, not outside the Logos but in the Logos, before the glory and in the glory. The Son of God becomes our brother, flesh of our flesh and bone of our bones, and in this fellowship of our flesh with the Son of God all Christian comfort and salvation consist. So the Apostle himself explains this assumption in the preceding words: the Son of God became a partaker [συγκοινωνῶ] of the flesh and blood of the children.

units.la: Scholasticorum quoque sermonem corrumpit. Assumtionis enim terminum ad quem, dicunt esse non naturam, sed personam: quia, vt loquuntur, vnio facta est non in natura, sed in persona, hoc est, quia per vnionem non coierunt duæ naturæ in vnam naturam, sed in vnā personam Filij Dei, prius in vna, nunc autem in duabus subsistentem naturis, inconfusis & integris, diuina & humana. Minimè gentium vero loquuntur, aut faciunt cum hoc Sophista: Carnem Saluatoris esse translatam in terminum assumtionis, hoc est, in illocalem Dei hypostasin, vt in ea fit ipsa illocalis. Pestilentes hæ sunt insidiæ. Hinc enim sophistæ inferre promtum esset: carnem in λόγῳ pari modo esse Deum, esse immensum, & vbique. Sed abstersò fuco reuocemus hanc prodigiosam sophisticam ad pauca. Sic igitur in summa argumentatur:
units.tr: He also corrupts the language of the Scholastics. For they say that the terminus to which the assumption is made is not the nature but the person, because, as they put it, the union was made not in the nature but in the person. That is, through the union the two natures did not come together into one nature, but into one person of the Son of God, who previously subsisted in one nature and now subsists in two natures, unconfused and whole, divine and human. But they by no means speak or act as this sophist does, saying that the flesh of the Saviour has been transferred into the terminus of the assumption, that is, into the unlocalised hypostasis of God, so that in it the flesh itself becomes unlocalised. These are pestilent snares. From here the sophist could easily infer that the flesh in the Logos is in the same way God, is immeasurable, and is everywhere. But let us wipe off the paint and reduce this monstrous sophistry to a few points. He argues in summary as follows:

units.la: Quod assumtum est in illocalem hypostasin λόγῳ, id assumtione ea illocalem existendi modum in λόγῳ sortitur, hoc est, fit illocale. Caro Saluatoris assumta est in illocalem hypostasin λόγῳ. Ergo caro Saluatoris in λόγῳ sortitur illocale existendi modum, hoc est, fit illocalis.
units.tr: Whatever is assumed into the unlocalised hypostasis of the Logos, by that assumption obtains an unlocalised mode of existing in the Logos, that is, it becomes unlocalised. The flesh of the Saviour has been assumed into the unlocalised hypostasis of the Logos. Therefore the flesh of the Saviour obtains in the Logos the unlocalised mode of existing, that is, it becomes unlocalised.

units.la: Maiorem probat thesi 36. quia in Deo Deiq; hypostasi omnis cogitatio loci & localitatis definit. Minorem Th. 34. quia illocalis hypostasis λόγῳ est terminus assumtionis, in quë per vnionem caro est translata. Item, authoritate Athanasij definientis vnionem hypostaticam assumtione humanitatis in Deum.
units.tr: He proves the major premise by thesis 36, because in God and in the divine hypostasis every thought of place and of localisation is excluded. He proves the minor by thesis 34, because the unlocalised hypostasis of the Logos is the terminus of the assumption into which, through the union, the flesh has been transferred. Likewise, he appeals to the authority of Athanasius, who defines the hypostatic union as the assumption of the humanity into God.

units.la: RESPOND. Sophisticam hic subesse, indicat manifesta falsitas conclusionis pugnantis cum tota historia Euangelica, quæ testatur humanam naturam Christi assumtam à λόγῳ semper lo-calem fuisse. Maior igitur tantum de eo vera est, quod assum-tum tum est vel conuersione in illocalem illam hypostasin λόγῳ, vel exæquatione cum ea: minime autem de eo, quod assumtum est vnione hypostatica tali, quæ assumentis & assumti naturam & proprietates relinquit & seruat integras & inconfusas. Quo modo & sensu carnem Saluatoris in hypostasin illocalem Filij Dei assumtam esse, nemo nisi Nestorianus vel Eutychianus hæreticus negauerit. Sic igitur sunt quatuor termini in argumento. Si Sophista distinctionem non admittit, ac de eo etiam verum esse Maiorem contendit, quod vnione hypostatica salvis proprietatibus assumtum est; tota vt salsissima negatur. Nam hypostasis λόγου, sicut est illocalis, sic etiam est infinita, æterna, incorporea, ex Patre genita, incarnata, natura Deus, nec tamen verum est, quicquid ab hypostasi tali & λόγῳ assumtum est, id pariter infinitum, æternum, incorporeum, ex Patre genitum, incarnatum, naturâ Deum esse.
units.tr: REPLY. That a sophistry lies hidden here is shown by the manifest falsity of the conclusion, which conflicts with the whole Gospel history, and which testifies that the human nature of Christ, once assumed by the Logos, was always localised. The major premise is therefore true only of what is assumed either by conversion into that unlocalised hypostasis of the Logos or by equalisation with it. It is by no means true of what is assumed by such a hypostatic union as leaves and preserves the natures and properties of the one who assumes and of what is assumed, whole and unconfused. In what sense and manner the flesh of the Saviour was assumed into the unlocalised hypostasis of the Son of God, no one but a Nestorian or Eutychian heretic would deny. So there are four terms in the argument. If the sophist does not admit this distinction, and insists that the major premise is true even of what has been assumed by a hypostatic union with its properties preserved, then the whole thing is rightly rejected as utterly absurd. For the hypostasis of the Logos, as it is unlocalised, so also it is infinite, eternal, incorporeal, begotten of the Father, incarnate, God by nature. Yet it is not true that whatever is assumed by such a hypostasis and the Logos is likewise infinite, eternal, incorporeal, begotten of the Father, incarnate, and God by nature.

units.la: Secundo etiam consequentia negatur: quia est manifesta fallacia non causæ vt causæ. Fingitur enim causa illohalitatis carnis esse assumtio carnis in illocalem λόγῳ, quæ causa nulla est. Neque enim λόγος assumsit carnem, quà vel quia est illocalis, sed quà vel quia est secunda hypostasis à Patre & Spiritu sancto distincta. Ratio huius firma & manifesta est, quam Sophista nullo sepiæ atramento infuscabit, quia assumtio carnis facta est non secundum proprietatem aliquam naturalem, vt est illocalitas, qua λόγῳ Patri & Spiritui sancto vnitur, sed secundum proprietates characteristicas, quibus à Patre & Spiritu sancto discernitur, vt præclare ostendit Damascenus: alioqui vel assumtio non esset à solo λόγῳ facta, sed à Patre & Spiritu sancto simul: vel certe reliqua attributa λόγῳ naturalia omnia, nullo excepto, carni per assumtionem seu vi vnionis tribuenda forent, ac πεγατωδῶς simul affirmare liceret, carnem in λόγῳ æterno, infinito, incorporeo, &c. omnem temporis, finitatis, corporeitatis, &c. rationem altissimè transcendisse, & æternum, infinitum, incorporeum existendi modum vere sortiri. Quid vero sic relinquet vbiquitariismus Eutychi? Vbi stabit aduersarij sexta thesis? vbi erit frater noster? caro nostra? fides & consolatio nostra?
units.tr: Secondly, the consequence is also denied, because it is a manifest fallacy of cause taken as cause. For the cause of the unlocalisation of the flesh is falsely made to be the assumption of the flesh into the unlocalised Logos, and that is no cause at all. For the Logos did not assume the flesh because he is unlocalised, but because he is the second hypostasis, distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit. The reason for this is firm and plain, and no ink of the cuttlefish will darken it. The assumption of the flesh was made not according to any natural property, such as unlocalisation, by which the Logos is united with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but according to the characteristic properties by which he is distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit, as Damascene clearly shows. Otherwise the assumption would not have been made by the Logos alone, but by the Father and the Holy Spirit together. Or else all the attributes natural to the Logos, without exception, would have to be ascribed to the flesh through the assumption, or by the force of the union, and one could rashly affirm at the same time that the flesh in the eternal, infinite, incorporeal Logos, and so on, has risen far above every condition of time, finitude and corporeity, and truly obtains an eternal, infinite, incorporeal mode of existing. What then will remain of the Eutychian ubiquitarianism? Where will the opponent's sixth thesis stand? Where will our brother be? Our flesh? Our faith and our comfort?

units.la: Quare quod tanta arte illocalitatem λόγου sophista vrget, inanis est fucus, quo carnem localem veram & solidam, vt ipse appellat, ab illocali λόγῳ non magis probat esse illocalem factam vi vnionis: quam si dicat, corpus humanum vi vnionis omnem densitatem, corporeitatem, mortalitatem, &c. altissimè transcendisse, & in anima rationalem, spiritualem, &c. immortalem existendi modum, verè sortiri: quia cum anima rationali, spirituali, immortali, &c. hypostaticè est vnitum. Apage nugas!
units.tr: Therefore, although the sophist presses so artfully the unlocalisation of the Logos, it is an empty varnish, by which he does not prove any more that the true and solid flesh, as he calls it, has been made unlocalised by the force of the union with the unlocalised Logos. It would be as if he said that the human body, by the force of its union with the rational, spiritual and immortal soul, had risen far above all density, corporeity and mortality, and truly obtains a rational, spiritual, immortal mode of existing in the soul, because it is hypostatically united with the rational, spiritual, immortal soul. Away with such trifles!

units.la: 1 3 Probatio Maioris nulla est, sed similis priori fallaciæ non causæ: quoniam illocalitas Dei assumentis non magis est causa illocalitatis carnis assumtæ: quam æternitas, simplicitas, immensitas eiusdem, carnem æternam, simplicissimam, immensam facit. Cessat in Deo non tantum omnis cogitatio loci & localitatis, sed & temporis, & finitatis, & humanitatis. Resp. An igitur cogitatio istorum in carne assumta etiam cessabit? Minime: quoniam unio facta est salvis & inconfusis naturis, & naturarum proprietatibus.
units.tr: The proof of the major premise is nothing, but it is like the earlier fallacy of cause taken as cause, since the unlocalisation of God who assumes does no more cause the unlocalisation of the assumed flesh than his eternity, simplicity and immensity make the flesh eternal, most simple and immense. In God, not only every thought of place and localisation ceases, but also of time, finitude and humanity. Reply: Will the thought of these things then cease also in the flesh assumed? By no means, since the union was made with the natures preserved whole and unconfused, and with the properties of the natures preserved.

units.la: Nec probatio Minoris ad rem facit. Nam illocalis hypostasis λόγου terminus est non Carnis, sed Assumtionis Carnis: nec caro facta est ipsa illocalis hypostasis λόγυ, vel in eam mutata: sed fictæ ab ea, & in eam assumta, ut in ea subsistat, & ab ea sustentetur ac gestetur, tanquam propria λόγυ caro. Interim sit & maneat, etiam in λόγῳ, vera & localis caro, qualis a λόγῳ & in λόγῳ assumta est.
units.tr: Nor does the proof of the minor premise bear on the matter. For the unlocalized hypostasis of the Word [λόγου] is the terminus not of the flesh but of the assumption of the flesh. Nor has the flesh become the unlocalized hypostasis of the Word [λόγου] itself, or been changed into it. Rather, it was formed by the Word and assumed into it, so that it subsists in the Word and is sustained and carried by it, as the Word's own flesh. Meanwhile the flesh is and remains, even in the Word [λόγῳ], a true and localized flesh, such as it was assumed by and into the Word [λόγῳ].

units.la: Neq; hæc sententia Scholasticorum est, ut prius monui, cum Terminum Assumtionis ad quem dicunt esse hypostasin, vel Vnionem terminari in hypostasi, quod natura assumta sit facta hypostasis, vel hypostasi terminetur & definiatur: sed quod cum assumente λόγῳ sit vnita in vnam hypostasin, quodque vnio ex duabus naturis non faciat vnam naturam, sed vnam personam: quo sensu etiam disputant, vnionem non fieri in natura, sed in persona. Frustra igitur sub hac larua Scholasticorum χρηστοφύσει quæritur. Porrò Athanasius sic assumtam intelligit humanitatem in Deum, ut non sit ipsa facta Deus, sed ut in hypostasi diuina ipsa subsistat, sitq; propria Dei caro, ut Deus vere sit homo & homo vere sit Deus.
units.tr: Nor is this the view of the Scholastics, as I warned earlier. They say that the terminus of the assumption, the point to which it tends, is the hypostasis, or that the union terminates in the hypostasis, because the assumed nature has become a hypostasis, or is terminated and defined by the hypostasis. Their view is rather that the flesh has been united with the assuming Word into one hypostasis, and that the union of two natures makes not one nature but one person. In this sense they also argue that the union takes place not in the nature but in the person. It is therefore in vain that this question is pursued under the mask of the Scholastics [χρηστοφύσει]. Moreover, Athanasius understands the humanity to be assumed into God in such a way that it is not itself made God, but subsists in the divine hypostasis itself and is God's own flesh, so that God truly is man and man truly is God.

units.la: Ampullas Chemnitij simplex Veritas nihil moratur: neque est, quod hunc clypeum obijciat Sophista: quia mutuum muli scabunt.
units.tr: Simple truth is not held up by Chemnitius' flasks, nor is there any reason for the sophist to oppose this shield, since mules rub each other's itches.

units.la: A Diuo Luthero, qui licet recte alicubi scripserit de vltimis verbis Domini, tamen Orthodoxi, ne videantur ab hominibus pendere, provocant ad Diuum Matthæum, Marcum, Lucam, Johannem, Paulum, Petrum, qui omnes testantur, carnem Salvatoris etiam in λόγῳ vere fuisse & mansisse localem. Provocant ad ipsum Saluatorem, qui post resurrectionem carne sua locali non extra λόγον, sed in λόγῳ, non extra vnionem, sed λόγῳ vnita, dixit: Videte, palpate, spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut videtis me habere. Provocant ab vtraq; confessione D. Lutheri ad vtrumq; Testamentum viuentis Dei: ad Augustanam confessionem, & saniora scripta ipsius D. Lutheri, quibus τὸ παντοχῆς carnis facessere iussit:
units.tr: Appeal is made to the divine Luther, who, although he wrote rightly in places about the last words of the Lord, nevertheless. The Orthodox, lest they seem to depend on men, appeal to the holy Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Paul and Peter, who all testify that the flesh of the Saviour, even in the Word, truly was and remained localized. They appeal to the Saviour himself, who after the resurrection, with his flesh localized, not outside the Word but in the Word, not outside the union but united to the Word, said: Behold, handle me, for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. They appeal, from both confessions of Dr. Luther, to both Testaments of the living God: to the Augsburg Confession and to the saner writings of Luther himself, by which he ordered the omnipresence [πανταχῆς] of the flesh to be dismissed. How the humanity is assumed into God. Finally, they appeal from the Concord of Bergen to the Concord, or Harmony, of the holy Evangelists and Apostles, which is known to have been publicly received in the Church of Christ.

units.la: Quomodo humanitas assumta in Deum. Prouocant deniq; à concordia Bergensi ad concordiam seu Harmoniam sanctorum Euangelistarum & Apostolorum, quam in Christi Ecclesiam publicè receptam esse constat.
units.tr: How the humanity is assumed into God. Finally, they appeal from the Concord of Bergen to the Concord, or Harmony, of the holy Evangelists and Apostles, which is known to have been publicly received in the Church of Christ.

units.la: XXXIX. Ex dictis apparet etiam, vnionem λόγῳ cum carne ipsarummet naturarum ad se inuicem κοινωνίᾳ vera solidaq; esse describendam. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XXXIX. From what has been said it also appears that the union of the Word with the flesh is to be described as a true and solid fellowship of the natures themselves with one another. REMARK.

units.la: Jam in calce προέγισμα deducit, quæ sano sensu suscepta nemo orthodoxus abijcit. Sed omnia sunt insidiarum plena, de quibus imperitiores breuiter monendi sunt.
units.tr: Now, at the end, he draws out the preliminary point, which no orthodox person rejects when taken in a sound sense. But all things are full of snares, and the less skilled must be briefly warned about them.

units.la: Primum πρόεγισμα est: Vnionem ipsarummet naturarum ad se inuicem κοινωνίας vera solidaq; describendam esse. Recte. Cur ergo hactenus sic non descripsit, sed tantum immanentiam definiuit: cum plane & integre fuerit definienda vnio, ne titulus mentiretur? Verum de hoc astu supra in argumento lectorem monui.
units.tr: The first preliminary point is that the union of the natures themselves with one another is to be described as a true and solid fellowship. Rightly so. Why then has he not so described it hitherto, but only defined indwelling, when the union ought to have been defined plainly and entirely, lest the title be false? But I have warned the reader about this trick above, in the argument.

units.la: Patribus Orthodoxis communio seu κοινωνία sæpe Vnionem significat; quia vnione facta est vna communis duarum naturarum κατάχρησις. Estq; hæc κοινωνία naturarum vera solidaq;: quia vere solideque, hoc est, realissime & arctissime communicata est deitati humanitas, & humanitati deitas, hoc est, vnita, vt sint vna persona: saluis manentib. naturis & proprietatibus. Sic Damascenus l. 3. c. 6. Diuinitas totaliter nobis in vna suiipsius χαρακτῆρα κοινωνῆς, id est communicauit seu vnita est. Fulgentius ad Donat. Nunquam homo à Deo gratiam salutis acciperet, si in vna persona Christi diuina & humana q; natura communio (hoc est, vnio) non maneret.
units.tr: With the Orthodox Fathers, communio or κοινωνία often signifies the union, because by the union one common communion of the two natures is made, a catachresis [κατάχρησις]. And this communion of the natures is true and solid, because the humanity has been communicated to the deity, and the deity to the humanity, truly and solidly, that is, most really and most closely, that is, united, so that they are one person, the natures and properties remaining safe. Thus Damascene, book 3, chapter 6: The divinity has communicated itself wholly to us in its own one character [χαρακτῆρα κοινωνῆς], that is, has been united. Fulgentius to Donatus: Man would never receive the grace of salvation from God, if the divine and human nature did not remain in communion (that is, in union) in the one person of Christ.

units.la: Crebrius tamen & proprie κοινωνία Patribus significat communem alterius naturæ & proprietatum eius prædicationem de tota persona in concreto: quæ κοινωνία non est ipsa vnio, sed vnionis effectus, seu consequens: estq; & hæc κοινωνία vera, solidaque, atque etiam, vt loquuntur, realissima in persona. Facit enim, vt Deus λόγος, vere solideque & realissime sit homo, passus, mortuus, excitatus, assumtus in gloria: & Homo vere solideque & realissime sit Deus æternus, omnipotens, immensus & ubique. Minime autem talis dici potest in naturis: quia non facit, vt Deitas vere solideque sit humanitas vel homo, sit passa, mortua excitata, assumta in gloria &c. neque etiam vt humanitas vere solideq; sit Deitas vel Deus, sit æterna, omnipotens immensa & ubique. Talis enim κοινωνία quid esset, nisi Eutychiana confusio proprietatum: proinde & naturarum: Hactenus datur primum πρόεγισμα.
units.tr: More often, however, and properly, κοινωνία signifies for the Fathers the common predication of the one nature's properties and the other's of the whole person in the concrete. This κοινωνία is not the union itself but the effect or consequence of the union, and it is true, solid and also, as they say, most real in the person. For it makes the Word of God truly, solidly and most really man, suffering, dead, raised, taken up in glory; and man truly, solidly and most really eternal God, almighty, immense and everywhere. But it cannot rightly be called such in the natures, because it does not make the Deity truly and solidly humanity or man, to suffer, die, be raised, be taken up in glory, and so on; nor the humanity truly and solidly Deity or God, eternal, almighty, immense and everywhere. For what would such a communion be, unless the Eutychian confusion of properties, and so of natures? So far the first preliminary point is given.

units.la: Sophista autem κοινωνίαν veram solidamque naturarum insidiose intelligit realem illam & mutuam communicationem Idiomatum in naturis factam, hoc est, transfusionem divinarum in carnem, & humanarum in deitatem: licet Chemnitius & saniores aliquot Vbiquitarij nondum absolute mutuam hanc κοινωνίαν idiomatum fateri velint, vnionis vere mutuę fingentes κοινωνίαν idiomatum non vere mutuam in naturis, sed in natura duntaxat humana: quod σοφὸν Φάρμακον seipsum satis elidit, & à Sophista astute hic occultatur, donec sequente disputatione, nitidiore tinctum fuco, si dis placet, in theatrum denuo producat.
units.tr: But the sophist insidiously understands the true and solid fellowship of the natures as that real and mutual communication of attributes made in the natures, that is, the transfusion of divine things into the flesh and of human things into the deity. Yet Chemnitius and some saner Ubiquitarians do not yet wish to admit absolutely this mutual fellowship of attributes, feigning a truly mutual fellowship of attributes not in both natures but in the human nature alone. That "wise remedy" [σοφὸν φάρμακον] destroys itself, and it is cunningly hidden here by the sophist, until in the following disputation he brings it back onto the stage, tinted with a brighter colour, if it please God.

units.la: XL. Itaque humanitati ipsam & λόγῳ personam & hypostasin communicatam, & (vt Diui Cyrilli vtar verbo) ineffabiliter collatam asserimus, ita, vt, Damasceno teste, hypostasis illa verbi sit etiam carnis facta hypostasis.
units.tr: XL. Therefore we assert that the person and hypostasis of the Word are communicated to the humanity and, to use the words of the divine Cyril, ineffably bestowed upon it, so that, according to the testimony of Damascene, that hypostasis of the Word becomes also the hypostasis of the flesh.

units.la: XLI. Si enim Deitas & assumptæ humanitatis natura sunt in Christo persona vna, necessum est, vt illa persona Deitatis λόγου sit vtriq; naturæ communis: Deitati quidem naturaliter, humanitati verò vi vnionis personaliter.
units.tr: XLI. For if the Deity and the assumed humanity are one person in Christ, it is necessary that that person of the Deity, the Word, be common to both natures: to the Deity indeed naturally, but to the humanity personally, by virtue of the union.

units.la: XLII. Et si λόγος non minus atque pueri realiter est particeps carnis & sanguinis, Hebr. 2. quidni caro vicissim ipsius quoque λόγου, seu (quod idem est) hypostaseos eius particeps euasit, idque non modò titulo, sed reuera & solide?
units.tr: XLII. And if the Word no less than the children is really a partaker of flesh and blood, Heb. 2, why should not the flesh in turn have become a partaker of the Word's own, or (which is the same) of his hypostasis, and that not only by title but in truth and solidly?

units.la: XLIII. Aut enim caro reipsa erit persona, quod absurdum est, aut (quod necessarium consequens est) personæ verbi assumentis realiter communicabit.
units.tr: XLIII. For either the flesh will itself be a person, which is absurd, or (which is the necessary consequence) it will really share in the person of the assuming Word.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Hoc alterum est πρῶτον. Humanitati ipsam hypostasin communicatam, & ineffabiliter collatam esse. Datur id quoque, modò sane intelligatur, quod hæc communicatio seu collatio facta sit per vnionem hypostaticam, qua vna eademque λόγου & carnis est facta hypostasis, salvis naturis, & naturarum proprietatibus. Hæc verò communicatio siue collatio hypostasis ministrat, proinde nec Deum, omnipotentem, immensam, illocalem, vbique, &c. quod insidiose inuit inde sequi & conficere tentabit Sophista. Pari sensu vt Orthodorhodoxum accipitur, quod dicit, carnem hypostaseos Ϝ λόγος participem euasisse verè & solidè: & hypostasi verbi assumentis realiter communicare. Neque erat, quod tam operose in probationem desudaret. Sed insidias Sophistæ de κοινωνία ubiquitaria, qua caro sit facta Deus, immensa, illocalis, ubique, quis non observet ac detestetur? Supra quoque Thesi III. faciebat carnem vi unionis personæ verbi capacem: de qua phrasi ibidem videatur Animaduersio.
units.tr: This is the second point, the first having been stated already: that the hypostasis itself has been communicated to the humanity and conferred on it in an ineffable way. This too is granted, provided it is understood that this communication or conferral is made through the hypostatic union, by which one and the same Word and flesh becomes one hypostasis, with the natures and their properties preserved. This communication or conferral of the hypostasis does not supply the flesh with God's omnipotence, immensity, non-locality, omnipresence, and so on, which the sophist will craftily try to infer and conclude from it. The statement that the flesh has truly and solidly become a partaker of the Word, and really communicates in the hypostasis of the assuming Word, is to be taken in the same sense as an orthodox statement. Nor was there any need for him to labour so hard in proving it. But who would not watch out for and detest the sophist's snares concerning the ubiquitarian communion [κοινωνία], by which the flesh is made God, immense, non-local, and everywhere? Above, in Thesis III, he also made the flesh capable through the power of the union of the person of the Word; on that phrase, see the Animadversion there.

units.la: XLIV. Quod si persona verbi communicata & collata est humanitati: vtiq; huius personæ Deitas quoq; communicata ei sit oportet, ne Deitatem λόγος ab illius hypostasi reipsa diuersum quid somniemus. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XLIV. If the person of the Word has been communicated and conferred on the humanity, then its Deity must surely be communicated to it as well, lest we imagine the Deity of the Word to be something really different from his hypostasis. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ne hoc tertium quidem πρόσλημμα negatur: Humanitati communicatam esse ipsam Deitatem Ϝλόγος, hoc est, personaliter vnitam. Nam Deitas λόγος & hypostasis λόγος sunt idem τῇ εἰναι, differunt saltem τῷ λόγῳ. Vt ergo hypostasis, ita etiam Deitas λόγου humanitati vere est & dicitur communicata, seu, vt ille maiuscule pingit, COLLATA, nempe vnione hypostatica, quæ facit, vt Homo, non autem vt Humanitas sit Deus, & ubique. Vnio enim communes facit naturas & proprietates, non naturæ vel naturis, in abstracto, vt vna natura sit altera, vel vtraque, vel habeat vtriusque proprietates: sed personæ in concreto, vt vtriusque naturæ sit persona vna, habens & expetens in se vtriusque proprietates.
units.tr: Not even this third proposition is denied: that the Deity of the Word, that is, the Word's Deity personally united, is communicated to the humanity. For the Deity of the Word and the hypostasis of the Word are the same in being [τῇ εἶναι], differing only in the mode of expression [τῷ λόγῳ]. Therefore, just as the hypostasis, so also the Deity of the Word is truly and rightly said to be communicated to the humanity, or, as he prints it in capitals, CONFERRED; namely by the hypostatic union, which makes the man, not the humanity, God and omnipresent. For the union makes the natures and properties common not in the abstract, so that one nature is the other, or both, or has the properties of both; but in the concrete, in the person, so that there is one person of both natures, having and claiming in itself the properties of both.

units.la: XLV. Ideo enim & Apostolus omnem plenitudinem Deitatis in Christo corporaliter habitare docet, summo post Trinitatis arcanum κοινωνίας modo, quem Scriptores Ecclesiastici similitudine animæ & corporis, necnon ignis & ferri candentis illustrant & explicant. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: XLV. For this reason the Apostle also teaches that all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily in Christ, in the highest mode of communion [κοινωνίας] after the mystery of the Trinity, which the ecclesiastical writers illustrate and explain by the likeness of soul and body, and also of fire and glowing iron. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Deitas λόγος, & plenitudo Deitatis λόγος, idem sunt. Est enim Deitas omnis diuisionis & multiplicationis expers. Vt ergo illa: ita hæc quoque communicata est humanitati, seu, vt Apostolus loquitur, habitat in Christo σωματικῶς, hoc est, corporaliter, seu personaliter: ita vt plenitudo Deitatis inhabitans, & hæc massa inhabitata, sint vnum σῶμα, vnum αὐτοσωπον, vnum suppositum, vt Scholastici vocant. Hæc verò inhabitatio quid ad fictitiam effusionem idiomatum diuinorum in carnem?
units.tr: The Deity of the Word and the fullness of the Deity of the Word are the same. For the Deity is free from all division and multiplication. Therefore, just as that Deity, so this fullness too has been communicated to the humanity; or, as the Apostle says, it dwells in Christ bodily [σωματικῶς], that is, corporeally or personally, so that the fullness of the Deity dwelling within and this indwelt mass are one body [σῶμα], one self-person [αὐτοσωπον], one suppositum, as the Scholastics call it. But what has this indwelling to do with the fictitious outpouring of the divine properties into the flesh?

units.la: De similitudine animæ & corporis, quatenus conueniat, annotarum est supra ad Thesin xx.
units.tr: How far the likeness of soul and body is apt has been noted above at Thesis XX.

units.la: Similitudo ferri seu carbonis, seu gladij igniti, ab Athanasio, Cyrillo & Damasceno, ad pœnitissimam, ac inseparabilem naturarum vnionem & κοινωνίαν declarandam vsurpatur: sed minime per omnia est similis: & si esset, non faueret communioni vbiquitariæ, & si faueret, nihil contra scripturas probaret. Vnio ibi est non duarum substantiarum, sed subiecti & accidentis formalis copulario, quæ vt calorem non facit ferrum, nec durum, nec grauem: ita nec ferrum facit calor, nec molle, nec leue, &c.
units.tr: The likeness of iron or charcoal, or of a glowing sword, is used by Athanasius, Cyril and Damascene to declare the most intimate and inseparable union and communion of the natures. But it is by no means alike in every respect; and even if it were, it would not favour the ubiquitarian communion, and if it did favour it, it would prove nothing against the Scriptures. There the union is not of two substances but a joining of a subject with a formal accident, which, just as heat does not make iron hard or heavy, so heat does not make iron soft or light, and so on.

units.la: XLVI. Sub hac plenitudine omnis Deitatis infalliBiliter omnis maiestas proprietatum verbi intelligitur. De cuius maiestatis κοινωνία adeoque idiomatum communicatione, sequente disputatione, Deo gubernante disseremus.
units.tr: XLVI. Under this fullness of all the Deity, the whole majesty of the properties of the Word is infallibly understood. On the communion of this majesty, and so on the communication of the properties, we shall speak in the following disputation, God willing.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: Animadversion.

units.la: Neque hoc postremum inficiantur Orthodoxi: sub plenitudine omnis Deitatis, omnem maiestatem proprietatum verbi intelligi. Quid enim proprietates verbi, seu naturales, seu characteristicæ sunt aliud, quàm ipsa plenissima Deitas λόγος? Sed facessant insidiæ sophisticæ: Maiestatem proprietatum verbi esse Deitatem, immensitatem, illocalitatem, vbiquitatem, vi vnionis à verbo in carnem realitet transfusam: quam si Sophista sequente disputatione astruere tentabit, Deo gubernante, errunt, qui solidissimis verbi diuini & piæ Antiquitatis argumentis destruent. Monetur interim, si nihil monstri alit, vt loquatur recto ore sine περιτολογίας. Nam ἀνυπέρμαντος σαφὴς.
units.tr: The Orthodox do not deny this last point either: under the fullness of all the Godhead, all the majesty of the Word's properties is understood. For what are the properties of the Word, whether natural or characteristic, other than the most full Godhead itself, the λόγος [Logos]? But let the sophistical snares go away. That the majesty of the Word's properties is the Godhead, immensity, non-locality, and ubiquity, transfused from the Word into the flesh in reality by the power of the union, is something the Sophist will try to establish in the following disputation, God willing. Those who will refute it with the most solid arguments of the divine Word and of pious antiquity will be in the right. Meanwhile, he is admonished, if he harbours nothing monstrous, to speak with an upright mouth, without perissology [περιτολογίας]. For the unanswerable is plain [ἀνυπέρμαντος σαφὴς].

units.la: EPISTOLA D. DAVIDIS PAREI AD ILLVSTREM ET GENEROSVM COMITEM, Dn. LVDOVICVM WITGENSTENIVM, &c. DE JUSTITIA CHRISTI actiua & passiua.
units.tr: LETTER OF D. DAVID PAREUS TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS AND NOBLE COUNT, LORD LUDWIG OF WITTGENSTEIN, ETC., ON THE ACTIVE AND PASSIVE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF CHRIST.

units.la: S.
units.tr: S.

units.la: QVod serius, quàm oportuit, postulationi tuæ re-spondeo, illustris ac Generose Comes, Domine Clemen-tissime: id primum oro, ne alicui culpæ, aut negligentiæ meæ ascribas. Tanta certè sunt tua in Ecclesiam, & in meipsum merita, vt vel nutui tuo totus seruiam merito aclubens. Concatenata negotiorum moles me totum hucusque varie distinuit: atque adeo à scriptione aliquoties incepta identidem retraxit.
units.tr: I reply to your request later than I should have, illustrious and noble Count, my most gracious Lord. Above all I ask that you not attribute this to any fault or negligence of mine. Your merits toward the Church and toward me are so great that I would gladly and rightly serve you entirely at a nod. A tangled mass of business has kept me occupied in various ways until now, and so I have repeatedly been drawn away from writing, though I had begun it several times.

units.la: Sed, vt quod res est, fatear, iudicium meum controuersiis non libenter interpono: tum quod agnoscam, quàm id sit exiguum: tum quod pro ea, quam semper colui, φιλαυτίᾳ[?] me litibus alienis non libenter admisceam: & huic præsertim, quæ est ἀεὶ δι-[?] ὑμάχη[?]: de qua nescio qui fiat, quod Ecclesiis nostris male metuam, ne quod dicitur, sit nobis ἀχαθὸς[?], ἐ ἀπνμα[?]. Scimus in hoc capite repurgationem doctrinæ nostro seculo coepisse. Vtinam in hoc non deficiat! Scripturæ phrasis plana sententia simplex est; nos iustificari propter sanguinem & mortem Christi, & iustificationem nostram esse remissionem peccatorum. Nunc disputatur, an morte Filij DEI iustificemur: an sola: immò an etiam temporaria: an res, qua imputata iustificamur, sit vna, an multiplex: simplex, an conflata ex partibus, duabus vel tribus: an imputatio sit vna, an duplex, vel triplex: an remissio peccatorum sit tota vel dimidia iustificatio, & nescio quid aliud: in quibus ego quidem iudico, plus periculosæ subtilitatis, quàm solidæ veritatis, plusque ingenij quàm fidei à plerisque adhiberi. Et hæc dissidia non solum in vicinia vestra palam vigent: sed passim nunc disseminantur, & prout ingenia inveniuntur, guta, varie agitantur. In alio angulo non ita procul à vobis remoto aliud glisćit certamen periculosius, de Iustitia DEI ἀνσμικῇ, insit ne Deo natura an tantum voluntate: ut sicut Deus vult cras pluere aut non pluere, natura eius neutrum horum exigente: ita velit aut non velit peccatum diabolorum & hominum auersari ac punire, natura quoque eius neutrum iustorum postulante: quod quidam Socinianis misti argutiis, nurum postulante: quod quidam Socinianis misti argutiis, per mouere cœperunt: per quem cuniculum satan necessitatem satisfactionis, ipsamque adeo satisfactionem Christi pro nobis, & sic una omnem fidem nostram labefactare, funditusque tandem euertere sine dubio conatur. Huc enim tendere Socinianas argutias minime obscurum est. Deus bone, quid sibi vult iste argutandi pruritus? & hæc nouandi omniaq; concuellendi libido? Quicquid heri somniarunt, hodie pro oraculis in Cathedras efferunt, & mordicus tuentur: cras aliud sentiunt: & quoties vestes toties sententias mutant: Quasi in Ecclesia opinionum, portentorum & litium non sit plus satis. Metuo nimis, ne istæ fauillæ in funestū breui erumpant incendiū, quo Ecclesiæ nostræ, nisi vigilemus, sensim correptæ, miserè tandē conflagrent. Præclara igitur laude dignum est studium tuum, curaque singularis tua, Generose Comes, quod pro eximia pietate & senili prudentia tua, glisćentia hæc mala non suspicere facis, sed sentis rem tuam agi, paries dum proximus ardet, vulneriq; recenti pro virili remedium quæris. Quod ad me attinet, etsi fateor, me hanc controuersiam non libenter attingetinet, etsi fateor, me hanc controuersiam non libenter attingere: tum quod iudico, re, ac modis omnibus consepultam cupere: tum quod iudico, eam Ecclesiis & scholis Euangelicis vehementer indignā esse, in hac præsertim scripturæ sacræ & doctrinæ repurgatæ clarissimæ luce: tum quod aduersarios iam pridem ex dissidiis nostris veritatis oppressionem captare video: tum deniq; quod in præcipiti est, quicquid dixero, ne oleum camino, quod dicitur, infundere velle videar, propter aliquorum calorem, qui hanc causam ita agunt, ut fratres, vel verbo dissentientes vix ferre possint: tamen cum videam, rem postulari ab officio & professione mea haud alienam, non grauabor de eo quod quæritur liberè sententiam meam eplicare. Atque ut ad omnia Generositatis tuæ interrogata ordine respondeam: Primò præcipua sententiarum & rationum controuersiæ huius momenta breuiter attingam: sola ne Iustistia Christi passiua, an etiam actiua ad iustitiam nobis imputetur. Tum quid de sententiis aliorum mihi videatur: paucis & quid ad sarciendam concordiam facto opus iudicem, paucis aperiam. Tertiò an sit consultum hoc argumentum ἁμαρτωλῶν ἢ ἀνα-μαρτήτων pro concione tractare. Et denique, an necesse sit in Catechesi & Agenda Palatina aliqua omittere, aut eradere, breuiter quoque monebo.
units.tr: But, to confess the truth, I do not willingly take sides in controversies. I know how small my judgment is, and because of the love of self (φιλαυτία) that I have always cultivated, I do not willingly mix myself into other people's quarrels, especially this one, which is an endless contest [ἀεὶ διαμάχη]. I do not know why, but I fear for our Churches that what is said is for us a kind of evil [ἀχαθός] and something unclear [ἀπνμα]. We know that the cleansing of doctrine on this point began in our age. Would that it did not fail here! The plain sense of Scripture is simple: we are justified on account of the blood and death of Christ, and our justification is the forgiveness of sins. Now it is disputed whether we are justified by the death of the Son of God, or by it alone; or indeed whether also by something temporary; whether the thing by which we are justified when it is imputed is one or many, simple or compounded of two or three parts; whether the imputation is single, double or triple; whether the forgiveness of sins is the whole or only half of justification, and a good deal else besides. In these matters I judge that more dangerous subtlety, than solid truth, and more cleverness than faith, is brought to bear by most people. And these dissensions not only flourish openly in your neighbourhood, but are now spread everywhere and are tossed about in various ways according to the wits that are found. In another corner, not far from you, a more dangerous contest is gaining strength, about the necessary [ἀναγκαίᾳ] justice of God: whether God has his nature necessarily or only by will, so that just as God wills whether it rains tomorrow or not, his nature requiring neither, so also he wills or does not will to turn away from and punish the sin of devils and men, his nature likewise demanding neither of the two of the just. Some have begun to move this idea, mixed with Socinian subtleties, by which path, without doubt, Satan tries to call into question the necessity of satisfaction, and indeed the satisfaction of Christ for us, and so to shake all our faith and at last overturn it from the foundations. For it is not at all obscure that the Socinian subtleties tend that way. Good God, what does this itch for arguing mean, and this lust for novelty and for overturning everything? Whatever they dreamed yesterday, today they bring forward from their chairs as oracles and defend stubbornly; tomorrow they think otherwise, and as often as they change their clothes they change their opinions. As if in the Church there were not already more than enough of opinions, monstrosities and quarrels! I greatly fear that these sparks will soon break out into a deadly conflagration, by which our Churches, unless we keep watch, will be gradually seized and at last wretchedly burned up. Your zeal, therefore, and your special care, noble Count, deserve praise of distinguished merit, because by your outstanding piety and old-age prudence you do not let these growing evils go unnoticed, but perceive that your own house is being threatened, since the wall next to you is burning, and you seek, as far as you can, a remedy for the fresh wound. As for me, although I confess that I do not willingly touch this controversy: because I judge that it is best buried in every way; because I judge it deeply unworthy of the Evangelical Churches and schools, especially in the very clear light of holy Scripture and of purified doctrine; because I see that our adversaries have long been hoping, from our dissensions, to seize the oppression of the truth; and finally because, whatever I say, it is a dangerous matter, lest I seem to want to pour oil on the fire, as they say, on account of the heat of some who handle this cause in such a way that they can hardly bear brothers who dissent even in words: nevertheless, since I see that the matter is required by my office and profession, which are not foreign to it, I will not hesitate to explain my opinion freely on what is asked. And so that I may answer all your questions in order: first, I will briefly touch on the main points of the opinions and arguments of this controversy: whether the passive righteousness of Christ alone, or also his active righteousness, is imputed to us for righteousness. Then I will briefly set out what seems right to me about the opinions of others, and what I judge needs to be done to restore concord. Thirdly, whether it is advisable to treat this subject from the pulpit, among sinners or among the sinless. And finally, I will also briefly advise whether it is necessary to omit or erase anything in the Catechism and the Palatine Agenda.

units.la: PRIMVM caput quod attinet, quo statvs controuersiæ intelligatur rectius, tenendum, in quo conueniant & dissideant disceptantes. Conuenit ergo inter omnes:
units.tr: As for the first point, so that the state of the controversy may be understood more rightly, we must note what the disputants agree on and where they differ. They agree, then, on all these points:

units.la: I. Iustificare forensi significatione esse idem quod à reatu absoluere & iustum reputare.
units.tr: I. To justify, in the forensic sense, is the same as to absolve from guilt and to reckon as righteous.

units.la: II. Nos peccatores iustificari coram Deo, non legaliter, sed euangelicè, hoc est, non operibus, sed fide: non nostra iustitia, sed aliena.
units.tr: II. We sinners are justified before God not legally but evangelically, that is, not by works but by faith; not by our own righteousness but by another's.

units.la: III. Hanc alienam iustitiam non infundi, sed imputari à Deo credentibus, idque gratis.
units.tr: III. This alien righteousness is not infused but imputed by God to believers, and that freely.

units.la: IV. Applicationem iustitiæ imputatæ fieri sola fide: & fide iustificari idem esse quod iustitia aliena imputata, & per fidem applicata, iustificari.
units.tr: IV. The application of the imputed righteousness is made by faith alone; and to be justified by faith is the same as to be justified by alien righteousness imputed and applied through faith.

units.la: V. Hanc denique alienam iustitiam esse solius Christi meritum & satisfactionem pro nobis seu iustitiam Christi nobis imputatam.
units.tr: V. Finally, this alien righteousness is the sole merit and satisfaction of Christ for us, or the righteousness of Christ imputed to us.

units.la: Dissident vero in huius meriti, seu iustitiæ Christi explicatione.
units.tr: But they differ in the explanation of this merit, or righteousness of Christ.

units.la: Primum enim sicut iustitia Dei in scriptura ὁμοιουμένως signi-ficat modo eam, qua Deus ipse iustus est, modo eam, qua nos iustificat: sic iustitia Christi ὁμοιουμένως dicitur tum ea, qua Christus θεάνθρωπος ipse iustus est, tum ea quam nobis est meritus, & quam nobis donet per fidem, ex cuius ὁμοιουμένως neglectu tota controuersia nascitur.
units.tr: For first, just as the righteousness of God in Scripture is used homonymously [ὁμωνύμως], sometimes for that by which God himself is just, and sometimes for that by which he justifies us, so also the righteousness of Christ is used homonymously, sometimes for that by which Christ, the God-man [θεάνθρωπος], is himself righteous, and sometimes for that which he has merited for us and gives us through faith. From neglect of this homonymy the whole controversy arises.

units.la: Deinde cum in Christo θείᾳ καὶ ἀνθρώπῳ à plerisque ponatur iustitia quadruplex: 1. Diuina essentialis. 2. Humana formalis, seu Originalis. 3. Actiua impletio legis. 4. Passiua obedientia: quæsitum est, omnes ne hæ iustitiæ, an aliquæ, an postrema sola sit res ea, qua imputata iustificamur.
units.tr: Next, since most people posit a fourfold righteousness in Christ, both divine and human [θείᾳ καὶ ἀνθρώπῳ]: (1) divine, essential; (2) human, formal or original; (3) active fulfilment of the law; (4) passive obedience. The question is whether all these righteousnesses, or some, or only the last, is the thing by which we are justified when it is imputed.

units.la: Aliqui materiam: alii formam iustitiæ nostræ appellant. Ego docendi causa Materiam appellabo.
units.tr: Some call it the matter of our righteousness, others its form. For the sake of teaching I will call it the matter.

units.la: Hæc quæstio secum traxit aliam de forma iustificationis nostræ, sitne remissio peccatorum tota an dimidia nostra iustificatio.
units.tr: This question has drawn with it another about the form of our justification: whether the forgiveness of sins is our whole justification or only half of it.

units.la: Et quantum recordari possum, hæc controuersia circa annum 64. primum inter Marchiacos quosdam Theologos agitari coepta est: deinde anno 70. interuentu Academiæ Witebergensis vtcumque sopita, vel potius suppressa. Prius vero Ecclesiis Euangelicis ignota fuit, neque in scriptis Lutheri, Melanchthonis, Zuinglii, Caluini, Martyris, Musculi, Hyperii, aliorumque huius seculi Theologorum quicquam iltius, quod sciam, disceptatum legitur: sed recepta fuit omnium consensu simplex illa scripturæ doctrina, nos mortis Christi iustificari, cum propter eam habeamus remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: And, as far as I can remember, this controversy was first stirred up around the year 1564 among certain Marchian theologians; then in 1570 it was somehow calmed, or rather suppressed, through the mediation of the University of Wittenberg. Before that it was unknown to the Evangelical Churches, and as far as I know nothing of it is read in the writings of Luther, Melanchthon, Zwingli, Calvin, Martyr, Musculus, Hyperius, or the other theologians of this age; but that simple doctrine of Scripture was received by the consensus of all: that we are justified by the death of Christ, and that on account of it we have the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Nunc sunt quasi quatuor sententiæ: quod scribens recordor Lombardi, vbi quatuor etiam sententias suorum de iustificatione recenseт, nesciens ipse quid sentiat.
units.tr: Now there are, as it were, four opinions. As I write this I recall Lombard, who also lists four opinions of his own school about justification, while not knowing himself what he thinks.

units.la: Primi sunt, qui omnes illas Christi iustitias vno complexu nobis imputari volunt. His igitur materia iustificationis est quadruplex illa CHRISTI iustitia: forma, quadripartita imputatio. Hanc tamen aliquando reuocant ad duas partes: remissionem peccatorum, propter mortem Christi, & imputationem iustitiæ Christi, diuinæ, humanæ, & actiuæ &c. Et ratio horum propria est, quod totus Christus Deus & homo sit noster sacerdos, rex, seruator &c. quodque dignitas meriti Christi cum primis à dignitate personæ, hoc est, à dignitate diuinitatis pendeat.
units.tr: The first are those who want all those righteousnesses of Christ to be imputed to us in one complex. For them, therefore, the matter of justification is that fourfold righteousness of CHRIST; the form is a fourfold imputation. Sometimes, however, they reduce this to two parts: the forgiveness of sins on account of the death of Christ, and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, divine, human, active, and so on. The reason for these people is peculiar: that the whole Christ, God and man, is our priest, king, saviour, and so on; and that the dignity of Christ's merit depends above all on the dignity of his person, that is, on the dignity of his divinity.

units.la: Alii, tres posteriores Christi iustitias materiam, & triplicem harum imputationem formam iustificationis statuunt: & docent, imputari nobis, Primo passiuam obedientiam ad hoc vt simus non iniusti, hoc est, ad remissionem peccatorum: Secundo, Actiuam obedientiam ad hoc, vt simus iusti, hoc est, ad iustitiam. Tertio, formalem siue habitualem, vt loquuntur, ad sanctitatem ad hoc, vt censeamur sancti, hoc est, ad sanctitatem perfectam.
units.tr: Others hold that the three latter righteousnesses of Christ are the matter, and that their threefold imputation is the form of justification. They teach that there is imputed to us: (1) his passive obedience, so that we may not be unrighteous, that is, for the remission of sins; (2) his active obedience, so that we may be righteous, that is, for righteousness; (3) his formal or habitual obedience, as they call it, for holiness, so that we may be counted holy, that is, for perfect holiness.

units.la: Tertii duas tantum Christi iustitias posteriores materiam, & geminam harum imputationem formam iustificationis faciunt.
units.tr: Those of the third view make only the two latter righteousnesses of Christ the matter, and their twofold imputation the form of justification.

units.la: Omnes tres isti hoc habent commune, quod remissionem peccatorum & iustificationem distinguunt, vt partem & totum: aliquando etiam vt partes integrales totius: & priorem mortem, posteriorem actiuæ obedientiæ, vendicant. Omnes etiam communibus fere scripturæ dictis & argumentis niuntur: ex quibus præcipua breuiter subiiciam.
units.tr: All three of these hold in common that they distinguish the remission of sins and justification as part and whole, sometimes also as integral parts of a whole. They assign the former to his death and the latter to his active obedience. All of them also rely on nearly the same sayings and arguments of Scripture, of which I shall briefly set out the chief ones.

units.la: I. Sicut vnius inobedientia peccatores facti sunt multi: sic vnius obedientia iusti constituuntur multi. Rom.5. At inobedientia Adami fuit actiua: Ergo & obedientia Christi actiua iustificamur.
units.tr: I. As by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by one man's obedience many are made righteous. Rom. 5. But Adam's disobedience was active; therefore we are justified also by Christ's active obedience.

units.la: II. Factus obediens vsque ad mortem crucis, Philipp. 2. Duplex hic Christi obedientia: vna ante mortem, altera in morte: Ergo vtraque imputatur.
units.tr: II. "Made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross," Phil. 2. Here there is a twofold obedience of Christ: one before death, the other in death. Therefore both are imputed.

units.la: III. Deus emisit Filium suum factum ex muliere, factum legi obnoxium, ut eos, qui legi erant obnoxij, redimeret. Galat. 4. Ergo actiua impletio legis à CHRISTO praestita nobis imputatur.
units.tr: III. God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law. Gal. 4. Therefore the active fulfilment of the law performed by Christ is imputed to us.

units.la: IV. Factus nobis à Deo sapientia, justitia, sanctificatio, &c. 1 Cor. 1. Ergo justitia & sanctitas nobis imputatur.
units.tr: IV. "Made unto us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, etc." 1 Cor. 1. Therefore righteousness and holiness are imputed to us.

units.la: V. Lex spiritus vitæ in Christo Jesu liberauit me à lege peccati & mortis, Rom. 8, 2. Ergo Christi vita seu obedientia actiua etiam imputatur.
units.tr: V. "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death," Rom. 8:2. Therefore Christ's life, or his active obedience, is also imputed.

units.la: VI. Totus Christus est justitia nostra, justificat nos. Ergo totus imputatur.
units.tr: VI. Christ whole is our righteousness; he justifies us. Therefore he is imputed whole.

units.la: VII. Justitia actiua non potest excludi à merito Christi, & à justificatione. Ergo imputatur.
units.tr: VII. Active righteousness cannot be excluded from the merit of Christ and from justification. Therefore it is imputed.

units.la: VIII. Lex obligat & ad obedientiam & ad poenam. Ergo oportuit Christum & obedientiam legis pro nobis implere, & poenam perferre.
units.tr: VIII. The law binds both to obedience and to punishment. Therefore it was necessary for Christ to fulfil the obedience of the law for us and to bear the punishment.

units.la: IX. Qualibus lex vitam promittit, tales necesse est nos Christi gratia effici, ut vitam consequamur. Lex vitam promittit non iis, qui legem non transgrediuntur, sed iis, qui totam implent. Atqui imputatione passiuæ obedientiæ censemur qui dem non injusti, non peccatores, seu legē non transgredientes: nondum verò censemur justi, seu legem implentes. Quid enim vanius, quàm justum arbitrari eum, qui legem non impleuit? Ergo oportet non solū imputari passiuam obedientiam ad hoc, ut simus non injusti, seu non transgressores legis, sed etiam actiuam ad hoc, ut simus justi, seu legem implentes. Qui enim pro non peccatore censetur in Christo, mortem quidem effugerit: sed quo jure vitam præterea petet, nisi omnem justitiam legis in eodem Christo impleuerit.
units.tr: IX. As the law promises life, so we must be made such by the grace of Christ that we may obtain life. The law promises life not to those who do not transgress it, but to those who keep all of it. Yet by the imputation of passive obedience we are indeed counted not unrighteous, not sinners, not transgressors of the law; we are not yet counted righteous, or fulfillers of the law. For what is more empty than to consider someone righteous who has not fulfilled the law? Therefore it is necessary that not only passive obedience be imputed, so that we are not unrighteous or transgressors of the law, but also active obedience, so that we are righteous, or fulfillers of the law. For he who is counted in Christ as a non-sinner will indeed escape death; but by what right will he claim life besides, unless he has fulfilled in the same Christ all the righteousness of the law?

units.la: X. Sacrificium & mors CHRISTI nos consolatur aduersus reatum & mortem æternam: sanctitas verò eius aduersus inhærentem adhuc impuritatem, seu reliquias peccatorum. Ergo ad consolationem nostram vtriusque imputatio est necessaria.
units.tr: X. The sacrifice and death of Christ comfort us against guilt and eternal death; but his holiness comforts us against the impurity still dwelling in us, or the remnants of sin. Therefore both imputations are necessary for our comfort.

units.la: XI. Denique Catechesis Palatina docent qq. LX. & LXI. perfectam satisfactionem, justitiam & sanctitatem Christi nobis imputari & donari, ut sit nostra justitia. Et q.XXXVI. Mediatorem sua innocentia ac perfecta sanctitate, nostra peccata, in quibus concepti sumus, tegere, ne in conspectum Dei veniant. Idem in Agenda Palatina passim repetitur.
units.tr: XI. Finally, the Palatine Catechism teaches in Q. 60 and 61 that Christ's perfect satisfaction, righteousness and holiness are imputed and given to us, so that they may be our righteousness. And in Q. 36 that the Mediator covers our sins, in which we were conceived, by his innocence and perfect holiness, so that they do not come into the sight of God. The same is repeated throughout the Palatine Agenda.

units.la: Exposui bona fide argumenta, quibus priores illi suas defendunt opiniones.
units.tr: I have set out in good faith the arguments by which those former men defend their opinions.

units.la: Restant quarti, qui solam passiuam Christi obedientiam justitiam nostram esse statuunt, & justificationem sola remissione peccatorum definiunt. Hi duobus praecipuè nituntur argumentis ex scriptura desumtis: vnum à materia: alterum à formis justificationis.
units.tr: There remain the fourth group, who hold that the passive obedience of Christ alone is our righteousness, and define justification by the remission of sins alone. They rely chiefly on two arguments drawn from Scripture: one from the matter, the other from the forms of justification.

units.la: Prius hoc est. Scriptura nostrae justitiae totam materiam ostendit in passione, cruce, sanguine, morte Christi. Ergo haec sola est res, propter quam justificamur.
units.tr: The first is this. Scripture shows the whole matter of our righteousness in the passion, cross, blood and death of Christ. Therefore this alone is the thing on account of which we are justified.

units.la: Antecedens probant testimonii scripturae: a Iustificamur gratis per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius. b Iustificamur sanguine ipsius. Reconciliati per mortem Filij eius. c Eum, qui non nouit peccatum, fecit peccatum, id est, hostiam pro peccato, vt nos fieremus justitia Dei in eo. d Factus pro nobis exsecratio in ligno, redemit nos ab exsecratione legis. e Habemus redemptionem per sanguinem eius, f Pacem reconciliauit in corpore carnis suae per mortem. g Redempti sumus preciosò sanguine Agni immaculati. h Cuius vibicibus sanati sumus. i Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato. k Redemisti nos per sanguinem tuum. Lauerunt stolas suas & dealbarunt in sanguine Agni.
units.tr: They prove the antecedent by testimonies of Scripture: (a) We are justified freely through the redemption made in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. (b) We are justified by his blood; we are reconciled through the death of his Son. (c) He who knew no sin he made to be sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. (d) Made a curse for us on the tree, he redeemed us from the curse of the law. (e) We have redemption through his blood. (f) He reconciled peace in the body of his flesh through death. (g) We were redeemed with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb. (h) By his stripes we were healed. (i) The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. (k) You redeemed us by your blood. They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

units.la: Posterius hoc est. Scriptura totam justificationem nostram definit remissione peccatorum propter sanguinem Christi. Ergo sola sanguinis effusio est id, cuius imputatione justificamur: & remissio peccatorum est tota nostra justitia.
units.tr: The second is this. Scripture defines our whole justification as the remission of sins on account of the blood of Christ. Therefore the shedding of blood alone is that by whose imputation we are justified, and the remission of sins is our whole righteousness.

units.la: Antecedens confirmant scripturae testimoniis. a Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori. Dico vobis, descendit hic justificatus in domum suam prae illo. b Notum sit vobis, vobis annunciari remissionem peccatorum per istum, & ab omnibus, à quibus per legem non potuistis absolui, per hunc omnem, qui credit, justificari.
units.tr: They confirm the antecedent with testimonies of Scripture: (a) "God, be merciful to me a sinner." "I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." (b) "Be it known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things from which you could not be absolved by the law."

units.la: Hic absolui, justificari, habere remissionem peccatorum idem valent. Dauid pronunciat beatum eum hominem, cui Deus imputat justitiam absq; operibus. a Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt peccata. Beatus vir, cui Deus non imputavit peccatum. b Quis intentabit crimina electis Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus est, qui mortuus est, &c. c Deus erat in Christo reconcilians sibi mundum, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum. d In quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem eius, hoc est, remissionem peccatorum, &c.
units.tr: Here to be absolved, to be justified, and to have the remission of sins mean the same. David pronounces blessed the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works. (a) "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin." (b) "Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is it that condemns? It is Christ who died, etc." (c) "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them." (d) "In whom we have redemption through his blood, that is, the remission of sins, etc."

units.la: Habent hi & alia argumenta, quae breuitatis causa non attinget. Allegant quoque pro se Catechesin Palatinam qq. XXXVII. XLV. LXVI. LVI. LVII. LXXII. LXXVI. LXXX. LXXXIV. &c. quibus docetur, nos remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & vitam aeternam bam obtinere propter vnicum Christi sacrificium in cruce peractum: & solum sanguinem Christi purgare nos ab omni peccato: quod ipsum in Agenda Palatina passim repetitur.
units.tr: They have other arguments too, which for the sake of brevity I will not touch. They also cite in their favour the Palatine Catechism, Q. 37, 45, 66, 56, 57, 72, 76, 80, 84, etc., in which it is taught that we obtain remission of sins, righteousness and eternal life on account of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross, and that the blood of Christ alone cleanses us from all sin. This too is repeated throughout the Palatine Agenda.

units.la: Hactenus discrepantes sententiae ἐξὶ δικαιώματος.
units.tr: So far the differing opinions concerning the one act of righteousness [ἐξ ἑνὸς δικαιώματος].

units.la: AD SECVNDVM caput transeo, ostensurus breviter, saluis aliorum judiciis, quid in his probare possim, vel secus.
units.tr: I come to the second chapter, intending to show briefly, saving the judgments of others, what I can prove in these matters, or otherwise.

units.la: Qui primam sententiam sequuntur, non video, quomodo ex scriptura probare possint essentialis justitiæ diuinæ imputationem: vel quorsum ea imputari dicatur, cum homo ad eam habendam vel praestandam nunquam fuerit obligatus. Nunquam enim Deus essentialem suam justitiam homini contulerat, nunquam homo eam amiserat. Faciunt ergo iniustum Deum, quasi ab homine postulet justitiam diuinam, quam nunquam ei derat, neque in aeternum est daturus.
units.tr: Those who follow the first opinion: I do not see how they can prove from Scripture the imputation of the essential righteousness of God, or why it should be said to be imputed, since man was never obliged to have or to render it. For God had never bestowed his essential righteousness on man, and man had never lost it. They therefore make God unjust, as if he demanded from man the divine righteousness, which he had never given him and will never give in eternity.

units.la: Ratio eorum est paralogismus non causæ. Etsi n. Christus totus est sacerdos, rex, seruator, & totus iustificat: notum tamen est, quod ἀποτελέσματος officii, inter quæ est Iustificatio, distinctis naturarum operationibus peragat. Totus igitur iustificat, sed aliter secundum Deitatem, nempe ut causa efficiens: aliter secundum humanitatem, nempe ut causa promerens. Et fluit quidem dignitas meriti à dignitate personæ: hoc est à divinitate mediatoris: verum hinc non sequitur diuinitatem venire in partem meriti, sed tantum esse meriti fontem. Oportebat enim Mediatorem esse Deum, non ut Deitas vel iustitia Deitatis nobis imputaretur, aut juxta Osiandri delirium, essentialiter in nobis habitans iustitia nostra fieret, sed propter causam in Catechesi q xvii. explicatam. Differunt igitur justitia Deitatis & meritum, ut efficiens & effectum.
units.tr: Their reasoning is a paralogism of cause. For although Christ is wholly priest, king and saviour, and wholly justifies, it is nevertheless known that he accomplishes the effects [ἀποτελεσμάτων] of his office, among which is justification, by the distinct operations of his natures. He therefore justifies wholly, but differently according to the Deity, namely as efficient cause, and differently according to the humanity, namely as meritorious cause. The dignity of the merit indeed flows from the dignity of the person, that is, from the divinity of the Mediator; but it does not follow from this that the divinity enters into the part of the merit, only that it is the fountain of the merit.
