For it was necessary that the Mediator be God, not so that the Deity or the righteousness of the Deity should be imputed to us, or, according to Osiander's raving, so that our righteousness should become one essentially dwelling in us, but on account of the cause explained in Catechism Q. 17. Therefore the righteousness of the Deity and the merit differ as efficient cause and effect.

units.la: Alia huius sententiae incommoda etiam ad duas sequentes pertinent. Secundam igitur & tertiam sententiam coniungo, nec differunt, nisi quod vna tres, altera duas partes facit iustitiae imputatae.
units.tr: Other drawbacks of this view also bear on the two following opinions. I therefore join the second and third opinions. They differ only in that one divides the imputed righteousness into three parts and the other into two.

units.la: Omnes vero hæ sententiæ iisdem incommodis laborant.
units.tr: All these opinions suffer from the same drawbacks.

units.la: I. Omnes confundunt justitiam personæ & meriti Christi, quam scriptura frequenter coniungit quidem, sed & manifeste distinguit, ut causam efficientem, vel ὡς ὁ ποιῶν, & causam materialem justitiæ nostræ: ut: seruus meus iustus notitia sui iustificabit multos. Talis nobis conueniebat pontifex qui esset sanctus, separatus a peccatoribus: ut non pro suis sed pro populi peccatis offerret. Eum qui non novit peccatum fecit pro nobis peccatum, ut nos, &c. 1. Petr. 3. Christus passus est semel iustus pro iniustis. Sic & Catechesis nostra: quæst. 15.16.
units.tr: I. They all confuse the righteousness of Christ's person with the merit of Christ, which Scripture frequently joins but also clearly distinguishes, as the efficient cause, or ὡς ὁ ποιῶν [as the one who does], and the material cause of our righteousness. For example: "My servant, the Righteous One, by his knowledge shall justify many" (Isa. 53:11). Such a high priest was fitting for us, one who was holy, separated from sinners, so that he might offer not for his own sins but for the sins of the people (Heb. 7:26–27). "He made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin" (2 Cor. 5:21), so that we, etc. "Christ suffered once, the just for the unjust" (1 Pet. 3:18). So also our Catechism, questions 15 and 16.

units.la: II. Distinctiones inter non iniustum & iustum esse, inter legem non transgredi, & legem implere, inter non mortuum & viuum esse : plus habent subtilitatis, quam veritatis, cum reuera sint termini æquipollentes, vt postea ostendam. Necessario enim qui coram Deo non est iniustus est iustus: qui legem non transgreditur implet: qui non est mortuus, viuit: siquidem hæc omnia sunt contraria ἀμιτα: quorum vno posito, vel negato, necesse sit poni vel negari alterum.
units.tr: II. The distinctions between not being unrighteous and being righteous, between not transgressing the law and fulfilling the law, and between not being dead and being alive, have more subtlety than truth. In fact they are equivalent terms, as I will show later. For whoever is not unrighteous before God is necessarily righteous; whoever does not transgress the law fulfils it; whoever is not dead lives. All these are opposites [ἀντικείμενα], so that when one is posited or denied, the other must necessarily be posited or denied.

units.la: III. Si passiuæ obedientiæ imputatione nondum sumus iusti, sed tantum non iniusti: quomodo verum illud: iustificati per sanguinem filii eius: reconciliati per mortem, &c.
units.tr: III. If by the imputation of passive obedience we are not yet righteous but only not unrighteous, how is that true which says: "justified by his blood" (Rom. 5:9), "reconciled by his death" (Rom. 5:10), etc.?

units.la: IV. Si remissio peccatorum non est iustificatio tota: quomodo verum illud: Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates: Rom.4.& quomodo Apostolus ibidem pro eodem sumit, imputare iustitiam, &, non imputare peccatum?
units.tr: IV. If the remission of sins is not the whole of justification, how is that true which says: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven" (Rom. 4:7)? And how does the Apostle in the same place take the same thing as "imputing righteousness" and "not imputing sin"?

units.la: V. Si omissio obedientiæ legis & imperfectio sanctitatis notæ non expiantur passiua obedientia Christi: sed necesse est, illam quidem actuali Christi obedientia, hanc vero natiua sanctitate tegi: quomodo rursus verum illud: Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato? nisi forte omissio & imperfectio illa non sint peccata.
units.tr: V. If the omission of obedience to the law and the imperfection of holiness are not expiated by the passive obedience of Christ, but must be covered, the former by his active obedience and the latter by his innate holiness, how is that true again which says: "The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7)? Unless perhaps those omissions and imperfections are not sins.

units.la: VI. Si non passiua sed actiua obedientia Christi iustificamur: quomodo Christus non est frustra mortuus? Quid enim necesse erat Christum mori, & moriendo mereri nobis remissionem peccatorum: si iuste & sancte viuendo iam meritus nobis iustitiam? Iustitia enim remissionem peccatorum necessario præsupponit.
units.tr: VI. If we are justified not by the passive but by the active obedience of Christ, then is Christ not dead in vain (Gal. 2:21)? For why was it necessary for Christ to die and by dying to merit for us the forgiveness of sins, if by living justly and holily he had already merited righteousness for us? For righteousness necessarily presupposes the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: VII. Manifestum est, omnem illam partitionem meriti Christi aut iustitiæ Dei in duo vel tria membra, aut morti Christi plurimum derogare. Nam duæ vel tres illæ iustitiæ nostræ partes, vel sunt tres perfectæ iustitiæ Christi satisfacientes legi per se singulæ: vel sunt totidem imperfectæ, ad vnam perfectam conflandam concurrentes. Si imperfectæ: an non aperte derogatur morti Christi? Si perfectæ, quomodo non iniustus Deus, qui pro vna culpa tres vel duas perfectas satisfactiones postulat, cum iustitia eius non nisi vnam requirat?
units.tr: VII. It is plain that every such division of the merit of Christ or of the righteousness of God into two or three members greatly detracts from the death of Christ. For those two or three parts of our righteousness are either three perfect righteousnesses of Christ, each satisfying the law by itself, or they are as many imperfect parts, combining to make up one perfect righteousness. If they are imperfect, is not the death of Christ plainly detracted from? If they are perfect, how is God not unjust, who for one fault demands two or three perfect satisfactions, when his justice requires only one?

units.la: VIII. Si pars iustitiæ nostræ quærenda est hic, pars ibi: pars in morte, pars in antegressa obedientia actuali, pars in natiua sanctitate Christi: quomodo non periculose distrahitur fides, & labefactatur consolatio nostra?
units.tr: VIII. If part of our righteousness is to be sought here, part there, part in his death, part in his preceding active obedience, part in the innate holiness of Christ, how is faith not dangerously torn apart, and our comfort not weakened?

units.la: IX. Denique, quod vnum me maxime hic impedit, nusquam legi, sacras scripturas sic tripartiri aut bipartiri iustitiã nostrã esse, nusquam legi, sanctitatem humanam Christi nobis imputari. esse iustitiam nostram, vel eius partem. Si quis legit, quæso mihi ostendat, vt & ego legam & credam. Nusquam etiam id lego de actuali obedientia. Neque quinque testimonia illa, quæ asse- runt, talem quid probant: quod ostendo paucis.
units.tr: IX. Finally, the one thing that above all hinders me here is this: I have never read that the holy Scriptures divide our righteousness into three or two parts; I have never read that the human holiness of Christ is imputed to us as our righteousness, or as a part of it. If anyone has read it, I beg him to show me, so that I too may read and believe. Nor do I read anything of this kind about active obedience. Nor do those five testimonies which they allege prove any such thing, as I will show briefly.

units.la: Ex dicto Rom. 5. plus concludunt quam sequitur. Neque enim valet consequentia: Justificamur obedientia Christi. Ergo actiua. Apostolus opponit [illegible, ~12 letters] Christi [illegible, ~10 letters] Adami, non vt actionem actioni, sed vt satisfactionem culpæ, vt remedium morbo: alioqui peccata omissionis, non forent [illegible, ~6 letters]. At culpa Adami non fuit tantum perpetratio mali, sed etiam omissio boni. Quam v. obedientiam hic intelligat, alibi expressius declarat, dicens: factus obediens vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Hæc vero fuit obedientia exinanitionis & mortis. Et de eadem etiam obedientia Theophylactus vtrumque locum interpretatur. Negatur igitur in hoc altero loco, quem secundo obiiciunt, de duabus obedientiis verba fieri. De vna enim continuata obedientia, vsque ad mortem crucis, Apostolum loqui, textus ostendit. Humiliationis ni- mirum obedientia, quæ formæ seruilis assumtione cœpit, & morte est terminata.
units.tr: From the passage in Romans 5 they conclude more than follows. For the inference is not valid: "We are justified by the obedience of Christ; therefore by his active obedience." The Apostle sets [...] of Christ [...] against Adam, not as action against action, but as satisfaction for guilt, as a remedy for a disease. Otherwise sins of omission would not be [...]. But the guilt of Adam was not only the commission of evil but also the omission of good. What obedience he means here, he declares more clearly elsewhere, saying: "Made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Phil. 2:8). This was the obedience of humiliation and death. Theophylact also interprets both passages of this same obedience. So in this second passage, which they bring forward second, it is denied that there is any talk of two obediences. For the text shows that the Apostle is speaking of one continuous obedience, extending to the death of the cross: the obedience of humiliation, which began with the assumption of the form of a servant and ended in death.

units.la: Nec locus Galat. 4. pro actiua obedientia aliquid facit. Quomodo enim Christus nostra causa fit factus obnoxius legi, Apostolus ipse clarius interpretatur cap. 3. redemit nos ab exsecratione legis, factus pro nobis exsecratio, vt in gentibus benedictio Abrahæ extet in Christo Iesu. Hoc vero de voluntaria demissione vsque ad mortem peccatis nostris à lege statutam intelligitur dictum. Quatenus tamen hic locus de totius legis seruitute accipi possit, infra monebo.
units.tr: Nor does the passage in Galatians 4 help the case for active obedience. How Christ was made subject to the law for our sake, the Apostle himself explains more clearly in chapter 3: "He redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us, that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus" (Gal. 3:13–14). This is understood to be said of the voluntary humbling, even to death, which the law laid upon him for our sins. However, I will note below how far this passage can be understood of the bondage of the whole law.

units.la: In dicto priore Corinth. 1. Apostolus res quatuor coniungit, minime vt partes imputatæ iustitiæ (quis enim in his numerabit sapientiam, aut ipsam redemtionem?) sed vt summa capita beneficiorum Christi, quorum alia tantum imputatione, vt iustitiam: alia etiam reali participatione nobis confert, in hac vt inchoate, in altera perfecte, vt reliqua. Nulla igitur hinc partitio probatur.
units.tr: In the earlier passage in 1 Corinthians 1, the Apostle joins four things together. He does this not as parts of imputed righteousness (for who would count wisdom among these, or redemption itself?), but as the chief heads of the benefits of Christ. Of these, some are conferred on us only by imputation, such as righteousness; others also by real participation: the one in this life inchoately, the other perfectly, as the rest. Therefore no division is proved from this.

units.la: In loco Roman. 8. est fallacia figuræ dictionis: neque enim lex Spiritus vitæ ibi significat vitam, vel actiuam obedientiam Christi, multo minus formalem sanctitatem eius, sed significat doctrinam vel gratiam vivificam Euangelii. Locus est obscurior. Ex scopo autem sententia simplex hæc patet: quod reliquiæ carnis non condemnent pios, modo eis per Spiritum reluctentur. (quod dixerat versu 1.) Probat Apostolus v. 2. in hypothesi suæ personæ ab effectu Euangelii: Lex, inquit, vitæ Spiritus, hoc est, doctrina vel gratia Evangelij, quod est ministerium spiritus vitæ seu vivificantis nos in Christo Jesu: liberum me reddidit: hoc est me & omnes credentes absoluit, liberos pronunciat: à lege peccati & mortis, hoc est, à condemnatione quam lex peccatoribus irrogat. Legem igitur spiritus & legem mortis hic opponit Apostolus, sicut opponit ministerium spiritus, & ministerium condemnationis, 2. Cor. 3. 8. Quasi dicat. Etsi lex illa mortifera iustificatis in Christo Jesu propter multa reliqua peccata, quibuscum adhuc luctantur, damnationem irrogare tentat: tamen lex spiritus vitæ, hoc est doctrina vel gratia Evangelii viuifica, eos à damnatione absoluit, non obstantibus illis peccatorum reliquiis, quandoquidem hæ quoque eis sunt remissæ propter Christum; sanguis enim Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato, & ab omnibus peccatorum reliquiis. Hæc saluo aliorum iudicio, mihi videtur genuina Apostoli sententia. Verum hoc obiter. Ad reliqua argumenta pergo.
units.tr: In the passage in Romans 8 there is a fallacy of the figure of speech. For "the law of the Spirit of life" does not there mean life, or the active obedience of Christ, much less his formal holiness, but means the doctrine or the life-giving grace of the Gospel. The passage is rather obscure. From the scope of the chapter, however, the simple sense is clear: that the remnants of the flesh do not condemn the godly, provided they resist them through the Spirit (as he had said in verse 1). The Apostle proves this in verse 2, from the effect of the Gospel, in the person of himself as a hypothetical example: "The law," he says, "of the Spirit of life," that is, the doctrine or grace of the Gospel, which is the ministry of the Spirit of life, or of him who quickens us in Christ Jesus, "has made me free," that is, has absolved me and all believers and pronounced us free, "from the law of sin and death," that is, from the condemnation which the law inflicts on sinners. So here the Apostle sets the law of the Spirit against the law of death, just as he sets the ministry of the Spirit against the ministry of condemnation (2 Cor. 3:8). As if he were saying: although that deadly law, against those justified in Christ Jesus, tries to inflict condemnation on account of the many remaining sins with which they still struggle, yet the law of the Spirit of life, that is, the life-giving doctrine or grace of the Gospel, absolves them from condemnation, notwithstanding those remnants of sin, since these too are forgiven them for Christ's sake; for "the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7), and from all the remnants of sin. This, with due deference to the judgment of others, seems to me the genuine sense of the Apostle. But that is by the way. I now pass on to the remaining arguments.

units.la: Sextum iam ante fuit solutum. Christus totus viuificat, sed aliter ut efficiens, aliter ut materia iustitiæ. Et totus nihominus iustificat, quantumvis passio vel mors tantum imputari dicatur. Totus enim est passus, mortuus. Neque excluditur à merito aut iustificatione actiua obedientia, licet non imputari dicatur; quod vult septima ratio. Quomodo enim causa efficiens vel sine qua non excluderetur à suo effectu? vtraque sane obedientia, actiua & passiua requirebatur in mediatore ad iustificationem nostri, sed diuerso modo: illa ut causa ης ςων αὐδο, sicut & natiua sanctitas: hæc ut materia.
units.tr: The sixth argument has already been answered. Christ quickens us wholly, but in one way as efficient cause, in another way as the matter of our righteousness. And he likewise justifies us wholly, however much it is said that only his passion or death is imputed. For he suffered and died wholly. Nor is active obedience excluded from merit or from justification, although it is said not to be imputed, which is what the seventh argument intends. For how could an efficient cause, or a cause without which nothing is done, be excluded from its effect? Both active and passive obedience were certainly required in the Mediator for our justification, but in different ways: the former as the efficient cause, just as innate holiness is; the latter as the matter.

units.la: In octaua ratione antecedens negatur: quia inauditum est legem obligare simul ad obedientiam & ad pœnam: sed omnis lex obligat (disiunctiue non copulatiue) vel ad obedientiam vel ad pœnam. Quamdiu enim præstatur obedientia, lex neminem obligat ad pœnam, id est, neminem pronunciat reum pœnæ, sed promittit vitam. Sed quando obedientia violatur, tum lex peccantem obligat ad pœnam. Hoc de legibus diuinis & humanis vniuersaliter verum est.
units.tr: In the eighth reason the antecedent is denied, because it is unheard of for a law to bind at the same time to obedience and to punishment. Every law binds either to obedience or to punishment (disjunctively, not conjunctively). For as long as obedience is rendered, the law binds no one to punishment; that is, it does not pronounce anyone liable to punishment but promises life. But when obedience is violated, the law then binds the offender to punishment. This is universally true of divine and human laws alike.

units.la: Sunt igitur hypotheses non veræ, & cum iustitia Dei pugnantes, quas hic assumunt. 1. Quod Adam ante lapsum obligatus fuerit simul & ad obedientiam & ad pœnam. 2. Quod homo post lapsum (& sic mediator pro homine) obligatus fuit ad præstandam legi obedientiam & ad luendam pœnam. Obedientia violata, homo peccator tenetur ad satisfactionem per pœnam. Hac persoluta cessat esse peccator, & obligatur ad obedientiam, non eam, pro cuius violatione satisfecit per pœnam, nam, sed ad aliam novam: vel si hanc rursus violet, ad novam poenam. Christus ergo nostram personam suscipiens obligabatur ad satisfaciendum pro nobis per poenam. Hac persoluta, & nobis imputata per fidem, nos sumus iusti: & obligamur porro ad novam obedientiam, vel ad novam poenam. Hanc novam obedientiam Christus etiam per regenerationem in nobis instaurat, sed imperfecte; & eam imperfectionem etiam tegit satisfactio Christi, ne nos condemnet: quia sanguis Jesu Christi mundat nos ab omni peccato, nempe tam sequente, quam antecedente iustificationem.
units.tr: The hypotheses they assume here are therefore untrue and at odds with the justice of God. (1) That Adam before the fall was bound at once both to obedience and to punishment. (2) That man after the fall (and so the mediator on behalf of man) was bound both to render obedience to the law and to pay the penalty. When obedience is violated, the sinful man is held to make satisfaction by punishment. Once this is paid, he ceases to be a sinner and is bound to obedience, not to the obedience whose violation he has satisfied by punishment, but to some new obedience; or, if he violates this again, to a new punishment. Christ, then, taking up our person, was bound to satisfy for us by punishment. When this is paid and imputed to us through faith, we are righteous, and we are further bound to new obedience or to new punishment. Christ also restores this new obedience in us through regeneration, but imperfectly; and his satisfaction also covers that imperfection, so that it does not condemn us, because the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin, namely both that which follows justification and that which precedes it.

units.la: Nona ratio videtur argutissima, sed revera nititur meris contradictionibus, & se ipsam elidit, estque adversa scripturae. Primo aperta contradictio est, cum dicitur: Lex promittit vitam implentibus legem: & non promittit vitam non transgredientibus legem. Ratio est: quia non transgredi legem, & implere legem revera sunt idem. Probatur ex contrario. Transgredi legem, est violare legem faciendo quod prohibet, vel omittendo quod praecipit. Ergo non transgredi legem est non violare legem, faciendo quod prohibet, vel omittendo quod praecipit. Hoc autem revera est implere legem. Qui enim nec contra legem facit, nec legem omittit, profecto legem implet. Quicunque igitur legem non transgreditur, legem implet. In πρῶτο- ἀλάστω Adamo ante lapsum res est manifesta. Is enim quamdiu non peccabat, legem implebat continuo actu in originali rectitudine perseverans. Et angeli beati in coelis, nonne implent legem eo ipso, quod nihil peccant? Nobis quoque in vita aeterna an non legem implere erit non peccare? Vel igitur haec sunt idem, vel ita certe connexa ut separare aut medium cogitare simpliciter sit impossibile. Secundo igitur ἀπούσως, id quoque est, quod dicitur, legem non promittere vitam non transgredientibus. Atqui promittit vitam implentibus legem. Non transgredi autem est implere. Tertio etiam contradictionem implicat, quod dicitur, obedientia passiva nos censeri non iniustos, seu non peccatores: nec tamen censeri iustos: Item non peccatores in Christo mortem quidem effugere, sed vitam petere non audere. Idem enim rursus affirmatur & negatur de terminis aequipollentibus. Nam certe qui coram Deo non est peccator, est iustus: & qui non est mortuus, seu qui mortem effugit, est vivus. Sunt enim contraria ἀντικεῖσθαι, ut dictum est. Quarto scripturis aperte repugnat, quod dicitur, nos passiva obedientia Christi non censeri iustos, hoc est, non iustificari. Nam contra expresse dicitur: Iustificati sanguine eius: reconciliati per mortem filii eius. Laverunt stolas suas in sanguine agni. Cum his & similibus bus dictis clarissimis, & inter se quoq; subtilitates illas & partitiones concilient qui possunt. Ego fateor me non posse.
units.tr: The ninth reason seems very subtle, but in truth it rests on mere contradictions and destroys itself, and it is contrary to Scripture. First, there is a plain contradiction in saying: the law promises life to those who fulfil the law, and does not promise life to those who do not transgress the law. The reason is that not transgressing the law and fulfilling the law are really the same. This is proved from the opposite. To transgress the law is to violate the law, by doing what it forbids or by omitting what it commands. Therefore not to transgress the law is not to violate the law, by doing what it forbids or omitting what it commands. But this is really to fulfil the law. For whoever neither acts against the law nor omits what it requires certainly fulfils the law. Whoever, therefore, does not transgress the law, fulfils it. In Adam before the fall the matter is clear: as long as he did not sin, he continually fulfilled the law by his action, persisting in original righteousness. And do not the blessed angels in heaven fulfil the law by the very fact that they sin not? Must not we too, in eternal life, fulfil the law simply by not sinning? Either these are the same, or they are so closely connected that to separate them, or to conceive a middle state, is simply impossible. Second, conversely, the statement that the law does not promise life to those who do not transgress is also false. Yet it promises life to those who fulfil the law, and not to transgress is to fulfil. Third, it is also self-contradictory to say that by passive obedience we are not counted unrighteous or sinners, yet are not counted righteous; likewise that in Christ we escape death as sinners, yet do not dare to seek life. For the same thing is again affirmed and denied in equivalent terms. For surely whoever is not a sinner before God is righteous, and whoever is not dead, or who escapes death, is alive. These are contraries, as has been said. Fourth, it openly contradicts Scripture to say that we are not counted righteous by the passive obedience of Christ, that is, are not justified. For on the contrary it is expressly said: Justified by his blood; reconciled by the death of his Son. They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Let those who can reconcile those subtleties and distinctions with these and similar most clear sayings, and with one another. I confess I cannot.

units.la: Ad decimam rationem respondetur ex dicto: sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato. Atqui certe impuritas sanctis adhærens peccatum est. Ergo ab ea etiam mundat nos sanguis Christi. Cur igitur trepidæ conscientiæ in tentatione à sanguine Christi ad aliud remedium quærendum relegantur contra tam manifestam scripturam?
units.tr: The tenth reason is answered from the saying: the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. But surely the impurity that clings to the saints is sin. Therefore the blood of Christ cleanses us also from this. Why, then, are troubled consciences in temptation sent away from the blood of Christ to seek some other remedy, against such plain Scripture?

units.la: Denique ad Catechesin Palatinam quod attinet, dicit ea quidem duobus locis satisfactionem, iustitiam & sanctitatem Christi nobis imputari: & semel, peccatum originale sancta conceptione & nativitate mediatoris tegi. Sed non venisse autoribus eius in mentem, iustitiæ imputatæ materiam tripartiti, vel sanguini Christi expiationem originalis peccati & iustificationem derogare, ex eo firmissime constat, quod alibi toties & tam aperte passioni morti, sacrificio Christi, & quidem soli atque unico merito iustitiæ & vitæ æternæ ascribunt & propter hoc meritum etiam peccatum inhærens nobis remitti testantur. Aut igitur pugnat secum Catechesis, quod absit, aut non tripartitur iustitiam imputatam neq; passiuæ obedientiæ meritum iustitiæ derogat.
units.tr: Finally, as far as the Palatine Catechism is concerned, it indeed says in two places that the satisfaction, righteousness and holiness of Christ are imputed to us, and once that original sin is covered by the holy conception and birth of the mediator. But it is most firmly evident from this that its authors had no intention of detracting from the tripartite division of imputed righteousness, or from the expiation of original sin and justification by the blood of Christ, since elsewhere they so often and so plainly ascribe righteousness and eternal life to the passion, death and sacrifice of Christ, and to that alone and unique merit, and attest that even indwelling sin is forgiven us on account of this merit. Either, then, the Catechism contradicts itself, which God forbid, or it does not divide imputed righteousness into three parts, nor does it detract from the merit of passive obedience.

units.la: Superest quarta sententia, quod iustitia nostra sit obedientia mortis seu poena filii Dei pro nostris peccatis: & quod iustificatio tota sit remissio peccatorum propter hanc satisfactionem nobis imputatam.
units.tr: There remains a fourth view: that our righteousness is the obedience of death, or the punishment of the Son of God for our sins, and that the whole of justification is the remission of sins on account of this satisfaction imputed to us.

units.la: Hanc sententiam, ut veriorem, simpliciorem ac tutiorem amplecti me profiteor, sic tamen ut recte & ad mentem sacræ scripturæ intelligatur & explicetur. Veriorem dico, quia constans vox est totius Evangelii, nos iustificari morte & sanguine filii Dei, & iustificationem nostram in sola remissione peccatorum consistere. Testimonia Euangelii supra sunt recitata.
units.tr: I profess that I embrace this view as truer, simpler and safer, provided it is understood and explained rightly and in accordance with the mind of Holy Scripture. I call it truer because it is the constant voice of the whole Gospel that we are justified by the death and blood of the Son of God, and that our justification consists in the remission of sins alone. The testimonies of the Gospel have been recited above.

units.la: At est synecdoche totius in vocabulo sanguinis, mortis, &c. Resp. Est sane. Sed non talis, quatres vel duæ iustitiæ planeinest, ut sunt sanctitas natiua, iustitia actiua, & obedientia passiua, in unum meritum consentur. Nulla enim est ratio, cur duæ priores sanguinis aut mortis nomine censeantur. Est vero Synecdoche totius humilitatis, ut dicetur. Dico & simpliciorem, quia nulla partitione meriti fidem huc illuc distrahit, nec consolationem turbat, sed in lucta conscientias ad unicam Christi mortem cum scriptura remittit: quippe qua sola plene satisfactum est iustitiæ & comminationi diuinæ: Morte morieris. Hac satisfactione per fidem nobis applicata, ipsi satisfecimus, sumus absoluti, iustificati, reconciliati Deo per sanguinem filii eius.
units.tr: But it is said that the word blood, death, etc. is a synecdoche of the whole. I reply: it certainly is, but not of such a kind that two or more righteousnesses are plainly included in it, such as natural holiness, active righteousness and passive obedience, which are reckoned together as one merit. For there is no reason why the first two should be named by the words blood or death. It is rather a synecdoche of the whole humiliation, as will be said. I call it simpler too, because by no division of merit does it draw faith hither and thither or disturb comfort; rather, in the struggle of conscience, it sends the soul back, in accordance with Scripture, to the unique death of Christ alone, since by that alone full satisfaction has been made to justice and to the divine threat: You shall surely die. When this satisfaction is applied to us through faith, we have satisfied him, and we are absolved, justified, and reconciled to God through the blood of his Son.

units.la: Ad At, inquis, ad iustitiam non satis est poena pro peccato, sed & requiritur impletio legis. Resp. Etiam poena est impletio legis. Ergo sufficit. Dupliciter enim lex impletur, vel per obedientiae perfectae praestationem, vel cum haec est violata, per sufficientis poenae perpessionem. Utraque satisfit iustitiae Dei. Utraq; igitur est legis impletio, est iustitia & δικαίωμα. De priore dicitur: Qui facit iustitiam iustus est. De posteriore: Qui mortuus est, iustificatus est à peccato. Priorem impletionem homo habuit ante lapsum, eaque fuit iustus: nec tenebatur ad alteram, quamdiu non peccabat: quia iustitia Dei non postulat simul utramque, sed alterutram: quando quidem lex, ut dictum est, creaturas rationales obligat non copulatiue ad obedientiam & ad poenam simul (esset enim iniquitas summa, obedientiam praestantes obligare ad poenam) sed disiunctiue ad obedientiam vel ad poenam. Priore vero impletione violata post lapsum homo tenetur ad implet ionem posteriorem, qua praestita iustificatur à peccato & Deo reconciliatur. Hanc impletionem Christus pro nobis praestitit moriendo, & donat eam nobis per fidem. Haec igitur ad iustificationem nobis sufficit: quia mortui cum Christo iustificari sumus à peccato. hoc docet Paulus Rom. 8. Condemnauit peccatum in carne, ut iustificatio legis ἐν ἡμῖν πληρωθῇ, & νόμος impleretur in nobis: & 2. Cor. 7. Eum qui non nouit peccatum fecit peccatum pro nobis, ut nos fieremus iustita Dei in eo. Iustificatos per poenam, Lex rursus obligat ad impletionem priorem per obedientiam; aut si non praestetur, ad posteriorem per poenam. Priorem igitur etiam recuperamus in Christo, sed inchoate tantum in hac vita perregenerationem: consummate vero in altera per glorificationem. Ex quibus manifestum est, iustificatis à peccato per mortem filii Dei impletionem legis nullo iure adimi posse: proinde neque iustitiam & vitam.
units.tr: You say: "But for righteousness it is not enough to have punishment for sin; the fulfilment of the law is also required." I reply: punishment too is a fulfilment of the law, and therefore it is sufficient. For the law is fulfilled in two ways: either by rendering perfect obedience, or, when this has been violated, by suffering a sufficient punishment. Both satisfy the justice of God. Both, therefore, are a fulfilment of the law, and are righteousness and a righteous requirement (δικαίωμα). Of the former it is said: He who does righteousness is righteous. Of the latter: He who has died is justified from sin. Man had the former fulfilment before the fall, and by it he was righteous; nor was he bound to the other as long as he did not sin, because the justice of God does not demand both at once, but one or the other. For the law, as has been said, binds rational creatures not conjunctively to obedience and to punishment at the same time (for it would be the greatest iniquity to bind to punishment those who render obedience), but disjunctively to obedience or to punishment. But when the former fulfilment has been violated after the fall, man is bound to the latter fulfilment, and when this is rendered he is justified from sin and reconciled to God. Christ rendered this fulfilment for us by dying, and gives it to us through faith. This, therefore, is sufficient for our justification, because we are justified from sin by being dead with Christ. Paul teaches this in Rom. 8.: God condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us [ἐν ἡμῖν πληρωθῇ], and the law might be fulfilled in us [νόμος]. And in 2 Cor. 7.: He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Having been justified through punishment, we are again bound by the law to the former fulfilment through obedience; or, if this is not rendered, to the latter through punishment. We therefore recover the former also in Christ, but only in the beginning, through regeneration in this life, and we shall have it perfectly in the other life, through glorification. From these things it is clear that the fulfilment of the law cannot be taken away by any right from those who are justified from sin through the death of the Son of God; and therefore neither their righteousness nor their life.

units.la: Tutiorem denique dico: quia nullum eorum incommodorum incurrit, quae sententiae aliae necessario secum trahunt, quamdiu iustitiam personae & meriti Christi confundunt, & meritum in partes tam ἐπιθέτως distrahunt.
units.tr: Lastly, I call it the safer view, because it does not run into any of the difficulties that the other opinions necessarily bring with them, so long as they confuse the righteousness of the person of Christ with the righteousness of his merit, and divide the merit into parts in an added, extrinsic way [ἐπιθέτως].

units.la: Possem huc afferre authoritates Patrum, qui iustitiam nostram similiter in sola ponunt remissione peccatorum propter Christi mortem: vt cum Augustinus dicit: Asylum nostrum remissio peccatorum. Quid est iustificari sanguine ipsius? Cum nobis trasceretur, Deus pater vidit mortem filii sui pro nobis, & placatus est nobis. Tota spes mea in morte Domini est. Mors eius meritum meum est, refugium meum, salus mea, vita, & resurrectio mea. Et Oecumenius: Quomodo fit iustificatio? per remissionem, quam in Christo Iesu consequimur. Et Ambrosius: Credere est salvus sola fi. de sine operibus, gratis accipiens remissionem peccatorum. Nec addq plures. Possem quoque afferre consensum Lutheri, Melanchthonis, Zvvinglii, Oecolampadii, Bullingeri, Caluini, Martyris, Musculi, Hyperii, Vrsini, Oleuiani, &c. à quorum doctrina de Justificatione latum vnguem non discedo. Neminem horum fecisse tripartitam aut bipartitam iustitiam imputatam certo est certius. Sed longum foret testimonia proferre. Sufficiat articulus quintus Augustanæ confessionis, cui in hoc capite omnes subscribunt: Homines iustificantur gratis propter Christum per fidem, cum credunt, se in gratiam recipi, & peccata remitti propter Christum, qui sua morte pro peccatis nostris satisfecit. Et in ditione posteriore. Cum Evangelium arguit peccata nostra, corda nostra perterrefacta statuere debent quod gratis nobis propter Christum donentur remissio peccatorum & iustificatio per fidem, quam credere & confiteri debemus, hac nobis donari propter Christum, qui pro nobis factus est hostia & placauit patrem. Hic iustificatio expresse tribuitur fiduciæ mortis Christi.
units.tr: I could cite the authority of the Fathers, who likewise place our righteousness solely in the remission of sins for the sake of Christ's death. Augustine says: "Our refuge is the remission of sins. What is it to be justified by his blood? When we were being transgressed against, God the Father saw the death of his Son for us, and was appeased toward us. My whole hope is in the death of the Lord. His death is my merit, my refuge, my salvation, my life, and my resurrection." And Oecumenius: "How does justification come about? Through the remission which we obtain in Christ Jesus." And Ambrose: "To believe is to be saved by faith alone, without works, receiving the remission of sins freely." I need not add more. I could also cite the agreement of Luther, Melanchthon, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bullinger, Calvin, Martyr, Musculus, Hyperius, Ursinus, Olevianus, and others, from whose doctrine of justification I do not depart a hair's breadth. It is quite certain that none of these ever taught a tripartite or bipartite imputed righteousness. But it would be tedious to produce their testimonies. The fifth article of the Augsburg Confession, to which all in this chapter subscribe, is enough: "Men are justified freely, for Christ's sake, through faith, when they believe that they are received into grace and that their sins are remitted for Christ's sake, who by his death has made satisfaction for our sins." And in the later edition: "When the Gospel accuses our sins, our terrified hearts ought to determine that the remission of sins and justification through faith are given to us freely for Christ's sake, which faith we must believe and confess: that this is given us for Christ's sake, who was made a sacrifice for us and appeased the Father." Here justification is expressly ascribed to faith in the death of Christ.

units.la: Coniunguntur autem remissio peccatorum, & iustificatio, non vt diversa, sed vt vnum beneficium σωὼν ὑμῶν [?] quod testatur Apologia, dicens: Consequi remissionem peccatorum & iustificari, iuxta illud: Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates.
units.tr: The remission of sins and justification are joined, however, not as different things but as one benefit. The Apology attests this, saying: "To obtain the remission of sins and to be justified, according to that saying: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven."

units.la: Et Melanchthon in locis: Iustificatio significat remissionem peccatorum seu acceptationem personæ ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: And Melanchthon in the Loci: "Justification signifies the remission of sins, or the acceptance of a person to eternal life."

units.la: Sic & Caluinus: Non aliter iusti coram Deo reputamur, nisi gratuita remissione peccatorum.
units.tr: So also Calvin: "We are not reckoned righteous before God except by the free remission of sins."

units.la: Et Confessio Gallicana: Credimus totam nostram iustitiam fundatam esse in remissione peccatorum nostrorum, in qua nostra quoque felicitas omnino consistit, vt dicit David, &c.
units.tr: And the French Confession: "We believe that all our righteousness is founded on the remission of our sins, in which our happiness also wholly consists, as David says, etc."

units.la: Et Catechesis Saxonica anno 71. Remissio peccatorum & iustificatio non differunt. Ideo iustificatio definitur, quod sit remissio peccatorum, reconciliatio cum Deo, imputatio iustitiæ, & acceptatio ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: And the Saxon Catechism of 1571: "The remission of sins and justification do not differ. Therefore justification is defined as the remission of sins, reconciliation with God, the imputation of righteousness, and acceptance to eternal life."

units.la: Quin sufficiat nobis Catechesis nostra, quæ initio statim secundæ partis docet, liberationis nullum esse alium modum, quam satisfactionem per pœnam sufficientem pro peccatis: & mediatorem sufficienter luendo hanc pœnam pro nobis nos redemisse, suaque passione tanquam vnico sacrificio propitiatorio nobis gratiam Dei, iustitiam & vitam æternam acquisiuisse.
units.tr: Indeed our own Catechism is enough for us, which at the very beginning of its second part teaches that there is no other way of deliverance than satisfaction through punishment sufficient for sins; and that the Mediator, by sufficiently bearing this punishment for us, redeemed us, and by his suffering, as the one propitiatory sacrifice, obtained for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.

units.la: At, inquies, Theologi prædicti docent iustificationem constare remissione peccatorum & imputatione iustitiæ. Ergo non constat remissione sola.
units.tr: But, you will say, the theologians named above teach that justification consists of the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. Therefore it does not consist of remission alone.

units.la: Resp. Nec ego nego his constare. Sed quomodo an ut partibus integralibus, quarum neutra sit tota justificatio? Nequaquam: sed vt actibus, ratione tantum, non subiecto differentitus, respectu differentiū terminorum à quo, & ad quem, qualibus constare solent actiones, quæ fiunt contrariorum immediatorum ἀεστί κὴ ἢ σει, quæq; cum reipsa & subiecto sint vna actio, tamen distinguuntur πὸ λόγῳ & respectu. Verbi causa, dealbatio parietis fit pulsione nigredinis, & aspersione albedinis: simul tamen & eadem actione, qua hæc aspergitur, illa pellitur, & contra. Ideo sunt vna actio ratione tantum differens. Repletio vasis fit pulsione vacui, & infusione liquoris: vtraque tamen fit vna actione. Vestitura, vt sic loquar, qua vestitur corpus, fit regendo nuditatem, & applicando vestem. Eadem tamen actione fit vtrumque. Sic igitur in justificatione (quæ vestituræ non est absimilis) concurrunt remissio peccatorum & imputatio justitiæ non vt diuersæ actiones vel partes, sed vt actus terminis differentes. Nam Deus remittendo nobis peccata propter justitiam Christi, eandem imputat, & eam imputando peccata remittit. Conjungi ergo hæc solent in justificatione non tam copulatiuè, quàm exegeticè, vt posterius declaret prius. Sic Calvinus: Justificationem (inquit) simpliciter interpretamur acceptationem, qua nos Deus in gratiam receptos pro justis habet, eamque in remissione peccatorum & imputatione justitiæ Christi positam esse dicimus. Hic copulam & exegeticè poni, ipse Calvinus non obscurè indicat sectione sequente: Vides (inquit) post remissionem peccatorum justificationem hanc velut interpretationis loco poni. Ideo idem alibi passim inculcat, justificationem nihil nisi remissionem peccatorum esse.
units.tr: Reply. Nor do I deny that it consists of these. But how? As integral parts, neither of which is the whole of justification? By no means. Rather as acts which differ only in concept, not in subject, with respect to the differing terms from which and to which, as actions usually consist which are performed in respect of immediate contraries [ἀεστί κὴ ἢ σει, privation and possession]; and which, although they are in reality and in subject one action, are nevertheless distinguished in concept and by relation. For example, the whitening of a wall is effected by the driving out of blackness and the spreading of whiteness; yet by the same action by which the whiteness is spread, the blackness is driven out, and conversely. So they are one action differing only in concept. A vessel is filled by the expulsion of emptiness and the pouring in of liquid; yet both are done by one action. The clothing of a body, so to speak, is done by removing nakedness and putting on a garment; yet both are done by the same action. So too in justification (which is not unlike being clothed), the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness concur, not as different actions or parts, but as acts differing in their terms. For God, by remitting our sins on account of the righteousness of Christ, imputes that righteousness to us, and by imputing it he remits our sins. Hence these are usually joined in justification not so much copulatively as explicatively, so that the latter explains the former. Thus Calvin: "We interpret justification simply as the acceptance by which God, receiving us into grace, holds us as righteous, and we say that it consists in the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ." That here the conjunction is used explicatively, Calvin himself indicates clearly in the following section: "You see," he says, "that after the remission of sins, justification is placed as it were in the position of an explanation." Therefore he elsewhere repeatedly insists that justification is nothing but the remission of sins.

units.la: Dixi denique, sententiam scripturæ, sanguini, morti, cruci CHRISTI, justitiam nostram tribuentis, rectè intelligendam & explicandam esse. Rectè intelligi voco, si nec latè, nec angustè nimis intelligatur. Latè nimis intelligitur, si etiam ad justitiam Deitatis essentialem, & humanitatis formalem vel actualem extendatur. Angustè nimis, si ad solam crucifixionem aut mortem triduanam exclusis perpessionibus antegressis restringatur. Declarationem igitur paucis positionibus subijcio.
units.tr: Finally, I have said that the sentence of Scripture which ascribes our righteousness to the blood, death, and cross of Christ must be rightly understood and explained. I say it is rightly understood if it is understood neither too broadly nor too narrowly. It is understood too broadly if it is extended to the essential justice of the Deity and to the formal or actual righteousness of the humanity. It is understood too narrowly if it is restricted to the crucifixion alone or to the three days of death, with the sufferings that went before excluded. I therefore append a declaration in a few propositions.

units.la: Prima. Justitia personæ & justitia meriti Christi vt non debent diuelli, ita nec debent confundi, sed distinguí in justificatione. Ratio est: quia scriptura distinguit inter qualitatem personæ Mediatoris merentis nobis justitiam: & inter meritum vel justitiam ipsam, tanquam inter prius & posterius, immò tanquam inter causam & effectum: vt Esa.53, 11. Seruus meus justus. Hebr. 7,26. Talis nobis conueniebat pontifex, qui &c. 2 Cor.5,20.
units.tr: First. The righteousness of the person and the righteousness of the merit of Christ ought not to be torn apart, but neither should they be confused; they must be distinguished in justification. The reason is that Scripture distinguishes between the quality of the person of the Mediator who merits righteousness for us, and the merit or righteousness itself, as between prior and posterior, or indeed as between cause and effect: as in Isaiah 53:11, "my righteous servant"; Hebrews 7:26, "such a high priest became us," etc.; 2 Corinthians 5:20.

units.la: Instit. lib. 3. c.11. f.2.
units.tr: Institutes, book 3, chapter 11, section 2.

units.la: ξυγν. Et interdum est Eum, qui non novit peccatum, &c. 1 Pet.3, 18. Christus semel passus est, justus pro injustis, &c. His & similibus locis tribuitur Christo duplex justitia, quasi duplex vestis: vna, qua ipse ornatus fuit, altera, quam nobis donat. Hac distinctione neglecta, multiplex confusio sequitur, & plurimis incommodis implicatur haec doctrina, vt difficilius contra Papistas & alios aduersarios defendatur.
units.tr: [ξυγν.] And at times it is said: "him who knew no sin," etc. (2 Cor. 5:21); "Christ died once for sins, the just for the unjust," etc. (1 Pet. 3:18). By these and similar passages a twofold righteousness is ascribed to Christ, as a twofold garment: one with which he himself was clothed, and the other which he gives to us. If this distinction is neglected, a manifold confusion follows, and this doctrine is entangled in many difficulties, so that it is harder to defend against the Papists and other adversaries.

units.la: Secunda. Justitia personae vocatur, quae requirebatur in persona Mediatoris, partim vt causa efficiens, partim vt ἡς ὁσὺς αὐδὸς, nostrae justitiae. Oportebat enim Mediatorem esse Deum & hominem justum, vt justitiam nobis mereri & conferre posset. Justitia meriti seu meritum vocatur λύτρον, & satisfactio Mediatoris pro nobis: & proprie est causa materialis justitiae nostrae, hoc est, res ea, quae ad justitiam nobis imputatur. Quod nisi concedatur, confusio multiplex, de qua est dictum, euitari nullo modo potest.
units.tr: Second. The righteousness of the person is the name given to the righteousness that was required in the person of the Mediator, partly as the efficient cause, and partly as the ἡς ὁσὺς αὐδὸς [source of our righteousness]. For the Mediator had to be God and a righteous man, so that he could merit righteousness for us and confer it. The righteousness of the merit, or the merit itself, is called the λύτρον [ransom], and the satisfaction of the Mediator for us; and it is properly the material cause of our righteousness, that is, the thing which is imputed to us for righteousness. Unless this is granted, the manifold confusion of which we have spoken cannot in any way be avoided.

units.la: Tertia. Sicut autem justitia personae non est tantum actualis obedientia Christi, sed complectitur totius personae θεανθρώπου justitiam diuinam & humanam, hoc est, essentialem Deitatis & formalem, atque actualem humanitatis conformitatem cum lege, tanquam summam personae Mediatoris perfectionem, absque qua pontifex & seruator noster esse non poterat: sic justitia meriti, seu λύτρον, non est tantum sanguis & mors Christi, sed complectitur totam obedientiam humiliationis ab articulo conceptionis vsque ad mortem crucis. Tota enim vita Christi miseriarum & dolorum plena, quid fuit nisi perpetua quaedam passio & poena peccatorum nostrorum? Nam ex ordine justitiae diuinae, cum Christus esset justissimus, vita eius non debuit esse misera & aerumnosa, sed plane ἄλυπος, fortunata, & felix. Quod vero misera fuit, poenae & satisfactionis rationem habuit pro nostris peccatis.
units.tr: Third. Just as the righteousness of the person is not merely the actual obedience of Christ, but embraces the divine and human righteousness of the whole θεανθρώπου [God-man] person, that is, the essential righteousness of the Deity and the formal and actual conformity of the humanity with the law, as the highest perfection of the person of the Mediator, without which he could not be our high priest and Saviour; so the righteousness of the merit, or λύτρον, is not merely the blood and death of Christ, but embraces the whole obedience of his humiliation from the moment of conception to the death of the cross. For the whole life of Christ, full of miseries and sorrows, what was it but a continual suffering and punishment for our sins? For by the order of divine justice, since Christ was most righteous, his life ought not to have been wretched and full of hardship, but altogether free from pain, fortunate and happy. That it was in fact wretched was for the sake of punishment and satisfaction for our sins.

units.la: Quarta. Cum igitur scriptura justitiam nobis monstrat in sanguine, cruce, morte Christi; non loquitur exclusiue, quasi perpessiones mortem antegressae ad meritum non pertineant: sed synecdochicè, complectens sub complemento λύτρου etiam omnes antecedentes gradus, hoc est, initium, incrementa & consummationem. Initium fuit in ipsa incarnatione, quando factus est pauper propter nos, &c. Incrementa seruí assumta fuerunt in tota vita, quam in perpetuis exegit miseriis, tentationibus, periculis, irae Dei obnoxius propter nos. Consummatio denique fuit in cruce & morte, quando spiritum emittens, clamauit: Consummatum est. Haec omnia in Christi λύτρον conjungit Esaias cap. 53. Verè languores nostros tulit, & dolores nostros portauit.
units.tr: Fourth. Since Scripture shows us the righteousness we have in the blood, cross and death of Christ, it does not speak exclusively, as though the sufferings that went before his death did not belong to his merit. It speaks synecdochically, embracing under the completion of the ransom [λύτρου] all the earlier stages as well: the beginning, the growth and the consummation. The beginning was in the incarnation itself, when he became poor for our sake, and so on. The growth of the servant was taken up in his whole life, which he spent in continual miseries, temptations and dangers, subject to the wrath of God on our account. The consummation came finally on the cross and in death, when, giving up the spirit, he cried: "It is finished." Isaiah 53 joins all these things together in Christ's ransom: Surely he has borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows.

units.la: portá portauit, vulneratus est propter prauaricationes nostras: attritus propter iniquitates nostras: & liuore eius sanati sumus. Et Apostolus 2 Corinth.cap.5. Cum esset dives, factus est pauper propter nos, vt nos eius pauperate ditesceremus. Et Hebr.2. Paulisper factus est inferior angelis, propter mortis perpessionem, &c. Præcipuè verò Philip. 2. Cum esset in forma Dei, exinaniuit seipsum formam serui assumta, & humiliauit seipsum, factus obediens vsque ad mortem crucis. Neque valet cauillatio: Apostolum hic non agere de materia nostræ justitiæ. Satis est, quod obedientiam, quam esse nostram justitiam alibi docuit, hic ad totam humiliationem extendit. Nec obstat locus Hebr. 9. verf.22. Absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Tantum hinc sequitur, a causa remissionis non excludi sanguinis effusionem; sed hanc esse causam, ῆς οὐκ ἄνευ; non autem sequitur, hanc esse causam solam, vel excludi mortem subsequentem, aut perpessiones antegressas. Tota igitur humiliationis obedientia vsque ad mortem crucis, ad mortem Christi pertinet.
units.tr: ...he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities, and with his stripes we are healed. And the Apostle, 2 Cor. 5: "Though he was rich, yet for our sakes he became poor, that we through his poverty might be made rich." And Heb. 2: "He was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death," and so on. Above all, Phil. 2: "Being in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross." Nor does the objection hold that the Apostle here is not dealing with the matter of our righteousness. It is enough that he extends to the whole humiliation the obedience which he elsewhere teaches is our righteousness. Nor does Heb. 9:22 stand in the way: "Without shedding of blood there is no remission." This only follows: the shedding of blood is not excluded from the cause of remission, but is this cause [ῆς οὐκ ἄνευ]. It does not follow that this is the only cause, or that the death that follows, or the sufferings that went before, are excluded. Therefore the whole obedience of humiliation, even to the death of the cross, belongs to the death of Christ.

units.la: Quinta. Cur vero scriptura meritum, quod toto obedientiæ suæ cursu Christus nobis acquisiuit, morti eius quasi peculiare ac proprium ascribat; causa est, quia in sola Christi morte meriti sufficientia consistit. Nam sine morte obedientia humiliationis non fuisset absoluta, nec fuisset satisfactum diuinæ commination i: Morte morieris: sine morte igitur reliqua Christi obedientia fuisset meritum insufficiens, neque nobis profuisset. Qui vero obedientiæ actiuæ aut sanctitati natiuæ meritum justitiæ asscribunt, mortem Christi sine dubio inanem reddunt.
units.tr: Fifth. Why Scripture ascribes to the death of Christ, as if it were peculiar and proper to it, the merit which Christ acquired for us through the whole course of his obedience, is because the sufficiency of merit consists in the death of Christ alone. For without death the obedience of humiliation would not have been complete, nor would the threat, "In dying thou shalt die" [Gen. 2:17], have been satisfied. Without death, therefore, the rest of Christ's obedience would have been an insufficient merit, and would not have profited us. Those, however, who ascribe the merit of righteousness to active obedience or to innate holiness, undoubtedly make the death of Christ empty.

units.la: Hac obseruata explicatione vera & consentanea scripturæ, manifestum euadit: Primo, ab vtraque controuertentium parte aliquid peccari: ab illis quidem, quod & justitiam personæ cum justitia meriti confundunt, & meritum in plura heterogenea diuidendo, non modo fidem & consolationem turbant, sed & morti CHRISTI justificationem contra scripturas derogant: ab istis vero, quod à justitia meriti totam CHRISTI vitam, humilitatem & perpessiones mortem antegressas excludunt, & particulam exclusiuam SOLA in phrasibus: sola mors justificat: solus sanguis purgat: opponunt vitæ & obedientiæ antegressæ; cum in genere causæ meritoriæ seu materialis partim quidem justitiæ personali, partim verò & præcipuè meritis humanis & omnibus causis aliis externis opponatur: nisi particulam SOLA ad sufficientiam restringant, de qua positione quinta est dictum. Deinde facilem hanc fore conciliandæ controuersiæ rationem: si omnes omnia illa communia, in quibus eos supra dixi conuenire, de justificatione gratuita fidei per justitiam CHRISTI imputatam, contra Papistas & merita humana consentienter doceant: nec de hac justitia, seu materia justitiæ imputatæ ad vulgus in concionibus scrupulose disputent, sed phrasibus scripturæ vtantur, & contenti sint, nos non operibus, sed fide, non justitia nostra, sed aliena obedientia, videlicet sanguine & morte Filii DEI nobis imputata, & per fidem applicata justificari, &c. Nam hæc ad consolationem veram, & ad refutanda merita humana omnibus sufficiunt.
units.tr: Once this explanation, which is true and consistent with Scripture, has been observed, it becomes clear: First, that each side of the disputants sins in something. Those indeed sin in that they confuse the righteousness of the person with the righteousness of merit, and by dividing merit into several heterogeneous parts they not only disturb faith and comfort, but also, contrary to Scripture, take away from the death of Christ its share in justification. The others sin in that they exclude from the righteousness of merit the whole life and humiliation of Christ and the sufferings that went before his death, and they set the exclusive particle SOLE in phrases such as "death alone justifies" and "blood alone cleanses" against his life and earlier obedience. Yet in the category of meritorious or material cause, merit is opposed partly to personal righteousness, and chiefly to human merits and all other external causes, unless they restrict the particle SOLE to sufficiency, about which the fifth position has been said. Next, this would be an easy way of reconciling the controversy, if all would teach in agreement all those common points in which I have said above they agree, concerning the free justification of faith through the imputed righteousness of Christ, against the Papists and human merits; and if they did not dispute scrupulously before the people in sermons about this righteousness, or the matter of imputed righteousness, but used the phrases of Scripture and were content that we are justified not by works but by faith, not by our own righteousness but by the alien obedience, namely the blood and death of the Son of God, imputed to us and applied through faith, and so on. For these phrases are sufficient for true comfort and for refuting human merits.

units.la: Quod ad scrupum ipsum attinet, si omnino in scholis tangendus sit, ad conciliationem tolerabilem obtinendum, necesse erit id caueri vtrinque, quod sententias maximè separat. Postremi offenduntur partitione meriti in tam diuersa: quia vident multa inde nasci absurda, & scripturis vim fieri. Priores contra offenduntur restrictione meriti ad mortem, quia metuunt, ne vita & obedientia antegressa excludatur contra scripturas. Quid ergo? Necesse est, alteri ne partiantur materiam meriti in duo, tria vel quatuor, vt fit: non adimant morti justitiæ meritum, nec remissioni peccatorum justificationem: alteri ne restringant meritum ad effusionem sanguinis in cruce, aut ad mortem triduanam, nec excludant vitam & obedientiam antegressam: ab vtrisque vero
units.tr: As for the scruple itself, if it must be touched upon at all in the schools, then to obtain a tolerable reconciliation it will be necessary for both sides to guard against what most divides their opinions. The latter are offended by the division of merit into such different parts, because they see many absurdities arising from it and violence being done to the Scriptures. The former, on the other hand, are offended by restricting merit to death, because they fear that the life and obedience that went before are excluded, contrary to Scripture. What then? One side must not divide the material of merit into two, three or four parts, as happens, nor take from the death of Christ the merit of righteousness, nor from the remission of sins its justification. The other must not restrict merit to the shedding of blood on the cross or to the three days of death, nor exclude the life and obedience that went before. But each side...

units.la: 1. Distinguatur cum scriptura, justitia personalis à merito tanquam causa efficiens, & sine qua non, à materiali: quandoquidem ex confusione necesse est nasci varia incommoda, quibus labefactatur sententia scripturæ, turbantur conscientiæ, & Papistis præbetur cauillandi occasio, vt est ostensum positione prima & secunda.
units.tr: 1. Let it be distinguished, with Scripture, the personal righteousness from the merit, as efficient cause and as "without which not" [sine qua non], and from the material cause. Since confusion necessarily gives rise to various inconveniences, by which the teaching of Scripture is weakened, consciences are troubled, and an occasion of cavilling is given to the Papists, as has been shown in the first and second positions.

units.la: 2. Rectè limitetur justitia personæ Mediatoris: juxta positionem tertiam.
units.tr: 2. The righteousness of the person of the Mediator should be rightly limited, according to the third position.

units.la: 3. Rite quoque definiatur justitia meriti: & synecdoche sanguinis, mortis, passiuæ obedientiæ, &c. de tota humiliatione Christi intelligatur, juxta pos. 4. & 5.
units.tr: 3. The righteousness of merit should also be properly defined, and the synecdoche of blood, death, passive obedience, and so on, should be understood of the whole humiliation of Christ, according to the fourth and fifth positions.

units.la: 4. Addatur pro conciliatione hoc insuper, sub humiliatione comprehendi seruitutem spontaneam legis, & sic etiam obedientiam actiuam, quam vocant, adeo vt hæc quoque certo respectu in meriti rationem veniat: quatenus nimirum, vt spontanea seruitus, à Filio DEI nostra causa suscepta & præstita, consideratur. Dupliciter enim obedientia illa consideratur. Primò, vt conformitas cum lege: & sic est justitia personæ Mediatoris. Deinde, vt seruitus legis, cui nostra causa Christus sponsponte se fecit obnoxium: & sic ad meritum pertinet. Etsi enim CHRISTUS, qua homo, ipse quoque obedientia legis tenebatur: tamen, qua justus, sanctus, & Filius Dei, etiam juxta humanitatem, ad pleraque tam primæ quam secundæ tabulæ officia non erat obligatus: quibus tamen se sponte subjecit: & sic totius legis servus est factus propter nos, ut nos à servitute, coactione & damnatione legis redimeret. Sic spontanea servitus fuit, quod est circumcisus, quod sabbata & festa servavit, quod subiectus fuit parentibus, & Cæsari didrachmum solvit, quod proximo servivit, &c. cum esset circumcisionis, sabbathi, parentum, Cæsaris & proximi Dominus. De hac servitute legis illud quoque Apostoli intelligi potest. Galat. cap. 4. DEVS emisit Filium suum factum ex muliere, factum legi obnoxium, &c. Sic minus valebit querela de exclusione actiuæ obedientiæ àmerito.
units.tr: 4. For reconciliation, let this be added besides: the humiliation includes the voluntary servitude to the law, and so also what they call active obedience, so that this too in a certain respect comes under the category of merit: namely insofar as it is considered as the voluntary servitude undertaken and rendered by the Son of God for our cause. For that obedience is considered in two ways. First, as conformity with the law, and so it is the righteousness of the person of the Mediator. Then, as the servitude of the law, to which Christ, for our cause, of his own accord made himself liable, and so it belongs to merit. For although Christ, as man, was himself also bound to obey the law, yet as righteous, holy, and the Son of God, even according to his humanity, he was not obliged to many of the duties both of the first and of the second table, to which nevertheless he voluntarily subjected himself. And so he became the servant of the whole law for our sake, that he might redeem us from the servitude, compulsion and condemnation of the law. Thus it was voluntary servitude that he was circumcised, that he kept the sabbaths and feasts, that he was subject to his parents, and paid the didrachma to Caesar, that he served his neighbour, and so on, although he was the Lord of circumcision, the sabbath, parents, Caesar and neighbour. This servitude of the law the Apostle's words may also be understood to mean, Gal. 4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made subject to the law," and so on. So the complaint about the exclusion of active obedience from merit will carry less weight.

units.la: Ista conciliationis ratio si forte scrupulosius non satisfaciet, saltem non omnino displicebit iis, qui hæc sententiarum dissidia sopita cupiunt: vel certè de rationibus pacis amplius cogitabunt, & meliora ostendent. Mihi hæc satisfaciunt.
units.tr: If perhaps this method of reconciliation does not satisfy the more scrupulous, it will at least not wholly displease those who desire these disagreements of opinion to be quieted; or they will certainly think more about the ways of peace and will show better ones. To me these satisfy.

units.la: Ex his porro liquet, quod tertio loco quæsitum fuit, quomodo hæc doctrina pro concione tractanda sit, & an [illegible, ~6 letters] de ea ad populum disputare conveniat. Ego sane hoc committendum non arbitror.
units.tr: From these things it further appears what was asked in the third place, how this doctrine is to be handled in a sermon, and whether it is fitting to dispute about it before the people [illegible]. For my part, I certainly do not think this should be entrusted to them.

units.la: Quid enim aliud ex eiusmodi disceptatione exspectari possit, quam ut rudiores turbentur in fide, & in eam descendant cogitationem, doctrinam, de justitia fidei hactenus tractatam in Ecclesiis Evangelicis, lubricam & incertam nobis esse, in qua tamen primum olim est factum à Papatu divortium? Et potest Ecclesia ædificari in fide & consolatione etiam absque antithesi: qua sane non adversarij, sed fratres perstringerentur, horum animi distraherentur in periculosas [illegible, ~2 letters]​διχοστασίας: & certamina atque scandala augerentur nostra culpa. Certè Pontificij hanc ansam utraque manu arriperent nos splendidè traducendi, nobis scilicet in eo capite non convenire, in quo proram & puppim Evangelij hactenus posuerimus. Accepit Papatus in emendatione doctrinæ de justificatione per Lutherum & alios primum, ut dixi, & luculentum vulnus. An vero nos hoc vulnus bestiæ iterum sanabimus? neque cogitabimus, quas DEO rationes simus reddituri [illegible, ~2 words] nostræ. At est periculum, ne error pro veritate in Ecclesia obtineat. Non est, modo retineantur & sedulo doceantur ea, quæ sunt in confesso: in reliquis adhibeatur moderatio & candor, audiantur placidè fratres, & conferantur sententiæ secum & cum verbo Dei: denique nodus in scirpo non quæratur.
units.tr: For what else could be expected from such a dispute, than that the more ignorant would be troubled in faith, and would come to think that the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, hitherto handled in the Evangelical Churches, is slippery and uncertain for us, although it was on this very point that the first divorce from the Papacy once took place? And the Church can be built up in faith and comfort even without antithesis, which would certainly not wound our adversaries but our brethren; their minds would be drawn away into dangerous [illegible] dissensions, and strife and scandals would be increased through our fault. Certainly the Papists would seize this occasion with both hands to traduce us splendidly, namely that we do not agree on that head on which we have hitherto placed the prow and stern of the Gospel. The Papacy received, as I said, its first and a grievous wound in the reform of doctrine concerning justification through Luther and others. Shall we then heal this wound of the beast again? And shall we not consider what accounts we shall have to render to God [illegible] of ours? But there is danger that error may prevail in the Church. There is not, provided that what is agreed is retained and diligently taught; in the remaining matters let moderation and candour be shown, let the brethren be heard calmly, and let opinions be compared with one another and with the Word of God. Finally, let no one seek a knot in a bulrush.

units.la: CAP. IV. Restat quartum caput de Catechesi & Agenda Palatina, an in his quædam omittere vel etiam eradere oporteat. Hic nescio mirer magis, an doleam quorundam αὐτοκεφάλων, qui sibi fas esse arbitrantur, sacra & profana omnia ad calculum, vel potius virgulam suam revocare, & quæ videtur obelo suo critico configere. Hæc libido ferenda non est. Si quid altius illi sapuerint, quam alij, suam potius Catechesin, vel Agendam novam sibi fabricarent: aut si quid erroris in Palatina peruiderunt, fraternè monerent de emendatione eos, ad quos ea cura pertinet, & qui parati erunt rationes reddere. Videtur sane præ-tensus ille zelus nec conscientiæ multum, nec scientiæ satis habere. Nam qua conscientia mutabunt illi non sua, sed aliena, eradent priuati ea, quæ publicè ad plures Ecclesias pertinent? Si scientiæ satis habent, hoc est, si Catecheseos mentem bene ubique perspexerunt, & candorem adhibere volunt, quem in ambiguis adhibere par est: intelligent nulla opus esse ratione: quia omnia satis conueniunt, modo dubia secundum manifestiora, & pauciora secundum plura, uti est æquum, accipiantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. The fourth chapter remains, concerning the Catechism and the Palatine Agenda, and whether certain things in them ought to be omitted or even erased. Here I do not know whether to wonder more or to grieve at certain self-appointed men [αὐτοκεφάλων], who think it right to bring all sacred and profane matters to their own reckoning, or rather their own rod, and to pierce whatever seems to them with their critical obelus. Such presumption is not to be tolerated. If they have tasted something deeper than others, they should rather compose their own Catechism or a new Agenda for themselves. Or, if they have perceived some error in the Palatine one, they should brotherly admonish those to whom that care belongs, and who will be ready to give an account. That pretended zeal certainly seems to have little conscience and not enough knowledge. For with what conscience will they change not their own things but those of others, and erase privately what publicly belongs to many churches? If they had enough knowledge, that is, if they had thoroughly grasped the mind of the Catechism everywhere, and wished to show the candour that ought to be shown in ambiguous matters, they would understand that there is no need for such a reason. Everything agrees well enough, provided that doubtful passages are taken in light of the clearer ones, and the fewer in light of the more numerous, as is fair.

units.la: At nihil dubium vel ambiguum in Catechesi esse oportuit. Fateor sane: nec tale quid irrepsisset, si postquam hic scrupus moueri coepit, scribenda fuisset.
units.tr: But nothing doubtful or ambiguous ought to have been in the Catechism. I grant this indeed. Nor would such a thing have crept in, if it had been written after this scruple began to be raised.

units.la: Manifestiora igitur & plura de iustitia meriti Christi in Catechesi occurrunt hæc:
units.tr: The clearer and more numerous statements about the righteousness of Christ's merit in the Catechism are these:

units.la: 1. Quæst. 12. & 14. docetur liberationis, & cum Deo reconciliationis modum nullum fuisse alium, quam ut vel ipse homo peccator, vel pro homine peccatore Mediator diuinæ iustitiæ satisfaceret per sufficientem pœnam. Ergo pœna Mediatoris pro nobis est satisfactio nostra, & res ea per & propter quam Deo reconciliamur & iustificamur: nam hæc duo apostolo idem valent, Rom. 5. v. 9, 10.
units.tr: 1. Q. 12 and 14 teach that there was no other way of deliverance and of reconciliation with God than that either man himself, a sinner, or a Mediator on behalf of sinful man should satisfy divine justice by a sufficient punishment. Therefore the punishment of the Mediator for us is our satisfaction, the thing through and on account of which we are reconciled to God and justified; for these two mean the same to the Apostle, Rom. 5:9, 10.

units.la: 2. Quæst. 15. & 16. docetur, Mediatorem oportuisse esse verum Deum, & verum hominem, perfecte iustum: idq; ut posset ἀντὶ pro nobis dependere, quod peccator non potuisset. Ergo iustitia personæ distinguitur à ἀντὶ, tanquam causa ab effectu, & iustitia formalis atque actualis mediatoris pertinet ad iustiam personæ, tanquam causa sine qua non.
units.tr: 2. Q. 15 and 16 teach that the Mediator had to be true God and true man, perfectly just; and this so that he could pay in place of us [ἀντί], which a sinner could not. Therefore the righteousness of the person is distinguished from the payment made in place of us, as cause from effect; and the formal and actual righteousness of the Mediator pertains to the righteousness of the person, as a cause without which the effect cannot be.

units.la: 3. Quæst. 21. docetur, propter hoc Christi λύτρῳ, omnibus credentibus donari remissionem peccatorum, æternam justitiam & vitam. Ergo Catechesis non ita partitur remissionem peccatorum & justitiam, vt illa propter λύτρον, hæc propter justitiam actiuam donetur.
units.tr: 3. Q. 21 teaches that on account of Christ's ransom [λύτρῳ] the forgiveness of sins, eternal righteousness and life are granted to all believers. Therefore the Catechism does not divide forgiveness of sins and righteousness so that the former is granted on account of the ransom and the latter on account of active righteousness.

units.la: 4. Qu. 37. docetur, Christū sua passione tanquam vnico sacrificio propitiatorio, nobis gratiam Dei, justitiam & vitam acquisiuisse: & quidem hanc passionē per totum vitæ tempus extendi, quo in terris egit, etsi præcipuus passionis actus fuerit in vitæ extremo. Rursus igitur meritum justitiæ & vitæ non actiuæ, sed passiuæ obedientiæ asscribitur, & simul passio synecdochicæ de tota humilitate intelligitur.
units.tr: 4. Q. 37 teaches that Christ, by his suffering as the one propitiatory sacrifice, acquired for us God's grace, righteousness and life; and indeed that this suffering extended through the whole time of his life on earth, although the principal act of the suffering was at the end of his life. Again, therefore, the merit of righteousness and life is ascribed not to active but to passive obedience, and at the same time the suffering is understood, by synecdoche, as the whole of his humiliation.

units.la: 5. Quæst. 40. iterum docetur, nullo alio pacto potuisse pro nostris peccatis satisfieri justitiæ & veritati diuinæ, quam ipsa morte Filij Dei. Rursus ergo confirmatur, mortem Filii Dei esse satisfactionem, hoc est, rem eam per & propter quam justificamur.
units.tr: 5. Q. 40 again teaches that satisfaction for our sins could be made to divine justice and truth in no other way than by the very death of the Son of God. Again, therefore, it is confirmed that the death of the Son of God is the satisfaction, that is, the thing through and on account of which we are justified.

units.la: 6. Quæst. 45. dicit Catechesis, ideo surrexisse Christum, vt posset nos suæ justitiæ, quam nobis morte sua pepererat, participes facere. Ergo mors CHRISTI nobis peperit justitiam, & imputationem eius censemur non tantum non injusti, sed etiam justi.
units.tr: 6. Q. 45 says that Christ therefore rose so that he might make us partakers of his righteousness, which he had won for us by his death. Therefore the death of Christ won us righteousness, and by its imputation we are counted not only as not unrighteous, but also as righteous.

units.la: 7. Quæst. 56. docet: Deum propter satisfactionem Christi (quæ est pœna & mors eius) omnium nostrorum peccatorum, etiam originalis memoriam depositisse; & nos justitiæ CHRISTI gratis donare. Rursus igitur confirmat, mortem esse non modo remissionis peccatorum omnium, etiam originalis, sed & justificationis meritum: neque necesse esse, originale peccatum tegi sanctitate humanitatis, ne in conspectum Dei veniat.
units.tr: 7. Q. 56 teaches that God, on account of Christ's satisfaction (which is his punishment and death), has laid aside the memory of all our sins, even original sin, and freely gives us the righteousness of Christ. Again, therefore, it confirms that death is the merit not only of the remission of all sins, even original sin, but also of justification; and that it is not necessary for original sin to be covered by the holiness of humanity, so that it does not come into the sight of God.

units.la: 8. Denique Quæst. 66.67.70.72.74.76.80. identidem petitur, nos propter vnum Christi sacrificium, sanguinem, mortem, habere remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & vitam æternam. In his igitur omnibus nulla docetur, nec cogitari potest talis partitio meriti, quasi imputatione mortis CHRISTI tantum remissionem peccatorum & , vt nonnulli recens loqui cœperunt, tantum priuatiua beneficia: imputatione vero actualis obedientiæ, justitiam demum & beneficia positiua consequamur. Catechesis omnia simul morti tribuit: sicut & scriptura Joh. 3. Dedit Filium vnigenitum, (nempe in mortem) vt omnis, qui credit, (nempe Filium pro se traditum & mortuum) non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam, &c. At inquis; Qu. 60. 61. justitiam imputatam expresse partitur in tria, perfectam satisfactiofactionem, iustitiam & sanctitatem, quæ nobis imputari dicit: & q.36.dicit, Mediatorem sua innocentia & perfecta sanctitate nostra peccata, in quibus concepti sumus, tegere ne in conspectum Dei veniant.
units.tr: 8. Finally, Q. 66, 67, 70, 72, 74, 76 and 80 repeatedly ask that we have forgiveness of sins, righteousness and eternal life on account of the one sacrifice, blood and death of Christ. In all these, therefore, no such division of merit is taught, nor can it be conceived, as if by the imputation of Christ's death we obtained only the forgiveness of sins and, as some have recently begun to say, merely privative benefits, but by the imputation of his actual obedience we obtained at last righteousness and positive benefits.
