Christ therefore did not command them to eat with the mouth in the bread what was not yet in the bread, or was not yet eatable. We say briefly: by the word eat only the oral eating of the external sacrament, or of the bread, is commanded; but by the word of promise, This is my body which is given for you, which promise agrees with John 6:52: The bread which I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world, there is required a spiritual eating of the body of Christ given for us, and a drinking of the blood of Christ shed for us for the remission of sins.

units.la: Rursus tamen Grammaticus conatur probare maiorem prosyllogismi: Vocabulum vnam habens significationem, in na est accipiēdum: Manducatio tam de pane, quam de corpore Christi vnam habet significationem: Ergo vna de vtroque est accipienda.
units.tr: Yet again the grammarian tries to prove the major of the prosyllogism: a word having one meaning must be understood in one way. Eating has one meaning both of the bread and of the body of Christ. Therefore it must be understood in one way of both.

units.la: Resp.1. Rursus deficit in probatione maioris: Quia neque syllogismi, neque prosyllogismi maiorem concludit vniuersali syllogismo in Barbara: sicut oportuit. 2. Minor habet petitionem principii: Sumit enim, tam de corpore quam de pane dici: Manducate: quod debet probare: & esse falsum historia institutionis docet. Corpore enim suo Christus non latebat in pane, sed sedebat ad mensam, cum de accepto, fracto & porrecto pane diceret discipulis: Manducate.
units.tr: Answer 1. Again he fails in proving the major, because neither the syllogism nor the prosyllogism draws the major as a universal syllogism in Barbara ought to do. 2. The minor begs the question: it takes it that Eat is said of the body as well as of the bread, which he ought to prove; and the history of the institution teaches that this is false. For Christ was not hidden in the bread with his body, but was sitting at the table, when he said to the disciples, speaking of the bread he had taken, broken and handed over: Eat.

units.la: TERTIA QVÆSTIO.
units.tr: THIRD QUESTION.

units.la: Quibus res offerantur: & à quibus percipiantur?
units.tr: To whom are the things offered, and by whom are they received?

units.la: Ad hanc duabus propositionibus respondetur: vtraque affirmante.
units.tr: To this question two propositions are given in response, both affirmative.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I. Res signata sacramenti corpus & sanguis Domini, licet omnibus offerantur, à solis tamen fidelibus percipiuntur.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I. The thing signified in the sacrament, the body and blood of the Lord, although it is offered to all, is received by the faithful alone.

units.la: Ratio 1. Quia soli fideles promissionem, qua res signatæ offeruntur, fide accipiunt.
units.tr: Reason 1. Because the faithful alone receive by faith the promise by which the signified things are offered.

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia soli credentes habent spiritum Christi, à quo caro eius viuifica separari nequit.
units.tr: Reason 2. Because the believers alone have the Spirit of Christ, from whom his life-giving flesh cannot be separated.

units.la: Ratio 3. Quia in solis credentibus Christus manet, & ipsi in eo, per fidem, Ephes.3.17.
units.tr: Reason 3. Because Christ dwells in the believers alone, and they in him, through faith, Eph. 3.17.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia soli credentes percipiunt & habent vitam æternam, Johan.3.& 6.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because the believers alone receive and have eternal life, John 3 and 6.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II. Impii vel increduli sine fide accedentes, symbolis sinerebus percipiunt, res vero oblatas infidelitate respuunt.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II. The impious or unbelieving, approaching without faith, receive the symbols indeed, but reject the things offered because of their unbelief.

units.la: Rationes vide Explicat. Catechet.q.81.titulo: Quid impii accipiant in Cœna Domini.
units.tr: For the reasons, see the Explicatio Catechetica, question 81, under the heading: What the impious receive in the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Obiectiones pro manducatione impiorum vide ibidem. D. D A-
units.tr: For the objections in favour of the eating of the impious, see the same place. D. D A-

units.la: D. DAVIDIS PAREI EPITOME ARMINIANISMI, SIVE EXAMEN QVINQVE ARTICVLORVM Ministrorum Remonstrantium in Belgio.
units.tr: D. DAVID PAREUS' EPITOME OF ARMINIANISM, OR AN EXAMINATION OF THE FIVE ARTICLES OF THE REMONSTRANT MINISTERS IN THE NETHERLANDS.

units.la: PRIMVS ARTICVLVS.
units.tr: THE FIRST ARTICLE.

units.la: DEVM æterno, immutabili decreto, in Iesu Christo filio suo, ante iactum mundi fundamentum, statuisse, ex lapso peccatis obnoxio humano genere, illos in Christo, propter Christum, & per Christum seruare, qui Spiritus S. gratia, in eundem filium eius credunt, & in ea fidei obedientia, per eandem gratiam in finem perseuerant: Contra vero eos, qui non conuertuntur, & infideles, in peccato & iræ subiectos relinquere, & condemnare, tanquam à Christo alienos: secundum illud Euangelii Ioh. 3. 36. qui credit in filium habet vitam æternam: qui vero filio non assentitur, non videbit vitam æternam, sed ira Dei manet super eum.
units.tr: God, by an eternal and unchangeable decree, determined in Jesus Christ his Son, before the foundation of the world was laid, concerning the human race fallen and subject to sin, to save in Christ, for Christ's sake and through Christ, those who by the grace of the Holy Spirit believe in the same Son of God and persevere to the end in that obedience of faith, through the same grace. On the other hand, he determined to leave and condemn as aliens from Christ those who are not converted and are unbelieving, subject to sin and the wrath of God, in accordance with the words of the Gospel, John 3:36: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not assent to the Son shall not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.

units.la: EXAMEN.
units.tr: EXAMINATION.

units.la: Hic articulus prima fronte nihil incommodi vel quæstionis habere videtur, sed summam Euangelii tradere, quales homines, qualibus mediis Deus ab æterno statuerit seruare, nempe, credentes in filium Dei, & in fide obedientiaque fidei per gratiam Spiritus sancti in finem perseuerantes: quales contra statuerit condemnare: nempe, non conuersos & infideles, à Christo alienos: Quorum utrumque Euangelio docetur.
units.tr: At first sight this article seems to contain nothing objectionable or questionable, but to set out the sum of the Gospel: what kind of people, and by what means, God from eternity determined to save, namely, those who believe in the Son of God and who persevere to the end in faith and in the obedience of faith through the grace of the Holy Spirit; and what kind of people, on the other hand, he determined to condemn, namely, those who are not converted and are unbelieving, aliens from Christ. Both of these are taught in the Gospel.

units.la: Sic multi boni, præsertim politici, de hoc articulo iudicant, neque controuersiam altiorem mouendam censent: præsertim cum omnia salutis media Deo, & Christo, & gratiæ luculenter adscribere videatur. Et reuera nulla hic quæstio esset, si
units.tr: So many good men, especially politicians, judge this article in this way, and think that no deeper controversy should be stirred up, especially since it seems to ascribe all the means of salvation clearly to God, to Christ and to grace. And indeed there would be no question here, if

units.la: autores hoc solum vellent, articulo hoc explicari popularem doctrinam de qualitatibus saluandorum & damnandorum. Quoniam vero in collatione profitentur, hunc articulum continere doctrinam de praedestinatione ad salutem: negant vero, qualitates saluandorum, fidem & perseuerantiam, ex praedestinatione tanquam ex fonte descendere: sed contendunt, eas praedestinatione seu electione ordine priores esse: nec obscure ab hominis voluntate suspendunt: unde necesse est, Deum solida salutis nostrae gloria spoliari, hominem superbia inflari, consolationem Christianam in vita & in morte labefactari, iustificationem gratuitam & salutis certitudinem abnegari, quicquid in contrarium verborum phaleris praetexatur: iccirco articulus hic simpliciter probari non potest: estque plenus aequivocationibus siue cothurnis periculosis, sub quibus Pelagianismus occulte in Ecclesiam inuehitur: Quae fraus ut lateret magis, vocabulo praedestinationis consulto abstinuerunt.
units.tr: the authors wished only this: that by this article the popular doctrine about the qualities of the saved and the damned be explained. But since in their collection they profess that this article contains the doctrine of predestination to salvation, yet deny that the qualities of the saved, faith and perseverance, flow from predestination as from a fountain, but contend that these are prior in order to predestination or election, and openly make them depend on the will of man, it is necessary that God be stripped of the solid glory of our salvation, man be puffed up with pride, Christian comfort in life and in death be weakened, and justification by grace and the certainty of salvation be denied, whatever is put forward in the way of words to the contrary. Therefore this article cannot be simply approved; it is full of equivocations, or dangerous buskins, under cover of which Pelagianism is secretly brought into the Church. In order that this trick might lie more hidden, they deliberately refrained from the word predestination.

units.la: Fuit autem Pelagianismus Augustini temporibus haeresis talis:
units.tr: Now Pelagianism in the times of Augustine was a heresy of this kind:

units.la: 1. Peccatum Adami nemini nocuisse nisi ipsi: nec deteriorem hominem nasci nunc, quam fuerat conditus.
units.tr: 1. The sin of Adam harmed no one but himself, nor is man now born worse than he was created.

units.la: 2. Christum fuisse missum & mortuum ad expianda omnia peccata imitatione Adami commissa.
units.tr: 2. Christ was sent and died to expiate all the sins committed by imitation of Adam.

units.la: 3. Salutem in Christo ita in medio propositam esse omnibus, ut quicunque ad fidem & ad baptismum accedere voluerint, salui esse possint.
units.tr: 3. Salvation in Christ is so set before all in the midst that whoever wishes to come to faith and to baptism may be saved.

units.la: 4. Qui vero credituri, bene operaturi, & in fide per Dei gratiam iuuanda mansuri essent, praescisse Deum ante mundi constitutionem, & eos praedestinasse in regnum suum, quos gratis vocatos prae aliis credituros, & dignos futuros electione, deque hac vita bono fine excessuros praeuiderit.
units.tr: 4. But those who would believe, work well, and remain in faith through the help of God's grace, God foreknew before the foundation of the world, and predestined them into his kingdom: those whom he foresaw would be called freely before others, would believe, and would be worthy of election, and would depart from this life with a good end.

units.la: 5. Gratiam Dei omnibus dari ex merito, pro bono vsu liberi arbitrii.
units.tr: 5. The grace of God is given to all on account of merit, for a good use of free will.

units.la: 6. Et quidem dari in tantum, ut homo in hac vita sine omni peccato esse possit, si velit.
units.tr: 6. And indeed it is given to such an extent that a man in this life can be without all sin, if he wishes.

units.la: Aduersus hanc haeresin Hieronymus & Augustinus multum disputarunt, & Augustinus quidem tria capita in opusculis suis todemo 7. omnia reuocauit. 1. De peccato originis. 2. De gratia & causa praedestinationis. 3. De perfectione iustitiae. Pelagius in synodo Palaestina damnatus reuocauit errorem in tantum, ut diceret: Anathema, qui vel sentit vel dicit, gratiam Dei, qua Christus venit in hunc mundum, peccatores saluos facere, non solum per singulas horas, aut per singula momenta, sed etiam per singulos actus nostros, non esse necessariam: Et qui hanc conantur auferre, poenas sortiuntur aeternas. nas. Quis Pelagium hic non absoluisset? sed fucum & fraudem Palæstinis Episcopis fecit cothurno gratia: ut Augustinus ostendit. Reliquit post se discipulos duos præcipue, acris ingenii iuuenes Cælestium & Iulianum, quibuscum multum Augustino fuit negotii in Africa. Transuolauit hæc pestis tandem mediterraneum mare in Siciliam & Galliam Massiliensem, non quidem integra, sed quantum ad caput de gratia & prædestinatione & morte Christi, cuius proinde assertores vocabantur Semipelagiani & Pelagianorum reliquiæ: de quibus extant Prosperi Aquitani & Hilarii Arelatensis Epistolæ ad Augustinum: & huius erudita duobus libris de prædestinatione sanctorum, & de bono perseuerantiæ, atque etiam tertio de correptione & gratia comprehensa responsio. Qua si articulorum Authores hodie stare vellent, vti stare possent ac deberent, (est enim tota Pauli-na) res iudicata iam haberetur. Reuera enim Massiliensium & Siracusanorum causam nonnihil interpolatam Arminius cum sequacibus hodie reassumpsit. Neque is ignorare id potuit: vn-de parum ingenua tergiuersatione scripsit in articulis, se nec Semipelagianismum sibi obiectum, nec dorantem, nec quincuncem vel trientem eius agnoscere.
units.tr: Against this heresy Jerome and Augustine disputed at length, and Augustine indeed in his small works, in the seventh volume, retracted all three chief points: 1. On original sin. 2. On grace and the cause of predestination. 3. On the perfection of righteousness. Pelagius, condemned at the Synod of Palestine, retracted his error so far that he said: Anathema to him who thinks or says that the grace of God, by which Christ came into this world to save sinners, is not necessary not only for each hour or each moment, but also for each of our actions; and those who try to take this away incur eternal punishments. Who would not have acquitted Pelagius here? But he played a trick and deceived the Palestinian bishops by the buskin of grace, as Augustine showed. He left behind him two disciples especially, young men of sharp wit, Caelestius and Julian, with whom Augustine had much trouble in Africa. This plague at last flew across the Mediterranean Sea into Sicily and Massilian Gaul, not indeed whole, but as far as the chief points concerning grace, predestination and the death of Christ; its supporters were therefore called Semipelagians and remnants of the Pelagians. Concerning them there survive the Letters of Prosper of Aquitaine and Hilary of Arles to Augustine, and his learned response in two books on the predestination of the saints and on the gift of perseverance, and also a third on rebuke and grace. If the authors of the articles wished to stand by this response today, as they could and ought to do (for it is wholly Pauline), the matter would already be considered settled. For indeed Arminius with his followers has today revived, somewhat altered, the cause of the Massilians and Syracusans. Nor could he be ignorant of this; hence in his articles he wrote, with rather disingenuous evasion, that he acknowledged neither Semipelagianism objected to him, nor its dorantes, nor its quincunx or triens.

units.la: Ad articulum vt reuertamur, æquiuocationes variæ sic patent:
units.tr: To return to the article, the various equivocations are evident as follows:

units.la: I. Cothurnus primus latet in immutabili Dei decreto. Iuxta scripturas immutabile Dei decretum est, quod absolute non muratur, nec à creaturis mutari potest. Sic enim Deus pronuntiat se immutabilem, & consilium suum immutabile: Ego DEVS, & non mutor: Consilium meum stabit, & omnem meam voluntatem fa-ciam. Illi vero intelligunt, Deum decreto immutabili quidem statuisse seruare credentes, quoad speciem, hoc est, nonnisi credentes: sed non omnino immutabili, quod indiuidua, hunc vel illum credentem: nisi sub conditione, si hic vel ille credens mutationem non inducat. Sentiunt enim (vt liquet Art. V.) eos qui hodie sunt vere credentes, cras posse fieri plane incredulos, rursusque ex incredulis fieri credentes. Consequenter igitur sentiunt, Deum eos, quos heri credentes immutabili decreto sub conditione statuerat seruare, hodie mutata conditione statuere non seruare, perendie rursus mutata conditione rursus statuere seruare: quod an sit Dei immutabile decretum statuere, ipsi viderint. Certe vertibilis umbra non magis mutabilis erit tali decreto: quod scriptura negat.
units.tr: I. The first buskin lies hidden in the immutable decree of God. According to the Scriptures, the immutable decree of God is that which is absolutely not changed, nor can be changed by creatures. For thus God declares himself immutable, and his counsel unchangeable: I am the LORD, and I change not; my counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure. But they understand that God, by an immutable decree, indeed determined to save believers, as to kind, that is, only believers; but not wholly immutable, as to individuals, this or that believer, unless under the condition that this or that believer does not bring about a change. For they hold (as is clear from Article V) that those who today are truly believers can tomorrow become plainly unbelieving, and again from unbelievers become believers. Consequently, they hold that God, who had determined by an immutable decree under condition to save those who were believers yesterday, today, the condition having changed, determined not to save them; the day after tomorrow, the condition having changed again, determined again to save them. Whether this is an immutable decree of God to determine, they themselves must see. Certainly a shadow that turns is no more changeable than such a decree; which Scripture denies.

units.la: Tale decretum in Deo ponunt Authores Decreti Holland. Matth. 11, 21. & 23, negantes, à Deo ad salutem inuitari quemquam, cuius salutem omnino non dare DECREVERIT. Hoc enim posito, dicendum est, 37. Deum ciuitatibus Galilææ & Iudææ, quas Christus prædicans ad salutem inuitabat, salutem omnino dare decreuisse. Atqui cum non crederent, salutem eis non dedit. Ergo vel salutem eis dare prius non decreuerat, vel postea decretum mutauit.
units.tr: The authors of the Holland Decree put such a decree in God, citing Matthew 11:21 and 23, denying that anyone is invited by God to salvation whose salvation he has absolutely not decreed to give. For if this is granted, it must be said that God decreed absolutely to give salvation to the cities of Galilee and Judea, to which Christ preaching invited them to salvation. But since they did not believe, he did not give them salvation. Therefore either he had not previously decreed to give them salvation, or he afterwards changed the decree.

units.la: II. Alius cothurnus, isque præcipuus, fundamentum reliquorum, summam totius causæ, differentiamque vtriusque partis continens, subest verbo statuisse. Hoc nobis, iuxta scripturas significat, Deum eos, qui in tempore credunt, & perseverant, & seruantur, ab æterno non solum seruare statuisse, sed etiam in Christo elegisse, & ad salutem prædestinasse, & qualitates ad salutem requisitas, puta, fidem, conuersionem & perseverantiam, per verbum & gratiam Spiritus sancti in eis efficere decreuisse, vt infallibiliter seruentur: idque ad laudem gloriosæ gratiæ declarandam: Contra vero eos, qui in tempore non credunt, neque perseuerant, neque seruantur, ab æterno statuisse non seruare, neq; in Christo elegisse, neq; ad vitam æternam ordinasse, neq; fidem & perseuerantiam eis dare, sed in cœcitate vel infidelitate originali eos relinquere, & propter peccata damnare decreuisse: idque ad ostendendam in eis iram & notam faciendam potentiam suam.
units.tr: II. Another buskin, and the chief one, the foundation of the rest, containing the sum of the whole cause and the difference between the two parties, lies under the word determined. According to the Scriptures this means to us that God determined from eternity not only to save those who in time believe, persevere and are preserved, but also in Christ to have chosen them and predestined them to salvation, and decreed to bring about in them, through the Word and the grace of the Holy Spirit, the qualities required for salvation, namely faith, conversion and perseverance, so that they are infallibly saved, and this to declare the praise of his glorious grace. On the other hand, he determined from eternity not to save those who in time do not believe, do not persevere, and are not saved, nor to choose them in Christ, nor to ordain them to eternal life, nor to give them faith and perseverance, but to leave them in blindness or original unbelief, and to condemn them on account of their sins; and this to show his wrath in them and to make known his power.

units.la: Vtrumq; diuini huius statuti membrum ex scripturis, & perpetua mundi historia atque experientia manifestum est. Prius membrum (quod Electio & Prædestinatio Sanctorum ad gloriam vocatur) traditur Rom.8.30. Eph.1.3. Act.13.48. Philip.2.13.1.Thess.1.4.2. Thess.2.13. Matth.24.24. &c. Posterius membrum (quod reprobationem & prædestinationem malorum ad poenam Theologi vocant) Matt.11.25. Ioh.10.26. Rom.9.21.22. Prou.16.4. 1.Pet.2.8. Iud.v.4. &c.
units.tr: Both parts of this divine decree are made plain from Scripture and from the constant history and experience of the world. The first part, which is called the election and predestination of the saints to glory, is taught in Rom. 8.30; Eph. 1.3; Acts 13.48; Phil. 2.13; 1 Thess. 1.4; 2 Thess. 2.13; Matt. 24.24, etc. The second part, which the theologians call the reprobation and predestination of the wicked to punishment, is taught in Matt. 11.25; John 10.26; Rom. 9.21, 22; Prov. 16.4; 1 Pet. 2.8; Jude v. 4, etc.

units.la: Testatur etiam perpetua mundi historia & experientia, Deum subinde sic discriminasse populos, vt vnum dignaretur gratia fœderis sui, & vocationis per verbum, alium non: discriminasse etiam vocatorum indiuidua, vt vnum efficace gratia donaret, fide, conuersione, perseuerantia & salute, alterum non: idque nullo populorum vel indiuiduorum merito, aut præstantiæ ingeniorum ratione habita: (omnia enim inuenit pariter à bono cœlesti auersa, omniaque pariter flectere & dirigere ad se potuit si voluisset) sed mero beneplacito & bonitate: Sic Israelitarum populum elegit peculium; gentibus aliis reprobatis. Psal. 147.19. Annunciat iudicia sua Israeli, non fecit taliter vlli nationi. Iesu.41.9. Elegi te, & non reprobaui te. Cur autem? Deut.7.7. Non quia plures essetis præ omnibus populis, amauit vos Iehoua, & elegit vos: sed quia diligebat vos Iehoua, &c. Rursus ex vocatis Israelitis, subinde alios elegit, alios reprobauit: Iacob dilexit, Esau odio habuit, &c. idque non ex operibus: sed vt propositum electionis firmum maneret, &c. Et hoc nostro seculo, nos Christianos solos dignatur vocare per verbum Evangelii: Turcas, Paganos, &c. non dignatur: Ex Christianis etiam vocatis alios donat vera fide, conuersione, perseuerantia & æterna salute, alios non donat, sed in ignorantia vel hypocrisi relinquit.
units.tr: The constant history and experience of the world also testify that God has at various times so distinguished between peoples that he deigned to grant one the grace of his covenant and calling through the Word, and not another. He has likewise distinguished between the individuals who are called, giving to one, by efficacious grace, faith, conversion, perseverance and salvation, and not to another. And he has done this with no regard to the merit of peoples or individuals, or to the quality of their minds. For he found all alike turned away from the heavenly good, and he could have bent and directed all alike to himself, had he willed it. He did it by mere good pleasure and goodness. Thus he chose the people of Israel as his peculiar possession and rejected the other nations. Ps. 147.19: "He declares his judgments to Israel; he has not done so for any other nation." Isa. 41.9: "I have chosen you and not rejected you." But why? Deut. 7.7: "Not because you were more numerous than all peoples did the LORD love you and choose you, but because the LORD loved you, etc." Again, from among the called Israelites he chose some and rejected others: he loved Jacob and hated Esau, etc., and this not on account of works, but that the purpose of election might remain firm, etc. And in our own age he deigns to call only us Christians through the word of the Gospel; he does not deign to call Turks, pagans, etc. Among the Christians who are called, he gives true faith, conversion, perseverance and eternal salvation to some, and does not give them to others, but leaves them in ignorance or hypocrisy.

units.la: Neque potest hæc populorum & personarum discriminatio diuinæ prouidentiæ derogari, & ingeniis hominum adscribi, citra blasphemiam. Secus pro discriminatione nostri per vocationem & adoptionem præaliis, nullis opus foret ad Deum precibus, nec Deo deberemus gratias: nec staret illud Apostoli: Quis te discreuit? quid habes quod non accepisti? quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Staret v. Atheismus, quem Pelagiana hæresis inuexit: Ego me discreui: habeo quod non accepi: quod est barathrum inferni.
units.tr: Nor can this distinction of peoples and persons be taken away from God's providence and ascribed to human abilities without blasphemy. Otherwise, if our distinction from others through calling and adoption depended on ourselves, there would be no need of prayers to God, and we ought not to give thanks to God. Nor would the Apostle's words stand: Who makes you to differ? What have you that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it? Rather the atheism would stand which the Pelagian heresy brought in: I made myself to differ; I have what I did not receive, which is the abyss of hell.

units.la: Est autem in Theologia indubitabilis regula, nitens S. Scripturæ autoritate: Quicquid Deus in tempore facit: id eum ab æterno facere decreuisse, cum in Deum nulla cadere possit mutatio. Quare discriminationem illam electorum & non electorum, sed reproborum: saluandorum & non saluandorum, sed propter peccata damnandorum, quam videmus Deum fecisse, & facere in tempore, eum ab æterno sic facere decreuisse, indubitabile Christianis esse debet: Spoliatus enim Deus (verba Lutheri sunt) virtute & sapientia eligendi, quid erit nisi idolum fortuna, cuius nutu omnia temere fiunt? Et tandem eò venietur, vt homines salui fiant & damnentur ignorante Deo: vt qui non discreuerit certa electione saluandos & damnandos, & oblata omnibus generali lenitate, tolerante & indurante, tum misericordia corripiente & puniente hominibus reliquerit, vtri velint salui fieri aut damnari: ipse interim forte ad conuiuium Æthiopum profectus, vt Homerus dicit. Atque hæc est orthodoxæ de prædestinatione doctrinæ summa: sicque verbum statuisse in Articulo est iuxta scripturas & experientiam prorsus intelligendum. Illis vero longe aliter significat, Deum eos, qui in tempore credunt & perseuerant, ab æterno quidem statuisse seruare, sub conditione, si crederent & perseuerarent: cæterum nec ad salutem eos magis quam alios omnes ordinasse, nec in Christo elegisse, nisi euentualiter, quatenus illi præaliis in Christum crederent & perseuerarent: (fidem enim & perseuerantiam electione priorem faciunt) vt vero illi potius quam alii crederent & perseuerarent, non statuisse Deum singulari aliqua gratia in illis efficere: sed decreuisse omnibus hominibus vniuersalem quandam, excitantem quidem & præuenientem, sed indifferentem & resistibilem gratiam offerre, cui... re: cui qui non resistunt, sed bono vsu liberi arbitrii assentiuntur & cooperantur, ad fidem concipiendam, & perseverantiam in finem vsque praestandam, illi sint in Christo electi & praedestinati, & hos proinde Deum ab aeterno euentualiter ex fide & perseuerantia praeuisa elegisse in Christo, atque ad salutem praedestinasse, seu seruare statuisse: qui v. eidem resistunt, vel non cooperari ad fidem & perseuerantiam volunt, illi non sint in Christo electi & praedestinati: & hos proinde Deum ab aeterno euentualiter ex praeuisa infidelitate ad damnationem praedestinasse, siue damnare statuisse. Hanc esse propriissimam illorum mentem, omnes eorum declarationes ostendunt. Eandem v. fuisse Semipelagianorum Massilienfium & Siracusanorum sententiam, legat apud August. locis prius dictis, qui non credit, vel dubitat. Manifestum autem est, quod, secundum eam, neque fides, conuersio, perseuerantia & salus nostra: neque discrimination nostri abaliis, gratiae Dei in solidum, sed nostrae voluntati atque cooperationi debeatur. Quando enim exempli gratia, in vna ciuitate ex pluribus eandem concionem audientibus, eandemque gratiam excitantem habentibus, hic credit ille non credit, hic perseverat, alter deficit, si Paulus Apost. quaerat ex credente & perseuerante: Quis te discreuit? Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Respondebit ille: Ego me discreui; quia gratiae excitanti cooperari volui: voluntatem cooperandi habui, non accepi. Quo blasphemo mendacio nonne homo se cum diabolo in infernum praecipitabit? Si autem fides & perseuerantia & salus nostra nostrae voluntati superaedificatur, quomodo iustificatio gratuita? & cum voluntate humana nihil sit mutabilis, nonne tota salus nostra stabit super arena, omnisque certitudo & consolatio Christiana redibit in nihilum? De altero cothurno satis.
units.tr: In theology there is an indubitable rule, resting on the authority of Holy Scripture: Whatever God does in time, he decreed from eternity to do, since no change can fall upon God. Therefore that distinction between the elect and the non-elect, or rather between the reprobate, those to be saved and those not to be saved but condemned for their sins, which we see God has made and is making in time, must be beyond doubt for Christians: that he decreed it from eternity. For God, stripped of power and wisdom to choose (these are Luther's words), what will he be but an idol of Fortune, at whose nod all things happen at random? And at last it will come to this, that men are saved and damned with God ignorant: since he has not distinguished by a certain election those to be saved and those to be damned, but, offering to all a general gentleness, tolerating and hardening, and then by mercy correcting and punishing, has left men to choose whether they will be saved or damned, while he himself perhaps has gone off to the feast of the Ethiopians, as Homer says. This is the sum of the orthodox doctrine of predestination, and so the word decreed in the article must be understood entirely in accordance with Scripture and experience. But to them it means something quite different: that God indeed decreed from eternity to save those who in time believe and persevere, under the condition that they would believe and persevere; but that he did not ordain them to salvation more than all others, nor elect them in Christ, except eventually, insofar as they believe and persevere in Christ rather than others (for they make faith and perseverance prior to election). And that God did not decree to bring about in them, by some singular grace, that they rather than others should believe and persevere; instead he decreed to offer to all men a universal grace, indeed arousing and preventing, but indifferent and resistible. Those who do not resist it, but by the good use of free will assent to it and cooperate with it, so as to conceive faith and furnish perseverance to the end, are elected and predestined in Christ. These God from eternity eventually elected in Christ, foreseeing their faith and perseverance, and predestined to salvation, or decreed to save. But those who resist the same, or are unwilling to cooperate for faith and perseverance, these are not elected and predestined in Christ; and these God from eternity eventually predestined to damnation, foreseeing their unbelief, or decreed to condemn. That this is their very own mind, all their declarations show. The opinion of the Semipelagians of Marseilles and Syracuse was the same. Whoever doubts or disbelieves this may read Augustine in the passages cited above. Now it is clear that, according to this view, neither our faith, conversion, perseverance and salvation, nor our distinction from others, is owed wholly to the grace of God, but to our will and cooperation. For when, for example, in one city among many people hearing the same sermon and having the same arousing grace, this one believes and that one does not, this one perseveres and the other falls away, if the Apostle Paul asks the believer and the perseverer, Who makes you to differ? What have you that you did not receive?, he will answer: I made myself to differ, because I was willing to cooperate with the arousing grace; I had the will to cooperate, I did not receive it. Will not a man, with this blasphemous lie, hurl himself into hell along with the devil? But if our faith, perseverance and salvation are built upon our own will, how is justification gratuitous? And since nothing is changeable with the human will, will not our whole salvation stand upon sand, and all Christian certainty and comfort come to nothing? Enough of the other buskin.

units.la: III. Est & aequiuocatio in verbis: Ex lapso, peccatis obnoxio, genere humano: Lapsum genus humanum Scriptura & Catechesis intelligit, ex lapsu Adae peccato originali perditum, hoc est, non solum in peccatis mortuum, sed & adeo vitiatum ac depravatum, vt ad bene agendum prorsus non sit idoneum, & ad omne malum procliue, donec per Spiritum sanctum renegeretur; quale Deus propagare, ex quali etiam sicut in tempore sibi colligit, sic ab aeterno sibi colligere decreuit, hoc est, in Christo elegit aeternam Ecclesiam. Isti intelligunt quidem lapsum, siue originali, (de quo nondum se declararunt) siue actuali bus peccatis obnoxium: non vero ita depravatum, quin possit libera voluntate velle & eligere bonum vel malum: Deum vocantem audire: pulsanti aperire: gratiae excitanti resistere, vel assentiri & cooperari: Qui sensus repugnat scripturæ & veritati: Quis te discreuit? Non sumus ex nobis idonei &c. Prudentia carnis est inimicitia aduersus Deum.
units.tr: III. There is also an equivocation in the words "from the fallen human race, subject to sin." Scripture and the Catechism understand the human race as fallen, lost through the fall of Adam by original sin. That is, it is not only dead in sins but so corrupted and depraved that it is wholly unfit to do good and prone to every evil, until it is regenerated through the Holy Spirit. God propagates such a race, and from such a race, just as he gathers to himself in time, so he decreed to gather from eternity; that is, he elected the eternal Church in Christ. Those men indeed understand the fall as subjecting humanity to sin, whether original (on which they have not yet declared themselves) or actual, but not so depraved that it cannot, by free will, will and choose good or evil, hear God calling, open to one knocking, and resist or assent to and cooperate with arousing grace. This sense is contrary to Scripture and truth: "Who makes you to differ?" "We are not sufficient of ourselves," etc. "The wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God."

units.la: IV. Est quoque notabilis cothurnus in relatiuo illos: Quod nos cum Apostolo, Rom.8.30. intelligimus de hominibus certis in individuo, de Petro, & Paulo, &c. prædestinatis a Deo non modo ad salutem & gloriam, sed etiam ad antecedentia media salutis, & ad qualitates in saluandis requisitas, vocationem externam & internam, ad fidem & iustificationem, ad conuersionem & perseuerantiam in finem: iuxta sententiam Apostoli: Quos prædestinauit, hos & vocauit; quos vocauit, hos & iustificauit; quos iustificauit, hos & glorificauit; Quorum (inquit Augustinus) ita est certus numerus, ut nec addatur eis quisquam nec minuatur ex eis: Quibus etiam solis datur infallibiliter, ut credant, & perseverent, & perire non possint: sicut dicitur: Crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam, hoc est, Interprete Chrysostomo prædestinati à Deo: Et: Qui cœpit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet in diem vsque Iesu Christi: Et: Impossibile est seduci electos.
units.tr: IV. There is also a notable buskin in the relative pronoun "those." We, with the Apostle (Rom. 8.30), understand it of certain men individually, of Peter and Paul, etc., predestined by God not only to salvation and glory but also to the antecedent means of salvation, and to the qualities required in those to be saved: external and internal calling, faith and justification, conversion and perseverance to the end. This is according to the saying of the Apostle: "Whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified; whom he justified, these he also glorified." Of these (says Augustine) the number is so certain that nothing is added to them and nothing taken from them. To these alone it is infallibly given to believe and persevere, and they cannot perish, as it is said: "As many as were ordained to eternal life believed" (that is, as Chrysostom explains, predestined by God). And: "He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ." And: "It is impossible for the elect to be led astray."

units.la: Illi intelligunt homines non certos, sed quoscunque eventualiter credituros, vel certos quidem, sed tantum in specie, non in individuo: credentes ante electionem: prædestinatos non ad fidem & perseverantiam, sed post fidem ad salutem eventualiter, si perseverent: Breuius: Nos intelligimus illos, quos electio seu prædestinatio facit credentes & perseverantes: Illi, quos electio inuenit credentes & perseverantes: Breuissime: Nos intelligimus credituros & credentes consequenter, seu post electionem: Illi credituros & credentes antecedenter, seu ordine, ante electionem: Quomodo nimirum currus trahit equos. Si enim fides non potest esse ante vocationem, quæ est electione & prædestinatione posterior: quomodo potest esse ante electionem: Atqui Apostolus contra: Elegit nos, vt essemus sancti: non, cum essemus sancti: sanctificationis vero nostræ principium fides est. Act.15,9.
units.tr: Those men understand by "men certainly saved" not persons who are certain individually, but whoever will believe eventually; or they grant that they are certain, but only in kind, not individually: that they are believing before election, and predestined not to faith and perseverance, but after faith to salvation eventually, if they persevere. More briefly: we understand those whom election or predestination makes believers and persevering; they understand those whom election finds believing and persevering. Most briefly: we understand those who will believe and do believe consequently, that is, after election; they understand those who will believe and do believe antecedently, that is, in order, before election. This is just as a cart draws the horses. For if faith cannot be before calling, which comes later than election and predestination, how can it be before election? Yet the Apostle argues the contrary: "He chose us that we should be holy," not "when we were holy"; and the beginning of our sanctification is faith. Acts 15:9.

units.la: V. Non dissimilis cothurnus latet in verbis: In Christo. Nos intelligimus cum Apostolo, Deum ante iacta mundi fundamenta nos elegisse in Christo consequenter, h.e. vt fide & spiritu inseremur Christo, tanquam membra capiti, essemusque in Christo post electionem: Mox enim declarat Apostolus v.4. Praedestinauit nos in adoptionem per Iesum Christum: Adoptio vero fit per fidem. Johan.1,12. Illi intelligunt Deum nos elegisse in Christo antecedenter, hoc est, ante electionem existentes in Christo per præuisam fidem. Vnde vero electis fides ordine ante electionem: Num ex gratia Dei? Non certe. Gratiam enim Apostolus facit electione & prædestinatione posteriorem, dicēs: Elegit prædestinauit nos ad laudem gloriosæ GRATIÆ SVÆ. Num non igi-tur ex libero arbitrio? Hoc cum Pelagio statuant necesse est, Videatur Augustinus de prædestin.sanct.cap.19.
units.tr: V. A similar buskin lurks in the words "in Christ." We understand, with the Apostle, that God before the foundation of the world chose us in Christ consequently, that is, that we are engrafted into Christ by faith and the Spirit, as members into the head, and so we are in Christ after election. For the Apostle soon declares (v. 4): "He predestined us to adoption through Jesus Christ"; but adoption comes by faith (John 1:12). They understand that God chose us in Christ antecedently, that is, that we, existing in Christ before election through foreseen faith. But whence do the elect have faith in order before election? From the grace of God? Certainly not. For the Apostle places grace after election and predestination, saying: "He chose and predestined us to the praise of the glory of his grace." Is it not therefore from free will? They must hold this with Pelagius. Let Augustine be consulted, On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 19.

units.la: VI.In verbis,per Christum & propter Christum: dubitari potest, an non etiam lateat cothurnus. Nos simpliciter intelligi-mus,per & propter Christi λύτρῳ satisfactorium. Illi de satis-factione Christi dissimiliter sentiunt & loquuntur. Constat e-nim,Vorstium,cum quo eundem funem trahunt, de satisfactio-ne Christi vel nulla, vel semipleua, nec necessaria, iampridem multa ex Socino Samosateniano scandalosè disputasse.
units.tr: VI. In the words "through Christ and on account of Christ" it may be doubted whether a buskin is not also hidden. We simply understand "through and on account of Christ" as the satisfying ransom [λύτρον]. They think and speak differently about the satisfaction of Christ. For it is established that Vorstius, with whom they pull the same rope, has for a long time scandalously disputed, following Socinus of Samosata, that Christ's satisfaction is either none or half-complete and not necessary.

units.la: VII.Cothurnus insignis latet in vocabulo Gratia: quod licet alias varie significet; in quæstione tamen de causa fidei, conuersionis & perseuerantiæ & salutis nostræ: Gratia proprie est efficax motus & tractus misericordiæ Dei, in mentibus & cordibus electorum; fidem, conuersionem & perseuerantiam ineffabili modo operantis. De qua Christus: Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Et Augustinus: Legant & intelligant, intueantur atque fateantur. Pelagiani, non lege atque doctrina forinsecus insonante, sed interna atque occulta, mirabili ac ineffabili potestate operari Deum in cordibus hominum, non solum nouas reuelationes, sed etiam BONAS VOLUNTATES. Illi intelligunt Gratiam tum externæ vocationis per verbum: tum interna suasionis moralis per Spiritum, sed indifferentis, quam pe-nes liberum hominis arbitrium sit bene vel male determinare, recipere, vel respuere. Ideo Resistibilem vocant, vt patebit Art. V quæ opinio & gloriæ Dei derogat, & hominem suo reti sacri-ficare h.e. contra Deum superbire facit, & certitudinem salutis & consolationem nostram in vita & morte conuellit, vt ostensum cothurno 11.
units.tr: VII. A notable buskin lurks in the word "grace," which, although it has various meanings elsewhere, in the question about the cause of faith, conversion, perseverance and our salvation means: grace properly is the efficacious motion and drawing of God's mercy in the minds and hearts of the elect, working faith, conversion and perseverance in an ineffable manner. Of this Christ says: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." And Augustine: "Let them read and understand, look and confess." The Pelagians, not by a law and teaching sounding from outside, but by an inner and hidden, wondrous and ineffable power, say God works in the hearts of men not only new revelations but also good wills. They understand grace as both the external calling through the Word, and the internal moral persuasion through the Spirit, but indifferent, such that it lies in the free will of man to determine it well or badly, to receive it or reject it. Therefore they call it "resistible," as will be clear in Article V. This opinion both detracts from the glory of God, and makes man sacrifice himself to his own net, that is, makes him proud against God, and overturns the certainty of salvation and our consolation in life and death, as shown under buskin 11.

units.la: VIII. Etiam in verbo credere, & nomine fidei haud dubie iu-ditur. Nobis credere est non tantum omni verbo Dei assentiri, sed præcipue & proprie promissione Euangelii de gratia & remissione peccatorum propter Christi sanguinem confidere. Mar. 5.26. Crede tantum modo, pro, confide. Et hunc sensum præsertim habet in phrasi, credere in Deum, in Christum, &c. Si creditis in Deum, etiam in me credite: pro, confidite: Consolatur enim ibi Apostolos. Domine quis est, vt credamus eum? pro, vt confidam in eo. Fides saluifica nobis est coniuncta cum fiducia promissionis Euangelii, seu promissæ misericordiæ Dei de remissione peccatorum propter Christi sanguinem: vt, cum dicimur fide iustificari, fides fiduciam significat: & fide iustificari, est fiducia meriti Christi à peccatis absolui: quem sensum Apostolus tra-dit, cum dicit: Quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine guine suo, ad declarandum justitiam suam, per remissionem peccatorum praecedentium: vbi fides in sanguine suo, non potest nisi fiduciam sanguinis Christi significare.
units.tr: VIII. Also in the word "believe" and the name "faith" they are undoubtedly misled. For us, to "believe" is not merely to assent to every word of God, but chiefly and properly to trust in the promise of the Gospel concerning grace and the remission of sins for the sake of Christ's blood. Mark 5:36: "Only believe," that is, trust. And it especially has this sense in the phrase "believe in God," "in Christ," etc.: "If you believe in God, believe also in me," that is, trust; for there he consoles the Apostles. "Lord, who is he, that we may believe on him?" that is, that I may trust in him. Saving faith is joined to the trust in the promise of the Gospel, or of God's promised mercy, of the remission of sins for the sake of Christ's blood; so that when we are said to be "justified by faith," faith signifies trust, and to be justified by faith is to trust in the merit of Christ to be absolved from sins. The Apostle hands down this sense when he says: "Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness through the remission of past sins" (Rom. 3:25), where "faith in his blood" can signify nothing but trust in the blood of Christ.

units.la: Illi vero, quod fidem tantum de assensu, credere tantum pro assentiri intelligant, tum hoc ostendit, quod in articulo verba Joh.cap.3.v.36. ὁ δὲ ἀπειθῶν τῷ υἱῷ, reddunt: Qui vero non assentitur Filio: pro, qui non credit Filio: tum lubricae ipsorum de fide disputationes docent. Quibus plerunque fiduciam in fide non requirunt: & fidem justificare, seu ad justitiam imputari volunt, non quia Christi meritum sibi applicat: sed quia ipse fidei actus pro impletione legis reputatur, quae Alberij Triuncuriani deplorati hominis fuit opinio.
units.tr: But they, who understand "faith" only of assent and "believe" only as "assent," show this in the passage John 3:36, where they render ὁ δὲ ἀπειθῶν τῷ υἱῷ as "he who does not assent to the Son," instead of "he who does not believe the Son"; and their slippery disputations about faith teach the same. They mostly do not require trust in faith, and they want faith to justify, or to be imputed for righteousness, not because it applies Christ's merit to us, but because the act of faith itself is reckoned as the fulfilling of the law. This was the opinion of the deplorable man Albert Trincurian.

units.la: Cum igitur tot aequivocationibus depravet veram, occultet falsam de praedestinatione doctrinam, hic Articulus, utique approbari simpliciter non potest.
units.tr: Since, therefore, with so many equivocations they corrupt the true doctrine of predestination and hide the false, this Article certainly cannot simply be approved.

units.la: An articulus (seposita praedestinatione) sufficere & tolerari possit?
units.tr: Whether the article can suffice and be tolerated when predestination is set aside?

units.la: Quid vero, inquies, de praedestinatione adeo est disputandum? Nonne ad salutem sufficit tenere summam Euangelij Articulo hoc traditam: Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet vitam aeternam. Qui non credit, super eo manet ira Dei? & annon hactenus tolerari possit Articulus?
units.tr: But, you will say, must there be so much debate about predestination? Is it not enough for salvation to hold the sum of the Gospel that this article sets forth: He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life; he who does not believe, the wrath of God remains upon him? And can the article not be tolerated up to this point?

units.la: Scio sic aliquos judicare: immo scripserunt viri alias eruditi & pij, de praedestinatione non esse disputandum in Euangelio, sed tantum praedicandum de promissionibus universalibus gratiae. Verum boni isti non observarunt, sic scribendo se contradicere Spiritui sancto, qui certe in Euangelio doctrinam de praedestinatione tradidit, ut supra cothurno II. locis allegatis videre est; videntur autem vel hoc praetextu imprudentes ipsi fundamentum fidei & consolationis nostrae labefactare, vel ab aliis labefactari non observare. Illud igitur siue Ambrosij siue Prosperi piissime dictum hic tenendum de praedestinatione: Quod Deus occulta esse voluit, non sunt scrutanda: quae autem manifesta fecit, non sunt neganda: ne in illis illicite curiosi; & in istis damnabiliter inveniamur ingrati. Sicut igitur illicita est curiositas, non revelata in Euangelio de praedestinatione velle scrutari: sic damnabilis est ingratitudo, quae de praedestinatione Deus in Euangelio revelavit, velle negare vel opprimere. Ad quaesitum vero sic respondetur.
units.tr: I know that some judge this way. Indeed, men otherwise learned and pious have written that predestination is not to be disputed in the Gospel, but only the universal promises of grace are to be preached. Yet these good men did not notice that by writing so they contradict the Holy Spirit, who certainly set forth the doctrine of predestination in the Gospel, as can be seen in the passages cited above in the second chapter. They seem, however, either through this pretext to undermine, unwittingly, the foundation of our faith and comfort, or not to notice that others are undermining it. Therefore that most pious saying, whether of Ambrose or of Prosper, is to be held here concerning predestination: What God has willed to be hidden is not to be searched into; what he has made manifest is not to be denied, lest we be found rashly curious about the former and culpably ungrateful about the latter. Just as it is an unlawful curiosity to wish to search into what is not revealed in the Gospel concerning predestination, so it is a culpable ingratitude to wish to deny or suppress what God has revealed in the Gospel concerning predestination. Now let us answer the question as follows.

units.la: Sufficientiam quod attinet, perinde quaeras in Ecclesia: Annon sufficiat ad salutem doctrina Catechetica, de miseria hominis, de liberatione per Christum, deque gratitudine? Quorsum igitur lectio Bibliorum, & sublimior Theologia?
units.tr: As for sufficiency, you may ask the same thing of the Church: Is not the catechetical teaching sufficient for salvation, concerning the misery of man, deliverance through Christ, and gratitude? Why then the reading of the Bible and the higher theology?

units.la: In Logica: An non sufficiat tenere, tot esse figuras syllogismorum, & tot modos? Quorsum igitur organo Aristotelico opus in Scholis.
units.tr: In logic: Is it not enough to know that there are so many figures of syllogisms and so many moods? Why then is the Aristotelian Organon needed in the schools?

units.la: In politica: An non sufficiat popularis scientia juris & æqui ad Rempubl. gubernandam? Quorsum igitur tantus Legum apparatus, tam operosa juris prudentia?
units.tr: In politics: Is not a popular knowledge of law and equity enough for governing the commonwealth? Why then such a great apparatus of laws, such laborious legal learning?

units.la: In Mathematica: An non sufficiat, nosse triangulum habere tres duobus, &c. diametrum ad circumferentiam esse in subtripla proportione superpartiente unam septimam, &c. Quorsum igitur tam arduæ & intricatæ demonstrationes Euclydis?
units.tr: In mathematics: Is it not enough to know that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, etc., and that the diameter is to the circumference in the sub-triple superparticular proportion of one seventh, etc.? Why then the so difficult and intricate demonstrations of Euclid?

units.la: Ad talia nemo non facile respondendum videt, aliquibus quidem prima disciplinarum istarum elementa, cognitionem nempe & σὺ satis esse posse: sed non omnibus.
units.tr: Nobody can fail to see that to such questions one may readily reply that for some people the first elements of these disciplines, namely knowledge and the "that" [τὸ ὅτι], may indeed be enough, but not for everyone.

units.la: Catechumenis in Ecclesia sufficere ad salutem possunt rudimenta Catecherica salutis, sicut lac infantibus sufficit pro nutrimento: non sufficit vero adultioribus in fide, qui cibum solidiorem requirunt: non doctoribus Scholarum, Pastoribus Ecclesiarum, quibus ex officio & conscientia, vberior Theologicarum rerum scientia est necessaria.
units.tr: For catechumens in the Church the catechetical rudiments of salvation may suffice for salvation, just as milk suffices as nourishment for infants. But it does not suffice for those more advanced in faith, who require more solid food, nor for teachers of the schools or ministers of the Churches, for whom, by their office and conscience, a fuller knowledge of theological matters is necessary.

units.la: Tironibus classicis in Logica ad syllogizandum sufficit tot figurarum & modorum cognitio. Philosophis necessaria est & τὸ διότι Organo Aristotelico tradita scientia, unde & cur tot sint, plures vero esse nequeant.
units.tr: For beginners in logic, knowledge of so many figures and moods is enough to make syllogisms. For philosophers the knowledge handed down in the Aristotelian Organon is necessary, the "why" [τὸ διότι] of things: whence and why there are so many, and why there can be no more.

units.la: Pedaneo judici vel Notario elementa juris & justitiæ sufficere possunt. Juris professori, causarum Aduocato vel Cancellario, &c. legum fontes necessario cognoscendi sunt.
units.tr: For a judge of the lowest court or a notary, the elements of law and justice may suffice. For a professor of law, an advocate or chancellor in causes, and so on, the sources of the laws must necessarily be known.

units.la: Mechanico illud τὸ ὅτι de trigono & circulo sufficiet ad opificium. Mathematarum Doctor vel studiosus demonstrationum & τὸ διότι scientiam desiderat.
units.tr: For a mechanic, that "that" [τὸ ὅτι] concerning the triangle and the circle will suffice for his craft. A doctor or student of mathematics desires the knowledge of demonstrations and of the "why" [τὸ διότι].

units.la: Pari ratione dicendum: Articulum hunc, (semotis nunc æquivocationibus) catechumenis & idiotis, mysteriorum sublimiorum non capacibus, sufficere ad salutem posse: satisque esse illud τὸ ὅτι, quales se esse, quibusque vti mediis ad salutem conquendam oporteat: credentes nempe in Christum, inque fide & obedientia fidei ad finem usque perseuantes: per verbi & sacramentorum ministerium & per huic cooperantem gratiam. Adultioribus vero in fide, inprimisque Scholarum & Ecclesiarum Doctoribus, qui nihil praeterea necessarium dixerit, jejunus profecto & imperitus rerum æstimator erit. Quinimmo juvat oportetque hos altius scripturas, penitiusque cognoscere ipsum doctrinæ prædictæ τὸ διότι, hoc est, fontem & causam primam scripturis revelatam: unde qualitates illæ mediaque salutis, cum gratia & salute ipsa originaliter in nos descendant: vnde etiam descendat ista, quam videmus, populorum & indiui-duorum seruandorum, à reliqua pereuntium multitudine, discriminatio: ne forte (quod ignorato vel derelicto fonte necesse est fieri) cisternas confractas, aquas non continentes nobis effodiamus, Jerem. 2,13. hoc est, vocationem, fidem, perseuerantiam, salutem nostram vel ingeniis, viribus & meritis humanis, vel gratiæ quidem, sed indifferenti, & libero arbitrio nostro ex parte, vel in totum, cum Dei contumelia, nostroque exitio adscribamus.
units.tr: By the same reasoning it must be said that this article, (with the ambiguities now set aside), can suffice for salvation for catechumens and laypeople, who are not capable of the higher mysteries; and that the "that" [τὸ ὅτι] is enough, namely what kind of persons we must be and what means we must use to obtain salvation: that is, believing in Christ, and persevering in faith and in the obedience of faith to the end, through the ministry of the Word and sacraments and through the grace cooperating with it. But for those more advanced in faith, and especially for the teachers of the schools and Churches, who would say that nothing more is necessary, will surely be a barren and unskilled judge of things. Indeed, it helps and is necessary that these men know the Scriptures more deeply and the very "why" [τὸ διότι] of the said doctrine, that is, the fountain and first cause revealed in the Scriptures, from which those qualities and means of salvation, together with grace and salvation itself, descend to us at their origin; from which also there descends that distinction, which we see, between peoples and individuals to be saved and the rest of the perishing multitude. Otherwise (which must happen when the fountain is ignored or abandoned) we shall dig for ourselves broken cisterns that hold no water, Jer. 2:13; that is, we shall ascribe our calling, faith, perseverance and salvation either to our own talents, strength and human merits, or to grace indeed but a neutral grace, and partly to our free will, or altogether, to the dishonour of God and to our own ruin.

units.la: Hic vero fons, hæcque causa suprema & prima, non est nisi æterna Dei prædestinatio, hoc est, æternum de nobis, præ aliis, in Christo seruandis consilium. Ex hoc enim fonte fluit saluando-rum omnium vocatio externa & interna ad fidem in Christum: fluit fides & resipiscentia, fluit justificatio, obedientia & perseuerantia fidei, fluit tota salus & glorificatio nostra: quod perspicue docet & confirmat scriptura his & similibus dictis: Quos prædestinauit, hos & vocauit, quos vocauit, hos & justificauit, quos justificauit, hos & glorificauit. Item: Electio assecuta est, reliqui obcaluerunt. Item: Crediderunt, quotquot ordinati erant ad vitam æternam. Item: Elegit nos in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta, vt essemus sancti & inculpati coram eo in dilectione: quos prædestinauit in adoptionem per Iesum Christum, ad laudem gloriosa gratiæ suæ, &c. Confirmat idem Augustinus, dicens: Hæc prædestinatio sanctorum nihil aliud est, quàm præparatio beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissime liberantur, quicunque liberantur. Confirmat etiam Lutherus valde emphatice his verbis: Ex æterna Dei prædestinatione vtrumque fluit, & quam originem habet, quis scilicet creditsurus sit, quis non creditsurus sit: quis à peccato absoluendus, quis non: vt id omne sit extra nostram potestatem, & in solius Dei manu, quod justificamur.
units.tr: But this fountain and this supreme and first cause is nothing other than the eternal predestination of God, that is, the eternal counsel concerning us, that we, rather than others, are to be saved in Christ. For from this fountain flows the external and internal calling of all who are saved to faith in Christ; from it flow faith and repentance, from it flow justification, the obedience and perseverance of faith, and from it flows our whole salvation and glorification. Scripture clearly teaches and confirms this by these and similar sayings: Whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified; whom he justified, these he also glorified. Likewise: The election obtained it, and the rest were hardened. Likewise: As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Likewise: He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love; who predestined us to adoption through Jesus Christ, to the praise of the glory of his grace, etc. Augustine confirms the same, saying: This predestination of the saints is nothing other than the preparation of God's benefits, by which surely all who are delivered are delivered. Luther also confirms it very emphatically in these words: From the eternal predestination of God both flow, and it has its origin in this, who is going to believe and who is not going to believe, who is to be absolved from sin and who is not; so that all of this, that we are justified, lies outside our power and in the hand of God alone.

units.la: Huc igitur fonte Theologis cumprimis, & quotquot in fide & consolatione juuat fieri confirmatiores, probe cognoscendum, Ecclesiæq; & Scholis perspicue & sobrie explicandum esse, quis dubitet? Idque duas potissimum ob causas:
units.tr: Who would doubt that, from this fountain, theologians above all, and all who are helped to become more firmly grounded in faith and comfort, ought to know it thoroughly, and that it must be explained to the Church and the schools clearly and soberly? And this for two main reasons:

units.la: I. Propter gloriam Dei: vt scientes, media causasque salutis, & qualitates saluandorum & salutem ipsam, non ex nostro ingenio, sed ex solo Dei beneplacito descendere, non nobis, sed diuinæ misericordiæ in solidam salutem nostram acceptam referamus.
units.tr: I. For the glory of God: so that, knowing that the means and causes of salvation, and the qualities of those to be saved and salvation itself, descend not from our own wit but from the sole good pleasure of God, we may ascribe them not to ourselves but to divine mercy, as our solid salvation.

units.la: II. Propter consolationem nostram: vt firmiter statuentes, fidem, perseuerantiam & salutem nostram non viribus, vel arbitrio nostro niti, sed in æterno, immutabilique Dei consilio fundari, eandem certam atque immobilem fore confidamus, & hac freti fiducia, precibus assiduis, bonisque operibus, tanquam mediis ad finem ordinatis à Deo vocationem & electionem no-stram firmam nobis reddere studeamus.
units.tr: II. For our comfort: so that, firmly establishing that our faith, perseverance and salvation rest not on our powers or our free will but are grounded in the eternal and unchangeable counsel of God, we may trust that it will be sure and immovable, and, relying on this confidence, we may strive by constant prayers and good works, as means ordained by God to that end, to make our calling and election firm to us.

units.la: Atqui fontem hunc limpidissimum cœno æquiuocationum conspurcat obstruitq; penitus hic articulus. Negat enim (videlicet collatio) fidem & perseuerantiam nostram ex æternæ electionis fonte, tanquam effectum ex causa prima descendere: vtramq; in speciem gratiæ Dei, reuera humanæ voluntati adscribit: quia voluntatem humanam gratiæ Dei resistibilis DOMINAM facit, liberum arbitrium gratiâ Dei resistibilis fortius & potentius constituit, totumq; saluandorum & damnandorum discrimen ab hominum voluntatibus suspendit. Qua ratione gloriam salutis humanæ Deo in solidum tribui non posse, sed necessariò derogari, manifestum est.
units.tr: Yet this article defiles and utterly blocks up this most limpid fountain with the mire of ambiguities. For it denies (namely by collation) that our faith and perseverance descend from the fountain of eternal election as an effect from a first cause; it ascribes both, in appearance a grace of God, in reality to the human will, because it makes the human will the mistress of grace that can be resisted, and it sets up free will as stronger and more powerful than grace that can be resisted, and it hangs the whole distinction between the saved and the damned upon the wills of men. It is plain that by this reasoning the glory of human salvation cannot be given wholly to God, but must necessarily be taken away from him.

units.la: Hinc & certitudinem gratiæ, fidei, justificationis, perseuerantiæ totiusq; salutis: proinde & vnicæ consolationis nostræ in vita & in morte funditus convellit. Cum gratia enim resistibili & voluntate hominis resistente, vel resistere valente, tanquam cum duobus principiis vel repugnantibus, vel in horas variantibus, perquis non intelligat, certam fiduciam gratiæ, justificationis, perseverantiæ, salutis, solidamq; in vita & in morte consolationem consistere nullo modo posse?
units.tr: Hence it also utterly overthrows the certainty of grace, faith, justification and perseverance, and of salvation as a whole, and therefore of our only comfort in life and in death. For if grace is resistible, and the human will either resists it or is able to resist it, as though there were two principles either opposed to each other or changing from hour to hour, who does not see that a certain trust in grace, justification, perseverance and salvation, and a firm comfort in life and in death, can in no way stand?

units.la: Hinc de Tolerantia quid statuendum sit, manifestum quoq; est. Articulum enim tam æquiuocum, tamq; periculosis captiosum cothurnis, quis tolerabilem dixerit? saccharum occulto tinctum veneno quis sciens volens emerit, vel comederit? Quis ecclesiis obijciendum, perpetuarum litium materiam futurum, vtile duxerit? Num medici in scholis ferent empiricos pathologicam doctrinam adulterantes, vel negantes? Mathematici mechanicorum ψευδογραφίας, quibus verbi gratia tetragoni sinum falsum pro vero inducunt, fontesque scientiæ conuellunt, num tolerari possint?
units.tr: From this it is also clear what must be decided about toleration. For who would call tolerable an article so equivocal and so dangerously deceptive in its tragic buskin? Who, knowing and willing, would buy or eat sugar secretly tinctured with poison? Who would think it useful to throw before the churches a matter that will be a source of perpetual strife? Will doctors in the schools bear with quacks who adulterate or deny pathological doctrine? Can mathematicians tolerate the pseudographia [ψευδογραφίας] of mechanics, by which, for example, they pass off a false sine of a square as true and undermine the sources of knowledge?

units.la: Longe minus in Ecclesia toleranda sunt dogmata æquiuoca, quibus prætextu gratiæ gratia negatur: principum salutis in homine collocatur: diuinæ voluntati voluntas hominis præfertur: vt ideo quis adiuuetur, quia voluit: non ideo quia adiuuatur, velit: originaliter malos receptionem boni non à summo bono, sed à semetipso inchoare creditur: aliunde deniq; Deo placari, quam ex eo, quod ipse donauerit, docetur. Hæc de æquiuocationibus primi Articuli. Quomodo vero is recte intelligi, explicatur, pleri, & formari possit, cothurno II. est explicatum.
units.tr: Far less must equivocal dogmas be tolerated in the Church, dogmas by which, under the pretext of grace, grace is denied; the first cause of salvation is placed in man; the human will is preferred to the divine will; so that a man is helped because he willed, and not that he wills because he is helped; and it is believed that those who are originally evil begin to receive the good not from the highest good but from themselves; and finally it is taught that God is reconciled in some other way than by what he himself has given. These things are said about the equivocations of the first article. How it may rightly be understood, explained, fully set forth and framed has been explained in the second buskin.

units.la: ARTICVLVS SECVNDVS
units.tr: THE SECOND ARTICLE

units.la: Proinde Jesum Christum mundi Seruatorem, pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse, atque id ita quidem, vt omnibus per mortē Christi reconciliationem & peccatorum remissionem impetrauerit: ea tamen conditione, vt nemo illa peccatorum remissione reipsa fruatur, præter hominem fidelem: & hoc quoq; secundum Euangelium. Joh.3,16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt quisquis credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Et 1 Ioh.2.verf.2. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: nec pro nostris solum, sed & pro totius mundi peccatis.
units.tr: Accordingly, that Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the world, died for all and each, and indeed in such a way that by the death of Christ he obtained reconciliation and the remission of sins for all; yet on this condition, that no one actually enjoys that remission of sins except the faithful man; and this also according to the Gospel. John 3:16: For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. And 1 John 2:2: He himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.

units.la: EXAMEN.
units.tr: EXAMINATION.

units.la: Rem non nouam agunt Remonstrantes hoc articulo. Olim enim Semipelagiani Massiliæ & Siracusis eundem tuebantur his verbis: Pro vniuerso genere humano mortuum esse Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, & neminem prorsus à redemtione sanguinis eius exceptum, etiamsi omnem hanc vitam alienissima ab eo mente pertranseat: quia ad omnes homines pertineat misericordia sacramentum: quo ideo plurimi non renouentur, quia quod nec renouari utile habeant, prænoscantur. Itaq; quantum ad Deum pertinet, omnibus paratam vitam æternam: quantum autem ad arbitrij libertatem, ab his eam apprehendi, qui Deo sponte crediderint, & auxilium gratiæ merito credulitatis acceperint.
units.tr: The Remonstrants do not bring forward anything new in this article. For long ago the Semipelagians of Marseilles and Syracuse defended the same thing in these words: That our Lord Jesus Christ died for the whole human race, and that no one whatever is excluded from the redemption of his blood, even if he passes through this whole life in a mind most alien to him; because the sacrament of mercy pertains to all men; by which indeed many are not renewed, because they are foreknown as those who have no use in being renewed. Therefore, as far as God is concerned, eternal life is prepared for all; but as far as freedom of the will is concerned, it is laid hold of by those who have believed God of their own accord, and have received the help of grace by the merit of their believing.

units.la: Quo articulo etsi in speciem Dei gratiam & Christi redemtionem amplificabant: reuera tamen vtrumque minuebant, Deo gratiam indifferentem, Christo redemtionis meritum, libero arbitrio efficaciam vtriusque tribuentes: & dum vellent doctrinam de prædestinatione, quam ex Apostolo tuebatur Augustinus, euertere, reuera totum euangelium couellebant, causam fidei & perseuerantiæ, proindeque salutis humanæ Deo & Christo indifferenter, ingenio & arbitrio humano determinatiue adscribentes; quod quale sit, à Deo docti intelligunt. Vbi enim illud Apostoli: Quis te discreuit? Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi qui non acceperis? Maledictus, qui ponit carnem brachium suum.
units.tr: Although in this article they seemed to magnify the grace of God and the redemption of Christ, in truth they diminished both, attributing to God a grace that is indifferent and to Christ a merit of redemption, and giving the efficacy of both to free will. And while they wished to overturn the doctrine of predestination, which Augustine defended from the Apostle, they in fact undermined the whole gospel, ascribing the cause of faith and perseverance, and therefore of human salvation, indifferently to God and Christ, and determinatively to human ingenuity and will. What sort of thing this is, those taught by God understand. For where is that saying of the Apostle: Who maketh thee to differ? And what hast thou that thou didst not receive? Now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? Cursed be the man who makes flesh his arm.

units.la: Similiter isti articulo hoc de vniuersali reconciliationis omnium hominū cum Deo per mortem Christi impetratione, in speciem, gratiam mortis Christi amplificant: reuera idem, quod illi agebant, agunt: & dum cogitant apostolicam Dei prædestinationem, discernentem saluandos à non saluandis, conuellere: contra, suam prædestinationem eventualem sponte credentium & perseuerantium, seu, ad fidem & perseuerantiam seipsos determinil-[?] terminantium, fide & perseuerantia posteriorem (quæ reuera Postdestinatio, non Prædestinatio dicenda esset) inducere: humanam voluntatem gratiæ resistibilis Dominam faciendo, & reconciliationem per Christi mortem, hominum voluntati exponendo, fidem Gratiæ euacuant, consolationem ex morte Christi eneruant.
units.tr: In the same way, these men, by this article on the universal obtaining of reconciliation of all men with God through the death of Christ, magnify in appearance the grace of Christ's death; in truth they do what the others were doing: and while they think to overthrow the apostolic predestination of God, which separates those who are to be saved from those who are not, on the contrary they introduce their own eventual predestination of those who believe and persevere of their own accord, or of those who determine themselves to faith and perseverance, a later predestination (which would really be called post-destination, not predestination) based on faith and perseverance. By making the human will the mistress of resistible grace, and by exposing reconciliation through the death of Christ to the human will, they nullify the grace of faith and weaken the comfort derived from the death of Christ.

units.la: Putant vero, sicut & illi, prædestinationem sic inde euerti: Si Deus Christum Filium suum mundo dedit, & non tantum pro aliquibus, sed pro omnibus pariter hominibus mori voluit: & Christus juxta voluntatem Patris, pro omnibus pariter est mortuus: Non igitur prædestinatione sua aliquos tantum Deus elegit ad vitam æternam aliis reprobatis: Neque Christus dici potest mortuus tantum pro aliquibus, seu pro solis electis.
units.tr: Indeed, they think, just as those others did, that predestination is thus overthrown: If God gave his Son Christ to the world, and willed that he should die not only for some but equally for all men; and if Christ, according to the will of the Father, equally died for all: then God did not choose some only to eternal life by his predestination, with others reprobated; nor can Christ be said to have died only for some, or for the elect alone.

units.la: Sed nihil prædestinatio æterna hinc læditur. Ea enim non obstante Deus Christum Filium suum, quem dedit mundo, mori voluit, & Christus juxta consilium Patris, mortuus est, aliter quidem, seu alio sensu pro omnibus pariter hominibus, sive electi & fideles illi sint, sive reprobi & infideles, aliter vero seu alio sensu pro solis electis & fidelibus.
units.tr: But eternal predestination is not harmed by this at all. For notwithstanding it, God willed that Christ his Son, whom he gave to the world, should die, and Christ according to the counsel of the Father died, indeed in one way, or in another sense, for all men equally, whether they are elect and faithful or reprobate and unbelieving; but in another way, or in another sense, for the elect and faithful alone.

units.la: Quod, ut intelligatur magis, atq; ostendatur, articulus accuratius est examinandus. Habet is quatuor membra.
units.tr: In order that this may be understood more fully and shown, the article must be examined more carefully. It has four parts.

units.la: I. Propositionem: quod Christus sit mortuus pro omnibus & singulis: quæ est ambigua.
units.tr: I. The proposition: that Christ died for all and each; which is ambiguous.

units.la: II. Glossam: quod omnibus reconciliationem & remissionem peccatorum impetrauerit: quæ est æquiuoca, & falsa.
units.tr: II. The gloss: that he obtained for all reconciliation and the remission of sins; which is equivocal and false.

units.la: III. Conditionem: quod nemo nisi homo fidelis reipsa fruatur reconciliatione: quæ est vera, & propositionem limitat, glossam vero euertit.
units.tr: III. The condition: that no one except the faithful man actually enjoys reconciliation; which is true, and limits the proposition, but overturns the gloss.

units.la: IV. Probationem per duo allegata scripturæ, quæ nihil ad propositionem directè. In neutro etiam allegato fit mortis Christi pro omnibus & singulis aliqua mentio: ut mirandum sit, authoribus aptiora non succurrisse: Prioris vero posterius membrum cogit etiam propositionem limitare, & glossam refellit.
units.tr: IV. The proof, by two passages of Scripture, which bear nothing directly on the proposition. Neither of the passages makes any mention of Christ's death for all and each, so that it is remarkable that the authors did not hit upon more suitable ones. Indeed, the latter part of the first proof forces us to limit the proposition as well, and refutes the gloss.

units.la: Miscenturigitur vera quædam ambigue dictis vel falsis.
units.tr: Therefore certain true statements are mixed ambiguously with false ones.

units.la: Verum, inquam, est, quod nemo peccatorum remissione reipsa fruatur, præter hominem fidelem. Qui enim non credit, super eo manet ira Dei, non remissio vel reconciliatio: Nisi quod verbis reipsa fruatur, subesse videtur cothurnus de duplici fruitione remissionis peccatorum seu reconciliationis: vna reali per fidem, fidelibus solis propria, quæ sola vera est: altera non reali, sine fide omnibus, etiam infidelibus communi: quæ est fictitia & nulla.
units.tr: Yet, I say, it is true that no one actually enjoys the remission of sins except the faithful man. For he who does not believe, upon him the wrath of God remains, not remission or reconciliation. Unless, by the words actually enjoys, a tragic buskin of a twofold enjoyment of remission of sins or reconciliation seems to lurk beneath: one real, through faith, proper to the faithful alone, which alone is true; the other not real, common to all, even the unbelieving, without faith, which is fictitious and nothing.

units.la: Hinc vero conficitur, Christum proprie pro omnibus & solis fidelibus, pro nullis infidelibus, & sic non absolutè pro omnibus bus & singulis hominibus mortuum esse. Nam mori pro aliquo, propriissime est, morte sua aliquem à morte liberare, seu mori alicuius loco, vt ipse viuat: quod liquet. 2 Sam.18,33. Vtinam mortuus essem pro te, hoc est, tuo loco, vt tu viueres. Et de Christo Rom.5,6.8.Mortuus est pro nobis, cum impij & peccatores essemus, hoc est, nostro loco, vt nos à peccato & morte liberati iustitiæ viua-mus, seu, vitam æternam habeamus. Sic 1 Cor.5,15. 1 Joh.3,16. 1 Joh.4,9. Joh.15,13. &c.
units.tr: From this, however, it follows that Christ properly died for all and only the faithful, and for no unbelievers; and so he did not die absolutely for all and each man. For to die for someone most properly means to free someone from death by one's own death, or to die in another's place, so that he may live; which is plain. 2 Sam. 18:33: Would God I had died for thee, that is, in thy place, that thou mightest live. And of Christ, Rom. 5:6, 8: He died for us when we were ungodly and sinners, that is, in our place, so that we, freed from sin and death, might live to righteousness, or might have eternal life. So 1 Cor. 5:15; 1 John 3:16; 1 John 4:9; John 15:13, etc.

units.la: Ambigua ex imperfectione est propositio, Iesum Christum Seruatorem pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse. Si addas: Credentibus: perspicua & vera erit propositio. Si hominibus: manet ambigua.
