Potest enim accipi vel de amplitudine meriti mortis CHRISTI omnibus hominibus ad reconciliationem sufficientissimi: vel de efficacia eiusdem omnes homines reconciliante.
units.tr: The proposition that Jesus Christ the Saviour died for all and each is ambiguous because of its imperfection. If you add for believers, the proposition will be clear and true. If you add for men, it remains ambiguous. For it can be taken either of the greatness of the merit of Christ's death, which is most sufficient for the reconciliation of all men, or of the efficacy of the same death in reconciling all men.

units.la: Priore sensu, vera etiam est propositio. Mors Christi enim tatione amplitudinis atque potentiæ suæ, remedium est peccatis omnium & singulorum hominum expiandis sufficientissimum: Neque ad realem reconciliationem deest quicquam omnibus & singulis eam fide accipientibus. Hoc sensu Christus pro omnibus & singulis hominibus mortuus esse dici potest: quomodo, verbi causa, medicus, vrbe totainfecta, antidotum omnibus ægris sufficientissimum præparans, pro omnibus præparasse diceretur, Hocque sensu dicta scripturæ, vbi Christus dicitur mortuus esse pro omnibus, 1 Tim.2,6. gustasse mortem pro omnibus, Hc.2.2. Propitiatio esse pro peccato totius mundi, 1 Joh.2,2. vulgo non incommode intelliguntur: licet etiam strictius accipi possint.
units.tr: In the former sense the proposition is also true. By the greatness and power of his death, Christ's death is the most sufficient remedy for expiating the sins of all and each of mankind, and nothing is lacking for real reconciliation to those who receive it by faith, all and each. In this sense Christ can be said to have died for all and each of mankind, just as a physician who prepares the most effective antidote for all the sick, when the whole city is infected, would be said to have prepared it for all. In this sense also the statements of Scripture, where Christ is said to have "died for all" (1 Tim. 2:6), to have "tasted death for all" (Heb. 2:9), and to be "the propitiation for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2), are commonly understood without impropriety, although they may also be taken more strictly.

units.la: Posteriore sensu de remedij sufficientissimi fructu seu efficacia, quæ est realis cum Deo reconciliatio, & ex morte in vitam resti-tutio, falsa est propositio: Dicere enim Christum pro omnibus & singulis sic mortuum esse, vt omnes & singulos promiscue, fideles & infidelis, qui Christum vel nesciunt, vel oppupnant, Deo reconciliauerit: repugnat Euangelio, quod magno consensu efficaciam mortis Christi solis & omnibus credentibus vendicat. Cui probando vel vna seruatoris Christi sententia in articulo allegata, Jo.3,16. vt omnis &c. sufficit: Non dicit enim: vt omnes & singuli homines habeant vitam æternam: sed, vt omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam, prout realis fruitio remissionis peccatorum in articulo etiam limitatur: vnde & in dictis præallegatis 1 Tim.2,6. Heb.2,9. 1 Joh.2,2. &c. cum de efficacia mortis Christi intelliguntur, vniuersalis omnes necessario ad vniuersitatem credentium & electorum astringenda est:de de qua vniuersitate scite scribens Prosper: In electis, inquit, atque ab omnium generalitate discretis speciali quadam censetur vniuersitas, & de toto mundo totus mundus liberatus, & de omnibus homi-nibus omnes homines videantur assumti.
units.tr: In the latter sense, concerning the fruit or efficacy of this most sufficient remedy, which is real reconciliation with God and restoration from death to life, the proposition is false. To say that Christ so died for all and each that he reconciled to God all and each, faithful and unbelieving alike, including those who either do not know Christ or oppose him, contradicts the Gospel, which with one voice ascribes the efficacy of Christ's death to believers alone, and to all of them. To prove this, a single saying of the Saviour cited in the article is enough, John 3:16, "that whosoever &c." For it does not say, "that all and each man should have eternal life," but "that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." Likewise, in the article the real enjoyment of the forgiveness of sins is restricted in the same way. Hence also in the passages cited above, 1 Tim. 2:6, Heb. 2:9, 1 John 2:2, and so on, when they are understood of the efficacy of Christ's death, the universal "all" must necessarily be confined to the totality of believers and the elect. Prosper, writing wisely of this totality, says: "Among the elect, and set apart from the generality of all, there is held to be a special totality; and the whole world is delivered from the whole world, and from all men all men are seen to be taken up."

units.la: Duabus hisce veritatibus Remonstrantes euidentissime con-stringuntur.
units.tr: The Remonstrants are most plainly bound by these two truths.

units.la: Primo Christum quoad sufficientiam λύτρου & meriti sui, pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse, & mori voluisse, & juxta consilium Patris debuisse.
units.tr: First, that Christ, as to the sufficiency of his ransom [λύτρου] and his merit, died and was willing to die for all and each, and ought to have done so according to the counsel of the Father.

units.la: Secundo; quoad fructum & efficaciam mortis suæ, h.e. realem cum Deo reconciliationem ac restitutionem, non pro omnibus & singulis, sed pro solis & omnibus credentibus mortuum esse & mori voluisse, & juxta consilium Patris debuisse.
units.tr: Second, that as to the fruit and efficacy of his death, that is, real reconciliation and restoration with God, he died and was willing to die, and ought to have done so according to the counsel of the Father, not for all and each, but for believers only, and for all of them.

units.la: Priorem veritatem in collatione nusquam quidem leguntur diserte probare: sed nec palam negare; neq; possunt negare, nisi insufficientiam meriti statuere velint.
units.tr: Indeed, in the Conference they are nowhere found expressly to prove the first truth, but neither do they openly deny it; nor can they deny it, unless they wish to assert the insufficiency of his merit.

units.la: Posteriorem concedunt, quoad euentum: non omnes homines Christo esse reipsa restauratos, & in statum gratiæ restitutos. Negant vero, quoad intentionem Seruatoris, & consilium Patris: quid absurdius & salsius? Quos enim Deus per mortem Filij sui non reipsa restaurat in tempore: eos nec reipsa restaurare intendit vel decreuit ab æterno. Certe enim Deus noster, omnia quæ voluit, fecit. Quicquid igitur non fecit, vel facit in tempore: id nec voluit ab æterno. Quos etiam Christus morte sua reipsa non restaurat: eos nec restaurare voluit, nec juxta consilium Patris debuit. At fatentibus illis, non omnes homines Christum reipsa restaurat, & in gratiæ statum restituit. Ergo Christum non omnes homines reipsa restaurare, & in statum gratiæ restituere voluisse, vel ex consilio Patris debuisse, fateantur necesse est: Secus dicant, Christum aliquid non facere, quod facere omni modo voluit, & negent omnipotentiam: vel quod ex consilio Patris facere debuit, & negent obedientiam. Si obijciant voluisse Christum congregare filios Ierusalem: nec tamen fecisse: dicant etiam, Christum omni modo voluisse eos congregare, non solum externa vocatione, & invitatione ad resipiscentiam per Prophetarum & suam atque Apostolorum prædicationem, sed etiam internæ gratiæ atque potentiæ suæ tractatione: nec quicquam tamen profecisse: viderint vero, quo pacto omnipotentem Dei filium impotentiæ non accusent, seipsos blasphemiæ crimine non alligent.
units.tr: The second they concede as regards the outcome: "that not all men have actually been restored to Christ and brought back into the state of grace." But as regards the intention of the Saviour and the counsel of the Father they deny it. What could be more absurd or insipid? For those whom God does not actually restore through the death of his Son in time, he neither intended nor decreed from eternity to restore. For surely "our God has done whatever he willed." Whatever he does not do, or does not do in time, therefore he did not will from eternity. Those whom Christ does not actually restore by his death, he neither willed to restore nor ought to have restored according to the counsel of the Father. But they, admitting that not all men are actually restored by Christ and brought back into the state of grace, must therefore admit that Christ did not will, or ought by the counsel of the Father, to restore all men and bring them back into the state of grace. Otherwise they must say either that Christ did not do something he wholly willed to do, and so deny his omnipotence, or that he failed to do what he ought to have done according to the Father's counsel, and so deny his obedience. If they object that Christ "willed to gather the children of Jerusalem" but did not do so, let them also say that Christ wholly willed to gather them, not only by the outward calling and invitation to repentance through the preaching of the Prophets, and of himself and his Apostles, but also by the working of his inward grace and power; and yet nothing was achieved. Let them see, however, how they do not accuse the omnipotent Son of God of impotence, and do not bind themselves with the crime of blasphemy.

units.la: Vtraque igitur veritate, nolint velint, constricti, consensum cum orthodoxis ingenue fateantur oportet, vel non. Si fatentur, quod ina-nibus consensum, quomodo non seipsos perfidiæ damnant, quod inahibus logomachiis ecclesias vnitas lacerent, rempublicam tranquillam perturbent? Si negant consensum in priore, quomodo non blasphemant mortem Filij Dei, quasi insufficiens λύτρον? Si in posteriore, quomodo non manifesta contradictione se inuolvunt? Si enim negant, Christum, quoad efficaciam & fructum mortis suæ, non pro omnibus & singulis hominibus, sed pro solis credentibus mortuum esse: vtique contra affirment necesse est: Christum, quoad fructum & efficaciam mortis suæ, pro omnibus & singulis hominibus, non pro solis credentibus mortuum esse, hoc est, omnes & singulos homines (non solos credentes) Deo reconciliasse, seu, quod idem est, omnes & singulos homines remissione peccatorum reipsa frui fecisse. Atqui hanc affirmationem diserte negant limitatione articuli, dicendo, neminem peccatorum remissione reipsa frui praeter fidelem hominem: & disertius in collatione, dicendo: Non omnes homines à Christo reipsa restaurati, & in statum gratiæ restitutos esse. Hac igitur contradictione tenentur: omnes reipsa reconciliatos seu restitutos: & : non omnes reipsa restitutos esse.
units.tr: Therefore, bound by either truth, whether they wish it or not, they must either frankly confess agreement with the orthodox, or not. If they confess it, how do they not condemn themselves for faithlessness, when they tear the unity of the churches and disturb the peace of the commonwealth with empty logomachies? If they deny agreement on the first point, how do they not blaspheme the death of the Son of God, as though it were an insufficient ransom [λύτρον]? If on the second, how do they not entangle themselves in plain contradiction? For if they deny that Christ died, as regards the efficacy and fruit of his death, for all and each man and not for believers only, then they must surely affirm the contrary: that Christ, as regards the fruit and efficacy of his death, died for all and each man and not for believers only; that is, that he reconciled all and each man (not only believers) to God, or, what is the same, caused all and each man to enjoy the forgiveness of sins in fact. Yet they expressly deny this affirmation, by the limitation of their article, saying, "no one enjoys the forgiveness of sins in fact except the faithful man," and more expressly in the Conference, saying: "Not all men have been actually restored by Christ and brought into the state of grace." They are therefore held in this contradiction: that all have actually been reconciled or restored, and that not all have actually been restored.

units.la: Hic vero receptum parabunt ad glossam propositionis, ita Christum pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse, vt omnibus morte sua reconciliationem & peccatorum remissionem IMPETRAVERIT: quasi hic fit tertius sensus, quo Christus præter sufficientiam & efficaciam mortis suæ respectum, pro omnibus mortuus esse dici possit, & ita distinctio superior eludatur: quia omnibus morte sua reconciliationem IMPETRAVERIT.
units.tr: Here, however, they will prepare a familiar escape, a gloss on the proposition: that Christ so died for all and each, that by his death he OBTAINED reconciliation and forgiveness of sins for all. As if there were here a third sense, in which Christ could be said to have died for all, apart from the sufficiency and efficacy of his death, and so the distinction above would be evaded, because he OBTAINED reconciliation for all by his death.

units.la: Sed dicant, quæso, nobis, quid sibi hic cothurnus velit, quo responsiones fratrum in collatione plus decies elusisse leguntur.
units.tr: But let them tell us, I beg, what this tragic buskin means here, the buskin by which the brothers' answers in the Conference are read to have dodged more than ten times.

units.la: Nusquam sic scriptura loquitur, Christum impetrasse omnibus reconciliationem: sed aperte dicit, Deum in Christo sibi reconciliasse omnia in cælo & in terra: reconciliasse sibi mundum: Christum reconciliasse omnia per sanguinem suum: significans Christum reipsa reduxisse in statum gratiæ mundum synecdochice, hoc est, omnes in mundo credentes: sicut in illis: Non veni condemnare mundum, sed seruare mundum: vt mundus cognoscat, me à te missum esse: vbi mundus non potest nisi de mundo electorum intelligi. Item, omnia, hoc est, omnes fide justificatos, vt patet Rom. 5, 11.
units.tr: Nowhere does Scripture speak in this way, that "Christ obtained reconciliation for all." Rather it plainly says that God reconciled to himself, in Christ, all things in heaven and on earth; that he reconciled the world to himself; that Christ reconciled all things through his blood. This signifies that Christ actually brought the world back into the state of grace, by synecdoche, that is, all believers in the world; as in those words: "I did not come to condemn the world, but to save the world, that the world may know that I have been sent by you" (John 3:17; 17:21), where "world" can only be understood of the world of the elect. Likewise "all things," that is, all justified by faith, as is clear from Rom. 5:11.

units.la: Hoc sensu, si volunt, Christum omnibus reconciliationem impetrasse, pro, omnes reipsa reconciliasse, cur non aperte loquuntur? & cur non exprimunt, quibus omnibus impetrauerit? Si omnibus credentibus, quid litigant? Si omnibus hominibus promiscue, dicant, quomodo impetrauerit; meriti amplitudine, an etiam efficacia? Si meriti amplitudine, rursus quid litigant? si & efficacia, dicant, absolute & sine fide, an sub conditione fidei? Si absolute omnibus, etiam sine fide; quomodo non rursus contradictione se implicant, ex limitatione sua conditionata; neminem reipsa frui reconciliatione praeter fidelem hominem? Si sub conditione fidei, quomodo non sic etiam nodo contradictionis constringuntur? Si enim omnibus impetrauit sub conditione fidei; destituitur igitur conditione fidei non impetrauit. At conditione fidei destituti, hoc est, infideles, sunt plurimi. Ergo plurimis his non impetrauit. Haec vero nonne rursus contradicentia sunt: omnibus impetrauit; plurimis non impetrauit. Quomodocunque igitur cothurnum vertant, vel logomachi turbatores deprehenduntur, vel contradictione aperta inuoluuntur.
units.tr: In this sense, if they wish, "that Christ obtained reconciliation for all," in the sense that "all were actually reconciled," why do they not speak openly? And why do they not state for whom, "for all," he obtained it? If for all believers, what are they quarrelling about? If for all men without distinction, let them say how he obtained it: by the greatness of his merit, or also by efficacy? If by the greatness of his merit, again, what are they quarrelling about? If also by efficacy, let them say: absolutely and without faith, or under the condition of faith? If absolutely for all, even without faith, how are they not again entangled in contradiction, through their own conditional limitation, "that no one enjoys reconciliation in fact except the faithful man"? If under the condition of faith, how are they not likewise bound in the knot of contradiction? For if he obtained it for all under the condition of faith, then those who lack the condition of faith did not obtain it. But many are lacking the condition of faith, that is, the unbelieving. Therefore he did not obtain it for these many. Are these not again contradictory statements: "he obtained it for all," and "he did not obtain it for many"? However they turn this buskin, they are caught either as troublers who play with empty words, or they are entangled in an open contradiction.

units.la: Videtur autem cothurnus hic aliquanto accuratius excutiendus: vt quam sit vtriq; pedi aptus, hoc est, verum & falsum sensum occultet, ex verborum significatione appareat.
units.tr: This buskin, however, must be examined somewhat more carefully, so that it may become clear from the meaning of the words how well it fits either foot, that is, how it conceals both a true and a false sense.

units.la: Reconciliatio est dissidentium in gratiam restitutio vel reditio: actiue Deo & Christo, passiue nobis tribuitur. Verbum impetrare aequiuocum est varie significans, modo exorare, modo praeparare, procurare, mereri, acquirere, obtinere, conferre, &c. Phrasis igitur Christum impetrasse omnibus reconciliationem valde aequiuoca sit oportet. Atqui aequiuocationibus ludere non est Theologorum, sed sophistarum, qui fallere volunt. Non potest tamen phrasis nisi triplicem sensum habere: vel quod Christus morte sua reconciliationem omnibus impetrauerit quadam metalepsei: merendo seu promerendo materiam reconciliationis omnibus sufficientissimam: quomodo, verbi causa, medicus, de quo supra, antidotum omnibus aegris sufficientissimum praeparans, vel aliunde impetrans, sanitatem omnibus praeparasse vel impetrasse diceretur: vel quod reconciliationem omnibus impetrauerit proprie, eandem conferendo omnibus, hoc est, omnes reipsa reconciliauerit: Idque vel absolute sine conditione; quomodo, verbi gratia, Ioab intercessione mulieris Tekoa, Absolomo parricidae apud Danidem impetrauit reconciliationem absolute, vt sine conditione reduceretur in conciliationem absolute, vt sine conditione reduceretur in conspectum regis, & pater osculaaretur filium: Quomodo etiam Esther Iudaeis impetrasse legitur securitatem absolute sine conditione: Vel sub conditione fidei in omnibus ponendae, vt si omnes credant in Filium, sint reipsa reconciliati: si non credant, reconciliationis sint expertes: quomodo, verbi causa, Adoniae seditioso apud Salomonem impetrata fuit impunitas, sub conditione innocentiae: Si fuerit filius virtutis, non cadet capillus de capite eius: si vero malum fuerit deprehensum in eo, moriatur.
units.tr: Reconciliation is the restoration or return of those at odds to favour. It is ascribed to God and Christ actively, and to us passively. The verb to obtain is ambiguous and has many meanings: sometimes to entreat, sometimes to prepare, procure, merit, acquire, secure, confer, and so on. The phrase Christ has obtained reconciliation for all must therefore be very ambiguous. Yet playing with ambiguities belongs not to theologians but to sophists, who wish to deceive. The phrase can, however, have only three senses. Either (a) by a kind of metalepsis, Christ by his death obtained reconciliation for all in the sense that he merited, or earned, material for reconciliation sufficient for all, just as a physician who prepares or procures an antidote, sufficient for all the sick (mentioned above), would be said to have prepared or obtained health for all. Or (b) he obtained reconciliation for all in the proper sense, by conferring it on all, that is, by actually reconciling all. And this may be done either absolutely, without condition, as when Joab, through the intercession of the woman of Tekoa, obtained for the murderer Absalom an absolute reconciliation with David, so that he was brought back without condition into the king's presence and his father kissed his son; or as Esther is read to have obtained absolute security for the Jews without condition. Or else (c) on condition of faith to be placed in all, so that if all believe in the Son they are actually reconciled, and if they do not believe they are without reconciliation; as, for example, impunity was obtained for the seditious Adonijah from Solomon on condition of his innocence: If he shall be a son of valour, not a hair of his head shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness be found in him, he shall die.

units.la: Dicam breuius: Christus impetrauit reconciliatione omnibus, vel quoad amplitudinem meriti, pro omnium reconciliatione sufficientissimi: vel insuper, quoad efficientiam reconciliationis omnium. Idq; vel absolute, siue credant, siue non, vel conditionaliter, si omnes credant. Neque dari potest quartus cothurni sensus. Quem enim Remonstrantes in collatione adferunt, Christum impetrasse omnibus reconciliationem, hoc est, effecisse, vt Deus homini peccatori ianuam iterum aperuerit gratiae suae: quamuis nemo ad illius gratiae communionem est ingressurus, nisi per fidem: vel est nouus cothurnus, seu schema aequiuocum, limitatione rursus anferens, quod prius posuit, (quomodo enim omnibus impetrauit reipsa reconciliationem, qui effecit, vt princeps seditiosis aperiat ianuam arcis suae: quam tamen nemo sit ingressurus, nisi per mille florenos: quibus fidei conditio longe praestantior) vel si est impetratio reconciliationis dicenda, ad conditionalem impetrationis modum tertium pertinet.
units.tr: To put it more briefly: Christ obtained reconciliation for all, either as regards the extent of his merit, being sufficient for the reconciliation of all, or moreover as regards the efficacy of reconciliation for all. And this is either absolutely, whether they believe or not, or conditionally, if all believe. Nor can a fourth sense of the buskin be given. For what the Remonstrants bring forward in their collation, Christ obtained reconciliation for all, that is, brought it about that God reopened to sinful man the door of his grace, although no one will enter into communion with that grace except through faith, is either a new buskin, or an ambiguous figure which, by a limitation, takes back again what it first asserted. (For how does he obtain reconciliation really for all, who brings it about that a prince opens the gate of his citadel to rebels, which, however, no one will enter except by paying a thousand florins, the condition of faith being far more excellent than this?) Or, if it is to be called an obtaining of reconciliation, it belongs to the third, conditional mode of obtaining.

units.la: Manent igitur tres tantum impetratae reconciliationis modi, quorum aliquo Christum omnibus reconciliationem impetrasse dicendum illis est.
units.tr: There remain, therefore, only three modes of obtained reconciliation, and it must be said of one of these that Christ obtained reconciliation for all.

units.la: Si primo, consentiunt Orthodoxis: quid igitur Ecclesiam & Rempublicam turbant?
units.tr: If in the first sense, they agree with the Orthodox; why then do they disturb the Church and the commonwealth?

units.la: Si secundo, contradictione se inuoluunt, affirmantes, Christum omnibus absolutam reconciliationem impetrasse, hoc est, omnes reipsa in statum gratiae restituisse: quomodo Ioab Absolomo reconciliationem cum patre absolute impetrauit, hoc est, in gratiam Patris eum restituit: contra vero limitatione articuli, sicut & in collatione, diserte negantes, omnes a Christo reipsa restauratos, & in gratiae statum restitutos. Quae contradictio non minus aperta est, quam si dicerent, Ioabum Absolomo gratiam Patris absolute impetrasse; & non absolute impetrasse: seu eum in gratiam Patris reipsa restituisse; & non reipsa restituisse.
units.tr: If in the second sense, they entangle themselves in contradiction, affirming that Christ obtained absolute reconciliation for all, that is, actually restored all to a state of grace, just as Joab obtained for Absalom an absolute reconciliation with his father, that is, restored him to his father's favour; yet, on the other hand, by the limitation of the article, as also in the collation, they plainly deny that all were actually restored by Christ and brought back into a state of grace. This contradiction is no less open than if they were to say that Joab obtained absolute favour of the Father for Absalom, and did not obtain it absolutely; or that he actually restored him to the Father's favour, and did not actually restore him.

units.la: Si tertio, contradictionis scopulo rursus alliduntur. Si enim Christus intentione sua omnibus reconciliationem sub conditione fidei in omnibus ponenda impetrauit: nullis igitur sine conditione fidei, seu fide destitutis, in quibus neque a Deo (qui fidem non dat omnibus, sed quibus vult) neque a libero arbitrio (quod Deo non viuificante mortuum est in peccato) euentualiter fuit ponenda vel ponitur, h.e. infidelibus impetrauit. Infideles autem semper fuerunt & sunt plurimi. Nonne igitur hic etiam manifestus conflictus: omnibus impetrauit, & plurimis non impetrauit? Quomodocunque igitur se habeat cothurnus, vel idem cum orthodoxis aequiuocationibus suis sibi volunt: & suae ecclesiae & reip. turbatores inueniuntur; vel contradictioni {a}ctionibus manifestis irretiti tenentur: vel denique (quicquid reten-giuerfentur) in Massilienfium Semipelagianorum castra, vniuer-salem omnium etiam sine agnitione & fide Christi vitam hanc pertransseuntium reconciliationem, ab Huberto nuper in Germania renouatam, tuentium, concedere coguntur.
units.tr: If in the third sense, they are again dashed on the rock of contradiction. For if Christ by his intention obtained reconciliation for all on condition of faith to be placed in all, then he did not obtain it for those destitute of faith, that is, for unbelievers, who are without faith, in whom faith neither has been nor is eventually to be placed either by God (who does not give faith to all, but to whom he wills) or by free will (which, unless God quickens it, is dead in sin). Unbelievers, however, always have been and are the majority. Is there not then here also a manifest conflict: that he obtained it for all, and did not obtain it for the majority? Therefore, however the buskin is worn, either they wish these same ambiguities to be shared with the Orthodox, and they are found to be disturbers of their own church and of the commonwealth; or they are caught in the net of manifest contradictions; or finally (whatever they try to retract) they are compelled to concede to the camp of the Semipelagians of Marseilles, who defend the universal reconciliation of all, even of those who pass through this life without knowledge and faith of Christ, a reconciliation lately revived in Germany by Hubert.

units.la: Atque huc profecto omnia fere eorum argumenta, ab Huberianis mutuata, collimant. Hinc Christum non fidelium tantum, sed & totius mundi, hoc est, infidelium quoq; Reconciliatorem voci-tant. Hac hypothesi nituntur classica illa absurda, quibus ortho-doxos gravare solent: quod alioqui increduli, nisi & his reconciliationem impetrarit, nihil haberent, quod crederent: aut si crederent, mendacium crederent: quae sunt salsissima. Licet enim Christus non sit mortuus pro omnibus, quoad efficiam mortis suae: est tamen mortuus pro omnibus, quantum ad sufficientiam meriti sui. Hoc habent omnes, etiam infideles, quod credant in Evangelio, Christum pro totius mundi peccatis sufficientissime fuisse, omnes in ipsum credentes Deo reconciliasse: proinde si quoque meriti & reconciliationis huius participes fore, siquidem ex incredulis credentes fiant. Hoc vero statuentes & credentes, nequaquam mendacium credunt. Mendacium vero crederent infideles, si statuere vellent, vel docerentur, sibi etiam in infidelitate manentibus per Christum reconciliationem impetratam esse. Mendacium enim hoc est, non veritas; Christum omnibus, etiam infidelibus, qua tales sunt & manent, reconciliationem impetrasse.
units.tr: Indeed almost all their arguments, borrowed from the Huberians, aim at this point. Hence they call Christ the Reconciler not only of the faithful, but of the whole world, that is, of unbelievers too. On this hypothesis rest those classic absurdities with which they are accustomed to burden the Orthodox: that otherwise unbelievers, unless reconciliation had been obtained for them too, would have nothing to believe; or if they believed, they would believe a lie. These are most insipid. For although Christ did not die for all as regards the efficacy of his death, yet he did die for all as regards the sufficiency of his merit. All, even unbelievers, have this: that they believe in the Gospel that Christ was most sufficiently given for the sins of the whole world, and that he reconciled to God all who believe in him; therefore, if they become believers from unbelievers, they will also be sharers in this merit and reconciliation. In holding and believing this, they by no means believe a lie. Unbelievers would indeed believe a lie if they were willing to hold, or were taught, that reconciliation had been obtained through Christ for them too while they remain in unbelief. For this is a lie, not the truth: that Christ obtained reconciliation for all, even for unbelievers, as such as they are and remain.

units.la: Etiam supponunt, multos, pro quibus omni modo mortuus est Christus, damnari. Id falsum esse, Apostoli exclamatio arguit: Quis condemnabit? Christus est, qui mortuus est. Haec enim apostolica consolatio vana esset, nisi supponeretur vniuersalis: neminem, pro quo Christus mortuus est, condemnari. Ad hanc enim piae mentes firmiter subsumere possunt; Pro me Christus est mortuus: & concludere; Igitur non condemnabor. Haec est Christiana consolatio ex Christi morte. Hanc vero isti destruunt, pro vniuersali particularem supponentes: Aliqui, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, non condemnantur. Ex puris enim particularibus, quae esset consecutio? quae consolatio? Frustra vero Impetrationis cothurno, & Massilianismo praetexunt verba Catechismi, dicentes: Si quis omnino vult, impetrare idem esse, quod restituere in statum gratiae, quid fiet Catechismo, qui resp. 37. eodem verbo vtitur.
units.tr: They also assume that many, for whom Christ died in every way, are condemned. That this is false the Apostle's exclamation proves: Who shall condemn? It is Christ who died. For this apostolic consolation would be empty unless the universal proposition were assumed: that no one for whom Christ died is condemned. For pious minds can firmly take up this proposition: Christ died for me; and conclude: Therefore I shall not be condemned. This is the Christian consolation from the death of Christ. But they destroy it, substituting a particular proposition for the universal: Some, for whom Christ died, are not condemned. For from purely particular propositions what consequence could follow? What consolation? And they vainly pretend, with the buskin of obtaining and with Massilian doctrine, the words of the Catechism, saying: If anyone wishes to say that to obtain is the same as to restore to a state of grace, what will become of the Catechism, which in answer 37 uses the same word?

units.la: Primo falsum est, quod Catechismus eodem verbo vtatur: non dicit enim, ut gratiam Dei, iustitiam & vitam aeternam impetraret vteretur, nihil sed ut acquireret. Deinde, si eodem verbo impetraret vteretur, nihil id faceret pro cothurno. Non enim dicit, pro omnibus, sed, ut nobis, nempe credentibus (de quibus est quæstio: Quid credis, cum dicit, passus est) gratiam &c. acquireret. Quin Catechismus evidenter eos contradictione constringit. Loquitur enim de reali acquisitione gratiæ, seu restitutione in statu gratiæ, quali Christus dicitur Ecclesiam Dei proporio sanguine acquisivisse, hoc est, in statum gratiæ restituisse. Si igitur acquisivit, idem est, quod impetravit; sequitur, impetrare idem esse quod restituere in statu gratia, quod negant: & omnibus impetrare reconciliationem, idem esse, quod omnes restituere in statum gratiæ: quod negando in collatione, nodo contradictionis denuo se induunt.
units.tr: First, it is false that the Catechism uses the same word: for it does not say that he might obtain for us the grace of God, righteousness and eternal life, but that he might acquire them. Next, even if it used the same word obtain, that would do nothing for the buskin. For it does not say for all, but that he might acquire for us, namely for believers (who are the subject of the question: What do you believe, when it says, he suffered) the grace, and so on. Indeed the Catechism plainly binds them in contradiction. For it speaks of the real acquisition of grace, or restoration to a state of grace, in the way that Christ is said to have acquired the Church of God with his own blood, that is, to have restored it to a state of grace. If therefore he acquired is the same as he obtained, it follows that to obtain is the same as to restore to a state of grace, which they deny; and that to obtain reconciliation for all is the same as to restore all to a state of grace, which, by denying it in the collation, they once again bind themselves in the knot of contradiction.

units.la: Neque se hoc nodo exsoluunt, obijciendo, quod eadem responsione Christus iram Dei adversus peccatum universi generis humani sustinuisse dicitur. Hæc enim verba non patiuntur se ita glossari vel torqueri, Christum universum genus humanum morte sua reconciliasse, vel universo generi humano reconciliationem & remissionem peccatorum impetrasse: (quibus enim hanc acquisiuerit, sive, ut loquuntur, impetrauerit, sequentia, demum verba docent, ut sua passione &c.) sed declarant atque amplificant causam & materiam passionis, fuisse nimirum hanc, sensum sive sustinentiam iræ Dei peccato non aliquorum hominum, sed universi generis humani concitatæ. Unde universitas quidem peccati & iræ Dei adversus illud à Christo toleratæ efficitur: vniuersitas vero reconciliationis impetratæ vel restitutæ omnibus, minime. Reconciliationis enim impetratio seu restitutio finem & fructum passionis declarat; verba vero illa non de fine & fructu, sed de efficiente & materia passionis loqui manifestum est. Manet igitur nodus, & frustra prætextum cothurno suo in Catechismo quærunt.
units.tr: Nor do they extricate themselves from this knot by objecting that, in the same way, Christ is said to have borne the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. For these words do not allow themselves to be glossed or twisted into meaning that Christ reconciled the whole human race to himself by his death, or obtained reconciliation and forgiveness of sins for the whole human race. (For what follows, namely the words that by his suffering and so on, teaches that he acquired it, or, as they say, obtained it.) Rather, these words declare and amplify the cause and matter of the passion: that is, that the wrath of God was aroused not by the sin of some men but by the sin of the whole human race, and that Christ bore it. Hence the universality of sin and of the wrath of God against it, borne by Christ, is established; but the universality of the reconciliation obtained or restored for all is by no means established. For the obtaining or restoring of reconciliation declares the end and fruit of the passion; but that it is clear those words speak not of the end and fruit but of the efficient cause and matter of the passion. The knot therefore remains, and in vain they seek a pretext for their buskin in the Catechism.

units.la: Vnam denique in collatione reperio strophám, ad contradictionis nodum eludendum excogitatam, vbi scribunt: Passionem & mortem Christi antecedere ordine ipsam fidem & infidelitatem. Itaq; Remonstrantes absurdum dictu existimare, Christum pro fidelibus vel infidelibus (qua talibus) mortuum esse: assentiri vero, mortuum esse pro omnibus hominibus, quorum postea quidam infideles, quidam fideles fiant. Discernere enim illos inter statum hominis peccatoris, ante infidelitatem, & in illa. Sic videntur satis cauisse contradictioni huic:
units.tr: Finally, in their conference I find one turn of phrase devised to evade the knot of contradiction, where they write: The passion and death of Christ precede in order faith and unbelief. Accordingly the Remonstrants think it absurd to say that Christ died for believers or unbelievers as such, but they agree that he died for all men, of whom some afterwards become unbelievers and some believers. For they distinguish between the state of man as sinner before unbelief, and his state within it. Thus they seem to have sufficiently guarded against this contradiction:

units.la: Christus pro omnibus & singulis hominib. est mortuus. Et:
units.tr: Christ died for all and each of men. And:

units.la: Christus pro infidelibus hominibus, qui sunt plurimi, non est mortuus:
units.tr: Christ did not die for unbelieving men, who are very many.

units.la: Verum enim vero his argutiis, & nouis cothurnis nodum minime soluunt: occultum vero animi vlcus, & nouæ prophetiæ mysterium produnt. Singula igitur excutienda diligentius.
units.tr: But by these subtleties and new buskins they in no way loosen the knot; rather they betray the hidden ulcer of their mind and the mystery of a new prophecy. Each point must therefore be examined more carefully.

units.la: Primò, passionem & mortem Christi antecedere ordine fidem esto : antecedere ordine infidelitatem est falsum. Infidelitas enim ordine antecedit impietatem & inimicitiam hominis adversus Deum, sicut causa ordine antecedit effectum. Impietas vero & inimicitia hominis adversus DEVM ordine antecedit passionem & mortem Christi, teste Apostolo: Christus enim cum adhuc nullis viribus essemus, suo tempore pro impiis mortuus est. Item: Cum adhuc peccatores & inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus per mortem Filij eius, &c. Ergo infidelitas etiam passionem & mortem Christi ordine antecedit.
units.tr: First, let it be granted that the passion and death of Christ precede faith in order; it is false that they precede unbelief in order. For unbelief precedes in order impiety and the enmity of man against God, just as a cause precedes its effect in order. Impiety and the enmity of man against God, however, precede in order the passion and death of Christ, as the Apostle witnesses: For Christ, when we were still without strength, died at the appointed time for the ungodly. Likewise: When we were still sinners and enemies, we were reconciled through the death of his Son, and so on. Therefore unbelief also precedes in order the passion and death of Christ.

units.la: Deinde, nulla est consecutio, Mors Christi ordine antecedit fidem & infidelitatem. Ergo absurdum dictu est, Christum pro fidelibus vel infidelibus (qua talibus) mortuum esse. Luditur enim fallacia non causæ : quoniam quicquid sit de ordine fidei vel infidelitatis ad mortem Christi, verissimum dictu est, Christum pro fidelibus vel infidelibus (qua talibus) mortuum esse: æquivocationibus, qui subsunt, remotis.
units.tr: Next, there is no valid consequence in this: the death of Christ precedes faith and unbelief in order; therefore it is absurd to say that Christ died for believers or unbelievers as such. For this is a fallacy of the non-cause, since whatever the order of faith or unbelief relative to the death of Christ may be, it is most true to say that Christ died for believers or unbelievers as such, once the ambiguities underlying it are removed.

units.la: De infidelibus ostensum est Apostoli testimonio. Si enim verissime dicitur: Christum esse mortuum pro impiis & inimicis, (qua talibus) nempe antecedenter, hoc est qui ordine ante mortem Christi erant impij & inimici: etiam verissime dicitur Christum mortuum esse pro infidelibus, (qua talibus) nempe antecedenter, hoc est, qui ordine ante mortem Christi erant infideles: postea per fidem impij, infideles, inimici esse desierunt.
units.tr: That for unbelievers has been shown by the testimony of the Apostle. For if it is most truly said that Christ died for the ungodly and enemies (as such), namely antecedently, that is, those who in order before Christ's death were ungodly and enemies, then it is also most truly said that Christ died for unbelievers (as such), namely antecedently, that is, those who in order before Christ's death were unbelievers; afterwards, through faith, they ceased to be ungodly, unbelieving and enemies.

units.la: De fidelibus idem est verissimum: idque sive mors Christi absolutè in se, sive relatè ad intentionem Seruatoris, & consilium patris consideretur.
units.tr: The same holds most truly of believers, whether the death of Christ is considered absolutely in itself, or relatively to the intention of the Saviour and the counsel of the Father.

units.la: Absolute mortem Christi considerando, ex eo quod mors Christi ordine antecedit fidem, conficitur quidem, absurdum dictu esse, Christum esse mortuum pro fidelibus (qua talibus) antecedenter, h. e. quorum fides ordine antecederet mortem Christi: Sic enim ἡ πίστις ordine antecederet τὸ πιστεύειν, h.e. fides esset prior re credita, quod est absurdum, cum in talib. relatis fides sit posterior re credita: sicut scientia scibili, sensus sensibili est posterior: juxta Aristotelis doctrinam: Minime vero conficitur, absurdum dictu esse, Christum esse mortuum pro fidelibus (qua talibus) consequenter, h. e. quorum fides mortem Christi intuens, sibique applicans, fructum eius atque efficaciam consequeretur. Hoc enim sensu Christus Seruator aperte dicit, se roqueretur. Hoc enim sensu Christus Seruator aperte dicit, se ponere vitam pro amicis, & pro quibus suis: nempe consequenter, qui ordine post mortē Christi creditam futuri essent fideles, amici & ουες.
units.tr: Considering the death of Christ absolutely, it follows from the fact that the death of Christ precedes faith in order that it is indeed absurd to say that Christ died for believers (as such) antecedently, that is, whose faith would precede in order the death of Christ. For thus pistis would precede in order pisteuein, that is, faith would be prior to the thing believed, which is absurd, since in such relative things faith is posterior to the thing believed, just as knowledge is posterior to the knowable and sense to the sensible, according to the teaching of Aristotle. Yet it does not follow that it is absurd to say that Christ died for believers (as such) consequently, that is, those whose faith, looking upon the death of Christ and applying it to themselves, would obtain its fruit and efficacy. For in this sense Christ the Saviour openly says that he lays down his life for his friends and for those for whom he lays it down: namely consequently, those who after the death of Christ is believed would be believers, friends and ouies.

units.la: Relate vero ad intentionem seruatoris & consilium patris, mortem Christi æstimădo, prout reuera in hac quæstione æstimari debet, & phrasin mori pro aliquo, propriissime intelligendo (vt supra est declaratum) verissimum est dictu: Christum mortuum esse, & mori voluisse ac debuisse, tantum pro fidelibus (qua talibus) h. e. iis qui fide mortem eius suam facerent: non pro infidelibus (qua talibus) h.e. iis qui infidelitate mortem eius negligerent vel contemnerēt: Contra est absurdum dictu, Christum (propriissimo illo sensu) non mortuum esse, nec mori voluisse & debuisse, tantum pro fidelibus: sed etiam mortuum esse & mori voluisse ac debuisse pro infidelibus (qua talibus). Hoc enim quod non modo scripturæ sacræ, & euentui (ex quibus de voluntate Seruatoris & consilio Patris iudicari oportet) reclamet, sed & manifestam contradictionem implicet, Remonstrantibus conscientia sua dictabit.
units.tr: Relatively, however, to the intention of the Saviour and the counsel of the Father, and reckoning the death of Christ as in truth it ought to be reckoned in this question, and understanding the phrase to die for someone most properly (as has been explained above), it is most true to say that Christ died, and was willing and bound to die, only for believers (as such), that is, for those who by faith would make his death their own; not for unbelievers (as such), that is, those who by unbelief would neglect or despise his death. On the contrary, it is absurd to say that Christ (in the most proper sense) did not die, nor was willing and bound to die, only for believers, but also died and was willing and bound to die for unbelievers (as such). For this, which contradicts not only Holy Scripture and the outcome (from which the will of the Saviour and the counsel of the Father must be judged), but also implies a manifest contradiction, their own conscience will dictate to the Remonstrants.

units.la: Tertio: Quod assentiuntur, Christum mortuum esse pro omnibus hominibus: de magnitudine pretii mortis Christi pro omnibus hominibus sufficientissimi bene habet. De fructu & efficacia eius omnibus hominibus impetrata vel acquisita etiamsi omnem hanc vitam alienissima à Christi mente pertranseant, non scripturæ sacræ, nec euentui, sed Semipelagiano Massilienfium errori assentiuntur.
units.tr: Thirdly: as to their agreeing that Christ died for all men: this is well and sufficiently true concerning the greatness of the price of Christ's death for all men. But concerning the fruit and efficacy of it, obtained or acquired for all men, even though they pass over all this life, most alien to the mind of Christ, they assent not to Holy Scripture nor to experience, but to the Semipelagian error of the Massilians.

units.la: Quarto: Quod ex omnibus hominibus ordine post mortem Christi quidam fiant fideles, recte est. Quod ordine post mortem Christi quidā fiant infideles, falsum est. Omnes enim Christus moriturus ordine inuenit in impietate, in peccato, in inimicitia. Rom. 5. v. 6. 8. 9. Omnes igitur inuenit in infidelitate.
units.tr: Fourthly: that some of all men become believers after the death of Christ in order is right. That some become unbelievers after the death of Christ in order is false. For Christ, about to die, found all men in order in impiety, in sin, in enmity. Rom. 5 vv. 6, 8, 9. Therefore he found all in unbelief.

units.la: Quod denique norunt discernere inter statum hominis peccatoris ante infidelitatem, & in illa: sane notitiam hanc ex scriptura sacra non hauserunt: quæ statum peccati seu hominis peccatoris ante infidelitatē, & sine infidelitate ignorat: omnes vero homines filios irę & filios incredulitatis atque contumaciæ nasci tenatur. Hoc est igitur illud τὸ ὕνακρο νoux προφητειας mysterium & ... cui articuli quinq; & plures alii manifesti vel occulti sunt superstructi, hominē nasci sine infidelitate, nec esse infidelitatem: nisi cum homo adultus Euangelium repellit: & hinc: peccatum originis, si quod fit, pœnā esse, nō culpā: & hinc: hominem animale habere liberum arbitrium ad bonum & ad malum: locus iniuria postulari fidem ab eo, qui facultatem credendi non habeat: hinc prædestinatio & electio ex fide præuisa: hinc impetratio vniuersalis reconciliationis ex morte Christi: hinc gratia resistibilis seu indifferens: hinc apostasia sanctorum, perseueran-tia incerta, salus dubia, & alia occulta, quæ dies manifestabit.
units.tr: Finally, as to their claim that they know how to distinguish between the state of sinful man before unbelief and within it: they certainly have not drawn this knowledge from Holy Scripture, which knows of no state of sin, or of sinful man, before unbelief and without unbelief; rather it holds that all men are born children of wrath and children of unbelief and obstinacy. This, then, is that mystery of the prophecy (to hypsilon nou tes prophēteias)... upon which the five articles and many others, manifest or hidden, are built: that man is born without unbelief, and that there is no unbelief except when an adult man rejects the Gospel; and hence: original sin, if it is anything, is a punishment and not a guilt; and hence: man in his animal nature has free will to good and to evil; and hence it is unjustly demanded of one who has no ability to believe that he should believe; hence predestination and election on account of foreseen faith; hence universal impetration of reconciliation by the death of Christ; hence grace is resistible or indifferent; hence apostasy of saints, uncertain perseverance, doubtful salvation, and other hidden things which the day will reveal.

units.la: Ex his omnibus duo habentur manifesta. Vnum, hac strophā de ordine fidei ad mortem Christi, minimè expediri vel eludi contradictionem, quā se hoc articulo implicare coguntur: Christum absolute pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse: omnibusq; reconciliationem impetrasse: & tamen pro infidelibus, qui plurimi sunt, mortuum non esse: neque his reconciliationem impetrasse: quod malæ causæ est evidens argumentum. Quando enim aduersarius ad contradictoria concedenda adigitur, victus est. Alterum: hunc proinde articulum, quia æquivocationibus & contradictionibus Ecclesiam turbat, seipsum elidit, in Ecclesia ferendum non esse.
units.tr: From all this two things are plainly established. First, that by this turn of phrase about the order of faith relative to the death of Christ the contradiction in which they are forced to entangle themselves in this article is in no way resolved or evaded: namely that Christ died absolutely for all and each, and obtained reconciliation for all; and yet that he did not die for unbelievers, who are very many, nor obtained reconciliation for them. This is clear evidence of a bad cause: when an opponent is driven to concede contradictories, he is already defeated. Second: this article, since it disturbs the Church with ambiguities and contradictions, destroys itself, and is not to be tolerated in the Church.

units.la: ARTICVLVS TERTIVS.
units.tr: THE THIRD ARTICLE.

units.la: Hominem vero salutarem fidem à seipso non habere: nec vi liberi sui arbitrij: quandoquidem in statu defectionis & peccati, nihil boni, quod quidem vere bonum est, quale quid est fides salutaris, ex se possit cogitare, vel facere: sed necessarium esse, eum à Deo in Christo per Spiritum eius sanctum regigni & renouari mente, affectibus, seu voluntate & omnibus facultatibus, vt aliquid boni possit intelligere, cogitare, velle & perficere, secundum illud Christi: Johan.15. vers.5. Sine me nihil potestis facere.
units.tr: Moreover, they hold that saving faith does not come from man himself, nor from the power of his free will, since in a state of defection and sin he cannot of himself think or do anything truly good, such as saving faith is. Rather, man must be born again and renewed by God in Christ, through his Holy Spirit, in mind, affections, or will, and in all his faculties, so that he can understand, think, will and accomplish something good, according to the saying of Christ: John 15:5, Without me you can do nothing.

units.la: ARTICVLVS QVARTVS.
units.tr: THE FOURTH ARTICLE.

units.la: Hanc Dei gratiam esse initium, progressum ac perfectionem omnis boni: atque id eo quidem vsque, vt ipse homo regenitus, absque hac præcedanea, seu adiuentitia, excitante, consequente & cooperante gratia neque boni quid cogitare, velle aut facere possit, neque etiam vlli malæ tentationi resistere. Adeo quidem, vt omnia bona opera, quæ excogitare possumus, Dei gratiæ in Christo tribuenda sint. Quoad verum modum operationis illius gratiæ, illa non est IRRESISTIBILIS: de multis enim dicitur, eos Spiritui sancto restitisse; Actor. 7. & alibi multis locis.
units.tr: This grace of God is the beginning, progress and perfection of all good. It is so much so that the regenerate man himself, without this preceding, accompanying, following and cooperating grace, can neither think, will nor do any good, nor resist any evil temptation. So much so that all the good works we can devise must be ascribed to the grace of God in Christ. As to the true manner of that grace's operation, it is not IRRESISTIBLE, for it is said of many that they resisted the Holy Spirit: Acts 7, and in many other places.

units.la: EXAMEN.
units.tr: EXAMINATION.

units.la: Quanquam hi duo articuli aliquatenus differant: quod tertius est de causa operante fidem & conversionem in homine non renato: quartus priore parte est de causa operante progressum, incrementa & perfectionem omnis boni in homine renato: posteriore parte est de modo, quo causa illa tum fidem & conversionem in non renatis, tum progressum, incrementa & perfectionem in renatis operatur: Tamen omnino cohærent, ideoq; à partibus conferentibus in collatione coniuncti fuerunt, imo & quintus, qui est de perseverantia sanctorum, cum quarto connexus est: eo quod modus operationis gratiæ tam ad perfectionem, quæ perseverantia obtinetur, quam ad initium & progressum refertur.
units.tr: Although these two articles differ somewhat, in that the third concerns the cause operating faith and conversion in a man not yet regenerate, while the fourth, in its first part, concerns the cause operating the progress, increase and perfection of all good in a regenerate man, and its latter part concerns the manner in which that cause operates faith and conversion in the unregenerate, and progress, increase and perfection in the regenerate, nevertheless they wholly cohere. For this reason they were joined together by the parties in the conference. Indeed the fifth article, which concerns the perseverance of the saints, is also connected with the fourth, because the manner of operation of grace is referred both to the perfection by which perseverance is obtained and to the beginning and progress.

units.la: Tertius non eget multo examine: si natiuum verborum sensum sequamur, vtraque parte est sacris literis consentaneus; 1. Quod causa procreans fidem salutarem in homine non sit ipse homo, vel liberum eius arbitrium: eo quod in statu peccati homo non est idoneus ad aliquid boni ex se cogitandum vel faciendum: iuxta scripturas. Eph. 2. 9. 2. Cor. 3. 5. &c. II. Quod necesse sit hominem a Deo in Christo per gratiam Spiritus S. regenerari, seu illuminari mente, renovari voluntate, affectibus, &c. ad bonum intelligendum, cogitandum, volendum, perficiendum, iuxta allegatum, Joh. 15. 6.
units.tr: The third article hardly needs much examination: if we follow the natural sense of the words, both parts agree with the sacred letters. (1) The cause that produces saving faith in a man is not the man himself or his free will, because in a state of sin man is not fit to think or do anything good of himself, according to the Scriptures: Eph. 2:9; 2 Cor. 3:5, etc. (2) It is necessary that a man be regenerated by God in Christ through the grace of the Holy Spirit, or be enlightened in mind and renewed in will, affections, etc., so that he may understand, think, will and accomplish good, according to the passage cited, John 15:6.

units.la: Quartus quoque priore parte, iuxta superficiem verborum verus est, & Deo gloriosus: quia initium, progressum & perfectionem omnis boni hominis regeniti Deo seu Gratiæ adscribit, iuxta dicta. Jac. 1. 7. Ephes. 2. 9. Phil. 1. 6. &c. Neque in collatione orthodoxi aliquid horum reprehendere voluerunt, modo iuxta scripturæ sacræ mentem intelligerentur. Sed in cauda venenum. Clausula de modo operationis illius gratiæ, quod prius datum est, totum aufert. Modum huNc operationis negant esse irresistibilem: in collatione vocant resistibilem: Hi termini ipso sono sunt horridi & barbari: Imo & soloeci. Barbari sunt, quia nec scriptoribus Latinis, quod sciam, nec diuinis literis noti; scholis etiam orthodoxorum, nescio an & Iesuitarum inauditi. Iesuitas omnes non legi. Bellarminus omnium antesignanus, auxilii generalis & specialis, motionis & gratiæ indifferentis vel non indifferentis accuratissimus disputator, in libris de gratia & libero arbitrio nusquam habet, quod meminerim. Vt videatur pars Arminii cothurnum irresistibilis gratiæ in magnum causæ suæ compendium excogitasse, ad conflandam veritati inuidiam: quasi nimirum orthodoxi gratiam irresistibilem, hoc est, coactivam vel coactionem docerent.
units.tr: The fourth article, too, in its first part, is true according to the surface of the words and glorious to God, because it ascribes the beginning, progress and perfection of all good in a regenerate man to God or to grace, according to the sayings: James 1:17; Eph. 2:9; Phil. 1:6, etc. Nor did the orthodox wish to find fault with any of these in the conference, provided they were understood according to the mind of Holy Scripture. But there is poison in the tail. The clause about the manner of that grace's operation takes away everything that was given before. They deny that this manner of operation is irresistible; in the conference they call it resistible. These terms are themselves harsh and barbarous in sound, indeed even ungrammatical. They are barbarous, because, as far as I know, they are known neither to Latin writers nor to the divine letters, and perhaps they are unheard of even in the schools of the orthodox, and of the Jesuits. I have not read all the Jesuits, but Bellarmine, the foremost of them all, the most accurate disputant on general and special help, on motion and on indifferent or non-indifferent grace, nowhere, as far as I remember, has these terms in his books on grace and free will. So it would seem that the Arminian party devised the buskin of irresistible grace as a great shortcut for their cause, to kindle hatred of the truth, as if the orthodox taught an irresistible grace, that is, a coactive grace or coercion.

units.la: Etiam sensu seu significatione barbari & soloeci sunt termini. Irresistibile enim, cui non possit resisti: Resistibile cui possit resisti, quo quaeso authore passiue dici probabunt? Quidni potius actiue irresistibile, quod non resistere: Resistibile, quod resistere possit, significabit? Multa quidem verbalia in bilis ab actiuis ducta passiue significant: amabilis, placabilis, visibilis, &c. sed nec pauca a neutris descendentia, non passiuae, sed neutrius significationis sunt: rationabilis, risibilis, hinnibilis, peccabilis, conducibilis, & habilis, pro eo qui ratiocinari, ridere, hinnire, peccare, condu-cere, habere potest. Sic & stabilis, quod haud dubie sequitur resistibilis, a resisto, quod est gradum sisto: est etiam repugno. Vt igitur stabilis item instabilis, repugnabilis, non est passiue, cui stari, instari (barbara) repugnari potest: sed neutraliter, qui diu stare, non stare, repugnare potest: Ita resistibilis non est cui resisti, sed qui resistere potest. Sic contra resistibilis erit valde resistens: sicut resonabilis Echo apud Sabinum est Echo valde resonans. Quo sensu clausula cum utroq; articulo dubio careret: non tamen ex mente Remonstrantium. De usu igitur tam barbarae & ambiguae vocis prius Grammatici consuluissent, quam Ecclesiam eadem turbarent.
units.tr: The terms are barbarous and ungrammatical also in sense or meaning. For irresistible means that which cannot be resisted, and resistible that which can be resisted. By whose authority, I ask, will they prove that they are used passively? Why should irresistible not rather signify actively that which does not resist, and resistible that which is able to resist? Many verbal adjectives in -bilis derived from active verbs have a passive sense: amabilis, placabilis, visibilis, etc. But not a few that come from neuter verbs are not passive but have a neuter sense: rationabilis, risibilis, hinnibilis, peccabilis, conducibilis, and habilis, meaning one who can reason, laugh, neigh, sin, be useful, or have. So too stabilis, which undoubtedly follows resistibilis from resisto, which is the frequentative of sisto and also means repugno. Just as stabilis, likewise instabilis and repugnabilis, is not passive, meaning that which can be stood or stood upon (barbarously), or be opposed, but neuter, meaning that which can stand long, not stand, or oppose, so resistibilis is not that which can be resisted, but that which can resist. Conversely, resistibilis will be very resisting, just as resonabilis Echo, in Sabinus, is an Echo that resounds greatly. In this sense the clause would be free of doubt in either article, though not according to the mind of the Remonstrants. Therefore, before disturbing the Church with such a barbarous and ambiguous word, the grammarians should have been consulted about its usage.

units.la: Sed sit sane barbarus ille terminus passiva significatione latinus. Sit inquam operatio gratia resistibilis vel irresistibilis, cui a voluntate hominis resisti potest vel non potest: seu quae libero arbitrio impediri potest vel non potest. De hac quid statuendum sit quaeritur: sine gratia operans haec omnia, quae utroque articulo gratia tribuuntur, RESISTIBILIS an IRRESISTIBILIS dicenda?
units.tr: But let that barbarous term be granted a Latin passive sense. Let it be, I say, the operation of grace resistible or irresistible, which can or cannot be resisted by the human will, that is, which can or cannot be impeded by free will. The question is what must be decided about this: are all those things that are attributed to grace in both articles, operated without grace, to be called RESISTIBLE or IRRESISTIBLE?

units.la: Remonstrantes prius affirmant: posterius negant. Orthodoxi in collatione vocem barbaram & ambiguam non agnoscunt: ramen quod attinet, prius negant, posterius contra affirmant: Si, inquiunt, per resistere intelligitur, Dei operationem penitus impedire, & expugnare, fatemur a nobis in hominis conuersione talem gratia operationem statui, quae hac significatione est IRRESISTIBILIS, id est quae non potest impediri, neque expugnari per voluntatem hominis repugnantem: idq; quoniam gratia Dei in Christo illam repugnantiam tandem expugnat, impedit & tollit. Hancq; sententiam decem scripturae sacrae argumentis firmiter probant. Remonstrantes contra suam gratiam resistibilem novem rationibus ostendere conantur, plerisq; aequivocis ex ambiguo gratia vocabulo: quo praecipue nititur ista sententiarum atque argumentorum collusio. Ad quam proinde facilius expediendam, & statum quaestionis rectius percipiendum, distinctione est opus triplicis gratiae, iuxta triplicem humanae voluntatis statum.
units.tr: The Remonstrants affirm the former and deny the latter. The orthodox, in the conference, did not recognise the barbarous and ambiguous word, yet as far as the matter goes they deny the former and affirm the latter. "If," they say, "by resisting is understood entirely impeding and overcoming God's operation, we confess that in the conversion of man we posit such an operation of grace as in this sense is IRRESISTIBLE, that is, which cannot be impeded or overcome by a resisting human will, because the grace of God in Christ at last overcomes, impedes and removes that resistance." They firmly prove this view by ten arguments from Holy Scripture. The Remonstrants, against their resistible grace, try to show by nine arguments, most of them equivocal, drawn from the ambiguous word grace, on which this whole collusion of sayings and arguments chiefly rests. Therefore, to unravel it more easily and to perceive the state of the question more correctly, a distinction of threefold grace is needed, according to the threefold state of the human will.
Conference, pp. 217, 238, 239.

units.la: Coll. pag. 218.
units.tr: Conference, p. 218.

units.la: Coll. pag. 226.
units.tr: Conference, p. 226.

units.la: Est enim humana voluntas consideranda, quid possit vel faciat ante conversionem, quid in ipsa conversione, quid post conversionem. Sic triplex gratia est: Prima gratia vocans seu vocationis externæ, primo statui: Altera operans seu motionis internæ, secundo statui: Tertia cooperans, motionis quoq; internæ, tertio statui voluntatis conveniens.
units.tr: For the human will must be considered in respect of what it can or does before conversion, what it does in conversion itself, and what it does after conversion. Thus there is a threefold grace. The first is the calling or external vocation grace, belonging to the first state. The second is the operating or internal motion grace, belonging to the second state. The third is the cooperating grace, also internal motion, belonging to the third state of the will.

units.la: Gratia vocans seu vocationis externę est, qua Deus homines nondum renatos foris dignatur vocare seu invitare ad fidem, obedientiam & salutem per vocem Legis: Audi Israel, &c. in præceptis meis ambulate, &c. Hæc facite, &c. & per conciones Evangelii: Venite ad me omnes, &c Resipiscite & credite Evangelio.
units.tr: The calling grace, or external vocation, is that by which God deigns to call or invite men not yet regenerate outwardly to faith, obedience and salvation, through the voice of the Law: Hear, O Israel, etc.; walk in my precepts, etc.; do these things, etc., and through the sermons of the Gospel: Come to me, all of you, etc.; repent and believe the Gospel.

units.la: Hac gratia (quæ prima, præveniens, præcedanea, excitans, invitans, & suadens vocari solet) Deus in veteri Testamento non dignatus fuit quovis populos, sed solos Israelitas: iuxta illud: Statuta sua annunciat Israeli: Non fecit sic vlli nationi: sicut in novo Testamento, non quovis hodie populos sed solos Christianos dignatur.
units.tr: This grace (which is usually called the first, preventing, preceding, stirring, inviting and persuading grace) God did not deign to bestow on every people in the Old Testament, but only on the Israelites, according to the saying: "He declares his statutes to Israel; he has not dealt so with any nation" (Ps. 147:19–20), just as in the New Testament he today deigns to bestow it not on every people but only on Christians.

units.la: De hac gratia ad quæsitum respondetur, quod minime sit irresistibilis, sed nimis resistibilis: imo quod voluntas non renata nihil possit, nisi gratiæ vocanti resistere: Quandoquidem prudentia carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum: & legi Dei non subiicitur: ac ne potest quidem. Hinc querelæ Dei, & prophetarum, & Christi, & Apostolorum, in utroque Testamento de vocatorum resistentia & contumacia: Locutus sum vobis, mane surgendo, & loquendo, & non audiuistis: vocavi vos & non respondistis: Vtinam populus meus obtemperasset mihi: Israel in viis meis ambulasset! Quoties volui te congregare, & noluisti! Vos semper resistitis Spiritui sancto, &c. Hanc & non aliam resistibilitatem gratiæ probant Remonstrantes argumento suo secundo, tertio, quarto, quinto, sexto, septimo, octavo. Nonne igitur tanto conatu siliquas, quod dicitur, triturant? Neque enim de huius gratiæ resistibilitate quæstio vel dubium est.
units.tr: To this grace the answer is that it is by no means irresistible, but far too resistible. Indeed, an unregenerate will can do nothing except resist the grace that calls it, since the wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God, and it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Hence the complaints of God, of the prophets, of Christ and of the apostles, in both Testaments, about the resistance and obstinacy of those who are called: I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking, and you did not listen; I have called you, and you did not answer. Oh that my people had obeyed me, that Israel had walked in my ways! How often would I have gathered you, and you would not! You always resist the Holy Spirit, and so on. The Remonstrants prove this and no other resistibility of grace by their second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh and eighth arguments. Do they not, as the saying goes, grind husks with such great effort? For there is neither question nor doubt about the resistibility of this grace.

units.la: Gratia cooperans (de hac prius dicendum) quæ & subsequens, abiitis consequens dicitur, est, qua Deus bonæ voluntati homi-nis regeniti intus cooperatur, quaque homo renatus in statu gratiæ corroboratur. De hac dicitur: Misericordia Domini subsequetur me omnibus diebus vitæ meæ: Dabo timorem meum in corda eorum, ut non recedant à me: Spiritus tuus rectus ducit me in viam rectam: Deus confirmabit vos usque in finem inculpatos. Hanc Paulus precatur Ecclesiis in omnium epistolarum clausulis.
units.tr: Co-operating grace (to be discussed first), which is also called subsequent, or consequent, is that by which God inwardly co-operates with the good will of the regenerate man, and by which the renewed man is strengthened in a state of grace. Of this it is said: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life; I will put my fear in their hearts, that they may not depart from me; your good Spirit leads me into the right land; God will establish you blameless to the end. Paul prays for this for the churches at the close of all his epistles.

units.la: De hac etiam proprie non est quæstio. Etsi enim Deus eam regeneratis (iuxta promissiones suas, & preces eorum) nunquam totaliter & finaliter subducit: tamen ita eam pro sapientia sua moderatur, vt subinde ad eos vel explicandos, vel humilian- dos, vel excitandos, vel castigandos, luctam quandam spiritus & carnis in eis relinquat, qua modo spiritus à carne, vicissim caro à spiritu superatur, id quod lapsus, & gemitus, & querelæ sanctorum testantur. Et Apostolus confirmat: Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, spiritus autem adversus carnem. Hanc igitur faci- le etiam patimur vocari Resistibilem, non simpliciter tamen, sed secundum quid. Neque enim hæc siue resistibilitas siue resisten- tia est (ut prior) inter voluntatem & gratiam, sed inter sensuali- tatem seu carnem in sanctis reliquam, & inter gratiam: testante Apostolo: Non quod volo hoc ago, sed quod odi, hoc facio. Non enim facio bonum, quod volo; sed malum quod nolo, hoc ago: & ita quidem ut caro à spiritu, sensualitas à bona voluntate, concupiscentia à gratia tandem superetur.
units.tr: Strictly speaking, there is no question about this either. For although God, according to his promises and the prayers of the regenerate, never wholly and finally withdraws this grace from them, yet in his wisdom he so governs it that at times, either to test them, to humble them, to rouse them or to chastise them, he leaves in them a certain struggle of spirit and flesh, in which now the spirit is overcome by the flesh, and now in turn the flesh by the spirit. The falls, groans and complaints of the saints bear witness to this. The Apostle confirms it: The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. So we readily allow this to be called resistible, though not simply, but in a qualified sense. For this resistibility or resistance (unlike the former) is not between the will and grace, but between the sensuality or flesh remaining in the saints and grace, as the Apostle testifies: What I want to do, I do not do; but what I hate, that I do. For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do. And so indeed the flesh is overcome by the spirit, sensuality by the good will, and concupiscence at length by grace.

units.la: Denique gratia operans, (quæ cum duabus prioribus ab his confunditur) est motus misericordiæ Dei (ut vocatur ab Augustino) quo intus in mentibus, voluntatibus vel cordibus non- dum regenitorum operatur ea, quæ ad conuersionem hominis pertinent. Hæc gratia seu motio Dei propria est, quæ in quæ- stionem venit, nec tota tamen. Testante enim scriptura & expe- rientia, sunt huius gratiæ tres distincti gradus. Aliquorum enim Deus miseretur usq; ad bonum illuminationis & fidei historicæ: aliquorum usque ad bonum fidei temporariæ & alicuius lætitiæ: aliquorum denique usque ad bonum fidei salvificæ & regenerationis.
units.tr: Lastly, operating grace (which is often confused with the two preceding kinds) is the motion of God's mercy (as Augustine calls it), by which he works inwardly in the minds, wills or hearts of those not yet regenerate, bringing about those things that pertain to the conversion of man. This grace, or motion, of God is peculiar, and it is this that is in question, though not the whole of it. For Scripture and experience both testify that there are three distinct degrees of this grace. For God shows mercy to some up to the good of illumination and historical faith; to some up to the good of temporary faith and a certain joy; and finally to some up to the good of saving faith and regeneration.

units.la: Primum gradum ne ipsi quidem Remonstrantes negant esse irresistibilem. Quando enim, inquiunt, Deus voluntatem suam pate- facit, irresistibilem spiritus sancti virtutem in nostra mente agnosci- mus: quoniam mens nostra ipsum scire non potest effugere: & in animo nostro, quando illam pulsat. Quia velimus nolimus, cogimur illud sentire.
units.tr: The Remonstrants themselves do not deny that the first degree is irresistible. For when, they say, God reveals his will, we recognise the irresistible power of the Holy Spirit in our mind, since our mind cannot escape knowing it, and in our soul when it strikes it. Because, whether we will it or not, we are compelled to feel it.

units.la: De secundi gradus Resistibilitate non est laborandum. Illu- minationem horum irresistibilem quoque esse non negant illi. De motione ad assensum & lætitiam aliqualem, per nos sentire eis licet, quod volent. Si resistibilem dicunt, quia motio vo- luntatem non omnino efficaciter afficit, nihil hoc ad quæsi- tum.
units.tr: Let us not labour over the resistibility of the second degree. They do not deny that the illumination of these people is also irresistible. As for the motion towards assent and a certain joy, they are free to feel about it as they wish. If they call it resistible because the motion does not affect the will wholly and effectually, this has nothing to do with the question.

units.la: Resistentiam finalem Scripturæ & exempla probant: Cum gaudio accipiunt sermonem: sed radicem non habent, qui ad tempus credunt, & tempore tentationis deficiunt. Ex eo multi discipulorum discesserunt ab eo: Nonnulli naufragium fidei fecerunt. Discedunt qui- dam à fide. Abnegantes Dominum, qui eos mercatus est; recedunt à sancta doctrina eis tradita. De tertii gradus operatione (quæ vocatio interna dicitur) totum quæsitum est: irresistibilem hanc Dei motionem esse firmissime probarunt orthodoxi.
units.tr: Scripture and examples prove a final resistance: They receive the word with joy, but have no root; they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away. From that time many of his disciples went back from him; some have made shipwreck of the faith; some depart from the faith; denying the Lord who bought them, they turn away from the holy doctrine delivered to them. The whole question concerns the operation of the third degree (which is called internal calling). The orthodox have most firmly proved that this motion of God is irresistible.

units.la: I. Quia Deus eos, quos efficaciter convertere intendit, sicut irresistibiliter illuminat: sic irresistibiliter non solum potentia, sed & actu credendi donat, Phil.1.29. & 2.13. Proinde efficacia motionis suæ non solum resistentiam, sed & resistibilitatem in eis tollit. Quod obiicitur: vobis datum pro Christo pati: non ad operantem, sed ad cooperantem gratiam pertinet, de cuius lucta modo dictum: proinde nihil ad rem.
units.tr: I. Because God, as he irresistibly enlightens those whom he intends effectually to convert, so irresistibly bestows on them not only the power but also the act of believing (Phil. 1.29; 2.13). Therefore the efficacy of his motion removes in them not only resistance but also resistibility. The objection, it has been given to you to suffer for Christ, pertains not to operating but to co-operating grace, whose struggle has just been described; therefore it is beside the point.

units.la: II. Quia Deus convertendo nos, dat cor novum, & spiritum novum: aufert cor lapideum, & dat carnem, facitque nos ambulare in præceptis suis. At cor novum, & spiritum novum, & actum ambulandi in præceptis Domini fingere cum resistentia vel resistibilitate absurdum est. Jerem.31.18. Deut.29.4. Ezech. 36.26. Contra quod nihil solidi adfertur, licet multa dicantur.
units.tr: II. Because when God converts us, he gives a new heart and a new spirit; he takes away the stony heart and gives a fleshly heart, and makes us walk in his precepts. But to imagine a new heart, a new spirit and the act of walking in the Lord's precepts together with resistance or resistibility is absurd (Jer. 31.18; Deut. 29.4; Ezek. 36.26). Nothing solid is brought against this, although many things are said.

units.la: III. Quia hominis animalis in peccatis mortui, vivificatio, regeneratio, conversio, nova creatio, cum resistibilitate non minus absurde, quam prima hominis creatio, vel quotidiana generatio, vel ultima resuscitatio, cogitatur vel fingitur. Joh.3.3. & 5. 2.5. Eph.2.5. &c. Quæ ratio verbositate nequicquam eluditur.
units.tr: III. Because the making alive, regeneration, conversion and new creation of a man dead in sins are conceived or imagined together with resistibility no less absurdly than the first creation of man, or his daily generation, or his final resurrection (John 3.3; 5.25; Eph. 2.5, etc.). This argument is vainly evaded by wordiness.

units.la: IV. Quia gratia operans conversionem cum resistibilitate non differret a persuasione oratoria, vel illicio moraliad fidem: quali vivificationem hominis in peccatis mortui fieri est impossibile: Quæ contra dicuntur, ...
units.tr: IV. Because conversion effected by grace with resistibility would not differ from oratorical persuasion, or moral enticement to faith; by which the making alive of a man dead in sins would be impossible. What is said against this...

units.la: V. Quia gratia operans fidem & conversionem, efficacia sua omnem hominum & rerum creatarum virtutem superat, eoque nec depravata voluntate humana est superabilis. Ephes.1,18.19. Col.2.12.13.2. Thes.1.11.2 Pet.1.3. Cuius rationis maior minime, ut dicitur, infirma est. Vis enim pravæ voluntati humanæ insuperabilis, certe eidem est irresistibilis.
units.tr: V. Because grace that works faith and conversion surpasses by its efficacy all the power of men and created things, and so it cannot be overcome even by a depraved human will (Eph. 1.18, 19; Col. 2.12, 13; 2 Thess. 1.11; 2 Pet. 1.3). The greater premise of this argument, as it is said, is by no means weak. For if a power is insuperable to a depraved human will, it is certainly irresistible to it.

units.la: VI. Quia si gratia regenerationis esset resistibilis, foret ea communis multis non renatis: At scriptura eam propriam filiorum Dei facit. Rom.8.14. 30. 1 Corinth.1.23.24. Johan.14. 17. Johan.6.36.45. 1. Johan.4. 17. quæ ratio non solum pro resistentia, ut prætenditur, sed etiam de irresistibilitate concludit.
units.tr: VI. Because if the grace of regeneration were resistible, it would be common to many who are not reborn; but Scripture makes it the peculiar possession of the sons of God (Rom. 8.14, 30; 1 Cor. 1.23, 24; John 14.17; John 6.36, 45; 1 John 4.17). This argument concludes not only for resistance, as is pretended, but also for irresistibility.

units.la: VII. Quia tractus Patris, sine quo nemo venit ad Christum, Joh.6.44. irresistibilitatem gratiæ supponit: secus nemo etiam tractus veniret: Nec ideo tamen trahimur à Patre inviti (quod obiicitur) magis, quam inviti illuminamur.
units.tr: VII. Because the drawing of the Father, without which no one comes to Christ (John 6.44), presupposes the irresistibility of grace; otherwise no one would be drawn at all.
